cards.definitions: \(\mathrm{NEXP}=\bigcup _{a\ge 1}\mathrm{NTIME}(2^{n^{a}}): a\) language is accepted by one nondeterministic Turing machine whose every computation branch halts within exponential time \(2^{n^{a}}\), up to a constant factor, for some fixed a. An input is in the language exactly when at least one branch accepts. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with n Boolean inputs, constants 0 and 1 and one output. AND and OR may have any positive fan-in; NOT has one input. A majority gate on m inputs outputs 1 when at least \(\lceil m/2\rceil\) of them are 1, including a tie when m is even. Fan-out is unrestricted. Size is the number of operation gates plus wires. Repeated connections count individually, so their multiplicities cannot encode uncharged weights. Depth is the maximum number of operation gates on an input-to-output path. All circuits compute exactly on every input; no average-case correctness or randomness is allowed. \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) consists of languages having one fixed depth bound and one polynomial size bound across all input lengths. The family may be nonuniform: no algorithm is required to construct its nth circuit. NEXP machines are uniform and have no oracle or advice. The formal quantifiers permit the lower bound to be witnessed at infinitely many input lengths, rather than requiring failure at every sufficiently large length.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves that one language in NEXP has no polynomial-size constant-depth majority-circuit family, with depth and polynomial exponent both unrestricted constants. A negative resolution proves \(\mathrm{NEXP}\subseteq \mathrm{TC}^{0}\). A bound ruling out only \(n^{k}\) gates for one fixed k, or only one fixed circuit depth, does not by itself establish the displayed separation.

context_blocks.title: Small depth still permits powerful gates
context_blocks.text: A constant-depth circuit applies only a bounded number of layers, but a majority gate can inspect many inputs at once. For three bits it returns 1 on 110 and 111, while returning 0 on 100. Thus majority is not a bounded-fan-in local operation. \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) permits many such gates in parallel and lets their outputs feed later layers. The depth bound stays fixed as input length grows, while the number of gates and wires may be any fixed polynomial.

context_blocks.title: Why parity is not enough
context_blocks.text: Parity is difficult for constant-depth circuits using only AND, OR and NOT, but it is easy for majority circuits. A threshold test for whether an n-bit input has at least t ones is implementable with a majority gate and suitable constants. Two adjacent threshold tests identify an exact number of ones, and taking an OR over odd counts gives parity with a polynomial number of gates in constant depth. This example shows why a lower bound for the weaker gate set cannot simply be reused after majority is added.

context_blocks.title: What NEXP contributes
context_blocks.text: The hard language need only have a nondeterministic exponential-time algorithm; it need not be in P or NP. That is a generous uniform computation budget, making the lack of a known separation striking. Nevertheless, counting the truth tables that have no small circuits does not automatically identify one language within this budget. The assertion requires one language that defeats every fixed polynomial size and every fixed depth, rather than a different unrestricted truth table for each desired bound.

context_blocks.title: The established nearby separation
context_blocks.text: Williams proves that NEXP does not have polynomial-size ACC circuits. ACC allows constant-depth Boolean circuits with gates testing the number of 1 inputs modulo a fixed integer. \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) can implement these modular tests by combining threshold comparisons. It is therefore a more permissive class, and excluding ACC does not exclude \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\). The original 2011 reference supports this nearby theorem, not the stronger conclusion asked here.

context_blocks.title: The 2026 results retain important restrictions
context_blocks.text: Chen, Tal and Wang prove super-quadratic gate lower bounds for depth-two linear-threshold circuits, with a hard function in \(E^{\mathrm{NP}}\), exponential time with an NP oracle. Their \(n^{2.5- \varepsilon}\) bound is still a fixed polynomial and addresses depth two. A September preprint claims near-cubic wire bounds in that setting; its source also carries a critical comment, and it is not independently verified here. Wire counts and gate counts are different quantitative parameters. Ren and Williams obtain near-maximum general circuit bounds with a promise-Merlin–Arthur oracle and one bit of advice. None of these statements supplies the required ordinary NEXP language outside all of nonuniform \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\).

cards.title: NL versus UL
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{NL}=UL\)? Equivalently, is there a single nondeterministic Turing machine that decides directed s–t reachability using \(O(\log  N)\) work space and polynomial time, has exactly one accepting computation on every reachable instance, and has no accepting computation on every unreachable instance, where N is the explicit input length?
cards.definitions: An input consists of a finite directed graph with labelled vertices and explicitly listed edges, together with vertices s,t. Reachability asks whether a directed path from s to t exists; the length-zero path is allowed when \(s=t\). A machine has a read-only two-way input tape, \(O(\log (N+2))\) read/write work-tape cells over a fixed finite alphabet, and a fixed finite nondeterministic transition relation. Every computation branch must halt within a polynomial in N. NL permits any positive number of accepting branches on yes inputs; UL permits exactly one. On no inputs both classes require zero accepting branches. A branch is a sequence of transition choices, not merely its endpoint or output. Rejecting branches need not be unique. Machines are uniform finite programs without advice, randomness, oracle access or additional catalytic storage. The equality asks whether every NL language has some equivalent UL machine; it does not require a computable compiler converting descriptions of arbitrary machines. Directed reachability is NL-complete under deterministic logspace reductions, so its UL membership suffices.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove a uniform \(O(\log  N)\)-space unambiguous algorithm for all directed reachability inputs, or prove that some NL language is not in UL. Any positive construction must remain unambiguous on every input without assuming that the supplied graph itself has a unique path. A polynomial-time algorithm using \(O((\log  N)^{3/2})\) space, nonuniform advice, catalytic memory, or an unproved hardness hypothesis is progress rather than a solution.
cards.why: Determine whether the multiplicity of accepting computations adds power to logarithmic-space computation.

cards.status_note: The checked general unconditional simulation still uses \(O(\log ^{3/2} N)\) space. The 2025–2026 hardness-based results remain conditional, catalytic results use additional resources, and Hoza’s July 2026 lower bound excludes only oblivious isolation. No settlement of uniform \(\mathrm{NL}=UL\) found through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: A nondeterministic reachability algorithm can guess the next vertex of a path, checking each edge as it goes. It needs only a current vertex and a step counter, so logarithmic memory suffices. The difficulty is that a graph can offer many successful sequences of guesses. An unambiguous algorithm must retain the ability to recognize a path while allowing only one successful computation.

This restriction is weaker than determinism. The machine may still branch many times and have many rejecting computations. On a reachable graph, only one complete branch may accept. Consequently, \(\mathrm{NL}=UL\) would explain something about the source of nondeterministic power without establishing \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{NL}\). A proof that \(\mathrm{NL}\ne UL\) would, however, also separate deterministic and nondeterministic logspace, since \(\mathrm{L}\subseteq UL\subseteq \mathrm{NL}\).

One approach is to assign positive integer weights to edges so that every reachable ordered pair has a unique minimum-weight path. Reinhardt and Allender show how such min-isolating weights support an unambiguous reachability algorithm. If the weights are polynomially bounded and can be generated in deterministic logspace from the graph, the resulting memory use remains logarithmic. Randomly choosing suitable weights can give isolation, but does not provide a uniform deterministic construction.

Reinhardt and Allender also prove NL/poly=UL/poly. Here a polynomial-length advice string may depend on the input length and be shared by every input of that length, without any requirement that the string be generated efficiently. This is evidence that isolation is possible in a broad nonuniform sense. Removing the advice is essential to the ordinary \(\mathrm{NL}=UL\) question.

The strongest checked unconditional general simulation uses more than logarithmic memory. Van Melkebeek and Prakriya give an unambiguous polynomial-time simulation of NL using \(O((\log  N)^{3/2})\) space. Their work reduces the randomness and weight-description costs of isolation. The remaining square-root-of-logarithm factor is small numerically, but it is an unbounded factor in the resource defining the target class.

The inherited 2025 paper by Doron, Pyne, Tell and Williams develops new hardness-versus-randomness tools for isolation. Its main conditional unambiguity theorem concerns the linear-space analogue \(\mathrm{NSPACE}[n]\subseteq\)USPACE\([O(n)]\), under uniform circuit lower bounds with specified oracle access. The March 2026 Pyne–Tell survey gives a refined version. These assumptions are unproved, and the linear-space conclusion should not be reported as an unconditional logspace equality.

A February 2026 revision by Arvind, Chakraborty and Datta gives reachability algorithms in a catalytic model with UL oracle access. Catalytic computation permits extra memory initially containing arbitrary data, provided that the data are restored at the end. This is an interesting way to use storage, but it supplies resources absent from a plain UL machine. The headline about derandomizing isolation therefore does not resolve this card.

Hoza proves a new limitation in July 2026. Suppose one weight assignment must work for every layered graph of given width w and length \(\ell\), without examining which edges are actually present. Such an oblivious min-isolating assignment requires weights of magnitude \(2^{\Omega (\log  w\cdot \log  \ell )}\), so polynomially bounded universal weights cannot solve the general problem by this route. This restriction does not cover assignments that depend on the actual graph or other unambiguous algorithms.

A solution would determine whether many successful paths are ever intrinsically necessary when computation has only logarithmic memory. It would also clarify how much information must be retained to select a unique witness from a large implicitly represented family. The challenge is not to name a canonical path mathematically, but to recognize one with the required uniqueness guarantee and very little working storage.

It would also clarify how much information must be retained to select a unique witness from a large implicitly represented family. The challenge is not to name a canonical path mathematically, but to recognize one with the required uniqueness guarantee and very little working storage.

cards.title: L versus NL
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine A and an absolute constant C such that, for every directed graph G on vertices \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\) and every s,t, A decides whether t is reachable from s while using at most $C\log_2(n+2)$ work-tape cells? G is supplied explicitly as a read-only adjacency matrix, together with s and t. The machine must halt and be correct on every input. This is equivalent to \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{NL}\).
cards.definitions: The graph may have self-loops; reachability allows a path of length zero, so \(s=t\) is a yes instance. Input access is two-way and read-only. Work tapes have a fixed finite alphabet; visited work-tape cells, including all counters and stored vertex identifiers, count toward space. The finite control and read-only input cells do not. There is no advice, random tape, oracle, writable copy of the input, or external storage. L is deterministic \(O(\log  N)\) work space on binary inputs of bit length N. NL uses the same space bound with nondeterministic transitions and accepts exactly when some computation branch accepts; all branches can be clocked to halt within polynomial time. Since the matrix encoding has \(N=Theta(n^{2})\) bits, \(O(\log  N)=O(\log  n)\). A halting deterministic machine with this space bound automatically runs in polynomial time: it cannot repeat a complete configuration.
cards.answer_criterion: Give an always-correct deterministic logarithmic-space reachability algorithm for all directed graphs, or prove that no such algorithm exists. By NL-completeness under deterministic logspace reductions, either direction settles L versus NL. An algorithm for undirected graphs, a nondeterministic algorithm, or an algorithm using a larger power of log n does not answer the stated question.
cards.why: Directed reachability is the canonical model of exploring possible computational states. Its space complexity determines whether nondeterministic logarithmic memory can be replaced by deterministic logarithmic memory, with consequences for low-memory graph algorithms and complexity theory.

importance.reason: A central space-complexity separation expressed by a basic graph problem. The contrast with solved undirected reachability isolates a fundamental role of edge direction and nondeterminism.

progress.text: Savitch proves that nondeterministic space s can be simulated deterministically in \(O(s^{2})\) space, for s at least logarithmic. Directed reachability consequently has an \(O(\log ^{2} n)\)-space algorithm.

Immerman and Szelepcsényi independently establish closure of nondeterministic space under complementation. In particular \(\mathrm{NL}=\mathrm{coNL}\), so both reachability and nonreachability admit nondeterministic logspace algorithms.
Reingold obtains deterministic logarithmic space for undirected connectivity, published at STOC 2005 and subsequently in JACM. Arbitrary directed graphs are outside that theorem.

Doron, Pyne, Tell, and Williams give two algorithms such that, on each directed graph, at least one succeeds: deterministic polynomial-time, polylogarithmic-space transitive closure, or nondeterministic logarithmic-space random-walk estimation. This per-graph alternative does not give the first algorithm on every graph or reduce its space to \(O(\log  n)\).

Bhadra and Tewari show NL-hardness even for directed graphs whose edges can be partitioned into two forests of directed paths of length at most two, including when the partition is supplied. Such a simple decomposition therefore does not make the general logspace obstacle disappear.

context_blocks.text: A graph search usually remembers which vertices it has visited. With only logarithmic space, it can store a constant number of vertex names and counters, but cannot keep a separate visited bit for every vertex. The input may be rescanned as often as necessary. The challenge is to organize those repeated scans so that arbitrary directed paths can be detected without retaining a large search frontier.

Nondeterminism gives a simple logarithmic-space procedure: keep the current vertex and a length counter, guess the next edge, and accept if t is reached within \(n- 1\) edges. Any reachable target has a simple path within that bound. For a general nondeterministic logspace computation, vertices can instead represent machine configurations. An accepting computation becomes a directed path, explaining why this graph problem captures the whole class NL.

Savitch’s algorithm recursively asks whether a path can pass through a candidate midpoint. It saves space by recomputing subproblems, but a logarithmic recursion depth with logarithmic information per level uses \(O(\log ^{2} n)\) space. Its running time is quasipolynomial. Reducing the storage to a single logarithmic factor would also force polynomial time in the stated machine model.

For undirected graphs, Reingold already achieved the logarithmic target. Edge direction is therefore a substantive part of this card. Likewise, \(\mathrm{NL}=\mathrm{coNL}\) shows that nonreachability has a nondeterministic logspace procedure; it does not remove nondeterminism. Recent connections with random-walk estimation make the landscape richer, while leaving the same deterministic directed question.

cards.title: Existence of TFNP-complete problems
cards.formal:
Does the class of total polynomially bounded search problems with polynomial-time verifiable answers contain a complete problem under deterministic polynomial-time many-one search reductions?

Writing this class as \(\mathrm{TFNP}\) and the reduction as \(\le_m^p\), the target is
\[\exists Q\in\mathrm{TFNP}\ \forall R\in\mathrm{TFNP},\qquad R\le_m^p Q.\]
The same fixed relation \(Q\) must work for every \(R\). For each \(R\), a reduction computes one \(Q\)-instance from the input and converts every valid answer to that instance into a valid \(R\)-answer. The question is unrelativized and concerns the whole class, including problems whose totality follows from different mathematical principles.

source_formulation.text: The search for a complete problem in TFNP is of primary concern to certain fields such as cryptography, but it remains open whether such a […]

cards.why: A complete problem would give one universal task against which the difficulty of every efficiently verifiable total search problem could be compared. Its nonexistence would establish a structural limitation on extending the completeness framework from decision problems to all total search. This is a central question connecting complexity classes defined by semantic conditions, mathematical existence principles and the strength of formal proof systems.

sentences: TFNP contains search problems with polynomially bounded, efficiently verifiable answers guaranteed to exist for every binary input.
The question asks whether one problem in this class is complete for all the others under deterministic polynomial-time many-one search reductions.
Each reduction makes one transformed instance and must decode every valid returned answer correctly.
The complete relation is fixed universally, while the reduction and its polynomial bounds may vary with the source problem.
Known subclass completeness and oracle results clarify the structure without settling this general existence question.

cards.definitions:
Let \(\Sigma=\{0,1\}\), let \(\Sigma^*\) include the empty string, and let \(|x|\) be bit length. A search relation is a subset \(R\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\Sigma^*\). An answer to input \(x\) is any string \(y\) satisfying \(R(x,y)\); no uniqueness or ordering of valid answers is required.

The relation belongs to \(\mathrm{TFNP}\) if all three conditions hold. First, there are positive integers \(a,b\), fixed for \(R\), such that every valid pair satisfies \(|y|\le a(|x|+1)^b\). Second, a deterministic algorithm decides \(R(x,y)\) in time at most \(C(|x|+|y|+2)^d\), for fixed positive integers \(C,d\). Third,
\[\forall x\in\Sigma^*\ \exists y\in\Sigma^*,\qquad R(x,y).\]
Thus totality applies to every binary input. A relation based on a structured encoding must also prescribe a valid answer for malformed instances; restricting the domain to inputs promised to have a solution is insufficient. The output bound is part of the relation: an overlong string is not a valid answer.

Algorithms use uniform finite-program deterministic multitape Turing machines over fixed finite alphabets, with binary input and output. Time counts bit operations, input handling and writing the output, in the worst case over all inputs. A pair can be encoded as \(\langle x,z\rangle=1^{|x|}0xz\), whose length is linear in \(|x|+|z|+1\); malformed encodings may be assigned an arbitrary fixed output. All functions used below are total and polynomial-time computable on their full encoded domains. There is no randomness, advice, nonuniform circuit family or external oracle available to these functions.

For \(R,Q\in\mathrm{TFNP}\), the reduction \(R\le_m^p Q\) means that there are functions \(f:\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*\) and \(g:\Sigma^*\times\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*\) computed in deterministic polynomial time such that
\[\forall x,z\in\Sigma^*,\qquad Q(f(x),z)\ \Longrightarrow\ R(x,g(x,z)).\]
The bound for \(f\) is polynomial in \(|x|\), and that for \(g\) is polynomial in \(|x|+|z|\). The decoder may use the original input \(x\). This is a single transformed instance with a single returned answer; correctness must hold for every possible valid answer, without controlling which answer is returned. The reduction does not itself compute an answer to \(Q\), and the quantification over valid answers is not an oracle supplied to \(f\) or \(g\). Multiple adaptive instance queries are not the reduction in this question.

The complete problem \(Q\), its verifier and its balance bound are fixed before \(R\) is chosen. The reduction functions and their polynomial constants may depend on \(R\) and \(Q\), but not on the particular input. No single effective procedure that recognizes TFNP membership or produces reductions from arbitrary verifier descriptions is required.

A negative answer is the exact opposite quantifier statement:
\[\forall Q\in\mathrm{TFNP}\ \exists R\in\mathrm{TFNP},\qquad R\not\le_m^p Q.\]
The target is completeness for a search class under the specified search reduction. Completeness of a decision language, completeness for a proper TFNP subclass, or an NP search problem that lacks answers on some inputs does not by itself satisfy it.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence statement. An affirmative answer must specify one relation \(Q\), prove its polynomial balance, deterministic polynomial-time verifiability and totality on all binary inputs, and establish the stated reductions from every \(R\in\mathrm{TFNP}\). A negative answer must prove that every candidate \(Q\in\mathrm{TFNP}\) fails to receive such a reduction from some relation in the class. No effective enumeration of all TFNP problems is additionally required. A subclass-completeness result, a separation relative to an oracle or a conditional consequence alone is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: The source states nonexistence of a many-one complete TFNP problem among the central conjectures connecting computational complexity and proof systems. This card asks the equivalent yes-or-no existence question, so the commonly stated conjecture predicts a negative answer.

Polynomial verifiability and a polynomial answer bound can be given by machine descriptions, but totality asserts a condition over all inputs. This semantic requirement prevents simply treating every polynomial-time verifier as a total search problem. Pudlák relates the general completeness question to the ability of fixed arithmetical theories to capture total search, and proves a universal-problem result for suitable classes whose totality is provable in a fixed theory.

Many important subclasses have complete problems tied to particular existence principles. The December 2025 manuscript studies further oracle hierarchies and collapses within TFNP; these subclass results do not supply a complete problem for the entire class.

The MFCS 2024 oracle permits a TFNP-complete problem while SAT has no polynomial-time optimal proof system. This separates two conjectures in that relativized setting; it neither constructs an ordinary TFNP-complete problem nor rules one out. Worst-case completeness alone also does not specify an average-case cryptographic hardness guarantee.

cards.title: Sliding-scale PCP conjecture
cards.formal: Do constants \(a,b,c>0\) and \(q\ge 1\) exist such that 3-SAT has a verifier using at most a \(\log _{2}(N+2)\) random bits and q queries to a proof of at most \((N+2)^{b}\) symbols over an alphabet of size at most \((N+2)^{b}\), with perfect completeness and soundness at most \((N+2)^{- c}\)?
cards.definitions: N is the bit length of an explicitly encoded 3-CNF formula. A uniform deterministic polynomial-time verifier receives the input, a uniform random bit string and oracle access to a fixed proof string. It reads at most q alphabet symbols, each encoded with \(O(\log  N)\) bits, and accepts or rejects. Queries may be adaptive. On a satisfiable formula some proof is always accepted; on an unsatisfiable formula every proof has acceptance probability at most \((N+2)^{- c}\). Polynomial bounds and all constants are universal. No cryptographic soundness assumption or interaction is allowed.

context_blocks.text: The PCP theorem achieves constant error with a constant number of queries. Driving soundness down to an inverse polynomial while retaining a constant number of queries would give substantially stronger verification and constraint-satisfaction gaps.

Dinur, Harsha and Kindler obtain inverse-polynomial error with polyloglogarithmically many queries. Their paper explicitly names the constant-query polynomial-alphabet endpoint as the sliding-scale conjecture in this regime. This is different from asking that a constant-error PCP have linear proof length.

cards.why: A central quantitative PCP barrier controlling the strength of gap amplification and inapproximability.

cards.title: \(\mathrm{P}_{R}\) versus \(\mathrm{NP}_{R}\) in the Blum–Shub–Smale model
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{P}_{\mathbb{R}}=\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb{R}}\) for the unit-cost Blum–Shub–Smale model over the ordered field of real numbers?
cards.definitions: Inputs are finite tuples \(x\in \mathbb{R} ^{n}\), with input size n. A machine has a finite program and finitely many fixed real constants. It can store and copy real numbers, perform +, −, ×, and division by a nonzero number, and branch on the sign or equality to zero of a stored real, at unit cost per operation; the ordinary BSS input, output and register-shift operations are included. \(\mathrm{P}_{\mathbb{R}}\) consists of subsets of the disjoint union of the spaces \(\mathbb{R} ^{n}\) decidable by one such deterministic machine in polynomially many steps as a function of n. \(\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb{R}}\) consists of sets for which membership of x is equivalent to existence of a real witness y of length bounded by a polynomial in n that is accepted by one deterministic BSS verifier in polynomially many steps. Machine constants are finite and independent of input length; witnesses may contain arbitrary reals. The target is equality of these classes, not equality in a finite-precision or bit-cost model.

context_blocks.text: The BSS model treats exact field operations and order tests as elementary computation. Its version of nondeterminism allows real witnesses and captures basic real algebraic feasibility problems.

This separation is a foundational question about algebraic computation over a continuum. Classical P versus NP does not by itself answer it: the input representation, cost model and certificates differ.

The recommended paper studies Boolean inputs to real computation. Proposition 1.1 identifies \(\mathrm{BP}(\mathrm{P}_{\mathbb R}^{0})=\mathrm{P}^{\mathrm{PosSLP}}\), where the superscript 0 permits only machine constants 0 and 1. PosSLP asks whether an arithmetic straight-line program using 0, 1, addition, subtraction and multiplication outputs a positive integer. Theorem 1.4 places PosSLP in the counting hierarchy.

With arbitrary fixed real constants, \(\mathrm{P}^{\mathrm{PosSLP}}/\mathrm{poly}=\mathrm{BP}(\mathrm{P}_{\mathbb R})\) is Conjecture 1.2 in that paper. These Boolean-input results do not settle equality of deterministic and nondeterministic BSS classes on arbitrary real inputs.

cards.title: \(\exists\mathbb{R}\) versus \(\mathrm{NP}\)
cards.formal: Is \(\exists\mathbb{R}=\mathrm{NP}\) under polynomial-time many-one reductions between finitely encoded decision problems?
cards.definitions: Let ETR be the following language of finite binary strings. An instance is an existential sentence \(\exists x_1,\ldots,x_m\in\mathbb R:\Phi(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\), where \(\Phi\) is an explicitly represented Boolean formula with atoms \(p=0\) or \(p>0\). Each \(p\) is an integer-coefficient polynomial, supplied as a list of monomials with coefficients and nonnegative exponents in binary. Parentheses, connectives, variable indices and all lengths are explicitly encoded; invalid encodings are rejected. Truth uses exact real arithmetic as mathematical semantics, not unit-cost computation. \(\exists\mathbb R\) is the class of languages reducible to ETR by a deterministic Turing machine in time polynomial in input bit length. \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of languages with polynomial-length binary witnesses checked by deterministic polynomial-time Turing machines. Equivalent fixed finite-tape machine conventions may be used. The question is unrelativized.

context_blocks.text: Real solutions describe geometric positions, distances and continuous parameters, but need not have short rational coordinate descriptions.
The complexity class organizes a large family of geometric recognition and realization problems. Its known containments are \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\exists\mathbb R\subseteq\mathrm{PSPACE}\).
Relativized structural results do not decide whether ordinary finite binary certificates suffice for the unrelativized class.

cards.title: DNF versus d-DNNF succinctness
cards.formal: Is the following nonuniform size separation true? For every \(C\geq1\), integer \(k\geq1\) and \(N\geq1\), there is a DNF formula \(F\) of size \(s\geq N\) such that every d-DNNF circuit computing exactly the same Boolean function on the same input variables has size greater than \(C(s+1)^{k}\). Equivalently, is there no single polynomial bound on the size of a d-DNNF representation of an arbitrary DNF? No efficient construction or conversion algorithm is required on either side of this size comparison.
cards.why: The question measures an inherent space cost of making overlapping explanations disjoint while retaining decomposable structure. It determines whether the simplest compact disjunctive representation can always remain compact in a form suited to exact counting, independently of how difficult that form is to find.

The question is about the existence of compact equivalent circuits, so hardness of efficiently finding a conversion or a separation for unrestricted DNNFs does not by itself answer this more specific size comparison.

cards.definitions: Inputs are Boolean variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\). A literal is \(x_i\) or \(\neg x_i\). A DNF is a finite disjunction of terms, each a conjunction of distinct literals with no contradictory pair; the empty conjunction is true and the empty disjunction false. Its size is one plus its number of terms and literal occurrences. An NNF circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with one designated output, leaves labeled by literals or the constants zero and one, and internal AND and OR gates of arbitrary finite fan-in. It may share subcircuits and have unrestricted depth. Its size is its total number of vertices and edges. The variable set of a gate comprises variables labeling leaves that reach it. Decomposability means that the variable sets of different children of every AND gate are pairwise disjoint. Determinism means that, for every OR gate and every assignment to the union of its children’s variable sets, at most one child evaluates to one. A d-DNNF satisfies both conditions. Equivalent circuits agree for every input assignment, with no error or auxiliary existentially quantified variables. There is no common variable order, tree-structured decomposition, restriction to decision gates, or uniformity requirement. Polynomial comparisons use the DNF representation size, including all literal occurrences; ordinary explicit gate/edge encodings give the same polynomial-versus-superpolynomial distinction. The family formulation using polynomial-size DNFs in the number of inputs is equivalent after permitting unused input variables as padding.

context_blocks.text: Decomposability separates the variable sets of conjunctions, while determinism makes the alternatives at each disjunction disjoint. These restrictions support exact model counting in time polynomial in the representation size. A DNF already satisfies decomposability after inconsistent terms are removed, but its terms need not be disjoint.

Capelli’s June 2026 habilitation explicitly asks for a superpolynomial d-DNNF lower bound for DNF formulas. The known separation of unrestricted DNNF from d-DNNF uses a broader source representation and therefore does not settle this DNF restriction.

Even if every DNF has a polynomial-size d-DNNF representation, finding one in polynomial time would have additional counting consequences. The source distinguishes this algorithmic conversion issue from the existence of small representations; conditional conversion hardness supplies no unconditional size separation.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the quantified superpolynomial size separation, or refute it by proving that one polynomial bounds the minimum equivalent d-DNNF size for every DNF. A negative answer need not give an efficient converter. A lower bound for decision-DNNF, structured d-DNNF, or a broader DNNF input family does not meet the stated unrestricted-output, DNF-input criterion.

cards.title: CLS versus FP
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{CLS}\subseteq\mathrm{FP}\)? Equivalently, does a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm solve the following Either-Solution problem: given an End-of-Line instance and an independent Localopt instance, return a valid solution of at least one of them?
cards.definitions:
Every circuit is an explicitly encoded acyclic Boolean circuit with fan-in-two \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}, \mathrm{NOT}\), constants, listed wires and ordered input/output nodes. An End-of-Line instance consists of \(S,\mathrm{P}:\{0,1\}^{n}	o \{0,1\}^{n}, n\ge 1\), satisfying \(\mathrm{P}(0^{n})=0^{n}\) and \(S(0^{n})
e 0^{n}\). An accepted output is a bit string \(v\in \{0,1\}^{n}\) with \(\mathrm{P}(S(v))
e v\), or with both \(v
e 0^{n}\) and \(S(\mathrm{P}(v))
e v\). In particular \(v=0^{n}\) is permitted only for the first condition. A Localopt instance consists of \(T:\{0,1\}^{m}	o \{0,1\}^{m}\) and \(V:\{0,1\}^{m}	o \{0,1\}^{r}\), with \(m,r\ge 1\). Treat V’s output as an unsigned binary integer; an accepted local-search output is w with \(V(T(w))\ge V(w)\). The joint instance contains both independent sets of circuits; n,m,r may differ. A solution is a tag selecting one instance and a string meeting that instance’s condition. On malformed encodings or failure of the two easily checkable End-of-Line conditions, output INVALID; on a valid joint instance INVALID is forbidden. The algorithm must halt within one fixed polynomial in the combined encoded length, including all circuit input/output nodes. It receives no advice, randomness or oracle. Total NP search problems are polynomially bounded input-output relations with polynomial-time verifiable outputs and at least one output for each input. A reduction maps an input to an instance and transforms every valid answer back to a valid original answer, using deterministic polynomial time for both maps. PPAD and PLS are the classes reducing to End-of-Line and Localopt respectively. The source proves that the either-solution problem is complete for their intersection and that CLS=PPAD∩PLS. These equalities give the stated equivalent discrete formulation of \(\mathrm{CLS}\subseteq\mathrm{FP}\); no new smoothness or numerical promise is introduced.

context_blocks.text: CLS captures total search tasks motivated by continuous local improvement. Fearnley, Goldberg, Hollender and Savani proved that it equals PPAD∩PLS, connecting this optimization class to two discrete existence principles.

The equivalent task presented here gives two independent succinct problems and asks for a solution to either one. The known completeness theorem means that an efficient algorithm for this task would solve every problem in CLS. The theorem identifies the class; it does not supply a polynomial-time solution algorithm.

cards.title: Polynomial-size circuits for EXP
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{EXP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\)? More explicitly, does there exist a language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\), decidable by one deterministic exponential-time algorithm, whose circuit complexity \(s_L(n)\) satisfies \[\forall C\geq1\;\forall k\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\;\forall N\geq1\;\exists n\geq N:\quad s_L(n)>C(n+1)^{k}?\]
cards.why: This is a central test of whether explicit computation can be proved to require large unrestricted Boolean circuits. Resolving it would cross the gap between uniform time hierarchy theorems and lower bounds that defeat arbitrary nonuniform circuit families.

cards.definitions: \(\mathrm{EXP}=\bigcup_{a\geq1}\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{n^{a}})\), with the usual multiplicative constants and polynomially equivalent deterministic multitape Turing-machine encodings. The input is an arbitrary binary string and the machine decides membership without a promise, advice or oracle. A Boolean circuit on \(n\) inputs is an acyclic graph using fan-in-two AND and OR gates, fan-in-one NOT gates, constants, and one output. Its size is the number of noninput gates; replacing this by its explicit gate-and-wire encoding length preserves polynomial size. The quantity \(s_L(n)\) is the minimum such size for exact agreement with membership in \(L\) on all \(n\)-bit strings. Circuit choices for different lengths are arbitrary and need not be computable. The class \(\mathrm{P/poly}\) comprises languages with \(s_L(n)\leq C(n+1)^k\) for all \(n\), for some constants \(C,k\) depending on the language. The quantifiers in the question require one language defeating every polynomial size bound; they do not require a lower bound at every sufficiently large length. The source uses exponential-time notation in a truth-table generation discussion; the card uses the standard union defining EXP. Using \(\mathrm E=\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{O(n)})\) instead gives the equivalent class-containment question by polynomial padding.

context_blocks.text: The deterministic time hierarchy separates polynomial from exponential uniform running time. It does not rule out small circuits chosen independently at each input length, which is the nonuniform issue in this conjecture.

Wigderson states the separation as Conjecture 8.6 in a discussion of explicit hard Boolean functions and pseudorandomness. Counting shows that many truth tables need large circuits, but the conjecture additionally places a hard language in a fixed uniform exponential-time class.

A 2026 preprint by Atserias and Müller proves a consistency result relating bounded arithmetic to \(\mathrm{EXP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\). Consistency of the separation with a formal theory is distinct from a proof of the separation itself.

The public note proposes a weaker upper-bound question: whether every EXP language has subexponential-size circuits. For example, one precise convention is \(\forall L\in\mathrm{EXP}\;\forall\varepsilon>0\;\exists N\;\forall n\ge N:\ s_L(n)\le 2^{\varepsilon n}\). Polynomial-size circuits would imply this upper bound. It is consequently weaker than the containment \(\mathrm{EXP}\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\), which is the negative answer to the present separation question, rather than a weaker form of the conjectured lower bound. The displayed convention specifies this contextual variant; it is not substituted for the card’s original target.

cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of \(\mathrm{EXP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\), including an EXP language and the quantified superpolynomial lower bound, or prove its negation \(\mathrm{EXP}\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\). Different hard languages for different fixed exponents, a lower bound for a restricted gate basis, or a consistency theorem alone do not settle the question.

cards.title: Exponential depth-three \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) lower bounds for E
cards.formal:
Does there exist a language \(L\in\mathrm E\) whose characteristic functions require exponential-size depth-at-most-three Boolean AND/OR circuits, with arbitrary fan-in and input negations, at infinitely many input lengths?

Let \(f_{L,n}(x)=1\) exactly when \(x\in L\), for \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), and let \(S_3(f)\) be the minimum number of AND/OR gates in such a circuit computing \(f\) exactly. The question is
\[\exists L\in\mathrm E\ \exists\delta\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\ \forall N\ge1\ \exists n\ge N:\quad S_3(f_{L,n})>2^{\delta n}.\]
Here \(N,n\) are integers. This makes the source’s class lower-bound target precise as failure of subexponential-size depth-three computation for one language in E. No almost-every-length strengthening is imposed.

sentences: The question asks for one language decidable in deterministic time exponential in input length but requiring exponential-size depth-three Boolean circuits.
The circuits use arbitrary-fan-in AND and OR gates with input negations, sharing and either top-gate orientation.
A fixed positive lower-bound exponent must hold at infinitely many lengths for the same E language.

cards.definitions:
The class \(\mathrm E\) consists of languages \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\) for which there are one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine \(M\) and a fixed positive integer \(c\) such that, on every binary string \(x\) of length \(n\), the machine halts within \(2^{c(n+1)}\) steps and outputs the membership bit of \(L\). The machine uses fixed finite alphabets, and time counts tape operations, input handling and output. There is no advice, oracle, randomness or promise restricting inputs. No separate space bound is imposed. The same \(M,c\) work at every length. This distinguishes E from unrestricted exponential time \(2^{n^{O(1)}}\) and from exponential-time computation with an NP oracle.

A circuit for an \(n\)-input function is a finite directed acyclic graph with one output. Its sources are constants \(0,1\) and literals \(x_i,\neg x_i\) for \(1\le i\le n\). Each internal gate is AND or OR of a nonempty finite list of predecessor values. Fan-in and fan-out have no fixed bound; computed values may be shared. A gate may also have a single predecessor. An output may be a literal or constant. The circuit must agree with the function on every assignment to all \(n\) variables.

Depth is the largest number of internal AND/OR gates on a source-to-output path and is at most three. Input negations do not contribute to depth; there are no internal NOT, parity, modular-counting, threshold or arbitrary truth-table gates. The size is the number of internal AND/OR gates, counting a shared gate once. Constants, literal sources and wires are not separately charged. The minimum over this class is \(S_3(f)\), which is defined for every Boolean function because a disjunctive normal form is available. Constant and literal outputs have size zero. Both possible top-gate orientations, including OR–AND–OR and AND–OR–AND, are allowed; the lower bound must cover the entire stated class.

All bottom gates have unrestricted fan-in. Neither the function nor the circuit is required to be monotone: a circuit can use both polarities of every variable. Although the notation refers to the depth-three AC-zero gate model, candidate circuits here are allowed exponential size; a polynomial-size restriction is not built into the minimization.

The circuits compared at different input lengths are completely nonuniform. They need not have computable descriptions or be produced by the machine deciding \(L\). The E condition applies to the single language whose membership functions are being computed. There is no extra algorithmic requirement to find a smallest circuit or compute its size.

The same language and the same positive exponent \(\delta\) must work for arbitrarily large lengths. A different hard function chosen independently at each length qualifies only if the resulting family has a single E decider. The displayed claim is equivalent to the existence of such an \(L\) with
\[\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2(S_3(f_{L,n})+2)}{n}>0.\]
Its negation says that every \(L\in\mathrm E\) has \(\log_2(S_3(f_{L,n})+2)/n\to0\). Thus a refutation permits the sublinear exponent and its rate to depend on \(L\), and does not require an effective procedure for constructing the circuits. The phrase exponential lower bound is interpreted at the class-noncontainment level; the source does not spell out an almost-every-length quantifier.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed existence statement. A proof must establish one E language, its uniform deterministic exponential-time bound and a positive constant exponent for a lower bound against every allowed circuit at infinitely many lengths. A refutation must prove sublinear logarithmic circuit size, as specified in the definitions, for every E language. Counting hard functions without an E evaluator, restricting bottom fan-in or monotonicity, allowing an oracle in the evaluator, or proving only a square-root-exponent lower bound is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: The source proves hardness for minimizing OR–AND–MOD circuits and discusses the resulting lower-bound consequences for that gate model. It explicitly separates those consequences from the open question for ordinary depth-three AND/OR circuits. Changing a modular-counting bottom layer to an unrestricted OR layer changes the relevant lower-bound problem.

The February 2026 manuscript describes the longstanding unrestricted depth-three lower-bound frontier at a square-root exponent. Its new matching result is for monotone circuits with bottom fan-in at most three, and its exponential dependence on the input length is in that restricted model. It does not cover all circuits minimized by this card.

The target language is allowed an E computation, whereas the related depth-three cards use NP explicitness and different exponent thresholds. Their statements therefore retain distinct evaluator and quantitative requirements; an implication should not be inferred solely from the word explicit.

The gate-count convention is used consistently in the target. Polynomial changes between ordinary gate, wire and description-size measures do not change existence of an exponential lower bound when its positive constant exponent is unspecified.

cards.title: Randomized evasiveness conjecture
cards.formal: Is there an absolute constant \(c>0\) and an integer \(n_0\ge 2\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge n_0\) and every nonconstant monotone graph property \(P\) on n vertices, its randomized adjacency-query complexity with two-sided error at most \(1/3\) satisfies \(R_{1/3}(P)\ge c n^2\)? Both c and \(n_0\) must be independent of P. This card asks for the bounded-error randomized evasiveness conjecture.
cards.why: This conjecture asks whether monotonicity and invariance under vertex names force essentially complete inspection even when random errors are allowed. It is a broad structural lower-bound question covering many graph recognition tasks at once. Its resolution would sharply delimit the power of randomized access to an exact graph property and explain why proximity testing can behave so differently.
cards.status_note: The bounded-error conjecture is explicit in the checked 2002 and 2020 sources and is restated as open in the Winter 2025 notes. The search is bounded and cited proofs were not independently verified.

importance.reason: A major longstanding structural conjecture in query complexity, asserting a universal quadratic barrier for randomized recognition across all nontrivial monotone graph properties.

sentences: A monotone graph property is invariant under vertex renaming and cannot be destroyed by adding edges.
The conjecture says every nonconstant such property needs a quadratic number of adjacency queries even with randomized error at most one third.
The query bound is worst-case over graphs and random choices, while the error guarantee holds separately for each graph.
Zero-error expected-cost lower bounds and the solved quantum analogue concern distinct computational models.
A resolution would establish or refute a universal information barrier for randomized exact graph recognition.

cards.definitions: Let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and let \(E_n\) be the set of unordered pairs of distinct elements of \([n]\). An input \(x\in\{0,1\}^{E_n}\) describes a finite simple undirected graph: \(x_e=1\) means e is an edge. Every one of the \(2^{\binom n2}\) assignments is a valid input. A graph property is a function \(P:\{0,1\}^{E_n}\to\{0,1\}\) invariant under every permutation of the vertices, with the permutation acting on each edge’s two endpoints. Monotone means \(x_e\le y_e\) for every e implies \(P(x)\le P(y)\). Nonconstant means some input has value 0 and another has value 1; for monotone P the empty graph has value 0 and the complete graph value 1. No monotonicity across different vertex counts is imposed. A deterministic query tree is a finite binary tree whose internal nodes name edges, whose outgoing branches carry the possible queried bits, and whose leaves carry output bits. On input x it follows the branch specified by each queried \(x_e\). Its cost on x is the number of queries along that path. A randomized query algorithm is a probability distribution \(\mu\), independent of x, on such trees. It has cost at most q if every tree with positive probability has depth at most q. It computes P with error at most \(1/3\) when \(\Pr_{T\sim\mu}[T(x)=P(x)]\ge 2/3\) for every input x. Define \(R_{1/3}(P)\) as the smallest such integer q. The distribution and trees may depend on P and n. Sampling, storage and all computation on previously obtained answers are uncharged; only queries revealing one adjacency bit are counted. There is no uniformity or efficient-construction requirement on the trees, and no description of P is part of the queried graph. Queries may be adaptive. Input distributions, promises that a no-instance is far from P, quantum access, certificates and other graph oracles are absent. Cost is worst-case over both the graph and trees in the support, not expected over those choices. The only approximation allowed is the stated probability of an incorrect membership bit. In particular, a graph missing P by a single edge still requires the same success guarantee.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed universal lower-bound proposition. A positive answer requires one c and one \(n_0\) working for all the indicated graph properties and all \(n\ge n_0\). Its negation is: for every \(c>0\) and every integer \(N\ge 2\), there exist an integer \(n\ge N\) and a nonconstant monotone graph property P on n vertices with \(R_{1/3}(P)<c n^2\). A refutation must establish this quantified failure, not just a constant-factor saving from querying every edge. A result only for zero-error randomized algorithms, deterministic algorithms, selected properties, or proximity testing does not by itself settle the bounded-error target.

context_blocks.text: Connectedness is monotone: adding edges cannot disconnect a connected graph. It is also independent of how its vertices are named. The conjecture encompasses every property with these two formal features, including properties chosen separately at different graph sizes, rather than only a fixed list of familiar algorithmic problems.

Recognition asks for the actual membership bit on every graph. Property testing changes the required distinction by allowing graphs close to the property to have unconstrained answers. Goldreich’s discussion emphasizes this difference: constant-query proximity testers do not contradict a quadratic lower bound for recognition.

The saved manuscript only briefly describes randomized recognition. This card explicitly adopts the bounded-error convention already used in its working summary, corroborated by Buhrman and de Wolf’s Open Problem 6 and Grossman, Komargodski and Naor’s Conjecture 3.14. The no-error expected-cost question is a distinct weaker variant and is preserved as context, not silently conflated with this target.

For zero-error computation, every sampled deterministic tree is correct on every input and complexity is the largest, over inputs, expected query count. Chakrabarti and Khot prove \(\Omega(n^{4/3}(\log n)^{1/3})\) in that model. Their definition is narrower than algorithms allowed to give a wrong answer. The cited theorem is therefore not itself a proof of the same bound for this card’s larger algorithm class.

The deterministic Aanderaa–Karp–Rosenberg conjecture asks for the exact value \(\binom n2\) for every property at every size. Here the target allows a fixed multiplicative saving and concerns randomized algorithms. A quadratic randomized lower bound would not automatically establish the exact deterministic value. A quadratic deterministic lower bound alone does not exclude randomized savings.

The quantum analogue has a different scale. The 2020 result proves a universal \(\Omega(n)\) quantum-query lower bound, and the property of having at least one edge admits \(O(n)\) quantum queries. Resolving that linear-scale analogue does not resolve the quadratic classical randomized conjecture.

cards.definitions:
SAT is the language of satisfiable finite Boolean formulas built from variables, NOT, binary AND and binary OR. Fix the following binary prefix encoding: a variable with positive index i is 00 followed by 1^l 0 and the l-bit binary representation of i, where l is the bit length of i; NOT is 01 followed by one encoded formula; AND is 10 followed by two encoded formulas; OR is 11 followed by two encoded formulas. A valid string must encode exactly one complete formula. Invalid strings are outside SAT. Truth assignments map the finitely many variables occurring in a formula to Boolean values, with the usual truth tables for the three connectives.

The sentence \(\sigma\) is the usual finite-computation arithmetization of: there exist a deterministic Turing machine M and positive integers c,k such that, for every binary string x, M halts within \(c(|x|+1)^k\) transitions and outputs 1 exactly when x is in SAT, and 0 otherwise. Machines have a finite transition table, a two-way infinite tape, a finite tape alphabet containing the binary input symbols and blank, a start state, and accepting and rejecting halting states; each transition reads and writes one symbol, changes state, and moves the head by at most one cell. The input is written consecutively starting at the initial head position, with blank elsewhere. There is no oracle, advice or randomness. Finite strings, transition tables and computation histories are encoded by natural numbers. Standard effective encodings of these finite objects give ZFC-provably equivalent sentences, so the target is invariant under their choice. SAT is NP-complete, making this the conventional P = NP sentence.

ZFC means classical first-order set theory in the language of membership and equality, with extensionality, empty set, pairing, union, power set, infinity, foundation, choice, and the separation and replacement schemas for all first-order formulas with parameters. Arithmetic is interpreted on its natural numbers, with finite strings and machine computations encoded there. The notation \(\mathrm{ZFC}\vdash\tau\) means that there is a finite derivation of \(\tau\) using these axioms in a sound and complete classical first-order proof calculus with equality; equivalent standard calculi give the same derivable sentences. There is no proof-length bound, extra soundness axiom, oracle, or restriction to a weak fragment of arithmetic. Both unprovability assertions range over all finite derivations in the ordinary metatheory.

The question asks for actual syntactic independence, without building a consistency hypothesis into the proposition. A positive answer entails that ZFC is consistent; inconsistency would make both sentences derivable and hence make this independence claim false. If an argument assumes Con(ZFC) or stronger principles, those assumptions must remain explicit. Choosing ZFC makes the source's general independence discussion into one definite yes/no question; it does not claim that independence from every possible axiom system is equivalent.

context_blocks.text: Fortnow’s further-reading section directs readers to Aaronson’s survey on formal independence. The general source discussion does not select a single axiom system; the target here explicitly fixes full ZFC.

Aaronson distinguishes independence for weak logical theories from the unresolved question for strong theories encompassing ordinary mathematical reasoning. Conditional bounded-arithmetic results do not establish either unprovability assertion for full ZFC.

Oracle results change the computational model by allowing machines to query an additional language. Opposite relativizations or independence of an oracle formulation do not establish independence of the ordinary SAT sentence used here.

The target concerns finite formal derivations in a specified theory. It does not say that the arithmetic statement lacks a truth value, and it does not restrict the length or the mathematical methods of a permitted ZFC derivation.

Actual syntactic independence implies consistency of the named theory. An independence theorem stated only under an unproved consistency assumption has a different logical form, so such an assumption must remain explicit in any proposed answer.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the two stated unprovability assertions, or their logical negation: \(\mathrm{ZFC}\vdash\sigma\) or \(\mathrm{ZFC}\vdash\neg\sigma\). Derivability must concern the specified SAT sentence and full ZFC. A proof only about a weaker theory, bounded-length proofs, an oracle version, or an unrelated strengthened statement does not settle this target. An independence theorem conditional on consistency settles only that explicitly conditional version unless its assumption is also established.

cards.title: Majority outside constant-depth modular circuits
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{MAJ}\notin\mathrm{ACC}^{0}\)? Precisely, for every fixed modulus \(m\geq2\), depth bound \(d\geq1\), constants \(C\geq1\), \(k\geq1\), and \(N\geq1\), is there an input length \(n\geq N\) for which no depth-at-most-\(d\) circuit over AND, OR, NOT and \(\mathrm{MOD}_{m}\), with at most \(C(n+1)^k\) gates, computes \(\mathrm{MAJ}_{n}\) exactly?
cards.why: Majority is a basic threshold operation. Showing that constant-depth modular circuits cannot compute it would separate ordinary threshold counting from the full fixed-modulus ACC⁰ model on a simple explicit function.
cards.status_note: The target is explicitly open in Jukna’s source. A 13 September 2026 small-text check of later modular-circuit work identified a symmetry-restricted AND result, not a solution for majority in unrestricted ACC⁰. No resolution was verified; status remains source_open.

sentences: Majority returns one when at least half of its input bits are one.
ACC⁰ circuits combine Boolean operations and modular-counting gates using constant depth and polynomial size.

cards.definitions: For \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\), \(\mathrm{MAJ}_{n}(x)=1\) if and only if \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\geq\lceil n/2\rceil\). An ACC circuit is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit with one output, unbounded-fan-in AND, OR and \(\mathrm{MOD}_m\) gates, fan-in-one NOT gates, and constants. A \(\mathrm{MOD}_{m}\) gate outputs one precisely when the sum of its Boolean inputs is divisible by \(m\). Depth is the maximum number of noninput gates on an input-output path, including NOT gates. Size is the number of noninput gates; counting wires instead gives the same polynomial-size class. The modulus, depth and polynomial-size constants are fixed for the whole family and cannot depend on \(n\). Circuits may be chosen separately for every length, without any construction algorithm, uniformity or bound on fan-out. The class \(\mathrm{ACC}^{0}\) is the union of these polynomial-size, constant-depth families over all fixed moduli. Allowing a fixed finite collection of moduli is equivalent, by using their common multiple with a constant-size gate substitution. All assignments must be computed correctly; no probability of error is allowed.

context_blocks.text: Jukna’s Research Problem 12.28 asks whether Majority lies outside ACC⁰. This is a lower bound for one concrete counting function, stronger in explicitness than separating a large uniform complexity class from the circuit class.

Prime-modulus lower bounds and the separation of nondeterministic exponential time from ACC⁰ concern different targets from the full majority question. In particular, results for prime moduli do not cover arbitrary composite moduli such as six.

Pago’s 2026 work proves lower bounds for computing AND using modular gates under syntactic symmetry assumptions. The permitted gate basis, target function and symmetry restriction differ from the unrestricted majority circuits in this card, so that result does not resolve this question.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal lower-bound statement, or refute it by proving the existence of fixed \(m,d,C,k\) and circuits of size at most \(C(n+1)^k\) computing majority for every input length. Refuting one fixed size exponent is insufficient for a positive answer. Results for a prime modulus, a restricted wiring symmetry, uniform circuits alone or a different hard function do not meet the complete criterion.

Pago’s 2026 work proves lower bounds for computing AND using modular gates under syntactic symmetry assumptions. The permitted gate basis, target function and symmetry restriction differ from the unrestricted majority circuits in this card, so that result does not resolve this question.

cards.title: Graph nonisomorphism in BPP
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform randomized Turing machine M and fixed positive integers C,k such that M halts on every binary input x and every random outcome within \(C(|x|+1)^k\) transitions, and outputs the correct membership bit for \(\mathrm{GNI}\) with probability at least \(2/3\) for each x? The language \(\mathrm{GNI}\) consists of valid encodings of two nonisomorphic finite simple undirected graphs. This asks whether \(\mathrm{GNI}\in\mathrm{BPP}\).
cards.why: This asks whether random computation alone can efficiently decide a canonical structural equivalence problem. Nonisomorphism has efficient interactive verification, but the help of an unbounded prover is an additional resource. Settling the BPP question would locate ordinary graph comparison more precisely between efficient deterministic algorithms, randomized algorithms and stronger forms of verification.

sentences: Graph nonisomorphism asks whether two graphs have no adjacency-preserving vertex bijection.
The target is one randomized polynomial-time algorithm with error at most one third on every encoded input.
Because BPP is closed under complement, the same question can be phrased for ordinary graph isomorphism.
Interactive proofs, quasipolynomial algorithms and algorithms for restricted graph classes do not provide the required decider.
A resolution would clarify whether random computation alone suffices for this central structural comparison problem.

cards.definitions: For \(n\ge 0\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]\) empty. A finite simple undirected graph G on \([n]\) has an adjacency matrix \(A_G\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) that is symmetric with zero diagonal. Its vertices are labeled; its edges are unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Encode a pair G,H by \(1^n0\), followed by the full row-major matrix of G, followed by \(1^m0\) and the full row-major matrix of H. The total binary length is \(N=n^2+m^2+n+m+2\). Extra trailing bits, missing entries, or nonsymmetric or nonzero-diagonal matrices make an encoding malformed. Graphs G,H are isomorphic, written \(G\cong H\), if there is a bijection \(\pi:[n]\to[m]\) such that \(A_G(i,j)=A_H(\pi(i),\pi(j))\) for every \(i,j\in[n]\). If \(n\ne m\), no such bijection exists; the two empty graphs are isomorphic. All valid graph pairs are in the domain, without degree, connectivity, automorphism, sparsity or random-input promises. Computation receives the entire binary string, rather than an oracle or succinctly generated adjacency matrix. The computation model is one uniform classical multitape Turing machine with a finite program, finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. In one transition each tape head moves at most one cell. Time counts all transitions, including input access and internal computation. Polynomial time means a bound \(C(N+1)^k\) for fixed positive integers C,k, independent of the input and of the graph sizes. There is no advice, prover, witness supplied with the input, graph-isomorphism oracle or uncounted preprocessing. At a randomized transition the machine may obtain one independent unbiased random bit, with this transition counted in its runtime. Success probability is over these internal bits for each fixed input, not over a distribution of graphs. BPP consists of binary languages for which such a machine has error at most \(1/3\) on every input and a polynomial worst-case clock over inputs and random outcomes. For \(\mathrm{GNI}\), acceptance is required with probability at least \(2/3\) when the encoding is valid and \(G\not\cong H\); it is at most \(1/3\) for isomorphic pairs and malformed strings. Distinct vertex counts form yes-instances for GNI. The output is only one membership bit, without a nonisomorphism certificate, quantum computation or interaction with another party. One machine and one polynomial must work at all graph sizes.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of \(\mathrm{GNI}\in\mathrm{BPP}\) or \(\mathrm{GNI}\notin\mathrm{BPP}\) in the model above. The positive case must supply one uniform polynomial-time bounded-error decider, or establish its existence, with the required probability bound on every input. The negative case must exclude every such randomized machine. Correctness only on typical graphs, an interactive verification protocol, a method with only expected polynomial time and no suitable clock conversion, or a restricted-model lower bound does not by itself settle this target.

context_blocks.text: Graph nonisomorphism asserts that no bijection of the vertex sets preserves adjacency. An isomorphism is an easily checked witness for the opposite answer; a failed attempt to find one does not certify nonisomorphism. The target requires a bounded probability of error on every graph pair, including highly symmetric instances.

Goldreich’s footnote uses graph nonisomorphism to contrast an interactive proof with a problem not known to have a BPP algorithm. The verifier in such a proof receives messages from a computationally unbounded party. The question here removes that assistance and asks about the verifier’s own randomized computation.

BPP is closed under complement: reversing the answer preserves its error bound and runtime. After checking that the encoding is valid, an algorithm for nonisomorphism can therefore be turned into one for isomorphism, and conversely. Validity checking is needed because both graph languages reject malformed strings. Thus this is exactly the randomized polynomial-time question for ordinary graph isomorphism, with its answer polarity reversed.

The deterministic and randomized targets are related but distinct. A deterministic polynomial-time isomorphism decider supplies a positive answer here. A negative answer here would exclude a deterministic polynomial-time isomorphism decider and, since isomorphism has efficiently checkable permutation witnesses, would imply P differs from NP. A positive answer here does not automatically derandomize the computation.

The general quasipolynomial upper bound also applies to nonisomorphism by reversing a validated input’s answer. Its January 2017 correction matters when interpreting the original arXiv manuscript. Parameterized algorithms and typical-instance performance must separately account for their promises before they can be compared with an all-input polynomial clock.

The 2026 survey concerns the general deterministic frontier and parameterized progress. It does not prove that randomized polynomial-time algorithms are impossible. The BPP question remains a dated source-open question after the bounded later-work check recorded here.

cards.title: Directed reachability in polynomial time and polylogarithmic space
cards.formal:
Is there one deterministic algorithm that decides directed reachability using polynomial time and polylogarithmic working space simultaneously?

Precisely, does there exist a uniform deterministic Turing decider \(M\) and fixed positive integers \(a,k,c\) such that, for every encoded instance \((G,s,t)\) of bit length \(N\), it correctly decides whether \(t\) is reachable from \(s\), while
\[\operatorname{time}_M(G,s,t)\le c(N+2)^a\qquad\text{and}\qquad\operatorname{space}_M(G,s,t)\le c\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil^k?\]
Both bounds must hold for the same computation on every input. This is the question whether directed reachability belongs to the class SC.
cards.why: Directed reachability captures nondeterministic logarithmic space and is a basic model of exploring a large state graph. The question asks whether exploration can be both computationally efficient and extremely economical in reusable memory. Its resolution would clarify the relationship between deterministic and nondeterministic space while separating a genuine simultaneous resource bound from two individually achievable guarantees.

The last check establishes only that the stated model includes extra catalytic memory. None of these results supplies the requested general deterministic simultaneous time-space bound, and bounded later-work searches found no matching resolution. Current openness is not exhaustively certified.

sentences: The problem asks for directed reachability to be decided simultaneously in polynomial time and polylogarithmic space.
One uniform deterministic machine must meet both bounds on every explicitly encoded graph and marked vertex pair.
No graph restrictions, randomness, advice or additional catalytic memory are allowed.
Separate efficient-time and small-space algorithms do not satisfy the joint requirement.
The target is equivalently inclusion of nondeterministic logspace in SC, and is weaker than L equaling NL.

cards.definitions:
For an integer \(v\ge1\), the directed graph \(G=([v],E)\) has \([v]=\{1,\ldots,v\}\) and \(E\subseteq[v]\times[v]\). Loops are allowed, and repeated edges have no separate meaning. The graph may have cycles, arbitrary in- and out-degree and arbitrarily many paths. No planarity, acyclicity, uniqueness, few-path or connectivity promise is imposed. The marked vertices satisfy \(s,t\in[v]\).

Reachability means that for some integer \(\ell\ge0\) there are vertices \(u_0,\ldots,u_\ell\) with \(u_0=s\), \(u_\ell=t\) and \((u_i,u_{i+1})\in E\) for every \(i<\ell\). The zero-edge path makes every vertex reachable from itself. Whenever reachability holds, a path with at most \(v-1\) edges also exists. The required output is one membership bit; a path itself need not be output.

Use the explicit binary encoding \(1^v0\), followed by the \(v^2\) adjacency-matrix bits in row-major order, followed by fixed-width binary encodings of \(s,t\). Each vertex field has \(b_v=\lceil\log_2(v+1)\rceil\) bits and must represent an integer between \(1\) and \(v\). The total length is
\[N=v+1+v^2+2b_v.\]
There are no trailing fields. Any binary string failing this format is rejected. The machine must also meet the same time and space bounds on malformed inputs, measured by their actual length. This representation is polynomially related to the vertex count; it is not a succinct circuit description of an exponentially large graph.

The machine has one two-way read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of ordinary work tapes over fixed finite alphabets, initially blank. Each step changes the finite control, reads or writes a bounded number of tape symbols and moves each head by at most one cell. Time is the total number of steps until its accept/reject halt, in the worst case. Space is the maximum number of work-tape cells ever visited during the run, multiplied by a fixed number of bits sufficient to encode a tape symbol. In particular all counters, indices, remembered input bits and temporary data count toward space. Input storage and the finite control do not count. The single decision bit is the halting state, so no uncharged output tape can be used as working memory.

No random bits, nondeterministic choices, quantum register, oracle, advice, writable input or extra catalytic memory are available. The same finite program and constants work for all graph orders and all valid and malformed inputs. An algorithm may depend on the fixed encoding, but cannot be chosen separately for each graph. The input is read sequentially by its head rather than supplied as a unit-cost adjacency oracle; scanning it is charged to time.

For an ordinary language of binary strings, SC means decidability by a single uniform deterministic machine with a polynomial time bound and a fixed-power logarithmic space bound as above. It differs from merely supplying one polynomial-time algorithm and another polylogarithmic-space algorithm. The exponent \(k\) is allowed to be any fixed positive integer; the target does not specifically demand logarithmic or squared-logarithmic space.

Equivalently, the question is \(\mathrm{NL}\subseteq\mathrm{SC}\). Here NL consists of languages decided by a nondeterministic Turing machine with logarithmic charged work space and a fixed polynomial clock on every branch, accepting an input exactly when at least one branch accepts. Directed reachability is NL-complete under deterministic logarithmic-space many-one reductions, and those reductions preserve membership in SC. In particular, \(\mathrm L=\mathrm{NL}\) would imply an affirmative answer, but this card asks only for the weaker simultaneous bounds and does not assert the converse.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the simultaneous-bound existence statement. An affirmative answer must give one exact deterministic decider for all directed graphs and prove its polynomial time and fixed-power logarithmic space bounds with constants independent of the instance. A negative answer must prove that no such decider exists: for every correct uniform decider and every proposed constants, some input violates at least one bound. Separate algorithms meeting separate bounds, a restriction to a special graph family, or a simulation with randomness, advice or catalytic memory is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: Exercise 9 explicitly asks whether PATH is in SC and points out that Savitch’s theorem does not settle this. The small-space simulation uses superpolynomial time, while usual graph traversal uses much more than polylogarithmic space.

Barnes, Buss, Ruzzo and Schieber give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm with space \(v/2^{\Theta(\sqrt{\log v})}\). This is sublinear but remains far larger than any fixed power of \(\log v\). Their introduction also separates lower bounds for restricted graph-exploration models from bounds for general Turing computation.

The 2025 paper studies quantum logspace on directed graphs with bounded path counts and reviews deterministic simultaneous bounds for such restricted instances. Its promises and computational model are different from an unrestricted deterministic reachability algorithm.

The February 2026 preprint trades ordinary workspace against an additional tape of catalytic memory. Catalytic storage is extra writable memory that must eventually be restored, and is absent from this card’s model; a small ordinary-workspace bound in that model is not the claimed SC containment.

cards.title: P versus NP intersect coNP
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\)? Equivalently, does there exist a language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) with polynomially bounded, polynomial-time verifiable certificates for both membership and nonmembership, but no uniform deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm?
cards.why: This asks whether computational difficulty can persist even when every yes answer and every no answer has a short efficiently checkable proof. It isolates a basic boundary between verification and decision that is finer than the usual one-sided NP condition.
