cards.title: Linear-time exact inversion counting
cards.formal: Do there exist one uniform deterministic word-RAM algorithm \(A\) and a constant \(C>0\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\) and every explicitly listed permutation \(\pi\) of \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(A\) outputs \[\operatorname{Inv}(\pi)=|\{(i,j)\in[n]^2:i<j\ \text{and}\ \pi(i)>\pi(j)\}|\] exactly, using at most \(Cn\) machine instructions in the worst case? The word length and allowed instructions are specified below. The constant and the program must be independent of \(n\) and \(\pi\).
cards.definitions: The input contains \(n\) and the array \(\pi(1),\ldots,\pi(n)\), promised to contain each integer from one through \(n\) exactly once. The output is the single integer inversion count, between zero and \(n(n-1)/2\). Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Choose \(d\ge3\), so the count fits in a word. All constants are independent of the permutation and \(n\). No randomness is allowed. The values are already ranks, so no conversion from arbitrary ordered keys is required. The array has one entry per word; no compressed representation, streaming restriction or comparison-only restriction is imposed. The algorithm may use auxiliary random-access memory, but allocating, initializing and accessing that memory consumes the counted steps. The output is one word containing the exact nonnegative integer. Neither a list of all inverted pairs nor individual per-position counts are required.

context_blocks.text: An inversion is a pair of positions whose values occur in decreasing order. Its total is the Kendall tau distance from the identity ordering and the minimum number of adjacent swaps required to sort the permutation.

Chan and Pătraşcu give a deterministic exact \(O(n\sqrt{\log_2 n})\)-time word-RAM algorithm. They also give a linear-time constant-relative-error approximation, which does not supply the exact output requested here.
Elmasry’s adaptive algorithm improves the time on inputs with fewer inversions, but retains a superlinear worst-case bound over all permutations.

Kempa and Kociumaka’s STOC 2025 paper again identifies inversion counting among the central problems whose fastest known algorithms have the square-root-logarithmic overhead. Theorem 1.3 transfers any improved inversion-counting time to a packed Dictionary Matching problem. Its bounded-integer array formulation and the permutation formulation have the same linear-time endpoint.

In that Dictionary Matching problem, the input consists of a packed binary text occupying a linear number of logarithmic-size words and a linear number of patterns, each of logarithmic bit length; the output says whether any pattern occurs. The connection is a conditional consequence for another task, not an unconditional superlinear lower bound. The linear exact endpoint remains the card’s explicit editorial formulation of the gap.

cards.why: Exact inversion counting compresses a permutation’s pairwise disorder into one integer and is a fundamental offline aggregation task. Its complexity remains separated from the cost of sorting already rank-bounded integers. The 2025 hardness connections show that a linear-time solution would also change the algorithmic frontier for packed-string processing.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence assertion or its negation. A positive answer must specify one fixed program and prove its exact count and linear worst-case running time for every legal permutation in the specified model. A negative answer must exclude all such programs and all fixed constants. A relative-error estimate, an algorithm that is linear only on nearly sorted inputs, an expected-time randomized algorithm, or an improvement still superlinear in the worst case does not meet this target. A conditional lower bound establishes only its stated conditional implication.

cards.title: Near-linear constant-factor minimum-degree spanning trees
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic algorithm \(A\), absolute constants \(K,C\ge1\), and an integer \(b\ge0\) such that, for every connected simple undirected graph \(G=([n],E)\) with \(n\ge2\) and \(m=|E|\), the algorithm outputs a spanning tree \(T\subseteq G\) satisfying \(\Delta(T)\le K\Delta^\star(G)\) in at most \(C(m+n)(\log_2(n+2))^b\) word-RAM operations? Here \(\Delta(T)=\max_{v\in[n]}\deg_T(v)\) and \(\Delta^\star(G)=\min\{\Delta(T):T\text{ is a spanning tree of }G\}\). All constants and the program must be independent of the graph. This is a static construction problem; the graph is supplied once, and no update sequence is part of the input.
cards.why: A low-degree spanning tree supplies a connected backbone while limiting the largest number of connections handled by one vertex. A constant approximation in near-linear time would make a strong structural guarantee available at a cost close to reading the graph. The target is substantially weaker than exact degree minimization, but stronger than bounds whose approximation grows with the graph size. This is a static construction frontier, despite the dynamic setting of the seminar collection.
cards.status_note: Reported resolution: arXiv:2607.11413v1 (13 July 2026), Theorem 1.1, states a deterministic near-linear construction meeting the source’s constant-factor target. The target correspondence, concluding proof and handling of unknown optimum were checked on 14 September 2026, but the full technical proof was not independently verified and no accepted publication of this particular result was confirmed. Status remains uncertain to express that verification limit; it should not be read as a newly certified open problem.

cards.definitions: The vertices are labelled \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), all edges are unweighted unordered pairs of distinct vertices, and the input has no repeated edges. A spanning tree is a connected acyclic graph with vertex set \([n]\) and edge set contained in \(E\); it has exactly \(n-1\) edges. Its degree counts incident tree edges. The minimum defining \(\Delta^\star(G)\) exists because the graph is finite and connected; for \(n\ge2\), it is at least one. Input is an explicit adjacency-list array with vertex offsets, an entry for each endpoint of each edge, and the integers \(n,m\); each identifier or offset occupies one word. Output is an explicit list of the tree’s \(n-1\) endpoint pairs. The algorithm is a single finite program independent of \(n,m\), with words of \(W=\lceil d\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits for a fixed integer \(d\ge4\). Each operation reads or writes constantly many addressed words, compares, branches, performs Boolean operations or shifts, adds, subtracts or multiplies modulo \(2^W\), or divides unsigned words by a nonzero divisor with quotient and remainder. Shifts by at least \(W\) return zero. Work memory initially contains zero. All input access, initialization performed by the program, preprocessing, addressing and output writes are charged; no oracle for the optimum, graph-dependent advice, real arithmetic or random coins is available. The time bound is worst-case for every valid input. Near-linear means the displayed bound with one fixed logarithmic exponent; the approximation factor is one universal constant, not a function of \(n\), \(m\) or the optimum. The deterministic convention makes explicit the type of algorithm in the currently reported resolution.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean establishing the algorithmic existence statement with explicit finite program, approximation constant and time-bound constants, or proving its negation. An affirmative proof must cover every connected input graph and produce the tree itself, without being given \(\Delta^\star(G)\). An estimate of the optimum, a guarantee restricted to dense graphs or large optimal degree, or an additive error growing with \(n\) does not by itself establish a universal constant ratio. This yes/no question does not ask to optimize \(K\) or approximate the integer optimum within \(1/100\). A cited theorem or an unformalized implementation is not a Lean-verified submission.

context_blocks.text: Saranurak’s question in Seminar 24471 concerns one input graph. It asks for a near-linear-time algorithm achieving a constant multiplicative approximation to the minimum possible maximum tree degree. Its occurrence in a seminar about distributed and dynamic algorithms does not add update operations to this particular question.

The classical Fürer–Raghavachari result has additive error at most one, but its \(O(mn)\)-scale running time is much larger than near-linear. Later near-linear constructions allowed additive terms logarithmic in the number of vertices; such terms do not yield a uniform constant ratio when the optimal degree is small.

Bhattacharya, Farokhnejad and Wang’s STOC 2026 result gives an additive-one approximation in \(\widetilde O(mn^{3/4})\) time. It improves the earlier construction time without itself meeting the near-linear target.

The July 2026 preprint by Bhattacharya, Farokhnejad, Saranurak and Wang states a deterministic construction with degree at most \(\lceil(1+\varepsilon)\Delta^\star\rceil+1\) in \(\widetilde O(m/\varepsilon^2)\) time. Its Theorem 1.1 explicitly identifies this as resolving the constant-factor question. For any fixed positive \(\varepsilon\le1\), this degree guarantee implies a universal constant factor because \(\Delta^\star\ge1\).

The preprint’s theorem, concluding proof and treatment of unknown optimum were inspected. Its full collection of technical lemmas and data-structure proofs has not been independently verified in this review, and the checked author record presents it as an arXiv manuscript. The card therefore records a reported resolution with uncertain verification status, rather than asserting that a new open gap remains or certifying a completed proof.

cards.title: Strongly polynomial planar minimum-cost flow
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic strongly polynomial algorithm for minimum-cost flow in a planar directed graph whose worst-case number of arithmetic operations and comparisons is \(o(n^{2}\log(n+2))\), where \(n\) is the number of vertices? The algorithm must return an exact minimum-cost feasible flow, or correctly report infeasibility, for all rational capacities, costs and vertex supplies.
cards.why: This asks how much planarity can accelerate exact flow optimization when numerical magnitudes cannot enter the operation count. It separates combinatorial graph structure from progress that relies on bounded capacities and costs.

sentences: Minimum-cost flow assigns capacity-respecting arc flows that meet prescribed supplies and minimize total cost.
The question asks for an asymptotic improvement over the quadratic-times-logarithmic bound on planar graphs.
The algorithm must be strongly polynomial, so numerical magnitudes cannot enter its arithmetic-operation bound.
A later nearly linear algorithm for polynomially bounded integer data does not by itself meet that requirement.
A resolution would show whether planar structure yields a faster exact algorithm independently of the size of the input numbers.

cards.definitions: The input is a finite directed graph with vertex set \([n]\), no loops and at most one arc for each ordered pair of vertices; opposite arcs are allowed. The underlying undirected graph is planar, and a combinatorial planar embedding is supplied. Thus the number of arcs is \(O(n)\). Each arc \(a\) has a finite rational capacity \(u_a\geq0\) and rational cost \(c_a\), and each vertex \(v\) has rational supply \(b_v\), with \(\sum_v b_v=0\). All numerators and positive denominators are encoded in binary; no magnitude bound is imposed. A feasible flow assigns rational \(f_a\) with \(0\leq f_a\leq u_a\) and \(\sum_{a\text{ out of }v} f_a-\sum_{a\text{ into }v}f_a=b_v\) at each vertex. Its cost is \(\sum_a c_a f_a\). Strong polynomiality means a bound polynomial in \(n\) on exact rational arithmetic operations, comparisons and index/memory operations, independent of all numeric bit lengths, together with a polynomial bound in total input bit length on every intermediate number’s encoding length. Arithmetic uses addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by nonzero values. The algorithm has finite uniform code and no advice, randomness or oracle. The little-o improvement means that there is a function \(T(n)\) bounding its operation count on every such \(n\)-vertex input with \(T(n)/(n^{2}\log(n+2))\to0\). The source’s instruction to beat the stated bound is interpreted as an asymptotic little-o improvement, not merely a smaller leading constant. The simple planar-network convention prevents arbitrarily many parallel arcs from hiding an unbounded input size in \(n\).

context_blocks.text: Erickson’s question in the 2013 seminar report explicitly asks for a strongly polynomial algorithm improving the quadratic-times-logarithmic bound. The supply-and-capacity formulation is stated there; all-zero supplies give its minimum-cost circulation special case.

A 2022 preprint gives a nearly linear algorithm for planar minimum-cost flow with polynomially bounded integer costs and capacities. Those numeric restrictions are material: this result does not by itself answer the strongly polynomial question for arbitrary rational input data.

cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof of existence of an algorithm with the exact flow guarantee, little-o operation bound and polynomial intermediate bit lengths, or prove that no such deterministic strongly polynomial algorithm exists. A speedup for bounded numerical data, an approximation algorithm, or a lower leading constant at the same asymptotic order does not answer the stated question.

cards.title: Set-system sparsifiers of size proportional to chain length
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that for every integer \(m\ge 1\), every family \(S\subseteq 2^{[m]}\), every weight vector \(w\in \mathbb{R} \ge 0^{m}\) and every \(0<\varepsilon <1\), there is a reweighting \(\tilde\{w\}\in \mathbb{R} \ge 0^{m}\) with at most \(C\cdot CL(S)/\varepsilon ^{2}\) nonzero coordinates and satisfying \((1- \varepsilon )\sum _{i\in A}w_{i}\le \sum _{i\in A}\tilde\{w\}_{i}\le (1+\varepsilon )\sum _{i\in A}w_{i}\) simultaneously for every \(A\in S\)?
cards.why: Would give a sharp structural bound for simultaneous multiplicative compression of arbitrary weighted set families. It asks whether chain length and squared inverse accuracy fully account for the necessary support, without logarithmic losses.
cards.status_note: Published definitions, main bound and Conjecture 23 checked through 11 September 2026, together with the related May 2026 report and subsequent searches. No matching logarithm-free universal bound or counterexample was located.

progress.text: The ICALP paper proves a universe-size-independent bound with logarithmic overhead and poses the \(O(CL(S)/\varepsilon ^{2})\) bound as Conjecture 23.

cards.definitions: Here \([m]=\{1,\ldots ,m\}\), and S is any finite collection of subsets, including possibly the empty collection. The support of w̃ is \(\{i:\tilde\{w\}_{i}>0\}\); coordinates outside it are dropped, while retained coordinates may receive arbitrary nonnegative real weights. No normalization such as \(\sum w_{i}=1\) is imposed. Following the source’s witness definition, a chain of length \(\ell\) consists of distinct coordinates \(a_{1},\ldots ,a_{\ell}\) and distinct sets \(A_{1},\ldots ,A_{\ell}\in S\) with \(a_{i}\in A_{i}\) for every i and \(a_{j}\notin A_{i}\) whenever \(i<j\). \(CL(S)\) is the maximum possible \(\ell\), allowing \(\ell =0\). Equivalently, take the union-closure \(U(S)=\{\bigcup T:T\subseteq S\}\), including the empty union; \(CL(S)\) is the largest number of strict inclusions in an ascending chain starting from \(\varnothing\) in \(U(S)\). Thus \(CL(S)=0\) when S is empty or contains only \(\varnothing\). It is not merely the largest chain in the original family. A \((1\pm \varepsilon )\) sparsifier is a reweighting satisfying the simultaneous inequalities in the statement. Sets of original weight zero must retain weight exactly zero. All data and weights are quantified mathematically; the question places no running-time, oracle-access, randomness or bit-complexity requirement on finding w̃. The same C must work independently of m, S, w and \(\varepsilon\). The source allows \(\varepsilon >0\); values \(\varepsilon \ge 1\) admit the zero reweighting, so restricting the nontrivial question to \(0<\varepsilon <1\) preserves it.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal existence bound with one absolute constant C, or refute it by showing that for every C there are a family, weights and an accuracy parameter for which every multiplicative sparsifier needs more than \(C\cdot CL(S)/\varepsilon ^{2}\) coordinates. Bounds with an additional unbounded logarithmic factor do not meet the conjecture; an efficient construction is not required.

context_blocks.title: Preserve all set weights with fewer coordinates
context_blocks.text: A coordinate can represent an edge, a constraint or a position of a codeword. A sparsifier removes coordinates and compensates by reweighting those it keeps. The same reweighting must preserve every specified set’s weight, including small-weight sets, which makes multiplicative error stronger than a global additive-error allowance.

context_blocks.title: One set can be represented by one weighted coordinate
context_blocks.text: If S contains only the whole nonempty universe, its chain length is one. Placing the entire total weight on any one coordinate preserves that sole set weight exactly. A large universe alone therefore does not force a large sparsifier.

context_blocks.title: Union-closure sees constraints absent from direct containment
context_blocks.text: If S consists of all m singleton sets, the original sets are pairwise incomparable. Their unions nevertheless form a chain of m strict inclusions, so \(CL(S)=m\). With unit original weights and \(\varepsilon <1\), every singleton must retain positive weight; all m coordinates are necessary. This explains why the conjecture uses chain length in the union-closure.

context_blocks.title: The current upper bound still has logarithmic overhead
context_blocks.text: The paper gives support \(O(CL(S)\cdot \log ^{2}(CL(S)/\varepsilon )\cdot (\log  \log (CL(S)/\varepsilon ))^{2}/\varepsilon ^{2})\), with the usual constant-size adjustments to logarithms near one. This already removes dependence on the universe size from the overhead. Conjecture 23 asks whether all remaining logarithmic factors can be removed.

context_blocks.title: Existence and computation remain separate
context_blocks.text: The source notes that its main existence bound is not efficiently implementable in full generality. The conjecture itself only asks whether a small reweighting exists. Proving such a bound for every set family would already sharpen broad cut, code and constraint sparsification principles.

cards.title: Complexity of directed detours
cards.formal: Classify the worst-case complexity of the following decision problem on unrestricted finite directed graphs: given distinct vertices s and t, is there a simple directed s-to-t path with at least \(\operatorname{dist}_{G}(s,t)+1\) edges? The requested distinction is polynomial-time solvability versus NP-completeness. This is the fixed \(k=1\) case of Longest Detour, not the problem with k supplied as part of the input.
cards.why: Pinpoints whether even the smallest departure from shortest-path length creates NP-complete difficulty under the simple-path constraint, a basic boundary in directed path algorithms.

cards.definitions: The input is a directed graph \(G=(V,E)\), with \(V=[n], n\ge 2\), no loops or parallel arcs, and distinguished \(s\ne t\). Both opposite arcs between two vertices are allowed. The graph is unweighted; every arc has length one. A simple s-to-t path is a sequence \(v_{0}=s,v_{1},\ldots ,v_{\ell}=t\) of pairwise distinct vertices with \((v_{j- 1},v_{j})\in E\) for \(1\le j\le \ell\), and its length is \(\ell\). If t is reachable from \(s, \operatorname{dist}_{G}(s,t)\) is the minimum length of such a path. If t is unreachable, the instance is a no-instance. The input lists all vertices and arcs using binary vertex labels; N is the full encoding length. Polynomial time means one deterministic multitape Turing machine that decides every instance in at most \(C(N+1)^{a}\) steps for absolute constants C,a. NP-completeness uses deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions; in particular, a hardness proof can give a map from Boolean satisfiability instances to these graph instances that preserves yes/no answers. The decision problem is in NP: an at-most-n-vertex path is a polynomial-size certificate, and reachability distance and the path conditions can be checked in polynomial time. No planarity, acyclicity, connectivity or uniqueness of shortest paths is promised.
cards.answer_criterion: Determine the problem’s complexity in the stated unrestricted directed, unweighted model. A deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm establishes tractability; a polynomial-time many-one reduction from SAT establishes NP-completeness, since membership in NP is known. The latter excludes a polynomial-time algorithm under \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). The question does not assume a \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{NP}\)-complete dichotomy in advance; any different established classification must explain the remaining boundary. Bounds only for planar graphs, or hardness when k is variable, do not classify the fixed \(k=1\) problem.

context_blocks.title: Another shortest path is not enough
context_blocks.text: The question asks for strictly greater length. A graph may have many different shortest s-to-t paths and still have no simple path longer than them. Finding a second distinct path therefore does not by itself decide the problem.

context_blocks.title: Repeated vertices change the task
context_blocks.text: Allowing a walk to revisit a cycle would make it possible to add length without producing the required simple path. The distinct-vertex condition is essential to this complexity question.

context_blocks.title: A minimal increase can still hide global structure
context_blocks.text: Shortest paths are efficiently computable, but deciding whether their length can be exceeded by a simple path constrains which vertices can be reused. Here even one additional edge is the unresolved threshold.

cards.title: Polynomial-time minimum-total-length disjoint paths for fixed k
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 3\), is there a polynomial-time algorithm that, given an undirected unweighted graph G and k prescribed terminal pairs \((s_{i},t_{i})\), outputs pairwise vertex-disjoint paths \(\mathrm{P}_{i}\) from \(s_{i}\) to \(t_{i}\) minimizing \(\sum _{i}|E(\mathrm{P}_{i})|\), or correctly reports that no such collection exists? Randomized algorithms with success probability at least \(2/3\) on every input are admitted in this reading, consistently with the randomized \(k=2\) baseline cited by the source. Polynomial degree and constants may depend on k; an FPT bound with exponent independent of k is not requested.
cards.why: Would determine whether exact length optimization preserves the polynomial-time solvability of undirected disjoint routing with a fixed number of prescribed terminal pairs.
cards.status_note: Checked the original graph model and concluding question, the full 2025 cycle-packing discussion, and the exact scopes of the 2024 grid and 2025 planar results. Searches through 12 September 2026 identified no general fixed-k polynomial-time algorithm. Randomized bounded-error solvability is explicitly admitted as in the source’\(s k=2\) comparison.

cards.definitions: G is a finite simple connected undirected graph with n numbered vertices and unit length on every edge, encoded by an adjacency matrix and the terminal labels. Take the 2k terminals to be distinct; repeated endpoints across different pairs make vertex-disjointness infeasible, and a pair with \(s_{i}=t_{i}\) uses the zero-edge path at that vertex and can be handled separately. A path is a sequence of distinct vertices with consecutive vertices adjacent. Vertex-disjointness includes endpoints and means \(V(\mathrm{P}_{i})\cap V(\mathrm{P}_{j})=\varnothing\) for \(i\ne j\). Pairings are fixed: connecting a source to a different pair’s target is not acceptable. Define OPT as the minimum sum of edge counts over all feasible collections and set OPT=∞ when there is none. The output consists of the k vertex sequences of an optimal collection, or an infeasibility answer. For each fixed k the algorithm is a probabilistic Turing machine, with one finite program handling all n and all inputs for that k, running in at most \(C_{k}(n+1)^{c_{k}}\) steps on every random-bit sequence. Constants \(C_{k},c_{k}\) are independent of n. With probability at least \(2/3\) over its independent fair bits, the full output must be correct, including exact optimality. A deterministic algorithm is included as the zero-error case. The formulation asks for polynomial time for each fixed k and does not demand a uniform procedure generating these programs as k varies. The source compares this target with k-DSP, which requires every \(\mathrm{P}_{i}\) separately to have length \(\operatorname{dist}_{G}(s_{i},t_{i})\). Such a collection, when it exists, has the smallest possible total length; minimum-total-length routing must also handle inputs where disjoint routes exist but no collection of individually shortest routes exists.
cards.answer_criterion: Establish or refute polynomial-time solvability, with the stated bounded-error allowance, for every fixed \(k\ge 3\). A positive answer must output an exactly optimal collection or detect infeasibility on all inputs. A conditional negative answer must state its assumption and imply that no such polynomial-time algorithm exists for at least one fixed k. Hardness only when k grows with n, an FPT lower bound, approximation, or an algorithm restricted to individually shortest paths does not decide this question.

cards.definitions:
In the bottleneck path problem (BP), the input is an explicit directed graph G=(V,E), a source s, a target t and a weight w(e) for every edge. Among all directed s-to-t paths P, output one minimizing max_{e∈P}w(e). Any optimal simple path is acceptable; ties require no prescribed choice. If t is unreachable, report that no path exists. When s=t the empty path is returned, with bottleneck conventionally −∞.

In the bottleneck spanning-tree problem (BST), the input is the same kind of directed weighted graph and a specified root s. Output an out-arborescence T spanning all vertices: s has indegree zero, every other vertex has indegree one in T, and there is a directed path in T from s to every vertex. Minimize max_{e∈T}w(e). If no such tree exists, report this. For a one-vertex graph, the empty tree has value −∞. This objective minimizes the single largest tree-edge weight, not the sum of weights. A tree minimizing that largest weight need not supply an individually optimal bottleneck path to every vertex.

Weights are arbitrary elements of a totally ordered set, such as arbitrary real numbers. They are opaque keys: they may be stored, copied and compared in constant time, but their digits, arithmetic values and integer ranks are not available for computation. Equal weights are allowed. The graph is given by adjacency lists with O(log(n+m+2))-bit vertex and edge indices; ordinary operations on these indices have unit cost. The algorithm is charged for all graph operations, comparisons, random sampling and writing its path or tree, not just the number of comparisons. There is no assumption that the weights are sorted, bounded integers, or machine words supporting bit operations.

The randomization convention is Las Vegas: on every fixed input the answer is exact, termination occurs with probability one, and the expected total work over the algorithm's internal random choices is at most C(n+m) for a universal constant C. This includes feasibility checks and output. A randomized algorithm with a small probability of an incorrect optimum would not meet this convention. For BP, isolated and unreachable vertices can be removed in O(n+m) work. A feasible nontrivial BST instance has m≥n−1. Thus O(n+m) makes the source's O(m) target meaningful also on degenerate explicit inputs without changing its substantive content.

The question asks for this guarantee for both tasks, but their expected-linear-time versions are equivalent through the reductions in Section 4 of the source. These reductions do not establish the corresponding deterministic equivalence: the BST-to-BP reduction uses randomness. The source's separate question about a deterministic O(mβ(m,n)) bound is not the target of this card. Neither all-pairs bottleneck paths nor finding every individual single-source bottleneck value is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Give always-correct comparison-based algorithms with expected O(n+m) total work for both directed tasks, or use the source reductions to derive both guarantees from one. Alternatively, rule out such algorithms, stating any assumptions used. An undirected algorithm, a word-RAM algorithm inspecting weight representations, a bound on comparisons alone, or a faster algorithm only for sufficiently dense graphs does not settle the unrestricted target. A deterministic lower bound alone does not rule out the permitted randomized algorithms.

cards.definitions:
Graphs are finite, undirected and simple. A forest has no cycle. In a nontrivial tree, a leaf has degree one; an isolated vertex is allowed as a component. A tree with at most three leaves is a path or a subdivided claw. A subdivided claw \(S_{a,b,c}\), for integers \(a,b,c\geq1\), consists of three internally disjoint paths of respectively \(a,b,c\) edges sharing one endpoint. That common endpoint has degree three, and the other endpoints are the three leaves.

The graph \(G\) is \(H\)-free if no vertex subset induces a graph isomorphic to \(H\). An induced copy must preserve both edges and nonedges. If \(H\) is disconnected, all its components must occur together with no extra edges between their chosen vertices. Excluding the whole forest is therefore not the same as separately excluding every component.

The input explicitly lists \(G\) and nonnegative integer vertex weights \(w(v)\), encoded in binary. The length \(L\) includes the graph and all weight bits; zero weights and the empty independent set are allowed. An independent set \(I\subseteq V(G)\) contains no pair joined by an edge. Its weight is
\[w(I)=\sum_{v\in I}w(v).\]
The required output is a set \(I\) attaining the largest possible weight, not merely an inclusion-maximal set or an approximation.

The forbidden graph \(H\) is fixed before the input varies. The algorithm, polynomial exponent and multiplicative constant may depend on \(H\). The question does not require one exponent independent of \(H\), or fixed-parameter tractability when \(H\) is treated as a variable input. It asks for ordinary polynomial bit complexity for each fixed class.

There is no bound on the maximum degree, clique size or biclique size of \(G\). No sparsity promise is imposed beyond the forbidden induced forest. Recognition of \(H\)-freeness can be done in polynomial time for fixed \(H\), but the optimization guarantee is required only on that class.

Computing the exact optimum value and outputting an optimum set are polynomial-time equivalent here by the usual self-reduction on induced subgraphs, which remain \(H\)-free. The primary source discusses the full family of forests; the symmetric long claws \(S_{t,t,t}\) are a central subfamily, not an unmentioned restriction of this formulation.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove polynomial-time solvability for every fixed forest in the stated family, or refute this assertion for at least one fixed forest. Any complexity assumption used for a negative result must be explicit. A quasipolynomial-time algorithm, an approximation scheme or a theorem requiring bounded degree or a forbidden biclique does not meet the full target.

cards.definitions:
The algorithm is given the entire vertex set, identified with \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and the fixed degree bound. The edge set is hidden. The graph is fixed throughout the execution and is promised connected; no random input distribution is assumed.

A query supplies two named vertices \(u,v\) and receives the integer
\[d_{G}(u,v)=\min\{\text{number of edges on a path from }u\text{ to }v\}.\]
The answer contains no path, intermediate vertices or distances to other destinations. An edge has distance one. Computing all distances from one vertex by querying this oracle costs \(n-1\) queries, rather than one query.

The algorithm may choose each new query using all previous answers and its private random bits. Its output must be exactly the set \(E(G)\) on the given vertex labels. Isomorphism type, an approximate metric, a graph consistent with only some answers, or a sample of edges is insufficient.

The randomized convention is Las Vegas: the output is correct whenever returned, and the procedure terminates with probability one. The query bound is an expectation over its internal randomness for each fixed allowed graph. This is not average-case complexity over randomly generated graphs. Deterministic algorithms also qualify.

The constants may depend on the fixed \(\Delta\), but not on \(n\) or the particular graph. The displayed bound specifies the meaning of \(\widetilde O(n)\): a linear number of vertices times a fixed power of a logarithm. A bound \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\) for a fixed positive \(\varepsilon\) does not meet it.

Only calls to the distance oracle are charged in this query-complexity question. The algorithm must be an effective finite procedure, but no separate polynomial bound on local computation or memory is imposed. No restriction is placed on the number of adaptive rounds. There is no additional promise of bounded treewidth, treelength, cutwidth or a planar graph.

Simplicity matters because distances cannot reveal edge multiplicities or loops. Connectedness is also part of the source model: allowing a graph with just one hidden edge and otherwise isolated vertices would already force a quadratic search for that edge.
cards.answer_criterion: Give algorithms with the displayed expected-query bound for every fixed degree bound, and prove exact reconstruction on every promised graph, or show that such bounds are impossible for at least one fixed degree bound. A lower bound against the source’s particular algorithm alone does not refute the general question.

cards.title: Spanners matching Thorup–Zwick emulator tradeoffs
cards.formal:
For every fixed integer \(k\ge1\), do there exist constants \(C_{k},D_{k}>0\) such that every finite simple undirected unweighted graph \(G=(V,E)\), with \(n=|V|\ge1\), has a spanning subgraph \(H=(V,E_{H})\), \(E_{H}\subseteq E\), satisfying
\[
|E_{H}|\le C_{k}n^{\,1+1/(2^{k+1}-1)}
\]
and, simultaneously for all distinct vertices \(u,v\) in the same connected component of \(G\),
\[
d_{H}(u,v)\le d_{G}(u,v)+D_{k}\,d_{G}(u,v)^{\,1-1/k}?
\]
The constants may depend on \(k\), but not on the graph, its size or the vertex pair. This is the fixed-\(k\) size and distance-error tradeoff achieved by Thorup–Zwick emulators, now required of an actual subgraph.
cards.why: Spanners retain real routes in the original network, while emulators can encode long routes as weighted shortcuts. Matching their size/error tradeoffs would establish that this structural restriction costs only constant factors at every fixed level of sublinear distance accuracy. The later almost-matching theorem makes the exact remaining loss especially concrete.

cards.definitions:
The distance \(d_{G}(u,v)\) is the number of edges on a shortest path in \(G\); it is \(+\infty\) if there is no path. A spanning subgraph keeps every vertex and may remove edges, but all retained edges still have unit length. It cannot insert shortcut edges or change weights. Consequently, \(d_{H}(u,v)\ge d_{G}(u,v)\) automatically.

The inequality for finite distances requires \(H\) to connect every pair originally connected in \(G\). Vertices in different components remain disconnected because \(H\subseteq G\). Equal vertices have distance zero in both graphs and need no separate distortion inequality. For distinct connected vertices, \(d_{G}(u,v)\ge1\), so the power is defined even at \(k=1\), where it equals 1.

There is one subgraph \(H\) for the entire graph and fixed \(k\). It must satisfy the bound for every distance scale and every pair simultaneously. The quantifier order is
\[
\forall k\ge1\ \exists C_{k},D_{k}>0\ \forall G\ \exists H\ \forall u,v.
\]
The size bound has no hidden logarithmic factor in \(n\), no \(n^{\delta}\) loss for positive \(\delta\), and no additional accuracy parameter affecting the selected subgraph. Dependence on a growing \(k=k(n)\) is not requested.

For \(k>1\), the allowed additive error is sublinear in the distance because \(d^{1-1/k}/d=d^{-1/k}\) tends to zero. It need not be a constant independent of distance. For example, \(k=2\) asks for \(O(n^{8/7})\) edges with additive error \(O(\sqrt d)\). The \(k=1\) case asks for \(O(n^{4/3})\) edges and constant additive error.

An emulator is a weighted graph on the same vertex set that may contain edges absent from \(G\). A shortcut between \(u,v\) can receive weight \(d_{G}(u,v)\), preserving the prohibition on underestimating original distances. A spanner must instead use only original edges. Replacing shortcuts by their full original paths can increase the number of retained edges and does not automatically preserve the size bound.

The main assertion is existential: it asks for the same structural tradeoff, not a prescribed transformation of a supplied emulator or a specified construction running time. A construction establishing these bounds qualifies. This follows the size/stretch question in the source; bounds on construction time are separate from this target.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed existence assertion for every fixed integer \(k\), or refute it by showing that for some fixed \(k\) no constants \(C_{k},D_{k}\) work for all graphs. A counterexample to one proposed construction is insufficient. A family with the stated edge exponent plus any fixed positive slack, or different spanners for different accuracy parameters, does not establish the exact target.

cards.title: Maximum reset threshold of synchronizing automata
cards.formal: For every integer \(n\ge 1\), determine \(T(n)=\max\){\(rt(A): A\) is a synchronizing complete deterministic finite automaton with n states and any finite nonempty alphabet}, where \(rt(A)\) is its shortest reset-word length.
cards.definitions: An automaton here is a finite transition system \(A=(Q,\Sigma ,\delta )\), with |\(Q|=n, a\) finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), and a total function \(\delta :Q\times \Sigma \to Q\). Extend \(\delta\) to words by \(\delta (q,\varepsilon )=q\) and \(\delta (q,wa)=\delta (\delta (q,w),a)\). A word w is a reset word when |\(\{\delta (q,w):q\in Q\}|=1\). The automaton is synchronizing if at least one such word exists; its reset threshold \(rt(A)\) is the minimum number of letters in a reset word. The quantification ranges over every n and every finite alphabet and total transition function satisfying this promise. The common final state need not be specified beforehand. Initial states and accepting states play no role. The empty word handles \(n=1\). No strong-connectivity, binary-alphabet, permutation-letter, or other structural restriction is imposed. Partial automata, nondeterministic transitions, and synchronizing only a prescribed proper subset of Q are different models. The maximum is well-defined: on n labeled states there are only \(n^{n}\) different letter transformations, and duplicate transformations may be removed without changing shortest reset lengths. Thus finitely many transition alphabets suffice. \(T(1)=0\). The target is the integer-valued function of n, not the running time of testing synchronization.
cards.answer_criterion: Specify a real-valued approximation g on the positive integers and prove in Lean that |\(g(n)- (T(n) : \mathbb{R} )|\le 1/100\) for every integer \(n\ge 1\), using the model and target defined here. Certified lower and upper functions \(\ell\)\((n)\le T(n)\le u(n)\) with \(u(n)- \ell (n)\le 1/50\) also qualify via their midpoint. The answer may use unambiguous mathematical expressions or certified bounds; g need not be integer-valued, and no simple exact formula for \(T(n)\) is required. An exact determination also qualifies. A one-sided bound, agreement at finitely many n, or an asymptotic estimate without the stated pointwise error guarantee does not meet this criterion.
cards.why: A central extremal problem in automata theory, with a simple finite-state formulation and a sharp explicit candidate bound. It tests whether local compression and algebraic structure can force globally short control sequences in every synchronizing system.

importance.reason: The flagship quantitative question about synchronizing automata, connecting finite-state control, extremal combinatorics, and linear-algebraic methods.

context_blocks.text: This card asks for the worst-case reset-length function with absolute approximation error at most 0.01 for every n. The Černý conjecture predicts \(T(n)=(n- 1)^{2}\). Determining a different function would also answer this card, but merely refuting the conjectured formula would not.

Synchronization asks how to restore a finite system to a known state when its current state is unknown. A fixed input sequence must work simultaneously from every possible starting state; it cannot observe the intermediate state and adapt its next letter. The length bound therefore measures the cost of an open-loop reset, rather than ordinary shortest-path navigation from a known vertex.

The proposed constant is forced by a concrete family. On states \(0,\ldots ,n- 1\), let a cyclically increment the state and let b send \(n- 1\) to 0 while fixing the other states. For \(n\ge 2\), the word \(b(a^{n- 1}b)^{n- 2}\) has length \((n- 1)^{2}\) and resets this automaton. Černý’s construction also proves that no shorter reset word works. This is the known lower bound for \(T(n)\); the Černý conjecture predicts equality for every n.

Knowing that a reset exists is much easier than establishing its sharp maximum length. Pairwise merging gives polynomial criteria for synchronizability, and successive compression of subsets gives general polynomial length bounds. The bottleneck is how much progress one can force as the current set of possible states shrinks. Adding separate worst-case bounds for these stages gives a cubic estimate and can lose information about how the stages interact.

The August 2026 open-problems survey records a general upper bound of approximately \(0.1654n^{3}+o(n^{3})\), due to Shitov’s refinement of Szykuła’s result. The gap is therefore in the exponent as well as the leading constant: the conjecture asks for the exact quadratic bound \((n- 1)^{2}\). Results for restricted transition systems do not establish that bound for all synchronizing automata.

A July 2026 preprint reports the conjectured bound for one-cluster automata: systems having a letter whose functional graph has exactly one directed cycle. Its sharper positive-level estimate uses the cycle length and the distance of off-cycle states from that cycle. This is a claim for a restricted class, and the later general survey still states the unrestricted conjecture as open.

cards.title: Sakoda–Sipser problem
cards.formal: Do universal constants \(C,k\ge 1\) exist such that, for every \(n\ge 1\), every finite nonempty input alphabet \(\Sigma\) and every two-way nondeterministic finite automaton A over \(\Sigma\) with at most n states, there is a two-way deterministic finite automaton D over the same alphabet with at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) states satisfying \(\mathrm{L}(D)=\mathrm{L}(A)\)? Equivalence must hold on all finite input words, without a length bound.
cards.definitions: The read-only input tape contains a left endmarker, a word \(w\in \Sigma\)*, and a right endmarker. Each automaton has one head, initially on the left endmarker, a finite set Q of states with a designated initial state and designated halting accepting states. In each nonhalting configuration it uses its current state and the scanned symbol to choose a new state and a head displacement in \(\{- 1,0,+1\}\); moves outside the endmarkers are forbidden. A missing transition rejects that branch. A word is accepted if some finite computation reaches an accepting state. Infinite nonaccepting branches do not count as acceptance. For a deterministic automaton there is at most one available transition in each state-symbol pair, and its unique infinite run, if any, rejects. There is no work tape, rewritable input, second head, stack, counter, randomness or advice. State count includes all control and halting states, but the bound is independent of word length and alphabet size. The target is existence of D for each A; computing D from A is not required to take polynomial time. Standard endmarker and stay-put conventions change these state bounds only by polynomial factors.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of universal constants C,k giving an equivalent 2DFA with at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) states for every n-state 2NFA, or prove that no such constants exist. In the negative direction, every proposed polynomial bound must fail on some source automaton; all language comparisons concern words of every length.
cards.why: A principal unresolved measure of the succinctness provided by nondeterminism. It isolates the issue in finite-state machines, connects to nonuniform space complexity, and asks whether revisiting read-only data can replace a large internal record of possible computations.

importance.reason: The flagship state-complexity problem for two-way finite automata, open since 1978, with unusually direct connections between finite-state descriptions and logarithmic-space complexity.

progress.text: Sakoda and Sipser formulate the polynomial-state simulation questions and conjecture that nondeterminism cannot always be removed with polynomial cost.
The Geffert–Mereghetti–Pighizzini simulation gives \(n^{O(\log  n)}\) states for unary two-way NFAs. It leaves a polynomial-versus-superpolynomial gap.
Kapoutsis characterizes polynomial-state simulation on short inputs by \(\mathrm{NL}\subseteq \mathrm{L}\)/poly, carefully distinguishing input-length restrictions and advice.
Clerici Lorenzini and coauthors obtain a polynomial-size normal form for two-way NFAs accepting letter-bounded languages.
Guillon and coauthors give polynomial-size complementation using self-verifying 1-limited automata, with rewritable annotations; the unrestricted read-only determinization question remains open.

Adeogun and Kapoutsis’ revised preprint establishes a quadratic 2DFA state lower bound for one-way liveness and the resulting NFA-to-2DFA conversion. This does not exclude a polynomial determinization bound.

context_blocks.text: All four basic finite-automaton models—one-way or two-way, deterministic or nondeterministic—recognize exactly the regular languages. Their descriptions can nevertheless have very different sizes. The familiar subset construction gives an exponential conversion from a one-way NFA to a one-way DFA. The open issue is whether the deterministic machine can avoid that cost by repeatedly revisiting the original input instead of remembering all possible nondeterministic states at once.

A simple example shows why a one-way lower bound is insufficient. Over \(\{0,1\}\), consider words whose r-th symbol from the right is 1. A one-way deterministic automaton must distinguish all binary suffixes of length r and therefore needs at least \(2^{r}\) states. A two-way deterministic automaton can scan to the right endmarker, walk left r positions while counting in its finite control, and inspect the symbol. It uses \(O(r)\) states. Rereading changes the representation cost even though the accepted language is unchanged.

Known unrestricted upper bounds still pass through a one-way representation and are exponential in a polynomial of the number of states. At the opposite end, exponential separations are known if the deterministic target has restricted head motion, such as reversing only at endmarkers. Those restrictions can themselves make deterministic automata exponentially larger. A lower bound using them therefore cannot be transferred to an unrestricted 2DFA without another argument.

The unary case remains meaningful: the input then consists of repetitions of one letter, and only its length can carry information. Unary two-way NFAs can be simulated by two-way DFAs with \(n^{O(\log  n)}\) states. This is far smaller than an exponential bound but still exceeds every fixed polynomial. It demonstrates that even removing almost all input syntax does not make the remaining determinization question routine.

Connections to logarithmic-space computation require careful quantifiers. Kapoutsis proves that polynomial-state deterministic simulation on inputs of length at most the source state count is equivalent to \(\mathrm{NL}\subseteq \mathrm{L}\)/poly. Here L/poly allows a deterministic logarithmic-space machine polynomially long advice depending only on input length. That theorem concerns bounded-length agreement, whereas this card requires agreement on every word. It should not be restated as an unconditional equivalence of the full Sakoda–Sipser question with \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{NL}\).

Clerici Lorenzini, Pighizzini, and Prigioniero study letter-bounded languages in 2025: languages contained in \(a_{1}*\cdots a_{t}\)* for fixed letters. They obtain a polynomial-cost normal form in which nondeterministic choices and head reversals occur at endmarkers. The source language restriction is crucial; the theorem does not put every two-way NFA into that normal form.

Guillon, Prigioniero, and Taheri’s STACS 2026 theorem complements arbitrary two-way NFAs with a polynomial-size self-verifying 1-limited automaton. Such a machine can annotate input cells on their first visit; the construction uses a shared guessed annotation that subsequent traversals can inspect. It remains a recognizer of regular languages, but its ability to retain those annotations is absent from a 2DFA. Their introduction explicitly leaves ordinary determinization and ordinary two-way-NFA complementation open.

Adeogun and Kapoutsis’ July 2026 revision proves a quadratic state lower bound for deterministic two-way automata solving one-way liveness. The problem encodes paths through successive layers of a graph; a small nondeterministic automaton can guess a path, whereas a deterministic one must use more control states. The lower bound also applies to conversion from one-way NFAs. Quadratic growth is compatible with the polynomial simulation asked here, so this strengthens the documented lower-bound picture without resolving the conjecture.

cards.title: Generalized star-height problem
cards.formal: Does there exist a finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\) and a regular language \(\mathrm{L}\subseteq \Sigma\)* such that every generalized regular expression denoting L has Kleene-star nesting depth at least two, when complement is allowed without increasing that depth?
cards.definitions: \(\Sigma\)* is the set of all finite words over \(\Sigma\), including the empty word \(\varepsilon\). A regular language is one accepted by a finite deterministic automaton. Generalized expressions are finite expressions built from \(\varnothing , \varepsilon\), and the letters \(a\in \Sigma\) using binary union \(E\cup F\), concatenation EF, complement \(E^{c}\), and Kleene star E*. Their meanings are respectively the empty language, \(\{\varepsilon\}, \{a\}\), language union, all concatenations uv with \(u\in \mathrm{L}(E)\) and \(v\in \mathrm{L}(F), \Sigma *\setminus \mathrm{L}(E)\), and the union of all finite concatenation powers of \(\mathrm{L}(E)\), including power zero \(\{\varepsilon\}\). Set \(h(\varnothing )=h(\varepsilon )=h(a)=0, h(E\cup F)=h(\mathrm{EF})=\max \{h(E),h(F)\}, h(E^{c})=h(E)\), and \(h(E*)=h(E)+1\). Define \(h_{g}(\mathrm{L})=\min \{h(E):\mathrm{L}(E)=\mathrm{L}\}\), which exists because every regular language has an ordinary regular expression. The question is whether \(h_{g}(\mathrm{L})>1\) for at least one such L. There is no bound on expression size, number of complements, union or concatenation depth, automaton size, or alphabet size. Intersection is permitted as the abbreviation \((E^{c}\cup F^{c})^{c}\) and does not add star depth. Backreferences, infinite words, additional predicates and auxiliary alphabets in the final expression are not part of the syntax.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that some regular language has generalized star height at least two, including a lower bound over all generalized expressions for that language, or prove that every regular language over every finite nonempty alphabet has a generalized expression of star height at most one. Expression size is unrestricted in both alternatives.
cards.why: A basic unresolved expressive-depth question for regular languages: determine whether Boolean operations eliminate every need for nested iteration, or whether a genuine second level exists.

importance.reason: A longstanding foundational problem connecting regular expressions, finite automata, algebraic language theory and logical descriptions.

cards.status_note: The checked author sources distinguish the open generalized question from the solved ordinary star-height problem. A later-work search on 11 September 2026 found no verified height-two example or universal height-one theorem. The inspected factor-counting results establish additional height-one subclasses only.

context_blocks.text: Kleene star represents arbitrary finite repetition. Nested stars arise naturally when repetitions occur inside other repeated blocks. The question is whether such nesting expresses a real hierarchy once a language can also be complemented at no cost to the height measure. Complement preserves regularity, so it does not enlarge the class recognized by finite automata. It may nevertheless radically change the shape of the shortest-depth expression for the same language.

Even elementary examples demonstrate that syntax and language height must be separated. Over \(\Sigma =\{a,b\}\), the language of all words has the ordinary expression \((a\cup b)\)*, with a star. With complement, it is simply \(\varnothing ^{c}\) and has height zero. The language avoiding the factor ab is \((\Sigma *ab\Sigma *)^{c}\); replacing each displayed \(\Sigma\)* by \(\varnothing ^{c}\) makes this a star-free expression. Infinitely many words can therefore belong to a language of generalized height zero.

Height zero does not capture all regular languages. Over the unary alphabet \(\{a\}\), the even-length language \((aa)\)* has generalized height exactly one. Its two-state automaton remembers length modulo two. Schützenberger’s theorem characterizes height zero through an aperiodic syntactic monoid, and this parity language has a nontrivial two-element group. Thus the first separation, between zero and one, is known; the question asks for the next separation.

The syntactic monoid packages how words behave inside arbitrary contexts: u and v are equivalent when puq belongs to L exactly when pvq does, for every pair of words p,q. Concatenation induces multiplication on the finitely many equivalence classes. A finite monoid is aperiodic when some exponent N makes \(x^{N}=x^{N+1}\) for every element x. Schützenberger’s characterization gives an effective algebraic test for star-freeness, but no corresponding complete height-one criterion is known.

The ordinary, or restricted, star-height problem disallows complement. In that setting, arbitrarily high heights exist and the minimum height is computable. These facts cannot be transferred to generalized height by reusing an ordinary expression or an automaton cycle measure: allowing complement introduces additional descriptions that the old lower-bound argument may not exclude. Pin’s problem page explicitly distinguishes these two versions and separately lists the existence of height two and the algorithmic computation of height.

Pin, Straubing and Thérien prove height at most one for several algebraic classes, including languages recognized by finite nilpotent groups of class at most two, and eliminate a proposed height-two example. They also show that every regular language is the inverse image of an ordinary height-one language under a suitable word morphism. That representation does not bound generalized height without an additional closure statement: inverse morphisms preserve regularity, but their preservation of generalized height one is part of the unresolved issue.

Bourne and Ruškuc extend the height-one territory using factor-counting arguments. Their results cover specified counting cases and languages recognized by Rees zero-matrix semigroups over abelian groups. A factor here is a contiguous occurrence of a word, which differs from counting scattered subsequences. The theorem handles a substantial recognizing-semigroup class, while leaving the existence of a language above height one unresolved.

Daviaud and Paperman study languages generated from sets u* with a single word u, under Boolean or lattice operations and, in some cases, quotients. They give effective equational characterizations of those particular classes. These are deliberately restricted families inside the broader problem: a full height-one expression may take the star of an arbitrary star-free language and combine the resulting languages by concatenation and Boolean operations. Their paper describes its result as a step toward that larger structural challenge.

Cotumaccio’s 2025 account of connections between compressed indexing and automata again identifies generalized star height as an open structural question. It does not supply a new separation or universal flattening theorem. The relevance extends beyond a formal-expression puzzle: a solution would clarify how finite-state iteration, modular behaviour and Boolean operations interact, while allowing descriptions to grow arbitrarily large.

cards.title: Decidability of every level of the dot-depth hierarchy
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 0\), is there an algorithm that, given a deterministic finite automaton over a finite alphabet A, always halts and decides whether its language belongs to \(DD_{k}(A)\), the k-th dot-depth level defined below?
cards.definitions: For each finite nonempty alphabet A, let A* be its finite words, \(\varepsilon\) the empty word, and \(A+=A*\setminus \{\varepsilon\}\). Set \(DD_{0}(A)=\{\varnothing ,\{\varepsilon\},A+,A*\}\). For a class C of languages over \(A, Pol(C)\) consists of all finite unions of marked products \(\mathrm{L}_{0}a_{1}\mathrm{L}_{1}\cdots a_{r} \mathrm{L}_{r}\), where \(r\ge 0\), each \(a_{i}\in A\), and every \(\mathrm{L}_{i}\in C; r=0\) gives \(\mathrm{L}_{0}\). Let \(Bool(C)\) be closure under finite union, finite intersection and complement relative to A*. Define \(DD_{k+1}(A)\)=Bool(\(Pol(DD_{k}(A))\)). The input automaton is given by finite explicit tables, including its alphabet, initial state and accepting states; its accepted language is \(\mathrm{L}(M)\). The question quantifies \(\forall k\exists a\) total Turing algorithm \(A_{k}\forall M\), with \(A_{k}(M)\)=yes exactly when \(\mathrm{L}(M)\in DD_{k}(A)\). Each \(A_{k}\) must handle arbitrary finite input alphabets. No polynomial-time or elementary-time bound is requested. This fixes the full integer levels and the four-language level-zero convention; it does not merge distinct concatenation hierarchies or leave the logical signature implicit. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that membership in \(DD_{k}\) is decidable for every fixed integer \(k\ge 0\), with each decider handling all finite alphabets, or prove that membership is undecidable for at least one fixed level k. The positive statement does not require an effective procedure that takes k as an additional input.
cards.why: Determine whether bounded logical alternation can be recognized effectively throughout a fundamental hierarchy of regular languages.

importance.reason: A longstanding structural decision problem linking finite automata, logical definability and finite monoids; a full solution would explain much more than the known low-level algorithms.

The January 2025 alternation-hierarchy announcement is still explicitly withdrawn because of a fatal flaw in Lemma 19. No corrected result settling every fixed full dot-depth level was located.

context_blocks.text: Finite automata provide a complete and effective representation of regular languages, but the number of states is only one measure of a language’s complexity. Another asks how complicated a logical description must be. Two automata with similar state counts can recognize languages requiring very different combinations of order, concatenation and negation. The dot-depth hierarchy measures that descriptive structure.

A marked product picks a sequence of distinguished letters and constrains the substrings around them. Over an alphabet containing a and \(b, A*aA*bA\)* says that some a occurs before some later b. Replacing the middle A* by \(\{\varepsilon\}\) requires the two distinguished letters to be adjacent. Boolean combinations can require several such patterns or forbid them. Iterating these operations permits the pieces between distinguished letters to satisfy properties that were already built at earlier levels.

The level is a minimum over all descriptions of the same language. Seeing four layers in a supplied expression does not prove the language needs four: another expression may be simpler. The input is therefore an automaton, rather than a proposed optimal expression. The algorithm must discover whether some description at the requested level exists, regardless of how the language was initially presented.

The union of the levels is the star-free class, whose membership is decidable through the aperiodicity of the syntactic monoid. This answers whether any finite level suffices, while the present question asks about a prescribed bound. Place and Zeitoun’s account of the dot-depth problem emphasizes this distinction between the classical star-free theorem and the finer unresolved classification.

There is a useful logical interpretation: full levels correspond to Boolean combinations of first-order formulas with bounded quantifier alternation, with the appropriate word predicates. The closely related Straubing–Thérien hierarchy starts from just the empty and universal languages and uses the order-only signature. Dot-depth also captures successor information. The card defines the language operations directly so that changing the basis or adding predicates cannot silently change its target.

Positive instances are effectively enumerable. Enumerate expressions at level k, convert each to a finite automaton, and check language equality with the input. If a suitable expression exists this eventually finds it. The obstruction is recognizing negative instances: continuing to search without success is not a certificate that every candidate fails. A decision theorem needs an effective stopping criterion or an equivalent finite characterization.

Separation asks whether a language from a prescribed class can contain one given regular language while avoiding another. Covering asks whether a given language can be covered by finitely many languages from the class such that each covering language is disjoint from at least one member of a given finite list of forbidden regular languages. These are stronger classification tasks than membership. Place and Zeitoun’s 2021 result decides separation and covering for dot-depth two.

Their 2024 result uses a generic algebraic characterization of Boolean polynomial closure. For levels at least two, it reduces membership at the next full level to covering at the preceding level. Together with the known covering result, this decides dot-depth three. The reduction does not by itself decide covering at every new level, so it cannot simply be iterated to settle the entire hierarchy.

A January 2025 preprint by Barloy, Cadilhac, Paperman and Straubing announced decidability of the first-order alternation hierarchy and related half-level results. It was withdrawn on January 31: the authors identify a fatal flaw in the proof of Lemma 19. The unchanged title and abstract still appear in search results, so they cannot be treated as an established resolution. No corrected replacement resolving this card was found in the present review.

MeSCaL implements established membership tests, including computations for level two and intermediate levels, while its 2025 account explicitly retains the general hierarchy problem. Such tools make existing decision theorems usable without implying that every level is decidable.

Lambert’s July 2026 paper develops effective methods that turn automata into logical descriptions for dot-depth one and specified extensions. Its target classes are fixed; it does not claim a procedure for every level of this hierarchy.

Settling the question would determine whether a major logical complexity measure for regular languages can always be recognized effectively at any prescribed finite level. It would also clarify which finite algebraic information is sufficient to describe bounded alternation. An undecidable level would be equally revealing: even these finite-state languages would resist a complete algorithmic classification by that natural form of descriptive simplicity.

cards.title: Equivalence of deterministic macro tree transducers
cards.formal: Is there a total algorithm that, given two deterministic macro tree transducers with the same finite ranked input and output alphabets, decides whether they define exactly the same partial function from finite ordered input trees to finite ordered output trees?
cards.definitions: Fix the ordinary inside-out, or call-by-value, semantics. A ranked alphabet assigns a nonnegative arity to each symbol; a tree node has exactly that many ordered children. A transducer has finitely many states q, each with one input-tree argument and \(m(q)\) output-tree parameters, and an initial state \(q_{0}\) with \(m(q_{0})=0\). For each state q and input symbol \(\sigma\) of arity k there is at most one rule \(q(\sigma (x_{1},\ldots ,x_{k}),y_{1},\ldots ,y_{m})\to r\). The finite right-hand side follows the grammar \(r ::= y_{j} | \delta (r_{1},\ldots ,r_{l}) | q' (x_{i},r_{1},\ldots ,r_{m(q' )})\), with \(\delta\) an output symbol of arity l and \(1\le i\le k\). Subtrees and parameters may be copied or deleted, and calls may be nested inside parameter arguments without a fixed nesting bound across instances. On input \(\sigma (t_{1},\ldots ,t_{k})\), evaluate parameter arguments to output trees, then evaluate a call \(q'\) on the indicated child \(t_{i}\) with those parameter values. A missing rule makes the corresponding evaluation undefined, and under call-by-value an undefined argument makes its enclosing evaluation undefined. There is no inspection or pattern matching on parameter trees. Every recursive call processes a proper input child, so evaluation terminates on each finite input, with either a finite tree or undefined. A transducer with a rule for every state/symbol pair is total. There is no regular look-ahead oracle in this chosen syntax. Equality requires identical domains and, on that domain, identical labelled ordered output trees, without identifying different trees by their leaf strings, shapes or origin annotations. Input alphabets, state sets, arities and rules are all part of the finite input to the desired decision algorithm.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that equivalence of the specified partial deterministic macro tree transducers is decidable by a total algorithm, or prove that this decision problem is undecidable. Equivalence requires equality of domains and of the labelled ordered output trees on every input in the common domain.
cards.why: Locate the decidability boundary for equivalence of terminating recursive tree programs with copying and nested output parameters.

importance.reason: A central longstanding transducer-equivalence problem, connecting functional program verification with finite-state methods, algebraic invariants and structural recursion.

cards.status_note: Primary-source review and a later-work search on 11 September 2026 found no decider or undecidability theorem for the unrestricted model stated here. The inspected 2025–2026 papers classify shape, growth or expressive power. Their claims do not decide ordinary functional equivalence of arbitrary pairs.

context_blocks.text: A macro tree transducer is a small recursive program for transforming structured data. Its input could be a syntax tree, and its output another syntax tree. A state examines the current input symbol and recursively processes child subtrees. Output parameters act as accumulated pieces of the result that can be inserted, duplicated or passed onward. This makes the model more expressive than a finite-state traversal that simply emits output around its recursive calls.

The restriction to proper input children guarantees termination. It does not bound output size by a polynomial, because a rule may copy a parameter or call a state repeatedly. For example, repeatedly replacing an accumulated tree y by \(b(y,y)\) along a unary input chain produces an exponentially large output from a small input. The equivalence question must account for that output implicitly if it hopes to avoid constructing every possible result.

The question asks about all finite inputs. Different rule tables can compute the same transformation through different intermediate structures, so syntactic comparison is too restrictive. Testing every tree up to a chosen height can discover a counterexample, but success on that finite collection proves nothing without a theorem giving an adequate height bound. There is no such bound built into the problem statement.

Non-equivalence is semidecidable: enumerate finite input trees, evaluate both programs, and stop when their definedness or outputs differ. Every individual evaluation terminates even if it takes a long time. The missing counterpart is a complete way to confirm equivalence. No terminating equivalence decider is supplied by this semidecision observation.

Maneth’s survey describes three substantial decidable subclasses: ordinary top-down tree transducers without output parameters, macro transducers of linear size increase, and macro transducers with both input and output alphabets monadic. Linear size increase connects to deterministic MSO-definable tree translations. These restrictions remove different difficulties and do not collectively cover all macro transducers. In particular, restricting the input to unary trees alone is not the same as restricting both alphabets.

The survey also records that inverse images of regular tree languages are effectively regular. Taking the inverse image of all output trees gives an effective description of the domain, so domain equality is already decidable. That useful fact does not decide whether two different output functions agree everywhere on their common domain. The hard part is comparing the unbounded structured outputs rather than merely determining where a computation is defined.

Seidl, Maneth and Kemper settle equivalence of deterministic top-down tree-to-string transducers using inductive invariants expressed through polynomial ideals. Their result combines a search for an equivalence proof with a search for a counterexample. That theorem concerns a particular tree-to-string formalism; the present target is the parameterized tree-to-tree model.

The inherited Maneth–Seidl paper studies origin equivalence: each output node also records which input node caused its creation. It decides this stronger equality test for weakly self-nesting transducers. An origin mismatch can occur even when the ordinary output trees are identical, so a negative answer to origin equivalence is not a negative answer to the present question. The paper further shows that for unrestricted unary-input macro transducers, origin equivalence is as difficult as ordinary equivalence.

Gallot and Maneth’s June 2025 paper decides shape preservation for compositions of total deterministic macro tree transducers. Shape preservation means that the output has the input’s ordered tree shape, although labels may change. This property concerns a transformation’s relation to its own input and does not decide equality of two arbitrary transformations.

Gallot, Lhote and Nguyên’s January 2026 revision decides polynomial size-to-height growth and computes its degree. Such a bound compares the height of the output tree with the number of input nodes. Two transformations can satisfy the same growth bound while differing in their output labels or branching, so growth classification is distinct from functional equivalence.

Dartois, Nguyên and Peyrat’s May 2026 paper characterizes a class of functions of linear size-to-height increase using tree-to-tree Hennie machines and a typed lambda calculus. Its equivalence proof concerns the expressive power of two models. It is not an algorithm for deciding whether two arbitrary macro tree transducers produce identical outputs. Keeping these senses of equivalence separate prevents a misleading reading of the recent abstract.

A resolution would locate an important boundary of automatic program comparison. These programs already terminate and have a disciplined recursive structure, but still support nested parameter passing and copying. Decidability would provide a foundation for validating transformations and optimizations in that model; undecidability would demonstrate that structural recursion alone does not make full semantic equality effectively recognizable.
