importance.reason: A longstanding geometric extremal problem whose elementary input model hides a large unresolved gap between universal coverage guarantees. It links continuous packing choices with arbitrary finite point configurations, and the demonstrated limitation of the familiar greedy algorithm separates general existence from that algorithm’s performance.

sentences: The target is the worst possible optimal coverage by rectangles anchored at their lower-left corners at arbitrary points of the unit square.
Every finite point set must include the origin, and each point receives a positive-area rectangle with no interior overlap.
The numerical answer must locate the universal coverage constant within one percentage point, with a complete Lean proof.
Freedman’s exact half-coverage conjecture remains the source question and is stronger than satisfying this approximation criterion.
The checked universal bounds are 39 and 50 percent, while the smaller upper bound in the 2021 paper concerns only its particular greedy algorithm.

cards.definitions: Write \(p=(x_p,y_p)\). A valid packing chooses real coordinates \(u_p,v_p\) satisfying \(x_p<u_p\le1\) and \(y_p<v_p\le1\) for every \(p\in P\), and uses \(R_p=[x_p,u_p)\times[y_p,v_p)\). For distinct points \(p,q\), the open sets \((x_p,u_p)\times(y_p,v_p)\) and \((x_q,u_q)\times(y_q,v_q)\) must be disjoint; boundaries may touch. Its total area is \(\sum_{p\in P}(u_p-x_p)(v_p-y_p)\). All points are distinct, their number is arbitrary, and coordinates may be any real numbers in the stated domain. Points may share an x-coordinate or y-coordinate; there is no general-position assumption. The origin is mandatory. The other three corners of a rectangle need not belong to \(P\). Every point anchors exactly one positive-area rectangle, and no rotations, other anchor corners, squares-only restriction, or overlaps of positive area are permitted. Valid packings exist for every such finite set, and their areas are bounded by one. Thus \(A(P)\) and \(\alpha\) are well-defined real suprema and infima. No optimum-attaining point set or packing is demanded by the definitions. There is no computational running-time requirement and no rational-coordinate or finite-precision restriction.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real value \(a\) and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that \(|a-\alpha|\le1/100\), with the quantifiers, positivity and boundary conventions above. Equivalently, certify an interval \([L,U]\) containing \(\alpha\) with \(U-L\le1/50\) and take its midpoint. A lower bound \(L\) must hold for every finite allowed point set through its packing supremum; an upper bound \(U\) must bound the infimum over all allowed point sets, allowing a sequence of sets approaching the bound. A value of \(A(P)\) for one selected instance, an uncertified experiment, or only a performance guarantee for a particular algorithm is insufficient. Exact determination is welcome but not required. This numerical benchmark does not claim that a one-percentage-point approximation proves or refutes the exact half-coverage conjecture.

context_blocks.text: Freedman’s original conjecture asks whether every permitted point set admits a packing covering at least \(1/2\) of the square. The ICALP 2021 source states this in its introduction and calls for algorithms reaching that guarantee in its conclusion. This card follows the authorized numerical formulation of extremal targets: it asks for the underlying universal coverage constant, retaining the exact conjecture here as the source question. The numerical acceptance criterion is a broadening, not a claim of logical equivalence to proving the conjecture.

The checked 2021 paper establishes a universal coverage guarantee of \(0.39\), while its introductory extremal comparison gives \(\alpha\le1/2\). Consequently the checked bounds are \(0.39\le\alpha\le0.5\). This interval is wider than the benchmark’s permitted \(1/50\) certified interval.

The same paper exhibits inputs on which its studied greedy packing algorithm covers less than \(0.433\). That is an upper bound on this particular algorithm’s worst-case guarantee. It is not an upper bound of \(0.433\) on the optimum packing constant \(\alpha\), and it does not refute Freedman’s conjecture.

A 2013 preprint announcing a proof was withdrawn on 28 April 2014 because its authors found a bug in Claim 5. Its unchanged abstract must be read together with the withdrawal notice; it is not a verified resolution.

Nölke’s 2023 dissertation still records the half-coverage conjecture as open and cites 0.39 as the best known universal guarantee. Its other anchored-packing variants have different allowed anchor positions and do not automatically settle the lower-left problem.

cards.title: Polygon visibility graph recognition
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite simple undirected graph \(G\) on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and a cyclic order \(C=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) of its vertices, decides whether some simple polygon with these labelled vertices in boundary order \(C\) has visibility graph exactly \(G\)? Here \(n\geq3\), the graph is given by its complete adjacency matrix and the cyclic order by an explicit list. Both visible and nonvisible pairs must be realized, and the polygon has no holes or additional vertices.
cards.why: The problem is a central inverse question about geometric visibility: whether pairwise sight-line information and a boundary order can be tested for realizability efficiently. It connects graph recognition with geometric representation complexity.
cards.status_note: The specified fixed-order recognition question remains explicitly open in the checked 2024 compendium. The bounded search through 13 September 2026 did not locate a later resolution. Closed visibility and permitted collinear labelled vertices are explicit formulation conventions; no unrestricted rational-witness assumption is used.

sentences: A polygon's visibility graph records which pairs of vertices can be joined by a segment lying inside the polygon.
The source supplies both a candidate graph and a Hamiltonian cycle specifying the intended polygon boundary.
It asks for an efficient decision procedure for whether a simple polygon realizes exactly that information.
Choosing coordinates must satisfy visibility and obstruction requirements simultaneously.
The problem tests whether a combinatorial record of sight lines contains enough accessible structure to reconstruct a genuine geometric environment.

cards.definitions: A realization assigns distinct points \(p_i\in\mathbb R^2\) to the labels. The union of the segments \([p_{v_i},p_{v_{i+1}}]\), with indices cyclic modulo \(n\), must be a simple closed polygonal curve: consecutive segments meet only at their common endpoint and nonconsecutive segments are disjoint. Let \(P\) be this curve together with its bounded complementary component. Vertices \(i\ne j\) are visible exactly when the entire closed segment \([p_i,p_j]\) is contained in \(P\). Visibility along the boundary is allowed, including through other labelled collinear vertices; redundant collinear boundary vertices are permitted as long as the curve remains simple. This closed-region convention is explicit and no general-position promise is imposed. The graph must contain every edge of the specified boundary cycle, otherwise the answer is no. Malformed matrices, a nonsymmetric matrix, loops, a nonpermutation order or \(n<3\) are rejected. The input is a binary encoding of the full matrix and list, of length \(N\); one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine must decide correctly in at most \(K(N+1)^a\) steps for fixed \(K,a\). Real coordinates are existential mathematical witnesses, with no rationality, grid-size or bit-length restriction. The requested algorithm returns a Boolean answer and need not produce coordinates.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the language of realizable graph/order pairs belongs to \(\mathrm P\), or that it does not, for the exact polygon and visibility conventions above. A positive answer must establish correctness and a polynomial worst-case bit-time bound for one uniform decision algorithm on every encoding. A negative answer must rule out every such algorithm; an NP-hardness or \(\exists\mathbb R\)-hardness result alone does not prove nonmembership in \(\mathrm P\) without the corresponding separation. A necessary graph condition, recognition of a special polygon class, or recognition with extra geometric data is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: The source problem supplies the boundary order as well as the graph. This removes the need to search for a Hamiltonian boundary cycle, but leaves the geometric realizability question. The statement above fixes simple closed polygons and closed-segment visibility explicitly.

Constructing the visibility graph of an already drawn polygon and recognizing a graph that could arise from some polygon are different tasks. Recognition has to account simultaneously for every edge and every absent edge without being given any coordinates.

The 2024 compendium by Schaefer, Cardinal and Miltzow explicitly retains polygon visibility recognition as open even when the boundary order is supplied. It defines visibility by containment of the complete joining segment in the polygon.

The same compendium distinguishes several related recognition problems with \(\exists\mathbb R\) hardness or completeness results, including polygons with holes and simultaneous interior/exterior visibility. Those results impose different objects or additional data and do not settle this simple-polygon problem. Here \(\exists\mathbb R\) denotes problems reducible in polynomial time to the existence of real solutions of finite systems of polynomial equalities and inequalities.

Lin and Skiena study coordinate requirements for realizing visibility graphs. The fact that a realization is a finite list of real points does not by itself make it a polynomial-length certificate in the Turing model.

A polynomial algorithm would identify when a purely combinatorial collection of sight lines can come from one polygonal environment. The fixed boundary order is part of the scientific question; discarding it or requiring a convex polygon would change the class being recognized.

cards.formal: Does there exist a universal real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), some set \(U_n\subset\mathbb R^2\) of at most \(Cn\) distinct points supports a crossing-free straight-line drawing of every simple planar graph on \(n\) vertices?

cards.definitions: The point set \(U_n\) is chosen as a function of \(n\) before the graph is supplied. For each finite simple undirected planar graph \(G\) with vertex set \([n]\), there must be an injective map \(\phi:V(G)\to U_n\). Every edge is drawn as the closed line segment between its endpoint images. Two edge segments may intersect only at the image of a shared endpoint, and the relative interior of an edge may contain no vertex image. Unused points in \(U_n\) are allowed. The injection may depend on \(G\); the same prescribed correspondence of labels to points is not required. The graph need not have a prescribed planar embedding. Coordinates are arbitrary reals, and no grid-size, computability or runtime constraint is imposed. A planar graph means one admitting a plane embedding by arcs with these same incidence and nonintersection requirements.

context_blocks.text: A universal point set is chosen before the graph is known. Once a graph arrives, its vertices may be assigned to any suitable distinct points of that same set. The question is whether a constant number of available points per graph vertex always suffices for every planar graph of that size.

Location matters even for four vertices. The complete graph on four vertices is planar, but putting all four vertices on the corners of a convex quadrilateral forces its two diagonals to cross. A planar straight-line drawing can instead place one vertex inside the triangle formed by the other three. Thus a large collection of points in convex position is not by itself universal for planar graphs.

Classical straight-line grid-drawing theorems give a universal \(O(n)\)-by-\(O(n)\) grid and therefore \(O(n^2)\) available points. Lower bounds exceeding \(n\) show that using exactly one point per vertex is too restrictive in general, but a constant-factor lower bound does not refute the existence of some larger universal linear constant.

The 2023 work gives linear-size sets for restricted classes of planar graphs. A host set for a class with additional structural constraints need not support all planar graphs. This is why the quantified graph family, as well as the number of points, is part of the target.

A preprint posted on 10 September 2026 claims universal sets of size \(n^{1+o(1)}\) for unrestricted planar graphs. This improves the stated general upper frontier if its proof is correct, but it does not assert \(Cn\) for a fixed constant. For example, \(n\log n\) also has the form \(n^{1+o(1)}\) while its ratio to \(n\) is unbounded. The preprint’s claim is recorded without an independent proof audit.

The input graph has no prescribed embedding or fixed correspondence between vertex labels and host points. Coordinates may be arbitrary real numbers. Allowing a bend in each edge, prescribing the vertex-to-point assignment, or requiring a small integer grid would change the existence question.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that a constant \(C>0\) and sets \(U_n\) with the stated universal drawing property exist for every \(n\), or prove the logical negation in Lean: for every \(C>0\), some \(n\) has the property that every point set of size at most \(Cn\) fails to support at least one simple planar graph on \(n\) vertices. The point set precedes the graph in the quantifiers, and each successful drawing may choose its own vertex assignment.

cards.title: NP recognition of closed hyperbolic three-manifolds
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and a polynomial p such that, for every finite PL-triangulation T of a compact connected three-manifold M, M is closed and admits a hyperbolic metric if and only if there exists a binary certificate w with |\(w|\le p(|T|)\) and \(V(T,w)=1\)?
cards.why: Would show that a global constant-curvature geometry can always be certified using polynomially bounded discrete evidence from an arbitrary triangulation. It would sharpen the complexity of a central geometric recognition problem beyond mere decidability.

cards.definitions: The input consists of t abstract tetrahedra and a finite list of affine face identifications, each encoded by two tetrahedron indices, face indices and a permutation of the face vertices. Unpaired faces are permitted. Identifying these faces produces the quotient space \(M=|T|\). The input is promised to be a PL-triangulation of a compact connected topological three-manifold, possibly with boundary; no orientability or irreducibility promise is imposed. Its encoding length |T| counts all bits in the explicit tetrahedron and face-pairing data, with binary indices. Closed means that M has empty boundary, since compactness is already promised. A hyperbolic metric means a Riemannian metric locally isometric to hyperbolic three-space \(H^{3}\); for example \(H^{3}\) is the upper half-space \(\{(x,y,z)\in \mathbb{R} ^{3}:z>0\}\) with metric \(ds^{2}=(dx^{2}+dy^{2}+dz^{2})/z^{2}\). Equivalently, the metric has constant sectional curvature −1. On closed M it is complete. The abstract tetrahedra in the input are topological data and are not supplied as geometric tetrahedra in that metric. V is one uniform deterministic Turing algorithm without advice or an oracle, and runs in time polynomial in |T|+|w| on all encoded inputs. Correctness is required on every promised manifold triangulation; no particular certificate format or method is prescribed. The polynomial certificate bound and verifier are fixed for the entire problem, not chosen separately for each manifold.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a polynomial certificate bound and a uniform polynomial-time verifier that accepts some bounded-length certificate for every closed hyperbolic input and accepts none for every other promised manifold input. Alternatively, prove that no such bound and verifier exist. A terminating recognition algorithm alone, or certificates for non-hyperbolicity, do not establish this NP membership.

context_blocks.text: Two very different gluing descriptions can represent the same manifold. A successful verifier must accept every description of a closed hyperbolic manifold with some certificate polynomial in that description’s size. cards.title: Efficient average-distortion embeddings of polyhedral norms
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time construction of a globally defined Euclidean embedding of the square-root metric of every rational polyhedral norm, with quadratic average distortion at most \(C\sqrt{\log_2 d}\) on any given finite rational point set, for one universal constant \(C\)? The construction must produce a finite description permitting polynomial-time evaluation to any requested precision. This is the explicitly encoded polyhedral-norm branch of the source’s algorithmic average-John question; the exact guarantees and complexity parameters are below.
cards.why: Average-distance preservation can be much better than preservation of every distance from below. Constructing such maps would make a strong structural theorem in metric geometry algorithmically usable. The global nonexpansion requirement matters because a later query point need not belong to the original data set.
cards.status_note: The broader constructive question is open in the 2021 seminar source. This card explicitly fixes a rational polyhedral bit-model specialization. Checked later sketching results have different output and nonexpansion guarantees, but bounded checks through 2026-09-16 do not independently establish current openness of this selected computational version.

progress.text: Naor’s published average John theorem establishes the geometric \(O(\sqrt{\log d})\) bound through an existence argument.
The seminar report asks for an explicit efficient map, and the near-neighbor paper gives constructions for specified norm families.

Version 3 of the average-distortion sketching preprint develops a more general sketch-and-decoder model and results for discrete subsets of fixed norm families. These guarantees are not the global Euclidean-map target.

The algorithmic question asks for an efficiently constructed map that is nonexpanding on the entire space, including future query points.
This card explicitly selects rational polyhedral norms and rational data points so that the input and computational cost have finite bit encodings.

cards.definitions:
An input consists of integers \(d\ge2\), \(r\ge d\), \(n\ge2\), a matrix \(A\in\mathbb Q^{r\times d}\) of column rank \(d\), and a list \(P=(p_1,\ldots,p_n)\) of pairwise distinct points in \(\mathbb Q^d\). Integers and rational coordinates are written in binary, with signed numerators and positive denominators; dimensions and lists are explicit. Let \(N\) be the total input bit length. Define a norm on the entire real space \(\mathbb R^d\) by
\[
\|x\|_A=\max_{1\le j\le r}|(Ax)_j|,
\qquad
\operatorname{dist}_A(x,y)=\sqrt{\|x-y\|_A}.
\]
Full column rank makes \(\|\cdot\|_A\) a norm. There is no bound on \(r\), coordinate magnitudes or geometric aspect ratios except what their input lengths express. The norm is supplied by the matrix, not by a unit-cost oracle. All arithmetic and norm evaluations are charged at bit cost.

The assertion asks for two fixed deterministic multitape Turing-machine programs \(B,E\), constants \(C,K\ge1\), and an integer \(a\ge1\), independent of every input. On each valid input, \(B\) must output an integer \(m\ge1\) and a finite binary description \(\sigma\) in at most \(K(N+1)^a\) steps, with \(m\) and \(|\sigma|\) at most \(K(N+1)^a\). That description must specify one continuous function \(f_\sigma:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^m\) satisfying
\[
\|f_\sigma(x)-f_\sigma(y)\|_2^2\le\|x-y\|_A
\quad\text{for all }x,y\in\mathbb R^d
\]
and
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n
\|f_\sigma(p_i)-f_\sigma(p_j)\|_2^2
\ \ge\
\frac{1}{C^2\log_2 d}
\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n\|p_i-p_j\|_A.
\]
Here \(\|\cdot\|_2\) is the Euclidean norm. Both sums are over ordered pairs, including the zero diagonal. The average is with respect to the uniform distribution on \(P\); the factor \(n^{-2}\) cancels on both sides. The first inequality is nonexpansion for the square-root metric on the whole space, including points outside \(P\). The second controls squared Euclidean distances on average. No individual lower bound on a pairwise distance or injectivity is required.

The meaning of a finite description is fixed by the second program. On input \((\sigma,x,1^k)\), where \(x\in\mathbb Q^d\) has binary description length \(b\) and \(k\ge1\), \(E\) must output a dyadic rational vector \(v\in\mathbb Q^m\) satisfying
\[
\|v-f_\sigma(x)\|_2\le2^{-k}
\]
in at most \(K(N+b+k+1)^a\) bit operations. Dyadic rationals are represented by an integer numerator and a power-of-two denominator, both explicitly encoded in binary. The approximations for all rational \(x\) and all precisions must correspond to the same continuous map; they are not separate independently chosen embeddings. Continuity and density of rational points determine that map on all of \(\mathbb R^d\). Its displayed geometric inequalities are exact mathematical requirements; rounding pertains only to evaluation.

The description may include the original matrix and point set. Both construction and evaluation may depend polynomially on their total bit length; no storage or query-time bound independent of \(n\) is imposed. No random bits, advice, noncomputable real constants, free preprocessing or oracle is available. The problem asks for construction of a map, not just a table of images of the input points.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of such uniform programs and constants, including their bit complexity, a single well-defined global map per output description, both geometric inequalities and the evaluation guarantee at every rational query and precision, or a complete Lean proof that the assertion is false. A nonconstructive embedding, a map defined only on \(P\), or a sketch whose decoder estimates distances without giving Euclidean coordinates does not meet this target. The distortion requirement is \(O(\sqrt{\log d})\) with a common constant; \(2^{-k}\) specifies computational output precision. Neither is replaced by the numerical-benchmark \(1/100\) tolerance.

cards.definitions:
A finite metric space consists of a finite set X and a symmetric function d:X×X→[0,∞) with d(x,y)=0 exactly when x=y and d(x,z)≤d(x,y)+d(y,z). Its half-snowflake is the metric space with distance √d(x,y). The square root applies to the original distances, not to the Wasserstein distance or to the dimension. Distances in the base space R³ are the usual Euclidean distances.

The set \(\mathcal P_p(\mathbb R^3)\) consists of Borel probability measures μ on R³ satisfying \(\int\|u\|_2^p\,d\mu(u)<\infty\). A coupling of μ and ν is a probability measure π on R³×R³ with these two marginals. Write Π(μ,ν) for all such couplings. The Wasserstein metric is \(W_p(\mu,\nu)=(\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\int\|u-v\|_2^p\,d\pi(u,v))^{1/p}\). Thus the transport cost uses the pth power of Euclidean distance and takes a pth root after minimizing. Images may be arbitrary measures of finite pth moment; no support-size, equal-mass, rational-coordinate or computability restriction is imposed.

The two-sided inequality means a bi-Lipschitz embedding of distortion at most C_p after a common rescaling s. It forces F to be injective when X has more than one point. Both F and s may depend on p and the entire finite metric. The quantifier order is ∀p>2 ∃C_p<∞ ∀(X,d) ∃F,s; there is no single bound required to work uniformly as p varies, and p=∞ is excluded. This is an existence question, with no algorithmic running-time target.

The source writes c_Y(X,√d)≤D_p, where c_Y is the infimum of the distortions of all embeddings. The infimum need not be attained. Existence of some finite uniform bound in that formulation is equivalent to the displayed formulation: increasing an available finite infimum bound, for example to twice its value, allows actual embeddings for each finite X. The source's stronger suggestion D_p=1 instead means distortion arbitrarily close to one for every finite metric. It must not be silently replaced by a demand for an attained isometric embedding, and neither strengthening is required here.

The already-proved theorem embeds the 1/p-snowflake, with distances d(x,y)^{1/p}, with distortion arbitrarily close to one. When p>2 its exponent is smaller than 1/2, so it does not answer this question. At p=2 it does give the half-snowflake result; that endpoint is background, outside the unresolved range.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the uniform-in-X finite-distortion assertion for every fixed p>2, or refute it by finding a fixed p>2 for which half-snowflake distortions into this exact target space are unbounded across finite metrics. A single finite metric with distortion greater than one does not refute the claim. Results allowing the distortion or base-space dimension to grow with |X|, or using exponent 1/p instead of 1/2, do not settle it. No optimal numerical value of C_p is requested.

references.authors: Bauer, Ulrich; Rathod, Abhishek; Spreer, Jonathan

cards.definitions:
A finite abstract simplicial complex is a finite collection of nonempty finite vertex sets, called simplices, closed under taking nonempty subsets. A simplex with \(r+1\) vertices has dimension \(r\). The input explicitly lists its simplices, or equivalently its maximal simplices and their vertex labels. The promise is that every simplex has at most three vertices. Edges and triangles need not form a manifold or embed in Euclidean three-space.

An elementary collapse removes a pair \((\sigma,\tau)\) of simplices, where \(\sigma\) is a codimension-one face of \(\tau\) and the only simplex properly containing \(\sigma\) is \(\tau\). An elementary expansion is the inverse: add such a pair so that the result is again a simplicial complex and that pair could be collapsed immediately.

Simple-homotopy equivalence to a point means that a finite sequence of expansions and collapses takes \(K\) to a complex consisting of a single vertex. New vertices may be introduced; intermediate complexes may be larger and have dimension greater than two. There is no prescribed bound on the number of moves, number of vertices or intermediate dimension. Relabeling vertices has no mathematical effect.

For comparison with the topological formulation, the geometric realization \(|K|\) is obtained by gluing an ordinary Euclidean simplex for each face along its common subfaces. It is contractible if its identity map can be continuously deformed to a constant map: there exist \(p\in|K|\) and a continuous
\[H:|K|\times[0,1]\longrightarrow |K|,\qquad H(x,0)=x,\quad H(x,1)=p.\]
For a finite complex, being contractible is equivalent to having the simple-homotopy type of a point, as recalled in the sources.

The algorithm is a single deterministic Turing machine acting on the finite encoding. It must give the correct yes/no answer and terminate on both contractible and noncontractible inputs. No polynomial-time or other running-time bound is required. There is no promise that \(K\) is already contractible or simply connected, and no contraction certificate is supplied.

This is specifically recognition of the simple-homotopy type of a point. The card does not ask to decide equivalence of an arbitrary pair of complexes. It also does not restrict allowed moves to collapses alone, or impose a fixed expansion budget.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of a total decision algorithm for this input class, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A procedure that eventually finds a contraction on yes-instances but may run forever on no-instances is insufficient. A hardness theorem ruling out efficient algorithms does not establish undecidability.

cards.title: Linear-size sample compression
cards.formal: Is there a universal integer \(C\ge1\) such that every nonempty Boolean concept class \(H\subseteq\{0,1\}^{X}\) on an arbitrary set \(X\), with finite VC dimension \(d\ge1\), admits a labeled sample compression scheme with nonnegative integer kernel and side-information bounds \(k,b\) satisfying \[k+b\le Cd?\] The scheme is exact on every finite \(H\)-realizable sample, stores an unordered subset of labeled sample records plus \(b\) bits, and may reconstruct a predictor outside \(H\). Its compressor, reconstructor, \(k\), and \(b\) may depend on the complete class, but the same scheme and bounds must work for all sample sizes. Only \(C\) must be universal. This preserves the card’s previously selected linear-size, counted-side-information formulation.
cards.definitions: A concept is a total Boolean function on \(X\). A finite set \(U\subseteq X\) is shattered by \(H\) if \(\{h|_U:h\in H\}=\{0,1\}^{U}\); the VC dimension is the largest cardinality of a shattered set. A finite labeled sample is a finite set \(S\subseteq X\times\{0,1\}\). It is \(H\)-realizable if some \(h\in H\) agrees with every pair in \(S\); in particular, a realizable sample has no contradictory labels at the same point. The empty sample is allowed. A scheme consists of deterministic set maps \(\kappa\) and \(\rho\). For every realizable \(S\), \(\kappa(S)=(T,z)\), where \(T\subseteq S\), \(|T|\le k\), and \(z\in\{0,1\}^{b}\). The reconstruction \(\rho(T,z):X\to\{0,1\}\) is a total predictor satisfying \[\rho(\kappa(S))(x)=y\qquad\text{for every }(x,y)\in S.\] The reconstructor is defined for all possible finite labeled kernels of size at most \(k\) and all \(b\)-bit strings, with consistency required only on actual compressed messages. It receives no original sample, sample size, omitted point, original index or ordering of retained examples. One retained labeled example costs one unit, even on a domain whose points have no finite binary descriptions; each side-information bit costs one unit. The retained set is unordered. A finite side alphabet \(I\) instead of bit strings costs \(\lceil\log_2|I|\rceil\) bits. Allowing variable-length strings of bounded length changes this linear-size question only by a constant factor if their lengths are encoded as part of the message. The compressor is required only on realizable samples. Reconstruction need not be proper, stable under deletion of unused records, computable, efficient, or measurable. No randomness or data-distribution promise is involved. Dimension zero is omitted from the display because a nonempty such class has one pointwise labeling and admits a scheme storing nothing. All classes of positive finite dimension, not just finite domains or finite classes, are included.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof of the stated universal linear bound, or of its logical negation. A positive answer must provide a single universal constant and, for each class, a valid compressor and reconstructor with the counted size bound holding on every realizable sample. A negative answer must show that for every integer \(C\ge1\), some class of positive finite VC dimension admits no such scheme of size at most \(Cd\). A lower bound against only proper, stable, efficient, or otherwise restricted reconstruction does not refute this unrestricted target. Neither does failure of a particular embedding construction. Free side information or free ordering of retained points is outside the model. The requirement is exact consistency and linear size with a universal constant; it asks for no additive numerical approximation.
cards.why: A central question connecting the combinatorial complexity of prediction with how many observations suffice to represent all training decisions. Its universality across concept classes, and its links to learning, extremal set systems and graph geometry, make the linear-versus-exponential gap fundamental.

importance.reason: A longstanding general conjecture asking whether VC dimension controls sample representation up to a constant factor; it reaches far beyond any one learning algorithm or geometric example.

context_blocks.text: The compressed object lets a fixed decoder reproduce every label in the original training sample. It need not identify the unknown target on points that were never observed. The same decoder must work at every sample size, so a bound depending only on the class’s VC dimension would be independent of how much training data was supplied.

The distinction between examples and bits is essential. A domain point may require arbitrarily many bits to describe, but sample compression charges one unit for retaining its labeled record. Conversely, an unbounded uncharged message would evade the intended resource bound. Both the retained kernel and the side information are therefore limited explicitly, and the kernel has no free ordering.

Moran and Yehudayoff prove that every binary class of VC dimension \(d\) has a scheme of total size \(2^{O(d)}\). Their sharper theorem also depends on dual VC dimension, which exchanges the roles of domain points and hypotheses by regarding a point as its vector of labels across the class. That dual dimension can grow exponentially in \(d\), leaving the general linear-versus-exponential gap. The checked result is from the corrected v2 and subsequent journal publication.

Chase and coauthors show that some finite classes require an exponential increase in dimension to be contained in an extremal class, a structured type of class with known tight compression. This limits a previously studied embedding-based route to compression. It does not prove that the original class itself requires an exponential-size scheme.

The April 2026 graph-ball paper explicitly retains the general linear conjecture. It gives proper compression of size \(O(t\log(t+1))\) for graph-ball classes whose underlying graph has treewidth at most \(t\), and an analogous cliquewidth result. The predictors are themselves balls, but the resource parameter is graph width and the family is restricted. These structured results are not a universal linear-VC theorem.

The 2025 reduction paper transfers some binary compression bounds to multiclass, regression and robust-learning settings. The sharper transfers need additional reconstruction or stability properties. The ordinary linear conjecture appears in its introduction; its later robust-compression open problem is a different target.

A March 2026 preprint first claimed a sample-compression breakthrough and later a no-clash teaching result. The current checked version, dated 3 August 2026, is withdrawn and identifies an incorrect proof of Lemma 2. Its stale search-result title and earlier abstract are not evidence that the conjecture has been resolved.

cards.title: Learning parity with noise in polynomial time
cards.formal: For every fixed rational \(\eta\in(0,1/2)\), does there exist a uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm that exactly recovers every hidden parity vector from independent uniform examples with independent label noise of rate \(\eta\)? More explicitly, is the following assertion true? \[\forall\eta\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1/2)\ \exists A_\eta,\ C_\eta,k_\eta\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge1\ \forall s\in\{0,1\}^n:\quad \Pr[A_\eta^{\operatorname{EX}_{n,s,\eta}}(1^n)=s]\ge\frac23,\] where every execution takes at most \(C_\eta(n+1)^{k_\eta}\) bit-computation steps, including all example requests and output writing, and \(\operatorname{EX}_{n,s,\eta}\) returns a fresh pair \[ (a,b),\qquad a\sim U_n,\quad e\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\eta),\quad b=\langle a,s\rangle\oplus e.\] All vectors, errors and machine coins are independent except for the displayed dependence of each label on its input and the same fixed secret. This retains the existing every-fixed-rate, every-secret search-LPN target.
cards.definitions:
The domain \(\{0,1\}^n\) is the vector space \(\mathbb F_2^n\), where addition is coordinatewise modulo two. The parity \(\langle a,s\rangle=(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i s_i)\bmod2\) is the XOR of exactly those input coordinates where \(s_i=1\); \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo two. \(U_n\) is the uniform distribution giving each input vector probability \(2^{-n}\), and \(e\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\eta)\) means \(\Pr[e=1]=\eta\). The secret is arbitrary, fixed before the samples and coins are drawn, and unchanged throughout one execution. Each call returns an independent sample under that fixed secret, including a fresh error bit. The learner may decide when to request more samples based on its previous observations, but cannot choose \(a\), observe the error bit, obtain a clean label, or query a coherent quantum example.

\(A_\eta\) is one classical probabilistic multitape Turing machine using fair independent coins and the specified example oracle. It receives the dimension in unary. The fixed rational rate may be built into the machine; there is no promise that one common algorithm or common exponent works uniformly over rates approaching one half with \(n\). The machine, positive integer constant \(C_\eta\), and positive integer exponent \(k_\eta\) are chosen before \(n\) and \(s\). They may depend on \(\eta\), but have no length-dependent advice. All reading, storing, revisiting examples, computation and output bits are charged; the oracle’s internal sample generation is not charged, and one request costs at least one step. The worst-case bound holds for all possible example and coin histories, not just in expectation. Thus time, samples and stored bits are polynomially bounded, while unrestricted repeated access to stored data is allowed. No single-pass or small-memory constraint is imposed.

The output is exactly one \(n\)-bit vector \(\widehat s\); malformed output is failure. Success means \(\widehat s=s\), not merely low noisy-label error or an unspecified prediction advantage. The probability is over the entire training sample stream and learner randomness for each fixed secret, with no distributional promise on \(s\). Neither \(s\) nor the sample inputs are promised sparse. Fixed confidence \(2/3\) is retained. The target is the existence of a polynomial-time search procedure, rather than the quantitative size of the best subexponential exponent or a numerical approximation requiring a precision convention.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof of the displayed assertion or its complete logical negation. A positive result must supply a machine and polynomial resource bound separately for every fixed rational noise rate, and prove exact recovery with the stated probability for every dimension and secret. A negative result must exhibit at least one fixed rational \(\eta\in(0,1/2)\) for which every candidate machine and polynomial bound fail on some dimension and secret, either in the resource guarantee or in recovery probability. Hardness only for a rate depending on \(n\), a restricted statistical-query or small-memory learner, sparse inputs, quantum examples, or under an unproved computational assumption is not the unconditional negation. Recovering a hypothesis with some advantage is sufficient only together with a proved conversion meeting the exact-secret criterion and the same polynomial-resource requirements.
cards.why: A canonical computational learning problem where a tiny amount of independent label noise defeats the obvious algebraic method, connecting efficient learning, random-code decoding and cryptographic hardness.

importance.reason: A fundamental boundary between information-theoretic learnability and efficient learning, with broad consequences for noise-tolerant algorithms and cryptographic assumptions.

cards.status_note: The checked classical and 2026 primary literature does not provide a matching polynomial-time algorithm or unconditional impossibility for every fixed rational constant noise rate. The May amplification changes parameters; the September worst-case reduction is conditional on a joint code/dual-code hardness premise. The 15 September optical paper’s publisher abstract reports finite structured sparse-constraint experiments, not the stated general guarantee; its full PDF was inaccessible through the publisher gateway. The rate-dependent polynomial convention, classical independent samples and exact every-secret recovery target are retained. Bounded checks through 16 September 2026 justify uncertain current status rather than proof of continued openness.

context_blocks.text: Without noise, random parity examples yield a consistent system of binary linear equations. Independent label errors remove that exact algebraic consistency while leaving the hidden rule exceptionally simple. The problem is a standard boundary between efficient noiseless learning and learning with random classification noise.

For every fixed noise rate below one half, \(O_\eta(n)\) examples suffice information-theoretically for exact recovery with constant confidence, although an unrestricted decoder may use exponential computation. The true secret agrees with a fresh noisy label with probability \(1-\eta\); every different parity agrees with probability \(1/2\) under uniform inputs. This statistical separation explains why a polynomial sample bound alone does not settle the computational question.

Collecting sample vectors as matrix rows gives \(b=As+e\) over \(\mathbb F_2\): the columns of the uniform matrix generate a random binary linear code, and the label string is a noisy codeword. Worst-case decoding hardness for arbitrary codes is not itself a hardness proof for this randomly generated sample distribution. The code, noise and sample-count quantifiers matter.

Blum–Kalai–Wasserman give a \(2^{O_\eta(n/\log n)}\)-time algorithm with a comparable subexponential number of examples at fixed noise. They also establish a separation between example-based noise-tolerant learning and statistical-query learning for a restricted parity class. A statistical-query lower bound therefore cannot be treated as a lower bound for every machine that observes individual examples.

Lyubashevsky gives time \(2^{O_{\eta,\gamma}(n/\log\log n)}\) using \(n^{1+\gamma}\) examples for every fixed \(\gamma>0\) in the constant-noise regime. This answers the older subexponential-time polynomial-sample question, but its time remains superpolynomial. Its sample regime must not be silently combined with the faster many-sample BKW exponent.

Garg–Kothari–Liu–Raz prove that noisy-parity learning in their streaming memory model needs either \(\Omega(n^2/(1/2-\eta))\) bits of memory or exponentially many samples. Their source uses \(\varepsilon=1/2-\eta\) for the noise bias. At fixed \(\eta\), quadratic memory is permitted by this card, so this unconditional storage lower bound does not exclude the target learner.

Aggarwal–Gupta–Li’s May 2026 paper amplifies success on a small fraction of LPN instances into success on almost all instances with changed dimension and noise parameters. It concerns transformations between hardness and success regimes; it neither constructs a polynomial-time algorithm for every fixed noise rate nor proves that none exists. The parameter changes prevent its abstract from being read as fixed-instance amplification without qualifications.

The September 2026 revision by Aggarwal and coauthors gives conditional low-noise LPN hardness from simultaneous worst-case assumptions about decoding a code from random noise and distinguishing noisy codewords of its dual. Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 4.1 retain this joint alternative; it is not an unconditional worst-case-hardness theorem for the stated constant-rate search problem.

cards.context:
Without noise, random parity examples yield a consistent system of binary linear equations. Independent label errors remove that exact algebraic consistency while leaving the hidden rule exceptionally simple. The problem is a standard boundary between efficient noiseless learning and learning with random classification noise.

For every fixed noise rate below one half, \(O_\eta(n)\) examples suffice information-theoretically for exact recovery with constant confidence, although an unrestricted decoder may use exponential computation. The true secret agrees with a fresh noisy label with probability \(1-\eta\); every different parity agrees with probability \(1/2\) under uniform inputs. This statistical separation explains why a polynomial sample bound alone does not settle the computational question.

Collecting sample vectors as matrix rows gives \(b=As+e\) over \(\mathbb F_2\): the columns of the uniform matrix generate a random binary linear code, and the label string is a noisy codeword. Worst-case decoding hardness for arbitrary codes is not itself a hardness proof for this randomly generated sample distribution. The code, noise and sample-count quantifiers matter.

Blum–Kalai–Wasserman give a \(2^{O_\eta(n/\log n)}\)-time algorithm with a comparable subexponential number of examples at fixed noise. They also establish a separation between example-based noise-tolerant learning and statistical-query learning for a restricted parity class. A statistical-query lower bound therefore cannot be treated as a lower bound for every machine that observes individual examples.

Lyubashevsky gives time \(2^{O_{\eta,\gamma}(n/\log\log n)}\) using \(n^{1+\gamma}\) examples for every fixed \(\gamma>0\) in the constant-noise regime. This answers the older subexponential-time polynomial-sample question, but its time remains superpolynomial. Its sample regime must not be silently combined with the faster many-sample BKW exponent.

Garg–Kothari–Liu–Raz prove that noisy-parity learning in their streaming memory model needs either \(\Omega(n^2/(1/2-\eta))\) bits of memory or exponentially many samples. Their source uses \(\varepsilon=1/2-\eta\) for the noise bias. At fixed \(\eta\), quadratic memory is permitted by this card, so this unconditional storage lower bound does not exclude the target learner.

Aggarwal–Gupta–Li’s May 2026 paper amplifies success on a small fraction of LPN instances into success on almost all instances with changed dimension and noise parameters. It concerns transformations between hardness and success regimes; it neither constructs a polynomial-time algorithm for every fixed noise rate nor proves that none exists. The parameter changes prevent its abstract from being read as fixed-instance amplification without qualifications.

The September 2026 revision by Aggarwal and coauthors gives conditional low-noise LPN hardness from simultaneous worst-case assumptions about decoding a code from random noise and distinguishing noisy codewords of its dual. Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 4.1 retain this joint alternative; it is not an unconditional worst-case-hardness theorem for the stated constant-rate search problem.

The publisher abstract of a 15 September 2026 optical-computing paper reports a 512-variable experiment with at most two variables per constraint and numerical comparisons. Those structured sparse constraints and finite physical experiments do not supply the arbitrary-dimension uniform classical polynomial-time guarantee requested here. Only its publisher abstract was accessible during this check.

cards.title: Learning Boolean juntas from uniform random examples
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform classical randomized learner \(A\) and universal positive integers \(B,C\) such that every Boolean \(k\)-junta on \(n\) variables can be learned from independent uniform noiseless examples in time polynomial in \(n,2^k\) and inverse error? Explicitly, for all integers \(n\ge1\), \(0\le k\le n\), \(t\ge3\), and every \(k\)-junta \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), the learner receives \(1^n,1^k,1^t\) and an independent-example oracle \(\operatorname{EX}_f\). Every execution takes at most \(B(n+2^k+t)^C\) steps and outputs an ordinary Boolean circuit \(h\) for which \[\Pr_{A,\,\operatorname{EX}_f}\left[\Pr_{x\sim U_n}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\frac1t\right]\ge\frac23.\] The exponent \(C\), constant \(B\) and machine are independent of \(n,k,t,f\). This preserves the existing full \(\operatorname{poly}(n,2^k,1/\varepsilon)\) target; it is not merely a separate polynomial-time statement for every fixed \(k\).
cards.definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A \(k\)-junta is a Boolean function for which there exist an unknown subset \(S=\{i_1<\cdots<i_r\}\subseteq[n]\), \(r\le k\), and an arbitrary Boolean table \(g:\{0,1\}^r\to\{0,1\}\) such that \[f(x)=g(x_{i_1},\ldots,x_{i_r})\quad\text{for all }x\in\{0,1\}^n.\] Neither \(S\) nor \(g\) is given to the learner. No monotonicity, sparsity of the truth table or lower bound on variable influence is assumed. For \(k=0\), the class consists of the two constant functions, using the unique empty input to \(g\). The public \(k\) is only an upper bound on the number of relevant coordinates; it need not be the minimal support size.

\(U_n\) gives each binary vector probability \(2^{-n}\). Each call to \(\operatorname{EX}_f\) supplies a new pair \((x,f(x))\) with \(x\sim U_n\), independent of all previous draws and the learner’s fair random coins. The unknown target is fixed before the data are drawn. The learner can request further independent examples adaptively, but cannot choose their inputs, obtain membership-query labels, or request coupled or neighboring examples. Labels are exact noiseless bits. The outer probability measures confidence over the complete learning execution; the inner probability is zero-one prediction error on a fresh independent input. Reciprocals of positive integers suffice to represent arbitrary desired positive error tolerances up to polynomial rounding overhead. The fixed confidence is \(2/3\).

The output is a finite acyclic ordinary Boolean circuit on the \(n\) input bits, using two-input AND/OR gates, one-input NOT gates and constants with a fixed effective binary encoding. It may depend on all coordinates and need not itself be a \(k\)-junta; this is improper learning. It is evaluated without the training oracle and with no stored target-dependent state other than its output description. The learner is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine, with no advice, receiving the displayed public integers in unary. All example reading, computation, stored-data access, fair random bits and output writing count in the worst-case bit-time bound, which also bounds the number of example requests and output length. The example generator’s internal sampling cost is not charged. Circuit evaluation is polynomial in the written circuit size under this encoding. Repeated access to stored examples and any polynomial amount of memory within the time bound are allowed. The requirement is predictive approximation; it does not require identifying the exact relevant set, giving a minimum representation or recovering every truth-table entry.

Polynomial dependence on \(2^k\) permits an exponential dependence on the number of relevant variables, since an arbitrary \(k\)-bit table already has \(2^k\) entries. It excludes a degree of \(n\) that grows with \(k\). For every fixed \(c>0\), the displayed guarantee would in particular be polynomial in \(n,t\) for all \(k\le c\log_2 n\); an algorithm that only handles each constant \(k\) with its own exponent need not satisfy it. The accuracy target is the explicitly bounded rational error \(1/t\); the problem asks for exact existence of the learner and universal exponent rather than a numerical optimal value.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof that such \(A,B,C\) exist, or prove the complete negation: for every proposed uniform machine and universal constants, some allowed \(n,k,t,f\) violates the worst-case resource bound, finite hypothesis condition or the stated PAC probability. A positive answer must handle all Boolean junta tables and all support sizes up to \(n\) with one exponent independent of \(k\). A learner using membership queries, correlated random-walk examples, a randomly perturbed marginal distribution, or only monotone targets does not meet the specified interface. A statistical-query, limited-memory or specified-neural-training lower bound does not exclude every allowed machine. Conditional cryptographic hardness must retain its unproved premise and is not the unconditional negation. Neither exact support recovery nor a prescribed proper output is an additional obligation.
cards.why: Determine whether arbitrary dependence on a small hidden set of variables can be learned efficiently from ordinary observations, separating computational search from sample sufficiency.

importance.reason: A central unresolved task in computational learning theory, isolating feature selection and serving as a prerequisite for efficient learning of general decision trees and DNF formulas.

progress.text: Mossel–O’Donnell–Servedio publish the first constant-factor improvement over the brute-force exponent for learning arbitrary juntas from uniform examples.

Beretta’s revised RANDOM paper distinguishes junta-distribution learning from noiseless function learning and records the continuing computational gap.
Servedio’s survey explicitly retains the uniform-example junta barrier and contrasts it with efficient learning using membership queries.
A new gradient-based learning result uses labelled samples from a lazy random walk; its temporal dependence is outside the independent-example model.

cards.status_note: The checked 2025 survey and NeurIPS introduction retain the independent-uniform-example junta barrier. The inherited OpenReview pointer was identified on 16 September 2026 as Chandrasekaran–Klivans, Learning Juntas under Markov Random Fields; its full theorem has a positive random-smoothing premise, with probability over that perturbation and the stated graph/width conditions. context_blocks.text: A junta uses only a few of the available input features, but its dependence on those features can be completely arbitrary. The problem asks for an efficient predictor from passive observations. It separates the small information content of the hidden rule from the computational cost of locating useful features among many irrelevant ones.

The finite class contains at most \((k+1)n^k2^{2^k}\) functions. At constant confidence, realizable finite-class learning therefore needs only \(O((2^k+k\log(n+1)+\log(k+1)+1)/\varepsilon)\) examples information-theoretically. This fits the desired polynomial resource scale; the unresolved requirement is efficient computation with those examples.

Mossel–O’Donnell–Servedio give exact learning in \(n^{(\omega/(\omega+1))k}\operatorname{poly}(n,2^k,\log(1/\delta))\) time, where \(\omega\) is a valid matrix-multiplication exponent. Using the exponent available in their paper gives roughly \(n^{0.704k}\) times polynomial factors. Their model uses independent uniform examples, so this is progress in the required access model.

Valiant’s Corollary 7 improves noiseless junta learning to a bound below \(n^{0.60k}\operatorname{poly}(n,2^k)\) for the matrix-multiplication exponent and constants used there. Servedio’s November 2025 survey still reports the roughly \(n^{0.6k}\) benchmark. The exponent of the ambient dimension continues to grow with support size, so this is not the universal polynomial in the formal statement.

Individual-coordinate correlation can vanish even for a relevant coordinate, as in the parity of three selected bits. That illustrates a limitation of certain correlation statistics, not an unconditional lower bound against all example-based learners: noiseless parity itself has an efficient algebraic learner. Statistical-query restrictions must remain distinct from unrestricted observation of the actual samples.

Membership-query algorithms and monotone-junta learners have stronger positive guarantees under their respective conditions. Membership queries let the learner choose which inputs are labeled, while monotonicity restricts the possible truth tables. Neither condition is assumed here.

Beretta’s RANDOM 2025 paper concerns distributions whose probability mass function depends on a small coordinate set and relates that density-learning task to sparse noisy parity. Its introduction separately describes the persistent difficulty of noiseless Boolean function learning under uniform examples. The distribution-learning equivalence is not a resolution of this card’s prediction problem.

The inherited OpenReview pointer has now been identified as Chandrasekaran–Klivans, Learning Juntas under Markov Random Fields, NeurIPS 2025. Its introduction explicitly retains the difficult uniform-example question. Its positive Theorem 1.3 assumes a smoothed Markov random field, a known bounded-degree dependency graph and the stated bounded-width parameters, with success probability also taken over the random external-field perturbation. Even though the unperturbed uniform distribution is a Markov random field, a guarantee over positive random smoothing does not imply a guarantee at that exact unperturbed distribution.

Cornacchia–Mikulincer–Mossel’s May 2026 Theorem 2 studies labeled samples along a lazy random walk on the hypercube. It gives nearly linear ambient-dimension sample dependence for each fixed support size, with the stated target-dependent constants. Consecutive examples are correlated even if each has a uniform marginal. An independent-example source does not provide that temporal information, so the theorem concerns a different learning interface.

A \(k\)-junta has a decision-tree or DNF representation of size at most \(2^k\) under the usual leaf/term convention, with polynomial overhead if literal occurrences are counted. Efficient uniform-example learning for those larger representation classes would therefore imply the requested bound. This explains the junta problem’s role as a basic obstacle within computational learning theory.

Wigderson’s Open Problem 17.9, inherited through the user-approved consolidation of TCS-0023, asks for polynomial-time uniform learning beyond constant support size, or hardness under a natural complexity assumption. The retained card asks for the specific stronger bound \(\operatorname{poly}(n,2^k,1/\varepsilon)\) for every \(k\). A positive answer handles \(k=O(\log n)\); success only in a slower-growing regime or a conditional negative answer is not the same assertion. This historical source remains a related milestone, and the earlier consolidation and reserved identifier are preserved as provenance.

cards.title: Polynomial-time distribution-free PAC learning of DNF
cards.formal:
Does there exist one uniform classical randomized learner \(A\) and absolute positive integers \(a,d\) such that the following holds for every pair of integers \(n,s\ge1\), every Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) representable by a DNF with at most \(s\) terms, every probability distribution \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\), and every pair of integers \(t,b\ge2\)? Given only \((n,s,t,b)\) and access to independent labeled examples \((x,f(x))\) with \(x\sim D\), the learner halts within
\[a(n+s+t+b+1)^d\]
steps on every run and outputs an explicitly encoded deterministic Boolean circuit \(h\) on \(n\) inputs such that
\[\Pr\!\left[\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}D(x)\,\mathbf 1[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\frac1t\right]\ge1-2^{-b}?\]
The outer probability includes the learner’s coins and sampled examples. Membership queries, equivalence queries and descriptions of \(f\) or \(D\) are not supplied. The output need not be a DNF; it must be an efficiently evaluable circuit as defined below.
cards.definitions:
A literal is a variable \(x_i\) or its negation, \(1\le i\le n\). A term is the conjunction of a subset of literals with at most one sign for each variable; the empty conjunction equals \(1\). A disjunctive normal form (DNF) is the disjunction of finitely many terms; the disjunction with no terms equals \(0\). Contradictory terms may be removed and repeated literals or terms ignored without increasing size. The size bound \(s\) counts terms, each of arbitrary width at most \(n\). The learner receives an upper bound \(s\), not a representation or a promise that the minimum DNF has exactly \(s\) terms. Both negated and unnegated literals are allowed.

The learner is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and unit-cost transitions. The integer parameters are in canonical binary notation with separators. The runtime is polynomial in their displayed values, not merely their encoding lengths. Apart from the example oracle, it has no oracle or advice and performs no quantum operations. Reading parameters, processing samples, generating random bits, storing data, arithmetic and writing the entire hypothesis all count toward the same worst-case time bound. Internal random bits are independent unbiased coins, independent of the example stream.

Each example-oracle request returns a fresh independent pair \((x,f(x))\) from the same fixed \(D\) and target \(f\). The learner can choose when to request or reuse an obtained example, but cannot choose or condition the next sampled point. Transferring its \(n+1\) bits costs \(n+1\) steps, and subsequent processing is also charged. One may equivalently supply an infinite independent example stream and charge for each read example. All answers are noiseless. The algorithm receives neither point probabilities nor a sampling program for \(D\). The distribution is an arbitrary assignment of nonnegative real masses summing to one on the finite Boolean cube; no product structure, uniformity, smoothness or efficient samplability is promised. Thus finite exact sampling is an idealized access model, and the cost of implementing a sampler for \(D\) is not part of the learning task.

A hypothesis is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit with input wires \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), constants \(0,1\), binary AND/OR gates, unary NOT gates and one designated output wire. It is encoded by its full topologically ordered gate list, gate types and binary indices of preceding wires, with separators, followed by the output index. The output is always valid circuit syntax. The number of written bits is bounded by the learner’s runtime; evaluation on any new \(n\)-bit input uses ordinary deterministic circuit evaluation, with time polynomial in \(n\) and the written circuit length. It uses no example oracle, target oracle or new randomness. A circuit that only describes a procedure for generating a much larger circuit is not an explicit output in this convention. No abstention output is allowed at prediction time.

The inner sum is the prediction error on a fresh point drawn from \(D\). The outer probability is over the finite sample/coin experiment bounded by the clock. The guarantee is required separately for every fixed \(f,D,n,s,t,b\); the same program and constants must work for all of them. No worst-case correctness on every point is required. With \(\varepsilon=1/t\) and \(\delta=2^{-b}\), the requirement is the usual polynomial dependence on \(n,s,1/\varepsilon,\log(1/\delta)\). Other \(0<\varepsilon,\delta<1\) are covered by rounding to reciprocal-integer accuracy and dyadic confidence at least as strong as requested. These encodings retain the original PAC target without an input representation for arbitrary real numbers.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence proposition or its full logical negation. An affirmative proof must specify one learner and universal polynomial bound, establish valid explicit circuit output and the all-run time bound, and prove the stated error/confidence inequality for every target, distribution and parameter choice. A negative proof must rule out every uniform learner and every fixed polynomial bound in this model. It must cover arbitrary circuit hypotheses, not only proper learners that return DNFs or a restricted algorithm class. A conditional lower bound whose computational assumption is left unproved, an algorithm with membership queries, a guarantee only for a special distribution or constant number of terms, and a superpolynomial runtime do not establish either full answer.

context_blocks.text: A DNF accepts a point when at least one conjunction of feature conditions holds. Learning predicts these labels from observations without receiving the rules. The unknown distribution can concentrate its probability on any subset of the Boolean cube, so uniform-input arguments do not automatically extend to this task.

The obstacle is computational rather than a shortage of samples: the finite DNF class admits sample complexity \(O((ns+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon)\). This statistical guarantee does not give a polynomial-time learner. The 2025 survey explicitly separates sample complexity from the cost of producing an evaluable hypothesis.

For each fixed term bound \(s\), a runtime \(n^{O(s)}\) is polynomial in \(n\), but the required single polynomial in both \(n\) and \(s\) is stronger. Servedio’s Theorem 8 records the general upper bound \(2^{\widetilde O(n^{1/3}\log s)}\), with accuracy and confidence dependence suppressed as specified in that survey; the tilde hides polylogarithmic factors. This remains superpolynomial for polynomially many terms.

Improper learning allows hypotheses outside the DNF class. A lower bound for outputting a small DNF can therefore leave this question open. Daniely–Shalev-Shwartz give an improper-learning hardness result under their random-K-SAT refutation assumption, including polynomially growing term bounds. That assumption is not an established unconditional lower bound.

Daniely–Vardi’s Theorem 3 rules out efficient learning of DNFs with a superconstant number of terms under their Assumption 1 on local pseudorandom generators. Their learning definition permits efficiently evaluable hypotheses outside the target class. The local-generator hypothesis is a specific average-case assumption, not merely \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) or an unconditional theorem.

The 2025 faster exact learner of Alman and coauthors has access to membership and equivalence queries. A membership query obtains the target value at a chosen point; an equivalence query can provide a counterexample to a proposed hypothesis. Those access guarantees differ from an independent random-example stream, even when the question still concerns small DNFs.

The May 2026 Iterative Chow Filtering result obtains quasipolynomial-time DNF learning in the PQ distribution-shift framework under a uniform training distribution. Its predictor may use a selector to abstain, and training labels and unlabeled test data have distinct roles. Those distribution, runtime and output guarantees do not supply the polynomial-time distribution-free predictor required here.

The January 2026 relative-error DNF result is a property tester: it distinguishes membership in the class from the specified notion of distance using function-query access. Testing whether an unknown function is a DNF is a different output task from learning an accurate predictive circuit from random examples.

Every \(k\)-junta, a Boolean function depending on at most \(k\) coordinates, has a DNF representation with at most \(2^k\) terms. Consequently, a learner meeting this target would give a learner polynomial in \(n,2^k,1/\varepsilon,\log(1/\delta)\) for juntas, including under the uniform distribution. This implication does not assert that learning juntas alone suffices for general DNF learning.

cards.why: DNF learning is a central question about whether compact Boolean rules can be inferred efficiently from observations. Polynomial sample complexity is available, but achieving polynomial computation for arbitrary input distributions remains the difficulty. A positive answer would also cover important target classes such as decision trees and juntas through their DNF representations.

cards.title: Efficient learning of well-separated Gaussian mixtures
cards.formal: Is there an end-to-end polynomial-time, polynomial-sample algorithm for learning the parameters of well-separated spherical Gaussian mixtures at the source’s square-root-logarithmic separation scale? More precisely, do there exist one uniform randomized learner \(A\) and universal constants \(C_{\rm sep},B,a\ge1\) such that the following holds for every integer \(k\ge3\), \(d\ge1\), \(s\ge k\), \(R\ge1\), \(t\ge3\)? For every mixture \[P=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\pi_i N(\mu_i,\sigma_i^2 I_d),\qquad \pi_i\ge1/s,\quad \frac{\max_i\sigma_i}{\min_i\sigma_i}\le R,\] whose means satisfy \[\|\mu_i-\mu_j\|_2\ge C_{\rm sep}\max\{\sigma_i,\sigma_j\}\sqrt{\log(sR)}\quad(i\ne j),\] the learner, given only \(d,k,s,R,t\) and independent unlabeled samples from \(P\), returns \(k\) estimated component parameters with probability at least \(2/3\) for which some permutation \(\tau\) of \([k]\) satisfies, for every \(i\), \[\frac{|\widehat\pi_{\tau(i)}-\pi_i|}{\pi_i}\le\frac1t,\qquad \frac{\|\widehat\mu_{\tau(i)}-\mu_i\|_2}{\sigma_i}\le\frac1t,\qquad \frac{|\widehat\sigma_{\tau(i)}-\sigma_i|}{\sigma_i}\le\frac1{t\sqrt d}.\] Require at most \(B(d+k+s+R+t)^a\) samples and total arithmetic operations, including output. The learner receives no initial estimates of the means, weights or variances. It need not attain the source’s sharper near-linear sample bound; the selected question asks for polynomial sample complexity and polynomial time simultaneously.
cards.why: Identifiable clusters need not be easy to locate. This problem asks whether the separation that makes parameter recovery statistically feasible also permits an efficient global algorithm. It is a basic test of the computational cost of fitting latent-variable models when the number of components grows.
cards.status_note: The source’s selected §4.3 question concerns a global polynomial-time algorithm at square-root-logarithmic separation, while Theorem9 supplies the parameter metric and a statistically efficient but potentially inefficient procedure. The strongest directly checked later polynomial-time identity-covariance result uses log^{1/2+c}(k) separation with fixed c>0. Low-dimensional Fourier results, the 2026 slow-characteristic-function family excluding Gaussians, and newer nonspherical clustering bounds do not match the full target. No matching resolution was found in this bounded review through 16 September 2026; current status remains uncertain rather than a proved assertion of openness. The public bound parameters and exact-real arithmetic convention are explicit and are not claimed equivalent to a finite-bit interface.

sentences: The card asks for globally learning well-separated spherical Gaussian mixtures with both polynomial samples and polynomial computation.
The weights, centers and unequal component scales are hidden, and all must be recovered to the source’s stated relative accuracy up to one permutation.
The source’s efficient local refinement requires initialization that its sample-efficient procedure does not find in polynomial time.
Later algorithms improve separation or dimension dependence but retain assumptions or parameter costs that do not meet the full target.
A Lean resolution must establish or refute one uniform end-to-end learner under the explicit separation, access and arithmetic-cost conventions.

cards.definitions:
Here \(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_k>0\) sum to one, \(\mu_i\in\mathbb R^d\), and \(\sigma_i>0\). The covariance matrix of component \(i\) is \(\sigma_i^2 I_d\), so \(\sigma_i\) is a standard deviation, not a variance. To draw an observation, select an index with probabilities \(\pi_i\) and then draw from that component; the index is never revealed. Different observations and learner coins are independent. Each component’s coordinates have independent variance \(\sigma_i^2\), but both its center and scale are unknown. Weights need not be equal and scales need not coincide. There is no bound on the absolute centers or on the common absolute scale, no general-position or linear-independence assumption on centers, and no target-specific advice.

\([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\), \(I_d\) is the identity matrix and \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_j v_j^2)^{1/2}\). The logarithm is natural. The same constant \(C_{\rm sep}\) applies to every instance and is independent of requested accuracy. In the balanced equal-scale special case \(s=k,R=1\), the separation is a constant times \(\sqrt{\log k}\) standard deviations. For general mixtures, the source’s separation (14) uses \(\sqrt{\log(\rho_\sigma/\pi_{\min})}\), where \(\rho_\sigma=\max_i\sigma_i/\min_i\sigma_i\) and \(\pi_{\min}=\min_i\pi_i\). The public integers \(s,R\) are conservative bounds on \(1/\pi_{\min}\) and \(\rho_\sigma\); the displayed separation is imposed with those supplied bounds. Rounding each true quantity upward increases it by at most a factor of two, absorbed by the universal separation constant. This is an explicit public-parameter convention for the source’s polynomial-resource question, not a restriction to balanced or known-variance mixtures.

All five integer parameters are supplied in unary. Accuracy is \(\varepsilon=1/t\); these reciprocal tolerances express arbitrary precision within a constant factor. The output is a finite list \((\widehat\pi_i,\widehat\mu_i,\widehat\sigma_i)_{i=1}^k\) with positive estimated scales, nonnegative weights summing to one, and real mean vectors. Its component order is immaterial: the same permutation must match all three parameter types. The loss is parameter recovery in the displayed relative/scaled units. Merely producing a distribution close in total variation, a good partition for some observations, or a sampler with a different representation does not by itself meet this output requirement.

Use a finite uniform exact-real register program, with rational constants in its fixed code. Copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division guarded at zero, comparison, branching, square root of a nonnegative number, and each random fair bit cost one operation. Integer control, input reading, register access and writing each output real are counted. Loading a \(d\)-coordinate observation costs \(d\) operations. The program has no component-label oracle, chosen-input density oracle, exact-moment oracle, free optimization procedure, floor/digit extraction or arbitrary real advice. Its single polynomial bound must hold for every target, sample history and coin history; the success guarantee accounts for the randomness. Constants, program and polynomial exponent are common to all parameters. The source does not specify coordinate-bit precision; this declared real-arithmetic convention does not assert an equivalent finite-bit algorithm. Any finite-precision version needs its own sample representation and justified rounding/error analysis.

The time bound explicitly allows polynomial dependence on the weight and scale-ratio bounds, while the separation depends on their logarithm. It is not polynomial time if the exponent on dimension or component count grows with \(k\), \(t\), or a separation parameter. A family of algorithms at separation \(\log^{1/2+c}k\) with constants or exponents depending on a fixed \(c>0\) does not imply a single algorithm at \(c=0\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean proof of the uniform existence proposition or its negation. A positive proof must include global initialization from unlabeled samples, every component’s mean/weight/scale guarantee under one permutation, the stated success probability, and a universal polynomial bound for samples and all arithmetic/output costs. A local convergence theorem with accurate starting parameters is not enough. A negative result must rule out every learner and universal constants for some allowed parameters and mixture, rather than merely a particular iterative method. A computational assumption must remain a hypothesis unless proved. Larger asymptotic separation, fixed component count, equal variances only, or a weaker distribution-learning output is not a complete answer. The requested parameter accuracy is explicitly \(1/t\), with the dimension factor in the standard-deviation error retained.

source_formulation.text: At the well-separated spherical-Gaussian regime of the paper, can parameter learning from unlabeled samples use both polynomial time and polynomial sample complexity?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase

context_blocks.text: Expectation maximization alternates between estimating component membership probabilities and updating parameters. The source proves strong local refinement guarantees and an information-theoretically sample-efficient initialization. The latter can be computationally expensive, which is why its final initialization discussion still asks for an end-to-end polynomial algorithm.

The source permits unknown unequal spherical variances and unequal weights. Its Theorem 9 measures mean error in units of each component’s standard deviation and asks for a smaller relative scale error as dimension grows. The completed statement preserves those parameter guarantees, rather than replacing them with a total-variation approximation or clustering-only task.

Li–Liu obtain polynomial-time learning for identity-covariance mixtures when separation is \(\Omega(\log^{1/2+c}k)\) for any fixed \(c>0\). Their parameter-estimation guarantee is a major improvement over earlier polynomial separation requirements. The theorem does not set \(c=0\), and its common known covariance differs from the full unequal-scale formulation.

Qiao and coauthors give a Fourier-based algorithm with stronger separation guarantees in the low-dimensional regime \(d=O(\log k/\log\log k)\). Their general runtime is polynomial in \(k\) multiplied by a function of dimension, separation and accuracy. This does not provide one polynomial bound over the full high-dimensional parameter range.

The 2026 sparse-Fourier method efficiently learns mixtures whose component characteristic functions decay sufficiently slowly. The main theorem explicitly excludes Gaussians. Its combined treatment of slow- and fast-decaying components retains separate separation and runtime dependencies for the latter, so it does not establish the present Gaussian threshold.

COLT 2026 gives substantial improvements for nonspherical centered mixtures and mixtures with identical unknown covariance. The centered result retains a nonpolynomial function of inverse minimum weight, and the equal-covariance result retains a weight-dependent exponent. Neither theorem supplies the fully polynomial growing-component guarantee specified here.
