cards.definitions: A concept is a function \(h:X\to\{0,1\}\); repeated copies are not distinct concepts. A set \(S\subseteq X\) is shattered by \(\mathcal C\) if every Boolean labelling of \(S\) is the restriction of some member of \(\mathcal C\). The VC dimension is the largest size of a shattered set, with value zero for the empty class. For a nonempty subclass \(\mathcal D\subseteq\mathcal C\) and \(h\in\mathcal D\), put \[t(h,\mathcal D)=\min\{|S|:S\subseteq X,\ \forall g\in\mathcal D,\ g|_S=h|_S\Rightarrow g=h\}.\] These are labelled teaching examples: the labels are those assigned by \(h\). The minimum exists, and for a singleton class it is zero. Set \(t_{\min}(\mathcal D)=\min_{h\in\mathcal D}t(h,\mathcal D)\), and define \(\operatorname{RTD}(\mathcal C)=\max_{\varnothing\ne\mathcal D\subseteq\mathcal C}t_{\min}(\mathcal D)\), with \(\operatorname{RTD}(\varnothing)=0\). Equivalently, repeatedly remove all concepts of minimum teaching-set size from the current class and take the largest such minimum encountered. No computational-efficiency, random-sampling or teacher-algorithm requirement is imposed. Restricting to finite \(X\) loses no instance for finite concept classes on an arbitrary domain: retain one domain point for each distinct vector of labels across the class. This preserves both dimensions and yields a finite domain.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal linear bound for some finite \(K\), or of its negation. A refutation must establish that for every \(K>0\) there is a finite class of positive VC dimension with \(\operatorname{RTD}(\mathcal C)>K\operatorname{VCdim}(\mathcal C)\); one class with \(\operatorname{RTD}>\operatorname{VCdim}\) only rules out constant one. The optimal constant need not be determined. A quadratic upper bound, a result for special concept classes, or a lower bound for one teaching-set construction does not resolve the statement.

cards.title: Statistical-query complexity of sparse halfspaces
cards.formal: Do there exist absolute constants \(C\ge 2\) and \(a,b>0\) such that, for every \(n\ge 2\) and \(1\le r\le n, SQ-DIM(Hn,r, 1/[C(r \log _{2} n)^{a}])\le C n^{b}\), where Hn,r is the class of r-sparse halfspaces on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) and SQ-DIM is the distribution-worst-case correlation parameter defined below?
cards.why: Clarifies whether a statistical-query learner can exploit sparsity while tolerating coarse, sample-efficient estimates. The problem isolates an informational obstruction from the cost of reading many irrelevant coordinates, without assuming a favorable data distribution.
cards.status_note: Source Problem 3 and its definitions checked, with subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026. No resolution of this worst-distribution, inverse-\(\operatorname{poly}(r \log  n)\) parameter question was located. Results for noisy, Gaussian, smoothed or ordinary sample-access learning do not automatically settle it. No exhaustive literature or proof audit is claimed.

cards.definitions: A member of Hn,r is a function \(h:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \{- 1,+1\}\) of the form \(h(x)=+1\) if \(\sum j w_{j}x_{j}\ge \theta\) and \(h(x)=- 1\) otherwise, where \(w\in \mathbb{R} ^{n}\) has at most r nonzero coordinates and \(\theta \in \mathbb{R}\). Different weight representations of the same function define one member. For any probability distribution D on the finite cube and \(0<\gamma <1, SQ-DIM(Hn,r,D,\gamma )\) is the largest integer d for which there are d distinct functions \(h_{1},\ldots ,hd\) in Hn,r satisfying |\(\sum x D(x)h_{i}(x)h_{j}(x)|\le \gamma\) whenever \(i\ne j\). Then \(SQ-DIM(Hn,r,\gamma )\) is the maximum of this integer over all D, without any uniformity, product-distribution or margin promise. These maxima exist because the Boolean function class is finite and each feasible correlation condition is a closed constraint on the finite probability simplex. The constants C,a,b must work simultaneously for all n,r and all distributions. This is exactly the polynomial-versus-superpolynomial parameter question in source Problem 3, with its \(O(1)\) exponents made explicit. It asks for an upper bound on this dimension, not polynomial time to enumerate the functions or evaluate real weights.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed universal polynomial bound for some fixed C,a,b, or prove its negation: for every choice of such constants there are n,r and a distribution supporting a family larger than \(Cn^{b}\) with pairwise absolute correlations at most \(1/[C(r \log _{2} n)^{a}]\). The target is this source-defined parameter statement, not a guarantee restricted to one distribution or to halfspaces with large margin.

cards.title: Improper compression for Gaussian-mixture reconstruction
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform randomized learning procedure with the following guarantee? For all integers \(d\ge1\), \(k>d\) and \(t\ge2\), and every Borel probability distribution \(D\) on the closed Euclidean unit ball \(B_d\), it learns a shared model \(w\) and an encoder–decoder pair \(E_w:B_d\to\{0,1\}^{b}\), \(Q_w:\{0,1\}^{b}\to B_d\) such that, with probability at least \(2/3\), \[\mathbb E_{x\sim D}\|Q_w(E_w(x))-x\|_2^{2}\le\operatorname{OPT}_k(D)+1/t,\qquad \operatorname{OPT}_k(D)=\inf_{\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_k\in B_d}\mathbb E_{x\sim D}\min_{i\in[k]}\|x-\mu_i\|_2^{2}?\] Training, sample count, model storage, encoding and decoding must all be polynomial in \(d,k,t\), while the number of bits per encoded point satisfies \(b\le C(1+\log_2 k+\log_2 t)^{q}\) for universal \(C,q>0\). This is the explicitly normalized, bounded-data version of the source's first reconstruction question, in the overcomplete regime \(k>d\).
cards.why: The task asks whether efficient unsupervised reconstruction can compete with a small optimal codebook while using only a polynomial in the logarithms of its size and accuracy per point. It separates the cost of discovering original mixture parameters from the cost of learning a useful compact representation.
cards.status_note: The first reconstruction question is open in the COLT 2018 source. The bounded-data real-RAM version is an explicit editorial specification, not a verbatim complete model supplied there. Bounded searches on 2026-09-14 found later Gaussian-mixture compression results for density estimation, whose objective and time guarantees differ. No matching resolution was verified, and the search is not exhaustive.

cards.definitions:
Here \(B_d=\{x\in\mathbb R^{d}:\sum_{j=1}^{d}x_j^{2}\le1\}\), \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\), and \(\|x\|_2^{2}=\sum_jx_j^{2}\). The comparator is the best set of \(k\) reconstruction centers; repeated centers are allowed. The distribution need not itself be a Gaussian mixture. There is no separation, covariance or minimum cluster-weight promise. Accuracy is additive squared Euclidean reconstruction error in these unit-ball coordinates. The integer \(t\) requests error \(1/t\); all positive accuracy levels are covered by rounding to a smaller reciprocal-integer tolerance.

Fix three finite programs, for training, encoding and decoding. They use a real RAM with rational program constants, exact addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero values, square roots of nonnegative values, comparisons and indexed memory access, each charged one operation. Integer counters and addresses use logarithmically many bits in \(d+k+t+2\), with a fixed constant factor allowed for each program. There is no floor operation, real-digit extraction, advice, or noncomputable real program constant. Training also has independent fair random bits and a sampling oracle returning independent points from \(D\). One sample request and reading each of its coordinates are charged. There must be one polynomial \(p\), independent of \(D,d,k,t\), bounding training operations, samples, and stored scalar or integer cells, and bounding operations for encoding any one point and decoding any codeword. All executions must halt within these bounds, even on the probability-of-failure event.

Training returns a finite shared parameter vector \(w\) and the integer code length \(b\); the two fixed evaluation programs use \(w,d,k,t,b\). They are deterministic after training. Every codeword has exactly \(b\) bits, with padding allowed. The decoder receives only that codeword and the shared model, and returns a point in \(B_d\). The original point and extra point-dependent information are unavailable to it. Model storage is charged to the polynomial storage bound, not again to each point's code length. Probability of training success is over its samples and random bits; the expectation in the successful guarantee uses a fresh independent point. No restriction to a nearest-center decoder or to \(k\) possible reconstructions is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence of the three uniform procedures and universal polynomial and code-length bounds, with the stated error guarantee, or a proof that no such procedures exist in this model. A negative result for a proper Gaussian-parameter estimator or a decoder restricted to exactly \(k\) centers does not refute this improper target. A multiplicative constant greater than one in front of \(\operatorname{OPT}_k(D)\) does not meet the required additive guarantee.

cards.title: Compression overhead for adversarial robustness
cards.formal: Is there a universal constant \(K>0\) such that the following implication holds for every nonempty domain \(X\), every nonempty total binary concept class \(\mathcal C\subseteq\{0,1\}^{X}\) of finite VC dimension, every integer \(k\ge1\), and every perturbation map \(U:X\to2^{X}\) satisfying \(x\in U(x)\)? If \(\mathcal C\) admits an ordinary labeled sample compression scheme of size at most \(k\), must it admit an adversarially robust labeled sample compression scheme of size at most \(\lceil Kk\rceil\)? The constant is independent of the class, domain, perturbation sets and sample length. Perturbation sets may be infinite. This makes the size-overhead assertion in Open Problem 28 explicit, with \(k\) denoting the available ordinary compression bound.
cards.why: Sample compression asks how much of a training set determines a predictor consistent with all its constraints. Adversarial robustness replaces each example by an entire set of required predictions. A constant-overhead theorem would connect these two information requirements without charging separately for the number of possible perturbations.
cards.status_note: Open Problem 28 in the ALT 2025 source. A bounded later-work search and the author bibliography checked on 2026-09-14 did not reveal a matching resolution. The finite-set and stable-scheme theorems and the separate robust-learnability counterexample have different hypotheses. No independent verification of all cited proofs is claimed.

sentences: The question asks whether ordinary sample compression can be made adversarially robust with only a universal constant factor in size.
A message contains original labeled examples and a counted auxiliary bitstring.

cards.definitions:
A sample \(S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n))\) is any finite sequence of points of \(X\) with labels in \(\{0,1\}\), including the empty sequence. A labeled compression scheme consists of fixed deterministic maps \(\kappa,\rho\). The compressor sends \(S\) to \((T,b)\), where \(T\) is a finite ordered sequence of labeled examples drawn from \(S\) and \(b\) is a finite binary string. Following the source's sequence convention, every entry of \(T\) must occur in \(S\); reordering or repetition is allowed, and every retained occurrence is counted. Size at most \(k\) means \(|T|+|b|\le k\) on every sample. The reconstructor maps only \((T,b)\) to a total binary predictor \(\rho(T,b):X\to\{0,1\}\). It does not receive the omitted examples, their original indices, or the original sample length for free. One labeled example counts as one unit regardless of its representation length; each auxiliary bit also counts as one unit. No computability or running-time restriction is imposed.

Ordinary realizability means that some \(c\in\mathcal C\) satisfies \(c(x_i)=y_i\) for every \(i\). An ordinary scheme must reconstruct a predictor satisfying those equalities for every realizable sample. Robust realizability means that some \(c\in\mathcal C\) satisfies \(c(z)=y_i\) for every sample position \(i\) and every \(z\in U(x_i)\). A robust scheme must have \(\rho(\kappa(S))(z)=y_i\) for all these positions and perturbations whenever the sample is robustly realizable. The compressed examples must be original labeled examples, not freely chosen perturbed points. Each pair of maps may depend on \(\mathcal C\) and, in the robust case, on the entire fixed map \(U\), but is selected once for all samples. Reconstructed predictors can lie outside \(\mathcal C\). There is no correctness requirement on nonrealizable samples, although the size bound still applies. Empty samples impose no correctness constraints.

A finite set is shattered by \(\mathcal C\) if all its binary labelings are restrictions of members of \(\mathcal C\). The VC dimension is the supremum of the cardinalities of shattered finite sets; it is required to be finite.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the universal constant-overhead implication, or a proof that no universal \(K\) works. A negative answer must establish ordinary compression of size \(k\) for its finite-VC class and a robust compression requirement exceeding \(\lceil Kk\rceil\), for arbitrarily large proposed constants \(K\); nonexistence of any bounded robust scheme for such a class also suffices. Bounds depending on perturbation-set size, or a conclusion for stable ordinary schemes alone, do not establish this implication.

context_blocks.text: The source writes the available ordinary size as a function of VC dimension. Here the available bound is called k so that the constant hidden in its proposed overhead is explicitly universal. The printed phrase that the domain has a compression scheme is read as referring to the concept class; sample compression is a property of a class together with its reconstructor.

The decoder knows the fixed perturbation map, but it must recover a predictor from original examples and auxiliary bits. Retaining one original example does not by itself identify which of its potentially many perturbations an ordinary compressor selected. This distinction is part of the information requirement, even when computation is unrestricted.

For uniformly finite perturbation sets, Theorem 26 gives an additional logarithmic dependence on their maximum cardinality. Theorem 27 removes this factor under the stronger premise of a stable ordinary compression scheme. Stability requires that discarding unselected examples leave the compressor’s message unchanged.

Theorem 29 establishes that robust learnability alone need not give a bounded robust compression scheme. Its construction starts from a partial concept class. It does not supply the ordinary bounded-compression premise for the resulting total class required here; it is therefore not a resolution of Open Problem 28.

cards.title: Local regularization for multiclass learning
cards.formal: Does every realizably PAC-learnable multiclass hypothesis class H admit a fixed local regularizer \(\psi :H\times X\to \mathbb{R} \ge 0\) such that every learner induced by \(\psi\), under the pointwise minimum-score rule below, PAC learns H? This is the existence part of the source question; optimal sample complexity is a separate refinement.
cards.why: Tests whether a fixed preference over hypotheses at each prediction point is a general principle for multiclass learning. A negative answer would identify a limit of regularization even when improper prediction is allowed; a positive answer would give a common template for all learnable multiclass classes.
cards.status_note: As of 11 September 2026, two checked preprints claim a negative resolution. Their theorem statements and local-regularization/PAC definitions match the main target, but the full impossibility proofs were not independently audited and no accepted publication was verified. Retained as uncertain rather than certified open or resolved.

cards.definitions: Let X be an instance space, Y a label space that may be infinite, and \(H\subseteq Y^{X} a\) nonempty class of predictors \(h:X\to Y\). A distribution D on labeled examples \(X\times Y\) is realizable by H if some \(h*\in H\) satisfies PrD\([h*(x)\ne y]=0\). The risk of a predictor g is \(LD(g)\)=PrD\([g(x)\ne y]\). A learner A maps a finite labeled sample S to a predictor \(A(S)\), which need not belong to H. It PAC learns H if, for every \(\varepsilon ,\delta \in (0,1)\), there is \(mA(\varepsilon ,\delta )<\infty\) such that for every H-realizable D and every \(m\ge mA(\varepsilon ,\delta ), a\) sample S of m independent draws from D satisfies \(\Pr [LD(A(S))>\varepsilon ]\le \delta\). Probability spaces, predictors and learners are understood with measurable error events, so these probabilities are defined. There is no running-time requirement. For a nonempty realizable sample S, the version space \(H[S]\) consists of all \(h\in H\) agreeing with every labeled example in S. A local regularizer assigns each pair \((h,x) a\) nonnegative real score \(\psi (h,x)\), fixed before observing S. It is admissible only if a minimum score on \(H[S]\) is attained at every test point x and the induced prediction rules are well-defined; an empty argmin cannot make the claim vacuously true. A learner is induced by \(\psi\) when \(A(S)(x)\) belongs to {\(h(x): h\in\)argmin \(g\in H[S] \psi (g,x)\)} for every such S,x. On empty or unrealizable samples its behavior is unrestricted. The quantifier “every induced learner” includes every valid tie-breaking rule; its sample bound may depend on that learner. The regularizer can depend on H and x, but not on S, its size, its unlabeled points, \(D, \varepsilon\) or \(\delta\).
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every realizably PAC-learnable H has such an admissible regularizer, or give a PAC-learnable class H and prove that every admissible local regularizer induces at least one learner that is not PAC consistent in the stated distribution-independent sense. A favorable tie-breaking rule alone is insufficient. Neither a transductive separation nor failure of proper learning alone settles this PAC question.

context_blocks.title: A different preference at each test point
context_blocks.text: A regularizer expresses which hypotheses the learning rule prefers. Local regularization lets that preference depend on the new point being classified. After training, only hypotheses that fit the sample remain eligible, and the rule predicts using a least-scored eligible hypothesis at that point.

context_blocks.title: Why the prediction can be outside the class
context_blocks.text: One hypothesis might be preferred in one region of X and another in a different region. The resulting predictor can combine their labels without being a single hypothesis from H. This flexibility matters because some multiclass problems are learnable only by allowing such improper output.

context_blocks.title: Ties carry a real quantifier
context_blocks.text: The source asks the regularizer to succeed for every induced tie-breaking learner. If all scores are zero, the rule imposes no preference among sample-consistent hypotheses. Selecting one specially chosen successful learner from those ties would not show that the regularizer itself learns the class. Likewise, score minima must exist for the prediction rule to be meaningful.

context_blocks.title: Sample-dependent regularization is a different model
context_blocks.text: The source reports a general positive result when a local regularizer may first use the unlabeled training points. Here the score function is fixed independently of the sample. The question tests whether that extra sample information is necessary for a general multiclass learning rule.

context_blocks.title: Two 2026 claims of a negative resolution
context_blocks.text: Hou’s July preprint claims a countable learnable class beyond all local regularizers. The August preprint by Asilis and coauthors independently claims a PAC counterexample under the same worst-case tie convention and acknowledges Hou’s work. The checked statements match the main question, but their full lower-bound proofs have not been independently verified in this review. The card therefore records a claimed negative resolution with uncertain status.

cards.title: Agnostic direct-sum learning rates
cards.formal: Does the single-instance agnostic learning rate determine all Cartesian-power learning rates up to constant factors? Precisely, for every two nonempty concept classes \(\mathcal C\subseteq Y^{X}\) and \(\mathcal D\subseteq Z^{W}\) on nonempty countable input and label sets, suppose there are \(a,b>0\) such that \[a\,e_{\mathcal D}(n)\le e_{\mathcal C}(n)\le b\,e_{\mathcal D}(n)\qquad\text{for every integer }n\ge1.\] Must there then be \(a',b'>0\), allowed to depend on the two classes but not on \(n\) or \(r\), such that \[a'\,e_{\mathcal D^{r}}(n)\le e_{\mathcal C^{r}}(n)\le b'\,e_{\mathcal D^{r}}(n)\qquad\text{for every }n,r\ge1?\] This is the constant-factor rate-determination form of the source's agnostic Open Question 3. The countable-domain convention and constant-factor interpretation are explicit editorial choices; the source paper also asks separate realizable-learning and compression questions.
cards.why: A direct-sum law would explain whether learning several tasks together has a statistical cost determined by the difficulty of one task. In the agnostic setting, whole-tuple loss and unrestricted correlations can make that question depend on class structure not visible in its ordinary learning rate.

cards.definitions:
For a nonempty class \(\mathcal H\subseteq V^{U}\) on countable sets \(U,V\), and any probability distribution \(P\) on \(U\times V\), let \(L_P(h)=\Pr_{(x,y)\sim P}[h(x)\ne y]\). Define \[e_{\mathcal H}(n)=\inf_{A_n}\sup_{P}\left(\mathbb E_{S\sim P^{n}}L_P(A_n(S))-\inf_{h\in\mathcal H}L_P(h)\right).\] Here \(A_n:(U\times V)^{n}\to V^{U}\) ranges over all deterministic learning rules and is chosen before \(P\); it may depend on \(\mathcal H\) and \(n\). It need not be computable, and may output a predictor outside \(\mathcal H\). The training sample consists of \(n\) independent pairs from \(P\). The outer expectation is over that sample; the risk uses a fresh independent pair. All countable sets have their discrete sigma-algebras. The countable sample space makes these expectations well-defined even when the hypothesis class is uncountable. Labels may have arbitrary noise. Infima are not assumed to be attained. The rate is a dimensionless minimax expected excess probability of error in \([0,1]\).

For \(r\ge1\), \(\mathcal H^{r}\) consists of all maps \((x_1,\ldots,x_r)\mapsto(h_1(x_1),\ldots,h_r(x_r))\) with \(h_1,\ldots,h_r\in\mathcal H\). Its input set is \(U^{r}\) and its label set is \(V^{r}\). Apply the same learning-curve definition to this class. Each of the \(n\) examples is now an entire input–label tuple. Its coordinates can be arbitrarily correlated: \(P\) ranges over every distribution on \(U^{r}\times V^{r}\), not just product distributions. A tuple prediction incurs loss one whenever any coordinate differs from the label tuple, and zero otherwise. This is whole-tuple zero-one loss, not a sum or average of coordinate losses. The learner for the product may also be improper, so its output need not act separately on each coordinate.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the rate-determination implication. A refutation must give two admissible classes with comparable single-instance curves but prove that no positive constants independent of both \(n\) and \(r\) compare their product curves. A positive answer must cover every such pair of classes and all positive sample sizes and product multiplicities. The target is a proposition about constant-factor rate information; it does not ask whether exact numerical single-instance curves encode additional information.

context_blocks.text: The inherited card contained the title of a paper posing several independent problems. This revision selects its agnostic rate question and makes the precision of the proposed relationship explicit. It does not assert that the other questions in that paper are equivalent or resolved.

The comparison is between expected error and the best predictor in the target class under the same distribution. Bounding the total error of separately learned coordinates does not automatically bound this excess error against the best whole-tuple predictor.

The order of quantifiers matters. Constants depending on the number of tasks would allow different behavior to be hidden as that number increases. This formulation requires a single pair of comparison constants for all sample sizes and multiplicities.

The August 2026 preprint claims a counterexample using \(X=Y=\{0,1\}\): one class contains the two constant functions, and the other contains the zero function and the identity function. It claims product rates respectively of order \(n^{-1/2}\) and \(\min\{1,\sqrt{r/n}\}\), while both single-instance rates are of order \(n^{-1/2}\). The claim concerns the exact whole-tuple, improper model used here, and would refute this implication.

cards.title: Dimension complexity of distribution-independent SQ learning
cards.formal: Is there a universal constant \(C>0\) with the following property? For every nonempty set \(X\), every nonempty binary concept class \(\mathcal H\subseteq\{-1,+1\}^{X}\), every integer \(m\ge1\), tolerance \(0<\tau<1\) and error \(0\le\varepsilon<1/4\), suppose a single randomized statistical-query learner makes at most \(m\) queries of tolerance \(\tau\) and, for every input distribution \(D\), target \(h\in\mathcal H\) and admissible oracle response rule, returns \(\hat h\) with \(\mathbb E[\Pr_{x\sim D}(\hat h(x)\ne h(x))]\le\varepsilon\). Must \(\operatorname{dc}(\mathcal H)\le C m/\tau^{2}\)? The learner is selected before the distribution, target and oracle replies. The constant is independent of all these objects and of the accuracy, domain size and class.
cards.why: This asks whether learning successfully from noisy expectation information under every distribution forces all targets to share a small linear representation. It connects a general information-access model with the geometric capacity of linear predictors, and tests whether known advantages of learned representations depend essentially on the input distribution.
cards.status_note: Open Question 2 in the COLT 2026 source. Bounded primary-source search on 2026-09-14 found the August 2026 VALG theorem, whose explicit additional rank hypothesis and polynomial bound do not settle the stated implication. The source also reports a flaw in the earlier 2025 claimed bound. This review compares theorem scope; it does not independently verify either paper’s proofs.

progress.text: Feldman, Kamath and Srebro state the linear dimension bound as Open Question 2. Their Section 3 reports that the claimed upper bounds of Karchmer and Malach (2025) have a proof flaw, citing a 2026 communication with those authors.

The VALG preprint presents Theorem 4.9 under the additional polynomial mean-response-rank hypothesis of Assumption 4.42. Its explicit qualification prevents treating it as a resolution of the unrestricted question. The theorem has not been independently proof-checked in this review.

sentences: The question asks whether successful distribution-independent statistical-query learning forces low dimension complexity.
The learner may adapt bounded expectation queries to previous noisy answers.
Its guarantee must hold for every distribution, target and valid response rule.
The desired conclusion is one deterministic feature map representing the entire class exactly in dimension proportional to the query count divided by squared tolerance.
Recent conditional results impose additional structure and do not establish the unrestricted implication.

cards.definitions:
Use the discrete measurable structure \(2^{X}\) on an arbitrary domain, and quantify over all countably additive probability measures on it. A tolerance-\(\tau\) query is an arbitrary bounded function \(q:X\times\{-1,+1\}\to[-1,1]\); its answer is any real \(v\) satisfying \(|v-\mathbb E_{x\sim D}q(x,h(x))|\le\tau\). Queries may depend on previous answers and an internal random seed independent of the instance. A response rule can depend on the public history, including the current query, but observes the hidden seed only through that history. It must obey the tolerance at every history that can occur for the fixed distribution and target. The guarantee holds for every such rule, with expectation over the learner's seed. Require the interactions and their resulting loss to be measurable, so that the stated expectations exist. These measurable-interaction conventions specify the source's abstract oracle model. Query count is the resource: there is no restriction on computation between queries, description length, adaptivity, or the class containing the output predictor. There are no free samples or additional distribution information.

The dimension complexity is the least integer \(d\ge0\) for which there is one map \(\phi:X\to\mathbb R^{d}\) such that, for each \(h\in\mathcal H\), some \(w_h\in\mathbb R^{d}\) satisfies \(h(x)=\operatorname{sgn}_{+}(\langle w_h,\phi(x)\rangle)\) for every \(x\in X\). Here \(\operatorname{sgn}_{+}(z)=+1\) when \(z\ge0\), and \(-1\) otherwise, and the inner product is the sum of coordinatewise products. Put \(\operatorname{dc}=+\infty\) if no finite dimension works. The feature map is deterministic, shared by all targets, and independent of \(D\); no construction or efficiency requirement is imposed on it. Offsets require a coordinate of the feature map. The representation must be exact at every point, even though the learner's premise allows positive expected error.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the universal implication, or of its negation. A positive answer must supply a universal finite \(C\). A negative answer must show that no such constant works: for every \(C>0\), exhibit or prove the existence of a class and admissible learner parameters satisfying the premise but with \(\operatorname{dc}(\mathcal H)>Cm/\tau^{2}\). An infinite dimension example also qualifies. A result assuming extra rank, margin or distribution conditions, or allowing only approximate or random feature representations, does not establish the stated implication.

context_blocks.text: The source poses separate questions about a specified neural-network training procedure and about statistical queries. This card selects its formal Open Question 2. The broader deep-learning motivation is retained here; the card does not assert that this SQ question is equivalent to the neural-network question.

Learning may choose different predictors after observing different distributions. A low-dimensional representation has a stronger order of choices: the same features must work before either the distribution or the target is selected. Exact representation also concerns points that may have negligible probability in a particular learning instance.

The statistical-query interface permits queries that depend jointly on the example and its label. Restricting queries to a label multiplied by an example function gives a different model. Similarly, replacing the requested bound by an unspecified polynomial, or adding dependence on the domain size, changes the question.

The August 2026 preprint gives a conditional polynomial dimension statement. It assumes a bound on the dimension of a space of averaged terminal predictions; that bound is an additional hypothesis, not a consequence established for arbitrary SQ learners. Its authors explicitly describe the remaining gap to the original question.

cards.title: Monotone empirical risk minimization
cards.formal: Does every nonempty Boolean concept class \(\mathcal H\subseteq\{0,1\}^X\) of finite VC dimension on a countable domain \(X\) admit a possibly randomized empirical risk minimizer whose expected population error never increases with sample size, under every data distribution? Precisely, for each such \(X,\mathcal H\), require learning rules \(A_n\), \(n\geq1\), that always return an empirical risk minimizer in \(\mathcal H\), and for every distribution \(D\) on \(X\times\{0,1\}\) satisfy \[\mathbb E_{S\sim D^{n+1},R}L_D(A_{n+1}(S,R))\leq\mathbb E_{S\sim D^n,R}L_D(A_n(S,R))\quad(n\geq1).\] The learner may depend on \(\mathcal H\), but not on \(D\).
cards.why: The problem asks whether exact empirical fitting is inherently compatible with the intuition that more independent data should improve expected predictions. It separates the behavior of ERM from general statistical consistency and from monotone wrappers that change the learning rule.
cards.status_note: The ERM existence question is explicit in the checked 2022 paper. The bounded review through 14 September 2026 found no proof or refutation for the specified countable-domain Boolean finite-VC family. The broader source also asks about other losses and models. Later statements about monotone unrestricted learners, maximum likelihood in well-specified families, or bound-derived risk distributions are not treated as resolutions of this exact ERM claim.

sentences: Expected prediction error can increase when a learner receives an additional independent training example.
This card asks whether every finite-VC Boolean class on a countable domain nevertheless admits a monotone empirical risk minimizer.
The learner may randomize and resolve ties, but must always output an empirically optimal hypothesis from the original class.
Monotonicity is required for every data distribution and every consecutive positive sample size, using actual population error.
A resolution would clarify whether exact empirical fitting can always be reconciled with monotone learning curves.

cards.definitions: The population zero-one loss of \(h:X\to\{0,1\}\) is \(L_D(h)=\Pr_{(x,y)\sim D}[h(x)\ne y]\). For an ordered sample \(S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n))\), its empirical loss is \(\widehat L_S(h)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf1[h(x_i)\ne y_i]\). Each \(A_n\) maps a sample and an independent uniform seed \(R\in[0,1]\) to an element of \(\arg\min_{h\in\mathcal H}\widehat L_S(h)\). This minimum exists because the attainable empirical errors form a nonempty subset of \(\{0,1/n,\ldots,1\}\). Ties may be resolved using the whole ordered sample and the seed; for every fixed sample and test point, the returned label is required to be a measurable function of the seed. With countable \(X\), these conditions make all displayed expectations well defined. No computational or storage bound is imposed. Samples are independent identically distributed draws from \(D\), repetitions are allowed, and the test observation defining population loss is independent of training and of the seed. Labels may be noisy: realizability by \(\mathcal H\) is not assumed. Finite VC dimension means a finite upper bound on the cardinalities of sets \(F\subseteq X\) for which \(\{h|_F:h\in\mathcal H\}=\{0,1\}^F\). The monotonicity compares expectations over samples and learner randomness; it is not a pathwise comparison for each particular sample extension, a statement only after a distribution-dependent threshold, or monotonicity of a generalization bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every class in the stated domain admits such a family of learning rules, or exhibit a class of finite VC dimension on a countable domain and prove that no family of randomized empirical risk minimizers has the displayed property for all \(D,n\). An affirmative proof must retain exact empirical minimization and membership of the output in \(\mathcal H\). For a negative answer, showing nonmonotonicity of one tie-breaking rule does not exclude all eligible ERMs. General monotone learners that need not minimize empirical risk, eventual monotonicity, or decreasing upper bounds on error do not meet this criterion.

context_blocks.text: Viering, Mey and Loog’s original paper asks broadly when learning is monotone and whether it can be made so, emphasizing empirical risk minimization. This card selects the Boolean classification ERM question on countable domains, keeping the broader research direction as provenance instead of presenting it as one unspecified characterization request.

Bousquet, Daniely, Kaplan, Mansour, Moran and Stemmer formulate the remaining ERM question explicitly in their 2022 open-questions section: whether every learnable class admits a monotone empirical risk minimizer. Their general monotone-learning theorem permits rules outside this constraint.

Finite VC dimension controls statistical learning in this setting, but convergence to the best population error need not imply improvement at each consecutive sample size. The quantifier over all distributions includes misspecified or noisy data as well as realizable classification problems.

The 2019 paper provides monotone and nonmonotone examples using the same loss for fitting and evaluation. Such counterexamples show that particular familiar procedures may fail, but do not automatically rule out every permissible ERM rule for a given class.

The 2025 PAC perspective studies distributions constructed from generalization bounds. In its Section 3, a bound-derived expression is used as a distributional model. Monotonicity of that expression alone does not establish the actual expected-risk inequality required here.

Randomization and tie resolution are part of the existence question. The learner can choose among all empirically optimal hypotheses, but cannot replace exact minimization with an arbitrary predictor or select its rule after learning the unknown data distribution.

cards.title: Identifiable elicitation complexity
cards.formal: Determine the identifiable elicitation-complexity function \(E(\mathcal P,\Gamma)\) defined below, throughout its full domain of nonempty convex families of real-outcome distributions and finite-dimensional statistical properties. Its value is the smallest positive number of intermediate real reports needed to recover \(\Gamma\) through an elicitable, identifiable property, or \(\infty\) if no finite number suffices. The numerical benchmark requires a real-valued approximation with absolute error at most \(1/100\) at every finite value, and a proof identifying exactly the infinite-value cases.
cards.why: A loss can recover a richer prediction than the statistic ultimately needed. The minimum dimension of that prediction measures an expressive limitation of loss-based estimation, independently of optimization time. A general classification would connect statistical functionals, forecast evaluation and the design of indirect prediction objectives.
cards.status_note: Question 3 is open in the 2016 source. The checked 2021 journal framework proves important families of complexity bounds, and the 2024 survey still lists unresolved examples. Bounded later checks through 2026-09-16 verified no classification over the full stated domain; restricted Lipschitz and calibration variants are not treated as resolving it.

The intermediate prediction must have a unique expected-loss minimizer and an identification function whose expected value vanishes exactly at the correct report.

cards.definitions:
Let \(\mathcal M\) be the set of Borel probability measures on \(\mathbb R\). A distribution family \(\mathcal P\) is any nonempty subset of \(\mathcal M\) that contains \(\lambda p+(1-\lambda)q\) whenever \(p,q\in\mathcal P\) and \(0\le\lambda\le1\). The domain consists of every such \(\mathcal P\), every positive integer \(d\), and every function \(\Gamma:\mathcal P\to\mathbb R^d\). The dimension \(d\) is part of the specification of \(\Gamma\). No finite encoding, computability, continuity, moment assumption or uniform support bound is imposed on this domain.

For a positive integer \(k\), an admissible intermediate property consists of a nonempty report set \(R\subseteq\mathbb R^k\), a surjective function \(h:\mathcal P\to R\), a loss \(L:R\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\), an identification function \(V:R\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^k\), and a link \(\psi:R\to\mathbb R^d\). For each report \(r\in R\), the functions \(y\mapsto L(r,y)\) and every coordinate of \(y\mapsto V(r,y)\) must be Borel measurable and absolutely integrable with respect to every \(p\in\mathcal P\). Write \(\mathbb E_p u(Y)=\int_{\mathbb R}u(y)\,dp(y)\). Elicitation means that, for every \(p\in\mathcal P\) and every \(r\in R\) distinct from \(h(p)\), \(\mathbb E_p L(h(p),Y)<\mathbb E_p L(r,Y)\). Thus the expected loss has the unique global minimizer \(h(p)\), with no approximate minimization or tie-breaking convention. Identification means that, for every \(p\in\mathcal P\) and \(r\in R\), \(\mathbb E_p V(r,Y)=0\) if and only if \(h(p)=r\). Finally, \(\Gamma(p)=\psi(h(p))\) must hold for every \(p\in\mathcal P\).

Set \(E(\mathcal P,\Gamma)\) to the least positive integer \(k\) for which these objects exist, and to \(\infty\) when there is no such finite \(k\). The unit is the number of scalar real coordinates of the intermediate report. Constant properties therefore have value \(1\), under the positive-dimension convention used here. Requiring \(R=h(\mathcal P)\) makes identification apply exactly to attainable reports; unused reports can be removed without losing elicitation. Neither convexity nor smoothness of \(L\), nor continuity of \(h\) or \(\psi\), is required. The single observation \(Y\) is the sole outcome argument of the loss and identification functions; a loss on several independent observations defines a different model. Statistical sample complexity and computational time for optimizing a loss are not the quantity being measured.

The symbol \(\infty\) here records failure of every finite report dimension. It does not assert the existence of a countably infinite-dimensional elicitable intermediate property. This convention extends the finite complexity classes to a total extended-valued function, including cases that the 2021 source leaves undefined when no allowed intermediate property exists.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of a full determination of \(E\) on the stated domain: specify an unambiguous function \(a(\mathcal P,\Gamma)\in[0,\infty]\), prove \(a=\infty\) exactly when \(E=\infty\), and prove \(|a(\mathcal P,\Gamma)-E(\mathcal P,\Gamma)|\le1/100\) for every finite value, interpreting the integer \(E\) as a real number. A structural characterization of all finite complexity classes together with all infinite cases may specify the answer. The approximation need not be integer-valued, and no efficient algorithm or predetermined formula grammar is required. Merely repeating the defining minimum over admissible losses and intermediate properties, a one-sided bound, or a classification of only selected statistics does not meet the criterion.

context_blocks.text: The 2016 paper poses three distinct questions: which properties are elicitable, which losses elicit a given property, and how to characterize elicitation complexity classes. This card selects Question 3. It makes the real-outcome, convex-distribution-family branch explicit and retains the source’s restriction to identifiable intermediate properties; it does not additionally demand a classification of every possible loss.

Without a restriction on intermediate properties, encodings of an entire distribution into one real report can make the dimension measure degenerate. Identifiability is part of the target definition, rather than an optional regularity assumption.

The later journal treatment distinguishes identifiable intermediates from other classes defined through linear expectations or smooth convex losses. Its theorems establish tight complexity values for several families, including suitable Bayes-risk examples, rather than a classification of all statistical properties.

The 2024 survey still records unresolved elicitation complexities for several statistical quantities, including higher central moments and financial risk measures. Results using multiple independent observations or a restricted class of losses concern different complexity functions.

cards.title: Uniform convergence under Dobrushin dependence
cards.formal: For every \(a\in\)[0,1), does there exist a finite constant \(C_{a}\) such that the following holds uniformly? Let \(m\ge 1\), let H be a nonempty class of measurable binary functions on a measurable instance space X with finite VC dimension d, and let \(\mathrm{P}_{m}\) be a joint law of \(S=(Z_{1},\ldots ,Z_{m}), Z_{i}=(X_{i},Y_{i})\in X\times \{0,1\}\), whose marginals all equal D and whose total-variation Dobrushin coefficient is at most a. For every \(\delta \in (0,1)\), require \(\Pr _{S\sim \mathrm{P}_{m}}[\sup _{h\in H}|\mathrm{L}_{S}(h)- \mathrm{L}_{D}(h)|>C_{a}\sqrt{(d+\log (2/\delta ))/m}]\le \delta\). Here \(\mathrm{L}_{S}\) and \(\mathrm{L}_{D}\) are zero-one losses and the conditional-kernel and measurability conventions below are part of the model. This card reads the source’s proposed extension quantitatively, using the iid-order finite-VC rate stated in equation (18) of its full version; it is not merely a claim that some unspecified convergence rate exists.

cards.title: Learning speedups from random examples
cards.formal: Does the low-end learning speedup hold using only independent uniform labeled examples? For each circuit family C specified below, suppose every polynomial-size subfamily has a randomized weak learner under the uniform distribution, with confidence \(1- 1/n\) and worst-case running time \(2^{n}/n^{\omega (1)}\). Must every polynomial-size subfamily then have, for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) and \(a\ge 1, a\) randomized learner with error at most \(n^{- a}\), confidence at least \(1- 1/n\), and worst-case running time \(O(2^{n^{\varepsilon}})\), still using only independent uniform labeled examples?
cards.why: Tests whether the sharp gap in possible circuit-learning runtimes is a structural feature of passive learning, or relies on being able to choose labels to request. It connects the computational cost of statistical prediction with major circuit classes while keeping the distribution and available information fixed.
cards.status_note: Read the conference model, low-end lemma and open-question passage, and the full preprint’s corresponding question. Read the later journal Theorem 5.1 and its access conventions. cards.definitions:
The unknown target is a Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \{0,1\}\). One example request supplies \((X,f(X))\), where X is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) and independent of all earlier examples and the learner’s private random bits. The learner receives \(1^{n}\) and the fixed parameters specifying the target class. It may decide when to stop sampling, but cannot choose, correlate, condition or relabel the oracle’s next input. Reading and storing examples, internal computation and writing the hypothesis all count toward the time bound. A standard randomized multitape Turing machine with an example tape suffices; polynomial overheads in n do not alter the time classes used here. On every run it halts within the bound, including runs with labels outside the target promise. Its output is an explicitly encoded Boolean circuit h, with no example oracle or target-function gates. The hypothesis may belong to a larger circuit family than the target.

The error of h is \(\Pr_{X\text{ uniform}}[h(X)\ne f(X)]\). Confidence is the probability, jointly over the sample and internal randomness, of obtaining a hypothesis satisfying the stated error bound, for every eligible f and every sufficiently large n. A weak learner has error at most \(1/2- n^{- b}\) for some fixed \(b\ge 1\). The exponent b and the learner may depend on the fixed target subfamily. A strong learner here means that for each fixed \(a\ge 1\) there is an algorithm attaining error \(n^{- a}\); this is not a claim of polynomial dependence on a variable accuracy input.

The circuit families are \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}, \mathrm{AC}^{0}[p]\) for a fixed prime \(p, \mathrm{ACC}^{0}, \mathrm{TC}^{0}, \mathrm{NC}^{1}\), Boolean formulas, and unrestricted Boolean circuits. Circuits have input bits and Boolean constants, and size is the number of wires. \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) uses \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}\) gates of unbounded fan-in and NOT gates; \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}[p]\) also permits gates testing whether the number of true inputs is 0 modulo p. \(\mathrm{ACC}^{0}\) permits such modular gates for fixed moduli, with the choice of moduli independent of n. \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) additionally permits unweighted majority gates, outputting 1 when at least half their inputs are 1. For these four families a subfamily fixes both a constant depth bound d and a size bound \(n^{k}\), where \(k\ge 1\) is constant; modular parameters are also fixed. Boolean formulas use fan-in-two \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}\) and NOT, have fan-out one except for input variables, and at most \(n^{k}\) wires. Unrestricted Boolean circuits use those same gate types, allow shared subcircuits and have at most \(n^{k}\) wires. \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) uses bounded fan-in Boolean gates, polynomial size and depth at most \(d \log _{2}(n+2)\) for fixed d. Taking all fixed k,d covers the source’s polynomial-size \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) convention. Every circuit description is finite, with gate types and wire endpoints in binary.

For each fixed family C, the premise quantifies over ALL its fixed polynomial-size subfamilies: for each k and any fixed depth/modular parameters, there exist b, a uniform learner A and a time bound \(T_{A}(n)\) such that for every constant \(M>0, T_{A}(n)\le 2^{n}/n^{M}\) for all sufficiently large n. Thus \(2^{n}/n^{\omega (1)}\) means a superpolynomial saving, not just \(2^{n}/n^{10}\) and not a different algorithm for each M. The conclusion quantifies over every target subfamily and every fixed \(\varepsilon >0,a\ge 1\); the algorithm and the hidden constant may depend on these fixed choices, but not on n or f. There is no requirement that one algorithm accept descriptions of arbitrary target families. Learners are uniform algorithms across input lengths; the target circuits themselves need not be uniformly generated. The implication is unconditional and applies separately to each listed family.

This card makes explicit the low-end, polynomial-target branch of conference Lemma 24. The source also has a high-end branch relating learning subexponential-size targets to quasipolynomial-time learning of polynomial-size targets. The generic extracted question referred to that lemma as a whole; the present target selects its main low-end branch rather than asserting that this one implication is equivalent to both branches together.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove or refute the stated implication for the listed circuit families, with only independent uniform labeled examples in both the premise and conclusion. A positive result must supply the all-\(\varepsilon\), all-fixed-accuracy speedup whenever the weak-learning premise holds. A negative result must establish failure of that implication for an eligible family; a lower bound in a restricted learning model, or an algorithm that needs membership queries, does not by itself refute or establish it. The separate high-end branch is not required by this card.

cards.title: Public-key encryption from one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of a classical cryptographic one-way function imply the existence of a classical public-key encryption scheme for one-bit messages, with negligible correctness error and security against every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time chosen-plaintext adversary, in the plain model specified below? This is an unrelativized existence implication. The construction and its security proof may inspect the program of the one-way function and need not be black-box.
cards.definitions:
The security parameter is \(\lambda\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\), supplied as the unary string \(1^{\lambda}\). All algorithms are uniform classical Turing machines on bits: one finite program works for every parameter, with no advice, oracle or quantum resource. A PPT algorithm uses independent fair random bits and halts within a fixed polynomial in its total input length on every input and every random tape. Each algorithm has its own polynomial bound. Reading, computing, random-bit generation, communication and output all have ordinary bit-machine costs. Bit-string tuples use the component encoding \(s\mapsto1^{|s|}0s\); finite lists prepend an encoded binary component count. Binary integers have no leading zeros except the representation of zero. Explicitly proved polynomial-time equivalent encodings are acceptable.

A function \(\nu:\mathbb N_{\geq1}\to[0,1]\) is negligible if \(\forall d\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\;\exists\lambda_0\;\forall\lambda\geq\lambda_0:\nu(\lambda)\leq\lambda^{-d}\). A one-way function is a total deterministic polynomial-time map \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) such that for every uniform classical PPT algorithm \(I\),
\[\Pr[\,|Y|=\lambda\ \land\ f(Y)=f(X)\,]\]
is negligible, where \(X\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\) and \(Y=I(1^{\lambda},f(X))\). The probability also includes the independent coins of \(I\). Any preimage of length \(\lambda\) counts as success; failure or a different output length does not. Injectivity and preservation of length are not required.

A candidate encryption scheme is a triple \((\mathsf{Gen},\mathsf{Enc},\mathsf{Dec})\) of uniform polynomial-time algorithms. The randomized algorithm \(\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda})\) returns two finite bit strings \((pk,sk)\), the public and secret keys. The randomized algorithm \(\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,b)\), for \(b\in\{0,1\}\), returns a finite ciphertext bit string \(c\). The deterministic algorithm \(\mathsf{Dec}(1^{\lambda},sk,c)\) returns \(0\), \(1\), or the failure symbol \(\bot\). Algorithms are total on well-formed inputs, including arbitrary key and ciphertext strings; malformed encodings return a fixed failure response in polynomial time. Their runtime bounds use the full input length, so all honestly generated keys and ciphertexts have length polynomial in \(\lambda\). Encryption uses fresh private coins on each invocation, independently of key generation.

Correctness requires, for each \(b\in\{0,1\}\), negligible
\[\Pr[\mathsf{Dec}(1^{\lambda},sk,\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,b))\ne b],\qquad (pk,sk)\leftarrow\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda}),\]
over key-generation and encryption coins; failure counts as an error. This is average correctness over honestly generated keys and coins, not a requirement that every key and every random tape decrypt correctly.

Security requires that for every uniform classical PPT algorithm \(E\) outputting a bit, its advantage
\[\left|\Pr[E(1^{\lambda},pk,c)=B]-\frac12\right|\]
be negligible, where \((pk,sk)\leftarrow\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda})\), \(B\) is an independent uniform bit, and \(c\leftarrow\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,B)\). All coins, including those of \(E\), are independent except for the displayed dependencies. The programs are public. The adversary may perform any polynomial amount of computation and generate encryptions of arbitrarily chosen bits using \(pk\) and its own fresh coins; it has no decryption oracle. This is the standard one-bit indistinguishability formulation of chosen-plaintext security for public-key encryption. Security holds for every such adversary, with its own negligible bound eventually at all sufficiently large parameters. There is no restriction to infinitely many parameters, to an average choice of the adversary, or to a particular fixed polynomial attack time.

There is no pre-existing shared secret, trusted setup, random oracle, auxiliary hardness assumption or quantum information. The quantifier order is: if some \(f\) satisfying the stated one-wayness condition exists, then some single scheme satisfying the format, cost, correctness and security requirements exists. Neither its algorithms nor its proof must use \(f\) through an oracle interface. A uniform compiler taking the code of \(f\) as input is not an additional requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this existence implication or its logical negation. A positive answer must obtain the stated uniform classical encryption scheme from the existence of one-way functions alone and prove the full correctness and chosen-plaintext guarantees. A negative answer must prove that a one-way function exists while no scheme in the stated class meets both guarantees. An oracle separation, a lower bound on a restricted class of reductions, a break of one proposed scheme, or a construction requiring some additional unproved hardness assumption does not settle the target. One-bit messages are the specified target; polynomially many independently encrypted bits yield the standard extension to longer messages with polynomial security loss. A cited or unchecked proof claim does not satisfy Lean acceptance.
cards.why: This asks whether the minimal generic assumption supporting private-key cryptography also supports encryption to a receiver whose encryption key is public. It tests whether the apparent need for additional structure in public-key constructions reflects a true difference in existence or only the known reductions. The distinction controls the foundational assumptions needed for confidential communication without a pre-existing shared secret.

context_blocks.text: Computing a one-way function is easy, while recovering a preimage of a random image is hard. Public-key encryption needs a different asymmetry: public information must enable encryption while related private information enables decryption. The question concerns the existence of that additional capability, rather than a performance improvement for a particular deployed scheme.

Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin and Luby establish that one-way functions and pseudorandom generators have equivalent existence. A pseudorandom generator deterministically expands a short uniform seed into a longer string that efficient tests cannot distinguish from uniform. Together with the standard consequences surveyed in their conclusion, this supports private-key encryption from one-wayness. Private-key encryption starts from shared secret information, which the present target does not provide.

The target retains the saved one-bit message convention. Public encryptability means an observer can generate its own chosen-plaintext examples, so concealing only a message from an observer denied that capability would be a weaker target. Indistinguishability also requires randomized encryption: a deterministic correct scheme would make the two publicly computable ciphertexts distinguishable. The card permits negligible average decryption error and does not silently impose perfect correctness.

A secure one-bit scheme extends to any prescribed polynomial message length under the same public key, with polynomial loss in correctness and distinguishing advantage. It also implies passive key agreement. General interactive key agreement permits more communication than the two-message interaction associated with public-key encryption, so the related key-agreement card has a separate conclusion. These implications concern existence and security; no additional transmission or authentication task is part of this card.

Impagliazzo and Rudich exhibit an oracle world with one-way permutations but no secure key agreement. Since public-key encryption implies key agreement, the separation also constrains public-key encryption in that world. The original result is from STOC 1989; this audit read the author manuscript dated 28 May 1994. Such a relativized separation does not assert that ordinary one-way functions exist without ordinary public-key encryption.

Barak and Mahmoody’s corrected April 2009 Theorem 1.1 quantifies the random-oracle limitation: if each party makes at most \(q\) queries and agreement probability is at least \(\rho\), then for every \(0<\delta<1\) an observer can recover Bob’s output with probability at least \(\rho-\delta\) using at most \((16q/\delta)^{2}\) oracle queries. Other computation is unbounded. The paper explicitly corrects an earlier proof and does not extend this quadratic bound unchanged to a random-permutation oracle. It is not a polynomial-time attack on all ordinary encryption schemes.

Chatterjee, Mu and Vasudevan’s EUROCRYPT 2026 construction assumes hardness of planted MinRank on random instances, equivalently a random rank-metric decoding problem. The matrices are random rather than masked members of a specially structured decodable code family. This broadens the available concrete foundations for encryption, but hardness of that specific distribution is not supplied merely by the existence of an arbitrary one-way function. The introduction and definitions were checked in the 2025 preprint; its full security proof was not independently verified.

Li, Ni and Zan’s August 2023 preprint explicitly claims a positive answer from one-way functions. Its statement was checked, but this review has not verified the proof or found a conclusive later assessment. The card therefore records an uncertain scientific status and remains active; neither an accepted resolution nor a refutation of that claim is asserted.

cards.title: One-way functions from \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\)
cards.formal:
Does \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) imply the existence of a classical one-way function secure against uniform probabilistic polynomial-time inversion? Precisely, under that premise alone, must there exist one total deterministic polynomial-time computable function
\[f:\{0,1\}^{*}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{*}\]
such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time inverter \(I\) and every real constant \(c>0\), there is an integer \(N\ge1\) for which every \(n\ge N\) satisfies
\[\Pr_{x\sim U_n,\,r}\!\left[z\in\{0,1\}^{n}\ \land\ f(z)=f(x),\quad z=I(1^n,f(x);r)\right]\le n^{-c}?\]
Here \(U_n\) is the uniform distribution on length-\(n\) binary strings, and \(r\) denotes the inverter’s independent fair random coins. Finding any length-\(n\) preimage counts as successful inversion. The function must be fixed before the inverter and security exponent are chosen.
cards.definitions:
All computation is by ordinary multitape Turing machines with fixed finite programs and finite tape alphabets, unit-cost transitions and explicitly encoded inputs/outputs. There are no oracles, nonuniform advice strings, quantum operations or external uncounted computations. Polynomial time means a bound \(a(m+1)^d\) on every input of length \(m\), for fixed positive integers \(a,d\) depending on the machine. Reading input, evaluating functions, generating random bits and writing outputs are included in the running time.

A language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) lies in \(\mathrm P\) if one deterministic polynomial-time machine decides membership on every input. It lies in \(\mathrm{NP}\) if membership is equivalent to existence of a binary certificate of polynomially bounded length accepted by one deterministic polynomial-time verifier. The verifier is total on all input/certificate pairs. The premise compares these uniform total decision classes, not circuit classes or average-case classes.

The function \(f\) is computed by one deterministic machine in polynomial time on every binary string, including the empty string; its output length is consequently polynomially bounded. No length-preserving or injectivity requirement is imposed. Its description is public and may be built into an inverter’s fixed program. Security is required at positive input lengths \(n\).

An inverter \(I\) receives the explicitly separated pair \((1^n,y)\), with the input length \(n\) in unary and \(y\) a binary string. It has one fixed program, obtains independent unbiased coin bits, and halts within one polynomial in \(n+|y|+1\) on every input and every coin sequence. It outputs a finite binary string or the failure symbol \(\bot\). Its polynomial may depend on \(I\) but not on \(n,y\). An output of the wrong length, \(\bot\), or a string whose image differs from \(y\) is a failure. The retained convention is same-length inversion: a preimage must have the sampled input length \(n\). The original sampled \(x\) need not be recovered if another such preimage exists.

The experiment first draws \(x\) uniformly from all \(2^n\) inputs, evaluates \(y=f(x)\), and runs \(I\) with fresh independent random coins. Thus outputs with more length-\(n\) preimages are encountered more frequently; \(y\) is not sampled uniformly from the range. The probability is a finite exact average, since the inverter has an all-path polynomial clock. The constants in the forward evaluation bound and the inverter bound can differ.

Negligible inversion probability means exactly the quantifier order
\[\exists f\ \forall I\ \forall c>0\ \exists N=N(f,I,c)\ \forall n\ge N.\]
Neither the inverter nor \(f\) can vary with the input length, although each may use the supplied length in its computation. Security at only infinitely many lengths is not the target. Failure of one-wayness for a fixed \(f\) means that some single polynomial-time inverter has success greater than \(n^{-c}\), for some fixed \(c>0\), at arbitrarily large lengths; the logical negation does not demand success at every sufficiently large length.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the implication in the statement or its full logical negation. An affirmative proof must establish, under \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) alone, a total function with one uniform polynomial-time evaluator and the stated eventual negligible-success guarantee against every permitted inverter. No additional circuit lower bound, average-case hardness assumption or conjectured cryptographic primitive may be left unproved. The proof may use the premise without proving it separately.

A negative proof must establish \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) and show that for every total deterministic polynomial-time function \(f\), there exist a single permitted inverter \(I\) and a constant \(c>0\) such that for every threshold \(N\), some \(n\ge N\) has inversion success greater than \(n^{-c}\). An oracle separation, a barrier to one reduction technique, or an efficient inverter for a particular candidate is insufficient. The target is an existence implication and imposes no black-box-construction requirement or prescribed proof method.

context_blocks.text: Existence of one-way functions implies \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). The converse asks for much more than a function with occasional difficult inputs: the security experiment generates inputs uniformly, and every efficient inverter must have negligible overall success at all sufficiently large lengths. Worst-case inversion difficulty by itself does not give that distributional guarantee.

Average-case decision hardness and one-wayness have distinct requirements. The former can concern a language paired with a chosen feasible instance distribution. Here instances are images of uniform inputs under the same efficiently computable function whose inversion is tested. The adversary may exploit collisions and only needs to find any permitted preimage; hard reconstruction of the original sampled input is not enough.

Håstad–Impagliazzo–Levin–Luby establish that one-way functions suffice for cryptographic pseudorandom generators, with the converse also holding. A cryptographic generator efficiently expands uniform random bits so that polynomial-time statistical tests cannot distinguish its outputs from uniform strings with nonnegligible advantage. This explains the broad consequences of the primitive without adding encryption, a trapdoor or injectivity to this question.

Known nonadaptive oracle-reduction barriers show that certain reductions from NP-complete worst-case problems to average inversion would collapse the polynomial hierarchy. Such reductions choose all their oracle questions before receiving answers and must work for every oracle satisfying the average-success promise. The barrier concerns that reduction class; it does not establish the negation of the unrestricted implication.

Liu–Pass give an unconditional equivalence between one-way functions and a particular boundary-hardness condition for randomized time-bounded description complexity. Their corresponding statement for deterministic description complexity uses an exponential circuit-hardness assumption. An equivalence with a specialized hardness condition does not by itself establish that condition from \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\); the inspected paper explicitly retains this missing connection.

The April 2026 Liu–Mazor–Pass paper derives conditional pseudorandom generators and restricted zero-knowledge consequences from hardness of specific gap-description problems. A conditional generator’s seed distribution may be inefficient to sample, whereas an ordinary cryptographic generator uses uniform seeds. The paper retains additional hardness hypotheses and says that obtaining ordinary one-way functions from plain worst-case gap hardness remains beyond its results.

The eventual security requirement matters to both sides of the question. To disprove one-wayness of a candidate, a fixed inverter with noticeable success at arbitrarily large lengths is enough. To prove one-wayness, security on a sparse infinite subsequence is insufficient. The requested implication therefore cannot be replaced by an infinitely-often variant without changing the target.

cards.title: Circuit obfuscation from polynomial-hard LWE
cards.formal: Does the decisional LWE assumption with the fixed polynomial parameters below imply the existence of indistinguishability obfuscation for all polynomial-size Boolean circuits, with no additional hardness, leakage-resilience, or circular-security assumption? The target is a classical polynomial-time obfuscator secure against classical polynomial-size adversaries.
cards.definitions: Fix \(q(n)\) to be the least prime at least \(n^{4}\) for every integer \(n\ge 2\). Let \(\chi _{n}\) be the discrete Gaussian on Z with probability of e proportional to \(\exp (- \pi e^{2}/n^{2})\). The assumed LWE statement is: for every polynomial \(m(n)\), the ensembles (\(A,A s+e\) mod q) and \((A,u)\) are computationally indistinguishable, where A is uniform in \(Z_{q}^{m\times n}, s\) is uniform in \(Z_{q}^{n}\), the m coordinates of e are independent \(\chi _{n}\) samples, and u is independent uniform in \(Z_{q}^{m}\). Indistinguishable means every polynomial-size classical circuit family has negligible advantage in n; negligible means smaller than \(n^{- c}\) eventually for every constant \(c>0\). No secret-dependent leakage is supplied. An obfuscator O is a uniform probabilistic algorithm running in time polynomial in \(\lambda +|C|\) that outputs a Boolean circuit \(O(1^{\lambda},C)\) of polynomial size. Circuits are finite acyclic \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}/\mathrm{NOT}\) circuits with fan-in at most two, a specified list of input and output bits, and explicit binary descriptions; |C| is description length. For every polynomial p, there is negligible \(\mu _{p}\) such that for every |\(C|\le p(\lambda )\), with probability at least \(1- \mu _{p}(\lambda )\) over the obfuscator’s coins the output circuit agrees with C on ALL inputs. For every pair of circuit sequences \(C_{0},\lambda\) and \(C_{1},\lambda\) with polynomially bounded, equal description lengths, the same input/output lengths and identical functions, their obfuscations are computationally indistinguishable against all polynomial-size circuit families. Both functionality and security quantify over all such circuits, without requiring an efficiently checkable proof of equivalence. There is no oracle, trusted setup, quantum state, or restriction to a special circuit family. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Asks whether a single basic noisy-linear-equation assumption supports general program obfuscation. Resolving the implication would clarify the strength of LWE and the assumption cost of a broad family of cryptographic constructions that currently use iO as a separate resource.

importance.reason: A central assumption-minimization problem for general obfuscation, with consequences throughout cryptography and a crucial distinction between ordinary LWE and strengthened LWE-based assumptions.

progress.text: Barak and coauthors establish impossibility for general virtual-black-box obfuscation while introducing weaker obfuscation notions, including the indistinguishability target.
Regev develops LWE, lattice-hardness connections and public-key encryption; these results supply the standard noisy-equation foundation, rather than general obfuscation.
Jain, Lin, and Sahai construct general iO from four well-founded assumptions with the quantitative security specified in their theorem. The JACM publication does not reduce the list to LWE.
Their follow-up removes LWE, obtaining iO from LPN over prime fields, DLIN, and local PRGs under subexponential security. It explicitly leaves minimal assumption sets open.

Brakerski and coauthors obtain iO from circular-security properties of LWE-based encryption, including randomness-leakage resilience. They also repair a limitation in a previous exponentially-efficient-obfuscation transformation.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No construction from the plain polynomial-hard decisional-LWE assumption fixed here was identified. Existing multi-assumption and circular-security constructions do not settle it. Polynomial hardness, polynomial modulus/noise ratio, classical adversaries, arbitrary circuits and no auxiliary leakage are explicit choices that make the broad LWE-alone question unambiguous.

context_blocks.text: Indistinguishability obfuscation compares two implementations of exactly the same function. After obfuscation, an efficient observer should not tell which implementation was used. Equality of size prevents a trivial distinction from the amount of code supplied; padding can put implementations under a common size bound. This definition does not say that every secret written into an arbitrary program is hidden. A secret that the function itself reveals through its outputs remains visible.

That distinction is necessary. Barak and coauthors rule out general obfuscation under the stronger virtual-black-box requirement, which would make code reveal no more than oracle access to its function. Their impossibility theorem does not rule out indistinguishability obfuscation. The weaker comparison between equivalent implementations has therefore become a central target, rather than an informal promise to make arbitrary software unreadable.

LWE supplies a particularly concrete potential foundation. Its samples are linear equations modulo a public integer, perturbed by small independent errors. Exact equations would reveal the secret by linear algebra; the errors obstruct that approach. Regev introduced reductions connecting LWE to worst-case lattice problems and used it to build public-key encryption. This card fixes a particular ordinary decisional-LWE ensemble so that the noise distribution, modulus, number of samples, and adversarial resources cannot vary silently.

Jain, Lin, and Sahai established general-circuit iO from a combination of four assumptions: LWE, LPN over large fields, a local Boolean pseudorandom generator, and a bilinear-group assumption. Their theorem uses stronger quantitative security than mere polynomial hardness. Its Journal of the ACM version appeared in February 2026, following the STOC 2021 work. That publication is an important foundation for iO, but is not a 2026 construction from plain LWE alone.

A follow-up by the same authors removes LWE from that combination, leaving the other three assumptions. Eliminating LWE from a sufficient set is logically different from eliminating all the other assumptions while retaining LWE. The follow-up explicitly poses the possibility that LWE alone might suffice, without claiming a resolution.

Brakerski, Döttling, Garg, and Malavolta give another route using LWE-based encryption with circular randomness-leakage resilience. The construction uses that stronger assumption. Its security experiment exposes structured information related to keys and encryption randomness, whereas ordinary LWE supplies only the noisy linear samples defined above. Calling the construction LWE-based therefore does not remove the extra security hypothesis.

A solution would unify the assumptions behind many uses of obfuscation with an established lattice-learning problem. The specific target here is deliberately demanding: ordinary polynomial security and a polynomial modulus-to-noise ratio. Even a construction from plain LWE with stronger quantitative hardness would be substantial progress, but the security loss would still need attention before it established this exact implication. The question concerns mathematical feasibility; it does not impose practical code size or execution speed.
