cards.title: Unleveled fully homomorphic encryption from LWE alone
cards.formal: Does ordinary polynomial-modulus decisional LWE, with the parameter convention below, imply a classical compact fully homomorphic encryption scheme whose keys are generated without an evaluation-depth bound, secure against nonuniform polynomial-size adversaries without any additional circular-security or key-dependent-message assumption?
cards.definitions: Fix the following ordinary LWE assumption: for every fixed integer \(c\ge 3\) and polynomial sample count \(M(d)\), let \(q(d)\) be the least prime at least \(d^{c}\), let s be uniform in \(Z_{q}^{d}\), let A be uniform in \(Z_{q}^{M(d)\times d}\), and let the coordinates of e be independent integers with probability proportional to \(\exp (- \pi z^{2}/(4d))\), reduced modulo q. The ensembles (A,As+e mod q) and \((A,u)\), for independent uniform \(u\in Z_{q}^{M(d)}\), are computationally indistinguishable against nonuniform classical circuits of size polynomial in d. Thus the error distribution is the discrete Gaussian \(D_{Z,2\sqrt{d}}\); only ordinary independently generated LWE samples are assumed hard. The FHE scheme has uniform classical polynomial-time algorithms \(Gen(1^{\lambda})\to\)(pk,evk,sk), \(Enc(pk,b)\), Eval(evk,\(C,c_{1},\ldots ,c_{t}\)), and \(Dec(sk,c)\), with bit plaintexts and Boolean circuits over AND, OR and NOT. Gen takes no circuit-size or depth bound. There is one fixed polynomial P such that keys, fresh bit ciphertexts, evaluated one-bit ciphertexts and the time to decrypt a valid output are bounded by \(\mathrm{P}(\lambda )\), independently of C and t. Evaluation is polynomial-time in \(\lambda\) and its total input length. For every polynomial p, uniformly over all circuits C of size and input count at most \(p(\lambda )\) and all input bits \(b_{1},\ldots ,b_{t}\), decrypting Eval on independent encryptions of these bits equals \(C(b_{1},\ldots ,b_{t})\), except with negligible probability over generation, encryption and evaluation. Ordinary decryption is correct with negligible error. Given both pk and evk, every nonuniform polynomial-size classical adversary has negligible advantage in distinguishing an encryption of 0 from one of 1. Negligible means smaller than \(\lambda ^{-a}\) eventually for every \(a>0\). No subsequent secret-key assistance, ideal oracle, external trusted setup, superpolynomial adversary-hardness assumption, functional-encryption assumption or obfuscation assumption is allowed. This fixes a polynomial-modulus version of “standard LWE”; it does not assume any encryptions of secrets or correlated hints are secure.

cards.why: Determine whether ordinary LWE alone supports compact encrypted computation at arbitrary polynomial depth with one fixed key set.

importance.reason: A central foundational gap in fully homomorphic encryption, separating established leveled LWE constructions from reusable fixed-depth-independent keys and their extra security assumptions.

cards.status_note: No classical unleveled compact FHE construction from the specified ordinary LWE assumption alone was found through 11 September 2026. Functional-encryption constructions use additional assumptions. The inspected February and April 2026 no-circularity proposals retain explicit level bounds; the latter also uses quantum evaluation. This card fixes polynomial-modulus LWE, nonuniform classical security and fresh-input FHE correctness.

context_blocks.text: Homomorphic encryption lets a server compute on encrypted data and return an encrypted answer. Compactness makes this substantive: the client should decrypt a short answer, rather than receive the original ciphertexts together with the whole circuit and perform the computation itself. Here all four algorithms are classical, and the ciphertext for one output bit remains bounded by a fixed polynomial in the security parameter.

The order of choices is the heart of the problem. In a leveled scheme, the user first chooses a maximum depth L and generates keys suitable for that level. This can support every circuit up to L without revealing the data. The present question asks for one key-generation algorithm that receives only the security parameter and supports every polynomial-depth circuit later supplied to the evaluator. Choosing \(\mathrm{L}=\lambda ^{10}\) during setup still leaves deeper polynomial computations outside the guarantee.

Lattice ciphertexts generally include small errors that hide the plaintext. Homomorphic operations transform the desired message and these errors together. Once the error exceeds the decryption tolerance, the output may no longer decode correctly. Gentry’s bootstrapping idea refreshes a ciphertext by homomorphically evaluating a decryption circuit, with the secret key itself provided in encrypted form. Micciancio’s teaching slides explain both this noise issue and the associated circular-security question.

A chain of independent keys avoids the immediate circularity. Encrypt the secret key at level i under the public key at level \(i+1\), then use the next level to refresh the current ciphertext. The usual hybrid proof can replace those encryptions in reverse order because the chain has an endpoint. But the public material grows with the number of refreshes planned in advance. Closing the chain into a cycle reuses a bounded collection of keys and changes the security argument.

Brakerski and Vaikuntanathan’s construction makes the distinction explicit in its journal abstract: ordinary LWE gives leveled FHE, while removing the depth restriction uses an additional weak circular-security assumption. Later bootstrapping work supports polynomial-modulus parameters and polynomial lattice approximation factors. Improvements in error growth and efficiency do not themselves justify exposing the secret-key encryptions needed to reuse the keys.

The requested proof need not avoid bootstrapping, or even avoid encrypted keys. It must justify the actual public evaluation information using ordinary LWE alone. Conversely, it is not enough to prove that some artificially designed CPA-secure encryption scheme becomes insecure when encrypting its own key. Such a counterexample refutes an automatic upgrade for every scheme; it does not rule out designing a particular FHE scheme with a valid ordinary-LWE proof.

Bitansky and Solomon obtain FHE without circular-security assumptions using functional encryption, under polynomial hardness assumptions. This is a significant positive result for a broader assumption set. In their ITCS 2023 construction, the available functional-encryption instantiation uses assumptions including LPN, bilinear SXDH and shallow pseudorandom generators, in addition to the LWE-based homomorphic component. The basic theorem protects against uniform adversaries; their nonuniform extension requires an additional worst-case complexity assumption. Neither version establishes LWE alone under the convention here.

Recent claims also require checking the formal setup. Wang, Huang and Tang’s February 2026 dynamic multi-key scheme advertises avoiding a common reference string and circular security. Definition 2.2 nevertheless gives Setup the depth parameter L, and the construction chooses its dimension and modulus using L. Its stated compactness also permits dependence on L. This is a leveled guarantee, even though the number of participating keys can change dynamically.

Liu and coauthors’ April 2026 quantum homomorphic proposal also advertises classical LWE and no circular-security assumption. Its Section 3.4 uses \(\mathrm{L}+1\) independent key layers; a later discussion explicitly preallocates L evaluation gadgets. It therefore retains a level bound, and its evaluator performs quantum operations. These scope differences already prevent it from settling the classical, depth-independent target; this review does not validate its separate efficiency or quantum-security claims.

There is a further definitional distinction between evaluating one arbitrary circuit on fresh ciphertexts and repeatedly evaluating new circuits on the resulting ciphertexts. Micciancio’s slides show that correctness for the first task does not automatically imply correctness for the second. This card asks for the usual fresh-input FHE guarantee. Establishing full composability would be an additional accomplishment, rather than an implicit condition that makes the target harder.

A solution would remove a central gap between the clean assumption used to prove the security of leveled lattice encryption and the extra assumption used to reuse a fixed key set indefinitely over polynomial computations. It would clarify the foundation of FHE independently of practical parameter optimization, and could improve the assumptions of constructions that use unrestricted encrypted computation as a component.

cards.title: Sub-square-root share-size exponents in perfect secret sharing
cards.formal: Do there exist real constants \(K>0\) and \(0<c<1/2\) such that, for every \(n\ge 1\) and every monotone access structure \(\Gamma\) on \([n]\) with \(\varnothing \notin \Gamma\) and \([n]\in \Gamma\), there exists a perfect secret-sharing scheme for a uniform one-bit secret with \(\max _{i} \log _{2}|S_{i}|\le K\cdot 2^{cn}\), where \(S_{i}\) is the finite alphabet of participant i’s share?
cards.why: A worst-case storage benchmark for information-theoretic access control, separating the power of general secret sharing from linear schemes. The newly reported bound directly addresses its strict exponential threshold.
cards.status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. The target and theorem were compared; the proof was not independently verified. This remains an uncertain claimed resolution.

cards.definitions: \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). An access structure \(\Gamma \subseteq 2^{[n]}\) is monotone when \(A\in \Gamma\) and \(A\subseteq B\subseteq [n]\) imply \(B\in \Gamma\). A scheme is a joint probability distribution of a secret B uniform on \(\{0,1\}\) and shares \(X_{i}\in S_{i}\), where each \(S_{i}\) is a finite nonempty set. For each \(A\in \Gamma\) there is a deterministic map \(r_{A}:\prod _{i\in A}S_{i}\to \{0,1\}\) such that \(r_{A}((X_{i})_{i\in A})=B\) with probability one. For each \(A\notin \Gamma\), the conditional distributions of \((X_{i})_{i\in A}\) given \(B=0\) and \(B=1\) are identical. This is exact reconstruction and perfect information-theoretic privacy, with arbitrary collusion within A. Share size is the base-two logarithm of its alphabet cardinality, not its Shannon entropy or the sum over participants. It is normalized by the secret size of one bit. There is no linearity, field, threshold, computation-time or uniform construction requirement. The scheme may depend on the whole finite access structure. K,c must be universal. Rounding \(\log _{2}|S_{i}|\) up to an integer encoding length changes K only by an absolute factor.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that some universal \(K>0\) and \(0<c<1/2\) satisfy the stated worst-share bound for every permitted access structure, or prove the logical negation in Lean. A negative answer must show that for every such \(K,c\) some access structure admits no perfect scheme with that bound, allowing all finite share alphabets and all joint distributions in the definition. The object quantified over is a general scheme; it need not be linear or efficiently constructed.

context_blocks.text: Status update: Nir’s August 2026 preprint states a directly matching positive result. Theorem 1.5 gives every n-party access structure a scheme for a one-bit secret with maximal share size \(2^{0.496n+o(n)}\). Taking any fixed c between 0.496 and \(1/2\) absorbs the sublinear exponent for large n; a universal K covers the finitely many smaller sizes. The proof has not been independently verified here, so the card records an uncertain claimed resolution.

An access structure describes which groups may reconstruct a secret. It need not depend only on group size: a designated participant may be essential, or several different combinations may be authorized. Monotonicity means that an authorized group stays authorized when more participants join. Perfect privacy requires even an unlimited observer holding every share of an unauthorized group to see the same distribution for either secret value.

For example, suppose participant 1 together with either participant 2 or participant 3 may reconstruct a bit B. Choose an independent uniform bit R and give shares R, B XOR R, B XOR R respectively. Either authorized pair recovers B by XOR. Participants 2 and 3 together see two copies of a uniform masked bit and learn nothing about B; participant 1 alone sees independent randomness. This simple access structure needs only one bit per share, but arbitrary patterns can be much harder.

The question concerns the largest participant’s stored alphabet, measured in bits. A share with M possible values costs \(\log _{2} M\), even if its probability distribution has smaller entropy. The total share size is between the largest share and n times that share; these measures have the same leading exponential rate. None of these conventions permits replacing perfect privacy by computational secrecy or small statistical leakage.

The classical construction treats authorized sets separately and can use exponentially large shares. Successive results reduced the exponent; Applebaum and Nir’s 2021 bound is \(1.5^{n+o(n)}\), equivalently \(2^{0.58496\ldots n+o(n)}\). This remains above the half exponent requested in the seminar question. The seminar list prints a different earlier upper exponent; the primary construction is used for the historical bound recorded here.

Linearity is a real restriction: shares are linear combinations of the secret and random field elements. Known exponential lower bounds for linear schemes do not apply to all joint distributions allowed in this card. Likewise, lower bounds for particular reconstruction degrees or graph access structures need their own hypotheses. A general upper bound must handle every monotone authorized-group pattern, with one universal exponent.

The same 2026 preprint gives a half-exponent linear construction and a strictly smaller nonlinear exponent. Its nonlinear theorem is the part relevant to this card; the linear theorem alone would not satisfy \(c<1/2\).

cards.title: Existence of one-way functions
cards.formal: Does there exist a total deterministic polynomial-time computable function \(f:\{0,1\}*\to \{0,1\}\)* such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm I and every integer \(d\ge 1\), there is \(n_{0}\) with \(\Pr [f(I(1^{n},f(X)))=f(X)]\le n^{- d}\) for all \(n\ge n_{0}\), where X is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) and the probability also includes the independent random coins of I?
cards.why: Asks for the unconditional existence of the basic computational asymmetry underlying much of modern cryptography.

cards.definitions: The security parameter \(n\ge 1\) is given in unary as \(1^{n}\). A single deterministic Turing machine computes f on every finite binary string in time polynomial in its input length. Each inverter I is one classical randomized Turing machine with a worst-case polynomial running-time bound; its input contains \(1^{n}\), so its running time and output length are polynomial in n. It receives \(f(X)\), not X, and has no advice, oracle or secret information. An output Y succeeds exactly when \(f(Y)=f(X)\); any preimage is accepted, even one of a different length from X. An explicit failure output is unsuccessful. No injectivity, permutation property or length preservation is imposed. A probability function is negligible if it is eventually at most \(n^{- d}\) for each integer \(d\ge 1\). The threshold \(n_{0}\) can depend on I and d. Security is averaged over the uniformly sampled input and the inverter’s coins, and must hold for all sufficiently large n, not merely an infinite subsequence.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves, without an unproved computational hardness assumption, that at least one f satisfies the stated efficiency and inversion bound. A negative resolution proves that every polynomial-time f has a polynomial-time inverter whose success is non-negligible: for some \(d\ge 1\) it exceeds \(n^{- d}\) for infinitely many n. A conditional construction or a failure of one particular candidate does not decide existence.

context_blocks.title: What must be hard
context_blocks.text: Computing an output and finding an input that produces it are different tasks. The experiment first generates an ordinary random input, computes its image, and asks an efficient algorithm for any matching input. The difficulty must survive every polynomial-time inverter on this distribution. A few exceptional hard inputs, or a single unsuccessful attack, do not establish this average-case guarantee.

context_blocks.title: Forgetting information is not enough
context_blocks.text: Suppose f keeps the first \(\lceil n/2\rceil\) bits of an n-bit input and discards the rest. Recovering the exact original random string would usually be impossible because the discarded bits are missing. Inversion as defined here is easy: append enough zero bits to obtain an n-bit string with the given prefix. Its image is the required value. This example explains why the success condition accepts any preimage and why simple information loss is not cryptographic hardness.

context_blocks.title: How strong is negligible success?
context_blocks.text: An inverter that succeeds with probability \(1/n^{10}\) still violates the requirement. A probability such as \(2^{- n}\) is negligible, while \(1/n^{10}\) is not. The quantifiers allow a different eventual threshold for each algorithm and each requested exponent. They do not ask for a single finite input length at which every conceivable polynomial-time program is already defeated. The forward computation and all adversaries here are classical; a quantum primitive with different inputs or outputs is a separate model.

context_blocks.title: Relation to other open questions
What the existing theorems establish
context_blocks.text: Levin gives a concrete complete function whose one-wayness follows if any one-way function exists. Completeness identifies a universal candidate; it does not establish the premise. Liu and Pass characterize existence through an average-case hardness property of time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity, the length of a shortest program producing a string within a time bound. Their equivalence does not prove that hardness property. Hirahara and Nanashima’s June 2026 revision characterizes Pessiland, the hypothetical situation with average-case hard problems but no one-way functions. This is another structural theorem, not evidence that either hypothetical world actually occurs. The checked sources do not resolve unconditional existence.

cards.context:
Computing an output and finding an input that produces it are different tasks. The experiment first generates an ordinary random input, computes its image, and asks an efficient algorithm for any matching input. The difficulty must survive every polynomial-time inverter on this distribution. A few exceptional hard inputs, or a single unsuccessful attack, do not establish this average-case guarantee.

Suppose f keeps the first \(\lceil n/2\rceil\) bits of an n-bit input and discards the rest. Recovering the exact original random string would usually be impossible because the discarded bits are missing. Inversion as defined here is easy: append enough zero bits to obtain an n-bit string with the given prefix. Its image is the required value. This example explains why the success condition accepts any preimage and why simple information loss is not cryptographic hardness.

An inverter that succeeds with probability \(1/n^{10}\) still violates the requirement. A probability such as \(2^{- n}\) is negligible, while \(1/n^{10}\) is not. The quantifiers allow a different eventual threshold for each algorithm and each requested exponent. They do not ask for a single finite input length at which every conceivable polynomial-time program is already defeated. The forward computation and all adversaries here are classical; a quantum primitive with different inputs or outputs is a separate model.

One-way functions would imply \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\), since \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) would permit efficient search for a polynomial-length preimage. Whether \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) alone implies their existence is separately recorded in TCS-0022. One-way functions are equivalent to several basic cryptographic primitives, including pseudorandom generators and suitable private-key encryption, but it is not known whether they suffice for public-key encryption; that implication is TCS-6545. The present question assumes neither \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) nor any candidate’s hardness.

Levin gives a concrete complete function whose one-wayness follows if any one-way function exists. Completeness identifies a universal candidate; it does not establish the premise. Liu and Pass characterize existence through an average-case hardness property of time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity, the length of a shortest program producing a string within a time bound. Their equivalence does not prove that hardness property. Hirahara and Nanashima’s June 2026 revision characterizes Pessiland, the hypothetical situation with average-case hard problems but no one-way functions. This is another structural theorem, not evidence that either hypothetical world actually occurs. The checked sources do not resolve unconditional existence.

cards.definitions: For security parameter \(n\ge 1, Gen(1^{n})\) samples a public key pk and a secret key sk. \(Enc(1^{n},pk,m)\) takes a bit \(m\in \{0,1\}\) and fresh independent coins and outputs a binary ciphertext; \(Dec(1^{n},sk,c)\) returns a bit or failure. All three algorithms have worst-case polynomial running time in their input length. Correctness means that max over \(m\in \{0,1\}\) of Pr[Dec(\(1^{n},sk,Enc(1^{n},pk,m)\))≠m] is negligible in n, with probability over key generation, encryption and any decryption coins. For IND-CPA, Gen runs first, and a uniform PPT adversary \(A_{1}\) receives \((1^{n},pk)\) and outputs bits \(m_{0},m_{1}\) and a state z. Independently choose a uniform bit b, generate \(c=Enc(1^{n},pk,m_{b})\), and give \((1^{n},pk,z,c)\) to its second stage \(A_{2}\), which outputs a bit \(b'\). For every pair \((A_{1},A_{2}), |\Pr [b' =b]- 1/2|\) must be negligible. A function \(\eta (n)\) is negligible if, for every integer \(d\ge 1, \eta (n)\le n^{- d}\) for all sufficiently large n. Adversaries may run the public encryption algorithm themselves polynomially many times before and after seeing c; there is no decryption oracle. The model has no trusted correlated setup, ideal oracle, secret advice or quantum algorithms. The receiver’s public key is given authentically; its replacement by an active attacker is outside this confidentiality experiment. One-bit message space fixes an equivalent existence question: independent bit encryptions and the standard hybrid argument extend IND-CPA security to every polynomial message length.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves existence of a scheme satisfying the stated correctness and computational indistinguishability bounds with no unproved computational assumption. A negative resolution proves that every efficient correct scheme fails that security requirement. An assumed-hardness construction, experimental resistance to attacks, or an impossibility theorem only for unbounded attackers does not settle this question.

context_blocks.title: Public information, private recovery
context_blocks.text: A sender receives the public key and can encrypt a message without knowing the secret key. The receiver can decrypt with that secret key. An observer has the same public encryption capability as the sender, so secrecy must come from a limitation on computation rather than from hiding the encryption algorithm. The question asks whether such a limitation can be proved to exist for some efficient scheme.

context_blocks.title: Why the challenge compares two messages
context_blocks.text: The adversary chooses two messages after seeing the public key, then receives an encryption of a fair random choice between them. Guessing always gives success \(1/2\). Security requires every efficient adversary’s additional advantage to be negligible. This is stronger than merely failing to recover a long message exactly: learning one distinguishing bit can already violate the requirement. Restricting the displayed experiment to message bits keeps the existence question concrete without requiring a particular practical ciphertext format.

context_blocks.title: A simple failure of deterministic encryption
context_blocks.text: Imagine that encryption uses no fresh randomness and the two possible messages are 0 and 1. Anyone with the public key can compute both ciphertexts and compare the challenge with them. On keys for which both messages decrypt correctly, the two ciphertexts must differ, so the comparison reveals the challenge bit. Randomized encryption avoids this immediate comparison attack, but randomness by itself is not a proof of security.

context_blocks.title: Which assumptions are still missing?
context_blocks.text: Regev’s lattice-based construction gives classical public-key encryption from learning-with-errors hardness. This is a theorem relating two computational tasks; it does not prove the assumed task hard. In March 2026, Lu, Poremba, Quek and Ramkumar gave another conditional route based on average-case hardness of quantum stabilizer decoding, with classical cryptographic algorithms. A new candidate assumption broadens the foundations available for constructions while leaving unconditional existence unresolved. The word quantum in the underlying decoding problem does not itself make the encryption algorithms quantum.

context_blocks.title: The boundary of the question
context_blocks.text: Secure public-key encryption implies one-way functions and hence \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). The converse implication from arbitrary one-way functions is a separate open question, TCS-6545; proving that implication alone would still leave their existence unproved. Computational security here permits an unbounded adversary to succeed. Consequently, the impossibility of information-theoretic secrecy from only public information does not answer the present question. Chosen-ciphertext security adds access to a decryption oracle and is also a different requirement. The requested theorem concerns precisely efficient classical attackers in the stated chosen-plaintext experiment.

cards.title: Key agreement from one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of a classical one-way function imply the existence of a classical two-party key-agreement protocol in the plain public-channel model below? The parties must output \(\lambda\)-bit keys with negligible disagreement, and either honest key must be computationally indistinguishable from an independent uniform key given the entire public transcript. This is the unrelativized existence implication, allowing arbitrary constructions and security proofs, including those that inspect the program implementing the one-way function.
cards.definitions:
The security parameter is an integer \(\lambda\geq1\), given as the unary string \(1^{\lambda}\). Every algorithm has one finite program for all parameters and is a classical Turing machine operating on bits; no nonuniform advice or oracle is available. A probabilistic polynomial-time (PPT) algorithm uses independent fair random bits and has a polynomial worst-case running-time bound on every input and every random tape. For standalone algorithms, the bound is in the total input length. Machine steps, reading and writing bits, and producing outputs all count. Each algorithm may have its own fixed polynomial bound. Tuples of bit strings use the prefix-free component encoding \(s\mapsto1^{|s|}0s\); a finite list is encoded by its number of components in the same encoding, followed by its encoded components, with integers represented in binary without leading zeros except for zero itself. Any explicitly proved polynomial-time equivalent encoding is acceptable.

A function \(\mu:\mathbb N_{\geq1}\to[0,1]\) is negligible if \(\forall d\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\;\exists\lambda_0\;\forall\lambda\geq\lambda_0:\mu(\lambda)\leq\lambda^{-d}\). A one-way function is a total deterministic polynomial-time function \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) such that, for every uniform classical PPT inverter \(I\), the function \(\Pr[\,|Y|=\lambda\ \land\ f(Y)=f(X)\,]\) is negligible, where \(X\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\) and \(Y=I(1^{\lambda},f(X))\). The probability includes the independent coins of \(I\). A failure output or a string of the wrong length is an unsuccessful inversion; recovering any preimage of the stipulated length suffices. The function need not be injective or length preserving. Its program is public.

A candidate protocol consists of two uniform interactive machines \(A,B\). On the common input \(1^{\lambda}\), they start with independent private coins and no other secret or correlated input. They exchange finite classical bit strings through a noiseless public channel. Fix the conventional alternating-message execution, with \(A\) first and empty messages permitted; public termination flags indicate when each machine has finished. A polynomial in \(\lambda\), fixed for the protocol, bounds the combined computation, messages, message lengths, and execution length on every pair of honest random tapes. Both parties always terminate with strings \(K_A,K_B\in\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\). The public transcript \(T\) is the finite ordered list of messages with sender labels, message boundaries and termination flags, encoded as above. Private working tapes and private coins are not part of \(T\). Communication occurs only through these messages; there is no additional timing channel. No trusted setup, preshared secret, correlated randomness, random oracle, quantum computation or quantum communication is permitted.

Correctness means that \(\Pr[K_A\ne K_B]\) is negligible in \(\lambda\), over independent honest coins. Passive secrecy means that for every uniform classical PPT algorithm \(D\) outputting a bit, the advantage
\[\left|\Pr[D(1^{\lambda},T,K_A)=1]-\Pr[D(1^{\lambda},T,U_{\lambda})=1]\right|\]
is negligible, where each experiment runs the honest protocol and \(U_{\lambda}\) is an independent uniform element of \(\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\). The coins of \(D\) are independent of all other randomness. Correctness makes the same requirement with \(K_B\) equivalent. The eavesdropper sees the whole transcript and the public programs but does not modify messages. Its polynomial running time allows it to store the entire polynomial-length transcript: there is no extra storage bound. Negligibility is required eventually at all sufficiently large parameters, not just along a subsequence; its thresholds may depend on the adversary. The quantifier order is: if some \(f\) satisfying one-wayness exists, then some single pair \((A,B)\) satisfying the resource bound, correctness and secrecy against every such \(D\) exists. No uniform compiler from descriptions of functions to protocols, black-box interface, fixed number of rounds or perfect correctness is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated existence implication or its logical negation. A positive answer must establish an unrelativized protocol satisfying all of the specified correctness, secrecy, uniformity and cost requirements from the one-way-function premise alone. A negative answer must establish that a one-way function exists and that no protocol in the stated class satisfies both correctness and secrecy. Failure of a particular protocol, an oracle separation, a restriction to black-box reductions, a result assuming perfect correctness, or an attack with polynomially many oracle queries but unbounded computation does not establish that negation. Additional unproved cryptographic assumptions and security only at infinitely many parameters do not settle the full target.
cards.why: This asks whether generic computational one-wayness suffices for two strangers to establish a shared classical secret through publicly visible interaction. It separates the minimal hardness underlying symmetric cryptography from the additional structure used for secret establishment, while allowing more interaction than public-key encryption. A resolution would determine whether that foundational gap concerns existence itself or the known forms of cryptographic reductions.

context_blocks.text: A one-way function concerns the difficulty of reversing a computation on a randomly generated input. Key agreement concerns a joint distribution generated by two initially independent parties: they must learn the same string while a public observer cannot distinguish it from a fresh uniform string. Hardness of inversion by itself does not directly assert this joint secrecy property.

The secrecy experiment includes the candidate key as well as the transcript. A key can be difficult to recover in full while still revealing predictable bits, so mere resistance to complete key recovery is not the chosen definition. The saved card already required indistinguishability from uniform; this review preserves that stronger standard formulation and makes the probability spaces and adversary-dependent negligible bounds explicit.

Impagliazzo and Rudich established an oracle world in which one-way permutations exist but secure key agreement does not. A one-way permutation is a length-preserving bijective special case of a one-way function. This separates the relativized primitives and obstructs reductions that continue to work in that world. It is not a proof that ordinary one-way functions exist without ordinary key agreement. The author manuscript checked here is dated 28 May 1994; the original conference publication was STOC 1989.

Black-box uselessness asks a further composition question: can adding a one-way-function primitive help obtain key agreement from some auxiliary primitive that did not suffice alone? Couteau, Farshim and Mahmoody prove restricted forms, rather than the general statement. Their ITCS 2021 Theorem 17 uses infinitely-often security, perfect correctness and a constant bound on one party’s queries to the one-way-function oracle; the other auxiliary oracle is still available. These restrictions and the paper’s specified reduction notions are part of that theorem. They are not assumptions of this card.

Public-key encryption implies passive key agreement, whereas the target here permits a general polynomial amount of interaction. The two existence questions are therefore closely related but have different conclusions. The agreed key must remain secret only against an observer; this does not assert authentication or security against a party that replaces the messages. The absence of pre-existing shared information is an essential part of the question.

Brzuska, Couteau, Egger and Quach obtain key agreement from one-way functions in a bounded-storage model. Their publisher abstract describes a large public stream and an a priori storage restriction on the observer, and reports polynomial storage gaps. That additional physical resource restriction is absent here: a PPT observer may retain the entire honest transcript. The abstract and publication metadata were checked; this review does not claim to have verified the full bounded-storage construction.

Li, Li, Li and Liu’s August 2026 preprint states a many-round quantum random-oracle impossibility result. With independent initial private states, classical messages, a Boolean-output random oracle and perfect agreement, it claims a classical eavesdropper making \(O((q_A+q_B)^{5})\) oracle queries when the parties make \(q_A,q_B\) quantum queries. The observer is allowed unbounded other computation. The statement was checked in the paper, but its proof was not independently verified. Its oracle, perfect-correctness and query-cost conditions differ from this card’s classical, negligible-error, polynomial-time target.

Li, Ni and Zan’s 2023 preprint explicitly claims public-key encryption from one-way functions. If valid, this would also settle the key-agreement implication. This audit checked the claim but did not verify its proof or find a conclusive later assessment. Its presence therefore changes the recorded scientific status to uncertain; it does not justify archival.

A one-way permutation is a length-preserving bijective special case of a one-way function. This separates the relativized primitives and obstructs reductions that continue to work in that world. It is not a proof that ordinary one-way functions exist without ordinary key agreement. The author manuscript checked here is dated 28 May 1994; the original conference publication was STOC 1989.

Black-box uselessness asks a further composition question: can adding a one-way-function primitive help obtain key agreement from some auxiliary primitive that did not suffice alone? Couteau, Farshim and Mahmoody prove restricted forms, rather than the general statement. Their ITCS 2021 Theorem 17 uses infinitely-often security, perfect correctness and a constant bound on one party’s queries to the one-way-function oracle; the other auxiliary oracle is still available. These restrictions and the paper’s specified reduction notions are part of that theorem. They are not assumptions of this card.

Public-key encryption implies passive key agreement, whereas the target here permits a general polynomial amount of interaction. The two existence questions are therefore closely related but have different conclusions. The agreed key must remain secret only against an observer; this does not assert authentication or security against a party that replaces the messages. The absence of pre-existing shared information is an essential part of the question.

Brzuska, Couteau, Egger and Quach obtain key agreement from one-way functions in a bounded-storage model. Their publisher abstract describes a large public stream and an a priori storage restriction on the observer, and reports polynomial storage gaps. That additional physical resource restriction is absent here: a PPT observer may retain the entire honest transcript. The abstract and publication metadata were checked; this review does not claim to have verified the full bounded-storage construction.

Li, Li, Li and Liu’s August 2026 preprint states a many-round quantum random-oracle impossibility result. With independent initial private states, classical messages, a Boolean-output random oracle and perfect agreement, it claims a classical eavesdropper making \(O((q_A+q_B)^{5})\) oracle queries when the parties make \(q_A,q_B\) quantum queries. The observer is allowed unbounded other computation. The statement was checked in the paper, but its proof was not independently verified. Its oracle, perfect-correctness and query-cost conditions differ from this card’s classical, negligible-error, polynomial-time target.

Li, Ni and Zan’s 2023 preprint explicitly claims public-key encryption from one-way functions. If valid, this would also settle the key-agreement implication. This audit checked the claim but did not verify its proof or find a conclusive later assessment. Its presence therefore changes the recorded scientific status to uncertain; it does not justify archival.

cards.title: Oblivious transfer from public-key encryption
cards.formal: In the classical plain model, does the existence of an IND-CPA-secure public-key encryption scheme for bits imply the existence of a polynomial-time 1-out-of-2 bit oblivious-transfer protocol secure against static semi-honest corruption of either party? Both primitives have negligible error and computational security as defined below. The implication may use arbitrary non-black-box techniques and a polynomial number of communication rounds.
cards.definitions: The security parameter is \(\lambda\), supplied in unary. Honest algorithms are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time Turing machines; adversarial distinguishers are polynomial-size classical circuit families. A function \(\mu\) is negligible if for every \(c>0, \mu (\lambda )<\lambda ^{- c}\) for all sufficiently large \(\lambda\). Public-key encryption consists of \(KeyGen(1^{\lambda})=(pk,sk), Enc(pk,m;r)\), and \(Dec(sk,c)\), for \(m\in \{0,1\}\); decryption fails with negligible probability over key generation and encryption coins, for each m. IND-CPA means that no such adversary given pk distinguishes \(Enc(pk,0)\) from \(Enc(pk,1)\) with nonnegligible advantage; public encryption is available to it. In OT, sender S has bits \((m_{0},m_{1})\), receiver R has a choice bit c, and R must output \(m_{c}\) except with negligible probability for every input triple; S has no output. The parties follow their prescribed algorithms but keep their entire views, including inputs, random tapes, and messages. There must be uniform probabilistic polynomial-time simulators \(Sim_{S}(1^{\lambda},m_{0},m_{1})\) and \(Sim_{R}(1^{\lambda},c,m_{c})\) whose outputs are computationally indistinguishable from the corresponding real views for every sequence of input triples. Thus S learns nothing about c and R learns nothing beyond \((c,m_{c})\). The parties have independent private randomness and exchange classical messages directly. There is no trusted setup, common reference string, random oracle, pre-shared correlated randomness, trusted hardware, or quantum resource.
cards.answer_criterion: Establish the stated existence implication without a second unproved hardness assumption, or refute that unrelativized implication. A construction may inspect and use the code of the encryption algorithms and use non-black-box security arguments. An oracle separation or a lower bound restricted to black-box reductions is a barrier, not a negative resolution of this question. A construction requiring an additional property of encryption must also derive that property from arbitrary IND-CPA encryption to settle the card.
cards.why: Determines whether the ability to send secrets to a designated receiver already suffices for general private computation between mutually distrustful parties. It is a basic boundary in the hierarchy of cryptographic assumptions, with a longstanding black-box barrier and no known unrestricted implication.

importance.reason: A foundational comparison between ordinary public-key confidentiality and a primitive complete for secure computation; resolving it would change which assumptions suffice for a broad range of protocols.

progress.text: Gertner and coauthors prove an oracle with PKE but no semi-honest OT, and give positive constructions when PKE has specified extra properties. Their oracle separations use uniform adversaries.

Maji and Wang prove limitations on optimal fair coin tossing from black-box PKE or key agreement; this is further evidence about restricted constructions, not an unrestricted separation.
Li, Zhang, and Lin construct OT from rerandomizable PKE, replacing oblivious sampling with a public ciphertext-rerandomization requirement.
The journal version of Tanishita and coauthors’ work derives OT from updatable encryption with additional sampling properties. It does not remove all extra assumptions on the starting primitive.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No unrestricted classical implication from arbitrary IND-CPA public-key encryption to OT was identified. Known oracle/black-box separations and positive results for rerandomizable or suitably samplable encryption do not settle this formulation. The card fixes semi-honest standalone security with classical communication and no setup.

context_blocks.text: Ordinary encryption protects a message from someone who lacks the secret key. Oblivious transfer must arrange a more selective situation: the receiver can read one of two messages, cannot read the other, and does not disclose which one it selected. This combines privacy for both participants. Merely encrypting both messages under a key generated by the receiver fails, because that receiver can decrypt both ciphertexts. Asking the receiver to reveal which key it can decrypt would instead reveal its choice.

Some encryption schemes offer the missing structure. If a receiver can create two indistinguishable-looking public keys while knowing a decryption key for just one, it can place the decryptable key in position c. The sender encrypts the two messages under the corresponding keys. Such an argument needs a suitable oblivious-sampling property, including security even given the sampler’s retained randomness. Gertner and coauthors identify sufficient properties and also prove an oracle separation between general PKE and even semi-honest OT. Their historical separation uses uniform adversaries.

That result constrains a style of construction, rather than deciding the unrestricted implication. In an oracle argument all algorithms are given access to an additional idealized operation. A construction based on the actual implementation of an encryption scheme may use features that do not survive replacement by an arbitrary oracle. Consequently, the qualifier allowing non-black-box techniques is substantive; removing it would turn the card into a question already addressed by known barriers.

The semi-honest target is already powerful. Haitner, Ishai, Kushilevitz, Lindell, and Petrank show how to transform semi-honest OT into OT secure against malicious parties, and obtain general secure computation without an honest majority. Their result fixes static corruption and standalone security; it does not promise fairness or guaranteed output delivery against a party that aborts. This explains why the basic passive-security implication matters without building stronger composition or fairness requirements into the question.

Progress continues through additional algebraic or sampling structure. Li, Zhang, and Lin construct OT from rerandomizable PKE: anyone with the public key can turn a ciphertext into a fresh encryption of the same plaintext. This avoids their predecessors’ oblivious-sampling requirement but introduces a different hypothesis. Ordinary IND-CPA security alone does not include a public rerandomization algorithm.

A 2026 journal paper by Tanishita and coauthors studies updatable encryption, where update tokens let a third party transform ciphertexts across keys. With specified oblivious-sampling properties, it derives two- or three-round OT. Those theorems refine the boundary for a structured encryption primitive. They do not give a transformation starting with an arbitrary public-key encryption scheme.

A related barrier concerns fair coin tossing. Maji and Wang show limits for protocols using public-key encryption or key agreement as black boxes, whereas OT supports optimally fair constructions. This gives another operational way to see the distinction between ordinary encrypted communication and primitives complete for secure computation. The fairness result has its own model and does not constitute a proof against all non-black-box OT constructions.

cards.title: Collision-resistant hashing from one-way functions
cards.formal: In the ordinary classical computational model, does the existence of a polynomial-time computable one-way function secure against all polynomial-size circuit families imply the existence of a publicly keyed collision-resistant hash family \(H_{k}:\{0,1\}^{2\lambda}\to \{0,1\}^{\lambda}\) secure against all polynomial-size circuit families?
cards.definitions: A one-way function is a deterministic uniformly polynomial-time computable map f on finite binary strings, with output length bounded by a polynomial in the input length, such that for every family of possibly randomized Boolean circuits \(A_{n}\) of size polynomial in n, Pr[\(f(A_{n}(1^{n},f(X)))=f(X)\) and |\(A_{n}(1^{n},f(X))|=n\)] is negligible in n, where X is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\). The same invocation of \(A_{n}\) supplies the candidate preimage in both parts of this event. A function \(\mu\) is negligible if for every \(c>0\) there is \(N_{c}\) such that \(\mu (n)\le n^{-c}\) for all \(n\ge N_{c}\). A hash family consists of a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time key generator \(Gen(1^{\lambda})\) producing a polynomial-length public key k, and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time evaluator \(H(1^{\lambda},k,x)\). For every key in the generator’s support, \(H_{k}\) maps every \(2\lambda\)-bit input to a \(\lambda\)-bit output. Collision resistance means that for every polynomial-size possibly randomized circuit family \(B_{\lambda}\), the probability that \(B_{\lambda}(1^{\lambda},k)\) outputs distinct \(x,x' \in \{0,1\}^{2\lambda}\) with \(H_{k}(x)=H_{k}(x' )\) is negligible in \(\lambda\), over \(k\leftarrow Gen(1^{\lambda})\) and the attacker’s coins. Both messages may be chosen after the attacker sees k. Circuit descriptions may depend on the security parameter, but not on the freshly sampled key. The implication permits arbitrary use of the description of f and arbitrary proof techniques; no random oracle, additional setup assumption, quantum resource, trapdoor, or stronger quantitative hardness assumption is supplied.
cards.answer_criterion: Establish the stated existence implication without additional assumptions, or refute it in the ordinary unrelativized model. A positive result may use non-black-box techniques. An oracle world where one-way functions exist but collision-resistant hashing fails proves only a relativizing barrier. Failure of a particular construction, even for a specific one-way function, is also insufficient to refute the existence implication. Producing only target-collision resistance, noncompressing injective functions, or a construction from stronger product-hardness assumptions does not settle the proposition.
cards.why: Determines whether a fundamental compressing cryptographic primitive needs assumptions beyond ordinary one-wayness, while exposing the gap between known black-box barriers and unrestricted constructions.

importance.reason: A central unresolved implication among cryptographic primitives, with consequences for authentication, data commitments and succinct verification.

cards.status_note: No unrestricted implication or refutation was found in the primary literature checked through 11 September 2026. Existing black-box separations do not settle this ordinary-model existence statement. The definitions explicitly use uniform honest algorithms, nonuniform classical adversaries, public fresh keys and factor-two compression.

context_blocks.text: A collision-resistant hash compresses its input while making it computationally difficult to find two distinct messages with the same digest. Collisions must exist by the pigeonhole principle: there are \(2^{2\lambda}\) possible inputs and only \(2^{\lambda}\) outputs. Security is therefore not a claim that collisions never occur, or that a digest uniquely identifies a message. It is a claim about what an efficient adversary can construct after learning the hash key.

A one-way function poses a different challenge. The attacker receives the image of a random input and must find any preimage. An injective one-way function can have no collisions at all, yet it is not a compressing hash. Conversely, a compressing map may have easily found collisions even if some inversion tasks look difficult. The question asks whether the minimal assumption of computationally hard inversion can always supply the more structured difficulty of finding collisions.

The public key matters to the asymptotic definition. If a single compressing function were fixed at each security parameter and security were required against nonuniform circuits, an attacker could hard-code one collision for each parameter. A fresh polynomial-length key prevents that pair from being selected in advance for the actual function used. The key is not secret: the adversary sees it before choosing either colliding message.

Target-collision resistance changes the order of moves. An attacker first commits to one message, then sees a random key and seeks a second message colliding with its committed target. Rompel constructs universal one-way hash functions of this kind from arbitrary one-way functions, as part of the route to secure signatures. That theorem does not give the present game, where both messages are chosen after the key is known. The order difference is small syntactically but central to the unresolved assumption gap.

Simon constructs an oracle setting with one-way permutations but no collision-resistant hash functions in the relevant relativized sense. It rules out building and proving the desired primitive by treating the assumed function purely as an oracle in the separated framework. The theorem does not rule out exploiting a function’s implementation or a proof that fails to relativize. The ordinary mathematical implication in this card therefore remains stronger than the black-box construction question already answered negatively.

Holmgren and Lombardi give a positive route under stronger assumptions about simultaneously inverting independent challenges. Their one-way product functions require quantitative batch hardness beyond ordinary one-wayness. They construct collision-resistant hashing from suitable such functions and connect the missing assumption to unusually strong parallel repetition. This identifies a concrete intermediate target without showing that every ordinary one-way function possesses the required batch security.

The separation also connects hashing to total search problems. Given a circuit for a compressing map, a collision is guaranteed to exist and can be checked efficiently. Folwarczný and coauthors study whether one-way functions can establish hardness for total NP search more generally, extending limitations for a class of single-query reductions. These are restrictions on reductions, not an unconditional proof that collision-resistant families cannot follow from one-wayness by any method.

Applications can sometimes avoid the full primitive. Rothblum’s July 2026 work constructs efficient interactive arguments for bounded-space computations from one-way functions. Communication depends on the space bound times a polynomial in log T and the security parameter, and the security loss depends polynomially on the computation time T. This weakens assumptions for that interactive application; it does not construct a publicly evaluable compressing hash that withstands arbitrary key-dependent collision attempts.

A resolution would clarify the foundations of many protocols that use short commitments to large data. It would either place full collision resistance on the same assumption level as ordinary one-wayness, or demonstrate a separation that survives beyond black-box barriers. The card asks for polynomial security only; requiring near-optimal exponential security or resistance to quantum attacks would introduce additional questions.

cards.title: One-way permutations from one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of classical one-way functions secure against nonuniform polynomial-size adversaries imply the existence of a classical, efficiently generated family of full-domain one-way permutations with the same security convention?
cards.definitions: A one-way function is a uniformly polynomial-time computable family \(f_{n}:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \{0,1\}^{\ell (n)}\), for a polynomially bounded, computable output length \(\ell\), such that for every randomized polynomial-size circuit family \(A_{n}, \Pr [f_{n}(A_{n}(1^{n},f_{n}(X)))=f_{n}(X)]\) is negligible in n for uniform \(X\in \{0,1\}^{n}\); outputs outside \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) fail. A function \(\mu\) is negligible if for every \(c>0, \mu (n)\le n^{-c}\) for all sufficiently large n. A permutation family consists of a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time key generator \(Gen(1^{n})\) and deterministic polynomial-time evaluation \(Eval(1^{n},pk,x)\), with a fixed polynomially bounded, polynomial-time computable integer \(m(n)\ge n\). For every pk in the support of \(Gen(1^{n})\), Eval defines a bijection \(\pi _{pk}:\{0,1\}^{m(n)}\to \{0,1\}^{m(n)}\). For every randomized polynomial-size adversary \(A_{n}, \Pr [\pi _{pk}(A_{n}(1^{n},pk,\pi _{pk}(X)))=\pi _{pk}(X)]\) must be negligible, with \(pk\leftarrow Gen(1^{n})\), independent uniform X and independent adversary coins. Malformed outputs fail. The public key is available to the attacker; no trapdoor is required or given. All security is classical. “Full-domain” fixes the input set to the whole Boolean cube; the valid public-key set need not be all bit strings of its length. The implication is an ordinary existence implication, without restrictions to black-box constructions and without extra assumptions such as obfuscation or subexponential security.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated existence implication, allowing any mathematical construction or proof technique, or refute that implication in the ordinary computational model. Proving that one-way functions do not exist would make the implication vacuously true. An oracle separation or a theorem excluding a restricted class of reductions is a construction barrier, not a refutation of the unrestricted implication. A permutation family on special sparse domains does not meet the full-domain convention fixed here; an additional trapdoor property would be a stronger positive result.
cards.why: Determine whether basic average-case inversion hardness necessarily supports efficient bijections, a rigid primitive at the foundation of cryptographic constructions.

importance.reason: A longstanding question about the structure obtainable from minimal cryptographic assumptions, with strong construction barriers and a recent full-domain breakthrough under additional assumptions.

progress.text: Rudich develops oracle barriers; the thesis’s one-way-function-to-permutation argument is conditional on a combinatorial conjecture.

Matsuda–Matsuura exclude fully black-box constructions from even one-bit-expanding injective one-way functions with adaptive one-wayness.
Asharov–Segev handle domains depending on the primitives in their OWF-only barrier, and separately study domain-invariant constructions using obfuscation.
Shmueli–Zhandry obtain full-domain trapdoor permutations from subexponentially secure iO and OWFs; Section 1.4 distinguishes input-domain from key-domain invariance.

context_blocks.text: A one-way function is easy to evaluate but hard to invert on a random input. It may identify many different inputs and need not cover its output space. A one-way permutation has exactly one preimage for every output in its domain. The extra requirement is structural: nothing is lost mathematically, yet efficiently recovering the uniquely determined input must remain infeasible.

This card fixes the full-domain, public-key family version because the original phrase “one-way permutation” leaves several conventions unspecified. A public key chooses a permutation of an entire Boolean cube; all input strings of that length are valid. A stronger unkeyed formulation asks for a single length-preserving permutation on all bit strings. A more permissive formulation allows key-dependent sparse domains. Results in those settings must be compared with their domain and sampling requirements visible.

Making a computation reversible is not enough. The map \((x,z)\mapsto (x,z \mathrm{XOR} f(x))\) is a bijection for any efficiently computable length-compatible f, but its inverse is obtained by applying exactly the same map. Likewise, simply attaching x to \(f(x)\) makes the output injective while revealing the desired preimage. The construction has to preserve computational difficulty while removing collisions and covering the domain, without publishing the information needed for inversion.

Many other forms of cryptographic structure can be derived from bare one-wayness. Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin and Luby show that every one-way function yields a pseudorandom generator. That success does not enforce bijectivity. The permutation question tests whether computational hardness can always be reorganized into a particularly rigid, uniquely invertible mathematical object.

Rudich’s 1988 thesis developed the oracle-separation approach and gave a barrier for this implication conditional on a combinatorial conjecture. The thesis abstract states that qualification explicitly. It is misleading to describe the original thesis alone as an unconditional separation of the ordinary existence assumptions. An oracle world changes what algorithms can access, so it diagnoses limitations of proof techniques rather than settling the actual implication.

Matsuda and Matsuura subsequently prove a fully black-box barrier even when the starting function is injective, increases length by only one bit, and satisfies their stronger adaptive one-wayness condition. Thus an apparently tiny departure from a permutation already defeats a broad class of generic constructions. Their result concerns constructions that treat the supplied primitive and adversary through specified interfaces; it does not exclude exploiting the code or other structure of a concrete function.

Asharov and Segev address another subtlety: earlier negative arguments could fail when the construction’s domains depended on the underlying primitives. They exclude black-box constructions from one-way functions even without that domain-invariance requirement. They also give a separate barrier for constructions using oracle-aided indistinguishability obfuscation, under domain-invariance conditions. The two statements have different assumptions and should not be merged into an unrestricted impossibility theorem.

There is significant progress with stronger assumptions. Shmueli and Zhandry’s July 2025 paper constructs full-domain trapdoor one-way permutations assuming subexponentially secure indistinguishability obfuscation and subexponentially secure one-way functions. It uses a new kind of pseudorandom permutation that supports controlled permutation of its outputs. The trapdoor guarantee is stronger than this card requests, but both the extra primitive and the stronger hardness assumptions prevent this from proving the target implication.

The same paper explains why its full-domain result is compatible with the earlier obfuscation barrier. Its input domain is the whole cube, but its public keys are obfuscated programs. The valid-key domain therefore depends on the building blocks. The older formal domain-invariance condition constrains both input and key domains. Keeping these two notions separate prevents an erroneous claim that a published barrier has been contradicted.

A positive answer would show that unique, length-preserving inversion hardness is available whenever basic cryptographic hardness exists. A negative answer would reveal a structural separation inside foundational cryptographic assumptions. Existing barriers make the problem especially informative: a successful construction from ordinary one-way functions would need to escape the established generic approaches, rather than merely improve their efficiency.

cards.title: Chosen-ciphertext security from ordinary public-key encryption
cards.formal: Does the existence of IND-CPA-secure public-key encryption imply the existence of IND-CCA2-secure public-key encryption in the plain model, with classical security against all nonuniform polynomial-size adversaries and no additional computational assumption?
cards.definitions: A public-key encryption scheme has uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithms \(Gen(1^{n})\to (pk,sk)\) and \(Enc(pk,m)\to c\) and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm \(Dec(sk,c)\to m\) or ⊥. It supports bit-string messages of any polynomially bounded length. For every polynomial p, the maximum decryption-error probability over messages |\(m|\le p(n)\) is negligible in n, with probability over key generation and honest encryption. In the IND-CPA game an adversary receives pk, chooses equal-length messages \(m_{0},m_{1}\) and state, receives \(c*=Enc(pk,m_{b})\) for an independent uniform bit b, and guesses b. Its advantage is |Pr[guess=b]−\(1/2|\). In the IND-CCA2 game it also has adaptive access to \(Dec(sk,\cdot )\), both before and after choosing the challenge messages and receiving c*. After the challenge, the oracle rejects the exact bit string c*; all other ciphertext queries are allowed. Security requires negligible advantage for every nonuniform probabilistic polynomial-time adversary, allowing any polynomial number of oracle queries. Negligible means eventually smaller than \(n^{-a}\) for every \(a>0\). Each adversary has its own polynomial resource bound, but the scheme is fixed independently of that bound. The plain model has no ideal random oracle, externally supplied common reference string, hardware or trusted setup beyond the recipient generating its own key pair. This is an unrestricted existence implication, not a requirement that a compiler treat the original scheme as a black box.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that an IND-CCA2 scheme with these guarantees exists whenever an IND-CPA scheme exists, or refute that implication in the ordinary computational model. A conversion assuming additional trapdoor functions, suitable proof systems, special pseudorandom generators or ideal random oracles does not by itself suffice. A theorem excluding a restricted class of black-box conversions is a barrier, not a negative answer to the unrestricted implication. Fixed-query bounded CCA2, pre-challenge-only CCA1 and non-malleability without adaptive decryption access are weaker targets.
cards.why: Determine whether public-key confidentiality alone can always be strengthened to resist adaptive decryption attacks, without importing another cryptographic assumption.

importance.reason: A central question about the minimal assumptions for robust public-key encryption, connecting encryption, proof systems, trapdoor structure and generic security transformations.

The revised threshold-encryption work retains additional-model or stronger-security requirements in its CPA-to-CCA transformations.

context_blocks.text: Public-key encryption already allows anyone, including the attacker, to create ciphertexts. Ordinary chosen-plaintext security protects the contents of an honestly generated challenge ciphertext. Chosen-ciphertext security additionally protects it while the attacker submits other ciphertexts for decryption and uses the responses to decide what to ask next. The only forbidden query is the challenge itself, because returning its plaintext would make confidentiality impossible by definition.

A simple modification illustrates the gap between definitions. Start with a secure ordinary scheme, append an unused bit to every ciphertext, and make decryption ignore that bit. The modification preserves chosen-plaintext security. A chosen-ciphertext attacker flips the challenge’s unused bit and submits the resulting different string to the oracle, which returns the challenge plaintext. This proves that a particular CPA scheme need not itself be CCA-secure; it does not rule out building another scheme from its existence.

This is why the question concerns a construction or existence implication. A successful transformation may change the ciphertext format, use many public keys, encode messages, and inspect the original algorithms’ descriptions. It must arrange that responses to every other ciphertext remain harmless. A proof faces the corresponding simulation problem: how can it answer decryption queries while relying only on a challenge from the weaker security game?

The source proposal points to Trevisan’s cryptography project list, which explicitly asks whether CCA security can be derived from CPA security by black-box techniques or by any techniques. Its bibliography juxtaposes partial negative results with positive results for non-malleability. That distinction remains important: an advance for one attack model should not silently be reported as a solution for another.

Gertner, Malkin and Myers give a black-box separation for constructions whose new decryption algorithm never calls the original encryption algorithm. This covers a substantial class of natural attempts. It still leaves constructions that re-encrypt during decryption, and does not cover arbitrary use of the source code. The scope of that restriction is central to the theorem, rather than a technical detail that can be omitted.

Choi, Dachman-Soled, Malkin and Wee construct non-malleable encryption from any semantically secure scheme and extend their approach to bounded chosen-ciphertext attacks. In the bounded version, the permitted number q of decryption queries is fixed before constructing the scheme. Full CCA2 instead asks for one scheme that withstands every polynomial-time attacker, whose query polynomial can be larger than any particular bound built into that scheme.

Another productive route adds a primitive that helps enforce ciphertext validity. Hohenberger, Koppula and Waters prove in CRYPTO 2020 that injective trapdoor functions suffice for CCA-secure public-key encryption, without requiring lossiness or correlated-product security. This removes significant earlier restrictions. An arbitrary encryption scheme is not automatically such a trapdoor function: its decryption need only recover the message, not a unique full input including encryption randomness.

Koppula and Waters obtain generic upgrades using a hinting pseudorandom generator, whose security survives a special kind of auxiliary information. Ordinary pseudorandomness does not state that guarantee. Their construction offers another way to organize the decryption proof, but applying it to arbitrary public-key encryption still requires establishing the additional hinting property from the original assumption.

Matsuda’s PKC 2025 work shows that a publicly verifiable noninteractive batch argument for NP can supply the additional ingredient. The May 2025 revision weakens the required proof-length savings: they need not be strong enough for currently known constructions of noninteractive zero knowledge. This is progress in reducing the extra structure needed for the upgrade. The paper still assumes the batch argument; it does not construct it from arbitrary CPA encryption.

A PKC 2026 paper by Brzuska, Klooß and Woo gives CPA-to-CCA transformations for threshold encryption, where several parties jointly decrypt. Its generic transform from arbitrary CPA-secure threshold encryption uses a random oracle. Its other route has additional requirements, including a stronger semi-malicious CPA notion. The July 2026 revision therefore does not establish the plain-model implication in this card.

Resolving the implication would clarify whether protection against active ciphertext manipulation is an additional foundational assumption or a consequence of ordinary public-key confidentiality. It would also explain why existing general approaches repeatedly need structure beyond the weak starting primitive. The target is a foundational security theorem; it does not ask that the resulting construction be practical or preserve the original scheme’s efficiency.

cards.title: Noninteractive zero knowledge from one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of classical one-way functions imply reusable, adaptively secure noninteractive zero-knowledge arguments for circuit satisfiability in the honestly generated common-reference-string model, with computational soundness and computational zero knowledge against nonuniform polynomial-size adversaries?
cards.definitions: A one-way function is a uniformly polynomial-time computable family \(f_{n}\) on uniform n-bit inputs with polynomial-length outputs, such that every nonuniform randomized polynomial-size adversary given \(1^{n}\) and \(f_{n}(X)\) finds any n-bit preimage with negligible probability. Circuit satisfiability has statements x encoding Boolean circuits and witnesses w assigning their inputs, with \(R(x,w)=1\) exactly when the circuit outputs 1. A proposed argument consists of uniform algorithms \(Setup(1^{\lambda},1^{B})\to\)crs, Prove(crs,x,w)→\(\pi\), and Verify(crs,\(x,\pi\))→\(\{0,1\}\); their time and output length are polynomial in \(\lambda +B\), where B bounds statement and witness lengths. Setup is independent of the later statements; its private coins are not published. For every polynomial \(B=B(\lambda )\), completeness error is negligible uniformly over valid \((x,w)\) of length at most B. Adaptive computational soundness means that every nonuniform polynomial-time adversary given crs has negligible probability of outputting an unsatisfiable x and an accepted \(\pi\). Reusable computational zero knowledge means there exist uniform polynomial-time SimSetup and SimProve such that no nonuniform polynomial-time distinguisher separates these experiments: \((i)\) it receives honest crs and can adaptively request Prove(crs,x,w) for polynomially many valid pairs; \((ii)\) it receives simulated crs from SimSetup, and each valid query is answered by SimProve using the simulation trapdoor and x, without receiving w. Both experiments reject invalid queries, and the distinguisher retains arbitrary polynomial-size auxiliary information. All negligible bounds are in \(\lambda\): for each \(a>0\) the error is eventually below \(\lambda ^{-a}\). Only crs is public in the real system, and one proof message is sent for each statement. No random oracle, extra cryptographic assumption, online verifier challenge, proof of knowledge or succinctness requirement is included. Circuit satisfiability covers every NP language through witness-preserving polynomial reductions.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated existence implication, or refute it in the ordinary computational model. The result may use the code of the one-way function and need not be black-box. A construction adding LWE, an appropriate batch argument, trapdoor hashing, or strong extra complexity assumptions does not suffice unless those ingredients are themselves derived from the same ordinary OWF premise. An interactive proof, a witness-indistinguishable argument, or a single-theorem result without a justified reusable upgrade is not the specified conclusion.
cards.why: Determine whether the minimal assumption supporting basic cryptography is sufficient for reusable, publicly verifiable proofs that reveal no witness and require no online interaction.

importance.reason: A fundamental boundary between interactive and noninteractive zero knowledge, with implications for the assumptions behind privacy-preserving proof systems and cryptographic transformations.

progress.text: Goldreich–Micali–Wigderson establish interactive zero knowledge for NP from one-way functions; the inherited survey distinguishes the noninteractive open question.
Peikert–Shiehian construct NIZK for NP from plain LWE using correlation-intractable hashing.
The revised Bradley–Waters–Wu work derives NIZK from adaptively sound BARGs plus OWFs, retaining the extra batch-argument premise.
Chen–Rothblum–Tell’s revised work gives NIZK with uniform soundness from subexponential OWFs and additional strong complexity assumptions.
Chakraborty–Hulett–Khurana–Tomer extend conditional implications from nontrivial NIZK to OWFs and error amplification; this is not OWF-to-NIZK.

Florentz–Konopnicki–Rothblum’s CRYPTO 2026 chapter appears online; its succinct OWF-based zero-knowledge proof remains interactive.
