cards.status_note: No construction of reusable adaptive NIZK arguments from ordinary OWFs alone, or refutation of that unrestricted implication, was found through 11 September 2026. The cited BARG, trapdoor-hash and derandomization constructions retain extra assumptions; recent OWF-only succinct proofs are interactive, and high-error characterizations run in the reverse direction.

context_blocks.text: An NP witness can be easy to check and sensitive to reveal. For circuit satisfiability, publishing a satisfying assignment gives a verifier complete evidence, but also exposes every bit of that assignment. Zero knowledge asks for convincing evidence whose visible distribution can instead be simulated without the assignment. It formalizes the requirement that verification disclose no additional information beyond the statement’s truth.

The common reference string is an explicit resource. An honest setup algorithm produces public parameters before any statements are selected. After that setup, a prover sends one message that anyone can verify. The setup may retain randomness while generating the string, but that randomness is not handed to users. The simulation trapdoor exists only in the security experiment. This model differs from asking for a noninteractive system with no setup at all.

The card allows computational soundness: a computationally unbounded attacker might find a false accepted proof, but efficient attackers must not. Such a system is called an argument. It also asks for a reusable reference string, with statements chosen after seeing the string and earlier proofs. These choices make the target precise without requiring short proofs or a way to extract a witness from a successful prover.

The classical Goldreich–Micali–Wigderson theorem already supplies interactive zero-knowledge proofs for NP from one-way functions. Interaction gives the verifier a role in challenging what the prover has prepared. The inherited Damgård–Nielsen survey explicitly asks whether one-way functions suffice in the noninteractive setting. That survey discusses a proof-system version with stronger soundness; the argument target here asks for protection only against efficient cheating.

Known positive constructions use more structure. Peikert and Shiehian construct NIZK for NP from ordinary LWE in 2019. Their method builds hash families whose correlation-intractability property supports a sound Fiat–Shamir transformation. The point is a proved property of a specially constructed family, not simply substituting an arbitrary hash function for a verifier’s random challenge. LWE is a sufficient assumption, but it has not thereby been derived from arbitrary one-way functions.

Bradley, Waters and Wu show that an adaptively sound noninteractive batch argument for NP, together with a one-way function, yields NIZK. Their TCC 2024 result also studies how to obtain the needed adaptive soundness from other batch-argument guarantees. The title “Batch Arguments to NIZKs from One-Way Functions” must be read with its starting resource intact: the batch argument is an additional primitive, rather than something their theorem constructs from a bare one-way function.

Branco and coauthors develop a vector-trapdoor-hash approach, with an updated version in March 2026. Their constructions use either LWE or a combination of DDH and LPN assumptions. The initial black-box constructions provide single-theorem zero knowledge, and their multi-theorem upgrade uses cryptography in a non-black-box way. This distinction is compatible with the target here, which allows any construction technique but requires the OWF-only assumption and reusable security.

Chen, Rothblum and Tell pursue a different route through derandomization and strong computational hardness. Their construction combines a subexponentially secure one-way function with an additional complexity assumption and obtains computational soundness against uniform adversaries. It is progress toward avoiding highly structured cryptographic primitives, but the extra hardness and the adversary convention both differ from this card.

Recent results in the reverse direction should not be read as a construction. Chakraborty, Hulett, Khurana and Tomer show in February 2026 that nontrivial NIZK arguments imply one-way functions under the hypothesis that NP is not contained in ioP/poly, even in a broad high-error regime. Their amplification consequences improve existing weak NIZK systems. Neither direction starts with an ordinary OWF alone and produces the desired NIZK system.

Another 2026 result gives succinct zero-knowledge proofs using one-way functions as black boxes. Florentz–Konopnicki and Rothblum’s protocol is interactive: its theorem explicitly bounds a number of public-coin rounds that depends on the relation’s parameters. Its noninteractive commitment component does not make the whole protocol noninteractive. A resolution of this card would isolate exactly how much cryptographic structure is needed to remove that interaction after a single reusable setup.

cards.context:
An NP witness can be easy to check and sensitive to reveal. For circuit satisfiability, publishing a satisfying assignment gives a verifier complete evidence, but also exposes every bit of that assignment. Zero knowledge asks for convincing evidence whose visible distribution can instead be simulated without the assignment. It formalizes the requirement that verification disclose no additional information beyond the statement’s truth.

The common reference string is an explicit resource. An honest setup algorithm produces public parameters before any statements are selected. After that setup, a prover sends one message that anyone can verify. The setup may retain randomness while generating the string, but that randomness is not handed to users. The simulation trapdoor exists only in the security experiment. This model differs from asking for a noninteractive system with no setup at all.

The card allows computational soundness: a computationally unbounded attacker might find a false accepted proof, but efficient attackers must not. Such a system is called an argument. It also asks for a reusable reference string, with statements chosen after seeing the string and earlier proofs. These choices make the target precise without requiring short proofs or a way to extract a witness from a successful prover.

The classical Goldreich–Micali–Wigderson theorem already supplies interactive zero-knowledge proofs for NP from one-way functions. Interaction gives the verifier a role in challenging what the prover has prepared. cards.title: One-way functions from errorless average-case NP hardness
cards.formal: Is the following implication true? \[(\mathrm{NP},\mathrm{PSamp})\not\subseteq\mathrm{AvgP}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{there exists a classical one-way function}.\] Here the antecedent means that some fixed NP language, under some fixed polynomial-time samplable distribution ensemble, has no deterministic exact decider with average polynomial running time in the moment sense below. The conclusion asks for a total polynomial-time computable function \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time inverter \(I\) and every integer \(c\ge1\), there exists \(n_0\) for which, for every \(n\ge n_0\), \[\Pr_{x\sim U_n,\ I}\bigl[|z|=n\ \land\ f(z)=f(x)\bigr]\le n^{-c},\qquad z\leftarrow I(1^n,f(x)).\] The statement is unrelativized and has no additional hardness, derandomization or cryptographic assumption.
cards.why: A problem can be difficult to decide on typical efficiently generated inputs without obviously providing an efficiently computed map that is hard to invert. Connecting these two kinds of difficulty would clarify the minimum computational assumptions needed for classical cryptography. The precise decision-error and security-length conventions are essential to that comparison.

None supplies a proof or refutation of the specified implication. Bounded review through 2026-09-15 is not an exhaustive certification of current openness.

sentences: This card selects the average-case-to-one-way-function branch of a broader question in Wigderson’s book.
The hardness assumption concerns exact deterministic decision under an efficiently samplable distribution, with average polynomial time defined by a runtime moment.
The conclusion requires a polynomial-time function that every uniform probabilistic inverter fails to invert with more than negligible probability at all sufficiently large lengths.
Recent heuristic-hardness characterizations, infinitely-often security results and oracle separations use different guarantees.
A resolution would clarify whether broad distributional hardness already forces the computational structure underlying classical one-wayness.

cards.definitions: A language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) is in NP if there are a fixed deterministic polynomial-time predicate \(R\) and a polynomial \(p\) such that \(x\in L\) exactly when some \(u\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}\) satisfies \(R(x,u)=1\). A sampler is one probabilistic Turing machine \(S\) that, on the unary size parameter \(1^n\), uses independent unbiased random bits and halts within \(q(n)\) bit steps on every random tape, for a fixed polynomial \(q\). Its exact output distribution is \(D_n\), over finite strings of length at most \(q(n)\). The ensemble parameter \(n\) need not equal the output length. PSamp is the class of these ensembles. A deterministic exact decider \(A\), given \((1^n,x)\), must halt and return the membership bit of \(L\) correctly for every \(n\ge1\) and every finite \(x\), including inputs outside the support of \(D_n\). Let \(T_A(1^n,x)\) be its number of bit steps. The pair \((L,D)\) belongs to AvgP if there exist \(A\), constants \(\alpha>0,C>0\), and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that \(\mathbb E_{x\sim D_n}[T_A(1^n,x)^\alpha]\le C(n+1)^k\) for every \(n\ge1\). These choices may depend on \(L,S\), but not on \(n\). This is an exact, deterministic moment-based notion, not merely a polynomial first moment or a heuristic allowed to misclassify a small fraction of inputs. The antecedent asserts the existence of one pair \((L,D)\) in the stated class failing this condition. In the conclusion, \(U_n\) is uniform on all \(n\)-bit strings, and the probability also includes the inverter’s independent unbiased coin flips. An inverter is a fixed finite probabilistic Turing program whose running time is polynomial in its input length on every random tape; all reading, writing and arithmetic are charged. It receives both \(1^n\) and \(f(x)\). It may output any preimage of \(f(x)\) of length exactly \(n\), not necessarily the original \(x\); malformed or wrong-length outputs fail. The function \(f\) is computed by one fixed finite deterministic polynomial-time program on all input strings, so output length is automatically polynomially bounded. All programs are uniform and have no advice or oracle. Security is required for all sufficiently large \(n\) for each inverter and exponent; security on only infinitely many lengths is a different guarantee.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the implication or its logical negation. A positive answer must derive the existence of a function with the full uniform, all-sufficiently-large-length inversion guarantee from the stated distributional hardness alone. The implication does not require an efficient black-box transformation from a description of the hard pair. A negative answer must establish the antecedent together with nonexistence of every such function in the unrelativized model; an oracle world, a barrier to one type of reduction or failure of one candidate construction is insufficient. A result assuming randomized heuristic hardness instead of the specified deterministic exact hardness, or yielding only infinitely-often security or a fixed polynomial security gap, does not alone settle this formulation.

cards.title: Public-key quantum money from LWE alone
cards.formal: Does quantum hardness of decisional Learning with Errors with the fixed polynomial parameters below imply reusable, unforgeable public-key quantum money in the standard model?
cards.definitions: For each integer \(\lambda\ge2\), let \(q(\lambda)\) be the least prime at least \(\lambda^4\), and let \(\chi_\lambda\) give integer z probability proportional to \(\exp(-\pi z^2/\lambda^2)\). The assumption states that, for every polynomially bounded sample count m, the distributions \((A,As+e\bmod q)\) and \((A,u)\) are computationally indistinguishable: A is uniform in \(\mathbb Z_q^{m\times\lambda}\), s is independently uniform in \(\mathbb Z_q^\lambda\), the coordinates of e are independent samples from \(\chi_\lambda\), and u is independent uniform in \(\mathbb Z_q^m\). Indistinguishability is against all nonuniform polynomial-size quantum circuit families with classical advice. Advantage is the absolute difference of acceptance probabilities and must be negligible in lambda, meaning eventually less than \(\lambda^{-c}\) for every constant c>0. Quantum circuits use a fixed universal Clifford-plus-T gate set, zero-state ancillas and computational-basis measurements; polynomial-size classical control is allowed. A money scheme consists of uniform quantum polynomial-time algorithms Gen, Mint and Verify. Gen on unary lambda outputs classical keys (pk,sk). Mint(sk) outputs a classical serial string s and a quantum register rho; their lengths are polynomial in lambda. Verify(pk,s,rho) returns an accept/reject bit and a residual note register, without secret information. For every polynomial t, an honestly generated note survives t successive verifications, all accepting, with probability at least one minus a negligible function, over key generation, minting and verification. For every polynomially bounded integer-valued k and every nonuniform polynomial-size quantum adversary with classical advice, give the adversary pk and k independently minted notes under the same key. The probability that it produces k+1 serial/register pairs all accepted by fresh local applications of Verify is negligible; its output registers may be jointly entangled and serials need not be distinct. This also applies to k=0. The construction has no ideal oracle, externally supplied setup, obfuscation assumption, leakage assumption, or additional hardness assumption. The target is the implication from the explicitly stated LWE assumption; a construction with an arbitrary computational reduction qualifies.

Known constructions with stronger assumptions and restricted impossibility results leave a gap. iO-based schemes and schemes founded on group-action assumptions do not establish the LWE-only implication specified here.
The 2025 obfuscation barrier applies to a particular black-box interface. It is evidence about a restricted class of constructions, not a refutation of this unrestricted implication.

cards.title: Average-case RSA inversion versus factoring for exponent 65537
cards.formal: For the fixed exponent \(e=65537\) and the balanced-prime ensemble below, does the existence of a uniform randomized polynomial-time RSA inverter with inverse-polynomial average success imply the existence of a uniform randomized polynomial-time factoring algorithm with inverse-polynomial average success?
cards.definitions: For each integer \(n\ge 3\) let \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) be the finite set of primes p with \(2^{n- 1}\le p<2^{n}\) and \(\gcd (e,p- 1)=1\). Choose an ordered pair \((p,q)\) uniformly from \(\{(p,q)\in \mathrm{P}_{n}^{2}:p\ne q\}\), and set \(N=pq\). All assertions are for sufficiently large n with at least two such primes. Conditional on N, choose x uniformly from \(\mathbb{Z}_{N}^{*}=\{a\in \{0,\ldots ,N- 1\}:\gcd (a,N)=1\}\), independently of algorithm coins, and set \(y=x^{e}\) mod N. The inverter I receives \((1^{n},N,y)\), in binary except for \(1^{n}\), and must output the unique \(x\in\mathbb{Z}_{N}^{*}\) with that image. Nonnegligible success here means that some integer \(a\ge 1\) and \(n_{0}\) exist such that \(\Pr [I(1^{n},N,y)=x]\ge n^{- a}\) for every \(n\ge n_{0}\). The factoring algorithm F receives \((1^{n},N)\) and succeeds by outputting p or q; require some \(b\ge 1\) and \(n_{1}\) such that \(\Pr [F(1^{n},N)\in \{p,q\}]\ge n^{- b}\) for every \(n\ge n_{1}\). Both machines use independent fair random bits and have worst-case running time bounded by their own fixed polynomials in their input lengths on every random tape. The probabilities average over the stated modulus ensemble as well as x and the coins, with no promise of success separately on each modulus. The assertion is the ordinary existence implication \((\exists I,a,n_{0})\Rightarrow (\exists F,b,n_{1})\). It does not restrict a proof to black-box reductions: a construction of F may use the fixed code of I and count all calls to it in F’s polynomial running time. No independent oracle or advice is supplied.

cards.title: Noninteractive SZK versus SZK
cards.formal: Does NISZK equal SZK? Equivalently, does there exist a uniform deterministic polynomial-time reduction that maps every promised pair of sampling circuits X,Y to a sampling circuit Z, preserving the near/far promises specified below?
cards.definitions: A sampling circuit is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit with AND and OR gates of fan-in two, NOT gates, constants, a specified list of random input bits and an ordered list of output bits. Its description explicitly lists gates and wires in binary. Fresh independent uniform bits are supplied to all random inputs; the output distribution is the resulting distribution on bit strings. X and Y may have different numbers of random inputs but have the same output length. For finite distributions P,Q on the same set, \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=\tfrac12\sum_z|P(z)-Q(z)|\). The source convention for Statistical Difference has YES instances with \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(X,Y)<1/3\) and NO instances with \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(X,Y)>2/3\). Inputs between these promises impose no correctness obligation. The reduction outputs one circuit Z with \(m\ge 3\) output bits. On every YES input require \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(Z,U_{m})<1/m\); on every NO input require \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(Z,U_{m})>1- 1/m\), where \(U_{m}\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{m}\). The reduction runs in a fixed polynomial of the combined encoded input length on every syntactically valid input, including inputs outside the promise; writing Z and all its input/output nodes counts in that time. It receives no advice or sampling oracle. These are the source’s Statistical Difference and Statistical Difference from Uniform promise problems. Their completeness under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions makes existence of this reduction equivalent to the original class equality. Thus the complete-problem formulation fixes the question without having to choose a new auxiliary-input or setup convention for protocols.

context_blocks.text: Statistical zero knowledge asks whether a verifier can be convinced while learning only information that a simulator could reproduce. The unresolved equality asks whether interaction adds power when a noninteractive protocol has an honestly sampled public random string.

The same question can be stated entirely in terms of finite sampling circuits. Statistical Difference is complete for SZK, while Statistical Difference from Uniform is complete for NISZK. The requested reduction therefore tests the original class equality with a fully discrete input and output contract.

cards.title: Fully homomorphic encryption from public-key encryption
cards.formal: Does the existence of IND-CPA-secure public-key bit encryption imply the existence of an IND-CPA-secure, compact, unleveled fully homomorphic bit-encryption scheme for every polynomial-size Boolean circuit, with the algorithms and security convention below?

All algorithms are uniform probabilistic Turing machines with worst-case polynomial bit running time in their explicit input lengths; decryption is deterministic. The security parameter \(\lambda\) is supplied in unary. An adversary is a nonuniform family of randomized Boolean circuits of size polynomial in \(\lambda\), including its advice and random-input nodes. All random bits are independent and fair. A function \(
u:\mathbb{N}	o [0,1]\) is negligible when for every positive integer a there exists \(\lambda _{0}\) such that \(
u (\lambda )\le \lambda ^{- a}\) for all \(\lambda \ge \lambda _{0}\). Security is quantified separately over every such adversary family, with a negligible bound allowed to depend on the family. A public-key bit-encryption scheme consists of \(Gen(1^{\lambda})=(pk,sk), Enc(pk,b)=c\) for \(b\in \{0,1\}\), and \(Dec(sk,c)\in \{0,1,\perp\}\). There is one negligible \(
u\) such that for every \(\lambda\) and b, \(\Pr[\operatorname{Dec}(sk,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,b))
e b]\le
u(\lambda)\), over key generation and encryption. In the IND-CPA experiment Gen is run, the adversary receives pk and selects bits \(b_{0},b_{1}\) and a state, an independent uniform \( eta \in \{0,1\}\) is chosen, \(c=Enc(pk,b_{ eta})\) is returned, and the adversary outputs \( eta '\). Require \(|\Pr[ eta\prime= eta]-1/2|\) to be negligible. The adversary may perform any polynomial number of public encryptions on its own before and after the challenge. For FHE, Gen outputs (pk,evk,sk); the evaluation key evk is public and is included with pk in the IND-CPA experiment. Gen receives no circuit size or depth bound. Eval(evk,\(C,c_{1},\ldots ,c_{t}\)) outputs one ciphertext for a circuit \(C:\{0,1\}^{t}	o \{0,1\}\), encoded as an acyclic \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}/\mathrm{NOT}\) circuit with listed wires. For every polynomial s there is a negligible \(
u _{s}\) such that for every \(\lambda\), every such C of description length and input count at most \(s(\lambda )\), and every \(m\in \{0,1\}^{t}\), independently of the generated keys, \(\Pr[\operatorname{Dec}(sk,\operatorname{Eval}(evk,C,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,m_1),\ldots,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,m_t)))
e C(m)]\le
u_s(\lambda)\). The probability includes key generation, fresh encryption coins for each bit, and evaluation coins. Eval’s time is polynomial in the entire supplied circuit and ciphertext encoding, with one algorithm for all C. There is one polynomial q, independent of C,t and s, bounding every evaluated ciphertext length and its decryption time by \(q(\lambda )\); keys also have polynomial length. cards.title: PZK versus SZK
cards.formal: Does PZK=SZK for classical single-prover interactive proofs of promise problems, with polynomial-time verifiers and simulators, negligible proof error, and zero knowledge against every polynomial-time verifier?
cards.definitions: A promise problem is a pair \((Y,N)\) of disjoint sets of finite binary strings. An interactive proof consists of a computationally unbounded prover P and a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time verifier V exchanging polynomially many bits on common input x. There is a negligible function \(\varepsilon\) such that on \(x\in Y\) the honest interaction accepts with probability at least \(1- \varepsilon (|x|)\), and on \(x\in N\) every prover strategy is accepted with probability at most \(\varepsilon (|x|)\). Negligible means smaller than |\(x|^{- d}\) for every fixed \(d>0\) at all sufficiently large lengths. No condition is imposed outside \(Y\cup N\). The view of a verifier consists of its random bits and exchanged messages. SZK requires that for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time verifier V* there is a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time simulator S* which, on x alone, produces a distribution within negligible total variation distance of the view of \((\mathrm{P},V*)(x)\), for every \(x\in Y\). Total variation distance is one half of the sum of absolute probability differences over possible views. PZK instead permits S* to output a failure symbol ⊥ with probability at most \(1/2\); conditioned on nonfailure, its output distribution must equal that view exactly. Every runtime bound is a strict polynomial bound over all random outcomes, with a polynomial allowed to depend on the fixed verifier or simulator. This is the ordinary input-only simulation convention of the cited definitions, without a shared random string, an oracle, a setup assumption, or a restriction to honest verifiers.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every promise problem admitting the stated statistical proof also admits a perfect one in this model, or exhibit a promise problem in SZK and prove that it has no PZK proof. The protocol may change completely in a positive result. An oracle separation, a failure of one proposed compiler, a perfect-zero-knowledge PCP, or an honest-verifier-only theorem does not resolve this unrelativized class equality.

context_blocks.text: Zero knowledge formalizes the idea that a verifier can reproduce what it sees without receiving help from the prover. Statistical simulation permits a negligible discrepancy between distributions. Perfect simulation requires exact agreement after the allowed failure event. Goldreich’s textbook asks whether this difference changes which statements can be proved.

The failure convention is part of the model. A strict polynomial-time perfect simulator that never fails is a different requirement, often called super-perfect zero knowledge. Allowing an expected polynomial runtime is also a separate definitional issue discussed in the source. Neither convention is silently substituted here.

PZK is contained in SZK: repeat the bounded-failure perfect simulator polynomially many times until it succeeds, and use an arbitrary output if every attempt fails. The remaining probability of failure is negligible, while successful outputs retain the exact distribution. The open direction asks whether negligible simulation error can always be eliminated by some proof system.

Bouland, Chen, Holden, Thaler and Vasudevan construct an oracle relative to which SZK is not contained in PZK. This supplies evidence against equality and rules out a proof that relativizes in the corresponding way. It does not separate the classes in the ordinary model specified here.

Gur, O’Connor and Spooner explicitly retain PZK versus SZK as open in their 2024 paper. Their perfect-zero-knowledge construction is for probabilistically checkable proofs, where a verifier queries a proof oracle. That achievement concerns a different access model from ordinary interactive proofs and leaves this equality unresolved.

The target asks for a class equality, not a quantitative improvement in a particular cryptographic protocol. Its resolution would determine whether exact distributional privacy has an intrinsic expressive cost. TCS-1929 instead concerns zero knowledge for streaming interactive proofs with a memory restriction.

cards.title: Low-noise LPN hardness from Nearest Codeword hardness
cards.formal: Does the following implication hold? If binary Nearest Codeword is not in BPP, then no uniform probabilistic polynomial-time distinguisher D has advantage at least $n^{-c}$, for any fixed $c>0$ and all sufficiently large square n, between $(A,As+e)$ and $(A,u)$. Here $A\in\mathbb F_2^{n^2\times n}$, $s\in\mathbb F_2^n$, and $u\in\mathbb F_2^{n^2}$ are independent uniform random variables, and the coordinates of e are independent Bernoulli variables with rate $1/\sqrt n$. Advantage is the absolute difference of D’s acceptance probabilities in the two experiments.
cards.why: A basic security assumption would obtain an explanation through independently studied hardness. The extra assumption in the new reduction makes the remaining target concrete.

progress.text: The revision gives a reduction for $\eta=n^{-\alpha}$, any constant $\alpha<1$, from simultaneous worst-case hardness of two tasks on a code and its dual. This advances beyond earlier near-half-noise reductions; the single-assumption target remains stronger.

cards.review_note: Editorial specialization of the NCP-only direction in Section 1.2 of the September 2026 revision. It fixes the starting problem, decision-LPN distribution, sample count, noise, uniformity, and asymptotic advantage, replacing the vague phrase natural worst-case problem. The source does not state this exact parameter specialization as a numbered conjecture.

context_blocks.text: LWE has strong connections to worst-case lattice problems. Establishing comparable foundations for LPN at cryptographically useful noise rates is more difficult.

Without noise, enough independent parity equations reveal the secret by linear algebra. Flipping some answers breaks that direct procedure: the learner must cope with equations whose right-hand sides may be wrong. At a low noise rate, most equations remain correct, which makes the precise source of hardness especially important.

A worst-case-to-average-case reduction would start with an arbitrary hard coding instance and turn it into the random samples used by LPN. It must preserve a usable noise regime and show how an LPN solver would solve the original task. Requiring two different coding tasks to be hard simultaneously is a stronger premise than deriving the guarantee from one standard worst-case problem.

cards.definitions: Binary Nearest Codeword receives a binary matrix G, a binary target y with the same number of rows, and an integer t, and asks whether $\min_z\operatorname{wt}(Gz-y)\le t$, with arithmetic over \(F_{2}\) and Hamming weight wt. BPP means a uniform randomized polynomial-time decider correct with probability at least \(2/3\) on every instance. The LPN side here is a decision problem with n-squared samples, random secret, and inverse-square-root noise. Restricting n to squares makes the noise parameter an exact rational; this is an explicit specialization of the source’s broader low-noise direction.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed complexity-theoretic implication, for example by a reduction turning such an LPN distinguisher into a BPP algorithm for Nearest Codeword, or prove that the implication is false. Invoking simultaneous hardness of an additional problem on the dual code does not establish this implication.

importance.reason: Would connect worst-case coding hardness to a central average-case cryptographic assumption in a concrete low-noise regime.

cards.title: One-way functions in \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\) from one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of a classical one-way function imply the existence of a classical one-way function computed by a polynomial-time uniform \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\) circuit family?
cards.definitions: The security parameter \(\lambda\) is supplied in unary. Algorithms are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time machines; security is against nonuniform polynomial-size classical circuit families. A function \(\nu (\lambda )\) is negligible if for every \(c>0, \nu (\lambda )\le \lambda ^{- c}\) for all sufficiently large \(\lambda\). Probabilities include setup, algorithm and adversary coins. No ideal oracle or additional trusted setup is supplied unless explicitly stated; arbitrary non-black-box implications are allowed. A one-way function is a deterministic polynomial-time map \(f:\{0,1\}*\to \{0,1\}\)* of polynomially bounded, length-dependent output size, such that every allowed inverter on \((1^{n},f(U_{n}))\) finds any n-bit preimage with negligible probability, for uniform \(U_{n}\). A polynomial-time uniform \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\) family is generated from \(1^{n}\) in \(\operatorname{poly}(n)\) time, has polynomial size and a universal constant depth, and uses fan-in-two \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}\) and unary NOT gates. Inversion security quantifies over all polynomial-size adversaries, not just shallow ones.

context_blocks.text: Local evaluation and global inversion difficulty are strikingly different requirements. An \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\) one-way function has each output bit depend on only a constant number of input bits, while inverting the full output must defeat every polynomial-size adversary.

Known locality transformations start from stronger assumptions such as one-way functions in \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\). Those constructions establish plausible \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\) cryptography, but they do not derive it from an arbitrary sequentially computable one-way function. The implication therefore asks whether cryptographic hardness can always be made local.

cards.why: Identify whether extreme locality is inherent in minimal cryptographic hardness or requires a stronger assumption.

Finally the adversary guesses \( eta\). Its absolute advantage over \(1/2\) must be negligible. The number and total length of queries are bounded by the adversary’s polynomial size. Illegal challenge or extraction queries abort the game with an independent fair guess, contributing zero advantage. There are no decryption queries; all public encryption calls can be performed by the adversary itself. The existence implication permits non-black-box constructions and provides no random oracle, extra setup or assumption beyond the stated PKE existence. The key generator is part of the IBE functionality, not an external assumption.

cards.title: Exponentially hard weak versus strong one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of an exponentially hard weak one-way function imply the existence of an exponentially hard strong one-way function, in the following nonuniform-adversary, negligible-success formulation? The premise is that there exist a uniform polynomial-time computable length-preserving function \(f\), a real \(a>0\), an integer \(k\ge1\), and \(n_0\), such that \[\operatorname{Inv}_f(C,n)\le1-n^{-k}\] for every \(n\ge n_0\) and every circuit \(C\) with \(n\) inputs, \(n\) outputs and at most \(2^{an}\) gates. The desired conclusion is that there exist another uniform polynomial-time computable length-preserving function \(g\) and a real \(b>0\) such that, for every integer \(d\ge1\), there is \(n_d\) with \[\operatorname{Inv}_g(C,n)\le n^{-d}\] for every \(n\ge n_d\) and every such circuit with at most \(2^{bn}\) gates. The constants and function in the conclusion may depend on those witnessing the premise.
cards.why: Ordinary hardness amplification equates weak and strong one-wayness at polynomial security scales. Preserving hardness exponential in the actual input length would extend that equivalence to a much stronger regime and clarify how fine-grained average-case hardness supports cryptographic security.

sentences: The premise is a polynomial-time function that defeats exponential-size inversion circuits on an inverse-polynomial fraction of inputs.
The question asks whether this already guarantees a function whose inversion success is negligible for exponential-size circuits.
An attacker succeeds by finding any preimage of a challenge sampled from a uniform input.
Ordinary repetition enlarges the input and can lose hardness exponential in the new length.

cards.definitions:
A length-preserving function is a single map \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) with \(|f(x)|=|x|\), computed by one deterministic multitape Turing machine in at most \(A(n+1)^r\) steps on every input of length \(n\), for some fixed constants \(A,r\). The same convention applies to \(g\). There is no oracle or advice in forward evaluation.

For a circuit \(C:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^n\), define its inversion success by \[\operatorname{Inv}_f(C,n)=\Pr_{x\leftarrow U_n}\bigl[f(C(f(x)))=f(x)\bigr],\] where \(U_n\) is uniform on all length-\(n\) bit strings. Finding any length-\(n\) preimage counts as success; the output need not equal the originally sampled \(x\). The challenge is sampled by applying \(f\) to a uniform input, not by choosing a uniform element of its image.

Circuits are finite directed acyclic graphs of fan-in-two AND and OR gates, fan-in-one NOT gates and constants, with named inputs and outputs. Size counts noninput gates, including constants; no restriction is placed on fan-out. Real size limits mean their integer floors. Every circuit is allowed independently at each input length, including circuits with information built into their wiring and constants. No uniform procedure for generating the attack circuits is required. Deterministic circuits suffice for the displayed average-success bound: a randomized attack is a distribution over such circuits, and averaging cannot exceed their common bound.

Weakness means a fixed inverse-polynomial fraction of the sampled challenges defeats every allowed attacker. Strongness here means that the maximum success of any allowed attacker is negligible: smaller than every fixed inverse power for sufficiently large lengths. The exponent \(b\) is fixed before \(d\). This explicitly uses negligible success against exponential-size circuits; it does not add a separate exponentially small success requirement. Security is measured against the input length of each function itself, on all sufficiently large lengths. Both functions are length-preserving, following the source's stated convention; arbitrary padding is not assumed to preserve exponential hardness.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of this implication, or a proof of its negation. A positive answer may use an arbitrary construction or existence argument and need not preserve the original security exponent. It must produce a single polynomial-time function with a positive linear exponential attack-size exponent and negligible inversion success. A negative answer must refute the existence implication itself; a barrier for black-box transformations or for a restricted amplification method is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: The reverse implication is immediate: negligible inversion success also leaves an inverse-polynomial fraction of inputs hard. The substantive question is the weak-to-strong direction. It does not ask to prove that one-way functions exist without assumptions.

The usual direct-product amplification evaluates the weak function on many independent blocks. Its enlarged input length can turn exponential security in a block length into only stretched-exponential security in the new length. The 2025 revision explicitly identifies this loss as the unresolved issue.

Security-preserving amplification is known under regularity assumptions: at a fixed input length, every value in the image of a regular function has the same number of preimages. The present premise includes arbitrary functions with unequal fiber sizes, so that special case does not establish the general implication.

The question is about existence of a suitable strong function. It does not demand a black-box reduction, restrict forward computation to constant depth, or require the new function to use the same input length as a single invocation of the old one. Its exponential guarantee is nevertheless measured in its own full input length.

cards.title: Subpolynomial-key perfectly secure three-server DPFs
cards.formal: Does there exist a fixed finite Abelian group \(G\), with \(|G|\ge2\), and a uniform three-server distributed point function with perfect correctness, perfect privacy against any one server, and worst-case key length \(\ell(N)=N^{o(1)}\)? For every integer \(N\ge2\), location \(\alpha\in[N]\), and value \(\beta\in G\), key generation must produce three binary keys \((k_0,k_1,k_2)\) such that \[\sum_{i=0}^{2}\operatorname{Eval}_i(k_i,x)=\begin{cases}\beta&x=\alpha,\\0_G&x\ne\alpha\end{cases}\qquad\text{for every }x\in[N]\] with probability one. For each individual \(i\), the distribution of \(k_i\) must be identical for all pairs \((\alpha,\beta)\) with the same \(N\). Every generated key must have at most \(\ell(N)\) bits. The fixed output group may be chosen as part of a positive answer; requiring all output groups is the source's separate question.
cards.why: Distributed point functions compress secret shares of a sparse vector while letting each holder evaluate its share locally. Resolving the three-server question would locate a basic boundary for information-theoretic compression and privacy, with consequences for private retrieval and secure computation that use additive reconstruction.
cards.status_note: Open in the 2022 source and still identified as lacking a perfectly secure three-party construction in the 2026 survey’s February literature snapshot. sentences: A distributed point function gives three servers compact shares of a vector supported at one secret location.
Each server can evaluate its own share, and the three outputs must add to the requested point function.
A single key must reveal exactly no information about either the location or the stored value.
The target is a key length smaller than every positive power of the domain size over some fixed nontrivial finite Abelian group.
Known subpolynomial constructions achieve perfect privacy with four servers or statistical privacy with three, a distinction retained in a 2026 survey.

cards.definitions:
Write \([N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}\). A finite Abelian group is a finite set with an associative and commutative addition, identity \(0_G\), and additive inverses. Its elements have fixed binary names, and its addition table is fixed with the scheme. The point function is zero away from one specified input and takes the specified value there. The case \(\beta=0_G\) is included.

A scheme consists of one randomized Turing machine \(\operatorname{Gen}\) and three deterministic Turing machines \(\operatorname{Eval}_i\), all fixed independently of \(N,\alpha,\beta\). The generator receives the binary encodings of \(N,\alpha,\beta\) and produces three finite bit strings. It may use independent fair bits and must halt with probability one. This convention permits exact sampling from a fixed group of odd order by rejection sampling. Each evaluation machine halts on every valid key and domain input and returns one element of \(G\). The key determines \(N\); its encoding, all public corrections, and any parameter descriptions used in evaluation count toward key length. The machines and the fixed group table are public. There is no additional shared random tape, hidden setup, or uncounted data depending on the particular point function.

This card asks for the information-theoretic key-length bound: it imposes no running-time bound beyond these algorithmic termination conditions. Perfect correctness means that the displayed identities hold simultaneously for all domain inputs with probability one over key generation. Perfect privacy means equality of each single key's entire probability distribution, including its length. Consequently even unlimited computation and arbitrarily many evaluations of that key cannot reveal the location or value. Privacy against a coalition of two servers is not required.

The bound is uniform over locations, values, server indices, and all keys having positive probability. Subpolynomial length means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\), some \(N_\varepsilon\) satisfies \(\ell(N)\le N^{\varepsilon}\) for all integers \(N\ge N_\varepsilon\). The same fixed group and algorithms must work for all \(N\). A security parameter is unnecessary because the privacy error is exactly zero.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such a scheme exists, or a proof that no such scheme exists. A positive answer must specify the algorithms and prove correctness, equality of all required key distributions, termination, and the asymptotic key-length bound. A negative answer must cover every fixed nontrivial finite Abelian output group. Statistical privacy with arbitrarily small positive error, or a construction using four servers, does not meet this target.

context_blocks.text: The source obtains subpolynomial keys with three servers when privacy has a small statistical error, and with four servers when privacy is perfect for suitable fixed output groups. This question asks whether three servers can also achieve exact privacy.

The requirement hides both the special location and its output value. Ordinary private information retrieval permits a client to reconstruct replies using additional private information; such a protocol is not automatically a distributed point function whose server outputs add directly to the desired value.

The card makes the output-group scope explicit: existence for some fixed nontrivial group. It does not require a bound uniform over growing groups. The later paper extends the groups supported by efficient information-theoretic constructions, but the checked statements use different server counts or permit statistical security.

The 2026 survey continues to distinguish the known four-party perfectly secure construction from the three-party statistically secure one. Its stated literature snapshot is February 2026, even though the arXiv version was submitted in July.

cards.title: Sublinear communication for perfectly secure two-party computation
cards.formal: Is there a uniform two-party protocol in the trusted correlated-randomness model that perfectly computes every Boolean circuit \(C:\{0,1\}^n\times\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) with polynomial setup and computation, and online communication \(O(n+g(s))\) for some function \(g(s)=o(s)\), where \(s\) is the circuit's supplied size? More precisely, seek fixed algorithms, constants \(K,q\ge1\), and \(g:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb R_{\ge1}\) with \(\lim_{s\to\infty}g(s)/s=0\), such that every circuit and every pair of inputs satisfy the correctness and privacy conditions below; dealer computation, total setup length and both parties' computation are at most \(K(n+s+1)^q\), while at most \(K(n+g(s))\) bits are exchanged online. The circuit is arbitrary, without a layering or depth restriction. The additive input-length term fixes the source's sublinearity question in a form that also covers circuits of linear size.

sentences: Two parties want to compute a Boolean circuit while keeping each input perfectly private.
A trusted dealer can distribute correlated randomness before either input is supplied.
The question asks whether polynomial setup and computation can give online communication sublinear in the circuit size, apart from the input-length cost.
Such savings are known for layered circuits, while completely optimal communication can require exponential setup.
The unresolved target covers arbitrary circuits with perfect passive privacy and shared outputs.

cards.definitions:
A circuit is an explicitly given finite directed acyclic graph with \(2n\) input vertices, Boolean constants, fan-in-two AND/OR gates, NOT gates, and one designated output. Fan-out is unrestricted. Let \(s\) count all vertices, including inputs and constants; in particular \(s\ge2n\). Gates and predecessors are encoded in topological order with binary indices. Both parties and the dealer know this public description. The inputs \(x_0,x_1\in\{0,1\}^n\) are private to their respective parties. The size in the bound is that of the supplied circuit; the protocol may optimize its computation, but cannot charge an artificially padded circuit to increase its communication allowance.

Before the parties receive their inputs, a trusted randomized dealer, given only \(C\), samples finite correlated strings \((r_0,r_1)\) and privately sends \(r_b\) to party \(b\). These strings may depend on \(C\) but not on either input. The dealer then takes no further part. Dealer randomness consists of independent fair bits; its computation and output length obey the polynomial bound on every run. Independent local random tapes can be included in these strings. After this phase the parties are deterministic machines on their input, setup string and message history. Their descriptions are fixed across all circuits and lengths, and their complete online runtimes obey the same polynomial bound. There is no other setup, oracle or computational hardness assumption.

The parties exchange binary messages and output private bits \(y_0,y_1\). Perfect correctness means
\[\Pr[y_0\mathbin\oplus y_1=C(x_0,x_1)]=1\]
for every input pair, where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. The task uses the source's shared-output convention: neither party is required to learn the reconstructed answer. Perfect privacy against one passive corruption means that, for each \(b\) and each fixed \(C,x_b\), the distribution of party \(b\)'s entire view is identical for every choice of the other party's input. Its view includes \(r_b\), all sent and received messages and its output. A passive adversary follows the protocol and may inspect that entire view with unlimited computation; the parties do not collude. Privacy and correctness have zero error.

Online cost is the worst-case number of bits sent in both directions, over inputs and all dealer outcomes of positive probability. Message boundaries, control information and input-dependent stopping must be encoded in this communication; timing and silence are not free channels. There is no separate round bound beyond polynomial runtime. The dealer's private deliveries are excluded from online communication but included in the setup-length bound. For every family whose circuit size is polynomial in \(n\), the stated \(\operatorname{poly}(n+s)\) resource bound is polynomial in the input length, as required by the source. A single choice of algorithms, \(K,q,g\) must work for all such families, not only a fixed function or depth.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence, including perfect privacy, correctness, polynomial setup/computation and a uniform sublinear \(g\), or prove that no such protocol and resource bounds exist. A protocol for layered circuits only, a computationally secure construction, or a truth-table protocol using setup exponential in \(n\) does not settle this target. A negative answer must rule out all sublinear savings allowed above, rather than only exactly optimal or one-round online communication.

context_blocks.text: The input-independent setup is a resource, not a free truth table of the function. Beaver-style evaluation uses linear-size correlated randomness and linear online communication. A one-time truth table can make communication linear in the input length, but its exponential setup falls outside this question.

Couteau gives perfect passive-security protocols for layered circuits with communication \(O(n+s/\log\log s)\) for a fixed number of parties and a constant-size output, using polynomial storage. In a layered circuit every edge joins consecutive layers. Transforming a general circuit into this form can increase its size and therefore does not automatically give sublinear cost relative to the original circuit.

cards.title: Polynomial-time computationally sound verification of \(\#\mathrm{SAT}\)
cards.formal: Do there exist deterministic uniform algorithms \(P,V\), integers \(C>c\ge1\), and a constant \(K\ge2\) giving the following plain-model argument system for exact \(\#\mathrm{SAT}\), without unproved hardness assumptions? On a Boolean formula \(\Phi\) encoded in \(N\) bits, \(P\) produces a proof of length at most \((N+1)^C\) in time \(T_P(N)=2^{K(N+1)^c}\). The verifier runs in time \(K(N+1)^C\) and outputs either the exact number of satisfying assignments or the rejection symbol \(\bot\). Completeness requires \(V(\Phi,P(\Phi))=\#\mathrm{SAT}(\Phi)\) on every valid formula. Soundness requires that every uniform randomized adversary running in any fixed polynomial in \(T_P(N)\) has only negligible probability, as a function of \(T_P(N)\), of generating a length-\(N\) formula and a proof on which \(V\) outputs an incorrect number. This card fixes the unconditional version of the source question; conditional constructions are recorded below.
cards.why: Exact counting requires certifying that no satisfying assignments were missed, as well as that counted assignments exist. This question tests whether computational soundness can give deterministic short verification of such global information while retaining an honest prover with a specified running time. It connects the power of proof systems with derandomization and the distinction between uniform computational attacks and arbitrary false witnesses.
cards.status_note: Open Problem 4.5 of the 2023 source was checked together with the 3 April 2025 revision of Chen–Rothblum–Tell on 2026-09-14. The latter gives conditional polynomial-time verification under strong hardness assumptions; this card explicitly selects unconditional existence with its honest-prover/adversary convention. A bounded later-work search found no unconditional resolution.

sentences: The task is to check the exact number of satisfying assignments to a Boolean formula in polynomial time.
An exponential-time honest prover supplies a short proof to a fully deterministic verifier.
Even adversaries running in any polynomial in the honest prover’s time must almost never find a false counting claim that the verifier accepts.

This card asks whether the specified counting-verification system exists without those unproved assumptions.

cards.definitions:
Fix a polynomial-time parsable binary encoding of formulas over AND, OR and NOT. An instance lists its \(n\) variables explicitly, so \(n\le N\), and its formula is a finite tree with leaves among those variables and Boolean constants. The value \(\#\mathrm{SAT}(\Phi)\) is the number of assignments in \(\{0,1\}^n\) on which the formula evaluates to one, including choices of any listed unused variables. The answer is written in binary and has at most \(n+1\) bits. Measuring resources in the full encoding length fixes the meaning of polynomial-size formulas and includes the cost of reading their descriptions.

The prover and verifier are deterministic multitape Turing machines with finite descriptions independent of input length. The proof is one finite binary string; there is no interaction, oracle, common reference string, advice, secret setup or verifier randomness. The verifier rejects malformed instances and overlong proofs. It halts within its stated bound on every input, reading at most one symbol beyond the permitted proof length to detect excess input. Increasing the fixed constant \(K\) absorbs encoding and rejection overhead. The honest prover must construct its proof in the stated exponential time; mere existence of a proof with no bound on its production is insufficient.

More explicitly, for every uniform probabilistic Turing machine \(A\) whose worst-case runtime on \(1^N\) is at most \(T_P(N)^a\) for some fixed \(a\ge1\), and for every integer \(d\ge1\), there is \(N_{A,d}\) such that, for every \(N\ge N_{A,d}\),
\[\Pr_{(\Phi,\pi)\leftarrow A(1^N)}\bigl[\Phi\text{ is valid},\ |\Phi|=N,\ V(\Phi,\pi)\notin\{\#\mathrm{SAT}(\Phi),\bot\}\bigr]\le T_P(N)^{-d}.\]
Probability is over independent fair random bits used by \(A\). Any output that is not a valid formula/proof pair is a failed attack. The adversary chooses both the formula and its proof, knows \(P,V\), and has no nonuniform advice or auxiliary input. The polynomial exponent \(a\) may be arbitrarily large and is not fixed by the protocol. Negligibility is measured in the honest prover's time, rather than merely inverse polynomial in the formula length. The constants \(c,C,K\) and the two machines must be fixed before quantifying over adversaries and accuracy exponents.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such a system exists, including all completeness, uniformity, running-time and soundness requirements, or prove that no such system exists. A positive answer must be unconditional. A construction assuming a conjectured hard function is progress but does not settle this selected version. Randomized verification, interaction, a setup string, soundness only against polynomial-in-input-length adversaries, or an unbounded honest prover changes the question.

context_blocks.text: Computational soundness permits incorrect proofs to exist, provided no adversary with the specified resources can generate a false instance together with an accepted proof. Ordinary NP soundness forbids every false proof. Allowing nonuniform advice would let an adversary hardwire a false pair at each input length, removing this distinction.

The honest prover is allowed exponential time, and the adversary is allowed every polynomial in that time. Requiring a polynomial-time honest prover would instead give a polynomial-time exact counting algorithm by composing prover and verifier. Allowing an arbitrarily stronger honest prover than the attacker would also distort the model; the later paper explains why.

The 2023 source gives, under strong assumptions, verification in time \(2^{\varepsilon n}\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), with an honest prover and adversaries using \(2^{O(n)}\) time. Its next question asks for a polynomial-time verifier.

The 2025 paper proves \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\subseteq\mathrm{cs}\text{-}\mathrm{NP}\) under strong assumptions about functions that remain hard for small-space computation on efficiently samplable inputs. Its Definition 1.1 explicitly allows a polynomial-time verifier with an exponential-time honest prover. Applying its polynomial-space verification result to exact-count claims gives conditional progress on this card, since exact counting can be performed in polynomial space. The paper does not prove the required hardness assumptions.

cards.definitions:
The common input is the full truth table \(x\) of a function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), with \(n\geq1\) and \(N=2^n\). Let \(C(f)\) be its minimum Boolean circuit size. Fix the standard basis of binary AND and OR and unary NOT, with constant inputs available, arbitrary fan-out, one output, and size equal to the number of gates. Circuits are acyclic and compute every truth-table entry correctly.

A yes-instance satisfies \(C(f)\leq N^\varepsilon\). A no-instance satisfies \(C(f)>N^{1-\varepsilon}\). Inputs between these thresholds have no required decision outcome. The strict no-threshold follows the formal definition in the later source; the thresholds need not be integers. The constant \(\varepsilon\) is chosen once, not supplied per instance. The task has both low-complexity and high-complexity promised inputs at arbitrarily large lengths.

An interactive proof has an honest prover \(P\) and a randomized verifier \(V\). Total communication, rounds and verifier computation are polynomial in \(N\), the explicit truth-table length. No computational bound is imposed on the prover. On every yes-instance, the honest interaction accepts with probability at least \(2/3\). On every no-instance, every cheating prover, including an unbounded one, causes acceptance with probability at most \(1/3\). This is a proof system; soundness only against efficient provers would be an argument system.

Computational zero knowledge requires that for every randomized polynomial-time verifier \(V^*\), including one given arbitrary polynomial-length auxiliary information \(z\), there is a randomized polynomial-time simulator \(S_{V^*}\). Given only \(x,z\), it produces a distribution computationally indistinguishable from the entire view of \(V^*\) in the honest-prover interaction on \(x\). That view includes the common input, auxiliary information, verifier randomness, messages and final output. The simulator is not given a small circuit or other witness.

Indistinguishability is required on all yes-instances: every polynomial-size distinguishing circuit has only negligible advantage in \(N\), uniformly over these instances and polynomial-length auxiliary strings. Negligible means smaller than \(N^{-c}\) for every fixed positive \(c\) at sufficiently large \(N\). The simulator and verifier use the ordinary polynomial-time convention of the later source. No setup, random oracle, trusted third party or hardness assumption is supplied.

The chosen circuit basis fixes a concrete representation. The existential constant-gap formulation tolerates constant-factor changes of standard finite bases by choosing a slightly wider gap and handling finitely many small lengths separately. It does not identify circuits with a shortest program: MINKT instead bounds the program length needed to print a string within a supplied time budget, and its gap parameters constitute a separate choice.

The target asks for one protocol meeting worst-case completeness, soundness and zero knowledge at every input length. A protocol that succeeds on most inputs from a particular distribution or only at infinitely many lengths is a weaker result.
cards.answer_criterion: Give some fixed admissible gap constant and a protocol with proofs of polynomial verifier and simulator cost, completeness, soundness against all provers, and computational zero knowledge against arbitrary efficient auxiliary-input verifiers, without assuming one-way functions or another hardness premise. A negative answer must rule out the specified protocols for every constant in this selected gap family. Failure for that family would not by itself refute all alternatives in the original broader question.

cards.title: Quantum PCP conjecture with classical reductions
cards.formal:
Do there exist fixed positive integers \(k,d\) and a rational constant \(0<\varepsilon<1\) for which the following promise problem \(\mathrm{LH}_{k,d,\varepsilon}\) is QMA-hard under deterministic classical polynomial-time many-one reductions? An instance specifies \(n\geq1\) qubits, \(1\leq m\leq(n+1)^d\) local terms \(H_1,\ldots,H_m\), and rational thresholds \(0\leq a<b\leq1\) with \(b-a\geq\varepsilon\). Each term acts on at most \(k\) qubits, has rational real and imaginary matrix entries, and satisfies \(0\preceq H_i\preceq I\). For the normalized Hamiltonian
\[H=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m H_i,\]
distinguish \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\leq a\) from \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\geq b\). The classical reduction requirement preserves the saved card’s variant; the cited survey’s standard formulation permits quantum reductions.
cards.why: This asks whether coarse average-energy estimation retains the full difficulty of verification with an arbitrary quantum witness. The per-term normalization prevents a numerical rescaling from creating the required gap. A positive result would give a robust quantum analogue of classical constraint-satisfaction hardness, with consequences for the computational structure of low-energy states. The saved classical-reduction version additionally requires that the hard physical instance be produced without quantum computation.

cards.title_en: Quantum PCP conjecture with classical reductions

context_blocks.text: Editorial scope: the existing card explicitly chose deterministic classical reductions. This review preserves that mathematical target and qualifies the title. Aharonov, Arad and Vidick instead state their Conjecture 1.3 under quantum polynomial-time reductions, and explain that permitting quantum reductions is needed for the known equivalence with their proof-verification formulation. The stronger reduction requirement here is therefore not attributed to their conjecture as an established equivalent formulation.

The classical PCP theorem gives constant-gap hardness for constraint satisfaction. Quantum local Hamiltonians replace local Boolean penalties by local operators, while a global state may be entangled across all qubits. The quantum Cook–Levin theorem establishes QMA-completeness at inverse-polynomial relative precision. The constant relative gap asked for here remains an additional claim. The no case rules out low average energy for every state, rather than only product states or a specified family of trial states.

Anshu, Breuckmann and Nirkhe proved the no-low-energy-trivial-states theorem, first announced in 2022 and published at STOC 2023. Their families have bounded-size local interactions and a fixed positive energy-density threshold below which state preparation needs depth \(\Omega(\log n)\). Depth counts layers of disjoint bounded-size quantum gates, with no geometric restriction. This establishes a strong structural phenomenon in low-energy states, but is not a reduction proving QMA-hardness of distinguishing high and low ground energies. In particular, their theorem’s Hamiltonians are frustration-free: they have a common zero-energy state.

The games version also requires care. Natarajan and Nirkhe’s 2024 status note identifies an error in an earlier Natarajan–Vidick energy-amplification argument that invalidates its claimed games PCP for a QMA-complete problem. Their note distinguishes efficient honest provers from arbitrarily powerful entangled provers. Neither the old claim nor general results about interactive games supply the Hamiltonian statement on this card.

Buhrman, Helsen and Weggemans give a detailed quantum reduction between constant-query proof checking and local Hamiltonians, and clarify adaptive-query and multiple-prover variants. Their 2025 theorem controls approximation of a verifier’s acceptance probability by an energy and can produce a fixed classical Hamiltonian description with high probability. The reduction itself is quantum. These structural results do not establish that all QMA problems have constant-query proofs, or that the needed Hamiltonian descriptions can always be computed by classical reductions.

The October 2025 Bergamaschi–Metger–Vidick–Zhang preprint proves a gap-amplification result with an increase in the locality of the resulting Hamiltonian. Its locality-gap tradeoff does not preserve a constant locality throughout the full conjectured gap increase. Thus it is a distinct partial result even though its reductions can be deterministic.

Sun and Vidick’s June 2026 preprint gives interactive oracle proofs for QMA with polynomial total communication, polylogarithmic query and round counts, and a constant soundness gap. The interaction and nonconstant query bounds are part of the theorem. It does not assert the noninteractive, constant-locality Hamiltonian hardness asked for here. Its full proof has not been independently verified in this review.

Nguyen’s July 23, 2026 Simons talk abstract explicitly keeps the general quantum PCP question open and reports amplification of a combinatorial gap. The checked abstract does not assert the full normalized energy-gap theorem. A matching full paper or video proof was not verified in this review.

Bafna and Vyas’s August 19, 2026 preprint also explicitly describes quantum PCP as open. It concerns classical private PCPs for NP, with nonconstant query complexity and additional parameter improvements conditional on a product-expansion conjecture. Its classical result does not verify quantum witnesses or settle this Hamiltonian problem.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the full stated existence of constants and classical QMA-hardness, or of its logical negation. A positive answer must prove the reduction guarantees and their uniform polynomial resource bounds for all QMA promise pairs with one fixed target triple \((k,d,\varepsilon)\). A negative answer must establish that for every allowed triple there is a QMA promise pair admitting no qualifying classical reduction to that target problem. The source pair may depend on the triple. A lower bound on one proposed reduction, a counterexample only to a particular construction, an oracle separation, or an algorithm for a restricted Hamiltonian family is not this negation. A proof allowing only quantum reductions does not by itself prove the saved classical-reduction variant; conversely, refuting the latter need not refute the weaker standard formulation. Constant-gap hardness with growing locality, a theorem solely about preparation depth of low-energy states, or an interactive verification theorem does not meet this answer criterion.
cards.definitions:
A qubit has state space \(\mathbb C^2\), with basis \(|0\rangle=(1,0)\) and \(|1\rangle=(0,1)\). The \(n\)-qubit state space is \(\mathcal H_n=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes n}\). A pure state is a vector of norm one; a general state is a positive semidefinite Hermitian operator \(\rho\) of trace one on that space. The adjoint \(M^*\) is the conjugate transpose, and \(M\) is Hermitian when \(M=M^*\). The order \(M\preceq N\) means that \(N-M\) is Hermitian and \(z^*(N-M)z\geq0\) for every complex vector \(z\). The symbol \(I\) denotes the identity on the relevant space.

A local term is specified by an increasing list of \(\ell\) distinct qubit indices, with \(0\leq\ell\leq\min(k,n)\), and the complete \(2^\ell\)-by-\(2^\ell\) matrix in lexicographic computational-basis order on these indices. It acts as that matrix on the listed tensor factors and as identity on all other factors. A zero-qubit matrix is a scalar multiple of the identity. The bounds \(0\preceq H_i\preceq I\) concern the embedded operator, equivalently its supplied local matrix. Different terms may overlap and need not commute. Repeated terms are allowed and counted in \(m\). No spatial geometry, bound on the number of terms touching one qubit, or common zero-energy state is required.

The ground energy is
\[\lambda_{\min}(H)=\min_{\|\psi\|=1}\langle\psi,H\psi\rangle
=\min_{\rho\succeq0,\,\operatorname{tr}\rho=1}\operatorname{tr}(H\rho).\]
Both minima range over all global states, including entangled ones; no circuit preparation or classical description bound is imposed on a state. The promise gap \(b-a\) separates the two input cases. It is not a gap between the first and second eigenvalues of one Hamiltonian. The normalization and the per-term bound fix the energy scale, so \(0\leq\lambda_{\min}(H)\leq1\).

The input is an explicit finite bit string. To fix an encoding, for a natural number \(u\) let \(w(u)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(w(0)=0\), and write \(E(u)=1^{|w(u)|}0w(u)\). Encode an integer by a sign bit followed by \(E\) of its absolute value: sign 0 is nonnegative and sign 1 is negative, with sign 0 for zero. Encode a rational by its integer numerator and its positive denominator in lowest terms. A complex entry is its real rational part followed by its imaginary rational part. The instance consists of \(1^n0\), then \(E(m)\), then the rationals \(a,b\), then the \(m\) terms. A term consists of \(E(\ell)\), its \(\ell\) indices encoded by \(E\), and its matrix entries in row-major order. There are no trailing bits. The entire length \(N\) counts every numerator, denominator, index and matrix entry. Matrix precision is part of \(N\), not a unit-cost real input. Strings failing these syntactic conditions or any stated matrix or threshold condition are outside the promise, as are valid instances with \(a<\lambda_{\min}(H)<b\).

Here QMA is the following class of promise pairs \(\Pi=(Y,N_0)\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^*\). A verifier has one deterministic classical Turing machine that, given \(x\), outputs a quantum circuit \(V_x\) and its register sizes in time polynomial in \(|x|+1\). The circuit has polynomially many qubits and gates, with a designated witness register of \(w(|x|)\) qubits and all other qubits initialized to \(|0\rangle\). The function \(w\) is polynomial-time computable and polynomially bounded. The generator and all resource bounds are fixed for \(\Pi\), valid on all inputs, and have no advice or oracle. The witness may be any density operator on its register and need not have an efficient description.

Circuits use the fixed gate set consisting of the Hadamard gate
\[W=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\]
the phase gate \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), and controlled-NOT, which sends \(|u,v\rangle\) to \(|u,u\mathbin{\oplus}v\rangle\) for bits \(u,v\), where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Gates are specified by their names and qubit indices. At the end a designated output qubit is measured in the computational basis; outcome 1 is acceptance. Probabilities are given by the Born rule applied to the witness and zero ancillas after the circuit. For every \(x\in Y\), some witness is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); for every \(x\in N_0\), every witness is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). There is no acceptance requirement outside \(Y\cup N_0\).

QMA-hardness under the required reductions means that for every such pair \(\Pi\), there is one deterministic classical multitape Turing machine \(R_\Pi\) that halts on every input \(x\) within \(C(|x|+1)^r\) bit steps for some fixed positive integers \(C,r\), outputs a classical binary string, and satisfies
\[x\in Y\Rightarrow R_\Pi(x)\in(\mathrm{LH}_{k,d,\varepsilon})_{\rm yes},\qquad
x\in N_0\Rightarrow R_\Pi(x)\in(\mathrm{LH}_{k,d,\varepsilon})_{\rm no}.\]
Output writing is included in the time bound. On promised source inputs the output must obey every target condition, including the common locality and term-count bounds. Off the source promise no output guarantee is required, but the runtime bound still holds. The reduction may depend on \(\Pi\); \(k,d,\varepsilon\) must be chosen once before quantifying over \(\Pi\). Thus the order is \(\exists k,d,\varepsilon\;\forall\Pi\in\mathrm{QMA}\;\exists R_\Pi\). No random or quantum computation is allowed in \(R_\Pi\).

cards.title: BPP versus BQP
cards.formal:
Is \(\mathrm{BPP}\subsetneq\mathrm{BQP}\)? Equivalently, does there exist one total decision language
\[L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\quad\text{such that}\quad L\in\mathrm{BQP}\ \text{and}\ L\notin\mathrm{BPP}?\]
Both classes require a correct membership bit with probability at least \(2/3\) separately on every input. The quantum and classical models are uniform and have fixed polynomial resource bounds as defined below. The established containment \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\) makes equality the other possible answer.
cards.definitions:
A language \(L\) is a set of finite binary strings, with membership bit \(\mathbf1_L(x)\); put \(n=|x|\), including \(n=0\). There are no excluded inputs or external promise.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BPP}\) means that one finite classical probabilistic multitape Turing-machine program \(R\) and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) satisfy the following for every input \(x\): every coin sequence makes \(R(x)\) halt within \(p(n)=C(n+1)^d\) steps with a bit output, and
\[\Pr[R(x)=\mathbf1_L(x)]\ge 2/3.\]
Each transition costs one bit step and can read at most one fresh independent fair bit. Equivalently, feed a uniform \(z\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\) and ignore unused bits; the probability condition is exactly
\[3\bigl|\{z:R(x;z)=\mathbf1_L(x)\}\bigr|\ge 2\cdot2^{p(n)}.\]
The time bound is worst case over all coin sequences, not expected time. The same program and constants work for all input lengths and all inputs of a length.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BQP}\) is defined using circuits over the fixed gates \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\). In the ordered one-qubit basis \((|0\rangle,|1\rangle)\),
\[H=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&(1+i)/\sqrt2\end{pmatrix},\qquad i^2=-1.\]
On two distinct addressed qubits, \(\mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin{\oplus}b\rangle\) for bits \(a,b\), where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Gates act as the identity on all other qubits. They may address any qubits; there is no geometric locality restriction.

There must exist one deterministic classical multitape Turing machine \(G\) and fixed positive integers \(K,e\) such that, on unary input \(1^n\), including the empty unary string at \(n=0\), \(G\) prints within \(K(n+1)^e\) bit steps a complete circuit description. The description specifies a register size \(q(n)\ge n+1\), an ordered list of \(m(n)\) gates with binary qubit addresses, and one designated output qubit \(j(n)\). Both \(q(n)\) and \(m(n)\) are at most \(K(n+1)^e\). Every listed address must be valid, and the list depends only on \(n\), not on the particular \(x\). The circuit may have unrestricted depth subject to this polynomial gate bound.

For \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), initialize the register to the computational basis state \(|x\rangle\otimes|0^{q(n)-n}\rangle\). A computational basis state \(|y\rangle\) is the unit coordinate vector indexed by \(y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}\) in \(\mathbb C^{2^{q(n)}}\). Apply the listed unitary matrices in order, obtaining
\[|\psi_x\rangle=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}}\alpha_y|y\rangle,
\qquad \sum_y|\alpha_y|^2=1.\]
Measure only qubit \(j(n)\) at the end. The probability of output \(b\in\{0,1\}\) is exactly \(\sum_{y:y_{j(n)}=b}|\alpha_y|^2\). For every \(x\), this probability must be at least \(2/3\) when \(b=\mathbf1_L(x)\). These equations specify the mathematical semantics; the machine is not asked to write down the exponentially long state vector or its amplitudes.

There is no advice, oracle gate, postselection, supplied quantum state or freely chosen real parameter. All auxiliary qubits start at zero. Only the stated finite gate set is primitive; gate descriptions and uniform generation are finite classical data. Both models are ideal; hardware noise is outside the model. Constants and exponents may depend on the fixed language's algorithms, but not on \(n\) or \(x\).

The target compares existence of a decider for each total language. It does not require a compiler transforming quantum circuit generators into classical programs, preservation of a particular polynomial exponent, sampling an entire quantum output distribution, or computing amplitudes. Correctness on an average input distribution is insufficient.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of either
\[\exists L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\quad L\in\mathrm{BQP}\land L\notin\mathrm{BPP},\]
or its logical negation, equivalently \(\mathrm{BQP}\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}\) and hence \(\mathrm{BPP}=\mathrm{BQP}\).

For strict containment, establish the uniform circuit family, its polynomial generation/size/register bounds and pointwise bounded-error correctness for one fixed language, then exclude every classical probabilistic program with any fixed polynomial worst-case bound and the stated correctness guarantee. A lower bound only against deterministic algorithms does not exclude BPP. For equality, prove that every total language satisfying the quantum definition has a classical decider satisfying the full BPP definition; reproducing its circuit amplitudes or output distribution is not required.

Conditional hardness, an oracle or query separation, a promise or sampling separation, and a lower bound against shallow or otherwise restricted classical circuits do not establish strict containment of these total-language classes. A faster quantum algorithm for a task without a matching classical lower bound is also insufficient. The error thresholds specify exact probabilities, not numerical acceptance tolerances.
