cards.definitions:
A promise problem is an ordered pair \(L=(L_{\mathrm{yes}},L_{\mathrm{no}})\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^*\). There is no requirement on inputs outside their union. A verifier is specified by one deterministic classical Turing machine that, on a string \(x\) of length \(n\), outputs in time polynomial in \(n\) the description of a quantum circuit \(V_x\), its witness-register lengths and a designated output qubit. All register lengths and the number of gates are bounded by a polynomial depending on the verifier, not on \(x\). Apart from its witness registers, the circuit starts with ancillary qubits in state \(|0\rangle\). It uses the fixed gate set \(\{H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\}\), acting on specified qubits, where \[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\] and \(\mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin\oplus b\rangle\) for bits \(a,b\); \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. The circuit accepts when its final computational-basis measurement of the output qubit is 1. Qubits are two-dimensional complex systems; an \(m\)-qubit pure state is a unit vector in \(\mathbb C^{2^m}\), with computational basis \(\{|z\rangle:z\in\{0,1\}^m\}\). A mixed state is a positive semidefinite, trace-one complex matrix on this space. For witness density matrix \(\rho\), acceptance probability is \[\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[\Pi_1V_x\bigl(\rho\otimes |0\rangle\langle0|^{\otimes a}\bigr)V_x^\dagger\right],\] where \(a\) is the number of ancillary qubits, \(V_x^\dagger\) is the conjugate transpose, and \(\Pi_1\) projects onto output-qubit value 1 and acts as identity on the other qubits. Positive semidefinite means \(v^\dagger\rho v\ge0\) for every vector \(v\); \(\operatorname{Tr}\) is the sum of diagonal entries. Witnesses may depend arbitrarily on the whole input and need not be efficiently preparable. Circuit uniformity forbids advice depending only on input length, and neither model receives an oracle. The witness is sent once, before verification, with no further interaction. The stated finite universal gate set fixes an encoding; bounded-error classes permit the usual polynomial-overhead approximations of other effective universal gate sets. A different verifier and polynomial bound may be used for each promise problem.

The class \(\mathrm{QMA}\), quantum Merlin–Arthur, consists of the promise problems with such a verifier and one polynomial-length quantum witness register for which both conditions hold: for every \(x\in L_{\mathrm{yes}}\), some witness state is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); for every \(x\in L_{\mathrm{no}}\), every witness state is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). The quantifiers apply to arbitrary mixed states, not merely the honestly intended state. Pure witnesses suffice for completeness by linearity of acceptance probability.

For \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\), the verifier instead has two witness registers, each of length bounded by a polynomial in the input length. For every yes-input there must exist density matrices \(\rho\) and \(\sigma\) on the respective registers such that the product state \(\rho\otimes\sigma\) is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\). For every no-input and every pair \(\rho,\sigma\), the acceptance probability on \(\rho\otimes\sigma\) is at most \(1/3\). The two factors can each have arbitrary internal entanglement among their own qubits; the restriction concerns the division between the two registers. Equivalent soundness quantification allows every separable state \(\sum_jp_j\rho_j\otimes\sigma_j\), where \(p_j\ge0\) and \(\sum_jp_j=1\), because acceptance is linear. The two witnesses need not be identical. Both may depend on the whole input and may be coordinated before they are sent, but their joint state at receipt must satisfy the indicated separability restriction. After receipt, the verifier may perform arbitrary allowed joint gates and create entanglement. It is not required to test separability of an arbitrary incoming state; separability is a promise on the states against which soundness is required. Neither class restricts amplitudes to be nonnegative or witness states to have short classical descriptions. Equality means equality of all disjoint promise pairs admitted by the two definitions.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\subseteq\mathrm{QMA}\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that some promise problem lies in QMA(2) but outside QMA. An equality proof must supply sound single-witness verification for every eligible two-witness problem; merely concatenating the intended honest witnesses is insufficient because the single-witness verifier must also resist entangled dishonest states. A separation must exclude every ordinary uniform polynomial-time QMA verifier for the same promise pair. A quantum- or classical-oracle separation, a result about a restricted-amplitude class, or a state-generation task does not alone settle this decision-class comparison.

source_formulation.text: Does the promise that two quantum witnesses are unentangled give more verification power than an unrestricted single quantum witness?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Section 6, Question 1

context_blocks.text: The two-witness condition changes which dishonest messages a verifier must handle. A verifier designed for a product state may be fooled by an entangled state on the same two registers. Treating both registers as one long witness preserves an honest proof but can invalidate soundness; this is why the class comparison is nontrivial.

There is no resource advantage just from having twice as many qubits: a single polynomial-length witness can already contain that many. Nor does the model provide two-way interaction or ask the verifier to certify that an arbitrary state is unentangled. The product-state restriction is part of the proof-system model.

The ordinary inclusions recorded in both the 2024 source and the September 2026 manuscript are \(\mathrm{QMA}\subseteq\mathrm{QMA}(2)\subseteq\mathrm{NEXP}\). Here NEXP is the class of promise problems decidable by a nondeterministic classical Turing machine in time \(2^{p(n)}\) for some polynomial \(p\), with an accepting branch on every yes-input and no accepting branch on any no-input. These inclusions alone neither prove nor refute equality of the first two classes.

Harrow–Montanaro establish error amplification and show that two unentangled proofs can simulate polynomially many. This explains why the two-proof class captures a broad finite-message regime, while still leaving comparison with one unrestricted quantum witness open.

The 2024 source studies witnesses whose relative phases are restricted, including nonnegative-amplitude variants at specified completeness and soundness parameters. It explicitly warns that those results do not immediately establish the relationship between ordinary QMA and QMA(2). A restriction on which dishonest states are allowed can increase verification power, so it cannot be transferred by treating it as an innocuous representation change.

The September 2026 manuscript gives the first separation relative to a unitary oracle. Both verifiers receive access to the same quantum black box, and the two-proof verifier gains power in that setting. This updates the 2024 paper’s statement that even such an oracle separation was unknown, but it does not separate the ordinary classes.

The new manuscript also draws consequences for approximate disentanglers and explicitly says a classical-oracle separation remains open. These are separate statements with their own parameters; neither is substituted for the unrelativized equality asked here. The recorded status is a manuscript claim checked for scope, not an independent validation of its proof.

cards.title: Quantum entropy inequalities beyond strong subadditivity
cards.formal:
Is there an unconditional homogeneous linear inequality for finite-dimensional quantum subsystem entropies that does not follow from the standard von Neumann inequalities? Precisely, do there exist an integer \(n\ge4\), real coefficients \((c_J)_{\varnothing
e J\subseteq[n]}\), and a vector \(v\in\mathcal V_n\), as defined below, such that \[\sum_{\varnothing
e J\subseteq[n]}c_J S(ho_J)\ge0\] for every choice of finite local dimensions and every \(n\)-party density matrix \(ho\), while \[\sum_{\varnothing
e J\subseteq[n]}c_Jv_J<0?\] The same coefficients must work in every local dimension. The party count is any one finite \(n\ge4\); the target is not restricted to exactly four parties or to a special class of states.
cards.why: This asks whether the established linear laws of quantum entropy are complete. A new unconditional inequality would reveal a universal restriction on sharing quantum information; completeness would characterize every finite-party entropy cone by finitely many standard inequalities, after taking closure.

These sources retain the unconditional general quantum entropy cone question. No universal inequality outside the standard cone or proof of equality in every party count was identified. Restricted-state and constrained inequalities are different targets. No cited proof was independently verified or formalized in Lean.

sentences: For a multipartite quantum state, the entropies of all subsystems form a vector subject to universal inequalities.
Positivity and strong subadditivity give basic constraints on those vectors.
This question asks whether additional inequalities are needed to describe the quantum entropy cone for four or more parties.
The cited stabilizer-state analysis relates the problem to classical non-Shannon inequalities and to states violating the Ingleton inequality.
New constraints or counterexamples would sharpen the mathematical description of how quantum information can be shared among several systems.

cards.definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Choose arbitrary positive integers \(d_1,\ldots,d_n\) and the Hilbert space \(\mathcal H=\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\mathbb C^{d_i}\), with its standard product basis. A density matrix is a Hermitian matrix \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\) that is positive semidefinite, meaning \(z^\dagger\rho z\ge0\) for every complex vector \(z\), and has trace one. Dagger denotes conjugate transpose and trace is the sum of diagonal entries. Arbitrary complex matrix entries and mixed states are allowed.

For a subset \(J\subseteq[n]\), the marginal \(\rho_J\) is obtained by tracing out its complement. In product-basis indices its entries are \[(\rho_J)_{a,b}=\sum_z\rho_{(a,z),(b,z)},\] where \(a,b\) index the factors in \(J\), \(z\) ranges over all basis indices of the complementary factors, and the tuples are placed in the original order of the parties. If \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_D\) are the eigenvalues of a density matrix, define its von Neumann entropy in bits by \(S=-\sum_{j=1}^D\lambda_j\log_2\lambda_j\), with \(0\log_2 0=0\). Define the empty-system entropy to be zero. The entropy vector \(s(\rho)\in\mathbb R^{2^n-1}\) has coordinates \(s(\rho)_J=S(\rho_J)\), indexed by the nonempty subsets.

The standard comparison cone \(\mathcal V_n\) consists of all real vectors \(v=(v_J)_{\varnothing\ne J\subseteq[n]}\), extended by \(v_\varnothing=0\), that satisfy \(v_J\ge0\) for every \(J\), and, for every pair of subsets \(A,B\subseteq[n]\), both \[v_A+v_B\ge v_{A\cap B}+v_{A\cup B}\qquad\text{(strong subadditivity)}\] and \[v_A+v_B\ge v_{A\setminus B}+v_{B\setminus A}\qquad\text{(weak monotonicity)}.\] Disjoint, overlapping, equal and empty subsets are all included. Thus familiar subadditivity and the Araki–Lieb inequalities are already among the consequences. Weak monotonicity follows from strong subadditivity after purifying a quantum state with an additional party; it is explicitly included here so it cannot be counted as a new inequality. Every actual quantum entropy vector lies in \(\mathcal V_n\), but a vector in this cone is only a list of real numbers and is not promised to come from a state.

An inequality is homogeneous linear if its left side is the displayed linear combination with constant coefficients and zero right side. It is unconditional if it holds for all states and dimensions, without extra entropy equalities, independence assumptions or a restriction to stabilizer, classical or holographic states. Not following from the standard inequalities means exactly that it fails at some vector of \(\mathcal V_n\), as required by the strict inequality in the target. This is semantic nonimplication; no choice of syntactic proof system is involved. Equivalently, since the closure of the set of quantum entropy vectors is a closed convex cone, the question asks whether this closure is strictly smaller than \(\mathcal V_n\) for at least one finite \(n\ge4\). Closure means approximation to arbitrary accuracy in the finite-dimensional real coordinate space; it is not exact realization by a single finite-dimensional state. No running-time or algorithmic discovery requirement is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated existence, including validity for every finite-dimensional state and an exact vector witnessing nonimplication by the standard cone, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. The negative outcome must show that for every finite \(n\ge4\), every universally valid homogeneous linear entropy inequality is nonnegative on every vector in \(\mathcal V_n\). Equivalently it proves equality of the closed quantum entropy cone and \(\mathcal V_n\) for every such \(n\). A positive outcome needs only one party count, but a negative result for exactly four parties does not settle all larger counts. An inequality valid under additional constraints, a restriction to some states, or failure of exact realization of a boundary vector without excluding arbitrarily close realizations does not establish the requested separation. Numerical searches alone and approximate versions of the strict separation are insufficient.

context_blocks.text: A multipartite state has one entropy for every nonempty subsystem. Universal linear inequalities limit which patterns of shared quantum information are possible, independently of the dimensions used to realize them. The question asks whether the familiar inequalities already exhaust these linear constraints.

Quantum entropy differs from classical entropy: adjoining a system can reduce entropy. For instance, a pure maximally entangled pair has zero joint entropy and positive one-party entropies. Classical monotonicity cannot be added to the comparison cone; the source uses weak monotonicity instead.

For at most three parties, the closure of the set of quantum entropy vectors is characterized by the standard inequalities. For four or more, the source explicitly distinguishes this closed-cone question from the exact set of realizable entropy vectors. Nonrealizability at a limiting boundary point alone is not a new universal linear inequality.

Classical non-Shannon inequalities demonstrate that the analogous classical outer cone is too large. That fact does not transfer directly to quantum states, because classical diagonal states form only a subclass and quantum conditional entropy can be negative.

The 2013 paper characterizes the four-party stabilizer entropy cone using an additional Ingleton inequality. General quantum states, including some classical diagonal states, need not satisfy Ingleton. The theorem therefore answers a restricted-state question and leaves the target here open.

Known constrained quantum entropy inequalities assume additional relations among entropies. Such a conclusion can fail to survive limits of states that only approach those relations. It does not automatically give an unconditional separating inequality for the closed entropy cone.

The 2025 Quantum Entropy Prover formalizes deduction from strong subadditivity and weak monotonicity using linear programming, and also handles supplied constraints. Its introduction explicitly retains existence of non-von-Neumann-type unconditional inequalities as an open question; an automated prover for the known cone does not characterize the actual quantum cone.

The 2026 holographic-cone paper also distinguishes the unresolved general quantum cone from the more restricted holographic setting. New graph realizations or inequalities for that restricted cone do not apply to every finite-dimensional quantum state.

cards.title: Bell nonlocality from finitely many copies of every entangled state
cards.formal: For every finite pair of local dimensions \(d_A,d_B\ge2\) and every entangled state \(\rho\) on \(\mathbb C^{d_A}\otimes\mathbb C^{d_B}\), do there exist a finite integer \(k\ge1\), local filters with strictly positive joint success probability, and finite families of local measurements for which the successfully filtered state obtained from \(\rho^{\otimes k}\) has Bell-nonlocal correlations? Both filters act before the measurement settings are chosen. No auxiliary shared entangled state is supplied. The number of copies, filters, output dimensions and measurement families may depend on \(\rho\).
cards.definitions:
A density matrix is a Hermitian matrix \(X=X^\dagger\) with \(v^\dagger Xv\ge0\) for all complex vectors \(v\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}X=1\). Dagger is conjugate transpose and trace is the sum of diagonal entries. A bipartite state is separable if it is a finite convex combination of product density matrices; entangled means not separable. No purity, rational-entry or efficient-preparation promise is imposed. The \(k\) copies are independent copies of the same state. Regroup the tensor factors of \(\rho^{\otimes k}\) into Alice's \((\mathbb C^{d_A})^{\otimes k}\) and Bob's \((\mathbb C^{d_B})^{\otimes k}\); each party may act jointly on all of its own copies.

A successful local filter is specified by finitely many rectangular complex matrices \(A_j\) from Alice's input space to a finite output space \(\mathbb C^{r_A}\), with \(\sum_jA_j^\dagger A_j\le I\). It maps \(X\) to \(\mathcal F_A(X)=\sum_j A_jXA_j^\dagger\). Bob's filter \(\mathcal F_B\) is defined by matrices \(B_l\) and \(\sum_lB_l^\dagger B_l\le I\), with output \(\mathbb C^{r_B}\). Here \(S\le I\) means \(I-S\) is positive semidefinite. These are precisely finite-dimensional completely positive trace-nonincreasing maps. Their joint success probability and conditional output are \[q=\operatorname{Tr}\bigl[(\mathcal F_A\otimes\mathcal F_B)(\rho^{\otimes k})\bigr]>0,\qquad \sigma=\frac{(\mathcal F_A\otimes\mathcal F_B)(\rho^{\otimes k})}{q}.\] No lower bound on \(q\) uniform over states or copy counts is required. The success flags may be compared before the measurement settings are chosen. The filters cannot depend on those settings. Local ancillary states are absorbed in the local maps; no entangled ancilla shared between the parties is permitted.

Let \(X,Y,O_A,O_B\) be finite nonempty sets of settings and outcomes. For each \(x\in X\), Alice's positive-operator-valued measurement is a family \((M_{\alpha|x})_{\alpha\in O_A}\) of positive semidefinite operators on \(\mathbb C^{r_A}\) summing to identity. Define Bob's \((N_{\beta|y})_{\beta\in O_B}\) similarly. The conditional correlation is \[p(\alpha,\beta\mid x,y)=\operatorname{Tr}\bigl[\sigma(M_{\alpha|x}\otimes N_{\beta|y})\bigr].\] Measurement settings are independently selected after successful preparation; no communication is allowed after they are supplied. All outcomes are retained in this distribution, with no further postselection on outcomes or settings.

The correlation is Bell-local if there are a finite set \(L\), nonnegative weights \(w_\lambda\) summing to one, and normalized conditional probability distributions \(u_\lambda(\alpha\mid x)\), \(v_\lambda(\beta\mid y)\), such that \[p(\alpha,\beta\mid x,y)=\sum_{\lambda\in L}w_\lambda u_\lambda(\alpha\mid x)v_\lambda(\beta\mid y)\] for every setting and outcome. The weights cannot depend on \(x,y\). For finite settings and outcomes this includes all local hidden-variable models, since deterministic response tables have a finite convex hull. Bell-nonlocal means no such representation exists. Equivalently, the distribution violates some linear Bell inequality valid for all local distributions. The target permits every finite Bell scenario, not only two settings or the CHSH inequality. Public shared randomness may select local procedures, but cannot turn a convex combination of Bell-local correlations into a nonlocal one; existence can therefore be tested for fixed filters and measurements as above. There is no computation, sample or circuit-size bound on the chosen operations.

context_blocks.text: Entanglement describes the shared state. Bell nonlocality describes observed correlations that cannot be reproduced by local response functions and shared randomness. The source explicitly asks whether collective use of repeated copies and preliminary local filtering always connects these two notions.

Liang, Masanes and Rosset prove that entanglement can activate a Bell violation when combined with a suitable auxiliary state. That auxiliary resource need not be a copy of the state being tested, so the theorem leaves the question in this card open.

Hirsch and coauthors exhibit entangled two-qubit states remaining Bell-local after every local filter on one copy, including general positive-operator-valued measurements. Their theorem rules out a universal one-copy claim; it does not give a state remaining local after arbitrary numbers of copies.

The December 2025 broadcast result places the original source in a four-party experiment and rules out quantum-realizable broadcast explanations with a separable source across the original cut. Its additional parties and causal assumptions differ from the ordinary two-party local hidden-variable definition here. Its universal entanglement-certification result therefore does not settle this repeated-copy question.

The original source also distinguishes arbitrary Bell inequalities from the CHSH test. The repeated-copy filtered CHSH criterion is tied to distillability, while the present target allows every finite setting and outcome configuration. Restricting the output test to CHSH would change the question.

cards.why: A positive answer would give every entangled bipartite state an intrinsic Bell-nonlocal manifestation using only repeated access to that same state. A negative answer would exhibit entanglement that remains Bell-local under every finite collective local test and preliminary filter. This separates the mathematical resource of entanglement from the observable nonlocal correlations used in device-independent information tasks.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal finite-copy assertion, or of its logical negation: there is one finite-dimensional entangled state for which every finite \(k\), every allowed pair of filters with positive success probability, and every finite family of local measurements produces a Bell-local distribution. A positive proof need not bound \(k\), filter success probability or violation size uniformly over states. A one-copy local model, including a model surviving every one-copy filter, does not establish the negative all-copy assertion. Activation with a different auxiliary entangled state, a network with additional parties, or a test with quantum inputs does not establish the specified bipartite target. Bell violation and filter positivity are exact mathematical conditions; approximate numerical evidence alone is insufficient.

source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the open repeated-copy question in the source introduction

sentences: Entanglement and Bell nonlocality are distinct properties of quantum states and measurement correlations.
The question asks whether every entangled bipartite state becomes Bell-nonlocal after local filtering of some finite number of copies.
The filter must succeed before measurement settings are selected, and no extra shared entangled state is provided.
Single-copy counterexamples, auxiliary-state activation and four-party broadcast results address different resource models.
A full answer would determine whether repeated copies of the state itself always make its entanglement observable through a conventional bipartite Bell violation.

cards.context:
Entanglement describes the shared state. Bell nonlocality describes observed correlations that cannot be reproduced by local response functions and shared randomness. The source explicitly asks whether collective use of repeated copies and preliminary local filtering always connects these two notions.

Liang, Masanes and Rosset prove that entanglement can activate a Bell violation when combined with a suitable auxiliary state. That auxiliary resource need not be a copy of the state being tested, so the theorem leaves the question in this card open.

Hirsch and coauthors exhibit entangled two-qubit states remaining Bell-local after every local filter on one copy, including general positive-operator-valued measurements. Their theorem rules out a universal one-copy claim; it does not give a state remaining local after arbitrary numbers of copies.

The December 2025 broadcast result places the original source in a four-party experiment and rules out quantum-realizable broadcast explanations with a separable source across the original cut. Its additional parties and causal assumptions differ from the ordinary two-party local hidden-variable definition here. Its universal entanglement-certification result therefore does not settle this repeated-copy question.

The original source also distinguishes arbitrary Bell inequalities from the CHSH test. The repeated-copy filtered CHSH criterion is tied to distillability, while the present target allows every finite setting and outcome configuration. Restricting the output test to CHSH would change the question.

cards.title: \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\) versus NEXP
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)=\mathrm{NEXP}\) for ordinary promise problems without an oracle? Equivalently, does every promise problem decidable by a nondeterministic classical Turing machine in time \(2^{p(n)}\), for some polynomial \(p\), admit a uniform polynomial-time quantum verifier with two polynomial-length unentangled witnesses, completeness at least \(2/3\), and soundness at most \(1/3\)? The known inclusion \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\subseteq\mathrm{NEXP}\) makes the reverse containment the unresolved direction. The verifier, its running time and both witness lengths must remain polynomial in the original binary input length.

source_formulation.text: Does ordinary QMA(2), with a constant completeness–soundness gap, equal nondeterministic exponential time?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Section 1.3, printed page 53:12

cards.why: Two short quantum messages may contain a highly structured encoding of a much longer computation, while their independence restricts how a dishonest prover can cheat. This question asks whether that resource reaches the full power of nondeterministic exponential time despite a polynomial-time verifier and a constant reliability gap. It locates the upper end of the unusually wide known range for QMA(2).

sentences: The question asks whether polynomial-time verification of two unentangled polynomial-length quantum proofs captures nondeterministic exponential time.
It compares ordinary promise classes with a fixed constant acceptance gap and no oracle or advice.
NEXP already contains QMA(2), so the unresolved direction is verification of every NEXP promise problem by the two-proof model.
Exponentially small-gap and nonnegative-amplitude variants have stronger known characterizations that do not automatically transfer to this model.
Recent amplification and oracle results retain those distinctions and do not establish ordinary QMA(2) equals NEXP.

cards.definitions:
A promise problem is an ordered pair \(L=(L_{\mathrm{yes}},L_{\mathrm{no}})\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^*\). There is no requirement on inputs outside their union. A verifier is specified by one deterministic classical Turing machine that, on a string \(x\) of length \(n\), outputs in time polynomial in \(n\) the description of a quantum circuit \(V_x\), its witness-register lengths and a designated output qubit. All register lengths and the number of gates are bounded by a polynomial depending on the verifier, not on \(x\). Apart from its witness registers, the circuit starts with ancillary qubits in state \(|0\rangle\). It uses the fixed gate set \(\{H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\}\), acting on specified qubits, where \[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\] and \(\mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin\oplus b\rangle\) for bits \(a,b\); \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. The circuit accepts when its final computational-basis measurement of the output qubit is 1. Qubits are two-dimensional complex systems; an \(m\)-qubit pure state is a unit vector in \(\mathbb C^{2^m}\), with computational basis \(\{|z\rangle:z\in\{0,1\}^m\}\). A mixed state is a positive semidefinite, trace-one complex matrix on this space. For witness density matrix \(\rho\), acceptance probability is \[\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[\Pi_1V_x\bigl(\rho\otimes |0\rangle\langle0|^{\otimes a}\bigr)V_x^\dagger\right],\] where \(a\) is the number of ancillary qubits, \(V_x^\dagger\) is the conjugate transpose, and \(\Pi_1\) projects onto output-qubit value 1 and acts as identity on the other qubits. Positive semidefinite means \(v^\dagger\rho v\ge0\) for every vector \(v\); \(\operatorname{Tr}\) is the sum of diagonal entries. Witnesses may depend arbitrarily on the whole input and need not be efficiently preparable. Circuit uniformity forbids advice depending only on input length, and neither model receives an oracle. The witness is sent once, before verification, with no further interaction. The stated finite universal gate set fixes an encoding; bounded-error classes permit the usual polynomial-overhead approximations of other effective universal gate sets. A different verifier and polynomial bound may be used for each promise problem.

The class \(\mathrm{QMA}\), quantum Merlin–Arthur, consists of the promise problems with such a verifier and one polynomial-length quantum witness register for which both conditions hold: for every \(x\in L_{\mathrm{yes}}\), some witness state is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); for every \(x\in L_{\mathrm{no}}\), every witness state is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). The quantifiers apply to arbitrary mixed states, not merely the honestly intended state. Pure witnesses suffice for completeness by linearity of acceptance probability.

For \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\), the verifier instead has two witness registers, each of length bounded by a polynomial in the input length. For every yes-input there must exist density matrices \(\rho\) and \(\sigma\) on the respective registers such that the product state \(\rho\otimes\sigma\) is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\). For every no-input and every pair \(\rho,\sigma\), the acceptance probability on \(\rho\otimes\sigma\) is at most \(1/3\). The two factors can each have arbitrary internal entanglement among their own qubits; the restriction concerns the division between the two registers. Equivalent soundness quantification allows every separable state \(\sum_jp_j\rho_j\otimes\sigma_j\), where \(p_j\ge0\) and \(\sum_jp_j=1\), because acceptance is linear. The two witnesses need not be identical. Both may depend on the whole input and may be coordinated before they are sent, but their joint state at receipt must satisfy the indicated separability restriction. After receipt, the verifier may perform arbitrary allowed joint gates and create entanglement. It is not required to test separability of an arbitrary incoming state; separability is a promise on the states against which soundness is required. Neither class restricts amplitudes to be nonnegative or witness states to have short classical descriptions. Equality means equality of all disjoint promise pairs admitted by the two definitions.

A nondeterministic classical Turing machine has finitely many tapes, a fixed finite tape alphabet and a fixed finite transition relation. An execution chooses one permitted transition at each step, and one step is charged for each such transition. A promise problem \(L=(L_{\mathrm{yes}},L_{\mathrm{no}})\) is in \(\mathrm{NEXP}\), nondeterministic exponential time, if there exist such a machine and an integer-valued polynomial \(p\) with the following properties. Every computation branch on every length-\(n\) binary input halts within \(2^{p(n)}\) steps; every yes-input has an accepting branch; and no no-input has an accepting branch. No correctness requirement is imposed outside the promise. The machine is fixed for the problem and has neither an oracle nor advice. The polynomial and machine may differ between promise problems. Here QMA(2) retains the constant error thresholds already defined. A class allowing an exponentially small difference between completeness and soundness is called a precise variant; that is not the class being compared in this card.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of \(\mathrm{NEXP}\subseteq\mathrm{QMA}(2)\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that a promise problem in NEXP is outside QMA(2). A positive proof must preserve polynomial verification and proof lengths with the fixed \(2/3\) versus \(1/3\) acceptance gap; a negative proof must exclude every ordinary uniform verifier with two unentangled polynomial-length witnesses. A protocol with an exponentially small gap, an exponentially long proof, extra oracle access, or a restriction to nonnegative dishonest witness amplitudes does not by itself satisfy this target. Equality or separation between QMA and QMA(2) alone does not answer their comparison with NEXP.

context_blocks.text: The comparison is about how much computation can be verified, not the physical size of a state vector’s written description. A polynomial number of qubits has exponentially many amplitudes, but an efficient verifier can access them only through its permitted quantum computation. A constant completeness–soundness gap is a substantive part of the claim.

The original source records equality between NEXP and a precise version of QMA(2) whose gap may be exponentially small. Such a verifier may distinguish its yes- and no-cases by a probability difference too small for polynomially many repetitions to resolve. The present card retains the ordinary constant-gap definition.

Known amplification for ordinary QMA(2) and equivalence of two to polynomially many unentangled proofs do not convert every exponentially small-gap protocol into a polynomial-time constant-gap one. The initial gap is a parameter of the amplification cost.

Nonnegative-amplitude proof systems impose additional conditions on the witnesses allowed in the soundness case. Results reaching NEXP in such models therefore concern a different collection of dishonest proofs. The 2024 source explicitly distinguishes those results from ordinary QMA(2).

The August 2026 preprint reports stronger amplification for the nonnegative-amplitude variant, approaching the one-quarter soundness threshold from above as completeness approaches one. Its abstract distinguishes that regime from the stronger-gap comparison with ordinary or real-amplitude witnesses. It does not state the unrestricted equality asked here.

The September 2026 manuscript still records the chain from QMA through QMA(2) to NEXP as the general ordinary-class information available. Its new theorem separates QMA from QMA(2) relative to a unitary oracle; that theorem neither puts all NEXP problems in ordinary QMA(2) nor separates them from it.

The neighboring single-witness question concerns the lower end of the containment chain. This card concerns the upper end. Their logical relationship is worth retaining, but they ask different equalities and a result about one pair does not automatically settle the other.

cards.title: Maximum randomized-versus-quantum gap for total functions
cards.formal: Determine the optimal polynomial separation exponent \[\alpha_{\mathrm{RQ}}=\inf\bigl\{a\ge0:\exists C>0\ \forall n\ge1\ \forall\text{ nonconstant }f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\},\ R(f)\le C\,Q(f)^a\bigr\}.\] Here \(R(f)\) and \(Q(f)\) are randomized and quantum bit-query complexities with worst-case error at most \(1/3\). The constant \(C\) must be independent of both \(n\) and \(f\). The known range is \(3\le\alpha_{\mathrm{RQ}}\le4\). This card makes the source's maximum-gap question precise at the level of its polynomial exponent; logarithmic factors are not part of this numerical target.
cards.why: This quantifies the greatest possible quantum query advantage when an algorithm must handle every input, without a promise. It tests a basic limitation on quantum speedups and distinguishes the role of classical randomization from that of deterministic computation.
cards.status_note: Open in Aaronson’s 2021 survey. The near-cubic lower-bound family and universal quartic bound were checked in their primary papers on 2026-09-14. A bounded later-work search found no resolution of the displayed exponent; the September 2026 paper Quantum Query Advantage Requires Space concerns an additional workspace restriction and does not close this gap.

Aaronson explicitly asks to close the gap between the cubic separation and quartic universal upper bound.

importance.reason: Determines the strongest quantum query advantage when the function has no promise, a basic limit on quantum computation.

sentences: The question asks for the largest polynomial quantum query advantage over randomized algorithms on total Boolean functions.
Both models must answer correctly with probability at least two thirds on every input.
Only queries to input bits are counted, with other computation and workspace unrestricted.
Known results put the optimal separation exponent between three and four.
The target is to certify that exponent within one hundredth, without resolving finer logarithmic factors.

cards.definitions:
A total Boolean function assigns one output bit to every length-\(n\) bit string, with no promise restricting the inputs. Nonconstant means that both output values occur. A deterministic decision tree adaptively chooses an input coordinate, receives its bit, and ultimately outputs a bit. Its depth is the maximum number of queries on a root-to-leaf path. A randomized query algorithm is a probability distribution over deterministic trees of depth at most \(T\). It must output \(f(x)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) for each fixed input \(x\). The least possible \(T\) is \(R(f)\); unlimited computation and storage between queries are free.

For an input \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), a quantum bit query is the unitary \(O_x|i,b,z\rangle=|i,b\mathbin{\oplus}x_i,z\rangle\), where \(i\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\), \(b\in\{0,1\}\), \(z\) is a work register, \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo two, and the dummy coordinate has \(x_0=0\). A \(T\)-query algorithm starts in a fixed state, alternates at most \(T\) calls to this oracle with input-independent unitary operations on a finite-dimensional workspace, and finally measures a designated output bit. Arbitrary finite workspace and unitary matrices are allowed. Only oracle calls are charged; all other computation is free. Intermediate measurements and classical random choices can equivalently be included by storing their outcomes coherently. Algorithms may depend on the function and input length, but their operations cannot depend on the unknown input except through oracle calls. No uniform circuit-generation or time bound is imposed. Write \(Q(f)\) for the least integer \(T\) that achieves error at most \(1/3\) on every input in the domain of \(f\). The query bound is a worst-case bound, not an expected number of calls.

Both complexities are positive integers for nonconstant functions and at most \(n\). The infimum takes all real nonnegative exponents with a universal multiplicative bound. An exponent at the infimum need not itself admit such a bound: logarithmic factors may prevent attainment. Removing constant functions avoids zero-complexity conventions. The approximation tolerance for \(\alpha_{\mathrm{RQ}}\) concerns the exponent itself, not a relative approximation to a query count.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a real number \(a_*\) and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that \(|a_*-\alpha_{\mathrm{RQ}}|\le1/100\). A certified interval of width at most \(1/50\) suffices via its midpoint. It must control the universal upper bound and the existence of sufficiently large separations to certify this accuracy; merely improving one currently known bound does not suffice. The benchmark does not require resolving logarithmic factors or proving that the infimum exponent is attained.

context_blocks.text: Quantum algorithms can exploit a special promise to obtain enormous advantages over randomized algorithms. Total functions remove that freedom. Every input string must have a specified correct answer, so both the quantum algorithm and its classical competitors must handle adversarial inputs.

The quartic upper bound follows from \(R(f)\le D(f)=O(Q(f)^4)\), where \(D(f)\) is deterministic decision-tree depth. A matching separation between deterministic and quantum queries does not automatically give a matching separation against randomized algorithms.

The near-cubic lower-bound family comes from stronger promise-problem separations combined with a construction turning them into total functions. This establishes an exponent of at least three; it does not supply a quartic randomized separation.

The exponent formulation intentionally ignores subpolynomial factors. For example, an additional logarithmic factor in a universal cubic bound would still be compatible with exponent three. Establishing the exact bound with exponent three and no extra factor is a finer question.

cards.title: Efficient approximation of the optimal dihedral measurement
cards.formal: Can the specific pretty good measurement \(\{E_0,\ldots,E_{N-1},E_{\bot}\}\) defined below be approximated by uniform polynomial-size quantum circuits to every requested inverse-polynomial accuracy? Precisely, does there exist one deterministic circuit generator and a polynomial \(p\) such that, for every integer \(N\ge2\), number of copies \(k\ge1\), and precision parameter \(m\ge2\), it runs in time at most \(p(\lceil\log_2N\rceil+k+m)\) and produces a circuit with at most that many gates and ancilla qubits whose output distribution satisfies \[\sup_{\sigma}\frac12\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z_N\cup\{\bot\}}\left|\Pr[C_{N,k,m}(\sigma)=j]-\operatorname{Tr}(E_j\sigma)\right|\le\frac1m?\] The supremum ranges over all input density matrices on \((\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^N)^{\otimes k}\). The circuit receives one such state and returns one classical outcome. The selected target concerns this concrete measurement, without requiring a particular unitary realization or a Subset Sum algorithm.

source_formulation.text: Can the optimal dihedral measurement be implemented efficiently without requiring the known coherent subset-sum-sampling construction?

cards.why: This isolates the cost of extracting the information already present in dihedral coset states. An efficient implementation would turn a provably optimal measurement into an algorithmic resource, while a general impossibility theorem would distinguish measurement optimality from computational feasibility.

Its input space contains several dihedral coset-state registers, and its outcomes are candidate hidden shifts plus a complementary outcome.
The measurement is defined by the inverse square root of the sum of the ensemble states, with an explicit convention on its kernel.
The required circuit must reproduce its outcome distribution uniformly on valid inputs to any requested inverse-polynomial accuracy.
Known subset-sum connections constrain particular unitary implementations and do not establish hardness for every measurement circuit.

cards.definitions:
Write \(\mathbb Z_N=\{0,\ldots,N-1\}\), with addition modulo \(N\). For a hidden shift \(s\in\mathbb Z_N\) and \(x\in\mathbb Z_N\), let \[|c_x^{(s)}\rangle=\frac{|0,x\rangle+|1,x+s\rangle}{\sqrt2},\qquad \rho_s=\frac1N\sum_{x\in\mathbb Z_N}|c_x^{(s)}\rangle\langle c_x^{(s)}|.\] Thus \(\rho_s\) is the mixed state obtained by a uniform unknown coset offset. For \(k\) independent samples with the same shift, the state is \(\tau_s=\rho_s^{\otimes k}\) on \(\mathcal H_{N,k}=(\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^N)^{\otimes k}\). The discrimination ensemble assigns prior probability \(1/N\) to each shift \(s\). Both this prior and the average over coset offsets are part of the definition; neither \(s\) nor the offsets are supplied to the implementing circuit.

For this ensemble define \[G=\sum_{s\in\mathbb Z_N}\tau_s,\qquad E_s=G^{-1/2}\tau_sG^{-1/2},\qquad E_{\bot}=I-P_G.\] The inverse square root is the inverse on the support: if \(G=\sum_\lambda\lambda P_\lambda\) is its spectral decomposition, then \(G^{-1/2}=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda^{-1/2}P_\lambda\), with value zero on the kernel, and \(P_G=\sum_{\lambda>0}P_\lambda\). Every \(E_s\) is positive semidefinite and \(\sum_sE_s=P_G\). Adding \(E_{\bot}\) makes the sum the identity on the entire input space. A positive operator-valued measure is such a finite collection of positive semidefinite operators summing to identity; its outcome probabilities on state \(\sigma\) are \(\operatorname{Tr}(E_j\sigma)\). A density matrix is Hermitian, positive semidefinite and of trace one. Hermitian means \(\sigma=\sigma^\dagger\), with dagger conjugate transpose, and positive semidefinite means \(v^\dagger\sigma v\ge0\) for all vectors \(v\). The above expression, including its kernel convention, fully specifies the measurement even when \(G\) is singular. On each \(\tau_s\), outcome \(\bot\) has probability zero. The source associates that complementary outcome with the trivial hidden subgroup, but optimality is asserted for the uniform ensemble of order-two subgroups.

The classical generator receives \(N\) in binary and \(k,m\) in unary. This makes the error tolerance \(1/m\) and the polynomial dependence on its reciprocal explicit. The target does not demand polynomial dependence on \(\log m\). Each \(N\)-dimensional register is embedded in \(q=\lceil\log_2N\rceil\) qubits by the binary basis encodings of \(0,\ldots,N-1\); the input therefore uses \(k(q+1)\) qubits. No correctness condition is imposed on states outside that valid encoded subspace. The given state can be mixed, entangled across copies, and unrelated to an actual hidden shift; the error bound specifies the measurement on its whole valid input space. The circuit receives no further copies or a state-preparation oracle. It may consume the input, and no condition is imposed on the remaining quantum state after it outputs the label. In particular, this is a guarantee for classical outcome distributions, not for a prescribed post-measurement state or a particular coherent circuit extension.

Ancillas start in zero, and the circuit uses the fixed gates \[H=2^{-1/2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\quad \mathrm{CNOT}|b,c\rangle=|b,b\oplus c\rangle.\] These act on the indicated wires and as identity elsewhere; \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two and \(i^2=-1\). A final computational-basis measurement produces a binary outcome label, with \(0,\ldots,N-1\) interpreted as shifts and every remaining label mapped to \(\bot\). Ordinary finite gates and classical bit operations have unit cost, so no arbitrary real matrix is supplied as one free gate. There is no nonuniform advice, extra oracle, postselection or unbounded repeat-until-success loop. The displayed half-sum is total variation distance between the actual and specified outcome distributions; it is the largest difference in probabilities of an event defined by a set of labels. The requirement is uniform in the input state and every finite \(N,k,m\), with one polynomial and generator for the whole family. It asks for a sample from the distribution, not an explicit list of its \(N+1\) probabilities.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the displayed uniform approximation family exists, including the circuit-generation and gate bounds and its total-variation guarantee, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such polynomially bounded family exists. A negative proof must cover all implementations of these outcome probabilities, not merely a prescribed subset-sum-basis unitary or a chosen extension to a larger Hilbert space. A different measurement with a good success probability for recovering the hidden shift does not by itself implement the specified POVM. Agreement only on the average success rate, or only on the coset ensemble without the uniform-input error guarantee, is insufficient for this precise implementation target. Exponential dependence on \(\log N\), \(k\), or the unary precision parameter does not meet the resource bound. This is a yes/no efficiency question with accuracy quantified in its definition, not a numerical output problem requiring only a fixed additive tolerance.

context_blocks.text: The imported card combined implementation of an optimal measurement with the broader relation between the dihedral problem and random Subset Sum at different densities. On 16 September 2026 the user selected efficient approximation of the specific measurement. The present target records that narrowing and explicitly fixes its statistical error criterion and unary inverse-accuracy parameter. The wider reduction question is not claimed answered.

Bacon, Childs and van Dam prove that the displayed pretty good measurement maximizes the probability of identifying a uniformly random hidden shift from the coset-state ensemble. Optimality is an information-theoretic statement: it does not bound the number of elementary gates needed to carry out the measurement.

Their Theorem 2 gives success probability at least \(1/8\) once \(k\ge\log_2N+4\), and bounds it above by \(2^k/N\) for every \(N,k\). Thus enough copies can contain useful information even while extracting that information efficiently remains difficult. The chosen implementation target permits all copy counts and does not select a random Subset Sum density.

The earlier implementation analysis connects coherent uniform sampling of subset-sum solutions with an implementation of the optimal measurement. Its converse imposes a particular refinement and unitary realization. The 2016 source studies further restricted types of subset-sum-basis unitaries and derives consequences for subset-sum collision problems. Those statements do not prove a lower bound for every possible circuit with the same measurement statistics.

The later dihedral survey continues to separate the existence and success rate of an optimal measurement from its efficient implementation. Its exact-recovery no-go statements concern deterministic recovery from nonorthogonal samples, not approximation of the probabilistic measurement defined here.

The August 2026 semidirect-product algorithms apply under explicit restrictions on the abelian factor and the acting prime. For the dihedral action that prime is two, and the required ratio condition does not cover arbitrary cyclic order. Those results therefore do not supply this general measurement implementation.

cards.title: Quantum versus classical nonuniform advice
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{BQP/qpoly}=\mathrm{BQP/poly}\) as classes of languages without an oracle? Explicitly, for every language decidable by a uniform polynomial-time quantum algorithm supplied with a polynomial-size quantum advice state depending only on input length, does some uniform polynomial-time quantum algorithm with polynomial-length classical advice decide the same language with error at most \(1/3\) on every input? The algorithm and polynomial advice bound may change. The reverse inclusion follows by encoding a classical advice string in the computational basis.
cards.why: This compares the computational value of quantum and classical information stored in advance for an entire input length. It asks whether a short quantum state can support useful computations that no polynomial-length classical record can support, even when preparing either kind of advice is free. The shared-advice requirement makes this a different resource comparison from per-instance witnesses.

context_blocks.text: Advice is fixed before the particular input is seen and is trusted to be the chosen length-specific information. It must support every input of that length. A witness, by contrast, may be selected for one instance and must be checked against dishonest alternatives. Neither comparison is obtained simply by changing the name of the auxiliary register.

Quantum advice is supplied as a fresh copy on each run. The definition does not assume the algorithm can clone an unknown state or preserve it for unlimited reuse. Classical advice can be copied, but the class comparison allows either algorithm to consume the supplied resource during its computation.

The advice families can be uncomputable in both models. The question concerns what polynomial-size information makes possible for the uniform computation, not how to construct that information. Allowing input-specific advice would remove the crucial requirement that one message works for all strings of a given length.

Aaronson proved \(\mathrm{BQP/qpoly}\subseteq\mathrm{PP/poly}\). PP permits polynomial-time classical randomized computation with acceptance probability strictly greater than one half on yes-inputs and at most one half on no-inputs, without an inverse-polynomial margin; poly again permits length-specific classical advice. This upper bound uses a different computation model from bounded-error BQP, so it is not the desired simulation in BQP/poly.

The 2007 quantum-oracle separation demonstrated an advice advantage when both computations share a quantum black box. This supplies evidence in that augmented computation model and retains the oracle as an essential part of its statement.

The 2024 result separates the advice classes with an oracle encoding a classical function, but restricts even quantum algorithms to classical queries. This is a genuine precursor to the later standard classical-oracle theorem. Permitting superposition queries gives the classical-advice algorithm more power, so the access conventions must not be conflated.

The February 2026 construction, checked in its April revision, separates the advice classes using a standard classical oracle that both quantum algorithms may query in superposition. It resolves that oracle question while leaving the ordinary language equality asked here unresolved.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of \(\mathrm{BQP/qpoly}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP/poly}\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that some language has quantum advice as defined but no eligible classical-advice algorithm and family. An affirmative proof need not produce the classical advice efficiently, but must establish one length-indexed family and a uniform algorithm that work for all inputs. A negative proof must rule out every polynomial advice length, every classical advice family and every uniform quantum algorithm. A separation of promise problems alone does not automatically meet this card’s retained total-language target. Oracle separations, a difficult-to-describe state, or an advantage for advice selected after seeing the input do not suffice.
cards.definitions: A language is a set \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\); here every binary string must be decided, with no promise excluding some inputs. For each \(n\ge0\), let \(m(n),a(n)\) be nonnegative integers bounded by a fixed polynomial. A single deterministic classical Turing machine, given an input string \(x\) of length \(n\), generates in polynomial time a quantum circuit \(U_x\) with an \(m(n)\)-qubit advice register, \(a(n)\) ancillary qubits initialized to \(|0\rangle\), polynomially many gates, and one designated output qubit. The generating machine has no advice and no oracle. It uses the fixed exact gates \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\), with \[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathrm{CNOT}|b,c\rangle=|b,b\mathbin\oplus c\rangle,\] where \(b,c\in\{0,1\}\) and \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. The circuit outputs the computational-basis measurement of its output qubit. The quantum advice family is a sequence \((\rho_n)_{n\ge0}\) of density matrices on \(\mathbb C^{2^{m(n)}}\). A density matrix is positive semidefinite with trace one; positive semidefinite means \(v^\dagger\rho_nv\ge0\) for all vectors \(v\), and trace is the sum of diagonal entries. The probability of output 1 is \[\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[\Pi_1U_x\bigl(\rho_n\otimes|0\rangle\langle0|^{\otimes a(n)}\bigr)U_x^\dagger\right],\] where \(\Pi_1\) projects onto output 1 and is identity on the remaining qubits, and dagger denotes conjugate transpose. The language belongs to \(\mathrm{BQP/qpoly}\) if some such generating machine, polynomial bounds and advice family satisfy output-1 probability at least \(2/3\) for every \(x\in L\) and at most \(1/3\) for every \(x\notin L\). The same fixed \(\rho_n\) must work for all \(2^n\) strings of length \(n\). A fresh copy of that state is supplied for each independent computation; no cloning or repeated reuse of a consumed copy is promised. Advice is trusted: the requirement concerns the selected family, not all possible advice states. There is no computability or efficient-preparation requirement on the family, and its preparation cost is not charged. The language belongs to \(\mathrm{BQP/poly}\) if the advice can instead be a binary string \(b_n\in\{0,1\}^{m(n)}\), supplied as the basis state \(|b_n\rangle\). Its length may have a different polynomial bound and the circuit may be different, but \(b_n\) still depends only on \(n\), need not be computable, and must work for every length-\(n\) input. Both classes use uniform quantum computation in addition to the explicitly allowed nonuniform advice. BQP abbreviates bounded-error quantum polynomial time; poly and qpoly indicate classical-bit and quantum-qubit advice of polynomial length.

cards.title: Quantum query complexity versus bounded approximate degree
cards.formal: Determine, up to universal multiplicative constants, the extremal function \[M(n,d)=\max\bigl\{Q(f):\varnothing\ne D\subseteq\{0,1\}^n,\ f:D\to\{0,1\},\ \operatorname{bdeg}_{1/3}(f)\le d\bigr\}\] for all integers \(n\ge1\) and \(1\le d\le n\). The bounded approximate degree \(\operatorname{bdeg}_{1/3}(f)\) is the least total degree of a real polynomial \(p\) satisfying \[|p(x)-f(x)|\le1/3\quad(x\in D),\qquad 0\le p(x)\le1\quad(x\in\{0,1\}^n).\] The query measure \(Q\) has worst-case error at most \(1/3\). This makes the source's largest-gap question a two-parameter extremal query bound. The source's additional question of whether an exponential gap exists was answered affirmatively in 2023.
cards.why: Bounded approximate degree is the main numerical object behind the polynomial method for quantum query lower bounds. Determining its worst possible discrepancy from actual quantum query complexity would quantify how much algorithmic difficulty this method can miss under promises.
cards.status_note: The exponential-separation part of the 2021 question was resolved by Ambainis and Belovs at CCC 2023. The card retains the broader maximum-gap target as the explicit extremal curve M(n,d). The source, published separation and 2024 follow-up were checked on 2026-09-14; their checked theorems do not determine this curve, and a bounded later-work search found no complete characterization.

sentences: The question compares quantum query complexity with polynomials that approximate a promised Boolean function.
The polynomial must remain between zero and one even on inputs outside the promise.
The target is the largest quantum query complexity possible at each input length and bounded-degree budget.
A 2023 theorem already proves that the gap can be exponential, so that subquestion is no longer open.
The remaining task is to determine the full extremal bound up to universal multiplicative constants.

cards.definitions:
A partial Boolean function has a nonempty promise domain \(D\) of valid inputs, with one prescribed output bit for each valid input. An algorithm knows the function and promise but receives the actual input only through its bit oracle. Correctness is required on \(D\). Its fixed query budget applies on every input, including inputs outside the promise, where the output bit may be arbitrary.

For an input \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), a quantum bit query is the unitary \(O_x|i,b,z\rangle=|i,b\mathbin{\oplus}x_i,z\rangle\), where \(i\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\), \(b\in\{0,1\}\), \(z\) is a work register, \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo two, and the dummy coordinate has \(x_0=0\). A \(T\)-query algorithm starts in a fixed state, alternates at most \(T\) calls to this oracle with input-independent unitary operations on a finite-dimensional workspace, and finally measures a designated output bit. Arbitrary finite workspace and unitary matrices are allowed. Only oracle calls are charged; all other computation is free. Intermediate measurements and classical random choices can equivalently be included by storing their outcomes coherently. Algorithms may depend on the function and input length, but their operations cannot depend on the unknown input except through oracle calls. No uniform circuit-generation or time bound is imposed. Write \(Q(f)\) for the least integer \(T\) that achieves error at most \(1/3\) on every input in the domain of \(f\). The query bound is a worst-case bound, not an expected number of calls.

A real polynomial is a finite linear combination of monomials in \(n\) real variables; its total degree is the largest sum of variable exponents in a monomial with nonzero coefficient. Multilinear polynomials suffice because \(x_i^j=x_i\) on Boolean inputs for \(j\ge1\). Their real coefficients have no bit-length or computability restriction. Boundedness is imposed only on the entire Boolean cube, not on all of \(\mathbb R^n\), and includes inputs outside the promise. Every partial Boolean function has a bounded exact representing polynomial of degree at most \(n\): extend its values to a total Boolean function and interpolate.

There are finitely many partial Boolean functions on a fixed cube, so the displayed maximum is over a finite set. It is nonempty and satisfies \(1\le M(n,d)\le n\) on the stated domain, using a single input-bit function for the lower bound and reading all bits for the upper bound. The parameter \(n\) counts individual Boolean oracle bits. A symbol from a larger alphabet is not available in one query. Neither the promise nor the polynomial is supplied as an additional input-dependent oracle.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a specified positive function \(H(n,d)\), universal constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\), and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of \(cH(n,d)\le M(n,d)\le CH(n,d)\) throughout the stated integer domain. The answer must identify the asymptotic dependence on \(n,d\), not merely rename the defining optimization over functions or algorithms. Both a universal upper bound and matching worst-case examples are required. Exponential separation alone is already known and does not settle this full extremal target.

context_blocks.text: A \(T\)-query quantum algorithm has an acceptance probability that is a polynomial of degree at most \(2T\), bounded between zero and one on every Boolean input. Hence bounded approximate degree is always at most twice quantum query complexity. The question asks how far the converse can fail.

The promise does not remove the full-cube boundedness condition. Omitting that condition changes the measure and permits simple examples with artificially low degree. For total Boolean functions the two measures are polynomially related, but promises permit much larger separations.

Ambainis and Belovs give Boolean promise functions on \(n\) bits with bounded exact polynomial degree \(O(\log n)\) and quantum query complexity at least \(n^{1/3}\) up to logarithmic losses along their family. Bounded exact degree also upper-bounds bounded approximate degree, so this answers the exponential-gap subquestion.

The 2024 paper reproves such a partial-function separation through total search problems and strengthens the polynomial measure in additional results. These results establish large gaps, but the checked theorems do not determine the full extremal dependence on the input length and degree budget.

cards.context:
A \(T\)-query quantum algorithm has an acceptance probability that is a polynomial of degree at most \(2T\), bounded between zero and one on every Boolean input. Hence bounded approximate degree is always at most twice quantum query complexity. The question asks how far the converse can fail.

The promise does not remove the full-cube boundedness condition. Omitting that condition changes the measure and permits simple examples with artificially low degree. For total Boolean functions the two measures are polynomially related, but promises permit much larger separations.

Ambainis and Belovs give Boolean promise functions on \(n\) bits with bounded exact polynomial degree \(O(\log n)\) and quantum query complexity at least \(n^{1/3}\) up to logarithmic losses along their family. Bounded exact degree also upper-bounds bounded approximate degree, so this answers the exponential-gap subquestion.

The 2024 paper reproves such a partial-function separation through total search problems and strengthens the polynomial measure in additional results. These results establish large gaps, but the checked theorems do not determine the full extremal dependence on the input length and degree budget.

cards.definitions: For \(n\ge 2\) let \(J_{ij}, 1\le i<j\le n\), be independent real normal random variables of mean 0 and variance 1. On \((\mathbb{C} ^{2})^{\otimes n}\), let \(Z_{i}\) and \(X_{i}\) act on the i-th qubit by the Pauli matrices \(Z=diag(1,- 1)\) and X with off-diagonal entries 1 and diagonal entries 0. Put \(H_{J}=n^{- 1/2}\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}Z_{i} Z_{j}\) and \(B_{n}=\sum_{i} X_{i}\). Let |+⟩=\((|0\rangle +|1\rangle )/\sqrt{2}\). For integer depth \(p\ge 1\) and fixed real angle vectors \(\gamma ,\beta \in \mathbb{R} ^{p}\), define |\(\psi _{p,J}\rangle =e^{- i\beta _{p} B_{n}}e^{- i\gamma _{p} H_{J}}\cdots e^{- i\beta _{1} B_{n}}e^{- i\gamma _{1} H_{J}}|+\rangle ^{\otimes n}\). Matrix exponentials have their usual convergent-series meaning; states have unit norm. Expectation is over J. The n limit exists for each fixed p and angles as established for this model in the source. Angles may depend on p but are fixed independently of n and J. First take the infinite-n ensemble limit for fixed angles, then optimize those angles, then take the supremum over finite depths. Supremum need not be attained. Identity layers imply that the optimized depth values are nondecreasing. They are bounded by \(\Pi *=\lim _{n\to \infty} E_{J}[\max _{z\in \{- 1,1\}^{n}} n^{- 1/2}\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}z_{i} z_{j}]/n\), the finite Parisi ground-state value in this normalization. Maximization, rather than minimization, fixes the sign convention.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous value a and a Lean proof that |\(a- A|\le 1/100\), or certified lower and upper bounds of width at most \(1/50\) with the midpoint as answer. Exact determination also qualifies. Merely restating the defining supremum, reporting floating-point optimization at finitely many depths, or interchanging depth and instance-size limits is insufficient. Equality with \(\Pi\)* is a stronger possible answer, not assumed by the target.

cards.definitions: Write \([d]=\{1,\ldots ,d\}, u_{d}(i)=1/d\) and \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,u_{d})=(1/2)\sum_{i}|p_{i}- 1/d|\). The algorithm receives d and \(\varepsilon\) and oracle access to a unitary \(U_{p}\) satisfying \(U_{p}|0^{k}\rangle =\sum_{i}\sqrt{p_{i}}|i\rangle |\psi _{i}\rangle\), where each garbage state |\(\psi _{i}\rangle\) is normalized. The extension of \(U_{p}\) away from |\(0^{k}\rangle\) and its garbage states are arbitrary; the tester must work for every valid oracle satisfying the promise. A query is one application of \(U_{p}, U_{p}\dagger\) or controlled-\(U_{p}\); intervening quantum operations, ancillas and measurements are unrestricted and do not count toward query complexity. The code is used as a black box: the tester does not get a classical description to inspect for free. Let \(Q(d,\varepsilon )\) be the minimum worst-case number of such queries among testers whose probability of the correct yes/no output is at least 0.99 for every oracle with \(p=u_{d}\) or \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,u_{d})>\varepsilon\), taking the worst case over allowed oracle-register sizes. No guarantee is required in the intermediate gap.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a positive function \(g(d,\varepsilon )\) and absolute constants \(a,A>0\) such that a \(g(d,\varepsilon )\le Q(d,\varepsilon )\le A g(d,\varepsilon )\) throughout the stated domain. Prove both bounds uniformly over its two parameters and all valid oracle implementations. A formula or certified evaluation rule may specify g; merely renaming Q is insufficient. This is an asymptotic query bound up to multiplicative constants, not pointwise additive 0.01 accuracy.

cards.title: \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\) versus \(\mathrm{BQEXP}\)
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\subseteq\mathrm{BQEXP}\)? In promise-problem terms, does every pair \(\Pi=(Y,N)\) of disjoint sets of binary strings that has a polynomial-time quantum verifier with two unentangled polynomial-size proofs also admit a uniform quantum algorithm running in time \(2^{p(n)}\), for some polynomial \(p\), with error at most \(1/3\) on every promised input? The algorithm receives no proofs. The polynomial may depend on \(\Pi\) and its verifier, but not on the individual input of length \(n\).
cards.why: Unentangled quantum proofs add a nonconvex constraint to quantum verification. An exponential-time quantum simulation would place a meaningful algorithmic limit on this model and clarify whether its power can be explained without nondeterministic exponential-time witness search.
cards.status_note: The source explicitly asks this inclusion in January 2026. Primary definitions and the NEXP upper bound were checked together with July 2026 hierarchy and stoquastic results on 2026-09-14. None of those checked results supplies a BQEXP simulation for general QMA(2); this is a bounded literature check.

sentences: The question asks whether every problem with two unentangled quantum proofs can be decided in quantum exponential time without proofs.
The verifier is polynomial-time and may process both proofs jointly, but the proofs must initially be a product state.
The deciding algorithm must be uniform and have bounded error on every promised input.
The standard upper bound uses nondeterministic exponential time, which does not give the requested algorithm.
Recent quantified and stoquastic results concern different upper-bound models and leave this inclusion unresolved.

cards.definitions:
A promise problem specifies yes-inputs \(Y\) and no-inputs \(N\); on inputs outside \(Y\cup N\), a deciding algorithm has no correctness requirement but must still obey its resource bound. A qubit has state space \(\mathbb C^2\). A pure state on \(w\) qubits is a unit vector in \(\mathbb C^{2^w}\). Two unentangled proofs have the tensor-product form \(|\psi\rangle\otimes|\phi\rangle\), where each vector describes at most \(w(n)\) qubits for some polynomial \(w\). Arbitrary entanglement within either proof is allowed, but entanglement between the proofs is excluded.

Membership in \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\) means that one deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine, on input \(x\), generates a quantum circuit \(V_x\) of polynomial size. The circuit takes the two proof registers and zero-initialized work qubits, and finally measures an output bit. Write \(a_x(\psi,\phi)\) for its acceptance probability. Its guarantees are \[x\in Y\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists\psi,\phi:\ a_x(\psi,\phi)\ge2/3,\qquad x\in N\ \Longrightarrow\ \forall\psi,\phi:\ a_x(\psi,\phi)\le1/3.\] The two proofs are sent once; there is no later interaction. The same definition results if mixed product states or convex mixtures of product states are permitted, by linearity of acceptance probability. The verifier need not certify that an arbitrarily supplied entangled pair is a product: unentanglement is the proof model's assumption.

Use the fixed finite gate set consisting of Hadamard \(H=2^{-1/2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), its inverse, and controlled NOT, acting on named wires. Circuit size counts every gate; every initialized or proof qubit counts toward the relevant qubit bound. Uniform generation outputs the full gate and wire list.

Membership in \(\mathrm{BQEXP}\) means that one deterministic circuit generator, on input \(x\) of length \(n\), runs in at most \(2^{p(n)}\) steps and outputs a circuit with at most \(2^{p(n)}\) gates and qubits, using the same finite gate set. The circuit begins with zero-initialized qubits, receives no proof or advice, and accepts yes-inputs with probability at least \(2/3\) and no-inputs with probability at most \(1/3\). Classical dependence on \(x\) is through the generator. Polynomial overheads in the generator and circuit can be absorbed into \(p\). No oracle or postselection is available. Probability in both models is ordinary quantum measurement probability.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the inclusion, or of its negation. Inclusion requires a bounded-error, uniform exponential-time quantum decision procedure for every problem satisfying the stated two-proof verification definition. Separation requires a promise problem in \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\) with no such decision procedure. Simulations only for restricted verifiers, shorter proofs, or a different completeness-soundness gap do not suffice.

context_blocks.text: Classically, two existential witnesses can simply be concatenated. In this quantum model, allowing an arbitrary joint state would remove the product restriction and give the ordinary single-proof model. That restriction is therefore part of the computational resource, rather than an incidental communication detail.

A known upper bound is \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\subseteq\mathrm{NEXP}\), where \(\mathrm{NEXP}\) allows nondeterministic time \(2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}\). Guessing sufficiently accurate classical descriptions of the two states and verifying them explains this bound. Enumerating all such descriptions is much more expensive, so this does not give a deterministic or quantum exponential-time algorithm.

The 2026 hierarchy result gives a structural upper bound using competing quantifiers over pure quantum states. Its stated containments still end at nondeterministic exponential time. An existential/universal characterization does not itself implement a bounded-error quantum decision procedure.

The July 2026 work obtains exponential-time algorithms for a stoquastic restriction, designed to remove destructive interference. Its verifier restrictions are substantive, so those algorithms do not yield the requested simulation for general quantum verifiers.

cards.title: Succinct entangled proofs with efficient provers
cards.formal: Does quantum circuit acceptance admit a uniform two-prover, one-round proof with a classical polynomial-time verifier, total classical communication \(O((\log(N+2))^k)\) for some fixed \(k\), completeness at least \(2/3\), and soundness at most \(1/3\) against arbitrary entangled provers, such that the honest provers can prepare and execute their strategy in quantum polynomial time given polynomially many copies of an accepting witness? Here \(N\) is the explicit circuit-instance length, and the instance, efficiency and soundness requirements are defined below.

source_formulation.text: The best of both worlds The essential reason that two-prover succinct verification remains an open problem is that nonlocal answer reduction is hard.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 3

cards.why: This asks whether a classical verifier can check general quantumly provable claims using very little communication while keeping the honest quantum resources polynomial. It joins three substantial demands—two separated provers, unconditional soundness and succinct communication—and would clarify the practical content of entangled proof systems beyond their unconstrained complexity-class power.

No matching resolution was found in the bounded search, and the cited proofs were not independently verified.
