cards.definitions: The matrix \(H=H^*\) is fixed, not part of a circuit input. Its entries are algebraic complex numbers, specified by finite integer-polynomial and isolating-region descriptions that may be hardcoded into an algorithm depending on \(H\). A circuit has \(N\ge1\) qubits initialized to an explicitly supplied computational-basis string \(b\in\{0,1\}^N\). Each gate chooses an ordered pair of distinct qubits and applies \(\exp(-itH)\) on that pair for a signed rational time \(t\); negative times give exact inverse evolution. There are no free single-qubit gates or intermediate measurements. At the end all qubits are measured in the computational basis, defining a probability distribution \(p_C\) on \(\{0,1\}^N\). The input explicitly lists the initial bits, gate sequence, ordered wire indices and rational numerators and positive denominators in binary. It also includes a unary integer \(B\ge1\) with \(|t|\le B\) for every gate. Let \(L\) be the full bit encoding length. This charges enough description length for polynomial physical evolution time, as required by the source model. The simulation branch requires a single uniform randomized Turing machine for this fixed \(H\), taking \(C\) and a binary rational \(0<\varepsilon<1\), that halts on every random tape within a fixed polynomial in \(L+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+\operatorname{len}(\varepsilon)\) and outputs a string with distribution \(s_C\) satisfying \(\tfrac12\sum_z|s_C(z)-p_C(z)|\le\varepsilon\). It uses independent fair coins and no oracle or advice. Define \(\operatorname{Post}(H)\) as follows. For a language \(K\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\), a uniform deterministic polynomial-time compiler maps each input \(x\) to such a circuit \(C_x\), a designated output bit, and a disjoint list of postselection bits with prescribed values. There is a polynomial \(p\) such that the prescribed event has probability at least \(2^{-p(|x|)}\) on every input. Conditional on it, the output is 1 with probability at least \(2/3\) for \(x\in K\) and at most \(1/3\) otherwise. Circuit descriptions, including the unary time bound, have polynomial length in \(|x|\). The postselection list and values may depend on the input through the compiler. PP consists of languages for which a uniform polynomial-time fair-coin Turing machine accepts with probability strictly greater than \(1/2\) on members and at most \(1/2\) on nonmembers. The second branch is the source’s postselected-computation criterion expressed via PP; the algebraic-entry, accuracy and exponentially bounded postselection conventions are explicit editorial choices. The alternatives need not be disjoint. No commutativity promise is imposed on \(H\).
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of the disjunction for every allowed fixed interaction, or a Lean counterexample interaction for which both branches fail. The proof must use the supplied finite-precision sampling and uniform postselection conventions. A classification with free local gates, arbitrary analog reductions, a commutativity promise or a different sampling error does not automatically settle this variant.

cards.title: Exponential repetition of two-player entangled games
cards.formal: Does every finite two-player, one-round game \(G\) with entangled value \(\omega^{*}(G)<1\) admit a constant \(c_{G}>0\) such that \[\omega^{*}(G^{\otimes n})\leq \exp(-c_{G}n)\qquad\text{for every integer }n\geq1?\] The repetition uses the unchanged game and requires winning every coordinate. The 2016 paper proves convergence to zero at a polynomial rate; an August 2026 manuscript claims the exponential bound, with verification limits recorded below.

references.title: A Parallel Repetition Theorem for All Entangled Games
references.locator: Explicit open question on PDF page 3

cards.definitions:
A game is specified by finite nonempty question sets \(X,Y\), finite nonempty answer sets \(A,B\), a probability distribution \(\mu\) on \(X\times Y\), and a winning predicate \(V:X\times Y\times A\times B\to\{0,1\}\). The referee samples \((x,y)\) from \(\mu\), sends \(x\) only to Alice and \(y\) only to Bob, and accepts their answers \(a,b\) exactly when \(V(x,y,a,b)=1\). The two questions may be correlated, and some pairs may have probability zero.

Before receiving their questions, the players may share any finite-dimensional bipartite quantum state \(\rho\) on \(\mathcal H_{A}\otimes\mathcal H_{B}\). On question \(x\), Alice applies a measurement \(\{E^{x}_{a}:a\in A\}\); on question \(y\), Bob applies \(\{F^{y}_{b}:b\in B\}\). Each measurement is a family of positive semidefinite operators summing to the identity. Their conditional answer probability is
\[\Pr[a,b\mid x,y]=\operatorname{Tr}\!\bigl(\rho(E^{x}_{a}\otimes F^{y}_{b})\bigr).\]
They cannot communicate after receiving the questions. Shared randomness is permitted and can be incorporated into the shared state.

The entangled value \(\omega^{*}(G)\) is the supremum of the winning probability over all such finite-dimensional states and local measurements. The dimensions have no fixed upper bound, and a strategy attaining the supremum need not exist. This is the finite-dimensional tensor-product model, not the possibly larger commuting-operator or general nonsignaling model. No efficiency restriction is placed on a strategy.

In \(G^{\otimes n}\), the referee samples \(n\) independent pairs from \(\mu\), sends the complete tuple of Alice's questions to Alice and the complete tuple of Bob's questions to Bob, and receives answer tuples in \(A^{n}\) and \(B^{n}\). Acceptance requires \(V(x_{i},y_{i},a_{i},b_{i})=1\) for every coordinate \(i\).

Each player may use one joint local measurement depending on their entire tuple. Their shared state and its dimension may depend on \(n\). Thus independent sampling by the referee does not force independent play. Product strategies give the lower bound \(\omega^{*}(G^{\otimes n})\geq\omega^{*}(G)^{n}\); this is not the requested upper bound.

The constant \(c_{G}\) may depend on the entire fixed game, including its soundness gap \(1-\omega^{*}(G)\). It must be positive and independent of \(n\), the strategy and its dimension. No universal optimal exponent or algorithm for computing \(c_{G}\) is requested. A transformed game with added questions is a different game and cannot replace \(G\) in this statement.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal exponential upper bound in the stated strategy model, or exhibit one fixed finite game with value below one for which no positive \(c_{G}\) works. A sequence of different games with progressively slower exponential constants is not a counterexample. Polynomial decay, convergence to zero, exponential decay only for a special game family, or amplification after changing the game does not settle the conjecture.

cards.title: Martin’s conjecture
cards.formal: Assume \(\mathsf{ZF}+\mathsf{DC}+\mathsf{AD}\). Is the following conjunction true for all total Turing-invariant functions \(f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}\)? Part I: every such \(f\) is constant in Turing degree on a cone or computes its input on a cone. Part II: the relation \(\leq_M\) of Turing reducibility on a cone prewellorders the set \(\mathcal F\) of all such functions above the identity on a cone, and for every \(f\in\mathcal F\), its pointwise Turing jump \(f'\) has rank exactly \(\operatorname{rank}_M(f)+1\) in that same prewellorder. All functions, cones, ordinals and quantifiers are interpreted within the stated set-theoretic universe.
cards.definitions:
Write \(\omega=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\) and \(2^{\omega}=\{x:\omega\to\{0,1\}\}\). Such a real is identified with the subset \(\{n:x(n)=1\}\) of \(\omega\). Fix an acceptable effective enumeration \((\Phi_e)_{e\in\omega}\) of ordinary oracle Turing programs with natural-number inputs and outputs. The oracle answers membership queries in a real. Define \(x\leq_T y\) to mean that some index \(e\) satisfies \(\Phi_e^y(n)\downarrow=x(n)\) for every \(n\in\omega\), with no time bound. The single index computes the entire real, and may depend on \(x,y\). Define \(x\equiv_T y\) by mutual reducibility. A Turing degree is an equivalence class for \(\equiv_T\). The jump \(y'\) is the characteristic real of \(\{e:\Phi_e^y(e)\text{ halts}\}\). Any acceptable effective numbering gives the same induced operation on degrees.

A total function \(f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}\) is Turing-invariant when \(\forall x,y:\ x\equiv_T y\Rightarrow f(x)\equiv_T f(y)\). No computability, measurability, Borel definability, order preservation or uniform production of reduction indices is required. The quantifiers concern functions on reals with this invariance property; no choice of a representative from every Turing degree is assumed.

For \(a\in2^{\omega}\), the cone with base \(a\) is \(C_a=\{x\in2^{\omega}:a\leq_T x\}\). Being constant in degree on a cone means
\[\exists a,b\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ f(x)\equiv_T b.\]
Being above the identity on a cone means
\[\exists a\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ x\leq_T f(x).\]
The base may depend on \(f\). Constancy is equality of degrees, not literal equality of output reals. A cone requirement holds for every real in that cone, not merely infinitely many reals or a set of full ordinary Lebesgue measure.

For invariant \(f,g\), define
\[f\leq_M g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists a\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ f(x)\leq_T g(x).\]
The base may depend on both functions; no single base must work for all comparisons. Set \(f\equiv_M g\) when both \(f\leq_M g\) and \(g\leq_M f\). Let \(\mathrm{id}(x)=x\) and \(\mathcal F=\{f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}: f\text{ is Turing-invariant and }\mathrm{id}\leq_M f\}\). The prewellorder clause means that \(\leq_M\) is reflexive, transitive and total on \(\mathcal F\), and that the induced order on the set \(\mathcal F/{\equiv_M}\) is a well-order: every nonempty subset of that quotient has a least member. Its strict order is \([g]<[f]\) when \(g\leq_M f\) and \(f\not\leq_M g\). When this clause holds, \(\operatorname{rank}_M(f)\) is the ordinal order type of the quotient classes strictly below \([f]\), with its least class having rank zero. The pointwise jump is \(f'(x)=(f(x))'\). The \(+1\) in Part II is ordinal successor, and the rank is computed in the full quotient above the identity, not a selected definable subclass.

The background \(\mathsf{ZF}\) is Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory without the axiom of choice. Full dependent choice \(\mathsf{DC}\) asserts that for every nonempty set \(S\), every relation \(R\subseteq S\times S\) with \(\forall s\in S\;\exists t\in S:\ sRt\), and every \(s_0\in S\), there is a sequence \((s_n)_{n\in\omega}\) starting at \(s_0\) with \(s_nRs_{n+1}\) for all \(n\). The axiom of determinacy \(\mathsf{AD}\) asserts that for every set \(W\subseteq\omega^{\omega}\), the following perfect-information game is determined. Players I and II alternate choosing natural numbers, with I moving at even-numbered stages starting at zero; I wins exactly when the resulting sequence belongs to \(W\). A strategy assigns a next move to every finite history at that player’s turn, and is winning if every infinite play compatible with it is won by that player. Determined means that one player has such a winning strategy. No regularity condition is imposed on \(W\). These are internal set-theoretic axioms; the full axiom of choice is not added to them.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of both parts of the conjunction under \(\mathsf{ZF}+\mathsf{DC}+\mathsf{AD}\), or a refutation of at least one part under that same background. A refutation of Part I must establish the existence of an invariant function that is neither constant in degree on any cone nor above the identity on any cone. A refutation of Part II must establish failure of the stated full prewellorder or, when that prewellorder exists, failure of the exact jump-successor clause. A result only for uniformly invariant, Borel, regressive or order-preserving functions does not prove the full conjunction. Counterexamples obtained with the full axiom of choice do not refute the stated determinacy version. The Lean formalization must represent the set-theoretic background faithfully, for example through an internal set universe and its satisfaction relation, with all reals and functions interpreted there; importing ambient choice into that universe and deriving a contradiction with determinacy is not a proof of this target. No unproved classification or uniformity principle may be substituted for a required part.
cards.why: Turing degrees encode relative computational power and have a highly non-linear structure. Martin’s conjecture asks whether invariance under mutual computability nevertheless forces every nontrivial operation into an ordered hierarchy once behaviour is compared on cones under determinacy. It gives a precise structural target behind the observed regularity of many degree operators, and connects computability with descriptive set theory and analogous hierarchies of logical strength.

importance.reason: A flagship conjecture about the global structure of Turing degrees and the classification of invariant computational operations.

progress.text: Steel proves Part II for uniformly invariant functions; the result and original publication are recorded in the checked survey’s Theorem 1.3 and reference [26].
Slaman–Steel establish uniform Part I, the regressive case and Borel order-preserving Part II, as recorded in the survey’s Theorems 1.2, 1.6 and 1.7.
Lutz–Siskind version 3 gives the order-preserving and measure-preserving Part I results. Its revision note corrects the proof of Theorem 4.12; this audit uses the corrected version.
Day–Marks version 2 records conditional structural results for a related decomposition question and many-one output degrees; it does not settle the unrestricted Turing-degree target.
Walsh’s Bulletin of Symbolic Logic survey presents the full target as Conjecture 6.4 and summarizes distinct partial cases in Theorems 6.6–6.7; the article first appeared online on 4 December 2025.

context_blocks.text: A function can assign different output reals to equivalent inputs while still inducing a well-defined operation on degrees. This is the invariance required here. The operation itself need not be computable: the Turing jump is a central example. The conjecture concerns the organization of such operations rather than an algorithm for listing or calculating their values.

The two parts have separate content. Part I is a dichotomy for all invariant functions. Part II concerns the full collection already above the identity and asserts both a well-order after identifying cone-equivalent functions and an exact successor rule. In particular, strict increase under the jump alone is weaker than the assertion that its rank is the next ordinal. No continuity rule at limit ordinals is included in that successor clause.

Determinacy gives a zero-one law for invariant sets: each contains a cone or its complement contains one. Martin measure assigns these cases values one and zero. Thus the phrase almost everywhere in the cited formulation means on a Turing cone. It does not refer to the usual probability measure from independent bits, and a comparison base need not work for unrelated functions.

Uniform invariance requires one map \(u:\omega^2\to\omega^2\) that converts any pair of indices witnessing \(x\equiv_T y\) into a pair witnessing \(f(x)\equiv_T f(y)\), independently of the reals. Even this index map is not required to be computable in the survey’s definition. Steel and Slaman–Steel establish the two parts for the uniform subclass. Ordinary invariance does not supply such a map.

The regressive case is already settled: if invariant \(f\) satisfies \(f(x)\leq_T x\) on a cone, then on a cone it is constant in degree or equivalent to the identity. Order preservation is a different restriction, namely \(x\leq_T y\Rightarrow f(x)\leq_T f(y)\). The saved full target includes neither restriction. Earlier extraction of only a regressive subcase was corrected before this audit; this review preserves the full conjecture.

Lutz and Siskind prove Part I for all order-preserving functions and for all measure-preserving invariant functions. Here the latter means \(\forall a\;\exists b\;\forall x\geq_T b:\ a\leq_T f(x)\), with the base allowed to depend on the fixed target degree. Their Theorem 3.7 and Theorem 4.8 use determinacy and dependent choice for reals, which follow from this card’s stronger fixed background. The older Part II theorem for order-preserving functions retains a Borel restriction; Borel means inverse images of open sets belong to the sigma algebra generated by the finite-prefix open sets of Cantor space.

The background cannot be replaced by \(\mathsf{ZFC}\). Lutz and Siskind’s §6.4 supplies choice-based counterexamples, including an invariant order-preserving function that is neither constant nor above the identity on a cone. These do not satisfy the determinacy setting. A faithful proof-assistant treatment must keep that internal set universe distinct from any ambient use of choice.

The author erratum to the Marks–Slaman–Steel survey withdraws Theorem 1.8, an asserted equivalence whose argument fails at limit ordinals. This audit therefore uses the actual two-part conjecture and checked restricted theorems, without importing the withdrawn equivalence as a fact about arbitrary invariant Borel functions.

Day and Marks’ February 2026 revision studies conditional consequences of an unresolved decomposition question for Turing equivalence, including nonuniformity for functions whose outputs are compared by many-one reducibility. These are related structural results with a different output reducibility and an additional open premise. They do not claim a counterexample to the full conjecture stated here.

Walsh’s March 2026 journal survey states the full conjecture explicitly as open and distinguishes the order-preserving Part I theorem from the Borel order-preserving Part II theorem. This supplies a dated status source; the bounded September follow-up search is recorded separately from verification of the underlying proofs.

cards.title: Kolmogorov–Loveland randomness versus Martin-Löf randomness
cards.formal: Is every Kolmogorov–Loveland random infinite binary sequence Martin-Löf random with respect to the fair-coin product measure?
cards.definitions: Work in Cantor space \(2^{N}\), with coordinates numbered \(0,1,\ldots\) and fair-coin product measure \(\mu\). For a finite binary string \(\sigma\), the cylinder \([\sigma ]\)={\(X:\sigma\) is a prefix of X} has measure \(2^{- |\sigma |}\). A Martin-Löf test is a sequence \((U_{k})_{k\ge 1}\) of open sets obtained by one algorithm enumerating pairs \((k,\sigma )\), with \(U_{k}\) equal to the union of its enumerated cylinders for index k and \(\mu (U_{k})\le 2^{- k}\). A sequence X is Martin-Löf random if for every such test \(X\notin \bigcap _{k} U_{k}\). A Kolmogorov–Loveland betting strategy starts with capital 1. From the finite history h of bits already revealed, a partial computable procedure outputs a previously unqueried coordinate j and a rational multiplier \(q\in [0,2]\), before seeing \(X(j)\). The selected coordinates can be reconstructed from the earlier history and the same procedure; no coordinate may be selected twice along any run. After \(X(j)\) is revealed, the capital is multiplied by q if the bit is 0 and by \(2- q\) if it is 1, and that bit is appended to h. Thus each bet preserves expected capital under a fresh unbiased bit and cannot create debt. \(q=1\) allows reading a bit without risking capital. The next coordinate may depend on all revealed values and need not exceed previous coordinates. If the procedure fails to produce its next action, no further capital is earned. There are no oracle, running-time or space allowances beyond ordinary partial computability. A strategy succeeds on X if its capital at completed bets has unbounded supremum. X is Kolmogorov–Loveland random if every such strategy has bounded capital on X; the bound may depend on both X and the strategy. Rational multipliers suffice for the standard notion, and allowing partial rather than total computable strategies does not change the resulting class.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A central equivalence problem for algorithmic randomness: determine whether adaptive computable prediction detects every failure of effective measure-theoretic randomness.

importance.reason: A defining open question linking computability, adaptive information access, fair betting and effective null tests; a resolution would settle the relationship between two foundational randomness notions.

cards.status_note: The revised 2025 primary paper and its journal version explicitly retain KLR=MLR as a major open problem. Its finite-family/open-set obstruction is not a separating infinite sequence. No later resolution found through 11 September 2026. The formulation fixes fair-coin measure, fresh adaptive coordinates, rational fair bets, partial computability and unbounded-capital success.

context_blocks.text: These are two ways to say that an individual infinite sequence behaves randomly. Martin-Löf tests describe effectively recognizable events of arbitrarily small probability, and a sequence is nonrandom if one test catches it at every level. The betting definition instead asks whether an algorithm can turn knowledge of selected bits into unbounded profit. It measures mathematical unpredictability of a whole sequence, rather than a statistical confidence score assigned to a finite data sample.

The betting order is adaptive. A strategy may inspect a faraway coordinate before deciding which earlier, still unseen coordinate to bet on. It may also read a coordinate with a zero wager to gather information. It cannot bet on a bit already revealed, since that would permit guaranteed profit even from a fair-coin sequence. Its choice of the next position must be computed using only the information it has actually observed.

The known implication from Martin-Löf randomness follows from the fairness of the bets. For a fixed strategy starting with capital one, the set of sequences on which capital ever reaches a threshold R has measure at most \(1/R\). Reaching a threshold is witnessed after finitely many completed actions and can be effectively enumerated. Taking increasing thresholds produces a Martin-Löf test covering the sequences on which this strategy succeeds. The unresolved direction would convert every effective failure of randomness into success of some permitted gambler.

Choosing the query order in advance is insufficient. Kastermans and Lempp show that randomness against computable injective query orders is weaker than Martin-Löf randomness; they also establish the separation for computable permutation orders. The full Kolmogorov–Loveland definition permits choices that depend on observed bit values. Consequently their separating sequences do not establish the separation requested here.

Merkle, Miller, Nies, Reimann and Stephan prove that Kolmogorov–Loveland random sequences have arbitrarily dense subsequences that are Martin-Löf random. A key splitting result says that when a computable set of coordinates and its complement are both infinite, at least one of the two resulting subsequences is Martin-Löf random. This places the notion close to Martin-Löf randomness, but the randomness of a subsequence does not by itself imply randomness of the original interleaving.

Generalized betting games use a different query model. Generalized betting games may split a current set of possible sequences into computably described pieces, instead of querying exactly one fresh bit. Petrović’s 2021 paper gives a pair of strategies in a generalized half-betting model that together succeed on every non-Martin-Löf-random sequence. The greater freedom of the query is part of that theorem, so it does not directly give two Kolmogorov–Loveland strategies.

Petrović’s 2025 result identifies a limitation of a method used for those more flexible games. Kolmogorov–Loveland strategies do not admit the same finite-family guarantee of uniformly forcing large capital on every sequence in a sufficiently small effective open set. The paper constructs small open sets containing sequences on which the relevant capital bounds are not exceeded. This is a barrier to that style of quantitative coverage argument.

The remaining quantifier matters: finding a suitable sequence inside each of arbitrarily small open sets need not produce one sequence lying in every level of a single Martin-Löf test. Likewise, excluding one fixed finite family of gamblers does not exclude a strategy chosen separately for each nonrandom sequence. The 2025 paper explicitly keeps the equivalence question open.

A positive answer would show that the ability to choose unseen coordinates adaptively compensates for the restrictions of an ordinary computable betting procedure. A negative answer would exhibit effective statistical nonrandomness that escapes every such procedure. Either outcome would resolve a basic mismatch between two precise definitions of randomness and sharpen our understanding of what information an adaptive algorithm can extract from an infinite object.

cards.title: Rigidity of the Turing degrees
cards.formal:
Let \(D_T=\mathcal P(\mathbb N)/{\equiv_T}\) be the set of all Turing degrees, ordered by Turing reducibility. Is this order rigid? The exact assertion is
\[\forall\pi:D_T\to D_T,\quad \Bigl[\pi\text{ is bijective}\ \land\ \forall a,b\in D_T\,\bigl(a\le_T b\iff\pi(a)\le_T\pi(b)\bigr)\Bigr]\ \Longrightarrow\ \forall a\in D_T\,\pi(a)=a.\]
The domain is the full quotient of all subsets of the standard natural numbers. The quantifier over \(\pi\) ranges over arbitrary functions on this quotient in ordinary classical set theory, with ZFC as the set-theoretic background.
cards.definitions:
Write \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\), \(\mathcal P(\mathbb N)\) for its full power set, and \(\chi_A:\mathbb N\to\{0,1\}\) for a set's characteristic function. A deterministic oracle Turing machine is a finite program with ordinary unbounded work tapes and an additional operation that receives \(\chi_B(k)\) when it asks whether \(k\) belongs to the oracle set \(B\). Each terminating computation takes finitely many steps and makes finitely many queries; no uniform bound on their number, time or space is imposed. Natural inputs and queries have the usual finite binary encodings. Any fixed effective enumeration \((\Phi_e)_{e\in\mathbb N}\) of all such programs gives
\[A\le_T B\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists e\in\mathbb N\ \forall n\in\mathbb N,\ \Phi_e^B(n)\text{ halts with output }\chi_A(n).\]
The same index must work on every input, but may depend on \(A,B\). Programs contain no additional oracle, infinite advice or noncomputable constants. All subsets are eligible oracle sets, including noncomputable ones.

Define \(A\equiv_T B\) by \(A\le_T B\) and \(B\le_T A\). A degree \([A]\) is the equivalence class of \(A\), and \([A]\le_T[B]\) means \(A\le_T B\); this is independent of the representatives. Equality of degrees is mutual reducibility, not equality of their representatives. The set \(D_T\) includes every degree, not just degrees containing computably enumerable sets, arithmetical degrees, or degrees below a selected bound. A set is computably enumerable if a program with no oracle lists exactly its members, with arbitrary repetition and delay allowed.

An order automorphism is a total injective and surjective map \(\pi:D_T\to D_T\) that preserves and reflects every reducibility comparison. It need not be computable, definable, continuous or induced by a prescribed operation on sets. A representation \(F:\mathcal P(\mathbb N)\to\mathcal P(\mathbb N)\), if used to specify it, must satisfy \([F(A)]=\pi([A])\) for every \(A\); the representation itself need not be bijective. The order language has only equality and \(\le_T\). Jump preservation is a known consequence of this order structure, not an extra assumption in the target.

For the dated context, \(\mathbf 0=[\varnothing]\). The join \([A]\vee[B]\) is \([A\oplus B]\), where \(A\oplus B=\{2n:n\in A\}\cup\{2n+1:n\in B\}\). Set \(A'=\{e:\Phi_e^A(e)\text{ halts}\}\); the Turing jump is \([A]'=[A']\), and \(\mathbf 0''=(\mathbf 0')'\). These degrees are independent of the chosen effective machine enumeration. The upper cone with base \(b\) is \(\{a:b\le_T a\}\). Its complement includes both degrees below \(b\) and degrees incomparable with \(b\).

The assertion concerns the degree order built from the full power set in the ambient universe, not a selected countable model's internally computed degrees. The continuum hypothesis and determinacy are not hypotheses of the target. There are no finite input sizes, efficiency bounds or numerical approximation parameters in this structural question.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed universal assertion or its exact negation. A positive answer must apply to every set-theoretic order automorphism of the entire \(D_T\). A negative answer must prove
\[\exists\pi:D_T\to D_T\ \exists a\in D_T,\quad\pi\text{ is bijective},\quad \forall b,c\in D_T\,\bigl(b\le_Tc\iff\pi(b)\le_T\pi(c)\bigr),\quad\pi(a)\ne a.\]
An existence proof is sufficient; no computable formula for the automorphism is required. A construction on representatives must establish that it descends to this full quotient and has all the stated properties. Proving rigidity only on a proper substructure or for a restricted family of maps does not meet the criterion. Nor does a non-surjective order embedding or a permutation of representatives that fixes every degree. Both answer directions retain the stated classical background without an unproved extra hypothesis; relative consistency or independence alone does not assert either of these two mathematical conclusions. All supporting formalized definitions and theorems needed for the chosen direction must be included or supplied by verified Lean libraries.
cards.why: Rigidity asks whether the entire ordering of relative computational power has any nontrivial global symmetry. context_blocks.text: Two oracle decision problems represent the same Turing degree precisely when each can compute the other. Their degree records computational power without committing to a particular set of integers as its encoding. This question asks whether all degrees can be consistently relabeled, changing at least one point while preserving every reducibility comparison. A nontrivial symmetry must work simultaneously across the whole structure.

The computable degree \(\mathbf 0\) and the join operation are fixed by every order automorphism. Shore and Slaman proved the stronger fact that the graph of the Turing jump is first-order definable using the degree order alone. Thus \(\pi(a')=\pi(a)'\) for every degree \(a\), and all finite jumps of \(\mathbf 0\) are fixed. Preservation of the jump is an established restriction, not a proof of full rigidity.

Slaman and Woodin proved that every automorphism fixes every degree at least \(\mathbf 0''\); their automorphism group is also at most countable. These are statements about restrictions of global automorphisms. They do not assert that an arbitrary automorphism of the upper cone extends to the full structure, and they do not cover degrees incomparable with its base. The underlying set of all degrees has cardinality \(2^{\aleph_0}\).

The same structural analysis connects rigidity with the Slaman–Woodin bi-interpretability conjecture: the degree structure and full second-order arithmetic would recover one another through logical interpretations, with the correspondence to degrees definable without parameters. The survey states equivalence with rigidity in its precise sense of bi-interpretability. This concerns the expressive power of the whole order.

Rigidity does not mean that every degree has its own parameter-free first-order definition. There are only countably many finite formulas in this language and uncountably many degrees. Most degrees therefore cannot be individually defined that way, even if the entire order is rigid.

Kjos-Hanssen proves that a coordinate permutation \(p:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\), acting on characteristic sequences by \(F_p(A)(n)=A(p(n))\), can induce an automorphism of all Turing degrees only when that automorphism is the identity; in fact \(p\) must be computable. He also excludes nontrivial automorphisms induced by homeomorphisms of \(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\) preserving every Bernoulli product measure. Here the topology is generated by finite initial segments, and the measure with parameter \(t\in[0,1]\) makes coordinates independent bits with probability \(t\) of being one. These representation and measure restrictions are absent from the main question.

Slaman and Soskova study the separate structure of degrees at most \(\mathbf 0'\), equivalently the \(\Delta^0_2\) degrees. They prove that this local structure has a finite automorphism base: agreement on a fixed finite tuple determines an automorphism. They obtain a countable automorphism group and an equivalence between local rigidity and bi-interpretability with first-order arithmetic. None of these conclusions states that the group is trivial. Their local arithmetic comparison is distinct from the full structure’s second-order comparison.

Ongay-Valverde’s 2021 preprint gives restrictions on the action of a hypothetical automorphism on generic degrees under the continuum hypothesis \(2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_1\). Theorem 7.4 additionally concerns families meeting a relative genericity condition above every degree, with jointly generic representatives for each degree and its image. Its Section 8 explicitly keeps the continuum-hypothesis assumption. This conditional restriction neither constructs a nontrivial automorphism nor proves that all automorphisms are trivial, even under that hypothesis.

Cooper’s 1999 Theorem 1.1 claims a nonidentity global automorphism fixing every degree at least \(\mathbf 0'\). This is a claim of a full negative answer, rather than merely a local example. The present review checked the statement in the author-uploaded text but did not verify its long construction.

Slaman’s later survey explicitly reports that Cooper’s construction had not been independently verified and treats the general problem as unresolved. The subsequent permutation paper also states the full question as open. The card therefore keeps the historical full-solution claim visible and uses uncertain status; it does not infer either correctness or a proved error from the announcement alone.

cards.title: Busy Beaver \(\mathrm{BB}(6)\)
cards.formal: Determine the exact value of $BB(6)=S(6)$ by specifying a machine $M_*\in\mathcal{M}_6$ that halts on the blank tape and proving that $T(M)\le T(M_*)$ for every $M\in\mathcal{M}_6$ that halts on the blank tape. Here $\mathcal{M}_6$ is the class of deterministic Turing machines with six nonhalting states, two tape symbols and one initially all-zero, bi-infinite tape, as defined below, and $T(M)$ counts transitions up to and including the first entry into the separate halting state. The answer is then $BB(6)=T(M_*)$; the witness runtime is an exact description of the value.
cards.definitions: The states are A, B, C, D, E, F and a separate halting state Z; Z is not one of the six states being counted. Tape cells are indexed by the integers and contain 0 or 1. Initially every cell contains 0, the head is at cell 0, and the state is A. For each nonhalting state and scanned symbol, the transition table specifies a symbol to write, a move by exactly one cell left or right, and a next state. Execution stops on entering Z, including that final write-and-move transition in \(T(M)\). Unreachable states are allowed. The finite set of these transition tables is $\mathcal{M}_6$. Here BB is the runtime (maximum-shift) function S, not the function $\Sigma$ that maximizes the number of 1s left on the tape. In the progress note, $2\uparrow\uparrow k$ is a tower of k twos, and $2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow 1=2$, $2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow(k+1)=2\uparrow\uparrow(2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow k)$. For a halting machine \(M, T(M)\) is the least positive integer t at which the execution enters Z. The answer convention never applies T to a nonhalting machine: halting of the proposed witness is a required part of its certificate. Its explicitly specified transition table together with that certificate defines a terminating step-counting computation and hence a unique exact integer, even when evaluating that computation is impractical.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply the complete twelve-entry transition table of a particular machine \(M_\ast\) in the stated class. Provide Lean-checked proofs that (1) \(M_\ast\) halts from the specified blank-tape initial configuration, and (2) every machine M in this class that halts from that initial configuration executes at most \(T(M_\ast)\) transitions. Together these certify \(\mathrm{BB}(6)=T(M_\ast)\) exactly. The runtime of this proved-halting concrete machine is an accepted finite description of the integer; a simple closed form, decimal expansion, separately evaluated integer literal or full execution trace is not required. Specifying a machine without proving its halting and universal maximality, restating the defining maximum over all machines, or giving only an approximate or one-sided bound does not meet this criterion.
cards.why: This is a defining concrete problem in computability: identify the longest finite computation possible in a fixed, exceptionally small universal machine formalism. A proof would advance the boundary of complete mathematical understanding of small programs and test methods for nontermination proofs, recurrence analysis, and formal verification. The significance lies in establishing the exact boundary, not merely constructing a machine with an enormous runtime.

context_blocks.text: Fixing the number of states leaves finitely many machines, so a maximum halting time exists. Nevertheless, enumerating their transition tables does not tell us when to stop waiting for the machines that never halt. The Busy Beaver function packages that obstruction into a sequence of finite integers. Noncomputability of the whole sequence does not prevent individual values from being established.

The five-state case provides a concrete precedent: the bbchallenge collaboration proved \(S(5)=47,176,870\) with the Coq proof assistant. Its proof combines a complete enumeration after symmetry reductions with methods that certify halting or nonhalting. The paper makes precise how a finite search can be accompanied by a universal proof.

Six states introduce obstacles beyond running a larger search. The Antihydra machine has a halting question expressed through an integer recurrence whose parity behavior is still unresolved. A probabilistic heuristic about that behavior is not a proof that the machine runs forever. An exact Busy Beaver bound would also decide its halting behavior in principle, even if the required finite computation were physically infeasible.

The target is the exact six-state runtime maximum. A concrete machine with proved halting and universal maximality specifies that integer through its runtime, without a simple closed form or decimal expansion. Runtime and final tape output are different extremal quantities, and machine conventions matter. Existing catalogue questions about Busy Beaver growth, logical thresholds, or population protocols therefore remain separate problems.

cards.title: Reversal of Hindman’s theorem to the \(\omega\)-jump
cards.formal: Over RCA\(_{0}\), does Hindman’s finite-sums theorem imply ACA\(_{0}^{+}\)? Equivalently, does RCA\(_{0}+HT\) prove that every set X has an \(\omega -th\) Turing jump?
cards.definitions: Work in classical two-sorted second-order arithmetic, with number variables and variables for sets of natural numbers. RCA\(_{0}\) has the usual elementary arithmetic axioms, \(\Sigma ^{0}_{1}\) induction and \(\Delta ^{0}_{1}\) comprehension, allowing set parameters. HT is the assertion that for every integer \(k\ge 1\) and every coloring c of the positive integers into \(\{0,\ldots ,k- 1\}\), there exist an infinite set H of positive integers and a color i such that \(c(\sum_{h\in F}h)=i\) for every nonempty finite subset F of H. Terms in a sum are distinct; there is no fixed upper bound on their number and no additional sparsity requirement on H. For a set X, its Turing jump \(X'\) is {e: the e-th oracle Turing machine with oracle X halts on input e}, using one fixed effective enumeration. The \(\omega\)-jump existence axiom says \(\forall X\exists Y\) [\(Y_{0}=X\) and \(\forall j(Y_{j+1}=Y_{j}' )\)], where \(Y_{j}=\{e:\langle j,e\rangle \in Y\}\) and \(\langle \cdot ,\cdot \rangle\) is a fixed primitive recursive pairing. ACA\(_{0}^{+}\) is RCA\(_{0}\) plus that axiom. The question is formal provability of this implication over the stated base, not truth of Hindman’s theorem in ordinary set theory and not a single-instance computability claim.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the \(\omega\)-jump existence axiom in RCA\(_{0}+HT\), or prove nonimplication by constructing a model of RCA\(_{0}+HT\) in which some set has no coded \(\omega\)-jump. A standard-natural-number model is sufficient for a separation but is not required. A lower bound of ACA\(_{0}\) alone, an upper bound of ACA\(_{0}^{+}\), or a theorem about only bounded-length sums does not decide this implication. A negative answer need not show that HT is equivalent to ACA\(_{0}\); an intermediate strength would also refute the implication.
cards.why: A longstanding gap in the computational and axiomatic strength of a central infinite combinatorial theorem, with a precise target at the \(\omega -th\) Turing jump.

importance.reason: A landmark reverse-mathematical calibration problem connecting finite-sums combinatorics, oracle computation and the hierarchy of set-existence axioms.

progress.text: Blass–Hirst–Simpson establish ACA\(_{0}^{+}\Rightarrow HT\Rightarrow\)ACA\(_{0}\) over RCA\(_{0}\), leaving the reversal in this card open.
Carlucci–Zdanowski characterize ACA\(_{0}^{+}\) using Ramsey’s theorem for exactly large sets; this supplies a comparison principle rather than an HT reversal.
Carlucci–Kołodziejczyk–Lepore–Zdanowski reach the ACA\(_{0}\) lower bound already for sums of at most two elements with four colors; conference precursor 2017, journal version 2020.
Csima and coauthors prove nontrivial computability and reverse-mathematical lower bounds for sums of exactly two elements, a weaker principle than full HT.
Liu–Patey prove new upper bounds and separations for variable-word and unordered Carlson–Simpson principles, without claiming a resolution of HT’s strength.
Le Houérou–Patey obtain a conservation theorem for a one-variable, two-color Carlson–Simpson principle.

context_blocks.text: Hindman’s theorem says that a finite coloring contains an infinite set whose entire collection of finite sums has one color. This is much more than finding an infinite monochromatic subset: the same color must work for single elements, pairs, triples and every larger finite selection. For parity coloring, the positive even numbers give an immediate example. The theorem must also handle colorings with no such simple arithmetic description.

The combinatorial statement is a theorem, not the unresolved claim on this card. Reverse mathematics asks which set-existence axioms are needed to prove it. One works over a deliberately weak base theory and compares stronger principles by implication. The inherited paper records the classical bounds ACA\(_{0}^{+}\Rightarrow HT\Rightarrow\)ACA\(_{0}\) and identifies closing this gap as a major open problem. This card asks specifically whether the upper implication reverses.

ACA\(_{0}\) allows arithmetic comprehension; equivalently over the base theory, every set has its Turing jump. An individual jump supplies answers to halting questions relative to the given set. Repeating that operation a fixed finite number of times yields increasingly strong information. The \(\omega\)-jump places every finite iterate into the sections of one set. Being able to discuss each fixed finite stage is not the same as having this whole sequence available as a single object.

The distinction is visible in the model consisting of the standard natural numbers together with all arithmetical sets. It is closed under the ordinary Turing jump, since jumping an arithmetical set still yields an arithmetical set. It does not contain the join of all finite jumps of the empty set. Thus ACA\(_{0}^{+}\) demands more set existence than ACA\(_{0}\). Whether Hindman’s theorem already forces that additional existence is the precise issue here.

The computability bounds show why ordinary computable colorings already matter. The account by Csima and coauthors recalls a computable coloring for which every finite-sums solution computes the halting set, and an upper bound placing a solution in the \((\omega +1)-st\) jump of the coloring. These are bounds on information in solutions. Neither identifies the exact reverse-mathematical strength, and noncomputability alone falls far short of an \(\omega\)-jump reversal.

Restricted sum lengths have provided substantial progress without closing the full gap. Carlucci–Kołodziejczyk–Lepore–Zdanowski prove that the version requiring monochromatic singletons and pairs already implies ACA\(_{0}\); four colors suffice without an additional sparsity condition. Their results for sums of exactly \(n\ge 3\) terms use an apartness condition on the binary supports of the chosen integers. These carefully specified variants should not be merged with unrestricted HT.

Even replacing “at most two” by “exactly two” changes the logical picture. Csima and coauthors construct a computable two-color instance of the exactly-two version with no \(\Sigma ^{0}_{2}\) solution and prove a lower bound through diagonally noncomputable functions relative to the halting set. Yet exactly-two sums follow from Ramsey’s theorem for pairs, placing that principle strictly below full HT over the base. This is a useful warning that small wording changes can alter the problem.

There is a separate combinatorial principle known to capture the desired upper level exactly. Carlucci–Zdanowski prove that Ramsey’s theorem for exactly large finite sets is equivalent to ACA\(_{0}^{+}\). A finite set F is exactly large when |\(F|=\min (F)+1\), so its dimension varies with its elements. This yields a potential comparison target: an implication from HT to this precisely defined Ramsey principle would suffice. Its equivalence does not itself supply that missing implication.

Recent results in the neighboring theory of variable words require the same care. Liu–Patey’s June 2026 preprint, revised in July, gives low\(_{2}\) solutions to the Ordered Variable Word theorem for colorings of ordinary words and proves each fixed-dimensional unordered Carlson–Simpson lemma in ACA\(_{0}\). The paper distinguishes these principles from ordered higher-dimensional counterparts and still describes ACA\(_{0}^{+}\) as the weakest known system proving HT. Its new upper bounds should not be transferred to Hindman’s theorem.

Le Houérou–Patey’s July 2026 preprint obtains a conservation result for a one-variable Carlson–Simpson principle with two colors. It controls which arithmetical consequences that particular principle adds to a weak theory. This is a different assertion from constructing the \(\omega\)-jump out of unrestricted finite-sums homogeneity. Together the recent papers sharpen nearby boundaries without answering the implication stated here.

A positive answer would make a concrete additive-combinatorial theorem a characterization of closure under all finite Turing jumps at once. A negative answer would show that known proofs use more set existence than the theorem itself entails. Either outcome would clarify the information content of an infinite combinatorial search principle, which is the reason for its place in the computability part of this catalogue.

cards.title: Universality of Turing equivalence
cards.formal: For every countable Borel equivalence relation E on a standard Borel space X, does there exist a Borel function \(f:X\to 2^{\mathbb{N}}\) such that x E y if and only if \(f(x)\equiv _{T} f(y)\), for all \(x,y\in X\)?
cards.definitions: The space \(2^{\mathbb{N}}\) consists of all infinite binary sequences, identified with subsets of \(\mathbb{N}\). For \(a,b\in 2^{\mathbb{N}}, a\le _{T} b\) means that some oracle Turing machine with oracle b computes every bit of a and halts on every input coordinate; \(a\equiv _{T} b\) means both \(a\le _{T} b\) and \(b\le _{T} a\). There is no time or space restriction on these computations. A standard Borel space is a set with the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra of some Polish topology. The relation E must be a Borel subset of \(X\times X\) and each equivalence class must be at most countable; X itself may be uncountable. The function f is Borel measurable: inverse images of Borel sets are Borel. It need not be computable, continuous, injective on points, or uniform on indices witnessing equivalence. It must preserve both equivalence and inequivalence on every input pair, not merely almost everywhere for a chosen measure. The quantifiers ask for a separate Borel reduction for each E, without requiring an algorithm that takes a code for E and outputs f. This is the ordinary ZFC formulation of Borel universality.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that Turing equivalence is universal by producing the requisite Borel reductions, or prove it is not by identifying one countable Borel relation that does not reduce to it. Equivalently, settle whether \(E_{\infty}\le _{B}\equiv _{T}\) for a fixed standard universal countable Borel relation \(E_{\infty}\). A negative theorem conditional on a form of Martin’s conjecture must be labeled conditional. Failure of reductions with an additional uniformity or computability requirement is not a negative solution to the unrestricted Borel question.
cards.why: A central bridge between computability and descriptive set theory, asking whether equality of computational power can encode every countable Borel classification problem.

importance.reason: A classical universality question with consequences for Martin’s conjecture and for the distinction between definable and uniform computational encodings.

context_blocks.text: Two infinite binary sequences have the same Turing degree when each can compute the other. This partitions all possible oracles by their computational power. The universality question asks how complicated that partition is as a classification problem: can every countable Borel pattern of equivalence be represented exactly by equality of Turing degrees? The objects being classified are infinite sequences, not finite machine descriptions.

There are countably many oracle programs. Consequently, for a fixed oracle b, only countably many sequences can be computed from b, and its Turing-equivalence class is countable. The relation is Borel because a claim that an oracle program computes a given sequence can be written using countably many conditions about finite computations. Thus Turing equivalence itself belongs to the class of relations compared on this card.

A Borel reduction is a structured assignment of invariants. If f reduces E to Turing equivalence, the Turing degree of \(f(x)\) is a complete invariant for the E-class of x: equivalent objects receive the same degree, and inequivalent objects receive different degrees. Distinct representatives of one E-class may receive different binary sequences, provided those sequences have the same degree. Injectivity on equivalence classes is essential; injectivity on individual points is not.

It suffices to study a single standard benchmark \(E_{\infty}\). One realization is the orbit relation for the shift action of the free group \(F_{2}\) on \(\{0,1\}^{F_{2}}\): two labelings x,y are equivalent when \(y(h)=x(g^{- 1}h)\) for some group element g and every \(h\in F_{2}\). This countable Borel relation is universal. A reduction of that one relation to Turing equivalence would therefore answer the full universally quantified question.

The inherited Caicedo–Löwe survey records the question as Question 6 in its discussion of Martin’s conjecture. It traces the universality problem to Kechris and distinguishes it from nearby statements about arithmetic equivalence and uniform coding. The source is a 2019 preprint; the later published chapter updates the year in its title. The card retains the exact inherited version and locator.

There are strong positive results for neighboring relations. Slaman and Steel proved that arithmetic equivalence is universal; Marks, Slaman and Steel provide a published proof and discussion. Arithmetic equivalence allows each sequence to be computed from some finite Turing jump of the other, with the finite jump levels depending on the pair. That extra allowance changes which sequences become equivalent.

In the other direction, Marks proved universality of polynomial-time Turing equivalence, as well as polynomial-time many-one equivalence. These compare arbitrary languages over finite strings by resource-bounded oracle reductions. The theorem concerns the entire space of languages, not only decidable languages or languages inside a familiar complexity class. It establishes universality for a finer relation than unrestricted Turing equivalence.

Finer and coarser relations do not give an automatic transfer here. A coding that keeps two outputs inequivalent under polynomial-time reductions may still make them equivalent under unrestricted oracle computation. Once that happens, the reverse implication required of a Borel reduction fails. Preserving the encoding under all additional computations is the missing task; simply reusing the polynomial-time result does not complete it.

There is also a structural obstruction to familiar coding approaches. With Turing equivalence generated in its usual way by oracle-program reductions, it is not uniformly universal. Roughly, uniformity would require indices for computations between encoded outputs to be chosen solely from the indices witnessing the original equivalence, independently of the particular objects. Marks develops this distinction and shows why the choice of generating maps must be specified.

The present problem permits arbitrary Borel reductions, so that uniform obstruction is not the desired nonuniversality theorem. Whether ordinary universality must entail appropriate stronger uniformity properties is itself part of the surrounding theory. A proof that rules out one common coding pattern therefore reveals a methodological barrier without exhausting all Borel encodings.

Martin’s conjecture supplies a competing prediction. Its Borel form implies that Turing equivalence is not universal; in particular, it obstructs reducing two disjoint copies of Turing equivalence into one copy. Conversely, a universality proof would contradict that prediction. The point is a genuine conditional connection between two major structural questions, not an unconditional settlement in either direction.

Day and Marks’ February 2026 revision investigates an older question about writing Turing equivalence as an increasing union whose stages omit certain uniformly computable infinite sequences. A positive answer would imply nonuniform invariant functions and universality of ordinary many-one equivalence. Their consequences remain conditional on that decomposition question, and concern distinctions among degree relations that must not be collapsed into a proof of Turing universality.

Settling the card would tell us whether mutual computability provides a universal language for countable Borel classification, or has a structural limitation absent from some nearby degree notions. Either outcome would matter beyond computability: it would constrain the ways orbit equivalence relations, invariants and definable encodings can interact. The answer criterion is a precise existence theorem for reductions, with no algorithmic-efficiency requirement hidden inside the word “Borel.”

cards.definitions: The input explicitly gives \(m\ge 0\) and all four entries of each \(A_{i}\) as signed binary integers. Entries have no magnitude or sign restriction, and m is part of the input, not a fixed constant. Products use ordinary exact integer matrix multiplication: \((AB)_{r,s}=\sum _{t=1}^{2} A_{r,t}B_{t,s}\). The target \(0_{2}\) is the matrix with all four entries zero. The product length \(\ell\) is finite but unbounded, and generator indices may repeat in any order. Only listed generators can be used; inverses are not supplied automatically. The empty product is excluded, and an empty list is a NO instance. The semigroup generated by the list is the set of all such nonempty products, so mortality means membership of \(0_{2}\) in that set. The machine must return YES exactly for mortal lists and NO otherwise, terminating on both kinds. No running-time or memory bound is imposed beyond finite termination; there is no oracle, numerical tolerance or real-arithmetic primitive.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer gives a uniform decision algorithm with proofs of correctness and termination on every finite input list. A negative answer proves that the stated decision problem is undecidable. A procedure that only certifies particular zero products, a bounded-length decision algorithm, or a lower bound against polynomial time does not settle the target.

context_blocks.title: Can a sequence erase every vector?
context_blocks.text: A product equal to the zero matrix sends every two-dimensional vector to zero at once. The question is whether some finite sequence of the allowed transformations has this effect. It is stronger than sending one specified vector to zero: a matrix can kill that vector while acting nontrivially on others.

context_blocks.title: Two small examples
context_blocks.text: Let \(A=[[1,0],[0,0]]\) and \(B=[[0,0],[1,0]]\). Neither is the zero matrix, but \(AB=0_{2}\), so the list \((A,B)\) is mortal. Reversing the order gives \(BA=B\), showing that order matters. The list containing only A is not mortal, since every positive power of A equals A. Thus the presence of a singular generator by itself does not answer the question.

context_blocks.title: Hardness and undecidability are different claims
context_blocks.text: Bell, Hirvensalo and Potapov established NP-hardness in 2012; their 2024 paper still identifies unrestricted two-dimensional mortality as an open decidability problem. NP-hardness leaves open the possibility of a terminating algorithm with very large running time. Mortality is already undecidable for general finite lists of three-dimensional integer matrices, placing dimension two at a basic boundary.

context_blocks.title: Restricted matrix classes have stronger results
context_blocks.text: Jaax and Kiefer prove NP-completeness when each determinant is either 0 or +1. This gives a decision procedure for that promise and does not cover arbitrary determinants. The 2024 membership theorem concerns generators in \(GL_{2}(\mathbb{Z} )\), whose determinants are ±1; their products are invertible and cannot equal zero. Neither theorem decides mortality when unrestricted singular and nonsingular generators are mixed.

context_blocks.title: Relation to other matrix questions
context_blocks.text: General semigroup membership, discussed in TCS-5921, allows a target matrix supplied as input; mortality fixes that target to zero. A solution of general membership would therefore decide mortality. The April 2026 work on complex matrix embeddings studies different algebraic representation questions and supplies no general resolution of the present integer-matrix target.

sentences: A finite list of two-by-two integer matrices generates all nonempty products with arbitrary order and repetition.
The question asks whether a terminating algorithm can decide if any such product is the zero matrix.
Matrix entries and the number of generators are unrestricted.
NP-hardness is known, while decidability results for restricted determinants do not cover the general case.
Resolving the question would locate a basic computability boundary for products of small matrices.

cards.context:
A product equal to the zero matrix sends every two-dimensional vector to zero at once. The question is whether some finite sequence of the allowed transformations has this effect. It is stronger than sending one specified vector to zero: a matrix can kill that vector while acting nontrivially on others.

Let \(A=[[1,0],[0,0]]\) and \(B=[[0,0],[1,0]]\). Neither is the zero matrix, but \(AB=0_{2}\), so the list \((A,B)\) is mortal. Reversing the order gives \(BA=B\), showing that order matters. The list containing only A is not mortal, since every positive power of A equals A. Thus the presence of a singular generator by itself does not answer the question.

Bell, Hirvensalo and Potapov established NP-hardness in 2012; their 2024 paper still identifies unrestricted two-dimensional mortality as an open decidability problem. NP-hardness leaves open the possibility of a terminating algorithm with very large running time. Mortality is already undecidable for general finite lists of three-dimensional integer matrices, placing dimension two at a basic boundary.

Jaax and Kiefer prove NP-completeness when each determinant is either 0 or +1. This gives a decision procedure for that promise and does not cover arbitrary determinants. The 2024 membership theorem concerns generators in \(GL_{2}(\mathbb{Z} )\), whose determinants are ±1; their products are invertible and cannot equal zero. Neither theorem decides mortality when unrestricted singular and nonsingular generators are mixed.

General semigroup membership, discussed in TCS-5921, allows a target matrix supplied as input; mortality fixes that target to zero. A solution of general membership would therefore decide mortality. The April 2026 work on complex matrix embeddings studies different algebraic representation questions and supplies no general resolution of the present integer-matrix target.

cards.title: Shannon feasibility from algorithmic network coding
cards.formal: For every fixed finite acyclic directed network with correlated finite-alphabet sources and specified source-reconstruction demands, does high-probability algorithmic feasibility on independent source blocks imply Shannon achievability at the same edge rates? The algorithmic model permits sample-dependent local programs of length \(O(\log N)\) and \(O(\log N)\) extra bits on each edge for a block of \(N\) samples. The Shannon model requires fixed local encoding and decoding maps for each block length, with vanishing error and arbitrarily small rate slack, as defined below.
cards.why: The question compares information transmission for random sources with transmission of their individual realized strings. A positive answer would show that logarithmic sample-dependent algorithmic descriptions cannot create new asymptotic network rates. A negative answer would expose a concrete operational distinction between Shannon and Kolmogorov descriptions of distributed information.

sentences: Several correlated sources must be transmitted through a fixed directed acyclic network to designated recipients.
Shannon coding chooses local encoding and decoding maps that work with high probability for random source blocks.
Algorithmic coding instead allows each realized block to have its own short local programs and compatible edge messages.
The question asks whether high-probability algorithmic feasibility with logarithmic overhead always implies Shannon feasibility at the same asymptotic rates.
The target is this general converse, with vanishing error and rate slack defined explicitly, rather than a finite-block equivalence inferred from the title.

cards.definitions: Fix a finite directed acyclic graph \(G=(V,E)\), an integer \(m\ge1\), nonempty finite alphabets \(\mathcal X_1,\ldots,\mathcal X_m\), and any joint probability law \(P\) for \(X=(X_1,\ldots,X_m)\) on their product. The law is fixed as block length varies; its coordinates may be arbitrarily correlated, and no computability assumption is imposed on its probabilities. Each vertex \(v\) has fixed sets \(S_v,T_v\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\): it initially receives the source coordinates in \(S_v\) and must reproduce the coordinates in \(T_v\). Require \(\bigcup_v S_v=\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Several vertices may know or demand the same source, and a vertex may both receive sources and relay messages. Each edge \(e\) has a fixed finite real rate \(r_e\ge0\), measured in bits per joint source sample. For \(N\ge1\), take \(N\) independent copies of the entire vector \(X\); write \(X_j^N\) for the resulting length-\(N\) word of coordinate \(j\). The block law is \(P^{\otimes N}\), not independence between different coordinates. All finite words, integers and tuples use fixed computable binary encodings; tuple components and incident edges are ordered once with the network. Let \(C(u\mid v)\) be plain conditional Kolmogorov complexity: the least length of a binary program for a fixed optimal interpreter that halts with output \(u\) on auxiliary input \(v\). There is no time bound. Optimal means that this interpreter simulates every other partial computable interpreter with an additive program-length overhead independent of \(u,v\). Let \(L_N=\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil\). For a realized source block and an integer \(K\ge1\), algorithmic feasibility means that there exist edge-message strings \(M_e\) with \(|M_e|\le\lfloor Nr_e\rfloor+K L_N\), such that at every vertex \(v\), \[C\bigl(( (M_e)_{e\in\operatorname{out}(v)}, (X_j^N)_{j\in T_v})\mid N,(X_j^N)_{j\in S_v},(M_e)_{e\in\operatorname{in}(v)}\bigr)\le K L_N.\] The demanded outputs in this formula are the true source words, so reconstruction is exact on a feasible realization. Messages and witnessing programs may depend on the whole realized source block; only their lengths and the displayed local conditional complexities are constrained. They need not arise from one choice of encoding functions used for every realization. Call the rate vector algorithmically feasible with high probability if there exists one \(K\) such that, for every \(\eta\in(0,1)\), some \(N_0\) makes the probability of this feasibility event at least \(1-\eta\) for all \(N\ge N_0\). The same \(K\) works for every block length, realization and error threshold. Shannon achievability means that for every rate slack \(\delta>0\) and every error tolerance \(\eta\in(0,1)\), there is \(N_0\) such that for every \(N\ge N_0\) there exist deterministic local encoding and decoding maps with the following properties. In a topological order, each vertex computes its outgoing edge messages from only its local source words and incoming messages; each demand is decoded from the same local information. Each edge message belongs to the finite set of binary strings of length at most \(\lfloor N(r_e+\delta)\rfloor\). For each edge this bounded-string alphabet is shared by the parties and the receiver observes the whole message, including its length; the same convention is used for algorithmic messages. The probability, under \(P^{\otimes N}\), that every demanded word is reconstructed correctly is at least \(1-\eta\). The local maps are fixed before observing the source realization; they may depend on the network, law, rates, block length and tolerances, and have no computational time or description-size bound. There is no feedback, extra channel, shared sample-dependent advice or communication other than the edge messages. This is an asymptotic rate-region converse. It does not assert equivalence with logarithmic finite-block overhead in the Shannon model.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the implication for every network, source law, demand pattern and finite rate vector just defined, or refute it. A refutation requires a fixed admissible network, joint law and rate vector for which algorithmic feasibility holds with one logarithmic-overhead constant and probability tending to one, but Shannon achievability fails. In particular, failure at a single block length or at a rate boundary without accounting for arbitrarily small positive rate slack is insufficient. Results for only one source, independent sources, one terminal, particular network shapes, or only information-cut inequalities do not settle the general converse. An inefficient Shannon code is allowed; the target is coding feasibility, not efficient construction.

context_blocks.text: A network code chooses how each relay transforms its received messages and local source data. The same code must handle many possible source realizations. Several correlated sources and several destinations can make compatibility between these local choices a substantial constraint.

The algorithmic version instead asks whether a particular tuple of strings admits suitable edge messages. A short program may certify each local transformation, and a different realized tuple may use different programs. Their permitted logarithmic length is small compared with the transmitted source block, but this nonuniform freedom is exactly what the converse must address.

Shen’s 2006 framework defines algorithmic requests on finite acyclic directed graphs, with message-length capacities and logarithmic conditional-complexity allowances. The graph, local-information and program conventions in this card make that model explicit.

The 2021 problem list compares the two settings by taking independent repeated samples of a joint source law. Question 13 asks whether algorithmic feasibility with high probability can occur even when the corresponding Shannon transmission is impossible. The earlier direction from Shannon codes to algorithmic requests is discussed with an explicit warning that logarithmic precision may be lost.

Accordingly, the main target here is the converse actually asked in Question 13. It fixes logarithmic algorithmic overhead and the standard Shannon closure under vanishing error and positive rate slack. It does not claim a two-way finite-block equivalence, and it keeps arbitrary correlation within each source sample.

The source surveys networks where both theories have strong positive coding theorems, including transmission with side information and the two-sender Slepian–Wolf problem. It also discusses networks where elementary cut constraints do not suffice. Agreement in these special cases does not supply a general translation between the models.

The distinction is operational rather than a change of terminology for entropy. The conclusion requires one collection of local maps that succeeds on almost all realizations, while the premise only asserts the existence of compatible short local descriptions separately for those realizations.

cards.title: Strong extractors for infinite sequences
cards.formal:
Does there exist one deterministic oracle Turing machine \(F\) such that for every pair of infinite binary sequences \(x,y\) with
\[\dim(x)=\dim(y)=\tfrac12\]
and global algorithmic independence as defined below, all computations \(F^{x\oplus y}(i)\), \(i\ge0\), halt with a bit, and the resulting sequence \(z(i)=F^{x\oplus y}(i)\) satisfies
\[\dim^x(z)=\dim^y(z)=1?\]
Here \(\dim^a\) is effective Hausdorff dimension measured with the entire sequence \(a\) available as an oracle. The same machine must work for all promised pairs; it receives no description of their independence constants.

This card takes the explicit dimension-one-half instance in the 2012 question and uses “independent” in the global oracle sense of Calude–Zimand's Definition 2.1. The weaker finitary prefix-independence notion is distinguished below; it is not silently substituted for this premise.
cards.why: The question asks whether two imperfectly random infinite sources can yield information of full asymptotic density that remains incompressible even after either entire source is disclosed. It tests how far the strong-extraction principle from finite information extends to arbitrary individual sequences. The distinction matters because an infinite oracle can expose information beyond any fixed pair of input prefixes.
cards.status_note: Checked on 2026-09-14: the full 2012 question, the 2007 ordinary extraction theorem, and Calude–Zimand’s global/finitary independence definitions and restricted positive result. The published finite-string abstract and July 2026 finite-state extraction abstract were checked for their scope. A bounded search found no matching strong global-oracle extractor or general impossibility for the fixed half-dimensional promise. The independence interpretation is explicit; source-open does not claim exhaustive present-status certification.
