cards.definitions: Variables are drawn from a countable set. A literal is a variable or its negation. A clause is a finite set of literals, interpreted as their disjunction, and a CNF formula is a finite set of clauses, interpreted as their conjunction. A \(k\)-CNF has at most \(k\) literals per input clause; derived clauses have no width bound. Define the size of \(F\) to be \(\sum_{A\in F}(1+|A|)\). Polynomial size means that some \(a>0,b\in\mathbb N\), fixed for the family, satisfy this size bound \(\le a(n+1)^b\) for every \(n\). The parameter \(n\) indexes the family; it need not equal the number of variables. There is no computability or uniform generation requirement on the family. A proof is a finite sequence of configurations \(\mathcal C_0,\ldots,\mathcal C_t\), each a finite set of clauses, starting at \(\mathcal C_0=\varnothing\). One step may add an input clause from \(F\); add the resolvent \(A\cup B\) when \(A\cup\{x\}\) and \(B\cup\{\neg x\}\) are both currently present, with \(x\) absent from \(A\) and \(\neg x\) absent from \(B\); add a weakening \(A\cup B\) when \(A\) is present and \(B\) is any finite clause; or erase one currently present clause. An inference adds its conclusion before any separate erasure, so premises and conclusion coexist in that configuration. The proof ends with the empty clause present. The clause space is \(\operatorname{Sp}(\pi)=\max_j|\mathcal C_j|\), counting input clauses only while they have been downloaded and retained. The length \(L(\pi)\) is the number of input-clause downloads and inference steps, including weakenings and rederivations, but excluding erasures. Erased clauses may be downloaded or derived again; their reappearance is charged again. There is no read-once, tree-like, regularity or restriction on reuse. Space counts clauses regardless of how many literals they contain: it is not total literal space, variable space, bit memory or width. Length counts proof lines as specified, not the bit cost of manipulating a long clause. The target concerns existence of proofs with the two simultaneous bounds, not an efficient algorithm that finds them.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated implication for every fixed width and every polynomial-size family, or prove its negation. A positive answer must produce or establish existence of refutations satisfying both resource bounds at once. Separate witnesses for polynomial length and constant clause space do not suffice. A negative answer must exhibit a fixed \(k\) and a polynomial-size family with a common constant-space refutation bound, but such that for every \(S\ge1,C>0,d\in\mathbb N\) some member has no refutation satisfying both \(\operatorname{Sp}(\pi)\le S\) and \(L(\pi)\le C(n+1)^d\). A polynomial length lower bound, a lower bound only for tree-like proofs, or a trade-off that disappears after increasing space by a fixed constant does not refute this statement.

context_blocks.text: Nordström’s Open Problem 16 asks this simultaneous length–clause-space question for polynomial-size fixed-width CNF families. It is distinct from the neighboring question about trade-offs when space is at least linear in formula size, whose later resolution is already noted in the survey.

The survey records that a constant clause-space bound guarantees some polynomial-length refutation, but that conclusion does not bound the clause space of the short refutation. The missing simultaneous guarantee is precisely the present target.

With total literal space in place of clause space, the corresponding simultaneous constant-space and polynomial-length statement is already known. A constant number of clauses may nevertheless contain many literals, so that result does not apply to this measure.

Papamakarios and Razborov’s ICALP 2022 paper revisits the same constant-clause-space question explicitly in Section 5. Theorem 4.7 gives formulas of linear size with clause-space-four tree-like refutations for which all tree-like refutations have a nearly quadratic length lower bound. A polynomial lower bound in that restricted proof system does not contradict the present unrestricted polynomial-length conclusion.

Their broader equivalences relate proof-space measures to tree-like proof size and identify stronger separation questions. The checked journal metadata places the expanded publication in November 2023; the theorem numbering quoted here is from the fully read ICALP version.

cards.title: Separating levels of bounded arithmetic
cards.formal:
Are there integers \(i>j\ge1\) and a closed first-order arithmetic sentence \(\theta\) such that
\[T_2^i\vdash\theta\qquad\text{and}\qquad T_2^j\nvdash\theta?\]
The theory \(T_2^r\) is BASIC together with induction for every \(\Sigma_r^b\) formula in the language defined below. The question asks for a separation as sets of provable sentences, with no assumed separation of computational complexity classes and no additional oracle symbols. One pair of levels is enough; it need not be fixed in advance, and proving strictness at every pair is not required.
cards.why: These theories organize arithmetic reasoning by the logical complexity permitted in induction hypotheses. Showing that even two positive levels prove different sentences would establish an unconditional difference in the strength of those reasoning principles. It would clarify how computational complexity is reflected in provability, beyond the known conditional connections.

Ježil–Tsintsilidas, arXiv:2602.19934v1 (February 2026), explicitly retain removal of assumptions in their hierarchy separations as an open problem. A bounded subsequent search found no matching unconditional separation or proof that all positive levels coincide. This records the checked sources and search limits, not exhaustive certification of present openness.

cards.definitions:
Use classical first-order logic with equality and the one-sorted language \(L=\{0,1,+,\cdot,H,\ell,\#,\le\}\). Here \(H\) and \(\ell\) are unary, \(+\), \(\cdot\), \(\#\) are binary, and \(\le\) is a binary predicate. Terms are the finite expressions formed from variables, these constants and these function symbols. Atomic formulas are equalities or inequalities between terms. The logical operations are negation, conjunction, disjunction and first-order universal/existential quantification; implication and equivalence abbreviate their usual Boolean expansions. The successor notation \(Sx\) abbreviates \(x+1\), \(2\) abbreviates \(1+1\), and \(2x\) means \(2\cdot x\).

The intended standard structure has domain \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,\ldots\}\), its usual addition, multiplication and order, \(H(x)=\lfloor x/2\rfloor\), \(\ell(0)=0\), \(\ell(x)=\lfloor\log_2 x\rfloor+1\) for \(x>0\), and \(x\#y=2^{\ell(x)\ell(y)}\). This interpretation explains the symbols; the theory's nonlogical axioms are exactly the following finite BASIC list and the specified induction scheme, rather than all sentences true in this standard structure. Every free variable in the following displays is universally quantified.

The order and successor axioms are
\[\begin{gathered}
a\le b\ \to\ a\le b+1,\qquad a\ne a+1,\qquad 0\le a,\\
(a\le b\land a\ne b)\ \to\ a+1\le b,\qquad a\ne0\ \to\ 2a\ne0,\\
a\le b\lor b\le a,\qquad (a\le b\land b\le a)\ \to\ a=b,\\
(a\le b\land b\le c)\ \to\ a\le c,\qquad a\le a+b,\\
(a\le b\land a\ne b)\ \to\ (2a+1\le2b\land 2a+1\ne2b).
\end{gathered}\]
The addition and multiplication axioms are
\[\begin{gathered}
a+b=b+a,\qquad a+0=a,\qquad a+(b+1)=(a+b)+1,\\
(a+b)+c=a+(b+c),\qquad a+b\le a+c\ \to\ b\le c,\\
a\cdot0=0,\qquad a\cdot(b+1)=a\cdot b+a,\qquad a\cdot b=b\cdot a,\\
a\cdot(b+c)=(a\cdot b)+(a\cdot c),\\
1\le a\ \to\ ((a\cdot b\le a\cdot c)\leftrightarrow(b\le c)).
\end{gathered}\]
The length, halving and smash axioms are
\[\begin{gathered}
\ell(0)=0,\qquad \ell(1)=1,\qquad a\le b\ \to\ \ell(a)\le\ell(b),\\
a\ne0\ \to\ (\ell(2a)=\ell(a)+1\land\ell(2a+1)=\ell(a)+1),\\
\ell(a\#b)=\ell(a)\cdot\ell(b)+1,\qquad 0\#a=1,\\
a\ne0\ \to\ (1\#(2a)=2(1\#a)\land1\#(2a+1)=2(1\#a)),\\
a\#b=b\#a,\qquad \ell(a)=\ell(b)\ \to\ a\#c=b\#c,\\
\ell(a)=\ell(b)+\ell(c)\ \to\ a\#d=(b\#d)\cdot(c\#d),\\
a\ne0\ \to\ \ell(a)=\ell(H(a))+1,\\
a=H(b)\ \leftrightarrow\ (2a=b\lor2a+1=b).
\end{gathered}\]
These are the 32 axioms in Krajíček's Definition 5.2.1, regrouped by operation, with \(H\) and \(\ell\) replacing the printed halving and length notation. No sequence function or oracle predicate is added.

For a term \(t\) not containing \(y\), write \(\exists y\le t\,\psi\) for \(\exists y(y\le t\land\psi)\), and \(\forall y\le t\,\psi\) for \(\forall y(y\le t\to\psi)\). These are bounded quantifiers. They are sharply bounded when the bound is explicitly \(\ell(t)\). The bound may contain other free variables. Let \(\Sigma_0^b=\Pi_0^b\) be all formulas built from atomic formulas using Boolean operations and only sharply bounded quantifiers. Recursively, \(\Sigma_{r+1}^b,\Pi_{r+1}^b\) are the smallest pair of classes satisfying: both contain \(\Sigma_r^b\cup\Pi_r^b\); both are closed under conjunction, disjunction and both sharply bounded quantifiers; \(\Sigma_{r+1}^b\) is closed under bounded existential quantification; \(\Pi_{r+1}^b\) is closed under bounded universal quantification; and negation sends either class into the other. These are the full formula classes, allowing sharply bounded quantifiers inside as well as outside the other quantifiers, rather than only a strict prenex fragment.

For a set \(T\) of closed axioms, \(T\vdash\theta\) means that the closed sentence \(\theta\) has a finite proof in classical first-order logic with equality from those axioms. Equivalently, every nonempty \(L\)-structure satisfying all axioms of \(T\) satisfies \(\theta\). This equivalence is first-order completeness; structures in this characterization are not restricted to the standard natural numbers. There is no bound on proof length. Equality of theories here means equality of their deductive closures in the same language.

For each integer \(r\ge1\), \(T_2^r\) has the displayed BASIC axioms and, for each \(\varphi(x,\vec a)\in\Sigma_r^b\), the universal closure over all parameter variables \(\vec a\) of
\[\bigl(\varphi(0,\vec a)\land\forall x(\varphi(x,\vec a)\to\varphi(x+1,\vec a))\bigr)\ \to\ \forall x\,\varphi(x,\vec a).\]
Parameters are allowed and are not required to be numerals. There are no induction axioms for formulas outside the specified class unless they are consequences of these axioms. Since the formula classes are nested, \(T_2^j\subseteq T_2^i\) in deductive strength when \(j<i\). A positive answer therefore gives a strict inclusion. The separating sentence may have unrestricted first-order quantifiers; no complexity or syntactic bound on that witness sentence is part of the target.

The indices, finite formulas and finite proofs in the question range over ordinary standard mathematical objects. The nonprovability claim is external: it means that no finite proof from the weaker theory exists, rather than asking the weaker theory itself to prove its inability. A countermodel for the weaker theory and the sentence is an equivalent way to certify that nonprovability. A positive answer must be unconditional in the usual mathematical metatheory; adding an unproved complexity assumption changes the requested statement.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed existential separation. A positive answer must establish one pair of standard integers \(i>j\ge1\), a closed sentence provable in \(T_2^i\), and its nonprovability in \(T_2^j\); the latter can equivalently be proved by a model of \(T_2^j\) falsifying the sentence. A negative answer must establish equality of the deductive closures for every pair \(i>j\ge1\). A difference between axiom lists, a lower bound on the shortest proof of a still-provable sentence, a relativized separation, or a separation conditional on an unproved complexity conjecture does not settle this target.

cards.title: Unprovability of polynomial circuit upper bounds in \(S_2^1\)
cards.formal:
Is the following unconditional unprovability statement true?
\[\forall k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \exists\eta\ \forall c\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}:\qquad S_2^1\nvdash\operatorname{UB}_{c,k}[\eta].\]
Here \(\eta(x,y)\) must be a \(\Sigma_1^b\) formula for which \(S_2^1\) proves that every \(x\) has exactly one output \(y\). It therefore represents a polynomial-time function. The sentence \(\operatorname{UB}_{c,k}[\eta]\), defined below with explicit coding, asserts that the predicate “the output is nonzero” has exact Boolean circuits of description size at most \(c n^k\) on every positive input length \(n\).

For each fixed exponent, the same represented function must resist provability for every fixed coefficient. The question concerns what this formal theory can prove; it does not ask directly for a circuit lower bound in the standard natural numbers or for unprovability of all possible upper bounds for one fixed function.
cards.why: Circuit upper bounds assert that small nonuniform computations exist, even when no efficient method for finding them is supplied. This question asks whether a theory designed to formalize polynomial-time reasoning can certify fixed-polynomial circuit bounds for every polynomial-time predicate. A positive result would expose an unconditional limitation on the power of such proofs without requiring the corresponding unconditional circuit separation.

for every \(\Sigma_1^b\) formula \(\varphi\). This is polynomial induction, with halving in the hypothesis; it is not unrestricted successor induction for these formulas.

To specify the polynomial-time predicate without leaving its formal representation implicit, let \(\eta(x,y)\) range over \(\Sigma_1^b\) formulas whose only free variables are among \(x,y\) and for which
\[S_2^1\vdash\forall x\,\exists y\bigl(\eta(x,y)\land\forall z(\eta(x,z)\to z=y)\bigr).\]
Thus the theory proves that \(\eta\) defines one total number-valued function. The associated language consists of numbers whose unique output is nonzero. By the definability/witnessing characterization of \(S_2^1\), these provably total \(\Sigma_1^b\) graphs represent polynomial-time functions. This is a base-language presentation of the source's polynomial-time function symbols in a conservative definitional extension. The formula \(\eta\), rather than just its extension in the standard natural numbers, is part of the witness being quantified over.

Here is an explicit arithmetic encoding of the circuits used in the upper-bound sentence. An \(n\)-input circuit has constants at nodes zero and one, inputs at nodes \(2,\ldots,n+1\), and \(g\ge0\) computational nodes \(n+2,\ldots,n+g+1\) in evaluation order. Each computational node has a two-bit operation tag: zero is AND, one OR, two NOT of the first predecessor, and three a copy of the first predecessor. It also has two predecessor indices, both less than its own index; the second is ignored for the last two tags. The output is any node. Shared values and unrestricted depth are allowed, with exact correctness on all inputs. Copy gates are only a serialization convenience and can be removed; this is an ordinary bounded-fan-in Boolean model.

Let \(w=\ell(n+g+2)\), \(q=2+2w\), and \(d=gq+w\). The circuit number \(C\) has binary length \(d+1\); its highest bit is a delimiter. In the lower bits, counted from position zero at the least significant bit, gate \(i\in\{0,\ldots,g-1\}\) has its tag at positions \(iq,iq+1\), first predecessor in the next \(w\) bits, and second predecessor in the next \(w\) bits. The output index occupies the \(w\) bits starting at \(gq\). A valid encoding has both predecessors below \(n+2+i\) and output below \(n+g+2\). Denote these conditions by \(\operatorname{Valid}(n,g,C)\). The description size charged in the sentence is \(\ell(C)+\ell(g)\); the input length is supplied separately. Thus the measure is a binary description length, not an unannounced change to an exact gate-count bound.

All bit and field operations in this description have the following fixed bounded-arithmetic expansion. For \(X\ge1\), define \(\operatorname{Field}(X,a,b,v)\) by the existence of \(z,t,u,r,s\), all at most \(X+(1\#X)+1\), such that
\[\begin{gathered}
z=1\#H(z),\quad \ell(z)=a+1,\quad t=1\#H(t),\quad \ell(t)=b+1,\\
X=uz+r,\quad r<z,\quad u=st+v,\quad v<t.
\end{gathered}\]
Here \(a\) is the starting position, \(b\ge1\) is field width, and \(u< v\) abbreviates \(u\le v\land u\ne v\). The equations select \(z=2^a\) and \(t=2^b\). Define \(\operatorname{Bit}(X,a,e)\), for \(e\in\{0,1\}\), as
\[(\ell(X)\le a\land e=0)\ \lor\ (a<\ell(X)\land\operatorname{Field}(X,a,1,e)).\]
This also defines the padded zero bits of \(X=0\). In \(\operatorname{Valid}\), each extracted tag or index is a bounded existential variable at most \(n+g+4\); gate checks are quantified over \(i<g\). These conventions expand validity into one definite arithmetic formula.

Define \(\operatorname{Eval}(N,n,g,C,x)\) to assert that the encoded circuit outputs one on the \(n\)-bit, zero-padded representation of \(x\). Its arithmetic expansion is: validity holds and there exists an integer
\[V\le (N\#N)\cdot(C\#C)\]
whose bits at node indices give a correct evaluation, with output bit one. Bits zero and one of \(V\) equal zero and one respectively; for each \(r<n\), bit \(r+2\) of \(V\) equals bit \(r\) of \(x\); and for each \(i<g\), the bit at \(n+2+i\) is the Boolean operation indicated by the tag applied to the predecessor bits. All field and bit occurrences use the preceding formulas, with Boolean auxiliary variables bounded by one and extracted indices bounded by \(n+g+4\). The four Boolean operations are specified by their truth tables. The output index is extracted from its field and its \(V\)-bit must be one. The quantifiers over nodes and gates are bounded by \(n\) and \(g\). Since validity implies \(g\le\ell(C)\) and \(n=\ell(N)\ge1\), the displayed bound is ample for the finite evaluation vector. This description fixes the formula through bounded quantifiers and Boolean combinations, and introduces no extra axioms about an opaque evaluator.

For fixed positive integers \(c,k\), let \(\operatorname{UB}_{c,k}[\eta]\) be the following closed \(L\)-sentence, with the defined predicates expanded:
\[\begin{split}
\forall N\ge1\ \exists g\ \exists C\ \bigl(&\operatorname{Valid}(n,g,C)\land\ell(C)+\ell(g)\le c\,n^k\\
&\land\forall x\ \forall y\bigl((\ell(x)\le n\land\eta(x,y))\to
(\operatorname{Eval}(N,n,g,C,x)\leftrightarrow y\ne0)\bigr)\bigr),
\end{split}\]
where every \(n\) abbreviates \(\ell(N)\). The fixed numeral \(c\) and fixed power \(n^k\) are expanded using multiplication. This is the source's Log convention: lengths come from the length of an arbitrarily quantified number, instead of treating their unary encodings as separately available objects. Zero input length is omitted. The quantifier \(\ell(x)\le n\) permits leading-zero padding; the represented function is a function of the number \(x\), exactly as in the source's unary function-symbol formulation.

The choices of \(k\), \(\eta\) and \(c\) in the main question are external standard integers/formulas. For each fixed exponent, one formula must work against every coefficient. The required conclusion is absence of any finite proof of each displayed upper-bound sentence, not that the theory proves its negation. The description encoding above makes a routine circuit serialization explicit; it is not a claim that the source printed this exact bit layout. Polynomially related standard circuit encodings yield the same all-exponents unprovability target after a fixed change of exponent and coefficient. No single EXP language or unproved complexity assumption substitutes for a provably total polynomial-time graph.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed metamathematical statement. A positive answer must, for every standard exponent \(k\ge1\), establish a permitted formula \(\eta\) with its \(S_2^1\)-provable totality and uniqueness and prove that no finite \(S_2^1\) proof of \(\operatorname{UB}_{c,k}[\eta]\) exists for any standard coefficient \(c\ge1\). A negative answer must establish an exponent \(k\) such that every permitted \(\eta\) has some coefficient \(c\) for which the corresponding upper-bound sentence is provable. The coefficient and proof may depend on \(\eta\). Nonprovability for a weaker theory, an EXP computation, one proposed proof, or one coefficient alone is insufficient. No unproved complexity hypothesis is part of the target.

cards.definitions:
A literal is \(x_{i}\) or its negation \(
eg x_{i}\). A clause is a disjunction of literals and a CNF F is a finite conjunction of clauses over variables \(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}\); unsatisfiable means no Boolean assignment satisfies every clause. Resolution derives \(C\lor D\) from \(C\lor x_{i}\) and \(D\lor 
eg x_{i}\), and allows weakening from C to \(C\lor D\); input clauses can be used as axioms. A refutation derives the empty clause. A tree-like proof uses each derived occurrence as a premise at most once, duplicating occurrences when necessary; \(S_{T}(F)\) is the minimum number of leaves, rather than total literal count. A configuration proof starts with no stored clauses and at each step downloads an input clause, erases a stored clause, or adds a resolvent/weakening of clauses currently stored; it ends with the empty clause stored. \(CSpace(F)\) is the minimum, over such proofs with unrestricted length, of the maximum number of simultaneously stored clauses. For PCR fix K and use the polynomial ring \(K[x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n},y_{1},\ldots ,y_{n}]\), where \(y_{i}\) represents \(
eg x_{i}\). A line P means \(\mathrm{P}=0\). Logical axioms are \(z^{2}- z\) for each z among \(x_{i},y_{i}\) and \(x_{i}+y_{i}- 1\). The encoding of a clause is the product of its false-literal indicators: \(x_{i}\) contributes \(y_{i}\) and \(
eg x_{i}\) contributes \(x_{i}\). From P,Q derive \(\alpha \mathrm{P}+ eta Q\) for \(\alpha , eta \in K\); from P derive zP for any literal variable z. A PCR refutation derives 1. Its configurations may download axioms, erase lines or add an inference whose premises are stored. The monomial space of a configuration is the number of distinct formal monomials with nonzero coefficients occurring anywhere in its stored polynomials, counted once across all lines; coefficients and exponents are not separately charged. \(MSpace_{K}(F)\) is the minimum maximum monomial space over all PCR refutations. Every proof is finite and minima concern the specified syntactic systems. The source’s relation \(A\preceq B\) permits \(A(F)\le ((B(F))\log  n)^{O(1)}; \approx\) means both directions. The harmless +1 terms here cover one-leaf or other constant-size cases. No polynomial-length restriction is imposed on the space-minimizing proof.
cards.answer_criterion: For each stated space measure, prove the universal polynomial/logarithmic simulation bound or refute it by showing that no constants C,a work for all unsatisfiable formulas (with K fixed in the PCR case). The two variants must be reported separately. A polynomial separation between raw measures does not refute a comparison that explicitly permits arbitrary polynomial and logarithmic factors.

cards.definitions: Targets are Boolean functions \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) computed by finite acyclic fan-in-two AND/OR and unary NOT circuits with constants and one output. The target description explicitly lists gates and wire indices; its binary length is at most a supplied bound \(s\). A single oracle Turing machine \(A\) receives \(1^n,1^s\) and binary rationals \(0<\varepsilon,\delta<1/2\), and may query \(f(x)\) at any chosen \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). Queries may be adaptive and cost the time to write the query plus one step for the answer. The learner has independent fair random coins and no advice, target description or additional oracle. It outputs an explicit deterministic Boolean circuit \(H\) over the same basis. For every permitted input and target it must satisfy \(\Pr_{A\text{ coins}}[2^{-n}|\{x:H(x)\ne f(x)\}|\le\varepsilon]\ge1-\delta\). There is one fixed polynomial \(p\) bounding its time, queries and output length on every random tape by \(p(n+s+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+\lceil\log_2(1/\delta)\rceil+\operatorname{len}(\varepsilon)+\operatorname{len}(\delta))\). The hypothesis need not lie within the target’s size bound; its encoding must obey this output bound. The quantifiers range over every \(n,s\ge1\) and every function with a target description of size at most \(s\). P is the class of languages decided by uniform deterministic polynomial-time Turing machines. NP consists of languages with polynomial-length witnesses checked by a uniform deterministic polynomial-time verifier. Equality concerns languages on all binary inputs, not promise classes. The conclusion is deterministic P equals NP even though the learner is randomized. The implication allows arbitrary proofs and use of the fixed learner code; it is not restricted to black-box reductions.

cards.definitions:
A language is a set of finite binary strings. It belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\) if membership has certificates of length polynomial in the string length that a fixed deterministic polynomial-time verifier can check.

A Cook–Reckhow proof system for \(L\) is a total deterministic polynomial-time computable function
\[f:\{0,1\}^{*}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad \operatorname{range}(f)=L.\]
The input \(\pi\) is a proof and \(f(\pi)\) is the statement it proves. Thus every output is in \(L\), and every member of \(L\) has some proof. The running time is polynomial in \(|\pi|\), including writing the output. No polynomial bound in the statement length is imposed on the shortest proof. The system is one uniform algorithm, with no nonuniform advice.

For two systems \(f,g\) for the same language, \(f\) simulates \(g\) if there is a polynomial \(p\) such that
\[\forall \pi\in\{0,1\}^{*}\ \exists \sigma\in\{0,1\}^{*}:\quad f(\sigma)=g(\pi),\quad |\sigma|\leq p(|\pi|).\]
The polynomial may depend on the two systems, but not on the individual proof. The system \(f\) is optimal if it simulates every total polynomial-time system \(g\) whose range is exactly \(L\).

Only the existence of these short translated proofs is required. Requiring a polynomial-time algorithm that computes \(\sigma\) from \(\pi\) defines the stronger notion of \(p\)-optimality, which is not the target here. Optimality also does not say that all statements have polynomial-length proofs: the comparison is against competing proof systems, not directly against statement length.

This card selects the existential question explicitly stated on page 2 of the source, making its broad page-3 discussion concrete. It asks for at least one language outside \(\mathrm{NP}\), without requiring arbitrarily high complexity or choosing the tautology language in advance. Such a language is automatically computably enumerable, because it is the range of \(f\); decidability is not an additional requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give an unconditional example of a language \(L\notin\mathrm{NP}\) and prove that it has an optimal system under the stated simulation relation, or prove that every language admitting such an optimal system belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\). A conditional existence theorem, an oracle construction, or an example using advice or a weaker simulation relation does not by itself settle this question.

cards.definitions:
A CNF formula is an explicit conjunction of clauses over finitely many Boolean variables. Each clause is a disjunction of literals, where a literal is a variable or its negation. Let \(|F|\) be its ordinary binary encoding length, including literal indices and clause boundaries. Variables may be renamed consecutively in polynomial time.

A Resolution derivation is a finite sequence of clauses. Each line is an input clause of \(F\), or follows from two earlier lines by
\[\frac{A\lor x\qquad B\lor\neg x}{A\lor B},\]
where neither \(A\) nor \(B\) contains the pivot variable \(x\). Repeated literals are identified. A refutation ends in the empty clause, which is false under every assignment. Its length is the number of clauses in the sequence. Earlier lines may be reused: this is general directed-acyclic-graph Resolution, with no tree-like or regularity restriction.

The integer \(s\geq1\) is encoded in unary, so the input length is proportional to \(|F|+s\). The short refutation is promised to exist but is not given to the algorithm. Counting total proof symbols instead of clauses changes this polynomial-time question only by polynomial factors, since every clause uses variables of \(F\).

One fixed uniform deterministic algorithm must halt within a fixed polynomial bound on every input. It must output SAT whenever \(F\) is satisfiable, and UNSAT whenever \(F\) has a refutation of length at most \(s\). These cases are disjoint by soundness of Resolution. If \(F\) is unsatisfiable but all its Resolution refutations have length greater than \(s\), either output is allowed. Malformed encodings can be rejected immediately.

No satisfying assignment or refutation has to be output. In particular, the task does not ask whether a refutation of length at most \(s\) exists on every input: an UNSAT output is allowed even when all Resolution refutations are longer. This promise distinction is the decision formulation of weak automatability, corresponding to allowing efficiently checkable proofs in another fixed proof system instead of insisting on Resolution output.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct the stated deterministic polynomial-time separator, or prove that no such separator exists. A conditional obstruction must state its hypothesis explicitly. Hardness of finding a Resolution refutation, estimating its minimum length, or solving unrestricted SAT does not establish hardness of this particular promise separator without a reduction that respects its two promised cases.

cards.title: Log-rank conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Do there exist integers \(C\ge1,k\ge1\) such that every total Boolean function \(f:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}\), for arbitrary nonempty finite sets X and Y, satisfies \(D(f)\le C\bigl(\log_2(r(f)+2)\bigr)^k\)? Here r(f) is the rank over the real numbers of its zero-one communication matrix, and D(f) is its exact deterministic communication complexity in bits.
cards.definitions: Alice receives \(x\in X\), Bob receives \(y\in Y\), and both know the complete function f, its finite domains and their chosen protocol. These shared data are not charged as communication. A protocol is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node specifies its sender and a function from that sender’s input set to \(\{0,1\}\). At that node the sender transmits this one bit, and both parties follow the corresponding edge; the node already records the preceding transcript. Every leaf is labeled 0 or 1. For every pair (x,y), the reached leaf must be labeled f(x,y), so both parties determine the exact answer. The cost is the maximum number of transmitted bits on any input pair, equivalently the tree depth after deleting unreachable branches. D(f) is the minimum cost among all correct trees; a finite protocol always exists. The protocol may depend arbitrarily on f, and its description length, local computation and number of communication rounds have no separate bound or charge. The communication matrix is \(M_f=(f(x,y))_{x\in X,y\in Y}\), treating its zeroes and ones as real scalars. Define \(r(f)=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb R}(M_f)\), the dimension of its column span over \(\mathbb R\). The particular enumeration of either domain does not matter. Rank zero means the all-zero function, which has D(f)=0, and the all-one function also has D(f)=0. The term r+2 avoids a zero or undefined logarithm at small ranks without changing the asymptotic conjecture. The same C and k must work for every choice of domains and function; the protocol need not be generated uniformly from the table. The statement has no promise pairs, missing matrix entries, distribution on inputs, randomness, quantum messages, approximation or one-way restriction. Rank over a finite field, approximate rank and sign rank are not the parameter used here. Some sources encode outputs by minus one and plus one. With \(A=2M_f-J\), where J is the all-one matrix, the two ordinary real ranks differ by at most one and the output relabeling does not change D(f); with the r+2 convention these formulations have the same polynomial-boundedness question. The explicit negation is: for every pair of integers C,k at least one, there exist nonempty finite X,Y and a total f such that \(D(f)>C(\log_2(r(f)+2))^k\). No effective generator of the counterexample functions is added.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a single pair of universal constants C,k satisfying the displayed inequality, or prove its quantified negation excluding every such pair. An affirmative proof must apply to every total function in the exact interactive protocol model; it need not compute an optimal protocol efficiently. A negative proof must give arbitrarily strong failures of polynomial dependence on log-rank, with examples permitted to depend on C and k. Failure of one proposed exponent, a result for partial functions, or a bound using approximate rank, sign rank, randomness or quantum communication does not meet this target.
cards.why: One of the central organizing conjectures of communication complexity. It asks whether a basic linear-algebraic quantity characterizes efficient exact communication, and connects protocols to rectangle partitions, discrepancy, graph structure, and cancellation in matrix decompositions.

importance.reason: A flagship structural conjecture linking deterministic protocols and matrix rank, with many equivalent combinatorial formulations and a large quantitative gap.

progress.text: Lovász and Saks pose the relation between real matrix rank and deterministic communication, as traced in the checked source papers.
Lovett establishes the general upper bound \(O(\sqrt r\log(r+2))\), substantially improving the linear-rank upper bounds.
Göös, Pitassi and Watson prove a nearly quadratic lower bound in log-rank. Their Theorem 2 first concerns one-sided partition number, with the real-rank consequence stated separately.
Sudakov and Tomon obtain \(D(f)=O(\sqrt{r(f)})\). The preprint dates from November 2023, the article appeared online in July 2024, and the journal volume is dated 2025.

Song reports \(\Omega((\log r)^2/\log\log r)\) for an explicit construction. This is a preprint claim with a specific quantitative comparison, not an independently verified catalogue assertion of the strongest bound over all constructions.
The checked third revision of Hambardzumyan–Lovett–Shirley proves the signed-rectangle decomposition theorem and equivalent formulations, and explicitly retains the general conjecture as open.

cards.status_note: The August 2026 equivalent-formulations paper explicitly states that the total deterministic log-rank conjecture remains unresolved, with the square-root-rank upper bound. A bounded primary-source search on 14 September 2026 found no verified resolution. The new lifting proof and its comparison of suppressed logarithmic factors were not independently verified; fixed polynomial lower bounds and partition reformulations do not settle the universal conjecture.

context_blocks.text: Matrix rank gives a general lower bound on communication. A protocol using at most d bits has at most \(2^{d}\) leaves, and the inputs reaching each leaf form a rectangle \(A\times B\). Summing the indicator matrices of the output-one rectangles represents \(M_{f}\) as a sum of at most \(2^{d}\) rank-one matrices. Consequently \(\log _{2}r(f)\le D(f)\) when \(r(f)\ge 1\). The conjecture asks whether this algebraic obstruction controls deterministic communication up to a polynomial.

An elementary upper bound goes in the other direction but is much larger. A rank-r Boolean matrix has at most 2ʳ distinct rows: choose r columns that determine every row, and record their Boolean entries. Alice can identify her row with at most r bits, after which Bob can determine the answer and send one output bit. This protocol makes clear why the question concerns the gap between rank and its logarithm.

A low-rank factorization permits arbitrary real coefficients and cancellation. A protocol instead needs a recursively organized partition into monochromatic rectangles. Moving between these kinds of structure is the main difficulty. Lovett used discrepancy to obtain an \(O(\sqrt{r} \log  r)\) communication bound; Sudakov and Tomon remove the logarithmic factor using a stronger discrepancy estimate for sparse matrices. The resulting \(O(\sqrt{r})\) remains far larger than a polynomial in log r.
Lower-bound constructions show that a linear bound in log-rank is too optimistic. Göös, Pitassi, and Watson obtain a nearly quadratic separation through query-to-communication lifting.

Song’s August 2026 preprint reports an explicit bound \(\Omega((\log r)^2/\log\log r)\) by refining the parameters in earlier constructions. This records the preprint’s stated result, whose proof and comparison of logarithmic losses were not independently verified here. In any event, a lower bound of this fixed polynomial order would not refute the conjecture, which permits a larger universal exponent.

Hambardzumyan, Lovett and Shirley prove that a rank-r Boolean matrix is a signed sum of \(O(r\log(r+2))\) rectangle indicator matrices. Their equivalent conjecture compares this with the minimum number of disjoint all-one rectangles that partition the one-entries. That one-sided partition number differs from both a partition of all entries into monochromatic rectangles and the leaves of a protocol tree. The equivalence is a proved reformulation, not an established bound for exact protocols.

A finite example disproving one proposed constant or exponent would still permit a different polynomial bound. A negative answer must exclude every universal polynomial, with the function and dimensions allowed to vary with that polynomial. A positive answer may choose a different protocol for each function; the conjecture imposes no efficient protocol-construction requirement.

cards.title: Fourier Entropy–Influence conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Does there exist one finite real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every positive integer \(n\) and every function \(f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\}\), \[H(f)\le C I(f),\] where \(H(f)\) is the Shannon entropy in bits of the squared Fourier spectrum and \(I(f)\) is total influence for uniformly distributed inputs? The same \(C\) must work for all dimensions and all Boolean functions.
cards.definitions: Let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and give each \(x\in\{-1,1\}^n\) probability \(2^{-n}\). For \(S\subseteq[n]\), define \(\chi_S(x)=\prod_{i\in S}x_i\), with empty product one, and \[\widehat f(S)=2^{-n}\sum_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}f(x)\chi_S(x),\qquad q_S=\widehat f(S)^2.\] These are real coefficients and \(\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}q_S=1\). Define \(\eta(0)=0\) and \(\eta(t)=t\log_2(1/t)\) for \(0<t\le1\), where \(\log_2 t=\ln t/\ln2\). Then \[H(f)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\eta(q_S).\] The sum includes the empty set and is not conditioned on nonempty spectral subsets or divided by the variance. For each \(i\in[n]\), let \(x^{\oplus i}\) negate coordinate \(i\) and retain all other coordinates. Set \[I_i(f)=2^{-n}\bigl|\{x\in\{-1,1\}^n:f(x)\ne f(x^{\oplus i})\}\bigr|,\qquad I(f)=\sum_{i=1}^n I_i(f)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}|S|q_S.\] Influence uses an actual bit flip, with no additional probability of leaving that coordinate unchanged. All scalar Boolean functions are allowed; no balance, monotonicity, circuit-size, degree or efficient-computability promise is imposed. Constant functions satisfy \(H(f)=I(f)=0\). The inequality is non-strict, so it includes them.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal inequality for some positive finite constant, or of its logical negation. A positive proof must use the specified uniform measure, full squared spectrum, base-two Shannon entropy and total bit-flip influence for every \(n\) and every scalar Boolean function. A negative proof must establish \[\forall C>0\ \exists n\ge1\ \exists f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\},\quad H(f)>C I(f).\] The dimension and function may depend on \(C\); equivalently, the entropy-to-influence ratios of nonconstant Boolean functions must be unbounded. Defeating one numerical constant or checking finitely many truth tables is insufficient. No optimal value of \(C\), algorithm for finding counterexamples or numerical approximation is required.
cards.why: A central structural conjecture connecting sensitivity to spectral information. Its resolution would sharpen our understanding of Boolean functions and spectral learning, while testing a relation that fails without the Boolean constraint.

importance.reason: A longstanding, broadly consequential conjecture in Boolean function analysis, with direct learning-theory implications and active 2026 progress that still leaves the universal classical inequality open.

cards.status_note: Open in the checked classical primary literature, explicitly reiterated in both August 2026 quantum papers. Bounded searches and version checks through 15 September 2026 found no proof or refutation of the universal scalar Boolean Shannon-entropy inequality. The June separated classes impose extra hypotheses, the coordinate-entropy estimates retain an extra term, and the August counterexamples are operator-valued or use non-Boolean complex phases. Li–Han’s December 2025 weaker-bound preprint was withdrawn for prior appearance of its result. Complete new preprint proofs were not independently verified.

context_blocks.text: A Fourier coefficient records correlation with a parity of selected input bits. Squaring these correlations gives a probability distribution on subsets of the coordinates. Its Shannon entropy measures dispersion among subsets; total influence is the expected cardinality of a subset from that distribution. The conjecture asks whether being the spectrum of a Boolean-valued function forces a universal linear relation between these two quantities.

This is not a generic fact about probability distributions on subsets. A distribution uniform on the n singleton sets has entropy \(\log _{2} n\) but expected set size one. It is the squared Fourier spectrum of the normalized real function \(g(x)=(x_{1}+\cdots +x_{n})/\sqrt{n}\), which is generally not Boolean. Conversely, a parity of all n inputs has entropy zero and total influence n. These examples explain both why Boolean-valuedness matters and why the proposed inequality has only one direction.

If FEI holds with constant \(C\), then for every \(0<\delta<1\), some family \(\mathcal T\) of at most \(2^{CI(f)/\delta}\) subsets satisfies \(\sum_{S\notin\mathcal T}q_S\le\delta\). Equivalently, retaining those Fourier coefficients approximates \(f\) with mean squared error at most \(\delta\) under the uniform measure. The support bound depends on the accuracy parameter; a guarantee independent of accuracy is not being asserted.

O’Donnell, Wright and Zhou prove FEI for symmetric Boolean functions, which are invariant under every permutation of coordinates, and for read-once decision trees, where the variables used in the two branches at each query are disjoint. The read-once condition is stronger than merely avoiding a repeated query along each path. Their application to a disjunction of \(m\ge2\) conjunctions of literals uses \(I(f)=O(\log m)\): FEI would give concentration on \(m^{O(1/\delta)}\) Fourier coefficients for each fixed error \(\delta\). This is a version of Mansour’s conjecture, not its stronger proposed logarithmic dependence on inverse error. It concerns uniform-measure spectral concentration and the associated query-learning setting.

Han’s Theorem 1 bounds \(H(f)\) by an absolute constant times \(I(f)+\sum_i I_i(f)\log_2(1/I_i(f))\), with zero terms when \(I_i(f)=0\). The journal version appeared online on 20 December 2024 in Combinatorica volume 45 (2025). The 10 December 2025 arXiv revision adds an acknowledgement of related prior work by Keller, Mossel and Schlank. The extra coordinate-entropy term can exceed a constant times total influence, so this bound leaves FEI open.

The earlier Keller–Mossel–Schlank paper already gives \(H(f)\le\sum_i h_2(I_i(f))\) in Claim 4.1, where \(h_2(t)=-t\log_2 t-(1-t)\log_2(1-t)\) with zero endpoint terms. The claim supplies the same general kind of coordinate-entropy control and applies beyond Boolean-valued spectra after normalization. This is why a later proof or refinement of that weaker bound must be distinguished from resolving FEI. Min-entropy, \(-\log_2\max_S q_S\), concerns just the largest coefficient and is a different, weaker target than Shannon entropy.

González, MacManus and Pereyra’s revision of 9 June 2026 reports FEI for the defined \(\delta\)-tribes class and for classes with recursive separation properties. The separation theorems retain hypotheses on their terminal functions and constants; they are not assertions for all monotone functions or unrestricted decision trees. The paper also exhibits failure of a stronger inequality involving a prescribed splitting coordinate. Those examples satisfy FEI, so that failure is not a counterexample to this card’s target.

Slote’s 2 August 2026 preprint reports a counterexample to the quantum extension, whose inputs are Hermitian unitary operators and whose coefficients come from tensor products of Pauli matrices. Theorems 1 and 5 give operators supported on degree-\(d\) Pauli terms with entropy \(\Theta(d^2)\) and influence \(d\). Classical Boolean functions form a restricted diagonal case of that operator setting. The operators constructed in the theorem therefore do not supply scalar Boolean counterexamples. The full new construction was not independently verified in this review.

A follow-up by Slote, Volberg and Zhang, revised 6 August 2026, also treats quantum counterexamples. Its §6.6 reports Hermitian involutions with total influence below two and spectral entropy \(\log_2 n+O(1)\) in its family parameter. The underlying auxiliary scalar functions take complex values of modulus one, rather than only the real values \(-1\) and \(1\). That domain change is essential, and §6 still describes classical FEI as open. These theorem scopes were checked without independently certifying the full proofs.

A positive solution would expose a strong restriction on the spectra of every Boolean computation, independently of how that computation is represented. A negative solution would identify Boolean functions whose spectral information greatly exceeds their sensitivity to input changes. Either outcome would clarify a basic link between combinatorial stability, harmonic analysis and the possibility of learning from sparse spectral descriptions.

cards.title: Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Does there exist an absolute constant \(C\ge 1\) such that, for all integers \(n\ge 1\) and \(1\le d\le n\) and every real multilinear polynomial f of degree at most d satisfying \(0\le f(x)\le 1\) for every \(x\in \{- 1,1\}^{n}\), some coordinate i satisfies \(Inf_{i}(f)\ge (\operatorname{Var}(f)/d)^{C}\)?
cards.definitions: All expectations use the uniform distribution on \(\{- 1,1\}^{n}\). Write \(f(x)=\sum_{S\subseteq [n]} \hat\{f\}(S)\prod _{j\in S}x_{j}\), with \(\hat\{f\}(S)=E_{x}[f(x)\prod _{j\in S}x_{j}]\); degree at most d means \(\hat\{f\}(S)=0\) when |\(S|>d\). Let \(x^{\oplus i}\) be x with just coordinate i negated. Define \(\operatorname{Var}(f)=E[(f- E f)^{2}]=\sum_{S\ne \varnothing}\hat\{f\}(S)^{2}\) and \(Inf_{i}(f)=E[(f(x)- f(x^{\oplus i}))^{2}]/4=\Sigma\)_{S∋i}\(\hat\{f\}(S)^{2}\). This is squared \(\mathrm{L}_{2}\) influence, with the factor \(1/4\) fixed explicitly. The pointwise range restriction holds on the entire cube, not merely with high probability. Coefficients may be arbitrary real numbers; no sparsity, coefficient-size, block structure, Boolean-valued-output or quantum-realizability promise is imposed. C must be independent of n,d,f and its variance. Constant polynomials satisfy the inequality trivially with both sides zero. The one-power notation is a normalized version of a polynomial lower bound in variance and inverse degree; because \(\operatorname{Var}(f)\le 1/4\), fixed positive prefactors can be absorbed by increasing C.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove one universal exponent C works for every admissible polynomial, or show that for every proposed C there is an admissible polynomial of positive variance for which every coordinate has influence smaller than \((\operatorname{Var}(f)/d)^{C}\). Refuting one particular exponent is insufficient to refute existence of some universal exponent. An exponential-in-degree influence bound, a theorem only after randomly fixing coordinates, or a result for a restricted subclass is partial progress.
cards.why: A central structural question about real-valued Boolean-cube functions, with direct consequences for when quantum query algorithms can have large classical simulation costs.

importance.reason: Connects a basic dimension-independent influence bound to almost-everywhere classical simulation of quantum queries, bringing Boolean analysis and quantum complexity together.

progress.text: Aaronson–Ambainis formulate the influential-variable conjecture and prove its implication for almost-everywhere classical query simulation.
Keller–Klein withdraw their claimed general proof; the arXiv notice identifies failure of Lemma 5.3.
Bansal–Sinha–de Wolf establish the conjectured behavior for completely bounded block-multilinear forms.
Bhattacharya proves junta approximation after random restrictions and influential-variable guarantees for a non-negligible fraction of restrictions.
Revision 2 of the random-restriction preprint updates presentation and references while retaining its restriction and variance hypotheses.
Blanc–Docter–Strassle–Tan prove almost-everywhere simulation for bounded-round quantum algorithms, with a round-dependent polynomial exponent.
Escudero Gutiérrez–Saucedo–Palazuelos sharpen completely bounded block-multilinear root-influence bounds to the optimal constant and obtain nonadaptive simulation in that setting.

references.authors: Francisco Escudero Gutiérrez; Miquel Saucedo; Carlos Palazuelos

cards.status_note: The 4 September 2026 primary paper explicitly leaves the unrestricted Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture open. Recent restricted-model and bounded-round results do not prove it; the 2019 general claim remains withdrawn. Checked through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: A low-degree polynomial contains interactions among only a few variables at a time, yet it may involve a very large number of variables overall. The question asks whether its variation must be detectably concentrated on at least one coordinate. The desired lower bound depends on the interaction degree and on how much the function varies, while having no dependence on the ambient number n of input bits.

Dependence on variance is essential. Consider \(f(x)=1/2+(x_{1}+\cdots +x_{n})/(2n)\). This degree-one polynomial always lies in \([0,1]\), but \(\operatorname{Var}(f)=1/(4n)\) and each coordinate has influence \(1/(4n^{2})\). No positive lower bound depending only on degree could work. The example is consistent with the conjectured polynomial dependence on variance. It also distinguishes an influential coordinate relative to the function’s variation from a coordinate with a constant absolute influence.

The quantum connection comes from acceptance probabilities. A quantum algorithm making t queries to input bits has an acceptance probability represented by a bounded polynomial of degree at most 2t. If the conjecture holds, a classical procedure can repeatedly query an influential coordinate and restrict the polynomial. After sufficiently many such queries, the remaining uncertainty has small variance, allowing its mean to estimate the acceptance probability on most uniformly sampled inputs.

That consequence concerns query complexity. It does not automatically supply polynomial-time classical computation between queries, nor does it promise accurate simulation on every input. A small exceptional set can contain the entire promise domain of a quantum speedup. Also, the influential-variable conjecture is stronger than the simulation statement it implies: not every bounded low-degree polynomial is the acceptance probability of a quantum algorithm with a comparable query budget.

The distinction between bounded real outputs and Boolean outputs is substantial. The conjectured polynomial behavior is known for Boolean-valued functions, but the general real-valued case remains harder. Classical Fourier-analytic techniques yield bounds with exponential dependence on degree. These already force some influence, yet they do not provide the polynomial guarantee needed here.

One productive restriction is complete boundedness. Roughly, this requires the polynomial to remain bounded even when suitable matrix contractions replace scalar inputs, with products taken in a specified order. It is much stronger than being bounded on the scalar Boolean cube. Bansal, Sinha and de Wolf prove influential-variable bounds for completely bounded block-multilinear forms, a class connected to algorithms querying separate input blocks.

Bhattacharya’s random-restriction theorem approaches the unrestricted class differently. Fix most coordinates independently to random signs and leave roughly a \(\log (d)/d\) fraction available. Under a lower bound on the original variance, a non-negligible fraction of restrictions have a polynomially influential remaining variable. The accompanying junta theorem approximates restricted functions using few coordinates. Neither assertion directly guarantees such a variable in the original, unrestricted function.

Two recent results clarify the frontier. Blanc and coauthors obtain the desired almost-everywhere classical simulation for a fixed number of quantum query rounds; their exponent depends on the number of rounds. This does not address arbitrary adaptivity or prove the full polynomial inequality. Escudero Gutiérrez, Saucedo and Palazuelos subsequently obtain an optimal root-influence inequality for completely bounded block-multilinear polynomials, improving simulation to allow nonadaptive classical queries for that setting.

The September inequality controls the sum of square roots of influences by the number of blocks times the completely bounded norm. Its extra norm hypothesis is precisely what prevents applying it to every polynomial in this card. The paper explicitly retains the unrestricted conjecture. A historical general proof claim by Keller and Klein is withdrawn because of an error in a key lemma, and is recorded as a withdrawal rather than progress establishing the conjecture.

cards.title: Mansour’s conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Does there exist an absolute constant \(C>0\) such that, for every \(n\ge 1\), integer \(s\ge 2\), Boolean function \(f:\{- 1,1\}^{n}\to \{- 1,1\}\) representable by a DNF with at most s terms, and \(\varepsilon \in\)(\(0,1/2\)], some family \(F\subseteq 2^{[n]}\) satisfies |\(F|\le \lceil s^{C \log _{2}(1/\varepsilon )}\rceil\) and \(\sum_{S\notin F} \hat\{f\}(S)^{2}\le \varepsilon\)?
cards.definitions: A DNF is an OR of conjunctions of literals \(x_{i}=1\) or \(x_{i}=- 1; a\) satisfied formula has value +1 and an unsatisfied formula value −1. Term widths, overlaps, and the number of occurrences of a variable are unrestricted. On the uniform probability space \(\{- 1,1\}^{n}, \chi _{S}(x)=\prod _{i\in S}x_{i}, \chi _{\varnothing}=1\), and \(\hat\{f\}(S)=2^{- n}\sum_{x} f(x)\chi _{S}(x)\). Parseval gives \(\sum_{S} \hat\{f\}(S)^{2}=1\). Thus \(\varepsilon\)-concentration on F means that the polynomial \(g=\sum_{S\in F}\hat\{f\}(S)\chi _{S}\) has \(E[(f- g)^{2}]\le \varepsilon\). The coefficients are ordinary Walsh coefficients, not a basis adapted to a different distribution. The same C must work for all \(n,s,\varepsilon\) and f. This is an existence question about the spectrum; no efficient algorithm for finding F is part of the proposition.
cards.answer_criterion: An affirmative resolution proves the stated bound with one universal C. A negative resolution must show that for every C some admissible \(s,n,\varepsilon\) and DNF require more than \(\lceil s^{C \log _{2}(1/\varepsilon )}\rceil\) coefficients to leave squared Fourier mass at most \(\varepsilon\). A polynomial bound whose exponent has an unspecified dependence on \(\varepsilon\) would settle only the weaker fixed-accuracy form.
cards.why: A fundamental bridge between short logical formulas, sparse spectral representations, and learning with queries. The strong accuracy parameter makes the question a precise test of how much analytic structure small DNF size forces.

importance.reason: A defining conjecture in Boolean function analysis and learning theory, connecting representation size to approximate Fourier sparsity and agnostic learning.

cards.status_note: Open in the strong logarithmic-accuracy form stated here, following the inspected primary sources and a later-result search through 11 September 2026. Fixed-error polynomial concentration, restricted DNF models, and generalized-basis learning results do not by themselves settle this formulation.

context_blocks.text: A DNF describes a function as a short list of sufficient conditions for acceptance. Its Fourier expansion describes the same function through parity correlations. Mansour’s question asks whether a short description in the first language forces an approximately short description in the second. The number n of available variables may greatly exceed the number s of terms, yet the proposed number of relevant correlations depends only on s and the permitted error.

The approximation is measured in squared error under uniformly random inputs. It does not require exact agreement everywhere, and the approximating polynomial need not have Boolean outputs. Keeping the largest squared coefficients is the best approximation with that many Walsh characters. Consequently the question is a statement about how rapidly the sorted Fourier mass decays, independent of an algorithm’s ability to identify the important characters.

Sparsity and degree are different resources. A parity involving every variable has just one nonzero Fourier coefficient but has degree n. Conversely, restricting a polynomial to degree d can leave a number of possible coefficients that grows like \(n^{d}\). A theorem saying that high-degree coefficients have little total mass therefore does not by itself give the requested bound, which must avoid such dependence on the ambient dimension.

Even one wide conjunction can have many nonzero coefficients exactly. This does not contradict the conjecture: if the conjunction fixes w distinct coordinates, its satisfying event has probability \(2^{- w}\). Approximating its ±1-valued function by the constant −1 incurs squared error \(4\cdot 2^{- w}\). Rare accepting terms can therefore produce an exactly dense spectrum while contributing very little approximation error. Combining many overlapping terms is where the simple observation stops being sufficient.

There are two common strengths of the named conjecture. The weaker one allows \(s^{K(\varepsilon )}\) coefficients for an arbitrary function K of the error. The stronger one in this saved record asks for \(K(\varepsilon )=O(\log (1/\varepsilon ))\). O’Donnell–Wright–Zhou explicitly distinguish these statements. The card preserves the stronger target instead of treating all polynomial concentration claims as interchangeable.

The connection to Fourier entropy explains that distinction. If the Fourier entropy were \(O(\log  s)\), Markov’s inequality applied to the surprisal \(\log (1/\hat\{f\}(S)^{2})\) would capture all but \(\varepsilon\) of the mass on at most \(s^{O(1/\varepsilon )}\) coefficients. The Fourier Entropy–Influence conjecture, combined with the influence bound for DNF, would supply such an entropy estimate. This implication gives the weaker form, but its exponent does not establish the logarithmic dependence required here.

Mansour’s classical general bound gives \(s^{O(\log  \log  s)}\) coefficients at fixed accuracy. Klivans–Lee–Wan proved polynomial concentration for a specified random-DNF model and for every fixed read number. These are substantial structural results, but randomness in the formula cannot be assumed in a worst-case statement about every DNF. Their final May 2010 revision corrects an earlier issue in the read-number argument.

Lecomte–Tan sharpen the fixed-accuracy general estimate to \(s^{O(\log  \log  k)}\), where k bounds the number of terms containing a variable. Their stronger small-read theorem gives \((s/\varepsilon )^{O(\log (1/\varepsilon ))}\) concentration for read number up to a stated roughly doubly logarithmic range. The explicit \(s/\varepsilon\) base should be retained when comparing accuracy parameters. Their work also explains how control of term covers improves Fourier estimates beyond a single global norm bound.

The learning consequences depend on access to the target. Through the agnostic-learning reduction described by Klivans–Lee–Wan, suitable sparse Fourier approximation yields efficient agnostic learning under the uniform distribution with membership queries, for fixed approximation accuracy. Such queries allow selected input points; they are stronger access than an ordinary stream of independently sampled labeled examples. This conjecture should not be advertised as automatically solving every version of passive DNF learning.

Recent neighboring results retain these distinctions. Han’s 2025 entropy estimate contains an additional sum involving individual influences, rather than the full conjectured constant times total influence. González–MacManus–Pereyra’s June 2026 revision proves FEI for further classes under structural separation conditions. Neither is a universal theorem with the strong DNF accuracy bound in the question.

Heidari–Khardon’s June 2026 revision studies generalized Fourier representations associated with Bayesian networks. Its DNF learning theorem uses membership queries and a restricted distributional model; its agnostic result concerns decision trees. These changes in basis, distribution and target class are mathematically meaningful, but they do not establish concentration of every DNF in the ordinary uniform Walsh basis used here.

cards.title: Maximum influence of polynomial threshold functions
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors jointly for all integers \(n\ge 1\) and \(1\le d\le n, M(n,d)=\max\){\(I(f): f=\operatorname{sign}(p):\{- 1,1\}^{n}\to \{- 1,1\}, \deg (p)\le d\), and p has no zero on the Boolean cube}, using total influence as defined below.
cards.definitions:
A realizing polynomial p is a real polynomial in n variables of total degree at most d, with \(p(x)
e 0\) at every Boolean input. The sign is +1 for positive values and −1 for negative values. Coefficients are unrestricted real numbers; no bound on coefficient magnitude, description length, margin or number of monomials is assumed. One may take p multilinear by reducing \(x_{i}^{2}\) to 1 on the cube. The nonzero convention loses no threshold functions under a fixed sign-at-zero convention, since a sufficiently small constant perturbation preserves all assigned signs. If x is uniform on \(\{- 1,1\}^{n}\), let \(x^{i}\) denote x with coordinate i flipped. Define \(Inf_{i}(f)=\Pr [f(x)
e f(x^{i})]\), pointwise sensitivity \(s_{f}(x)=|\{i:f(x)
e f(x^{i})\}|\), and \(I(f)=\sum_{i} Inf_{i}(f)=E[s_{f}(x)]\). The constants in the requested matching asymptotic bounds must be independent of n,d,f and the realizing polynomial. Constant functions have zero influence; allowing \(d=0\) adds only these trivial cases. The maximum exists because only finitely many Boolean functions occur on a fixed cube; realizing polynomials may have arbitrary real coefficients. The earlier asymptotic Gotsman–Linial question asks for \(M(n,d)=O(d\sqrt{n})\), while an exact symmetric-extremizer conjecture was disproved.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a positive function \(h(n,d)\) and universal constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\) with \(c h(n,d)\le M(n,d)\le C h(n,d)\) for all \(n\ge 1\) and \(1\le d\le n\), and prove both bounds in Lean. This must determine the joint parameter dependence, including saturation at large degree, within constant factors. No particular extremizing Boolean function is prescribed; merely refuting one candidate formula does not determine M.
cards.why: A basic unresolved relation between algebraic threshold complexity and the edge boundary of a Boolean function, central to noise sensitivity, learning and threshold-circuit analysis.

importance.reason: A foundational and quantitatively sharp Boolean-function conjecture whose surviving asymptotic form matters even though the original exact extremizer was disproved.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The exact symmetric-maximizer conjecture is false, but the universal \(O(d\sqrt{n})\) influence bound remains open in the checked primary literature, including the April 2026 revisions on rational degree and Boolean surface area.

context_blocks.text: The quantitative target is the maximum influence as a function of dimension and degree. The following history concerns the asymptotic Gotsman–Linial conjecture and the separately disproved exact-extremizer claim.

A polynomial threshold function first evaluates a low-degree real polynomial and then keeps only its sign. Linear threshold functions include majority votes and weighted voting rules. Quadratic threshold functions can also include pairwise interactions between inputs. The conjecture asks whether this algebraic simplicity forces the function to change its output relatively rarely along the edges of the Boolean cube.

Total influence counts those changes in an averaged way. If D is the number of undirected cube edges joining opposite outputs, then \(I(f)=2D/2^{n}\). The maximum possible influence of an arbitrary Boolean function is n, achieved by parity. A degree-d bound of \(C d\sqrt{n}\) would sharply restrict the boundary when d is small compared with \(\sqrt{n}\); once \(d\ge \sqrt{n}\), the elementary bound \(I(f)\le n\) already suffices with \(C=1\).

Majority shows why a square root is unavoidable. For odd n, flipping a coordinate changes majority exactly when the other \(n- 1\) coordinates split evenly, giving I(\(MAJ_{n}\))=\(n\cdot \operatorname{binom}(n- 1,(n- 1)/2)/2^{n- 1}\), asymptotic to \(\sqrt{2n/\pi}\). Thus even degree one permits influence growing with dimension. The target is not a constant influence bound for every fixed-degree function.

There is a natural higher-degree candidate: place d parallel threshold hyperplanes between consecutive central Hamming layers, then take the sign of the product of their linear equations. The sign alternates at those layers. When the layers lie near the center, their boundaries together have order \(d\sqrt{n}\). Gotsman and Linial proposed the much stronger assertion that this symmetric construction maximizes influence exactly.

Chapman disproved that exact assertion for most parameter pairs, including quadratic examples in every odd dimension at least five. The paper carefully separates its exact conjecture from Conjecture 1.2, the asymptotic statement discussed here, and leaves the latter open. Its SODA publication was in 2018; the arXiv copy was uploaded in 2021. Neither date turns the disproved exact formulation into a refutation of the remaining asymptotic question.

Products of d linear threshold signs satisfy the desired order by a simple union bound: if the product changes across an edge, at least one factor changes. Summing the factors’ influence bounds gives \(O(d\sqrt{n})\). But a general degree-d polynomial need not factor into d linear forms, and its sign need not admit such a representation. This identifies one tempting argument and the missing structural fact it would need.

Kane proved the near-optimal dimensional estimate \(I(f)\le \sqrt{n}\cdot (\log  n)^{O(d \log  d)}\cdot 2^{O(d^{2} \log  d)}\) for \(d\ge 2\). For each fixed d, this is \(\sqrt{n}\) times a polylogarithmic factor, establishing the correct exponent of n. The extra logarithms can still grow without bound, while the dependence on d is much larger than linear. Removing these losses is exactly what the displayed conjecture demands.

The proof program uses random restrictions and comparisons between Boolean and Gaussian polynomial behavior. Anti-concentration helps ensure that a small perturbation rarely carries the polynomial through zero. Such transfers must deal with coordinates of high influence and with the discrete cube’s concentrated mass. The continuous analogue is informative, but it is not a direct proof for arbitrary Boolean threshold polynomials.

For quadratic functions there are useful structural subcases. Kim, Maldonado and Wellens analyze the graph whose edges indicate nonzero quadratic coefficients and establish asymptotic estimates under restrictions such as low fractional chromatic number or few edges. This connects the influence question to the interaction graph, while leaving general dense quadratic interactions outside those special guarantees.

A 2026 paper by Chang, Slote, Volberg and Zhang proves a polylogarithmic bound, for fixed degree, on Boolean surface area \(BSA(f)=E[\sqrt{s_{f}}(x)]\). The April 27 revision strengthens its original subpolynomial estimate. This is significant new control of boundary geometry, but BSA is a different moment from \(I(f)=E[s_{f}(x)]\). A bound on the expectation of the square root does not directly bound the expectation by its square.

Indeed, pointwise \(s_{f}(x)\le \sqrt{n}\cdot \sqrt{s_{f}}(x)\) yields only \(I(f)\le \sqrt{n}\cdot BSA(f)\). Substituting the new polylogarithmic surface-area bound still leaves a factor depending on log n, with degree-dependent constants. This calculation explains why that recent theorem is compatible with the influence conjecture remaining open, without diminishing its improvement for the different boundary measure.

Kothari, Kovacs-Deak, Wang and Yang’s April 2026 revision on rational degree also restates the influence conjecture and proposes a weaker version using nondeterministic degree. Their theorem resolves a separate polynomial relation between rational and ordinary degree, rather than this threshold-degree inequality. These connections help explain the conjecture’s importance for the relationships among Boolean complexity measures, in addition to its learning and circuit applications.

cards.title: Aanderaa–Karp–Rosenberg conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: For every integer \(n\ge 2\) and every nonconstant function f from the simple undirected graphs on \([n]\) to \(\{0,1\}\) that is invariant under every permutation of \([n]\) and monotone under adding edges, is \(D(f)=n(n- 1)/2\), where \(D(f)\) is its deterministic worst-case adjacency-query complexity?
cards.why: This asks whether every nontrivial monotone graph property can force complete inspection of its adjacency data, even when all computation between queries is free. A resolution would identify an exact limit of adaptive information gathering imposed by graph symmetry.

progress.text: Kahn, Saks and Sturtevant, Theorem 1, establish exact evasiveness for every nontrivial monotone graph property when the number of vertices is a prime power.
Aaronson and coauthors, Theorem 5, prove the optimal universal \(Omega(n)\) bounded-error quantum query lower bound. This is a separate query model.
Elekes and coauthors, version 3, Section 1.1, retain the finite conjecture as open while studying failures of infinite-vertex extensions.

Benedetti’s CATA IV abstract announces a counterexample to topological evasiveness. No finite graph-property counterexample is specified in the abstract; the related author publication list still labels the manuscript in preparation at this review.

cards.definitions: Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\) and \(U_{n}=\{\{i,j\}:1\le i<j\le n\}; a\) graph is an arbitrary edge set \(E\subseteq U_{n}\), with no loops, parallel edges or input promises. Nonconstant means that f takes both values 0 and 1. Monotonicity means \(E\subseteq F\) implies \(f(E)\le f(F)\). Invariance means \(f(\pi (E))=f(E)\) for every permutation \(\pi\) of \([n]\), where \(\pi (E)=\{\{\pi (i),\pi (j)\}:\{i,j\}\in E\}\). A deterministic query algorithm is a finite rooted binary decision tree. Each internal node names an unordered pair in \(U_{n}\) and its two outgoing edges correspond to the answer 0 or 1 for absence or presence of that pair; each leaf carries an output bit. Following the answers supplied by E must end with output \(f(E)\) for every \(E\subseteq U_{n}\). The cost on E is the number of internal nodes visited, and \(D(f)\) is the minimum, over all such correct trees, of the maximum cost over E. Repeated queries can be omitted. The tree may depend arbitrarily on n and f; f is the fixed task, not an additional unknown input. Only queries count: computation, storage and the size of the tree are unrestricted, and no uniform procedure for constructing trees across n or f is required. The model is deterministic and exact, with no probability distribution over inputs. Reading every pair gives \(D(f)\le |U_{n}|\).
cards.answer_criterion: Prove \(D(f)=|U_{n}|\) for every n and f satisfying the stated conditions, or refute this universal claim. A finite refutation consists of one n, a completely specified invariant nonconstant monotone f, and a correct decision tree whose depth is at most |\(U_{n}|- 1\). A lower bound only up to a constant factor, or a theorem restricted to particular properties or vertex counts, does not settle the full claim.

context_blocks.text: Imagine receiving a graph behind an interface that answers only whether a chosen pair of vertices is joined. The algorithm can choose its next pair after seeing earlier answers. The conjecture says that, for every qualifying property, even the best such strategy has some input on which it must inspect every possible pair.

For a concrete example, consider the property of having at least one edge. Finding an edge establishes a yes answer immediately. On the empty graph, however, every pair must be inspected: an unexamined pair could hide the only edge. Evasiveness is thus a worst-case requirement; it does not say that every graph forces a complete scan.

The hypotheses specify which questions qualify. A constant answer needs no queries, so it is excluded. Asking whether the particular pair \(\{1,2\}\) is an edge needs one query but depends on vertex labels, so it is excluded by isomorphism invariance. Monotonicity requires a yes answer to survive the addition of edges; connectivity and containing a triangle have this feature, whereas having exactly one edge does not.

Symmetry says that relabeling the graph cannot change the answer. It does not prevent the algorithm from using labels to decide which pair to inspect first. Moreover, the difficult input can depend on the algorithm. These distinctions make the conjecture much stronger than the observation that all edge positions are potentially relevant.

The older quadratic lower-bound question is settled. The remaining target is exact equality with the total number of pairs, including the last possible query. Kahn, Saks and Sturtevant prove this equality whenever n is a prime power, meaning \(n=p^{k}\) for a prime p and an integer \(k\ge 1\). Their result covers every qualifying property at those sizes, but not every integer n.

Aaronson and coauthors establish the optimal universal lower bound of order n for bounded-error quantum queries. Quantum access and a permitted error probability change the model; the theorem does not establish the exact deterministic all-pairs bound.

Elekes and coauthors investigate countably infinite graphs, where versions of the monotone conjecture fail. Their October 2025 revision explicitly states the finite conjecture as open. Infinite-vertex counterexamples do not refute this card.

A June 2026 talk announces a counterexample to a broader topological evasiveness conjecture. That formulation assumes transitivity among the vertices of a simplicial complex; this card requires invariance under every relabeling of an underlying graph. The announcement does not exhibit the latter kind of counterexample, and the associated manuscript is listed as in preparation. It is therefore recorded as related announced work, without treating it as a resolution of this card.

sentences: An algorithm learns an unknown graph by asking whether individual pairs of vertices are edges.
The conjecture asks whether every nonconstant monotone property invariant under vertex relabeling has some input requiring all possible pairs to be queried.
Queries may be adaptive and all computation between them is free.
The example of looking for one edge illustrates how an easy positive instance can coexist with an empty graph that requires a complete scan.

The exact claim is known for prime-power vertex counts, while results about quantum queries, infinite graphs and broader topological symmetry must be distinguished from the full finite deterministic question.
