cards.title: Real Grothendieck constant
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Determine the real Grothendieck constant \(K_{G}^{\mathbb R}\), defined as the least universal comparison factor between the vector and sign bilinear optima below.
cards.definitions: For positive integers m,n and a real matrix \(A=(a_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), define \(S(A)=\max_{\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}^{m},\,\delta\in\{-1,1\}^{n}}|\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{ij}\varepsilon_i\delta_j|\) and \(V(A)=\max_{u_1,\ldots,u_m,v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\mathbb R^{m+n},\,\|u_i\|_2=\|v_j\|_2=1}|\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{ij}\langle u_i,v_j\rangle|\). The inner product and norm are Euclidean. Define \(K_{G}^{\mathbb R}=\sup_{m,n\ge1,\,A\ne0}V(A)/S(A)\). The denominator is positive for nonzero A. Grothendieck’s inequality makes the supremum finite. The vector dimension m+n permits every possible Gram matrix of these m+n vectors; this is the unrestricted real constant, with no fixed dimension, complex vectors, computational restriction, or asymptotic input model.

context_blocks.text: The two optima compare a discrete sign assignment with its vector relaxation. The universal loss quantifies a basic limitation of this relaxation across all real bilinear objectives.

The earlier strict improvement over Krivine’s bound disproved a proposed value without determining the constant. A 2026 preprint reports a lower bound of \(6\pi/11\) and a further quantitative upper bound; their separation still exceeds the benchmark tolerance.

cards.why: Determining this constant would settle a foundational quantitative barrier shared by functional analysis, semidefinite optimization and quantum correlations.

cards.title: Polynomial relation between classical and quantum communication
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Are randomized classical and entanglement-assisted quantum communication polynomially related for every total Boolean function? Precisely, do universal constants \(C\ge1\) and integer \(k\ge1\) exist such that \[R^{\mathrm{cc}}_{1/3}(F)\le C\bigl(Q^{\mathrm{cc},*}_{1/3}(F)+1\bigr)^k\] for every pair of nonempty finite sets \(X,Y\) and every function \(F:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}\)?
cards.why: The problem delineates quantum advantage in a basic distributed model with unrestricted local computation.

progress.text: The revised AND-functions paper proves the restricted \(O((Q^{\mathrm{cc},*})^7\log^2 n)\) deterministic bound while explicitly retaining the general Log-Equivalence Conjecture.
Hasegawa–Le Gall report polynomial separations using constant-round quantum communication. The claimed advantage does not exceed every polynomial.

Gavinsky posts a claimed exponential quantum–classical separation for an explicit total Boolean family, using two quantum messages and no prior entanglement. This matching claim was missed by the previous bounded status check.

Le Gall posts stronger claimed total-function separations and explicitly specifies public randomness, worst-case communication and per-input error. Pending proof verification, these claims would refute the universal polynomial relation.

context_blocks.text: Communication complexity isolates the information that must cross between two parties who already have unlimited ability to process their own inputs. A quantum advantage in this setting is therefore a saving in transmitted information, rather than a faster local computation. The shared entanglement in the quantum model is a free, input-independent resource.

For a total function, every combination of an Alice input and a Bob input must be handled. Promise problems may omit difficult combinations, and relations may accept several different answers. These distinctions prevent the known much larger advantages for those models from automatically providing a counterexample here.

The polynomial has to be the same for all functions. Examples in which the classical cost is a fixed power of the quantum cost are compatible with the conjecture, even if that power exceeds two. The negation requires advantages that defeat every fixed polynomial bound.

Bhattacharya and coauthors state this as the Log-Equivalence Conjecture, attributed to Shi and Zhu. Their earlier 2026 paper explicitly retains the general total-function question and studies a restricted composed family.

For \(F(x,y)=f(x_1\land y_1,\ldots,x_n\land y_n)\), their revised Theorem 1.2 gives \(D^{\mathrm{cc}}(F)=O((Q^{\mathrm{cc},*}_{1/3}(F))^7\log^2 n)\), where \(D^{\mathrm{cc}}\) denotes exact deterministic communication. This restricted AND-composition result, with its additional input-length factor, differs from the universal polynomial in quantum cost alone.

Hasegawa and Le Gall’s August 2026 preprint obtains a polynomial quantum advantage for a total function using a constant number of quantum communication rounds. Its improvement concerns interaction: the size of the communication gap remains polynomial. It therefore does not refute the general polynomial-relation conjecture.

Resolving the conjecture would determine whether total Boolean communication imposes a general limit on quantum savings. The comparison permits arbitrary prior entanglement and unrestricted interaction, so such a limit would apply beyond particular algorithms or graph-like compositions.

Gavinsky's preliminary August 2026 preprint claims an explicit total-function family with quantum cost \(O(\log^3 N\log\log N)\) and randomized classical cost \(\Omega(N^{1/6}/\log^{7/3}N)\), where \(N\) is the input length of each party. The stated quantum protocol has two transmissions and no prior entanglement; the classical lower bound permits any number of rounds. Polynomial growth in \(N\) defeats every fixed power of its logarithm, so this would refute the displayed conjecture if the proof is correct.

Le Gall's preprint of 15 September 2026 claims \(\operatorname{polylog}(n)\) quantum communication and \(\widetilde\Omega(\sqrt n)\) randomized communication with two quantum messages, and \(\widetilde\Omega(n^{1-1/j})\) classical cost for every fixed integer \(j\ge2\) with a larger constant number of quantum messages. Section 2 explicitly uses public randomness, unrestricted classical rounds, worst-case message costs and error at most \(1/3\) per input. These are total Boolean functions, not promise problems or relations. The full proof has not been independently verified here.

The new claims also apply to the comparison with free prior entanglement: a protocol using no prior entanglement is admissible when that resource is permitted. A protocol whose final receiver is Alice can send its output bit to Bob, adding at most one to the communication cost without changing the error probability. These model correspondences establish a match to the stated target; they do not certify the new lower-bound arguments.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal polynomial bound or of its negation. A negative answer must show that for every \(C\ge1\) and integer \(k\ge1\), some finite total Boolean function satisfies \(R^{\mathrm{cc}}_{1/3}(F)>C(Q^{\mathrm{cc},*}_{1/3}(F)+1)^k\). A superpolynomial separating family can witness this; one fixed polynomial separation cannot. A bound with an extra input-length factor, a promise-problem or relation separation, or a comparison imposing a fixed round limit does not resolve the stated all-functions, unrestricted-round target.
cards.definitions: Alice receives \(x\in X\), Bob receives \(y\in Y\), and Bob must output \(F(x,y)\). A protocol is agreed in advance for the entire function \(F\). Local computation and storage are unrestricted and free; only communication is charged. The protocol may depend on \(F\), but its shared resources are independent of the actual inputs. In the classical model the parties exchange bits and may use shared public randomness and private randomness. In the quantum model they exchange qubits, may use arbitrary finite-dimensional local quantum operations and measurements, and may start with any finite-dimensional shared entangled state independent of \((x,y)\). There is no fixed upper bound on the amount of this prior entanglement; its preparation is not charged. Local quantum operations are completely positive trace-preserving maps, with measurement outcomes retained in local registers, and the final output is a two-outcome measurement at Bob. Classical bits sent by a quantum protocol count as transmitted qubits. Neither model receives free input-dependent advice or any communication through timing, message length, silence or postselection. One may use a fixed finite alternating schedule of transmissions, padding unused transmissions; local branches cannot signal through the schedule. Arbitrarily many rounds are allowed, with no input-length-dependent round restriction imposed by the question. The cost is the worst-case total number of bits or qubits transmitted, including all rounds and all randomness or measurement branches. In either model the output must equal \(F(x,y)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) on every pair \((x,y)\). The quantities \(R^{\mathrm{cc}}_{1/3}(F)\) and \(Q^{\mathrm{cc},*}_{1/3}(F)\) are the least costs among protocols with this guarantee. Total means that all of \(X\times Y\) is the correctness domain; no additional joint promise is allowed. The additive one in the polynomial handles zero-communication functions. The constants \(C,k\) must be independent of the function, the domains, any bit encoding of the inputs, and the amount of shared entanglement.

cards.title: Fourier Min-Entropy–Influence conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Does there exist a finite universal constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\) and every Boolean function \(f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}\), some set \(S\subseteq[n]\) satisfies \(\widehat f(S)^2\ge 2^{-C I(f)}\)? Here \(I(f)\) is total influence under the uniform distribution. Equivalently, the conjecture asserts \(H_\infty(f)\le C I(f)\), with Fourier min-entropy defined below. The same constant must work for every dimension and every function.
cards.why: Total influence measures how often individual bit changes alter an output, while Fourier min-entropy measures how weak even the strongest parity correlation can be. A universal relation would constrain all Boolean functions without representation or balance assumptions. Its distinction from full Fourier entropy matters: controlling a single coefficient asks for less than controlling the entire spectral information, yet retains a connection to fundamental influence inequalities.
cards.status_note: The unrestricted conjecture is explicit in the 2021 primary paper and is still treated as a conjecture in the checked July 2026 Li–Tang publication. Their reported constant lower bound and Han’s general bound do not settle existence of a finite universal FMEI constant. This bounded source review does not independently verify every later proof or certify an exhaustive literature search.

importance.reason: A broad structural conjecture connecting sensitivity with a guaranteed spectral coefficient for every Boolean function. It is a consequential weakening of Fourier entropy–influence with an independent connection to KKL, and recent lower bounds on its universal constant emphasize a substantial unresolved barrier rather than a single construction parameter.

sentences: The FMEI conjecture says that every Boolean function has a parity whose squared Fourier correlation is exponentially large in minus its total influence.
Both influence and Fourier coefficients use the uniform distribution on the Boolean cube.
One universal constant must cover every dimension and truth table, including constant and unbalanced functions.
The conjecture is weaker than full Fourier entropy–influence and remains meaningful because of its connection to fundamental influence inequalities.
Recent constructions force the universal constant to be at least four, while leaving the existence of any finite constant unresolved.

cards.definitions: Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). For \(S\subseteq[n]\), define the parity \(\chi_S(x)=\prod_{j\in S}x_j\), with \(\chi_\varnothing(x)=1\), and the normalized Fourier coefficient \(\widehat f(S)=2^{-n}\sum_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}f(x)\chi_S(x)\). Set \(p_f(S)=\widehat f(S)^2\); these nonnegative masses sum to one. Define \(H_\infty(f)=-\log_2\bigl(\max_{S\subseteq[n]}p_f(S)\bigr)\), measured in bits. The maximum is positive, so this logarithm is always defined, even if some coefficients vanish. If \(x^{\oplus j}\) is obtained by changing the sign of coordinate \(j\), define \(I_j(f)=2^{-n}|\{x\in\{-1,1\}^n:f(x)\ne f(x^{\oplus j})\}|\) and \(I(f)=\sum_{j=1}^n I_j(f)\). Equivalently \(I(f)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}|S|p_f(S)\). Quantification includes constant functions, for which \(I(f)=H_\infty(f)=0\), as well as unbalanced, nonmonotone and arbitrarily complex functions. The witnessing set may be empty and may depend on the entire function. There is no algorithmic requirement to find it. In particular, the target is the largest squared Fourier coefficient, not the entropy of the truth table, the largest individual coordinate influence, or the Shannon entropy \(H(f)=\sum_{S:p_f(S)>0}p_f(S)\log_2(1/p_f(S))\). Changing the base from two to the natural exponential only rescales the universal constant.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated universal-constant inequality or its negation. A positive answer must establish one finite \(C>0\) for every dimension and Boolean function, with the normalized Fourier distribution and uniform influences above. A negative answer must prove that for every \(C>0\) there exist \(n\ge1\) and a nonconstant Boolean function \(f\) with \(H_\infty(f)>C I(f)\). Disproving one proposed constant, checking finitely many truth tables, or establishing a bound with a dimension-dependent factor does not settle this existence question. Determining the smallest possible constant is not required.

context_blocks.text: The named conjecture is stated explicitly as Conjecture 4.1 by Arunachalam, Chakraborty, Koucký, Saurabh and de Wolf. The draft’s saved O’Donnell book locator instead points to the Kahn–Kalai–Linial theorem and its surrounding influence theory. That book remains background provenance; the explicit research statement is anchored to the conjecture in the checked paper.

The full Fourier Entropy–Influence conjecture implies this one because \(H_\infty(f)\le H(f)\). A proof of the present target would not by itself establish the full Shannon-entropy inequality. Conversely, a refutation of this target would also refute that stronger conjecture.

The same paper verifies the conjecture for DNFs in which each variable occurs only a fixed bounded number of times. This supplies a representation-restricted result; the universal conjecture allows every Boolean truth table.

Biswas and Sarkar obtain a Boolean function with \(H_\infty(f)/I(f)=128/45\). Li and Tang’s 2026 paper reports a family with ratios tending to \(4\) from below, which forces any universal constant to be at least \(4\). These are lower bounds on a possible constant, not an unbounded sequence of ratios and hence not a refutation.

Han’s general Fourier-entropy bound contains the additional term \(\sum_j I_j(f)\log(1/I_j(f))\), with zero terms omitted. Its dependence on the separate coordinate influences does not supply the universal multiple of \(I(f)\) asked for here.

cards.title: Multiparty Clique lower bounds in compression games
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Do there exist a constant \(\varepsilon>0\) and an integer round bound \(r(N)\to\infty\) such that every nonuniform, deterministic, polynomial-party \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\)-compression protocol family deciding Clique with at most \(r(N)\) rounds has cost \(\Omega(N^\varepsilon)\)? Here \(N\) is the graph’s number of vertices. In each round, Alice sends messages to independent computationally unrestricted Bobs, receives their replies, and eventually computes the answer herself with an \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) circuit. Cost is the sum over rounds of the maximum length of an Alice-to-Bob message in that round.

source_formulation.text: We conjecture that such a lower bound holds for the Clique function.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 6

cards.why: This asks whether many unrestricted helpers can compensate for Alice’s constant-depth computation using short messages and an increasing number of interactions. The source connects a positive answer for Clique to a major nonuniform circuit lower bound. The unusual communication measure makes precise model recovery essential to that connection.
cards.status_note: The conjecture is explicit in the 2015 primary source. Its proved fixed-round Majority results and logarithmic-depth simulation do not settle the selected growing-round Clique bound. Bounded subsequent-result searches through 2026-09-15 identified no resolution, but this dated review does not certify present openness exhaustively.

progress.text: Oliveira and Santhanam define the multiparty model in Section 2 and state the growing-round Clique conjecture on printed page 129.

Corollary 5.6 gives the \(n^{O(1/r)}\) compression upper bound for nonuniform logarithmic-depth functions for every fixed \(r\). The paper’s established Majority lower bounds do not close the selected Clique question.

category_assignment.reason: The core model is communication by circuit-restricted players to a referee.

importance.reason: The model isolates whether interaction with unrestricted computation can overcome constant-depth limitations at low communication cost. The conjectured Clique bound would separate NP from nonuniform logarithmic-depth circuits, giving this precise communication question consequences far beyond a single compression scheme.
importance.basis: Individual review of Oliveira–Santhanam Sections 1.2, 2 and 5, especially Corollary 5.6; importance is an editorial assessment of its structural and circuit-complexity consequences.

sentences: Alice sees a graph and a requested clique size, but her computation is limited to polynomial-size constant-depth Boolean circuits.
She can exchange messages with polynomially many unrestricted helpers, each of whom sees only its own conversation.
Alice must compute the correct final answer on every input.
Communication cost sums the longest message from Alice in each round, and the question asks for a polynomial lower bound even under a growing round budget.
The source shows that such a Clique lower bound would separate NP from nonuniform logarithmic-depth circuits.

cards.definitions: For each integer \(N\ge2\), the input consists of the \(\binom N2\) adjacency bits of a simple undirected graph \(G\) on \([N]\), listed in lexicographic order of pairs \(i<j\), followed by \(\ell=\lceil\log_2(N+1)\rceil\) bits encoding a nonnegative integer \(k\) in ordinary most-significant-bit-first binary. The input length is \(L_N=\binom N2+\ell\). Clique is 1 if \(0\le k\le N\) and some \(k\)-vertex set has every pair joined by an edge; it is 0 when \(k>N\). The empty set makes the answer 1 for \(k=0\). Alice receives all input bits, while \(b_N\ge1\) Bobs receive no input. A protocol has a fixed number \(R_N\le r(N)\) of rounds. In round \(t\), Alice simultaneously sends a fixed-length binary string \(a_{t,j}\) to each Bob \(j\). Each Bob replies with a fixed-length binary string \(z_{t,j}\). Message lengths and all strategies are fixed before the input is known; empty strings are permitted. Bob \(j\)’s reply is an arbitrary deterministic function of the sequence \(a_{1,j},\ldots,a_{t,j}\), with no computational restriction. Bobs cannot communicate with each other or observe other Bobs’ messages. Each message \(a_{t,j}\) is computed by a Boolean circuit using the original input and all messages in earlier completed rounds. After the final replies, an additional circuit at Alice computes the single output bit from the input and the complete transcript. All of Alice’s circuits use only AND and OR gates of arbitrary finite fan-in, unary NOT gates, and constants. There are constants \(d\in\mathbb N\), \(A>0\) and \(a\in\mathbb N\), fixed across \(N\) for the protocol family, such that every Alice circuit has depth at most \(d\), and the sum of their gate, wire, input and output counts, the number \(b_N\) of Bobs, and the total number of transmitted bits are each at most \(A(N+1)^a\). Reply bits are not charged to communication cost, but remain subject to these polynomial length bounds. Alice’s circuits and all Bob functions may depend arbitrarily on \(N\); no uniform construction is required. No player uses randomness. Correctness means the output equals Clique on every input of length \(L_N\). Define \(c_\Pi(N)=\sum_{t=1}^{R_N}\max_{1\le j\le b_N}|a_{t,j}|\). The target quantifiers are \(\exists\varepsilon>0\;\exists r:\mathbb N_{\ge2}\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) with \(r(N)\to\infty\) and \(r(N)\le\lceil\log_2(N+1)\rceil\), such that \(\forall\Pi\) in the specified model deciding Clique, \(\exists C_\Pi>0\;\exists N_\Pi\ge2\;\forall N\ge N_\Pi,\ c_\Pi(N)\ge C_\Pi N^\varepsilon\). The constants governing polynomial circuit size, constant depth and the number of parties are arbitrary and may depend on \(\Pi\), while \(\varepsilon,r\) are chosen before \(\Pi\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the quantified lower-bound statement, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. The affirmative proof must cover every polynomial-size constant-depth Alice family and every collection of unrestricted Bob strategies, for the stated growing round budget and some exponent independent of the protocol family. A fixed-round lower bound whose exponent tends to zero as the chosen round count grows does not establish the target. Bounds on the total sum of all parties’ message lengths, a single-Bob model, average-case correctness or a different function do not establish this Clique statement.

context_blocks.text: The selected sentence follows the source’s conjecture of a polynomial communication lower bound with a growing number of rounds. This card interprets it as the existence of one growing round budget and one positive exponent that work against every polynomial-size constant-depth protocol family, with the lower-bound constant and starting length allowed to depend on the family.

The source uses input-bit length \(n\). This statement fixes a standard graph-and-threshold encoding and uses vertex count \(N\), with \(L_N=\Theta(N^2)\); a fixed positive polynomial exponent remains a fixed positive polynomial exponent under this normalization. The growing budget is capped at \(\lceil\log_2(N+1)\rceil\): existence of a lower bound for any growing budget also entails it for a smaller growing budget. Aggregate polynomial circuit and transcript bounds agree with the source’s polynomial resources in this round range.

In the multiparty model, Alice computes the final answer. An unrestricted Bob does not act as a referee who receives everyone’s messages. The Bobs are independent helpers with access only to their respective conversations with Alice, and only messages from Alice contribute to the stated cost.

Corollary 5.6 states that every function in \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}/\mathrm{poly}\) has polynomial-party \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) compression games of cost \(n^{O(1/r)}\) for each fixed positive integer \(r\). Here \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}/\mathrm{poly}\) means Boolean functions computed by nonuniform polynomial-size, bounded-fan-in circuits of depth \(O(\log n)\).

The paper consequently identifies the conjectured Clique lower bound as sufficient to separate \(\mathrm{NP}\) from \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}/\mathrm{poly}\). Its Majority bounds have round-dependent exponents and do not establish the required fixed exponent for Clique with an unbounded round budget.

cards.title: Sharp low-degree Fourier weight of halfspaces
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: For every integer \(n\ge 1\) and every linear threshold function \(f:\{- 1,1\}^{n}\to \{- 1,1\}\), is \(\mathrm{W}^{\le 1}(f)=\hat\{f\}(\varnothing )^{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat\{f\}(\{i\})^{2}\ge 2/\pi\)?
cards.why: A sharp universal low-degree Fourier inequality for all halfspaces describes the spectral structure of a foundational Boolean function class.

sentences: A halfspace is the sign of a weighted sum of input bits and a threshold.
Its degree-zero and degree-one Fourier coefficients measure its mean and coordinate correlations.
The question asks whether their squared weight is always at least \(2/\pi\).
Majority functions approach that proposed universal constant as dimension grows.
The exact inequality is retained because a general algorithm for merely approximating the extremal constant is already known.

cards.definitions: A linear threshold function has \(f(x)=\operatorname{sign}(\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_{i} x_{i}- \theta )\) for some real weights \(w_{i}\) and threshold \(\theta\), with \(\operatorname{sign}(t)=1\) when \(t\ge 0\) and −1 otherwise. Constant functions are included. Under the uniform measure on \(\{- 1,1\}^{n}\), define \(\hat\{f\}(S)=2^{- n}\sum_{x} f(x)\prod _{i\in S}x_{i}\), with empty product 1. Thus \(\hat\{f\}(\varnothing )\) is the mean and \(\hat\{f\}(\{i\})\) is the correlation with the i-th coordinate. The displayed squared coefficients are the Fourier weight in degrees zero and one. There is no bound on dimension, weights or bias, and no regularity assumption on the halfspace. The constant \(\pi\) is the usual circle constant.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the exact universal inequality or give a threshold function with a rigorous proof that its low-degree weight is strictly less than \(2/\pi\). Approximation of the extremal constant to 0.01 would not settle this universal proposition. An algorithm for approximating that constant is already known; the retained target is the source’s sharp inequality.

cards.title: Removing low-influence directions from convex sets
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Does there exist a function \(\tau :(0,1)\to [0,1]\) with \(\lim _{\varepsilon \to 0^{+}}\tau (\varepsilon )=0\) such that the following holds for every \(n\ge 1\), every centrally symmetric convex Borel set \(K\subseteq \mathbb{R} ^{n}\), every unit vector v and every \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\)? If \(Inf_{v}[K]\le \varepsilon\), then there exists a centrally symmetric convex Borel set \(C\subseteq v\perp\) such that \(\gamma _{n}(K \triangle  (C+\mathbb{R} v))\le \tau (\varepsilon )\). The same \(\tau\) must work in all dimensions and for all such sets and directions.

cards.definitions: \(\gamma _{n}\) is standard Gaussian probability measure, the law of X with independent \(N(0,1)\) coordinates. Central symmetry means \(K=- K\), with symmetry about the origin. Convexity means \(tx+(1- t)y\in K\) for \(x,y\in K\) and \(t\in [0,1]\). Write \(1_{K}\) for the indicator of K. The convex influence in a Euclidean unit direction v is \(Inf_{v}[K]=(1/\sqrt{2}) E[1_{K}(X)(1- \langle v,X\rangle ^{2})]\). This is nonnegative for centrally symmetric convex K. The orthogonal subspace is \(v\perp =\{y:\langle v,y\rangle =0\}\), and \(C+\mathbb{R} v=\{y+tv:y\in C,t\in \mathbb{R}\}\) is a cylinder whose membership depends only on the projection \(x- \langle v,x\rangle v\). The symmetric difference \(K\triangle \mathrm{L}\) consists of points in exactly one of K and L, so its Gaussian measure is the probability that their membership indicators disagree. Empty sets and the whole space are permitted. No lower or upper bound away from zero or one is imposed on \(\gamma _{n}(K)\), and no bound on total influence is assumed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove a single modulus \(\tau\) tending to zero that bounds the Gaussian approximation error uniformly over the stated sets, dimensions and directions, or prove that no such modulus exists. Equivalently for a negative answer, exhibit a sequence with directional influence tending to zero while its Gaussian distance from every symmetric convex cylinder in that direction stays bounded below by a positive constant. A dimension-dependent modulus or a cylinder in some other direction does not suffice.

sentences: A De Morgan formula computes a Boolean function with an expression tree whose leaves are literals.
Its partition measure counts disjoint rectangles pairing accepting and rejecting inputs, each certified by one differing coordinate.
The question asks whether formula leaf size is always bounded by a fixed polynomial in that rectangle count.

cards.definitions: A De Morgan formula on \(n\) variables is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node is AND or OR; each leaf is one literal \(x_i\) or \(\neg x_i\), \(i\in[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Evaluation uses the usual Boolean operations. Repeated occurrences of the same literal count as separate leaves, and subtrees cannot be shared. The leaf size is the total number of leaves. Define \(L(f)\) as the minimum leaf size among formulas evaluating to \(f(x)\) on every \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). Formulas need not be monotone, balanced, depth-bounded or uniformly constructible. Let \(A=f^{-1}(1)\) and \(B=f^{-1}(0)\), both nonempty because \(f\) is nonconstant. A rectangle is a nonempty Cartesian product \(U\times V\) with \(U\subseteq A\) and \(V\subseteq B\). It is coordinate-monochromatic if there are a coordinate \(i\in[n]\) and a bit \(b\in\{0,1\}\) such that \(u_i=b\) for every \(u\in U\) and \(v_i=1-b\) for every \(v\in V\). Equivalently, a single literal separates the two sides, with either orientation permitted. A partition is a finite collection of such rectangles whose union is all of \(A\times B\), with distinct rectangles pairwise disjoint as subsets of ordered pairs. Row sets may overlap across rectangles, and column sets may overlap, provided the products do not. Define \(\chi(f)\) as the minimum number of rectangles in any such partition; coordinate labels and the descriptions of the row and column sets have no additional cost. Every pair \(a\in A,b\in B\) differs in some coordinate, so a singleton partition exists and \(\chi(f)\ge1\) is finite. No recursive or protocol-tree condition is imposed on a partition. The statement quantifies \(\exists C,d\;\forall n\;\forall f\) with the domains above. Both measures are nonuniform finite mathematical minima; no algorithm converting a partition into a formula is required. Restricting to nonconstant functions removes the empty-rectangle convention for constants without changing the substantive comparison.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of a universal polynomial bound \(L(f)\le C\chi(f)^d\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that \(\forall C\ge1\;\forall d\in\mathbb N\;\exists n\ge1\;\exists f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) nonconstant with \(L(f)>C\chi(f)^d\). Refuting one proposed exponent or giving a constant-factor gap is insufficient to refute all polynomial bounds. A result for arbitrary communication relations, overlapping covers, positively oriented monotone partitions or algebraic tilings does not automatically establish the target for the defined partitions of total Boolean functions.

context_blocks.text: The imported early draft states the question as Research Problem 6.24 after Rychkov’s lemma. Its tiling number is a coordinate-labelled partition of accepting versus rejecting inputs, rather than a partition of the Boolean input cube or a tiling by constant output bits.

Rychkov’s lemma gives \(\chi(f)\le L(f)\). The question asks whether the reverse comparison holds with one fixed polynomial for every Boolean function. The known bound recorded by the source is \(L(f)\le\chi(f)^{2\log_2\chi(f)}\), which is quasipolynomial rather than polynomial.

Disjointness is essential to the measure: overlapping coordinate rectangles can cover every accepting–rejecting pair using only twice the number of variables. The task concerns the minimum disjoint partition, not the size of such an unrestricted cover.

Neither the formulas nor the functions are required to be monotone. Both orientations of a differing coordinate are allowed in a partition rectangle. The source separately defines positively monochromatic partitions for monotone formula questions.

Jukna’s second expanded edition draft dated 14 September 2026 retains the exact question as Research Problem 6.1 on printed page 277. It again states that the polynomial inverse is unknown and records the same quasipolynomial upper bound. This is a dated author draft, not a claim of publication of the second edition.

cards.title: Large zero rectangles in low-rank real matrices
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\) and every matrix \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) of rank \(r\) with at least \(n^2/2\) zero entries, there are nonempty sets \(I,J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) satisfying \[A_{ij}=0\quad(i\in I,\ j\in J),\qquad |I|\,|J|\ge n^2\exp(-C\sqrt r)?\]
cards.why: The question asks whether low real rank forces a large exact combinatorial pattern when zeros are dense. This connects linear-algebraic complexity to the rectangles that control communication protocols, while extending beyond Boolean matrices. Its value is the proposed general structural principle; the question is not merely to speed up a search for a rectangle.

sentences: The question concerns square real matrices with low rank and at least half their entries equal to zero.
It asks for a Cartesian block consisting entirely of zeros whose area is a square-root-exponential fraction of the whole matrix.
The constant in that guarantee must be the same for every matrix and dimension.
The rank is over the real numbers, and entries may have arbitrary signs and magnitudes.
Recent results establish related guarantees under additional entry restrictions, while the checked sources retain the general real-matrix question.

cards.definitions: The rank is the dimension over \(\mathbb R\) of the span of the columns. A zero entry means exact equality to zero. Apart from the zero-density condition, entries may be arbitrary real numbers of either sign and magnitude; there is no finite-alphabet or integrality assumption. A rectangle is a Cartesian product \(I\times J\) of row and column index sets, and its size is its number of entries \(|I||J|\). The sets need not be consecutive, equal, or of the same cardinality. This is an area guarantee, with no separate lower bound prescribed for each side. The exponential is the real exponential function and \(\sqrt r\) is the nonnegative square root. The same constant must work for all dimensions, ranks, entries and zero patterns. When \(r=0\), the entire matrix is zero and the displayed bound asks for the whole matrix. The target is an existence theorem about matrices, not an algorithm with a specified input representation or running time.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal statement, or of its negation. A negative answer must establish that for every real \(C>0\) there exist \(n\ge1\) and an admissible real matrix of rank \(r\) such that every all-zero rectangle has area strictly below \(n^2\exp(-C\sqrt r)\). One finite example violating a chosen constant does not refute the conjecture. A result restricted to Boolean, nonnegative integer, bounded-entry or intersection matrices does not settle the stated arbitrary-real target. No numerical approximation of matrix entries or of a zero test substitutes for exact equality.

context_blocks.text: A matrix can have many zero entries without those entries forming a large Cartesian block. The question asks whether a small dimension of the column span forces such a block, and specifies how much of the matrix it must occupy.

The conjectured area fraction is \(\exp(-C\sqrt r)\). It depends only on rank, even when the number of rows and columns is much larger. The constant is uniform: allowing it to depend on the particular matrix would remove the quantitative content of the question.

Lovett posed this precise half-zero-density, real-matrix, rectangle-area version in the 2013 Dagstuhl report. That report also states that the square-root dependence in the exponent would be best possible. The present formulation keeps its area target rather than requiring a balanced square.

For Boolean communication matrices, a constant rectangle is a collection of input pairs on which the answer is fixed. Low-rank real matrices allow a much wider range of entry values, so a theorem for Boolean matrices alone does not cover this question.

Hunter, Milojević, Sudakov and Tomon retain a broader sparse-real-matrix conjecture as Conjecture 1.8: when at most an \(\varepsilon\) fraction of entries are nonzero, a zero square of side \(n\exp(-O(\sqrt{\varepsilon r}))\) is predicted. That additional density parameter and square-side target are useful context, not replacements for the fixed-density area statement here.

Their Theorem 1.12 proves a related bound for nonnegative matrices whose nonzero entries are at least one and whose average entry is at most one half. In particular it gives the desired rank dependence for Boolean matrices with at least half their entries zero. A density of zeros does not impose the required average-entry bound on an arbitrary real matrix, and arbitrary signed entries fall outside the theorem.

Their Theorem 1.10 also resolves a related cross-disjoint-set-family conjecture, with its exponent measured by the size of the ground set. This result does not identify the ground-set size with the real rank of every matrix. Sudakov’s 2025 Oberwolfach report continues to list the general sparse-real-matrix statement as Conjecture 5.

cards.title: Quadratic decision-tree bounds from block sensitivity
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that every total Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), for every integer \(n\ge1\), satisfies \[D(f)\le C\,\operatorname{bs}(f)^2?\] Here \(D(f)\) is deterministic worst-case bit-query complexity and \(\operatorname{bs}(f)\) is block sensitivity, with both measures defined below. The constant must be independent of \(n\) and of the function, and no logarithmic or dimension-dependent multiplier is allowed.
cards.why: The two quantities measure different aspects of the information needed to determine a Boolean output: the worst adaptive query cost and the number of disjoint ways to change the output at one input. Their known cubic general upper bound and quadratic examples leave a basic gap. A uniform quadratic relation would sharpen the structure of query complexity across every total Boolean function.
cards.status_note: The unrestricted inequality is posed in the checked Jukna draft and remains explicitly unresolved in the 2023 primary paper. The 2026 primary result checked here concerns block number and decision-tree size, not this general depth bound. Bounded searches through 2026-09-15 found no resolution; this does not independently certify an exhaustive later literature review.

sentences: The target is a universal quadratic upper bound on deterministic decision-tree depth in terms of block sensitivity.
A decision tree adaptively reads individual bits and must compute a total Boolean function correctly on every input.
Block sensitivity counts disjoint blocks whose separate flips all change the value at one common input.
The known general bound is cubic, while quadratic bounds hold for several restricted classes.
The proposed constant must work for every function and dimension, and recent results on tree size or counts of minimal blocks do not settle this depth question.

cards.definitions: A deterministic decision tree is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node is labeled by an input coordinate \(i\in[n]\), with its two outgoing edges labeled zero and one; each leaf is labeled by an output bit. On input \(x\), the tree queries the bit \(x_i\) at the current node and follows the matching edge until it reaches a leaf. It computes \(f\) if the reached leaf equals \(f(x)\) for every \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). Its worst-case query cost is the maximum number of internal nodes visited on any input, and \(D(f)\) is the minimum such cost over all trees computing \(f\). Repeated coordinate queries are permitted and count again. A leaf-only tree has cost zero. The tree may be chosen separately for each known function, and its number of leaves or total nodes is not the measured resource. No efficient construction of the optimal tree from a truth table or circuit is required. For \(B\subseteq[n]\), let \(x^{\oplus B}\) denote the input obtained from \(x\) by flipping exactly the bits in \(B\). A nonempty block \(B\) is sensitive at \(x\) if \(f(x)\ne f(x^{\oplus B})\). Define \(\operatorname{bs}(f,x)\) as the largest number \(t\) of pairwise disjoint nonempty blocks \(B_1,\ldots,B_t\) that are each sensitive at this same input \(x\), and let \(\operatorname{bs}(f)=\max_x\operatorname{bs}(f,x)\). Each block is tested by flipping it alone from the common input, not by a cumulative sequence of flips. Blocks need not be singletons or have a specified size. This maximum disjoint collection is different from the number of all minimal sensitive blocks and from fractional block sensitivity. All total Boolean functions are included: monotonicity, symmetry, graph invariance, bounded alternation, balanced output and succinct circuit representation are not assumed. Constant functions have \(D(f)=\operatorname{bs}(f)=0\) and satisfy the proposed bound. Randomized and quantum queries are outside the definition of \(D(f)\).
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal quadratic inequality or of its negation. A positive answer must establish one finite \(C\) that works for every dimension and every total function. A negative answer must establish that for every \(C>0\) there exist \(n\ge1\) and a total nonconstant Boolean function \(f\) for which \(D(f)>C\,\operatorname{bs}(f)^2\). Thus disproving the coefficient-one inequality is insufficient unless the ratios \(D(f)/\operatorname{bs}(f)^2\) are unbounded. A result for a subclass, a bound on decision-tree size instead of depth, or a bound with a dimension-dependent factor does not meet the criterion. The smallest possible constant and an efficient tree-construction algorithm are not required.

context_blocks.text: Jukna’s early draft poses \(D(f)=O(\operatorname{bs}(f)^2)\) as Research Problem 14.10 after Corollary 14.9 gives the general cubic upper bound. This card retains that constant-factor universal inequality, rather than asking only whether some polynomial relation exists.

Chugh, Podder and Sanyal’s 2023 paper states that the known general upper bound is cubic and the widest known separation is quadratic. Their Question 1 keeps the unrestricted gap open. Polynomial equivalence among measures, including the sensitivity theorem, does not by itself fix this exponent.

Their Theorem 4 establishes the quadratic bound for zebra functions, defined by having the same number of output changes along every increasing path from the all-zero input to the all-one input. This includes monotone and symmetric functions but is a restriction on the truth table. Their Theorem 5 also gives the quadratic bound when the maximum number of such changes is bounded by a fixed constant.

Chakraborty and Gál’s February 2026 paper improves bounds for the number of minimal sensitive blocks, and obtains consequences for the total size of decision trees. Those quantities differ from both the maximum number of disjoint sensitive blocks and the worst-case query depth in the present target. Its stated results do not establish the unrestricted quadratic inequality here.

cards.definitions: A sign matrix \(A\in \{- 1,+1\}^{r\times s}\) has positive finite numbers r,s of rows and columns and has every entry specified. Its sign-rank rank±\((A)\) is the least \(D\ge 1\) for which there are unit vectors \(u_{1},\ldots ,u_{r},v_{1},\ldots ,v_{s}\in \mathbb{R}\)ᴰ with \(A_{ij}\langle u_{i},v_{j}\rangle >0\) for all i,j. Equivalently it is the minimum real rank of a matrix B satisfying \(A_{ij}B_{ij}>0\) entrywise; zero entries do not realize either sign. The margin \(m(A)\) is the supremum, over such unit-vector representations in all finite dimensions D, of \(\min _{i,j} A_{ij}\langle u_{i},v_{j}\rangle\). It lies in (0,1]. In optimizing margin, the representation dimension is unrestricted; the representation of least dimension need not maximize margin. The requested d may grow arbitrarily rapidly as \(\rho\) tends to zero, but for each fixed positive \(\rho\) it must bound all matrix sizes. Equivalently, one can use a finite nondecreasing bounding function \(\eta\):[\(1,\infty\))→\(\mathbb{N}\). This uniform bounded-margin interpretation is explicitly restated in the later source’s Open Problem 1.3. Matrices with missing or promise-restricted entries are excluded.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove a finite size-independent bound \(d(\rho )\) for every positive margin threshold \(\rho\), or prove there is a fixed \(\rho >0\) and a sequence of fully specified finite sign matrices with margins at least \(\rho\) and unbounded sign-ranks. No efficient procedure for producing the low-dimensional representation is required. Unbounded sign-rank with margins tending to zero, or only for partial matrices, does not refute the statement.

cards.title: Fourier rank versus sparsity
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Does there exist a sequence of integers \(n_{j}\ge 1\) and Boolean functions \(f_{j}:\{- 1,1\}^{n_{j}}\to \{- 1,1\}\) such that \(k(f_{j})\to \infty\) and \(r(f_{j})/\sqrt{k}(f_{j})\to \infty\) as \(j\to \infty\), where k is Fourier sparsity and r is Fourier rank over \(F_{2}\)? Equivalently, is the ratio \(r(f)/\sqrt{k}(f)\) unbounded over all finite-dimensional Boolean functions?
cards.why: Would determine whether sparse Boolean Fourier support necessarily occupies only square-root-many independent parity directions, or whether the familiar quadratic relation misses a growing separation.

references.title: Tight Chang’s-Lemma-Type Bounds for Boolean Functions

cards.definitions: For \(n\ge 1\) and \(S\subseteq [n]\), put \(\chi _{S}(x)=\prod _{i\in S}x_{i}\), with \(\chi _{\varnothing}=1\). The Fourier coefficient is \(\hat\{f\}(S)=2^{- n}\sum _{x\in \{- 1,1\}^{n}}f(x)\chi _{S}(x)\), so \(f=\sum _{S\subseteq [n]}\hat\{f\}(S)\chi _{S}\). The support is \(\operatorname{supp}(\hat\{f\})=\{S:\hat\{f\}(S)\ne 0\}\), and \(k(f)=|\operatorname{supp}(\hat\{f\})|\). It is at least one. Identify a subset S with its incidence vector in \(F_{2}^{n}\) and define \(r(f)=\dim _{F_{2}}\) span\(\{1_{S}:S\in \operatorname{supp}(\hat\{f\})\}\). The empty set contributes the zero vector; it may count towards k but never increases r. This rank is not a real linear-span dimension of functions. The limit \(r(f_{j})=\omega (\sqrt{k}(f_{j}))\) means that for every real \(M>0\), the ratio eventually exceeds M. No bound on \(n_{j}\) in terms of j, explicit construction algorithm, or computational efficiency is requested. The negation is the existence of a universal constant C such that \(r(f)\le C\sqrt{k}(f)\) for every n and every such f. Since \(r(f)\le k(f)\), unbounded ratios necessarily require unbounded sparsities.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer must prove the existence of functions with unbounded \(r(f)/\sqrt{k}(f)\), equivalently a sequence with the displayed limits. A negative answer must prove a universal constant-factor square-root bound for every Boolean function. A fixed larger constant, finitely many examples, or a bound retaining a growing logarithmic factor does not decide the question.

cards.definitions: Alice receives \(x\in X\) and Bob receives \(y\in Y\). Both know \(f\) and the finite domains. A public-coin protocol selects a deterministic binary communication tree using a finite string of independent shared fair random bits, independent of the inputs. At a node, the designated player sends one bit determined by that player’s own input, the public string and the transcript so far. At termination Bob outputs a bit determined by his input, the public string and transcript. The worst-case cost is the maximum number of communicated bits over all inputs and public strings. Local computation and the public random string are free; its finite length may depend on the protocol. There is no message to reveal the public seed, no advice depending on private inputs and no restriction to one-way communication. The complexity \(R_{1/3}(f)\) is the minimum cost of a protocol whose output equals \(f(x,y)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input pair. It is finite because Alice can send an encoding of her input. Protocols may depend nonuniformly on the finite function; no uniform construction from its truth table is requested. For \(f^{\otimes k}:X^k\times Y^k\to\{0,1\}^k\), Alice and Bob receive their full tuples and Bob must output \((f(x_1,y_1),\ldots,f(x_k,y_k))\). Success probability at least \(2/3\) concerns the entire vector simultaneously on every tuple pair. The inputs need not be independent draws from a distribution: the cost and error guarantees are worst-case. The protocol may communicate across coordinates in any way. The constant \(c\) must work for all domains, functions and copy counts; a different constant for each fixed function is insufficient. Zero-communication functions impose the vacuous lower bound zero.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of the universal constant-factor inequality, or a Lean proof of its negation: for every positive proposed constant there are a total Boolean function and copy count violating it. Refuting a version for relations, partial functions, distributional inputs or per-coordinate error alone does not refute this selected assertion. Expected communication is not the cost used here.

cards.title: Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis
cards.formal: For every real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist an integer \(q\ge3\) such that no q-SAT decider A has a bound \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) for every valid q-CNF formula F, for any fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\)? The width q may depend on epsilon but is fixed independently of the input. Equivalently, is \(\lim_{q\to\infty}s_q=1\)? This is the deterministic Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis.
cards.definitions: Fix an integer clause-width bound \(q\ge 3\). A q-CNF formula is a finite list of clauses, each a finite list of at most q literals. A literal is a variable \(x_i\) or its negation \(\neg x_i\), with \(1\le i\le n\). The variables that occur are exactly \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), so n counts distinct variables, not clauses or input bits. Repeated literals, repeated clauses and clauses containing both signs of a variable are allowed. A Boolean assignment satisfies the formula if every clause has at least one true literal. An empty clause is false; the empty conjunction is true and has n=0. For a completely specified binary encoding, let \(\operatorname{code}(a)\), for a nonnegative integer a, be \(1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary expansion of a+1, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). Encode n and the number m of clauses with this code, then each clause by its coded length followed by its literals. Each literal is a sign bit (0 for positive, 1 for negated) and the code of its variable index. All indicated lists must be fully present, with no trailing bits, valid indices and every declared variable occurring. Let L be the complete bit length. Ill-formed strings, including clauses wider than q, are rejected. No density, satisfiability-count, occurrence or input-distribution promise is imposed. A q-SAT decider A is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program and fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. Each transition reads or writes only the cells at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. The total transition count includes parsing, input access and all internal work. A must halt on all inputs, decide satisfiability exactly on valid q-CNF formulas, and reject malformed strings in polynomial time in their length. It receives no advice, random bits, quantum operations, oracle or precomputed instance information. The machine may depend on the fixed q. For a valid formula F, let \(t_A(F)\) be its runtime and \(n(F),L(F)\) its variable count and bit length. An exponent \(\alpha\ge 0\) is attainable at width q if there exist such a decider A and fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\) with \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{\alpha n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) for every valid q-CNF formula F. The constants are independent of F. Define \(s_q\) as the infimum of all attainable exponents. This set is nonempty because exhaustive assignment testing gives an attainable exponent 1, so \(0\le s_q\le1\). The infimum need not itself be attainable. Polynomial factors in L remain explicit, including when clauses are repeated many times. The chosen explicit syntax and malformed-input normalization do not impose a new satisfiability promise; they fix the bit model for the source’s exponential-rate question. The sequence \(s_q\) is nondecreasing: a decider for width q+1 also decides the width-q restriction after checking its syntax. Since every \(s_q\le1\), its limit exists. The quantified statement says that no fixed positive saving from the exponent 1 works for all fixed widths. Its negation is that there exists one real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) such that for each integer \(q\ge3\) there are a q-SAT decider \(A_q\) and constants \(C_q,d_q\) with \(t_{A_q}(F)\le C_q2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}(L(F)+1)^{d_q}\) for every q-CNF formula F. The algorithm and polynomial factor may depend on q and the selected epsilon. There is no added requirement of one algorithm receiving q as an input, nor of an effective procedure generating \(A_q\) from q. Each individual machine is uniform over its formula inputs. Infima need not be attained; the equivalence uses the available slack between a limit below 1 and 1.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed deterministic all-width proposition, equivalently a proof that \(\lim_{q\to\infty}s_q=1\) or that this limit is strictly below 1. A refutation must establish one positive exponential saving valid at every fixed width, with the algorithm and polynomial factors allowed to depend on that width. A positive answer must exclude such a shared saving. Improvement at finitely many widths, a randomized algorithm, or a lower bound only under another unproved hypothesis does not by itself meet this criterion. The target is a yes/no assertion about the limit, not its numerical approximation.
cards.why: SETH is one of the main assumptions used to explain why specific polynomial running-time exponents resist improvement. Settling it would test the foundation of a broad network of tight conditional bounds in strings, graphs, data structures, and exact exponential-time algorithms.

importance.reason: A principal organizing hypothesis of fine-grained complexity, connecting exact SAT complexity to tight running-time barriers across many algorithmic areas.

progress.text: Impagliazzo and Paturi study the optimal exponential rates of fixed-width satisfiability and their limiting rate, proving relations among widths under ETH. They do not prove the limiting rate equals one.
The textbook states deterministic SETH as Conjecture 14.2, distinguishes separate fixed-width algorithms from a single unrestricted CNF-SAT algorithm, and proves that SETH implies ETH.
Vassilevska Williams surveys fine-grained reductions from satisfiability hypotheses to polynomial-time problems, explicitly tracking the relevant models and forms of hypotheses.

Jiang and Cai report the randomized general-3-SAT bound \(O^*(1.307031578^n)\) and a separate stronger Unique-3-SAT bound. Their Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2 concern fixed width; these preprint claims do not settle the deterministic all-width hypothesis.

context_blocks.text: Exhaustive search tries all \(2^{n}\) assignments and checks the formula each time. Restricting clause width supports much faster algorithms, particularly for small k. SETH accommodates these speedups: it says that no positive constant saving in the exponent survives uniformly across arbitrarily large fixed widths. It does not assert that 3-SAT needs essentially \(2^{n}\) time.

The order of quantifiers separates this statement from several nearby claims. A \(2^{0.9n}\)-time algorithm for every fixed k would refute SETH even if the polynomial factors and implementations depended on k. A family of bounds \(2^{(1- 1/k)n}\) would be compatible with it. A fast algorithm for unrestricted CNF-SAT would also refute it, but the failure of such an unrestricted algorithm is not the definition being used here.

ETH asks for a positive optimal exponential rate already at width three; SETH additionally asks that the rates approach one as width grows. Sparsification relates bounded-width formulas to bounded-density formulas and helps transfer these hypotheses through reductions. It does not make the two hypotheses equivalent. Proving either would go beyond \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\), which by itself allows intermediate running times such as \(2^{\sqrt{n}}\).

Fine-grained reductions turn this hypothesis into precise conditional barriers for familiar polynomial-time problems, including Orthogonal Vectors, edit distance, and graph-distance questions. The reduction must preserve the intended exponential saving, not merely be polynomial-time as in an NP-hardness reduction. When a reduction or resulting algorithm uses randomness, the corresponding randomized hypothesis must be tracked separately.

Jiang and Cai’s July 2026 preprint reports randomized bounds \(O^*(1.306969598^n)\) for Unique-3-SAT and \(O^*(1.307031578^n)\) for general 3-SAT, where \(O^*\) suppresses polynomial input factors. These are stated preprint results whose proof and numerical certification have not been independently verified here. In either case, fixed width three and internal randomness differ from a deterministic saving that holds at every fixed width.

The 2015 textbook explicitly cautions that its limiting-rate definition is more precise than the informal question about one unrestricted CNF-SAT algorithm. A negative answer may consist of separate algorithms for all fixed widths, sharing one positive saving in the exponential rate but not necessarily a uniform generator or a common polynomial input factor.

cards.title: Truly subcubic APSP
cards.formal: Is there a uniform randomized algorithm \(A\), a fixed rational constant \(0<\varepsilon\le1\), and a fixed constant \(C>0\) such that, on every directed \(n\)-vertex graph with arbitrary real edge weights and no negative-weight cycle, \(A\) outputs the entire exact shortest-distance matrix with probability at least \(2/3\), while every run takes at most \(Cn^{3-\varepsilon}\) steps? Here \(n\ge2\), and steps are measured in the comparison-addition real RAM with logarithmic-size index words defined below. The same program, exponent improvement and time constant must work for every graph size and every real weight assignment.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated algorithm-existence proposition or its full logical negation in this exact machine model. A positive proof must exhibit one finite uniform program and fixed constants, prove the promised-graph distance semantics and joint correctness probability, and charge every operation to the worst-case \(Cn^{3-\varepsilon}\) bound. A negative proof must rule out every such program and every fixed positive exponent saving, including randomized programs.

A result for bounded integer weights, a restricted graph family, approximate distances, a single source, or additional accurate predictions does not settle this target. Neither does a lower bound restricted to one reduction method or to machines lacking the permitted word operations. An unproved APSP hardness hypothesis cannot serve as the proof of its own consequence here. A bound \(n^3/f(n)\) with only a subpolynomial saving \(f(n)=n^{o(1)}\) does not establish a fixed exponent saving; expected running time alone does not establish the specified worst-case bound. There is no additive or multiplicative error allowance in the distance output.
cards.why: All-pairs distances are a basic graph primitive. A fixed improvement over the cubic exponent would also change the complexity of several equivalent path, matrix and weighted-triangle problems. Their reductions make the exact weight and machine assumptions essential to interpreting claimed improvements.
cards.definitions:
The vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The input gives \(n\) and an \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix in vertex order. Each entry has a presence flag and, when present, one exact finite real weight. Thus there is at most one edge for each ordered pair; self-loops are allowed. Missing edges have no weight and are represented by the flag, not by a large finite number. There is no bound on the magnitude, sign or precision of a real weight. The graph is promised to have no directed cycle of negative total weight, including negative self-loops.

A finite directed walk \((v_0,\ldots,v_k)\) has weight \(\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}w(v_i,v_{i+1})\). The empty walk from a vertex to itself has weight zero. For each ordered pair \((u,v)\), the distance \(d_G(u,v)\) is the minimum weight of a walk from \(u\) to \(v\), or the separate symbol \(+\infty\) if none exists. The no-negative-cycle promise ensures that every reachable minimum is finite and attained; nonnegative cycles can be removed, so a simple path suffices for distinct endpoints. In particular \(d_G(u,u)=0\). Zero-weight cycles and equal shortest distances are allowed. Output consists of all \(n^2\) exact distances in vertex-pair order, each a real value or an unreachable flag. Printing the vertices of every shortest path is not required.

The machine has one fixed finite program and two kinds of random-access memory cell: exact real cells and finite index-word cells. One real-cell load, store or copy, addition, subtraction, or comparison costs one step; comparison returns its trichotomy result as a word. These are the only operations inspecting real values. Real constants built into the finite program are restricted to \(0\) and \(1\); there are no arbitrary advice constants. A real value cannot be converted to its digits, an integer address, or its floor. Multiplication or division of real cells and operations packing several arbitrary reals into one word are not available.

For some fixed integer \(a\ge4\) chosen as part of the program's model, an index word has \(b(n)=\lceil a\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Word loads, stores, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, and addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{b(n)}\) cost one step. Unsigned integer quotient and remainder by a nonzero word also cost one step; division by zero is an invalid computation. A shift of at least \(b(n)\) positions returns zero. Addresses are words. All accessed cells must fit in this address range; a new work cell starts at zero and each access is charged. Word operations can process indices, counters and comparison results; they do not reveal the representation of a real edge weight. The input matrix and initially empty work memory are the only input-dependent initial state.

The randomized instruction obtains one fresh independent fair bit per step. All preprocessing, table construction, memory access, random-bit generation, input reading and output writing are charged to the same runtime. There is no nonuniform table supplied for free, extra prediction, oracle, parallel work unit or quantum operation. The bound is worst case over the input and every coin sequence. For each fixed promised graph, the probability that the whole output matrix is correct must be at least \(2/3\); separate success probabilities for individual entries are insufficient. A deterministic algorithm is included by ignoring the coins.

The bound depends on \(n\), not the bit length or magnitude of weights, because the real operations are exact primitives. This is a classical real-operation question, not an ordinary bit-time algorithm for arbitrary real encodings. Restricting \(\varepsilon\) to rational values in \((0,1]\) preserves existence of a fixed positive exponent saving; any positive saving implies a smaller such rational saving. No behavior is required on graphs violating the no-negative-cycle promise.

progress.text: Subcubic equivalences connect APSP to min-plus products, negative triangles and several other tasks; the full manuscript distinguishes integer-range reductions from its strongly polynomial randomized reduction.
Williams obtains randomized time \(n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}\) on the real RAM; STOC publishes the result in 2014 and an expanded journal version appears in 2018.
The few-weights manuscript gives deterministic improvements under restrictions on the number of outgoing weights per vertex, with explicit weight-model conventions.
ICALP publishes the matrix-multiplication-time node-weighted zero-triangle result; independently weighted edges remain a different target.
The prediction-assisted APSP preprint gives a fixed exponent saving when its supplied certificate has sufficiently few erroneous or unverifiable pairs.
The black-box-reduction preprint establishes barriers for reductions uniform over arbitrary triangle relations; it does not establish an unrestricted APSP lower bound.

context_blocks.text: If the edges from u to v, u to z and z to v have weights 8, 5 and −2, and there are no other edges, then the shortest u-to-v distance is 3. Negative edges are compatible with a finite exact answer. By contrast, a negative cycle reachable on a u-to-v walk would make its weights unbounded below; the input promise excludes that case. An unreachable ordered pair is reported separately from every finite distance.

The corresponding min-plus matrix operation is \((X\star Y)_{ij}=\min_k(X_{ik}+Y_{kj})\). This uses minimum and addition, whereas ordinary matrix multiplication uses addition and multiplication. Vassilevska Williams and Williams establish subcubic equivalences among APSP, min-plus products, negative edge-weighted triangles and related tasks. Their integer-range theorem carries weight-length factors; Section 4.3 separately gives a randomized strongly polynomial reduction whose overhead depends on the matrix dimension instead. These equivalences preserve existence of some positive saving, not necessarily its exact exponent.

Williams gives a randomized real-RAM bound \(n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}\), and a deterministic subpolynomial improvement with a different exponent in the denominator. These are substantial savings over cubic time. Nevertheless, for each fixed \(c>0\), the expression \(n^3/2^{c\sqrt{\log_2 n}}=n^{3-c/\sqrt{\log_2 n}}\) has an exponent tending to three. That bound alone does not establish \(O(n^{3-\varepsilon})\) for any fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). The algorithms permit ordinary computation on finite words as well as comparisons and additions of weights.

Abboud and coauthors study graphs with at most \(d\) distinct weights on the outgoing edges of each vertex. Their Theorem 1.4 gives a fixed exponent saving when \(d\le n^{3-\omega-\delta}\) for a fixed \(\delta>0\), where \(\omega\) is the ordinary matrix-multiplication exponent. This theorem is stated in their bounded-integer word-RAM setting. Theorem 1.2 for one outgoing weight per vertex also has an explicitly stated real-weight extension in Section 4.4. Neither statement covers unrestricted arbitrary real edge weights with up to \(n\) different outgoing weights per vertex.

Akmal and Fischer’s ICALP 2026 Theorem 1 solves zero-sum node-weighted triangle detection in \(O(\mathrm{MM}(n))\) time. Here a triangle’s value is the sum of three vertex weights, and \(\mathrm{MM}(n)\) denotes an admissible running-time bound for ordinary matrix multiplication, with the paper’s monotonicity convention. This is different from independently weighting every edge. The introduction explicitly retains the unresolved fixed-exponent improvement for minimum edge-weighted triangles. The paper uses \(\mathrm{MM}(n)\), rather than asserting that the infimum exponent \(\omega\) must be attained.

Polak and Schmidt’s July 2026 preprint gives an exact APSP algorithm with supplied prediction certificates and running time \(O(n^{2.83}+\eta n)\) for its chosen parameters. The error measure \(\eta\) counts vertex pairs whose induced distance estimates are incorrect or fail the paper’s verification condition. It can be as large as \(n^2\), so this guarantee can still be cubic. Obtaining a sufficiently accurate certificate at no charged cost is an additional input assumption, not a uniform worst-case solution of this card.

Sheffield, Vassilevska Williams and Xi’s August 2026 preprint proves limits on reductions that treat a triangle relation as a black box and must work for every such relation. Its Definition 1 makes this uniformity across relations essential. These limits concern the strength of a particular reduction model, not a lower bound excluding every algorithm for the fixed shortest-path problem.

cards.title: Orthogonal Vectors Hypothesis
cards.formal: Is it true that for every \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\) there is a fixed integer \(c\ge 1\) for which no uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm decides bichromatic Orthogonal Vectors on two lists of n vectors in \(\{0,1\}^{d}\), with \(d=\lceil c \log _{2} n\rceil\), in worst-case time \(O(n^{2- \varepsilon})\) and with error probability at most \(1/3\) on every input?
cards.definitions: Here \(n\ge 2\) and the two input lists A and B each have length n; repeated vectors are allowed. The answer is YES exactly when some \(a\in A\) and \(b\in B\) satisfy \(\sum_{j=1}^{d} a_{j} b_{j}=0\) as an integer sum, equivalently their supports are disjoint. This is not an inner product over the field with two elements. Inputs are explicitly supplied as packed binary vectors. Computation uses a uniform classical RAM with words of \(\Theta (\log (n+d))\) bits, ordinary constant-time word arithmetic, Boolean operations, shifts, comparisons, memory access and generation of a random word. Each program uses a fixed word-length constant; arbitrary-precision unit-cost operations, nonuniform advice and free preprocessing tables are excluded. Reading, preprocessing and all subsequent computation count in the time bound. For fixed \(\varepsilon\) and c, hidden time constants and the program may depend on these parameters, but not on n. There is no promise on vector weights, overlap or input distribution. Randomness is internal to the algorithm; correctness must hold for every pair of lists.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated lower-bound proposition, or refute it by exhibiting one fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) such that for every fixed integer \(c\ge 1\) an algorithm \(A_{c}\) meets the \(n^{2- \varepsilon}\) time and error bounds. This quantifier order matters: the algorithms and constants may depend on c, but the exponent saving \(\varepsilon\) must work for every c. Giving a different positive saving \(\varepsilon _{c}\) that tends to zero with c, shaving logarithmic factors from quadratic time, or proving lower bounds only for restricted circuit models does not settle the proposition.
cards.why: A basic disjointness problem anchors a large part of fine-grained complexity. Settling its uniform exponent barrier would reshape conditional lower bounds for strings, geometry and data structures.

importance.reason: One of the principal hypotheses organizing polynomial-time lower bounds across multiple algorithmic areas, with an elementary explicit task and precise dimension dependence.

cards.status_note: The July 2026 primary literature explicitly states the unrestricted OV conjecture as open while proving restricted-model variants. Low-dimensional and average-case improvements do not negate its quantifier order. Checked through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: Each vector can be viewed as a subset of a universe of d coordinates. The task is to find a disjoint pair across two collections. Although checking one pair is easy, there are \(n^{2}\) possible pairs. For logarithmic dimension, packed coordinates make a single check take only a constant number of machine operations when c is fixed. The hypothesis asks whether there is an unavoidable exponent arbitrarily close to two as that fixed dimension constant grows.

The dependence on c is the main subtlety. There are already truly subquadratic algorithms for each fixed c, with a saving that can deteriorate as c increases. The polynomial-method algorithm of Abboud, Williams and Yu runs in time \(n^{2- 1/O(\log  c)}\) in the relevant large-c regime. This is consistent with the hypothesis: selecting a sufficiently large c can make that known saving smaller than any proposed universal \(\varepsilon\). The source is SODA 2015; some later bibliographies mistakenly label it 2014.

Very small dimension permits another strategy: enumerate possible coordinate patterns and aggregate the input instead of considering all pairs separately. The 2026 low-dimensional algorithms achieve a randomized bound of \(\widetilde{O}\)\((1.25^{d} n)\), with a further reported \(O(1.16^{d} n)\) bound obtained through computer-aided parameter evaluation. These improve the useful range of the pattern-based approach, but their exponential dependence on d becomes a power of n when \(d=c \log _{2} n\).

For example, substituting \(c=2\) into \(1.25^{d} n\) gives, up to constant and logarithmic factors, \(n^{1+2 \log _{2} 1.25}\), whose exponent is about 1.644. Increasing c increases this exponent. Thus an impressive subquadratic algorithm for one small logarithmic dimension does not supply one exponent saving for all logarithmic dimensions. This numerical example illustrates the quantifiers; it is not an additional algorithmic theorem.

The hypothesis is useful because disjointness can encode compatibility between partial solutions. In the standard split-and-list SAT reduction, each half-assignment produces a vector marking clauses it fails to satisfy. Two half-assignments extend to a satisfying assignment exactly when their vectors are disjoint. Sparsification controls the number of clause coordinates. For the randomized version stated here, the corresponding randomized Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis supplies a conditional justification; a deterministic-only SAT assumption must not silently be used to exclude randomized solvers.

Reductions then transfer the conjectured time barrier to problems that look quite different. Rohatgi’s Earth Mover Distance paper, the inherited source for this record, develops one such geometric application. The significance of OV is its role as a common intermediate problem: a new algorithm can overturn a collection of conditional barriers, while an unconditional proof would establish a strong lower bound for a concrete problem already known to be in polynomial time.

Restricted-model lower bounds provide evidence without establishing that unrestricted conclusion. Choudhury and coauthors prove near-quadratic monotone-circuit lower bounds for the negation of OV at logarithmic dimension. This negated predicate says every cross-pair intersects and is monotone in the input bits. Their July 2026 paper also strengthens formula and branching-program bounds. General RAM programs can use operations and intermediate representations beyond those restrictions, so these theorems do not prove the hypothesis as formulated here.

Distributional improvements are a separate frontier. Alman, Andoni and Zhang obtain faster algorithms when vector coordinates are independently sampled with a specified Bernoulli bias, including difficult parameter ranges. Such a result can explain why random instances are easier while leaving adversarial instances unresolved. The card deliberately requires correctness and the stated running time on every input rather than only on a random input distribution.

cards.title: Algebraic k-Clique Hypothesis
cards.formal: Let \(\tau (k)\) be the infimum of worst-case time exponents of randomized algorithms deciding k-Clique, as specified below, and let \(\omega\) be the arithmetic matrix-multiplication exponent over C. Is \(\liminf _{k\to \infty} \tau (k)/k=\omega /3\)?
cards.definitions: For each fixed integer \(k\ge 3\), the input is the adjacency matrix of a simple undirected graph on \(n\ge k\) labeled vertices; accept iff some k distinct vertices are pairwise adjacent. A uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input, and its time bound must hold for every random tape. Set \(\tau (k)=\inf\){\(a\ge 0\): such an algorithm runs in \(O(n^{a})\) time as \(n\to \infty\)}. The program and hidden constants may depend on k, but not on n. Words have \(C_{k}\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits for some fixed constant \(C_{k}\); arithmetic modulo the word range, division with remainder, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts and indirect memory access cost one step, and a fresh random word costs one step. Initial memory apart from the input is zero; preprocessing counts; there is no nonuniform advice, giant-word operation or free oracle. For \(\omega\), let \(M(N)\) be the smallest number of binary +,−,× gates in a circuit over C that computes all entries of the product of two formal \(N\times N\) matrices. Arbitrary complex constants and sharing are allowed, but division and branching are not. Define \(\omega =\inf \{a:M(N)=O(N^{a})\}\). This fixes the characteristic-zero arithmetic convention, separately from the bit-based graph algorithm. The question concerns the coefficient of k in the exponent; it does not fix k proportional to n or treat the latest published numerical upper bound on \(\omega\) as its exact value.
cards.answer_criterion: The matrix-multiplication reduction gives the upper asymptotic benchmark \(\omega /3\). An affirmative answer therefore proves that, for every \(\delta >0\), there is K such that \(\tau (k)\ge (\omega /3- \delta )k\) for every fixed \(k\ge K\). A negative answer proves a strict saving in this coefficient, for example via algorithms with \(\tau (k)\le (\omega /3- \delta )k\) for arbitrarily large k and one \(\delta >0\). Saving logarithmic time factors or an additive \(o(k)\) in the exponent does not refute this leading-exponent formulation.
cards.why: A basic quantitative hardness hypothesis for graph patterns and many reductions in fine-grained complexity, precisely testing whether the matrix-multiplication exponent gives the optimal leading coefficient.
