cards.status_note: Open in the stated unrestricted randomized leading-exponent form, following the inherited hypothesis and later primary sources checked through 11 September 2026. The liminf and machine conventions make the asymptotic claim explicit. Logarithmic speedups, matrix-exponent improvements and conditional lower bounds do not settle it.

context_blocks.text: For each fixed k, clique detection is already a polynomial-time problem: one can inspect every k-element subset. The issue is which polynomial is necessary. An exponent near k and an exponent near 0.79k differ dramatically as the fixed pattern size increases. This is why ordinary NP-hardness, which allows k to vary with the input, leaves the main quantitative question unanswered.

The arithmetic reduction groups the vertices of a candidate clique into three parts. For \(k=3r\), create auxiliary vertices representing r-cliques and join two auxiliary vertices when their represented sets are disjoint and their union is a clique. A triangle in this auxiliary graph represents a 3r-clique in the original graph. There are \(O(n^{r})\) auxiliary vertices, so matrix-based triangle detection gives the familiar leading time exponent \(\omega k/3\).

When k is not divisible by three, the groups have unequal sizes. Rectangular matrix multiplication gives more refined bounds for individual k; padding to the next multiple of three already changes the exponent by only a constant. Because this card asks for the leading coefficient as k grows, those residue-class effects do not alter the target. They would matter in a card asking for the exact exponent at a particular small k.

The inherited source states the hypothesis in the \(n^{\omega k/3- o(k)}\) form and allows both randomized and deterministic algorithms. The explicit liminf formulation records the order of limits: first study \(n\to \infty\) for each fixed k, then ask about large k. The model definitions make time, error and machine operations explicit. This avoids relying on an informal distinction between which graph algorithms count as combinatorial.

A negative answer would identify a way to exploit the clique decision task beyond the matrix-multiplication benchmark, potentially changing many currently conditional optimality claims.

cards.title: Hyperclique Hypothesis
cards.formal: For every fixed pair of integers \(h\ge 3\) and \(k>h\) and every constant \(\varepsilon >0\), is there no classical randomized \(O(n^{k- \varepsilon})\)-time algorithm deciding whether an n-vertex h-uniform hypergraph contains a k-clique, with error at most \(1/3\) on each input?
cards.definitions: The input hypergraph \(H=([n],E)\) is simple and unweighted, with E a subset of the h-element subsets of \([n]\). It is given by a dense table containing one Boolean membership entry for each h-element subset, in a fixed computable order. A k-clique is a set \(S\subseteq [n]\) of k distinct vertices such that every h-element subset of S belongs to E. The task outputs one yes/no bit and requires neither counting nor listing cliques. Fix the classical word-RAM with \(O(\log (n+2))\)-bit words, constant-time arithmetic, bitwise operations and random access on words; the word-length constant and runtime constants may depend on the fixed \(h,k,\varepsilon\). Random bits are allowed, but quantum operations, nonuniform advice and precomputed input-dependent tables are not. All processing of the input and construction of auxiliary data are charged. The excluded algorithm must run in \(O(n^{k- \varepsilon})\) steps on every execution and answer correctly with probability at least \(2/3\) for every input. The quantifiers concern each fixed pair h,k separately, not only a limit as k tends to infinity. The card explicitly uses the bounded-error randomized version of the classical hypothesis.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated exclusion of all such algorithms, or refute it by giving one fixed pair \(h\ge 3,k>h\), one fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) and a correct algorithm with the required worst-case time and per-input success probability. A conditional confirmation must name the stronger assumption. A logarithmic-factor speedup, an algorithm for a sparse or promised subclass, or a circuit-size bound in a restricted algebraic model is not a resolution of the full claim.
cards.why: A principal fine-grained hypothesis for higher-order combinatorial interactions, supporting conditional lower bounds beyond ordinary graph clique and shortest paths.

importance.reason: A foundational unresolved exponent question with consequences for Max-CSP optimization, algebraic identity checking and sparse graph/hypergraph algorithms.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No classical bounded-error algorithm with a fixed positive exponent saving for a covered h,k pair was found in the checked sources. The 2025 regularization and 2026 reductions use or relate the hypothesis; they do not prove it unconditionally.

context_blocks.text: A graph records pairwise compatibility. An h-uniform hypergraph records compatibility of h vertices at a time. For \(h=3\) and \(k=4, a\) positive instance contains four vertices whose four triples are all hyperedges. Knowing that every pair participates in some hyperedge is insufficient: the compatible triples must be exactly those supported on the same four vertices. This is the smallest parameter pair covered by the hypothesis.

For fixed h and k, exhaustive search takes \(O(n^{k})\) time: enumerate all k-element vertex sets and check the fixed number of required hyperedges. The problem is therefore already polynomial-time for every individual card parameter pair. The conjecture asks whether that polynomial exponent can be reduced by a positive constant. Ordinary NP-hardness when k varies would not establish such a fine-grained statement.

The graph case \(h=2\) behaves differently. Matrix multiplication gives algorithms beating the direct k-tuple search for many clique sizes. Lincoln–Vassilevska Williams–Williams explain why the corresponding higher-order operation for hypergraphs is a separate obstacle and formulate hyperclique-based lower bounds. This distinction is the reason the present hypothesis starts at \(h=3\), instead of extending a graph-clique bound mechanically to all uniformities.

Their connections to satisfiability concern optimization problems such as Max-h-SAT: find an assignment satisfying as many clauses as possible. A suitable hyperclique speedup would also improve exhaustive-search algorithms for these problems. This must be distinguished from deciding whether every clause of a fixed-width SAT instance is simultaneously satisfiable, for which exponential improvements are already known. The Max-h-SAT hypothesis is an additional assumption, not an unconditional proof.

The fixed exponent saving is essential. A running time \(n^{k}\) divided by any fixed power of log n would not contradict the card. Nor would an improvement available only when k grows with n. Conversely, an \(O(n^{3.99})\) algorithm for 4-cliques in 3-uniform hypergraphs would be enough to refute the universally quantified statement, without resolving every other h,k pair.

The dense encoding prevents an implicit promise about sparsity. Its size is \(\Theta (n^{h})\) table entries, which is below the exhaustive-search exponent because \(k>h\). Any refuting exponent saving can be reduced to a smaller positive saving so that reading this table still fits the claimed time. Thus routine conversions between explicit dense representations do not provide an artificial refutation.

The inherited paper works with k-partite hypergraphs. This is essentially equivalent for fixed k: make k copies of the vertex set and place an edge between copies in distinct parts whenever their distinct original vertices form an input hyperedge. Selecting one vertex from each part then tests the original clique condition. The vertex blowup depends only on k, preserving a positive polynomial exponent saving.

Fischer–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß go further in their ICALP 2025 regularization theorem. They transfer algorithms between general k-partite hypergraphs and a strongly regular class in which each transversal \((h- 1)\)-tuple has the same number of extensions to a hyperedge. Controlling these overlapping incidences without introducing false cliques is the substantive part of the construction. The result shows that this regularity promise does not remove the conjectured difficulty.

The same work uses regularization to classify optimization of Boolean CSPs over assignments with exactly k nonzero variables. The degree of the constraint functions separates easy linear cases, graph-clique cases and higher-degree cases with exhaustive-search lower bounds under a 3-uniform hyperclique assumption. This supplies a reason to study the hypothesis beyond the clique problem itself.

Dudek and coauthors’ STOC 2026 work gives another connection: a refutation for the 3-uniform, 4-clique case would yield a truly subquadratic algorithm for detecting four-term arithmetic progressions in an integer universe. Their paper studies verification of algebraic identities and uses this relationship for conditional lower bounds. It supplies a new consequence or conditional foundation, rather than establishing the hyperclique lower bound outright.

Fritsch–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß’s ICALP 2026 paper studies when sparsity helps for small independent sets in hypergraphs and Boolean CSPs. Its algorithms have separate vertex-count and edge-count terms, with matching bounds under clique hypotheses. Improved running time on sparse forbidden-hyperedge inputs is compatible with the dense worst-case statement here; taking a complement can turn a sparse instance into a dense one.

The hypothesis expresses a possible computational divide between pairwise and higher-order interactions. Its value is that precise reductions turn it into concrete runtime barriers for other tasks. The proper status is a conjectural foundation for those barriers. Repeated applications and increasingly robust reductions strengthen its usefulness, while a proof or one genuine exponent-saving algorithm would be a qualitatively different result.

cards.definitions: An edit inserts one symbol, deletes one symbol, or substitutes one symbol by the other; each operation costs 1. \(ED(x,y)\) is the minimum total number of edits transforming the entire string x into the entire string y. Equal symbols can be retained at cost 0. The output is this integer, not necessarily a sequence of edits. Both strings have length n and are provided explicitly, one symbol per word. The word-RAM has \(w=\operatorname{ceil}(4 \log _{2}(n+2))\) bits per word, zero-initialized addressable memory of w-bit words, and a fixed finite program independent of n. One operation reads or writes one addressed word, branches or compares words, or applies unsigned addition, subtraction or multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer division by a nonzero word with rounding down, a bitwise Boolean operation, or a logical shift by fewer than w positions. Constants are fixed by the program, and words cannot hold arbitrarily large integers in one step. The running time includes every memory access and arithmetic operation; no oracle, advice or input-dependent precomputed table is supplied. All preprocessing is charged. The time guarantee is worst-case over inputs, with no random coins or probability of error. The constant exponent saving \(\varepsilon\) cannot tend to zero with n. The chosen binary alphabet is an explicit specialization of the imported phrase “a fixed finite alphabet”, supported by Bringmann–Künnemann’s binary-alphabet formulation; a unary alphabet would make the equal-length problem trivial.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution supplies one algorithm with a proof of exact correctness for every binary input pair and a worst-case \(O(n^{2- \varepsilon})\) bound for some fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) in the specified model. A negative resolution rules out every such deterministic algorithm and every fixed positive exponent saving. A lower bound conditional on an unproved hypothesis is not an unconditional negative resolution. Faster approximation, special-case performance and logarithmic-factor savings do not meet the target.

context_blocks.title: Edits can shift an entire alignment
context_blocks.text: The strings 0101 and 1010 disagree at all four positions, but their edit distance is 2: delete the first 0 and append a 0. One edit cannot suffice, because the lengths are equal and a single substitution would leave other disagreements. Edit distance therefore measures more than the number of mismatched positions. Insertions and deletions let long portions of the two strings line up at different offsets.

context_blocks.title: What the quadratic barrier means
context_blocks.text: The classical dynamic-programming computation compares prefixes of the two strings and takes \(O(n^{2})\) time. The question concerns the best possible algorithm, not the necessity of evaluating every entry in that particular computation. A bound such as \(n^{2}/\log  n\) is smaller than \(n^{2}\) but does not give a fixed positive saving in the exponent. The target asks for \(n^{2- \varepsilon}\) with one \(\varepsilon >0\) that remains valid for arbitrarily long strings.

context_blocks.title: A precise conditional obstacle
context_blocks.text: The Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis, SETH, states that for every \(\delta >0\) there is a clause width k for which Boolean k-SAT on N variables cannot be decided deterministically in \(O(2^{(1- \delta )N} \operatorname{poly}(\mathrm{L}))\) time, where L is the formula length. Backurs and Indyk relate a truly subquadratic exact edit-distance algorithm to a faster satisfiability algorithm. Bringmann and Künnemann establish the conditional obstruction even for binary strings. This is strong evidence for a barrier, but SETH is an assumption. The reduction does not prove unconditionally that the requested algorithm is impossible.

context_blocks.title: Why recent approximation is different
context_blocks.text: Mao and Rubinstein’s March 2026 result gives a randomized \((1+\eta )\)-approximation for each fixed \(\eta >0\), with running time \(n^{2}/2^{\log ^{\Omega}(1) n}\). A multiplicative approximation can return a nearby value rather than the exact minimum. Its error guarantee and its dependence on \(\eta\) cannot simply be replaced by exact correctness at no cost. Thus this progress does not supply the deterministic exact algorithm requested here.

context_blocks.title: Scope of the benchmark
context_blocks.text: The alphabet is explicitly binary, the edit costs are all one, and the guarantee is for every input pair. Results for typical strings, a bounded number of edits, weighted substitution schemes, or a supplied good alignment may have different complexity. Computing the distance is already a polynomial-time task. The unresolved issue is the finer rate within polynomial time and its connection to the exponential-time cost of satisfiability.

A bound such as \(n^{2}/\log  n\) is smaller than \(n^{2}\) but does not give a fixed positive saving in the exponent. The target asks for \(n^{2- \varepsilon}\) with one \(\varepsilon >0\) that remains valid for arbitrarily long strings.

The Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis, SETH, states that for every \(\delta >0\) there is a clause width k for which Boolean k-SAT on N variables cannot be decided deterministically in \(O(2^{(1- \delta )N} \operatorname{poly}(\mathrm{L}))\) time, where L is the formula length. Backurs and Indyk relate a truly subquadratic exact edit-distance algorithm to a faster satisfiability algorithm. Bringmann and Künnemann establish the conditional obstruction even for binary strings. This is strong evidence for a barrier, but SETH is an assumption. The reduction does not prove unconditionally that the requested algorithm is impossible.

Mao and Rubinstein’s March 2026 result gives a randomized \((1+\eta )\)-approximation for each fixed \(\eta >0\), with running time \(n^{2}/2^{\log ^{\Omega}(1) n}\). A multiplicative approximation can return a nearby value rather than the exact minimum. Its error guarantee and its dependence on \(\eta\) cannot simply be replaced by exact correctness at no cost. Thus this progress does not supply the deterministic exact algorithm requested here.

The alphabet is explicitly binary, the edit costs are all one, and the guarantee is for every input pair. Results for typical strings, a bounded number of edits, weighted substitution schemes, or a supplied good alignment may have different complexity. Computing the distance is already a polynomial-time task. The unresolved issue is the finer rate within polynomial time and its connection to the exponential-time cost of satisfiability.

cards.title: Online matrix–vector multiplication conjecture
cards.formal: Given a Boolean matrix $M\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}$, receive vectors $v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\{0,1\}^n$ one at a time. Output each Boolean product $(Mv_t)_i=\bigvee_{j=1}^{n}(M_{ij}\wedge(v_t)_j)$ before receiving $v_{t+1}$. Is there any constant $\varepsilon>0$ and randomized algorithm with total running time $O(n^{3-\varepsilon})$ and error probability at most $1/3$? The OMv conjecture asserts that there is no such algorithm. In this formulation the total includes preprocessing of $M$.
cards.why: I include this because it is one of the central assumptions used to explain why many dynamic data structures resist fast updates and queries simultaneously. Refuting it would invalidate a large collection of conditional barriers; proving it would give a major unconditional lower bound for an explicit polynomial-time problem.
cards.definitions: The product uses OR and AND, not addition modulo two. The matrix remains fixed throughout the sequence. The word-RAM has logarithmic-size words. Success concerns the complete online computation. This is distinct from multiplying over a field, updating the matrix itself, or answering one query after an uncharged preprocessing phase.

progress.text: Henzinger, Krinninger, Nanongkai, and Saranurak formulate OMv and derive conditional lower bounds for dynamic problems, including reachability and variants of connectivity.
Larsen and Williams give randomized online multiplication in total time $n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$. This improves the algorithmic baseline without refuting the conjecture.

Hu and Polak show fine-grained equivalences between Boolean OMv and several online non-Boolean products, including min-max, dominance, and equality. These broaden the supporting connections; they do not prove the conjecture.

context_blocks.text: If all vectors were available together, they would form another matrix and fast matrix multiplication could batch the work. The online requirement forbids waiting for future columns. A data structure can learn and preprocess the fixed matrix, but it must answer a sequence of queries whose later values have not yet arrived.

A small graph construction explains the relevance to dynamic algorithms. Make one vertex for each matrix column and one for each row; put a directed edge from column j to row i exactly when the matrix entry is one. Add a source with edges to the columns activated by the current query vector. The rows reachable from the source are exactly the one-entries of the answer vector. Changing the active columns turns each matrix query into a sequence of graph updates followed by reachability questions.

The conjecture is about a polynomial saving in the exponent. An improvement from $n^3$ to $n^3/\log n$ is significant but compatible with it. Even the stronger documented saving $2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$ is only $n^{o(1)}$, so it leaves the total time in the $n^{3-o(1)}$ range.

The graph reduction gives intuition, not a universal update-time theorem by itself. To derive a particular data-structure lower bound, one must account for preprocessing, the number of updates and queries, and how the graph size relates to the matrix dimension. These are precisely the parameters handled in the original reductions.

cards.title: Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis
cards.formal: Does there exist a constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) such that, for every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), a uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm computes the min-plus convolution of any two length-\(n\) integer arrays with entries in \([-n^{a},n^{a}]\) in \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) worst-case time?
cards.why: A central fine-grained hypothesis supporting quadratic barriers in knapsack and dynamic programming.

references.authors: David Bremner; Timothy M. Chan; Erik D. Demaine; Jeff Erickson; Ferran Hurtado; John Iacono; Stefan Langerman; Mihai Pătraşcu; Perouz Taslakian

importance.reason: A central fine-grained hypothesis supporting quadratic barriers in knapsack and dynamic programming.

category_assignment.reason: The fixed polynomial exponent improvement is a fine-grained complexity target.

cards.definitions: For \(n\ge2\), input arrays \(A=(a_{0},\ldots,a_{n-1})\) and \(B=(b_{0},\ldots,b_{n-1})\) are explicitly listed. Output all \(2n-1\) integers \(c_{k}=\min\{a_{i}+b_{j}:0\le i,j<n,\ i+j=k\}\), for \(0\le k\le2n-2\). Inputs need not be sorted or monotone. Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Randomness consists of independent uniform random words, each generated at unit cost. On every input, the whole output must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). The time bound holds for every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. The exponent saving \(\varepsilon\) is common to all fixed magnitude exponents \(a\); the program, word-size constant and hidden time constant may depend on \(a\). Signed entries and exact output sums use a constant number of words.

context_blocks.text: Min-plus convolution combines two cost profiles: entry \(c_k\) is the cheapest way to split the total index \(k\) between them. For \(A=(3,1)\) and \(B=(4,2)\), the output is \((7,5,3)\). The middle entry compares two different splits, while an endpoint has only one. All output positions are required simultaneously.

The direct computation checks every pair of input entries, producing a quadratic amount of work for a linear-size output. Unlike ordinary convolution, replacing sums of products by minima of sums changes the algebraic operation. The hypothesis is a computational barrier for this exact cost-combination primitive.

The 2026 paper records an unrestricted upper bound \(n^2/2^{\Theta(\sqrt{\log n})}\), obtained from earlier results. This is an improvement over quadratic time, but its exponent saving tends to zero with input length. The requested algorithm must save a fixed positive exponent, not merely a growing subpolynomial factor.

The same paper gives \(n^{1.5+o(1)}\) deterministic time when the arrays are monotone and their values obey the specified bounded-range condition. Neither monotonicity nor that special linear range is assumed by this card. Structured convolution is therefore a restricted positive result rather than an unrestricted resolution.

The established hypothesis name predicts a negative answer to the displayed algorithm-existence question. The card fixes a precise polynomially bounded integer formulation: one exponent saving works for every fixed magnitude exponent \(a\), while the implementation and constants may depend on \(a\). There is no claim about arbitrary real-number inputs or bit lengths growing faster than \(O(\log n)\).

The probability guarantee is for the entire output on each fixed input. A small error probability for each entry separately would not automatically give that guarantee for the full array. Likewise, average performance over an input distribution is different from the worst-case time and per-input correctness requirements.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that some fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) permits the stated family of uniform algorithms for every fixed magnitude exponent \(a\), with worst-case time and whole-output success guarantees, or prove the logical negation in Lean. In the negation, every proposed saving \(\varepsilon\) fails for at least one fixed \(a\), allowing all permitted algorithms and their constants. Neither a conditional hardness implication nor a theorem for monotone inputs proves that negation.

cards.title: Truly subquadratic algorithms for 3SUM
cards.formal:
Is there a constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) such that, for every fixed integer \(B\ge1\), a uniform randomized Las Vegas algorithm solves integer 3SUM with worst-case expected time \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) on the word RAM defined below? An input consists of three lists \(A,B',C\), each containing at most \(n\) integers in \([-n^B,n^B]\), and the task is to decide whether
\[\exists a\in A\ \exists b\in B'\ \exists c\in C:\quad a+b=c.\]
The algorithm and hidden constant may depend on the fixed universe exponent \(B\); the saving \(\varepsilon\) must be independent of \(B\). This selects the polynomial-universe integer version of the source's question, with the expected-time convention used by Kopelowitz–Pettie–Porat.
cards.why: 3SUM is a central test of whether apparently quadratic search over pairs can admit a fixed polynomial improvement. Its conjectured hardness supports fine-grained lower bounds for many geometric, graph and data-structure problems. The exact model matters: removing a logarithmic factor, changing integer size or omitting preprocessing costs can make a result look stronger than the improvement asked for here.
cards.status_note: The source problem list and Kopelowitz–Pettie–Porat’s modern expected-time formulation were checked on 2026-09-14, together with 2026 preprocessed-3SUM work. A bounded later search found no from-scratch Las Vegas algorithm or general lower bound resolving the explicitly selected polynomial-universe variant.

Kopelowitz, Pettie and Porat develop reductions from the modern expected-time 3SUM conjecture to set-intersection, graph and data-structure tasks.
ICALP work obtains improved subquadratic-space tradeoffs for preprocessed 3SUM; the model retains a preprocessing phase and does not establish a truly subquadratic from-scratch algorithm.

sentences: 3SUM asks whether a value in one integer list is the sum of values from two other lists.
The target is a fixed polynomial improvement over quadratic running time on a precisely specified word RAM.
The selected variant allows every fixed polynomial integer universe and requires a common exponent saving.
Randomization may change the running time but must never produce an incorrect answer.

cards.definitions:
The size parameter \(n\ge2\) bounds the length of each of the three lists. Repeated values are allowed and do not affect the answer; each chosen value comes from its prescribed list. A triple may contain equal numerical values from different lists. There is no single-list distinctness condition. Integers are supplied explicitly in signed binary and fit in one word of
\[w=\left\lceil(B+3)\log_2(n+1)\right\rceil\]
bits. The target equation is equality of ordinary integers, not congruence modulo the word size.

For each fixed \(B\), a uniform word-RAM algorithm has a finite program independent of \(n\) and of all list contents. Its memory cells contain \(w\)-bit words and are addressed by words. Initially only the input and its lengths are present; other cells are zero. Unit-cost instructions are reading or writing a word, copying, comparing, branching, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts by a word-specified amount; a shift by at least \(w\) yields zero. Division by zero can be defined to return zero. The program may obtain an independent uniformly random \(w\)-bit word at unit cost. There is no arbitrary-precision unit-cost arithmetic, real-number operation, oracle or nonuniform lookup table. Any table construction, sorting and preprocessing count toward the runtime. Arithmetic on more than one word must be implemented by these instructions.

Las Vegas means that the program halts with probability one and every output produced is correct; randomization affects its runtime, not its answer. The required bound means that for each \(B\) there are \(K_B,n_B\) such that the expected number of instructions is at most \(K_B n^{2-\varepsilon}\) on every valid instance with \(n\ge n_B\). Expectation is over the program's random words, followed by a worst case over the input lists. All smaller valid instances must also be decided correctly with finite expected time. No average-case input distribution or reusable preprocessing is supplied.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the existence claim, including one positive exponent saving uniform over every fixed \(B\), correctness, almost-sure termination and the expected instruction bound; or prove its negation. Negation means that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) some fixed polynomial universe admits no algorithm meeting that saving. An improvement by logarithmic factors alone, a fast data-structure query after expensive preprocessing, a restricted comparison-tree lower bound, or a Monte Carlo algorithm without the stipulated zero-error guarantee does not settle this selected target.

context_blocks.text: Known algorithms beat \(n^2\) by logarithmic factors. Such bounds are \(o(n^2)\), but they do not give \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) for a fixed positive \(\varepsilon\). The modern conjecture concerns this latter, truly subquadratic improvement.

The three-set input convention follows the source. The integer word-RAM and polynomial-universe choices distinguish this target from real-RAM variants and from decision trees that charge only selected comparisons. The lower-bound claim is not restricted to a comparison-only instruction set.

Kopelowitz, Pettie and Porat formulate the modern conjecture even for expected running time and use Las Vegas complexities in their reductions. The zero-error convention here follows that formulation; it is made explicit rather than silently identifying different randomized models.

Recent work improves time–space tradeoffs after sets have been preprocessed. This is useful progress for data structures, but the present input arrives from scratch, so the entire preprocessing time must be included in its complexity.

cards.title: Hitting Set conjecture
cards.formal:
Is the randomized Hitting Set conjecture true? For every \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist an integer \(c\ge1\) such that no uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm decides the following problem in worst-case time \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\)? The input is two lists \(A,B\), each of \(n\) subsets of \([d]\), where \(n\ge2\) and \(d=\lceil c\log_2 n\rceil\). Decide whether
\[\exists a\in A\ \forall b\in B:\quad a\cap b\ne\varnothing.\]
The chosen set must be one of the supplied sets in \(A\). This is the source's fine-grained two-list problem, not the general optimization problem of selecting a small hitting set from the universe.
cards.why: This hypothesis captures a quadratic barrier with an existential choice followed by a universal test. It supports fine-grained lower bounds for graph radius, centers and quantified geometric problems where the more familiar two-existential-quantifier orthogonal-vectors hypothesis does not directly match the task. Settling it would clarify the role of quantifier order in fine-grained complexity.
cards.status_note: The original 2016 conjecture and the 2021 logarithmic-dimension formulation were checked on 2026-09-14. A bounded later search, including 2026 graph-center work, found continuing conditional applications and no resolution of the selected randomized bounded-error hypothesis.

cards.definitions:
Write \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\). Sets are supplied explicitly as \(d\)-bit incidence vectors; lists may contain repetitions and empty sets. Equivalently, the answer is yes if some vector \(a\in A\) has integer inner product \(\sum_{j=1}^d a_j b_j>0\) with every \(b\in B\). The coordinate sum is over integers, not modulo two. The dimension constant \(c\) is fixed independently of input size.

Use a word RAM with word length \(w=\lceil4\log_2(n+2)\rceil\). Incidence vectors are packed into consecutive words, with unused bits zero. A machine has a finite program independent of \(n\), word-addressed memory, and unit-cost word reads/writes, copies, comparisons, branches, arithmetic addition/subtraction/multiplication modulo \(2^w\), quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations and shifts. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero; division by zero may return zero. A uniformly random independent \(w\)-bit word is available at unit cost. Memory initially contains only the instance; any further preprocessing or lookup-table construction is charged. There are no oracles, advice or unit-cost operations on arbitrarily long integers.

A bounded-error algorithm must output the correct yes/no answer with probability at least \(2/3\) on every valid input. Its runtime bound applies to every random tape and every input, not only in expectation. For fixed \(\varepsilon,c\), a forbidden algorithm would have constants \(K,n_0\) such that it takes at most \(Kn^{2-\varepsilon}\) instructions for every \(n\ge n_0\); the constants and program may depend on \(c,\varepsilon\). Finite smaller instances must also be decided correctly within finite time.

The order \(\forall\varepsilon\,\exists c\) is essential. Refutation requires one \(\varepsilon>0\) such that for every fixed \(c\) there is an algorithm with that same exponent saving; it does not require the same program or multiplicative constant for all \(c\). Conversely, a faster algorithm at one small dimension constant does not refute the conjecture. Choosing integral \(c\) is harmless because extra zero coordinates pad smaller dimensions.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the conjecture or its negation in the stated bounded-error word-RAM model. A refutation must supply a common positive exponent saving across all fixed dimension constants. A proof conditional on another unproved hypothesis is not a proof of this conjecture. A lower bound only for deterministic algorithms, a restricted instruction set, or an isolated value of \(c\) does not suffice.

context_blocks.text: For fixed \(c\), comparing every pair of packed vectors gives an \(O(cn^2)\)-time baseline. The conjecture permits savings that vanish as dimension grows; it rules out one fixed polynomial saving valid across all dimension constants.

Orthogonal Vectors asks whether some pair has zero inner product. Here one supplied vector must have nonzero inner product with every vector on the other side. Exchanging these quantifiers changes the question, just as finding a graph center differs from finding a distant pair of vertices.

The 2021 source transfers this hypothesis to model checking with an existential–universal–existential quantifier pattern. Such reductions establish consequences of the conjecture, not an unconditional lower bound for Hitting Set.

cards.title: ETH versus Gap-ETH
cards.formal: Does the deterministic Exponential Time Hypothesis imply the deterministic Gap Exponential Time Hypothesis for sparse 3-CNF formulas?
cards.definitions: For a 3-CNF formula F with n variables, let \(\operatorname{val}(F)\) be the maximum fraction of clauses simultaneously satisfiable. The ETH convention here asserts that there is \(c>0\) for which no deterministic algorithm decides satisfiability of all 3-CNF formulas in time \(O(2^{cn} \operatorname{poly}(\mathrm{L}))\), where L is the binary encoding length. Gap-ETH asserts that there exist constants \(B\ge 1, \delta \in (0,1)\) and \(c' >0\) for which no deterministic algorithm in time \(O(2^{c' n} \operatorname{poly}(\mathrm{L}))\) distinguishes \(\operatorname{val}(F)=1\) from \(\operatorname{val}(F)\le 1- \delta\) on formulas with at most Bn clauses. Its inputs are promised to satisfy one of those two alternatives. Empty formulas are satisfiable. All constants are fixed independently of F; randomized versions are not asserted.

context_blocks.text: ETH concerns exact satisfiability, while Gap-ETH postulates comparable exponential hardness even when unsatisfiable inputs violate a fixed fraction of clauses. Their equivalence would unify many exact and approximation lower-bound assumptions.

Bitansky and coauthors distinguish ETH from the stronger gap hypothesis while obtaining exponential hardness for particular approximation tasks. Hardness for those tasks does not imply a gap-preserving sparse 3-CNF statement. This implication is distinct from asking whether either hypothesis is true.

cards.title: Min-Weight k-Clique hypothesis
cards.formal: Is the following hypothesis true? For every fixed integer \(k\ge3\) and every real \(\varepsilon>0\), there is no uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every simple undirected \(n\)-vertex graph with integer edge weights in \([-n^{100k},n^{100k}]\), outputs a minimum-total-edge-weight \(k\)-clique, or correctly reports that no \(k\)-clique exists, with probability at least \(2/3\), and has worst-case running time \(O(n^{k-\varepsilon})\). The time bound is over both input graphs and all random choices, with \(k\) fixed and \(n\to\infty\). This is the fixed weight-range version of Hypothesis 7 in the cited survey.
cards.why: Weighted clique optimization is a basic way to express interactions among several selected objects. Its conjectured exponent underlies exact-time lower bounds for problems far beyond clique detection. A polynomial exponent improvement would change those conditional barriers, while a proof would establish strong unconditional limits for a family of explicit polynomial-time tasks. The question also separates the difficulty of arbitrary edge costs from that of merely requiring all pairwise adjacencies.
cards.status_note: The survey explicitly poses this fixed-range randomized hypothesis in 2018. Related min-weight clique assumptions continue to be used in ITCS 2026, with different weight-constant quantifiers. A bounded later-work search through 14 September 2026 did not identify a resolution of this exact formulation; conditional reductions and continuing use are not an independent proof of openness.

cards.definitions: An instance has an integer \(n\ge k\), labelled vertices \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), a set \(E\subseteq\binom{[n]}2\), and weights \(w:E\to\mathbb Z\) satisfying \(|w(e)|\le n^{100k}\). A feasible answer is a set \(S\in\binom{[n]}k\) with \(\binom S2\subseteq E\); its weight is \(\sum_{e\in\binom S2}w(e)\). Any minimizing set is acceptable, and a special failure symbol is correct exactly when no feasible set exists. The input is a read-only array consisting of \(n\) and, in lexicographic order for all unordered vertex pairs, an adjacency bit, sign bit and unsigned weight magnitude, each in its own word; absent edges use zero sign and magnitude. The output is the sorted list of \(k\) vertex labels or the failure symbol. For each fixed \(k\), an algorithm is one finite program independent of \(n\), using words of \(W=\lceil d\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits for some fixed integer \(d\ge100k+4\). The constant \(d\) may depend on the program and \(k\), but not on \(n\) or the input graph. One operation reads or writes a constant number of addressed words, branches or compares, performs a word-level Boolean operation or shift, adds, subtracts or multiplies modulo \(2^W\), divides unsigned words with quotient and remainder when the divisor is nonzero, or obtains one fresh uniform random \(W\)-bit word. Shifts by at least \(W\) produce zero. All work memory initially contains zero, and arbitrary precomputed tables depending on \(n\) are not supplied. A fixed number of registers, addressing, input reads, all preprocessing and output writes are charged. Random words are mutually independent. There is no real arithmetic, oracle, quantum operation or nonuniform advice. Uniformity is with respect to \(n\); a different finite program is allowed for each fixed \(k\). Formally, the prohibited bound would give constants \(C,n_0\), depending on the program, \(k\) and \(\varepsilon\), such that every run on every valid instance with \(n\ge n_0\) uses at most \(Cn^{k-\varepsilon}\) operations, while the full output is correct with probability at least \(2/3\) on each instance.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the hypothesis with all its quantifiers, or of its negation. A refutation must supply some fixed \(k\ge3\), some \(\varepsilon>0\), and a finite algorithm with a proved \(O(n^{k-\varepsilon})\) worst-case time bound and the stated per-instance success probability for the full weight range. A proof of the hypothesis must exclude every such algorithm for every fixed \(k\ge3\). A conditional reduction from another unproved hypothesis does not prove it unconditionally. Polylogarithmic or other \(n^{o(1)}\) savings, algorithms only for smaller weights or vertex weights, and approximations to the optimum do not refute it. The integer weights and exact combinatorial output define the algorithmic task; this yes/no hypothesis is not a numerical estimation problem with additive tolerance.

context_blocks.text: The source fixes the weight range \([-n^{100k},n^{100k}]\) and asks whether the exponent \(k\) can be decreased by any positive constant. For fixed \(k\), these are polynomially bounded integers with logarithmic bit length, not unbounded-precision real costs. The constant \(100\) is retained from the source rather than replaced by an unspecified polynomial.

The elementary \(O(n^k)\) bound gives a reference scale for fixed \(k\). The hypothesis permits smaller factors such as powers of logarithms: it only excludes a fixed positive saving in the exponent. Consequently, an \(n^{k-o(1)}\) algorithm can coexist with the claim.

Edge weights are essential. The survey distinguishes unweighted clique detection and vertex-weighted clique optimization, whose algorithmic bounds need not match the edge-weighted problem. It also separates minimum weight from the requirement that a clique have total weight exactly zero. These related tasks must not be substituted in the formal statement.

The three-vertex case is closely connected to all-pairs shortest paths through subcubic reductions. Higher clique sizes provide additional hardness assumptions used for sequence alignment, geometric optimization and graph problems across density ranges. This makes the family useful beyond a single graph-search task.

Abboud, Bringmann, Dell and Nederlof establish implications connecting weighted clique hardness to the Orthogonal Vectors conjecture. Such conditional connections strengthen the network of evidence but do not prove the hypothesis. Hu, Nogler and Saha still use a min-weight clique conjecture in ITCS 2026; their nonnegative weight range has a differently quantified exponent constant, so it is recorded as a related formulation rather than asserted to be identical to the fixed range here.

cards.title: Directed unweighted APSP below \(n^{5/2}\)
cards.formal: Do there exist a constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\) and a uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm computing the full exact all-pairs distance matrix of every unweighted directed graph on \(n\) vertices in \(O(n^{5/2-\varepsilon})\) worst-case time?
cards.definitions: The graph is given by its vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge2\), and an explicit list of \(m\) arcs. It has no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair; opposite arcs are allowed. Every arc has length one. For each ordered pair \((u,v)\in V\times V\), output the minimum number of arcs on a directed path from \(u\) to \(v\), or infinity if no path exists; diagonal entries are zero. The output is an explicit \(n\times n\) array. Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Randomness consists of independent uniform random words, each generated at unit cost. On every input, the whole output must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). The time bound holds for every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. The constant \(\varepsilon\) and all other constants are independent of the graph. No assumption about the matrix multiplication exponent \(\omega\), or about additive combinatorics, is included in the claim.

cards.title: Balanced dense NFA Acceptance Hypothesis
cards.formal: For the balanced dense binary NFA acceptance problem and word-RAM model below, is it true that for every constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) no uniform randomized algorithm has worst-case running time \(O(n^{3-\varepsilon})\) and error at most \(1/3\) on every input?
cards.definitions:
An instance supplies \(n\ge2\), states \(Q=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\), a start state \(q_0\in Q\), accepting states \(F\subseteq Q\), transitions \(\Delta\subseteq Q\times\{0,1\}\times Q\), and an explicit binary word \(x=x_1\cdots x_n\) of length exactly \(n\). There are no empty-word transitions and no repeated copies of a transition. Require \(n^2\le|\Delta|\le2n^2\). The transition relation is given as two \(n\times n\) Boolean matrices, with entry \((a,b)\) for symbol \(s\) indicating whether \((a,s,b)\in\Delta\). The accepting set is an \(n\)-bit indicator vector. The word is accepted exactly when \[ \exists q_1,\ldots,q_n\in Q:\quad q_n\in F\ \text{ and }\ \forall j\in\{1,\ldots,n\},\ (q_{j-1},x_j,q_j)\in\Delta.\]

The matrices are stored in row-major order, one Boolean entry per word; \(n,q_0\), the indicator entries and the input characters likewise occupy one word each in a fixed layout. Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\), where the fixed integer \(d\ge8\) is chosen with the algorithm. The input is read-only, random-access memory; auxiliary memory initially contains zeros. Its addresses and individual values fit in one word. The algorithm is a fixed finite program with no advice or precomputed input-dependent data.

Unit-cost instructions are word reads and writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and unsigned integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computations pay for their constituent instructions. Each random instruction returns an independent uniform \(w\)-bit word. All initialization, preprocessing, table construction and final output are charged. Arbitrary algebraic algorithms in this instruction model are allowed; no combinatorial restriction is imposed.

Correctness means that for every valid fixed input, the output equals its acceptance bit with probability at least \(2/3\). Running time is a worst-case bound over valid inputs and all random choices, not an expected bound. For a fixed \(\varepsilon\), a putative algorithm, \(d\), and constants \(C,n_0\) may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but not on \(n\) or the input. The excluded guarantee is that all valid instances with \(n\ge n_0\) terminate within \(C n^{3-\varepsilon}\) instructions while every valid instance, including smaller ones, is correctly decided with the stated error.

context_blocks.text: The automaton records possible state changes under each symbol. Acceptance asks whether one possible trajectory follows the entire supplied word and ends in an accepting state. Here both the number of states and the word length grow together, and the transition relation has quadratic size.

The 2024 source formulates a broader hypothesis with transition count \(\Theta(n^\alpha)\), word length \(\Theta(n^\beta)\), and a subpolynomial alphabet. It identifies \(\alpha=2,\beta=1\) as a core regime. This card retains its previously selected specialization to a binary alphabet, exactly \(n\) symbols, and the explicit density interval \([n^2,2n^2]\). It does not identify that one proposition with every parameter regime of the broader hypothesis.

The elementary bound in this balanced regime is \(O(n^3)\). The source reports subpolynomial-factor improvements for dense automata, which are compatible with excluding every fixed power saving. Its sparse-automaton bounds use SETH, and its combinatorial lower bounds have a restricted algorithm model. Neither type constitutes the unconditional all-algorithm lower bound requested here.

The broader framework connects automaton acceptance to context-free language reachability, Word Break and the online matrix-vector multiplication hypothesis. These are consequences of the source’s stated hypothesis and reductions; they should not be attributed without qualification to every editorially restricted variant.

Bille and Gørtz study the amount of nondeterministic activity during a particular regular-expression simulation. That density differs from the number of transitions in a general dense NFA. Their work explains the researcher connection recorded at import, rather than authorship of the NFA Acceptance hypothesis.

A refutation supplies some fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), a uniform algorithm in the stated RAM model, and proofs of its worst-case time and per-input correctness guarantees on all promised instances. A positive answer excludes all such algorithms without an unproved complexity assumption. The negation of this asymptotic statement is not a single hard or easy finite instance. A bound restricted to combinatorial or deterministic algorithms, or a subpolynomial improvement of cubic time, does not meet the target.

The automaton records possible state changes under each symbol. Acceptance asks whether one possible trajectory follows the entire supplied word and ends in an accepting state. Here both the number of states and the word length grow together, and the transition relation has quadratic size.

cards.title: Linear-size Circuit-SAT below exhaustive search
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(c\ge 1\), do \(\varepsilon _{c}>0\) and a deterministic algorithm exist deciding satisfiability of every Boolean circuit with n inputs and at most cn gates in time \(O((2- \varepsilon _{c})^{n}\cdot n^{O(1)})\)?
cards.definitions: Use uniform classical deterministic Turing computation, with no advice or oracle. Integers and rational numerators and denominators are encoded in binary; L denotes the total input bit length. A polynomial bound has constants independent of the input. Circuits are finite acyclic directed graphs with input bits and one output, binary AND and OR gates and unary NOT gates; gates have unrestricted fan-out. Size counts non-input gates. The input lists every gate and predecessor index. Satisfiability means that some assignment to the n input bits makes the output one. The algorithm and the constants in its polynomial factor may depend on c, but \(\varepsilon _{c}\) must be positive and independent of n. There is no depth restriction.

context_blocks.text: Exhaustive assignment search works in roughly \(2^{n}\) time regardless of circuit structure. Linear-size circuits restrict the amount of computation performed on each assignment while retaining arbitrary depth and sharing.

Obtaining a fixed exponential saving for every fixed size density would establish a general algorithmic benefit of that restriction. The question is part of the algorithms-to-lower-bounds landscape described by Wigderson. Algorithms for bounded-depth or threshold-restricted circuits do not settle the stated general model.

cards.title: Fine-grained comparability of permanent and SETH
cards.formal: Are exact binary-matrix permanent computation and the family of fixed-width satisfiability problems comparable by deterministic fine-grained oracle reductions at the \(2^n\) scale? Ask whether at least one of the following two fixed directions exists. In the SAT-to-permanent direction, for every rational \(0<\varepsilon<1\), there is a rational \(0<\delta<1\), independent of the clause width, such that for every fixed \(k\ge3\) a reduction decides \(k\)-SAT on \(n\) variables, using an exact binary-permanent oracle, with ordinary bit time \(T\) and queried matrix dimensions \(N_j\) satisfying \[T+\sum_j2^{(1-\varepsilon)N_j}\le C\,2^{(1-\delta)n}(L+1)^a.\] Here \(L\) is the formula encoding length, and \(C,a\) and the reduction may depend on \(\varepsilon,k\). In the permanent-to-SAT direction, for every rational \(0<\varepsilon<1\), there exist rational \(0<\delta<1\), a fixed \(k\ge3\), and a reduction computing the permanent of every \(N\times N\) binary matrix using a \(k\)-SAT decision oracle, with queried variable counts \(n_j\) and \[T+\sum_j2^{(1-\varepsilon)n_j}\le C\,2^{(1-\delta)N}(N+1)^a.\] In this direction \(\delta,k,C,a\) and the reduction may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but not on \(N\) or the matrix. A single direction must satisfy its condition for every \(\varepsilon\).
cards.why: The permanent is a canonical exact counting problem with a natural exponential algorithm, whereas SETH organizes the difficulty of satisfiability decision across clause widths. A quantitatively efficient connection would reveal whether their exponential barriers have a common source. Ordinary counting completeness does not determine how a constant improvement in one exponential base transfers to the other problem.

sentences: The permanent of a binary matrix counts its perfect matchings exactly.
The source asks whether its exponential-time difficulty can be related to SETH in either direction.
This card makes that comparison precise using deterministic oracle reductions that preserve a constant saving in the exponential rate.
A reduction from SAT must preserve a saving uniform across clause widths, while the reverse direction may choose a fixed width for each saving.
The preferred binary-matrix case and exact counting oracle are distinguished from general matrix variants, ordinary completeness and counting SAT.

cards.definitions:
For \(A\in\{0,1\}^{N\times N}\), \(N\ge1\), define \(\operatorname{per}(A)=\sum_{\pi\in S_N}\prod_{i=1}^N A_{i,\pi(i)}\), where \(S_N\) is the set of permutations of \([N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}\). The exact integer, between zero and \(N!\), is returned in binary. Encode the input as \(1^N0\) followed by its \(N^2\) entries in row-major order. The parameter is the matrix dimension \(N\), not the number of entries or nonzero entries. For fixed \(k\), \(k\)-SAT asks whether a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most \(k\) signed Boolean variables from a declared set of \(n\ge1\) variables, has a satisfying assignment. Empty clauses are allowed. Remove tautological clauses and duplicate literals and clauses; a clause never contains both signs of a variable. Use this concrete canonical encoding: prefix \(1^n0\), followed by one bit for each possible normalized clause of size at most \(k\), indicating whether it occurs. Order these clauses first by size, then lexicographically by their increasing lists of variable indices and signs, with negative sign before positive sign. The formula length is \(L=n+1+\sum_{j=0}^{\min(k,n)}2^j\binom nj\), polynomial in \(n\) for each fixed \(k\). Unused declared variables are permitted. A queried SAT instance uses the same fixed \(k\) and encoding. This representation fixes all encoding choices; ordinary sparse representations differ by only polynomial factors for fixed \(k\).

A reduction is a deterministic multitape oracle Turing machine with a finite program for its stated fixed parameters, no advice and no random bits. It must be correct on every valid input when its oracle returns the correct value. It may make finitely many adaptive calls, meaning later calls may depend on previous answers. The permanent oracle returns the exact binary integer, while the SAT oracle returns only the YES/NO decision, not a witness or a satisfying-assignment count. The ordinary time \(T\) counts all machine transitions, including writing queries, processing answer bits, preprocessing, arithmetic and final output; only the internal oracle computation is excluded. The displayed sum charges every oracle call separately at its hypothesized improved exponential cost. The constants satisfy \(C\ge1\), \(a\in\mathbb N\), and the bound must hold on every valid input. No effective dependence of a reduction program on the external constant \(\varepsilon\) or on \(k\) is required; each chosen machine itself is uniform over input lengths. The forward quantifiers are \(\forall\varepsilon\,\exists\delta\,\forall k\,\exists R,C,a\). The reverse quantifiers are \(\forall\varepsilon\,\exists\delta,k,R,C,a\). In neither direction may an exponent improvement shrink with the input length.

For context, deterministic SETH asserts that there is no constant \(\eta>0\) for which every fixed \(k\ge3\) has a deterministic \(k\)-SAT algorithm in time \(2^{(1-\eta)n}n^{O(1)}\); the polynomial exponent and algorithm may depend on \(k\). The binary-permanent hypothesis here means that no constant \(\eta>0\) permits exact permanent computation in time \(2^{(1-\eta)N}N^{O(1)}\). The reduction target is explicit quantitative reducibility, rather than the bare propositional disjunction of two implications between these hypotheses. The polynomial factors are harmless under the universal quantification over exponent savings: an algorithm with a fixed larger saving can supply the oracle budget for a smaller saving.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked family of reductions satisfying one of the two directions, including exact correctness and the stated ordinary-time-plus-oracle-cost bounds for all parameters and inputs, or a complete Lean proof that neither direction exists. A positive answer must identify the direction and its quantifier dependence. Polynomial-time counting completeness without the exponential budget, a reduction using a counting-SAT oracle in the reverse direction, or a forward saving \(\delta\) depending on \(k\) is insufficient. A conditional obstruction to a restricted reduction model establishes only that obstruction.

context_blocks.text: Cygan’s seminar question asks for a relation in either direction and explicitly prefers binary matrices. This card keeps both directions as one comparability question and selects that preferred matrix domain. The explicit oracle budgets are a documented fine-grained interpretation of the source’s informal hardness comparison; general weighted matrices remain a different version.

A SAT-to-permanent reduction of the stated strength would make a fixed exponential improvement for permanent contradict SETH. A permanent-to-SAT reduction would make a failure of SETH yield a fixed exponential improvement for permanent. The two directions have different clause-width quantifiers.

The question concerns constructing reductions with a resource guarantee. Merely asking whether one of two unqualified logical implications holds would lose that content: the disjunction of the implications between any two propositions is classically tautological.

Belova and coauthors define fine-grained reductions by charging the sum of the improved running-time budgets over all oracle calls. Their SETH-hardness definition requires a saving independent of the SAT clause width. These conventions motivate the precise forward direction here.

The same SODA 2024 work relates strong co-nondeterministic lower bounds for Binary Permanent to lower bounds for explicit arithmetic polynomial families. That is a distinct conditional connection, not a proof of either deterministic SAT/permanent reduction demanded here.

cards.title: Time exponents for multiple-string LCS over fixed alphabets
cards.formal: Determine the optimal deterministic polynomial-time exponent function \(\tau(\sigma,k)\) for longest common subsequence of \(k\) strings over an alphabet of size \(\sigma\), on the entire domain \(D=\{(\sigma,k)\in\mathbb N^2:\sigma\ge2,\ k\ge2\}\). For each fixed pair, let \[\tau(\sigma,k)=\inf\bigl\{c\ge0:\ \exists A\ \exists C>0\ \exists n_0\ \forall n\ge n_0\ \forall(s_1,\ldots,s_k)\in(\{1,\ldots,\sigma\}^{\le n})^k,\ A\text{ outputs an LCS within }Cn^c\text{ operations}\bigr\},\] where \(A\) ranges over the correct uniform deterministic word-RAM algorithms defined below, and \(n,n_0\) are integers. Supply a function \(g:D\to\mathbb R\) and a complete Lean-checked proof that \(|g(\sigma,k)-\tau(\sigma,k)|\le1/100\) for every \((\sigma,k)\in D\). This explicitly broadens the source’s proposed constant-fraction exponent improvement into determination of the underlying exponent function; it is not claimed to be equivalent to that yes/no question.
cards.why: Multiple-string alignment has a rapidly growing dependence on the number of sequences, even though it is polynomial-time solvable when that number is fixed. A small alphabet may constrain the combinatorial choices enough to change the leading exponent. Determining the full exponent function would separate the cost of coordinating many strings from the expressiveness supplied by a growing alphabet, and would sharpen the fine-grained limits behind exact sequence comparison.
cards.status_note: The 2017 source explicitly poses the fixed-alphabet exponent-saving question. This card records a transparent quantitative broadening to the underlying exponent function, not an equivalent reformulation or a claim that every parameter pair is unresolved. Bounded later-work checks through 14 September 2026 found conditional bounds and different string variants, but no unconditional determination of this entire function.

progress.text: Abboud, Backurs and Vassilevska Williams, Theorem 2, show that an exponent improvement for k-LCS with alphabet size proportional to k would refute the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis. The alphabet dependence is part of the result.

Bringmann poses the fixed-alphabet fractional-exponent improvement in Section 4.3, Open Problem 3, printed page 120. Section 4.2 defines the common-subsequence task and asks a different time-space question.

Golan et al., CPM 2026, review the multiple-string worst-case bounds in Section 1 and obtain algorithms for a hybrid that also imposes a substring requirement. Their result does not determine the exponent function here.

sentences: Multiple-string LCS finds a longest string that occurs as a subsequence of every input.
The target is the optimal deterministic time exponent for every fixed alphabet size and fixed number of strings.
It makes the source’s question about a fractional exponent saving into an explicitly broader quantitative function.

cards.definitions: A subsequence of a string \(s\) is any string obtained by deleting positions while preserving the order of the retained symbols. An LCS of \(s_1,\ldots,s_k\) is a string that is a subsequence of every input and has maximum possible length. The algorithm must output one such string exactly, with arbitrary tie-breaking; inputs may have unequal lengths or be empty. The input includes an integer bound \(n\ge2\), the \(k\) lengths and all symbols, stored explicitly in a read-only array with one length or symbol per word; each length is at most \(n\). Output symbols and output length are written explicitly. For each fixed \((\sigma,k)\), the algorithm is one finite program independent of \(n\), with no nonuniform advice or tables supplied as a function of \(n\). Its word width is \(W=\lceil d\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) for some fixed integer \(d\ge\sigma+k+4\), allowed to depend on the program and the fixed pair. A constant number of word reads, writes, comparisons, branches, Boolean operations, shifts, additions, subtractions, multiplications modulo \(2^W\), or unsigned divisions with quotient and remainder by a nonzero word each cost one operation. A shift by at least \(W\) returns zero. Work memory starts at zero; all input access, preprocessing, addressing and output are charged. Each local operation accesses only constantly many words, and no real arithmetic, oracle, quantum operation or random coins are allowed. Running time is worst-case over all valid tuples for the stated length bound. The constants \(C,n_0,d\) and program may depend on \(\sigma,k\), but not on \(n\) or the input strings. An admissible algorithm must be correct and terminate on every valid input, including sizes below \(n_0\). The alphabet and string count remain fixed when taking the exponent; neither is hidden as a growing function of \(n\). The infimum is finite: exact multiple-string LCS has an \(O(n^k)\) algorithm for each fixed pair, while explicitly outputting a length-\(n\) common string requires linear time. Thus \(1\le\tau(\sigma,k)\le k\). No algorithm attaining the infimum is assumed to exist.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide one unambiguous mathematical function \(g\) on all of \(D\), together with a complete correct proof checked in Lean of the pointwise absolute bound \(1/100\) in exponent units. A family of certified intervals of width at most \(1/50\) covering every pair qualifies through their midpoints. The answer may be an expression or certified evaluation rule; merely repeating the defining infimum is not a determination. Bounds on the infimum must respect its possible nonattainment: a claimed endpoint need not be achieved by one algorithm with exactly that exponent. A result only for one alphabet, one number of strings, average-case inputs, approximations, or substring variants does not meet the entire criterion. Conditional bounds alone do not give an unconditional determination. The tolerance concerns the real-valued exponent function, not an approximation to the output subsequence or a constant-factor characterization of the full running time.

context_blocks.text: Bringmann’s Open Problem 3 asks whether \(k\)-LCS has an \(O(n^{(1-\varepsilon_\Sigma)k})\) algorithm for a fixed alphabet \(\Sigma\). The surrounding paragraph contrasts this with conditional \(n^{k-o(1)}\) hardness when the alphabet can grow linearly with \(k\). Recovering this alphabet dependence is essential; the inherited title alone omitted it.

The benchmark’s permitted quantitative broadening is used here to ask for \(\tau(\sigma,k)\). The original proposed fractional saving remains a separate sourced question. In particular, approximating every exponent to \(1/100\) need not decide whether an arbitrarily small strict exponent improvement exists or whether an infimum is attained. No equivalence between those targets is asserted.

Subsequences retain order while allowing gaps. Requiring a contiguous substring, an increasing sequence, a compressed representation, or a multiplicative approximation changes the task. The unrestricted worst case also differs from parameter bounds that become fast only when the optimum is very close to the input length.

Abboud, Backurs and Vassilevska Williams give conditional exponent lower bounds when the alphabet size is allowed to depend linearly on the number of strings. Their result does not supply the same uniform exponent barrier while one alphabet is held fixed and the number of strings varies. The source also records weaker parameterized hardness for constant alphabets, which leaves room between different linear coefficients in the exponent.

Golan, Kraus, Porat and Shalom review exact multiple-string LCS in CPM 2026 and study a hybrid subsequence–substring requirement. The faster algorithm for that hybrid does not solve unrestricted multiple-string LCS. Their discussion also distinguishes exact algorithms from recent two-string approximation results.

cards.title: P versus BPP
cards.formal:
Does \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{BPP}\)? Equivalently, is the following statement true?
\[\forall L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad L\in\mathrm{BPP}\ \Longrightarrow\ L\in\mathrm P.\]
Here \(\mathrm{BPP}\) requires one randomized polynomial-time machine whose probability of a correct answer is at least \(2/3\) separately on every input, including both members and nonmembers of \(L\). The proposed deterministic machine must decide the same total language correctly on every input in polynomial time.
cards.definitions:
A language \(L\) is a set of finite binary strings; its membership bit is \(\mathbf1_L(x)\in\{0,1\}\). Put \(n=|x|\), allowing \(n=0\). Computation uses finite multitape Turing-machine programs over fixed finite tape alphabets. Each ordinary tape transition costs one step. A randomized transition may read at most one fresh independent unbiased bit. There is no oracle, advice, quantum operation, input distribution or promise excluding some inputs.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BPP}\) means that there exist one randomized program \(R\) and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) such that, with \(p(n)=C(n+1)^d\), both of the following hold for every \(x\):
\[\begin{gathered}
 R(x)\text{ halts within }p(n)\text{ steps on every random tape and outputs a bit},\\
 \Pr[R(x)=\mathbf1_L(x)]\ge 2/3.
\end{gathered}\]
The probability is only over the internal fair bits. An exact finite interpretation is to supply a uniformly distributed string \(z\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\), ignoring its unused suffix. The probability condition is then the integer inequality
\[3\bigl|\{z\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}:R(x;z)=\mathbf1_L(x)\}\bigr|\ \ge\ 2\cdot 2^{p(n)}.\]
The time bound is worst case over both the input and every random tape, rather than an expectation. The error bound is pointwise: success on almost all inputs of a length does not suffice. The same constants apply at every length; an input-dependent exponent is not polynomial time in this definition.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm P\) means that there exist one deterministic program \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(C',d'\) such that for every binary string \(x\), the program halts within \(C'(|x|+1)^{d'}\) steps and outputs \(\mathbf1_L(x)\). Reading, writing, arithmetic and tape access all count toward time. The deterministic program and its constants may depend on the language and its randomized decider, but not on the particular input or its length.

The requested deterministic computation may use a different algorithm and a different polynomial exponent. The target does not require an effective compiler taking descriptions of randomized machines to deterministic ones. It asks for existence of a polynomial-time deterministic decider for each language in the class. Deterministic programs are also randomized programs that ignore their coins, so \(\mathrm P\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}\) holds directly. Sampling a distribution, returning a valid witness, and answering only promised inputs are different tasks from deciding this total membership bit.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated inclusion, or of its logical negation
\[\exists L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad L\in\mathrm{BPP}\ \land\ L\notin\mathrm P.\]
A positive proof must establish existence, correctness and a uniform polynomial time bound for a deterministic decider of every language satisfying the randomized definition. A negative proof must give one fixed language with a single randomized decider meeting the full pointwise error and worst-case polynomial time guarantees, and prove that no deterministic program with any fixed polynomial time bound decides that language.

A result conditional on an unproved hardness assumption, a nonuniform circuit simulation, an oracle separation, a promise-problem separation, or a simulation valid only at some lengths does not settle the target. A lower bound for one simulation rule or one generator family does not exclude every deterministic decider. The probability threshold is exact; this is a yes/no question with no numerical approximation tolerance.
cards.why: This asks whether independent random bits increase the set of total decision problems solvable efficiently. An equality would identify deterministic and randomized polynomial-time decision power; a separation would exhibit an inherent benefit of randomness even when a different deterministic algorithm is allowed.

context_blocks.text: A randomized answer is allowed to be wrong with probability at most one third on any specified input. For example, correctness on 99% of all strings of each length would still fail this definition if a remaining string were always answered incorrectly. The uncertainty belongs to the machine’s internal choices, not to which inputs the user may supply.

Adleman’s theorem gives \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\). Here \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\) allows a separate polynomial-size Boolean circuit at each input length, without requiring one efficient procedure that constructs these circuits. This is a nonuniform existence statement; the target requires one finite deterministic program for all lengths.

Impagliazzo and Wigderson prove a conditional equality: if a Boolean function computable in deterministic time \(2^{O(n)}\) has worst-case circuit complexity at least \(2^{\varepsilon n}\), for some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) and all sufficiently large \(n\), then \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{BPP}\). Circuit complexity here counts gates of unrestricted nonuniform Boolean circuits over a fixed complete finite basis that compute the function correctly on every input of that length. The exponential lower-bound hypothesis is part of the theorem; this is not an unconditional equality or a theorem assuming only \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\).

Doron, Moshkovitz, Oh and Zuckerman’s May 2026 preprint obtains finer conditional derandomization bounds for algorithms with a specified insensitivity property. For each fixed input, changing one uniformly chosen coin coordinate of a correct tape must rarely make the answer incorrect. Their two-sided version additionally constrains incorrect tapes that have a correct neighbor. Theorem 9.10 retains explicit circuit-hardness, insensitivity and error assumptions; these structural conditions are not properties required of every BPP program. The paper distinguishes hitting-set and pseudoentropy generators from general pseudorandom generators.

Tianrong Lin’s July 2026 revision states a direct claim of \(\mathrm P\subsetneq\mathrm{BPP}\) in Theorem 1.1, with additional claimed separations. That would answer this card negatively if its proof were valid. This review read the claimed theorem and checked its version history, but has not certified its proof or located independent primary validation in the bounded searches. It is therefore recorded as an unverified claim, and the card retains uncertain status.
