sentences: A lossless condenser compresses a weak random source while preserving its guaranteed entropy together with the seed entropy.
This question asks for a logarithmic seed and an output only a constant number of bits longer than that preserved entropy.
The output may be nonuniform, but it must be within one hundredth in statistical distance of a distribution with the required min-entropy.
The equivalent graph target has nearly lossless expansion and only a constant factor more right vertices than the number of outgoing edges from a source set.
Recent multiplicity-code and two-sided-expansion results improve related structure without meeting this constant-overhead target.

cards.definitions:
All lengths are integers in bits and all logarithms have base two. The min-entropy of a finite distribution is \(H_{\infty}(X)=-\log_2\max_x\Pr[X=x]\). The input promise therefore says that every point has probability at most \(2^{-k}\). Input distributions may be arbitrary; their coordinates need not be independent, and they need not have efficient samplers. The input to the condenser is a sample string and a seed, not a distribution description. \(U_t\) is uniform on all \(t\)-bit strings, with the single empty string when \(t=0\). Statistical distance is
\[\operatorname{TV}(P,Q)=\tfrac12\sum_z|P(z)-Q(z)|.\]
The comparison distribution \(Y_X\) may depend on the entire source distribution. Its existence is a mathematical guarantee; no algorithm for producing or sampling it is required.

Explicitness means that two fixed deterministic multitape Turing machines compute the lengths from \((1^n,k)\) and the full output from \((1^n,k,x,y)\), respectively. The entropy parameter is binary, \(|x|=n\), and \(|y|=d(n,k)\). For some fixed positive integers \(K,q\), each computation uses at most \(K(n+1)^q\) transitions, including preprocessing and output writing. No advice, oracle, randomized choice of construction or free length-dependent table is allowed. The machines and constants are fixed before \(n,k,X\); the comparison distribution is quantified after \(X\).

Lossless means that the comparison distribution preserves all \(k+d\) guaranteed input-and-seed entropy bits. The bounded quantity \(m-(k+d)\) is the output entropy gap, or output overhead, not lost entropy. The condenser is not required to output an almost-uniform string: it only has to be close to a distribution with the specified min-entropy. Uniformity conditional on a separately disclosed seed is not imposed.

There is an equivalent graph view for these parameters. Let \(N=2^n\), \(D=2^d\), \(M=2^m\), and \(K_0=2^k\). Treat the condenser as a neighbor function \([N]\times[D]\to[M]\), identifying integers with fixed-length binary strings. It defines a left-regular bipartite multigraph; seeds label edges, and repeated neighbors are permitted. The lossless condition is equivalent to requiring at least \((99/100)DK_0\) distinct neighbors for every set of exactly \(K_0\) left vertices. The size bounds become \(D\le(2n)^C\) and \(DK_0\le M\le2^{\Delta}DK_0\). Only this source-equivalent one-sided expansion is required; neither right-regularity nor right-to-left expansion is an additional condition.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed uniform condenser-family claim. A construction must specify its algorithms and constants and establish all length, time, distance and entropy requirements over the entire domain. An equivalent graph construction qualifies with a proved translation to these guarantees. A negative answer must rule out every such family. A constant fraction of output entropy gap, a superlogarithmic seed, or a construction only for a restricted entropy regime does not meet the target.

context_blocks.text: Open Problem 5.36 asks for degree polynomial in \(\log N\), expansion \(0.99D\), and only \(O(K_0D)\) right vertices. Proposition 6.33 translates the powers-of-two case into lossless condensation. The card fixes the binary representation and the exact fixed-error condenser formulation of Open Problem 6.35.

The 2022 Kalev–Ta-Shma construction gives a different lossless condenser with logarithmic seed length. Its Theorem 2 allows an output entropy gap proportional to the source entropy, with parameter restrictions; it does not establish an absolute constant gap. The paper explicitly distinguishes entropy loss from entropy gap and describes small-gap extraction as an outstanding challenge.

The September 2026 paper proves that the Kalev–Ta-Shma graph also expands losslessly in the reverse direction and characterizes its expansion. This additional two-sided property concerns a different resource. Its stated right-side size still has a power loss relative to the source set size in the checked parameters, so it does not give the constant output overhead requested here.

The source relates a positive answer to improved extraction with constant total entropy loss, the separate target TCS-1015. A condenser is allowed a nonzero output entropy gap; an extractor instead asks that the output itself be close to uniform. The card preserves that distinction.

cards.title: Promise-AM derandomization via targeted hitting sets
cards.formal: Is the following equivalence true? \[\mathrm{prAM}=\mathrm{prNP}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{a uniform nondeterministic polynomial-time targeted hitting-set generator exists for co-nondeterministic Boolean circuits.}\] The promise classes and generator are defined below. The generator receives the full description of the circuit it must hit. It must have at least one successful computation branch on every valid circuit, and every successful branch must output a hitting set whenever the circuit accepts at least half of its ordinary inputs. The target permits multiple distinct valid outputs but no input-dependent advice.
cards.why: Derandomization removes the need for public random challenges in efficient proof protocols. A targeted hitting set is a concrete finite object tailored to a verifier. An equivalence would determine whether eliminating randomness necessarily gives such tailored objects in the Arthur–Merlin setting, extending a known structural characterization of ordinary randomized computation.

sentences: The question compares promise-Arthur–Merlin derandomization with the existence of targeted hitting sets.
A generator receives a co-nondeterministic circuit and must hit its accepting ordinary inputs whenever they occupy at least half the domain.
Nondeterministic generation must always have a successful branch, and every successful output must satisfy the required hitting guarantee.

cards.definitions: A promise problem is a pair \((Y,N)\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^{*}\); inputs outside \(Y\cup N\) have no correctness requirement. Membership in \(\mathrm{prNP}\) means that there are a fixed deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) and a polynomial \(p\) such that, for every \(x\in Y\), some \(u\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}\) satisfies \(V(x,u)=1\), and for every \(x\in N\), every such \(u\) is rejected. Membership in \(\mathrm{prAM}\) means that there are a fixed deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(W\) and a polynomial \(q\) such that Arthur sends a uniformly random \(r\in\{0,1\}^{q(|x|)}\) to Merlin, who sees \(x,r\) and responds with \(u\in\{0,1\}^{q(|x|)}\); for \(x\in Y\), \(\Pr_r[\exists u:W(x,r,u)=1]\ge2/3\), and for \(x\in N\), this probability is at most \(1/3\). Merlin has no computational restriction. Equality means equality of the sets of promise problems recognized in these senses, with a potentially different verifier for each problem. A co-nondeterministic circuit is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit \(C(r,u)\), using constants, fan-in-two AND and OR gates and unary NOT gates, with one output, ordinary input bits \(r\in\{0,1\}^a\), and universally quantified input bits \(u\in\{0,1\}^b\). Its size counts all input and internal gates; put \(m=\max\{2,\operatorname{size}(C)\}\), so \(a,b\le m\). Encode its gates in topological order, with binary predecessor indices and designated ordinary/universal inputs. For \(z\in\{0,1\}^m\), set \(D_C(z)=1\) exactly when \(C(z_1,\ldots,z_a,u)=1\) for every \(u\in\{0,1\}^b\); extra ordinary bits are ignored. Empty universal inputs mean one empty assignment. Define density \(\mu(C)=2^{-m}|\{z:D_C(z)=1\}|\). A targeted generator is one finite nondeterministic Turing machine \(H\), and constants \(K,d\), whose every branch on a valid description \(C\) halts in at most \(K(m+1)^d\) bit steps, either with a distinguished failure symbol or with an explicit nonempty finite list \(S\) of strings in \(\{0,1\}^m\). At least one branch must output a list on every \(C\). If \(\mu(C)\ge1/2\), then every branch that outputs a list must satisfy \(\exists z\in S:D_C(z)=1\). If \(\mu(C)<1/2\), no hitting property is required, but the branch and output-format requirements still apply. All descriptions, nondeterministic choices, list entries and output writes are charged. No random bits, oracle or advice is supplied. The machine can depend on its particular circuit input, not merely on circuit size. Explicit polynomial-length output lists are the table representation of the source’s generators with \(O(\log m)\) seed bits; no compact representation of an exponentially large list is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the equivalence or its logical negation under these definitions. The nontrivial unresolved implication is from promise-AM derandomization to the stated generator; the reverse implication is already established in the cited framework. A positive answer must obtain a single uniform generator with polynomial cost, at least one successful branch for every circuit and no incorrect successful branch on any dense circuit. A generator requiring advice, working only for infinitely many input lengths, using superpolynomial time or handling ordinary deterministic circuits alone does not establish the target. A relativized separation or a counterexample to one proposed generator does not by itself refute the unrelativized equivalence.

context_blocks.text: Chen and Tell’s Open Problem 2.5 restates a question introduced by Goldreich in 2011. It asks for the equivalence with nondeterministically computed targeted hitting-set generators for co-nondeterministic circuits. The input circuit and the treatment of unsuccessful branches are essential parts of that formulation.

The source contrasts this open characterization with the established equivalence between promise-BPP derandomization and deterministic targeted pseudorandom generators. That deterministic-circuit result does not automatically provide the universal-witness circuit guarantee needed here.

The 2025 journal paper of van Melkebeek and Mocelin Sdroievski gives a precise nondeterministic definition: there is a successful branch on every input, and all successful outputs must hit a dense circuit. Its Definitions 3.8 and 3.9 supply the output-list convention used here.

The same journal paper’s Theorem 1.10 derives a targeted generator from a stronger high-time derandomization assumption, with an infinitely-often simulation and nonuniform advice. It is evidence toward the connection but leaves the uniform polynomial-time equivalence unresolved.

cards.title: Polynomial-time derandomization of randomized \(\mathrm{AC}^0\)
cards.formal: Does \(\mathrm{BPAC}^0\subseteq\mathrm P\) hold for polynomial-time-uniform circuit families? Equivalently, must every Boolean function on finite binary strings that is computed with error at most \(1/3\) on each input by a uniform polynomial-size, constant-depth randomized AND–OR circuit family admit an exact deterministic polynomial-time algorithm?
cards.why: Constant-depth AND–OR circuits are a central restricted model for which strong lower bounds are known, yet fully eliminating their randomness in uniform polynomial time remains a distinct challenge. The question tests whether those structural restrictions suffice to remove random choices while allowing a much more flexible deterministic simulator.
cards.status_note: Checked on 14 September 2026. The source explicitly poses the polynomial-time-uniform containment. The checked later generator and earlier weak-derandomization results have different quantitative or correctness guarantees. No proof or refutation of the stated containment was found in the bounded search; this does not certify exhaustive current openness.

progress.text: Shaltiel obtains explicit weak derandomization for constant-depth computations, preserving correctness on most inputs rather than every input.
The source records quasipolynomial simulation and explicitly asks whether polynomial-time uniform simulation is possible.
Lyu proves the \(O((\log S)^{d-1}\log(S/\varepsilon)\log\log S)\) seed bound for fooling fixed-depth circuits. The theorem does not give the polynomial-time class containment requested here.

sentences: The question asks whether randomness can be removed from uniform shallow AND–OR computations using deterministic polynomial time.
Each randomized circuit must answer correctly with probability at least two thirds on every input.
A single polynomial-time procedure constructs the family’s circuit descriptions from the input length.
The deterministic simulator may use arbitrary polynomial-time computation and need not remain a constant-depth circuit.
Quasipolynomial simulation, correctness on most inputs and nonuniform deterministic circuits do not meet the full target.

cards.definitions: A Boolean function here is a total function \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}\). A randomized circuit \(C_n(x,r)\) is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated output, \(n\) data input bits \(x\), and \(m(n)\) random input bits \(r\). Input nodes may contain these bits, their negations, and constants zero and one. Internal nodes are unbounded-fan-in AND or OR gates. There are no parity, majority, threshold or oracle gates. The depth is the maximum number of internal gates on an input-to-output path, and the size is the number of internal gates. Repeated wires into one gate are omitted. The entire circuit is encoded by an explicit ordered list of nodes, labels and predecessor lists with binary indices. A family witnesses \(f\in\mathrm{BPAC}^0\) if there exist fixed positive integers \(a,b,d\), a constant \(K\ge1\), and one deterministic algorithm \(M\) such that, for every \(n\ge0\), \(M\) given \(1^n\) outputs the circuit \(C_n\) in at most \(K(n+2)^a\) Turing-machine steps; its depth is at most \(d\), and both its size and \(m(n)\) are at most \(K(n+2)^b\). On every \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), independent fair random bits \(R\), uniform in \(\{0,1\}^{m(n)}\), satisfy \(\Pr[C_n(x,R)=f(x)]\ge2/3\). The constants, circuit-generation algorithm and random-bit bound may depend on the family but not on \(n\), \(x\) or the random choices. Polynomial-time uniformity is required; merely having a circuit at each length is insufficient. The class \(\mathrm P\) consists of the functions computed correctly on every binary input by one deterministic multitape Turing machine in at most \(K_0(n+2)^{b_0}\) worst-case steps, for some constants \(K_0,b_0\). That machine has no random bits, advice or oracle. It may depend on the randomized family, and its polynomial exponent need not be the same for all families. The target concerns class containment, with no additional demand for an algorithm that takes arbitrary family-generating programs and produces their deterministic simulators. The notation \(\mathrm{AC}^0\), used in the context below, means the analogous polynomial-time-uniform family with no random inputs.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of \(\mathrm{BPAC}^0\subseteq\mathrm P\), or of its negation under the stated uniformity convention. A positive answer must give exact, all-input polynomial-time simulation for every such family. A negative answer requires a total function in uniform \(\mathrm{BPAC}^0\) with no deterministic polynomial-time algorithm. Average-case correctness, quasipolynomial simulation, deterministic circuits without a uniform construction, or a failure to build one particular pseudorandom generator is insufficient. A proof of the stronger uniform equality \(\mathrm{BPAC}^0=\mathrm{AC}^0\) also answers the stated containment question, but preservation of constant depth is not required.

context_blocks.text: The randomized computation is shallow, but its random input can contain polynomially many bits. Trying every possible random string can therefore require far more than polynomial time. The desired simulator need only compute the same final bit; it is not required to retain the shallow circuit shape.

Uniformity is essential. A polynomial-time algorithm must be able to obtain the description for each length from that length alone. An existence theorem for a separately chosen circuit or separately chosen good random strings at every length does not provide such an algorithm.

Vadhan’s Definition 7.26 explicitly permits polynomial-time uniform construction. Open Problem 7.31 asks for the stronger equality \(\mathrm{BPAC}^0=\mathrm{AC}^0\), or at least containment in \(\mathrm P\). This card selects the latter, already stated alternative, matching its original polynomial-time title.

The source’s Corollary 7.30 gives a deterministic quasipolynomial-time simulation: time \(2^{(\log(n+2))^{O(1)}}\), with constants depending on the fixed family. It also records a quasipolynomial-size constant-depth simulation. Neither guarantee supplies polynomial time.

Shaltiel’s work gives uniform weak derandomization for constant-depth computations, where the deterministic result is correct on most inputs. It also notes that the nonuniform randomized and deterministic constant-depth classes coincide. Those statements leave this card’s simultaneous uniformity and all-input correctness requirement unresolved.

Lyu’s 2022 Theorem 1 constructs generators fooling depth-\(d\), size-\(S\) circuits within error \(\varepsilon\), with seed length \(O((\log S)^{d-1}\log(S/\varepsilon)\log\log S)\), for fixed \(d\) and \(S\) large enough. Here “fooling” means that every circuit’s acceptance probability changes by at most \(\varepsilon\). This is a substantial quantitative improvement, but its general fixed-depth seed bound is not \(O(\log S)\).

A pseudorandom generator is a useful comparison point, but its optimal construction is a separate, stronger-looking formulation. This question permits any deterministic simulator meeting the stated time and correctness requirements, without prescribing a generator or any other proof method.

cards.title: Universal traversal sequences under arbitrary labels
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic algorithm \(A\) and absolute positive integers \(C,b\) such that, for every pair of integers \(n,d\ge1\), on input \((1^n,1^d)\) the algorithm outputs in at most \(C(n+d+2)^b\) steps a word \(w=w_1\cdots w_T\in[d]^T\), with \(T\le C(n+d+2)^b\), satisfying the following universal property? For every connected undirected \(d\)-regular port-labeled multigraph on \(n\) vertices in the convention below and every starting vertex \(s\), the walk that successively takes absolute port numbers \(w_1,\ldots,w_T\) visits all vertices.
cards.why: A universal traversal sequence replaces all random choices in a walk by one short deterministic instruction list, without inspecting the graph. Efficient construction under arbitrary local labels would expose how far randomness can be removed when a walker cannot use information about its incoming edge or leave memory on vertices.
cards.status_note: The construction question is explicit in Vadhan’s 2012 text. The 2025 full exploration manuscript and September 2026 journal abstract/introduction were checked for model differences; neither states a matching polynomial-time UTS construction. The May 2026 weighted-PRG report concerns a different generator guarantee and was not treated as a traversal theorem. Bounded searches through 14 September 2026 located no matching resolution. This does not exhaustively certify current openness.

progress.text: The textbook records the existence of short universal traversal words and asks for efficient construction under arbitrary labels; its two numbered questions refer to the same target.
The revised exploration paper distinguishes UTS, incoming-port-based UXS and local computation costs. Its algorithm model includes vertex memory.
The journal publication retains a self-stabilizing exploration setting with agent and vertex memory; its abstract and introductory model were checked.

sentences: A universal traversal sequence is one list of absolute local port numbers that visits every vertex of every graph of a specified size and degree.
The graph may have parallel edges and self-loops, and its local port labels are arbitrary.
The question asks for a deterministic polynomial-time constructor given only the size and degree parameters.
Short sequences are known to exist, but incoming-port-based exploration and polynomial cover time with expensive local computation are different guarantees.
An efficient construction would remove randomness from graph-independent traversal under severely restricted information.

cards.definitions:
Use \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\). A port-labeled multigraph is specified mathematically by a map \(h:[n]\times[d]\to[n]\). The \(d\) ports at each vertex are distinct local labels; different ports may lead to the same neighbor. Undirectedness means \[ \forall u,v\in[n]:\quad |\{i:h(u,i)=v\}|=|\{j:h(v,j)=u\}|.\] This represents equal directed multiplicities in opposite directions. A self-loop is allowed and consumes one port, following the textbook’s directed-edge convention. A graph is connected when any two vertices are joined by a finite walk through its ports. No compatibility between the port numbers at opposite ends of an edge is imposed.

For a word \(w\) and start \(s\), define \(v_0=s\) and \(v_t=h(v_{t-1},w_t)\) for \(1\le t\le T\). Universality requires \(\{v_0,\ldots,v_T\}=[n]\). The same word must work for all maps \(h\) obeying those conditions and for every start. At step \(t\), the word specifies the absolute outgoing port \(w_t\), independently of the vertex, prior walk, or the port through which the walker arrived. There is no incoming-port-dependent offset, backtracking instruction, mutable vertex memory, or graph-dependent change to the word.

The constructor receives only the unary size and degree parameters, not \(h\), \(s\), a graph oracle, advice or a random seed. It is one finite deterministic multitape Turing program; all its work, preprocessing and output are counted. Each port number is output in binary with a delimiter, so writing the entire sequence is included in the polynomial time bound. The polynomial is in the values \(n,d\), not their binary encoding lengths. This card selects the polynomial-time construction explicitly offered in Open Problem 3.9; a logarithmic-workspace constructor is a stronger possible outcome, not an additional requirement. The target is exactly \(n\) vertices as in Example 3.8. For a parameter pair admitting no connected graph in this convention, the universal condition is vacuous.

cards.definitions: A language is a subset of \(\{0,1\}^*\); \(U_n\) is uniform on length-\(n\) binary strings. BPP consists of languages decided by a uniform randomized Turing machine in polynomial worst-case time on every random tape, with error at most \(1/3\) on each input and independent fair coins. Each \(A_{L,k}\) is one deterministic Turing machine with no advice and a worst-case polynomial time bound; its code, exponent and sufficiently-large-length threshold may depend on \(L,k\). No joint polynomial dependence on \(k\) is required. The displayed error is an input fraction at every sufficiently large length, not a probability over simulation coins. NEXP consists of languages recognized by nondeterministic Turing machines in time \(2^{n^a}\) for some fixed integer \(a\ge1\), allowing constant factors and finitely many small lengths. P/poly consists of languages whose length-\(n\) characteristic functions have polynomial-size Boolean circuits, with no uniformity between lengths. Boolean circuits are finite acyclic networks of fan-in-two AND and OR, unary NOT, input bits and constants, with one output. Circuit size is the length of an explicit binary gate-and-wire encoding. For \(m\ge1\), \(\operatorname{Perm}_m(X)=\sum_{\pi\in S_m}\prod_{i=1}^m X_{i,\pi(i)}\) is a formal polynomial in \(m^2\) indeterminates, where \(S_m\) is the set of permutations of \([m]\). Arithmetic circuits use fan-in-two addition, subtraction and multiplication, variable leaves and only the constants 0 and 1; there are no divisions or other field constants. They must compute the permanent as a formal polynomial over the integers, not merely on Boolean matrices. Polynomial size means one polynomial bound in \(m\) for all sufficiently large dimensions; the individual circuits need not be uniformly constructible. Thus a non-polynomial circuit conclusion excludes every fixed polynomial bound, rather than demanding an eventual exponential lower bound. The assertion is an ordinary logical implication, with no restriction to a black-box proof.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of this exact implication, or a Lean refutation establishing the heuristic premise together with polynomial-size circuits for every NEXP language and for the permanent in the stated arithmetic model. An unconditional proof of either circuit lower-bound conclusion suffices. A uniform time-class separation, a different simulation premise or an impossibility restricted to a chosen proof method does not settle the assertion.

cards.definitions:
The input \(1^{n}\) is unary: a string of \(n\) copies of the symbol 1. The output is the ordinary binary representation of an integer. An \(n\)-bit prime is an integer \(p\) in \([2^{n-1},2^{n})\) whose only positive divisors are 1 and \(p\). The domain begins at \(n=2\), since there is no one-bit prime.

The machine is a single classical probabilistic Turing machine, with independent unbiased random bits and a polynomial worst-case running-time bound on every random tape. There is no advice depending on \(n\), precomputed table of primes, oracle, or free preprocessing. All computation, including any primality tests, counts toward its time bound.

Pseudodeterminism means that for each fixed length there is one fixed prime \(p_{n}\) returned with the stated probability across independent executions. The prime may depend on the algorithm and on \(n\), but not on the execution’s random bits. It need not be the smallest \(n\)-bit prime or a prime prescribed in advance. The remaining probability mass may produce a failure symbol, another prime, or an invalid output.

The guarantee is required at every length. Success on infinitely many unbounded lengths alone does not suffice. A guarantee for all sufficiently large lengths would suffice, since finitely many shorter lengths can be handled by a fixed finite part of the algorithm.

The constant success probability is the usual bounded-error convention for pseudodeterminism. Independent repetitions followed by a majority output can amplify concentration on the same canonical prime with polynomial overhead. Merely finding some prime with high probability, while different runs usually return different primes, does not meet the requirement.

The source lists several distinct search tasks. This card explicitly selects prime generation as its main target; it does not assert that solving it is equivalent to making every randomized search problem pseudodeterministic.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct such an algorithm and prove the polynomial bound and concentration on a fixed valid prime at every length, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A result conditional on a number-theoretic or complexity assumption must identify that assumption. Infinitely-often correctness, nonuniform advice, or ordinary randomized prime generation does not settle the stated unconditional question.

cards.title: FPT versus \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic algorithm A, a total computable function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), and an integer \(c\ge0\), such that A decides whether G contains a k-clique and uses at most \(f(k)(N+2)^c\) steps for every encoded pair (G,k) of total bit length N? The exponent c is independent of both k and G. Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{FPT}=\mathrm{W}[1]\) under parameterized many-one reductions?
cards.definitions: A graph G is finite, simple and undirected, with vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), including n=0. A k-clique is a subset of exactly k vertices with an edge between each pair of distinct vertices. The empty subset is a 0-clique; no k-clique exists when k>n. For a fixed binary encoding, write \(1^n0\), then the n by n adjacency matrix in row order, then the ordinary binary representation of the nonnegative integer k (0 is written as 0, and otherwise there are no leading zeroes). A valid matrix is symmetric with zero diagonal, and the entire remaining suffix is the representation of k. N counts all bits, including k. A rejects any malformed string in time polynomial in its bit length. The bound in the statement applies to every valid pair, including k>n. The parameter is k alone; there is no promise on density, degree, clique number or any other graph property. A is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program and fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input and initially blank work tapes; each transition reads or writes only at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. The runtime includes parsing, input access and all internal work. Correctness is exact, and no advice, randomness, oracle or quantum operations are supplied. The same A, f and c work for every pair; f must be computable by a machine that halts on every nonnegative integer input, but its growth and the time needed to compute it have no prescribed bound. Constant multiplicative overhead can be absorbed into f. Using full input length rather than n gives the usual FPT question: for k at most n the two lengths are polynomially related, and k>n is rejected after parsing. For completeness, a parameterized language is a set of pairs \((x,k)\in\{0,1\}^*\times\mathbb N\), with both components explicitly encoded. It belongs to FPT if one uniform deterministic machine decides it within \(h(k)(M+2)^a\) steps for a total computable positive h, a fixed nonnegative integer a and complete encoding length M. A parameterized many-one reduction computes a single output pair \((y,k^{\prime})\) in such a time bound, preserves yes versus no membership, and satisfies \(k^{\prime}\le g(k)\) for a total computable function g; writing the output counts toward its runtime. The class W[1] can equivalently be defined as all parameterized languages admitting such a reduction to the Clique problem just specified. This characterization fixes the reduction convention without a change of target. It includes FPT, and Clique belongs to it, so FPT membership of Clique is equivalent to equality of the two classes.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the single algorithm, computable multiplier and constant exponent in the statement, or prove their joint nonexistence. In the affirmative case, prove correctness and the uniform worst-case bound on all pairs, together with the malformed-input convention. In the negative case, exclude every such algorithm, computable f and exponent c; a conditional lower bound, a bound for a restricted algorithm model, or failure at one proposed multiplier and exponent does not settle this target. An algorithm whose polynomial exponent depends on k also does not satisfy the displayed quantifiers.
cards.why: This is the principal boundary question for algorithms whose exponential difficulty is confined to a small parameter. It determines the force of thousands of parameterized hardness reductions and separates efficient small-solution search from algorithms whose input-size exponent grows with the solution size.

importance.reason: The defining unresolved tractability separation of parameterized complexity, with Clique as a precise and widely used complete problem.

progress.text: The textbook specifies parameterized reductions and proves the completeness framework for Clique, via its complement relation with Independent Set. Theorem 14.21 derives the stronger exclusion of \(f(k)n^{o(k)}\) Clique algorithms assuming ETH.

Bottesch identifies the FPT-versus-W[1] separation as the central conjecture, explains its known implications relative to P versus NP and ETH, and proves structural results with explicitly specified oracle conventions. These do not prove the unrelativized separation.
Lin gives a gap reduction showing that a constant-factor FPT approximation of Clique would imply an exact FPT algorithm. The consequence remains conditional on FPT differing from W[1].

Chen, Feng, Laekhanukit and Liu give a combinatorial proof of the \(k^{o(1)}\) parameterized inapproximability consequence under W[1]-hardness. The checked August 2024 revision precedes the SOSA 2025 publication.

Abboud, Fischer and Shechter improve combinatorial fixed-k Clique bounds by logarithmic factors. Their August 2024 author revision retains a polynomial exponent depending on k; the institutional record lists the Algorithmica publication on 22 May 2026.

cards.status_note: The textbook and Bottesch explicitly state the unresolved separation, and the later approximation papers retain it as an assumption. The checked fixed-k algorithm paper and its 2026 publication metadata provide no FPT algorithm. A bounded primary-source search on 14 September 2026 found no verified resolution; the review does not independently reprove the cited results.

context_blocks.text: For each fixed k, exhaustive search over vertex subsets decides Clique in polynomial time. The exponent grows with k, so this observation gives a different kind of tractability: increasing the target clique size can increase the power of n in the running time. The question asks whether all dependence on k can instead be moved into one multiplicative function. For example, \(2^{2^{k}}n^{3}\) meets the requested form, while \(n^{k/10}\) does not.

The unrestricted Clique problem is NP-complete, but this alone cannot rule out fixed-parameter tractability. The permitted function f can grow much faster than any polynomial when k grows with n. If \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) then Clique is certainly FPT; the converse implication is not known. Thus \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\) is a stronger separation conjecture than \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) in the direction currently proved.

Parameterized reductions keep the output parameter controlled solely by the original parameter. Since Clique is complete under these reductions, an FPT Clique algorithm would solve every \(\mathrm{W}[1]\) problem in FPT time. This is why a \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hardness proof is useful evidence against a parameterized algorithm for another problem. The evidence is conditional on the separation being true, even when the reduction theorem itself is unconditional.

The Exponential Time Hypothesis supplies a stronger quantitative barrier: it rules out \(f(k)n^{o(k)}\) algorithms for Clique. That conclusion excludes FPT, but uses an assumption that is itself open. Matrix-multiplication methods and improved combinatorial methods accelerate Clique for fixed k while leaving an exponent that grows with the parameter. Their progress does not eliminate the central gap.

Approximation has become another way to measure the reach of the conjecture. Lin proves that even fixed-factor parameterized approximation of Clique is \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hard. Later constructions strengthen the factor and simplify the reductions. These results enlarge the consequences of a separation; they do not prove \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\).

Uniformity is essential: one finite program must handle every k. Neither a separately chosen algorithm for each fixed k nor a bound with an exponent that increases with k establishes FPT. Conversely, the allowed computable multiplier can be enormous; this is a structural tractability question and does not assert that an affirmative algorithm would be practical.

For each fixed k, exhaustive search over vertex subsets decides Clique in polynomial time. The exponent grows with k, so this observation gives a different kind of tractability: increasing the target clique size can increase the power of n in the running time. The question asks whether all dependence on k can instead be moved into one multiplicative function. For example, \(2^{2^{k}}n^{3}\) meets the requested form, while \(n^{k/10}\) does not.

The unrestricted Clique problem is NP-complete, but this alone cannot rule out fixed-parameter tractability. The permitted function f can grow much faster than any polynomial when k grows with n. If \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) then Clique is certainly FPT; the converse implication is not known. Thus \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\) is a stronger separation conjecture than \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) in the direction currently proved.

Parameterized reductions keep the output parameter controlled solely by the original parameter. Since Clique is complete under these reductions, an FPT Clique algorithm would solve every \(\mathrm{W}[1]\) problem in FPT time. This is why a \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hardness proof is useful evidence against a parameterized algorithm for another problem. The evidence is conditional on the separation being true, even when the reduction theorem itself is unconditional.

The Exponential Time Hypothesis supplies a stronger quantitative barrier: it rules out \(f(k)n^{o(k)}\) algorithms for Clique. That conclusion excludes FPT, but uses an assumption that is itself open. Matrix-multiplication methods and improved combinatorial methods accelerate Clique for fixed k while leaving an exponent that grows with the parameter. Their progress does not eliminate the central gap.

Approximation has become another way to measure the reach of the conjecture. Lin proves that even fixed-factor parameterized approximation of Clique is \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hard. Later constructions strengthen the factor and simplify the reductions. These results enlarge the consequences of a separation; they do not prove \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\).

Uniformity is essential: one finite program must handle every k. Neither a separately chosen algorithm for each fixed k nor a bound with an exponent that increases with k establishes FPT. Conversely, the allowed computable multiplier can be enormous; this is a structural tractability question and does not assert that an affirmative algorithm would be practical.

benchmark_focus.reason: The defining unresolved tractability separation of parameterized complexity, with Clique as a precise and widely used complete problem.

cards.title: Exponential Time Hypothesis
cards.formal: Is \(s_3>0\) in the deterministic bit model defined below? Equivalently, does there exist one real \(c>0\) such that no 3-SAT decider A has a runtime bound \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{c n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) on every valid 3-CNF formula F for any fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\)? The same positive c must exclude all such algorithms. This is the deterministic Exponential Time Hypothesis.
cards.definitions: Fix an integer clause-width bound \(q\ge 3\). A q-CNF formula is a finite list of clauses, each a finite list of at most q literals. A literal is a variable \(x_i\) or its negation \(\neg x_i\), with \(1\le i\le n\). The variables that occur are exactly \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), so n counts distinct variables, not clauses or input bits. Repeated literals, repeated clauses and clauses containing both signs of a variable are allowed. A Boolean assignment satisfies the formula if every clause has at least one true literal. An empty clause is false; the empty conjunction is true and has n=0. For a completely specified binary encoding, let \(\operatorname{code}(a)\), for a nonnegative integer a, be \(1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary expansion of a+1, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). Encode n and the number m of clauses with this code, then each clause by its coded length followed by its literals. Each literal is a sign bit (0 for positive, 1 for negated) and the code of its variable index. All indicated lists must be fully present, with no trailing bits, valid indices and every declared variable occurring. Let L be the complete bit length. Ill-formed strings, including clauses wider than q, are rejected. No density, satisfiability-count, occurrence or input-distribution promise is imposed. A q-SAT decider A is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program and fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. Each transition reads or writes only the cells at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. The total transition count includes parsing, input access and all internal work. A must halt on all inputs, decide satisfiability exactly on valid q-CNF formulas, and reject malformed strings in polynomial time in their length. It receives no advice, random bits, quantum operations, oracle or precomputed instance information. The machine may depend on the fixed q. For a valid formula F, let \(t_A(F)\) be its runtime and \(n(F),L(F)\) its variable count and bit length. An exponent \(\alpha\ge 0\) is attainable at width q if there exist such a decider A and fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\) with \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{\alpha n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) for every valid q-CNF formula F. The constants are independent of F. Define \(s_q\) as the infimum of all attainable exponents. This set is nonempty because exhaustive assignment testing gives an attainable exponent 1, so \(0\le s_q\le1\). The infimum need not itself be attainable. Polynomial factors in L remain explicit, including when clauses are repeated many times. The chosen explicit syntax and malformed-input normalization do not impose a new satisfiability promise; they fix the bit model for the source’s exponential-rate question. This card specializes q to 3. Its negation, \(s_3=0\), means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a 3-SAT decider \(A_\varepsilon\) with fixed constants \(C_\varepsilon,d_\varepsilon\) satisfying \(t_{A_\varepsilon}(F)\le C_\varepsilon 2^{\varepsilon n(F)}(L(F)+1)^{d_\varepsilon}\) on every valid formula. The machine and constants may depend on epsilon. This statement does not require one machine with a single subexponential runtime bound, nor a computable map from epsilon to a machine.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of \(s_3>0\) or of \(s_3=0\) for the explicitly defined rate. A positive answer requires a positive constant excluding every valid deterministic decider at that exponential rate, with any polynomial input factor. A negative answer must establish arbitrarily small attainable positive exponents with the stated quantifiers. A fixed improved positive exponent, a bound for a restricted algorithm class, or a conditional lower bound does not settle this question. No numerical estimate of \(s_3\) is requested: the target is its strict positivity.
cards.why: ETH is the central hypothesis for ruling out subexponential exact algorithms and many fixed-parameter speedups. It turns the qualitative P versus NP question into a quantitative claim that can be transferred through carefully sized reductions.

importance.reason: A foundational quantitative hardness hypothesis underlying exact, parameterized, graph, and geometric algorithm lower bounds.

progress.text: Impagliazzo and Paturi define the exponential rates of bounded-width satisfiability and relate positive rate at width three to positive rates at other fixed widths. These are structural results about the hypothesis, not a proof of it.
The authors’ IPEC survey explicitly defines ETH by a positive infimum and distinguishes the number of variables from the complete input length.

The parameterized-algorithms textbook retains the positive-infimum definition, explains its distinction from ruling out a single subexponential algorithm, and gives consequences for parameterized complexity.

Liu gives a deterministic \(1.32793^n\) upper bound for 3-SAT up to polynomial factors, recorded in the checked March 2020 revision of the ICALP 2018 work. This leaves the positivity of the optimal rate unresolved.

Aggarwal, Gupta, Morolia and Zhang derive new lattice approximation hardness under ETH or randomized ETH, with different assumptions for their closest-vector and shortest-vector results. The paper still treats these as assumptions and distinguishes Gap-ETH.

cards.status_note: The original sources and the July 2026 ICALP paper continue to use ETH as an unproved hypothesis. The optimal-rate definition and cited algorithmic upper bound were checked against the full relevant source passages. Targeted later-work searches on 14 September 2026 found no verified resolution; bounded searches do not independently verify the cited proofs or exhaust all later literature.

context_blocks.text: NP-completeness describes the possibility of polynomial-time algorithms and does not itself impose a positive exponential rate. Even if P differs from NP, a running time such as \(2^{\sqrt{n}}\) remains possible for 3-SAT. ETH asks for a stronger obstruction: some fixed amount of exponential work must remain unavoidable when complexity is measured by the number of Boolean choices.

That parameter must be preserved carefully by a reduction. An ordinary polynomial-time reduction may turn an n-variable formula into an instance of size \(n^{3}\), which can destroy a claimed exponential lower bound in the new parameter. Sparsification supplies a controlled disjunction of bounded-density formulas, allowing variables and clauses to be related without an arbitrary polynomial blowup. This is a main reason ETH can support sharp bounds across many problems.

The infimum over all algorithms matters. Excluding one \(2^{o(n)}\) algorithm is the common informal wording, but the textbook explicitly keeps the stronger positive-infimum statement because the converse is unclear. ETH would be false if arbitrarily small constant exponents were attainable, even if the known algorithms depended on the desired exponent. A card that omitted this distinction would change the quantified question.

Liu’s deterministic algorithm has runtime \(O(1.32793^n)\) up to polynomial input factors. It therefore supplies an upper bound on \(s_3\); it establishes neither a positive lower bound nor the value of \(s_3\). The existence of one algorithm with a positive exponential rate does not rule out a much faster algorithm. Empirical solver success and promises on the formula are also distinct from this all-input infimum.

ETH is weaker than SETH, whose optimal rates approach one as the fixed clause width grows. It also differs from randomized ETH and from Gap-ETH, which asks for hardness of distinguishing fully satisfiable formulas from formulas with a constant unsatisfied fraction. Recent lattice reductions illustrate the value of tracking these distinctions: some approximation hardness can be obtained from deterministic ETH, while other results use randomized ETH. They extend the consequences of assumptions without proving the assumptions.

A single fixed exponent in ETH must obstruct every algorithm. Refuting one proposed lower-bound constant does not suffice, because another smaller positive constant could still work. Conversely, a refutation may use a different finite algorithm for each desired exponent; no effective procedure generating those algorithms is added to the target.

cards.title: Breaking the \(2^{n}\) barrier for weighted TSP
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(\varepsilon \in (0,1), c\ge 1\) and a uniform classical randomized algorithm that, for every complete undirected graph on \(n\ge 3\) labelled vertices with nonnegative binary-encoded integer edge weights of total encoding length L, outputs a minimum-weight Hamiltonian cycle with probability at least \(2/3\) in worst-case time \(O((2- \varepsilon )^{n}(n+\mathrm{L})^{c})\)?
cards.definitions: Each unordered pair of distinct vertices has one explicitly listed weight. A Hamiltonian cycle visits each vertex exactly once before returning to its first vertex, and its weight is the sum of its n edge weights. Output the cyclic list of vertex labels. The input has no metric, bounded-weight, planarity or sparsity promise. Use a random-access word RAM with \(w=B\lceil n+\log _{2}(\mathrm{L}+2)\rceil\) bits per word for one fixed sufficiently large integer B; unit-cost operations are reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction, multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\) and integer division by nonzero words. Integers occupying several words incur the cost of all word operations. This word size permits addressing exponential-space subset tables; its polynomial bit-operation overhead is already permitted by the polynomial factor in \(n+\mathrm{L}\). The running-time bound includes reading weights, preprocessing, random bits and output and holds on every execution. Only independent private fair random bits are allowed; there is no quantum access, advice or oracle. The constants \(\varepsilon ,c,B\) and the implicit multiplicative constant are independent of n,L and the weights. A deterministic algorithm also qualifies. Dependence polynomial in the numerical maximum weight, rather than its binary length, does not qualify.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
cards.why: Locate the fundamental exponential-time cost of exact weighted routing beyond the long-standing subset barrier.

importance.reason: A central exact-algorithm question with a sixty-year base-two barrier and a modern improvement that carefully distinguishes prefactor from exponent. It is separate from metric TSP approximation and from Hamiltonian-cycle detection.

progress.text: The Bellman and Held–Karp subset formulation gives the classical \(O(2^{n} n^{2})\) bound, recalled by the 2024 primary paper.
Stoian v2 states deterministic time \(2^{n} n^{2}/2^{\Omega (\sqrt{\log  n})}\), retaining base two.

context_blocks.text: The exact travelling salesman problem asks for a cheapest tour through all vertices. In the general weighted setting, discovering a Hamiltonian cycle is not enough: the input is complete, so tours certainly exist, but their costs can vary greatly. The computational target is the minimum among them.

The classical subset dynamic program has a base-two dependence on the number of vertices. Stoian’s 2024 algorithm improves the familiar \(O(2^{n} n^{2})\) time by a factor \(2^{\Omega (\sqrt{\log  n})}\). Its bound retains the exponential base two and does not yield \(O*((2- \varepsilon )^{n})\) for any fixed positive \(\varepsilon\).

This distinction is substantial even though both bounds are exponential. A fixed base reduction saves an exponential factor on increasingly large instances, whereas savings in the polynomial or subexponential prefactor do not. The card asks about unrestricted classical algorithms, not about the optimality of the original dynamic-programming recurrence.

Weight encoding separates this target from several related exact questions. A method whose time is polynomial in the maximum integer weight can be very expensive when a large weight has a short binary representation. Likewise, faster algorithms for unweighted Hamiltonicity or for special weighted graph classes do not establish the general weighted guarantee.

No asserted reduction from SETH is built into the question. The desired algorithmic existence is itself the target; a conditional lower bound must state its assumption separately. The Parameterized and exact algorithms bucket is appropriate because the defining issue is the exponential dependence on n, rather than polynomial-time approximation of a tour.

cards.title: Set Cover conjecture
cards.formal:
Is the Set Cover conjecture true? For every \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist a fixed integer \(d\ge1\) such that no uniform randomized bounded-error algorithm solves \(\le d\)-Set Cover on an \(n\)-element universe in worst-case time
\[O\!\left((2-\varepsilon)^n(n+1)^r\right)\]
for any fixed exponent \(r\)? An instance supplies a family \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^{[n]}\) with \(|S|\le d\) for every \(S\in\mathcal F\), and an integer \(t\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\). The task is to decide whether some subfamily \(\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal F\) of at most \(t\) sets satisfies \(\bigcup_{S\in\mathcal H}S=[n]\). Sets chosen for the cover may overlap. The randomized interpretation is explicit in the later primary sources.
cards.why: Set Cover is a central example of an exact algorithm whose natural dynamic-programming base remains two. The conjecture provides barriers for other exponential-time problems and is not merely a restatement of the familiar SAT hypotheses. Its incompatibility with the asymptotic rank conjecture links this algorithmic barrier to fundamental questions in algebraic complexity.
cards.status_note: The 2024 SCC formulation and both STOC 2024 asymptotic-rank connections were checked on 2026-09-14, together with a bounded later-work search. The rank-based algorithms are conditional; no unconditional proof or refutation of the selected randomized SCC was identified.

progress.text: Cygan and coauthors develop Set Cover-based lower bounds for exact exponential-time algorithms, keeping this assumption separate from the proved SAT equivalences.
Can Esmer and coauthors formulate the at-most-d Set Cover conjecture and characterize corresponding barriers for triangle partitioning and packing with structural parameters.
Björklund and Kaski show that the asymptotic rank conjecture and SCC cannot both hold.
Pratt improves the conditional Set Cover exponential base to arbitrarily close to 3/2^{2/3}, still assuming the asymptotic rank conjecture.

sentences: Set Cover asks whether a few supplied sets can cover a given universe.
The conjecture concerns exact algorithms when each available set has a fixed maximum size.
It says that no constant improvement over exponential base two works across all such size bounds.
The target allows bounded-error randomization and polynomial factors that depend on the fixed bound.
Recent results show that a major conjecture about tensor rank would refute SCC, but neither side is settled unconditionally.

cards.definitions:
Let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge1\). Each set is represented by its sorted list of distinct element indices in binary; the family is an explicitly supplied list without duplicate sets. Empty sets and an empty family are allowed. Write \(m=|\mathcal F|\). For fixed \(d\),
\[m\le\sum_{j=0}^{\min(d,n)}\binom nj\le(n+1)^d,\]
so the entire valid input has length polynomial in \(n\), with its degree allowed to depend on \(d\). The threshold can be capped at \(n\), since any cover contains a subcover of at most \(n\) sets. The question counts the universe size, not the number of available sets or selected sets, in the exponential part of the time bound.

Use a uniform random-access machine with finite program, binary words of length \(w=\lceil4(n+\log_2(m+2)+1)\rceil\), and word-addressed memory. This allows the usual exponential-size dynamic-programming tables while keeping each word polynomially many bits long. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copies, branches, comparisons, addition/subtraction/multiplication modulo \(2^w\), integer division with remainder by a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, shifts, and obtaining a uniformly random independent word. Shifts by at least \(w\) and division by zero may return zero. Initially memory holds only the input and otherwise zeroes. Every table construction and preprocessing operation is counted. The machine has no oracle or nonuniform advice, and no operation acts on an exponentially long bit string as one word. Charging polynomial bit cost for scalar word operations only alters the allowed polynomial factor.

A randomized algorithm must return the correct decision with probability at least \(2/3\) on every valid input and halt within its asserted time bound on every random tape. The bound means that for a fixed \(d,\varepsilon\), there are constants \(K,r,n_0\) for which runtime is at most \(K(2-\varepsilon)^n(n+1)^r\) whenever \(n\ge n_0\). All finite smaller valid instances must also be correctly decided. These constants and the program may depend on \(d,\varepsilon\), but not on \(n,\mathcal F,t\).

The negation is a single \(\varepsilon>0\) that works for every fixed \(d\), allowing a different algorithm and polynomial factor for each \(d\). An improved base for one particular set-size bound does not refute the conjecture. The decision version used here and the source's minimum-cover optimization version have the same exponential base: searching thresholds and recovering a cover uses only polynomially many calls for fixed \(d\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the conjecture or its negation in the stated randomized computational model. A refutation must give a uniform positive improvement of the exponential base across every fixed maximum set size. Proving a lower bound assuming SETH or another conjecture, restricting to deterministic algorithms, improving one bounded-size case, or counting only arithmetic operations on unbounded-size objects does not settle this target.

context_blocks.text: A subset dynamic program solves the problem in \(2^n\operatorname{poly}(n,m)\) time. The target asks whether the base two can be reduced by a constant independent of the maximum allowed set size. Polynomial factors are explicitly permitted and may grow with that fixed size bound.

The family is given explicitly and each set has at most d elements. This is distinct from requiring exactly d elements, requiring a partition into disjoint sets, or bounding how many sets contain each element. The 2024 source studies reductions between such variants, but the card fixes the at-most-d covering version.

Cygan and coauthors use the Set Cover assumption for tight conditional bounds on several exact algorithms. Their work does not prove that the ordinary Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis implies this Set Cover conjecture.

Björklund and Kaski prove that Strassen’s asymptotic rank conjecture would yield a randomized sub-two-base algorithm and hence refute SCC. Pratt strengthens the conditional algorithm. These are incompatibility and conditional-algorithm theorems, not unconditional resolutions of either conjecture.

cards.title: FPT approximation of twin-width
cards.formal: Do there exist total computable functions \(f,g:N\to N\) and a constant \(c\ge 1\), and one deterministic Turing machine A, such that for every finite nonempty simple graph G on n vertices and integer \(k\ge 0, A\) halts within \(f(k)(n+1)^{c}\) bit operations and either correctly reports \(tww(G)>k\) or outputs a contraction sequence of G of width at most \(g(k)\)? No order, decomposition or contraction sequence is supplied with G.
cards.definitions: The input gives n, the \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix of G, and k in binary. A contraction sequence is a sequence of partitions of \(V(G)\), starting with the singleton partition and ending with \(\{V(G)\}\), each obtained from its predecessor by merging two parts. For distinct parts X,Y, their pair is mixed if there exist both an adjacent pair \(x\in X,y\in Y\) and a nonadjacent pair \(x' \in X,y' \in Y\) in the original graph. The red degree of a part is the number of other parts with which it has a mixed pair. The sequence width is the maximum red degree over every part of every partition. Twin-width \(tww(G)\) is the minimum sequence width; a one-vertex graph has twin-width zero. The output lists the \(n- 1\) merges using integer part labels. Both f and g depend only on k, whereas c is independent of k and G. If \(tww(G)\le k\), rejection is forbidden. If \(tww(G)>k\), either a correct rejection or the stated bounded-width sequence is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. cards.title: Polynomial kernel for Edge Multiway Cut
cards.formal:
Does undirected Edge Multiway Cut, parameterized only by the allowed number \(k\) of edge deletions, admit a randomized polynomial kernel? Specifically, do there exist a uniform randomized algorithm \(R\) and positive integers \(C,a,b\) such that for every explicitly encoded instance \(I=(G,T,k)\) of length \(N\), on every random tape \(R\) halts within \(C(N+1)^a\) steps and outputs a well-formed instance \(I'=(G',T',k')\) of the same problem with
\[|I'|\le C(k+1)^b,\qquad k'\le C(k+1)^b,\]
and
\[\Pr_R[I\text{ is a yes-instance}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ I'\text{ is a yes-instance}]\ge2/3?\]
A yes-instance has a set of at most \(k\) edges whose removal leaves no connected component containing two terminals. The number of terminals is unbounded and is not an extra parameter. The constants, including the exponent \(b\), must be independent of \(|T|\).
cards.why: Kernelization asks whether the information relevant to a small cut budget can be compressed before solving the remaining hard instance. Edge Multiway Cut is a central test of that principle because it combines many terminal-separation requirements while parameterizing only the number of removed edges. A polynomial kernel would replace arbitrarily large graphs by uniformly small equivalent instances without fixing the number of terminals.

cards.definitions:
An input graph is a finite undirected unweighted loopless multigraph \(G=(V,E)\). Vertices are labeled \(1,\ldots,n\); edges are an explicitly listed sequence of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Parallel edges are distinct listed objects, each costing one deletion. The terminal set \(T\subseteq V\) consists of distinct designated vertices. The budget \(k\ge0\) is an integer in binary. Encode \(n\) in unary, the edge-list length and endpoints in a self-delimiting binary format, the terminal set as an \(n\)-bit membership vector, and \(k\) in self-delimiting binary. The total encoding length \(N\) includes every listed edge, vertex and terminal and the budget. The output uses the same format; succinct circuits, binary edge multiplicities and binary weights are not allowed.

A cut is a subset \(F\subseteq E\) of edge identities with \(|F|\le k\). The graph \(G-F\) retains every vertex and terminal. It must contain no path between any two distinct terminals. Terminals cannot be deleted, and terminal labels carry no further pairing data: every terminal must be separated from every other. Disconnected graphs, empty graphs, zero budgets and fewer than two terminals are included. The kernel need only preserve the decision answer, not the optimum cut value or every terminal-partition cut. It may relabel vertices and change the terminal set and budget.

The multigraph convention permits the contractions used in kernelization. It does not change polynomial-kernel existence relative to explicit simple graphs: replacing every edge by its own two-edge path through a fresh nonterminal gives a simple graph of polynomial encoding size with the same minimum number of edge deletions needed to separate terminals. Either part of such a path can be deleted at unit cost, while deleting both never helps beyond deleting one.

Use a uniform multitape probabilistic Turing machine with independent fair random bits and one transition per time unit, charging for writing the output. There is no advice, oracle or separately provided preprocessing. Runtime, output-format and size guarantees hold on every random tape. The probability of preserving equivalence is at least \(2/3\) for each fixed input, with two-sided error permitted. This explicitly fixes the saved card's allowance of randomized preprocessing; deterministic or one-sided-error polynomial kernels also qualify. The failure probability is not averaged over a distribution of graphs.

A polynomial kernel has size bounded solely by a fixed polynomial in \(k\), even when the original graph and terminal set are much larger. A bound such as \(k^{|T|+1}\) does not satisfy this condition, since its exponent changes with the input. A size bound \(k^{\log^{O(1)}k}\) is quasipolynomial and is likewise insufficient. Both bounds use the full encoding length, not just the number of vertices while ignoring labels, edges or weights.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the randomized polynomial-kernel claim. A positive proof must provide the preprocessing algorithm and verify the all-tape polynomial runtime, output size and parameter bounds, and per-instance equivalence probability for arbitrary terminal sets. A negative proof must rule out every algorithm in this model. A kernel for a fixed number of terminals, a reduction to a different decision language, quasipolynomial preprocessing or output size, or a conditional exclusion relying on an unproved complexity assumption does not by itself settle the stated unconditional claim.

The same work distinguishes a smaller nonconstructive mimicking-network bound from the network size achievable by randomized polynomial-time preprocessing.

The source’s mimicking networks preserve a richer family of terminal cut values. The benchmark asks only for an equivalent Edge Multiway Cut decision instance, so a solution does not need to construct such a stronger universal network.

The 2025 MFCS paper obtains deterministic kernels using quasipolynomial-time preprocessing for several problems whose randomized polynomial kernels were already known. It explicitly treats Multiway Cut with deletable terminals and separately mentions quasipolynomial-size Edge Multiway Cut kernels. cards.definitions: The input is \(n\ge1\), a target \(t\ge0\), and an explicitly listed multiset \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\) of positive integers, all in binary with delimiters; \(L\) is the bit length of that full encoding. Accept if and only if there is \(I\subseteq[n]\) with \(\sum_{i\in I}x_{i}=t\). Each index is used at most once, repetitions of values are permitted, and the empty subset is allowed. Use a uniform random-access machine with \(w=d(n+\lceil\log_{2}(L+2)\rceil)\)-bit words for fixed \(d\ge1\), large enough to address exponential memory. Unit-cost instructions are word read/write, copy, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, comparisons, Boolean operations and shifts; shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword integers are handled through charged component operations. Input packing, preprocessing and memory initialization are charged. Random words are independent and uniform and cost one instruction each. A fixed finite program receives no advice or tables. It answers correctly with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input and the time bound holds on every random execution. Constants are independent of all input values and \(n,L\). Quantum operations and random-instance promises are absent.

context_blocks.text: Subset Sum asks whether some selection of the supplied indices adds to the target exactly. For values \((3,3,5)\), target \(6\) is attainable by taking both occurrences of \(3\); an occurrence cannot be used twice. Target zero is always attainable by the empty subset. The input multiplicities and the exact integer comparison are part of the problem.

The classical meet-in-the-middle benchmark is \(2^{n/2}\) times polynomial factors. The question asks for a smaller fixed exponential rate on every input, not an improvement in one polynomial factor. A bound such as \(2^{n/2}/n^{100}\) would still leave the requested exponent saving unresolved.

Pseudopolynomial algorithms depend on the numerical target rather than just the number of bits needed to write it. They can be excellent when the target is small, but binary input values can be exponentially large relative to their descriptions. Chan’s 2026 work improves this separate regime while explicitly retaining the worst-case exponential question.

An August 2026 preprint claims a quantum \(O^{\ast}(2^{2n/7})\) algorithm and still identifies the classical half-exponent benchmark. The star notation hides polynomial factors. The use of quantum computation is decisive: this does not supply the classical algorithm quantified over here. The new preprint proof was not independently checked.

Random instances, uniqueness promises and restrictions on the magnitude or density of the numbers can also alter exponential complexity. This target has none of those input promises and permits bounded-error classical randomness on every instance. Exponential memory is allowed and addressable in the specified RAM; a polynomial-space restriction would ask a different question.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that one uniform classical randomized algorithm, constants \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), \(c\ge1\), and a constant multiplier meet the stated \(2^{(1/2-\varepsilon)n}L^c\) time bound on every random execution and success probability at least \(2/3\) on every input, or prove in Lean that no such choices exist. The theorem must allow unrestricted binary magnitudes, repeated positive values, all targets, and the full permitted RAM model.

cards.title: Single-exponential Directed Feedback Vertex Set
cards.formal: Do there exist a uniform deterministic algorithm and constants \(A,c>0\), \(d\in\mathbb N\), which decide Directed Feedback Vertex Set on every \(n\)-vertex directed graph and deletion budget \(0\le k\le n\) within \(A\,2^{ck}(n+1)^d\) bit-computation steps? The answer must be YES exactly when deleting at most \(k\) vertices makes the graph acyclic. The exponential dependence is solely on the solution-size budget, and the polynomial exponent is independent of \(k\).
cards.why: Deleting a small number of vertices to destroy every directed cycle is a basic model of repairing cyclic dependencies. Fixed-parameter algorithms make small deletion budgets tractable in principle, but the known factorial dependence is much larger than a fixed exponential base. The target asks whether directed cycle structure inherently causes that additional parameter cost.

cards.definitions: The input digraph is \(D=([n],E)\), \(n\ge1\), with \(E\subseteq[n]\times[n]\). Self-loops and opposite arcs are allowed; repeated copies of an arc are not represented and have no effect. A directed cycle is a sequence of distinct vertices \(v_1,\ldots,v_t\), \(t\ge1\), with arcs \((v_j,v_{j+1})\) for \(j<t\) and \((v_t,v_1)\). Thus self-loops are cycles of length one, and opposite arcs give a cycle of length two. For \(S\subseteq[n]\), the remaining graph is the induced digraph \(D[[n]\setminus S]\). A feedback vertex set is a set \(S\) for which this remaining digraph contains no directed cycle. Its cost is the cardinality \(|S|\); no vertex weights are present. There are no promises of planarity, bounded degree, bounded treewidth, a supplied solution or bounds on cycle length. Use a deterministic multitape Turing machine with one finite program for all \(n,k,D\), no advice and no random bits. A valid input consists of the prefix \(1^n0\), followed by the \(n^2\) adjacency bits in row-major order, followed by exactly \(\ell=\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits encoding \(k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\) in most-significant-bit-first binary. The machine must halt and return the correct decision on every valid input. Each Turing-machine transition costs one step, including all input processing and preprocessing. No running-time condition on malformed strings is part of the target. The fixed encoding has length polynomial in \(n\), so ordinary polynomial-time changes of explicit graph encoding only alter the permitted polynomial factor. The quantified constants \(A,c,d\) are independent of \(n,k,D\). The target is worst-case exact decision, including NO instances; it requires neither an optimal deletion set nor enumeration of all solutions.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked construction of the specified deterministic algorithm with its correctness and \(A2^{ck}(n+1)^d\) worst-case bound, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm and constants exist. A \(2^{O(k\log k)}n^{O(1)}\) algorithm, an exponent depending on \(k\) in the polynomial input-size factor, an approximation, or a result for restricted graph classes is insufficient for the affirmative answer. A lower bound conditional on an additional unproved hypothesis establishes only that conditional version of the negative statement.

cards.definitions: A k-expression is a finite expression building a labeled graph using labels from \(\{1,\ldots ,k\}\). It can create one isolated vertex with a chosen label; take the disjoint union of two previously constructed labeled graphs; add all edges between the vertices labeled i and those labeled j for distinct i,j; or change every label i to j. Edge insertion leaves existing edges in place without duplicating them. Relabeling changes no edges. The two operands of a disjoint union may both be arbitrary expressions, so this is ordinary clique-width, not linear clique-width. For a nonempty graph \(G, \operatorname{cw}(G)\) is the least k for which some k-expression produces a graph isomorphic to G after labels are erased. Set \(\operatorname{cw}(\varnothing )=0\). The input contains \(n\ge 0\) and the \(n\times n\) symmetric zero-diagonal \(0/1\) adjacency matrix for the graph on \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). It contains no construction expression or promise about its width. \(A_{k}\) outputs YES exactly when \(\operatorname{cw}(G)\le k\) and NO otherwise, always halting with the stated worst-case bit bound. The quantifier order is \(\forall k \exists A_{k},C_{k},c_{k} \forall G: k\) is fixed for each machine, and the polynomial exponent may depend on it. Each \(A_{k}\) is a single finite program with no advice depending on graph size; the statement imposes no effective map from k to its program and no uniform exponent.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove polynomial-time exact recognition for every fixed threshold k in the model stated, or prove that for at least one fixed k the language \(\{G:\operatorname{cw}(G)\le k\}\) has no deterministic polynomial-time decider. An expression with more than k labels does not establish a YES answer; failure of one construction does not establish NO. Variable-k NP-hardness, or fixed-k hardness under an unproved assumption, does not alone unconditionally refute this proposition.

context_blocks.title: A width that permits dense graphs
context_blocks.text: Clique-width counts reusable labels in a construction, not the size of a largest clique. Every nonempty edgeless graph has width 1. Complete graphs with at least two vertices have width 2, regardless of their size. Thus even very dense graphs can have small clique-width; the parameter captures how uniformly groups of vertices can be assembled.

context_blocks.title: Fixed thresholds versus the general optimization problem
context_blocks.text: Fellows and coauthors prove NP-completeness when both G and k are input. The present statement allows a different polynomial bound for each fixed k. For example, a hypothetical bound \(N^{k+2}\) would be polynomial for each such threshold, while not giving a polynomial bound when k grows with N. The source lists fixed-threshold recognition separately from the stronger FPT question, which asks for one algorithm with runtime \(f(k)N^{c}\) and c independent of k.

context_blocks.title: Small thresholds are understood
context_blocks.text: Polynomial-time recognition is known through \(k=3\), with the full three-label algorithm published by Corneil and coauthors in 2012. The cited sources retain \(k=4\) as the first unresolved threshold. A solution only for four labels would still leave the card’s quantification over every fixed k.

context_blocks.title: Approximate or supplied decompositions serve a different purpose
context_blocks.text: A procedure that returns an expression with \(f(k)>k\) labels for graphs of width at most k can enable other graph algorithms, yet leave the exact threshold undecided. Likewise, the July 2026 feedback-vertex-set result assumes a k-expression is already supplied. These results explain the usefulness of clique-width without providing the recognizer requested here.

cards.title: Independent set algorithms from tropical circuit size
cards.formal: Do there exist one deterministic Turing machine A and constants \(C,c\ge 1\) such that for every finite simple graph G on \(n\ge 1\) vertices and nonnegative integer weight vector w, A outputs the maximum independent-set weight within \(C(\tau (G)+n+\mathrm{L}+1)^{c}\) bit operations, where L is the total binary encoding length of w and \(\tau (G)\) is the minimum size of a tropical MWIS circuit defined below? Only G and w are supplied; neither \(\tau (G)\) nor a circuit is part of the input.
cards.definitions: G is given by its \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix. The n nonnegative weights are binary integers with delimiters, all counted in L. A vertex set I is independent when no edge has both endpoints in I. \(MWIS(G,w)=\max\)_{I independent}\(\sum_{v\in I}w_{v}\), allowing \(I=\varnothing\) with weight zero. A tropical circuit for G is a finite acyclic circuit with one designated output, arbitrary fan-out, input gates labeled \(x_{v}\) or the constant 0, and binary internal gates labeled max or + with their ordinary real-number meanings. No other constants or operations are allowed. Size counts every gate, including input and constant gates. An MWIS circuit must output \(MWIS(G,x)\) for every vector \(x\in R_{\ge}0^{n}\), so its topology depends only on G. Define \(\tau (G)\) as the minimum size of such a circuit. This minimum exists because finitely many independent sets can each be summed and their maximum computed. The output algorithm may use general deterministic computation, not only tropical operations. Constants C,c are uniform over all graphs and weight vectors.
