cards.title: Fixed-parameter tractability of graph isomorphism by rank-width
cards.formal: Do a computable function \(f:\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}\), an absolute constant c and a deterministic algorithm exist which decide isomorphism of graphs G,H in time \(f(k)(|V(G)|+|V(H)|+2)^{c}\), where \(k=\max (\operatorname{rw}(G),\operatorname{rw}(H))\)?
cards.definitions: Graphs are finite simple undirected graphs given by adjacency matrices. Isomorphism is a vertex bijection preserving adjacency. For a graph G and \(X\subseteq V(G)\), the cut-rank is the rank over the two-element field of the adjacency submatrix with rows X and columns \(V(G)\setminus X\). A rank decomposition is a tree of maximum degree three whose leaves are bijectively labeled by \(V(G)\). Every tree edge partitions the leaves and hence defines a cut-rank; the decomposition width is the maximum of those ranks. Rank-width \(\operatorname{rw}(G)\) is the minimum width, with \(\operatorname{rw}(G)=0\) for at most one vertex. No decomposition or parameter value is supplied to the algorithm. The exponent c is independent of the rank-width.

context_blocks.text: Rank-width measures graph complexity through low-rank adjacency cuts and supports many structural algorithms. Graph isomorphism on bounded rank-width is tractable at each fixed width, but that does not by itself yield one exponent independent of the parameter.

cards.title: Polynomial exact metric sparsifiers with a crossing-edge budget
cards.formal: Do there exist absolute constants \(C,c>0\) such that the following holds? For every finite simple undirected unweighted graph \(G=(V,E)\), terminal set \(T\subseteq V\) of size r, and integer \(p\ge 0\), there is a set \(Z\subseteq E\) with |\(Z|\le C(1+p+r)^{c}\) having this universal property: for every finite nonempty label set D, every metric \(\mu :D\times D\to R_{\ge 0}\), and every terminal labeling \(\tau :T\to D\), if there exists a labeling \(\lambda :V\to D\) extending \(\tau\) with at most p crossing edges, then some labeling \(\lambda\)* of minimum \(\mu\)-cost among all such budget-feasible extensions has all its crossing edges in Z. The same Z must work simultaneously for every \(D,\mu ,\tau\) and depends only on G,T,p. This is the polynomial-size version of the contraction-based metric-sparsifier property in the source’s Theorem 22; that theorem’s earlier quasipolynomial upper-bound claim was later retracted.

cards.definitions: A crossing edge of \(\lambda\) is an edge uv with \(\lambda (u)\ne \lambda (v)\). Write \(X(\lambda )=\{uv\in E:\lambda (u)\ne \lambda (v)\}\) and \(\operatorname{cost}_{\mu}(\lambda )=\sum_{uv\in E}\mu (\lambda (u),\lambda (v))\). A metric has \(\mu (a,b)=\mu (b,a), \mu (a,b)=0\) exactly when \(a=b\), and \(\mu (a,c)\le \mu (a,b)+\mu (b,c)\). The admissible labelings for a query are \(B(G,T,p,D,\tau )\)={\(\lambda :V\to D:\lambda |_{T}=\tau\) and |\(X(\lambda )|\le p\)}. If B is nonempty, the finite set \(D^{V}\) ensures that \(\min _{\lambda \in B}\operatorname{cost}_{\mu}(\lambda )\) is attained. The universal requirement is that this minimum equals the minimum with the additional constraint \(X(\lambda )\subseteq Z\); in particular the latter feasible set must be nonempty. The number p bounds crossings, not the real-valued metric cost. Labeling \(\tau\) need not be injective or surjective, and |D| is unbounded independently of \(p+r\). The constants C,c may not depend on the graph, budget, label set, metric or terminal labeling. Using \(1+p+r\) only handles zero parameters and is asymptotically equivalent to polynomial size in \(p+r\). Restricting all edges outside Z to have equal endpoint labels is exactly the labeling constraint imposed by contracting those edges; Z measures the original retained edges. The question is existence of this universal set, not the running time to find it, so it neither assumes rational metric entries nor a numerical oracle for them. Exact equality of optimum values is required; no multiplicative or additive error is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated universal polynomial bound, or refute it by showing that no fixed constants C,c can bound the required retained edges over all G,T,p. A negative result must respect the quantifier order: every candidate small Z must fail for some label set, metric and terminal labeling with a feasible budgeted extension. Hardness of finding a small Z does not disprove its existence. Bounds for one fixed metric, a fixed number of labels, ordinary terminal cut values, or approximate values do not settle this target.

cards.title: Polynomial kernels for minor-free edge deletion
cards.formal: Does every fixed finite family \(\mathcal H\) of finite simple undirected graphs admit a deterministic polynomial kernel for \(\mathcal H\)-Minor-Free Edge Deletion, parameterized only by the number \(k\) of edges that may be deleted? An instance is a finite simple undirected graph \(G\) and an integer \(k\ge0\). It is a yes-instance if there exists \(F\subseteq E(G)\) with \(|F|\le k\) such that \(G-F\) contains no graph from \(\mathcal H\) as a minor. The kernel must return one equivalent instance of this same problem with total encoding length and output parameter bounded by a polynomial in \(k+1\), as specified below.
cards.why: A polynomial kernel would bound all information relevant to the deletion decision by a polynomial in the allowed number of changes, irrespective of the size of the original graph. This would make minor exclusion a broad source of effective preprocessing for edge repair. The distinction from vertex deletion matters because deleting a few edges can leave all vertices present and does not provide the same structural control as removing a small set of vertices.
cards.status_note: Explicitly open in the 2020 source and retained in the 2023 published survey. Bounded later-work checks through 2026-09-15 did not identify a deterministic polynomial kernel for every fixed forbidden-minor family, or an unconditional refutation. Existing vertex-deletion kernels and algorithms assuming minor-free inputs have different scopes.

It tests whether fixed-parameter tractability can be strengthened to polynomial preprocessing for edge modifications, a substantially different setting from established vertex-deletion results.

sentences: The problem deletes at most k edges so that the remaining graph excludes every member of a fixed forbidden-minor family.
It asks whether every such family permits a polynomial-time reduction to one equivalent instance of polynomial size in k.
The input graph is arbitrary, and all vertices remain available during edge deletion.
A general kernel would provide a broad preprocessing guarantee for structural graph repair beyond known fixed-parameter algorithms.
The card restores the family quantifier and distinguishes vertex deletion, promised minor-free inputs and more general compressions.

cards.definitions: A graph \(H\) is a minor of \(G\) if it can be obtained by deleting vertices, deleting edges and contracting edges; after contraction, loops are discarded and parallel edges are merged. These operations define containment only. In the deletion problem itself, the permitted modifications are deletions of original edges: \(G-F\) retains every vertex. A graph is \(\mathcal H\)-minor-free when no \(H\in\mathcal H\) is its minor. Families and their graphs may be disconnected; no member is required to be planar. The empty family and empty graphs are allowed under the stated minor definition, including their trivial cases. The family is fixed before the input graph and budget and is not counted as an input parameter. Graph \(G\) has labelled vertices \([n]\), possibly \(n=0\), and is encoded by a length-delimited binary integer \(n\) and its upper-triangular adjacency-bit array. The budget is a length-delimited binary integer \(k\); let \(L\) be the total input bit length. A polynomial kernel for fixed \(\mathcal H\) means that there exist one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A_{\mathcal H}\), constants \(C_{\mathcal H}\ge1\), and integers \(b_{\mathcal H},d_{\mathcal H}\ge1\) such that for every \((G,k)\) it outputs a graph \(G^{\prime}\) and integer \(k^{\prime}\ge0\) in at most \(C_{\mathcal H}(L+2)^{b_{\mathcal H}}\) bit steps, with \[(G,k)\text{ is yes}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ (G^{\prime},k^{\prime})\text{ is yes},\qquad |\operatorname{enc}(G^{\prime},k^{\prime})|+k^{\prime}\le C_{\mathcal H}(k+1)^{d_{\mathcal H}}.\] The output uses the same graph and budget encoding and the same fixed forbidden family. The machine has a fixed finite number of tapes and a finite alphabet, with initially blank work tapes; input, output and all preprocessing are charged. No randomness, oracle, graph-dependent advice, extra weights or annotations, or calls to an instance-solving oracle are allowed. Constants and the finite program may depend on the entire fixed family, but not on \(G\) or \(k\); a uniform procedure compiling an arbitrary family into its kernel is not additionally required. Input graphs have no promise of being minor-free initially. The parameter bound includes \(k=0\) through \(k+1\). Binary encoding of very large budgets does not authorize time polynomial in their numerical value; the task has only \(|E(G)|\) possible edge deletions, so budgets above this value are equivalent to that capped budget.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universally quantified kernel-existence statement, or of its negation. An affirmative proof must establish a finite deterministic polynomial-time kernel for every fixed finite forbidden family, together with the equivalence and size/parameter bounds on every input. A negative proof must establish failure for at least one specified fixed family. A result for a family containing a planar graph alone, a vertex-deletion kernel, a kernel on already minor-free input graphs, a randomized compression, or a polynomial Turing kernel does not establish the full target. A kernel with output in a different annotated or weighted problem does not suffice unless the conversion to the stated unweighted problem and its size bound are proved. Conditional lower bounds remain conditional unless their additional assumptions are proved. This is a yes/no preprocessing question, not an estimate of the optimum deletion count.

context_blocks.text: The survey’s notation uses a family of forbidden graphs, not just one forbidden graph. Its Open Problem 2.13 follows the separate planar-deletion question and concerns removing edges to obtain a minor-free graph. The card restores that family scope and uses minor containment, which is distinct from the induced-subgraph containment discussed elsewhere in the survey.

The source records fixed-parameter tractability for the deletion task, but asks for the stronger polynomial-kernel property. An algorithm with an arbitrary parameter-dependent factor can decide small-budget instances without providing a polynomial-size equivalent instance in polynomial input time.

The 2023 published survey retains Open Problem 2.13. It contrasts the edge problem with kernels for deleting vertices when the forbidden family includes a planar graph. Those vertex results neither remove the edge-versus-vertex distinction nor cover every forbidden family required here.

A kernel must preserve the decision on arbitrary input graphs, including graphs that already satisfy the target property and those far from it. It is not enough to assume the input is minor-free or to return a list of oracle queries. Changes to the graph representation, allowable modifications or parameter must be included in the equivalence and size proof.

The 2025 robust contraction-decomposition result obtains algorithms for several deletion and cut problems on graphs that are already minor-free. Here minor-freeness is the desired output property after modifications, so that result’s input restriction describes a different task and does not settle the kernel question.

cards.title: ETH barrier to single-exponential treewidth computation
cards.formal: Assuming the deterministic Exponential-Time Hypothesis (ETH) defined below, is an exact single-exponential parameterized algorithm for Treewidth impossible? Specifically, let \(\mathrm{FastTW}\) mean that there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(A\), constants \(C\ge1\), and integers \(a,b\ge1\) such that, for every simple undirected graph \(G\) on \(n\ge1\) vertices and every integer \(0\le k<n\), \(A(G,k)\) decides whether \(\operatorname{tw}(G)\le k\) correctly within \(C\,2^{ak}(n+2)^b\) steps. Under the assumption ETH, determine whether \(\neg\mathrm{FastTW}\) or \(\mathrm{FastTW}\) holds. This selects the explicit single-exponential example in the source’s broader request for lower bounds.
cards.why: Treewidth is a central measure of how close a graph is to a tree, and a decomposition is often the prerequisite for running efficient parameterized algorithms. The cost of finding the optimum can therefore dominate the cost of using the structure. Establishing whether a single-exponential dependence is compatible with ETH would locate a major boundary between structural preprocessing and algorithms that work once a decomposition is already known.
cards.status_note: The 2014 source explicitly asks whether ETH excludes a single-exponential parameterized exact algorithm. The checked 2023 upper bound has quadratic parameter dependence in the exponent, while Bonnet’s 2025/2026 lower bound excludes subexponential dependence but not single-exponential dependence. Bounded checks through 2026-09-15 did not locate a resolution of this remaining conditional question.

progress.text: Bodlaender poses the explicit ETH question about exact single-exponential parameter dependence in Seminar 14451, Section 4.7, printed page 18.
Korhonen and Lokshtanov’s STOC 2023 result gives exact treewidth in \(2^{O(k^2)}n^{O(1)}\) time. The checked arXiv version 2 is dated 17 August 2023.

Bonnet’s arXiv version 2 proves the ETH-tight exponential lower bound in the vertex count and explicitly leaves the gap to quadratic parameter dependence in the exponent. This is not a super-single-exponential parameter lower bound.

The Journal of the ACM posts Bonnet’s accepted manuscript; the publisher records acceptance on 19 July 2026. These publication dates concern the established exponential lower bound, not a new resolution of the single-exponential parameter question.

sentences: Treewidth is the smallest maximum bag size minus one among tree decompositions of a graph.
The target asks whether ETH rules out exact decision in single-exponential time in the requested width and polynomial time in graph size.
The algorithm must handle every input without receiving a decomposition or a promise that the width threshold is met.
Resolving the question would clarify the cost of discovering the structural information used by many parameterized algorithms.
The new exponential lower bound in the number of vertices is recorded separately because it does not exclude the requested parameter dependence.

cards.definitions: A tree decomposition of \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite nonempty tree \(T\) together with bags \(B_t\subseteq V\) for \(t\in V(T)\), such that every graph vertex belongs to some bag, every edge has both endpoints in one bag, and for each \(v\in V\) the set \(\{t:v\in B_t\}\) induces a connected subtree. Its width is \(\max_t|B_t|-1\), and \(\operatorname{tw}(G)\) is the minimum width over all decompositions. Graphs may be disconnected, with isolated vertices. Their input representation is the binary integer \(n\), the upper-triangular adjacency-bit array on labelled vertices \([n]\), and the binary integer \(k\), using length-delimited fields. The task is exact decision on every input, including graphs with treewidth larger than \(k\); there is no supplied decomposition or promise that the answer is yes. A Turing machine has a fixed finite number of tapes over a fixed finite alphabet, a read-only input tape, initially blank work tapes and a binary output. Each transition moves each head by at most one cell, and all input processing is charged. Programs and constants are uniform in both \(n\) and \(k\); no advice, randomness, oracle or unbounded-precision unit-cost operation is available. The single-exponential class here allows arbitrary constant polynomial factors in \(n\). ETH means that there exists a real \(\delta>0\) such that no deterministic machine in this model decides every 3-CNF formula \(F\) in time \(C\,2^{\delta N}(L+2)^b\) for any fixed \(C\ge1\) and integer \(b\ge1\). Here \(N\ge1\) is the number of Boolean variables, \(L\) is the full binary encoding length, and each clause is a disjunction of at most three literals, each literal being a variable or its negation. The input gives \(N\) in unary and the clauses as length-delimited lists of signed binary variable indices; repeated clauses are permitted. The treewidth and ETH time bounds are worst-case. Exponential dependence on the parameter alone is the target, distinct from an exponential dependence on the entire vertex count.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean, with ETH as the explicit assumption, of either \(\neg\mathrm{FastTW}\) or \(\mathrm{FastTW}\). A proof of impossibility must rule out every constant \(a,b,C\) and every uniform machine meeting the full exact decision specification. A constructive answer must supply such a machine and prove the bound and correctness; an unconditional construction is sufficient for that direction. The accepted theorem must clearly retain its conditional scope and must not claim to establish ETH itself. Ruling out \(2^{o(k)}n^{O(1)}\) time does not rule out \(2^{O(k)}n^{O(1)}\) time. Approximate decompositions, algorithms assuming a decomposition is supplied, or bounds for another problem parameterized by treewidth do not meet this target. This is a binary complexity question, not a numerical approximation of the integer treewidth.

context_blocks.text: Bodlaender’s source asks broadly for time lower bounds and explicitly highlights whether \(2^{O(k)}n^{O(1)}\) time can be ruled out under ETH. The present target retains that conditional single-exponential question, rather than treating any lower bound as a resolution. The exact decision formulation makes the parameter and both yes and no instances explicit.

Korhonen and Lokshtanov improve the exact parameter dependence to \(2^{O(k^2)}n^{O(1)}\), breaking the earlier cubic dependence in the exponent. Their faster approximation result has a different output guarantee. Neither result supplies an exact single-exponential algorithm.

Bonnet establishes an ETH-based \(2^{\Omega(n)}\) lower bound for exact treewidth on \(n\)-vertex graphs. In particular this excludes a subexponential dependence on the treewidth parameter with a polynomial factor in \(n\). It still permits a single-exponential parameterized algorithm, so it does not settle Bodlaender’s explicit example.

The decision formulation is the standard parameterized exact treewidth task. Optimal value computation and finding a suitable decomposition have close algorithmic connections, but the theorem requested here is explicitly about exact decision with a threshold input. It does not impose an additional restriction on polynomial space, polynomial degree or a supplied structural certificate.

The 2026 journal acceptance of Bonnet’s paper confirms publication progress for the lower bound, while its further-work discussion distinguishes the remaining parameter gap. Recent dynamic approximation and algorithms for other tasks on bounded-treewidth graphs address different questions.

The source question asks for an exact algorithm whose running time has a fixed exponential base below two in the number of vertices.
The card specifies deterministic bit complexity, arbitrary unweighted directed graphs and an actual optimum arc set as output.

A resolution would clarify whether this basic precedence-ordering problem can beat the longstanding base-two exact-algorithm benchmark.

cards.definitions:
An input consists of \(n\ge0\) and an \(n\times n\) binary adjacency matrix with zero diagonal. It represents \(D=([n],A)\), with one possible arc for each ordered pair of distinct vertices. Both opposite arcs between a pair may occur. There are no parallel copies, loops, weights, bounds on degree or density, connectivity promises, or restrictions to tournaments or planar graphs. The vertex number is encoded in binary along with the full matrix; the empty graph is allowed.

For \(B\subseteq A\), the spanning subgraph \(([n],B)\) is acyclic when it contains no directed cycle: there are no pairwise distinct vertices \(v_1,\ldots,v_k\) with \(k\ge2\) and arcs \((v_i,v_{i+1})\in B\) for every cyclic index \(i\). All original vertices remain, including isolated vertices. Define
\[
\operatorname{mas}(D)=\max\{|B|:B\subseteq A,\ ([n],B)\text{ is acyclic}\}.
\]
The output is the binary incidence vector of a subset \(B\subseteq A\) with \(|B|=\operatorname{mas}(D)\). Merely producing an inclusion-maximal acyclic set does not meet this task.

An algorithm is one finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program, with ordinary bit-cost input access, computation and output. Its worst-case running time, including all preprocessing, is bounded as stated on every valid graph. It has no oracle, random instructions or advice depending on \(n\), and there is no independent polynomial-space requirement. The constants \(c,K,a\) and the program are independent of the graph and its order. Polynomial factors in the input size can be written as polynomial factors in \(n+1\), since the matrix has \(n^2\) entries.

The required improvement is a fixed exponential base below two. Equivalently one can absorb the polynomial factor into a slightly larger base still below two and require a bound \(K'(c')^n\) with \(c'<2\). A factor saving that leaves exponential base two is insufficient. Exact output is part of this computational task, rather than an invitation to estimate a numerical benchmark value.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of such an algorithm, its exact optimal output and the worst-case bit-complexity bound for all valid inputs, or a complete Lean proof that no such constants and algorithm exist. Conditional lower bounds do not prove this unconditional negation. Algorithms for a proper graph subclass, approximation algorithms, or bounds exponential in the number of deleted arcs rather than vertices do not by themselves settle the assertion. No \(1/100\) additive tolerance applies to the asymptotic running-time target.

cards.definitions: A parameterized decision problem Q is a subset of \(\{0,1\}*\times N\), with input \((x,k), n=|x|\) and k supplied in binary. XNLP consists of those Q decided by one nondeterministic multitape Turing machine using time \(g(k)(n+2)^{a}\) and working space \(g(k)\log _{2}(n+2)\) for some total computable g and constant a, simultaneously on every branch. An input is accepted exactly when some branch accepts; all branches halt within the bound. The input tape is read-only and excluded from working space, which counts visited cells on the fixed finite-alphabet work tapes. A parameterized logspace reduction \(Q_{1}\le Q_{2}\) is a deterministic halting transducer mapping \((x,k)\) to \((y,k' )\), preserving the yes/no answer, with \(k' \le h(k)\) for a total computable h and space \(h(k)+C \log _{2}(n+2)\) for an absolute C. Its output is write-only and is not counted as working space. Q is XNLP-hard when every problem in XNLP has such a reduction to Q. In the conjectured forbidden deterministic algorithm there is no randomness, oracle or advice, and a single program handles all parameters. Constants, including c and the code computing f, are fixed for that program; f may grow arbitrarily fast but must be computable. Using different computable functions in the time and space bounds is equivalent, since one common f can dominate both. Replacing n by \(n+2\) only handles short inputs. Slice-wise polynomial time allows its exponent to depend on k; the conjectured space bound permits dependence on k only in a multiplicative factor.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the simultaneous resource obstruction for every XNLP-hard problem, or refute it by an XNLP-hard problem and one uniform deterministic algorithm satisfying both bounds for explicit computable f and fixed c. A space bound achieved by a different algorithm, a time bound with a superpolynomial exponent in n at fixed k, or a result for only bounded parameter values does not meet the criterion.

cards.title: Disjoint-union closure of tractable forbidden patterns
cards.formal: For every pair of fixed nonempty finite simple graphs \(H_{1},H_{2}\), is the following implication true? If Independent Set parameterized by the requested set size k is fixed-parameter tractable on \(H_{1}\)-free graphs and is fixed-parameter tractable on \(H_{2}\)-free graphs, then it is fixed-parameter tractable on \((H_{1}\sqcup H_{2})\)-free graphs. Here exclusion is as an induced subgraph, ⊔ is disjoint union of the forbidden patterns, and fixed-parameter tractability has the deterministic meaning defined below. The two forbidden graphs may themselves be disconnected and may be isomorphic.
cards.why: A closure theorem would reduce the classification of parameterized Independent Set with one forbidden induced pattern to its connected components. It would organize many currently separate tractability results through one general structural principle.
cards.status_note: Read the original conjecture, induced-exclusion definition and parameter convention, the expanded journal manuscript’s conclusion, and the later ISAAC paper’s individual-pattern results and randomness qualification. Searched subsequent work without finding a resolution of the full closure implication. This is a source-grounded open status, not an exhaustive absence proof. No independent proof verification.

references.title: Parameterized Complexity of Independent Set in H-Free Graphs
references.authors: Bonnet, Édouard; Bousquet, Nicolas; Charbit, Pierre; Thomassé, Stéphan; Watrigant, Rémi
references.locator: Unresolved-question passage on page 12; PDF page 12

cards.definitions: For a fixed graph H, an input to Independent Set on H-free graphs is a finite simple undirected graph G on n labeled vertices, encoded by its adjacency matrix, and a binary integer k with \(0\le k\le n\), under the promise that no subset of \(V(G)\) induces a graph isomorphic to H. The answer is YES exactly when there is a set \(S\subseteq V(G)\) with |\(S|\ge k\) and no edge between distinct members of S. Only k is the parameter; H is fixed in the definition of the restricted problem and is not supplied as a variable-size input. Call H tractable if there exist a deterministic algorithm \(A_{H}, a\) total computable function \(f_{H}:\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}\) and a constant \(c_{H}\ge 0\) such that \(A_{H}\) correctly decides every promised input in at most \(f_{H}(k)(n+1)^{c_{H}}\) bit operations. The algorithm is uniform over n,k and its guarantees are worst-case and exact. Behavior outside the H-free promise is unrestricted. Constants, algorithms and computable functions may depend on H, while \(c_{H}\) cannot depend on k or n. For \(H_{1}\sqcup H_{2}\) take disjoint copies of their vertex sets, preserve the edges within each copy, and put no edges between copies. Thus a graph contains an induced \(H_{1}\sqcup H_{2}\) precisely when it has disjoint induced copies of \(H_{1}\) and \(H_{2}\) with no cross-edge between them. Excluding this one disconnected pattern is weaker than simultaneously excluding both \(H_{1}\) and \(H_{2}\). The conjecture says that the set of tractable forbidden patterns is closed under ⊔. Its quantifier is over existence of algorithms for each fixed pair; it does not additionally demand one effective transformation that constructs an algorithm from descriptions of \(H_{1},H_{2}\) or from the two assumed algorithms. Input graphs G are not promised to be disconnected. Weighted Independent Set and randomized fixed-parameter algorithms define different variants; this card uses the source’s unqualified deterministic FPT convention.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that for every fixed \(H_{1},H_{2}\) satisfying the two tractability premises there exist an algorithm A, a computable f and a constant c, all allowed to depend on that pair, deciding the \((H_{1}\sqcup H_{2})\)-free problem in \(f(k)(n+1)^{c}\) time; or refute this universal implication. A refutation must establish both premises and failure of the conclusion for its pair. A \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hardness proof for the conclusion is only a conditional refutation unless the relevant FPT-versus-\(\mathrm{W}[1]\) separation is assumed explicitly. A result for the intersection of the two graph classes or for disjoint input components does not settle this statement.

cards.title: Expected FPT delay from small-witness decision
cards.formal: Does every self-contained \(k\)-witness problem whose decision version is fixed-parameter tractable admit an always-correct randomized enumeration algorithm with expected delay \(f(k)L^{O(1)}\), where \(L\) is the encoded input length and \(f\) is a computable function? This selects the expected-delay branch of the source question; deterministic delay and the weaker incremental bounds are distinct companion questions.
cards.why: Tests how far an efficient existence test can be converted into a reliably responsive generator of all small solutions. The distinction between total work and delays matters when a solution set is large and users need successive answers before enumeration finishes.

references.title: Randomised Enumeration of Small Witnesses Using a Decision Oracle
references.locator: Unresolved-question passage on page 11; PDF page 11

cards.definitions:
A problem instance I has an explicitly represented finite universe U and a parameter k≥1. Its witnesses form a family W(I,k) of k-element subsets of U, not a family of ordered tuples or of certificates attached to the same subset. For example, when a witness is a k-vertex set supporting a path, several paths on that same vertex set do not create several witnesses. Each output is one subset, represented by its sorted list of element indices. The output order among subsets is unrestricted. Let N=|W(I,k)|; the algorithm is not given N. Instances with k>|U| have no witnesses.

“Self-contained” means that restricting the instance to X⊆U preserves exactly the witnesses contained in X: W(I|X,k)={W∈W(I,k):W⊆X}. The restriction examines only the retained elements and their relationships, is computable in polynomial time, and has encoded length polynomial in the original length L. A decision procedure on I|X therefore answers whether X contains a witness of the original instance. This is the inclusion query INC(I,X,k). Witnesses whose validity depends on their relationships to deleted elements, such as a vertex cover of the original graph, do not automatically satisfy this property.

The premise is a deterministic algorithm deciding whether W(I,k) is nonempty in time g(k)L^a, for some computable g and constant a independent of k and I. It thus also implements inclusion queries with an FPT bound. The desired enumerator may depend on the fixed witness problem, as may f and its constant polynomial exponent, but all of them must be uniform over its instances and parameter values. This is an implication between algorithmic existence statements; it does not additionally require an effective compiler from arbitrary decision-program code, or restrict the enumerator to a black-box oracle.

For a fixed input, let τ_i be the time when the ith distinct witness has finished being written, τ₀=0, and τ_{N+1} the termination time. Expected FPT delay requires E[τ_{i+1}−τ_i]≤f(k)(L+1)^b for every i=0,…,N, with a constant b independent of k,I,i,N. When N=0 it bounds the whole time to termination. Expectation is over the internal randomness on this fixed input, without conditioning on a particular random execution history. The algorithm never outputs a false or duplicate witness and finishes the complete list with probability one. Its bound charges all work, including any preprocessing, inclusion-query execution, duplicate handling and writing outputs. The question imposes no additional polynomial-space requirement.

An expected-incremental-FPT bound instead allows E[τ_{i+1}−τ_i]≤h(k)(L+i+1)^c, which grows with the number already output. An expected-output-FPT bound controls only the final expected time by h(k)(L+N+1)^c. Such a total bound may conceal a long wait before the next output. Dropping “expected” requires the corresponding deterministic bound. These notions are not identified with each other here. An extension query additionally asks whether some witness W satisfies Y⊆W⊆X for a prescribed Y; the premise provides no such forced-inclusion operation.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated implication for all self-contained k-witness problems, or exhibit a problem satisfying its decision premise and prove that no enumerator with the stated expected-delay guarantee exists, with any complexity assumption made explicit. A bound only on final expected running time, a delay allowed to grow polynomially with the number already output, a randomized list that can omit witnesses, or a result assuming an efficient extension oracle does not settle this selected branch. The source’s deterministic and incremental companion questions require separate conclusions.

cards.definitions:
The family \(\mathcal F\) is fixed before inputs are supplied; it is not part of the parameterized input. Its members are finite nonempty undirected graphs and may be disconnected. The original source allows parallel edges, as in its two-vertex examples. Use finite undirected loopless multigraphs with all edge copies explicitly listed for the general convention here; simple graphs are included.

A graph \(H\) is a minor of \(G\) if it can be obtained from a subgraph by contracting edges. Contraction identifies their endpoints, removes resulting loops and retains parallel edges. It is not induced-subgraph containment or topological-minor containment.

The input consists of \(G\) and a nonnegative integer \(k\). It is a yes-instance if there is \(S\subseteq V(G)\) with \(|S|\leq k\) such that \(G-S\) contains no member of \(\mathcal F\) as a minor. All vertices have unit deletion cost. There is no planarity, degree, connectivity or sparsity promise on \(G\). The empty forbidden family is trivial and may be omitted. Since every forbidden graph is nonempty, \(k\geq |V(G)|\) is immediately a yes-instance.

A polynomial kernel is a deterministic algorithm that runs in a polynomial in the total binary input length and outputs a single pair \((G^{\prime},k^{\prime})\) for the same fixed family. It must preserve the yes/no answer exactly on every input. There must be constants \(C_{\mathcal F},c_{\mathcal F}\) such that the total bit length of the output and the numerical value \(k'\) are at most \(C_{\mathcal F}(k+1)^{c_{\mathcal F}}\). Vertex labels can be renumbered. Counting only vertices while leaving arbitrarily many explicit parallel edges or a large encoded parameter would not suffice.

The algorithm, its polynomial running-time degree and the output exponent may depend on \(\mathcal F\). The question does not require one exponent that works for all families, nor an effective procedure constructing the kernel algorithm from an arbitrary family description. Such uniformity requirements would strengthen the target.

The parameter is the solution budget \(k\). It is not the size of a supplied vertex cover, a set whose removal leaves bounded treedepth, or another structural parameter. A kernel supplies one smaller equivalent instance, unlike an algorithm querying many small instances. Approximate kernels that lose a constant factor in deletion cost do not satisfy the exact equivalence requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove a polynomial kernel for every fixed finite forbidden family in this solution-budget model, allowing family-dependent exponents, or establish that some fixed family does not admit one. A conventional lower bound of the form “a polynomial kernel would imply NP is contained in coNP/poly” must retain that complexity assumption and is a conditional obstruction, not an unconditional separation. Special-family algorithms and approximate or structural-parameter kernels alone do not establish the universal claim.

cards.title: Polynomial kernels for Directed Feedback Vertex Set
cards.formal:
Does Directed Feedback Vertex Set admit a deterministic polynomial kernel parameterized solely by the deletion budget? More precisely, do there exist a deterministic algorithm \(K\), constants \(C,c>0\), and a polynomial \(p\), such that for every finite digraph \(D\) and nonnegative integer \(k\), \(K\) runs in at most \(p(L)\) steps on the explicit input of bit length \(L\), and outputs one instance \((D^{\prime},k^{\prime})\) of the same problem satisfying
\[
D\text{ has a directed feedback vertex set of size at most }k
\iff
D^{\prime}\text{ has one of size at most }k^{\prime},
\]
with the entire output encoding having at most \(C(k+1)^{c}\) bits? The constants and algorithm must work for all inputs. No additional structural parameter or promise on the input or the remaining acyclic graph is permitted.

references.authors: Mnich, Matthias; van Leeuwen, Erik Jan
references.locator: Explicit open question on PDF page 2

cards.definitions:
A digraph \(D=(V,A)\) has a finite explicitly listed vertex set and an arc set \(A\subseteq V\times V\). Self-loops and opposite arcs are allowed; repeated copies of an arc have no effect and need not be represented. A directed cycle is a sequence of distinct vertices \(v_{0},\ldots,v_{r-1}\), with \(r\ge1\), having arcs from each vertex to the next, including from \(v_{r-1}\) to \(v_{0}\). Thus a self-loop is a cycle and two opposite arcs form a cycle.

A directed feedback vertex set is a subset \(S\subseteq V\) such that the induced digraph \(D[V\setminus S]\) has no directed cycle. The decision instance is YES exactly when some such set has \(|S|\le k\). The remaining graph may be any directed acyclic graph, including a disconnected one.

Encode vertices by integers \(1,\ldots,n\), list all vertices and arcs, and encode \(k\) in binary using a fixed ordinary self-delimiting binary encoding. Measure preprocessing time on a deterministic multitape Turing machine in the total input length \(L\). The output uses the same encoding, with newly numbered vertices and a nonnegative binary integer \(k^{\prime}\). Bounding only the number of output vertices while permitting arbitrarily much auxiliary information would not meet the stated size requirement.

A kernel preserves the YES/NO answer, not necessarily the optimum value, the original vertex labels, or every solution. The output budget may differ from the input budget. The requirement is a single small instance of this same unweighted decision problem; a list of oracle queries or a compression into a different language is a different notion.

The preprocessing time must be polynomial in \(L\), uniformly for all \(k\). A procedure taking \(f(k)L^{d}\) time for an unrestricted computable function \(f\) is not by itself a polynomial-time kernelization. The case \(k=0\) is covered by the bound \(C(k+1)^{c}\). Allowing loops makes the model explicit and does not change the question: each loop forces its vertex into any deletion set, while repeated arcs can be removed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of an algorithm with the stated uniform polynomial preprocessing, exact answer equivalence, and polynomial output bit bound depending only on the original deletion budget, or refute that existence. A conditional lower bound must state its complexity assumption explicitly; it is not an unconditional refutation. A kernel using a larger structural parameter does not settle this target.

context_blocks.title: Fixed-parameter tractability does not give a polynomial kernel
context_blocks.text: The 2016 source recalls a \(k^{O(k)}\)-size kernel following from fixed-parameter tractability, while explicitly leaving a polynomial-size kernel open. The missing improvement concerns how small a polynomial-time preprocessing can make every instance, rather than whether exponential dependence on the solution budget is possible.

context_blocks.title: Restricting the deletion target changes the problem
context_blocks.text: The source proves polynomial kernels when deletion must leave an out-tree, an out-forest, or a directed pumpkin. These are stronger conditions than merely destroying directed cycles, so the results do not constitute a kernel for general Directed Feedback Vertex Set.

context_blocks.title: Later kernels use additional structure
context_blocks.text: The WADS 2019 result, subsequently published in the 2025 journal article, gives a polynomial kernel with parameter \(k+\ell\), where \(\ell\) is the size of a supplied vertex set whose removal leaves an underlying undirected graph of fixed bounded treewidth. Here treewidth at most \(\eta\) means that there are vertex bags indexed by a tree, each of size at most \(\eta+1\), covering all vertices and both endpoints of every edge, with the bags containing each vertex forming a connected subtree. The constant \(\eta\) is fixed. The extra \(\ell\) need not be bounded by a polynomial in \(k\); the general question therefore remains distinct.

context_blocks.title: The parameter in a negative result also matters
context_blocks.text: The same work distinguishes the combined parameter \(k+\ell\) from parameterization by \(\ell\) alone. Its conditional obstruction for the latter does not rule out a polynomial kernel in the solution budget \(k\).

cards.title: Constant-factor approximation for Densest k-Subgraph
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Do there exist a universal constant \(C\ge 1\) and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm A such that, for every finite simple undirected unweighted graph \(G=(V,E)\) and every integer \(1\le k\le |V|, A(G,k)\) outputs a set \(S\subseteq V\) with |\(S|=k\) and |\(E(G[S])|\ge \operatorname{OPT}(G,k)/C\), where \(\operatorname{OPT}(G,k)=\max _{T\subseteq V, |T|=k}|E(G[T])|\)?
cards.definitions: G is explicitly represented by its vertices and edges, and k is supplied in binary as part of the input. \(G[S]\) contains all edges of G with both endpoints in S; loops and parallel edges are absent. The running time is polynomial in the full input length with a fixed exponent independent of k. The same finite C must work for all graphs, all graph sizes and all choices of k; it cannot increase with \(n=|V|\) or with k. The output must be a vertex set, not only an estimate of the optimum. When OPT=0, every k-set meets the requirement. Because all feasible sets have the same cardinality, maximizing edge count, average degree \(2|E(G[S])|/k\), or edges per selected vertex gives the same approximation objective. No promise of a clique, graph expansion, metric edge weights or a random input distribution is supplied. This card fixes deterministic algorithms; a randomized constant-factor guarantee would be major progress but has a distinct derandomization requirement. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Densest k-Subgraph is a basic test of how well algorithms can identify a concentrated combinatorial structure. Its unresolved approximation landscape influences many reductions and separates strong evidence of difficulty from the hardness consequences currently obtainable from \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\).

importance.reason: A flagship approximation problem with a simple objective, a large algorithmic gap, strong conditional and relaxation barriers, and consequences for several other optimization problems.

progress.text: Bhaskara and coauthors obtain \(O(n^{1/4+\varepsilon})\) approximation in polynomial time for each fixed \(\varepsilon\); the exact quarter-power endpoint has quasipolynomial running time in this work.
Bhaskara and coauthors prove polynomial integrality gaps for strong SDP hierarchies, establishing barriers for those relaxations.
Manurangsi proves almost-polynomial-ratio hardness under ETH, with perfect completeness; the revised April 2017 manuscript appears at STOC 2017.
Chuzhoy and coauthors publish a 2-CSP conjecture and conditional superconstant NP-hardness for DkS, together with reductions to related graph objectives.
Liu, Liu, Ma and Konar publish an exact continuous penalization and a nonconvex optimization method; no general constant-factor polynomial-time guarantee is established.
Laekhanukit, Manurangsi and Trabelsi give reductions to Densest At-Least-k-Subgraph and explicitly retain the missing NP-hardness of even 1.001 approximation for DkS.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The constant-factor algorithm is already ruled out assuming ETH, which remains unproved. The May 2026 primary source explicitly notes the absence of NP-hardness of approximation even at factor 1.001. This card asks about a deterministic constant-factor algorithm on all unweighted graphs, and preserves the distinction between conditional evidence and an unconditional resolution.

context_blocks.text: The task asks for a fixed-size collection of vertices containing as many internal interactions as possible. The cardinality restriction is what turns an otherwise tractable density objective into a central approximation problem. Without a prescribed size, maximizing edges per vertex can be solved in polynomial time. Allowing at least k vertices also changes which solutions compete: a large moderately dense region may be a valid answer even when no comparably useful k-vertex portion can be extracted.

Exact optimization contains CLIQUE: a graph has a k-clique precisely when \(\operatorname{OPT}(G,k)=k(k- 1)/2\). This observation alone gives almost no multiplicative approximation gap. A k-set missing only one possible edge is nearly optimal as k grows, even though it is not a clique. To rule out a constant-factor algorithm, a reduction must create a substantial separation between the best densities of its YES and NO instances, not merely a one-edge difference.

Bhaskara, Charikar, Chlamtac, Feige and Vijayaraghavan achieve \(O(n^{1/4+\varepsilon})\) approximation in \(n^{O}(1/\varepsilon )\) time for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\). Their method uses small tree patterns and a hierarchy of conditioned information to identify a dense region. The \(O(n^{1/4})\) phrase in the paper’s title needs care: attaining that endpoint in their analysis takes quasipolynomial \(n^{O}(\log  n)\) time. Neither rate is a constant approximation.

There is substantial evidence against the target. Manurangsi proves that ETH rules out even approximation within \(n^{1/(\log  \log  n)^{a}}\), for a universal constant \(a>0\). ETH asserts that 3SAT has no \(2^{o}(N)\)-time algorithm on N variables. This is a stronger assumption than \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\); the result therefore already excludes every fixed constant under ETH, while leaving the weaker-assumption hardness problem unresolved. Its YES instances can contain a k-clique, a property called perfect completeness.

Semidefinite-programming lower bounds supply a different kind of evidence. Bhaskara, Charikar, Guruswami, Vijayaraghavan and Zhou construct polynomial integrality gaps for strong hierarchies of relaxations. A relaxation can assign a large fractional or vector-valued objective even when no genuine k-set has comparable density. Such a gap limits approximation guarantees obtained from that relaxation, but it is not a theorem excluding every polynomial-time combinatorial algorithm.

Chuzhoy, Dalirrooyfard, Grinberg and Tan propose a 2-CSP hardness conjecture that would imply NP-hardness of approximating Densest k-Subgraph within \(2^{(\log  n)^{\varepsilon}}\) for some \(\varepsilon >0\). Their paper also connects its approximability to graph partitioning, dense coloring and bounded-crossing subgraphs. Some connections use quasipolynomial reductions, so they should not be read as constant-factor polynomial-time equivalences. The conjectural premise remains a real part of the hardness claim.

Laekhanukit, Manurangsi and Trabelsi’s May 2026 paper still reports that no NP-hardness of approximation is known for Densest k-Subgraph even at factor 1.001. They show that the absence of any constant-factor DkS algorithm implies a \((3/2- \varepsilon )\) barrier for the at-least-k density problem. This transfers a hypothetical negative answer to a neighboring objective; the neighboring problem’s known 2-approximation does not answer this card.

An AAAI 2026 result by Liu, Liu, Ma and Konar gives an exact continuous penalization reformulation and an efficient nonconvex proximal-gradient method. Exactness concerns the relationship between optima of the formulations. It does not mean the method finds a global optimum, or even a fixed approximation ratio, on every graph in polynomial time. The distinction explains how useful practical progress can coexist with the unresolved worst-case guarantee.

Chuzhoy, Dalirrooyfard, Grinberg and Tan propose a 2-CSP hardness conjecture that would imply NP-hardness of approximating Densest k-Subgraph within \(2^{(\log  n)^{\varepsilon}}\) for some \(\varepsilon >0\). Their paper also connects its approximability to graph partitioning, dense coloring and bounded-crossing subgraphs. Some connections use quasipolynomial reductions, so they should not be read as constant-factor polynomial-time equivalences. The conjectural premise remains a real part of the hardness claim.

Laekhanukit, Manurangsi and Trabelsi’s May 2026 paper still reports that no NP-hardness of approximation is known for Densest k-Subgraph even at factor 1.001. They show that the absence of any constant-factor DkS algorithm implies a \((3/2- \varepsilon )\) barrier for the at-least-k density problem. This transfers a hypothetical negative answer to a neighboring objective; the neighboring problem’s known 2-approximation does not answer this card.

An AAAI 2026 result by Liu, Liu, Ma and Konar gives an exact continuous penalization reformulation and an efficient nonconvex proximal-gradient method. Exactness concerns the relationship between optima of the formulations. It does not mean the method finds a global optimum, or even a fixed approximation ratio, on every graph in polynomial time. The distinction explains how useful practical progress can coexist with the unresolved worst-case guarantee.

benchmark_focus.reason: A flagship approximation problem with a simple objective, a large algorithmic gap, strong conditional and relaxation barriers, and consequences for several other optimization problems.

cards.title: Unique Games Conjecture
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: For every pair of rational constants \(\varepsilon ,\delta >0\) with \(\varepsilon +\delta <1\), does there exist an integer \(q\ge 2\) such that it is NP-hard to distinguish Unique Games instances with $\operatorname{val}(G)\ge1-\varepsilon$ from instances with $\operatorname{val}(G)\le\delta$? Here q is the alphabet size, fixed independently of the input graph, and \(\operatorname{val}(G)\) is the largest fraction of constraints simultaneously satisfied by any labeling.
cards.definitions: An instance has finitely many vertices and a nonempty explicit list E of directed edges between distinct vertices; repeated edges are allowed and counted separately. Every vertex receives a label in \([q]=\{1,\ldots ,q\}\). An edge \(e=(u,v)\) carries an explicitly given permutation \(\pi _{e}:[q]\to [q]\) and is satisfied exactly when \(\pi _{e}(\ell (u))=\ell (v)\). Thus \(\operatorname{val}(G)=\max _{\ell} |\){e satisfied by \(\ell\)}|/|E|. There are no graph expansion or degree promises. NP-hardness means a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction from 3SAT mapping every satisfiable formula into the \(\ge 1- \varepsilon\) case and every unsatisfiable formula into the \(\le \delta\) case. The reduction, its running-time exponent, and q may depend on \(\varepsilon ,\delta\). Inputs with value strictly between the thresholds are outside the promise. The question is the NP-hardness proposition itself; \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) is needed when drawing the usual conclusion that no polynomial-time distinguishing algorithm exists. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: UGC would turn many conditional approximation thresholds into NP-hardness theorems and explain the optimality of a general SDP framework. Its very simple permutation constraints isolate a fundamental boundary between exact consistency, approximate consistency, and hardness amplification.

importance.reason: An organizing conjecture for approximation thresholds, with consequences for whole families of constraint satisfaction problems and strong connections to SDP algorithms, PCPs, and analysis.

progress.text: Khot proposes the conjecture. Perfect satisfiability is polynomial-time decidable; the conjectured hard regime has positive completeness error and an alphabet depending on both gap parameters.

Raghavendra gives a general SDP and rounding framework for fixed finite-domain CSPs and transfers SDP integrality gaps to Unique-Games-based hardness. Under UGC, its achievable thresholds are optimal up to any fixed accuracy, unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).

Arora, Barak, and Steurer give, for an absolute \(\alpha >0\), an \(\exp (q n^{\varepsilon ^{\alpha}})\)-time algorithm finding a \((1- \varepsilon ^{\alpha})\)-satisfying labeling in a \((1- \varepsilon )\)-satisfiable q-label instance on n vertices. In the small fixed-\(\varepsilon\) regime this is subexponential, but not polynomial.

The line of work proving the 2-to-2 Games Theorem yields NP-hardness of Unique Games at completeness \(1/2\) and arbitrarily small soundness. Khot’s exposition states this explicitly as Theorem 2.20; it leaves the near-one completeness of UGC unresolved.

The journal version of Dinur, Khot, Kindler, Minzer, and Safra’s second installment documents its role in the proof sequence, while retaining the full Unique Games statement as Conjecture 1.4. Its publication is not a new proof of full UGC.

context_blocks.text: Each constraint is locally simple: fixing either endpoint label determines exactly one compatible label at the other endpoint. Exact satisfiability of all constraints is decidable in polynomial time. Allowing a small fraction of constraints to fail changes the question sharply.

The conjecture says that an instance admitting an almost perfect assignment can nevertheless be hard to distinguish from one where every assignment fails almost everywhere. These are two promised regimes, rather than a request to compute the exact optimum. The alphabet is allowed to grow as the desired gap becomes more demanding. Indeed, a uniformly random labeling satisfies a \(1/q\) fraction in expectation, so a soundness threshold below \(1/q\) is impossible.

Raghavendra’s theorem connects such reductions to a general semidefinite-programming framework: under UGC, that framework achieves the approximation thresholds of fixed finite-domain constraint satisfaction problems, to arbitrary constant accuracy.

The strongest relevant hardness milestone must be read with its completeness parameter. The 2-to-2 Games Theorem implies hardness for Unique Games with value at least one half versus arbitrarily small value. It does not make the yes instances almost perfectly satisfiable. Raising completeness from one half to arbitrarily close to one is precisely a remaining gap relevant to this card.

Algorithmic progress also matters even when it is slower than polynomial time. Subexponential algorithms exploit spectral decompositions of the constraint graph, limiting what quantitative hardness reductions could establish. Because a polynomial reduction can enlarge the instance by a parameter-dependent power, these algorithms coexist with the NP-hardness conjecture.

cards.title: Polylogarithmic approximation for Directed Steiner Tree
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(a\ge 1\) and \(C\ge 1\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, for every feasible Directed Steiner Tree instance with k terminals, outputs a feasible subgraph of cost at most \(a(\log _{2}(k+2))^{C}\) times optimum with probability at least \(2/3\)?
cards.definitions: An instance consists of a finite directed graph \(G=(V,E), a\) root \(r\in V, a\) nonempty terminal set \(T\subseteq V\setminus \{r\}\) with \(k=|T|\), and nonnegative rational arc costs \(c_{e}\) given exactly in binary. Every terminal is promised reachable from r; this can also be checked in polynomial time, with infeasibility reported otherwise. A feasible solution is an arc subset \(F\subseteq E\) such that \((V,F)\) contains a directed path from r to every \(t\in T\). Its cost is \(\sum_{e\in F}c_{e}\), counting an arc once even if many paths use it. OPT is the minimum such cost. The algorithm must output a feasible subset on every execution and satisfy the approximation guarantee on every instance with probability at least \(2/3\) over its internal randomness. Its bit running time on every execution is bounded by one fixed polynomial in the entire input encoding length, including cost bits. The constants a,C and the polynomial are independent of \(n=|V|, k\) and the costs. If OPT=0, the successful output must also have zero cost. Local computation is ordinary uniform classical computation without advice or free optimization oracles. There is no planarity, acyclicity, bounded depth, bounded treewidth, metric, or supplied fractional-solution promise. The word tree refers to the optimization problem: any feasible subgraph may be returned, and redundant edges can be removed.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct an algorithm and fixed constants satisfying these bounds, or prove that no such randomized polynomial-time algorithm exists. An \(O(k^{\varepsilon})\)-approximation for every separately fixed \(\varepsilon >0, a\) polylogarithmic approximation taking quasipolynomial time, or a guarantee on a restricted graph class is partial progress. A gap for a particular LP relaxation limits that relaxation, not every algorithm. A hardness result ruling out only some smaller powers of log k does not exclude all fixed powers and therefore does not refute this proposition.
cards.why: A defining gap in directed network-design approximation: determine whether a shared directed connection network can be approximated within a polylogarithmic factor using only polynomial time.

importance.reason: A central approximation problem encompassing covering and rooted network design, with a persistent gap between polynomial and quasipolynomial algorithms.

context_blocks.text: The problem asks how cheaply a root can reach many destinations through one shared directed network. Buying a common initial segment can save cost across many root-to-terminal paths, but the directions restrict which branching structures are usable. With one terminal the problem is shortest path. With many terminals, selecting where the paths should share infrastructure becomes the central optimization challenge.

A simple reduction explains why ordinary reachability is insufficient. For a set-cover instance, create a vertex for each set and each element, an arc of cost one from the root to every set vertex, and zero-cost arcs from each set to its elements. Make all element vertices terminals. A feasible network must buy a collection of set arcs covering all elements, and its cost equals the number of chosen sets. The directed graph can thus encode a nontrivial covering problem even with only two layers after the root.

The familiar polynomial-time approximation frontier is \(O(k^{\varepsilon})\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\), from the classical directed Steiner algorithms. The running-time exponent depends on the chosen accuracy parameter. Setting \(\varepsilon\) to a quantity that shrinks with k is not a free improvement: it changes that dependence and can produce quasipolynomial time. A power of k, however small and fixed, eventually exceeds every fixed power of log k.

Grandoni, Laekhanukit and Li obtain an \(O(\log ^{2} k/\log  \log  k)\)-approximation in quasipolynomial time. Their techniques combine a structured reduction with a hierarchy of strengthened linear relaxations and dependent rounding. This establishes that a good approximation exists at a slower time scale. The requested advance is to achieve some polylogarithmic factor with a fixed polynomial running-time exponent; matching the sharper quasipolynomial factor is not required.

The same work gives near-matching quasipolynomial-time hardness under additional complexity assumptions, including the Projection Games Conjecture. This does not show that every polynomial-time polylogarithmic approximation is impossible: a larger fixed logarithmic power is allowed in this card. The issue is a gap between what can currently be computed in polynomial time and what is known with more time, rather than the already settled hardness of exact optimization.

A natural flow relaxation buys a fractional capacity \(x_{e}\) for each arc and, separately for each terminal, sends a unit flow from the root using at most \(x_{e}\) on that arc. Different terminals may reuse the same purchased capacity because a network edge is bought once. In general graphs this relaxation has polynomial-size integrality gaps, including \(\Omega (\sqrt{k})\) examples. Those examples explain why a straightforward LP-rounding strategy cannot guarantee a polylogarithmic factor against that relaxation on every instance. They do not rule out stronger relaxations or a different algorithm.

The inherited Laekhanukit reference requires careful version tracking. Its December 2024 general claim was withdrawn in version 2. Version 3, submitted in October 2025, presents itself as a rectification restricted to a relatively integral fractional solution: each terminal flow on an edge is either zero or the entire purchased capacity. The record still displays the earlier withdrawal comment about a reachability-proof error. This card treats the later restricted statement as a reported claim, not an established general approximation; finding an appropriate fractional solution is an additional requirement.

Planarity changes the picture substantially. Friggstad and Mousavi give a polynomial-time \(O(\log  k)\)-approximation for planar directed graphs, using shortest-path separators. Later work extends the structural approach to other rooted planar network-design problems and bounds a natural planar LP gap by \(O(\log ^{2} k)\). These theorems show that directedness alone does not preclude the requested factor, but their separator arguments do not apply to arbitrary directed graphs.

Chekuri and Jain’s July 2026 work extends planar results to length-constrained network design. Its guarantees are bicriteria: they approximate cost while allowing an \(O(\log  k)\) multiplicative violation of the path-length constraint. The paper explicitly retains the general Directed Steiner Tree approximation question as open. Removing a length constraint or changing the objective does not remove the planarity hypothesis needed by those algorithms.

cards.definitions: Use finite simple undirected d-regular graphs \(G=([n],E), n\ge 2\) and \(d\ge 1\), given explicitly by their adjacency matrices. Regular means that every vertex has exactly d neighbours; d is not a fixed constant or an extra promise. For nonempty \(S, \partial _{G} S\) is the set of edges with exactly one endpoint in S, and \(\Phi _{G}(S)=|\partial _{G} S|/(d|S|)\). Internal edges contribute twice to d|S| and zero to the boundary. This is normalized edge expansion, not the number of outside neighbours. The graph has no promised connectivity, geometry or spectral gap. The constants \(\eta ,\delta\) are chosen before the input; they are not parameters tending to zero with n. For \(\delta =a/b\) in lowest terms, inputs have n a positive multiple of b, so exact set size has no rounding ambiguity. The YES and NO cases are disjoint since \(\eta <1/2\); inputs meeting neither case have no required decision answer. NP-hardness means that for every language L with polynomially checkable witnesses, a deterministic polynomial-time map sends each \(x\in \mathrm{L}\) to a YES graph and each \(x\notin \mathrm{L}\) to a NO graph. Equivalently, it suffices to supply such a reduction from Boolean satisfiability. Reduction constants and the polynomial exponent may depend on \(\eta\) and its chosen \(\delta\). The card fixes the unweighted regular-graph, exact-cardinality version of the imported question; weighted-volume, randomized-hardness and size-interval versions must be identified when cited.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves the stated NP-hardness for every \(\eta\) by choosing \(\delta\) and giving a valid promise-preserving reduction. A negative resolution refutes this quantified hardness statement for some fixed \(\eta\). Polynomial-time algorithms for every fixed \(\delta\) at that \(\eta\) would refute the hardness claim under \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\); an algorithm alone must not be called an unconditional disproof of NP-hardness. Results restricted to special graph classes or allowing a different output set size do not automatically settle this formulation.

context_blocks.title: What expansion measures
context_blocks.text: Choose a vertex uniformly from S, then choose one of its neighbours uniformly. The probability of leaving S is exactly \(\Phi _{G}(S)\). A set with expansion near zero is a group whose connections mostly remain inside it. Expansion near one means that almost every connection goes out. The promise asks whether one unusually insulated set exists at the specified size, or whether every set of that size is almost completely exposed.

context_blocks.title: Small means a fixed fraction
context_blocks.text: If \(\delta =1/1000\), the target has one thousand vertices in a million-vertex graph and one million vertices in a billion-vertex graph. Its size still grows linearly with n. Enumerating all sets of a fixed number of vertices therefore does not give a polynomial-time algorithm for the question. The order of constants also matters: \(\delta\) may depend on the desired expansion gap \(\eta\), and an algorithm for one convenient pair of constants would not refute the full hypothesis.

context_blocks.title: A sparse large cut can miss the issue
context_blocks.text: Take the disjoint union of two complete graphs on 50 vertices. Either whole component has expansion zero. Yet a two-vertex set contained in one component has expansion \(48/49\), and a two-vertex set split between the components has expansion one. Thus every set of the specified small size expands very well even though a larger zero-expansion cut exists. Optimizing over all sets up to half the graph can answer a different question from the exact small-size promise.

context_blocks.title: Why a large gap remains difficult
context_blocks.text: For a proposed set, its size and edge boundary are easy to count. The universal NO condition ranges over all sets of that size. The hypothesis asserts hardness even though YES and NO graphs are separated by a wide gap, with many intermediate graphs excluded by the promise. A graph expansion construction, a bound on one spectral parameter, or an algorithm with an uncontrolled change in set size is not automatically a distinguisher for this promise.

context_blocks.title: Connections and current boundary
context_blocks.text: Raghavendra and Steurer reduce small-set expansion to Unique Games, making this hypothesis a sufficient foundation for Unique Games hardness. Raghavendra, Steurer and Tulsiani relate it to a version of Unique Games with an additional expansion requirement and derive conditional hardness for graph partitioning and arrangement problems. This does not establish equivalence to unrestricted Unique Games in both directions. In August 2026, Lin, Mirrokni and Woodruff use a randomized, weighted, exact-volume variant to prove a sparse least-squares hardness result. Such an application assumes an SSE statement; it does not prove the statement itself, and its modeling conventions should not be silently transferred to this card. The checked sources leave the hypothesis unresolved.

sentences: Is it NP-hard to distinguish one poorly expanding small set from uniformly strong expansion at the same set size?
The target set occupies a fixed fraction \(\delta\) of the graph, with \(\delta\) chosen after the gap parameter \(\eta\).
Expansion is the fraction of incident edges that leave the set.
A sparse cut of a larger size does not necessarily reveal any poorly expanding set of the target size.
Known reductions connect the hypothesis to Unique Games and conditional hardness without resolving it.

cards.title: Subtour-LP integrality gap for metric TSP
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Determine \(\Gamma =\sup _{n\ge 3,c} \operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{TSP}}(c)/\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}(c)\), where c ranges over every metric on n labeled points and \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}\) is the symmetric subtour relaxation defined below.
cards.definitions: For \(V=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\) and \(E=\{\{u,v\}:u\ne v\}, a\) metric has \(c_{uu}=0, c_{uv}=c_{vu}>0\) for \(u\ne v\), and \(c_{uv}\le c_{uw}+c_{wv}\). Costs are arbitrary real numbers; no Euclidean embedding is assumed. \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{TSP}}\) is the minimum sum of edge costs on a Hamiltonian cycle of the complete undirected graph. For \(S\subseteq V, \delta (S)\) contains edges with exactly one endpoint in S, and \(x(F)=\sum_{e\in F}x_{e}\). Define \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}=\min  \sum_{e} c_{e} x_{e}\) subject to \(x(\delta (\{v\}))=2\) for every \(v, x(\delta (S))\ge 2\) for every nonempty proper \(S\subsetneq V\), and \(0\le x_{e}\le 1\) for every e. The LP is feasible and has positive optimum. The supremum ranges over every finite size, not one fixed n. This is the symmetric metric subtour-LP integrality gap, not an approximation ratio measured only against \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{TSP}}\), an asymmetric TSP relaxation, or a restricted geometric metric.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |\(a- \Gamma |\le 1/100\). The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds \(\ell\)\(\le u\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell +u)/2\). An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The \(1/100\) tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture.
cards.why: The exact strength of the principal relaxation for a canonical optimization problem, joining polyhedral structure, probabilistic rounding and approximation. A resolution would explain a longstanding gap between fractional connectivity and integral tours.

importance.reason: A defining integrality-gap conjecture in combinatorial optimization with consequences for LP rounding and the limits of metric TSP approximation methods.

cards.status_note: The general \(4/3\) equality remains open through the primary-source review of 11 September 2026. The established explicit upper bound recorded here is \(3/2- 2.18\cdot 10^{- 34}; a\) September 2 preprint claims a further small improvement, clearly separated from verified literature. Restricted-class theorems and finite-size verification do not resolve the universal conjecture. The 12 September 2026 edit adopts absolute 0.01 benchmark acceptance; the saved open-status evidence concerns the underlying exact question and does not independently certify openness at that tolerance.

context_blocks.text: The target is the value of the universal integrality gap. The classical \(4/3\) conjecture proposes \(\Gamma =4/3; a\) larger determined value is also an answer to this quantitative question.

The relaxation allows fractional edge purchases while retaining two elementary properties of every tour: each vertex has degree two, and every nontrivial cut is crossed at least twice. It therefore knows much more than a disconnected cycle-cover relaxation, but its feasible points need not be convex combinations of Hamiltonian cycles. The conjecture asks for the exact worst loss caused by that remaining freedom.

For example, a feasible fractional vector may put positive weight on several alternative connections at one vertex without choosing a single predecessor and successor. The cut inequalities ensure aggregate connectivity, yet they do not force these local choices to assemble into one integral cycle. The proposed factor \(4/3\) says that, in a metric, repairing all such inconsistencies never costs more than one third of the fractional optimum.

The metric assumption is what makes shortcutting possible. If a connected Eulerian multigraph visits a vertex several times, replacing a detour by the direct edge between its endpoints does not increase cost. One can consequently search for a suitably cheap Eulerian structure rather than construct a Hamiltonian cycle at every intermediate step. This observation explains why spanning trees and parity correction recur in approximation algorithms for the problem.

A minimum spanning tree followed by a minimum-cost matching on its odd-degree vertices yields the classical \(3/2\) guarantee. Wolsey’s analysis measures both components against the LP: the tree costs at most the fractional optimum, and the matching at most half that value. The inherited July 2026 paper recalls this argument before studying a particular randomized refinement.

An algorithmic ratio and an integrality-gap ratio must use the correct denominator. A guarantee cost\(\le \alpha \cdot \operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{TSP}}\) does not establish \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{TSP}}\le \alpha \cdot \operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}\), since the fractional optimum can be smaller. Karlin–Klein–Oveis Gharan’s FOCS 2022 result explicitly supplies an LP-relative guarantee below \(3/2\), extending the earlier approximation breakthrough. It is this later theorem that directly improves the general gap bound.

The modern approach samples a spanning tree from a distribution constrained by fractional edge marginals, then corrects its parity. Tree cost and parity-repair cost interact, so treating the two separately can lose the desired saving. Gurvits–Klein–Leake strengthen probability estimates using capacities of real stable polynomials. Their Lemma 4.5 is explicitly LP-relative and yields the certified bound \(\Gamma \le 3/2- 2.18\cdot 10^{- 34}\). The small constant reflects a worst-case proof, not a claim that practical tours are that close to \(3/2\).

A class can have a better integrality gap than the worst ratio of a particular algorithm on it. Jin–Klein–Williamson prove the \(4/3\) bound for half-integral cycle-cut instances using a specialized construction. Half-integral means that nonzero fractional coordinates are \(1/2\) or 1, with an additional restriction on the hierarchy of tight cuts. This result does not cover every half-integral instance, still less every subtour solution.

Their July 2026 paper, which supplied the inherited reference, proves a \(10/7\) guarantee for the maximum-entropy algorithm on that same restricted class. Since \(10/7\) exceeds \(4/3\), it improves understanding of the chosen algorithm rather than improving the already-known class gap. The authors also identify examples giving a lower bound of \(11/8\) on the algorithm’s performance. Such an algorithm-specific obstruction cannot refute the conjecture about the cheapest possible tour.

Two complementary approaches restrict the fractional solution in other ways. Villa–Vercesi–Barta–Mastrolilli prove the \(4/3\) bound when an optimal solution has at most \(n+6\) nonzero components, combining structural reasoning and computation. This is a support-size condition, not a theorem for every instance on at most \(n+6\) vertices. Larger support remains outside its stated guarantee.

Cook–Hougardy–Petrich’s September 8, 2026 revision reports exact verification for all metric instances through \(n=16\) and for half-integral extreme points through \(n=18\). It also repairs omissions in earlier extreme-point lists. This is stronger evidence than sampling finitely many random metrics, because the computation organizes the relevant polyhedral cases. It still leaves unbounded n, and the catalogue has not rerun that enumeration.

A September 2 preprint by Zhao Song claims a larger universal saving, \(\varepsilon\)★>\(2.05522\cdot 10^{- 30}\), through a refined maximum-entropy analysis. Its main theorem is explicitly relative to \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}\). The statement was checked, but the lengthy proof and numerical certificate were not independently verified here, so the value is recorded as a recent claim rather than silently replacing the established bound. Even if confirmed, it would remain far above the conjectured ratio \(4/3\).
