cards.title: Optimal polynomial-time approximation ratio for metric k-Median
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Determine \(\rho _{\mathrm{med}}=\inf\){\(r\ge 1: a\) uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm always opens at most k facilities and has cost at most \(r\cdot\)OPT with probability at least \(2/3\) on every metric k-Median instance}, in the model below.
cards.definitions: An input consists of a finite set V, a full table of nonnegative rational distances d on V encoded in binary, nonempty subsets \(C,F\subseteq V\) of clients and allowable facilities with \(C\cup F=V\), and an integer \(1\le k\le |F|\). The table is promised to satisfy \(d(u,v)=d(v,u), d(u,v)=0\) exactly when \(u=v\), and the triangle inequality. Each client has unit demand. For nonempty \(S\subseteq F\) define \(\operatorname{cost}(S)=\sum_{c\in C}\min _{s\in S}d(c,s)\), and OPT=\(\min \{\operatorname{cost}(S):S\subseteq F,1\le |S|\le k\}\). L is the total bit length of the input. For each fixed guarantee r in the infimum, require one uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A_{r}\), with constants \(K_{r},d_{r}\) such that every execution takes at most \(K_{r} \mathrm{L}^{d_{r}}\) bit operations. It always returns an explicit nonempty \(S\subseteq F\) with |\(S|\le k\), and on each input \(\Pr [\operatorname{cost}(S)\le r\cdot \operatorname{OPT}]\ge 2/3\). Here e is the base of the natural logarithm. The algorithm and constants may depend on r but not on k, |C|, |F| or distance precision. No Euclidean, low-dimensional, stability, capacity or input-distribution promise is made. Candidate facilities are part of the input and cannot be enlarged. The guarantee also covers OPT=0. The infimum need not be attained by one algorithm. An exact value \(\rho\) means that feasible guarantees approach \(\rho\) from above and no algorithm in the stated class guarantees a factor smaller than \(\rho\).
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |\(a- \rho _{\mathrm{med}}|\le 1/100\). The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds \(\ell\)\(\le u\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell +u)/2\). An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The \(1/100\) tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture. Any additional complexity assumption must be explicit; a conditional hardness theorem proves only the corresponding conditional value or bound.

The FPT algorithm, Euclidean schemes and 2026 k-Means results do not settle the polynomial-time target here. The 12 September 2026 edit adopts absolute 0.01 benchmark acceptance; the saved open-status evidence concerns the underlying exact question and does not independently certify openness at that tolerance.

context_blocks.text: The target is the optimal approximation ratio itself, with the exact facility budget and randomized polynomial-time model fixed. The previously selected \(1+2/e\) threshold is a candidate value motivated by the hardness evidence described below.

Metric k-Median selects a limited number of service locations and minimizes total distance to the nearest selected location. The number of clients and the number of candidate facilities may differ, and the distance table need not come from a Euclidean embedding. The same formulation models representative selection for clustering and placement of facilities. Its simplicity makes the unresolved approximation threshold a central benchmark for algorithm design.

The two endpoint numbers are approximately 1.73576 and 2. The lower endpoint is the classical hardness threshold \(1+2/e\); the best general feasible guarantee in the checked literature is \(2+\varepsilon\). The inherited STOC 2025 paper explicitly asks for a tight approximation result after obtaining that upper bound. Asking for \(1+2/e+\varepsilon\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon\) avoids requiring that an infimum approximation ratio be achieved exactly.

The coverage origin of the lower endpoint can be seen directly. Represent each set as a candidate facility and each universe element as a client. Give a client–facility pair distance one when the set contains the element and distance three otherwise, and give distinct pairs on the same side distance two. These distances satisfy the triangle inequality. A collection of k sets covering a fraction p of the elements then has clustering cost \((3- 2p)\) times the universe size.

Feige’s Max k-Cover gap distinguishes complete coverage from coverage of at most \(1- 1/e+\eta\), for any fixed \(\eta >0\). Under the preceding metric construction this becomes a gap between cost one per client and cost at least \(1+2/e- 2\eta\) per client. This is why the constant is not an arbitrary numerical target. A randomized algorithm beating that gap on every input would yield randomized algorithms for the underlying NP-hard decision problem; the appropriate exclusion is \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{RP}\) for this card’s success convention.

Jain–Mahdian–Saberi’s 2002 paper gives the classical metric k-Median lower bound through a reduction to approximating Set Cover. Its historical statement uses the then-known slightly-superpolynomial-time assumption for Set Cover hardness. The coverage reduction above explains the stronger ordinary NP-hardness formulation without silently changing the assumption in the original theorem. Neither lower-bound route excludes approximation from just above \(1+2/e\).

The 2025 algorithm combines two components. One permits a logarithmic number of extra centers while retaining a \(2+\varepsilon\) cost bound; another handles instances where deleting one optimal center increases the optimum substantially. Combining them returns a feasible solution opening at most k centers. The full paper’s May 2026 revision retains this result. It is therefore incorrect to describe the headline \(2+\varepsilon\) theorem as only a bicriteria approximation.

The usual linear relaxation has a separate barrier near two. It uses fractional openings \(y_{s}\), assignments \(x_{c,s}\le y_{s}\), unit total assignment for each client, and \(\sum_{s} y_{s}\le k\). For a star with \(q\ge 3\) leaves, all vertices available as facilities, clients at the leaves and \(k=q- 1\), every integral optimum has cost two. Set the central opening to \(1/(q- 1)\), each leaf opening to \((q- 2)/(q- 1)\), and assign each client’s remaining fraction to the center. This feasible LP solution costs \(q/(q- 1)\), giving an integrality gap approaching two.

That explicit example limits a guarantee measured against this relaxation, not every polynomial algorithm measured against OPT. A sharper algorithm might use additional constraints, a different relaxation, or another method. Likewise, a lower bound for one rounding framework is not a computational impossibility theorem for the original optimization problem. The card’s target is deliberately stated using the true integral optimum.

There is already a matching-threshold algorithm in a different runtime regime. Cohen-Addad–Gupta–Kumar–Lee–Li’s ICALP 2019 work achieves \(1+2/e+\varepsilon\) in fixed-parameter time with respect to k. The potentially large dependence on the number of opened facilities is permitted there. This does not supply a polynomial-time algorithm when k grows as part of the input, but it shows that the target ratio has meaningful algorithmic support.

A 2026 development concerns geometric input. Cohen-Addad and coauthors improve approximation-scheme runtimes in low-dimensional Euclidean spaces, where additional structure is available. Such a scheme does not apply to arbitrary distance tables.

Anand and coauthors’ July 2026 spectral dual-fitting paper improves k-Means guarantees, including in general metrics. That objective sums squared distances; squaring changes both the analysis and the hardness constants. It does not establish the stated k-Median ratio.

Determining the optimal ratio would locate the computational price of general metric clustering. A value at the coverage threshold would match the known obstruction, whereas a larger value would require a different limiting obstruction. The exact facility budget is essential to either conclusion: averaging an excessive number of facilities over random choices changes the feasible problem.

cards.title: Vertex Cover approximation below factor two
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Do a constant \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\) and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm exist which, on every finite simple undirected graph G, output a vertex cover of size at most \((2- \varepsilon )\tau (G)\)?
cards.definitions: Use uniform classical deterministic Turing computation, with no advice or oracle. Integers and rational numerators and denominators are encoded in binary; L denotes the total input bit length. A polynomial bound has constants independent of the input. A vertex cover is a subset S of the vertices containing at least one endpoint of every edge; \(\tau (G)\) is the minimum size of such a set. The graph is represented by its adjacency matrix. The same \(\varepsilon\) and algorithm must work for graphs of all sizes, with no promise on degree, coloring or graph class. An edgeless input requires the empty cover. The question asks for an unconditional algorithm or unconditional refutation of its existence.

context_blocks.text: Vertex Cover is one of the canonical NP-hard covering problems and has a simple factor-two approximation. The absence of a fixed improvement despite extensive work makes the factor a central approximation barrier.

Unique Games implies hardness below two, while unconditional NP-hardness leaves a gap. A restricted graph-class algorithm does not answer the universal target. The source seminar situates the question in the development of approximation algorithms and primal-dual methods.

e j\) and no loops. A Hamiltonian cycle visits every vertex once before returning to its start; its cost is the sum of its n arc costs. \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(c)\) is the minimum over all such cycles. For \(S\subseteq V, \delta ^{+}(S)=\{(i,j):i\in S,j

otin S,j\in S\}\); for a set of arcs F write \(x(F)=\sum_{(i,j)\in F} x_{ij}\). \(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(c)\) minimizes \(\sum_{i
e j} c(i,j)x_{ij}\) over real variables \(x_{ij}\ge 0\) subject to \(x(\delta ^{+}(\{v\}))=x(\delta ^{-}(\{v\}))=1\) for every v, and \(x(\delta ^{+}(S))\ge 1\) for every nonempty proper \(S\subsetneq V\). The degree equalities imply \(x(\delta ^{+}(S))=x(\delta ^{-}(S))\), so an additional incoming-cut inequality would be redundant. No integrality restriction is placed on x. The feasible set is nonempty and compact; both optima are attained. Zero-LP instances are excluded from the ratio; they also have zero tour optimum. Indeed, the positive support of a zero-cost feasible solution is strongly connected by the cut constraints, and directed triangle inequalities then give zero distance between every ordered pair. For positive LP value, the integrality ratio is \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(c)/\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(c)\), and the overall gap is its supremum over all n and directed metrics. The question is a universal comparison of optimum values, without a running-time restriction on finding the tour. It concerns closed tours, not a prescribed-start/end path. The supremum is over every finite size and is not required to be attained. The usual factor-two conjecture asserts \(\Gamma _{\mathrm{ATSP}}=2\), taking account of known approaching lower-bound families.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |\(a- \Gamma _{\mathrm{ATSP}}|\le 1/100\). The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds \(\ell\)\(\le u\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell +u)/2\). An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The \(1/100\) tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture.

context_blocks.text: This card determines the universal subtour-LP integrality gap. The factor-two conjecture is a proposed exact answer; refuting that factor alone would not determine a larger gap.

context_blocks.title: Buying fractions of directed arcs
context_blocks.text: A tour buys each used arc completely. The relaxation permits fractional amounts of several arcs, while requiring one unit to enter and leave every city and at least one unit to leave every proper group of cities. Every tour is feasible for the LP, so the LP gives a lower bound on the tour cost. The quantity measures the largest possible multiplicative loss when converting fractional cost into an actual tour; the classical conjecture sets that loss at two. A fractional solution need not be a probability distribution over whole tours.

context_blocks.title: Why subtour constraints matter
context_blocks.text: Suppose six cities form two groups of three, with travel cost 1 within a group and 10 between groups. Two separate three-city directed cycles satisfy every degree condition and cost only 6, but do not form a tour visiting all cities. The cut inequality for either group rules out this disconnected solution. These inequalities therefore add a global requirement to the local degree constraints; whether that requirement is strong enough to keep the full gap at two is the unresolved issue.

context_blocks.title: The current general gap
context_blocks.text: Families of directed instances have ratios tending to 2, so no smaller universal factor can work. Traub and Vygen’s 2022 article establishes an upper bound of 22. Their 2024 book improves the proved bound to 17 and explicitly retains the factor-2 question. Its circulation LP has the same optimum as the degree-constrained LP on directed metrics, so the model matches this card. The book also notes room for a small further numerical improvement; 17 is a stated theorem, not a claim that no refinement exists.

context_blocks.title: Finite computations and half-integral vertices
context_blocks.text: Vercesi and coauthors construct improved lower-bound instances at particular sizes. The June 2026 revision by Sosso, Bernardelli and Gualandi computes the gaps for all half-integral extreme points through twelve vertices, where half-integral means coordinates in \(\{0,1/2,1\}\). An extreme point is a feasible LP solution that cannot be written as a nontrivial convex combination of two distinct feasible solutions. Other denominators and arbitrarily large instances remain outside that enumeration. These computations add evidence without proving the universal conjecture.

context_blocks.title: What a resolution would establish
context_blocks.text: The comparison measures the strength of this specific relaxation. A polynomial-time method achieving cost at most twice the LP optimum would settle the inequality and give an approximation guarantee, but the existence inequality itself does not promise an efficient construction. The symmetric metric TSP has a different classical \(4/3\) conjecture; its constants and finite verifications do not transfer to the larger family in which travel costs can depend on direction.

cards.title: Constant-factor approximation for uniform Sparsest Cut
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Do a universal \(C\ge 1\) and a randomized polynomial-time algorithm exist which, on every finite simple undirected graph G on \(n\ge 2\) vertices, output a nonempty proper set S with \(\varphi _{G}(S)\le C \min _{\varnothing \ne T\subsetneq V} \varphi _{G}(T)\), with probability at least \(2/3\)?
cards.definitions: Here \(\varphi _{G}(S)=|E(S,V\setminus S)|/(|S|\cdot |V\setminus S|)\), where \(E(S,V\setminus S)\) is the set of edges having exactly one endpoint in S. The graph is supplied explicitly by an adjacency matrix. Polynomial time is measured in bit operations on every random tape; the same algorithm and constant must work for all graphs. The zero-optimum disconnected case requires returning a zero cut. Uniform refers to equal demand for each pair of vertices, not regularity of the graph.

context_blocks.text: Uniform Sparsest Cut balances a cut’s edge boundary against the number of separated pairs. It is a basic measure of the decomposability of a graph and a major test case for approximation algorithms.

The ARV result gives an \(O(\sqrt{\log  n})\) approximation, with a bound growing with the graph size. A constant factor would cross the remaining qualitative approximation barrier. Nonuniform pair demands, conductance normalized by volumes, and Small-Set Expansion have different targets and are not silently substituted here.

cards.title: Unconditional NP-hardness at the Goemans–Williamson Max-Cut threshold
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: For every rational \(\varepsilon\) with \(0<\varepsilon <1- \alpha _{\mathrm{GW}}\), do rationals \(0<b<a\le 1\) with \(b/a<\alpha _{\mathrm{GW}}+\varepsilon\) exist such that distinguishing Max-Cut value at least a from value at most b is NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions?
cards.definitions: For a finite simple undirected graph with at least one edge, its Max-Cut value is the maximum fraction of edges crossing a bipartition. Let \(\alpha _{\mathrm{GW}}=\min _{0<\theta \le \pi} 2\theta /(\pi (1- \cos  \theta ))\). NP-hardness means there is a polynomial-time map from 3-CNF formulas to graphs mapping satisfiable formulas to the at-least-a case and unsatisfiable formulas to the at-most-b case. The reduction and constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\). No Unique Games or other hardness conjecture is assumed.

context_blocks.text: The Goemans–Williamson approximation ratio is a landmark in semidefinite optimization. Matching hardness from ordinary NP-hardness would identify that ratio as an intrinsic computational threshold under \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\).

Known optimal hardness follows from Unique Games; it is not an unconditional NP-hardness theorem. The target deliberately concerns the reduction itself, so a conditional implication from UGC does not count as a solution. This separates the problem from the Unique Games conjecture and from improving a particular rounding algorithm.

cards.title: Optimal polynomial-time approximation ratio for metric TSP

cards.formal: Determine \(\rho_{\mathrm{TSP}}\), the infimum of achievable expected polynomial-time approximation ratios for the symmetric metric traveling salesman problem.
cards.definitions: An instance is an integer \(n\ge3\) and an explicitly listed symmetric rational distance matrix \(d\in\mathbb Q_{\ge0}^{n\times n}\), with \(d(i,i)=0\), \(d(i,j)>0\) for i unequal to j, and \(d(i,k)\le d(i,j)+d(j,k)\) for all triples. cards.title: Constant-factor approximation for Dasgupta’s hierarchical clustering objective
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Do there exist real constants \(C\ge1\), \(K>0\), an integer \(a\ge1\), and one deterministic multitape Turing machine which, on every explicitly encoded nonnegative rational similarity graph \(G\), outputs a hierarchy \(T\) with \(\operatorname{cost}_G(T)\le C\operatorname{OPT}(G)\) within \(K(N+1)^a\) bit operations, where \(N\) is the total input bit length and the cost and allowed hierarchies are defined below?
cards.definitions:
An input is an integer \(n\ge2\) and a finite simple undirected graph \(G=([n],E,w)\), where \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(E\subseteq\{\{u,v\}:1\le u<v\le n\}\), and \(w:E\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\). The encoding explicitly lists all \(n\) vertices, including isolated ones, and all edges with their endpoints and weights. Integers use ordinary binary notation with delimiters; each rational weight is a nonnegative integer numerator and positive integer denominator in binary. The explicit vertex list ensures \(N\ge n\). There are no loops or repeated edges. An absent edge has weight zero. The graph need not be connected and has no metric, clusterability, density or sampling promise.

A hierarchy is a finite rooted full binary tree whose leaves are labeled bijectively by \([n]\); every internal node has exactly two children. For a node \(z\), let \(L_T(z)\subseteq[n]\) be its descendant leaf labels. For distinct leaves \(u,v\), let \(\operatorname{lca}_T(u,v)\) be their least common ancestor. Define
\[
\operatorname{cost}_G(T)=\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E}w(\{u,v\})\,|L_T(\operatorname{lca}_T(u,v))|,
\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(G)=\min_T\operatorname{cost}_G(T).
\]
Each unordered edge contributes once. The minimum is over all such trees, with no restriction on height or balance. The output explicitly lists the root, child edges and leaf labels of one tree. If all weights are zero, the required cost is zero and any valid hierarchy qualifies.

The same finite machine and constants must work for every \(n\), graph and weight encoding. All input reads, binary arithmetic, preprocessing and output writes count in the worst-case running time. The machine has no random bits, advice, external comparison or cluster-label oracle, or uncharged preprocessing. The factor \(C\) is independent of \(n\), the number of edges and the sizes or ratios of the weights; it is not an input parameter. Only the tree is required as output, and its stated cost guarantee is mathematical, using exact rational weights.

context_blocks.text: The source defines a cost for a complete hierarchy of pairwise similarities. This card retains the previously selected deterministic polynomial-time, constant-factor question. The explicit rational encoding and vertex list fix bit complexity and output size; they do not impose a structural promise.

The general approximation guarantee of Charikar and Chatziafratis is \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\). Their Theorem 3.4 proves Small-Set-Expansion hardness of approximation within every constant factor, already on unweighted graphs. This is a conditional complexity barrier, not an unconditional proof that the requested machine cannot exist.
The ICALP 2025 sublinear result assumes a clusterable graph and access to cluster labels of sampled seeds. Its input model and guarantee do not supply the unrestricted algorithm asked for here.

The July 2026 generalized clustering paper permits a leaf cluster to remain a whole graph from a specified class, such as a tree. Its objective can consequently vanish on inputs for which singleton-leaf hierarchies have positive cost. Those results concern a different stopping rule.

A constant-factor guarantee for the complementary revenue-maximization objective does not, just from that guarantee, give a constant-factor bound for this minimization objective. The target here is the displayed cost itself.

cards.why: A hierarchy must represent similarity at every scale, so optimizing a single flat partition is insufficient. A constant approximation for this canonical objective would give a uniform quality guarantee on arbitrary similarity data and would cross a major graph-partitioning hardness barrier.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the existence of a machine and fixed constants satisfying every stated guarantee, or a complete Lean proof of their nonexistence. An approximation factor growing with the input size, a result for a promised graph class, or a guarantee with an additional oracle does not settle this target. A conditional hardness result establishes its implication but does not by itself prove the unconditional negative answer.

cards.title: Min-CSP approximation at the SDP integrality gap
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal:
For every fixed finite domain \(D\), positive arity \(k\), and finite set \(\Lambda\) of nonnegative rational cost functions \(f:D^k\to[0,1]\), is the following true? For every rational \(\varepsilon>0\), there is a randomized polynomial-time algorithm which, on every \(n\)-variable minimization \(\Lambda\)-CSP instance \(I\) with finite \(n\)-variable SDP integrality gap \(\alpha_\Lambda(n)\), returns an assignment \(\sigma\) such that
\[\Pr\bigl[\operatorname{cost}_I(\sigma)\leq (1+\varepsilon)\alpha_\Lambda(n)\operatorname{OPT}(I)\bigr]\geq\tfrac23?\]
The same algorithm handles all \(n\); it also halts and returns an assignment on the sizes where the gap is infinite, but no multiplicative guarantee is imposed there. The gap and the basic SDP are defined below.
cards.why: A universal theorem would extend the general SDP approximation framework to multiplicative minimization guarantees, including instances whose optimum vanishes with input size. It would connect a geometric obstruction of a standard relaxation to actual polynomial-time approximation across all finite cost languages. A counterexample would identify a limit to interpreting integrality gaps as achievable algorithmic benchmarks.
cards.status_note: The 2017 chapter explicitly poses this n-dependent multiplicative question after distinguishing it from the 2009 additive rounding theorem. The February 2026 robust-satisfiability paper supplies results under additional template hypotheses, not the universal statement. A bounded primary-source search checked on 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution; this does not establish that the historical question remains open beyond the checked sources.

sentences: A minimization CSP assigns finite-domain values to variables to minimize the average of fixed local nonnegative costs.
Its basic SDP can achieve a lower cost using consistent local distributions and vectors than any actual assignment.
The question asks whether a randomized polynomial-time algorithm can match the SDP’s worst gap at each number of variables within every factor 1+ε.
The multiplicative guarantee must also protect zero or very small optimum values, which existing additive universal rounding does not do.
A resolution would clarify whether size-dependent SDP gaps universally predict achievable approximation for minimization CSPs.

cards.definitions:
Fix \(D=\{1,\ldots,q\}\), with \(q\geq1\), and a finite nonempty \(\Lambda\). Its rational cost tables and \(k\geq1\) are fixed, not input. The nonnegative rational convention gives a finite effective version of the source’s generalized nonnegative predicates; negative costs do not define the multiplicative approximation question. An instance has variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), \(n\geq1\), and a finite list of \(m\) constraints \(C=(f_C,(i_1,\ldots,i_k))\). Every \(f_C\in\Lambda\), and each \(i_j\in[n]\). Repeated coordinates and repeated occurrences are allowed, with each occurrence having unit weight. There are no hard constraints, infinite costs, extra unary pins or input-dependent predicates. For an assignment \(\sigma:[n]\to D\), set
\[\operatorname{cost}_I(\sigma)=\frac1m\sum_C f_C(\sigma(i_1),\ldots,\sigma(i_k)),\qquad \operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min_\sigma\operatorname{cost}_I(\sigma).\]
For \(m=0\), cost and optimum are zero. A zero-one cost table records violation by value one and satisfaction by value zero. Different arities can be represented by a common maximum arity with unused arguments; the question is not restricted to Boolean predicates.

Define the basic semidefinite relaxation as follows. Choose real vectors \(v_0,u_{i,a}\in\mathbb R^{1+nq}\), for \(i\in[n],a\in D\), satisfying
\[\langle v_0,v_0\rangle=1,\qquad \sum_{a\in D}u_{i,a}=v_0,\qquad \langle u_{i,a},u_{i,b}\rangle=0\quad(a\ne b).\]
For each constraint occurrence \(C\), let \(S_C\) be its set of distinct variables and choose a local distribution \(\mu_C:D^{S_C}\to\mathbb R_{\geq0}\) with total mass one. Impose
\[\sum_{z:z(i)=a}\mu_C(z)=\langle u_{i,a},u_{i,a}\rangle\quad(i\in S_C),\]
\[\sum_{z:z(i)=a,\ z(j)=b}\mu_C(z)=\langle u_{i,a},u_{j,b}\rangle\quad(i,j\in S_C,\ i\ne j).\]
Thus all local one- and two-variable marginals agree with the common vector inner products. Repeated occurrences of a variable in a constraint use the same value \(z(i)\). The SDP value \(\operatorname{SDP}(I)\) is the minimum of
\[\frac1m\sum_C\sum_{z\in D^{S_C}}\mu_C(z)f_C(z(i_1),\ldots,z(i_k)),\]
with value zero when \(m=0\). This is a finite semidefinite program via its Gram matrix; the stated vector dimension suffices for every such matrix. It is feasible and compact in Gram-matrix and distribution coordinates. Every assignment gives a feasible point, so \(0\leq\operatorname{SDP}(I)\leq\operatorname{OPT}(I)\). No higher level of an SDP hierarchy is included.

For a fixed instance define its gap ratio as \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)/\operatorname{SDP}(I)\) if the denominator is positive, as one if both values are zero, and as \(+\infty\) if only the denominator is zero. Let \(\alpha_\Lambda(n)\) be the supremum of these ratios over all lists of constraints on exactly \(n\) labelled variables; unused variables are counted. Then \(1\leq\alpha_\Lambda(n)\leq+\infty\), and the gap may grow with \(n\). The algorithm is not supplied with its value or an oracle for it. This is an instance-size gap, not a single constant supremum over every size.

Encode \(n,m\) in unary and each constraint by its fixed-table index and its \(k\) variable indices in binary; the total bit length is \(L\). The algorithm is a finite probabilistic multitape Turing machine using independent fair coin bits. For each fixed \(D,k,\Lambda,\varepsilon\), one program has worst-case running time \(C(L+1)^c\) on every input and every coin sequence; \(C,c\) may depend on these fixed parameters. Malformed strings may be rejected. The output explicitly gives all \(n\) labels. No polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\), common exponent across languages or effective algorithm for finding the program from \(\Lambda\) is required. The probability convention is the explicit bounded-error interpretation of the source’s randomized approximation framework.

The guarantee is multiplicative, relative to the actual optimum. When that optimum is zero and the size-dependent gap is finite, the algorithm must find a zero-cost assignment with probability at least \(2/3\). There is no additive error term, and no assertion that it must round a supplied SDP point or achieve the stronger bound with \(\operatorname{SDP}(I)\) in place of \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal algorithmic assertion, or of its logical negation. A positive proof must establish one polynomial-time machine for every fixed language and positive accuracy, working at all input sizes with the stated success probability, size-dependent gap and zero-optimum convention. A negative proof must establish a fixed finite language and positive accuracy for which no such machine exists. A constant additive guarantee for normalized cost, an algorithm restricted to one predicate family, or a conditional obstruction to one rounding scheme does not settle the universal statement. An unproved complexity assumption may support partial progress but is not part of this unconditional target.

source_formulation.text: If the minimization SDP gap at n variables is α_n, can a polynomial-time algorithm attain approximation factor (1+ε)α_n for every positive ε?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Chapter 11, §7, Open Problem 4; the n-dependent gap is retained, with finite cost encoding, zero cases and success probability made explicit.

context_blocks.text: The integrality gap measures a relaxation’s worst discrepancy from a genuine assignment. In minimization, the SDP can make local constraints appear cheaper than any global assignment. This question asks whether an efficient algorithm can always match the resulting size-dependent benchmark to arbitrarily small relative slack; it does not ask to compute the gap itself.

The source distinguishes maximization and minimization with nonnegative predicates. For maximization, a random assignment provides a positive baseline for each nonzero fixed predicate, allowing additive approximation losses to become relative losses. For minimization, satisfiable or nearly satisfiable instances can have optimum zero or arbitrarily close to zero, so the same argument fails.

Raghavendra and Steurer’s universal rounding theorem obtains the integrality-gap curve with an additive error in both its argument and its returned objective. Its running-time dependence on that additive accuracy can be very large. Taking the accuracy to shrink with the instance size therefore does not yield the polynomial-time multiplicative guarantee asked here.

The source explicitly permits α_n to depend on n. Replacing it by one global constant would discard major minimization examples, while a generic additive approximation to a normalized objective would leave zero and very small costs unprotected. These are essential parts of the question, not presentation choices.

The 2026 robust-satisfiability work obtains quantitative guarantees for specified majority and plurality preservation classes, along with separate conditional hardness for a particular promise problem. Those results concern selected families and loss curves. They do not assert a universal algorithm matching the exact n-variable multiplicative SDP gap for every finite nonnegative cost language.

cards.title: Square-root logarithmic approximation for metric labeling
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Does a randomized polynomial-time algorithm exist giving an \(O(\sqrt{\log (k+2)})\) approximation for every metric-labeling instance with k labels?
cards.definitions: An instance consists of a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), nonnegative rational edge weights \(w_{uv}, a\) metric d on \([k]\) supplied by its rational distance matrix, and nonnegative rational assignment costs \(c(v,i)\). A labeling \(f:V\to [k]\) has cost \(\sum_{v} c(v,f(v))+\sum_{uv\in E}w_{uv} d(f(u),f(v))\). The guarantee is \(\operatorname{cost}(f)\le C\sqrt{\log (k+2)}\cdot\)OPT with probability at least \(2/3\) for a universal C. Running time on every random tape is polynomial in the entire binary input length; k is part of the input. No restriction on the metric or graph is promised.

context_blocks.text: Metric labeling combines local assignment costs with penalties for assigning far-apart labels to neighboring vertices. It captures a broad family of classification and partitioning objectives.

General algorithms give logarithmic approximation, while the square-root logarithmic scale arises in hardness. Closing the gap would identify the approximation power of this general model. Results for a uniform, line or truncated metric leave arbitrary label metrics unresolved.

cards.definitions: A digraph \(D=(V,A)\) has labeled vertex set \(V=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\), no loops, and at most one arc in each direction between distinct vertices; opposite arcs are allowed. Its binary encoding explicitly lists vertices and arcs. A directed cycle has at least two distinct vertices \(v_{1},\ldots ,v_{\ell}\) and arcs \(v_{i}\to v_{i+1}\), with indices modulo \(\ell\). A k-dicoloring is a map \(c:V\to \{1,\ldots ,k\}\) such that each color class induces an acyclic digraph, equivalently no directed cycle is monochromatic. The dichromatic number is the least k admitting such a map. The promise problem for k accepts inputs with dichromatic number at most 2 and rejects those with dichromatic number greater than k; inputs with values \(3,\ldots ,k\) are outside the promise. The NP-hardness claim means that for each fixed k there is a deterministic algorithm \(R_{k}\) and constants \(c_{k},C_{k}\) such that, on a 3-CNF formula F of bit length \(N, R_{k}\) outputs a digraph in time at most \(C_{k}(N+1)^{c}_{k}\), with satisfiable F mapped to the accepting side and unsatisfiable F mapped to the rejecting side. A 3-CNF is a conjunction of clauses of at most three literals, each a variable or its negation. The reduction and its polynomial may depend on k, but not on F or N; k is not an input-size parameter. A promised coloring algorithm is given the graph without a 2-coloring and must return a valid k-dicoloring. A gap reduction of the stated kind rules out such a polynomial-time algorithm unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), since validity of an output coloring can be checked in polynomial time.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated NP-hardness for every fixed \(k\ge 4\), or refute that universal hardness assertion. A polynomial-time k-coloring algorithm for some fixed k would contradict the claim under \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). Hardness for \(k=3\), bounds for a growing number of colors, or hardness without the two-colorability completeness promise do not suffice.

cards.definitions: A binary constraint satisfaction instance has k variables, a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) of size n, and explicitly given binary relations specifying the allowed pairs for constrained variable pairs. Its finite input length includes these relation tables. An assignment chooses one alphabet value for each variable; \(\operatorname{val}(\Pi )\) is the maximum fraction of its constraints satisfied by an assignment. The promise is \(\operatorname{val}(\Pi )=1\) or \(\operatorname{val}(\Pi )\le 1- \varepsilon\); no answer is prescribed for intermediate values. For an instance of encoded size L, fixed-parameter tractable means time \(f(k)\mathrm{L}^{C}\) for some computable f and constant C independent of k and L. In the standard representation with one binary relation per constrained pair, this is equivalent to \(f(k)n^{O(1)}\) after absorbing polynomial k-factors into f. Here \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\) is the standard deterministic hypothesis, equivalently that deciding whether a finite graph has a k-clique has no \(f(k)\mathrm{L}^{C}\) algorithm. PIH asserts the existence of one fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) for which the promised approximation task has no such algorithm, irrespective of the computable function f or constant exponent C. The question is the implication from exact parameterized hardness to that constant-gap hardness, not an unconditional assertion of \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\).
cards.answer_criterion: Establish the stated implication using only \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\) as the complexity assumption, with a constant gap independent of k and n, or refute that implication. A result assuming ETH or Gap-ETH, a gap shrinking with k, or hardness for a list-assignment variant does not settle this target.

cards.title: Almost 3-colorable graphs versus graphs with no large independent set
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation

references.title: NP-Hardness of Almost Coloring Almost 3-Colorable Graphs
references.authors: Hecht, Yahli; Minzer, Dor; Safra, Muli
references.locator: Conjecture 23; PDF page 10

cards.definitions: G is a finite nonempty simple undirected graph, represented by its adjacency matrix or edge list. An independent set is a set of vertices containing no edge; \(\alpha (G)\) is its maximum size. The subgraph induced by \(U\subseteq V(G)\) contains all edges of G with both endpoints in U. It is properly 3-colorable if a map \(U\to \{1,2,3\}\) gives adjacent vertices different labels. Define iCol\(_{3}(G)=N^{- 1}\max\){|\(U|:G[U]\) is 3-colorable}. The yes case is iCol\(_{3}(G)\ge 1- \eta\), and the no case is \(\alpha (G)/N<\varepsilon\). Fractions refer to vertices, not edges or color classes of a fixed coloring. The parameters \(\varepsilon ,\eta\) are fixed before the reduction and are not part of the graph input. In the usual deterministic NP-hardness formulation, for each pair there must be a deterministic polynomial-time map from Boolean satisfiability instances to graphs that sends satisfiable inputs into the yes case and unsatisfiable inputs into the no case. The polynomial may depend on \(\varepsilon\) and \(\eta\). An algorithm for the promise problem may behave arbitrarily on graphs in neither case. Since a 3-colorable set has an independent subset of at least one third its size, the displayed parameter restriction ensures disjoint cases. The paper’s already proved weaker theorem allows randomized reductions; that distinction must be retained when assessing a claimed resolution.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated gap NP-hardness for every fixed admissible \(\varepsilon ,\eta\), with a reduction and its completeness and soundness guarantees, or refute the universal hardness assertion. If a claimed hardness result uses randomized reductions, state that convention explicitly and distinguish it from deterministic NP-hardness. A polynomial-time algorithm would contradict the deterministic hardness claim under \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\); without a complexity separation, it alone is not a logical refutation of NP-hardness.

cards.definitions:
The unit-cost Levenshtein edit distance \(\operatorname{ED}(X,Y)\) is the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions and substitutions needed to transform \(X\) into \(Y\). Each operation costs one, including substitution. There are no transpositions, moves of blocks, or cheaper substitution costs. The two strings can have different lengths or be empty.

The input consists of both strings in full, with their lengths. Let \(n=|X|+|Y|\). Characters can be encoded by integer labels in \(\{1,\ldots,\max\{1,n\}\}\); only equality of labels matters. This allows arbitrary alphabets occurring in the input, rather than a binary-alphabet promise. Renaming polynomially bounded integer symbols takes only a near-linear preprocessing cost, which is included.

Use the usual sequential random-access model with \(O(\log(n+2))\)-bit words: a word read or write, comparison, Boolean operation, shift, or arithmetic operation on a constant number of words costs one step. Memory is initially empty except for the input; reading the input, all preprocessing and writing the output are charged. The algorithm has independent fair random bits, but no advice or uncharged preprocessed strings, distance oracle, parallel processors or quantum operations.

One uniform algorithm and fixed constants must work at every input length, for every input pair and every distance regime. Its running-time bound holds for every random tape. The probability of meeting the approximation guarantee is over its internal randomness alone; the inputs need not be random or generated by a mutation model.

The estimate may be an integer: rounding a valid nonnegative rational estimate down preserves the inequalities because the true distance is an integer. No edit script or alignment has to be returned. When the strings are identical, a successful estimate must be exactly zero.

Truly subquadratic means a fixed positive exponent saving \(\eta\), independent of \(n\). A bound such as \(n^{2}/\log n\), or a stated improvement of the form \(n^{2}/2^{(\log n)^{c}}\) with fixed \(0<c<1\), does not supply such a saving. A polylogarithmic overhead on an already fixed-power saving can be absorbed by decreasing \(\eta\).

The approximation factor is at most three, uniformly over the input size. A guarantee of \(3+\varepsilon\) for every fixed positive \(\varepsilon\), or \(3+o(1)\), does not itself establish this endpoint. The main question is existence of some positive runtime saving, not its optimal value.
cards.answer_criterion: Give an algorithm meeting the factor-three guarantee and some fixed positive exponent saving for all inputs in the stated model, or prove that no such randomized algorithm exists. State any hypothesis of a conditional negative result explicitly. An arbitrary constant approximation, a factor exceeding three, an average-case result, or a subpolynomial rather than fixed-power runtime saving is insufficient.

context_blocks.title: The approximation endpoint remains a distinction
context_blocks.text: Goldenberg, Rubinstein and Saha obtain a \(3+o(1)\) approximation in \(n^{1.6+o(1)}\) time without preprocessing. Despite the paper’s title, this is a result in the ordinary input model. Its approximation factor approaches three from above and therefore does not certify the exact factor-three guarantee.

context_blocks.text: Mao and Rubinstein give a randomized \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), in time \(n^{2}/2^{(\log n)^{\Omega(1)}}\), with high probability. The demonstrated saving is subpolynomial in \(n\). Their theorem crosses the factor-three accuracy threshold but does not establish \(O(n^{2-\eta})\) time for any fixed \(\eta>0\).

Andoni and Nosatzki obtain \(O(n^{1+\gamma})\) time for every fixed \(\gamma>0\), with an approximation constant depending on \(\gamma\). Their theorem does not bound that constant by three. This is the known result preceding the source’s truncated question.

Goldenberg, Rubinstein and Saha obtain a \(3+o(1)\) approximation in \(n^{1.6+o(1)}\) time without preprocessing. Despite the paper’s title, this is a result in the ordinary input model. Mao and Rubinstein give a randomized \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), in time \(n^{2}/2^{(\log n)^{\Omega(1)}}\), with high probability. The demonstrated saving is subpolynomial in \(n\). Their theorem crosses the factor-three accuracy threshold but does not establish \(O(n^{2-\eta})\) time for any fixed \(\eta>0\).

The original paper also studies edit distance with cheaper substitutions and bicriteria guarantees involving substitution and insertion/deletion budgets. Those positive results concern a different cost model or additional parameters. The selected introductory question uses ordinary unit-cost distance on unrestricted inputs.

cards.definitions:
The input explicitly lists the vertices and edges of an unweighted graph. Parallel edges are permitted and counted separately, as in the source. Self-loops can be omitted because they can be drawn locally without crossings. There is no bound on degree, genus or crossing number, and no planar subgraph or embedding is provided. Running time is polynomial in the full input length on every random tape.

A drawing places vertices at distinct points and represents each edge by a simple polygonal curve joining its endpoints, without passing through any other vertex. The objective \(\operatorname{cr}(D)\) is the total number of pairwise edge crossings, summed over the entire drawing. The crossing number \(\operatorname{cr}(G)\) is its minimum over all drawings. One may restrict to good drawings: adjacent edges do not cross, two edges cross at most once, and no three edges cross at one point.

The output must specify a drawing, rather than only an unsupported estimate of its value. A finite combinatorial representation suffices: list crossings in order along each original edge and give a planar embedding of the graph obtained by replacing crossings with degree-four vertices. At each such vertex, the two segments of each original edge must be opposite in the cyclic order. This records the original curves and their crossings without requiring real-number coordinates.

Randomization with bounded error is explicitly allowed, in keeping with the later approximation literature; a deterministic algorithm would also qualify. The success probability is over internal coins for each fixed graph. The constant \(C\) and the polynomial time bound are independent of the graph. In particular, a factor depending on its maximum degree does not meet the target. When \(\operatorname{cr}(G)=0\), the approximation guarantee requires a drawing with no crossings.

This is ordinary topological crossing number. Edges need not be straight, there is no prescribed rotation system, and the objective is not the maximum number of crossings on any one edge. The source’s Multiple Edge Insertion problem additionally keeps a specified subgraph planar; that constraint is absent here.
cards.answer_criterion: Give such an algorithm and prove its running time and universal constant-factor guarantee, or prove that none exists. A conditional impossibility result must state its complexity assumption and cover randomized algorithms in the stated model. Hardness for a particular small approximation factor alone does not exclude all constant factors.

context_blocks.text: Cabello proves that there is a constant \(c_{0}>1\) for which deterministic polynomial-time \(c_{0}\)-approximation is impossible unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), even on cubic graphs. This does not rule out an algorithm with some larger fixed factor. A randomized algorithm is not excluded merely by assuming \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\).

context_blocks.title: Subpolynomial progress for low degree
context_blocks.text: Chuzhoy and Tan give a randomized approximation factor \(2^{O((\log n)^{7/8}\log\log n)}\operatorname{poly}(\Delta)\) for simple graphs with \(n\) vertices and maximum degree \(\Delta\). For bounded degree this is subpolynomial in \(n\), but still does not supply a universal constant.

context_blocks.title: Dense graphs admit much sharper approximation
context_blocks.text: Solé-Pi’s Theorem 1.2 constructs drawings with \(\operatorname{cr}(G)+O(n^{4}/(\log\log n)^{\delta})\) crossings, for an absolute \(\delta>0\), in randomized polynomial time. This yields asymptotic factor \(1+o(1)\) for dense simple graphs, but the additive error does not yield a constant multiplicative guarantee on arbitrary graphs with small crossing number.

cards.definitions: An instance has an explicit finite list of variables with values in \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\), and an explicit finite list of constraints. Each constraint names at most \(k\) distinct variables and gives the full Boolean truth table of its predicate on those variables. A repeated constraint counts separately. All variables, indices, delimiters and table entries count in the input bit length \(L\); there is no succinct predicate circuit or implicit list. The value of an assignment is the number of satisfied constraints, and \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) is the maximum value. For fixed \((k,d)\), an admissible algorithm is a uniform fair-coin Turing machine that outputs an assignment and halts within \(C_{k,d}(L+1)^{a_{k,d}}\) steps on every input and random tape, including output time. Its code and constants may depend on the fixed parameters, but not on the instance. Define \(\rho(k,d)\) as the supremum of \(r\in[0,1]\) for which some admissible algorithm satisfies \(\mathbb E[\operatorname{val}(A(I))]\ge r\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) on every instance; zero-optimum instances impose no additional ratio condition. The supremum is not presumed attained. Logarithms in \(q\) are natural. A constant-factor answer consists of a positive function \(g(k,d)\) and one \(C\ge1\) such that \(C^{-1}g(k,d)\le\rho(k,d)\le Cg(k,d)\) for all \(k,d\ge2\). No hidden constant may depend on either parameter. Here the Unique Games Conjecture means: for every rational \(0<\eta,\gamma<1/2\), there is a fixed label count \(R\ge2\) for which it is NP-hard to distinguish unique-game instances of optimum satisfied fraction at least \(1-\eta\) from those of optimum at most \(\gamma\). A unique-game instance is an explicitly listed finite bipartite multigraph with at least one edge, a label in \([R]\) at each vertex, and a permutation \(\pi_e:[R]\to[R]\) at each oriented edge; an edge is satisfied when its endpoint labels obey that permutation. The objective is the fraction of satisfied edges, counting multiplicity. NP-hardness of this promise problem means that every language with polynomial-time verifiable polynomial-length witnesses has a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction mapping members to the first promise and nonmembers to the second. BPP consists of languages decided by a uniform randomized polynomial-time machine with error at most \(1/3\) on every input. The additional assumption \(\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}\) makes the NP-hardness premise exclude bounded-error randomized polynomial-time decision procedures. Both assumptions and the fixed-parameter algorithm convention are explicit editorial choices.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a positive comparison function and a Lean proof, conditional only on the two stated hypotheses, of both universal constant-factor bounds for the entire arity/domain range. A ratio established for each fixed parameter with uncontrolled parameter-dependent comparison constants does not suffice. Bounds only for Boolean domains or only for one parameter regime do not determine this target. The answer concerns a supremum of achievable expected ratios and does not require an optimum-attaining algorithm. Numerical 0.01 tolerance does not apply to the asymptotic scale.

cards.title: Deterministic competitiveness of k-server
cards.formal:
For every integer \(k\ge1\), determine the universal deterministic competitive-ratio infimum
\[R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)=\inf\mathcal R_k,\]
where
\[\mathcal R_k=\Bigl\{r\in[1,\infty):\ \forall(M,d)\in\mathcal M_k\ \forall C_0\in M^k\ \exists A\ \exists\beta\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\ \forall\sigma\in M^{<\omega},\quad
\operatorname{cost}_{A}(\sigma;C_0)\le r\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma;C_0)+\beta\Bigr\}.\]
Here \(\mathcal M_k\) consists of all finite or infinite metric spaces having at least \(k+1\) points, \(A\) is a deterministic online rule in the serving model below, and \(M^{<\omega}\) is the set of all finite request sequences, including the empty sequence. Give a real-valued function \(g\) and a complete Lean proof that
\[\forall k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1},\qquad |g(k)-R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)|\le\frac1{100}.\]
The tolerance is absolute in the competitive ratio and is the same for every \(k\).
cards.definitions:
A metric space here consists of a set \(M\) and a function \(d:M\times M\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) with finite values, satisfying \(d(x,y)=0\) exactly when \(x=y\), symmetry, and \(d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)\). The space is known to the rule. It need not be finite, bounded, discrete, complete, compact, or given by computable distances. The quantifier ranges over ordinary set-based metric spaces.

There are exactly \(k\) servers with equal movement costs. For precise bookkeeping label them by \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\) and write a configuration as a tuple \(C=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\in M^k\). Several servers may occupy the same point. Labels only identify which server moves and confer no different costs or service capabilities; the physical configuration is a multiset. The initial tuple \(C_0\) is specified before the first request and is identical for the online rule and the offline comparator.

For a request sequence \(\sigma=(q_1,\ldots,q_T)\), request \(q_t\) must be served before \(q_{t+1}\) is revealed. If a server already occupies \(q_t\), all servers stay put and the cost of that step is zero. Otherwise the rule chooses one index \(i_t\in[k]\), moves that server from its current position \(x_{i_t,t-1}\) to \(q_t\), and pays \(d(x_{i_t,t-1},q_t)\). All other positions remain unchanged. Let \(\delta_t\) denote this step cost. The total cost is \(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\delta_t\). These are lazy moves; for the ordinary sum-of-movement-distances objective, the classical laziness lemma shows that this restriction does not worsen the attainable competitive guarantees.

A deterministic online rule is a function assigning a legal next move to each nonempty revealed request prefix, with the current configuration determined recursively from earlier moves. On two sequences with the same prefix it must make the same decisions through that prefix. It may use the known metric, \(k\), the initial tuple, and the whole revealed history. No random bits, future-dependent advice, request horizon or next request are provided. All finite sequences are included, of arbitrary length; the definition also covers requests chosen adaptively from the rule's past moves. Covered requests may remain in the remembered history.

This is a question about existence of online decision rules, without any time, space, computability, finite-program or finite-precision restriction. In particular, a rule on a specified real metric is an abstract function; no unmentioned representation of all real distances is required. The ratio \(r\) depends only on \(k\). The chosen rule and finite constant \(\beta\) may depend on \(k,r,(M,d),C_0\), but neither may be chosen after seeing the future sequence. The same \(A,\beta\) must satisfy the inequality for all sequence lengths and contents on that metric and initial placement.

The quantity \(\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma;C_0)\) is the minimum total cost of all legal lazy move sequences serving \(\sigma\) from \(C_0\), with all requests known in advance. There are at most \(k^T\) choices of server indices, so the minimum is attained and finite even when \(M\) is infinite. Both costs are zero for the empty sequence. There is no final return requirement and no prescribed terminal configuration. The competitive inequality is used directly, including when \(\operatorname{OPT}=0\); it is not a quotient by a possibly zero cost.

Movement costs and \(\beta\) have the same distance units, while \(r\) and \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\) are dimensionless. Multiplying all distances by a positive constant rescales costs and the allowed additive constant, but does not change the competitive ratio. No normalization of metric diameter is imposed.

The known universal upper bound gives \(2k-1\in\mathcal R_k\), so this set is nonempty and its real infimum exists; the deterministic lower bound gives \(k\le R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\le2k-1\). The infimum need not be attained. For \(u\ge1\), an upper bound \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\le u\) means that for every \(\eta>0\), the ratio \(u+\eta\) belongs to \(\mathcal R_k\). The selected rules and additive constants may depend on \(\eta\). A lower bound \(\ell\ge1\) means that for every \(r\in[1,\ell)\) there exist a metric and initial placement such that every online rule and every finite additive constant fail the competitive inequality on some finite sequence. The obstructing metric may depend on \(r\); no single metric witnessing attainment of a supremum is required.
cards.answer_criterion:
Specify an unambiguous function \(g:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb R\) and give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of
\[\forall k\ge1,\quad |g(k)-R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)|\le1/100.\]
Both sides of the error interval must be proved with the metric, rule, additive-constant and sequence quantifiers above. In particular, certified functions \(\ell,u\) satisfying \(\ell(k)\le R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\le u(k)\) and \(u(k)-\ell(k)\le1/50\) for every positive integer \(k\) qualify through their midpoint. Exact determination also qualifies. An upper bound on an infimum must not silently be replaced by existence of a rule attaining its endpoint.

The absolute error must remain at most \(1/100\) as \(k\) grows; relative error \(k/100\), a constant-factor asymptotic estimate, or finitely many solved server counts does not meet it. A rule for a particular metric family or one named algorithm establishes only the corresponding restricted guarantee. A lower bound must rule out all allowed deterministic rules on its witnessing metric, rather than only one proposed algorithm or proof certificate. No unproved additional hypothesis is part of the target. There is no fixed formula grammar or polynomial evaluation requirement for \(g\), but repeating the defining infimum without determining its value is not an answer. The benchmark precision does not assert the classical exact equality \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)=k\) or endpoint attainment.
cards.why: The k-server problem measures the movement cost of responding to demand without knowing future requests. It includes paging and serves as a basic problem in competitive analysis, with the same number of resources available to the online rule and the offline optimum.

context_blocks.text: On the uniform metric, where every two different points have distance one, the covered points represent pages currently in a cache. A request at an uncovered point incurs a page replacement. General metrics permit different movement costs between different demand locations. The comparison here always gives exactly \(k\) servers to both parties.

Manasse, McGeoch and Sleator prove the deterministic lower bound \(k\) and a matching algorithm for two servers. Their original paper also handles metrics with exactly \(k+1\) points. The lower-bound argument permits an offline starting-position change at a finite additive cost, so requiring the same initial placement does not remove the asymptotic obstruction. Together with the direct one-server case, the established initial values are \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(1)=1\) and \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(2)=2\).

Koutsoupias and Papadimitriou establish a universal \((2k-1)\)-competitive deterministic rule, the work-function algorithm. Their manuscript explicitly allows infinite metrics and repeated server locations. As the classical bound before the September 2026 claim, this yields \(k\le R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\le2k-1\). The result concerns competitive movement cost; it does not supply a polynomial running-time guarantee, and the present target does not require one.

The classical conjecture predicts an actual \(k\)-competitive rule for every metric, which would imply \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)=k\). Knowing only the infimum value need not imply endpoint attainment. The new preprint claims the stronger actual competitiveness statement, so its stated theorem would also determine this card's function exactly, rather than merely approximate it within \(1/100\).

Chrobak and Larmore obtain the optimal factor \(k\) on tree metrics, whose distances are the lengths of unique connecting paths in an edge-weighted tree. This covers the line as a special case. It is a guarantee for that geometry rather than for every metric.

Huang and Zhang prove that the work-function algorithm is 3-competitive on a circle. For circumference \(L>0\), this metric is \([0,L)\) with \(d(x,y)=\min\{|x-y|,L-|x-y|\}\). Their separate computer-assisted limitation concerns a precisely defined family of potential certificates under a specified universal condition. It does not disprove 3-competitiveness of all online rules or exclude every proof for the work-function algorithm. The inspected text is the 2022 preprint; the journal article appeared in 2024.

Bubeck, Coester and Rabani give metrics on \(k+1\) points with randomized competitive ratio \(\Omega(\log^2 k)\). This refutes the randomized \(O(\log k)\) conjecture. Their ratio compares expected movement cost to the offline optimum with a sequence-independent additive constant. It neither refutes the deterministic factor \(k\) nor determines the deterministic infimum function.

Frei and coauthors' ISAAC 2025 result has a deterministic lower bound \(2k-1\) for a different objective: each request costs the maximum simultaneous server movement, rather than the sum of movements. That time objective can reward moving several servers at once, so the lazy distance model in this card is not an interchangeable formulation. The new lower bound is not a matching lower bound for \(R_{\mathrm{det}}\).

The April 2026 k-server-bench preprint evaluates candidate proof certificates on finite instances, including four-server circle instances. It explicitly distinguishes passing those finite checks from a proof covering all configurations and request sequences. Its reported experiments do not resolve the remaining general case.

Coester and Cosson's ICALP 2026 theorem gives a polynomial-time randomized \(O(\log n\log^2 k)\)-competitive algorithm on \(n\)-point metrics. Its reduction uses few random bits, but does not eliminate randomness. A separate deterministic consequence supplies advice that depends on the instance. Neither extra input nor randomization is present in this card, so these computational improvements do not determine its universal deterministic ratio.

Coester, Koutsoupias and Zbysiński's preprint submitted on 14 September 2026 states in Theorem 1.2 that, for every metric and every finite request sequence,
\[\operatorname{WFA}_{C_0}(\sigma)\le k\operatorname{OPT}_{C_0}(\sigma)+\sum_{1\le i<j\le k}d(s_i,s_j).\]
Here \(s_1,\ldots,s_k\) are the initial server locations. The additive term is finite and depends only on the initial placement, as permitted here. The paper explicitly handles coincident positions with distinct location labels and a pseudometric, and states the theorem for any metric space. Its lazy implementation agrees with the serving convention of this card. The matching claim changes the current status to uncertain pending verification; this review has not independently certified the whole proof.

cards.title: Optimal approximation ratio for unrelated-machine makespan
cards.formal:
For offline makespan minimization on unrelated parallel machines, determine the real number
\[\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}=\inf\mathcal R,\qquad \mathcal R=\Bigl\{r\in[1,\infty):\exists A\ \exists c,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall I\in\mathcal I,\ \begin{array}{l} A(I)\text{ halts in at most }c(L(I)+2)^k\text{ bit steps,}\\ A(I)\text{ outputs a feasible schedule }\sigma_I,\\ C_{\max}(\sigma_I)\le r\operatorname{OPT}(I)\end{array}\Bigr\}.\]
Here \(\mathcal I\) is the full class of finite rational processing-time matrices defined below, \(L(I)\) is the full binary input length, and \(A\) ranges over finite deterministic Turing-machine programs. Approximate \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\) within absolute error \(1/100\), with a complete Lean proof. No complexity hypothesis is included in the definition of this number.
cards.definitions:
An instance has integers \(m\ge1\), \(n\ge0\), machine set \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), job set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and a fully listed matrix \(p\in(\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\cup\{\infty\})^{m\times n}\). Set \([0]=\varnothing\). Each job has at least one finite entry. The symbol \(\infty\) forbids that machine–job assignment; it is not an arithmetic input with finite cost. Entries may differ arbitrarily between both machines and jobs. All processing times use the same time unit.

A feasible schedule is a function \(\sigma:[n]\to[m]\) such that \(p_{\sigma(j),j}<\infty\) for every job. Its load on machine \(i\) is \(\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i}p_{ij}\), with an empty sum equal to zero. Define
\[C_{\max}(\sigma)=\max_{i\in[m]}\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i}p_{ij},\qquad \operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min_{\sigma\text{ feasible}}C_{\max}(\sigma).\]
This minimum is finite and attained because the feasible set is finite and nonempty. Jobs are independent, available at time zero and indivisible. A machine executes its assigned jobs consecutively, one at a time, without preemption; their order does not affect the objective. There are no release dates, precedence constraints, setup times, communication costs or additional scheduling promises. For \(n=0\), the unique empty assignment has makespan zero.

Fix the following concrete binary encoding. For an integer \(u\ge0\), let \(b(u)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\), and put \(E(u)=1^{|b(u)|}0b(u)\), where juxtaposition denotes concatenation. A finite entry \(a/b\) is represented in lowest terms with \(a\ge0\), \(b\ge1\), as the tag bit \(0\) followed by \(E(a)E(b)\); \(\infty\) is the single tag bit \(1\). The input is \(E(m)E(n)\) followed by the \(mn\) entry encodings in row order. Its total bit length is \(L(I)\). The output is \(E(\sigma(1))\cdots E(\sigma(n))\) in job order; the empty schedule has an empty output. Equivalent ordinary encodings with polynomial-time translations give the same approximation-ratio infimum.

A program is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with no advice, random bits, optimization oracle or noncomputable constants. Input reading, work-tape computation and writing the full output count toward its bit running time. Arithmetic on the encoded rationals must be performed within that bound; an arbitrary-precision arithmetic operation is not a unit-cost primitive. Guarantees are required on every valid instance; invalid strings are outside \(\mathcal I\). The algorithm receives the complete matrix in advance, regardless of the category’s historical online-algorithms label.

For each fixed achieved ratio \(r\), the same program and constants \(c,k\) must work for all \(m,n,p\). They may depend on \(r\), but \(r\) is not additional advice or an input to the program. A different program for each input length is not allowed. The set \(\mathcal R\) concerns an absolute multiplicative guarantee on each instance, with no additive slack and no asymptotic or average-case exception. If \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)=0\), the output must also have makespan zero; no quotient by zero is used. All these conventions include empty instances.

The ratio is dimensionless. The established factor-two algorithm gives \(2\in\mathcal R\), so \(\mathcal R\) is nonempty and \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le2\). The infimum need not be attained: \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le u\), for \(u\ge1\), means that for every \(\eta>0\) some program achieves a ratio at most \(u+\eta\), without requiring one program to attain \(u\) or one uniform procedure generating all these programs. A lower bound \(\ell\ge1\) means that no program achieves any fixed \(r\in[1,\ell)\) on every instance. The numerical tolerance applies to this infimum, not to the feasibility or objective guarantee of a proposed schedule.
cards.answer_criterion:
Specify a real value \(a\) and give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that
\[|a-\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}|\le\frac1{100}.\]
Both sides of the claimed error interval must be certified for the full deterministic polynomial-bit-time model above. In particular, proved bounds \(\ell\le\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le u\) with \(u-\ell\le1/50\) qualify through \(a=(\ell+u)/2\); exact determination also qualifies. Upper and lower bounds must have the infimum quantifiers specified above, without silently requiring attainment or substituting a fixed machine count. An unambiguous mathematical expression or certified specification of \(a\) is acceptable without a decimal expansion, but simply restating the defining optimization is not a determination. A one-sided algorithmic improvement or relaxation gap alone does not meet the criterion.

No unproved complexity assumption is implicit in this target. A theorem proved only under \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) is a conditional bound, not an unconditional certification of this number. An answer expressed by cases must establish the required error bound in every case. Here \(\mathrm P\) denotes languages decided by deterministic polynomial-time Turing machines and \(\mathrm{NP}\) languages having polynomial-length witnesses verified in polynomial time. The \(1/100\) allowance is benchmark precision on the ratio; it need not decide whether the exact infimum equals two.
cards.why: This is a central approximation question for allocating heterogeneous work to heterogeneous machines. The long gap between achievable guarantees and conditional hardness also has formal consequences for max-min fair allocation, making its resolution informative beyond scheduling.

importance.reason: A decades-old central scheduling problem with a large hardness gap, robust LP barriers and formal consequences for fair allocation.

context_blocks.text: The original source question asks whether some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), independent of the instance, permits a polynomial-time \((2-\varepsilon)\)-approximation. The user-authorized quantitative reformulation of 12 September 2026 instead asks for the full infimum of achievable ratios with absolute \(1/100\) benchmark precision. This broader quantity retains the original scheduling model. An approximation to that quantity can satisfy the benchmark while leaving the exact below-two threshold unanswered.

Unrelated machines need not have any common ranking by speed. A job can be fast on one machine and slow on another, while a second job has the reverse pattern. The makespan measures when all work has finished, so a schedule must balance indivisible loads rather than minimize their sum. Eligibility restrictions are included by forbidding selected assignments.

Their hardness already uses a finite positive-integer subcase. Thus the unconditional bounds here are \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le2\); assuming \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), they become \(3/2\le\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le2\). If \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), the finite rational scheduling optimization admits exact polynomial-time search and \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}=1\). The hardness assumption cannot be omitted from the lower endpoint.

Shchepin and Vakhania achieve ratio \(2-1/m\) for \(m\) machines. The same formula is below two for each finite \(m\), but its supremum over all machine counts is two. It therefore gives no fixed universal improvement. Likewise, the polynomial approximation scheme of Lenstra, Shmoys and Tardos fixes the number of machines in advance; its running-time dependence is different from the single polynomial required for unbounded \(m\).

For a target time \(T\), the configuration linear program has one nonnegative variable \(y_{i,S}\) for each machine and each job subset \(S\) whose total processing time on that machine is at most \(T\). It requires \(\sum_S y_{i,S}=1\) for each machine and total fractional coverage one for every job. Verschae and Wiese show that the supremum of the integral optimum divided by the least feasible relaxation time is two, even when each job has at most two eligible machines with potentially different processing times. This is a statement about that relaxation, not an impossibility result for every polynomial-time algorithm.

Restricted assignment requires a job to have the same processing time on every eligible machine. The SODA 2024 work of Bamas and coauthors gives a \((7/4+\delta)\)-approximation for its two-size subcase. For general two-value matrices with entries in \(\{u,w,\infty\}\), it gives \(2-1/n^{\delta}\) for every fixed \(\delta>0\), where \(n\) is the number of jobs. The exponent is on \(n\), not on the whole ratio. These guarantees preserve their restrictions and instance-size dependence.

The same paper proves that a polynomial-time \((2-1/\alpha)\)-approximation for unrestricted makespan, for any fixed \(\alpha\ge2\), yields a polynomial-time \((\alpha+\delta)\)-approximation for general Santa Claus allocation for every fixed \(\delta>0\). In that problem indivisible items have nonnegative player-dependent values, and the objective is to maximize the minimum total value received by a player. The reduction preserves the algorithmic significance of any fixed improvement here; the paper’s converse equivalence is confined to the two-value variants.

Baba, Bampis and Mitropoulos’ June 2026 preprint supplies an additional predicted partial job assignment. Its guarantee improves when prediction errors relative to an optimum are small and retains a worst-case factor two. The stated running time has a factor \((mn)^K\), so the search budget \(K\) must remain fixed for its polynomial-time claim. The inspected model uses positive processing times; neither good predictions nor a growing budget are supplied by the classical target.

The \(3/2\) result in Proportionally Fair Makespan Approximation concerns a mechanism’s fairness guarantee using an optimal initial allocation. The June 2026 revision explicitly states that its transformation is polynomial time given an allocation, while obtaining an optimal initial allocation is NP-hard. Consequently this existence result does not establish \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le3/2\). Fairness or incentive constraints and their separate existence bounds must be distinguished from computing a schedule with the complete polynomial-time guarantee in this card.

cards.title: Optimal approximation ratio for precedence-constrained makespan
cards.formal: Determine \(\rho _{\mathrm{prec}}=\inf\){\(r\ge 1: a\) uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm returns a feasible solution of objective value at most \(r\cdot\)OPT on every identical-machine precedence-constrained scheduling instance}, in the input and output model below.
cards.definitions: An input specifies \(n\ge 1\) jobs, a positive integer processing time \(p_{j}\) for each job, a directed acyclic graph of precedence constraints, and a positive integer machine count m. All numbers are encoded in binary and the graph is given explicitly. The machine count is not fixed in advance; one may cap it at n because additional machines cannot help. A feasible schedule chooses a machine \(a_{j}\in \{1,\ldots ,m\}\) and a nonnegative start time \(s_{j}\) for every job. Job j occupies that machine continuously during [\(s_{j},s_{j}+p_{j}\)), without preemption or migration. Intervals assigned to the same machine must be disjoint. For every precedence edge \(i\to j\), require \(s_{j}\ge s_{i}+p_{i}\). Every job can run on every machine and its processing time is independent of the chosen machine. There are no release dates, deadlines, communication delays, setup costs or extra resource constraints. The makespan is Cmax=\(\max _{j}(s_{j}+p_{j})\); OPT is the minimum over feasible schedules using the same m unit-speed machines. With integer processing times, an optimal schedule with integer start times exists, so the algorithm can output binary-encoded integer starts. Polynomial time is measured in the full input bit length, not in \(\sum_{j} p_{j}\). Each fixed achieved ratio r must apply for all n, all m, all processing times and all precedence DAGs. The algorithm receives the whole instance before constructing the schedule. For each fixed ratio r in the defining set, one finite deterministic algorithm and one time polynomial must work on every instance; both may depend on r. The infimum is over these globally uniform guarantees and need not be attained. There is no per-input-size choice of algorithm, advice or free optimization oracle.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |\(a- \rho _{\mathrm{prec}}|\le 1/100\). The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds \(\ell\)\(\le u\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell +u)/2\). An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The \(1/100\) tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture. Any hardness assumption must be stated explicitly; a conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional conclusion.
cards.why: Determine whether arbitrary precedence constraints allow a constant improvement over the classical factor-two makespan guarantee on identical machines.

cards.status_note: No polynomial-time fixed \((2- \varepsilon )\) improvement found through 11 September 2026. Svensson’s factor-two hardness requires the specified possibly stronger Unique Games variant. Recent fixed-machine approximation schemes and exact unit-job algorithms have narrower scope, while July 2026 UMPS hardness imposes machine eligibility restrictions absent here.
