cards.title: Randomized competitive ratio of list update
cards.formal: Determine the optimal randomized competitive ratio of online list update against an oblivious adversary in the full-cost model: \[\rho_{\mathrm{LU}}=\inf\{r\in[1,\infty):r\text{ is achievable under the definition below}\}.\] Give its value to absolute error at most \(1/100\). The same competitive factor must work for lists of every finite size, with an additive constant allowed to depend on the size and initial order. No predictions or advice about future requests are supplied.
cards.definitions: For \(n\ge1\), the item set is \([n]\) and an initial list \(L_0\) is a permutation of these items. A request sequence \(\sigma=(x_1,\ldots,x_T)\in[n]^T\) has arbitrary finite length \(T\ge0\), is fixed independently of all online randomness, and is revealed one request at a time. The online rule must finish serving \(x_t\) before learning \(x_{t+1}\); it is not told the remaining sequence or its length. Accessing an item in current position \(j\), counting from one, costs \(j\). After this access, that item may be moved any distance toward the front at zero cost. Each other exchange of adjacent items costs one. Paid exchanges may be performed between accesses, including before serving a revealed request, and every such exchange is charged. The free move changes only the accessed item’s position and preserves the relative order of all other items. Items are never inserted or deleted. The total cost is the sum of access costs and paid exchanges. The offline optimum \(\mathrm{OPT}_{n,L_0}(\sigma)\) is the minimum cost of a legal schedule starting from the same \(L_0\), with advance knowledge of all of \(\sigma\), under exactly these access and exchange rules. A randomized online rule chooses each finite legal service action using only the revealed request prefix, its previous actions and its private random state. Abstract probability distributions over actions are permitted, with no bound on computational work or memory; all expectations must be well defined. Each request is served with finitely many exchanges on each realization. A real \(r\ge1\) is achievable if \[\forall n\ge1\ \forall L_0\ \exists A_{n,L_0,r}\ \exists\beta_{n,L_0,r}\in[0,\infty)\ \forall T\ge0\ \forall\sigma\in[n]^T:\quad \mathbb E[\mathrm{cost}_{A_{n,L_0,r}}(\sigma)]\le r\,\mathrm{OPT}_{n,L_0}(\sigma)+\beta_{n,L_0,r}.\] The rule and finite additive constant are chosen before the future requests, so neither may depend on \(\sigma\) or \(T\). Expectation is over the algorithm’s randomness alone. The infimum is over such common factors \(r\); it need not be attained. This is the full-cost convention \(j\), not the partial-cost convention \(j-1\). All costs and the ratio are dimensionless.
cards.why: List update is a basic model of a data structure adapting to changing demand without knowing future accesses. Its optimal randomized ratio would quantify the value of randomization in a simple online problem whose deterministic analogue is well understood. The unresolved constant gap makes it a precise long-standing benchmark in competitive analysis.

context_blocks.text: The 2025 primary source states the classical randomized bounds \(1.5\le\rho_{\mathrm{LU}}\le1.6\) and defines access cost by the position counted from one. This interval has width \(0.1\), so it does not certify the required absolute error \(0.01\).

The same paper investigates algorithms assisted by predictions. Their guarantees involve additional information unavailable in the ordinary online problem specified here; those results do not settle the classical optimal ratio.

A related lower bound of \(1.50084\), proved by Ambühl, Gärtner and von Stengel, is explicitly for the partial-cost model, where the first item costs zero to access. Changing the charge by one on every request can change a competitive ratio, so that theorem is not asserted here as a stronger full-cost lower bound.

The additive constant is independent of the entire request sequence and its length. It permits a fixed initial-order cost but cannot absorb a cost that grows with the number of requests. The infimum formulation also permits a limiting optimal ratio without assuming that a best online rule exists.

cards.title: Adaptive regret in misspecified linear bandits
cards.formal: Do there exist universal constants \(C>0\) and an integer \(p\ge0\) such that, for every \(d,k,T\in\mathbb N\) with \(d,T\ge1\) and \(k\ge d^2\), and every known feature matrix \(\Phi\in\mathbb R^{k\times d}\), there is one bandit policy \(\pi\) satisfying, simultaneously for every unknown mean-reward vector \(\mu\in\mathbb R^k\) with \(\max_i\mu_i-\min_i\mu_i\le1\), \[R_T(\pi,\mu)\le C[\log(2kdT)]^p\min\left\{T,\ d\sqrt T+\varepsilon(\Phi,\mu)T\sqrt d,\ \frac{k}{d}\sqrt T\right\}?\] Here \(\varepsilon(\Phi,\mu)=\inf_{\theta\in\mathbb R^d}\|\Phi\theta-\mu\|_\infty\). The policy may depend on \(\Phi,d,k,T\), but cannot be given \(\mu\), a fitting parameter \(\theta\), the misspecification level \(\varepsilon\), or an upper bound on that level. Use the Gaussian-noise model below.
cards.why: Features let a learner transfer information between arms, but approximation errors can make that transfer misleading. A policy that adapts to unknown error while preserving a controlled fallback would identify how much statistical benefit an imperfect model can safely provide. The requirement that one policy meet the bound at every error level is central: independently choosing a policy after learning the true error would answer a different question.
cards.status_note: Current openness is uncertain. The precise bound is speculative in the 2020 book; checked later primary results establish important related adaptation guarantees, but this review has not verified the full displayed simultaneous bound as a theorem or excluded its coverage by existing work. This card is individually formulated and retains that status limitation explicitly.

category_assignment.reason: The question asks for sequential prediction, exploration or regret guarantees under online feedback.

importance.reason: A substantial robustness and adaptation question for a foundational sequential-learning model. The simultaneous guarantee tests whether useful linear structure can be exploited without sacrificing controlled performance when that structure is inaccurate, across arbitrary known action geometries. Its importance is broader than optimizing a bound for one fixed action set.

sentences: The question asks for one bandit policy that adapts to unknown error in a linear reward model.
It must exploit accurate features while simultaneously obeying a uniform fallback bound when those features fit poorly.
The model has finitely many indexed arms, independent Gaussian observation noise and a known feature matrix of arbitrary geometry.
The displayed tradeoff comes from an explicit speculation in Bandit Algorithms, while later papers prove closely related partial guarantees.
The formulation is now precise, but the current openness of the complete simultaneous bound remains uncertain.

cards.definitions: There are \(k\) indexed arms, with \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\); row \(\Phi_i\) gives the known feature vector of arm \(i\). Different arms may have the same feature vector, and no full-rank assumption or bound on the entries of \(\Phi\) is imposed. The mean vector is fixed before play and does not change with time or the learner’s choices. In round \(t\in[T]\), the policy chooses \(A_t\in[k]\), then observes only \(Y_t=\mu_{A_t}+Z_t\), where \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_T\) are independent standard real Gaussian random variables with mean zero and variance one, independent of the learner’s randomness. A policy for fixed known \((\Phi,d,k,T)\) is a collection of Borel-measurable maps from the history \(([k]\times\mathbb R)^{t-1}\) to the probability simplex \(\Delta_k=\{q\in[0,1]^k:\sum_iq_i=1\}\), one for each round; the selected arm is sampled from that distribution using fresh private randomness. These maps do not take the unknown environment as an argument. Thus the same policy must work for all allowed \(\mu\) for that fixed known instance. Expected regret is \(R_T(\pi,\mu)=\mathbb E_{\pi,\mu}[\sum_{t=1}^T(\max_{i\in[k]}\mu_i-\mu_{A_t})]\), with expectation over observation noise and policy randomness. It compares to the best fixed arm’s mean, not the largest realized noisy reward. For \(v\in\mathbb R^k\), \(\|v\|_\infty=\max_i|v_i|\). The infimum in the misspecification definition ranges over all real \(\theta\), with no norm constraint. The reward-range normalization bounds regret by \(T\); it does not bound the realized Gaussian observations. Logarithms in the displayed guarantee are natural. The single exponent \(p\) and multiplicative constant \(C\) are chosen before all instance parameters, so all hidden logarithmic losses are uniform powers of \(\log(2kdT)\). This is an information-theoretic policy-existence question: the number of reward observations is the resource, and no running-time, finite-precision representation or efficient implementation requirement is imposed on the measurable policies.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this policy-existence statement or its negation. A positive answer must provide the policy family and prove the simultaneous expected-regret bound with one universal \(C,p\), over the entire stated domain and without access to the misspecification level. A negative answer must rule out every universal pair \(C,p\), with an instance on which every policy has some admissible mean vector violating the bound; the violating mean vector may depend on the policy but is fixed before play. A guarantee only at zero misspecification, only for a known misspecification bound, or without the second uniform fallback term does not meet the target. No additive numerical tolerance applies to this asymptotic existence question.

context_blocks.text: The draft grouped two directions from the book. Section 24.4 makes the concrete conjectural claim with the minimum of \(d\sqrt T+\varepsilon T\sqrt d\) and \((k/d)\sqrt T\) when \(k\ge d^2\). This explicit simultaneous-adaptation statement is the card’s main target. Section 24.5 also asks more broadly for action-set-dependent regret characterizations; that broader direction is retained as context rather than silently folded into a second answer criterion.

The mathematical conventions are fixed against the chapter’s Gaussian model and the companion paper’s unit reward-range normalization. Indexed arms allow repeated feature rows, as in the book’s own lower-bound example. The additional T term records the trivial regret ceiling, and the explicit logarithmic factor spells out the book’s soft-O convention. These choices are recorded rather than left to the solver.

Lattimore, Szepesvári and Weisz’s Proposition 5.1 gives a finite-action guarantee of order \(\sqrt{dT\log(Tk)}+\varepsilon T\sqrt d\log T\) without requiring the error level as an input. This supports the first component of the desired tradeoff, but that theorem does not state the simultaneous \((k/d)\sqrt T\) fallback for all mean vectors.

Cutkosky, Das and Purohit’s Section 6.2 proves a frontier for performance on exactly linear rewards versus arbitrary rewards. Its Corollary 6 distinguishes these two cases. The present displayed bound also tracks every intermediate misspecification level; the two-case theorem alone is not recorded as a proof of that complete bound.

Hu, Yao, Zhang and Zhou’s July 2026 preprint uses misspecification-dependent guarantees for nonstationary bandits with changing feasible actions. Its principal claims concern dynamic regret and the variation of a time-dependent reward parameter. The checked statements do not directly assert the finite-action stationary bound on this card.

Current openness remains uncertain. The original book labels the displayed tradeoff speculative, and later work proves closely related adaptation results. This review recovers the exact target and checks several relevant theorem statements; it does not establish that no existing combination or later theorem already gives the complete guarantee.

cards.title: One forecaster with the optimal regret rate for every proper loss
cards.formal: For each fixed number \(K\ge 2\) of outcomes, does there exist one randomized online forecaster A, not given the loss function, such that for every bounded proper loss \(\ell\) its worst-case expected regret satisfies \(R_{A},\ell (T)\le C_{\ell},K\cdot (1+R*_{\ell},K(T))\cdot (\log (T+2))^{c_{\ell},K}\) for all \(T\ge 1\), for some constants \(C_{\ell},K>0\) and \(c_{\ell},K\ge 0\) independent of T? Here \(R*_{\ell},K\) is the minimax regret achievable by a forecaster tailored to that particular loss. This spells out the source’s “optimal up to constant or logarithmic factors in T” target; the additive one covers losses with zero or bounded optimal regret.
cards.why: Would establish whether a general-purpose probability forecaster can match every downstream user’s best possible learning rate without knowing that user’s loss. It refines universal sublinear regret into adaptation to the intrinsic difficulty of each scoring rule.
cards.status_note: Full forecasting model, proven simultaneous bounds and concluding question checked with the June arXiv record and subsequent searches through 11 September 2026. cards.definitions: The prediction space is the simplex \(\Delta _{K}=\{p\in \mathbb{R} ^{K}:p_{i}\ge 0,\sum p_{i}=1\}\). At round t, A chooses a possibly random \(\mathrm{P}_{t}\in \Delta _{K}\) from earlier revealed outcomes, then observes \(y_{t}\in \{e_{1},\ldots ,e_{K}\}\), where \(e_{i}\) is the ith unit vector. The adversary fixes \(y_{1},\ldots ,y_{T}\) in advance, knowing A but not its random bits. For a measurable loss \(\ell\):\(\Delta _{K}\times \{e_{1},\ldots ,e_{K}\}\to [- 1,1]\), propriety means \(E_{Y\sim p}\ell (p,Y)\le E_{Y\sim p}\ell (q,Y)\) for every \(p,q\in \Delta _{K}\); the minimizer need not be unique. Define \(Reg_{A},\ell (y_{1}:T)=E_{A}[\sum _{t=1}^{T} \ell (\mathrm{P}_{t},y_{t})]- \inf _{p\in \Delta _{K}}\sum _{t=1}^{T}\ell (p,y_{t})\). The expectation is over forecasting randomness, while the comparator is the best single fixed probability prediction in hindsight. Propriety makes the empirical outcome distribution a minimizing comparator. Set \(R_{A},\ell (T)=\sup _{y_{1}:T}Reg_{A},\ell (y_{1}:T)\), and \(R*_{\ell},K(T)=\inf _{B} R_{B},\ell (T)\), where B ranges over randomized online prediction strategies allowed to know \(\ell ,K\) and T. The desired A may know K and the horizon T, but its predictions are independent of which downstream loss is evaluated. Constants and logarithmic exponents may depend on the fixed loss and K; the asymptotic comparison is in T. This is an expected-regret comparison for each loss, not one simultaneous high-probability event over all losses. The question does not impose a particular polynomial running-time bound or a finite-precision implementation model; the target is the attainable online regret rate.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a loss-independent forecaster and prove the comparison for every bounded proper loss, or show that every such forecaster has some bounded proper loss for which its worst-case expected regret exceeds every allowed logarithmic-factor comparison with that loss’s minimax rate. Achieving \(\widetilde{O}\)\((\sqrt{T})\) for all losses alone does not settle the question, because some individual losses admit logarithmic or smaller regret.

cards.title: Additive-one approximation for bin packing
cards.formal:
Is there a polynomial-time approximation algorithm for one-dimensional offline bin packing that uses at most one more bin than optimum? Explicitly allowing randomization, the target is one uniform probabilistic algorithm \(A\) and a polynomial \(p\) such that, for every finite input list \(I=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{n})\) of rational sizes \(0<s_{i}\le1\), \(A\) runs within \(p(L)\) steps for every coin sequence, always outputs a feasible packing, and satisfies
\[
\Pr\bigl[B(A(I))\le\operatorname{OPT}(I)+1\bigr]\ge\tfrac23.
\]
Here \(L\) is the total binary input length, \(B\) is the number of bins used, and probability is over the algorithm’s independent fair random bits for each fixed input. A deterministic algorithm with the same bound on every input also qualifies.
cards.why: A one-extra-bin algorithm would show that a strongly NP-hard packing problem can nevertheless be solved to a uniformly tiny additive error. The question tests a much sharper notion of approximation than a ratio tending to one and is a long-standing benchmark for understanding the structure of feasible packings.
cards.status_note: Checked the complete two-page source question and the full Hoberg–Rothvoss author manuscript, especially Theorem 2 and its expected-time randomization convention. Confirmed the SODA 2017 publication date from publisher metadata. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no algorithm achieving the stated one-extra-bin target; newer results for online, dynamic or other packing variants do not establish it. The dated known bound is not presented as a newly proved 2026 theorem.
cards.review_note: Defined explicit binary rational inputs, offline packing output, integer optimum, exact capacity, additive-one guarantee and uniform bit complexity. Explicitly allows bounded-error randomization; preserves the source’s constant-additive discussion as partial progress.

cards.definitions:
All items and their sizes are given before computation starts. Each item is listed separately, including repetitions. Write \(s_{i}=a_{i}/b_{i}\), where \(a_{i},b_{i}\) are positive binary integers and \(a_{i}\le b_{i}\). Input length includes the item list, numerators, denominators and separators; arithmetic precision is not free.

A packing partitions the item indices \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) into nonempty bins \(B_{1},\ldots,B_{q}\) such that
\[
\sum_{i\in B_{j}}s_{i}\le1\quad\text{for every }j.
\]
Items are indivisible and must each appear in exactly one bin. The output explicitly assigns every item to a bin. The integer \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) is the minimum feasible number \(q\); the empty input has optimum zero and can be packed in zero bins. Zero-size items, if allowed by an alternative convention, can be handled separately without changing the existence question.

Running time is worst-case bit complexity on a uniform probabilistic multitape Turing machine. There is no input advice, supplied optimal packing or promise on the size distribution, number of distinct sizes or optimum. The input is an explicit list, not binary multiplicities representing exponentially many separate output items.

The additive allowance is exactly one bin with capacity exactly 1. It does not grow with the instance, and it is not a multiplicative factor \(1+\varepsilon\). Neither larger bin capacities nor discarding an item is permitted. The target concerns the integer optimum of the packing problem, not the optimum of a fractional relaxation.

The probability convention makes explicit an algorithmic interpretation that includes randomized approximation algorithms, as in the later logarithmic-additive result. Its theorem gives expected polynomial runtime with its quality guarantee; that is a separately reported form of the known result. For the target here, the output must always be feasible and only the one-extra-bin guarantee may fail with probability at most \(1/3\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give one algorithm and a proof of all stated time, feasibility and probability guarantees, or refute the existence of such an algorithm. A conditional impossibility result must expose its assumption, including any assumption needed to exclude randomized algorithms. An \(\operatorname{OPT}+C\) bound with unspecified constant \(C>1\), an asymptotic approximation scheme, or a nonconstructive fractional-integrality-gap bound alone does not meet the target.

context_blocks.title: Fractional packing is a related comparison
context_blocks.text: The Gilmore–Gomory relaxation permits a nonnegative fractional number of copies of each feasible bin pattern and requires enough total coverage of each item type. Statements comparing its optimum to integer packings concern an integrality gap; an existence bound for that gap does not by itself specify the efficient algorithm required here.

cards.title: Planted clique conjecture
cards.formal: Is the following hardness statement true? For every fixed real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), with \(k_n=\lfloor n^{1/2-\varepsilon}\rfloor\), there is no uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) for which \[\Pr[\widehat b=b]\geq\frac23\] in the balanced one-graph experiment below for every sufficiently large integer \(n\).
cards.definitions:
For \(n\geq2\), let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The null distribution \(N_n\) is the distribution of a simple undirected labeled graph on \([n]\) in which each unordered pair of distinct vertices is an edge independently with probability \(1/2\). For \(0\leq k\leq n\), the planted distribution \(P_{n,k}\) chooses \(S\) uniformly among all \(k\)-element subsets of \([n]\), includes every edge inside \(S\), and chooses each other edge independently with probability \(1/2\). There are no loops. The planted set has exactly \(k\) vertices; it is not formed by independently including each vertex.

In the experiment, first choose a fair bit \(b\). If \(b=0\), sample \(G\sim N_n\); if \(b=1\), sample \(G\sim P_{n,k_n}\). Give \(A\) only \((n,k_n,G)\), and let \(\widehat b\in\{0,1\}\) be its output. All randomness of the sampling and of \(A\) is independent. Success is averaged over \(b\), the graph, the planted set when present and the algorithm’s random bits. Writing \(s_A(n,\varepsilon)\) for this probability, \[s_A(n,\varepsilon)=\tfrac12\big(\Pr_{G\sim N_n,A}[A(n,k_n,G)=0]+\Pr_{G\sim P_{n,k_n},A}[A(n,k_n,G)=1]\big).\] This is not a separate \(2/3\) guarantee on each individual graph or on each of the two distributions. The algorithm receives one sampled graph, without the label \(b\), the set \(S\), sample access to the unknown distribution or other side information.

For \(u\geq0\), define \(\operatorname{code}(u)=1^a0\operatorname{bin}(u+1)\), where the binary expansion has \(a\) bits and no leading zeroes. The input is \(1^n0\operatorname{code}(k)\), followed by the full \(n^2\) adjacency matrix in row order, with no trailing bits. A valid input has \(n\geq2\), \(0\leq k\leq n\), a symmetric matrix and zero diagonal; let \(L\) be its full bit length. An allowed algorithm is one probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and tape alphabet, using fresh independent fair bits and no oracle or advice. For some integers \(C,c\geq1\), on every input and every random-bit sequence it outputs one bit within \(C(L+1)^c\) transitions. Malformed encodings return 0 within this bound. Input processing, bit arithmetic and any additional graphs generated by the algorithm count toward time. On valid inputs \(L=\Theta(n^2)\), so polynomial time in \(L\) and in \(n\) are equivalent.

For each fixed \(\varepsilon\), the forbidden guarantee is \(\exists A,C,c,N\ \forall n\geq N:\ s_A(n,\varepsilon)\geq2/3\), with the global clock condition just specified. The program and constants may depend on this fixed \(\varepsilon\), but cannot change with \(n\); \(\varepsilon\) is not supplied as an oracle or an infinite advice string. The supplied integer \(k_n\) removes any need to compute a real power to construct the input. The conjecture therefore says that every allowed algorithm has success below \(2/3\) for arbitrarily large \(n\), for every fixed \(\varepsilon\). It does not assert that its success tends to \(1/2\).
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of this hardness proposition or its logical negation. To refute it, give some fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), one allowed polynomial-time algorithm and a proof that its balanced success is at least \(2/3\) for every sufficiently large \(n\). To prove it, exclude every such algorithm for every fixed \(\varepsilon\). Success only on infinitely many sizes does not satisfy the refutation target. A limitation on sum-of-squares relaxations, local searches or another restricted model does not establish hardness against all allowed machines. A recovery result must imply the stated detection guarantee; a change of planting distribution or a conditional theorem must not be treated as an unconditional resolution of this exact experiment.
cards.why: A foundational average-case hardness hypothesis, planted clique isolates a gap between statistical information and efficient computation. The hidden clique is far larger than cliques arising by chance, yet no unrestricted polynomial-time detector is established in this regime. Related assumptions support hardness results for estimation, clustering and other inference tasks. Proving this formulation would imply Boolean \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\): a polynomial-time general clique decider would distinguish these distributions once \(k_n\) exceeds the typical null clique size.

importance.reason: A canonical computational threshold with broad consequences in average-case complexity, statistical inference, and the study of algorithmic lower-bound frameworks.

cards.status_note: No unconditional proof or unrestricted polynomial-time refutation of this exact fixed-size, balanced constant-success hypothesis was located in a bounded check through 14 September 2026. The cited sum-of-squares theorem is a relaxation/refutation lower bound; the optimal-advantage and September 2026 topology results are conditional, and several newer recovery results use other random graph models. Source/model review does not independently certify every cited proof.

context_blocks.text: The original provenance paper discusses statistical–computational gaps and proves lower bounds for low-degree polynomial procedures in latent models. The card retains the concrete fixed-size, balanced constant-success detection question already selected here. Those choices specify one version of the planted-clique hypothesis; they are not an unrestricted hardness theorem of the provenance paper.

There is enough information to distinguish the distributions. For \(r=\lceil3\log_2 n\rceil\), a union bound gives \(\Pr_{N_n}[\text{an }r\text{-clique exists}]\leq n^r2^{-r(r-1)/2}\to0\), while the planted graph contains such a clique for all sufficiently large \(n\), since \(k_n\geq r\). Thus exhaustive testing of all \(r\)-subsets gives success tending to one in \(n^{O(\log n)}\) time. The unresolved requirement is polynomial time.

Alon, Krivelevich and Sudakov give polynomial-time recovery of the hidden clique at every fixed positive constant times \(\sqrt n\), with success tending to one. Checking the reported clique gives detection as well. The polynomial exponent may depend on that constant; substituting the vanishing quantity \(n^{-\varepsilon}\) for it does not produce a fixed polynomial bound below the square-root scale.

Barak and coauthors show that degree-\(d\) sum-of-squares relaxations on a null random graph assign clique value \(n^{1/2-o(1)}\) when \(d=o(\log n)\), despite actual cliques being logarithmic in size. Their Remark 1.2 explicitly separates search, refutation and detection. The integrality gap rules out certain certificates of absence of a large clique; it is not an unrestricted lower bound for the balanced detector defined here.

Gheissari, Jagannath and Xu prove recovery by discrete gradient descent initialized at the full vertex set for \(k\geq C\sqrt n\), where \(C\) depends on the desired fixed error probability and the penalty parameter. Their Theorem 1.1 also analyzes a low-temperature chain. The theorem operates at the square-root scale and allows intermediate vertex sets that are not cliques.

Nagda and Raghavendra derive sharp efficient distinguishing advantages conditionally on a planted-clique hypothesis. Their model plants each vertex independently with probability \(k/n\), so clique size fluctuates; their advantage convention and eventual hardness hypothesis also differ from the exact guarantee here. The result strengthens consequences of its assumed hypothesis, without proving this card’s fixed-size hardness assertion.

Göbel, Ruff and Schiller’s COLT 2026 work concerns multiple overlapping planted cliques in random intersection graphs, with robust recovery for \(k\gg\sqrt{n\log n}\). Both its random graph distribution and signal regime differ from this single fixed-size planted-clique experiment.

A preprint posted on 11 September 2026 by Strelchuk, Subramanian and Wesołowski reports average-case hardness for Betti-number estimation through a planted-clique reduction. Its §3.2 uses a uniformly chosen planted set of fixed size. The reported hardness is conditional on a planted-clique conjecture, with a separate hypothesis for quantum algorithms; this review has not independently verified the new reduction.

cards.title: Average-case NP hardness from \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\)
cards.formal:
Is the following implication true in the ordinary uniform Turing-machine model?
\[\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists L\in\mathrm{NP}\ \exists S\in\mathrm{PSamp}\ :\ (L,D^S)\notin\mathrm{AvgP}.
\]
Here \(S\) is one exact polynomial-time sampler, \(D^S=(D^S_n)_{n\ge1}\) its output distribution ensemble, and \(\mathrm{AvgP}\) means deterministic, always-correct computation with the positive-moment runtime bound below. Thus the conclusion requires one fixed language and one fixed feasible sampling procedure for which no exact deterministic decider has average polynomial running time. No additional hardness or derandomization hypothesis may be assumed.
cards.definitions:
All algorithms have one fixed finite program, use ordinary multitape Turing machines with finite tape alphabets and unit-cost transitions, and receive explicit binary strings. There is no oracle or nonuniform advice. Randomized machines obtain independent fair coin bits; reading input, generating coins, computing intermediate data and writing output all take time.

A language is a set \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\). It belongs to \(\mathrm P\) if one deterministic machine decides membership on every input \(x\) within \(a(|x|+1)^d\) steps for fixed positive integers \(a,d\). It belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\) if there are a deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) and fixed positive integers \(a,d\) such that \(x\in L\) exactly when some binary certificate \(y\) of length at most \(a(|x|+1)^d\) satisfies \(V(x,y)=1\). The verifier is total and polynomial time in its full input length. The premise concerns these total decision classes.

A sampler \(S\in\mathrm{PSamp}\) is one randomized machine which, on unary input \(1^n\), \(n\ge1\), halts on every random tape within \(q(n)=a(n+1)^d\) steps, for fixed positive integers \(a,d\) depending on \(S\). It outputs a finite binary string of length at most \(q(n)\), possibly the empty string. Put \(D^S_n(x)=\Pr[S(1^n)=x]\). Sampling is exact, not an approximation, and its time bound holds for every coin sequence. The parameter \(n\) need not equal the sampled string length. These probabilities form a finite distribution: one may regard the random tape as \(q(n)\) fair bits, with unused bits ignored.

An exact decider \(A\) for \(L\) is one deterministic machine that, on the explicitly separated pair \((1^n,x)\), halts and returns \(1\) exactly when \(x\in L\), for every \(n\ge1\) and every binary string \(x\), including strings of zero probability under \(D^S_n\). It cannot answer 'unknown'. Let \(T_A(1^n,x)\) be its number of transitions, charged at least one step. There is no worst-case polynomial-time requirement on this decider. By definition,
\[(L,D^S)\in\mathrm{AvgP}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists A\ \exists\eta>0\ \exists C>0\ \exists k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge1:
\sum_x D^S_n(x)T_A(1^n,x)^{\eta}\le C(n+1)^k,
\]
where \(A\) must be an exact decider and \(\eta,C\) are real constants. The sum is over the finite support of \(D^S_n\). The algorithm and constants may depend on \(L,S\) but not on \(n\). Nonmembership means that for every such \(A,\eta,C,k\), some \(n\ge1\) violates the inequality. It is not necessary to violate it at every sufficiently large length.

This is the positive-moment convention for average polynomial time. It allows \(\eta\ne1\); the definition is not a bound on expected runtime itself and does not permit incorrect membership answers. The existentially selected sampler is part of the distributional problem, not input to the decider, which may have its fixed description built into its program.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed implication or its logical negation, under the stated uniform models and quantifiers. An affirmative result must, from \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) alone, establish a fixed \(L\in\mathrm{NP}\) and a fixed exact strict-polynomial-time sampler for which every deterministic exact decider fails every positive-moment polynomial bound. The sampler and language cannot depend on the decider being challenged. A negative result must prove \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) together with \((L,D^S)\in\mathrm{AvgP}\) for every permitted \(L,S\); an oracle separation or a barrier for one reduction method is not that negation. A complete proof of the implication may use the premise without separately proving it. Partial improvements, an additional unproved hardness assumption, or a failure of one particular algorithm do not establish the target.
cards.why: Worst-case hardness alone does not explain whether feasible procedures can generate instances that remain difficult on average. Resolving this implication would connect the central decision-class separation to robust limits on exact computation under efficiently generated inputs.

importance.reason: One of the central missing implications in complexity theory, connecting worst-case lower bounds to feasible instance generation and the limits of algorithms on typical inputs.

progress.text: Levin’s robust average-time theory and the Impagliazzo–Levin completeness extension provide the background for distributional NP with samplable inputs.
Bogdanov–Trevisan establish a polynomial-hierarchy consequence for the specified nonadaptive oracle reductions.
The inspected Wigderson edition states the general implication as Open Problem 4.6.
The revised Bogdanov–Trevisan survey retains the open question and specifies strict exact samplers, the ensemble parameter and the positive-moment definition.

Liu–Mazor–Pass’s ECCC report studies conditional generators and other consequences of specific gap-description hardness; no general NP implication is claimed.

context_blocks.text: Worst-case intractability only says that no single polynomial-time decider works on every input. It gives no immediate frequency statement about difficult inputs under a feasible sampler. The conclusion therefore quantifies over a language together with a fixed distribution ensemble; a different hard input chosen noncomputably at each length is not an admissible sampler.

The positive-moment definition is robust under polynomial changes in running time and machine representation. Rare long computations can affect the first moment much more strongly than a smaller positive moment. Heuristics that sometimes give a wrong answer have a different success condition from the total exact deciders required here.

Distributional completeness is available for polynomial-time samplable ensembles. It identifies problems whose average tractability would imply average tractability throughout the corresponding distributional NP class. Completeness alone does not establish that this class contains a hard problem under \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). Likewise, easiness under a particular familiar distribution need not reflect worst-case complexity.

Bogdanov–Trevisan show that certain nonadaptive worst-case-to-average-case oracle reductions for NP would collapse the polynomial hierarchy. Nonadaptive means that all oracle questions are chosen before their answers are read; the reduction must work for arbitrary oracles satisfying its average-correctness promise. This restriction concerns a proof mechanism, not the truth of the unrestricted implication.

Time-bounded description complexity asks how short a program can be while producing a given string within a prescribed time. Liu–Pass obtain a worst-case-to-average-case connection for a deterministic description problem under an additional exponential circuit-hardness assumption. Section 5 also gives a connection for randomized description complexity without that derandomization assumption, but still assumes worst-case hardness of that particular promise problem. Neither premise has been obtained from \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) alone in the inspected work.

The Liu–Pass paper uses AvgP for a promise-problem notion based on polynomial-time errorless heuristics, separately chosen for each inverse-polynomial failure threshold. This notation must not silently replace the card’s single exact decider and positive-moment bound. The source review records its specific model and hypotheses rather than inferring the requested general implication from a shared class name.

Liu–Mazor–Pass’s April 2026 results concern specific gap versions of description complexity, additional nonuniform hardness or derandomization assumptions, and conditional pseudorandom generators. Their hidden seed distribution can be inefficient to sample. Such a distribution does not meet the efficient sampling requirement in this question merely by existing.

cards.title: Computational threshold for tensor PCA
cards.formal: Is the following computational impossibility statement true? For every fixed integer \(k\ge3\), rational \(0<\varepsilon<(k-2)/4\), and rational \(0<c<1\), no uniform randomized polynomial-time classical algorithm can, for all sufficiently large \(n\), recover a vector with absolute correlation at least \(c\) with a uniformly random hidden unit direction from the single rounded tensor observation \[Y=\lambda_n v^{\otimes k}+Z,\qquad \lambda_n=n^{k/4-\varepsilon},\qquad v\sim\operatorname{Unif}(S^{n-1}),\] where all \(n^k\) ordered entries of \(Z\) are independent \(N(0,1)\) variables. Recovery must succeed with probability at least \(2/3\), averaged over the hidden direction, noise and algorithm coins. Rounding, output normalization and the uniform bit-cost model are defined below. The fixed power saving \(n^\varepsilon\) and the spherical prior are parts of the existing target, not replaced by a threshold for one algorithm family.
cards.definitions:
\(S^{n-1}=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\sum_i v_i^2=1\}\), with its rotation-invariant probability measure. A tensor is an array indexed by all ordered tuples \((i_1,\ldots,i_k)\in[n]^k\), including repeated indices. Its rank-one signal has entry \(\lambda_n v_{i_1}\cdots v_{i_k}\). The Gaussian noise entries, the direction and learner coins are independent. In particular the noise is not symmetrized: entries indexed by different permutations remain independent. The learner has exactly one tensor observation, with no labeled coordinates, informative starting vector, auxiliary graph or additional independent noise samples. The fixed constants \(k,\varepsilon,c\) are known to its program, but \(v\) and \(Z\) are hidden.

For \(n\ge2\), put \[b_n=\lceil10k\log_2 n\rceil,\qquad Q_b(x)=2^{-b}\left\lfloor2^b\max\{-2^b,\min\{x,2^b\}\}\right\rfloor.\] The actual input is \(n\) and the complete list \((Q_{b_n}(Y_{i_1,\ldots,i_k}))_{[n]^k}\) in lexicographic tuple order. Each entry is encoded by its signed integer numerator with the common denominator \(2^{b_n}\); the numerator has at most \(2b_n+2\) bits. The clipping interval and rounding direction are fixed, not chosen adaptively by the algorithm. The exact real tensor exists only in the sampling experiment; the machine receives no oracle for its discarded digits. The input length is \(O(n^k\log n)\) at fixed \(k\). This is the previously adopted explicit finite-precision version of the Gaussian question, not a theorem asserting equivalence to every exact-real formulation.

An allowed algorithm is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with independent fair random bits. There exist constants \(B,a\ge1\), possibly depending on the fixed triple, such that it terminates within \(Bn^a\) bit operations on every encoded input of this dimension and every random tape. Reading, storage operations, arithmetic, writing the output and its rational encodings are included. The single program and polynomial work for all \(n\), with no advice depending on dimension. Since \(k\) is fixed, this is polynomial in the complete input length. There are no exact-real or quantum operations.

The output is a list of \(n\) rational coordinates \(w_i\), each a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator. A malformed vector or \(w=0\) fails. Otherwise interpret \(u=w/\|w\|_2\), where \(\langle w,v\rangle=\sum_i w_i v_i\) and \(\|w\|_2=(\sum_i w_i^2)^{1/2}\). The success event is the mathematically defined inequality \[|\langle w,v\rangle|\ge c\|w\|_2.\] The learner need not compute that event, since it does not know the planted direction. Absolute correlation permits a global sign flip, including the inherent even-order ambiguity. The output need not encode the irrational normalized vector exactly; its rational representative determines the direction.

Write \(p_A(n;k,\varepsilon,c)\) for the probability of this event in the specified experiment. The target is \[\forall(k,\varepsilon,c)\ \forall A\text{ of polynomial bit cost}\ \forall N\ge2\ \exists n\ge N:\quad p_A(n;k,\varepsilon,c)<2/3.\] Thus the conjecture rules out eventual success on all dimensions; it does not claim that every algorithm fails at every large dimension, or that its success probability must tend to zero. Conversely, a refutation needs one fixed triple and one machine with eventual success at least \(2/3\). The range of \(\varepsilon\) ensures \(\lambda_n/\sqrt n=n^{(k-2)/4-\varepsilon}\to\infty\), placing the signal above the usual statistical scale in the unrounded model.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of the full quantified impossibility statement, or a Lean-verified counterexample consisting of one fixed triple, a single algorithm, polynomial worst-case bit/output bounds and an \(N\) for which \(p_A(n)\ge2/3\) for every \(n\ge N\). A lower bound against low-degree estimators, one iterative method, or a different prior is not the universal statement. Detection and recovery must not be interchanged without a proved reduction. Any normalization, symmetrization, multiple-sample or precision transfer must be justified in the same success and resource model. A conditional hardness reduction is partial progress until its premise is proved. Logarithmic threshold improvements or a constant-prefactor improvement at \(n^{k/4}\) do not supply the fixed exponent saving. The desired output quality is a fixed absolute correlation, not coordinatewise numerical recovery.

cards.status_note: No checked result through16 September2026 settles the displayed unrestricted finite-bit spherical recovery statement. The 2024 cumulant reconstruction theorem is restricted to odd order and low-degree estimators; the May2026 general-prior result assumes independent coordinates and both of its degree conditions. Random-start power iteration has scale n^{(k−1)/2}, while multiple-observation gradient and constant-prefactor critical-scale improvements do not produce a fixed power saving below n^{k/4}. The 2026 XOR reductions use Boolean spikes and conditional hardness premises. The checked Hastings2026 paper proves detection guarantees with a stated spectral-property caveat, not this recovery theorem. All such results remain context, and unrounded-to-rounded equivalence is not claimed.

context_blocks.text: Ordinary principal component analysis looks for a hidden direction in a noisy matrix. Tensor PCA asks the analogous question when observations have three or more indices. Here the clean signal has rank one: every entry is a product of coordinates of the same hidden unit vector. Gaussian noise obscures those products. The goal is only a constant correlation with the direction, much weaker than estimating every coordinate accurately.

For fixed tensor order, information-theoretic recovery in the standard Gaussian model becomes possible at a signal scale of order \(\sqrt{n}\). Montanari and Richard established the basic statistical-versus-computational distinction while studying tensor unfolding, power iteration and message-passing methods. Their noise normalization differs from the variance-one convention used in this card; their constant statistical threshold corresponds to order \(\sqrt{n}\) here.

Known polynomial-time methods reach signal strength around \(n^{k/4}\), up to factors that do not change this leading exponent. Wu and Zhou’s 2024 introduction records both this algorithmic scale and the conjectured gap from \(\sqrt{n}\). The interval for \(\varepsilon\) deliberately places our target strictly between them: \(\lambda /\sqrt{n}=n^{(k- 2)/4- \varepsilon}\) grows without bound. There is therefore ample statistical signal in the usual model, while efficient recovery remains unproved.

For example, at order four and \(\varepsilon =1/8\), the observation contains \(n^{4}\) noisy numbers and signal strength \(n^{7/8}\). The statistical scale is \(n^{1/2}\), and the conjectured efficient scale is n. A polynomial-time algorithm below that latter scale would have to exploit structure that current threshold evidence misses. Merely reading all \(n^{4}\) entries is allowed: the question concerns computation polynomial in the complete input, not a sublinear-access restriction.

Low-degree polynomial estimators provide one rigorous way to test proposed computational barriers. Kunisky, Moore and Wein establish the predicted degree-versus-signal tradeoff for detection with a spherical spike and derive a matching reconstruction lower bound for odd tensor orders. Their reconstruction theorem is specifically for odd orders; they explain that even orders require a sign-invariant estimand such as \(vv^{T}\) and additional work. Detection and recovery are separate tasks, and a detection lower bound should not silently be relabelled as their reconstruction theorem.

Fu and Sohn’s May 2026 preprint advances low-degree estimation bounds for tensor PCA with independent, mean-zero, variance-one spike coordinates and bounded moments. Its general-prior theorem controls estimation of fixed products of coordinates and obtains the predicted signal-versus-degree scaling within a stated degree range. Independent-coordinate priors are different from a vector conditioned to have unit norm. The result strengthens evidence for the computational gap without establishing an unrestricted polynomial-time lower bound for this card’s spherical prior.

Randomly initialized power iteration has a different benchmark from the best known general methods: Wu–Zhou analyze its scale \(n^{(k-1)/2}\) and improve it by a polylogarithmic factor. For \(k\ge3\), this is a larger leading exponent than \(k/4\). That algorithm-specific improvement is not an improvement below the card’s general computational threshold.

Ding–Gu–Liu–Fang study \(N\) independent observations and a normalized stochastic-gradient method, with a sufficient condition \(N\lambda^2\ge\widetilde\Omega(n^{\lceil k/2\rceil})\). For even order, normalizing the average to variance-one Gaussian noise gives signal strength \(\sqrt N\lambda\) at the familiar \(n^{k/4}\) scale. Their theorem neither proves an unrestricted lower bound nor supplies this card’s fixed power saving from one observation.

The rounding convention prevents an ambiguity about algorithms operating on exact Gaussian real numbers. Each coordinate is given with logarithmically many bits. Outside the clipping event, the total rounding error in Euclidean norm across the tensor is at most \(n^{k/2}2^{- b}\), an extremely small inverse power of n; clipping has vanishing probability. This is a specified computational model, rather than an assertion that every exact-real algorithm automatically transfers to it. Likewise, polynomial-estimator theorems for unrounded observations do not by themselves cover arbitrary algorithms that process rounded entries.

A resolution would clarify whether a simple, highly symmetric random model can hide statistically recoverable information from every efficient algorithm. A successful method would challenge a widely used picture of algorithmic thresholds. A full impossibility proof would require a complexity argument beyond the restricted algorithm families currently understood. Both outcomes would inform how computational hardness assumptions are formulated for inference problems.

Li’s 2025 theorem reaches a constant-prefactor critical scale for a Rademacher spike and symmetric noise, with a polynomial exponent depending on that fixed prefactor. After normalizing a sign vector to unit length, the leading signal exponent is \(k/4\). Replacing a fixed prefactor by \(n^{-\varepsilon}\) is not justified by a theorem whose runtime exponent depends on it. The spike prior also differs from the sphere.

The 2026 Bresler–Harbuzova reductions connect noisy planted XOR problems with Boolean-spike tensor PCA and transport algorithms or hardness hypotheses between parameter regimes. They preserve and compare conjectured barriers; they do not prove an unconditional barrier for the spherical prior or eliminate the specified finite-precision interface.

Hastings’s February2026 paper concerns detection rather than a proved recovery guarantee. Its added note also withdraws an unqualified provable speedup comparison after a sharper spectral-norm bound became known, retaining a spectral-property condition. It does not settle this classical recovery statement.

For \(k\ge3\), this is a larger leading exponent than \(k/4\). That algorithm-specific improvement is not an improvement below the card’s general computational threshold.

Ding–Gu–Liu–Fang study \(N\) independent observations and a normalized stochastic-gradient method, with a sufficient condition \(N\lambda^2\ge\widetilde\Omega(n^{\lceil k/2\rceil})\). For even order, normalizing the average to variance-one Gaussian noise gives signal strength \(\sqrt N\lambda\) at the familiar \(n^{k/4}\) scale. Their theorem neither proves an unrestricted lower bound nor supplies this card’s fixed power saving from one observation.

The rounding convention prevents an ambiguity about algorithms operating on exact Gaussian real numbers. Each coordinate is given with logarithmically many bits. Outside the clipping event, the total rounding error in Euclidean norm across the tensor is at most \(n^{k/2}2^{- b}\), an extremely small inverse power of n; clipping has vanishing probability. This is a specified computational model, rather than an assertion that every exact-real algorithm automatically transfers to it. Likewise, polynomial-estimator theorems for unrounded observations do not by themselves cover arbitrary algorithms that process rounded entries.

A resolution would clarify whether a simple, highly symmetric random model can hide statistically recoverable information from every efficient algorithm. A successful method would challenge a widely used picture of algorithmic thresholds. A full impossibility proof would require a complexity argument beyond the restricted algorithm families currently understood. Both outcomes would inform how computational hardness assumptions are formulated for inference problems.

Li’s 2025 theorem reaches a constant-prefactor critical scale for a Rademacher spike and symmetric noise, with a polynomial exponent depending on that fixed prefactor. After normalizing a sign vector to unit length, the leading signal exponent is \(k/4\). Replacing a fixed prefactor by \(n^{-\varepsilon}\) is not justified by a theorem whose runtime exponent depends on it. The spike prior also differs from the sphere.

The 2026 Bresler–Harbuzova reductions connect noisy planted XOR problems with Boolean-spike tensor PCA and transport algorithms or hardness hypotheses between parameter regimes. They preserve and compare conjectured barriers; they do not prove an unconditional barrier for the spherical prior or eliminate the specified finite-precision interface.

Hastings’s February2026 paper concerns detection rather than a proved recovery guarantee. Its added note also withdraws an unqualified provable speedup comparison after a sharper spectral-norm bound became known, retaining a spectral-property condition. It does not settle this classical recovery statement.

cards.title: Computational Kesten–Stigum threshold
cards.formal: Do there exist a fixed integer \(q\ge 5\), fixed rational constants \(a>b>0\) satisfying \((a- b)^{2}<q(a+(q- 1)b), a\) constant \(\delta >0\), and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm A such that, for every sufficiently large n, A weakly recovers the communities of the symmetric stochastic block model \(SBM(n,q,a,b)\), with expected overlap at least \(1/q+\delta\)?
cards.definitions: Generate the hidden labels \(\sigma _{1},\ldots ,\sigma _{n}\) independently and uniformly from \([q]=\{1,\ldots ,q\}\). Conditional on these labels, each unordered pair of distinct vertices is independently an edge with probability \(a/n\) if its labels agree and \(b/n\) otherwise. Thus the graph is simple and undirected; take \(n\ge a\). Equal prior probabilities make communities asymptotically balanced, but their sizes are not conditioned to equal \(n/q\). The algorithm receives this one graph and knows q,a,b; it receives no planted labels or auxiliary samples. It outputs a label vector \(\hat\{\sigma\}\in [q]^{n}\). Define \(overlap(\hat\{\sigma\},\sigma )=\max\) over permutations \(\pi\) of \([q]\) of \(n^{- 1}\sum_{i} 1\{\hat\{\sigma\}_{i}=\pi (\sigma _{i})\}\). The expectation in the question is over labels, graph edges and the algorithm’s random bits. Weak recovery means a fixed positive advantage over the limiting chance baseline \(1/q\). Running time is worst-case polynomial in n on a standard bit model, for every graph and random tape; the algorithm and polynomial exponent may depend on the fixed parameters but not on n. Put \(d=(a+(q- 1)b)/q\) and \(\theta =(a- b)/(a+(q- 1)b)\). The strict inequality is \(d\theta ^{2}<1\), below the Kesten–Stigum threshold. All three model parameters remain constant as n grows.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer must exhibit one fixed parameter choice below the threshold and prove the stated polynomial running time and nonvanishing expected overlap for all sufficiently large n. A negative answer must rule out every such algorithm at every fixed parameter choice in the formulation. Recovery with unlimited computation does not answer the question. An algorithm with q growing with n, a result only above the threshold, or a lower bound conditional on an unproved computational hypothesis is partial progress. The question does not impose an extra promise of information-theoretic recoverability: any positive algorithmic example automatically has that property.
cards.why: Determine whether the canonical local signal threshold is a true barrier for every efficient algorithm in a basic model of network inference.

importance.reason: A central, sharply parameterized computational-versus-statistical gap linking sparse random graphs, inference, message passing and average-case complexity.

cards.status_note: Efficient recovery above the threshold and information-theoretic recovery below it in suitable fixed-q assortative regimes are proved. The checked fixed-community computational lower bound remains conditional on an unproved low-degree conjecture. Growing-community algorithms in the August 2026 revision concern a different quantifier regime. No unconditional settlement of this precise fixed-q question found through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: Community detection asks whether the edges of a network reveal an underlying partition. Here every vertex has the same expected degree, regardless of its group. Consequently, sorting vertices by degree cannot directly identify their communities. The signal is in the pattern of connections between vertices, and each vertex has only a constant expected number of observations even as the network grows.

The target is deliberately much weaker than recovering every label. A constant-degree graph has many isolated vertices, whose memberships cannot be inferred from their incident edges. Weak recovery asks only for a fixed improvement over random guessing on average. Permuting all community names must be allowed: renaming the hidden groups changes neither the graph distribution nor the quality of an inferred partition.

The quantity \(d\theta ^{2}\) compares the growth in the number of observed neighbours with the decay of label information along an edge. In a local tree approximation, d describes branching and \(\theta\) describes how much a child’s label remembers its parent’s label. This explains why the value one is a natural boundary for algorithms based on propagation of small correlations. It does not by itself prove an impossibility result for algorithms that use the whole graph.

Abbe and Sandon prove efficient recovery above this boundary for every fixed number of communities. Their method uses an acyclic form of belief propagation and addresses the effect of cycles in the finite graph. This supplies the algorithmic side of the proposed threshold. The question asks whether a qualitatively different method can succeed strictly below it in the assortative case \(a>b\).

There really are parameters for which the graph contains useful information below the Kesten–Stigum threshold. Banks, Moore, Neeman and Netrapalli establish such regimes for at least eleven groups in the assortative model. Their recovery argument permits exponential computation, searching over sufficiently plausible partitions. Their five-group statement concerns the disassortative case, where between-group edges are more likely; that is a different parameter range from this card.

This produces a concrete computational-versus-statistical puzzle. The missing labels are not intrinsically unidentifiable everywhere below the boundary, yet known efficient methods do not recover them throughout the information-theoretically possible region. An affirmative answer to this card would refute the universal fixed-community barrier with a single parameter example. A negative answer would establish that the obstruction is computational wherever recovery is statistically possible.

Ding, Hua, Slot and Steurer give conditional evidence in 2025. In their parameterized symmetric model, a low-degree conjecture implies a strong computational lower bound for recovery below the threshold by a fixed margin. Their recovery definition uses correlation with the centred membership matrix. The result is a reduction from a conjecture about testing to recovery hardness, not an unconditional exclusion of polynomial-time algorithms. Its model and hypothesis restrictions matter when applying it to a particular choice of a,b.

The precise conjecture in that paper also matters. Its bounded test functions must have expectation bounded below under the planted distribution. The authors explain that a broader earlier version was refuted using rare events. Thus citing a generic “low-degree conjecture” without stating that a hypothesis remains unproved would erase both the conditional nature of the result and an actual correction in the underlying evidence.

A 2026 revision of work by Chin, Mossel, Sohn and Wein gives efficient recovery below the usual boundary when the number of communities grows sufficiently quickly, in particular in a regime above \(\sqrt{n}\). This is an important warning against treating the threshold as universal over every block model. Here q is fixed before n tends to infinity. Even a very large fixed q eventually lies below \(\sqrt{n}\), so the growing-community algorithm does not supply the fixed-parameter example requested.

Settling this problem would test whether a threshold suggested by local propagation describes all efficient global algorithms in a basic random graph model. A new algorithm would identify exploitable structure missed by the familiar threshold calculation. A rigorous barrier would give a particularly clean example in which unlimited inference and efficient inference have different capabilities, with the data distribution specified by only three constants.

cards.title: Polynomial-time refutation of random 3-SAT at constant density
cards.formal:
Do there exist an integer \(C\geq6\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) such that \(A\) never outputs \(\mathrm{UNSAT}\) on any satisfiable \(3\)-CNF formula, and
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\Pr_{F\sim R_3(n,Cn),\,\rho}
 [A(F;\rho)=\mathrm{UNSAT}]=1?
\]
The distribution \(R_3\), exact soundness, and worst-case time bound are defined below. The constant \(C\), machine and its time polynomial must be fixed before \(n\); the probability includes the algorithm’s independent random bits \(\rho\).
cards.definitions:
A Boolean variable takes values in \(\{0,1\}\). A literal is a variable or its negation, a clause is a disjunction of literals, and a CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses. General inputs are explicitly listed \(3\)-CNF formulas, with at most three literals in each clause; repeated clauses, repeated literals and empty clauses are allowed. The empty clause is false. The number \(n\) of named variables and the list length are encoded in binary, followed by binary indices and sign bits with delimiters. Valid indices lie in \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\); unused variables are allowed. Let \(L\) be the complete encoded length. Malformed encodings receive \(\mathrm{UNKNOWN}\) in polynomial time.

For \(n\geq3\), the random distribution \(R_3(n,m)\) is an ordered list of \(m\) independent clauses sampled with replacement. For each clause choose a uniformly random three-element subset of \([n]\), and independently negate each selected variable with probability \(1/2\). Write its three variables in index order. Thus each random clause has three distinct variables, duplicate clauses may occur, and signs in all clauses are independent. This fixed-size distribution is not a planted distribution or a distribution conditioned on unsatisfiability.

The algorithm always outputs either \(\mathrm{UNSAT}\) or \(\mathrm{UNKNOWN}\). Exact soundness means that for every satisfiable input formula \(F\) and every sequence \(\rho\) of its random bits, \(A(F;\rho)=\mathrm{UNKNOWN}\). On an unsatisfiable formula it may also return \(\mathrm{UNKNOWN}\); the required frequency of success applies only to the stated random distribution. Even on exceptional input formulas or random choices there is no allowed false assertion of unsatisfiability.

Use a uniform randomized multitape Turing machine with independent fair bits and no advice or external oracle. There must be integers \(K,d\geq1\) such that every computation takes at most \(K(L+1)^d\) bit operations on every input and every random-bit sequence, including adversarial formulas. Reading random bits and producing the answer are charged, so only polynomially many bits may be used. This is a worst-case bound, not an expected-time bound on random formulas. Deterministic machines are included.

The probability limit requires that for every real \(\eta>0\) there is an integer \(n_0\) such that for every integer \(n\geq\max\{3,n_0\}\), the probability of \(\mathrm{UNSAT}\) is at least \(1-\eta\). The rate of convergence need not be supplied as an algorithm. The density \(C\) is an absolute constant, not a function tending to infinity with \(n\). Choosing integer \(C\geq6\) loses no successful smaller constant-density regime: on a denser input the algorithm can run a lower-density refuter on the appropriate clause prefix, whose distribution is exactly the lower-density model. Unsatisfiability of a prefix implies unsatisfiability of the full formula, preserving soundness.

No named proof system or explicit derivation format is imposed. The output \(\mathrm{UNSAT}\) must be justified by the proven soundness of the algorithm; the machine need not print a resolution or sum-of-squares proof. Existence of short unsatisfiability certificates without an efficient way of finding them does not meet this definition.

context_blocks.text: Typical unsatisfiability has a short counting proof. For any fixed assignment, a random clause is satisfied with probability \(7/8\), so the expected number of satisfying assignments in \(R_3(n,Cn)\) is \(2^n(7/8)^{Cn}\). For \(C\geq6\), this tends to zero exponentially. Markov’s inequality therefore shows that the formula is unsatisfiable with probability tending to one. Always printing UNSAT would exploit that statistical fact but would violate soundness on satisfiable inputs.

The task asks for a certificate on a particular input while exploiting its typical structure. Search and proof existence are separate: a family of short refutations does not by itself give a polynomial-time algorithm that finds one. The 2015 source explicitly separates these possibilities in its comparison of efficient refutation algorithms and nondeterministically available certificates.

Spectral and semidefinite methods give efficient refutation at much higher clause counts, around \(n^{3/2}\) for random \(3\)-SAT in the source’s historical account. The relevant density is the number of clauses divided by \(n\), so this regime grows like \(\sqrt n\), in contrast to the constant required here. A bound for other predicates, such as not-all-equal clauses, cannot be substituted for ordinary disjunction clauses.

Gap refutation proves that every assignment violates a positive fraction of clauses. It must therefore remain silent even on suitable nearly satisfiable formulas. Barak’s cited formulation of Feige’s hypothesis uses this stronger soundness requirement. The present target retains the previously approved requirement of soundness only on satisfiable formulas, so consequences of a gap hypothesis must be checked separately.

The 2026 work extends the density, relaxation degree and refutation-strength tradeoff to more general random CSP distributions without uniformly random literals. Its sum-of-squares lower bounds restrict a particular family of algebraic relaxations; its generalization of the upper bounds does not supply the unrestricted constant-density algorithm asked for here. The paper treats binomial random-instance models in its displayed theorems, another reason to avoid identifying them verbatim with this fixed-size target.

The August 2026 ECCC report states stronger lower bounds for resolution extended to bounded-width disjunctions of conjunctions. Such a result blocks algorithms restricted to those refutations, but it does not rule out a different sound polynomial-time computation. The claim is recorded at the abstract level rather than as an independent full-proof audit.

If \(\mathsf P=\mathsf{NP}\), a deterministic polynomial-time SAT decision algorithm can refute every unsatisfiable input, and the elementary counting argument gives the required average-case success. Consequently an unconditional negative answer here would imply \(\mathsf P\ne\mathsf{NP}\). A positive answer would be a distribution-specific algorithm and would not itself decide worst-case SAT.

cards.why: This problem isolates the gap between knowing that a typical sparse formula is unsatisfiable and efficiently proving unsatisfiability without ever making a false claim. A resolution would identify a major limit of average-case certification or produce an algorithm beyond the methods underlying existing refutation barriers.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must supply one constant \(C\), one uniform algorithm, its worst-case polynomial time bound, exact soundness for every satisfiable input and every random-bit sequence, and the success limit for \(R_3(n,Cn)\).

A negative answer must rule out every such constant and every such algorithm. Equivalently, for every proposed sound polynomial-time \(A\) and every integer \(C\geq6\), there must be some \(\eta>0\) such that failure probability is at least \(\eta\) for arbitrarily large \(n\). Showing failure for a single algorithm, proof system or finite set of inputs is insufficient. A conditional theorem under an unproved complexity assumption is partial progress on this unconditional target. Algorithms requiring a growing clause density, allowing erroneous refutations on rare satisfiable inputs, or merely distinguishing a planted distribution do not satisfy the criterion.

importance.reason: A foundational average-case refutation problem with documented connections to proof complexity, learning and approximation. It supplies a different average-case task from planted recovery or detection. The exact-satisfiability variant is recorded without importing consequences of stronger gap hypotheses.

cards.title: Infinitely-often one-way functions from average-case NP hardness
cards.formal: Does $\mathrm{DistNP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{HeurBPP}$ imply the existence of a polynomial-time computable function f with the following property? For every probabilistic polynomial-time inverter I and every constant \(c>0\), infinitely many lengths n satisfy $\Pr[|z|=n\ \land\ f(z)=f(x)]<n^{-c}$, where $x\sim U(\{0,1\}^n)$ and $z\leftarrow I(1^n,f(x))$. The probability includes inverter randomness. This card fixes the infinitely-often security convention used by the cited characterization.

context_blocks.text: Hardness of deciding typical instances and hardness of finding preimages are different requirements. The assumption \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\) alone is weaker and belongs to a separate existing question.

An average-case decision problem asks an algorithm to classify instances drawn from a specified distribution. A one-way function creates a different experiment: sample an input, reveal its efficiently computed image, and ask an adversary to find any valid preimage. The sampling process and the form of the required answer both matter.

A reduction has to turn the first kind of difficulty into the second while preserving efficient generation and a meaningful success probability. It cannot simply use a hard yes/no question as a function and assume its inverse is hard. The question is whether some average-case hardness can exist without yielding the basic inversion obstacle on which one-way-function cryptography is built.

cards.definitions: DistNP consists of pairs \((\mathrm{L},D)\) with L in NP and \(D_{n} a\) polynomial-time samplable distribution on n-bit inputs. Such a pair is in HeurBPP if a single randomized algorithm A runs in time polynomial in n and 1/delta and, for every n and $0<\delta<1$, at least a $1-\delta$ fraction of x drawn from \(D_{n}\) have $\Pr[A(x,\delta)=L(x)]\ge2/3$. The output is a decision bit. Infinitely-often security is weaker than requiring negligible inversion probability at all sufficiently large lengths; the latter is a distinct stronger target.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the implication under the two explicit distributional and security definitions, or prove that average-case NP hardness can hold while every polynomial-time function fails that infinitely-often inversion guarantee. A result only about an oracle world does not settle the unrelativized implication.

importance.reason: Links average-case NP hardness to the existence of a basic cryptographic primitive; resolving it would clarify the foundations of complexity-based cryptography.

cards.definitions: The graph and one Lebesgue-measurable density \(f_{e}\) for each edge are chosen adversarially before the random weights. Each \(f_{e}\) is nonnegative, integrates to 1 on \([- 1,1]\), and is at most \(\varphi\) almost everywhere; weights \(w_{e}\) are sampled independently once from these densities and then held fixed. They may be negative and need not be identically distributed. A cut is a subset \(S\subseteq V\), with value \(\mathrm{W}_{w}(S)=\Sigma\)_{\(uv\in E\): exactly one of u,v lies in S} \(w_{uv}\). A legal step replaces S by \(S\triangle \{v\}\) for one vertex v, and requires a strictly larger cut value. Define \(\mathrm{L}(G,w)\) as the largest number of steps in any such path, maximized over all starting cuts and all choices of improving vertices after w is known; set \(\mathrm{L}=0\) if there is no step. There are finitely many cuts and strict improvement prevents revisiting one, so \(\mathrm{L}\le 2^{n}- 1\) and its expectation is well-defined. The expectation is over w alone, with the maximum over paths inside it. The resource counted is improving steps, not the bit cost of exact real arithmetic or of sampling distributions. The target concerns all graphs and all allowed densities with one common polynomial. A run ends at a single-flip local maximum, which need not maximize cut value globally.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed universal polynomial bound on \(E_{w}[\mathrm{L}(G,w)]\), or prove its logical negation by exhibiting admissible families that exceed every such polynomial. A bound for selected graph classes or for one favorable pivot rule does not establish the proposition. A rare long path or an unperturbed worst-case instance alone does not refute an expected bound under these density constraints.

context_blocks.title: What FLIP improves
context_blocks.text: The procedure repeatedly moves a vertex to the opposite side when this increases the weight crossing the cut. Different choices can produce different paths, so the question controls the longest one. This includes starting cuts and choices made after seeing the sampled weights, rather than relying on a particular implementation to avoid a bad path.

context_blocks.title: Local optimality has a different goal
context_blocks.text: Consider a four-cycle 1–2–3–4–1 with weights 0.9 on edges 12 and 34 and weights 1 on edges 23 and 41. The cut \(\{1,2\}\) has weight 2, and moving any single vertex decreases it by 0.1. Nevertheless, the alternating cut \(\{1,3\}\) has weight 3.8. Fast termination here would mean finding a state with no improving single move, without asserting that FLIP finds a global maximum.

context_blocks.title: What the smoothing parameter permits
context_blocks.text: The adversary chooses the graph and the distributions, while independent draws supply the randomness. Density bounded by \(\varphi\) prevents a distribution from putting too much probability in an arbitrarily short interval: an interval of length h has probability at most \(\varphi h\). Larger \(\varphi\) permits more concentrated weights, and the requested running-time bound may grow polynomially with \(\varphi\).

context_blocks.title: Known bounds cover only part of the target
context_blocks.text: The general-graph theorem of Chen and coauthors gives \(\varphi n^{O(\sqrt{\log  n})}\) steps with high probability, uniformly over improving paths. Schwartzman proves polynomial expected length when arboricity is \(O(\log ^{1- \delta}n)\) for fixed \(\delta >0\); arboricity is the minimum number of forests needed to partition the edges. This includes sparse graph classes but not arbitrary graphs. The expectation requirement matters: a high-probability statement by itself does not bound the contribution of a long tail.

context_blocks.title: A nearby negative result uses larger moves
context_blocks.text: Michel and Scott show superpolynomial smoothed behavior for 3-FLIP, where a step may move up to three vertices together. Their single-FLIP exponential examples instead concern the setting without random perturbations. Neither statement refutes polynomial expected length for the single-vertex, independently perturbed model here.

cards.title: Algorithmic threshold for the symmetric binary perceptron
cards.formal:
Does the Gaussian symmetric binary perceptron's polynomial-time search threshold satisfy
\[\alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(\kappa)=\widetilde\Theta(\kappa^2)\qquad\text{as }\kappa\downarrow0?\]
Precisely, are there constants \(C\ge1\), an integer \(a\ge0\), and \(\kappa_0\in(0,1/2]\) such that for every rational \(\kappa\in(0,\kappa_0]\),
\[\frac{\kappa^2}{C(\log(1/\kappa))^a}\ \le\ \alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(\kappa)\ \le\ C\kappa^2(\log(1/\kappa))^a?\]
For fixed margin \(\kappa>0\) and density \(\alpha>0\), an instance is an \(\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor\)-by-\(n\) matrix \(G\) with independent standard Gaussian entries. A successful search returns \(\sigma\in\{-1,1\}^n\) with
\[\max_{1\le i\le\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor}\left|\sum_{j=1}^{n}G_{ij}\sigma_j\right|\le\kappa\sqrt n.\]
The threshold is the supremum of fixed rational densities at which a uniform polynomial-time algorithm succeeds with probability tending to one as \(n\to\infty\), in the real-arithmetic model specified below.

The polylogarithmic tolerance restores the tilde lost in the imported excerpt. To make the source's informal efficient-algorithm class definite on exact Gaussian inputs, this card explicitly selects rational-constant randomized real-arithmetic computation. It does not assert equivalence with every discretized or machine-specific version of the conjecture.
