cards.status_note: The ordinary Hadwiger conjecture is explicitly open in Liu–Luo v2 of 9 September 2026, still its latest arXiv version on 14 September. Its triple-logarithmic coloring theorem is a recent preprint claim, not independently verified here. The December 2025 disproof and its September 2026 citation concern the stronger odd-minor version. Checked source formulations and a bounded later-work search do not certify all cited proofs.

context_blocks.text: A complete minor can be much larger than any complete subgraph: contraction groups connected regions into single vertices. Hadwiger asks whether the resulting complete graph can always have as many vertices as the original graph needs colors. For every \(t\ge2\), the graph \(K_{t-1}\) has no \(K_t\) minor and needs exactly \(t-1\) colors, so the conjectured bound for the excluded-minor class is sharp.

The exact cases through \(t=6\) are known. The \(t=5\) case is equivalent, via Wagner’s theorem, to the Four-Color Theorem for planar graphs. Robertson, Seymour and Thomas established the \(t=6\) case: without assuming four-colorability, their structural result makes a minimal counterexample apex, meaning that deleting one vertex leaves a planar graph. The Four-Color Theorem then gives five colors for that graph. Their paper indexes the conjecture by the allowed number of colors, one less than the clique-minor order used on this card.

Kostochka and Thomason obtained an \(O(t\sqrt{\log t})\) bound on degeneracy, where a graph is \(d\)-degenerate if every nonempty subgraph has a vertex of degree at most \(d\). Such a graph is \((d+1)\)-colorable. The order of this degeneracy bound is tight, but that fact is not a chromatic lower bound of the same order and does not disprove Hadwiger. Delcourt and Postle’s Theorem 1.5 gives \(O(t\log\log t)\) colors for arbitrary \(K_t\)-minor-free graphs; its quantification has no bound on the number of vertices.

Liu and Luo’s version 2, submitted on 9 September 2026, states in Theorem 1.1 that an absolute constant \(C\) satisfies \(\chi(G)\le Ct\log\log\log t\) for every integer \(t\ge16\) and every \(K_t\)-minor-free graph. Their logarithms are natural. This is recorded as a recent preprint claim whose proof has not been independently verified here. It does not establish either the weakening \(\chi(G)=O(t)\) or the exact bound \(t-1\); the introduction still identifies clique-minor orders starting at seven as open.

For the odd-minor variant, the disjoint branch trees must each have a proper two-coloring, with an edge joining vertices of the same color between every pair of trees. Forgetting these extra requirements yields an ordinary minor, so absence of an ordinary minor implies absence of an odd minor; the reverse implication need not hold. Kühn, Sauermann, Steiner and Wigderson’s December 2025 preprint states that for each fixed \(\delta>0\) and every sufficiently large \(t\), some graph has no odd \(K_t\) minor and has \(\chi(G)\ge(3/2-\delta)t\). This refutes the stronger odd-minor conjecture. Odd-minor absence by itself does not certify the ordinary-minor absence required for a negative answer here.

cards.title: Deterministic linear-time minimum spanning tree
cards.formal: Is there one deterministic comparison-based algorithm that, on every connected simple undirected graph with n vertices, m edges and arbitrary real edge weights, outputs a minimum spanning tree in \(O(m+n)\) worst-case time in the comparison RAM model below?
cards.definitions: The graph is explicitly supplied as vertex and edge records, with vertices numbered \(1,\ldots ,n\) and edges given distinct identifiers. An edge record contains its two endpoints and a weight key representing an arbitrary real number. A spanning tree is a set T of \(n- 1\) edges connecting all vertices without a cycle; it is minimum when \(\sum_{e\in T}w(e)\) is smallest among all spanning trees. For \(n=1\) the output is empty. Equal and negative weights are permitted, and any minimum tree is acceptable. Weight keys may be copied and compared, but their bit representations cannot be inspected, and arithmetic on their numerical values is unavailable. Each comparison has unit cost. Nonweight data, addresses and indices use \(O(\log (m+n+2))\)-bit words on a random-access machine, with unit-cost reads, writes, comparisons, standard word arithmetic, bitwise Boolean operations and shifts; arithmetic is restricted to these words. All ordinary operations count in the running time, not just weight comparisons. The algorithm has a fixed finite description and no input-length-dependent advice or free precomputed tables. Any tables it constructs, as well as writing the output, are charged to its time. The hidden linear-time constant must be independent of graph topology, n,m and the weights. This fixes a conventional uniform sequential comparison model. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A central unresolved boundary between deterministic and randomized algorithms for a classical graph optimization problem, and a rare case where a provably optimal algorithm exists before its exact asymptotic complexity is understood.

cards.status_note: The deterministic linear-time comparison problem remains open in the primary-author material checked through 11 September 2026. Integer-word algorithms, high-girth results and the optimal-decision-tree theorem do not settle this formulation.

context_blocks.text: A minimum spanning tree connects a graph as cheaply as possible without redundant cycles. It is among the basic examples where a local greedy rule produces a global optimum, and it appears in network design and clustering. The optimization objective is well understood; the unsettled issue is how much computation is fundamentally needed to identify the right \(n- 1\) edges when the input already contains m edge records.

Sorting every edge is sufficient for Kruskal’s algorithm, but sorting is a stronger task than the required output. On a graph that is itself a tree, every edge belongs to the answer regardless of their relative weights. On a triangle, only the identity of a largest-weight edge is needed: discard it. Thus the familiar comparison lower bound for sorting all keys does not automatically become a lower bound for finding an MST. A faster algorithm must exploit the graph’s structure to avoid unnecessary ordering information.

The cut and cycle rules make this possible. A lightest edge across a cut can be selected safely, and a strictly heaviest edge on a cycle can be discarded. Equal weights can be handled consistently by comparing pairs consisting of the weight and the edge identifier. These rules avoid numerical arithmetic on weights, so the problem is meaningful for arbitrary real keys even though the objective is expressed as a sum.

Karger, Klein and Tarjan combine random sampling with linear-time MST verification to obtain a Las Vegas algorithm with expected \(O(m+n)\) running time. It always returns a correct tree; randomness controls the work spent on recursive filtering. The target here is a deterministic guarantee for every input, so fixing an arbitrary random seed does not inherit the expected-time theorem.

Chazelle’s deterministic algorithm achieves \(O(m\alpha (m,n))\) time, where \(\alpha\) is a slowly growing inverse-Ackermann function. Its soft-heap machinery deliberately permits a controlled set of key increases inside an auxiliary data structure while the surrounding algorithm preserves the exact MST answer. The extra factor is tiny for practical input sizes, yet unbounded asymptotically. Removing it asks for an exact structural understanding of the problem’s complexity, not merely an implementation improvement.

Pettie and Ramachandran establish a different kind of optimality: total algorithmic running time can match, within a constant factor, the optimal worst-case number of edge comparisons for MST. Their algorithm is uniform; it constructs the small optimal decision trees it needs within the time analysis. But the asymptotic size of that optimum is itself unknown. Consequently a proof that linear-size comparison decision trees always suffice would settle the algorithmic question through their theorem.

The graph family also matters. Eisenstat and coauthors show that it is enough to solve graphs with at most \(3n/2\) edges, and separately relate the general problem to graphs with any fixed lower bound on girth, the length of a shortest cycle. Their available high-girth algorithm requires a lower bound that grows with n. That difference between a fixed girth threshold and a slowly growing threshold leaves the general deterministic question open.

Changing the access model can remove the obstacle. Fredman and Willard give a deterministic linear-time algorithm using integer-word operations on the weights. That theorem can exploit their binary representation, which the real-key comparison model deliberately withholds. Similarly, an algorithm that is fast for a random graph topology has an average-instance guarantee, even if the algorithm itself is deterministic; it does not bound the work on every graph.

The remaining challenge can therefore be stated without ambiguity: retain exactness, arbitrary real-key weights and all graph topologies, and make every part of the computation linear without random choices. A negative answer would be equally significant, by establishing an intrinsic cost for deterministic comparison-based optimization that expected-time random sampling avoids.

cards.title: Erdős–Hajnal conjecture
cards.formal: For each integer \(h\ge 2\) and each undirected simple graph \(H\) on \([h]\), is there a real constant \(c_H>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge 1\) and every undirected simple graph \(G\) on \([n]\) containing no induced copy of \(H\), \[\max\{\alpha(G),\omega(G)\}\ge n^{c_H}?\] The exponent is chosen after the entire forbidden graph \(H\) and before the host graph \(G\); the assertion must hold for all such \(H\).
cards.definitions: Write \([m]=\{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}\). A simple undirected graph on \([m]\) is a symmetric irreflexive adjacency relation on this set; it has no loops or multiple edges. An induced copy of \(H\) in \(G\) is an injection \(f:[h]\to[n]\) such that \(u\) and \(v\) are adjacent in \(H\) if and only if \(f(u)\) and \(f(v)\) are adjacent in \(G\), for every distinct \(u,v\in[h]\). Both edges and nonedges must be preserved. A clique is a vertex subset in which every distinct pair is adjacent, and an independent or stable set is one in which every distinct pair is nonadjacent. The integers \(\omega(G)\) and \(\alpha(G)\) are their respective maximum cardinalities; a homogeneous set in this card means a clique or an independent set. The right side \(n^{c_H}\) is an ordinary positive-real power, and the integer on the left is compared as a real number. The constant \(c_H\) may depend on all of \(H\), but not on \(G\) or \(n\). There is no additional degree, density, dimension or algorithmic promise. All positive host sizes, including \(n<h\), are included. This is an existence statement, with no required algorithm for computing \(c_H\) or finding the homogeneous set. A hereditary graph class is closed under isomorphism and induced subgraphs; a proper such class omits some finite graph.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer proves existence of a positive exponent for every finite forbidden graph and the homogeneous-set guarantee for every permitted host graph. A negative answer proves that there is one fixed graph \(H\) with \(|V(H)|\ge2\) such that, for every real \(c>0\), some positive integer \(n\) and some \(H\)-free graph \(G\) on \([n]\) satisfy \(\max\{\alpha(G),\omega(G)\}<n^c\). The witness host graph may depend on \(c\), but the forbidden graph must be the same for all \(c\). Failure of one proposed exponent or verification of finitely many host sizes does not establish this negation. No numerical approximation to an optimal exponent is being requested.
cards.why: This central conjecture asks whether every proper hereditary restriction forces a polynomial-size clique or independent set, far beyond the logarithmic scale possible in arbitrary graphs. It would provide a common structural guarantee across all forbidden-induced-subgraph classes and clarify the relation between local exclusions, large nearly uniform vertex sets and neighborhood complexity. These are basic objects in structural and algorithmic graph theory; the assertion itself is an existence theorem, not an efficient clique or independent-set algorithm.

importance.reason: A major unifying conjecture for hereditary graph classes, with a sharp qualitative gap between general bounds and the target and substantial recent progress on special cases.

context_blocks.text: Ramsey theory guarantees homogeneous sets on the logarithmic scale in arbitrary graphs, and random graphs show that a polynomial guarantee is impossible without restrictions. The Erdős–Hajnal conjecture asks whether excluding any one fixed induced pattern always changes that scale to \(n^{c_H}\) for some positive constant. A proper hereditary class omits a graph \(H\) and hence every induced copy of it, so the conjecture is equivalently a polynomial homogeneous-set guarantee for every proper hereditary class.

The conjecture is traced to 1977 in the checked modern primary papers, and Erdős and Hajnal developed it in their 1989 Ramsey-type paper. Their general bound is \(2^{a_H\sqrt{\log_2 n}}\) for a suitable positive constant. Bucić, Nguyen, Scott and Seymour improved this to \(2^{b_H\sqrt{\log_2 n\,\log_2\log_2 n}}\) for all \(n\ge2\). Their journal article appeared online on 6 May 2024. This still has a sublinear exponent in \(\log_2 n\) and does not yield a fixed positive power of \(n\).

Nguyen, Scott and Seymour proved the conjecture for the five-vertex path \(P_5\), whose only edges join consecutive vertices of a path. The preprint began in December 2023; the checked accepted revision is from 23 February 2026, and the journal publication is dated 23 March 2026. Together with the earlier bull and five-cycle cases and the known preservation properties, it completes all forbidden graphs on at most five vertices. The theorem concerns every \(P_5\)-free graph, with one positive exponent independent of its size.

The separate all-path theorem gives the following weaker guarantee: for every fixed path \(P\) and every real \(d\) with \(0<d<1\), there is \(a_{P,d}>0\) such that every \(P\)-free graph with \(n\ge2\) vertices has a homogeneous set of size at least \(2^{a_{P,d}(\log_2 n)^d}\). The constant can depend on both the path and \(d\). This explains the source notation \(2^{(\log n)^{1-o(1)}}\); its assertion for all fixed \(d<1\) does not include the required fixed-power case \(d=1\).

The 31 August 2026 revision by Huang, Ju and Zhou reports two further six-vertex cases. Both can be specified using the path \(a-b-c-d-e\) and a sixth vertex \(f\): the E-graph adds only \(cf\), while the Bird adds only \(bf\) and \(cf\). These definitions match Figures 4 and 5 of that revision. Each forbidden graph contains an induced \(P_5\), so its exclusion allows a larger host class than excluding \(P_5\). Theorems 1.10 and 1.11 concern these particular patterns, not every six-vertex graph.

Tran and Nguyen posted a further case on 28 August 2026. Their forbidden graph has vertex set \(\{a,b,c,d,e,f\}\) and exactly the edges \(\{ab,bc,cd,de,af,bf,df\}\); Theorem 1.1 states its Erdős–Hajnal property. It is distinct from both the E-graph and the Bird. The checked introduction still describes the general conjecture as open. The complete proofs of this preprint and the two cases in the preceding paragraph were not independently verified in this review.

Bucić, Fox and Pham prove, for each fixed forbidden graph, equivalence with two polynomial quantitative properties. The polynomial Rödl property requires that for every \(0<\varepsilon\le1/2\), an \(H\)-free graph on \(n\) vertices contain at least \(\varepsilon^{C_H}n\) vertices inducing edge density at most \(\varepsilon\) or at least \(1-\varepsilon\), for a fixed positive \(C_H\). The polynomial Nikiforov property permits a polynomially small proportion of induced copies of \(H\) instead of none. Their Theorem 4 proves the equivalence of these properties with Erdős–Hajnal; it does not establish any of them for every graph.

A July 2026 preprint of Sun, Wang and Zeng sharpens a result under an extra neighborhood restriction. For a graph \(G\), the open-neighborhood family is \(\{N_G(v):v\in V(G)\}\). It shatters \(S\subseteq V(G)\) if every \(A\subseteq S\) equals \(N_G(v)\cap S\) for some vertex \(v\); VC-dimension is the maximum size of a shattered set. Theorem 1.2 reports an absolute \(C\ge1\) such that dimension at most an integer \(d\ge1\) ensures a homogeneous set of size at least \(n^{(Cd)^{-d}}\). This improves the exponent in a previously proved bounded-dimension theorem. General \(H\)-free hosts in this card have no such dimension bound. The new proof was checked for scope, not independently certified.

Sági claims the full conjecture in Theorem 3.20 of the revision listed as arXiv v3, submitted 18 August 2017. The arXiv history records withdrawal of the earlier proof on 24 July 2017, and the author explicitly acknowledges a serious error in the 2012 version while offering different technical details in the revision. The withdrawal therefore cannot itself be treated as a refutation of v3. The revised full proof has not been verified here, while the checked 2026 primary literature continues to treat the general conjecture as open. This card is marked uncertain to record that unresolved proof claim accurately.

The polynomial Rödl property requires that for every \(0<\varepsilon\le1/2\), an \(H\)-free graph on \(n\) vertices contain at least \(\varepsilon^{C_H}n\) vertices inducing edge density at most \(\varepsilon\) or at least \(1-\varepsilon\), for a fixed positive \(C_H\). The polynomial Nikiforov property permits a polynomially small proportion of induced copies of \(H\) instead of none. Their Theorem 4 proves the equivalence of these properties with Erdős–Hajnal; it does not establish any of them for every graph.

A July 2026 preprint of Sun, Wang and Zeng sharpens a result under an extra neighborhood restriction. For a graph \(G\), the open-neighborhood family is \(\{N_G(v):v\in V(G)\}\). It shatters \(S\subseteq V(G)\) if every \(A\subseteq S\) equals \(N_G(v)\cap S\) for some vertex \(v\); VC-dimension is the maximum size of a shattered set. Theorem 1.2 reports an absolute \(C\ge1\) such that dimension at most an integer \(d\ge1\) ensures a homogeneous set of size at least \(n^{(Cd)^{-d}}\). This improves the exponent in a previously proved bounded-dimension theorem. General \(H\)-free hosts in this card have no such dimension bound. Sági claims the full conjecture in Theorem 3.20 of the revision listed as arXiv v3, submitted 18 August 2017. The arXiv history records withdrawal of the earlier proof on 24 July 2017, and the author explicitly acknowledges a serious error in the 2012 version while offering different technical details in the revision. The withdrawal therefore cannot itself be treated as a refutation of v3. The revised full proof has not been verified here, while the checked 2026 primary literature continues to treat the general conjecture as open. This card is marked uncertain to record that unresolved proof claim accurately.

cards.title: Reed’s conjecture
cards.formal: Does every nonempty finite simple undirected graph \(G\) satisfy \[\chi(G)\leq\left\lceil\frac{\Delta(G)+1+\omega(G)}{2}\right\rceil?\] The quantification is over every number of vertices and every edge set, with no restriction on maximum degree or graph class.
cards.definitions: For an integer \(n\geq1\), let \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(E\) be any set of two-element subsets of \(V\). Thus \(G=(V,E)\) has no loops or parallel edges, and an edge has no direction. Vertices \(u,v\) are adjacent exactly when \(\{u,v\}\in E\). A proper \(k\)-colouring, for an integer \(k\geq1\), is a function \(c:V\to\{1,\ldots,k\}\) with \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every edge; colours need not all be used. The chromatic number \(\chi(G)\) is the least such \(k\), which exists since \(k=n\) always suffices. Write \(d_G(v)=|\{u\in V:\{u,v\}\in E\}|\) and \(\Delta(G)=\max_{v\in V}d_G(v)\). A clique is a subset \(S\subseteq V\) whose distinct vertices are pairwise adjacent, and \(\omega(G)=\max\{|S|:S\text{ is a clique}\}\). Both maxima are over finite sets, and a singleton is a clique. The ceiling \(\lceil x\rceil\) is the least integer at least the real number \(x\); the division by two in the displayed bound is real division before rounding. Disconnected graphs, isolated vertices and all nonempty edgeless graphs are included; the latter have \(\chi=\omega=1\) and \(\Delta=0\). Labelling the vertices imposes no structural restriction. One may also include the empty graph with \(\chi=\omega=\Delta=0\), for which the inequality is immediate. This is an existence question about one ordinary proper colouring per graph, with no input algorithm, running-time, randomness, list assignment or recolouring requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal displayed inequality, or a complete Lean-checked refutation: a specified integer \(n\geq1\), a specified finite simple graph \(G\) on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and a proof that \(\chi(G)>\lceil(\Delta(G)+1+\omega(G))/2\rceil\). In the negative case the exact graph parameters, or certified bounds that imply this strict inequality, must be established; in particular, merely exhibiting a clique gives a lower bound on \(\omega(G)\), whereas an upper bound on the right-hand side is needed for a refutation. Equivalently, the proof may certify the absence of any proper colouring with the specified threshold number of colours. A positive proof must include every maximum degree and every graph size, including bounded-degree cases. The target is the exact universal proposition, not an estimate of an optimal coefficient, so no numerical approximation tolerance replaces it. An additive error, a smaller clique coefficient, a theorem for only sufficiently large maximum degree, or success for a restricted graph class does not meet the criterion unless the full statement follows. The existence proof need not give a polynomial-time colouring algorithm.
cards.why: A defining question about how a local degree constraint and a global clique obstruction jointly control ordinary graph colouring. A positive resolution would give a sharp universal guarantee for partitioning vertices into independent colour classes, while a counterexample would reveal a colouring obstruction beyond this proposed relationship among three basic graph parameters. Its significance is structural even without an efficient algorithm for finding the guaranteed colouring.

importance.reason: A defining universal conjecture linking three basic graph parameters, with sharp examples and broad influence on colouring theory and its algorithmic methods.

cards.status_note: Checked through 14 September 2026. The latest listed directed-paper revision, 8 September 2026, explicitly retains the full ordinary graph statement as Conjecture 1.1. Its proved directed interpolation, the large-degree 0.119/0.113 results, and the checked Kempe-recolouring theorem do not imply the missing universal half-average. Bounded later-work searches found no full matching resolution; this is dated primary-source evidence of openness, not an independent proof of current status or verification of every cited theorem.

context_blocks.text: The basic bounds are \(\omega(G)\leq\chi(G)\leq\Delta(G)+1\): a clique requires different colours at all its vertices, while the upper bound follows from the usual greedy-colouring theorem. Reed asks whether the rounded average of these two scales is always an upper bound. The conjecture concerns the global partition into independent sets, meaning vertex sets containing no edge, rather than a separate choice of colours within each neighbourhood.

The ceiling matters. A five-cycle has \(\Delta=\omega=2\) and \(\chi=3\), whereas the unrounded average is \(5/2\). Complete graphs attain the proposed rounded bound as well. These examples distinguish the exact statement from an asymptotic estimate with an unspecified additive constant.

The coefficient \(1/2\) cannot be increased in a universal interpolation \(\lceil(1-\varepsilon)(\Delta+1)+\varepsilon\omega\rceil\). Replace each vertex of a five-cycle by a clique of size \(t\geq1\), and put all edges between two replacement cliques exactly when their original cycle vertices are adjacent. This graph has \(5t\) vertices, \(\Delta=3t-1\), \(\omega=2t\), and no independent set larger than two vertices, hence \(\chi\geq\lceil5t/2\rceil\). For any fixed \(\varepsilon>1/2\), the proposed interpolation would be smaller than this lower bound for sufficiently large \(t\). This explicitly defined clique blowup is the example intended in the source; its description there as a Cartesian product is inaccurate.

Reed proved that some universal \(\varepsilon>0\) does give the weaker bound \(\chi(G)\leq\lceil(1-\varepsilon)(\Delta(G)+1)+\varepsilon\omega(G)\rceil\) for every graph. Thus a saving proportional to the gap between degree plus one and clique number is known; the unresolved target is the sharp half-average. The September 2026 digraph paper restates the original conjecture and this result as Conjecture 1.1 and Theorem 1.2, respectively.

Hurley, de Joannis de Verclos and Kang give \(\chi(G)\leq\lceil0.881(\Delta(G)+1)+0.119\omega(G)\rceil\) when \(\Delta(G)\geq\Delta_0\) for a universal threshold \(\Delta_0\). Their published 2022 Remark 3.1 explicitly says that an ingredient attributed to Delcourt and Postle had not then completed peer review; it also records an alternative published ingredient giving coefficients \(0.887\) and \(0.113\). This is a dated qualification about the 2022 argument, not a claim about the present review status of that ingredient. Neither variant provides coefficient \(1/2\), and the stated large-degree restriction must be retained.

Bonamy, Kelly, Nelson and Postle prove a different kind of improvement, \(\chi(G)=O(\Delta\sqrt{\ln\omega/\ln\Delta})\), for graphs of maximum degree at most \(\Delta\) and clique number at most \(\omega\), in the large-\(\Delta\) regime with \(\omega\geq2\). The implicit constant is universal. This becomes substantially smaller than the degree bound when \(\ln\omega/\ln\Delta\) is small; it does not give the exact half-average for every parameter range. The theorem in the 2018 author preprint also bounds the list-chromatic number, where every vertex has its own list of allowed colours.

A Kempe change swaps two colours on one connected component of the subgraph induced by those colours. The 2025 recolouring paper studies whether every pair of proper \(k\)-colourings is connected by a sequence of such changes. Its general conjectured clique coefficient is \(1/3\), due to obstructions to moving between colourings; this is a separate property from the existence of one colouring. For odd-hole-free graphs, meaning graphs with no induced odd cycle of length at least five, Theorem 4 guarantees recolourability above a local threshold, and in particular for \(k>\lceil(\omega+\Delta+1)/2\rceil\). The strict inequality leaves the equality case open in that recolouring question.

The September 2026 revision of Kawarabayashi and Picasarri-Arrieta replaces undirected colour classes by acyclic colour classes in a digraph, where acyclic means containing no directed cycle, including no two-cycle of opposite arcs. In the symmetric digraph obtained by replacing each edge by both opposite arcs, this is exactly ordinary proper colouring. Their proposed directed half-average bound therefore implies Reed’s conjecture, but their proved general interpolation has only some positive coefficient. Conjecture 1.1 of this revision still lists the full undirected half-average as open.

cards.title: Graph isomorphism in polynomial time
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic Turing machine M and fixed positive integers C,k such that on every binary input x, M halts within \(C(|x|+1)^k\) transitions and accepts exactly when x encodes two isomorphic finite simple undirected graphs? Equivalently, is the language \(\mathrm{GI}\) defined below in deterministic polynomial time?
cards.definitions: For \(n\ge 0\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]\) empty. A finite simple undirected graph G on \([n]\) has an adjacency matrix \(A_G\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) that is symmetric with zero diagonal. Its vertices are labeled; its edges are unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Encode a pair G,H by \(1^n0\), followed by the full row-major matrix of G, followed by \(1^m0\) and the full row-major matrix of H. The total binary length is \(N=n^2+m^2+n+m+2\). Extra trailing bits, missing entries, or nonsymmetric or nonzero-diagonal matrices make an encoding malformed. Graphs G,H are isomorphic, written \(G\cong H\), if there is a bijection \(\pi:[n]\to[m]\) such that \(A_G(i,j)=A_H(\pi(i),\pi(j))\) for every \(i,j\in[n]\). If \(n\ne m\), no such bijection exists; the two empty graphs are isomorphic. All valid graph pairs are in the domain, without degree, connectivity, automorphism, sparsity or random-input promises. Computation receives the entire binary string, rather than an oracle or succinctly generated adjacency matrix. The computation model is one uniform classical multitape Turing machine with a finite program, finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. In one transition each tape head moves at most one cell. Time counts all transitions, including input access and internal computation. Polynomial time means a bound \(C(N+1)^k\) for fixed positive integers C,k, independent of the input and of the graph sizes. There is no advice, prover, witness supplied with the input, graph-isomorphism oracle or uncounted preprocessing. The machine is deterministic and must always answer correctly. The language \(\mathrm{GI}\) contains exactly the valid encodings with \(G\cong H\); malformed encodings are rejected. P is the class of all binary languages decided under these uniform deterministic polynomial-time conventions. Ordinary vertex-permutation isomorphism is the equivalence relation in the target.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the specified language \(\mathrm{GI}\) belongs to P, or that \(\mathrm{GI}\notin\mathrm P\). A positive answer must establish one deterministic machine, fixed polynomial bounds and correctness on every input, including rejection of malformed strings. A negative answer must exclude every such polynomial-time machine; a lower bound for only one algorithm, invariant or representation does not suffice. No isomorphism witness or canonical representative must be output: the target is decision.
cards.why: Tests whether the central equivalence problem for finite combinatorial structures can be recognized in deterministic polynomial time after the quasipolynomial barrier was broken.

context_blocks.text: The same graph can appear under many vertex names. For example, renumbering a cycle leaves its adjacency relations unchanged as an unlabeled structure. Isomorphism asks whether this explains the entire difference between two inputs. A proposed bijection can be checked efficiently, but a negative instance requires ruling out all bijections. This places the decision problem in NP, the class with polynomially bounded certificates verifiable in polynomial time.

Simple summaries can agree on different graphs: a six-cycle and two disjoint triangles both have six vertices and every vertex has degree two. They are not isomorphic because one is connected and the other is disconnected. Any complete decision procedure must distinguish every nonisomorphic pair, including pairs with much stronger coincident invariants.

Babai’s general upper bound has the form \(\exp((\log(n+2))^{O(1)})\). This is a quasipolynomial upper bound, whose permitted exponents go beyond the fixed polynomial bound requested here. It does not prove a superpolynomial lower bound on the problem or on every implementation of that method.

Efficient algorithms on restricted graph classes provide substantial structure without settling the unrestricted target. In particular, a runtime with a degree or width parameter in the exponent is polynomial when that parameter is fixed, but it need not be polynomial when the parameter grows with the input. The 2026 survey explicitly separates these parameterized bounds from the general open problem.

A randomized polynomial-time algorithm with bounded error for ordinary isomorphism would settle the neighboring BPP question. It would not by itself provide the deterministic algorithm asked for here. A quantum algorithm deciding the same ordinary relation is another computational variant; the distinct relation called quantum graph isomorphism is a different mathematical target.

The two consolidated MFCS 2021 sources independently restate the general polynomial-time question. Butti and Dalmau discuss it beside fractional homomorphisms and linear-programming relaxations. Dawar and Vagnozzi discuss its equivalence to computing automorphism-orbit partitions and compare algebraic relaxations. These source contexts are preserved without substituting a conjecture about one relaxation for general graph isomorphism.

cards.context:
The same graph can appear under many vertex names. For example, renumbering a cycle leaves its adjacency relations unchanged as an unlabeled structure. Isomorphism asks whether this explains the entire difference between two inputs. A proposed bijection can be checked efficiently, but a negative instance requires ruling out all bijections. This places the decision problem in NP, the class with polynomially bounded certificates verifiable in polynomial time.

Simple summaries can agree on different graphs: a six-cycle and two disjoint triangles both have six vertices and every vertex has degree two. They are not isomorphic because one is connected and the other is disconnected. Any complete decision procedure must distinguish every nonisomorphic pair, including pairs with much stronger coincident invariants.

Babai’s general upper bound has the form \(\exp((\log(n+2))^{O(1)})\). This is a quasipolynomial upper bound, whose permitted exponents go beyond the fixed polynomial bound requested here. It does not prove a superpolynomial lower bound on the problem or on every implementation of that method.

Efficient algorithms on restricted graph classes provide substantial structure without settling the unrestricted target. In particular, a runtime with a degree or width parameter in the exponent is polynomial when that parameter is fixed, but it need not be polynomial when the parameter grows with the input. The 2026 survey explicitly separates these parameterized bounds from the general open problem.

A randomized polynomial-time algorithm with bounded error for ordinary isomorphism would settle the neighboring BPP question. It would not by itself provide the deterministic algorithm asked for here. A quantum algorithm deciding the same ordinary relation is another computational variant; the distinct relation called quantum graph isomorphism is a different mathematical target.

The two consolidated MFCS 2021 sources independently restate the general polynomial-time question. Butti and Dalmau discuss it beside fractional homomorphisms and linear-programming relaxations. Dawar and Vagnozzi discuss its equivalence to computing automorphism-orbit partitions and compare algebraic relaxations. These source contexts are preserved without substituting a conjecture about one relaxation for general graph isomorphism.

cards.title: Tutte’s 5-flow conjecture
cards.formal: Does every finite loopless bridgeless undirected multigraph \(G=(V,E)\) admit an orientation \(D\) of all its edges and a function \(f:E\to\{1,2,3,4\}\) such that, at every vertex \(v\in V\), \[\sum_{e\in E:\,\operatorname{head}_D(e)=v}f(e)=\sum_{e\in E:\,\operatorname{tail}_D(e)=v}f(e)\] as an equality of integers?
cards.definitions: A finite loopless undirected multigraph has a finite vertex set \(V\) and a finite set \(E\) of distinct edge identities, each assigned an unordered pair of two distinct vertices. Multiple edges with the same pair of endpoints are allowed and counted separately in every sum. Two vertices lie in the same connected component when a finite sequence of incident edges joins them; a vertex is joined to itself by the empty sequence. A bridge is an edge whose deletion, with the vertex set retained, increases the number of connected components. Bridgeless means that no edge has this property. Disconnected graphs, isolated vertices and the graph with no vertices are allowed. An orientation chooses, for each edge, one endpoint as its tail and the other as its head. The orientation and all values are chosen together for the whole graph; conservation must hold at all vertices simultaneously. Empty sums equal zero. For an integer \(k\ge2\), a nowhere-zero \(k\)-flow in this convention has the same conservation law and values in \(\{1,\ldots,k-1\}\). Thus a 5-flow uses four possible positive integer values; it may use any subset of them. Equivalently, after fixing an arbitrary reference orientation, signed integer values \(z(e)\) with \(1\le|z(e)|\le4\) may be used: a negative value is represented by reversing that edge and taking its absolute value. Values are scalar integers, not vectors, and conservation is exact, not merely a congruence. There are no sources, sinks, externally prescribed demands, capacities, embedding, degree restrictions or construction-time requirements. The proposition is universal over finite graphs, with the orientation and values allowed to depend on the graph.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this universal existence proposition, or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: there exists a finite loopless bridgeless undirected multigraph \(G\) such that for every orientation \(D\) and every assignment \(f:E(G)\to\{1,2,3,4\}\), at least one vertex violates the integer conservation equality. A negative answer must prove both the graph hypotheses and the nonexistence of every permitted flow; failure of one orientation, one search method or a finite collection of trial assignments is insufficient unless it establishes that universal nonexistence. A positive answer must cover every size and all allowed parallel edges and components. A 6-flow, an assertion only for graphs with an additional restriction, or a statement conditional on an unproved conjecture does not settle this target. An alternative formulation can qualify only with a Lean-checked implication establishing the exact proposition or its negation. No efficient procedure for constructing the witness is required.
cards.why: The conjecture asks whether the necessary absence of bridges always permits bounded nonzero integer circulation, with the universal value limit improved from five to four. It connects flow existence with graph coloring through planar duality and has a quantitative consequence for packing sets of arcs that meet every directed cut.

importance.reason: A defining flow-existence conjecture with consequences for graph decompositions, orientations and directed-cut packing.

progress.text: Seymour’s universal 6-flow theorem and Younger’s algorithmic version give the neighboring upper bound with integer values at most five, as recalled in the inspected 2025 Theorem 5.

context_blocks.text: Flow conservation models circulation with no accumulation at any vertex. If an edge is a bridge, summing conservation on one side of that bridge would force its value to be zero. Bridgelessness is therefore necessary. The issue is whether it is sufficient with the fixed range \(1,2,3,4\), independently of graph size. Components can be treated separately, and edgeless components satisfy conservation with the empty assignment. This extends the connected formulation in Conjecture 3 without changing the mathematical target.

Seymour’s 1981 6-flow theorem supplies values in \(\{1,2,3,4,5\}\) for every bridgeless graph. Younger’s 1983 work gives a polynomial-time construction, as recalled in Theorem 5 of the 2025 paper. The missing assertion is the universal reduction of the maximum value from five to four. The construction-time improvement in the known theorem is additional to the existence requirement on this card.

Tutte’s integer/group-flow theorem equates existence of a nowhere-zero integer 5-flow with existence of a flow over \(\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z\), the residues modulo five, using nonzero values and conservation in that group. This equivalence is an existence theorem; simply interpreting the same residues as positive integers need not preserve integer conservation. Theorem 2.3 in the 2026 reconfiguration paper recalls the lifting statement.

For a connected bridgeless graph drawn in the plane without crossings, the dual graph has a vertex for each face and an edge crossing each original edge between its incident faces. Tutte’s duality identifies existence of an integer \(k\)-flow with a proper \(k\)-coloring of that dual: adjacent dual vertices receive different colors. This explains why flow questions extend coloring phenomena beyond graphs with a planar embedding.

A directed cut consists of all arcs crossing a nontrivial vertex partition when every crossing arc points in the same direction; a dijoin is a set of arcs meeting every such cut. Cornuéjols, Liu and Ravi’s Theorem 3 implies that, when the underlying graph admits a 5-flow, a digraph with finite minimum directed-cut size \(\tau\ge2\) contains \(\lfloor\tau/5\rfloor\) pairwise arc-disjoint dijoins. The established 6-flow theorem yields \(\lfloor\tau/6\rfloor\). The 5-flow conjecture would improve this guarantee without asserting Woodall’s full packing equality.

Li and Su’s 2025 publisher abstract reports a 5-flow for every bridgeless graph of Euler genus at most 20. Euler genus is the least surface parameter admitting a crossing-free drawing: twice the number of handles for an orientable closed surface, or the number of crosscaps for a nonorientable one. This is a restricted graph class; no uniform bound on genus is assumed here. The present review inspected that abstract, not the full proof.

Esperet and coauthors’ July 2026 revision gives a graph with existing nowhere-zero 5-flows that cannot all be connected by steps changing a flow only along a cycle, while keeping every intermediate flow nowhere zero. Their Theorem 3.4 refutes this reconfiguration property in both the integer and modulo-five settings. It does not refute existence of a 5-flow; their introduction retains Tutte’s conjecture and the 6-flow theorem as the general benchmark.

Li, Li, Luo and Su’s January 2026 paper defines flows with vector values in several real dimensions and proves bounds on their norms. Its Conjecture 1.3 separately states the ordinary one-dimensional 5-flow question. A higher-dimensional flow has additional freedom and does not itself supply the scalar integer assignment required here.

cards.title: Almost-linear-time exact maximum matching in general graphs
cards.formal: Is there one randomized sequential algorithm that, on every explicitly represented finite simple undirected graph G with n vertices and m edges, outputs an exact maximum-cardinality matching with probability at least \(2/3\) and has expected running time \((n+m+2)^{1+o(1)}\) in the word-RAM model below?
cards.definitions: A matching \(M\subseteq E(G)\) is a set of edges no two of which share an endpoint. Its size is |M|, and \(\nu (G)=\max\){|M|:M is a matching in G}. The algorithm must output valid edge identifiers forming a matching on every terminating execution, and |\(M|=\nu (G)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) on each input. It must terminate with probability one. Vertices are labelled \(1,\ldots ,n\) and the input is an adjacency-list or edge-list representation of size \(O(n+m)\); isolated vertices are included in n. Put \(N=n+m+2\). Use a random-access machine with \(\Theta (\log  N)\)-bit words, supporting constant-cost reads, writes, comparisons, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations and shifts on words, and fresh uniform random words. Intermediate larger integers require multiple words and their processing is charged. Preprocessing and output writing are included. The program is uniform, with no advice or free precomputed tables. The time statement means that this same algorithm satisfies: for every real \(\varepsilon >0\) there are constants \(C\varepsilon\) and \(N\varepsilon\) such that for every input with \(N\ge N\varepsilon\), its expected number of operations is at most \(C\varepsilon  N^{1+\varepsilon}\). The expectation is over its own random choices, not a distribution on graph inputs. No edge weights, degree restriction, bipartiteness promise, approximation slack or auxiliary communication model is assumed. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A major remaining exact graph-optimization problem beyond the almost-linear flow framework. It asks whether odd-cycle and blossom structure impose a real asymptotic cost, even when randomization is allowed.

importance.reason: A core combinatorial optimization primitive with a large gap between general graphs and the fast bipartite case, connecting augmenting paths, polyhedral methods and algebraic algorithms.

Chen and coauthors achieve almost-linear exact flow algorithms, giving the corresponding bipartite matching consequence.

The catalytic-logspace revision constructs general maximum matchings with a polynomial-time bound, a different resource guarantee.

Bipartite flow algorithms, approximation schemes and the 2026 catalytic-space result do not meet the stated target. This card explicitly permits bounded-error randomization and expected running time.

context_blocks.text: Maximum matching is a basic model of pairing compatible objects while using each object at most once. General graphs allow compatibility patterns that cannot be separated into two sides. Edmonds’ blossom method established that this optimization is polynomial-time solvable. The remaining question is how close its exact computational cost can come to the size of the graph that must be read.

Maximum and maximal have different meanings. A maximal matching merely cannot be extended by adding a single edge. On a four-vertex path, the middle edge alone is maximal, while the two outside edges form a maximum matching of size two. A greedy linear-time procedure can therefore solve maximal matching and still fail the exact task on a tiny input. The card requires the global optimum, with no allowed loss of even one matched pair.

Alternating paths explain how a nonmaximum matching can improve. Such a path alternates edges outside and inside the matching and starts and ends at unmatched vertices. Flipping its edge membership increases the matching size by one. In general graphs, odd cycles complicate the search for shortest augmenting paths; contracted structures called blossoms keep track of these possibilities. Micali and Vazirani’s classical algorithm achieves \(O(m\sqrt{n})\) time, with later work developing its proof and presentation.

Bipartite graphs have a particularly effective flow formulation. Direct each edge from the left side to the right, join a source to left vertices and right vertices to a sink, and give every edge capacity one. Integral maximum flow gives a maximum matching. Almost-linear exact flow algorithms therefore solve bipartite matching within the desired time scale. There is no supplied bipartition in the present question, and the same construction does not automatically encode odd-cycle constraints.

A triangle illustrates the polyhedral obstacle without requiring a large example. If a fractional variable of one half is placed on each edge, every vertex has total incident value one, but the total value is \(3/2\) while an integral matching has size at most one. For any odd vertex set S, an integral matching uses at most \((|S|- 1)/2\) edges entirely inside S. Handling these additional odd-set restrictions efficiently is part of what distinguishes general matching from its bipartite counterpart.

Algebraic algorithms offer another route. Mucha and Sankowski use Gaussian elimination to construct maximum matchings in randomized time governed by matrix multiplication, conventionally written \(O(n^{\omega})\) for an available exponent \(\omega >2\). This is a major improvement over combinatorial bounds on dense graphs. It still does not yield input-size almost-linear time on all sparse graphs, where a dense n-by-n matrix representation can itself exceed the input size by a large factor.

Approximation also behaves differently. Duan, Pettie and Su obtain a \((1- \delta )\)-approximation for maximum weight matching in \(O(m\delta ^{- 1} \log  \delta ^{- 1})\) time, hence linear time for fixed \(\delta\); unit weights cover cardinality. To force exact cardinality purely by rounding this guarantee, one would need \(\delta\) small enough that the possible loss is below one edge. When the optimum is \(\Theta (n)\), that requires \(\delta =O(1/n)\), so substituting it into the approximation running time loses the desired almost-linear bound.

Ansaripour, Danaei and Mehlhorn’s 2024 implementation study is useful for interpreting experiments: the observed behaviour on random graphs can be close to linear, while specially constructed inputs expose substantial differences between algorithms. Empirical speed and average graph behaviour therefore cannot establish the bound quantified over every input here. Their paper also keeps the distinction between the faster bipartite results and general matching explicit.

A June 2026 revision by Chakraborty and coauthors places construction of a general maximum matching in polynomial-time catalytic logspace. This model permits a large auxiliary tape with arbitrary initial contents, provided those contents are restored. It is progress on space and reversible use of auxiliary memory. The polynomial-time statement is not an almost-linear running-time theorem, so it does not resolve this card.

cards.title: Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture
cards.formal: For every finite nonempty tree T and every integer \(r\ge 1\), does there exist a finite integer \(B(T,r)\) such that every finite simple undirected graph G with clique number at most r and no induced subgraph isomorphic to T has chromatic number at most \(B(T,r)\)?
cards.definitions: A tree is a connected graph with no cycle. All graphs here are finite, simple and undirected. The clique number \(\omega (G)\) is the largest number of pairwise adjacent vertices, and the chromatic number \(\chi (G)\) is the least number of colours in a proper vertex colouring, in which adjacent vertices receive distinct colours. Both parameters are zero for the empty graph. For \(S\subseteq V(G)\), the induced graph \(G[S]\) retains all edges of G with both endpoints in S. Saying that G contains an induced T means there is an injective map \(\varphi :V(T)\to V(G)\) such that xy is an edge of T if and only if \(\varphi (x)\varphi (y)\) is an edge of G. Extra edges between image vertices are forbidden. The quantifier order is \(\forall T \forall r \exists B \forall G\): the integer B may depend arbitrarily on T and r, but not on |\(V(G)|\), maximum degree or any additional parameter of G. Equivalently, for each T there is a function \(f_{T}:N\to N\) with \(\chi (G)\le f_{T}(\omega (G))\) for every induced-T-free graph G. No prescribed polynomial growth, computability requirement for \(f_{T}\), or efficient colouring algorithm is part of the target. The statement concerns ordinary chromatic number, not fractional, list, oriented or domatic colouring parameters.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated bound for all finite trees and all fixed clique bounds, or exhibit one fixed tree T and one fixed integer r together with induced-T-free graphs \(G_{k}\) satisfying \(\omega (G_{k})\le r\) and \(\chi (G_{k})\to \infty\). A single finite graph can disprove a proposed numerical bound but cannot refute the existence of some larger bound. A bound that still grows with |\(V(G)|\), or a theorem with a different excluded object or extra host-graph promise, is not a full resolution.
cards.why: Determine whether every fixed induced tree is an unavoidable pattern in graphs whose chromatic number grows while their clique number stays bounded.

importance.reason: A central organizing conjecture for hereditary graph colouring and forbidden induced subgraphs, defining the proposed forest boundary for χ-boundedness.

context_blocks.text: A clique explains one elementary reason for needing many colours: its vertices must all receive different colours. But graphs can require arbitrarily many colours even when every clique has size at most two. The conjecture proposes that forbidding any one fixed induced tree eliminates this unbounded gap. Once the tree and clique bound are fixed, the same finite palette should suffice no matter how many vertices the graph has.

The induced condition is essential. A copy of a tree as an ordinary subgraph can ignore unwanted edges between its vertices. An induced copy must reproduce both adjacency and nonadjacency. Complete graphs contain every sufficiently small tree as an ordinary subgraph, while most of those trees do not occur as induced subgraphs. The difficult step in building the desired tree is therefore arranging its branches without creating extra edges among them.

Trees are the natural boundary for this kind of one-forbidden-pattern statement. High-girth graphs can have arbitrarily large chromatic number while containing no short cycles. If a fixed forbidden graph contains a cycle, choosing larger girth avoids that graph while retaining an unbounded chromatic number and a bounded clique number. The corresponding obstruction is absent for forests. This is why the conjecture is a proposed classification, rather than an arbitrary choice of forbidden shape.

There are substantial positive cases. Kierstead and Penrice proved the conjecture for every tree of radius at most two: some central vertex is within distance two of every other vertex. Paths and further tree families are also known. Scott and Seymour subsequently strengthen the radius-two result under exclusion of a fixed complete multipartite subgraph, with polynomial bounds in its part size. Such results exploit restrictions on how branches can interact.

Nguyen, Scott and Seymour’s 2023 preprint, published in 2024, obtains a copy of any fixed rooted tree under the conjecture’s high-chromatic-number hypotheses, with every path from the root induced. This controls unwanted edges along ancestor–descendant paths. It still permits edges between different branches, and those edges may prevent the whole vertex set from inducing a tree. The distinction isolates one of the remaining obstacles.

Their later work on near-linear stable sets applies to every fixed excluded forest and fixed clique bound. It proves an independent set of size \(n^{1- o(1)}\), and consequently a chromatic bound \(n^{o(1)}\), where n is the number of vertices. Thus every fixed positive power \(n^{\varepsilon}\) eventually exceeds the available upper bound. Nevertheless, a function such as log n is also \(n^{o(1)}\) and is unbounded, so subpolynomial growth does not establish the constant \(B(T,r)\) sought here.

That work also proves a bounded fractional chromatic number for multibrooms, formed by identifying the roots of several paths that have additional leaves at their far ends. Fractional colouring covers vertices by weighted independent sets and minimizes the total weight. Ordinary colouring requires an actual partition into colour classes. The paper retains the full conjecture for general multibrooms despite its stronger fractional conclusion.

Davies and Yuditsky establish the conjecture, with a polynomial bound in the clique number, for intersection graphs of axis-aligned boxes in every fixed dimension d. Their result first appeared in 2024 and was published in April 2026. Both the excluded forest and dimension are fixed parameters. Allowing the dimension to grow with the input would let the bound vary with an extra parameter, so the theorem does not cover arbitrary graphs with the uniform bound required here.

For algorithms, this conjecture identifies a structural source of bounded colouring complexity and large independent sets. It does not itself promise that a suitable colouring can be found efficiently. A proof with an effective construction would offer additional algorithmic information; a counterexample would reveal a family of sparse-clique graphs whose chromatic obstruction survives exclusion of one fixed induced tree. The size-independent existence statement is already fundamental.

cards.title: Optimal bounds in the Excluded Grid Theorem
cards.formal: For each integer \(r\ge 2\), let \(f(r)\) be the least nonnegative integer t such that every finite simple undirected graph of treewidth at least t contains the \(r\times r\) square grid as a minor. Determine the asymptotic order of \(f(r)\) up to universal constant factors, including the correct logarithmic dependence.
cards.definitions: The \(r\times r\) grid has vertex set \(\{1,\ldots ,r\}^{2}\), with an edge between \((i,j)\) and \((i' ,j' )\) exactly when |\(i- i' |+|j- j' |=1\). It has \(r^{2}\) vertices; r denotes side length. A graph H is a minor of G if H can be obtained by deleting vertices, deleting edges and contracting edges, after removing loops and merging parallel edges. Equivalently, a model of H consists of one nonempty connected vertex set in G for each vertex of H, all pairwise disjoint, with an edge of G joining the corresponding sets for every edge of H. Additional edges are permitted. A tree decomposition of G is a tree T with bags \(B_{t}\subseteq V(G)\), such that every vertex belongs to some bag, the endpoints of every edge belong together to some bag, and the bags containing any given vertex form a connected subtree of T. Its width is \(\max _{t} |B_{t}|- 1\); treewidth \(\operatorname{tw}(G)\) is the minimum such width. Robertson–Seymour’s Grid-Minor Theorem guarantees that \(f(r)\) is finite. The quantifier over G includes graphs of arbitrary size, degree and genus. This is an extremal existence threshold; no efficiency requirement for finding the grid model is imposed. Polylogarithmic factors mean \((\log  r)^{c}\) for a fixed constant c, and matching bounds here must resolve such factors rather than suppress them.
cards.answer_criterion: Identify an explicit asymptotic function \(h(r)\) and universal constants \(a,b>0\) such that a \(h(r)\le f(r)\le b h(r)\) for all sufficiently large r. The upper bound must force a grid minor in every graph above the stated threshold; the lower bound must give graphs of comparable treewidth that exclude it. In particular, this determines whether \(f(r)=O(r^{2}(\log  r)^{c})\) for some fixed c. Merely improving a nonmatching polynomial exponent, solving the planar-host case, or replacing minors by a different containment relation is progress rather than a complete answer.

importance.reason: A central quantitative problem in graph minor theory with direct implications for structural decompositions, routing, packing and parameterized algorithms.

cards.status_note: The checked general bounds remain \(\Omega (r^{2} \log  r)\) and \(O(r^{9} \operatorname{polylog} r)\). The November 2025 product-structure result and SODA 2026 fixed-minor result refine different aspects and do not determine the all-graphs threshold. No matching asymptotic bounds found through 11 September 2026. The problem does not assume that either the near-quadratic or cubic conjecture is correct.

context_blocks.text: Treewidth measures how large the interacting pieces of a graph must be when organized along a tree. Many algorithms work by dynamic programming across the bags of a tree decomposition, with a strong dependence on bag size. A grid provides a canonical obstruction to small treewidth: its rows and columns create many overlapping connections that cannot be separated into very small bags. The Excluded Grid Theorem states that every graph of sufficiently large treewidth contains such an obstruction as a minor.

The unknown quantity is how much treewidth must be spent to force a grid of a given side length. The qualitative theorem only says that some finite threshold exists. A sharp quantitative bound would explain how efficiently general tangled connectivity can be organized into a planar grid. This is not a statement that the graph itself is planar, or that a grid must appear as an induced subgraph.

A vertex-count example already rules out a linear threshold. The complete graph on \(r^{2}- 1\) vertices has treewidth \(r^{2}- 2\), but cannot contain an \(r\times r\) grid minor because taking a minor cannot increase the number of vertices. Thus \(f(r)\ge r^{2}- 1\). Its many edges cannot replace the need for \(r^{2}\) disjoint nonempty branch sets in a minor model. This is why the fact that the \(r\times r\) grid itself has treewidth r does not imply a linear bound for arbitrary host graphs.

The known lower bound is stronger: \(f(r)=\Omega (r^{2} \log  r)\). Robertson, Seymour and Thomas obtain it using bounded-degree expanders of logarithmic girth. Such graphs have treewidth proportional to their number of vertices, while every cycle is long. A large grid contains quadratically many vertex-disjoint small cycles; lifting those cycles through a minor model requires quadratically many disjoint long cycles in the host. This consumes a logarithmic factor of additional vertices.

Chekuri and Chuzhoy obtain the first polynomial upper bound, replacing an enormous quantitative gap by a polynomial relationship between treewidth and grid size. Their proof is constructive: a randomized polynomial-time algorithm finds a grid model at the scale established by their theorem. This makes the result useful both as a structural guarantee and as a subroutine, although this card asks only for the optimal existence threshold.

Chuzhoy and Tan improve the general upper bound to \(O(r^{9}(\log  r)^{c})\) for an absolute constant c. Their SODA 2019 paper, published in journal form in 2021, builds on well-linked sets and paths of connected clusters. Well-linkedness supplies many disjoint connections; the challenge is arranging them into the grid’s particular pattern without losing too much width at successive stages. The lower and upper bounds still differ by a large power of r.

The same paper records competing predictions: Robertson–Seymour–Thomas conjectured that the \(r^{2} \log  r\) lower bound is tight, while Demaine and coauthors proposed a cubic threshold. Consequently, the catalogue target is the actual asymptotic order. A near-quadratic upper bound would be a major result, but should not be described as the only conjectured answer. Even \(r^{2}\) times an unspecified power of log r would leave part of the present target unresolved.

The 2025 paper The Grid-Minor Theorem Revisited strengthens the structural description of graphs excluding a fixed planar minor. It represents them inside clique blow-ups of graphs whose treewidth is controlled by the excluded graph’s treedepth. The blow-up size is an unspecified function of the excluded graph. This gives useful product structure and colouring applications, while leaving the optimal numerical threshold \(f(r)\) undetermined.

Catching Rats in H-minor-free Graphs, presented at SODA 2026, makes another substantial refinement under an extra host-graph restriction. For a fixed excluded graph H with t vertices and Euler genus g, a graph excluding both H and the \(r\times r\) grid has treewidth \(O(gr+t^{2304})\), hence \(O(t^{2}r+t^{2304})\). This is linear in r when H is fixed. General graphs in our question need not exclude any fixed H, so that additional parameter cannot be treated as a universal constant.

The threshold influences the quantitative strength of grid-based routing arguments, packing-versus-covering theorems and parameterized algorithms. Better bounds can improve how a large-treewidth case yields useful structure, or how a no-grid case bounds the state space for dynamic programming. A matching lower bound would be equally informative: it would identify an unavoidable loss in converting unrestricted graph connectivity into a planar obstruction.

cards.title: Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture
cards.formal: For every pair of integers \(n\ge 2\) and \(1\le r\le n- 1\), does every simple loopless digraph D on n vertices with minimum outdegree at least r contain a directed cycle of length at most \(\operatorname{ceil}(n/r)\)?
cards.definitions: A simple loopless digraph has a finite vertex set V and an arc set \(A\subseteq \{(u,v)\in V\times V:u\ne v\}\); each ordered pair occurs at most once. Both \((u,v)\) and \((v,u)\) are allowed. The outdegree \(d^{+}(v)\) is |\(\{u:(v,u)\in A\}|\) and minimum outdegree is \(\min _{v\in V}d^{+}(v)\). A directed cycle of length \(\ell\)\(\ge 2\) is a sequence of pairwise distinct vertices \(v_{1},\ldots ,v_{\ell}\) with \((v_{i},v_{i+1})\in A\) for every i and \(v_{\ell +1}=v_{1}\). Thus an opposite pair of arcs is a directed 2-cycle. \(\operatorname{ceil}(n/r)\) is the least integer not smaller than \(n/r\). There is no planarity, regularity, connectivity or algorithmic assumption.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.

cards.title: Almost-linear triangle detection
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every finite simple undirected graph with n vertices and m edges given by adjacency lists, decides whether a triangle exists with success probability at least \(2/3\) and worst-case running time \((n+m+2)^{1+o(1)}\)?
cards.definitions: A triangle is a set of three distinct vertices u,v,w for which all three unordered edges \(\{u,v\},\{v,w\},\{w,u\}\) are present. The input gives labelled vertices \(1,\ldots ,n\) and explicit adjacency lists; it is promised to describe a simple undirected graph, and can be disconnected or contain isolated vertices. The RAM has words of \(w=\lceil 4 \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits, random-access memory, and unit-cost word reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo 2ʷ, and integer division by a nonzero word. Independent random words may be generated at unit cost. Input reading and all preprocessing count toward time. The running-time bound holds for every graph and every random tape, while correctness probability is over the algorithm’s internal randomness. The \(o(1)\) is a function tending to zero as \(n+m\) tends to infinity, for this one fixed algorithm; equivalently, for every \(\varepsilon >0\) the same algorithm eventually uses at most \((n+m+2)^{1+\varepsilon}\) operations. There is no promise on density, degree, arboricity or triangle count. Matrix multiplication and other algebraic techniques are allowed if their implementation fits this machine model. Only one yes/no answer is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct and analyze an algorithm meeting the stated all-input time and probability guarantees, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A deterministic \(O(n+m)\) algorithm would be an even stronger positive answer. A fixed exponent above one, an \(O(n^{2})\) bound that is only input-linear on dense graphs, output-sensitive listing, or an algorithm restricted to bounded-arboricity graphs does not settle the question. The target fixes the original draft’s “linear or at least almost-linear” alternative at the precise almost-linear threshold.
cards.why: Determine whether detecting the simplest cyclic graph pattern requires a superlinear amount of computation beyond reading the input.

importance.reason: A fundamental graph primitive and fine-grained hardness assumption with consequences for dynamic data structures, joins and string matching.

context_blocks.text: Triangle detection is among the smallest nontrivial pattern-finding tasks in a graph. The pattern has only three vertices, but a graph may contain an enormous number of possible triples. The question asks whether all the relevant combinations can be handled in essentially the time required to read the graph. It must also handle triangle-free instances, where an algorithm cannot stop upon finding a convenient local witness.

Detection is different from listing. A complete graph has \(\Theta (n^{2})\) input edges and \(\Theta (n^{3})\) triangles, so explicitly listing every triangle cannot take linear time in the input size. A yes/no answer has constant output size and faces no such output-size obstruction. Likewise, approximate counting or finding triangles in a distribution of random inputs does not supply an exact decision guarantee on every adversarial graph.

Chiba and Nishizeki give triangle listing in \(O(m\cdot a(G))\) time, apart from reading isolated vertices, where arboricity \(a(G)\) is the minimum number of forests needed to cover the graph’s edges. This gives linear time on any family of bounded arboricity, including planar graphs. General graphs can have arboricity of order \(\sqrt{m}\), so this approach has a superlinear worst-case cost. A sparse graph can still contain a dense, difficult region.

Alon, Yuster and Zwick improve the general sparse-graph bound using a degree threshold. Handle triangles touching a low-degree vertex by local enumeration, and use matrix multiplication on the smaller set of high-degree vertices. For an available square matrix-multiplication exponent \(\tau\), the resulting standard bound is \(O(n+m^{2\tau /(\tau +1)})\), roughly \(O(n+m^{1.407})\) at familiar current exponents. The optimization balances the cost of the two parts.

Even setting the matrix-multiplication exponent to two in this particular reduction leaves exponent \(4/3\) in m. Thus faster dense multiplication alone, inserted into the same degree-splitting argument, would not make the sparse algorithm almost linear. This is an observation about the upper-bound method, not a proof that a different graph algorithm cannot do better.

Abboud and Vassilevska Williams formulate a no-almost-linear triangle hypothesis and use it to derive conditional lower bounds for dynamic problems. The conjecture concerns general algorithms on logarithmic-word RAMs. Their separate combinatorial Boolean-matrix-multiplication conjecture restricts the kinds of techniques used; it should not be substituted for the unrestricted question here. Reductions transfer assumed hardness, rather than establish an unconditional superlinear lower bound.

The distinction remains useful in current work. Kumabe and Uezato’s ICALP 2026 paper reduces triangle detection to matching certain fixed regular expressions with two backreference uses. Consequently, an almost-linear algorithm for that matching task would also give an almost-linear triangle algorithm. This illustrates why a small graph pattern can govern complexity in a seemingly unrelated setting.

Search results require source checks. Dumitrescu’s March 2024 claim of faster combinatorial triangle algorithms was withdrawn three days after posting; the author states that the algorithm may fail and identifies an invalid case analysis. It is not an established improvement.

I also checked the parent-edge rule in Vega’s August 2025 linear-time proposal. Consider the path 0–1–2–3–4–5–6 plus edges 0–3, 3–6 and 0–6. A legal DFS follows the whole path. Its unique triangle is \(\{0,3,6\}\), consisting entirely of back edges. No test restricted to a DFS parent, its child and a common neighbour can find it. A local simulation and exhaustive triple check confirm this counterexample to the stated rule; this is not a test of later replacement implementations.

A separate September 2026 Aegypti revision claims \(O(n^{2})\) time via bucket reduction. That claimed bound is not almost linear for every sparse input, even if its correctness were established. I have not adjudicated its different proof. An all-density statement must keep both n and m visible: a dense-case breakthrough and an input-linear sparse algorithm are distinct achievements.

A resolution would identify whether a basic three-way adjacency condition inherently requires substantial work beyond scanning an explicit graph. A positive algorithm would affect graph-pattern routines and invalidate hardness assumptions used by many reductions. A negative result would provide a major unconditional lower bound for a simple polynomial-time graph problem on a strong, standard machine model.

cards.title: Seese’s conjecture
cards.formal: For every isomorphism-closed class C of finite simple undirected graphs, does decidability of its MSO\(_{1}\) satisfiability problem imply that some constant k bounds the clique-width of every graph in C?
cards.definitions: An MSO\(_{1}\) sentence is built from vertex equality, adjacency \(E(x,y)\), membership \(x\in X\) in vertex sets, Boolean connectives, and quantification over individual vertices and subsets of the vertex set. There is no built-in vertex order, edge-set quantification, parity predicate or other counting extension. For a fixed class \(C, Sat_{MSO_{1}}(C)\) consists of all finite encoded MSO\(_{1}\) sentences \(\varphi\) for which some \(G\in C\) satisfies \(\varphi\). Decidable means that one Turing machine, allowed to depend on C, halts and answers correctly for every input sentence. C itself is not an input to that machine; no complexity bound is required. By negating sentences this is equivalent to deciding the theory \(Th_{MSO_{1}}(C)\)={\(\varphi\): every \(G\in C\) satisfies \(\varphi\)}. A k-expression builds a labeled graph from single vertices with labels in \([k]\), disjoint union, relabeling every vertex of one label to another, and adding all edges between two distinct labels. The clique-width \(\operatorname{cw}(G)\) is the smallest k permitting such an expression after labels are forgotten; set \(\operatorname{cw}(\varnothing )=0\). The conclusion is \(\exists k\forall G\in C \operatorname{cw}(G)\le k\), with k depending on C. No hereditary, minor-closed, bounded-degree or finite-forbidden-subgraph assumption is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the implication for every such graph class, or give one class of unbounded clique-width together with a correct terminating algorithm for its entire MSO\(_{1}\) satisfiability problem. A single finite graph cannot refute a uniform width bound for a class. Model checking on a supplied graph, or decidability with a promise about sentence size, is not the premise. Results requiring parity predicates or restricted graph classes do not prove the full statement.
cards.why: A major proposed structural necessity for logical decidability, connecting graph decompositions, finite model theory and algorithms over infinite families of finite inputs.

importance.reason: A foundational conjecture asking whether bounded clique-width is unavoidable whenever an entire graph class has decidable vertex-set monadic logic.

progress.text: Seese establishes foundational connections between decidable monadic graph theories and bounded structural width, and formulates the conjectural MSO\(_{1}\) boundary.
Courcelle–Oum prove that decidable MSO\(_{1}\) with parity predicates implies bounded clique-width.
Dawar–Sankaran develop the antichain/minimal-hereditary-class reduction for the stronger grid-interpretation conjecture; preprint 2020, CSL 2022, journal volume 2025.
Mählmann characterizes bounded shrub-depth through logical expressiveness and records a stronger MSO-dependence conjecture that would imply Seese’s.
Duron–Mählmann–Toruńczyk prove bounded clique-width for hereditary 2-WQO classes; the hypothesis differs from decidability of MSO\(_{1}\) satisfiability.
