cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. Seese’s MSO\(_{1}\) decidability implication remains unresolved in the checked primary literature. The parity extension, the shrub-depth expressiveness characterization and the July 2026 2-WQO result have distinct hypotheses or conclusions.

context_blocks.text: An MSO\(_{1}\) sentence can describe a graph property by quantifying over sets of vertices. Three-colorability, for example, can be expressed by choosing three sets that partition the vertices and requiring each set to be independent. Checking such a sentence on one finite graph is always decidable by exhaustive search. The premise here is much stronger: from a sentence alone, decide whether it holds in at least one member of an entire, potentially infinite graph class.

Clique-width measures how many vertex labels are needed to construct a graph using a small repertoire of operations. Labels identify groups of vertices that receive the same future edge additions. Dense graphs can have small clique-width: a complete graph can be built with two labels by inserting one vertex, joining it to all previous vertices, and merging its label. Thus the conjectured structural restriction is not a sparsity condition.

The classical treewidth theorem provides the motivation. Seese proves structural restrictions from decidability of monadic theories, and the version allowing quantification over edge sets forces bounded treewidth. Grid-minor machinery supports that argument. The MSO\(_{1}\) conjecture replaces edge-set quantification by vertex-set quantification and asks for bounded clique-width instead. Transferring the proof requires a logical way of recovering the appropriate obstruction.

Bounded-width descriptions support decidability because graph properties can be translated into properties of construction trees. In particular, for each fixed k the full class of graphs of clique-width at most k has decidable MSO\(_{1}\) satisfiability. But the conjecture is only a necessary-condition statement for an arbitrary class C. One cannot infer that every subclass of a bounded-width class has decidable theory.

For a simple reason, such a converse would be false. Choose an undecidable set S of positive integers, and let C contain exactly the edgeless graphs whose numbers of vertices belong to S. All those graphs have clique-width one. A sentence specifying exactly n vertices would decide whether \(n\in S\) if satisfiability over C were decidable. Restricting which sizes occur can encode undecidability even when each individual graph has trivial structure.

Courcelle–Oum prove the implication after extending MSO\(_{1}\) with the predicate \(Even(X)\), saying that a vertex set has even cardinality. Their vertex-minor and isotropic-system machinery establishes bounded clique-width from decidability of this stronger logic. This strengthens the premise: a decision procedure for ordinary MSO\(_{1}\) sentences need not handle parity sentences. Therefore their theorem supplies substantial progress while leaving the exact statement here open.

Hereditary classes, which are closed under taking induced subgraphs, are a useful focus even though the card quantifies over all classes. If satisfiability is decidable on C, it is also decidable on its hereditary closure: ask whether some vertex subset induces a graph satisfying the input sentence, using a relativized MSO\(_{1}\) formula. Unbounded clique-width is preserved on passing to that larger class. Thus a proof covering all hereditary classes would suffice.

Dawar–Sankaran develop a stronger route through interpreting arbitrarily large grids. Their Theorem 3.2 reduces that stronger assertion to two settings: antichains of unbounded clique-width under induced-subgraph containment, and minimal hereditary classes of unbounded clique-width. They verify the grid interpretation for the known minimal families studied in their paper. This is a research program and collection of cases, not a completed classification of all such families.

The inherited ICALP 2025 paper by Mählmann settles a different boundary: on hereditary classes, bounded shrub-depth characterizes coincidence of first-order and monadic second-order expressive power. Its conclusion formulates a stronger conjectural relationship between clique-width and MSO dependence, explaining how parts of that conjecture would imply Seese’s. Shrub-depth and clique-width are distinct parameters, and a theorem about expressive power does not by itself decide satisfiability.

Duron–Mählmann–Toruńczyk’s July 2026 preprint proves that every hereditary 2-WQO class has bounded clique-width. Here 2-WQO means that every infinite sequence of graphs with two possible vertex labels contains an earlier graph embedding as a label-preserving induced subgraph of a later one. This resolves a related structural conjecture, but it starts from a well-quasi-ordering hypothesis. It does not turn an arbitrary MSO\(_{1}\) decision procedure into such an ordering property.

The unresolved implication asks whether decidable graph theories always have bounded constructional complexity. A proof would show that broad logical decidability cannot arise from some entirely different mechanism on classes of unbounded clique-width. A counterexample would reveal precisely such a mechanism. Either outcome would change how structural graph theory explains the limits of automated reasoning over whole families of finite structures.

cards.title: Exact directed maximum flow in \(O((m+n) \operatorname{polylog} n)\) time
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(a\ge 1\), do there exist a constant \(k\ge 0\) and a uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A_{a}\) that, on every directed graph with \(n\ge 2\) vertices, m arcs, distinguished distinct vertices s,t and integer capacities in \(\{0,\ldots ,n^{a}\}\), outputs an exact maximum s–t flow with probability at least \(2/3\) in worst-case time \(O((m+n)(\log (n+2))^{k})\)?
cards.definitions: The graph is explicitly given by its labelled vertex set \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\) and an arc list, with no loops and at most one arc per ordered vertex pair; opposite arcs are allowed. A flow assigns an integer \(f_{e}\) to each arc, with \(0\le f_{e}\le u_{e}\) and equal incoming and outgoing sums at every vertex other than s,t. Its value is the outgoing sum at s minus the incoming sum at s; maximum refers to the largest such value. Output the m flow values, not only an approximate value. Use a word RAM with word length \(B_{a}\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) for a fixed integer \(B_{a}\) large enough to store capacities, total flow and memory addresses. Unit-cost operations are random-access word reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction, multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\) and integer division of nonzero divisors. Multiword computations are charged for their component operations. Independent fair random bits are allowed, with each generated word charged. All preprocessing and output are included, and the time bound holds on every random execution. context_blocks.text: Maximum flow is a basic model for routing through capacity constraints. A feasible solution must obey conservation at intermediate vertices, and optimality measures the largest transferable amount between two terminals. Even a graph with small integer capacities can require globally coordinated changes to a feasible routing. The question asks whether finding the exact optimum can cost only a polylogarithmic factor more than reading the graph.

Almost-linear algorithms already represent a major qualitative advance. Chen and coauthors obtained exact maximum flow and minimum-cost flow in \(m^{1+o(1)}\) time for polynomially bounded integral data. Li and Wice’s August 2026 preprint obtains an almost-linear maximum-flow bound through a different framework. Neither stated asymptotic guarantee is \(O(m \operatorname{polylog} n)\).

The distinction concerns the remaining overhead. For example, \(\exp (\sqrt{\log  n})\) is subpolynomial in n but exceeds every fixed power of log n. A running time containing that factor can be almost linear without satisfying this card. Removing the residual gap would identify a sharper computational cost for a central graph optimization primitive.

Exactness is also a substantive part of the target. A flow whose value is within a fixed relative error of optimum does not determine the optimum integer value when that value is large. Conversely, restricting capacities to polynomial magnitude means their binary encodings occupy logarithmically many bits each. The question is therefore not asking an algorithm to read arbitrarily long capacities in a graph-size-only time bound.

The primary topic is a static graph algorithm, so the current catalogue places the question in Structural graph theory and graph algorithms. Dynamic maintenance, parallel computation and strong polynomiality for unbounded-bit linear programming impose different requirements. No existing maximum-matching or dynamic-connectivity card represents this flow target.

cards.definitions: A finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) has a finite vertex set V and an edge set E consisting of unordered two-element subsets of V; there are no loops or parallel edges. An isomorphism from G to H is a bijection \(f:V(G)\to V(H)\) such that \(\{u,v\}\) is an edge of G if and only if \(\{f(u),f(v)\}\) is an edge of H. Write \([G]\) for its isomorphism class. For \(v\in V(G), G- v\) is the induced graph on \(V(G)\setminus \{v\}\): remove v and exactly the edges incident with v. Define \(D(G)\) to be the multiset \(\{[G- v]:v\in V(G)\}\), with one entry for every deleted vertex. Thus \(D(G)=D(H)\) means that for each isomorphism class K of graphs on \(n- 1\) vertices, the number of vertices v with \([G- v]=K\) equals the corresponding number for H. Each entry forgets all original vertex labels, including the identity of the deleted vertex; repeated isomorphism classes retain their multiplicities. All graphs, including disconnected graphs and graphs with isolated vertices, are included. The question is a structural uniqueness statement and imposes no running-time requirement on an algorithm.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that equal vertex decks imply isomorphism for every \(n\ge 3\), or refute the conjecture by exhibiting two nonisomorphic finite simple undirected graphs with \(n\ge 3\) and identical decks, with proofs of those properties.

context_blocks.text: Imagine receiving every graph obtained by deleting one vertex from an unknown graph, with the vertex labels erased in each view. Different deletions can yield identical-looking graphs, and their number of occurrences remains part of the data. The conjecture says this complete collection determines the original graph uniquely up to relabeling.

For a path on three vertices, deleting either endpoint leaves a single edge, while deleting the middle vertex leaves two isolated vertices. Its deck therefore consists of two copies of the edge and one edgeless two-vertex graph. The triangle instead has three copies of the edge. The lower limit of three vertices is necessary: an edge and an edgeless graph on two vertices both have a deck of two isolated single vertices.

Some global information survives deletion automatically. If \(n\ge 3\), every original edge appears in exactly \(n- 2\) members of the deck, so the total number of edges is the sum of the edge counts in the deck divided by \(n- 2\). Comparing each member’s edge count with that total also recovers the multiset of vertex degrees. These counts do not specify how all vertices fit together; that missing arrangement is the substance of the question.

Uniqueness has a different meaning from efficient recovery. There are finitely many graphs of a fixed order, so one can always enumerate those whose decks match the input. The conjecture says there is just one matching isomorphism class whenever the input is the deck of a graph with at least three vertices. It does not require that this enumeration be replaced by a polynomial-time algorithm.

McKay reports exhaustive verification through 13 vertices, and the 2026 revision by Heinrich and coauthors proves reconstruction for every interval graph with at least three vertices. Neither a finite range nor this particular graph class covers all finite graphs. The computations and proofs were not independently reproduced in this review.

A 2026 AI-assisted result concerns a structured bipartite incidence-deletion analogue: it retains the deleted vertex as an isolated vertex, preserves a given bipartition in isomorphisms, and assumes 2-connectivity and pairwise distinct vertex types. Its theorem is not the unrestricted vertex reconstruction conjecture.

The status record also preserves a 2024 general proof claim by O’Shea and Wilkins. Its publisher abstract was checked, but the full argument was inaccessible and is not validated here. Later specialist sources still formulate the general conjecture as open, so this review does not label it resolved.

cards.title: Berge–Fulkerson conjecture
cards.formal: Does every finite loopless bridgeless cubic multigraph G have an ordered list \((M_{1},\ldots ,M_{6})\) of perfect matchings such that for every edge \(e\in E(G), |\{i\in \{1,\ldots ,6\}:e\in M_{i}\}|=2\)?
cards.definitions: Edges of a multigraph have distinct identities and may share their unordered pair of endpoints; loops are forbidden. Cubic means every vertex has degree three, counting incident edge identities with multiplicity. A bridge is an edge whose deletion increases the number of connected components, and bridgeless graphs have none. Disconnected graphs are allowed. A matching is a subset of edges no two of which share an endpoint. It is perfect if every vertex is incident with exactly one of its edges. The six matchings may repeat; membership counts positions in the list, not just distinct subsets. The conclusion requires every edge to occur exactly twice, with no omitted edge and no extra coverage. No algorithmic bound is required.

cards.title: Barnette’s conjecture
cards.formal: Is every finite simple undirected graph that is 3-connected, cubic, bipartite and planar Hamiltonian?
cards.definitions: A simple graph has neither loops nor parallel edges. It is 3-connected if it has at least four vertices and deleting any set of at most two vertices leaves a connected graph. Cubic means every vertex has degree exactly three. Bipartite means its vertices admit a partition into two sets with no edge having both endpoints in the same set. Planar means it has a drawing in the plane whose edge interiors do not intersect and contain no vertices; different edges may meet only at shared endpoints. A Hamiltonian cycle is a cyclic ordering \(v_{1},\ldots ,v_{n}\) of all vertices, each appearing exactly once, such that \(\{v_{i},v_{i+1}\}\) is an edge for every i, with \(v_{n+1}=v_{1}\). The cycle must use only edges already present in the graph. No algorithmic running-time guarantee is requested.

cards.title: Seymour’s second-neighborhood conjecture
cards.formal: Does every finite nonempty oriented graph D contain a vertex v for which |\(N^{++}(v)|\ge |N^{+}(v)|\), where \(N^{+}(v)\) consists of vertices at directed distance one from v and \(N^{++}(v)\) consists of vertices at directed distance exactly two?
cards.definitions: An oriented graph is a finite vertex set V and an arc set \(A\subseteq V\times V\) with no loops and with at most one of \((u,v),(v,u)\) present for each distinct pair. Arc multiplicities are not allowed. \(N^{+}(v)=\{u:(v,u)\in A\}\). \(N^{++}(v)\)={\(w\in V\setminus (N^{+}(v)\cup \{v\})\): there exists u with \((v,u)\in A\) and \((u,w)\in A\)}. Thus a vertex already in the first neighborhood is not counted in the second, even if it is also reachable by a length-two walk. Cardinalities count vertices rather than paths or arcs. A sink has both sets empty and satisfies the inequality. No lower bound on outdegree, connectivity or planarity is imposed.

cards.title: Strongly polynomial near-linear negative-weight shortest paths
cards.formal: Do there exist a uniform randomized comparison-addition algorithm and constants \(C>0\), \(k\ge0\) that compute all exact distances from one specified source in every directed graph with arbitrary real arc lengths and no negative directed cycle, using at most \(C(m+n)(\log(n+2))^{k}\) operations and succeeding with probability at least \(2/3\)?
cards.definitions: The graph is given by its vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge2\), and an explicit list of \(m\) arcs. It has no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair; opposite arcs are allowed. Arc lengths may be positive, zero or negative. A path length is the sum of its arc lengths; the empty path has length zero. Output the minimum source-to-vertex path length for every vertex, or an infinity marker if unreachable. The promise excludes negative cycles anywhere in the graph. Use a uniform comparison-addition RAM. Real cells contain exact real numbers and support copying, addition, subtraction and comparison at unit cost; fixed rational program constants are allowed. Real multiplication, division, floor, bit extraction and conversion of an input-dependent real to an integer are not primitives. Integer control and address words have \(d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits for a fixed constant \(d\), with unit-cost Boolean operations, shifts, comparison and arithmetic on words. Integer operations cannot inspect real encodings. A fixed finite program receives no advice or free tables. Memory accesses, control, preprocessing and output all count. Bounds are uniform over all real edge values. Randomness consists of independent uniform random words, each generated at unit cost. On every input, the whole output must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). The time bound holds for every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. The operation bound is independent of all magnitudes and numerical encoding lengths. On rational inputs, intermediate values must have bit length polynomial in the total binary input length; this is the usual additional encoding condition for strong polynomiality.

context_blocks.text: Negative lengths allow shortest paths to express costs, credits and difference constraints. They make the numerical model essential: a graph-size bound uniform over real weights is stronger than a bound depending on the number of bits in integer weights.

Bernstein, Nanongkai and Wulff-Nilsen obtained near-linear integer-weight shortest paths with a \(\log W\) dependence. Bringmann, Cassis and Fischer improve the logarithmic factors and explicitly ask whether strong polynomiality can remove that dependence.

The February 2026 preprint by Li, Li and Zhang gives \(n^{2+o(1)}\) time for real weights. This is almost linear for dense graphs, but it neither has polylogarithmic overhead nor gives the requested sparse-graph bound.
Mareš supplies the shortest-path background; the endpoint and status distinctions here come from the later research papers.

cards.why: Removing numerical scaling dependence in a nearly input-linear bound would settle a central gap in exact shortest-path computation over arbitrary real data.

cards.title: Strongly polynomial maximum flow below the \(mn\) barrier
cards.formal: Do there exist a constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\) and a uniform randomized strongly polynomial algorithm that computes an exact maximum flow in every directed network with arbitrary nonnegative rational capacities, \(n\ge2\) vertices and \(m\ge n-1\) arcs, in \(O((mn)^{1-\varepsilon})\) worst-case arithmetic-RAM operations with success probability at least \(2/3\)?
cards.definitions: The graph is given by its vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge2\), and an explicit list of \(m\) arcs. It has no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair; opposite arcs are allowed. A feasible flow assigns a value \(f_{e}\) to every arc with \(0\le f_{e}\le u_{e}\) and equal incoming and outgoing total flow at each vertex except the distinct specified source \(s\) and sink \(t\). Its value is outgoing minus incoming flow at \(s\). The required output is a feasible flow attaining the largest possible value, including every arc value. Capacities and output values are finite rationals. Use exact rational cells with unit-cost copying, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero rational and comparison. Integer control and addresses use \(O(\log(n+m+2))\)-bit words with unit-cost arithmetic, Boolean operations and shifts; they cannot inspect rational encodings or apply floor to rationals. Fixed rational constants and a fixed finite program are allowed, with no advice or free tables. Charge all arithmetic, control, memory access, random-word generation and output operations, treating each rational input or output as one cell. The count is independent of capacity magnitudes and binary lengths. For input bit length \(L\), every intermediate numerator and denominator and the total used bit space must be polynomially bounded in \(L\), including on unsuccessful executions. Independent fair random words are allowed. The bound holds on every execution; the entire flow must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). Constants and the polynomial bit-space bound are uniform over all instances.

context_blocks.text: Strongly polynomial flow bounds count arithmetic operations without making large numerical capacities a source of extra iterations. This distinguishes combinatorial network size from the bit complexity of the capacities.

Dadush, Orlin, Sidford and Végh explicitly ask for an \(O((mn)^{1-\varepsilon})\) strongly polynomial algorithm. Their SODA 2026 work improves structured networks while identifying \(O(mn)\) as the general bound.

Almost-linear algorithms for polynomially bounded integral capacities answer a different numerical-complexity question. Here one fixed exponent saving must hold for arbitrary rational capacities and every edge density.

cards.why: A polynomial improvement over the general strongly polynomial maximum-flow barrier would separate a central combinatorial optimization primitive from its longstanding arithmetic complexity bound.

cards.title: Erdős girth conjecture
cards.formal: For every fixed integer $k\ge 2$, do there exist a constant $c_k>0$ and arbitrarily large simple undirected graphs $G$ with $n$ vertices, at least $c_k n^{1+1/k}$ edges, and no cycle of length at most $2k$? Equivalently, can the $O_k(n^{1+1/k})$ extremal upper bound for girth greater than $2k$ be attained up to a constant factor for every $k$? The first unsettled value is $k=4$: girth at least nine and $\Omega(n^{5/4})$ edges.
cards.why: This is a structural problem with a short, rigorous reduction to an algorithmic limit. I include it because many claims that a distance-preserving graph representation is optimal depend on precisely this unproved construction. A proof would establish those lower bounds; a counterexample would force a re-examination of the expected stretch–space tradeoff.
cards.definitions: The girth is the length of a shortest cycle, with infinite girth for a forest. A $t$-spanner is a spanning subgraph $H\subseteq G$ satisfying $d_G(u,v)\le d_H(u,v)\le t\,d_G(u,v)$ for every reachable pair. The parameter $k$ is fixed as $n$ grows, and constants may depend on $k$. The question asks for existence; an efficient explicit construction would be a stronger result.

progress.text: Althöfer, Das, Dobkin, Joseph, and Soares give sparse multiplicative spanners: every weighted $n$-vertex graph admits stretch $2k-1$ with $O_k(n^{1+1/k})$ edges. High-girth graphs give the corresponding obstruction to improving size.

Bodwin and Lopez review the remaining girth conjecture in Section 1.1. Their degree-fault-tolerant spanner lower bound is unconditional, separating a new algorithmic result from the still-open underlying conjecture.

cards.status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The general conjecture remains unresolved; several individual values of k are settled.

context_blocks.text: High degree tries to make short cycles unavoidable. In a graph whose small neighborhoods contain no cycles, a breadth-first search keeps discovering new vertices rather than revisiting old ones. Sustaining large branching for several levels consumes the available vertices rapidly. This is the reason a ban on short cycles forces an upper bound on density; the conjecture asks whether graphs can pack edges as efficiently as that counting argument permits.

The algorithmic connection is direct. Suppose a unit-weight graph has girth greater than $2k$. If a subgraph omits an edge $uv$, every remaining $u$–$v$ path has at least $2k$ edges: a shorter path together with $uv$ would create a forbidden cycle. Thus any $(2k-1)$-spanner must keep every edge. A dense graph of this kind is a certificate that no smaller spanner can preserve the required distances.

For example, a triangle-free graph alone is not enough for the $k=2$ application: a four-cycle allows one edge to be replaced by a three-edge detour. Excluding both triangles and four-cycles makes every edge indispensable for stretch three. This example explains why the exact girth threshold appears in the conjecture.

The conjecture is not an established law of graph sparsification. The 2026 source records that only the parameters 1, 2, 3, and 5 are known and discusses reasons to question the general statement. Its new fault-tolerant lower bound bypasses the conjecture for that model; it does not construct the missing high-girth families.

cards.title: List edge-coloring conjecture
cards.formal: For every finite loopless multigraph G and every assignment L of finite sets of colors to its edges with |\(\mathrm{L}(e)|\ge \chi ' (G)\) for every edge e, does there exist a proper edge coloring c with \(c(e)\in \mathrm{L}(e)\) for every e? Equivalently, is \(\chi ' _{\ell}(G)=\chi ' (G)\) for every such G?
cards.why: The conjecture asks whether local restrictions on available edge colors ever increase the number of choices each edge must receive beyond the optimum with a shared palette. It tests whether ordinary scheduling feasibility is robust to arbitrary per-job availability, across all finite loopless multigraphs.

progress.text: Galvin proves \(\chi ' _{\ell}(G)=\chi ' (G)=\Delta (G)\) for bipartite multigraphs; publisher abstract and Kahn’s discussion checked.

Kahn, Theorem 1.1, proves asymptotic equality of list and fractional chromatic indices for multigraphs; because the ordinary index lies between them, list and ordinary indices also have ratio tending to one.
Molloy’s seminar abstract announces the simple-graph bound \(\Delta +\Delta ^{2/5} \operatorname{poly}(\log  \Delta )\). This still allows an additive gap; only the abstract was checked.
Jafari’s version 1, Theorems 1.1–1.2, claims the conjectured exact values for \(K_{p- 1}\) and \(K_{2p}, p\) an odd prime. These partial claims do not cover all complete graphs or all multigraphs.

cards.definitions: A finite loopless multigraph consists of finite sets V and E and a map \(\partial\) assigning to each edge \(e\in E a\) two-element subset \(\partial e\subseteq V\). Distinct edges may have the same endpoints and are still distinct objects. Two distinct edges are adjacent if their endpoint sets intersect. A proper edge coloring assigns different colors to any two adjacent edges. For an integer \(k\ge 0\) let \([k]=\{1,\ldots ,k\}\), with [0] empty; \(\chi ' (G)\), the chromatic index, is the least k admitting a proper map \(E\to [k]\). A list assignment is a function \(e\mapsto \mathrm{L}(e)\) where each \(\mathrm{L}(e)\) is a finite subset of the positive integers, used only as distinct color names. Lists may differ, overlap arbitrarily and have an arbitrarily large finite union. The list chromatic index \(\chi ' _{\ell}(G)\) is the least \(k\ge 0\) such that every assignment with |\(\mathrm{L}(e)|\ge k\) admits a proper edge coloring from those lists. Both indices are zero when E is empty and are at most |E| otherwise; hence these minima exist. Requiring lists of exactly k colors is equivalent, since larger lists can be restricted to k colors. Any finite collection of abstract colors can be renamed by distinct positive integers without changing feasibility. Isolated vertices, disconnected graphs and arbitrary parallel-edge multiplicities are allowed. The maximum degree \(\Delta\) counts edges incident with a vertex, including parallel copies separately, and is zero for an empty vertex set. The target concerns existence, with no required algorithm, running time or bound on color-name bit lengths.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated universal list-colorability assertion, or refute it. A finite counterexample can specify a multigraph with ordinary chromatic index k and lists of k colors on every edge, together with a proof that no proper coloring from those lists exists. Equality only up to a vanishing relative error, a result for a restricted graph class, or successful coloring of selected list assignments does not resolve the universal claim.

context_blocks.text: Think of an edge as a job requiring its two endpoint resources at the same time, and a color as a time slot. Jobs sharing a resource must use different slots. Ordinary edge coloring offers every job the same collection of slots. List edge coloring lets each job have its own availability restrictions and asks for a compatible schedule.

For two edges sharing one endpoint, ordinary edge coloring needs two colors. Lists {red,blue} and {blue,green} still each have size two, although their union has size three; choosing red for the first edge and blue for the second is valid. The conjecture compares the number of choices available to each edge, not the total number of distinct color names used across all lists.

Identical lists are permitted, so \(\chi ' _{\ell}(G)\) is always at least \(\chi ' (G)\). The question is whether arbitrary overlaps among different lists can ever create an additional obstruction. An ordinary coloring alone does not answer this, since a color assigned to an edge may be absent from that edge’s list.

The reference quantity is the chromatic index, rather than just maximum degree. A triangle has maximum degree two but needs three edge colors. If each of its three edges is doubled, the multigraph has maximum degree four, yet all six edges are pairwise adjacent and need six colors. Allowing parallel edges therefore matters to the target.

Galvin proves the conjecture for every bipartite multigraph, whose vertices split into two parts with all edges crossing between them. In that class both indices equal maximum degree. The theorem permits arbitrary lists and parallel edges; restricting lists to one shared palette would miss its main content.

Kahn’s theorem settles the general multigraph question asymptotically. In particular, for every \(\varepsilon >0\), all multigraphs of sufficiently large maximum degree satisfy \(\chi ' _{\ell}(G)\le (1+\varepsilon )\chi ' (G)\). This leaves the exact question intact: a relative gap tending to zero can still allow an extra color.

The August 2026 preprint of Jafari claims exact equality for the complete graphs \(K_{p- 1}\) and \(K_{2p}\) whenever p is an odd prime; \(K_{r}\) denotes the simple graph with every pair of its r vertices adjacent. The respective claimed values are \(p- 2\) and \(2p- 1\). These are specific families, and the paper itself leaves the general even-order complete-graph case open. Its proofs have not been independently verified in this review.

sentences: A proper edge coloring assigns different colors to edges that share an endpoint.
In list edge coloring, each edge must choose its color from its own finite set of allowed colors.
The conjecture asks whether giving every edge as many choices as the ordinary chromatic index always suffices, even with arbitrary list overlaps and parallel edges.
It holds for bipartite multigraphs, and a general asymptotic theorem leaves only a vanishing relative gap.
Exact equality for every finite loopless multigraph would show that local availability restrictions never impose an additional per-edge palette requirement.

If each of its three edges is doubled, the multigraph has maximum degree four, yet all six edges are pairwise adjacent and need six colors. Allowing parallel edges therefore matters to the target.

Galvin proves the conjecture for every bipartite multigraph, whose vertices split into two parts with all edges crossing between them. In that class both indices equal maximum degree. The theorem permits arbitrary lists and parallel edges; restricting lists to one shared palette would miss its main content.

Kahn’s theorem settles the general multigraph question asymptotically. In particular, for every \(\varepsilon >0\), all multigraphs of sufficiently large maximum degree satisfy \(\chi ' _{\ell}(G)\le (1+\varepsilon )\chi ' (G)\). This leaves the exact question intact: a relative gap tending to zero can still allow an extra color.

The August 2026 preprint of Jafari claims exact equality for the complete graphs \(K_{p- 1}\) and \(K_{2p}\) whenever p is an odd prime; \(K_{r}\) denotes the simple graph with every pair of its r vertices adjacent. The respective claimed values are \(p- 2\) and \(2p- 1\). These are specific families, and the paper itself leaves the general even-order complete-graph case open. Its proofs have not been independently verified in this review.

cards.title: Triangle covering-to-packing ratio
cards.formal: Determine \(\Gamma _{\triangle}=\sup\){\(\tau _{\triangle}(G)/\nu _{\triangle}(G): G\) is a finite simple undirected graph with at least one triangle}, where \(\tau _{\triangle}\) and \(\nu _{\triangle}\) are defined below.
cards.definitions: A simple graph has no loops or parallel edges. A triangle is a set of three distinct vertices together with all three edges between them. An edge set F meets every triangle if each triangle contains at least one edge of F; equivalently, deleting F makes G triangle-free. Define \(\tau _{\triangle}\) as the minimum cardinality of such \(F\subseteq E(G)\). A packing is a family of triangles whose three-edge sets are pairwise disjoint; triangles in a packing may share vertices. Define \(\nu _{\triangle}\) as the maximum cardinality of a packing. Both values are zero when G has no triangles, including the empty graph. The inequality concerns integral edge sets and integral packings, with no fractional weights and no running-time requirement. Restricting the ratio to graphs containing a triangle avoids a zero denominator; triangle-free graphs already satisfy every nonnegative-factor comparison. The supremum is finite: deleting every edge of a maximal triangle packing gives \(\tau _{\triangle}\le 3\nu _{\triangle}\). Attainment of the supremum is not required.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |\(a- \Gamma _{\triangle}|\le 1/100\). The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds \(\ell\)\(\le u\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell +u)/2\). An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The \(1/100\) tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture.

cards.title: Deterministic Exact Matching
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm, polynomial in the input bit length, that decides the following problem? Given a simple undirected graph G on an even number n of vertices, each edge colored red or blue, and an integer $0\le k\le n/2$, determine whether G has a perfect matching containing exactly k red edges. The algorithm must be correct on every input. No bipartition is promised, and no randomness or computational hardness assumption is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that this decision problem belongs to P, or prove that it does not. A randomized polynomial-time algorithm, an approximation to the red count, or an algorithm restricted to bipartite graphs does not establish the positive answer.
cards.why: I include this because it is a concrete combinatorial derandomization target with a short, checkable definition. It asks whether randomness is necessary for an exact constraint on top of an otherwise tractable optimization problem, connecting matching algorithms to algebraic identity testing.
cards.definitions: P denotes languages decidable by a uniform deterministic Turing machine in time polynomial in the ordinary adjacency-list encoding and the binary encoding of k. A perfect matching is a set of disjoint edges covering every vertex. If a polynomial-time decision algorithm exists, a matching can also be recovered by polynomially many decisions on residual instances. This target concerns sequential polynomial time, not deterministic NC.

progress.text: Mulmuley, U. Vazirani, and V. Vazirani provide the randomized algebraic matching framework underlying polynomial-time Exact Matching algorithms.
El Maalouly surveys algorithms and related problems while retaining general deterministic polynomial-time Exact Matching as open.
Du claims a deterministic bipartite algorithm. Version 3 states eight explicit hypotheses in its Lean formalization. That paper does not claim a general-graph solution.

Sato and Yamaguchi’s revised preprint tests all possible red counts simultaneously with high probability using \(O(n^{\omega})\) finite-field operations, where \(\omega\) denotes the matrix-multiplication exponent used by their algebraic routines. The algorithm remains randomized; the introduction explicitly retains deterministic polynomial-time Exact Matching as open.

context_blocks.text: Perfect matching already has efficient deterministic algorithms on general graphs. Requiring a prescribed number of red edges adds an exact constraint that the ordinary matching objective does not express. A minimum-red matching and a maximum-red matching only identify two ends of the attainable range; intermediate counts can be missing.

For example, color a six-cycle alternately red and blue. Its two perfect matchings have respectively three and zero red edges. Neither one nor two is attainable. This obstruction appears even in a bipartite graph; allowing odd cycles adds further structure that a general algorithm must handle.

A yes answer is easy to verify once a matching is supplied: check that every vertex is covered once and count the red edges. The difficulty is finding a deterministic procedure that also certifies no instances in polynomial time. The existing algebraic route uses random choices to prevent the cancellation that can hide a feasible matching.

The graph class is essential. A 2026 preprint claims a deterministic solution for bipartite Exact Matching, and the separate catalogue entry records that claim and its formalization limits. This card concerns all graphs. Even a validated bipartite theorem would need another argument before it could settle the proposition here.

cards.title: Neumann–Lara conjecture
cards.formal: For every finite oriented graph D whose underlying undirected graph is planar, is there a coloring \(c:V(D)\to \{0,1\}\) such that neither color class induces a directed cycle?
cards.definitions: An oriented graph has no loops or parallel arcs and contains at most one of \((u,v)\) and \((v,u)\) for each unordered pair of distinct vertices. Its underlying simple undirected graph joins u,v exactly when one of these arcs is present. Planarity means that graph admits a drawing in the plane with edges intersecting only at common endpoints. For a vertex set X, the induced subdigraph \(D[X]\) retains every arc of D whose two endpoints lie in X. A directed cycle is a cyclic sequence of distinct vertices with all successive arcs oriented forward. A digraph is acyclic if it has no directed cycle. Color classes may be empty. This is not proper coloring: an arc may have endpoints of the same color provided no monochromatic directed cycle results. The assertion asks only for existence, without an algorithmic running-time bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.

cards.definitions: A graph G on \(n\ge 0\) vertices is given by n and the symmetric zero-diagonal binary adjacency matrix on \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). Two such graphs G,H are isomorphic, written \(G\cong H\), if a bijection between their vertex sets preserves both adjacency and nonadjacency. The oracle takes two graphs in this encoding and returns YES exactly when they are isomorphic. Each oracle answer costs one step; writing the query and all other computation count toward the polynomial bound, so query lengths and number of calls are polynomial in N. Adaptive queries are allowed. The output \(F(G)\) is an adjacency matrix of a graph on \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\), with \(F(G)\cong G\). For every pair of input graphs, \(G\cong H\) must imply \(F(G)=F(H)\) as labeled matrices; the reverse implication then follows automatically. Thus one algorithm chooses a single representative for every isomorphism class. No particular representative, lexicographic minimum or vertex permutation is prescribed. The same deterministic machine and polynomial bound apply to all graphs; it has no other oracle or nonuniform advice. The empty graph has the empty matrix as its canonical form.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer gives such an oracle algorithm and proves its worst-case polynomial running time, isomorphism preservation and identical outputs on every isomorphic pair. A negative answer rules out every deterministic polynomial-time algorithm with this decision oracle that computes any canonical-form function satisfying these conditions. A reduction that only finds an isomorphism between two supplied graphs does not suffice.

context_blocks.title: Recognizing a shape versus naming it consistently
context_blocks.text: Isomorphism asks whether two presentations describe the same graph after renaming vertices. Canonization takes just one presentation and returns a fixed presentation of that graph’s shape. For example, every relabeling of a three-vertex path must produce exactly the same three-by-three output matrix. It is insufficient to return a different isomorphic matrix depending on the input names. This consistency makes canonical forms useful for indexing and comparing stored structures.

context_blocks.title: The decision oracle gives only a bit
context_blocks.text: The oracle can compare any two explicitly constructed graphs, but returns only YES or NO. The question grants this ability at unit cost and asks whether polynomially much additional work can select consistent representatives. Finding a vertex matching for one given isomorphic pair has a different output requirement: its choices need not agree across every possible presentation of the same graph.

context_blocks.title: Known algorithms do not settle the reduction
context_blocks.text: Babai’s 2019 result gives general graph canonization in quasipolynomial time, meaning \(\exp (O((\log  n)^{d}))\) for a fixed constant d. It adapts the structure of an isomorphism algorithm and includes additional work to make choices canonical. Having quasipolynomial algorithms for both tasks does not establish a polynomial-time reduction that uses only decision answers.

context_blocks.title: Recent special cases
context_blocks.text: The ICALP 2026 paper obtains efficient canonical labelling for random regular graphs with high probability and recalls general quasipolynomial bounds. A guarantee for almost all graphs in a random model leaves exceptional and arbitrary input graphs uncovered. The present target is a deterministic worst-case reduction for every finite graph, and remains separate from the unrestricted question whether graph isomorphism itself lies in polynomial time.

cards.title: Steiner Shortcut Conjecture
cards.formal: Are there absolute constants \(C>0\) and integers \(a,b\ge0\) such that every finite directed graph \(G=(V,E)\), with \(n=|V|\ge2\), \(m=|E|\ge1\) and no isolated vertices, has an augmentation \(G_{+}=(V\cup V_{+},E\cup E_{+})\) with \(|E_{+}|\le Cm(\log(n+2))^{a}\), preserving reachability between every ordered pair of original vertices exactly, in which every reachable original pair is joined by a directed path of at most \(C(\log(n+2))^{b}\) arcs?
cards.definitions: Graphs are unweighted, finite and simple as directed graphs; opposite arcs are allowed. An isolated vertex is incident to no arc. The finite set \(V_{+}\) is disjoint from \(V\), and added arcs may have endpoints in either set. Reachability allows the empty path. Preservation means that for every \(u,v\in V\), a path from \(u\) to \(v\) exists in \(G_{+}\) if and only if it exists in \(G\). The path-length bound counts arcs and applies only to pairs in \(V\times V\). No thickness bound is imposed on consecutive Steiner vertices. Constants precede the quantifier over graphs. This is an existence statement with no construction-time requirement; unused isolated Steiner vertices may be omitted.

context_blocks.text: A long directed path represents a long chain of dependencies. Shortcuts ask how compactly the same reachability relation can be represented with short paths.

The original conjecture allowed extra arcs only between old vertices and was refuted. Conjecture 2 of the cited paper permits additional Steiner vertices; the known old-vertex lower bounds do not settle this statement.

The representation may preserve a large reachability relation without listing every reachable pair. Existence would settle a structural compression question, while efficient parallel construction is a separate algorithmic demand.

cards.title: Deterministic almost-linear vertex connectivity
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm computing the exact vertex connectivity and a minimum vertex separator of every simple unweighted undirected graph in \((m+n)^{1+o(1)}\) worst-case time on a word RAM?
cards.definitions: The input is a finite simple undirected graph with labelled vertex set \([n]\), \(n\ge2\), and an explicit list of \(m\) edges; isolated vertices are included. For \(S\subseteq V\), delete its vertices and incident edges. The vertex connectivity \(\kappa(G)\) is the minimum \(|S|\) for which the remaining graph is disconnected or has at most one vertex. For a disconnected input it is zero, and \(\kappa(K_{n})=n-1\). Output both \(\kappa(G)\) and an attaining set \(S\). Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Write \(N=m+n\). Almost-linear time means that there exist one algorithm, a constant \(C\) and a function \(h:\mathbb{N}\to[1,\infty)\), independent of the input graph, with \(\lim_{N\to\infty}\log h(N)/\log N=0\), such that the time is at most \(CNh(N)\) for every input. All hidden constants are independent of the graph. No randomness is allowed, and the bound must hold for all connectivity values, including those growing with the graph size.

Both lines build on the earlier vertex-connectivity algorithms of Henzinger, Rao and Gabow. The remaining demand is a uniform deterministic bound over all graphs.

cards.title: Constant-factor treewidth preservation by subcubic subgraphs
cards.formal: Does there exist a real constant \(C\ge 1\) such that every finite nonempty simple undirected graph G contains a nonempty subgraph H with maximum degree at most 3 and \(\operatorname{tw}(H)\ge \operatorname{tw}(G)/C\)?
cards.definitions: A subgraph \(H=(V_{H},E_{H})\) satisfies \(V_{H}\subseteq V(G)\) and \(E_{H}\subseteq E(G)\cap \{\{u,v\}:u,v\in V_{H},u\ne v\}\). Edges and vertices may be deleted, but no edge is contracted and no new vertex or edge is introduced. H need not be induced, connected or spanning. Its maximum degree is \(\max _{v\in V_{H}}|\{u:\{u,v\}\in E_{H}\}|\). A tree decomposition of a nonempty graph F consists of a finite tree T with vertex bags \(B_{t}\subseteq V(F)\), such that every vertex lies in a bag, both endpoints of each edge lie in a common bag, and the nodes whose bags contain a fixed vertex induce a nonempty connected subtree. Its width is \(\max _{t}|B_{t}|- 1\). Treewidth \(\operatorname{tw}(F)\) is the minimum width over all such decompositions; nonempty edgeless graphs have treewidth zero. C is independent of G and its treewidth. No bound on the number of vertices of H and no construction-time requirement is imposed.

cards.title: Linear-time directed shortest paths with nonnegative real weights
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic comparison-addition algorithm computing all exact distances from a specified source in every directed graph with arbitrary nonnegative real arc lengths in \(O(m+n)\) worst-case time?
cards.definitions: The graph is given by its vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge2\), and an explicit list of \(m\) arcs. It has no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair; opposite arcs are allowed. Each arc length belongs to \(\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\). The length of a path is the sum of its arc lengths; the empty path has length zero. Output the minimum source-to-vertex path length for every vertex, with an infinity marker for unreachable vertices. Zero-length arcs and cycles are permitted. Use a uniform comparison-addition RAM. Real cells contain exact real numbers and support copying, addition, subtraction and comparison at unit cost; fixed rational program constants are allowed. Real multiplication, division, floor, bit extraction and conversion of an input-dependent real to an integer are not primitives. Integer control and address words have \(d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits for a fixed constant \(d\), with unit-cost Boolean operations, shifts, comparison and arithmetic on words. Integer operations cannot inspect real encodings. A fixed finite program receives no advice or free tables. Memory accesses, control, preprocessing and output all count. Bounds are uniform over all real edge values. The algorithm must halt correctly on every input without randomness, with a universal time constant.

context_blocks.text: Reading a graph and writing its source distances already requires linear time. The question asks whether arbitrary nonnegative real lengths and direction can be handled within that exact input-and-output budget.
Duan and coauthors broke the sorting barrier in 2025. The 2026 improvement gives \(O(m\sqrt{\log n}+\sqrt{mn\log n\log\log n})\) time, still with superlinear overhead.
Exact reals can be added and compared, while their bit representations cannot be inspected. This makes the model substantive: integer bit operations do not supply a real-weight algorithm.

cards.title: Single-exponential exact cut mimicking networks
cards.formal: Does there exist an absolute constant \(C>0\) such that every finite undirected graph \(G\) with nonnegative real edge weights and a specified terminal set \(T\) of size \(k\ge2\) has an undirected nonnegatively real-weighted graph \(H\) containing the same labelled terminals, with \(|V(H)|\le2^{Ck}\), that preserves every minimum terminal bipartition cut value exactly?
cards.definitions: Graphs are finite and simple, with finite edge weights. For every nonempty proper subset \(A\subset T\), define \(\lambda_{G}(A)=\min\{\sum_{e\in\delta_{G}(S)}w_{e}:S\subseteq V(G),\ S\cap T=A\}\), where \(\delta_{G}(S)\) is the set of edges with exactly one endpoint in \(S\). Define \(\lambda_{H}\) in the same way, using the weights of \(H\). Preservation means \(\lambda_{H}(A)=\lambda_{G}(A)\) simultaneously for every such \(A\). New nonterminal vertices and arbitrary nonnegative real weights are allowed; \(H\) need not be a subgraph, minor or contraction of \(G\). Its vertex bound includes the terminals. The constant is independent of \(G\), its weights and \(k\). No algorithm or construction-time bound is requested.

context_blocks.text: A terminal cut function records how expensive it is to separate any chosen group of terminals from all the others. An exact mimicking network stores this whole function as a smaller graph.
For general graphs, the reviewed size gap is \(2^{\Omega(k)}\) versus \(2^{2^{O(k)}}\). Chen and Tan review this gap and improve bounds for special graph classes.
Requiring a contraction would change the answer: doubly exponential lower bounds are known in that restricted representation. The question permits an arbitrary replacement graph.

A Gomory–Hu tree preserves pairwise minimum cuts. A terminal bipartition constrains many vertices to each side simultaneously, so pairwise cut preservation does not establish this stronger representation property.

cards.why: Resolving the exponential-versus-doubly-exponential gap would determine how compactly an arbitrary network can represent all exact terminal separation costs.

cards.definitions: A finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) has a finite vertex set V and an edge set E consisting of unordered pairs of distinct vertices; loops and parallel edges are excluded. Isolated vertices and disconnected graphs are allowed. For \(e\in E\), let \(G- e=(V,E\setminus \{e\})\): deleting an edge retains every vertex, including vertices that become isolated. Two graphs are isomorphic, written \(G\cong H\), if a bijection of their vertex sets preserves adjacency in both directions. Write \([G- e]\) for the isomorphism class with vertex labels forgotten. The edge deck is the multiset \(D_{E}(G)=\{[G- e]:e\in E\}\); each edge contributes one entry, so repeated isomorphism classes retain their multiplicities. Deck equality requires each isomorphism class to occur equally often. Entries have no common vertex labeling and do not identify the deleted edge. The question concerns uniqueness from a deck known to arise from a graph, with no efficiency requirement on reconstruction.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the implication for all finite simple graphs with at least four edges, or give two nonisomorphic such graphs and prove that their complete edge decks agree with multiplicities. A result for a bounded number of vertices, a promised graph class or decks pooled from multiple graphs does not settle the universal claim.

context_blocks.title: What information survives
context_blocks.text: Think of making one copy of a network for each connection and deleting a different connection from each copy. The copies are shuffled and their vertex names erased. The conjecture says their shapes and repetition counts still identify the original network. For a four-cycle, the deck consists of four copies of the path on four vertices.

context_blocks.title: Why at least four edges
context_blocks.text: The threshold excludes a real ambiguity. A triangle together with one isolated vertex and the three-leaf star are nonisomorphic four-vertex graphs with three edges. Deleting any edge from either leaves a three-vertex path together with an isolated vertex. Their edge decks therefore agree, each containing three copies of the same graph.

cards.title: Lovász conjecture
cards.formal: Does every finite nonempty connected vertex-transitive simple undirected graph have a Hamiltonian path?
cards.definitions: A graph is vertex-transitive if for every u,v there is a bijection of its vertex set preserving adjacency and sending u to v. cards.title: Almost-linear exact directed global minimum cut
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), is there a uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every directed graph with positive integer arc weights at most \(n^{a}\), outputs a nonempty proper set \(S\subset V\) minimizing \(\sum_{e\in E(S,V\setminus S)}u_{e}\), and its exact value, in \((m+n)^{1+o(1)}\) worst-case time?
cards.definitions: The graph is given by its vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge2\), and an explicit list of \(m\) arcs. It has no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair; opposite arcs are allowed. Here \(E(S,V\setminus S)\) consists of arcs directed from \(S\) to its complement, and the objective counts each such arc once. There are no prescribed terminals. Zero optimum is allowed, including when the graph is not strongly connected. Weights are explicitly given integers in \(\{1,\ldots,n^{a}\}\). Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Randomness consists of independent uniform random words, each generated at unit cost. On every input, the whole output must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). The time bound holds for every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. Write \(N=m+n\). Almost-linear time means that there exist one algorithm, a constant \(C\) and a function \(h:\mathbb{N}\to[1,\infty)\), independent of the input graph, with \(\lim_{N\to\infty}\log h(N)/\log N=0\), such that the time is at most \(CNh(N)\) for every input. All hidden constants are independent of the graph. The program, word-size constant, overhead function and time constant may depend on \(a\), but not on the graph or its weights.

cards.title: Almost-linear directed vertex connectivity
cards.formal: Is there a uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm computing the exact vertex connectivity and an attaining vertex separator of every simple unweighted directed graph in \((m+n)^{1+o(1)}\) worst-case time?
cards.definitions: The graph is given by its vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge2\), and an explicit list of \(m\) arcs. It has no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair; opposite arcs are allowed. For \(S\subseteq V\), remove \(S\) and all incident arcs. Define \(\kappa(G)\) as the smallest \(|S|\) for which the remainder is not strongly connected or contains at most one vertex. Strong connectivity means reachability for every ordered pair of remaining vertices. Thus an input that is not strongly connected has value zero, and a complete bidirected graph has value \(n-1\). Output the value and an attaining \(S\). Whenever at least two vertices remain, failure of strong connectivity is equivalent to a partition \((L,S,R)\) with nonempty \(L,R\) and no arc from \(L\) to \(R\). Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Randomness consists of independent uniform random words, each generated at unit cost. On every input, the whole output must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). The time bound holds for every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. Write \(N=m+n\). Almost-linear time means that there exist one algorithm, a constant \(C\) and a function \(h:\mathbb{N}\to[1,\infty)\), independent of the input graph, with \(\lim_{N\to\infty}\log h(N)/\log N=0\), such that the time is at most \(CNh(N)\) for every input. cards.title: Boolean dimension of posets with planar cover graphs
cards.formal: Does there exist an integer \(d\ge 1\) such that every finite poset \(\mathrm{P}=(V,<)\) with a planar undirected cover graph admits strict total orders \(\mathrm{L}_{1},\ldots ,\mathrm{L}_{d}\) on V and a Boolean function \(\varphi :\{0,1\}^{d}\to \{0,1\}\) satisfying, for all distinct \(x,y\in V, x<y\) if and only if \(\varphi (1[x<_{\mathrm{L}_{1}}y],\ldots ,1[x<_{\mathrm{L}_{d}}y])=1\)?
cards.definitions: A finite poset is specified by an irreflexive transitive relation < on a finite set V. The undirected cover graph has vertex set V and an edge \(\{x,y\}\) when \(x<y\) with no z satisfying \(x<z<y\), or the reverse relation. Planarity means that this undirected graph has a drawing in the plane whose edge interiors do not intersect; an upward planar drawing of the order is not required. A strict total order compares every distinct pair in exactly one direction and is transitive. The orders \(\mathrm{L}_{i}\) need not extend the partial order. Each indicator \(1[x<_{\mathrm{L}_{i}}y]\) is a bit. Both the d orders and \(\varphi\) may depend on P, but the bound d is universal and independent of |V| and the height of P. The least possible number of orders is Boolean dimension. The claim is purely existential, with no algorithmic requirement.

cards.title: Strongly explicit Ramanujan families for every degree
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(d\ge 3\), is there one deterministic algorithm that computes the port rotation map of connected d-regular Ramanujan graphs for an unbounded set of vertex counts n in time polynomial in log n, with the effective family and graph conventions below?
cards.definitions: The graphs are undirected multigraphs on \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\); parallel edges and loops are permitted, as in the source’s graph convention. Each vertex has ports \([d]\). A rotation map \(Rot_{n}:[n]\times [d]\to [n]\times [d]\) is an involution: if \(Rot_{n}(v,i)=(w,j)\), then \(Rot_{n}(w,j)=(v,i)\). Paired ports encode an undirected edge; a fixed port encodes a loop. Define the symmetric integer adjacency matrix A by \(A_{vw}=|\{i\in[d]:\operatorname{first}(\operatorname{Rot}_n(v,i))=w\}|\), so every row sum is d and a fixed-port loop contributes one to the diagonal and degree. Connectivity means the underlying undirected graph is connected. List the real eigenvalues with multiplicity in decreasing order \(d=\lambda _{1}\ge \cdots \ge \lambda _{n}\). Require \(|\lambda_i|\le2\sqrt{d-1}\) for \(i\ge 2\), except that the single eigenvalue −d is permitted when the graph is bipartite. For each fixed d the answer supplies a decidable infinite set \(N_{d}\) of positive integers, a single total deterministic bit algorithm \(R_{d}\), and constants \(C_{d},a_{d}\). On input \((n,v,i)\) in binary, \(R_{d}\) runs in at most \(C_d(1+\log_2 n)^{a_d}\) steps for valid \(v\in [n],i\in [d]\). For every \(n\in N_{d}\) its outputs constitute the rotation map of such a graph. No graph-dependent advice, preprocessing or tables are supplied to \(R_{d}\); its fixed program may depend on d. The family’s size-membership decider must halt on all binary n but has no prescribed running-time bound. No bound on gaps between successive \(n\in N_{d}\) is required. Outputs at n outside \(N_{d}\) carry no graph promise. This retains the imported infinite-family target, which is weaker than requiring every admissible size; it does not impose simple-graph or non-bipartite restrictions.

cards.title: Bipartite Exact Matching: deterministic polynomial time
cards.formal: Given a bipartite graph $G=(L\cup R,E)$ with $|L|=|R|=n$, a red/blue coloring of its edges, and $k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$, decide whether $G$ has a perfect matching containing exactly $k$ red edges. The historical question asks for a deterministic algorithm polynomial in the ordinary bit encoding of $(G,k)$. An April 2026 preprint claims such an algorithm. This entry records that claimed resolution and its verification limits; it is no longer labeled as a confirmed open problem.
cards.why: I retain and expand this entry because exact cardinality constraints can remain difficult even when unconstrained optimization is easy. It is also a useful status correction: a research catalogue should preserve the problem and the claimed advance, while distinguishing an attributed preprint theorem from a proof that has been independently checked.
cards.definitions: A perfect matching consists of pairwise vertex-disjoint edges covering every vertex. Exactly k is an equality constraint, not an upper bound or an approximation target. This card concerns sequential deterministic polynomial time. Ordinary bipartite perfect matching in NC and Exact Matching on general graphs are separate questions.

context_blocks.text: An ordinary perfect matching assigns every left vertex to a different right vertex. Here an additional equality constraint counts how many selected edges are red. Minimizing or maximizing the red-edge count does not decide whether a particular intermediate count is attainable.

Consider two left vertices and two right vertices, with every possible edge present. Color the two diagonal edges red and the two off-diagonal edges blue. The only perfect matchings have either two red edges or none. There is no perfect matching with exactly one red edge, although one lies between the minimum and maximum attainable counts. Even this small example defeats an interval-based feasibility test.

The randomized algebraic approach encodes matchings in a polynomial and tests whether a relevant coefficient vanishes. Finding a deterministic replacement has made the problem a particularly concrete meeting point of graph algorithms and polynomial identity testing. Approximation results relax the equality constraint and therefore answer a different question.

cards.title: 3-colorability of diameter-two graphs
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, for every finite simple connected undirected graph \(G\) of diameter at most \(2\), decides whether \(G\) has a proper vertex coloring with three colors? The input does not promise that such a coloring exists. Precisely, there must be one Turing machine and constants \(C>0,b\in\mathbb N\), independent of the graph, whose worst-case running time on every valid \(n\)-vertex graph is at most \(C(n+1)^b\), and whose output is correct on every such graph.
cards.definitions: For \(n\ge1\), the vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The input is the ordinary binary encoding of \(n\), a delimiter, and an \(n\times n\) matrix of bits in row order. Valid graph matrices are symmetric with zero diagonal; a one in position \((u,v)\) means that \(\{u,v\}\) is an edge. Edges are unweighted, and distance is the number of edges in a shortest path. The graph is connected if every pair has a path, and its diameter is the maximum distance over all vertex pairs; a singleton has diameter zero. A proper three-coloring is a map \(c:[n]\to\{1,2,3\}\) satisfying \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) whenever \(\{u,v\}\) is an edge; use of fewer than three colors is permitted. The decision output is one exactly when the input is a connected graph of diameter at most two admitting such a map, and zero otherwise. Malformed encodings, nonsimple graph matrices, disconnected graphs and graphs of larger diameter are rejected. Thus the problem is a total language; checking the structural promise does not change its polynomial-time classification. The machine has one finite deterministic program, ordinary finite-alphabet tapes, no oracle or advice, and no random choices. Costs include reading the explicit adjacency matrix and writing the answer, and are worst-case over all encodings with the given vertex count. There are no vertex lists, precolored vertices, restrictions on degrees, triangle exclusions or four-cycle exclusions. The number of colors and the diameter bound are fixed, while the number of vertices is unbounded. The source’s diameter-exactly-two version has the same polynomial-time question, because connected graphs of diameter zero or one are complete and constitute a polynomial-time decidable additional class.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that this total language belongs to deterministic polynomial time, or prove that it does not. A positive answer must specify a uniform algorithm and prove its worst-case polynomial bound and exact correctness on all permitted graphs, including those with no proper three-coloring. A negative answer must rule out every deterministic polynomial-time algorithm. An NP-completeness theorem is a meaningful conventional hardness classification, but by itself gives a negative answer only under the additional assumption \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\); it is not an unconditional proof of nonmembership in \(\mathrm P\). A subexponential upper bound or an algorithm on a narrower forbidden-subgraph class does not settle the stated target.
cards.why: Three-colorability is a basic constraint-satisfaction problem, and diameter is one of the simplest measures of graph connectivity. This single unresolved boundary tests whether very short distances enforce exploitable structure without any sparsity assumption. Either an algorithm or a hardness reduction would explain a fundamental limit of structural restrictions in graph algorithms.

importance.reason: A longstanding concrete tractability boundary for a canonical NP-complete problem: two colors and diameter one are easy, while three colors at diameter three are hard. It supports the broader study of algorithms on structurally restricted graphs.

progress.text: Mertzios and Spirakis give a \(2^{O(\sqrt{n\log n})}\)-time diameter-two algorithm and NP-completeness at diameter three. The 2021 paper recalls these results in its introductory classification.

context_blocks.text: Paulusma’s 2019 open-problem discussion identifies three colors and diameter two as the outstanding tractability boundary. The same section contains further questions with extra graph restrictions or a variable number of colors. Those are distinct targets; this card keeps the existing unrestricted three-color decision problem.

The boundary is striking because diameter-one connected graphs are complete, whereas three-colorability is NP-complete already for diameter-three graphs, including triangle-free inputs. Requiring every pair of vertices to be at distance at most two leaves considerable global structure available, and its effect on the fixed three-color decision problem remains unresolved in the checked sources.

Dębski, Piecyk and Rzążewski’s Theorem 3 gives a \(2^{O(n^{1/3}\log^2 n)}\)-time algorithm for list three-coloring of diameter-two graphs, and hence for ordinary three-colorability. The statement is subexponential, not polynomial. No methods from its proof are part of the problem’s answer requirements.

Murakami’s July 2026 preprint proves polynomial-time list three-coloring when the graph has diameter two and contains no four-cycle as a subgraph. Its introduction and conclusion explicitly leave the unrestricted diameter-two case open. Forbidding a four-cycle as a subgraph is stronger than excluding only induced four-cycles, and neither restriction is present in this target.

cards.title: Polylogarithmic treewidth with forbidden induced minors
cards.formal: For every integer \(t\ge 2\), does there exist an integer \(c_{t}\ge 1\) such that every n-vertex graph G with \(n\ge 2\), no clique of size t and neither Kt,t nor Wt as an induced minor satisfies \(\operatorname{tw}(G)\le c_{t}(\log _{2} n)^{c_{t}}\)?

cards.definitions: All graphs are finite, undirected and simple. Write \(n=|V(G)|\) and take logarithms in base two. An induced subgraph \(G[S]\) retains precisely all edges of G whose endpoints are in S. Kt is the complete graph on t vertices; Kt,t is the complete bipartite graph with two independent sets of t vertices and every edge between the sets. A tree decomposition consists of a finite tree T and bags \(Bx\subseteq V(G)\), one per node x of T, such that every vertex occurs in a bag, both endpoints of every edge occur together in some bag, and the bags containing any fixed vertex form a connected subtree of T. Its width is maxx |\(Bx|- 1\). Treewidth \(\operatorname{tw}(G)\) is the minimum width of such a decomposition. For a concrete wall convention, construct Wt from vertices \((i,j), 0\le i\le t\) and \(0\le j\le 2t+1\): include all horizontal edges \((i,j)(i,j+1)\), and vertical edges \((i,j)(i+1,j)\) exactly when \(i+j\) is even, then repeatedly delete vertices of degree at most one until none remain. This is a fixed elementary hexagonal-wall family. Standard wall-size conventions differ by a fixed reindexing; since the source statement quantifies over every fixed t and allows its constants to depend arbitrarily on t, this indexing does not change the family-level claim. An induced minor is obtained by deleting vertices and contracting edges, with loops discarded and parallel edges merged, but without arbitrary edge deletions. Equivalently, its vertices can be represented by pairwise disjoint nonempty connected branch sets in G, with an edge between two branch sets exactly when their corresponding vertices are adjacent in the induced minor. The clique exclusion is an ordinary clique/induced-subgraph condition; the exclusions of Kt,t and Wt are induced-minor conditions. There is no bound on maximum degree. The constant \(c_{t}\) and the exponent \(c_{t}\) may depend on t, but not on n or G. Allowing separate constants for the multiplier and exponent is equivalent by increasing \(c_{t}\), since \(\log _{2} n\ge 1\). The statement is structural existence of tree decompositions and requests no algorithm for finding them. Restricting to \(t,n\ge 2\) removes only trivial small or undefined-log cases.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed bound for every t with constants depending only on t, or refute it by finding one fixed t for which, for every integer \(c\ge 1\), there is an admitted graph G with \(\operatorname{tw}(G)>c(\log _{2} |V(G)|)^{c}\). A subpolynomial upper bound or a bound on independence number inside bags does not establish the requested polylogarithmic bound on bag size.

context_blocks.title: Treewidth measures the size of the pieces
context_blocks.text: A tree decomposition organizes overlapping vertex sets along a tree. Vertices may appear in several bags, but their occurrences must remain connected. A path has treewidth one, whereas a complete graph on n vertices has treewidth \(n- 1\). Small bags allow many graph problems to be processed through their interactions along the decomposition.

context_blocks.title: Which large structures are excluded
context_blocks.text: The question removes large cliques and two specific induced-minor patterns: a complete bipartite graph and a hexagonal wall. Induced minors permit edge contractions but preserve the presence of edges between surviving branch sets. This makes their exclusion different from forbidding an ordinary graph minor, where arbitrary edges may also be deleted.

context_blocks.title: A polylogarithmic target
context_blocks.text: For each fixed t, the requested bound is a constant times a fixed power of log n. The power can grow with t. The statement does not ask for a constant treewidth bound and does not impose the maximum-degree restriction of the separate logarithmic-degree question.

context_blocks.title: Subpolynomial progress leaves a gap
context_blocks.text: The March 2026 version of Chudnovsky and coauthors’ preprint states \(\operatorname{tw}(G)\le 2^{a_{t}(\log _{2} n)^{1- \varepsilon _{t}}}\) for constants \(a_{t}\) and \(\varepsilon _{t}>0\) under these same exclusions. It states the polylogarithmic bound separately as Conjecture 1.1. The reported upper bound is subpolynomial in n, but does not establish that conjecture.

context_blocks.title: Other bag measures have different meanings
context_blocks.text: The May 2026 coarse-decomposition preprint bounds how many vertices in a bag can be far apart in the original graph. A bag can contain many nearby vertices while that number remains small. Such bounds are not bounds on the number of vertices in the bag, which is what treewidth counts.
