cards.definitions: For fixed \(n,b\), a permitted decoder is a function \(D:\{0,1\}^b\times\{0,1\}^b\to\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\). The same \(D\) must work for every connected unweighted simple undirected planar graph \(G\) with vertex set \([n]\): there must be a label assignment \(\lambda_G:[n]\to\{0,1\}^b\) such that \(D(\lambda_G(u),\lambda_G(v))=\operatorname{dist}_G(u,v)\) for all vertices, where distance counts edges on a shortest path. The decoder may depend on \(n\) and \(b\), but not on \(G\), and receives no shared graph data, vertex identifiers or additional input. Both the decoder domain and graph class are finite for fixed \(n,b\); no efficiency bound is imposed on constructing labels or decoding. The target measures label information alone, with arbitrary values on label pairs never used by an assignment. Known efficient schemes provide upper bounds in this unrestricted model as well. Here \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\); simple means no loops or parallel edges, and planar means admitting a drawing by nonintersecting arcs except at shared endpoints. Labels have the common fixed length \(b\); the target is the largest per-vertex bit length, not the sum over vertices. A finite admissible \(b\) always exists: each label can contain the whole finite graph description together with its vertex index, and a common decoder can recover graph distances from that description. Thus the least integer in the definition is well-defined.

context_blocks.text: A label is the information a vertex carries when the graph itself is unavailable. To answer a distance query, the decoder sees exactly the two endpoint labels. Its rule is common to the whole graph family, so it cannot have a different hidden graph stored for every labeling assignment.

Even the diagonal query constrains labels: a vertex is at distance zero from itself, while two distinct vertices in a connected unweighted graph are at positive distance. Two different vertices therefore cannot share a label. This simple observation only forces \(\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\) bits, far below the known polynomial lower bound.

The reviewed upper bound is \(O(\sqrt n)\) bits per vertex, while the general lower bound is \(\Omega(n^{1/3})\). The gap is polynomial in \(n\), not just a missing logarithmic factor. An exact constant-factor answer must identify a rate that is both attainable and necessary for the same two-label model.

Decoding speed is a separate resource. The 2023 paper also gives a variant with polylogarithmic decoding time and \(O(\sqrt{n\log n})\)-bit labels. This card permits an arbitrary finite decoder for each \(n,b\), so a lower bound that applies only to fast decoders would not establish its information-theoretic optimum.

A shared distance oracle can distribute information between vertex identifiers and one common data structure; that common structure is absent here. Approximate distances, weighted graphs, and distances after a failure similarly change the information a pair of labels must provide. This target fixes connected, simple, unweighted planar graphs and exact edge counts.

The graph can determine its entire label assignment, but it cannot determine the decoder. The order of these choices permits graph-dependent labels while preventing the graph from being supplied for free through a query routine. No efficiency requirement is imposed on finding the labels or evaluating the decoder.

cards.answer_criterion: Supply a specified asymptotic rate \(f(n)>0\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of constants \(c,C>0\), \(n_0\), such that \(cf(n)\le\ell_{\mathrm{planar}}(n)\le Cf(n)\) for all \(n\ge n_0\). cards.context:
A label is the information a vertex carries when the graph itself is unavailable. To answer a distance query, the decoder sees exactly the two endpoint labels. Its rule is common to the whole graph family, so it cannot have a different hidden graph stored for every labeling assignment.

Even the diagonal query constrains labels: a vertex is at distance zero from itself, while two distinct vertices in a connected unweighted graph are at positive distance. Two different vertices therefore cannot share a label. This simple observation only forces \(\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\) bits, far below the known polynomial lower bound.

The reviewed upper bound is \(O(\sqrt n)\) bits per vertex, while the general lower bound is \(\Omega(n^{1/3})\). The gap is polynomial in \(n\), not just a missing logarithmic factor. An exact constant-factor answer must identify a rate that is both attainable and necessary for the same two-label model.

Decoding speed is a separate resource. The 2023 paper also gives a variant with polylogarithmic decoding time and \(O(\sqrt{n\log n})\)-bit labels. This card permits an arbitrary finite decoder for each \(n,b\), so a lower bound that applies only to fast decoders would not establish its information-theoretic optimum.

A shared distance oracle can distribute information between vertex identifiers and one common data structure; that common structure is absent here. Approximate distances, weighted graphs, and distances after a failure similarly change the information a pair of labels must provide. This target fixes connected, simple, unweighted planar graphs and exact edge counts.

The graph can determine its entire label assignment, but it cannot determine the decoder. The order of these choices permits graph-dependent labels while preventing the graph from being supplied for free through a query routine. No efficiency requirement is imposed on finding the labels or evaluating the decoder.

cards.definitions: A simple undirected graph consists of a finite vertex set and a set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices; loops and repeated edges are not allowed. A cycle of length \(\ell\)\(\ge 3\) has \(\ell\) distinct vertices and the edges joining them cyclically. The girth is the length of the shortest cycle, and is +∞ for a forest. Thus “girth at least \(2k+2\)” forbids every cycle of lengths \(3,\ldots ,2k+1\), including non-induced cycles. \(M_{s}(n)\) is a maximum over all such graphs on the vertex set \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\); connectedness, regularity and efficient construction are not required. The quantifier order is \(\forall k \exists c_{k},N_{k} \forall n\ge N_{k} \exists G\). Constants may depend on k, but not on n; k remains fixed as n tends to infinity. The target is the stated constant-factor asymptotic density, not merely \(n^{1+1/k- o(1)}\), nor a claim for an arbitrarily sparse subsequence of n. This at-least-girth convention reproduces the source’s definition.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed existence claim for every fixed integer k, or refute it for at least one fixed k. Refutation means that no positive \(c_{k}\) and threshold \(N_{k}\) work at that k; a construction for only selected k or a smaller exponent does not settle the universal conjecture.

cards.title: Dynamic optimality conjecture
cards.formal: Fix n ordered keys and an access sequence X. In the root-BST model, an access is served by rotations until its key is at the root; its cost is one plus the number of rotations. Let \(\operatorname{OPT}(X)\) minimize total cost over offline executions, allowing an optimal initial tree. Is there a universal constant C such that, for every initial splay tree \(T_{0}\) and every X, \(\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_0)\le C(\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)\)? The additive term allows an arbitrary initial configuration.

context_blocks.text: A balanced search tree guarantees logarithmic time per access, but that worst-case guarantee ignores the sequence. Repeatedly accessing one key, or scanning nearby keys, can be much cheaper if the tree adapts. Dynamic optimality asks for one online rule that exploits every such pattern without being told which pattern will occur.

The benchmark is itself allowed to rotate its tree and knows all future requests. Competing with the best fixed tree only captures access frequencies; competing with a changing tree also captures temporal structure. Splaying uses only local zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rotations after each access, with no explicit prediction of the future.

For a concrete example, consider a chain on n keys with the requested key at its bottom. The first splay can cost \(\Theta (n)\), whereas an offline comparator can put that key at the root initially. The additive n allowance accounts for this starting discrepancy. Repeating the same request then costs one per access in both trees. A large cost for one badly initialized access therefore does not refute the statement.

The July 2026 preprint bounds splay cost by \(O((\operatorname{OPT}(X)+n) \log  \log  n \cdot  \log ^{2} \log  \log  n)\). Its competitive factor depends only on the number of keys, so the result covers every access pattern; that factor nevertheless grows without bound. A constant bound would be strictly stronger. The theorem is stated asymptotically, with the finitely many small values of n absorbed into constants.

Competitiveness concerns the total cost of a sequence. It does not require every individual access to be cheap, and it does not compare against an arbitrary RAM program with a hash table. Both executions must maintain binary search trees and pay for the specified rotations. Within those rules the offline execution can depend on the complete sequence, while the splay rule reacts only to the current request and tree.

cards.why: It asks whether a simple local adjustment rule can match every legal strategy with complete knowledge of the future. The issue is fundamental to instance-sensitive data structures: success would replace a growing competitive penalty by a constant for all access patterns. A counterexample would identify a limitation of splaying that its many separate locality guarantees fail to reveal.
cards.definitions: Keys are \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}, n\ge 1\), ordered by their integer values. A binary search tree has one node per key, every key in a left subtree smaller than its root and every key in a right subtree larger. A rotation on a parent-child edge exchanges those two nodes while reattaching the intermediate subtree so that the order is preserved. To splay a requested key x, repeatedly apply the following bottom-up rule until x is root. If its parent is root, rotate the edge from x to its parent (zig). Otherwise let p be its parent and g its grandparent. If x and p are both left children or both right children, first rotate p above g and then x above p (zig-zig). Otherwise rotate x above p and then x above g (zig-zag). Each access costs one plus its number of rotations. The tree after the access is the initial tree for the next access. For a finite sequence \(X\in [n]*, \operatorname{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_{0})\) is the sum of these costs starting from \(T_{0}\). A comparator execution may start with any tree, knows X in full, and serves each request by any finite sequence of parent-child rotations anywhere in the current tree whose final root is the requested key. Its cost is the same one-plus-rotations sum. \(\operatorname{OPT}(X)\) is the minimum cost over all such initial trees and executions; it is zero for the empty sequence. There are no insertions, deletions or additional node operations. This root-BST cost convention is the one used in the saved source, with the additive n term accounting for the initial tree.

progress.text: Splaying has logarithmic amortized access cost and stronger guarantees for useful special patterns. These do not establish competitiveness against an arbitrary changing offline tree.

The preprint proves \(O((\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)\log\log n\,\log^2\log\log n)\) total splay cost. Theorem 1 includes the initialization term explicitly. Constant competitiveness remains the target.

cards.title: Superlogarithmic static cell-probe lower bounds
cards.formal: Does there exist a fixed integer \(k\ge 2\) and a uniformly polynomial-time computable family of Boolean functions \(F_{n}\) on an n-word database and a \(k\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil\)-bit query such that its optimal deterministic static cell-probe query complexity \(t*F(n)\), with word size \(\lceil 4\log _{2} n\rceil\) bits and \(n\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil ^{2}\) memory cells, satisfies \(t*F(n)/\log _{2} n\to \infty\) as \(n\to \infty\)?
cards.definitions: For each integer \(n\ge 2\) put \(w=\lceil 4\log _{2} n\rceil\) and \(s=n\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil ^{2}\). A database is \(D\in (\{0,1\}^{w})^{n}, a\) query is \(q\in \{0,1\}^{k\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil}\), and \(F_{n}(D,q)\in \{0,1\}\). Explicit means that a single deterministic Turing machine computes \(F_{n}(D,q)\), given \((1^{n},D,q)\), in time polynomial in n; no advice is allowed in this definition. A data structure may preprocess D by any map \(E_{n}\) into s cells of w bits each. Preprocessing time is unrestricted, and this encoding may be nonlinear and nonuniform. For each query, a deterministic adaptive decision tree reads cells, choosing the next address from the query and previously read contents, and must output \(F_{n}(D,q)\) exactly for every database. Computation between probes is free. The trees may depend on n, F and the query, but their only access to D is through \(E_{n}(D)\). Each query starts without free database-dependent private information; memory is static and read-only. Define \(t*F(n)\) as the minimum, over all such encodings and trees, of the maximum number of probes over all D and q. All memory cells count toward s. This card fixes a near-linear-space, short-query, one-bit-answer specialization of the broader static lower-bound challenge; it does not assert equivalence to every space or word-size variant.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that some fixed k and admissible uniform family F satisfy: for every real \(B>0\) there is N such that \(t*F(n)>B \log _{2} n\) for every \(n\ge N\). Alternatively, prove the exact negation: for every fixed k and every admissible family F, there is a finite \(B>0\) such that \(t*F(n)\le B \log _{2} n\) for arbitrarily large n. In particular, the negative answer need not establish an \(O(\log  n)\) bound for all sufficiently large n.
cards.why: A central unconditional lower-bound bottleneck for data structures: establish that a short, explicitly defined static query fundamentally needs more than logarithmically many memory accesses despite unrestricted preprocessing.

cards.status_note: Primary sources and later-result searches checked on 11 September 2026 did not supply a resolution of the stated static specialization. The STOC 2026 paper retains the broader static barrier as Open Problem 1.1. The fixed near-linear space, short-query Boolean output and uniform polynomial-time family are an expressly recorded specialization; conditional proof barriers and bounds for dynamic memory or superpolynomial query sets do not resolve it.

context_blocks.text: A static data structure pays an initial cost to organize a database and then answers queries against that fixed information. In the cell-probe model, only the number of memory cells read during a query matters. The query algorithm has unlimited computational power between reads. Consequently, a lower bound must identify information that cannot be made locally accessible even by an ingenious encoding; showing that a particular search procedure or arithmetic computation is slow is insufficient.

The space allowance is central. With enough space, preprocessing could store every answer in a table, giving constant-probe queries. Here there are at least \(n^{2}\) possible queries, while the stored representation has only \(O(n \log ^{3} n)\) bits. Conversely, the database itself fits in n cells, so reading all n cells always suffices. The target therefore lies strictly between two elementary strategies: an unrestricted table with one entry for every possible query exceeds the budget, but the problem is always solvable without a computational-time obstruction.

The one-bit answer avoids obtaining a large probe bound merely because the output contains many independent bits. The query length is \(O(\log  n)\), with a fixed constant k. Increasing the query length to n bits can create communication lower bounds of an entirely different magnitude. Likewise, allowing only linear combinations in preprocessing or forbidding adaptive reads changes the collection of encodings and algorithms that a lower bound must defeat.

Koucký, Loff, Molli and Saks formulate the broad static challenge explicitly as Open Problem 1.1. Away from storage that is extremely close to the information-theoretic minimum, familiar general lower-bound approaches have not exceeded the logarithm of the number of queries. The present card turns this challenge into one yes/no proposition by fixing the word size, storage overhead, output alphabet and uniform meaning of an explicit problem. Its stricter conventions should be kept in mind when transferring results from a survey.

Korten, Pitassi and Impagliazzo obtain stronger tradeoffs through local pseudorandom generators. Their improvements are especially informative when the number of probes is small and the cells contain few bits. Their general bound includes an explicit dependence on word size. A gain proved for one-bit cells therefore cannot simply be carried over unchanged to \(\Theta (\log  n)\)-bit words. These results advance the tradeoff frontier without proving the superlogarithmic lower bound at the parameters fixed here.

Ko’s 2025 result illustrates another important parameter distinction. For random linear operators with m possible row queries, the lower bound is \(\Omega (\min \{\log (m/s), n/\log  s\})\) in a bit-cell formulation. It can exceed log n when the number m of queries grows sufficiently rapidly. With only polynomially many queries, the first term is at most \(O(\log  n)\). The random choice of an operator also does not by itself supply the uniformly polynomial-time explicit family required in this card.

The STOC 2026 natural-proofs paper supplies conditional obstacles to a broad class of proof methods. Such a proof recognizes a sufficiently large, efficiently testable property of function tables that implies data-structure hardness; conjectured local pseudorandom functions would obstruct that recognition. This is not an unconditional impossibility theorem for stronger lower bounds. The authors’ errata also flag a new sampling method whose coverage had not been checked and explain why a previously cited rigidity consequence no longer constitutes an unachieved barrier.

Static and dynamic memory have different sources of hardness. Larsen, Weinstein and Yu crossed the logarithmic barrier for dynamic Boolean problems, where updates limit how information can be reorganized. Ko’s March 2026 preprint claims a further \(\Omega ((\log  n/\log  \log  n)^{2})\) bound for a dynamic multiphase problem. Those update constraints are absent here: the whole database may be preprocessed without a time bound before any query arrives. Neither dynamic result automatically gives the requested static lower bound.

A positive solution would identify a uniformly computable query whose information cannot be recovered with only logarithmically many reads, even after unrestricted preprocessing. This separates a memory-access bottleneck from the running time of known implementations. The limit in the statement is stronger than an arbitrarily large ratio on an infinite subsequence: the ratio must eventually exceed each fixed constant and remain above it. That distinction also affects the exact negative answer.

cards.title: Deterministic linear-time static dictionaries
cards.formal: Is the following proposition true? For every fixed integer \(d\ge 1\) there are uniform deterministic construction and query programs \(A_{d},Q_{d}\) and a constant \(C_{d}\ge 1\) such that, for every \(n\ge 2\), every word length \(\lceil \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil \le w\le d\lceil \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil\), and every n-record input with distinct w-bit integer keys and w-bit values, \(A_{d}\) builds a static dictionary in at most \(C_{d} n\) operations and \(C_{d} n\) words of total space, and \(Q_{d}\) answers every membership-and-value query in at most \(C_{d}\) operations.
cards.why: Exact constant-time lookup is a basic component of many larger data structures. The unresolved cost is obtaining the representation deterministically in optimal time, so a resolution would settle whether randomness is essential to this combination of construction, storage and lookup guarantees.

cards.definitions: The universe is \(U_{w}\)={\(0,\ldots ,2\)ʷ−1}. An input is a list of n pairs \((x_{i},v_{i})\in U_{w}\times U_{w}\) with pairwise distinct \(x_{i}\) and arbitrary \(v_{i}\); the input order is unrestricted. On query \(q\in U_{w}\) the output is \((1,v_{i})\) if \(q=x_{i}\) and \((0,0)\) if q is absent. The stored set and values do not change after construction. The machine is a sequential word RAM with w-bit registers and cells. The primitive unit-cost instructions are memory reads and writes, copies, comparisons, conditional branches, addition and subtraction modulo 2ʷ, multiplication returning the full product in two words, integer quotient and remainder of two words with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and logical shifts. A shift by at least w returns zero; otherwise shifted-out bits are discarded. Addresses may occupy a fixed number of words, and all operations computing them are charged. Programs have finitely many instructions and constants, may receive n and w, and contain no input-size or word-size advice, random instruction, free table or special hashing primitive. Every table, parameter computation, memory initialization and output write performed by construction counts toward its time; input storage, the resulting dictionary and temporary storage count toward its space. Query reads the constructed representation and may use temporary workspace, with every operation charged; all retained information about the input is in the counted representation. The query must be correct on every q, including absent keys. Programs and constants may depend on d but not on n, w, the input or query. This spells out the saved \(w=\Theta (\log  n)\) convention as a claim for every fixed polynomial-size universe; Pagh’s broader arbitrary-word-length formulation is not asserted equivalent here.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition with deterministic algorithms meeting all three bounds for every fixed d, or disprove it for at least one fixed d. The negation says that no pair of admissible correct programs has simultaneously linear worst-case construction time, linear total space and constant worst-case query time for all inputs in that word-length range. Failure of a particular hash family, an average-input lower bound, or a lower bound in a comparison-only model is not that negation.

context_blocks.text: A dictionary is an exact lookup table for a sparse set of keys. For example, records \((12,5), (47,9)\) and \((103,2)\) require the answers 9 on key 47 and absent on key 48. The values need not be unique. The problem is to prepare a representation in time proportional to the number of records and then answer every lookup in a bounded number of machine steps, regardless of whether the key is present.

Direct addressing uses the key itself as an array index. This achieves constant lookup time, but an array for a universe of \(n^{2}\) possible keys occupies \(n^{2}\) cells even if only n keys are present. Such space is outside the target. At the opposite extreme, keeping the keys in sorted order uses linear space but ordinary binary search needs logarithmically many comparisons. These examples show why construction, storage and query time must be required simultaneously.

Randomized perfect hashing already gives linear expected construction time, linear storage and constant worst-case lookup time. The randomness concerns finding a suitable representation during construction; once a valid dictionary has been built, lookup can be exact and have a worst-case bound. Thus the open issue is not whether every query can avoid probabilistic errors, but whether the construction time can be bounded linearly without any random choices.

Pagh obtained deterministic \(O(n \log  n)\) construction for logarithmic-size words. Ružić subsequently related construction cost to integer sorting with only a log log n overhead. The latter is a much smaller overhead, but it still grows with n. The source question asks for its complete removal while retaining the other two guarantees. A representation whose existence is known but whose parameters take longer to find does not meet the construction requirement.

The dependence on word length matters even when keys occupy one machine word. Here a fixed polynomial-size universe is intended: the constant relating w to log n is fixed before the inputs vary. Constants in the guarantees may depend on that fixed bound. This is the logarithmic-word version already selected for this card; it does not silently claim a solution for word lengths growing faster than log n.

Uniformity also matters. Earlier dictionary results sometimes supplied word-size-dependent constants at no construction cost. The present formulation charges for computing every table and parameter that is not part of a fixed program. A one-time computation on a particular physical machine cannot disappear from an asymptotic bound that covers arbitrarily large inputs.

The dependency remains visible in modern applications. The 2024 internal-pattern-matching paper uses constant-time deterministic dictionaries with a general \(O(m(\log  \log  m)^{2})\) construction bound for a dictionary of size m, and treats very small dictionaries separately. The surrounding text length can be much larger than m, so that application must not be read as fixing word length to \(\Theta (\log  m)\). Kosolobov’s 2026 compressed index likewise records a slowdown when dictionary randomness is removed.

These applications explain the scientific stakes: a basic lookup operation can determine whether a larger construction remains deterministic within its intended time bound. The 2026 index is evidence that the issue remains useful, rather than a theorem resolving this static linear-construction question.

cards.title: Constant-time deterministic dynamic dictionaries
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(c\ge2\), does there exist a uniform deterministic word-RAM dictionary with capacity \(N\), word size \(w=\lceil c\log_2(N+2)\rceil\), \(O(N)\) words of space, \(O(1)\) worst-case lookup time and \(O(1)\) amortized insertion and deletion time? The guarantees must hold for every valid online sequence on \(w\)-bit keys and values, starting empty, after \(O(N)\) initialization.
cards.definitions: A uniform sequential word RAM has a fixed finite program, word-sized registers and addressed memory cells. Unit-cost instructions are reads and writes, comparisons, branching, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division with nonzero divisor, Boolean bit operations and logical shifts. Arithmetic stored in one word is modulo \(2^w\); shifts by at least \(w\) yield zero. Addresses must fit the available word size. All table construction and input-dependent auxiliary memory count; there is no free advice or input-dependent oracle. Randomized programs may generate independent uniform random words. The program receives \(N\ge2\) and \(w\). Insert supplies a new key and a value, Delete names a present key, and Lookup returns its value or an absent marker. At most \(N\) keys are simultaneously stored. No random instruction is allowed in this deterministic target. For each fixed \(c\), constants may depend on \(c\) but not on \(N\), input keys or sequence length. The joint amortized bound is total cost \(O(N+q+u)\) for \(q\) queries and \(u\) updates, while every query individually costs \(O(1)\). All retained input information, including any direct-address table, counts toward the \(O(N)\) space bound. This logarithmic-word, fixed-capacity formulation asks already for constant amortized updates; it does not demand constant worst-case updates.
cards.why: This is a basic possible separation between the power of randomization and determinism in a general-purpose data-structure primitive.

cards.title: Multiphase conjecture
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(\gamma>1\) and \(\delta>0\) such that every always-correct Las Vegas word-RAM solution of the following three-phase problem has overhead \(\tau(n)=\Omega(n^\delta)\) for \(k=\lceil n^\gamma\rceil\)? Phase I preprocesses \(S_1,\ldots,S_k\subseteq[n]\) in expected \(O(kn\tau(n))\) time; Phase II receives \(T\subseteq[n]\) and takes expected \(O(n\tau(n))\) time; Phase III receives \(i\in[k]\) and decides whether \(S_i\cap T=\varnothing\) in expected \(O(\tau(n))\) time.
cards.definitions: A uniform sequential word RAM has a fixed finite program, word-sized registers and addressed memory cells. Unit-cost instructions are reads and writes, comparisons, branching, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division with nonzero divisor, Boolean bit operations and logical shifts. Arithmetic stored in one word is modulo \(2^w\); shifts by at least \(w\) yield zero. Addresses must fit the available word size. All table construction and input-dependent auxiliary memory count; there is no free advice or input-dependent oracle. Randomized programs may generate independent uniform random words. A candidate program chooses a fixed integer \(a\ge2\) and uses words of \(w=\lceil a\log_2(n+k+2)\rceil\) bits. All its addresses must fit in one word, so the available address space is polynomial; the lower-bound claim quantifies over every such fixed \(a\). Sets may be given as incidence vectors, so their input lengths are \(kn\) and \(n\) bits. One uniform finite program for each phase must work for all \(n\) in the selected \(k=\lceil n^\gamma\rceil\) regime. The program may retain its computed memory between phases; all computation, initialization and copying are charged to the phase performing them. Phase I does not know \(T\) or \(i\), Phase II does not know \(i\), and Phase III receives only the index plus the retained state. Inputs are fixed independently of the random bits. Answers are always correct and each phase terminates almost surely; expected bounds hold for every fixed complete input. Define overhead as the maximum of 1 and the three worst-input expected phase costs divided respectively by \(kn,n,1\). A constant-factor asymptotic lower bound is required for all sufficiently large \(n\); a conditional hardness proof is not an unconditional resolution.
cards.why: The multiphase conjecture is a central candidate for proving polynomial operation lower bounds for dynamic data structures.

cards.title: Randomized complexity of online labeling
cards.formal: Determine, up to constant factors, the optimal amortized expected number of relabelings per insertion or deletion for randomized online list labeling with at most \(n\) live items and labels in \([2n]\), against an oblivious adversary. importance.reason: The problem measures the unavoidable movement needed to maintain a sorted array with spare capacity, a primitive used throughout ordered storage and indexing.

sentences: An ordered list is stored using a fixed range of numerical labels.
Insertions and deletions must preserve label order while keeping spare labels available.
The cost counts how many existing items receive a different label.
Randomization achieves nearly logarithmic expected amortized cost in the cited result.
The remaining task is to determine the optimal asymptotic rate for constant slack.

cards.definitions: Fix a capacity \(n\ge2\) and start with an empty ordered list. An insertion specifies the rank at which a new distinct item enters the list; a deletion names a live item. The list never contains more than \(n\) items. After each update the algorithm assigns distinct labels from \(\{1,\ldots,2n\}\) to the live items, in strictly increasing list order. Cost is one for the update plus the total number of relabelings of surviving items during it; assigning a label to the new item costs at most one additional unit. The input sequence is fixed independently of all random choices. Only relabelings are charged: local computation, rank search and auxiliary metadata are free, so this is a movement-cost model, not a word-RAM running-time target. An upper rate \(f\ge1\) means a uniform online algorithm and a constant \(C\) satisfy expected total cost at most \(C(n+M f(n))\) for every capacity and every finite valid sequence of \(M\) updates. For tightness, every algorithm and every rate \(g\) permitting such a bound must have \(g(n)=\Omega(f(n))\). Constants are independent of the sequence and capacity. The array has fixed constant slack; other label-universe regimes are outside this card. The algorithm is a fixed finite computable program taking the capacity as input, without advice or an oracle, and may use independent fair random bits. It receives updates sequentially, has no access to future updates, and must finish each operation almost surely with a valid ordered labeling. Its finite local computation and auxiliary storage are not charged by the movement objective. An oblivious sequence may depend on the algorithm and the capacity but not on the sampled random bits or observed random labels. The expectation is over the algorithm’s random choices for that fixed full sequence. A surviving item changed more than once during an update is counted for each relabeling; labels of live items must be valid at the end of the update. Here \(f(n)\) and competing rates \(g(n)\) concern integer capacities \(n\ge2\), and the asymptotic lower comparison is as \(n\to\infty\).

context_blocks.text: List labeling represents order by positions in an array with empty slots. An insertion supplies a new position in the logical order, but an empty array slot need not already be available between its neighbors. Other items may have to move. Deletions create space without prescribing where future insertions will occur.

The capacity is fixed and the array has twice that many slots. This gives a constant fraction of spare space even at maximum occupancy. A nearly full array or a polynomially larger label universe can have different bounds, so neither can silently replace this regime.

Movement and computation are separate resources here. A program can spend arbitrary finite effort deciding which labels to change; the objective counts the changes themselves. Similarly, expected amortized cost allows occasional expensive updates provided every fixed full sequence has the required expected total cost. It does not assert a worst-case time bound for each individual call.

The See-Saw theorem gives \(O(\log n(\log\log n)^3)\) amortized expected cost at any fixed positive constant slack. Its stated slack parameter may be fixed below one and its smaller array embedded in \([2n]\), giving the upper bound for this card. The paper records a general randomized lower bound of \(\Omega(\log n)\). Removing the remaining growing factor is the unresolved tight-bound issue.

Lower bounds for deterministic, history-independent, or other restricted labeling algorithms do not automatically apply to all randomized online algorithms. The adversary here commits to the whole sequence without observing random labels; adaptive choices based on those labels would change the game.

The original seminar question concerned randomized online labeling broadly. The retained benchmark selects constant slack, both insertions and deletions, and an oblivious adversary, matching the subsequently specified researcher-linked variant. The answer requires a tight asymptotic rate, rather than just the analysis of one named algorithm.

cards.answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguously defined rate \(f:\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\to\mathbb R_{\ge1}\) and complete Lean-checked upper and matching lower bounds up to constant factors in the stated expected amortized movement model. The upper bound must provide one uniform online algorithm with expected total cost \(O(n+Mf(n))\) for every capacity and oblivious valid sequence. The lower bound must establish the stated \(g(n)=\Omega(f(n))\) requirement for every competing permitted algorithm and achievable rate. An unbounded polylogarithmic factor or a lower bound only for a restricted algorithm family does not meet the target.

cards.title: Amortized decrease-key complexity of standard pairing heaps
cards.formal: Determine, up to constant factors, the amortized decrease-key bound \(d(N)\) of the standard two-pass pairing heap, while insert, meld and find-min are charged \(O(1)\) and delete-min is charged \(O(\log(2+N))\). The bound is required for every finite sequence starting from empty heaps with at most \(N\) live items in all heaps combined.
cards.definitions: A heap is a rooted heap-ordered tree. Link compares two roots and makes the larger root the new leftmost child of the smaller. Insert links a singleton to the root; meld links the two roots. Decrease-key receives a handle, reduces its key and, if it is not a root, cuts its whole subtree and links it to the root. Delete-min removes the root, links consecutive children from left to right in disjoint pairs, leaving an unpaired last child unchanged, then combines the resulting roots from right to left by successive links. Find-min reads the root. Keys are opaque ordered values; ties follow a fixed identity order. Constant-size nodes have enough sibling and parent pointers for a cut in constant time. Charge comparisons, links, cuts and pointer work. An admissible upper bound is a function \(d\ge1\) for which a universal \(C\) bounds total cost by \(C(a+b\log(2+N)+c d(N))\), where \(a\) counts the constant-cost operations, \(b\) delete-min operations and \(c\) decreases. A tight answer must also prove that every admissible charge function dominates the supplied rate within a universal constant for sufficiently large \(N\); the constants cannot depend on the sequence. Variants changing either pass, rank metadata or the linking discipline are different algorithms.
cards.why: A tight analysis would resolve the central complexity uncertainty for one of the simplest and most widely studied self-adjusting priority queues.

cards.title: Space-query exponent curve of 3SUM indexing
cards.formal: Determine \(\tau_{\mathrm{3SI}}(s)\) for every real \(s\in[1,2]\), where \(\tau_{\mathrm{3SI}}(s)\) is the infimum of real \(t\ge0\) for which, for every rational \(\eta>0\), a uniform randomized 3SUM index uses \(O(n^{s+\eta})\) words and answers queries in \(O(n^{t+\eta})\) worst-case time.
cards.definitions: The input is two sets \(A,B\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n^4-1\}\), each of size \(n\ge2\), supplied explicitly. A query \(z\in\{0,\ldots,2n^4-2\}\) asks whether \(z=a+b\) for some \(a\in A,b\in B\), using ordinary addition. Set \(L=n\) and fix \(d=10\) in the word-RAM model below. Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. Randomized algorithms, when explicitly permitted, may generate independent uniform random words. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. Preprocessing may take arbitrary time but must terminate almost surely; this preserves the preexisting card’s space-hardness convention. Every retained input, table and random seed is counted. Each fixed input/query is answered correctly with probability at least \(2/3\) over preprocessing and query randomness, and space and query time bounds hold on every random outcome. Queries cannot communicate input-dependent state for free. For each chosen \(s,t,\eta\), one finite program pair and constants handle every \(n\); there is no per-size choice of advice. Parameters select programs and are not real-number computational inputs. The infimum need not be attained. The quantity is a dimensionless query exponent, and it ignores subpolynomial factors only through the displayed quantifiers.

previous.definitions: A uniform sequential word RAM has a fixed finite program, word-sized registers and addressed memory cells. cards.title: Strong SetDisjointness conjecture
cards.formal: Is it true that every static word-RAM data structure for SetDisjointness with space \(S(N)\) and worst-case query time \(T(N)\) satisfies \(S(N)T(N)^2=\widetilde\Omega(N^2)\)? The input is a list of nonempty sets \(S_1,\ldots,S_m\subseteq[N]\) with total size \(N=\sum_i|S_i|\), and a query \((i,j)\) asks whether \(S_i\cap S_j\) is empty.
cards.definitions: A uniform sequential word RAM has a fixed finite program, word-sized registers and addressed memory cells. Unit-cost instructions are reads and writes, comparisons, branching, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division with nonzero divisor, Boolean bit operations and logical shifts. Arithmetic stored in one word is modulo \(2^w\); shifts by at least \(w\) yield zero. Addresses must fit the available word size. All table construction and input-dependent auxiliary memory count; there is no free advice or input-dependent oracle. Randomized programs may generate independent uniform random words. The sets are supplied as lists without repeated elements within a set, with \(m\le N\) and \(N\ge2\). Word size is \(w=\lceil10\log_2(N+2)\rceil\). Restrict attention to \(N\le S(N)\le N^2\), rounding up and padding unused cells if needed. Preprocessing may use arbitrary finite time; all input-dependent information retained afterwards counts toward \(S(N)\). A query reads this static representation and begins without input-dependent private state. Randomized preprocessing and query algorithms are allowed; the answer to each fixed input/query must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). Space and query time bounds hold for every random outcome. The notation means that, for each admissible data structure, there are constants \(c>0\), \(b\ge0\), and \(N_0\) such that \(S(N)T(N)^2\ge cN^2/(\log(2+N))^b\) for all \(N\ge N_0\). All sizes are measured in words and time in word-RAM steps. Uniform programs and exact empty/nonempty semantics are required; reporting the intersection is another problem.
cards.why: This conjecture underlies many space-query conditional lower bounds for text indexes, graph oracles and set systems.

cards.title: Unified bound for binary search trees
cards.formal: Does a deterministic online BST algorithm exist with total access cost \(O(n\log(2+n)+U(X))\) for every sequence \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in[n]^m\), where \[U(X)=\sum_{t=1}^{m}\log_2\!\left(2+\min\left\{n,\min_{1\le s<t}(t-s+|x_t-x_s|)\right\}\right)?\] The minimum over an empty set is \(+\infty\); the initialization term is independent of \(m\).
cards.definitions: The keys are the fixed ranks \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A BST has one node per key in symmetric order. Each access begins with a pointer at the root; primitive costs are moving it to a parent or child, performing a rotation incident to the pointer, and visiting the requested key. Other input-dependent state must be kept in the tree with constant-size fields per node. The algorithm sees requests only as they arrive; it may restructure the tree but may not use arbitrary jumps, an auxiliary search structure or advance knowledge. Begin with a balanced tree, constructed within the initialization allowance. There are no insertions or deletions. The target uses the elapsed-access definition of the unified bound in the 2024 paper; the cap by \(n\) and the additive constants cover first accesses. A uniform algorithm and universal multiplicative constant must work for all \(n,m,X\).
cards.why: The unified bound asks one search tree to exploit temporal and rank locality together, beyond proving separate working-set and dynamic-finger guarantees.

cards.title: Superconstant word-RAM time for prefix-\(U_1\)
cards.formal:
Is it impossible to maintain a length-\(n\) bit sequence under substitutions and answer prefix-AND queries using a deterministic uniform word-RAM data structure with \(O(n)\) preprocessing and \(O(1)\) worst-case time for each update and each query?

An update \(\operatorname{set}(i,b)\) replaces the bit at position \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) by \(b\in\{0,1\}\). A query at \(k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\) must return
\[\operatorname{prefix}(k)=\bigwedge_{i=1}^{k}b_i,\qquad\operatorname{prefix}(0)=1.\]
The word length is \(w=\lceil c\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) for a fixed integer constant \(c\ge1\). The impossibility is to hold for every such fixed constant and every correct data structure in the model below.

This retains the source's worst-case time convention. The target is absence of any constant bound, not a prescribed logarithmic lower-bound rate or the stronger exclusion of amortized constant time.

source_formulation.text: There is no structure for prefix-U1 with complexity \(O(1)\).

cards.why: This small dynamic problem isolates whether maintaining even threshold information about a changing minimum requires more than a constant number of actual word operations. Its hardness would complete conditional classifications of dynamic regular-language membership, and newer work extends that connection to tree languages. The challenge concerns computation inside the machine as well as memory access, making it a foundational word-RAM question.

cards.definitions:
The sequence length \(n\ge1\) remains fixed for the lifetime of the structure. Its initial bits are supplied explicitly, one per input cell. Preprocessing receives \(n\) and that sequence and must run in at most \(K(n+1)\) word operations for one fixed constant \(K\). It builds the state from which all subsequent operations are served. The two-element monoid \(U_1=\{0,1\}\) has multiplication Boolean AND, with identity one and absorbing element zero. Hence a nonempty prefix has product zero exactly when it contains a zero.

Equivalently, the zero positions form a changing subset \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Substitution adds or removes a supplied position, and the complemented prefix answer says whether \(S\cap\{1,\ldots,k\}\) is nonempty. Repeating a substitution with the present value is allowed and must also meet the cost bound. Queries do not ask for the minimum element itself or a predecessor of the query position. No insertion or deletion of sequence positions, change of \(n\), or restriction on which positions may change is included.

Use a finite-program unit-cost random-access machine whose cells and addresses are unsigned \(w\)-bit words. One operation can read or write one addressed cell, copy a word, compare two words or branch, apply word addition, subtraction or multiplication, apply unsigned integer division or remainder by a nonzero word, apply bitwise AND, OR, XOR or NOT, or shift a word left or right by a supplied integer amount. Arithmetic results are reduced modulo \(2^w\), except that division and remainder have their usual unsigned integer meanings; left shifts discard overflowing bits, right shifts insert zeros, and shifts by at least \(w\) give zero. Division by zero must be avoided or handled as an error, not an extra operation. Constant literals are fixed by the finite program. The program can use \(n\) and \(w\); both are supplied at initialization. Each listed operation has unit cost. No other arbitrary word function or input-dependent instruction is provided.

There are at most \(2^w\) addressable cells, all initially zero except the supplied input. Every read, write and table construction counts; no nonuniform precomputed table or advice depending on \(n\) is supplied free of charge. There is no additional linear-space requirement: the machine may use its polynomially many addressable cells, even if many were populated by previous updates. The fixed program, positive integer \(c\) and preprocessing constant \(K\) may depend on the data structure, but never on the input length, initial bits or future history. These explicit word operations instantiate the source's unit-cost arithmetic RAM convention, with only logarithmically many bits per word.

Updates and queries arrive one at a time. The answer to each query must be exactly correct for the state after all earlier updates, before a later operation is revealed. Every finite operation history is allowed, including histories selected using earlier answers and histories much longer than \(n\). All operation invocations must terminate. The structure is deterministic, with no error probability and no random or expected-time convention.

A constant-time structure would have one constant \(T\) bounding the work of every individual update and query, for every initial sequence, every length and every history. The work done by one operation cannot be charged to earlier or later operations. Allowing an onset \(n_0\) rather than all lengths gives the same existence question, since the finitely many smaller lengths can be handled separately. Consequently a positive impossibility result can be expressed as follows: for every correct linear-preprocessing structure, every proposed bound \(B\) and every onset \(N\), there is a length \(n\ge N\), an initial sequence and a finite operation history in which an individual operation takes more than \(B\) steps. No particular function tending to infinity is prescribed in advance.

The cell-probe model, mentioned in the context, charges only memory accesses and allows arbitrary computation on values already read at no cost. It is more permissive than the word-operation model just defined; a counting argument that ignores all such computation cannot automatically establish the requested word-RAM barrier.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the claimed nonexistence. A proof must exclude every correct deterministic uniform structure with linear preprocessing and fixed logarithmic word-length constant from having a common constant worst-case bound for both operations. It may give a quantitative lower bound, but must justify that it excludes all constants in this model. A refutation must give a single finite-program structure, some fixed word-length constant, linear preprocessing and exact constant worst-case bounds for both updates and queries on every history. An amortized or expected constant upper bound alone does not refute the specified worst-case conjecture. A lower bound for a stronger query task, larger monoid, smaller instruction set or stricter space limit does not alone prove it.

cards.title: Logarithmic fully retroactive priority queues
cards.formal: Does a deterministic fully retroactive priority queue exist with \(O(m+1)\) space and \(O(\log(2+m))\) amortized time per operation, where \(m\) is the number of operations in its represented history? It must support adding or removing a historical insertion or extract-min and asking for the minimum immediately after any supplied historical time.
cards.definitions: The comparison pointer machine stores constant-size records with a fixed number of pointer and data fields, accessed through a constant number of pointer registers. A step can follow or change a pointer, allocate a record, compare two keys or perform a constant-size control operation. Keys are opaque members of a totally ordered set; pointer arithmetic, array indexing by computed integers and unit-cost unbounded counters are unavailable. All work, including rebuilding, is charged. A history consists of insertion records \((t,x)\) and extract-min records \(t\), with pairwise distinct timestamps in an opaque totally ordered time domain. Replay records by timestamp from an empty queue. Inserted items have distinct identities and ordered priorities; ties are resolved by identity. Histories supplied after each edit are promised valid: extract-min never acts on an empty queue. An edit adds a record at an unused time or removes a named existing record. A query at \(t\) returns the minimum surviving item after replay through \(t\), or an empty marker. Removing a past operation changes the interpretation of all subsequent records. There is no monotonicity promise on inserted or extracted priorities. Space includes every retained historical record and index. For each finite edit/query sequence, the sum of \(1+\log(2+m)\) over operations bounds total computation within one universal constant; initialization is constant.
cards.why: This asks whether complete access to a changeable operation history can cost only as much asymptotically as an ordinary priority queue.

context_blocks.text: Demaine, Iacono and Langerman introduced the retroactive model, which edits the past rather than merely preserving snapshots.

The April 2026 revision reports \(O(\log^2m\log\log m)\) time and \(O(m\log m)\) space for the general case. It attains logarithmic time and linear space for monotonic priority queues, leaving the unrestricted target open.

cards.title: Optimal randomized memory-reallocation overhead
cards.formal: Determine, up to absolute constant factors as \(\varepsilon\to0\), the optimal worst-case expected reallocation overhead \(F(\varepsilon)\) for online allocators with load at most \(1-\varepsilon\). The allocator stores objects in contiguous intervals of a fixed array and may relocate live objects after each insertion or deletion.
cards.definitions: For every fixed real \(0<\varepsilon\le1/2\) and integer array length \(M\ge1\), a request inserts a fresh object of positive integer size \(s\), or deletes a named live object. Valid finite sequences start empty and have total live size at most \((1-\varepsilon)M\) after every request. At each operation boundary, every live object occupies one contiguous interval of its size in \(\{0,\ldots,M-1\}\), and these intervals are disjoint. On an update involving an object \(x\), cost is \(1+\sum_y s(y)/s(x)\), where the sum is over objects live both before and after the update whose starting addresses change. This counts allocation changes at operation boundaries; local computation and allocation metadata are uncharged. The online rule may know \(M,\varepsilon\) but no future requests, and may use private randomness. A sequence is fixed independently of that randomness; allocations must always be valid. For a family of rules covering all \(M\), its overhead is the supremum, over all capacities, valid finite request sequences and individual update indices, of expected update cost. \(F(\varepsilon)\) is the infimum of those overheads over all such families. No history-independence or resizability constraint is imposed. The target measures each update’s expectation, rather than expected amortized cost or a high-probability bound.
cards.why: A tight result would establish the intrinsic price of fragmentation when a general-purpose allocator operates close to full capacity.

context_blocks.text: The 2024 work studies low-overhead memory reallocation and its relationship with stronger resizability and history-independence guarantees. Those extra guarantees are not required for the target here.

Jin’s February 2026 paper gives an upper bound \(O((\log(1/\varepsilon))^4(\log\log(1/\varepsilon))^2)\) and a lower bound \(\Omega(\log(1/\varepsilon))\) for general allocators. The new general lower bound improves the scope of earlier bounds restricted to resizable allocators.

cards.title: Deque conjecture
cards.formal: Start from an arbitrary binary search tree containing \(n\) ordered keys, and perform \(m\) legal double-ended queue operations. Insert-min creates a new minimum as the root with the old tree as its right child; insert-max is symmetric. Delete-min splays the minimum to the root, removes it, and keeps its right subtree; delete-max is symmetric. Is the total number of primitive pointer operations and rotations always \(O(n+m)\), with a universal constant? This is Tarjan’s deque conjecture for the specified splay implementation.
cards.why: I include this because it tests whether one general-purpose adaptive representation can recognize a workload whose optimal cost is linear. The remaining gap is tiny numerically but significant mathematically: a proof would explain why expensive local restructuring cannot accumulate across arbitrary alternations of the two ends.
cards.definitions: Splaying uses the standard zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rules. Deletions are allowed only on a nonempty tree, and an inserted key must be outside the current key range at the specified end. Amortized cost is a bound on the total sequence, not a worst-case guarantee for each deletion. The initial tree may have any shape.

progress.text: Pettie proves \(O((n+m)\alpha^*(n+m))\) total cost, where \(\alpha^*\) counts how many iterations of the inverse-Ackermann function reduce the argument to a constant.
Levy and Tarjan connect the deque conjecture to a subsequence property sufficient for dynamic optimality. This provides a structural route to a proof, not the required linear bound itself.
The new analysis of splay competitiveness still describes the deque guarantee as nearly constant per operation. Its general search bound does not supply constant amortized deque cost.

cards.status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026, including the July 2026 splay result. The conjecture asks for linear total cost under insertions and deletions at either end.

context_blocks.text: A deque allows insertion and deletion at either end of a sequence. A linked representation can implement this abstract interface in constant time per operation. The conjecture concerns what happens when the same interface is implemented by a self-adjusting search tree: it asks whether the tree automatically achieves the linear total cost available for this restricted workload.

Deleting the minimum of a long left spine can require many rotations in a single operation. That does not disprove the conjecture, because the initial tree contributes an additive budget proportional to its size. The real difficulty is to understand whether alternating insertions and deletions at opposite ends can repeatedly rebuild expensive configurations.

For a concrete contrast, deleting keys in increasing order is a sequential-access pattern. A deque workload can switch ends after every operation and introduce new extreme keys between deletions. A bound for one monotone scan therefore does not immediately control this more flexible sequence.

The known total bound has an iterated inverse-Ackermann factor, which grows extraordinarily slowly but is asymptotically unbounded. Removing it would answer a structural question about how rotations reuse earlier work. This is a focused subproblem of the broader study of splaying, with updates included explicitly rather than only searches.

cards.title: Constant-update working-set heaps on pointer machines
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic online priority queue in the pointer-machine model below and an absolute constant C such that every legal sequence of M operations, starting from an empty queue, has total cost at most \(C(M+\sum_{x\ \mathrm{extracted}}\log \Gamma(x))\)? The operations are insert, find-min, decrease-key, and extract-min. For an extracted item x, define \(\Gamma(x)=1+\) the number of insertions strictly after x was inserted and before it was extracted, including inserted items that have already been removed. An insertion creates a distinct item and returns its handle; decrease-key receives that handle and its new key. Require exact answers for all sequences; melding is not required.
cards.definitions: Keys are opaque values in a totally ordered set and can only be compared; ties are broken by a fixed order on item identities. Find-min returns the minimum live item; extract-min also removes it. Decrease-key changes the key of an existing item to a no-larger value and does not reset its insertion time. A pointer machine has records containing O(1) pointers and O(1) auxiliary bits, together with the supplied key records. A fixed program operates through O(1) pointer registers. Charge one step for a key comparison, a pointer traversal or change, a constant-bit operation, or allocation of one constant-size record. It cannot perform address arithmetic or unit-cost operations on an unbounded auxiliary integer; larger counters must be explicitly represented and manipulated. All work between requests is charged. Amortization is over every finite sequence, including sequences leaving items in the queue.
cards.why: This is a basic test of whether temporal adaptivity and cheap priority changes can coexist without word-level machine tricks. A solution would clarify a model distinction in a fundamental graph-algorithm primitive. The small remaining factor makes it a sharper structural question than simply asking for a faster heap.

context_blocks.text: The usual priority-queue guarantee charges for extraction according to the number of stored items. A working-set guarantee instead takes account of how recently the extracted item entered the queue. For example, keep a large collection of expensive items present, repeatedly insert one smaller item, and immediately extract it. Each of these recent items has Gamma equal to one, so the proposed budget charges only a constant per such pair of requests. This illustrates the adaptive behavior that the question asks the implementation to exploit.

Fast decreases matter independently of these insertion times. A graph algorithm can discover a better tentative distance for an item that has been waiting for a long time. The interface gives the algorithm a handle to that item, but the queue still has to update the organization used to find its next minimum. Efficient extraction alone therefore does not settle the requested operation sequence bound.

The pointer restriction isolates the contribution of machine operations to this adaptivity. The July 2026 revision of van der Hoog and coauthors gives constant amortized insertion and working-set extraction, with inverse-Ackermann amortized decrease-key. That remaining factor is very slowly growing, but is asymptotically different from a constant.

A separate July 2026 construction achieves constant decrease-key with a stronger, stack-like extraction guarantee, while charging an iterated-log-star overhead to insertion. Its different trade-off is useful progress, but the joint constant-update target here still requires another argument. This card fixes the insertion-count definition of the working set and expresses the amortized question as a single total-cost inequality.

cards.title: Buffered fully persistent search trees
cards.formal: For every fixed \(0<\varepsilon<1\), can deterministic fully persistent comparison search trees in external memory support amortized update cost \(O(B^{\varepsilon-1}L_v)\), amortized successor queries \(O(L_v)\), sorted range reporting \(O(L_v+K/B)\), and cloning an arbitrary historical version in \(O(1)\) I/Os, with linear total space? Here \(L_v=1+\log_B(2+N_v)\), \(N_v\) is the size of the accessed version and \(K\) is the output size.
cards.definitions: The I/O model has block size \(B\ge2\), internal memory \(M\ge2B\) and unlimited external memory; only transfers of blocks between them are charged. Keys and version handles occupy constant space, and keys support comparisons only. Begin with an empty version. A branch may be extended by inserting or deleting a key, preserving every preceding version; cloning an arbitrary version creates a new independently extendible branch with the same set. All historical versions remain queryable. Search returns the least key at least the supplied key, or an empty marker; Range returns keys in a closed supplied interval. Require correctness for every online sequence. For \(U\) updates and \(C\) clones, linear total space means \(O(1+(U+C)/B)\) external blocks, including version metadata. All bounds may depend on the fixed \(\varepsilon\), but not on sizes, block parameters or the operation sequence. Amortized bounds must hold jointly over every finite history; buffering cannot postpone a query answer past its operation.
cards.why: Efficient historical branching together with buffered writes would combine two major capabilities of storage indexes without sacrificing their I/O savings.

context_blocks.text: The 2025 result obtains the buffered bounds with partial persistence: every historical version can be queried, but only the newest can be extended.

The paper separately describes constant-I/O cloning for unbuffered fully persistent trees and leaves efficient cloning with buffered full persistence open. This card fixes the simultaneous target rather than treating persistence and buffering separately.

cards.title: Combined depth and size bounds for confluently persistent tries
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge2\), does there exist a deterministic uniform functional trie representation and a constant \(C_k>0\) that supports the version, finger-navigation and subtree-copy interface below, with worst-case navigation time \(C_k\log_2(2+\Delta)\), no new permanent records from navigation, and both worst-case modification time and newly permanent record count at most \(C_k[1+\min\{D\log_2(2+\Delta),\log_2(2+N)\}]\) for every valid operation sequence?
cards.definitions:
A logical trie is a finite rooted tree, including its root, with distinct totally ordered labels on the outgoing edges of each node and one constant-size data atom per node. Logical occurrences are counted separately even when their physical representations share records. For each fixed integer \(k\ge2\), every stored version has \(k\) finger positions, possibly coincident. Selecting a version restores those positions in at most \(C_k\) operations; navigation changes a working copy of them. Reading a node’s data also costs at most \(C_k\) operations. These calls do not permit uncharged preprocessing. It can reset a finger to the root, move it to its parent, follow a child with a supplied label, or read the data at a finger. A failed parent or child move reports failure and leaves the finger unchanged. A modification creates a new stored version and leaves every previous version usable. It can change data at a finger, add a new leaf with an unused child label, remove the non-root subtree at a finger, or copy the subtree at a finger of any source version as a child with an unused label at a destination finger. The source and destination versions may coincide. The copy is a logical duplicate, so later changes to either occurrence do not change the other. Surviving destination fingers keep their logical positions; fingers in a removed subtree reset to the root. A copy may replace any specified subset of the resulting finger slots by counterparts of source fingers inside the copied subtree. Thus at most \(k\) fingers are stored in the resulting version. All parameters are supplied through version handles, finger indices and constant-size atoms; arbitrary logical nodes cannot be addressed directly.

Use a deterministic uniform pointer program with a fixed number of fields per record. A field holds a pointer, an opaque label or data atom, or an integer counter. Reading a field, comparing or copying atoms or pointers, comparing labels, and adding, subtracting or comparing counters cost one operation. New records may be initialized, but a previously initialized record is never overwritten. There is no pointer arithmetic, address-indexed array lookup, arithmetic on labels, random choice, oracle or nonuniform table. Counters have magnitude polynomial in the largest logical version size and operation count so far; costs count record operations, not their bit implementation. The program and field count are independent of all versions and operation sequences; constants may depend on the fixed finger bound \(k\). The initial version is a single root and costs \(O(k)\) operations and records.

For a modification, let \(N\) be the sum of the logical node counts of its participating input versions and its output version, counting a shared input only once. Let \(\Delta\ge2\) be the maximum of two and all node outdegrees in those versions. Let \(D=1+\sum_f\operatorname{depth}(f)\), summing the depths of the \(k\) stored or working fingers in each participating input version; root depth is zero. Define \(B=1+\min\{D\log_2(2+\Delta),\log_2(2+N)\}\). For navigation, \(\Delta\) is instead the maximum of two and the outdegrees in the selected logical version. Navigation must cost at most \(C_k\log_2(2+\Delta)\) operations, and a modification at most \(C_kB\) operations, in the worst case for every individual call in every finite valid sequence.

A record is permanent when reachable from any stored version handle, including that version’s stored finger representation. All stored versions remain available. Navigation may allocate temporary records but must leave the set of permanent records unchanged. A modification is charged every record newly made permanent by its result, including records allocated during earlier navigation; this count must be at most \(C_kB\). Existing permanent records shared by the new version are not charged again. Temporary allocation time is always charged to the call performing it; the permanent-space guarantee is not a bound on peak temporary storage. All logarithms and bounds use logical version sizes, not the number of previously allocated physical records.
cards.why: The question concerns whether persistent hierarchical data can exploit shallow or local changes while also protecting users against arbitrarily deep versions.

context_blocks.text: Version control must preserve old directory trees while allowing a whole directory to be copied between branches. A logical subtree copy can contain very many nodes, yet a representation can initially share their unchanged contents. Confluent persistence requires both source versions and all older versions to remain usable after this operation.

The source gives two functional representations. One exploits locality of finger operations with \(O(\log\Delta)\) time and allocation per call; navigation records can later become permanent. The other uses \(O(\log n)\) time and permanent space per modification, with \(O(\log\Delta)\) navigation time and no permanent navigation space. These are different guarantees because navigation may be followed by either another query or a modification.

An arbitrarily long path illustrates the size/depth distinction. A change near its root has small root depth even when the version is enormous, whereas a change near the bottom has large depth. The requested minimum would retain a shallow-update bound and also cap deep-update costs logarithmically in logical size. The question concerns one representation with simultaneous guarantees, not choosing a separate representation after seeing the next operation.

Charging only the records allocated inside the final update would conceal part of the first representation’s cost. Records produced by earlier finger moves count against the update if the new stored version retains them. Conversely, a navigation-only sequence produces no new stored versions, so discarded temporary work does not count as permanent history.

Editorial specification: Section 6 states the combined depth/size goal but leaves the multi-finger parameters implicit. This benchmark uses the sum of participating finger depths, a maximum degree over participating versions, and the sum of input/output logical sizes. With a fixed number of fingers these specify a single bound for copies and deletions; a one-finger point modification retains the root-depth scale \(1+d\). They are explicit conventions for the combined variant, not definitions quoted verbatim from the authors.

The source’s constant-time comparison of labels and functional pointer-record model are retained. This is not a claim about the cost of comparing arbitrary file-name strings, storing file contents, or implementing large counters in a bit machine. The documented temporary/permanent distinction is part of the target, rather than an unrecorded memory exemption.

cards.title: Deterministic fully dynamic connectivity with polylogarithmic worst-case updates
cards.formal:
Does there exist a finite deterministic word-RAM program \(A\), with fixed positive integer constants \(C,c,d,a\), such that for every integer \(n\ge2\) it maintains an initially empty simple undirected graph on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) under every finite valid online sequence of edge insertions, edge deletions and pairwise connectivity queries, with all the following guarantees?
\[\begin{aligned}
 \text{initialization time}&\le Cn^d,\\
 \text{total stored words at every time}&\le Cn^d,\\
 \text{time of each individual operation}&\le C(\log_2 n)^c.
\end{aligned}\]
Every query must return the exact connectivity bit. Initialization receives only \(n\); the word size is \(w=\lceil a\log_2 n\rceil\), and computation uses the machine conventions below. All constants and the same finite program are chosen before \(n\) or the operation sequence. Give a complete Lean proof of this existence proposition or its logical negation.
cards.definitions:
A graph state is a set \(E\subseteq\{\{u,v\}:u,v\in[n],\ u\ne v\}\), initially empty. An operation has a tag and two vertex labels, each supplied as one word. A valid \(\operatorname{insert}(u,v)\) requires distinct endpoints and an absent edge, and adds that edge. A valid \(\operatorname{delete}(u,v)\) requires a present edge and removes it. A query \(\operatorname{connected}(u,v)\) is valid for any \(u,v\in[n]\) and outputs one bit. Its answer is one exactly when there is a finite sequence \(u=x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_k=v\), with \(k\ge0\), whose consecutive pairs are edges of the current graph. In particular, a vertex is connected to itself. The graph has no additional promise on density, planarity, degree or expansion.

The machine must finish the current operation before the next is supplied. No operation count, future sequence, or complete input graph is available during initialization. The guarantee applies to every finite valid sequence of arbitrary length, including sequences selected using all previously observable states and answers. Persistent memory is bounded in terms of \(n\) alone, independently of the elapsed number of operations. Past output is write-only and cannot serve as free external storage.

Fix a word RAM with a finite instruction list and a fixed finite number of word registers. Words are unsigned integers in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\); memory addresses are also words. Each indirect load or store, register copy, comparison, conditional branch, Boolean bitwise operation, shift, and arithmetic operation on at most two words costs one step. Arithmetic primitives are addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer quotient and remainder. Addition, subtraction and multiplication return their result modulo \(2^w\); quotient and remainder use unsigned integer division and a zero divisor causes failure. A left shift discards bits outside the word; a right shift fills with zeros; either returns zero when the shift amount is at least \(w\). Reading an input word and writing the query bit also cost one step. The finite program can contain fixed integer constants, interpreted modulo \(2^w\), but has no oracle, random instruction, advice string or input-size-dependent instruction table. Any longer arithmetic computation pays for all constituent instructions.

Mutable registers and allocated memory, including every table and representation of the graph, count toward the stated space bound. Initially they contain only zeros except for the input \(n\); data-dependent initialization, allocation and zeroing of allocated words are charged. Every addressed location must be allocated and have a representable address. The fixed coefficient \(a\) may be chosen sufficiently large for the program's polynomial space; it cannot depend on \(n\) or sequence length. Polynomial preprocessing may depend only on \(n\), and all its computation and stored output count toward the initialization and space bounds. The program and its fixed finite control are independent of \(n\).

Time includes all graph maintenance, rebuilding, memory management, query computation and response output performed during that operation. No background work between operations is free. The operation bound is a worst-case bound for each individual call, not an average over a sequence or an expectation. Using positive integer constants is a normalization of the original polynomial-space and polylogarithmic-time bounds: enlarging constants or exponents absorbs fixed factors and small input sizes. It imposes no graph restriction.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of either
\[\exists A\ \exists C,c,d,a\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge2\ \forall s\in\mathcal S_n,\quad \operatorname{Guarantees}(A,C,c,d,a,n,s),\]
or its logical negation. Here \(A\) ranges over the finite deterministic programs just defined, \(\mathcal S_n\) is the set of all finite valid operation sequences, and \(\operatorname{Guarantees}\) includes initialization, termination, exact answers, memory use and the per-operation bounds in the statement. A positive answer must establish all guarantees for one program and constants that work for every \(n,s\). A negative answer must rule out every such program and every constant choice, equivalently show that each candidate fails a required guarantee for some size and finite valid sequence, with the empty sequence also testing initialization. Failure to terminate is a failure of the applicable time bound.

All memory and running-time statements must refer to the specified machine semantics. A lower bound for a restricted family of implementations, a single counterexample to one proposed algorithm, or a theorem requiring an unproved complexity assumption does not negate the full proposition. An amortized, randomized, expected-time, restricted-graph or offline guarantee does not prove it. This is an existence question, with no numerical tolerance or weaker intermediate target.
cards.why: Exact dynamic connectivity is a basic test of whether a graph data structure can guarantee uniformly low latency without randomness. The question separates efficient processing of a long sequence from a fast response after every individual change, and is relevant to graph algorithms that call connectivity as a subroutine.

importance.reason: A foundational dynamic-graph frontier directly relevant to data structures, with a new randomized breakthrough and an explicit remaining deterministic bottleneck.
