cards.title: Preprocessing exponent of binary jumbled indexing
cards.formal: Determine \(\alpha_{\mathrm{BJ}}\), the infimum of real \(a\ge1\) for which, for every rational \(\eta>0\), a uniform deterministic index for binary strings of length \(n\) has \(O(n^{a+\eta})\) worst-case preprocessing time, \(O(n)\) words of stored space and \(O(1)\) worst-case query time.
cards.definitions: The input is an explicit string \(T\in\{0,1\}^n\), with \(n\ge2\). A query is a pair of nonnegative integers \((u,v)\) with \(1\le u+v\le n\), and asks whether a contiguous substring has exactly \(u\) zeroes and \(v\) ones. Answers must be exact. All retained text and tables count toward space. Set \(L=n\). Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. Randomized algorithms, when explicitly permitted, may generate independent uniform random words. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. For each proposed \(a,\eta\), one finite construction/query pair and its constants must work for every \(n\) and every string; it receives no real parameter as input and may depend only on the chosen parameters. The infimum need not be attained. The cost of the original explicit input, indexing and output is included. The target is an exponent measured in powers of \(n\); no additive tolerance is applied to a big-O expression.

context_blocks.text: Jumbled matching ignores order inside a substring and retains only its symbol counts. A single index must answer queries of all lengths.
The binary case differs from the larger-alphabet variants for which Amir and coauthors prove conditional preprocessing/query barriers.
The 2026 monotone-convolution result yields deterministic preprocessing exponent at most \(3/2\) for the binary application.
The infimal exponent records the remaining asymptotic construction gap without counting a solved first-subquadratic result as open.

cards.why: A sharp construction exponent would identify the true cost of a basic order-insensitive text-search primitive and clarify its relation to structured convolution.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number \(a\) and a complete Lean-checked proof that its absolute distance from the defined exponent is at most \(1/100\). A certified enclosing interval of width at most \(1/50\) qualifies through its midpoint. Exact determination also qualifies. Both sides must concern the unrestricted quantity in this card; an assumed hardness conjecture proves only a conditional statement. Repeating the defining infimum or giving only an upper bound is insufficient.

cards.title: Polynomial-time construction of minimum-density DNA minimizers
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm and a universal constant \(C\) that, for all integers \(k,w\ge2\), output a total order \(\rho\) on the \(4^k\) DNA k-mers minimizing expected minimizer density exactly, in \(O((4^k+w)^C)\) bit operations?
cards.definitions: The fixed alphabet is \(\Sigma=\{A,C,G,T\}\). The input supplies \(k\) in binary and \(w\) in unary. The output lists every member of \(\Sigma^k\) once in order. For \(X\in\Sigma^{k+w}\), let \(p_0(X)\) be the smallest starting position in \(\{0,\ldots,w-1\}\) attaining the least k-mer under \(\rho\), and define \(p_1(X)\) in the same way over \(\{1,\ldots,w\}\). Define \(d(\rho)=4^{-(k+w)}|\{X:p_0(X)\ne p_1(X)\}|\). This is the expected sampling density on an independent uniform DNA sequence with leftmost tie-breaking. Optimality requires \(d(\rho)\le d(\pi)\) for every total order \(\pi\) on \(\Sigma^k\). Time is measured on a deterministic finite-tape Turing machine and includes all output bits and preprocessing. The same finite machine handles all \(k,w\), with no advice. The resource parameter is the explicit order-table size plus the unary window parameter; no claim of polynomial time in \(\log k+\log w\) is made.

context_blocks.text: Minimizers keep one selected k-mer from each sliding window, often reusing the same position across neighboring windows. Lower sampling density reduces the number of retained seeds.
GreedyMini asks whether minimum-density minimizers can be generated efficiently.
OptMini already provides exact exponential search and resolves various small parameter families.
The proposed target is efficient generation of a provably optimal order. Mere finite computability of the minimum density is already established and is not the question.

cards.title: Linear-space LZ77 random access
cards.formal: Given the greedy LZ77 parse with z phrases of a string $S[1..N]$ over an integer alphabet of size at most N, is there a deterministic word-RAM data structure using \(O(z)\) words in total that returns \(S[i]\) for any $1\le i\le N$ in worst-case \(O(\log  N)\) time? Words have $\Theta(\log N)$ bits. A phrase is a new literal or a longest prefix of the unparsed suffix having an occurrence starting earlier in S; overlapping copies are allowed. Space includes the stored parse and all query-support information. The uncompressed string is unavailable at query time.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a uniform data structure meeting both bounds for every greedy LZ77 parse, or prove that no such structure exists in the stated model. Linear space measured by a larger grammar or an LZ-End parse does not meet the \(O(z)\) requirement.
cards.why: I include this because compression is most useful when a small representation remains usable for selective queries. This question asks whether an extra logarithmic storage cost is an inherent price of navigating repeated data or a consequence of converting to a more convenient representation.
cards.definitions: All asymptotic constants are universal. The model permits standard arithmetic, multiplication, shifts, bitwise operations, comparisons, and indirect addressing on a constant number of words. A copied phrase beginning at b and referring to \(a<b\) is decoded sequentially, so self-overlap is well-defined. Preprocessing may take polynomial time in N; the target concerns final storage and query time, not construction in compressed time. Use \(1+\log  N\) at the smallest lengths.

progress.text: Ganardi, Jeż, and Lohrey show that a straight-line grammar can be balanced to logarithmic derivation depth with only constant-factor size growth. This settles the corresponding logarithmic-access target in terms of grammar size.
Gawrychowski explicitly asks for linear space in the Lempel–Ziv representation and logarithmic-time character access.

Boneh and Gawrychowski obtain deterministic \(O(z_{\mathrm{end}})\)-space random access in $O(1+\log^2(N/z_{\rm end}))$ time for LZ-End. Their introduction retains classical LZ77 random access as open and records $O(z\log(N/z))$-space solutions for it.

cards.status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026, including the July LZ-End result. The stated parse convention, space parameter, and deterministic query guarantee are explicit.

context_blocks.text: Lempel–Ziv compression replaces a repeated block by its earlier starting position and length. This can encode a long text with few phrases, but a position inside one copied phrase may lead to another copy, and then another. Random access asks for just one character without expanding the whole text.

The challenge is not that every deeply referenced string is hard. A long run of one repeated character can be accessed immediately once its simple structure is recognized. The target must work for arbitrary mixtures of copied material, where both the reference chains and the phrase lengths vary. Any shortcuts used to navigate those chains must fit in the compressed-space budget.

Converting the parse to a balanced grammar supplies a route to fast navigation, but the grammar can be larger than the original parse by a logarithmic factor. A space bound proportional to that grammar therefore need not be linear in z. Balancing a grammar already supplied as input is a different, solved representation problem.

The July 2026 LZ-End result is close in spirit: it obtains linear space and improved polylogarithmic access for a variant that restricts copy endpoints. Its parameter counts LZ-End phrases. Since the parsing rule and the number of phrases differ, those guarantees cannot be substituted directly for the classical LZ77 target.

cards.title: Faster elastic-degenerate string intersection
cards.formal: Does there exist a constant \(\varepsilon>0\) and a uniform classical randomized algorithm deciding intersection of two elastic-degenerate strings in \(\widetilde O(N_1+N_2+n_2N_1^{\omega-1-\varepsilon}+n_1N_2^{\omega-1-\varepsilon})\) worst-case time, with probability of correctness at least \(2/3\) on every input?
cards.definitions: An elastic-degenerate string \(E_i\) is an explicit list of \(n_i\ge1\) finite sets of distinct strings. Each set contains a nonempty string and may additionally contain the empty string. Its language consists of concatenations obtained by choosing one alternative from each set in order. Let \(N_i\) be the sum of the lengths of all alternatives, so \(N_i\ge n_i\). Delimiters are included in the encoding; the number of alternatives is at most \(2N_i\). Blocks containing only the empty string are omitted from this input convention. Symbols lie in \([0..(N_1+N_2)^2)\). The output says whether the two languages share any string; neither language is explicitly expanded. Set \(L=N_1+N_2\). Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. Randomized algorithms, when explicitly permitted, may generate independent uniform random words. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. Soft-O permits one fixed power of \(\log(L+2)\). Here \(\omega\) is the infimum of real exponents \(a\) such that square matrix multiplication over the rationals has uniform algebraic algorithms using \(O(t^{a+\eta})\) field operations for every fixed \(\eta>0\), with \(t\) the matrix dimension. The string algorithm need not be combinatorial. All constants and its finite program are independent of the input sizes.

context_blocks.text: A pangenome representation can store a sequence of alternative sequence fragments. Its represented language can be exponentially larger than the explicit alternatives.
The source gives an upper bound involving \(n_2N_1^{\omega-1}+n_1N_2^{\omega-1}\) and explicitly asks about a polynomial improvement in section 9.

The separate linear input term makes the target meaningful when the algebraic expression falls below the cost of reading the alternatives. It changes no requirement to compare entire represented languages.

cards.title: Input-optimal construction of compact inverse suffix arrays
cards.formal: Do there exist a uniform deterministic construction algorithm \(B\), a uniform deterministic query algorithm \(A\), and constants \(C_B,C_S,C_A>0\), such that for every \(n\ge2\) and every packed binary text \(T\in\{0,1\}^n\), \(B\) constructs a static index in at most \(C_B(1+n/\log_2(n+2))\) worst-case word-RAM steps, the retained index and query workspace together occupy at most \(C_S n\) bits, and \(A\) answers every query \(i\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) with \(\operatorname{ISA}_T[i]\) in at most \(C_A\) worst-case steps? All three constants and the programs are independent of \(n,T,i\). Both algorithms use the common word model specified below.
cards.definitions: The input supplies \(n\) and the consecutive bits of \(T\), packed into words with only the last word padded. \(\operatorname{ISA}_T[i]\) is the zero-based lexicographic rank of \(T[i..n)\) among all nonempty suffixes, with \(0<1\) and shorter proper prefixes first.  Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. No random bits are available. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. Every bit retained after construction, including the input if retained, counts toward the index. Query work storage is also charged to this bit bound. The construction time includes reading the packed input and writing every index word; no prebuilt instance-dependent structure is supplied. Query outputs are the exact integer rank in \(\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\), written in a word. The query routine has access only to the retained index, the size parameter and its query index. Its input-dependent working state does not persist as an additional uncharged store between queries. Construction workspace need not satisfy a separate linear-bit bound, but allocating, initializing and accessing it consumes the stated construction time. Space is measured in bits of all occupied words, including word padding. Binary input bits have a fixed agreed order within each word, and unused bits of the last word are zero. The logarithmic time bound is the packed-input scale in this word model.

context_blocks.text: The input-optimal construction endpoint is the editorial question approved for this card’s import. It strengthens the sublinear-construction questions discussed in the August 2026 source, which the source itself answers. The stronger endpoint is retained explicitly rather than attributed verbatim to the paper’s numbered questions. Its present openness has not been independently certified.

Kempa and Kociumaka’s August 2026 preprint states a deterministic \(O(n\log_2\sigma)\)-bit inverse suffix-array index with constant worst-case query time and construction time \(O(n\min\{1,\log_2\sigma/\sqrt{\log_2 n}\})\) for alphabet size \(2\le\sigma\le n\). For binary texts this gives \(O(n/\sqrt{\log_2 n})\), which is slower than the card’s \(O(n/\log_2 n)\) endpoint. Theorem 1.1 also bounds peak preprocessing space, an additional property of that result rather than an extra requirement on this card.

The preprint states that improving the construction time below its binary-text bound, while retaining sufficiently fast inverse queries, would improve the known time for Dictionary Matching. That is a conditional connection to another algorithmic task, not an unconditional lower bound excluding this card’s construction target.

Munro, Navarro and Nekrich’s CPM 2020 paper establishes sublinear deterministic construction for a compact text-search index. Its pattern-counting and occurrence-reporting guarantees concern different queries; that result does not itself give the constant-time inverse suffix-array functionality requested here.

cards.why: An inverse suffix-array query identifies the lexicographic position of a suffix without storing all ranks explicitly. A compact index with constant query time would be especially useful if its construction were as fast as processing the packed representation. The remaining construction gap tests a substantive barrier shared with other packed-string tasks.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence assertion or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify both fixed finite programs and prove exact suffix ranks for every binary text and every legal query, the construction bound, the total retained-bit bound and the constant worst-case query bound together. A negative answer must rule out all pairs of programs and all choices of their fixed constants in this model. A conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional implication. Linear space with slower queries, constant queries with more space, or sublinear construction slower than the displayed packed-input bound does not meet the full target.

cards.title: Linear-time LZ77 pattern matching
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, given a valid LZ77 representation of z phrases of a text T of length N and an explicit nonempty pattern P of length m, decides whether P occurs contiguously in T in \(O(z+m)\) worst-case time? Self-referencing copy phrases are allowed. Symbols are integers in $\{1,\ldots,(z+m)^c\}$ for a fixed constant c. Use a word RAM with word size $\Theta(\log(N+m+2))$, the operations specified below, and \(O(z+m)\) working words. The input is the compressed text and the explicit pattern; all preprocessing is included.
cards.answer_criterion: Give one uniform algorithm with the stated bounds for every valid input, or prove that no such algorithm exists in this model. The output is one yes/no answer. An algorithm linear in the uncompressed text length, or in a potentially larger grammar representation, does not attain this target.
cards.definitions: Each phrase is either one literal symbol or a pair \((s,l)\) instructing the decoder to append l symbols copied sequentially from an earlier starting position s in the text. For a phrase beginning at p, require \(1 \le  s < p\); the copied interval may overlap the phrase being produced. Phrase boundaries and references occupy \(O(1)\) words per phrase. No promise of a greedy parse is needed. The RAM has random access, comparisons, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division, and bitwise Boolean operations and shifts on a word at unit cost; arithmetic results are restricted to a word. There is no access to a separately stored decompressed text or precomputed index.
cards.why: This is a basic test of whether computation can follow the compressed input size rather than the size of the object it describes. Settling it would also clarify whether the representation gap between LZ77 and grammars creates an unavoidable algorithmic cost for a fundamental string operation.

progress.text: Gawrychowski gives deterministic \(O(z(1+\log (N/z))+m)\) time for LZ-compressed occurrence detection, including self-referential parses.
Ganardi and Gawrychowski obtain \(O(g+m)\) time when the supplied text representation is a grammar of size g. This resolves the grammar-input version.
Gawrychowski asks whether the Lempel–Ziv version can be solved in time linear in compressed-text size plus pattern length.

context_blocks.text: Ordinary pattern matching scans the text and pattern in linear time. That guarantee can be too expensive for compressed input: a short sequence of copy instructions may describe a text many orders of magnitude larger than the representation. Here the algorithm only has to determine whether an occurrence exists, so a large number of matches does not force a large output.

A match can cross phrase boundaries or occur inside a repeated region. For example, a pattern may start near the end of one copied block and finish in the next. Inspecting each phrase in isolation therefore misses valid occurrences. The challenge is to summarize enough boundary and periodicity information while charging only constant total work per input phrase and pattern symbol.

Grammar compression provides an instructive comparison. Linear-time pattern matching is known when the input is a straight-line grammar, but converting an LZ77 representation to an appropriate grammar can increase its size. The existing grammar algorithm therefore does not immediately give linear time measured in z.

The 2025 seminar question explicitly retains the Lempel–Ziv target. This card fixes the decision version, permits self-references, and charges preprocessing. These choices prevent a reporting cost or an uncharged text index from changing the question.

cards.title: Grammar random access in \(O(g \log  g)\) bits
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic data structure that, for every binary straight-line program G with g rules generating a binary string T of length N, stores a representation in $O(g\log(g+2))$ bits and returns \(T[i]\) for any $1\le i\le N$ in $O(\log(N+2))$ worst-case time? Preprocessing must take time polynomial in g and is given G, not an expanded copy of T. The space bound includes every persistent index and any retained grammar. Use the word-RAM model below. The representation may replace G; it need only answer queries to T correctly.
cards.definitions: A binary straight-line program has ordered variables \(X_{1},\ldots ,X_{g}\), one rule per variable, and start variable \(X_{g}\). A rule is \(X_{j} -> 0, X_{j} -> 1\), or \(X_{j} -> X_{a} X_{b}\) with \(a,b < j\). All variables must be reachable from the start variable. Expansion is unique and finite; g counts rules, not expanded occurrences. The input specifies rule types and indices in \(O(g \log (g+2))\) bits. Machine words have $\Theta(\log(N+g+2))$ bits; random access, comparisons, word addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division, Boolean operations, and shifts cost one step. Arithmetic results are restricted to a word. Stored bits may be packed; charge the final partially filled word as well. Queries may use \(O(\log (N+2))\) temporary words, initially empty and discarded afterward; this workspace contains no persistent advice. Every input-dependent table retained between queries counts toward the representation budget.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a uniform representation, preprocessing algorithm, and query algorithm satisfying all bounds for every valid G, or prove that no such data structure exists. Space linear in g machine words is insufficient when log N is asymptotically larger than log g. A scheme whose preprocessing first expands an exponentially longer T does not meet the polynomial-in-g preprocessing requirement.
cards.why: Random access is the simplest useful operation on a compressed string. Resolving this target would determine whether the extra address-length information is an inherent price of efficient access or an artifact of current representations, and would make the distinction between compressed bits and machine words precise.

importance.reason: A basic compressed-space versus access-time frontier at the bit level, relevant to many grammar-based operations. The fixed logarithmic target gives a sharper scope than the broader random-access trade-off landscape.

progress.text: Navarro asks whether efficient grammar random access can avoid the extra space used to store all expansion lengths.
Takasaka and I obtain space-efficient SLP encodings supporting logarithmic access; their leading expansion-length term remains g log N in this card’s notation.

Duyster and Kociumaka sharpen and largely match grammar random-access trade-offs in their stated parameter regimes. Theorem 1.1 assumes a space budget above g log N bits; it does not supply the representation asked for here.

context_blocks.text: A grammar rule stores references to smaller pieces, so its two references need only logarithmically many bits in the number of rules. A position in the expanded string can require many more bits. For example, a short chain of doubling rules can describe an exponentially long string. This difference is why a space bound stated in machine words can hide a substantial overhead relative to the grammar encoding.

To locate a position inside a concatenation, the usual navigation step compares that position with the length of the left expansion. Storing an exact expanded length with every variable is straightforward, but can consume g log N bits. The target asks whether this information can be organized or recovered using a representation comparable in bits to the original grammar, while keeping logarithmic access time.

The April 2026 encoding result improves the grammar representation and keeps logarithmic query time, but retains a g log N expansion-length term. The authors explicitly distinguish their encoding savings from removing that term. Their observation supports treating the latter as a separate question.

ICALP 2026 gives much sharper time-space trade-offs in a broad range of parameters. Its main upper-bound theorem uses a space budget above the g log N scale. Consequently, the optimality statements in that range do not automatically settle the smaller bit budget here. This card fixes logarithmic query time, a binary alphabet, polynomial preprocessing, and explicit workspace rules as a concrete specialization of the seminar’s fewer-auxiliary-bits direction.

cards.title: Fully functional suffix trees in BWT-run-linear space
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic static representation of the compact suffix tree of every binary text with a terminal sentinel, using \(O(r)\) words and supporting every operation listed below in \(O((\log(n+2))^c)\) worst-case time for one fixed constant \(c\), where \(n\) is text length and \(r\) its number of BWT runs?
cards.definitions: The input is \(T\in\{0,1\}^{n-1}\#\), with \(n\ge2\) and \(\#<0<1\). Its suffix tree is the trie of all nonempty suffixes with maximal nonbranching paths contracted; edge labels are nonempty substrings. Leaves are ordered by suffix lexicographic rank. The suffix array \(\operatorname{SA}[i]\) is the starting position of leaf rank \(i\), and \(\operatorname{ISA}\) its inverse. Define \(\operatorname{BWT}[i]=T[(\operatorname{SA}[i]-1)\bmod n]\); \(r\) counts maximal nonempty intervals of equal BWT symbols. A node is identified by its inclusive interval of descendant leaf ranks, two word-sized integers. Required operations return the root; parent; lexicographically first child; next sibling; child whose edge starts with a supplied symbol; edge-count depth; root-to-node string length; lowest common ancestor of two nodes; and, for a nonroot internal node with path label \(aU\), the suffix-link node with label \(U\). Also required are a leaf by rank, \(\operatorname{SA}\), \(\operatorname{ISA}\), and \(T[i]\). Missing parents, children and siblings return a distinguished marker. Set \(L=n\). Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. Randomized algorithms, when explicitly permitted, may generate independent uniform random words. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. All text, samples, handles retained internally, and temporary query work count toward space. Externally supplied or returned node handles have constant word size. Construction takes polynomial time in \(n\), including all tables. The terminal sentinel is unique and included in \(n\) and \(r\).

cards.title: Certifying Karp–Rabin fingerprints
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(c\ge2\), is there a uniform randomized algorithm that, given a string \(T\in\{0,\ldots,\sigma-1\}^n\), with \(n\ge2\), \(2\le\sigma\le n^c\), and a supplied prime \(p\le n^c\), certifies in \(O(n\log n)\) worst-case time whether the Karp–Rabin fingerprint modulo \(p\) is collision-free on all equal-length substrings of \(T\)? No input having a collision may ever be certified; every collision-free input must be certified with probability at least \(2/3\).
cards.definitions: A uniform sequential word RAM has a fixed finite program, word-sized registers and addressed memory cells. Unit-cost instructions are reads and writes, comparisons, branching, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division with nonzero divisor, Boolean bit operations and logical shifts. Arithmetic stored in one word is modulo \(2^w\); shifts by at least \(w\) yield zero. Addresses must fit the available word size. All table construction and input-dependent auxiliary memory count; there is no free advice or input-dependent oracle. Randomized programs may generate independent uniform random words. The input symbols and prime are given as integers; primality is promised. Use \(w=\lceil(4c+10)\log_2(n+2)\rceil\)-bit words, so a constant number of words suffices for all modular products. For length \(\ell\ge1\) and start \(0\le i\le n-\ell\), define \(h_p(T[i..i+\ell-1])=\sum_{j=0}^{\ell-1}T[i+j]\sigma^j\bmod p\). A collision is a triple \((i,j,\ell)\) of valid starts and a length for which the two strings differ but their fingerprints are equal. Equal strings with equal fingerprints are not collisions; fingerprints of different lengths need not be separated. The algorithm returns CERTIFIED or REJECT. The probability is over its internal random bits for each fixed \((T,\sigma,p)\); false rejection is permitted only with probability at most \(1/3\) on collision-free inputs. The given prime and base must be preserved. All preprocessing counts toward time, space is at most the number of words writable in that time, and there is no externally supplied suffix index or precomputed table.
cards.why: Efficient certification could turn a widely used probabilistic string primitive into a reliable one while preserving a chosen fingerprint representation.

cards.title: Constant-factor universally truthful auctions for submodular bidders
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C\ge 1\) and a randomized, universally truthful combinatorial-auction mechanism that, for every number n of bidders, number m of items and normalized monotone submodular valuation profile, uses polynomial communication and produces an allocation of expected social welfare at least OPT/C?
cards.definitions: There are \(m\ge 1\) distinct indivisible items and \(n\ge 1\) bidders. Bidder i privately knows \(v_{i}:2^{[m]}\to Q_{\ge 0}\), with \(v_{i}(\varnothing )=0, v_{i}(S)\le v_{i}(T)\) for \(S\subseteq T\), and \(v_{i}(S)+v_{i}(T)\ge v_{i}(S\cup T)+v_{i}(S\cap T)\) for all S,T. To make communication in bits precise, a public integer \(B\ge 1\) bounds the binary lengths of the numerator and positive denominator of each value. This is a bound per value, not permission to transmit the exponential table. One uniform protocol must work for every n,m,B with at most \(\mathrm{P}(n,m,B)\) communicated bits in the worst case, for one fixed polynomial P. Arbitrary interactive messages and demand queries are allowed; all query descriptions, replies, allocations and payments count toward communication. Local computation by bidders and auctioneer is unrestricted but must terminate. An outcome consists of pairwise disjoint bundles \(S_{1},\ldots ,S_{n}\) and rational payments \(p_{1},\ldots ,p_{n}\); unallocated items are allowed. Utilities are quasilinear, \(u_{i}=v_{i}(S_{i})- p_{i}\). There are no private budgets or distributional assumptions. Universal truthfulness means the mechanism is a report-independent distribution over deterministic dominant-strategy truthful mechanisms: for every fixed random seed r, every i, every admissible true and alternative reported type \(v_{i},v_{i}'\), and every \(v_{- i}, v_{i}(S_{i}(v_{i},v_{- i};r))- p_{i}(v_{i},v_{- i};r)\ge v_{i}(S_{i}(v_{i}' ,v_{- i};r))- p_{i}(v_{i}' ,v_{- i};r)\). A low-communication protocol implements this outcome and payment rule on the distributed reported types. OPT=\(\max  \sum_{i} v_{i}(T_{i})\), where the maximum is over pairwise disjoint \(T_{i}\subseteq [m]\). context_blocks.text: A bidder may value several items as substitutes. For example, a coverage valuation assigns each item a set of useful features and values a bundle by the total weight of features covered at least once. Receiving an item has less marginal value when many of its features are already covered. Submodularity abstracts this diminishing-returns property without requiring the valuation to be supplied as an explicit coverage instance.

The auctioneer must allocate the items using information held by strategic bidders. Maximizing the sum of their values is the social-welfare objective; maximizing the auctioneer’s revenue would be a different problem. Payments influence what information bidders choose to provide, but are transfers and do not enter the welfare objective. Even a very poor revenue guarantee would be acceptable here if incentives and welfare met the stated requirements.

Two established results cover separate parts of the requirements. With complete reports and unrestricted resources, the Vickrey–Clarke–Groves mechanism obtains optimal welfare and truthful incentives. If incentives are omitted, submodular welfare admits constant-factor approximation from compact queries. The difficulty is combining the guarantees while avoiding communication of exponentially many bundle values. The 2026 graph-auctions paper describes this communication perspective explicitly.

Universal truthfulness is a strong use of randomization: each mechanism obtained after fixing the coins must itself make truthful reporting optimal. Truthfulness in expectation requires only that the average utility discourage lying. The distinction has mathematical force; Dobzinski and Dughmi separate the two notions in a restricted multi-unit setting. Their separation is useful background, but their multi-unit approximation scheme does not supply a mechanism for arbitrary heterogeneous submodular valuations.

A demand query offers item prices and asks a bidder to choose a bundle maximizing its value minus its total price. Sending that bundle requires only m membership bits, even when finding it takes enormous local computation. This is why allowing demand queries changes the problem substantially. The formulation deliberately measures communication: an algorithm that delegates difficult optimization to a bidder can qualify. It would need further work to become computationally efficient for that bidder.

Dobzinski’s impossibility theorem rules out universally truthful \(m^{1/2- \varepsilon}\)-approximation using polynomially many value queries, for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\). A value query reveals only one specified bundle’s value. The theorem is a genuine barrier in that access model, but it cannot be extended by simply treating a demand query as one more value query. A demand answer can encode the result of comparing exponentially many bundles.

Assadi and Singla reached an expected \(O((\log  \log  m)^{3})\) approximation using \(O(n)\) demand queries, at FOCS 2019. Assadi, Kesselheim and Singla subsequently improved the submodular guarantee to \(O((\log  \log  m)^{2})\), while obtaining \(O((\log  \log  m)^{3})\) for the broader subadditive class. These asymptotic factors grow with the number of items, despite growing very slowly.

The latter mechanism learns approximate item prices through random groups of bidders. A bidder participates in a single fixed-price auction, so its own report cannot manipulate the menu it faces. Some price-learning rounds can become the final allocation rather than merely gathering information; the analysis accounts for welfare earned in those rounds. This makes price discovery compatible with truthfulness, but leaves a loss between the learned allocation and optimal welfare.

Recent positive results for graph auctions restrict each item to a small set of eligible bidders. For example, the 2026 paper gives a truthful factor-two mechanism when each item has two eligible bidders and valuations are subadditive. This structural restriction supplies information absent in a general auction, so it does not settle the present question. A general constant-factor mechanism would show that exact incentive compatibility need not impose an unbounded welfare loss in this central communication model.

cards.title: Existence of complete EFX allocations for additive valuations
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: For all integers \(n\ge4\) and \(m\ge0\), and every matrix \((v_{ig})_{i\in[n],g\in[m]}\) of nonnegative real values, does there exist a complete allocation \((A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) such that \(\sum_{h\in A_i}v_{ih}\ge\sum_{h\in A_j\setminus\{g\}}v_{ih}\) for every \(i,j\in[n]\) and every \(g\in A_j\) satisfying \(v_{ig}>0\)?
cards.why: Asks whether an indivisible allocation can always control every agent’s envy after the removal of any positively valued good, while distributing all goods. It tests a stronger fairness guarantee than EF1 even before imposing computational efficiency.

cards.definitions: For an integer \(k\ge0\), write \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). There are \(n\) agents and \(m\) indivisible goods. The finite nonnegative real number \(v_{ig}\) is agent \(i\)'s value for good \(g\); her value for a bundle \(S\subseteq[m]\) is \(v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S}v_{ig}\). A complete allocation is an ordered partition \((A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) into pairwise disjoint subsets whose union is \([m]\); empty bundles are allowed and every good is allocated exactly once. Envy-freeness up to any positively valued good (EFX) means that, for all agents \(i,j\) and all \(g\in A_j\) with \(v_{ig}>0\), one has \(v_i(A_i)\ge v_i(A_j\setminus\{g\})\). Both the positivity test and the comparison use agent \(i\)'s valuation. If all goods in \(A_j\) have value zero for \(i\), there is no inequality for that pair. Values need not be rational or strictly positive. No payments, chores, discarded goods, randomized allocations, or efficiency requirement are present. This uses the positive-good convention of Definition 5 in the cited survey; the stronger per-allocation condition EFX-zero also tests goods with value zero.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence for every valuation matrix in the stated domain, or prove its negation in Lean: there are finite \(n\ge4\), \(m\ge0\), and nonnegative additive valuations for which every complete partition violates at least one of the stated EFX inequalities. The target is existence, with no algorithmic, efficiency or stronger fairness requirement.

context_blocks.text: Indivisibility prevents ordinary envy-freeness even in the smallest examples. If four people all value a single good at one, whoever receives it is envied by the others. The allocation nevertheless satisfies EFX: removing that good leaves an empty bundle. EFX permits this unavoidable envy while limiting envy that survives the removal of any positively valued item. The removal is a hypothetical comparison; the actual allocation still assigns every good.

The word “any” makes the guarantee demanding. Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 4 and another bundle’s two goods at 6 and 1. Removing the 6-valued good eliminates her envy, so this pair satisfies the weaker EF1 test. Removing the 1-valued good leaves value 6, so this pair violates EFX. All comparisons use the potentially envious agent’s values, which can differ from the recipient’s.

Zero values require a convention. If an agent has value zero for her own bundle and values the goods in another bundle at 1 and 0, removing the positively valued good passes this card’s test. Requiring removal of the zero-valued good to pass as well would fail. That stronger condition on an individual allocation is often called \(\mathrm{EFX}_{0}\). The problem statement retains the survey’s positive-good EFX convention.

For three additive agents, Chaudhury, Garg and Mehlhorn prove complete EFX existence for any number of goods. Thus the universal question starts at four agents; it is the unrestricted number of goods at that first unresolved agent count that already presents a difficulty.

The four-agent theorem of Berger, Cohen, Feldman and Fiat leaves at most one good unassigned. Completeness matters: adding that final good can create new envy, so an almost complete allocation does not itself answer the stated question.

In August 2026, Alkassar, Fouz and Mehlhorn reported complete \(\mathrm{EFX}_{0}\) existence for four agents and at most nine goods, allowing arbitrary nonnegative real values. Their theorem uses reductions and a computational certificate corpus. \(\mathrm{EFX}_{0}\) implies the EFX condition here, but the bounded number of goods leaves the unrestricted target open. The theorem’s stated scope was checked; its computations were not rerun.

Recent nonexistence results concern broader valuation classes. Mackenzie and Suzuki give counterexamples with submodular and subadditive valuations, where the value of a bundle need not equal the sum of its individual goods’ values. Such examples do not meet the additive hypothesis on this card. Likewise, a chores result concerns unwanted items and a different fairness comparison.

The issue is existence for every input valuation matrix, without an efficiency requirement. An affirmative theorem would guarantee a complete allocation with this strong relaxation of envy-freeness. A negative answer needs one additive instance in the stated domain for which every complete partition fails; finding a poor allocation or a failing allocation algorithm is insufficient.

cards.title: Constant-factor approximation for Santa Claus
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: Is there a universal constant \(C\ge 1\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that allocates indivisible items with arbitrary nonnegative additive agent-specific values so that, with probability at least \(2/3\), every agent receives total value at least OPT/C, where OPT is the largest achievable minimum agent value?
cards.definitions: An input consists of \(n\ge 1\) agents, \(m\ge 1\) items and an explicit \(n\times m\) matrix \((v_{ij})\) of nonnegative rational values, encoded by binary numerators and positive binary denominators. Agent i values a bundle \(S\subseteq [m]\) at \(v_{i}(S)=\sum_{j\in S}v_{ij}\). An allocation is a tuple of pairwise disjoint bundles \((S_{1},\ldots ,S_{n})\); unallocated items are permitted. Its value is \(F(S_{1},\ldots ,S_{n})=\min _{i\in [n]}v_{i}(S_{i})\), and OPT is the maximum of F over all allocations. Let L be the total input bit length. There must be one algorithm, one C independent of n,m and all numerical values, and one polynomial P such that the algorithm always outputs a feasible allocation within \(\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{L})\) bit operations, for every random tape, and \(\Pr [F\ge \operatorname{OPT}/C]\ge 2/3\) on every input. The probability refers only to the algorithm’s independent internal random bits and requires the guarantee for all agents simultaneously. A deterministic algorithm is allowed as a special case. Zero values and OPT=0 are allowed, and no positive lower bound on OPT is supplied. The input values are used as given: one may not rescale each agent separately without changing the optimization problem. No identical-valuation, restricted-assignment, bounded-number-of-agents, bounded-number-of-values or bounded-item-degree assumption is imposed. All values are available to a centralized algorithm; incentives, payments and valuation oracles are not part of this problem.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a polynomial-time algorithm achieving the stated guarantee for some fixed C, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Hardness results conditional on a complexity assumption must identify that assumption, including the distinction between deterministic and randomized algorithms. A factor depending on the number of items or agents, a quasi-polynomial-time constant approximation, an estimate without an allocation, or an expected-value guarantee separately for each agent does not meet the target.

cards.status_note: The SODA 2024 reduction paper and SODA 2025 submodular paper explicitly retain the general additive constant-approximation question. Later checked constant guarantees concern restricted assignment or identical valuations, not arbitrary additive matrices. No general resolution found through 11 September 2026. context_blocks.text: The objective protects the least satisfied participant. Suppose two agents value each of two items at one. Allocating one item to each gives minimum value one, whereas giving both items to either agent gives minimum value zero. A lottery that gives both items to a uniformly chosen agent gives each agent expected value one, but its minimum value is always zero. This illustrates why the guarantee must concern the quality of one simultaneous allocation.

Even additive values allow substantial heterogeneity: an item can be extremely valuable to one agent, moderately valuable to another, and worthless to a third. Maximizing total welfare would assign each item to an agent valuing it most, independently of the other items. Maximizing minimum welfare couples those decisions because every agent needs adequate value from resources that cannot be reused. The valuations are inputs to the optimization problem, without strategic reporting constraints.

The name Santa Claus is used differently across papers. Some reserve it for restricted assignment, where each item j has a single intrinsic value \(w_{j}\) and \(v_{ij}\) is either \(w_{j}\) or zero. This card uses the broader max-min allocation problem with arbitrary entries. The difference is decisive: constant-factor algorithms are known for restricted assignment, while the general constant-factor question remains open.

Chakrabarty, Chuzhoy and Khanna give an approximation within \(m^{\varepsilon}\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\), where m is the number of items in this card’s notation. Their approximation–time tradeoff also yields a polylogarithmic factor in quasi-polynomial time. Choosing a smaller fixed \(\varepsilon\) improves the approximation exponent but increases the polynomial running-time exponent. Letting \(\varepsilon\) depend on m to try to force a constant factor does not preserve the known polynomial-time guarantee.

Their work also highlights a limitation of a standard configuration relaxation. For a target T, a configuration for agent i is a bundle worth at least T; fractional variables select configurations while respecting item capacities in aggregate. Integral feasible configurations would give every agent enough value. In the general setting, however, the relaxation can overestimate the integral optimum by a factor of order \(\sqrt{n}\). The algorithm uses the relaxation recursively on transformed instances, instead of relying on a constant-loss rounding of its original optimum.

Restricted assignment has stronger structure. This is a bound on the distance between fractional and integral optima in the restricted model. It does not assert a 3.534 algorithm for the arbitrary-value matrix, and an existence argument for a good integral solution must be distinguished from an efficient way to construct it.

There is a striking link with minimizing makespan on unrelated machines. Bamas, Lindermayr, Megow, Rohwedder and Schlöter show that a \((2- 1/\alpha )\)-approximation for unrelated makespan, for fixed \(\alpha \ge 2\), would yield an \((\alpha +\delta )\)-approximation for general Santa Claus for every fixed \(\delta >0\). Thus any fixed improvement below two in that scheduling problem would answer this question positively. Their general implication goes in this direction; equivalence is established for a specified two-value case.

Bamas, Morell and Rohwedder’s SODA 2025 result extends the \(m^{\varepsilon}\) and quasi-polynomial polylogarithmic guarantees to arbitrary monotone submodular valuations. It uses a recursively structured LP with exponentially many variables and constraints. This broadens the class of preferences that can be handled, while retaining a growing approximation factor even on the additive instances considered here.

More recent constant guarantees also require attention to their input promise. Boehmer’s April 2026 paper obtains value at least 0.4OPT for identical monotone submodular valuations. Identical preferences are a substantial restriction, even though submodularity is more general than additivity. The outstanding question concerns unrestricted disagreement about item values. Settling it would clarify whether balancing heterogeneous indivisible resources admits a constant loss at polynomial computational cost.

cards.title: Randomized truthful unrelated-machine scheduling
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors as \(m\to \infty\), the function \(R(m)\): the infimum worst-case expected-makespan approximation ratio achievable by truthful-in-expectation mechanisms with monetary payments for m unrelated machines and an arbitrary number of indivisible jobs. The infimum ranges over all mechanisms, without a computational or communication restriction. In particular, is \(R(m)=\Theta (1)\)?
cards.definitions: There are \(m\ge 2\) machines and \(n\ge 1\) jobs. Machine i privately knows a vector \(t_{i}\in R_{\ge 0}^{n}\); processing a set S costs it \(\sum_{j\in S}t_{ij}\). Every entry is finite. A direct-revelation mechanism maps reported vectors \(b=(b_{1},\ldots ,b_{m})\) to a distribution over assignments \(\sigma :\{1,\ldots ,n\}\to \{1,\ldots ,m\}\) and payments to the machines. Jobs are indivisible and every job is assigned exactly once. Let \(x_{ij}(b)=\Pr [\sigma (j)=i]\) and let \(p_{i}(b)\) be the finite expected payment to i. Risk-neutral utility is payment minus true processing cost. Truthfulness in expectation means that for every i, true \(t_{i}\), alternative report \(b_{i}\) and fixed reports \(b_{- i}, p_{i}(t_{i},b_{- i})- \sum_{j} t_{ij}x_{ij}(t_{i},b_{- i})\ge p_{i}(b_{i},b_{- i})- \sum_{j} t_{ij}x_{ij}(b_{i},b_{- i})\). This is a dominant-strategy condition against arbitrary fixed reports, without a prior on types. The makespan is \(C(\sigma ,t)=\max _{i} \sum_{j:\sigma (j)=i}t_{ij}\), and \(\operatorname{OPT}(t)=\min _{\sigma} C(\sigma ,t)\). For each m, consider a family \(M=(M_{m,n})_{n\ge 1}\) satisfying this incentive condition for every n and report profile. Its ratio is \(\sup _{n,t:\operatorname{OPT}(t)>0} E[C(M_{m,n}(t),t)]/\operatorname{OPT}(t)\), and it must also have expected makespan zero when \(\operatorname{OPT}(t)=0\). \(R(m)\) is the infimum of those ratios. Random assignments may be correlated across jobs. No budget balance, bound on transfers, individual-rationality constraint, anonymity, task independence or efficient representation is imposed. Since only expected utilities matter, payments can equivalently be deterministic amounts \(p_{i}(b)\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give an explicit asymptotic scale \(f(m)\) and universal constants \(a,b>0\) such that a \(f(m)\le R(m)\le b f(m)\) for all sufficiently large m, with matching incentive-theoretic lower bounds and mechanisms achieving the upper scale. A constant-factor mechanism for all numbers of machines and jobs would settle the target as \(\Theta (1)\). Showing only that \(R(m)\) is unbounded would rule out that possibility but would not determine the requested asymptotic order without matching bounds. Restrictions on the mechanism class or input distributions must not be silently added.

cards.status_note: The Nisan–Ronen proof, now published in JACM in February 2026, resolves only deterministic truthful mechanisms. Its randomized discussion records \(2- 1/m\) and \((m+5)/2\) bounds. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no matching unrestricted randomized bounds; results for task-independent mechanisms, fractional objectives, Bayesian types or no-payment models do not resolve this formulation.

context_blocks.text: A machine has a reason to exaggerate how long jobs take: receiving fewer jobs reduces its work. Payments are intended to counteract that incentive while keeping the overall schedule short. The private information is a whole vector, since a machine may be fast on one job and slow on another. A single speed parameter would describe a different and substantially more structured scheduling model.

The optimization objective creates the difficulty. Minimizing total processing cost can be implemented truthfully by a VCG mechanism, which assigns each job to a cheapest machine. But total cost and makespan differ. The largest load is at most the total cost, while the total cost of an optimal makespan schedule is at most m times its makespan. Thus this familiar truthful rule gives an m-approximation. Without incentive constraints and with unlimited computation, one could simply choose an optimal assignment.

Christodoulou, Koutsoupias and Kovács prove that the factor m is unavoidable for deterministic truthful mechanisms, resolving the Nisan–Ronen conjecture. Their result appeared as a 2023 preprint and in the Journal of the ACM in February 2026. It is an unconditional incentive restriction, independent of computational hardness. The paper’s related-work discussion expressly separates the unresolved randomized setting from this deterministic conclusion.

There are two different ways to randomize truthfully. A universally truthful mechanism draws a deterministic truthful mechanism before seeing the reports. Truthfulness in expectation only asks that honest reporting maximize expected utility; individual random outcomes need not implement truthful rules on their own. Universal truthfulness implies the latter condition, but the definition in this card permits the larger class. Mu’alem and Schapira nevertheless prove a lower bound of \(2- 1/m\) even for that larger class.

Randomization already helps when there are two machines. Lu and Yu’s STACS 2008 mechanism is universally truthful and beats the deterministic factor two. Their later WINE 2008 paper gives a truthful-in-expectation mechanism with ratio \((m+5)/2\) for general m, using a fractional allocation and a suitable rounding procedure. The improvement is substantial in its leading constant, but the guarantee still grows linearly with the number of machines.

The WINE paper also proves a lower bound \((m+1)/2\) for its task-independent class. A mechanism in the full question may use all reported jobs together and correlate their assignments. Consequently, a lower bound that treats each job separately does not close the gap between the general constant lower bound and linear upper bound. Whether such global dependence can change the asymptotic answer is part of what makes this question interesting.

Expected makespan must be distinguished from the largest expected machine load. Consider m identical machines and m unit jobs. Assigning all jobs to one uniformly random machine gives expected load one on every machine, yet the makespan is always m. Assigning one job per machine has makespan one. Thus the same marginal load target can conceal a factor-m difference in the objective. A truthful fractional solution, or an argument that controls only marginal probabilities, needs a valid rounding analysis before it yields a guarantee for this card.

Fine numerical results for small cases illuminate mechanisms without settling the asymptotic problem. Kuryatnikova and Vera obtain almost matching bounds near 1.505996 for two machines and two jobs within a class of randomized monotone scale-free algorithms. Their paper does not identify the optimal ratio over every truthful-in-expectation mechanism, every job count and a growing number of machines. Both the input restriction and mechanism restriction matter when interpreting the result.

The final question is whether allowing random outcomes fundamentally reduces the price of truthful multidimensional cost reporting. A constant answer would permit useful load balancing despite unrestricted private processing times. A growing lower bound would show that even risk-neutral incentives and unrestricted payments cannot recover the efficiency available to a scheduler who knows the true costs. Matching bounds would quantify that loss as a function of system size.

cards.title: Polynomial query complexity of exact envy-free cake cutting
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: Do absolute constants \(C,d>0\) and a deterministic Robertson–Webb protocol exist that, for every n and every profile of n nonatomic additive cake valuations, use at most \(Cn^{d}\) queries to produce a complete exactly envy-free allocation, allowing disconnected pieces?
cards.definitions: The cake is \([0,1]\). Agent i has an arbitrary nonatomic Borel probability measure \(\mu _{i}\): values are nonnegative, countably additive, \(\mu _{i}([0,1])=1\) and \(\mu _{i}(\{x\})=0\) for every point x. No density formula, bounded-density promise or random valuation model is supplied. The protocol learns valuations only through exact queries: \(Eval(i,x,y)\) returns \(\mu _{i}([x,y]); Cut(i,x,\alpha )\), with \(0\le \alpha \le \mu _{i}([x,1])\), returns a point \(y\ge x\) for which \(\mu _{i}([x,y])=\alpha\). Endpoints used by the protocol are 0, 1 and previously returned cut marks; interval values can be combined by additivity. If several cut points satisfy a query, the protocol must remain correct for any valid response. Count each evaluation or cut query as one; finite exact computation on the transcript is allowed without a bit-complexity bound. Output a partition \((A_{1},\ldots ,A_{n})\) of the entire cake into finite unions of intervals with endpoints among the known marks. Assign cut endpoints arbitrarily, since every agent values them at zero. Require \(\mu _{i}(A_{i})\ge \mu _{i}(A_{j})\) for every ordered pair i,j. There is no unallocated residue, approximation error, randomization, or connected-piece requirement. The bound \(Cn^{d}\) is uniform over all valuation profiles and valid query responses.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a deterministic protocol with the stated worst-case polynomial query bound, or prove that every such protocol has superpolynomial worst-case query complexity as n grows. A lower bound on the number of queries used by one known protocol is not a general impossibility result. A finite bound depending arbitrarily on n, an average-case polynomial bound, or a polynomial protocol permitting positive envy or discarded cake leaves this question open.
cards.why: A central information-complexity question in fair division: how many exact preference queries are necessary to allocate an entire divisible resource without envy?

importance.reason: The main worst-case complexity gap for exact envy-free cake cutting; recent single-exponential and average-case results sharpen the boundary without settling polynomial query complexity.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. Polynomial worst-case query complexity remains open. The latest checked general upper bound is the \(n^{O(1)}2^{n}\) protocol reported in the Ye–Bai preprint of 4 September 2026; Chèze’s polynomial result is over random valuation profiles.

context_blocks.text: Envy-freeness asks each person to compare the allocated pieces using their own valuation. It does not require different people to agree on values or to receive pieces of equal geometric length. For two agents, cut-and-choose works: one divides the cake into two equally valued parts and the other selects a preferred part. Extending this idea while controlling every pairwise comparison becomes much harder as the number of agents grows.

Completeness prevents a trivial answer. If the protocol could discard everything, giving everyone an empty piece would create no envy. Allocating the full cake also makes envy-freeness imply proportionality: for each agent, the value of their own piece is at least the average value of the n allocated pieces, namely \(1/n\). The converse fails because receiving a fair share does not prevent preferring someone else’s larger-valued share.

Disconnected pieces are essential to the computational question being asked. Exact envy-free allocations with connected pieces cannot, in general, be obtained by finite Robertson–Webb protocols once there are at least three agents. That obstruction does not apply when an agent may receive several intervals. Likewise, a bound on the number of final cut locations alone is not a bound on the number of valuation questions needed to discover suitable locations.

Nonatomicity gives the cut oracle its power: an interval can be cut to achieve any intermediate value. It does not impose a simple shape on preferences. A valuation may put almost all its mass in a very small region or have intervals of zero value. Exact comparisons must remain valid on these profiles, so a fixed numerical mesh or a small positive tolerance cannot silently substitute for an exact protocol.

Procaccia’s general lower bound is \(\Omega (n^{2})\) Robertson–Webb queries. This already separates envy-free division from the \(\Theta (n \log  n)\) query complexity of proportional division, but it remains compatible with a polynomial protocol. A quadratic lower bound cannot justify describing the target as impossible or necessarily exponential.

Aziz–Mackenzie’s FOCS 2016 breakthrough establishes a bound depending only on n for every profile, resolving the earlier question of whether any bounded protocol exists. Their displayed upper bound is a tower of six copies of n. This is stronger than merely terminating on each profile: earlier finite procedures could require arbitrarily many queries while n stayed fixed. The existence of a bounded protocol leaves the growth rate of that bound open.

Sokolov’s June 2023 preprint revises parts of the protocol and sharpens the analysis to \(n^{8n^{2}(1+o(1))}\). That is a major quantitative reduction, equal to \(2^{(8+o(1))n^{2} \log _{2}n}\), although it remains far above polynomial. The inherited \(2025/2026\) average-case article still quotes the older tower benchmark; the progress account here therefore also checks subsequent and separately posted algorithmic work.

A very recent advance is Ye–Bai’s September 4, 2026 preprint. Its Theorem 1.1 states a deterministic protocol using \(n^{O(1)}2^{n}\) queries for complete envy-free allocation with arbitrary nonnegative additive nonatomic valuations. The proof replaces a very large family of partial allocations by a polynomial-sized collection and controls how their pieces can be reassigned without conflicts. This is the latest reported general upper bound found in the review, and is identified as a preprint.

The same paper distinguishes query complexity from local computation. A helper construction uses exhaustive search after the relevant values have been elicited; Appendix C explains its deterministic choices and implementation through ordinary Robertson–Webb queries. Expensive transcript processing is allowed in the present question. Thus the reported single-exponential query bound should not be advertised as an equally fast bit-time algorithm, and it still does not give polynomially many queries.

Chèze’s inherited article studies a probability distribution on valuation profiles, following a full-independence framework. Under its uniform model, the probability of needing at least \(n^{12}\) queries tends to zero. This probability concerns the sampled preferences, rather than random bits used by a protocol facing an arbitrary fixed profile. Rare or specially chosen valuations remain relevant to the worst-case question. The article appeared online in September 2025 and in the 2026 journal volume.

Approximate envy-freeness creates another distinct regime. Bounds polynomial in n and inverse tolerance can produce small positive envy, including versions with connected pieces. Sending the tolerance to zero does not yield a finite exact protocol if the query count diverges. Exactness, completeness, access through queries and unrestricted disconnected allocations are therefore all part of this card’s answer criterion.

The fundamental issue is the amount of preference information needed for an exact global fairness guarantee. A polynomial protocol would show that the enormous historical bounds reflect limitations of the constructions rather than an intrinsic elicitation barrier. A superpolynomial lower bound would reveal a sharp information cost of exact envy-freeness even when computational work between queries is unrestricted.

cards.context:
Envy-freeness asks each person to compare the allocated pieces using their own valuation. It does not require different people to agree on values or to receive pieces of equal geometric length. For two agents, cut-and-choose works: one divides the cake into two equally valued parts and the other selects a preferred part. Extending this idea while controlling every pairwise comparison becomes much harder as the number of agents grows.

Completeness prevents a trivial answer. If the protocol could discard everything, giving everyone an empty piece would create no envy. Allocating the full cake also makes envy-freeness imply proportionality: for each agent, the value of their own piece is at least the average value of the n allocated pieces, namely \(1/n\). The converse fails because receiving a fair share does not prevent preferring someone else’s larger-valued share.

Disconnected pieces are essential to the computational question being asked. Exact envy-free allocations with connected pieces cannot, in general, be obtained by finite Robertson–Webb protocols once there are at least three agents. That obstruction does not apply when an agent may receive several intervals. Likewise, a bound on the number of final cut locations alone is not a bound on the number of valuation questions needed to discover suitable locations.

Nonatomicity gives the cut oracle its power: an interval can be cut to achieve any intermediate value. It does not impose a simple shape on preferences. A valuation may put almost all its mass in a very small region or have intervals of zero value. Exact comparisons must remain valid on these profiles, so a fixed numerical mesh or a small positive tolerance cannot silently substitute for an exact protocol.

Procaccia’s general lower bound is \(\Omega (n^{2})\) Robertson–Webb queries. This already separates envy-free division from the \(\Theta (n \log  n)\) query complexity of proportional division, but it remains compatible with a polynomial protocol. A quadratic lower bound cannot justify describing the target as impossible or necessarily exponential.

Aziz–Mackenzie’s FOCS 2016 breakthrough establishes a bound depending only on n for every profile, resolving the earlier question of whether any bounded protocol exists. Their displayed upper bound is a tower of six copies of n. This is stronger than merely terminating on each profile: earlier finite procedures could require arbitrarily many queries while n stayed fixed. The existence of a bounded protocol leaves the growth rate of that bound open.

Sokolov’s June 2023 preprint revises parts of the protocol and sharpens the analysis to \(n^{8n^{2}(1+o(1))}\). That is a major quantitative reduction, equal to \(2^{(8+o(1))n^{2} \log _{2}n}\), although it remains far above polynomial. The inherited \(2025/2026\) average-case article still quotes the older tower benchmark; the progress account here therefore also checks subsequent and separately posted algorithmic work.

A very recent advance is Ye–Bai’s September 4, 2026 preprint. Its Theorem 1.1 states a deterministic protocol using \(n^{O(1)}2^{n}\) queries for complete envy-free allocation with arbitrary nonnegative additive nonatomic valuations. The proof replaces a very large family of partial allocations by a polynomial-sized collection and controls how their pieces can be reassigned without conflicts. This is the latest reported general upper bound found in the review, and is identified as a preprint.

The same paper distinguishes query complexity from local computation. A helper construction uses exhaustive search after the relevant values have been elicited; Appendix C explains its deterministic choices and implementation through ordinary Robertson–Webb queries. Expensive transcript processing is allowed in the present question. Thus the reported single-exponential query bound should not be advertised as an equally fast bit-time algorithm, and it still does not give polynomially many queries.

Chèze’s inherited article studies a probability distribution on valuation profiles, following a full-independence framework. Under its uniform model, the probability of needing at least \(n^{12}\) queries tends to zero. This probability concerns the sampled preferences, rather than random bits used by a protocol facing an arbitrary fixed profile. Rare or specially chosen valuations remain relevant to the worst-case question. The article appeared online in September 2025 and in the 2026 journal volume.

Approximate envy-freeness creates another distinct regime. Bounds polynomial in n and inverse tolerance can produce small positive envy, including versions with connected pieces. Sending the tolerance to zero does not yield a finite exact protocol if the query count diverges. Exactness, completeness, access through queries and unrestricted disconnected allocations are therefore all part of this card’s answer criterion.

The fundamental issue is the amount of preference information needed for an exact global fairness guarantee. A polynomial protocol would show that the enormous historical bounds reflect limitations of the constructions rather than an intrinsic elicitation barrier. A superpolynomial lower bound would reveal a sharp information cost of exact envy-freeness even when computational work between queries is unrestricted.

cards.definitions: An election E consists of disjoint finite labeled sets V of \(n\ge 1\) voters and C of \(m\ge 1\) candidates, and a strict total order ≻_v on C for each \(v\in V\). A consistent distance d is a pseudometric on \(V\cup C: d(x,x)=0, d(x,y)=d(y,x)\ge 0\), and \(d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)\) for all points, with a≻_v b implying \(d(v,a)\le d(v,b)\). Distinct named points may be colocated. Equal distances may be broken in any order in the reported ranking; the guarantee must hold for every consistent pair \((E,d)\). The social cost \(SC_{d}(a)=\sum_{v\in V} d(v,a)\), and \(\operatorname{OPT}_{d}=\min _{a}\in C SC_{d}(a)\). A randomized ordinal rule f assigns each election E a lottery \(p=f(E)\), where \(p_{a}\ge 0\) and \(\sum_{a} p_{a}=1\). Its expected cost is \(\sum_{a} p_{a} SC_{d}(a)\). The lottery depends only on n,m and the full rankings, not on d or additional distance queries. It may use arbitrary real probabilities and unbounded computation. No anonymity, neutrality, incentive-compatibility or tournament-only restriction is imposed. Define \(Dist(f)=\inf\){\(D\ge 1\): for every E and every consistent \(d, \sum_{a} f(E)_{a} SC_{d}(a)\le D\cdot \operatorname{OPT}_{d}\)}, taking \(\inf \varnothing =+\infty\). This inequality requires zero expected cost if \(\operatorname{OPT}_{d}=0\) and avoids dividing by zero. Set \(D*=\inf _{f} Dist(f)\), over single rule families defined on all finite elections. The expectation is over the selected candidate, while elections and consistent metrics are worst-case choices. Replacing total cost by average cost divides both sides by n and gives the same distortion.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |\(a- D*|\le 1/100\). The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds \(\ell\)\(\le u\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell +u)/2\). An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The \(1/100\) tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture.

context_blocks.title: Rankings hide the size of a preference
context_blocks.text: Two voters rank candidates a and b in opposite orders. Put a at 0 and b at 2 on a line. If voter 1 is at 0 and voter 2 at 1, the total costs of a and b are 1 and 3; if voter 1 is at 1 and voter 2 at 2, they are 3 and 1. Both arrangements fit the same rankings when a distance tie is resolved in the reported direction. The rule therefore has to make one choice of lottery that works in both possible geometries.

context_blocks.title: What randomization changes
context_blocks.text: If the lottery selects a with probability p, its distortion in these two examples is respectively \(3- 2p\) and \(1+2p\). At least one is at least 2. Choosing each candidate with probability one half reaches 2 for this pair of examples, whereas a deterministic choice suffers factor 3 in one of them. This demonstrates why randomization can help, but it is only a small lower-bound example. It does not establish the optimum over all elections.

context_blocks.title: The old value-2 conjecture is false
context_blocks.text: Charikar and Ramakrishnan construct larger elections giving a universal randomized lower bound of approximately 2.11264. Consequently, the target is to identify the optimal value above two, not prove the former conjecture. The lower bound concerns all randomized rules that use rankings, with no restriction to a particular named procedure or to pairwise summaries.

context_blocks.title: Recent upper bounds leave a smaller gap
context_blocks.text: Frank’s August 2026 preprint gives an upper bound of 2.5. Shah’s revision of 6 September improves this to 2.1441; its first version had the weaker value 2.3282. The 8 September preprint of Cai and coauthors states an upper bound of 2.13713, leaving a gap of less than 0.025 above the reported general lower bound. These are recent theorem claims with checked model matches; this review has not independently verified their proofs or numerical certificates. They still leave an interval rather than an exact value.

context_blocks.title: Restricted rules answer different questions
context_blocks.text: A weighted tournament records how many voters prefer a to b for each pair. It need not preserve all the information in their complete rankings. The optimal factor 3 for randomized tournament rules therefore does not bound what full-ranking rules can achieve. Similarly, Shah’s lower bound of 2.136 concerns his random-size-stable-lottery family; it is not a new universal lower bound for every rule. The scope of both upper and lower bounds matters when comparing them with D*.

context_blocks.title: Why this constant matters
context_blocks.text: D* measures how much total distance can be lost solely because a decision rule knows the order of preferences but not their intensities. It makes no assumption that voters behave strategically, and it does not require a truthful mechanism. The mathematical guarantee is robust across every metric consistent with the ballots, rather than an average over a chosen model of elections.
