cards.title: VP versus VBP over the complex numbers
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}=\mathrm{VBP}_{\mathbb C}\)? More explicitly, let \((m_n,f_n)_{n\ge1}\) be any family with integers \(m_n\ge0\) and commutative polynomials \(f_n\in\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_{m_n}]\). Suppose that some positive integer \(a\) satisfies \[m_n\le(n+2)^a,\qquad \deg f_n\le(n+2)^a,\qquad c(f_n)\le(n+2)^a\quad\text{for all }n\ge1,\] where \(c\) is minimum arithmetic-circuit size in the model below. Must there exist a positive integer \(b\), depending on the whole family, such that \[\operatorname{abp}(f_n)\le(n+2)^b\quad\text{for all }n\ge1?\] Computation is exact and nonuniform over the complex field, and the competing branching programs are unrestricted.
cards.definitions:
A polynomial is a finite complex linear combination of commutative monomials in the listed variables. Its total degree is the maximum sum of exponents among nonzero monomials, with degree zero assigned to the zero polynomial. An arithmetic circuit is a finite acyclic graph with one designated output. Input gates are labelled by one listed variable or one arbitrary complex constant. Every other gate has two ordered input ports and is labelled by addition or multiplication in the polynomial ring; both ports may refer to the same predecessor, and any predecessor may be reused. There are no division gates. Size is the number of gates plus the number of wires, counting each input port’s wire separately; constant and variable input gates each have unit cost. Intermediate degrees are not separately bounded: the degree hypothesis is on the output polynomial after cancellations. The minimum of this size among circuits computing \(f\) is \(c(f)\).

An algebraic branching program (ABP) is a finite directed acyclic multigraph with distinct designated vertices \(s,t\), no edges entering \(s\), and no edges leaving \(t\). Each edge \(e\) is labelled by an affine form \(\lambda_e=\alpha_{e,0}+\sum_{j=1}^{m}\alpha_{e,j}x_j\), with arbitrary complex coefficients. It computes \(\sum_{\pi:s\leadsto t}\prod_{e\in\pi}\lambda_e\), where distinct paths include their edge choices and an empty sum is zero. Its size is \[|V|+|E|+\sum_{e\in E}\left(\mathbf1_{\alpha_{e,0}\ne0}+2\bigl|\{j\in[m]:\alpha_{e,j}\ne0\}\bigr|\right).\] Here \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), including the empty set if \(m=0\), and \(\mathbf1_P\) is one when \(P\) holds and zero otherwise. Thus every nonzero scalar coefficient and its variable occurrence are charged; labels are not arbitrary polynomial oracles. There is no width, layering, variable-order, read-once, syntactic multilinearity, symmetry, homogeneity or monotonicity requirement. The minimum size computing \(f\) is \(\operatorname{abp}(f)\).

Both minima concern formal polynomial identities, not agreement on finitely many inputs or convergence of coefficients. Sizes count algebraic objects and field elements, not bits encoding complex numbers; coefficients need not have bounded or computable bit descriptions. No algorithm generating a family’s circuits, programs or constants is required. Every polynomial has finite representations in both models. Positive integer exponents in \((n+2)^a\) absorb multiplicative constants and finitely many initial values of any polynomial bound. The families meeting the circuit hypotheses define \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\); polynomially many variables and a polynomial ABP bound define \(\mathrm{VBP}_{\mathbb C}\). ABP size already bounds output degree, and ABPs have polynomial-size circuit simulations, so only the displayed converse inclusion is at issue.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed inclusion or its negation, with the specified field, polynomial identities, resource accounting and quantifiers. A positive proof establishes a polynomial ABP bound for every family satisfying the circuit and degree hypotheses; it need not produce an efficient uniform converter. A negative proof establishes one family \((m_n,f_n)\) and one fixed positive integer \(a\) satisfying all three circuit-side bounds, but such that \[\forall b\ge1\ \forall N\ge1\ \exists n\ge N,\quad \operatorname{abp}(f_n)>(n+2)^b.\] The lower bound must cover every permitted ABP over \(\mathbb C\), including arbitrary constants, reuse of variables and cancellations. There is no required effective generator for a separating family. A lower bound in a restricted ABP model, a family of exponential output degree, or a border-complexity separation does not meet this criterion.
cards.why: The question compares unrestricted arithmetic circuits with path-sum computation inside the class of efficiently representable polynomials. Equality would make polynomial-size determinants of affine matrices sufficient to express every polynomial-degree circuit family. Inequality would establish a fundamental separation within efficient algebraic computation, isolating power supplied by general multiplication together with reuse of intermediate results.

Bounded searches and version checks through 15 September 2026 found no resolution for unrestricted commutative exact nonuniform computation over C. The January/June symmetry separation uses orbit complexity, prescribed variable symmetries and no degree bound; the multilinear report studies a syntactically restricted model; min-plus-semiring results have different operations. context_blocks.text: Circuits combine previously computed polynomials by both addition and multiplication, with unrestricted reuse. An ABP records sums of products along paths with affine labels. ABPs are polynomially equivalent to skew circuits, where each multiplication gate has at least one operand that is an input variable or constant. The conjectural gap concerns the size of exact representations under these two forms of computation, rather than which individual polynomials can be represented at all.

The polynomial-degree condition is essential. Small general circuits can have output degree exponential in their size, whereas an ABP with affine labels has degree at most its longest source-to-sink path. Such degree alone cannot separate the classes in this card because it is explicitly required to stay polynomial. The stated bounds concern the final polynomial; intermediate cancellations and degrees in a competing circuit are allowed.

Determinants give an equivalent structural description of \(\mathrm{VBP}\): a family belongs to this class exactly when it has representations \(f_n=\det(A_{n,0}+\sum_j x_j A_{n,j})\) with polynomially bounded matrix dimension and complex constant matrices. The determinant itself admits polynomial-size ABPs. Thus \(\mathrm{VP}=\mathrm{VBP}\) would make determinants universal for the circuit families in the statement. This is distinct from permanent versus determinant: the permanent is not known to have the polynomial-size general circuits required on the easy side of a separation here.

The classical Valiant–Skyum–Berkowitz–Rackoff depth reduction yields quasipolynomial simulations among formulas, ABPs and circuits for polynomial-degree families. The ITCS 2024 paper recalls that their quasipolynomial versions coincide, where a quasipolynomial bound means \(n^{(\log n)^{O(1)}}\). A polynomial bound \(n^{O(1)}\) is stronger. Approximation in coefficient space also defines separate border-complexity classes and does not supply an exact ABP identity.

Sinhababu and Thierauf prove factor closure over fields of characteristic zero: every factor of a nonzero polynomial with ABP size \(s\) has ABP size polynomial in \(s\). The result appeared at CCC 2020 and in Computational Complexity in October 2021. This gives ABPs a closure property already known for general circuits, without equating the models. The revised factoring survey of June 2026 still records that no inclusion in \(\mathrm{VF}\subseteq\mathrm{VBP}\subseteq\mathrm{VP}\) is known to be strict.

Dwivedi, Pago and Seppelt separate symmetric analogues of these three classes in their STOC 2026 work. Three differences matter: their polynomials obey a prescribed matrix-variable symmetry, their circuits are measured by the largest orbit of gates rather than total size, and their symmetric classes have no polynomial degree bound. The symmetry action must extend from input variables to the computation. These classes therefore cannot simply be substituted for the unrestricted classes in this card. The skew class is named symVBP in the January preprint and symVS in the conference abstract. Their additional completeness results for homomorphism polynomials are separate from an unconditional ordinary VP–VBP separation.

The January 2026 report by Fabris, Limaye, Srinivasan and Yehudayoff studies syntactically multilinear ABPs: on each source-to-sink path, a variable appears in at most one affine edge label. It characterizes aspects of a restricted lower-bound measure and recovers a separation of multilinear formulas from multilinear ABPs. Its own introduction still leaves superpolynomial lower bounds for general multilinear ABPs open. In this card even an output that happens to be multilinear may be computed using nonmultilinear intermediate expressions and cancellations. Lower bounds excluding those representations do not establish the unrestricted target.

The size conventions here make the algebraic model explicit. Counting all affine-label occurrences and using binary circuit gates changes customary vertex-only or edge-only presentations by polynomial overhead in the representation size and number of variables. It does not impose bit complexity or uniform constructibility on field constants. A complete answer must preserve these distinctions; a theorem about a min-plus semiring or a fixed-width program would concern different allowed operations or representations.

cards.context:
Circuits combine previously computed polynomials by both addition and multiplication, with unrestricted reuse. An ABP records sums of products along paths with affine labels. ABPs are polynomially equivalent to skew circuits, where each multiplication gate has at least one operand that is an input variable or constant. The conjectural gap concerns the size of exact representations under these two forms of computation, rather than which individual polynomials can be represented at all.

The polynomial-degree condition is essential. Small general circuits can have output degree exponential in their size, whereas an ABP with affine labels has degree at most its longest source-to-sink path. Such degree alone cannot separate the classes in this card because it is explicitly required to stay polynomial. The stated bounds concern the final polynomial; intermediate cancellations and degrees in a competing circuit are allowed.

Determinants give an equivalent structural description of \(\mathrm{VBP}\): a family belongs to this class exactly when it has representations \(f_n=\det(A_{n,0}+\sum_j x_j A_{n,j})\) with polynomially bounded matrix dimension and complex constant matrices. The determinant itself admits polynomial-size ABPs. Thus \(\mathrm{VP}=\mathrm{VBP}\) would make determinants universal for the circuit families in the statement. This is distinct from permanent versus determinant: the permanent is not known to have the polynomial-size general circuits required on the easy side of a separation here.

The classical Valiant–Skyum–Berkowitz–Rackoff depth reduction yields quasipolynomial simulations among formulas, ABPs and circuits for polynomial-degree families. The ITCS 2024 paper recalls that their quasipolynomial versions coincide, where a quasipolynomial bound means \(n^{(\log n)^{O(1)}}\). A polynomial bound \(n^{O(1)}\) is stronger. Approximation in coefficient space also defines separate border-complexity classes and does not supply an exact ABP identity.

Sinhababu and Thierauf prove factor closure over fields of characteristic zero: every factor of a nonzero polynomial with ABP size \(s\) has ABP size polynomial in \(s\). The result appeared at CCC 2020 and in Computational Complexity in October 2021. This gives ABPs a closure property already known for general circuits, without equating the models. The revised factoring survey of June 2026 still records that no inclusion in \(\mathrm{VF}\subseteq\mathrm{VBP}\subseteq\mathrm{VP}\) is known to be strict.

Dwivedi, Pago and Seppelt separate symmetric analogues of these three classes in their STOC 2026 work. Three differences matter: their polynomials obey a prescribed matrix-variable symmetry, their circuits are measured by the largest orbit of gates rather than total size, and their symmetric classes have no polynomial degree bound. The symmetry action must extend from input variables to the computation. These classes therefore cannot simply be substituted for the unrestricted classes in this card. The skew class is named symVBP in the January preprint and symVS in the conference abstract. Their additional completeness results for homomorphism polynomials are separate from an unconditional ordinary VP–VBP separation.

The January 2026 report by Fabris, Limaye, Srinivasan and Yehudayoff studies syntactically multilinear ABPs: on each source-to-sink path, a variable appears in at most one affine edge label. It characterizes aspects of a restricted lower-bound measure and recovers a separation of multilinear formulas from multilinear ABPs. Its own introduction still leaves superpolynomial lower bounds for general multilinear ABPs open. In this card even an output that happens to be multilinear may be computed using nonmultilinear intermediate expressions and cancellations. Lower bounds excluding those representations do not establish the unrestricted target.

The size conventions here make the algebraic model explicit. Counting all affine-label occurrences and using binary circuit gates changes customary vertex-only or edge-only presentations by polynomial overhead in the representation size and number of variables. It does not impose bit complexity or uniform constructibility on field constants. A complete answer must preserve these distinctions; a theorem about a min-plus semiring or a fixed-width program would concern different allowed operations or representations.

cards.title: VP versus VNP
cards.formal: Over the field $\mathbb C$, do there exist constants C,k such that, for every integer \(n\ge 1\), the polynomial $\operatorname{perm}_n(X)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^n x_{i,\sigma(i)}$ can be computed by an arithmetic circuit with at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) gates? Equivalently, is $\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}=\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}$? The usual conjecture is that the answer is no.
cards.definitions: X has \(n^{2}\) independent indeterminates and \(S_{n}\) is the set of permutations of \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input nodes labeled by variables or arbitrary complex constants, binary +, −, × operation gates, and one output. Its size counts operation gates; intermediate results can feed any number of later gates. Division, comparisons, oracle gates, approximation, and limits of circuits are absent. The output must equal the permanent as a formal polynomial. Circuits may depend on n without a uniform construction algorithm; constants have unit arithmetic cost, with no bit-encoding restriction. VP consists of polynomial families with polynomially bounded numbers of variables and total degrees, computed by polynomial-size circuits. VNP consists of polynomial families \(f_{n}(x)=\sum_{y\in \{0,1\}^{p(n)}} g_{n}(x,y)\), for some polynomial p and some such polynomial-size, polynomial-degree circuit family g. The witness sum is over Boolean strings even though the coefficients lie in C.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct the stated circuit family, or prove that the minimum circuit size of the permanent is not bounded by any polynomial in n. A lower bound for every polynomial-size general circuit family suffices. Lower bounds only for formulas, monotone circuits, bounded-depth circuits, or determinantal representations do not by themselves settle this formulation.
cards.why: This is the central separation question for arithmetic computation. It tests whether summing exponentially many efficiently describable algebraic contributions inherently requires more computation than evaluating one polynomial-size circuit, and organizes lower-bound research across algebra, geometry, and pseudorandomness.

importance.reason: A foundational separation for general arithmetic circuits, with a complete concrete target in the permanent and consequences across algebraic complexity and explicit lower-bound constructions.

progress.text: Ryser’s inclusion-exclusion expression gives an exponential-size formula, for example \(O(n^{2}2^{n})\) arithmetic operations. This substantially improves direct enumeration of n! permutations but remains far above a polynomial bound.
Valiant establishes algebraic completeness of the permanent over fields of characteristic different from two. Over C this yields the equivalence between polynomial-size permanent circuits and VP=VNP.

Limaye, Srinivasan, and Tavenas prove superpolynomial lower bounds against arithmetic circuits of every constant depth in characteristic zero. Those circuits may have unbounded fan-in, with size accounting for their description; the fixed depth is an essential restriction. The result does not separate general VP and VNP.

Narayanan relates elusive polynomial maps to expansion of iterated sumsets and obtains improved superlinear bounds in certain sublogarithmic-depth regimes. An explicit elusive-curve construction has exponential degree; the paper explains that its parameters do not yet imply \(VP\ne\)VNP.

context_blocks.text: The permanent sums one product for every perfect matching in a complete bipartite graph. Substituting a zero-one adjacency matrix counts perfect matchings. This card asks for an exact symbolic arithmetic computation valid on all complex matrices. The model permits cancellations and unrestricted reuse of intermediate results, so it captures substantially more than enumerating matchings.

The permanent and determinant have the same permutation products, but the determinant attaches a sign to each one. Determinants have polynomial-size division-free circuits despite their factorially many displayed terms. Thus counting the monomials in the permanent is not a circuit lower bound: the question is whether an equally effective algebraic compression exists for its unsigned sum.

Valiant makes this example universal. Every family in VNP reduces to a polynomially larger permanent by substitutions of variables and constants. A polynomial circuit for the permanent would therefore compress every efficient Boolean-witness sum in the definition of VNP. Conversely, separating these classes forces the permanent to escape polynomial circuit size.

Important partial results restrict how computations are organized. A formula cannot reuse an intermediate result; a constant-depth circuit permits only a fixed number of operation layers. Even proving that the permanent has no small determinant representation would rule out only that representation model. None of these restrictions is part of the circuit model in this card.

Recent lower bounds illustrate both the progress and the gap. Superpolynomial bounds are known at every fixed depth, and new work constructs polynomial maps that evade low-complexity parametrizations. The latter can yield stronger circuit lower bounds if its degree and dimension parameters improve sufficiently. The constructions currently cited do not give the required unrestricted superpolynomial bound.

cards.title: Polynomial-size arithmetic formulas for the determinant
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(K,C\ge 1\) such that for every \(n\ge 1\) the symbolic determinant \(Det_{n}(X)=\sum_{\pi \in S_{n}}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi )\prod _{i=1}^{n} x_{i,\pi (i)}\) has an arithmetic formula over the complex numbers with at most \(K n^{C}\) nodes?
cards.definitions: The \(n^{2}\) entries \(x_{ij}\) of X are distinct commuting indeterminates. \(S_{n}\) is the set of permutations of \([n]\), and \(\operatorname{sgn}(\pi )\) is +1 or −1 according to the parity of \(\pi\). An arithmetic formula is a rooted binary tree. Leaves are labelled by input variables or arbitrary constants from \(\mathbb{C}\); internal nodes apply addition, subtraction or multiplication. The output must equal \(Det_{n}\) as a formal polynomial in \(\mathbb{C} [x_{11},\ldots ,x_{nn}]\). Size counts every node, including each repeated occurrence of a variable, constant or copied subformula. Intermediate results cannot be shared between different parents. Constants are charged unit size, without a bound on their bit description; this is nonuniform algebraic complexity, so no algorithm generating the family is required. Division, comparisons, branching and input-dependent constants are not allowed. Intermediate polynomials may contain higher powers of individual variables and cancellations of those powers; only the final polynomial is required to be the determinant. There is no multilinearity, homogeneity, fixed-depth, monotonicity or bounded-coefficient restriction on intermediate computation. The fixed field \(\mathbb{C}\) is an explicit characteristic-zero specialization of the inherited question.
cards.answer_criterion: Exhibit polynomial-size formulas with one fixed size exponent for all n, or prove that the minimum formula-size function is not bounded by any polynomial: for every \(K,C\ge 1\) there is an n for which every allowed formula has more than \(K n^{C}\) nodes. A fixed-power lower bound such as \(\Omega (n^{3})\) is insufficient to refute polynomial size. A lower bound restricted to multilinear formulas, noncommuting variables, or bounded depth does not settle this unrestricted commutative formula question.
cards.why: The canonical test of whether reusing intermediate expressions gives a superpolynomial advantage over arithmetic expression trees, even for an efficiently computable polynomial.

importance.reason: A fundamental separation inside algebraic computation, equivalent to the formula-versus-branching-program question through determinant completeness and linked to many explicit polynomial families.

progress.text: Berkowitz gives division-free polynomial-size, \(O(\log ^{2} n)\)-depth determinant circuits; unfolding yields quasipolynomial-size formulas.

Raz establishes \(n^{\Omega (\log  n)}\) lower bounds for formulas that remain multilinear at every gate; the original ECCC report precedes the journal publication.
Chaugule and coauthors relate formula complexity of Schur polynomials and generalized Vandermonde determinants to the generic determinant.
Boyapati–Chillara–Vempati’s sparse-determinant preprint retains the strong multilinear lower bound with \(\Theta (n \log ^{6} n)\) nonzero entries; it appears at CCC 2026.
The updated factoring primer explicitly records that polynomial-size symbolic determinant formulas are still unknown, despite new formula-factoring results.

context_blocks.text: The determinant is computationally easy when an algorithm may save intermediate work and reuse it. A formula imposes a stricter discipline: each computed quantity has only one consumer. To use the same expression twice, the expression must be copied. This can turn a compact computation graph into a much larger tree. The problem asks whether the determinant has an alternative expression that avoids this potential blow-up.

The familiar permutation expansion has n! terms, but this does not prove that every formula is that large. Algebraic identities can compress a sum dramatically, just as a product of short sums can represent many expanded monomials. Conversely, Gaussian elimination is not itself a small formula: its usual presentation reuses entries, performs divisions and selects pivots. Its numerical running time therefore cannot answer the stated symbolic question.

Berkowitz’s division-free construction gives polynomial-size arithmetic circuits of depth \(O(\log ^{2} n)\). Unfolding a bounded-fan-in circuit of that depth into a tree gives a formula of size \(2^{O(\log ^{2} n)}=n^{O(\log  n)}\). This is quasipolynomial, already far below the permutation expansion, but still larger than a fixed power of n. A polynomial-size formula would close this remaining gap.

The determinant is also a complete problem for polynomial-size algebraic branching programs, whose outputs are sums of products of edge labels along directed source-to-sink paths. Consequently, polynomial-size determinant formulas would imply VF=VBP: every polynomial family having polynomial-size branching programs would have polynomial-size formulas. The larger class VP allows general arithmetic circuits. The June 2026 factoring primer still lists \(VF\subseteq\)VBP\(\subseteq VP\) without a known strict containment and explicitly leaves small determinant formulas unresolved.

An unrestricted lower bound is known, but it is only a fixed power. Kalorkoti proves \(\Omega (n^{3})\) formula size for the n by n determinant, even in a model allowing division. Here n is the matrix dimension; there are \(n^{2}\) independent variables. Thus the bound is cubic in dimension and only a power \(3/2\) in the number of variables. It must not be described as a cubic lower bound in the input-variable count.

Raz proves a much stronger \(n^{\Omega (\log  n)}\) lower bound when every intermediate polynomial is multilinear. This restriction is substantive even though the final determinant is multilinear. For a simple illustration, \((x+y)^{2}- x^{2}- y^{2}\) equals 2xy, a multilinear output obtained through nonmultilinear intermediate terms. The example does not establish a size advantage, but it shows why output multilinearity alone cannot justify applying a theorem that assumes multilinearity throughout a computation.

Recent progress tests which determinant features are needed for that restricted lower bound. Boyapati, Chillara and Vempati prove the existence of sparse n by n symbolic matrices with only \(\Theta (n \log ^{6} n)\) nonzero entries whose determinants still require \(n^{\Omega (\log  n)}\) multilinear formulas. This shows that the dense \(n^{2}\)-variable presentation is not essential to Raz’s obstruction. It leaves the permission to use nonmultilinear intermediate computations untouched.

The question also organizes complexity outside generic matrices. Chaugule and coauthors connect small formulas for Schur polynomials and generalized Vandermonde determinants to small formulas for the general determinant. Such reductions make the determinant a useful benchmark for whether apparently special algebraic expressions really admit efficient tree computations. A separation would reveal a basic cost of forbidding reuse, already within problems that possess efficient arithmetic circuits.

cards.title: Word problem for one-relation monoids
cards.formal: Is the uniform word problem for ordinary one-relation monoids decidable? Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine which, given any finite alphabet \(A\) and four finite words \(u,v,s,t\in A^*\), always halts and decides whether \(s\) and \(t\) represent the same element of the monoid \(\langle A\mid u=v\rangle\)? The presentation and the word pair are all parts of the input; no running-time bound is prescribed.
cards.definitions:
The free monoid \(A^*\) consists of all finite literal strings over \(A\), including the empty word \(\varepsilon\), with concatenation as multiplication and \(\varepsilon\) as identity. The monoid \(\langle A\mid u=v\rangle\) is the quotient \(A^*/{\equiv}\), where \(\equiv\) is the least equivalence relation containing \(u\equiv v\) and satisfying \(p\equiv q\Rightarrow xpy\equiv xqy\) for all words \(x,y\). Equivalently, \(s\equiv t\) if and only if some finite sequence \(s=w_0,w_1,\ldots,w_k=t\) exists in which every adjacent pair is \((xuy,xvy)\) or \((xvy,xuy)\) for some \(x,y\in A^*\). A zero-step sequence is allowed.

The four words are fully supplied literal strings, not variables to be instantiated by unknown strings. The two relation sides and the tested words may be empty. Replacing an empty side means inserting the other side at a gap in the current finite word. The relation may have equal sides and may preserve or change length. The alphabet itself may be empty, in which case every word is empty. There are no inverse symbols with automatic cancellation, group axioms, cancellation laws or commutativity laws beyond consequences of the single stated monoid relation.

The input explicitly gives an integer alphabet size \(a\ge0\), identifies \(A\) with \(\{1,\ldots,a\}\), and lists all four words with binary letter indices and lengths. This is finite ordinary string input, with malformed encodings rejectable. One ordinary deterministic program must give exact YES/NO answers for all valid presentations and all pairs, terminating on both answers. It receives no oracle, nonuniform advice, random coins or unbounded precomputed data for a presentation. No numerical approximation arises. This is uniform decidability across presentations; a separate non-effectively chosen algorithm for each fixed presentation has different quantifiers.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean proof that the displayed language of presentation-and-word-pair instances is decidable by a total computable function, or a proof of its undecidability. A positive proof must formalize finite words, the single-relation contextual congruence, finite encoding and a uniform algorithm whose termination and both correctness directions hold for all allowed empty and nonempty inputs. A negative reduction must stay inside ordinary one-relation monoids and preserve equality in both directions. A single fixed one-relation monoid with undecidable word problem suffices for a negative answer but is stronger than necessary to refute uniform decidability. A semidecision procedure that halts only on equal words, an unproved termination claim, an exponential derivation-length lower bound, or a negative theorem for inverse monoids, submonoid membership or equations with unknowns does not by itself settle the target. No Lean resolution is asserted by this review.
cards.why: A foundational decidability boundary for rewriting: can reachability under one literal reversible string rule already escape every terminating uniform algorithm?

importance.reason: One of the central minimal-presentation decision problems, connecting string rewriting, algebraic normal forms, computability and reductions between monoids, inverse monoids and groups.

progress.text: Magnus solves the one-relator group word problem; later work solves major ordinary-monoid special cases, without providing a general procedure.
Nyberg-Brodda surveys the unresolved problem, reduction methods, special cases and gaps in earlier claimed arguments.
The survey’s corrigendum fixes historical attributions and technical wording, including nontermination versus literal looping of Adian’s procedure.
Nyberg-Brodda gives monadic one-relation monoids with exponential Dehn functions but decidable word problems, separating short derivations from decidability.

cards.status_note: Gray–Reilly, 5 August 2026, explicitly retain the ordinary one-relation-monoid word problem as open. Their inverse-monoid theorem, the 2025/2026 submonoid-membership results and the August 2026 Diophantine theorem do not decide equality of two supplied words in the card’s ordinary presentation model. The saved card asks for one uniform machine; the source’s per-presentation wording is distinguished. Bounded checks through 16 September found no matching uniform resolution, not an exhaustive proof of openness.

context_blocks.text: This is a minimal string-transformation problem. There is only one reversible replacement rule, and it can be applied inside any surrounding context. Starting with a word, repeated replacements can generate many others. Equality asks whether the target lies in this reachability set. The alphabet symbols themselves have no hidden arithmetic meaning; any complicated computation would have to emerge from overlaps and repeated applications of this one rule.

An equality has a finite certificate: a sequence of contextual applications of the defining relation connecting the two words. Inequality has no analogous certificate supplied by the presentation itself. A long search with no successful derivation does not decide whether one exists, since intermediate words can have unbounded length.

Length-preserving relations, where \(|u|=|v|\), form a decidable special case. The general problem allows length-changing replacements. Termination of an oriented shortening rule is not sufficient by itself: different irreducible words may still represent the same element. The requested algorithm has no efficiency requirement, so a large computable time bound would still be a positive answer.

The surrounding algebra offers major positive results. Magnus proved decidability for one-relator groups in 1932. For ordinary monoids, classical work handles important cases such as a single relation equating a word to the identity, and presentations satisfying appropriate cycle-free conditions. Group algorithms cannot simply be applied to every monoid presentation: adjoining inverses may identify additional words, so equality in a related group can lose information.

The historical source needs its correction. Nyberg-Brodda’s survey traces the string-rewriting background to Thue, while its 2022 corrigendum identifies Novikov’s 1957 question as the earliest explicit formulation known to the author. The correction also replaces an informal claim that Adian’s procedure may loop with the more precise statement that it may fail to terminate. An infinite computation need not repeat a previously seen state.

There is concrete evidence that short relations can require very long equality proofs. Nyberg-Brodda constructs the family \(\langle a,b | baa(ba)^{N}=a\rangle\) for \(N\ge 2\) with at least exponential Dehn function. Here the Dehn function measures the maximum, over equal word pairs of bounded total input length, of the minimum number of relation applications needed to connect them. Nevertheless, the same paper proves that every monoid in this family has decidable word problem.

Gray and Reilly’s August 2026 paper proves the existence of a two-generator one-relator inverse monoid with undecidable word problem. Inverse monoid presentations are interpreted in a different algebraic theory that includes a generalized inverse operation and its identities. One displayed relation in that theory is not one ordinary string relation in the present sense. The paper’s introduction explicitly retains the ordinary-monoid problem and the relevant reduced-relator inverse-monoid case as open.

Foniqi–Gray–Nyberg-Brodda prove undecidability of submonoid membership for families of one-relation monoids, in a paper published online in 2025 and in the 2026 journal volume. Submonoid membership asks whether an element equals some product of members of a supplied finite generating list. That existential product choice is absent when comparing just two supplied words.

The August 2026 Diophantine result proves undecidability of solving systems of equations with unknown monoid elements and fixed coefficients in certain one-relation monoids. The word problem is a special case of that broader task, so the broader negative theorem does not imply undecidability of the special case on this card. This also distinguishes equality modulo one literal relation from ordinary word equations over a free monoid.

The current card retains its saved uniform target: the presentation varies with the input to one machine. The sources often phrase the general question as decidability for every fixed one-relation monoid. An affirmative uniform theorem would imply all those individual conclusions; a uniform negative theorem need not exhibit a single fixed undecidable monoid. The August 2026 inverse-monoid paper explicitly leaves the ordinary-monoid question open, and the bounded subsequent search found no matching uniform resolution.

cards.title: Deterministic polynomial-time factorization over finite fields
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic Turing algorithm that, for every explicitly represented finite field \(F_{q}\) and every nonzero dense univariate \(f\in F_{q}[x]\) of degree \(n\ge 1\), outputs its complete irreducible factorization using \((n+\log _{2}q)^{O(1)}\) bit operations, with one absolute polynomial bound?
cards.definitions: The field is supplied as \(F_{q}=F_{p}[t]/(h(t))\), where p is a binary-encoded prime, \(h\in F_{p}[t]\) is a supplied monic irreducible polynomial of degree \(e\ge 1\), and \(q=p^{e}\). These field promises are part of the input specification; no algorithm for constructing h is required. An element is represented by its e coefficients of degree below e, each in \(\{0,\ldots ,p- 1\}\). The polynomial f is given by all \(n+1\) coefficients in this representation. Output a unit \(u\in F_{q}\)\{0}, pairwise distinct monic irreducible polynomials \(g_{1},\ldots ,g_{r}\in F_{q}[x]\), and positive integer multiplicities \(m_{1},\ldots ,m_{r}\) with \(f=u\prod _{i} g_{i}^{m_{i}}\). Output order is irrelevant. Arithmetic, conversions, preprocessing and writing the factors all count in bit time. Repeated factors and characteristic-p inseparability are allowed. The running-time exponent must be independent of n,p,e and f. No randomness, number-theoretic hypothesis, factorization oracle or precomputed field-specific advice is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: An affirmative answer gives a correct complete-factorization algorithm with the stated uniform worst-case polynomial bit bound for every valid input. A negative answer proves no such algorithm exists in this model; failure of a particular deterministic strategy is insufficient. Polynomial dependence on q or p instead of log q, average-case bounds, fixed-degree results, or conditional algorithms do not resolve the claim.
cards.why: A canonical exact derandomization problem in computer algebra, with broad consequences wherever finite-field factorization is used as a subroutine.

importance.reason: A defining open problem in algebraic computation: randomized polynomial-time search is known, while uniform deterministic polynomial bit complexity remains unresolved even for basic root-finding cases.

cards.status_note: Open unconditionally for all explicitly represented finite fields and dense univariate inputs, based on sources checked through 11 September 2026. GRH alone is not known to give the requested general polynomial bound. Amortization over primes, fixed characteristic, special Galois groups and multivariate bounds retaining a univariate oracle do not resolve this exact question.

context_blocks.text: Finite-field polynomial factorization is a setting where randomization already gives efficient exact algorithms. The desired output has a short representation and is unique up to ordering after normalizing the factors. The open issue is therefore whether random choices are essential for guaranteed efficiency, rather than whether factorization is possible or whether its answer is too large to write down.

The logarithm of the field size is the relevant parameter because one coefficient occupies about \(\log _{2}q\) bits. Enumerating all q field elements may be reasonable for a tiny field, but is exponential in the coefficient length when q grows. This distinction is already visible for quadratics over a prime field: the general problem includes finding roots of \(x^{2}- a\) modulo an arbitrary large odd prime when a is a quadratic residue.

The field presentation makes a potentially hidden prerequisite explicit. Supplying an irreducible h gives a concrete way to add, multiply and invert extension-field elements using polynomial arithmetic modulo h. The algorithm is not being asked to discover a field representation. At the same time, arithmetic operations are not free: the requested complexity includes their bit cost and must remain polynomial as the extension degree and characteristic vary.

Classical algorithms organize the work into squarefree factorization, separation by irreducible-factor degree, and splitting products whose factors have equal degree. The first two stages have deterministic polynomial-time methods. Randomized equal-degree splitting then completes the factorization efficiently. This organization, surveyed by von zur Gathen–Panario, isolates a concrete source of the derandomization difficulty.

A proposed answer can be checked efficiently without solving the search problem from scratch. Multiplying the claimed factors verifies their product, and finite-field irreducibility tests use modular powering and gcd computations. For a monic polynomial g of degree d, one checks divisibility by \(x^{q^{d}}- x\) and excludes common factors with \(x^{q^{d/\ell}}- x\) for prime divisors \(\ell\) of d. The huge exponents are handled by repeated powering modulo g, not by writing enormous polynomials.

Unconditional deterministic methods do work in time polynomial in n, log q and the characteristic p. Consequently fixed characteristic is already a tractable regime even when the extension field is large. The general obstacle is a large characteristic encoded in only log p bits. Guo’s account records a \(p^{1/2}\) dependence up to factors polynomial in n and log q for the best general deterministic methods discussed there.

GRH does not currently remove every obstacle. Evdokimov’s algorithm gives quasipolynomial degree dependence under GRH, and Galois-theoretic methods obtain polynomial time for certain supplied lifts with controlled groups. Guo’s P-scheme framework extends those special cases and unifies earlier methods. Neither its polynomial-time subclass theorem nor the general quasipolynomial bound is a general deterministic polynomial-time factorization theorem.

The inherited September 2025 paper by Altman changes the averaging question. Starting from one integer polynomial f, it factors its reductions for every prime below a bound N. The average cost per prime is polynomial in the input parameters and the degree m of the splitting field over Q. This gives a strong amortized result when m is polynomially bounded, but m can be as large as n!, and processing all primes below N does not give a polynomial-time algorithm for one arbitrary prime supplied in binary.

Altman also distinguishes averaging over primes from older averaging over input polynomials. A deterministic procedure can run quickly on most randomly selected polynomials and still have hard individual inputs. The present question requires a worst-case bound for every f over every supplied field. Neither kind of averaging can silently replace that quantifier.

Recent multivariate factorization results sometimes suppress the underlying univariate cost in their headline bounds. Chuyoon–Shpilka’s March 2026 paper explicitly restores this dependence in Remark 1.7 and §2.2. Its finite-field subroutine runs in time polynomial in p, log q and the degree; its multivariate theorem includes a factor T for univariate factorization. Specializing the number of variables does not erase that cost.

Umans–Wang’s November 2025 work pursues a different improvement: a number-theoretic conjecture could reduce the degree exponent in fast polynomial-factorization algorithms below the familiar three-halves bound. It also has a separate consequence for deterministic integer factoring. Those are valuable quantitative directions, but the abstract’s deterministic integer result must not be misread as a general derandomization theorem for finite-field polynomials.

The problem is fundamental because polynomial factorization is repeatedly used as a subroutine in symbolic computation and computational number theory. A deterministic solution would make many algorithms independent of randomized splitting choices. A proof that no such solution exists would instead establish a striking separation for an exact algebraic search problem whose answers are efficiently verifiable.

cards.title: Conjugacy problem for one-relator groups
cards.formal: Is there a total algorithm which, on input a finite one-relator group presentation \(G=\langle x_{1},\ldots ,x_{k} | r=1\rangle\) and two words u,v, decides whether some word w satisfies \(w^{- 1}uw=v\) in G?
cards.definitions: The input consists of an integer \(k\ge 1\) and three explicitly written finite words r,u,v over the letters \(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{k}\) and their formal inverses. The group is the quotient of the free group \(F(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{k})\) by the normal subgroup generated by r. The relator may be empty, in which case G is free. Equality in the displayed equation is equality in this quotient, rather than literal equality of strings. A conjugating word w may have any finite length. The algorithm is a single deterministic Turing machine that must halt with the correct yes/no answer for every valid input; the presentation is part of the input. No polynomial-time or other specified resource bound is imposed. This is the uniform decision formulation; a separate algorithm for each fixed group, without an effective way to obtain it from a presentation, is not by itself sufficient.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a uniform terminating decision procedure for all such presentations and pairs of words, or prove that this input language is undecidable. A one-relator group with an undecidable fixed-group conjugacy problem would suffice for a negative answer. A result only for torsion groups, a decision procedure for word equality, or undecidability of a different equation or membership problem does not settle this question.
cards.why: A central decision problem at the boundary between decidable symbolic equality and existential reasoning in finitely presented algebraic structures.

importance.reason: One of Dehn’s classical algorithmic problems, still unresolved in a basic class defined by a single relation; it tests how far decidability survives beyond word equality.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The general conjugacy problem remains open in the checked primary literature. This card fixes the uniform presentation-input formulation. The 2026 undecidability results cited concern different equation, membership or inverse-monoid problems.

context_blocks.text: A finite presentation describes a group through generators and identities. Here there is just one defining identity, but it can be reused inside arbitrarily long products. The conjugacy question asks whether two elements become equal after a change of reference element: u and v are equivalent when \(v=w^{- 1}uw\). It is one of Dehn’s classical decision problems. The 2025 survey explicitly identifies the general one-relator conjugacy problem as unresolved.

Conjugacy is already different from equality in a free group. The words ab and ba are conjugate, since \(a^{- 1}(ab)a=ba\), although they represent different free-group elements. At the opposite extreme, the identity element is conjugate only to itself. Consequently, a conjugacy algorithm also decides whether an input word represents the identity, by setting v to the empty word. The reverse implication is the difficult part.

Magnus’s 1932 theorem supplies a uniform algorithm for word equality in one-relator groups. Its inductive approach, clarified through the Magnus–Moldavanskii hierarchy, decomposes presentations into simpler group constructions. The corresponding transfer of conjugacy algorithms is much more delicate: the survey gives examples of HNN extensions and amalgams with undecidable conjugacy even though the relevant word problems are decidable. These examples explain a barrier to extending the proof; they are not one-relator counterexamples.

The known word algorithm does at least give a positive semidecision procedure for the present question. Enumerate all finite words w and test whether \(w^{- 1}\)uwv\(^{- 1}\) represents the identity. If u and v are conjugate, a witness eventually appears. If they are not, this search continues forever. A complete decision procedure must also provide a way to terminate on every negative input.

Equivalently, one could give a computable uniform bound on the length of a shortest necessary conjugator as a function of the input length. Such a bound permits a finite search. Conversely, a decision procedure permits computing a bound: enumerate the finitely many inputs of bounded encoding length, identify the positive ones, and search for one witness for each. Each assignment defines a homomorphism to a finite group, where conjugacy can be checked exhaustively. In a conjugacy-separable group, this search eventually finds a separating image for every nonconjugate pair. Run it alongside the search for a conjugator. Undecidability for those tasks does not imply undecidability here.

Neither result contradicts Magnus’s word algorithm or supplies a conjugacy counterexample.

The significance is a sharp computability boundary inside an extremely economical symbolic formalism. One defining group relation is sufficient to create complicated infinite behavior, yet ordinary equality remains decidable. Settling conjugacy would determine whether this additional existential search can always be controlled. A very slow total algorithm would answer the card; an efficient algorithm for a broad but restricted subclass would be progress without completing it.

cards.title: Isomorphism problem for one-relator groups
cards.formal: Is there a total algorithm which, given any two finite one-relator group presentations \(G=\langle x_{1},\ldots ,x_{k} | r=1\rangle\) and \(H=\langle y_{1},\ldots ,y_{\ell} | s=1\rangle\), decides whether G and H are isomorphic as abstract groups?
cards.definitions: The input consists of integers \(k,\ell \ge 1\) and explicitly written finite words r and s in the respective generators and formal inverses. The groups are the free groups on these generators modulo the normal closures of r and s. An empty relator is permitted and presents a free group. An isomorphism is a bijective homomorphism of the resulting abstract groups; it need not carry a listed generator to a listed generator, preserve the spelling of a relator, or come from an automorphism of a free group on the given generators. The numbers of displayed generators may differ. The sought procedure is one deterministic Turing machine which halts and answers correctly on every valid pair of presentations. No polynomial-time, elementary-time or other quantitative runtime bound is imposed. There is no promise of torsion, hyperbolicity, nontrivial center, genericity or a supplied geometric decomposition.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a uniform terminating decision procedure for all such pairs, or prove that the isomorphism language on these one-relator presentations is undecidable. A procedure that halts only for isomorphic pairs, or one correct only on a specified subclass or almost all random presentations, is insufficient. Undecidability for arbitrary finite presentations, systems of equations or other algebraic structures must be connected to this exact input class by a valid reduction to count as a negative solution.
cards.why: One of the central decision problems for finitely presented groups, testing whether a single defining relation permits effective recognition of abstract algebraic structure.

importance.reason: A classical unresolved computability boundary with deep connections to geometric group theory, effective classification and the limitations of presentation-based invariants.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No uniform algorithm or undecidability theorem for isomorphism of arbitrary one-relator group presentations was found in the checked sources. The 2026 generic algorithms and Diophantine undecidability result do not settle this all-input isomorphism question.

context_blocks.text: A group presentation is a finite description of an often infinite algebraic object. The same group can have quite different descriptions: for example, \(\langle a,b | b=a^{2}\rangle\) and \(\langle x |\) empty relator⟩ both describe an infinite cyclic group. The question is whether one defining relation leaves enough structure to recognize abstract equality of group types algorithmically, even when the supplied generators and words look unrelated.

This is the third of Dehn’s classical decision problems. Word equality compares elements within one fixed presentation; conjugacy asks for a particular kind of equivalence between elements; isomorphism compares the entire groups. Linton and Nyberg-Brodda’s survey records the general one-relator isomorphism problem as open, despite broad positive results for subclasses.

The known uniform word algorithm gives a useful positive semidecision procedure. Enumerate possible word images \(u_{1},\ldots ,u_{k}\) for the generators of G in H and \(v_{1},\ldots ,v_{\ell}\) for the generators of H in G. Check that the images satisfy each defining relation and that the two compositions fix every generator. Every check is a finite collection of word-equality tests. If mutual inverse homomorphisms exist, their finite descriptions eventually appear.

The missing part is termination on nonisomorphic inputs. Searching longer for generator images cannot certify that none exist. Equivalently, an effective bound on the lengths of some pair of mutually inverse generator-image tuples, depending only on the input length, would permit a finite search. Conversely, a total isomorphism algorithm would allow such a computable bound to be assembled by checking the finitely many inputs of bounded length and finding witnesses for the positive cases.

Easily computable invariants can reject some pairs. Abelianization, for example, takes the exponent sums of the relator and gives a finitely generated abelian quotient whose isomorphism type can be computed by integer linear algebra. But it is incomplete: the free group on two generators and \(\mathbb{Z} ^{2}\) have the same abelianization, whereas one is nonabelian and the other is abelian. The free group is represented here using the allowed empty relator, and \(\mathbb{Z} ^{2}\) by the commutator relation.

Another tempting simplification is to ask whether an automorphism of the free group carries one relator to the other, allowing inversion. Whitehead’s algorithm handles the corresponding orbit question. The survey explains that this sufficient condition is not necessary for isomorphism of the quotient groups: the Magnus conjecture asserting such a converse was disproved, and some groups have infinitely many inequivalent one-relator descriptions.

Hyperbolic groups form a large positive case. Dahmani and Guirardel solve isomorphism uniformly for all hyperbolic groups, including those with torsion. Their result also handles peripheral structures and automorphism computations, reflecting how geometric decompositions can organize otherwise unbounded searches. It is a decision theorem, not merely a heuristic for finding likely isomorphisms.

All one-relator groups with torsion are hyperbolic, so this theorem covers that entire subclass. The survey also records decidability for one-relator groups with nontrivial center and other structured families. General torsion-free one-relator groups remain beyond these combined results. Even elementary examples such as \(\mathbb{Z} ^{2}\) show that the one-relator condition does not imply hyperbolicity.

Generic-case results explain why many randomly generated instances may nevertheless be tractable. Kapovich, Schupp and Shpilrain establish rigidity for large classes of random one-relator presentations: isomorphism can be forced by simple transformations of the displayed generators and relator. The exceptional inputs are small in a specified distributional sense, but an undecidable set of inputs could still lie among such exceptions.

Kapovich’s August 18, 2026 preprint extends a generic rigidity program to fixed numbers of generators and relators. It gives an algorithmically recognizable generic family and a quadratic-time generic isomorphism algorithm, using small-cancellation stability and rigidity under free-group automorphisms. Its one-relator specialization is relevant progress, while its guarantee remains a generic one rather than a terminating decision procedure for every input.

A different August 2026 result by Nyberg-Brodda proves undecidability of the Diophantine problem for certain one-relator Baumslag–Gersten groups. That task asks whether arbitrary systems of equations with coefficients have solutions. It demonstrates that one relation does not ensure decidability of every natural algebraic question. However, it supplies no automatic reduction to isomorphism between two one-relator presentations, so the present problem remains distinct.

A resolution would clarify whether this very economical presentation format has an effective classification in principle. The positive answer could be extremely slow and still be decisive. The negative answer would require encoding undecidable information into abstract group type while retaining a single defining relator—a much more specific construction than demonstrating difficult equations inside one fixed group.

cards.title: Derandomizing polynomial identity testing
cards.formal: Is polynomial identity testing for explicitly represented arithmetic circuits over the integers in deterministic polynomial time? More precisely, do a deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\), a real constant \(C>0\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) exist such that, on every valid circuit encoding of bit length \(N\), \(A\) decides whether the output is the zero formal polynomial and halts within \(C(N+2)^k\) steps?
cards.why: Polynomial identity testing is a central concrete derandomization problem: a polynomial may be identically zero because of cancellations invisible in the circuit syntax. A deterministic polynomial-time test would affect symbolic computation and numerous algebraic algorithms, and is known to imply major circuit lower bounds. This places the question at the intersection of efficient verification of algebraic identities and fundamental complexity limitations.
cards.status_note: Checked on 14 September 2026. The original source explicitly identifies the circuit version as unresolved. The 2026 primary papers retain the general PIT question and supply reductions or restricted-model progress, rather than a general deterministic polynomial-time algorithm. No matching proof or refutation was found in the bounded search; cited proofs were not independently verified.

sentences: An arithmetic circuit may compute the zero polynomial even when cancellation is difficult to see from its graph.

cards.definitions: An arithmetic circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated output. Each input node is either one of the explicitly listed variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) or a signed integer constant given in binary. Each internal gate has two ordered predecessors and computes addition, subtraction or multiplication over \(\mathbb Z\). Intermediate results may be used by several later gates; the graph need not be a formula. A topological list of all nodes, their labels, predecessor indices and the output index is supplied, with the full variable list and all bits of every constant included in the input length \(N\). Repeated use of a variable or predecessor is allowed. Gates compute in the commutative polynomial ring \(\mathbb Z[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), and the zero polynomial means that every coefficient is exactly zero. No division, exponentiation, comparison, oracle or approximate-arithmetic gate is present. There is no depth restriction, multilinearity promise or bound on the number of nonzero monomials. No separate polynomial bound on total degree is promised: repeated multiplication can give a degree exponential in the circuit description length. The algorithm has access to the complete graph and labels, not only an oracle for evaluations. Its running time counts bit-level Turing-machine operations, including all work on constants and any integers it computes; unbounded-size integer operations are not free. Correctness is exact on every valid encoding, with no randomness or advice. Malformed encodings are rejected within the same polynomial bound. One fixed machine and one fixed polynomial bound must work for all numbers of variables, circuits, degrees and integer constants.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm exists, or prove that no such algorithm exists in the stated bit model. A positive answer requires a uniform algorithm correct for every allowed circuit, including those of exponential degree. A negative answer must exclude every deterministic machine with any fixed polynomial time bound; a lower bound for one procedure does not suffice. Results only for formulas, restricted depth, bounded-read circuits, sparse polynomials or a restricted degree regime do not resolve the full target. An evaluation-only lower bound without the explicit circuit-description promise also does not refute it. Numerical agreement at sampled inputs does not establish a formal identity.

context_blocks.text: Two very different circuit expressions can represent the same polynomial. For instance, \((x+y)^2-x^2-2xy-y^2\) is zero as a formal polynomial. Identity testing asks for this conclusion without first expanding an expression that may contain exponentially many monomials.

The circuit description is part of the input. Its reuse of intermediate values can compress a large polynomial into a small graph, but the algorithm may inspect that graph. This differs from access only to a polynomial’s values, without any representation-size promise.

Strozecki’s enumeration survey explicitly identifies deterministic polynomial-time identity testing for arithmetic-circuit representations as a major unresolved step. The discussion explains why identity tests arise in procedures that generate the monomials of an implicitly represented polynomial.

The card adopts the standard integer-circuit, bit-complexity version of that direction, as explicitly defined in the 2026 STACS paper. Binary integer constants are included with their encoding cost. The target neither gives free arbitrary field constants nor silently bounds the circuit’s degree.

Randomized polynomial-time identity testing is known with one-sided error: the zero polynomial is always recognized as zero, while a nonzero polynomial is rejected with a fixed probability bounded away from zero. The requested change is a fully deterministic, all-input guarantee in polynomial time.

Kabanets and Impagliazzo prove that a polynomial-time deterministic identity test would force a major lower bound for Boolean circuits or for arithmetic circuits computing the permanent. This implication explains why removing randomness here is consequential. It does not make the task identical to proving any one chosen arithmetic lower bound.

Černý and Seppelt’s 2026 work shows that the same general identity-testing problem governs certain equivalence questions for graphs and weighted tree automata. Their reductions retain identity testing as a derandomization condition; they do not supply the requested deterministic test.

Shpilka and Tal’s February 2026 preprint gives deterministic identity tests for special expressions \(\sum_{i=1}^{r} f_i^d\), where the \(f_i\) are sparse low-degree polynomials and the common power \(d\) is sufficiently large relative to \(r\). The input structure and parameter conditions are essential, and its polynomial bounds in those degree parameters do not cover all circuits in time polynomial in their bit length.

cards.context:
Two very different circuit expressions can represent the same polynomial. For instance, \((x+y)^2-x^2-2xy-y^2\) is zero as a formal polynomial. Identity testing asks for this conclusion without first expanding an expression that may contain exponentially many monomials.

The circuit description is part of the input. Its reuse of intermediate values can compress a large polynomial into a small graph, but the algorithm may inspect that graph. This differs from access only to a polynomial’s values, without any representation-size promise.

Strozecki’s enumeration survey explicitly identifies deterministic polynomial-time identity testing for arithmetic-circuit representations as a major unresolved step. The discussion explains why identity tests arise in procedures that generate the monomials of an implicitly represented polynomial.

The card adopts the standard integer-circuit, bit-complexity version of that direction, as explicitly defined in the 2026 STACS paper. Binary integer constants are included with their encoding cost. The target neither gives free arbitrary field constants nor silently bounds the circuit’s degree.

Randomized polynomial-time identity testing is known with one-sided error: the zero polynomial is always recognized as zero, while a nonzero polynomial is rejected with a fixed probability bounded away from zero. The requested change is a fully deterministic, all-input guarantee in polynomial time.

Kabanets and Impagliazzo prove that a polynomial-time deterministic identity test would force a major lower bound for Boolean circuits or for arithmetic circuits computing the permanent. This implication explains why removing randomness here is consequential. It does not make the task identical to proving any one chosen arithmetic lower bound.

Černý and Seppelt’s 2026 work shows that the same general identity-testing problem governs certain equivalence questions for graphs and weighted tree automata. Their reductions retain identity testing as a derandomization condition; they do not supply the requested deterministic test.

Shpilka and Tal’s February 2026 preprint gives deterministic identity tests for special expressions \(\sum_{i=1}^{r} f_i^d\), where the \(f_i\) are sparse low-degree polynomials and the common power \(d\) is sufficiently large relative to \(r\). The input structure and parameter conditions are essential, and its polynomial bounds in those degree parameters do not cover all circuits in time polynomial in their bit length.

cards.definitions: For every integer \(n\ge 1\) the input consists of two length-n binary strings encoding integers a,b with \(0\le a,b<2^{n}\); leading zeroes are allowed. The required output is the ordinary binary representation of ab, padded to length 2n. The machine has a fixed finite program, a fixed finite tape alphabet, and a fixed finite number of one-dimensional tapes with one head per tape. Input strings and end markers occupy designated tapes initially, other tapes are blank, and the output must be written explicitly on a designated output tape. In one transition the machine reads and writes at most one cell per tape and moves each head by at most one cell. The cost is the number of transitions, including access, data movement and output. The same machine must halt correctly for every n and every input pair; its tape count and alphabet cannot grow with n. For a fixed correct machine M, let \(t_{M}(n)\) be its maximum running time over the \(2^{2n}\) pairs of n-bit strings. Bounds concern these fixed-machine functions as n tends to infinity. A matching rate \(g(n)>0\) means some correct M has \(t_{M}(n)=O(g(n))\), while every correct M has \(t_{M}(n)=\Omega (g(n))\); constants and thresholds may depend on M. A fresh hardcoded machine for each n is not allowed. No random access, unit-cost arithmetic on arbitrarily long integers, advice, oracle or quantum operations are part of the model. Changing the padded output convention to ordinary unpadded binary changes the cost by only \(O(n)\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give an asymptotic rate \(g(n)\) and prove both the existence of a single correct deterministic multitape machine running in \(O(g(n))\) worst-case time and an \(\Omega (g(n))\) worst-case lower bound for every correct machine. This asks for matching bounds up to multiplicative constants, not necessarily the particular rate n log n. An upper bound without a matching universal lower bound, or a lower bound for a restricted computational model, is a partial result.

context_blocks.title: A familiar operation with an unknown limit
context_blocks.text: For example, \(11_{2}\) multiplied by \(11_{2}\) is \(1001_{2}\): the input integers are 3 and 3, and the exact product is 9. The question asks how the cost grows when each input contains millions or many more bits. The school multiplication procedure performs quadratically many elementary digit operations. That describes one procedure, not a lower bound on every possible algorithm.

context_blocks.title: Bits and data movement are charged
context_blocks.text: A machine instruction that multiplies two arbitrarily large integers in one step would make the question trivial by placing the entire task inside the instruction set. Here each tape head accesses one cell at a time. Arithmetic on long numbers and rearranging their bits therefore take time. The explicit output alone gives a linear lower bound. It does not establish the additional logarithmic factor in the best known upper bound.

context_blocks.title: What the O(n log n) theorem settles
context_blocks.text: Harvey and van der Hoeven proved that binary integer multiplication takes \(O(n \log  n)\) time in this multitape model. Their 2021 theorem settles the upper-bound conjecture associated with Schönhage and Strassen. It does not prove that all algorithms require this much time. The 2025 paper by the same authors states that even a superlinear lower bound remains unknown in the unrestricted multitape model. The gap is between a linear lower bound and an n log n upper bound.

context_blocks.title: The matrix-transposition connection
context_blocks.text: A 2025 theorem relates multiplication to moving data: transposing an \(s\times s\) binary matrix written row by row. Even a \(2\times 2\) matrix with entries a,b,c,d changes its row-order encoding from abcd to acbd. If every multitape machine needs \(\Omega (s^{2} \log  s)\) time for the general transposition task, their theorem implies \(\Omega (n \log  n)\) time for multiplication. The transposition premise is itself unproved, so this is a conditional relationship between lower bounds, not an unconditional proof of multiplication’s optimality.

context_blocks.title: Which later results concern this question
context_blocks.text: Qin’s August 2026 result bounds the width of ordered binary decision diagrams computing a middle product bit on restricted inputs. Width in that model does not bound the running time of every multitape machine. Likewise, arithmetic-operation counts and performance on typical or small inputs answer other questions. This card concerns exact products, the worst input at each length, and one fixed algorithm working at all lengths.

cards.title: Strassen’s asymptotic rank conjecture
cards.formal: For every \(n\ge 1\) and every tensor \(T\in \mathbb{C} ^{n}\otimes \mathbb{C} ^{n}\otimes \mathbb{C} ^{n}\) whose three flattenings all have rank n, is \(\lim _{k\to \infty} R(T^{\otimes}k)^{1/k}=n\)?
cards.definitions: \(R(T)\) is the least r such that \(T=\sum_{i=1}^{r} a_{i}\otimes b_{i}\otimes c_{i}\) with \(a_{i},b_{i},c_{i}\in \mathbb{C} ^{n}\). Each flattening views the tensor as a linear map from the dual of one factor into the tensor product of the other two. In \(T^{\otimes}k\) the first, second and third tensor factors are respectively grouped, producing a tensor with three factors \(\mathbb{C} ^{n^{k}}\). Submultiplicativity of rank makes the displayed limit equal to \(\inf _{k\ge 1} R(T^{\otimes}k)^{1/k}\). This is exact rank over \(\mathbb{C}\), not border rank, and there is no explicitness or computational requirement on T.

context_blocks.text: Matrix rank has a simple algebraic characterization, whereas tensor rank changes substantially when many independent copies are considered jointly. Strassen’s conjecture says that in the asymptotic setting the three flattening dimensions already determine the answer.

The cubic concise formulation is the target proposed in the personal list. It includes matrix-multiplication tensors, so a positive resolution would imply matrix multiplication exponent two; the reverse implication is not claimed. The 2024–2026 source studies structural properties of asymptotic rank without proving this equality.

cards.title: Derandomizing black-box depth-four PIT
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic uniform polynomial-time construction of hitting sets for all size-\(s\), \(n\)-variable \(\Sigma\Pi\Sigma\Pi\) arithmetic circuits, in the field-operation model specified below? Precisely, one algorithm and constants \(C>0,b\in\mathbb N\) must work for every \(n,s\ge1\), every working field \(K\), and every supplied list \(T\) of \(2s^2+1\) distinct elements of \(K\). In at most \(C(n+s+1)^b\) operations it must output a list \(H\subseteq K^n\) such that every nonzero formal polynomial computed by any allowed circuit over \(K\) has a nonzero evaluation at some point of \(H\). The algorithm receives no circuit description, coefficients, or evaluation oracle for a particular polynomial.
cards.why: Identity testing asks whether a compact arithmetic computation represents the zero polynomial. A uniform collection of evaluations would remove randomness without inspecting the computation itself. The depth-four case is especially consequential because of its established relationship to much more general arithmetic circuits, and its unrestricted fan-ins distinguish it from several recent positive results.
cards.status_note: The unrestricted problem is posed in the 2010 survey. The checked 2021 and 2026 primary results give restricted-family algorithms and do not cover the target’s unrestricted fan-ins and arbitrary working fields. Bounded searches through 2026-09-15 found no general resolution. This records the scope of sources checked, not an independent certification of every later proof.

The same generated set must work for every circuit of the given size without seeing its coefficients or gates.

cards.definitions: An allowed circuit is a finite directed acyclic arithmetic circuit with one output, four alternating layers of unbounded-fan-in arithmetic gates, and input leaves labeled by variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) or arbitrary constants of \(K\). From output to inputs the operations are sum, product, sum, product. Fan-in-one gates may pad smaller depth. Gates and subexpressions may be shared; the size is the total number of wires, including wires from input leaves and with repeated uses counted separately. There are at most \(s\) wires. Addition and multiplication are the only polynomial operations; division gates, exponentiation gates with compressed exponents, and tests inside the hidden circuit are excluded. In expression form the output is a sum of products of sparse polynomials, with no fixed bound on the top fan-in or on the bottom monomial degrees beyond the wire budget. The total degree is at most \(s^2\), since each bottom product has degree at most \(s\) and each upper product has at most \(s\) factors. Homogeneity, multilinearity, and bounded variable occurrence are not assumed. A nonzero polynomial means one with at least one nonzero coefficient, not merely a function that is nonzero somewhere on the original base field. The construction uses one finite program with ordinary discrete control and registers holding opaque elements of \(K\). A field addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a tested nonzero element, equality test, copy, or access to a supplied field element costs one operation; discrete control is charged by its ordinary bit operations. The only initial field values are zero, one and the entries of \(T\). Field representations carry no readable extra advice. The constants \(C,b\) are independent of characteristic, field, \(T,n,s\) and all circuit coefficients. The cost includes writing every coordinate of every output point; existence of a small set without an efficient construction does not qualify. No randomness, parameter-dependent advice, or uncharged preprocessing is allowed. The input list \(T\) makes the source’s sufficiently-large-field convention explicit. For a smaller base field \(F\), evaluations may instead take place in a supplied extension \(K\supseteq F\) with such a list; the circuit is then viewed over \(K\). Constructing or encoding that extension is outside this field-operation target. This is not a claim about bit complexity over arbitrary field presentations or an algorithm confined to evaluations inside a too-small field.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the uniform hitting-set construction and its polynomial resource bound, or prove that no such construction exists in the stated model. A positive proof must handle every allowed coefficient assignment, every working field with the supplied distinct elements, and every size and variable count. It must establish that evaluating on all of \(H\) distinguishes the zero polynomial from every nonzero polynomial in the class. A negative proof must rule out every finite uniform algorithm and polynomial bound; failure of one candidate hitting set is insufficient. A white-box algorithm, a nonconstructive existence proof, a construction with superpolynomial running time, or a construction restricted to bounded top fan-in or bottom degree does not meet this target.

context_blocks.text: Open Problem 18 explicitly asks to derandomize black-box depth-four PIT. Definition 1.1 counts wires and permits unbounded fan-in at bounded depth; Remark 1.1 uses arbitrary fields by default. Section 4 permits extension-field evaluations, while Section 4.1 defines hitting sets. These conventions are made explicit in the field-operation target here.

Theorem 4.9, attributed to Agrawal and Vinay, relates polynomial-time explicit hitting sets for depth-four circuits to quasipolynomial-size explicit hitting sets for general arithmetic circuits. This is a stated consequence of solving the restricted-depth target; the card does not add a general-circuit result to the required answer.

Dutta, Dwivedi and Saxena’s 2021 Theorem 2 gives quasipolynomial-time black-box testing for bounded-top-fan-in depth-four circuits with either sums of univariates or bounded-degree bottom polynomials. Their polynomial-time theorem is white-box and for the sums-of-univariates subclass.

Garg, Oliveira, Sengupta, Shalmon and Shpilka’s 2026 Corollary 1.4 gives polynomial-time black-box PIT in characteristic zero when top fan-in is fixed and bottom degree is at most two. Its polynomial dependence is for each fixed top fan-in; it is not a polynomial-time guarantee uniform in unrestricted fan-in.

Shpilka and Tal’s February 2026 preprint gives explicit hitting sets for sums of \(r\) powers of sparse polynomials when the common power \(d\) satisfies \(d>r^2\), over characteristic zero or sufficiently large characteristic. Upper product gates in the present card may multiply unrelated factors, so the powering result covers a different restricted family.
