Its polynomial dependence is for each fixed top fan-in; it is not a polynomial-time guarantee uniform in unrestricted fan-in.

Shpilka and Tal’s February 2026 preprint gives explicit hitting sets for sums of \(r\) powers of sparse polynomials when the common power \(d\) satisfies \(d>r^2\), over characteristic zero or sufficiently large characteristic. Upper product gates in the present card may multiply unrelated factors, so the powering result covers a different restricted family.

cards.title: Unrestricted arithmetic lower bounds for the discrete Fourier transform
cards.formal: Let \(S(n)\) be the minimum size of a complex arithmetic straight-line program that computes all n coordinates of the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) exactly, in the model below. Do constants \(c>0\) and N exist such that \(S(n)\ge c n \log _{2}n\) for every power of two \(n\ge N\), with no bound on the magnitudes of the constants used in the program?

cards.definitions: For \(n\ge 1\) set \(\omega _{n}=\exp (- 2\pi i/n)\), and define \(DFT_{n}(x)_{j}=\sum_{k=0}^{n- 1}\omega _{n}^{jk}x_{k}\) for \(j=0,\ldots ,n- 1\) and \(x\in \mathbb{C} ^{n}\). This is the unnormalized cyclic DFT. A straight-line program is a finite acyclic list of scalar instructions. Each instruction either adds, subtracts or multiplies two previously available values, or multiplies one value by a fixed complex scalar. Input coordinates and any fixed complex constants are available initially. Values may be reused without limit, and all n required output coordinates must occur among the computed values. Size is the number of instructions; each complex scalar operation costs one, regardless of operand magnitude. The sequence and all constants may depend on n but not on x. Constants need not be efficiently generated or have a bounded bit representation. There is no restriction on circuit depth, reuse, storage, intermediate magnitudes or numerical conditioning. Operations are exact and must compute the required polynomial identities for every complex input. This is the standard division-free arithmetic-circuit formulation used to make the imported model precise; subtraction and multiplication by any reciprocal constant are allowed. No comparison, branching, floor, bit extraction, approximation or quantum operation is present. For this linear output map, allowing products of input-dependent intermediate values changes minimum size by at most a constant factor compared with linear circuits using only addition, subtraction and scalar multiplication, as stated in the cited circuit reference. Counting a two-input linear combination as one instruction instead of at most three also changes cost only by a constant factor.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the uniform lower bound for every sufficiently large power-of-two length and every program in the stated model, or refute it. Precisely, a refutation must show that for every \(c>0\) and every threshold N there is a power of two \(n\ge N\) and a program of size less than \(c n \log _{2}n\). A family using \(o(n \log  n)\) operations would suffice, but the full logical negation does not require a uniformly generated family or such a bound at every length. A lower bound requiring bounded coefficients, unitary gates, limited storage or numerical stability does not establish the target.

context_blocks.title: A fast transform reuses intermediate values
context_blocks.text: For four inputs, form \(a=x_{0}+x_{2}, b=x_{1}+x_{3}, c=x_{0}- x_{2}\) and \(d=x_{1}- x_{3}\). The four Fourier outputs are \(a+b, c- id, a- b\) and \(c+id\). Shared sums let the same work serve several output coordinates. The classical FFT extends this reuse to obtain \(O(n \log  n)\) operations; the question is whether a different unrestricted program can do asymptotically better.

context_blocks.title: Normalization should not decide this question
context_blocks.text: Dividing all outputs by \(\sqrt{n}\) gives the normalized DFT. In the unbounded-scalar model, converting either normalization to the other costs at most n extra operations, so the conjectured asymptotic lower bound is equivalent for the two. A lower-bound argument tied to one normalization may nevertheless fail for the other when its coefficients are restricted.

context_blocks.title: What the classical lower bound assumes
context_blocks.text: Morgenstern’s lower bound, recalled in both full sources, gives order n log n for the unnormalized transform when scalar magnitudes have a fixed bound. The determinant magnitude of that transform is \(n^{n/2}\), whereas the normalized matrix has determinant magnitude one. Arbitrarily large scalars invalidate the bounded per-operation growth used by that result. Thus the known theorem does not already settle this card.

context_blocks.title: Unitary and well-conditioned models
context_blocks.text: Ailon proves an n log n bound for normalized Fourier computation with two-coordinate unitary gates and no extra storage. Subsequent results relate possible speedup to numerical ill-conditioning. These are meaningful restrictions on computations; the present model permits general arithmetic, arbitrary reuse and large intermediate values, so those lower bounds have a narrower scope.

context_blocks.title: Related tasks use different cost measures
context_blocks.text: The 2026 source studies necessary divisions in Toom-Cook interpolation at integer evaluation points and division-aware costs. It does not give an unrestricted DFT operation lower bound. Counting only multiplications, approximating Fourier outputs at fixed precision, or applying a quantum Fourier transform to state amplitudes also asks a different question from computing this entire classical complex output vector.

cards.title: Uniform exact permanent circuits below base two
cards.formal:
Does there exist a rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), an integer \(C\ge1\), and one deterministic circuit generator \(G\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), \(G(1^{n})\) outputs a division-free rational arithmetic circuit \(\mathcal C_{n}\) with at most \(C(2-\varepsilon)^{n}\) nodes, within at most \(C(2-\varepsilon)^{n}\) Turing-machine steps, and
\[\forall K\text{ of characteristic zero}\ \forall A\in K^{n\times n},\qquad \mathcal C_{n}(A)=\operatorname{per}(A)=\sum_{\pi\in S_{n}}\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}A_{i,\pi(i)}?\]
Here \(S_{n}\) is the set of permutations of \(\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\), and every rational circuit constant is interpreted through the canonical embedding \(\mathbb Q\to K\). This fixes the uniform rational-circuit version of the saved characteristic-zero arithmetic-operation question.

sentences: The permanent is the unsigned sum of permutation products of a square matrix.
This card asks whether exact division-free rational circuits can beat exponential base two while being generated uniformly within the same exponential bound.
The generated polynomial must work for every matrix over every characteristic-zero field, with bit costs for circuit construction separated from field-operation costs for evaluation.
Checked recent results give conditional circuit improvements, finite-ring algorithms, bounded-entry bit-time savings or lower bounds for restricted formula classes.
A complete Lean proof must establish the specified uniform circuit family with a fixed positive base saving or rule out every family meeting these conventions.

cards.definitions:
A field \(K\) has characteristic zero when the sum of any positive number of copies of its multiplicative identity is nonzero; this gives a unique injective field homomorphism \(\mathbb Q\to K\). The domain contains every square matrix over every such field, including rational, real and complex matrices, with no sign, magnitude, sparsity, rank, symmetry or integrality promise. The permanent is the unsigned permutation sum above; it is not the determinant. All evaluations must be exact.

An arithmetic circuit is a finite list of nodes in topological order, with the last node the output. Each node is either an input variable \(x_{i,j}\) with \(0\le i,j<n\), a rational constant, or a binary \(+\), \(-\), or \(\times\) gate whose two ordered parent indices refer to earlier nodes. Repeated use of the same parent is allowed, so shared intermediate values and squaring are permitted. Unused nodes may be omitted. The size counts all nodes, including constants and variable nodes. On a matrix \(A\), an input node evaluates to its entry, constants are embedded in \(K\), and internal gates perform the indicated field operations. Each internal gate costs one arithmetic operation, independently of the sizes of field elements; a rational constant is a permitted circuit input. There is no division by an input-dependent value, branching on an input entry, rounding, bit extraction, transcendental gate, oracle gate, or limit computation. Subtraction is equivalently addition using the constant \(-1\), so it does not introduce an extra algebraic operation type beyond the source circuit convention.

The generator is one finite deterministic multitape Turing machine over fixed finite alphabets, given only \(1^{n}\). It receives neither matrix entries nor a description of the field. Its program and clock constants are fixed independently of \(n\). For definiteness, for a nonnegative integer \(t\), let \(b(t)\) be its ordinary binary expansion with \(b(0)=0\), and encode \(t\) by \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\). The output begins with the encoded positive node count. Each node then has a three-bit tag: 000 for a variable followed by \(E(i)E(j)\); 001 for a constant followed by a sign bit and \(E(u)E(v)\), representing \((-1)^{s}u/v\), with \(u\ge0,v\ge1\) in lowest terms and zero having sign zero; 010, 011 or 100 for addition, subtraction or multiplication followed by the two encoded parent indices. Indices start at zero, and the output must be a well-formed list with no trailing bits. Every generator transition, including writing every constant and index bit, is charged. Thus a separate unbounded search or arbitrary nonuniform circuit choice is not hidden outside the construction bound.

Circuit generation and field evaluation are different costs: the first is bounded binary computation on the dimension, while the second counts exact field operations on abstract entries. There is no claim of a bit-time bound independent of entry length when evaluating on encoded integers or rationals. The same generated rational polynomial must work in all characteristic-zero fields; no field-dependent or noncomputable constants are allowed. This is a specified uniform circuit model, not an assertion that all branching arithmetic algorithms or all field-specific circuit models are equivalent to it. The fixed base saving is uniform in dimension. Polynomial prefactors may be absorbed by a smaller positive base saving, but \(2^{n-o(n)}\) alone does not meet the target. This is an exact complexity-existence question, so absolute numerical tolerance does not apply.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify the finite generator, rational \(\varepsilon\), integer \(C\), valid output circuits and their two bounds for every dimension, and prove their exact evaluation identity for every matrix over every characteristic-zero field. A polynomial identity proof over \(\mathbb Q\), together with its transfer under the canonical field embedding, can establish the required universal identity. A negative answer must exclude every permitted generator and every fixed positive base saving, rather than one construction, bounded circuit depth or coefficient pattern. It need not be a single finite counterexample matrix. A conditional implication is only conditional unless its hypotheses are also proved. Approximate permanent values, algorithms only for bounded integer entries or finite rings, a sublinear saving in the exponent, and small circuits with no generator meeting the bound do not suffice. A negative result for this precise circuit model is not automatically a lower bound for every stronger arithmetic model.

context_blocks.text: Ryser’s classical upper bound uses \(O(n2^{n})\) field operations to compute the permanent. A fixed improvement from exponential base two would change the scale of exact algebraic counting, while still allowing exponential running time. Exact #P-completeness on zero–one integer matrices explains the absence of an expected polynomial-time counting algorithm, but it does not rule out a fixed exponential-base improvement in this arithmetic model.

For a \(2\times2\) matrix with rows \((a,b)\) and \((c,d)\), the permanent is \(ad+bc\), whereas the determinant is \(ad-bc\). Removing alternating signs changes the algebraic complexity substantially. On nonnegative entries the permanent also counts weighted bipartite perfect matchings, but this card allows every field entry and asks for exact evaluation. The randomized or deterministic relative approximations in the neighboring cards do not give this circuit family.

The proposal cited the uniform-circuit results of Björklund, Kaski, Koana and Nederlof. Their Section 2.2 uses division-free arithmetic circuits, and Theorem 1.3 bounds both construction time and circuit size. This card makes the previously unstated coefficient and uniformity conventions concrete by choosing a finite generator of rational circuits that works throughout characteristic zero. This portable rational model and the fixed exponential-base target are explicit editorial choices; they are not presented as identical to every possible reading of Knuth’s broader arithmetic-operation question quoted in that source.

The ICALP 2026 paper proves that a sufficiently low rank growth rate for a sequence of balanced tripartitioning tensors yields a uniform permanent circuit construction with a fixed exponential improvement. It relates the needed rank bounds to Strassen’s asymptotic rank conjecture. A tensor rank here is the least number of products of three linear forms needed to express the associated trilinear form. These are conditional upper bounds with a specified underlying field; the paper does not establish the required rank hypothesis unconditionally or identify every coefficient model. Its result is relevant evidence about the barrier, not a completed positive answer.

Björklund and Williams give a deterministic \(2^{n-\Omega(n/r)}\)-time permanent algorithm over a finite ring with \(r\le n\) elements. For fixed \(r\) this is a fixed base improvement, but a finite field has positive characteristic and is outside this card’s domain. They also obtain faster exact counting on regular zero–one matrices, where the saving depends on the degree. Those input restrictions must be retained when comparing the theorem to an unrestricted characteristic-zero circuit family.

Baitian Li’s revised paper of 3 May 2026, published at ICALP 2026, gives \(2^{n-\Omega(\sqrt n)}\)-type bit-time bounds for integer permanents, with polynomial dependence on the bit bound for entries. Its hafnian formulation uses a \(2n\times2n\) symmetric matrix; a permanent of order \(n\) is a special case at that size. The theorem is a significant exact speedup, but its sublinear exponent saving is not a fixed \((2-\varepsilon)^{n}\) guarantee, and its numerical operations are not this input-oblivious characteristic-zero circuit model. The revised title and more general hafnian scope replace the older title in the proposal’s reference trail.

Fonollosa’s July 2026 preprint compares Ryser, Glynn and Fourier evaluation formulas at the same \(\Theta(n2^{n})\) arithmetic scale. Its revised Corollary 1 gives a lower bound on the number of evaluations for the particular row-product evaluation schemes considered in that paper. That restricted-formula bound does not rule out general arithmetic circuits with reused intermediate values and unrestricted depth. The new proof was not independently verified in full during this review.

The fixed base, the dimension, the field, the coefficient representation and uniform construction all matter. A finite-ring computation, an experiment on structured matrices, a smaller constant number of exponential terms or a better approximate count may be useful without answering this question. A resolution would clarify the exact algebraic cost of one of the central counting polynomials.

Björklund and Williams give a deterministic \(2^{n-\Omega(n/r)}\)-time permanent algorithm over a finite ring with \(r\le n\) elements. For fixed \(r\) this is a fixed base improvement, but a finite field has positive characteristic and is outside this card’s domain. They also obtain faster exact counting on regular zero–one matrices, where the saving depends on the degree. Those input restrictions must be retained when comparing the theorem to an unrestricted characteristic-zero circuit family.

Baitian Li’s revised paper of 3 May 2026, published at ICALP 2026, gives \(2^{n-\Omega(\sqrt n)}\)-type bit-time bounds for integer permanents, with polynomial dependence on the bit bound for entries. Its hafnian formulation uses a \(2n\times2n\) symmetric matrix; a permanent of order \(n\) is a special case at that size. The theorem is a significant exact speedup, but its sublinear exponent saving is not a fixed \((2-\varepsilon)^{n}\) guarantee, and its numerical operations are not this input-oblivious characteristic-zero circuit model. The revised title and more general hafnian scope replace the older title in the proposal’s reference trail.

Fonollosa’s July 2026 preprint compares Ryser, Glynn and Fourier evaluation formulas at the same \(\Theta(n2^{n})\) arithmetic scale. Its revised Corollary 1 gives a lower bound on the number of evaluations for the particular row-product evaluation schemes considered in that paper. That restricted-formula bound does not rule out general arithmetic circuits with reused intermediate values and unrestricted depth. The new proof was not independently verified in full during this review.

The fixed base, the dimension, the field, the coefficient representation and uniform construction all matter. A finite-ring computation, an experiment on structured matrices, a smaller constant number of exponential terms or a better approximate count may be useful without answering this question. A resolution would clarify the exact algebraic cost of one of the central counting polynomials.

cards.title: NP-hardness of PosSLP
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{PosSLP}\) NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Concretely, does there exist one deterministic Turing-computable map \(g\) and constants \(C>0,d\in\mathbb N\) such that \(g\) runs in time at most \(C(N+1)^d\) on every input of bit length \(N\), outputs a valid integer straight-line program, and for every encoded 3-CNF formula \(F\), \[F\text{ is satisfiable}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{value}(g(F))>0?\] The reduction must be unconditionally correct on all inputs, with no algebraic conjecture, randomness, oracle or advice. Malformed input encodings are treated as no-instances and must also map to nonpositive outputs.

source_formulation.text: And finally, can we prove unconditional hardness results for PosSLP?
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 14

cards.why: A short sequence of elementary integer operations can represent numbers whose binary expansions are enormous. PosSLP isolates the task of deciding the sign of such a number. Its connections to numerical computation make a conventional hardness classification consequential well beyond the particular instruction format.
cards.status_note: The checked 2024 primary papers leave unconditional PosSLP hardness open, and Miltzow’s March 2026 discussion still describes the NP-hardness evidence as conditional. Bounded later-work checks through 2026-09-15 found no proof or refutation of the specified deterministic many-one NP-hardness target. The source’s broader hardness direction is preserved separately and is not claimed equivalent to this concrete specialization.

importance.reason: PosSLP is a central bridge between exact arithmetic computation and discrete complexity, yet no general NP-hardness result is established in the checked literature. An unconditional reduction would materially clarify the computational strength of succinct integer sign testing and the interpretation of many PosSLP-hard numerical tasks.

sentences: The target is unconditional NP-hardness of deciding whether a succinctly represented integer is positive.
The integer is produced by a straight-line program starting from one and using only addition, subtraction and multiplication.
The required reduction must deterministically convert each 3-SAT instance to one such program in polynomial bit time.
Known conditional consequences for randomized algorithms and unconditional hardness of polynomial variants do not supply this reduction.
A complete answer would clarify the discrete complexity of exact sign testing without also requiring a proof that P and NP differ.

cards.definitions: An integer straight-line program consists of an implicit initial value \(b_0=1\) and a finite sequence of \(m\ge0\) instructions. Instruction \(i\), for \(1\le i\le m\), is a triple \((j_i,k_i,\circ_i)\), where \(0\le j_i,k_i<i\) and \(\circ_i\in\{+,-,\times\}\); it defines \(b_i=b_{j_i}\circ_i b_{k_i}\). The output value is the exact integer \(b_m\), with output one when \(m=0\). Values may be negative or zero, and previous values may be reused arbitrarily. The program contains no input variables, divisions, roots, sign tests, branches, loops, separately supplied integer constants or compressed repetition instructions. The program is encoded by a self-delimited binary encoding of \(m\), followed in order by binary predecessor indices and an operation symbol for each instruction. All delimiters use a fixed finite alphabet; standard binary encodings of that alphabet are equivalent within constant factors. The PosSLP language accepts exactly valid encodings with positive output, and rejects valid zero or negative outputs and malformed programs. There is no promise on the sign or magnitude. A 3-CNF input is an explicit finite list of clauses, each containing at most three signed positive binary variable indices, with delimiters; repeated occurrences are allowed. Satisfiability means that some Boolean assignment to all occurring variables makes at least one literal in every clause true. An empty clause is false, and a conjunction with no clauses is true. The source input size \(N\) is its full encoded bit length. The reduction is one finite deterministic program on ordinary finite-alphabet Turing tapes; all reading, writing and index manipulation are charged by ordinary bit steps. Its time bound includes writing the entire straight-line program. It need not output the exponentially long binary expansion of the integer represented by that program. A many-one reduction makes one output instance with the displayed exact equivalence; it is not an adaptive oracle computation or a randomized transformation. Since 3-SAT is NP-complete under these reductions, this specific reduction is equivalent to NP-hardness, meaning that every language accepted by a polynomial-time nondeterministic Turing machine has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to PosSLP.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction exists, or prove that none exists. A positive answer must specify one reduction and prove its polynomial bit complexity, output validity and exact preservation of both satisfiable and unsatisfiable inputs. It must discharge every assumption needed for correctness. A negative answer must rule out all reductions of this form; failure of one construction does not suffice. NP-hardness is a relationship between decision problems and by itself does not establish \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), membership in NP, or NP-completeness of PosSLP. A conditional implication about randomized algorithms, an oracle reduction with no conversion to many-one form, or hardness for a polynomial-positivity variant does not meet this specified target.

context_blocks.text: The imported FSTTCS 2024 conclusion asks broadly for unconditional hardness results for PosSLP. To make that direction a single reviewable target, this card selects the concrete NP-hardness question explicitly posed in Bürgisser and Jindal’s earlier SODA 2024 conclusion, and fixes deterministic many-one reductions. It does not equate every possible hardness advance in the source direction with this particular target.

Bürgisser and Jindal show that a randomized polynomial-time algorithm for PosSLP would yield randomized polynomial-time algorithms for all NP languages, assuming an unproved constructive univariate-radical conjecture. This is a conditional complexity consequence and does not itself provide the unconditional deterministic reduction asked for here.

Bläser, Dörfler and Jindal prove unconditional coNP-hardness for a variant whose input represents a univariate polynomial and whose question is positivity at every real point. The quantification over real points changes the problem from testing the sign of one fixed integer. Their conclusion retains unconditional hardness of PosSLP as an open direction.

Miltzow’s March 2026 introduction to real computation again defines PosSLP by constant-one integer straight-line programs and describes the known NP-hardness results as conditional on assumptions that are far from resolved. Its informal discussion is used as a later status check; the complete input and reduction conventions here are stated independently.

cards.title: Cubic min-plus circuit lower bounds for shortest paths
cards.formal: For \(n \ge  2\), assign an arbitrary nonnegative real weight \(x_{ij}\) to every unordered edge \(\{i,j\}\) of the complete undirected graph on vertices 1,...,n. Define $f_n(x)=\min_{P:1\leadsto n}\sum_{e\in P}x_e$, where P ranges over simple paths. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input gates \(x_{ij}\) and optional constants 0 and infinity, binary gates \(\min (a,b)\) or \(a+b\), unrestricted reuse of gate outputs, and one designated output. Its topology depends on n but not on x, and it must compute \(f_{n}\) exactly for every permitted weight assignment. Let \(s(n)\) be the minimum number of binary gates in such a circuit. Is \(s(n)=Omega(n^{3})\)? Equivalently, do there exist constants \(c>0\) and n0 such that every such circuit has at least \(c n^{3}\) gates for every \(n\ge n0\)?
cards.definitions: A simple path visits no vertex twice. The two occurrences \(x_{ij}\) and \(x_{ji}\) denote the same input, because the graph is undirected. Infinity is an optional internal constant with min(a,infinity)=a and a+infinity=infinity; all input edge weights are finite and nonnegative. The circuit has no subtraction, tests with separate Boolean outputs, conditional routing, or input-dependent memory access. A min gate directly returns the smaller of its two numerical arguments. Input gates, wires, and reuse of an already computed value are free; binary arithmetic gates are counted. Circuits need not be generated uniformly by an efficient algorithm, so the proposed lower bound is nonuniform and imposes no depth restriction.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the quantified cubic lower bound, or refute it by proving its negation: for every \(c>0\) and every n0 there is an \(n\ge n0\) with a correct circuit using fewer than \(c n^{3}\) gates. An \(o(n^{3})\)-size circuit family for all sufficiently large n would suffice for a negative answer. A lower bound for a more restricted circuit class, for all-pairs output, or for shortest paths allowing negative input weights does not establish this statement.
cards.why: This is a basic unconditional lower-bound question for dynamic programming. A resolution would clarify whether the standard cubic relaxation computation is intrinsically necessary even for one distance when computation is restricted to minimum and addition, and would illuminate why monotone lower-bound methods struggle with paths of varying lengths.

importance.reason: A central explicit lower-bound problem for tropical circuits, linking shortest paths, pure dynamic programming, and provenance computation. The gap concerns a basic polynomial-time task rather than a specialized graph family.

progress.text: Jukna gives the \(O(n^{3}) \min\)-plus upper bound and explicitly asks for a cubic lower bound for the single-pair connectivity polynomial; his framework distinguishes nonnegative tropical evaluation from formal polynomial production.

The author’s book supplements discuss the known cubic all-pairs lower bound and the unresolved single-source and single-pair optimality questions. The all-pairs argument does not directly settle one output.

Koutris restates the question for complete undirected graphs over absorptive semirings, recording the \(O(n^{3})\) upper bound and the quadratic input-dependence lower bound, with the gap open already over the tropical semiring.

context_blocks.text: The numerical task is elementary to state: return one shortest-path distance. The difficulty is understanding what can be done by a fixed network of minimum and addition operations. An algorithm that chooses which vertex to process next using comparisons may use information to control its future computation. This circuit model cannot turn the identity of a minimum into arbitrary control flow. Consequently, a fast implementation of a graph-search algorithm does not automatically supply a circuit of comparable size.

A concrete upper bound comes from repeated relaxation. Initialize \(d_{0}(1)=0\) and \(d_{0}(v)\)=infinity otherwise, and compute \(d_{k}(v)=\min\)(\(d_{k-1}(v), \min\) over u distinct from v of \(d_{k-1}(u)+x_{uv}\)). After n-1 layers, output \(d_{n-1}(n)\). Each layer uses \(O(n^{2})\) gates. Nonnegative weights ensure that deleting cycles cannot increase a walk’s cost, so these layers suffice for the simple-path optimum. This gives \(O(n^{3})\) gates.

Every edge can influence the answer: choose a simple source-to-target path through that edge, make its other edges cheap, and all edges outside the path expensive. Thus dependence on the quadratic number of inputs gives a quadratic lower bound, but does not charge separately for repeated reuse of intermediate computations. The missing factor n is the substantive issue.

For all-pairs shortest paths, a cubic lower bound is known in the same general min-plus framework. Its many required outputs are essential to the usual argument; requesting only the distance from 1 to n leaves room for different sharing. The database formulation places the question in absorptive semirings, where adding an unnecessary detour is absorbed. This card fixes the nonnegative tropical instance so that its allowed operations and output are unambiguous.

cards.title: Linear-size circuits for integer multiplication
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(C>0\) and \(n_{0}\ge 1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge n_{0}, a\) Boolean circuit of at most Cn gates maps every pair of n-bit unsigned integers to all 2n bits of their exact product?
cards.definitions: The circuit has input bits \(a_{0},\ldots ,a_{n- 1},b_{0},\ldots ,b_{n- 1}\), representing \(a=\sum_{i}a_{i}2^{i}\) and \(b=\sum_{i}b_{i}2^{i}\), and output bits \(c_{0},\ldots ,c_{2n- 1}\) satisfying \(\sum_{j}c_{j}2\)ʲ=ab. Gates are two-input AND and OR and one-input NOT; constants 0 and 1 are allowed. Size counts gates, excluding input nodes and output wires. Fan-out and depth are unrestricted. There is one circuit for each n, with no uniformity requirement on how these circuits are generated. Every input must be answered exactly, with no randomness. Leading zeros are permitted. Let \(M(n)\) be the minimum gate count in this model; the proposition is \(M(n)=O(n)\). Changing to any other fixed functionally complete bounded-fan-in Boolean basis changes size by only a constant factor.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the quantified linear-size upper bound, or prove its negation: for every C and every \(n_{0}\) there is \(n\ge n_{0}\) with \(M(n)>Cn\). A lower bound \(c\cdot n\) with fixed c, a lower bound for bounded depth or restricted wiring, or a limitation of a particular multiplication algorithm does not give the required negative answer. A uniform linear-bit-time algorithm would imply the upper bound, but is a stronger demand than the existence of these nonuniform circuits.

context_blocks.text: Addition admits circuits whose gate count grows linearly with the input width. Multiplication is another elementary arithmetic operation, but the corresponding linear-size bound remains unknown. Goldreich singles it out immediately after the general challenge of proving a superlinear Boolean-circuit lower bound for an explicit function.

The circuit computes every output bit, including carries and the most significant half of the product. Treating a multiplication instruction on a whole machine word as one operation would hide the work being measured. The target concerns exact Boolean computation at individual-bit granularity.

Viola’s author manuscript, carrying a 2023–2026 revision notice, explicitly retains the linear-size multiplication question in Section 4.2. It also proves that multiplication and squaring are equivalent for this linear-size threshold: multiplication gives squaring immediately, and the converse uses squares together with linear-size addition and subtraction.

A negative answer would give a superlinear lower bound for a particularly concrete, efficiently computable family of multi-output Boolean functions. It would apply even to circuits tailored separately to each input length. A positive answer would show that the familiar logarithmic overhead of fast multiplication constructions is not necessary in this circuit model.

The existing TCS-7174 asks for optimal time on a deterministic multitape Turing machine. This card asks only about nonuniform gate count. The archived Karatsuba entry TCS-5168 concerns a reversible pebbling tradeoff, and TCS-6494 asks for a particular reduction from matrix transposition; neither is this unrestricted linear-size question.

cards.title: Optimal multilinear-formula size of the permanent
cards.formal: Determine the growth of \(\log _{2} F(n)\) up to universal multiplicative constants as \(n\to \infty\), where \(F(n)\) is the minimum size of a multilinear arithmetic formula over \(\mathbb{C}\) computing \(\operatorname{perm}_{n}\). Equivalently, find a positive function \(g(n)\) and constants \(a,A>0,n_{0}\) such that \(2^{a g(n)}\le F(n)\le 2^{A g(n)}\) for every integer \(n\ge n_{0}\).
cards.definitions: The permanent is \(\operatorname{perm}_{n}(X)=\sum_{\pi \in S_{n}}\prod _{i=1}^{n} x_{i,\pi (i)}\). An arithmetic formula is a finite rooted tree with variable or complex-constant leaves and binary addition or multiplication gates, evaluated as a commutative polynomial. Every gate must compute a multilinear polynomial: every variable has degree at most one in every monomial after cancellation. The formula must agree identically with \(\operatorname{perm}_{n}\) on \(\mathbb{C} ^{n^{2}}\), not merely on Boolean inputs. Size counts all gates, including leaves. No restriction on the numerical complexity of complex constants is imposed. Let \(F(n)\) be the minimum such size; it is attained because sizes are positive integers and the defining sum of monomials is a valid finite multilinear formula. The independent variables are the \(n^{2}\) entries of the matrix; n denotes its row count. Internal computations are required to be multilinear as polynomials after cancellation, not just at the output. Sharing of subexpressions is forbidden by the tree model. The requested precision is constant factors in \(\log _{2} F(n)\), not constant factors in \(F(n)\).

context_blocks.text: Multilinear formulas give a restricted but important setting in which superpolynomial lower bounds are known for an explicit central polynomial. The exponential target asks how far that separation can be taken even after substantial algebraic structure is imposed.

Raz’s lower bound grows as \(n^{\Omega (\log  n)}\), which is superpolynomial but not exponential in n. The broader permanent circuit problem permits sharing subcomputations and intermediate nonmultilinear polynomials, so these are not interchangeable targets. The survey records the unresolved exponential strengthening.

context_blocks.title: The full exponent instead of one proposed endpoint
context_blocks.text: The original conjecture asks for \(F(n)\ge 2^{cn}\). The retained card asks for its actual growth on the logarithmic scale, allowing an intermediate answer. Raz’s lower bound is \(n^{\Omega (\log  n)}\); the standard inclusion-exclusion formula gives an upper bound \(2^{O(n)}\) and is multilinear at every gate because its factors use different rows. No equivalence between the new determination task and the original conjecture is asserted.

cards.why: Establish a qualitatively stronger explicit algebraic lower bound in one of the few models already admitting superpolynomial separations.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a positive function \(g(n)\) and prove the two bounds displayed in the statement for the specified formula model, with constants independent of n. Merely restating \(\log _{2} F(n)\), proving a bound for constant depth or prohibiting cancellation adds restrictions not present here. This is an asymptotic exponent target, not a pointwise 0.01 approximation. The original exponential lower-bound conjecture would give \(g(n)=n\), using the known exponential-size upper bound.

sentences: A multilinear polynomial uses each variable with exponent at most one in every nonzero monomial.
Semantic multilinearity requires this property at every arithmetic-circuit gate after cancellation.
Syntactic multilinearity instead requires the variable-occurrence sets entering each multiplication to be disjoint.
The question asks whether one polynomial family over a fixed field can have polynomial semantic circuits but no polynomial syntactic circuits.
Formulas admit size-preserving conversion, while the checked 2026 discussion retains the possibility of greater semantic power for circuits with shared outputs.

cards.definitions: A field is a commutative field with \(0\ne1\); it may be finite or infinite and is chosen once for the entire family. An arithmetic circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated output. Input gates are labelled by variables in \(\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\) or by arbitrary elements of \(F\). Every internal gate has two input wires and is labelled \(+\) or \(\times\). Wires may reuse gate outputs, including as the two inputs of a gate, and both wires are then counted. Every gate lies on a path to the output. Size is one plus the number of wires; a field constant occupies one input gate irrespective of any representation length. There is no bound on depth or fan-out, no division gate, and no requirement that a circuit or its constants can be computed from \(n\). Each gate computes its formal polynomial in the polynomial ring \(F[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\). A polynomial is multilinear if every monomial with nonzero coefficient has exponent at most one in each variable; the zero polynomial is multilinear. A circuit is semantically multilinear if every gate computes such a polynomial, after all cancellations in \(F\). For each gate \(g\), let \(\operatorname{Var}(g)\) be the set of variable labels occurring at input gates from which there is a directed path to \(g\), whether or not those variables cancel from its polynomial. A circuit is syntactically multilinear if \(\operatorname{Var}(g_1)\cap\operatorname{Var}(g_2)=\varnothing\) at every product gate with children \(g_1,g_2\). No such disjointness is required at addition gates. Let \(s_{\mathrm{sem},F}(f)\) and \(s_{\mathrm{syn},F}(f)\) be the minimum sizes of the respective circuits computing exactly \(f\). Equality means equality of formal polynomials, including over finite fields. Both minima are finite for a multilinear polynomial. Precisely, the target asks for \(F,(f_n)_{n\ge1},C>0,k\in\mathbb N\) such that \(\forall n\ge1,\ s_{\mathrm{sem},F}(f_n)\le C(n+1)^k\), while \(\forall B>0\;\forall d\in\mathbb N\;\forall N\ge1\;\exists n\ge N,\ s_{\mathrm{syn},F}(f_n)>B(n+1)^d\). Thus superpolynomial separation means failure of every polynomial bound for the family, with violations arbitrarily far out; an eventually exponential lower bound is not required. The field and family are existentially quantified before these asymptotic bounds.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the stated fixed-field family separation, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. A positive answer must establish polynomial semantic size and failure of every polynomial syntactic size bound for one family over one fixed field. A negative answer must show that over every field, each polynomial-size semantically multilinear family also has polynomial-size syntactically multilinear circuits, with polynomial constants allowed to depend on that field and family. No effective circuit-conversion algorithm is additionally required. A separation involving unrestricted intermediate polynomials, formulas only, bounded-depth circuits only or Boolean-function equality does not settle this comparison.

cards.title: Decidability of freeness in automaton groups
cards.formal: Is abstract freeness of an automaton group decidable? Does one deterministic Turing machine, given any finite complete deterministic invertible Mealy automaton \(\mathcal A\), always halt and return YES exactly when \[\exists r\in\mathbb N\quad G(\mathcal A)\cong F_r,\] where \(G(\mathcal A)\) is generated by all state transformations and their inverses and \(F_r\) is the free group of rank \(r\)? Rank zero, the trivial group, is included. The question does not require the supplied state transformations themselves to be a free basis.
cards.why: Automata give finite descriptions of groups that can have complex infinite structure and need not have finite presentations by relations. Recognizing a free group tests a fundamental structural property in this representation. The problem isolates the effect of invertibility on decidability and distinguishes structural recognition from equality of individual represented elements.
cards.status_note: The MFCS 2024 final section and the 12 March 2026 St Andrews handout explicitly retain abstract automaton group freeness as open. The original §7.2.1(b) and current definition quantify over some free basis, not necessarily the input states. Positive-relations undecidability and general semigroup/monoid freeness do not resolve this predicate. The search through 16 September 2026 found no matching later resolution and is not exhaustive.

sentences: A finite invertible Mealy machine describes bijections of all finite words, whose compositions and inverses form an automaton group.
The question asks for an always-terminating algorithm deciding whether that whole group is isomorphic to a free group of some finite rank.
The supplied states may be redundant or act trivially, so they are not required to form the free basis.

A resolution would locate a basic limit of structural recognition from finite automaton descriptions.

cards.definitions:
A finite complete deterministic Mealy automaton is \(\mathcal A=(Q,\Sigma,\delta,\lambda)\), with finite nonempty state set \(Q\), finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), and total tables \(\delta:Q\times\Sigma\to Q\), \(\lambda:Q\times\Sigma\to\Sigma\). Invertibility means that for each state \(q\), the map \(a\mapsto\lambda(q,a)\) is a permutation of \(\Sigma\). No reversibility assumption is made on the maps \(q\mapsto\delta(q,a)\), and the numbers of states and letters are unbounded parts of the input. There are no designated initial or accepting states: all states are generators. The input is the full finite table, with binary state/letter indices and cardinalities. Invalid or noninvertible tables may be rejected.

The set \(\Sigma^*\) contains all finite words, including the empty word \(\varepsilon\). Each state defines a transformation recursively by \(T_q(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon\) and \(T_q(aw)=\lambda(q,a)T_{\delta(q,a)}(w)\). Invertibility makes each \(T_q\) a bijection of \(\Sigma^*\), preserving lengths and prefixes. The group \(G(\mathcal A)\) consists of all finite compositions of these functions and their inverses, including the empty composition, with function composition as multiplication. Equality means agreement on every finite input word of every length. This uses synchronous, total, one-letter-in/one-letter-out machines, rather than partial or asynchronous transducers.

The free group \(F_r\) has generators \(b_1,\ldots,b_r\) and their formal inverses. Its elements are finite reduced words, meaning adjacent inverse pairs have been cancelled; multiplication concatenates words and cancels such pairs, the empty word is the identity, and inversion reverses the word and flips each sign. Freeness of \(G(\mathcal A)\) means existence of a bijection to this group preserving multiplication and identity. A possible free basis may consist of arbitrary group elements rather than the given state list, which can contain identities, duplicates or dependent generators. Since the group is finitely generated, allowing all finite ranks is sufficient; no basis, rank, isomorphism or bound on relation length is supplied as an input promise or required as output.

The target is exact uniform decidability on every valid automaton table, with termination on both free and nonfree cases and no resource bound. One ordinary algorithm must work for all input sizes. No oracle, nonuniform advice, randomness, numerical tolerance or restriction to bounded input-word lengths is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean proof that this predicate admits a total computable decider on the encoded complete invertible Mealy tables, or prove that it does not. The formalization must connect the state recursion, generated group of all-word transformations and existence of an abstract free-group isomorphism, including rank zero, to the algorithm's correctness and termination. A negative reduction must preserve complete deterministic invertibility. Deciding whether the named states freely generate, checking absence of a positive relation, or proving semigroup freeness undecidable does not by itself meet the abstract group target. Failure of one bounded relation search is not a proof that every total algorithm is impossible. The card review does not claim a verified Lean resolution.

source_formulation.text: Is there an algorithm deciding whether the group generated by a given complete invertible finite automaton is a free group?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the abstract group-freeness question

context_blocks.text: A state table supplies a compact recursive description of transformations on a rooted tree of all finite words. Deciding equality of two specified products is possible in this representation, but recognizing the abstract structure of the entire infinite group is a separate problem.

The original 2000 list asks about the group’s structural properties, and the March 2026 handout defines freeness as isomorphism to a free group over some basis. This confirms that the target is not an injectivity test for the map from the free group on the names of all states.

For example, the usual adding machine generates an infinite cyclic group together with an identity state. The group is free of rank one, while the given state list is not a free basis and already contains a positive relation because the identity state acts trivially. Redundant state generators must therefore not force a NO answer.

Theorem 3.7 of the 2020 paper proves undecidability of checking absence of positive relations, which are nonempty products of state generators acting as the identity without using inverses. The same paper explicitly distinguishes this presentation-dependent property from abstract group freeness. Its appended erratum retracts other freeness claims, and was checked with the theorem.

The MFCS 2024 result proves undecidability of freeness for general complete automaton semigroups and monoids. Its final section still lists automaton group freeness as open. Allowing noninvertible state actions in the negative construction is not the promised group input class.

The 12 March 2026 specialist handout again records group freeness as open while listing semigroup/monoid freeness as undecidable. A bounded search through September found no checked later resolution; the card reports this dated evidence rather than claiming an exhaustive status proof.

cards.title: Approximate polynomial satisfiability in AM under GRH
cards.formal: Assuming the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, is approximate polynomial satisfiability for rational-coefficient arithmetic circuits in AM? An instance consists of division-free circuits computing \(f_{1},\ldots ,f_{m}\in \mathbb{Q} [x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}]\). It is a YES instance if, for every real \(\eta >0\), there is a point \(a\in \mathbb{C} ^{n}\) with \(\max _{i} |f_{i}(a)|<\eta\); otherwise it is a NO instance. Equivalently, for every polynomial \(A\in \mathbb{Q} [y_{1},\ldots ,y_{m}]\), the identity \(A(f_{1},\ldots ,f_{m})=0\) must imply \(A(0,\ldots ,0)=0\). This equivalent decision predicate is AnnAtZero. Ask for one uniform public-coin protocol with verifier time, random-tape length and prover-message length polynomial in the full binary input length, with completeness at least \(2/3\) and soundness at most \(1/3\) on every instance.

cards.definitions:
The integers n,m are positive and part of the instance. Each circuit is a finite acyclic graph with input gates \(x_{j}\) or rational constants and binary +,−,× gates; no division by expressions is allowed. The encoding lists gates in topological order, their input indices, their types, and the output gates. A rational constant is given by signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator. The bit length L counts this entire finite description, including constants and gate references. Variables can be relabeled so n is at most the description length; unused variables do not affect the predicate. Shared gates are allowed. Neither total degree nor the magnitudes of intermediate coefficients are promised polynomial in L. The target is a Turing bit-complexity bound, not unit-cost arithmetic with arbitrary complex constants.

An annihilator is a nonzero polynomial \(A(y_{1},\ldots ,y_{m})\) over \(\mathbb{Q}\) such that substituting the \(f_{i}\) yields the zero polynomial. Equivalently one can quantify over all A, including zero as in the formal statement. AnnAtZero asks whether every such A has zero constant term, not whether some annihilator exists. In particular, algebraically independent \(f_{i}\) satisfy it vacuously. The same condition holds if the annihilator coefficients are allowed in the algebraic closure \(\bar\{\mathbb{Q}\}\). A further equivalent algebraic formulation is: there are finite Laurent polynomials \(\beta _{j}(t)\in \bar\{\mathbb{Q}\}[t,t^{- 1}]\) such that \(f_{i}(\beta _{1}(t),\ldots ,\beta _{n}(t))\in t\bar\{\mathbb{Q}\}[t]\) for every i. Negative powers in the \(\beta _{j}\) are permitted, but all nonpositive powers must disappear after evaluation of each \(f_{i}\). There is no input error tolerance or promised bound on the exponents, coefficient descriptions or sizes of these witnesses. The Laurent formulation is equivalent to the rational-function formulation in the source. Geometrically, the origin belongs to the Zariski closure of the polynomial image \(f(\mathbb{C} ^{n})\): the smallest set defined by polynomial equations containing that image. For complex polynomial maps this is also equivalent to membership in its Euclidean closure, giving the \(\eta\) formulation. The approximating points may escape every bounded region; the target does not require an exact common zero in \(\mathbb{C} ^{n}\).

AM means the following. There are a deterministic polynomial-time bit algorithm V and polynomials r,p such that Arthur samples a uniformly random string \(u\in \{0,1\}^{r(\mathrm{L})}\) and sends it to Merlin, who returns \(w\in \{0,1\}^{p(\mathrm{L})}\); then V(instance,u,w) accepts or rejects. Merlin knows the instance and u and has unlimited computation. All verifier randomness is in u; the verifier has no remaining private coins. For every YES instance, \(\Pr _{u}\)[\(\exists w:V\)(instance,u,w)=1]\(\ge 2/3\), and for every NO instance this probability is at most \(1/3\). Constants and polynomial exponents are universal across n,m,L. Shorter messages may be padded. GRH here is the usual number-field form: every nontrivial zero in \(0<Re(s)<1\) of the Dedekind zeta function \(\zeta _{K}(s)\) of every number field K has real part \(1/2\). It is an assumption, not an oracle supplied to the verifier. The task asks for the stated inclusion under that assumption; no certificate of the truth of GRH is demanded.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove, under GRH, that one AM protocol satisfying the stated bounds decides every encoded instance, or refute the inclusion under the same assumption. A protocol only for exact common-root existence, algebraic dependence, bounded-degree special cases, or finite fields does not establish the target. A PSPACE algorithm or a test at one fixed positive numerical tolerance is insufficient. Failure of a proposed protocol is not a proof that APS is outside AM.

cards.title: Linear-time unit-Monge distance multiplication
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic \(O(n)\)-time algorithm which, given two permutations \(\pi,\tau\) of \(\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\), returns a permutation \(\rho\) satisfying \(A_\rho(i,j)=\min_{0\le h\le n}(A_\pi(i,h)+A_\tau(h,j))\) for all \(0\le i,j\le n\)?
cards.definitions:
For a permutation \(
u\), define \(A_
u(i,j)=|\{t:i\le t<n,\ 
u(t)<j\}|\). This counting matrix is the implicit simple unit-Monge representation used here. The input is the two permutation arrays, and the output is the array \(ho\); no \((n+1)\)-by-\((n+1)\) matrix is supplied or requested explicitly. The product of two such matrices has a representation of this form. Set \(L=n\ge2\). Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(L+2)ceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. Randomized algorithms, when explicitly permitted, may generate independent uniform random words. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. Require \(O(n)\) working words, with all preprocessing charged. All bounds are worst-case with universal constants and no randomness.

cards.title: Polynomial-time computation of addition-chain length
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(K>0\), \(a\in\mathbb N\) and one deterministic multitape Turing machine that, on every positive integer \(n\) supplied in binary, outputs the exact shortest addition-chain length \(\ell(n)\) in binary within \(K(b+1)^a\) steps, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor+1\) is the input length?
cards.definitions:
An addition chain for \(n\ge1\) is a finite strictly increasing sequence of positive integers
\[
1=a_0<a_1<\cdots<a_r=n
\]
such that for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,r\}\) there exist indices \(j,k\in\{0,\ldots,i-1\}\) with \(a_i=a_j+a_k\). The two indices may coincide, and an earlier entry may be reused any number of times. The length is the number \(r\) of additions, not the number \(r+1\) of entries. Define \(\ell(n)\) as the minimum such length; in particular, \(\ell(1)=0\). The only initially available number is \(1\). Subtraction, division, multiplication of chain entries and additional initial constants are not chain operations. The sum need not use the immediately preceding entry.

The machine receives just the ordinary binary expansion of \(n\), with no leading zeros. Its output is the ordinary binary expansion of the integer \(\ell(n)\), with \(0\) written as a single zero bit. The same finite program and constants must work for all valid inputs. The program has the usual unrestricted finite alphabet and binary work tapes of a multitape Turing machine, but all work, input reads and output writing count in its worst-case step bound. It has no advice, oracle, random bits or uncharged preprocessing. Invalid input strings must be rejected within the same bound with \(b\) interpreted as their string length. No addition chain or auxiliary number-theoretic data are supplied.

The requested machine may use any deterministic computation to find the length; the restrictions on chain operations define the quantity being optimized, rather than restricting the machine's internal calculations. The output is only the optimal length, not a chain attaining it. The input is a single binary target, not a list of targets and not a unary string of length \(n\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of an algorithm and fixed polynomial bound satisfying the exact-output task for every \(n\ge1\), or a complete Lean proof that no such algorithm exists. Exact integer output is part of this computational existence question, not an extra accuracy restriction on a numerical-value benchmark. A fast approximation, a heuristic, polynomial time in \(n\) instead of its bit length, or a result for special targets does not meet the stated guarantee. Conditional hardness must retain its assumption; hardness of forming several prescribed targets is a different problem.

context_blocks.text: Erickson’s exponentiation discussion distinguishes asymptotically short multiplication programs from computing the absolute minimum number of multiplications. The current book chapter still states the latter question. This card retains the earlier length-only target and does not infer an unproved equivalence with constructing an optimal chain.

The elementary bounds are \(\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\le\ell(n)\le2\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor\), including \(n=1\). Thus an optimal chain has \(O(b)\) entries of at most \(b\) bits. The existence of short certificates does not supply a deterministic polynomial-time optimizer.

The cryptographic arithmetic paper distinguishes single-target optimality from multiple-target addition sequences. Its procedures for selected exponents are not a proof of the general exact polynomial-time claim.

The 2025 assembly-theory article describes the shortest-addition-chain complexity as unknown. Only that dated observation is used here; its broader claims about complexity classes and assembly models are not part of this card’s mathematical premises.

Wallner’s 2026 result concerns the expected decompressed size of restricted chain structures, including Brauer chains. An average over chains of a fixed length does not compute the unrestricted minimum length for a supplied target.

The separately catalogued Scholz–Brauer conjecture concerns a structural inequality for special exponents. That conclusion differs from a uniformly efficient computation of the optimum on every binary input.

cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given an explicitly represented finite field \(\mathbb F_q\), integers \(n\ge2,d\ge1\), and arbitrary matrices \(A_1,\ldots,A_d\in\mathbb F_q^{n\times n}\), computes the rational number \[\alpha(A_1,\ldots,A_d)=\min_{\substack{V\le\mathbb F_q^n\\1\le\dim V\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor}}\frac{\dim(A_1V+\cdots+A_dV)}{\dim V}\] exactly? Polynomial time is measured in the total input bit length, uniformly over the field, dimension and number of maps. This is the finite-field polynomial-time branch of the source’s broader computation-complexity question.
cards.why: The expansion guarantee quantifies over every low-dimensional subspace, including subspaces with no coordinate description. Explicit constructions can prove that certain families expand without yielding an efficient procedure to evaluate arbitrary supplied matrices. The question asks whether this global algebraic property has a polynomial-time exact evaluation algorithm.

cards.definitions:
Write \(q=p^e\), where \(p\ge2\) is prime and \(e\ge1\). The field is supplied as \(\mathbb F_p[X]/(h(X))\), with a monic irreducible polynomial \(h(X)=X^e+\sum_{j=0}^{e-1}h_jX^j\) over \(\mathbb F_p\). Its elements are the coefficient vectors of representatives of degree less than \(e\), with coefficients in \(\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\); addition and multiplication mean polynomial addition and multiplication modulo \(p\) and \(h\). Primality and irreducibility are promises, not extra input-search tasks. Fix the following bit encoding. Give \(n,d,e\) as three unary strings terminated by zero, then the bit length \(\ell\) of \(p\) in unary terminated by zero, then the \(\ell\)-bit ordinary binary expansion of \(p\). Give \(h_0,\ldots,h_{e-1}\), followed by the entries of \(A_1,\ldots,A_d\) in matrix order and row-major order, each residue coefficient as an \(\ell\)-bit unsigned block. Matrix entries use their \(e\) coefficients in increasing degree. Let \(L\) be the length of this complete representation. All arithmetic cost is bit cost; field operations are not free unit-cost oracle calls.

A subspace \(V\) is any linear subspace over this supplied field, not merely the span of a subset of coordinate vectors. \(A_iV=\{A_iv:v\in V\}\), and the sum \(A_1V+\cdots+A_dV\) is their linear span, not a union or the intersection of their images. All dimensions are over \(\mathbb F_q\). The range \(1\le\dim V\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor\) is nonempty because \(n\ge2\); the finite field makes the minimum range finite. Each candidate ratio has numerator between zero and \(n\) and denominator between one and \(\lfloor n/2\rfloor\). Hence the output has a polynomial-length exact representation as a reduced nonnegative fraction with positive denominator, both in binary. No subspace attaining the minimum needs to be output. The original subspace is not automatically added to its image: \(V+\sum_iA_iV\) would be a different quantity unless an identity map were included. Matrices need not be invertible, contain the identity, be distinct, or already form an expander. The value can be below one, including zero; in that case the tuple meets none of the source’s expander conditions requiring an expansion factor at least one.

The algorithm is a single finite-program deterministic multitape Turing machine, with no advice, random bits or external oracles. Ask for constants \(C,c\ge1\) independent of \(p,e,n,d,h,A_i\) such that it halts on every valid promised input, returns the exact specified fraction and uses at most \(C(L+1)^c\) transitions, including preprocessing, field arithmetic and output. No claim for characteristic-zero fields or a black-box field representation is included.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked algorithm and proof of exact output and the stated uniform polynomial bit bound, or a complete Lean proof that no such algorithm and constants exist. The numerical output here is part of an exact computational task; the question asks for polynomial-time solvability, not the value on one input. A construction of particular expanding matrix families, a spectral sufficient condition, or an approximation to a different expansion parameter does not meet this target. A hardness result under an additional unproved complexity assumption establishes only a conditional negative answer.

context_blocks.text: Question 5 in the original paper asks for the complexity of computing the largest half-dimension expansion factor over a field. This card specifies its finite-field setting and asks the polynomial-time existence question. Definition 11 uses the span of all image subspaces. It reserves the word expander for factors at least one; the displayed minimum extends the evaluation task to arbitrary tuples, returning a value below one when no such factor exists.

The source develops explicit matrix families and rank-condensation constructions. Those guarantees concern the constructed families and do not themselves compute the optimum expansion of arbitrary input maps.

The 2025 work of Li, Qiao, Wigderson, Wigderson and Zhang separates dimension expansion from quantum expansion and compares linear-algebraic analogues of vertex, edge and spectral expansion. Its dimension parameter includes the original subspace and subtracts its dimension, so it must not be silently substituted for the original paper’s image-span ratio.

cards.definitions: A sparse representation of f lists its nonzero rational coefficients and corresponding nonnegative integer exponent vectors; s is the number of listed monomials and d bounds the sum of exponents in each monomial. The candidate divisor g is supplied by its coefficients and exponent vectors; because \(\delta\) is fixed, it has at most \(binomial(n+\delta ,\delta )\) monomials, so dense and sparse explicit encodings are polynomially related. Divisibility means that a polynomial \(h\in Q[x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}]\) exists with \(f=gh\). The quotient need not be sparse and need not be output. The polynomial running-time exponent may depend on the fixed \(\delta\), but not on the input n,s,d. The source counts exact arithmetic operations over Q at unit cost. In particular, the requested bound is polynomial in the numerical degree d, not merely in log d, and is not a bound on rational-coefficient bit complexity. There is no promise that g is irreducible. The cases \(f=0\) or nonzero constant g have immediate affirmative answers; the first unsettled divisor degree is two.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a deterministic divisibility decision algorithm with the stated polynomial arithmetic cost for every fixed \(\delta\), or establish an obstruction to that precise guarantee. Randomized testing, quasipolynomial time, or a bound requiring the dividend f to have constant individual degree does not answer the question.

cards.title: Algebraic branching programs versus formulas
cards.formal: For a fixed field F, is \(VF_{F} a\) proper subclass of \(VBP_{F}\)? Equivalently, is there a family \((f_{n})\) of polynomials of polynomially bounded degree in polynomially many commuting variables that has polynomial-size algebraic branching programs over F but no polynomial-size algebraic formulas over F? The field is a parameter of the question, as in the source; a result must state the fields to which it applies.
cards.why: Separates two fundamental models of algebraic computation and asks whether sharing path computations gives a polynomial-versus-superpolynomial advantage over arithmetic trees.
cards.status_note: Recovered the exact containment from the source and checked subsequent work through 12 September 2026, including the January 2026 multilinear paper. cards.definitions: A polynomial family has \(f_{n}\in F[x_{1},\ldots ,x_{m(n)}]\), where \(m(n)\) and the total degree of \(f_{n}\) are at most \(n^{a}+a\) for some fixed a. An algebraic formula is a finite rooted tree whose leaves are variables or constants in F and whose internal gates are binary addition or multiplication. Its output is a formal polynomial; equality means coefficientwise equality in \(F[x]\), also when F is finite. Its size is its number of nodes. An algebraic branching program is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated source and sink and affine-linear polynomial labels on edges. It computes the sum, over all source-to-sink paths, of the product of the labels on that path. Count vertices, edges and the nonzero coefficients used to describe edge labels as its size; these choices differ only polynomially from the usual size conventions. Field constants have unit algebraic cost, with no bit-length bound. \(VF_{F}\) and \(VBP_{F}\) consist respectively of the polynomial families with formula size and branching-program size bounded by \(n^{b}+b\) for some constant b independent of n. These are nonuniform classes: a different finite computation may be chosen for each n, with no requirement to generate it algorithmically. The separation asks for one family in \(VBP_{F}\) for which, for every b, some n requires formula size greater than \(n^{b}+b\). There is no restriction to multilinear computation, bounded depth, homogeneous intermediate gates or noncommuting variables.
cards.answer_criterion: For the stated field F, prove \(VF_{F} \subsetneq  VBP_{F}\) by exhibiting a family in \(VBP_{F}\) and proving that its formula sizes are not polynomially bounded, or prove \(VF_{F}=VBP_{F}\) by showing that every polynomial-size branching-program family has polynomial-size formulas. Any characteristic or field restriction must be stated as part of the scope of the answer. A lower bound only for bounded-depth or multilinear formulas does not resolve the unrestricted question.

cards.title: A uniform exponent saving for arbitrary generalized convolution
cards.formal: Does there exist an absolute \(\varepsilon >0\) such that, for every fixed finite domain D with \(d=|D|\ge 2\) and every fixed function \(f:D\times D\to D\), the entire f-convolution of two integer tables on \(D^{n}\) can be computed exactly in \(\widetilde{O}\)\((d^{(2- \varepsilon )n}\cdot \operatorname{polylog}(2+M))\) time? The same \(\varepsilon\) must work for all domains and operations; n is unbounded and M bounds the absolute input values. No associativity, commutativity or algebraic structure of f is assumed.
cards.why: Would give a broadly applicable improvement for table-merging computations without requiring an algebraic law on the state-combination operation, strengthening a common primitive in exact and parameterized algorithms.
cards.status_note: Read the IPEC question and the improved Algorithmica version, including its retained Section 6 question. cards.definitions: Identify D with \(\{0,\ldots ,d- 1\}\). For \(u,w\in D^{n}\) set \((u\oplus _{f} w)_{j}=f(u_{j},w_{j})\) for \(1\le j\le n\). Input tables \(g,h:D^{n}\to \{- M,\ldots ,M\}\), with \(n\ge 1\) and \(M\ge 1\), list every signed integer in binary. The output is the full table \(C:D^{n}\to Z\), where \(C(v)=\sum_{u,w\in D^{n}: u\oplus _{f} w=v}g(u)h(w)\); an empty sum is zero. All arithmetic is ordinary integer arithmetic. In the source’s fixed-operation convention, D and the finite \(d^{2}\)-entry table of f specify the convolution problem; the growing inputs are g,h. More explicitly, the requested bound means a deterministic algorithm, uniform in n and the input tables, taking at most \(C_{D,f} d^{(2- \varepsilon )n}(1+n \log  d+\log (2+M))^{a_{D,f}}\) bit operations, for constants \(C_{D,f},a_{D,f}\) depending only on D,f. Any finite preparation of that fixed table can be included in \(C_{D,f}; \varepsilon\) is chosen before D,f. This states the fixed-domain asymptotic question from the source, not a bound for reading an arbitrary operation table when \(n=1\). Standard random-access storage of the listed tables is permitted, with arithmetic charged for operand bit length; addressing costs are absorbed in the displayed polynomial factor. Each output has \(O(n \log  d+\log (2+M))\) bits. The target concerns every output entry, not a query for a single specified v.
cards.answer_criterion: Establish the bound with one positive \(\varepsilon\) independent of D and f, for all fixed finite operations and all input tables, or refute that universally quantified existence claim in the stated deterministic exact-computation model. An exponent saving that tends to zero with d, a theorem restricted to selected operations, or a faster single-entry query algorithm does not suffice.

cards.title: Efficient equations for VP with unrestricted complex coefficients
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(c\ge 1\), do there exist nonzero polynomials \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) in \(N_{n}=\operatorname{binom}(n+n^{c},n)\) coefficient variables, with degree and algebraic circuit size at most \(C_{c} N_{n}^{a_{c}}\), such that for every fixed integer \(b\ge 1\) there is \(n_{0}(c,b)\) for which \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\)(\(coeff(f)\))=0 whenever \(n\ge n_{0}(c,b)\) and \(f\in \mathbb{C} [x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}]\) has total degree at most \(n^{c}\) and an algebraic circuit of size at most \(n^{b}\)? Constants \(C_{c},a_{c}\) and the family \((\mathrm{P}_{n})\) may depend on c, but not on b. Coefficients of f may be arbitrary complex numbers. This expresses the source’s eventual vanishing on every polynomial-size family, without demanding a common finite threshold across all circuit-size exponents.
cards.why: Would clarify whether a broad family of algebraic lower-bound certificates can recognize all efficiently computable polynomials once arbitrary coefficients are allowed.

cards.definitions: An algebraic circuit over \(\mathbb{C}\) is a finite directed acyclic graph with inputs \(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}\) and arbitrary complex constants, binary addition and multiplication gates, and one output. Subtraction is allowed via multiplication by −1; there are no division gates. Its size is its number of vertices. It computes an exact formal polynomial, and each constant is one field element regardless of its bit description. \(VP_{\mathbb{C}}\) consists of polynomial families with polynomially bounded total degree and polynomially bounded nonuniform algebraic circuit size. For \(d=n^{c}\), list all monomials \(x_{1}^{\alpha _{1}}\cdots x_{n}^{\alpha _{n}}\) with \(\alpha _{i}\ge 0\) and \(\sum_{i}\alpha _{i}\le d\) in a fixed lexicographic order of exponent vectors. There are \(N_{n}=\operatorname{binom}(n+d,n)\) such monomials. \(coeff(f)\) is the full vector of their coefficients, including zeros. \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) is a polynomial over \(\mathbb{C}\) whose variables are these \(N_{n}\) coordinates. Nonzero means not the zero formal polynomial; over \(\mathbb{C}\) it is equivalent to being nonzero at some coefficient vector. Both degree and circuit size of \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) are bounded by a fixed polynomial in \(N_{n}\), not in n. The equations themselves are nonuniform: there is no additional requirement to construct their circuits in polynomial time from n. Vanishing must hold for all circuits under each fixed polynomial size bound eventually; the threshold can depend on that bound. Restricting c,b to positive integers covers arbitrary fixed polynomial exponents by increasing them. The statement imposes no bound on output coefficients of f or on constants used inside its circuit, and requests no explicit hard polynomial on which \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) is nonzero.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove existence of such a nontrivial polynomial-degree, polynomial-circuit-size family for every c, or refute the universal existence statement for at least one c. Vanishing only on polynomials with bounded integer coefficients, or only on a fixed restricted circuit architecture, does not establish the claim. Nonexistence of equations for VNP alone does not refute existence for VP.

cards.definitions:
A graph group, also called a right-angled Artin group, has one generator for every vertex in A. An edge specifies that its two generators commute. I is symmetric and has no loops. The displayed presentation imposes these commutation relations and the group axioms, with no additional relations such as a²=1. The alphabet A±1 contains each generator and a formal inverse. Products are identified under insertion or deletion of adjacent inverse pairs and interchange of adjacent commuting letters, including their inverses. The identity is the class of the empty word. For instance aba⁻¹b⁻¹ is the identity when a and b are joined by an edge; without that edge, it is nontrivial in the two-generator free group.

A straight-line program is an acyclic sequence of string assignments. In a convenient normal form, X_i is assigned an alphabet letter, the empty word, or a concatenation X_jX_k with j,k<i. A designated final variable produces val(S). Reusing a variable means reusing its whole generated string; it does not introduce a new unknown group element. General finite right-hand sides can be put in this form with polynomial overhead. The expanded string can have exponential length in the program size and is not given explicitly.

Vertices and variables have binary indices. The graph is given explicitly, for example by its vertex and edge lists, and every program instruction is listed explicitly. Let L be the total bit length of this representation. The requested bound is L^{O(1)} bit operations on a deterministic machine, with one exponent and one algorithm for the entire input family. It cannot hide an arbitrary dependence on |A| or the commutation graph in a supposedly fixed constant. Equivalent explicit encodings differing by polynomial factors give the same P-membership question. Ill-formed graphs or cyclic programs may be rejected in polynomial time.

For the weaker NP question, every identity instance would need a certificate of length polynomial in L verifiable deterministically in polynomial time; nonidentity instances must have no accepting certificate. The known coRP result instead gives a randomized polynomial-time identity test that always accepts identities and accepts any nonidentity with probability at most 1/3. This does not by itself put identity instances in NP. The target concerns an arbitrary compressed word, not merely a product u₁^{z₁}⋯u_t^{z_t} of explicitly written words with given binary integer exponents, and not the existence of unknown exponents.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove uniform deterministic polynomial-time decidability for arbitrary input commutation graphs and SLPs, or prove that no such algorithm exists, stating any complexity assumption used by a conditional obstruction. An NP upper bound is progress on the weaker branch and must not be reported as a positive answer to P-membership. A bound polynomial only for each fixed group, or an algorithm restricted to power words, does not settle this card.
