cards.title: Decidability of unconditional Shannon information inequalities
cards.formal: Does a Turing algorithm exist that, given \(n\ge 1\) and rational coefficients \((a_{S})\) for nonempty subsets \(S\subseteq \{1,\ldots ,n\}\), always halts and decides whether \(\sum_{\varnothing \ne S\subseteq [n]}a_{S} H(X_{S})\ge 0\) holds for every joint distribution of n finite-valued discrete random variables?
cards.definitions: The finite input lists n and all nonzero coefficients, each as a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator, with its subset S encoded explicitly; omitted coefficients are zero. \(X_{S}\) is the tuple \((X_{i})_{i\in S}\). Its Shannon entropy in bits is \(H(X_{S})=- \sum_{x} p_{S}(x)\log _{2} p_{S}(x)\), with \(0\log _{2}0=0\). Each variable has a finite alphabet, but alphabet sizes are unrestricted and are not supplied as bounds in the input. Joint probabilities may be arbitrary real numbers in \([0,1]\) summing to one. No independence, conditional-independence, functional-dependence, fixed-marginal or support-size promise is imposed. The inequality is a single homogeneous linear inequality, with non-strict \(\ge 0\) and no affine constant, premise, disjunction or nonlinear entropy term. Runtime may be any computable function of the input length; polynomial time is not required. The number n varies with the input.
cards.answer_criterion: An affirmative answer supplies a total effective procedure for exact validity of every such rational inequality. A negative answer proves that this language of valid inequalities is undecidable. Finding a false input inequality or proving an individual new valid inequality answers an instance, not the meta-question. A procedure that may run forever on valid inputs, or requires a promised numerical gap, does not resolve exact decidability.
cards.why: A basic computability question about the laws of Shannon information, with consequences for automated proofs, network and coding bounds, and database query reasoning.

importance.reason: A foundational decision problem at the intersection of information theory, computability and database theory; it asks whether exact universal entropy reasoning can be fully automated.

cards.status_note: Open for a single unconditional homogeneous rational linear inequality over all finite-valued distributions, based on primary sources and a later-result check through 11 September 2026. Invalidity is semidecidable. Conditional undecidability, restricted set-function domains and inequality-generation algorithms do not establish undecidability or decidability of this exact problem.

context_blocks.text: For a given distribution, each subset of variables has an entropy. Collecting these numbers produces one point in a space with \(2^{n}- 1\) coordinates. The question asks whether an input linear halfspace contains every such point, across all finite alphabets and distributions. It is therefore a question about all possible information structures, rather than about estimating entropies from a dataset.

Familiar examples are easy to express in this format. Subadditivity is \(H(X_{1})+H(X_{2})- H(X_{1},X_{2})\ge 0\). Conditional mutual information is \(H(X_{1},X_{3})+H(X_{2},X_{3})- H(X_{3})- H(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3})\ge 0\). Both hold without a premise. A negative coefficient is perfectly legitimate; it is the full linear combination, rather than each individual summand, whose sign is being decided.

The standard Shannon inequalities give a finite linear-programming proof method for each n. They express nonnegative conditional entropies and conditional mutual informations, or equivalently normalized monotone submodular set functions. If a candidate follows from them, it is universally valid. But the first non-Shannon inequality of Zhang–Yeung showed in 1998 that this proof method is incomplete. Rejecting an attempted Shannon derivation therefore cannot be used as a negative answer about entropy validity.

The unrestricted alphabet quantifier is a major part of the difficulty. A computation on binary variables explores only a small portion of the permitted distributions. Increasing a guessed alphabet bound may discover new counterexamples, but an unsuccessful search at every bound examined so far provides no effective stopping criterion. A solution cannot quietly replace all finite alphabets by one fixed support limit depending on a heuristic.

There is a rigorous semidecision procedure for invalidity. If an inequality is false, it is strictly negative at some distribution with finite alphabets. Entropy is continuous on that finite probability simplex, so a sufficiently close rational distribution still violates it. Enumerate alphabet sizes and rational distributions, and compute certified entropy approximations of increasing precision. Eventually the negative value is certified. The arithmetical-hierarchy study of Abo Khamis–Kolaitis–Ngo–Suciu places validity in co-r.e.

This explains precisely what a positive solution would add: a way to halt on every valid inequality as well. A complete effective enumeration of proofs of all valid inequalities, coupled with the counterexample search, would suffice. Existing automated methods can produce many correct certificates, but no completeness theorem for all rational unconditional inequalities is supplied by the inspected sources.

Taking the topological closure of the entropic region does not change this particular validity problem. A continuous linear form nonnegative on every entropic point is nonnegative on every limit point, and the reverse implication is immediate. Thus the same unconditional linear inequalities hold for entropic and almost-entropic vectors. This observation depends on the exact logical form; it does not authorize replacing the domain inside arbitrary conditional statements.

Cheuk Ting Li’s 2023 theorem establishes undecidability for conditional information inequalities and conditional-independence implication. Those inputs include premises that must hold exactly. Merely deleting a premise changes the statement. The theorem therefore does not by itself establish undecidability of a single unconditional inequality.

Adding a fixed penalty for violating a premise need not capture its limiting behavior. Kaced–Romashchenko explicitly show essentially conditional inequalities that do not extend to unconditional linear inequalities in the proposed manner. Their results explain why this seemingly direct route from conditional to unconditional validity needs additional justification.

Hannula’s 2024 work studies useful decidable simplifications: different classes of set functions and syntactic forms connected to database bounds. Its coNP-completeness result is for normal polymatroids, a restricted semantic domain, while another polynomial-time result uses monotone functions. These are precise complexity results for different domains, not a classification of validity over all entropy vectors.

The connection to databases gives the question an algorithmic role beyond coding theory. Entropy inequalities constrain how large a relational join can be under information about its inputs and degrees. Related logical forms occur in query containment and dependency implication. Understanding which constraints admit complete reasoning procedures helps explain why some query bounds can be computed effectively while broader formulations encounter undecidability.

The 2025 exploration by László Csirmaz compares the Copy Lemma, maximum-entropy constructions and the Ahlswede–Körner method, and leaves their completeness unresolved. Előd P. Csirmaz and László Csirmaz’s 2026 paper derives two infinite collections of five-variable inequalities and computes consequences through nine generations of its construction. Its enumeration concerns that method’s extremal inequalities; even the proposed characterization of the method is not a characterization of the entire entropy region.

cards.definitions: A channel has nonempty finite alphabets \(\mathcal X_1,\mathcal X_2,\mathcal Y_1,\mathcal Y_2\) and arbitrary real probabilities \(W(y_1,y_2\mid x_1,x_2)\ge0\), summing to one over outputs for each input pair. Conditional on input sequences, an \(n\)-use output sequence has law \(\prod_{t=1}^n W(y_{1,t},y_{2,t}\mid x_{1,t},x_{2,t})\). Messages \(M_1,M_2\) are independent and uniform on \([K_{1,n}]\) and \([K_{2,n}]\), where \([K]=\{1,\ldots,K\}\) and message counts are positive integers. Encoder \(i\) is a deterministic map \([K_{i,n}]\to\mathcal X_i^n\); its decoder is a deterministic map \(\mathcal Y_i^n\to[K_{i,n}]\). Error means at least one incorrectly decoded message, averaged over both messages and channel randomness. A pair \((R_1,R_2)\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^2\) is achievable if there are codes with block lengths \(n_j\to\infty\), error tending to zero, and \(\liminf_{j\to\infty}n_j^{-1}\log_2K_{i,n_j}\ge R_i\) for both users. The capacity region \(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{IC}}(W)\) is the closure of these achievable pairs. The channel and both codebooks are known to all terminals. There is no common message, feedback, terminal cooperation, input cost or computational bound. Predetermined time sharing is allowed. The region is compact, convex and downward closed, so all its nonnegative upper supporting values determine it. The function is measured in weighted bits per joint channel use. Channel laws and weights are mathematical real objects; no finite-precision input or algorithmic evaluation model is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function \(g(W,\lambda)\) on the entire stated domain and a Lean proof of \(|g(W,\lambda)-F_{\mathrm{IC}}(W,\lambda)|\le1/100\) for every channel and weight. The proof must control both sides of the error; exact determination also qualifies. The guarantee concerns the support value in bits per joint use, with the coding model unchanged. Sample values, a plot or a restatement of the defining optimization or limit are insufficient. No prescribed formula syntax or polynomial evaluation-time bound is required.

cards.title: Constant-rate binary locally decodable codes with logarithmic query complexity
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(r\in\)(0,1], \(\delta \in (0,1/2)\) and \(A>0\) such that, for arbitrarily large message lengths k, there are an integer n with \(k\le n\le k/r\), an encoding \(C:\{0,1\}^{k}\to \{0,1\}^{n}\), and randomized local decoders \(Dec_{i}\) for \(i\in \{1,\ldots ,k\}\), satisfying the following? For every message x, every received word \(z\in \{0,1\}^{n}\) differing from \(C(x)\) in fewer than \(\delta n\) positions, and every requested index \(i, Dec_{i}\) with oracle access to z outputs \(x_{i}\) with probability at least \(2/3\) while making at most \(\lceil A \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil\) bit queries on every execution.
cards.why: A central locality-versus-redundancy barrier with consequences for private information retrieval and matrix rigidity.
cards.status_note: The 2 April 2026 source explicitly identifies this binary problem as open. The January 2026 HDX result has different decoding guarantees. cards.definitions: Here k counts message bits and n counts stored codeword bits; rate is \(k/n\) and Hamming distance counts unequal coordinates. “Arbitrarily large” means that every threshold K is exceeded by an admissible k; the constants \(r, \delta\) and A must be fixed before K. The encoding is deterministic and injective. A decoder knows C, k, n and the requested index, but learns the received word only by querying named coordinates, each returning one bit. Queries may be adaptive. A randomized decoder can be represented as a probability distribution over finite binary decision trees with the stated depth bound, whose leaves output 0 or 1. Computation, description length and encoding time are unrestricted: this is the source’s existence question, without an additional requirement of efficient uniform construction. The success guarantee is separate for each triple \((x,z,i)\); it does not require one random seed to recover all bits simultaneously. The adversary may choose corruptions knowing x and C, but z is fixed before the decoder’s private randomness. There is no secret key, channel-computation bound or input-dependent auxiliary information. The decoder must return the requested bit, rather than an erasure or a list of candidates.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove existence of a family with all the stated fixed constants and guarantees, or prove its logical negation. A negative result must exclude every choice of positive constant rate, positive constant error tolerance and logarithmic-query constant for unbounded message lengths. A construction over a growing alphabet or a decoder that may fail on some requested positions under the allowed corruption guarantee does not establish the proposition.

context_blocks.title: Recover one item without reading everything
context_blocks.text: A file can be protected by adding redundant bits, yet reading the whole encoded file to retrieve one bit defeats the purpose of local access. Constant rate limits the storage overhead to one fixed factor. Constant error tolerance requires recovery even when a fixed positive fraction of the stored bits have been changed adversarially.

context_blocks.title: Why simple repetition does not suffice
context_blocks.text: Repeating every message bit three times gives constant rate and a three-query majority decoder. However, an adversary can spend just three corruptions on the requested bit’s copies. For large files this fits within any fixed positive global error budget and makes those copies look like a different message. Local redundancy alone therefore does not supply the guarantee for every requested position.

context_blocks.title: The remaining query gap
context_blocks.text: The April 2026 source records a logarithmic lower bound at constant rate, while the known binary high-rate construction uses \(2^{O(\sqrt{\log  n\cdot \log  \log  n})}\) queries. A bound of this latter form is subpolynomial but still larger than logarithmic. Its large-alphabet construction reaches polylogarithmic symbol queries; one such symbol can contain many bits, so it does not give the binary result here.

context_blocks.title: Related decoding guarantees
context_blocks.text: The January 2026 HDX paper gives approximate local list decoding and low-depth list decoding. A list may contain several plausible messages, and circuit depth measures parallel stages rather than bits inspected. Those results do not supply the single requested message bit with this card’s worst-case query and success guarantees.

cards.definitions: The source alphabets \(\mathcal X_i\) and reproduction alphabets \(\widehat{\mathcal X}_i\), for \(i=1,2\), are nonempty finite sets. The pairs \((X_{1,t},X_{2,t})\) are independent identically distributed draws from an arbitrary real probability table \(P\) on \(\mathcal X_1\times\mathcal X_2\). Distortions are finite-valued functions \(d_i:\mathcal X_i\times\widehat{\mathcal X}_i\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\). Write \(P_i\) for the marginal source law and \(D_{i,\min}=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X_i}P_i(x)\min_{z\in\widehat{\mathcal X}_i}d_i(x,z)\). The domain requires finite real \(D_i\ge D_{i,\min}\). An \(n\)-block code consists of deterministic encoders \(f_{i,n}:\mathcal X_i^n\to[M_{i,n}]\), where \([M]=\{1,\ldots,M\}\) and \(M_{i,n}\ge1\), and a deterministic decoder from the pair of indices to \(\widehat{\mathcal X}_1^n\times\widehat{\mathcal X}_2^n\). Each encoder sees only its own source block. For the resulting reproductions define \(\Delta_{i,n}=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n\mathbb E[d_i(X_{i,t},\widehat X_{i,t})]\). A nonnegative pair is achievable if, along some \(n_j\to\infty\), codes satisfy \(\limsup_{j\to\infty}n_j^{-1}\log_2M_{i,n_j}\le R_i\) and \(\limsup_{j\to\infty}\Delta_{i,n_j}\le D_i\) for both sources. The region \(\mathcal R\) is the closure of achievable pairs. There is no interaction, extra side information, computational restriction or variable-length encoding; distortion is expected per-symbol distortion. Predetermined time sharing is allowed. Transmitting both source blocks and selecting minimum-distortion reproductions establishes feasibility on the stated domain; smaller distortion targets, which would give an empty region, are excluded. cards.definitions: The channel has nonempty finite input alphabets \(\mathcal X_1,\mathcal X_2\), output alphabets \(\mathcal Y_1,\mathcal Y_2\), and a table of arbitrary real probabilities \(W(y_1,y_2\mid x_1,x_2)\ge0\), summing to one over outputs for every input pair. In an \(n\)-use code, terminal \(i\) holds a message \(M_i\) uniform on \([K_{i,n}]=\{1,\ldots,K_{i,n}\}\), with positive integer message counts and independent messages. At time \(t\), its input is \(X_{i,t}=f_{i,t}(M_i,Y_i^{t-1})\), where \(f_{i,t}\) is deterministic and \(Y_i^{t-1}=(Y_{i,1},\ldots,Y_{i,t-1})\). Given the current inputs and full past history, the current output pair has distribution \(W\). Terminal 1 estimates \(M_2\) from \((M_1,Y_1^n)\), and terminal 2 estimates \(M_1\) from \((M_2,Y_2^n)\), by deterministic decoders. Error is the probability that either estimate is wrong, averaged over messages and channel draws. A nonnegative rate pair is achievable if codes along \(n_j\to\infty\) have error tending to zero and \(\liminf_{j\to\infty}n_j^{-1}\log_2K_{i,n_j}\ge R_i\) for both terminals. Thus \(R_1\) is the rate from terminal 1 to terminal 2, and \(R_2\) is the reverse rate. The region \(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{TW}}(W)\) is the closure of achievable pairs. The law and all coding functions are public. There are no extra communication links, shared messages, input constraints or computational bounds. The received outputs provide the permitted feedback. Predetermined time sharing is allowed. The capacity region is compact, convex and downward closed, so its nonnegative upper supporting values determine it. Rates are in bits per simultaneous joint channel use, without an extra factor of two. The channel table and weight are mathematical real objects, not finite-precision algorithmic inputs.

cards.definitions: Encode G with vertices \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}, n\ge 0\), by n and its symmetric zero-diagonal \(n\times n\) binary adjacency matrix; encode k, a and b as signed or unsigned binary integers as appropriate. For \(m\ge 1\), the strong power \(G^{\boxtimes m}\) has vertex set \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}^{m}\). Distinct tuples x,y are adjacent exactly when, for every coordinate j, either \(x_{j}=y_{j}\) or \(\{x_{j},y_{j}\}\) is an edge of G. An independent set contains no adjacent pair; \(\alpha (H)\) is its maximum cardinality, with \(\alpha\) of the graph with no vertices equal to zero. Define \(\Theta(G)=\sup_{m\ge1}\alpha(G^{\boxtimes m})^{1/m}\). For nonempty G the supremum equals the limit as \(m\to \infty\), and \(1\le \Theta (G)\le n\); set \(\Theta (G)=0\) when \(n=0\). The desired output approximates \(\Theta\) itself, not its logarithm. The same machine must work for all graphs and precision requests, with no oracle or graph-dependent advice. It may use arbitrarily much finite time and memory on each input.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer supplies a single algorithm and proves termination and the stated absolute-error bound for every valid graph and precision. A negative answer proves that no such uniform algorithm exists. Hardness of exact independent-set computation, failure of a particular approximation scheme, or failure of any finite power to attain the limit does not by itself answer this computability question.

context_blocks.title: Zero-error communication as a graph
context_blocks.text: Vertices represent symbols, and an edge means that the channel can confuse the two symbols. An independent set is therefore a collection of distinguishable messages for one use. Over several uses, messages are tuples and must be distinguishable in at least one coordinate. The strong power records exactly this possibility of confusion, while the root normalizes message counts per use.

context_blocks.title: Why longer blocks matter
context_blocks.text: A complete n-vertex graph has capacity 1, since every pair of distinct symbols can be confused. An edgeless n-vertex graph has capacity n. Between these extremes, coding across several uses can help: the five-cycle has independence number 2 but Shannon capacity \(\sqrt{5}\). For nonempty graphs, \(\log _{2}\Theta (G)\) is the corresponding zero-error rate in bits per use.

context_blocks.title: A limit needs an effective error guarantee
context_blocks.text: Every finite strong power has a finite independence number, but the definition takes a supremum over unbounded lengths. Alon and Lubetzky show that a long fixed prefix of these values can seriously underestimate the eventual capacity. This result rules out an unjustified stopping inference from apparent stabilization; it does not rule out every algorithm with a graph-dependent running time.

context_blocks.title: Recent progress and the scope of the question
context_blocks.text: The October 2025 paper explicitly retains general computability as unknown. Lavi and Sason’s January 2026 results provide exact values for special families and connected examples where no finite strong power attains capacity. Nonattainment does not preclude effective approximation: a computable real can be the limit of unequal approximants. The exact capacity of \(C_{7}\) is a separate card, and computing that one value would not settle the uniform question for all finite graphs.

cards.title: Efficient explicit constant-rate tree codes
cards.formal: Do there exist a fixed finite output alphabet \(\Sigma\), constants \(0<\delta<1\) and \(0<\alpha<\delta/2\), and uniform deterministic polynomial-time encoding and decoding algorithms for binary tree codes of every height \(N\ge1\), with relative tree distance at least \(\delta\) and decoding from suffix error fraction at most \(\alpha\)? Both \(|\Sigma|\) and the two positive distance parameters must be independent of \(N\). The binary information rate \(1/\log_2|\Sigma|\) is therefore a positive constant. The precise causal and decoding requirements are specified below.
cards.why: Tree codes protect communication whose later symbols depend on earlier interaction. A constant alphabet and positive tree distance would keep redundancy bounded while maintaining distinguishability after every possible divergence. cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked construction of the fixed alphabet, positive constants, uniform encoder and decoder, and proofs of prefix consistency, the distance inequality, the promised decoding guarantee and polynomial bit complexity; or give a complete Lean-checked proof that no such collection exists. An existence proof for labels without efficient encoding and decoding does not fulfill the target. A growing alphabet, vanishing distance or decoding guarantee for selected input histories alone is insufficient. A limitation of an additional property not required above does not refute the stated existence claim.

context_blocks.text: Wigderson’s Open Problem 15.34 explicitly requests efficient encoding and decoding, constant rate and constant relative distance. The card keeps all four requirements and uses the standard finite-height binary-input formulation.

The 2018 interactive-coding paper defines efficient tree-code decoding through suffix distance: a received prefix is decoded when every suffix has sufficiently few errors. This supplies a concrete promise for the otherwise unspecified decoding clause in the source question.

The checked May 2026 version of Cohen, Schulman and Srivastava records that constant-rate positive-distance tree codes exist nonconstructively, while the explicit constructions discussed there achieve rate \(\Omega(1/\log\log N)\) at constant distance. That rate tends to zero as the horizon grows.

Their rate–immediacy theorem rules out constant rate for codes satisfying an additional immediacy property under the theorem’s hypotheses. General tree codes need not satisfy that property, so the result does not prove impossibility of the encoder and decoder requested here.

cards.formal: For every fixed finite adversarial channel \(A\) with rational polyhedral input and noise constraints, and every fixed integer \(L\ge2\), does the existence of a nonconfusable completely positive order-\(L\) distribution with admissible input marginal imply a uniform deterministic polynomial-time encodable family of positive-rate \((L-1)\)-list-decodable codes for that same channel? cards.why: The information-theoretic criterion identifies when a channel permits a linear amount of information with a fixed ambiguity bound. Making that criterion explicit would turn a broad existence theorem into efficiently usable encoders without changing the channel or relaxing the list bound.

sentences: A fixed adversarial channel restricts the types of transmitted words and noise words and transforms each input symbol through a specified table.
The source gives a completely positive distribution criterion ensuring that positive-rate codes with a fixed list bound exist.
The question asks whether every channel satisfying that criterion also admits deterministic encoders running in polynomial time in blocklength.

cards.definitions:
A channel \(A=(X,\Lambda_X,S,\Lambda_S,Y,W)\) has finite alphabets \(X=\{1,\ldots,a\}\), \(S=\{1,\ldots,b\}\), \(Y=\{1,\ldots,c\}\), where \(a\ge2\) and \(b,c\ge1\). Its deterministic transition rule is a table \(W:X\times S\to Y\). For a finite set \(T\), write \(\Delta(T)=\{p\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{T}:\sum_{t\in T}p(t)=1\}\). The nonempty sets \(\Lambda_X\subseteq\Delta(X)\) and \(\Lambda_S\subseteq\Delta(S)\) are closed rational polytopes, each given by finitely many linear equalities and non-strict inequalities with rational coefficients. The table, alphabet sizes, signed integer numerators and positive denominators have ordinary binary encodings. These are fixed channel data, independent of blocklength.

The type of \(u\in T^n\) is \(\tau_u(t)=|\{j:u_j=t\}|/n\). An input word \(x\in X^n\) is admissible if \(\tau_x\in\Lambda_X\). Given \(x\), any \(s\in S^n\) with \(\tau_s\in\Lambda_S\) is allowable noise, and the output is \(y_j=W(x_j,s_j)\) for \(j=1,\ldots,n\). The adversary may choose the entire noise word with knowledge of the entire input word. There is no causality restriction, random channel transition, feedback, shared randomness, insertion or deletion.

A code \(C\subseteq X^n\) consists of admissible input words. It is \((L-1)\)-list-decodable when, for every \(y\in Y^n\), at most \(L-1\) distinct words \(x\in C\) admit an allowable noise word producing \(y\). Different candidate input words may use different noise words. This is a zero-error combinatorial guarantee over every output; it imposes no running-time bound on finding the list.

The promise on \(A,L\) is that there exist a probability vector \(p\in\Lambda_X\), a finite integer \(h\ge1\), probability vectors \(p_1,\ldots,p_h\in\Delta(X)\), and real numbers \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_h\ge0\) with \(\sum_j\lambda_j=1\), such that
\[
Q(x_1,\ldots,x_L)=\sum_{j=1}^{h}\lambda_j\prod_{i=1}^{L}p_j(x_i),
\qquad p=\sum_{j=1}^{h}\lambda_jp_j,
\]
is nonconfusable. This is the completely positive distribution condition. The component distributions \(p_j\) need not individually satisfy the input constraints; their common resulting marginal \(p\) must.

Precisely, \(Q\) is confusable if there exists a joint probability distribution \(Z\) on \(X^L\times S^L\times Y\) whose marginal on \(X^L\) is \(Q\), whose \(i\)-th noise-coordinate marginal belongs to \(\Lambda_S\) for every \(1\le i\le L\), and which gives probability one to \(y=W(x_i,s_i)\) simultaneously for all \(i\). Nonconfusable means that no such \(Z\) exists. These distributions are real probability vectors; the promise does not require their entries to be rational or supplied to an encoder.

An explicit positive-rate family means that there exist a rational \(R>0\), an infinite set \(B\subseteq\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\) of blocklengths, two finite deterministic Turing-machine programs \(H,E\), and constants \(K,t\ge1\), with the following properties. On unary input \(1^n\), \(H\) decides whether \(n\in B\) in at most \(K(n+1)^t\) bit operations. For every \(n\in B\), set \(k_n=\lceil Rn\rceil\). On input \((1^n,m)\), with \(m\in\{0,1\}^{k_n}\), the encoder \(E\) outputs \(E_n(m)\in X^n\) in at most \(K(n+1)^t\) bit operations, using binary encodings for output symbols. The map \(E_n\) is injective and its image \(C_n\) is an admissible \((L-1)\)-list-decodable code. Thus the rate \(\log_2|C_n|/n\), measured in information bits per channel use, is at least \(R\).

The programs, constants, rate and infinite length set may depend on the fixed \(A,L\), but not on the particular blocklength or message. Both programs are uniform across lengths and have no advice, oracle, random bits or precomputed codebook supplied as input. The cost bound includes all preprocessing done on that input. No polynomial dependence on the binary description length of a varying channel is required, and there is no demand for a uniform algorithm that produces the programs from the channel. An infinite decidable set of lengths permits divisibility restrictions from exact type constraints; no positive density of those lengths is assumed. The output alphabet is exactly \(X\); replacing it or changing the channel is not allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of this universal explicit-construction assertion, including polynomial bit complexity, positive rate and the fixed \((L-1)\) list bound, or a complete Lean proof of its negation for the stated class of channels. A random existence proof, exhaustive construction taking time polynomial only in the exponentially large codebook, or a construction after changing the alphabet does not meet the assertion. Efficient list decoding is not an additional requirement. The asymptotic polynomial-resource and positive-rate requirements do not carry a \(1/100\) numerical tolerance.

context_blocks.text: Section 18, item 4 asks for explicit positive-rate codes whenever a nonconfusable completely positive distribution exists. Theorem 47 already establishes positive-rate existence; the unresolved part is explicit construction.

This card specifies the deterministic finite-alphabet channel branch used in the paper. It explicitly restricts the convex type constraints to fixed closed rational polytopes, so that the channel has finite exact data. It does not claim to cover arbitrary real, length-dependent constraints or stochastic transition rules.

“Explicit” is interpreted as one polynomial-time encoder per fixed channel and list bound, on an infinite polynomial-time recognizable set of lengths. The source’s positive-rate convention permits an infinite sequence of blocklengths. The length-set and Turing-machine clauses make that convention algorithmic, without requiring a code for every length or an efficient list-decoding procedure.

The completely positive condition involves mixtures of independent equal-marginal products. Confusability allows a different noise explanation for each of the candidate codewords, provided that all explanations yield the same output. This is more general than a single Hamming-distance threshold.

The 2025 zero-rate result bounds code size above the list-decoding or list-recovery threshold. Its matching constructions in that regime do not provide positive-rate families for every channel below the threshold.

Later explicit constructions reproduce broad classes of local properties of random linear codes. The checked AEL-based theorem increases the alphabet, and the checked folded Reed–Solomon construction uses an alphabet growing with length. These statements do not by themselves supply codes for every fixed channel and fixed alphabet in this card.

cards.title: Full-length Reed–Solomon list decoding beyond Johnson
cards.formal: Do there exist real constants \(\varepsilon,\rho\in(0,1)\) with \(\varepsilon<\sqrt{\rho}\), a constant \(K\ge1\), an integer \(c\ge1\), and infinitely many prime powers \(q\), such that for every function \(r:\mathbb F_q\to\mathbb F_q\), \[\left|\left\{f\in\mathbb F_q[X]:\deg f\le\lfloor\rho q\rfloor,\;\bigl|\{x\in\mathbb F_q:f(x)=r(x)\}\bigr|>\varepsilon q\right\}\right|\le Kq^c?\] The zero polynomial is included among the degree-bounded polynomials. All four constants are fixed independently of \(q\) and of the received function \(r\). This is the combinatorial full-length Reed–Solomon question from Open Problem 5.20, without a requirement for an efficient decoding algorithm.
cards.why: Reed–Solomon codes are a central algebraic code family, and their list size expresses an intrinsic information limit even when computation is unrestricted. The full-length requirement fixes the evaluation set completely. Determining whether any constant-rate infinite family surpasses the Johnson threshold would resolve a basic distinction between this rigid algebraic family and the punctured variants for which capacity results are known.
cards.status_note: The precise target is open in Vadhan’s 2012 source. The checked 2025 primary papers explicitly distinguish full-length codes from the punctured families covered by their positive results. Bounded searches through 2026-09-15 found no proof or refutation of the displayed full-length existence statement. This review does not claim that all later parameter regimes or proofs were exhaustively checked.

cards.definitions: A prime power is \(q=p^m\), where \(p\) is a prime and \(m\ge1\) is an integer; the characteristic may vary along the infinite set. The field \(\mathbb F_q\) has exactly \(q\) elements. Let \(d=\lfloor\rho q\rfloor\). The code consists of evaluations of all formal polynomials \(\sum_{j=0}^{d}a_jX^j\), with \(a_j\in\mathbb F_q\), at every element of the field. Its block length and alphabet size are both \(q\), its dimension is \(d+1\), and its rate is \((d+1)/q\), which tends to \(\rho\) as \(q\) grows. Because \(d<q\), distinct allowed polynomials give distinct codewords. Coordinates are indexed by field elements, so no ordering choice matters. A received word is an arbitrary function on this entire field and need not be a low-degree polynomial. Its agreement fraction with a codeword is \(q^{-1}|\{x:f(x)=r(x)\}|\); the normalized Hamming distance is one minus this fraction. The displayed list uses strict agreement \(>\varepsilon\), equivalently distance \(<1-\varepsilon\), following the source’s LIST convention. Thus a boundary with exactly \(\varepsilon q\) agreements is excluded. The list is a set of distinct polynomials, not a list with repetitions. The polynomial bound \(Kq^c\) is uniform over all received words and all selected field sizes. Infinitely many prime powers means an unbounded set of distinct values of \(q\); it does not mean every sufficiently large prime power. No efficient method for selecting that infinite set, constructing field representations, finding the list, or encoding its members is required. The evaluation set may not be punctured or replaced by a random proper subset; neither folded symbols, derivatives, restricted message spaces, nor an average over received words is part of the target.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed existence statement or its negation. A positive proof must establish one fixed admissible pair \((\varepsilon,\rho)\), one polynomial list bound and infinitely many field sizes, and the bound must hold for every received word at each of those sizes. It need not supply a decoder. A negative proof must show that for every admissible pair and every \(K\ge1,c\ge1\), only finitely many prime powers have the uniform list bound. Equivalently, beyond a threshold depending on those constants, every prime power must admit some received word with more than \(Kq^c\) qualifying polynomials. Hard instances for only one rate, one characteristic, or an infinite but not exhaustive subsequence do not by themselves refute the existence statement. Results for randomly punctured codes, list recovery with multiple candidate symbols per coordinate, or only algorithmic hardness do not settle this combinatorial full-length target.

context_blocks.text: Vadhan’s Construction 5.14 defines the full-length code by evaluating every degree-at-most-\(d\) polynomial over the entire field. Definition 5.18 uses strict agreement, and Open Problem 5.20 asks for fixed \(\varepsilon<\sqrt{\rho}\) with degree \(\lfloor\rho q\rfloor\) and polynomial list size along an infinite sequence. The rate convention differs slightly from writing the degree as the dimension.

The Johnson bound and the algorithms recalled in the textbook provide the familiar square-root threshold. The open question asks whether some fixed constant parameters can do strictly better at the level of list cardinalities, including with inefficient decoding.

The 2025 joint journal paper of Alrabiah, Guo, Guruswami, Li and Zhang establishes capacity results for randomly punctured Reed–Solomon codes over fields whose sizes are linear in the block length. “Linear-sized” does not mean equal to the block length. Theorem 1.1 explicitly requires a field size strictly greater than the block length when the dimension is positive, so it does not apply to the full-length codes here.

That paper’s introduction distinguishes combinatorial obstructions for some full-length parameter regimes, due to Ben-Sasson, Kopparty and Radhakrishnan, from the later positive puncturing results. A restriction in some regimes does not refute the present existence quantifiers over parameters and infinitely many field sizes.

Li and Shagrithaya’s 2025 paper addresses list recovery, where each received coordinate may specify several acceptable symbols. Its discussion of full-length Reed–Solomon lower bounds concerns that stronger task. Ordinary list decoding here has exactly one received symbol at each coordinate.

cards.title: Polyhedrality of linear-rank inequality cones
cards.formal: For every integer \(n\ge6\), is the cone \(L_n\) of linear rank inequalities valid over every commutative field polyhedral? Equivalently, for each fixed \(n\ge6\), do finitely many valid coefficient vectors generate every universally valid homogeneous linear inequality on the dimensions of all nonempty sums of \(n\) subspaces by nonnegative real linear combination? The finite generating family may depend on \(n\); no common bound on its size as \(n\) varies is assumed.
cards.why: Dimensions of subspace sums describe the information profiles available to linear coding and linear secret-sharing systems. Finite generation would give a finite complete system of universal linear constraints for each fixed number of subspaces. Nonpolyhedrality would show an intrinsic need for infinitely many constraints even after that number is fixed.
cards.status_note: Open in the checked 2022 seminar Problem (4.4). The complete five-variable result does not extend to all n>=6, and the checked scope of later 2025 work on rank inequalities does not settle polyhedrality. Bounded later checks through 2026-09-16 verified no resolution.

cards.definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(\mathcal S_n=\{S\subseteq[n]:S\ne\varnothing\}\). A subspace arrangement consists of a commutative field \(F\), a nonnegative integer \(m\), and subspaces \(V_1,\ldots,V_n\) of \(F^m\). Finite and infinite fields, every characteristic, arbitrary ambient dimension, repeated subspaces and the zero subspace are all allowed. Its rank vector \(r\in\mathbb R^{\mathcal S_n}\) has coordinate \(r_S=\dim_F(\sum_{i\in S}V_i)\), where the sum denotes the linear span of the listed subspaces and each finite dimension is embedded in \(\mathbb R\).

A real vector \(a=(a_S)_{S\in\mathcal S_n}\) is a universally valid linear rank inequality if \(\sum_{S\in\mathcal S_n}a_Sr_S\ge0\) for every such arrangement, including every choice of \(F\). Define \(L_n\) to be the set of all these coefficient vectors. All inequalities are homogeneous and non-strict; no additive constant, normalization, integrality constraint on coefficients or restriction to a fixed characteristic is included. The empty-set coordinate is omitted because its dimension is always zero. In particular \(L_n\) is a closed convex cone in the finite-dimensional real vector space \(\mathbb R^{2^n-1}\).

Here a cone is polyhedral if it is the intersection of finitely many closed homogeneous real halfspaces. For \(L_n\), this is equivalent to finite generation: there exist a nonnegative integer \(M_n\) and vectors \(a^{(1)},\ldots,a^{(M_n)}\in L_n\) such that
\[
L_n=\left\{\sum_{j=1}^{M_n}\lambda_j a^{(j)}:\lambda_j\in\mathbb R,\ \lambda_j\ge0\right\}.
\]
The empty sum is zero. These generators may have arbitrary real coordinates. No effective procedure for finding them, rationality of a generating family or computational bound is requested.

For clarity, the coefficient cone \(L_n\) is the dual of the closed conic hull \(C_n\) of all rank vectors: \(C_n\) is the Euclidean closure of the set of all finite nonnegative real combinations of arrangement vectors, allowing different fields for different arrangements. Then \(L_n=\{a:\langle a,x\rangle\ge0\ \text{for all }x\in C_n\}\). Polyhedrality of \(C_n\) and \(L_n\) is equivalent. The question does not assert that every point of \(C_n\) is itself the rank vector of one arrangement, or that the unclosed conic hull is already closed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof that \(L_n\) is polyhedral for every integer \(n\ge6\), or a complete Lean proof that \(L_n\) is not polyhedral for at least one fixed integer \(n\ge6\). A positive answer may establish the existence of finite generating families without an efficient construction. A growing number of required inequalities as \(n\) increases does not by itself refute polyhedrality at any fixed \(n\). Neither a result for unrestricted entropy inequalities nor a result confined to one field characteristic settles the stated all-fields target by itself.

context_blocks.text: Problem (4.4), attributed to Alexander Shen in the 2022 seminar report, asks about the inequality cones for \(n\ge6\). This card uses the field-independent convention for linear rank inequalities from the subspace-arrangement literature. The report separately asks about field-size and characteristic dependence in Problem (8.3); those restricted cones are not silently substituted for \(L_n\).

The coefficient cone of valid inequalities and the closed cone of admissible rank profiles are dual objects. Making the closure and dual convention explicit prevents a claim about a discrete set of integer rank vectors from being mistaken for the polyhedrality question.

Dougherty, Freiling and Zeger give a complete finite set of inequalities on five variables, including 24 additional types beyond the Shannon and Ingleton inequalities. Their six-variable discussion gives further inequalities without a complete finite description.

Later work studies additional rank inequalities and distinctions between representability and common-information conditions, including in the broader setting of skew fields. Such results about individual inequalities or proof methods do not alone determine whether the full all-fields cone is polyhedral.

cards.title: Effective classification of polynomially testable hereditary graph properties
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic Turing machine that, on input a finite list \(\mathcal F\) of finite simple graphs, always halts and correctly decides whether \(\mathcal F\) has the polynomial sampling property below? The input is the finite list of forbidden induced patterns. No running-time bound is imposed on this classification algorithm. The constants in the sampling property may depend on the whole fixed list, but must hold simultaneously at every graph order and proximity parameter.
cards.definitions: A finite simple graph is an undirected graph with no loops or multiple edges. Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). A valid input list \(\mathcal F=(F_1,\ldots,F_r)\), \(r\ge0\), is encoded by the orders and full Boolean adjacency matrices of its members on \([|V(F_i)|]\); the matrices are symmetric with zero diagonal. Integer orders and list lengths are binary encoded with delimiters. Repeated graphs and the graph of order zero are allowed. For \(n\ge1\), let \(\mathcal P_{\mathcal F,n}\) consist of all graphs on \([n]\) with no induced copy of any \(F_i\). An induced copy of \(F_i\) is an injection \(\phi:V(F_i)\to[n]\) such that for every distinct \(u,v\), \(\{u,v\}\in E(F_i)\) if and only if \(\{\phi(u),\phi(v)\}\in E(G)\). For a graph \(G\) on \([n]\), define \[d_{\mathcal F}(G)=\frac{1}{n^2}\min_{H\in\mathcal P_{\mathcal F,n}}|E(G)\mathbin{\triangle}E(H)|\] when the set is nonempty, and \(d_{\mathcal F}(G)=+\infty\) otherwise. Symmetric difference counts each added or deleted undirected edge once. A graph is \(\varepsilon\)-far if \(d_{\mathcal F}(G)>\varepsilon\), with strict inequality. For an integer \(s\ge1\), the canonical sampling test chooses a uniformly random subset \(S\subseteq[n]\) of size \(\min\{n,s\}\), queries all \(\binom{|S|}{2}\) adjacency bits within it, and rejects exactly when \(G[S]\) contains an induced member of \(\mathcal F\). Local sampling and finite pattern checking are not charged as adjacency queries. The polynomial sampling property means that there exist integers \(C,a\ge1\) such that for every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), every \(n\ge1\), and every \(\varepsilon\)-far graph \(G\), this test with \(s=\lceil C\varepsilon^{-a}\rceil\) rejects with probability at least \(2/3\). Probability is solely over the uniform subset. For every member of \(\mathcal P_{\mathcal F,n}\), the test accepts with probability one. There is no extra promise on the host graph. The empty forbidden list defines all graphs; if the list contains the order-zero graph, every test rejects since the empty induced copy exists in every sample. These conventions also specify empty property classes at individual orders. The classifier takes only \(\mathcal F\), not \(n,\varepsilon,C\) or \(a\), and need not output the constants. It is one finite program with no advice or oracle, required to output YES exactly for lists with the sampling property and NO for all other valid lists. It may reject malformed encodings; it must halt on every input string.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that such a total classifier exists, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such classifier exists. The affirmative answer must establish termination and both directions of correctness on every finite forbidden list. The negative answer must rule out every deterministic Turing program as a total correct classifier. An equivalent condition that still quantifies over unbounded host graphs and all accuracy parameters is not by itself a decision algorithm. Proving polynomial testability for one family or a finite collection of families does not meet the universal classification target.
cards.why: Asks whether the efficient sampling regime of hereditary graph testing can be recognized from a finite description, turning a broad classification programme into a precise decidability target.

context_blocks.text: Each finite forbidden list defines an elementary graph-membership test: search the input graph for the listed induced patterns. The classification problem has a different input and quantifier structure. Given the list alone, it asks whether every sufficiently distant host graph has a small random sample witnessing a violation, with a single polynomial bound across all host orders and accuracy parameters.

The inherited card added an effectiveness requirement to the source’s structural characterization programme. This review preserves that choice and makes its machine model explicit. The source does not itself assert the decidability statement or its negation, so the current scientific status of this effective target is recorded as uncertain.

Hereditary properties are closed under taking induced subgraphs, and every forbidden-induced-pattern property here is hereditary. General hereditary testing gives some size-independent sample bound. It does not guarantee polynomial dependence on reciprocal distance, which is the distinction the classifier must recognize.

The finite list remains fixed during each sampling problem. Reading every pair in a sample squares the sample size, so polynomial vertex sampling and the resulting polynomial adjacency-query bound agree at this level of precision. The classifier itself is allowed arbitrary finite time; it is not a polynomial-time recognition question.

For nonempty finite families in the usual nontrivial setting, the checked sufficient condition is that the family contain a bipartite graph, a co-bipartite graph and a split graph. Bipartite means a partition into two independent sets; co-bipartite means a partition into two cliques, with arbitrary edges between them; split means a partition into a clique and an independent set. One graph may fill several roles. A necessary condition requires bipartite and co-bipartite members.

The necessary and sufficient conditions do not coincide. The paper provides families meeting the former that are hard to test, and the split-graph property supplies a positive case outside the latter. For split graphs the forbidden list consists of the four-cycle, its complement and the five-cycle; none is itself split. These examples prevent turning either condition into a complete classification.

Even among single forbidden patterns, the induced four-cycle and its complement are the outstanding polynomial-testability cases identified by the survey. The four-vertex path case, whose free graphs are cographs, has a polynomial tester.

The checked induced-four-cycle theorem gives single-exponential reciprocal-distance dependence. It is relevant progress on a member of the class being classified, but does not establish the polynomial sampling property for that member.

The August 2026 container characterization supplies explicit quantitative translations between tester bounds and combinatorial container parameters. Its premises still range over all large host graphs and accuracy parameters. The inspected statements do not give a procedure that halts on each finite forbidden list and decides whether polynomial parameters exist.

An effective positive classification would turn a finite pattern description into a reliable recognition method for the polynomial testing regime. An undecidability result would instead limit such systematic recognition, even though checking any particular finite host graph against the list is straightforward.

cards.title: Polynomial testability versus distance estimation
cards.formal: Is every polynomially testable property of finite simple graphs also polynomially estimable in the dense graph model? Precisely, for every graph property \(\mathcal P=(\mathcal P_n)_{n\ge1}\) satisfying the definitions below, does existence of a uniform randomized tester and integers \(C,a\ge1\) with worst-case adjacency-query bound \(Ct^a\) imply existence of a uniform randomized distance estimator and integers \(D,b\ge1\) with bound \(Dt^b\)? The guarantees must hold for every graph order \(n\), every integer \(t\ge2\), and every input graph, with proximity and additive accuracy \(\varepsilon=1/t\). Programs and polynomial constants may depend on \(\mathcal P\), but not on \(n,t\) or the input graph.
cards.definitions: A finite simple graph on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is an undirected graph whose edges are unordered pairs of distinct vertices. For each integer \(n\ge1\), \(\mathcal P_n\) is a nonempty collection of these graphs invariant under every permutation of \([n]\). No closure under vertex or edge deletion is assumed. For \(n\ge2\), define \[d(G,\mathcal P_n)=\frac{1}{\binom n2}\min_{H\in\mathcal P_n}|E(G)\mathbin{\triangle}E(H)|.\] Here \(E(G)\) is the edge set and symmetric difference \(\triangle\) counts each added or deleted edge once. Set \(d(G,\mathcal P_1)=0\). The minimum exists because \(\mathcal P_n\) is nonempty and finite. Distance lies in \([0,1]\); it is normalized by all possible unordered pairs, not by the number of present edges. A tester receives \(n,t\) in binary and can query whether any chosen pair of distinct vertices is an edge. Queries may depend on previous answers and independent fair random bits. It accepts each \(G\in\mathcal P_n\) with probability at least \(2/3\) and rejects each \(G\) with \(d(G,\mathcal P_n)\ge1/t\) with probability at least \(2/3\). Either answer is permitted when \(0<d(G,\mathcal P_n)<1/t\). An estimator has the same input and oracle access and outputs a binary-encoded rational number \(z\) such that \[\Pr\bigl[|z-d(G,\mathcal P_n)|\le1/t\bigr]\ge2/3\] on every graph, with no distance promise. Each algorithm is one finite probabilistic Turing oracle program with no advice or additional oracle. It must terminate on every execution. Local computation, storage and output length have no quantitative bound; the charged resource is the total number of adjacency queries, bounded on every input and every random execution. Each probability is over the program's random bits for the fixed input graph. The algorithm does not receive a description of \(\mathcal P\): its fixed program may depend on that property. The implication asks for existence of the estimator, not a uniform meta-algorithm taking a tester's code as input. Accuracy is required at every reciprocal integer; this discretization fixes the parameter encoding without imposing a graph-size-dependent bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated universal implication or of its logical negation. An affirmative proof must provide the full estimator guarantees whenever the tester hypothesis holds. A negative proof must establish a property with a polynomial-query tester for which every uniform estimator fails every fixed polynomial query bound under the same model. A separation between particular algorithms, or a conversion with exponential rather than polynomial query overhead, is insufficient. This is a yes/no question about algorithms at arbitrarily small accuracy, not a request for one distance estimate at the numerical benchmark tolerance.
cards.why: A decision tester recognizes only a large violation, whereas a distance estimator measures the minimum repair needed at every distance scale. A general polynomial implication would transfer efficient sampling guarantees to quantitative assessment across the dense-graph model. A separating property would establish an information-cost distinction between these two basic tasks even when unlimited local computation is allowed.

importance.reason: A direct quantitative frontier between two central tasks in property testing, with a universal implication that would organize many existing polynomial-testing results.

context_blocks.text: A tester can answer arbitrarily on inputs that are close to a property but do not satisfy it. A distance estimator must still provide an accurate number there. For example, its output must distinguish small, moderate and large repair costs on the same scale, rather than merely certify a sufficiently large violation.

The input contains \(\binom n2\) potential edge bits. A polynomial-in-\(t\) query bound is independent of \(n\), so for large graphs the algorithm reads only a small part of the adjacency relation. This is an information constraint; difficult computation on the observed sample is not excluded.

The existing card explicitly selected the polynomial implication from the stronger quantitative question in the source. Problem 5.4 asks for a conversion preserving an arbitrary testing complexity after polynomial rescaling of accuracy. Such a conversion would imply this card, but a proof of this card would not by itself establish that stronger relationship for nonpolynomial testing functions. The present review preserves this previously recorded target.

The source defines estimation through tolerance thresholds. Returning an additive-distance estimate, as used here and by Fiat–Ron, captures the polynomial-query regime as well: a polynomial number of threshold comparisons at finer accuracy, with amplified success probabilities, suffices to obtain a distance estimate. The factor between pair-count and squared-order normalization is bounded for every order at least two.

The general Fischer–Newman theorem establishes qualitative tester-to-estimator conversion. Its original quantitative loss is of tower type. This does not yield a polynomial estimator from a polynomial tester.

The later conversion improves that loss to double exponential for general properties and to single exponential for hereditary properties. Hereditary means closed under taking induced subgraphs; the universal target here has no such restriction.

Polynomial estimators are known for several particular graph classes, including the stated induced-path and chordal examples. They show that the stronger task can be efficient, but do not settle its cost for every polynomially testable graph property.

cards.context:
A tester can answer arbitrarily on inputs that are close to a property but do not satisfy it. A distance estimator must still provide an accurate number there. For example, its output must distinguish small, moderate and large repair costs on the same scale, rather than merely certify a sufficiently large violation.

The input contains \(\binom n2\) potential edge bits. A polynomial-in-\(t\) query bound is independent of \(n\), so for large graphs the algorithm reads only a small part of the adjacency relation. This is an information constraint; difficult computation on the observed sample is not excluded.

The existing card explicitly selected the polynomial implication from the stronger quantitative question in the source. Problem 5.4 asks for a conversion preserving an arbitrary testing complexity after polynomial rescaling of accuracy. Such a conversion would imply this card, but a proof of this card would not by itself establish that stronger relationship for nonpolynomial testing functions. The present review preserves this previously recorded target.

The source defines estimation through tolerance thresholds. Returning an additive-distance estimate, as used here and by Fiat–Ron, captures the polynomial-query regime as well: a polynomial number of threshold comparisons at finer accuracy, with amplified success probabilities, suffices to obtain a distance estimate. The factor between pair-count and squared-order normalization is bounded for every order at least two.

The general Fischer–Newman theorem establishes qualitative tester-to-estimator conversion. Its original quantitative loss is of tower type. This does not yield a polynomial estimator from a polynomial tester.

The later conversion improves that loss to double exponential for general properties and to single exponential for hereditary properties. Hereditary means closed under taking induced subgraphs; the universal target here has no such restriction.

Polynomial estimators are known for several particular graph classes, including the stated induced-path and chordal examples. They show that the stronger task can be efficient, but do not settle its cost for every polynomially testable graph property.

benchmark_focus.reason: A universal polynomial tester-to-estimator implication would convert robust graph-property recognition into quantitative distance measurement across the dense model.

cards.title: Sublinear testing of bounded-degree graph isomorphism
cards.formal:
Can isomorphism between two arbitrary bounded-degree graphs be tested with a sublinear number of adjacency-list queries? Precisely, does there exist a uniform randomized tester \(A\), with explicit inputs \(n\ge1\), a degree bound \(d\ge1\), and an integer \(q\ge2\), satisfying the following guarantees for every pair of allowed \(n\)-vertex input graphs \(G_1,G_2\)?
\[G_1\cong G_2\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pr[A\text{ accepts}]\ge2/3,\]
\[\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{iso}}(G_1,G_2)\ge1/q\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pr[A\text{ rejects}]\ge2/3.\]
For each fixed \(d,q\), its worst-case query bound \(Q(n,d,q)\) must satisfy
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{Q(n,d,q)}n=0.\]
Both graphs are given only through oracles. The graph model, distance and query accounting are specified below. The target retains the sublinear-existence question in the saved card, which is one part of the source’s broader request to determine the full query complexity.
cards.why: The problem asks whether two large sparse structures can be compared without reading a linear fraction of their neighborhoods. It isolates the information needed to recognize structural similarity when both objects are unknown. A resolution would locate a basic boundary of sublinear access and explain whether large connected components create an obstruction beyond the known distribution-like examples.

cards.definitions:
The graphs \(G_i=([n],E_i)\), where \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), are undirected and simple, with maximum degree at most \(d\). Disconnected graphs and isolated vertices are allowed. There is no expansion, hyperfiniteness, component-size or randomness promise on their structure.

Graph \(G_i\) is represented by an incidence oracle \(g_i:[n]\times[d]\to[n]\cup\{\bot\}\). Its first \(\deg_{G_i}(v)\) entries at vertex \(v\) list the distinct neighbors of \(v\) in an arbitrary fixed order, and the remaining entries are \(\bot\). The oracles are promised consistent with undirected simple graphs. One adjacency query chooses \(i\in\{1,2\}\), \(v\in[n]\), and \(j\in[d]\), and receives \(g_i(v,j)\). Queries may depend on earlier answers. Correctness must hold for every permitted neighbor ordering.

For a permutation \(\sigma\) of \([n]\), put \(\sigma(E_2)=\{\{\sigma(u),\sigma(v)\}:\{u,v\}\in E_2\}\). Define
\[\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{iso}}(G_1,G_2)=\frac1{dn}\min_{\sigma\in S_n}|E_1\mathbin{\triangle}\sigma(E_2)|,\]
where \(S_n\) is the set of all permutations and \(\triangle\) denotes symmetric difference. Each deleted or added undirected edge counts once. Thus distance zero means graph isomorphism, and the rejection promise means at least \(dn/q\) edge edits are needed after the best vertex relabelling. Neighbor-list positions do not affect this distance. For nonisomorphic pairs at distance strictly below \(1/q\), either output is allowed.

The tester is a probabilistic oracle Turing algorithm given binary \(n,d,q\), access to both incidence oracles, independent fair random bits and a primitive returning an independent uniformly sampled vertex label in \([n]\). Count every incidence-oracle call and every such vertex-sampling call as one query. All other finite local computation is unrestricted, and the tester must halt. The bound \(Q(n,d,q)\) holds on every allowed pair, every representation and every sequence of random outcomes. Success probabilities include all internal randomness and vertex samples. No graph-dependent advice or full description of either graph is provided; any preprocessing uses only \(n,d,q\).

The degree and reciprocal proximity are fixed when taking the sublinear limit. There is no requirement for one bound uniform in growing \(d\) or \(q\), and no polynomial runtime requirement beyond the query guarantee. Using reciprocal integer accuracies covers all fixed positive proximities by choosing a smaller reciprocal threshold. The edge-edit normalization follows the saved card; the source also uses a convention with a factor of two in the edge threshold. That constant rescaling does not change the all-fixed-proximities existence question.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence of a tester with the stated correctness, access and sublinear-query guarantees, or a Lean-checked refutation of that existence statement. A positive answer must cover every pair of bounded-degree input graphs and every fixed proximity, with two-sided error at most \(1/3\). A near-linear bound that is not \(o(n)\), a guarantee for almost all graphs, a known-target tester, or a result only for small connected components is insufficient. A lower bound of order \(n^{2/3}\) up to logarithmic factors alone does not rule out sublinear testing.

context_blocks.text: Open Problem 2.4 explicitly separates testing against a known fixed graph from testing a pair of oracle inputs. This card chooses the latter, as in its saved formulation, and retains two-sided error.

Goldreich proves upper and lower query bounds of order \(n^{2/3}\), up to polylogarithmic factors and proximity dependence, when connected components have polylogarithmic size. The lower bound also applies to general inputs, but the upper bound retains its component-size restriction.

Goldreich and Tauber obtain a \(\widetilde O(\sqrt n)\) tester for almost all fixed regular target graphs, with a matching lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Their model supplies the target graph in advance; it neither supplies both graphs only by oracle nor covers every possible target.

The relevant resource here is query complexity. A tester may perform extensive finite computation on its observations. Therefore a fast algorithm for explicit graph isomorphism does not, by itself, meet the oracle-query target, and a query bound does not by itself assert fast total runtime.

cards.title: Polynomial testing of induced four-cycle freeness
cards.formal: Do there exist integers \(C,a\ge1\) such that the canonical sampling test below, with sample size \[s(\varepsilon)=\lceil C\varepsilon^{-a}\rceil,\] rejects every finite simple graph that is \(\varepsilon\)-far from having no induced four-cycle with probability at least \(2/3\), for every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\)? The constants must be independent of the graph order and of \(\varepsilon\). The test always accepts graphs with no induced four-cycle, so this asks for polynomial-query one-sided testing in the dense graph model.
cards.why: This is the unresolved concrete case, up to complementation, in the classification of polynomial testing for a single forbidden induced graph. It asks whether a globally expensive repair necessarily leaves violations visible in a polynomial-sized random sample. The answer would separate two very different quantitative regimes of dense-graph testing for one small and fully specified pattern.

sentences: The question asks whether induced four-cycle freeness can be tested from a random sample whose size is polynomial in reciprocal proximity.
An induced four-cycle has its four cycle edges and neither diagonal, and repairing the graph permits both edge additions and deletions.
The canonical tester rejects when its sampled induced subgraph contains such a cycle and must reject every far graph with probability at least two thirds.

cards.definitions: A finite simple graph is an undirected graph \(G=([n],E)\), where \(n\ge1\), \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(E\) is a set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. An induced four-cycle consists of four distinct vertices \(v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4\) whose edges among those vertices are exactly \(\{v_1,v_2\},\{v_2,v_3\},\{v_3,v_4\},\{v_4,v_1\}\); the two diagonals are absent. Let \(\mathcal P_n\) be the graphs on \([n]\) with no such induced subgraph. Define \[d(G,\mathcal P_n)=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\min_{([n],E')\in\mathcal P_n}|E\mathbin{\triangle}E'|.\] Here \(\triangle\) is symmetric difference, so both edge additions and deletions are allowed and each undirected edit is counted once. The minimum exists because \(\mathcal P_n\) is nonempty and finite. The graph is \(\varepsilon\)-far when \(d(G,\mathcal P_n)>\varepsilon\), with strict inequality. This uses the edge-count-over-\(n^{2}\) convention of the selected survey; it is half the adjacency-matrix-entry distance in the original Goldreich question. The tester is given \(n\) and rational \(\varepsilon\), and has oracle access to the adjacency bit of any unordered vertex pair. For a positive integer \(s\), the canonical test chooses a uniformly random subset \(S\subseteq[n]\) of cardinality \(\min\{n,s\}\), queries every unordered pair in \(S\), and rejects exactly when \(G[S]\) contains an induced four-cycle. All \(\binom{\min\{n,s\}}{2}\) adjacency queries count; the property check on the finite sampled graph has no additional query cost, and no running-time bound is requested. Uniform subset sampling is the stated finite probability distribution, with sampling and local computation not charged as adjacency queries. If \(n\le s\), the entire graph is inspected. In particular, orders below four are always accepted and never far. No behavior is required for nonsatisfying graphs at distance at most \(\varepsilon\). Every host graph is allowed; no degree, density, chordality or other promise is imposed. The deterministic sampling-size formula and rejection rule specify a single uniform family of tests once \(C,a\) are fixed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the formal proposition or its logical negation with a complete Lean-checked proof. A positive answer must exhibit fixed polynomial constants and establish rejection probability at least \(2/3\) for every far input and every permitted proximity parameter. A negative answer must show that for every choice of \(C,a\) there are a proximity parameter and a graph at the stated distance for which that sampling test rejects with probability less than \(2/3\). A merely exponential sample bound, a result for ordinary four-cycle freeness, or a tester with an additional host-graph promise does not meet the target.

context_blocks.text: An induced four-cycle is a cycle without either diagonal. A complete graph on four vertices contains ordinary four-cycles, but no induced four-cycle. This distinction changes both the set of valid graphs and the repair task: adding a diagonal can destroy an induced cycle, while adding edges cannot eliminate an ordinary subgraph copy.

The tester does not try to find every violation or to reconstruct a repaired graph. It distinguishes graphs satisfying the property from graphs requiring more than \(\varepsilon n^{2}\) edits. A polynomial sample bound would mean that the number of queried adjacencies remains polynomial in reciprocal proximity even when the host graph is arbitrarily large.

The induced removal lemma relates edit distance to the number of forbidden induced copies. For a fixed pattern, polynomial bounds on that density and polynomial bounds for canonical one-sided sampling are equivalent up to changes in polynomial exponents. The known four-cycle removal bound is exponential in a power of reciprocal distance, which is far larger than the polynomial dependence conjectured here.

Alon and Shapira classified the polynomial and superpolynomial cases for single forbidden induced graphs apart from a few small patterns. Alon and Fox settled the four-vertex-path case, leaving the induced four-cycle and its complement as the remaining case. Complementing all adjacencies preserves edit distance and transfers the sampling question between those two patterns.

On 15 September 2026 the user authorized replacing the inherited classification programme by a concrete narrower statement. The selected target is Conjecture 3.6 of the 2025 survey. Goldreich's Open Problem 8.26 concerns all dense-graph properties, permits two-sided error, and asks for a characterization; it is strictly broader in scope and is not asserted equivalent to this testability conjecture. The separate active finite-family classification card also remains a different target.

The 2026 container characterization connects one-sided tester complexity to quantitative combinatorial parameters. It supplies an equivalence, rather than polynomial values of those parameters for every particular property. Consequently, the existence of that characterization does not itself settle the induced-four-cycle bound.

cards.title: Planar graphs from local neighborhoods
cards.formal: For every real \(\varepsilon>0\), does there exist a positive integer \(D=D(\varepsilon)\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\) and every pair of finite simple planar graphs \(G,H\) on \(n\) vertices, equality of their multisets of rooted radius-\(D\) neighborhoods implies \[\min_{\phi:V(G)\cong V(H)}\left|\phi(E(G))\mathbin{\triangle}E(H)\right|\le\varepsilon n?\] The minimum is over all vertex bijections, and \(\triangle\) denotes symmetric difference of edge sets. There is no maximum-degree bound; the radius may depend only on \(\varepsilon\).
cards.why: This asks whether local structure determines approximate global structure throughout the planar family, even around vertices of very high degree. It isolates a structural obstruction behind extending sparse-graph testing beyond bounded-degree and outerplanar settings.
cards.status_note: Source-open. The user selected this specific source question on 16 September 2026. No resolution of the all-planar, unbounded-maximum-degree implication was identified. Positive bounded-degree and outerplanar results have different scopes. No cited proof was independently verified or formalized in Lean.

sentences: The question compares two planar graphs through the rooted neighborhoods around all their vertices.
It asks whether a radius depending only on the allowed error makes identical neighborhood multisets imply closeness under edge edits and vertex relabeling.
No maximum-degree bound is imposed, so even a small-radius neighborhood may be large.
The source proves the analogous result for outerplanar graphs, while bounded-degree planar theorems allow the radius to depend on the degree bound.
This specific structural question replaces the original broad classification target by an explicitly selected yes/no assertion.

cards.definitions:
A finite simple undirected graph is a finite vertex set \(V\) and a set \(E\) of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Thus loops and multiple edges are excluded. A planar graph admits a drawing in the plane with distinct points for vertices and curves for edges whose interiors neither intersect one another nor meet a vertex. A drawing is not part of the data, and it is not used to compare neighborhoods. Graphs need not be connected. Their order is \(n=|V|\), and the two graphs in the question have the same order.

The graph distance \(\operatorname{dist}_G(u,v)\) is the minimum number of edges in a path from \(u\) to \(v\), with distance infinity when no path exists. The rooted radius-\(D\) neighborhood \(B_G(v,D)\) is the subgraph induced by \(\{u\in V(G):\operatorname{dist}_G(u,v)\le D\}\), together with the distinguished root \(v\). An induced subgraph retains every edge whose two endpoints belong to that set. Rooted graphs are isomorphic when a bijection of their vertices preserves edges and sends one root to the other. Vertex labels, the planar drawing, any ordering of neighbors, and edges leaving the neighborhood are not part of its rooted isomorphism type.

The multiset of radius-\(D\) neighborhoods records each rooted isomorphism type with its multiplicity among the \(n\) possible roots. Equality means that, for every finite rooted graph \(F\), the number of vertices \(v\) for which \(B_G(v,D)\) is isomorphic to \(F\) equals the corresponding number in \(H\). Thus multiplicities matter. Although corresponding roots can be paired, their individual neighborhood isomorphisms need not agree on overlapping vertices. In particular, such a pairing is not already a global graph isomorphism. Even a radius-one neighborhood may contain arbitrarily many vertices, because degrees are unrestricted.

For a vertex bijection \(\phi:V(G)\to V(H)\), define \(\phi(E(G))=\{\{\phi(u),\phi(v)\}:\{u,v\}\in E(G)\}\). The symmetric difference consists of edges in exactly one of its two arguments. Its cardinality counts edge deletions plus edge additions, each at unit cost, after a free relabeling of vertices. Taking the minimum over bijections gives the edit distance to isomorphism. There are no vertex edits or isolated-vertex padding in this equal-order question. Intermediate graphs during edge editing are not required to be planar. The permitted number of edits is at most \(\varepsilon n\), normalized by vertex count rather than by the number of possible edges or by a degree bound. For \(n=1\) the conclusion is automatic. No algorithm for finding the bijection, a computable bound on \(D\), or property-testing oracle is requested; this is a structural existence statement.

source_formulation.text: Do identical sufficiently large rooted local-neighborhood multisets force two planar graphs of the same order to be close to isomorphic under edge edits?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the specific question in §5, selected in place of the adjacent broad classification question

context_blocks.text: The broad imported question asked for a classification of graph properties testable with sublinear query complexity. This card now adopts the separate, concrete planar local-neighborhood question from the same source. The change of scope was explicitly selected on 16 September 2026; it does not claim to complete the original general classification programme.

The structural issue is whether sufficiently large local views determine a sparse planar graph up to a small linear number of edge edits. The neighborhoods carry no consistent global labels. Matching their multiplicities therefore supplies statistical local information, not a ready-made global correspondence.

For planar graphs with a fixed maximum degree, earlier local-to-global results provide a radius depending on both the error tolerance and that degree bound. The selected question asks whether the degree dependence can be removed completely. Planarity bounds average degree, but permits individual degrees growing with the graph order.

Babu, Khoury and Newman prove the required local-view implication for outerplanar graphs, with no maximum-degree bound. Outerplanar means that the graph has a plane drawing with every vertex incident to the exterior face. Their Theorem 4.4 states the same qualitative radius-versus-edge-distance conclusion for that subclass.

The source extends its methods to graphs with a fixed number of edge-removal outer layers. It distinguishes this from removing exterior vertices layer by layer, and explicitly retains the ordinary 2-outerplanar case as open at publication. Those positive results therefore must not be read as covering every planar graph.

The paper also obtains polylogarithmic-query property testers for its unbounded-degree subclasses, using ordered-neighbor and degree access. These algorithmic results explain the motivation for the structural question, but the selected target itself asks only for the stated finite-graph implication.

Basu, Kumar and Seshadhri sharpen the dependence on proximity for testing properties of bounded-degree planar graphs and show matching exponential behavior for isomorphism testing. Their results retain a maximum-degree bound and therefore do not settle the unbounded-degree local-view question.
