context_blocks.text: Nonprivate PAC learning at constant accuracy and confidence has sample complexity governed by VC dimension. Approximate private learnability instead has a qualitative connection to finite Littlestone dimension. This equivalence says that a finite sample bound exists; it does not identify how large the bound must be.

For finite classes, the 2026 source summarizes a lower scale \(\Omega(v+\log^{*}d)\) and upper scales \(\min\{O(\log|\mathcal C|),\widetilde O(d^{5})\}\), suppressing privacy and learning parameters. The proposed bound depends polynomially on \(v\) and \(\log^{*}d\), so replacing \(d\) by another fixed power does not answer it. The source presents this as one concrete formulation following its broader characterization question.

Lyu’s improved PAC learner has a bound \(\widetilde O(d^{5}\log(1/\delta)/(\varepsilon\alpha))\), with the remaining confidence and logarithmic factors specified in the paper. Its dependence on \(d\) is polynomial but is still much larger than a polynomial in \(\log^{*}d\). The result was published at STOC 2026; the checked detailed theorem is in the 2025 author manuscript.

Yan proves a nearly matching iterated-logarithmic bound when \(v=1\), including an improper learner and explicit parameter dependence. The 2026 problem paper also discusses thresholds, rectangles and halfspaces where the privacy overhead is relatively small. These positive special cases do not supply a bound uniform over unbounded VC dimension.

The card retains the earlier editorial normalization \(\varepsilon=1\), error \(1/10\), failure probability \(1/10\), and \(\delta=1/(100m^{2})\). In particular, \(\delta\) is tied to the actual sample size, rather than silently treated as a fixed constant while \(m\) grows. The source suppresses these parameters, so its displayed summary bounds are context rather than claims that every hidden factor is independent of this normalization.

cards.definitions: A concept is a binary function; the learner knows \(\mathcal X\) and \(\mathcal C\). The VC dimension \(v\) is the largest cardinality of a subset \(S\subseteq\mathcal X\) on which the restrictions of \(\mathcal C\) realize every binary labeling. A complete binary tree of depth \(r\) has an instance point at each internal node and its two outgoing edges labeled 0 and 1. It is shattered by \(\mathcal C\) if every root-to-leaf edge-label sequence is produced by one fixed concept on that path's instance points. The Littlestone dimension \(d\) is the greatest shattered depth. For \(z\ge1\), \(\log^{*}z\) is the least number of successive base-two logarithms needed to obtain a value at most one; in particular \(\log^{*}1=0\). The dimension-zero case is excluded only to avoid a logarithm convention: on a fixed nonempty domain such a class contains a single distinct concept and has a data-independent exact predictor. A learner is an arbitrary probability kernel from \((\mathcal X\times\{0,1\})^m\) to the finite set \(\{0,1\}^{\mathcal X}\). It need not return a member of \(\mathcal C\). For every pair of labeled sample lists \(S,S'\) differing at one position and every subset \(E\) of output hypotheses, require \[\Pr[L(S)\in E]\le e\Pr[L(S')\in E]+1/(100m^{2}).\] Privacy holds even on samples not realizable by the class. The sample size is chosen before the target and distribution; the probability in the PAC guarantee includes both independently drawn examples and the learner's randomness. There are no runtime or representation bounds, and no uniform program across classes is required. The integer-power bound is equivalent to an unspecified universal polynomial in \(1+v\) and \(1+\log^{*}d\). A finite class on an arbitrary domain can be reduced to the finite domain of distinct label vectors \((h(x))_{h\in\mathcal C}\), of which there are at most \(2^{|\mathcal C|}\); both dimensions and these unrestricted learning/privacy requirements are preserved. Thus the finite-domain convention introduces no additional sample-complexity restriction on finite classes.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof of the universal polynomial bound or its logical negation under the exact privacy and PAC conventions above. A positive answer must supply, for every class, a sample size and private learner satisfying the guarantee simultaneously for all targets and distributions. A negative answer must show that for every proposed pair of universal integers \(A,k\), some finite class admits no such learner at any positive integer sample size within the proposed bound. Computational lower bounds, proper-learning obstructions that disappear for improper learners, or a result only for one fixed VC dimension do not refute the statement.

cards.context:
Nonprivate PAC learning at constant accuracy and confidence has sample complexity governed by VC dimension. Approximate private learnability instead has a qualitative connection to finite Littlestone dimension. This equivalence says that a finite sample bound exists; it does not identify how large the bound must be.

For finite classes, the 2026 source summarizes a lower scale \(\Omega(v+\log^{*}d)\) and upper scales \(\min\{O(\log|\mathcal C|),\widetilde O(d^{5})\}\), suppressing privacy and learning parameters. The proposed bound depends polynomially on \(v\) and \(\log^{*}d\), so replacing \(d\) by another fixed power does not answer it. The source presents this as one concrete formulation following its broader characterization question.

Lyu’s improved PAC learner has a bound \(\widetilde O(d^{5}\log(1/\delta)/(\varepsilon\alpha))\), with the remaining confidence and logarithmic factors specified in the paper. Its dependence on \(d\) is polynomial but is still much larger than a polynomial in \(\log^{*}d\). The result was published at STOC 2026; the checked detailed theorem is in the 2025 author manuscript.

Yan proves a nearly matching iterated-logarithmic bound when \(v=1\), including an improper learner and explicit parameter dependence. The 2026 problem paper also discusses thresholds, rectangles and halfspaces where the privacy overhead is relatively small. These positive special cases do not supply a bound uniform over unbounded VC dimension.

The card retains the earlier editorial normalization \(\varepsilon=1\), error \(1/10\), failure probability \(1/10\), and \(\delta=1/(100m^{2})\). In particular, \(\delta\) is tied to the actual sample size, rather than silently treated as a fixed constant while \(m\) grows. The source suppresses these parameters, so its displayed summary bounds are context rather than claims that every hidden factor is independent of this normalization.

cards.definitions: For an integer \(T\ge 2, a\) mechanism is a family of Borel probability distributions \(M_{x}\) on \(\mathbb{R} ^{T}\), one for each binary stream \(x\in \{0,1\}^{T}\). Its output \(Y_{t}\) is released immediately after observing \(x_{t}\). Causality means that whenever x and \(x'\) have the same first t bits, the marginal distributions of \((Y_{1},\ldots ,Y_{t})\) under \(M_{x}\) and \(M_{x}'\) are equal. The horizon T is known before the first output. Streams are fixed inputs, not adaptively chosen in response to outputs. Neighbors differ in exactly one bit, and pure privacy requires \(M_{x}(S)\le \exp (1/2)M_{x}' (S)\) for every pair of neighbors and every Borel \(S\subseteq \mathbb{R} ^{T}\). This protects the entire joint transcript, with no additive failure allowance. There is no restriction on computation, memory, real precision, output integrality or monotonicity; internal randomness may be correlated across times. A different family of probability distributions may be chosen for each T. The maximum over streams is outside the expectation; the maximum over time is inside it. The infimum is used without assuming attainment. \(E(T)\) is finite, for example because a data-independent all-zero transcript has error at most T. All logarithms in asymptotic comparisons may use any fixed base greater than one.

context_blocks.text: Continual counting publishes a running total as events arrive. For the stream \((1,0,1,1)\), the exact outputs are \((1,1,2,3)\). Changing its second bit gives \((1,1,1,1)\) and exact outputs \((1,2,3,4)\): one protected event changes several releases. Privacy must therefore hold for the whole visible transcript. Separate guarantees for isolated timestamps do not establish the stated joint guarantee.

The causal requirement forbids using future events to improve earlier releases. It also concerns their joint distribution, not merely the marginal law of each single output; otherwise correlations among old outputs could reveal future data. The offline query-release problem may inspect the complete database before producing any answer and consequently asks for a different capability.

The order of maximum and expectation is central. Imagine an error vector that equals one at a single uniformly random timestamp and zero elsewhere. Its expected maximum is one, but the largest expected absolute error at any predetermined timestamp is only \(1/T\). This example concerns error criteria, not a proposed private mechanism. Squared-error bounds and average-over-time bounds also cannot be substituted without checking the conversion.

For the fixed privacy budget here, the July 2026 Bairaktari–Larsen result gives the lower benchmark \(\Omega (\log ^{3/2}T)\), while the best upper bound summarized in their Table 1 is \(O(\log ^{2}T)\). The binary-tree mechanism aggregates intervals and reuses their noisy counts across prefixes. The paper closes the dependence on T for approximate privacy at fixed parameters, but its pure-privacy row retains the square-root-of-logarithm gap.

Arkhipov and Kalinin improve constants for mean and maximum per-coordinate squared error using matrix mechanisms. Those criteria take expectations before choosing the worst coordinate, or average squared errors. Improving them is useful, but does not by itself determine the expected largest absolute error of the entire transcript.

Bhowmik and Hasan’s August revision claims tight squared-error order for arbitrary real factorizations within Laplace matrix mechanisms. It explicitly excludes expected maxima and unrestricted non-matrix mechanisms. Thus even accepting its claimed theorem would not settle this card’s minimax quantity.

Lin, Mirrokni and Woodruff independently give a near-optimal lower bound for a prefix-matrix factorization cost. Its quantification is over factorizations, while this card allows every causal private output distribution. The distinction remains essential when reading a result advertised as optimal for a class of mechanisms.

A matching order for \(E(T)\) would identify the unavoidable worst-time accuracy cost of a basic continually released statistic under pure privacy. The target is a minimax information bound: it does not additionally ask for an efficient implementation or restrict the form of a candidate mechanism.

cards.answer_criterion: Determine an asymptotic rate \(g(T)\) and prove constants \(c,C>0\) and \(T_{0}\) such that \(c g(T)\le E(T)\le C g(T)\) for every \(T\ge T_{0}\). The upper guarantee must be achievable by permitted causal pure-private mechanisms, and the lower guarantee must cover all such mechanisms. Constants may not depend on T. The expected maximum absolute-error criterion must be the same on both sides.

cards.title: Polynomial-time private release of all marginals
cards.formal: Do there exist an integer \(C\ge1\), a function \(\alpha:\mathbb N_{\ge2}\to[0,1]\) with \(\lim_{d\to\infty}\alpha(d)=0\), a uniform randomized mechanism \(M\), and a uniform deterministic evaluator \(E\) satisfying the following statement? For every integer \(d\ge2\), put \(n=d^{C}\). For every explicitly given database \(D\in(\{0,1\}^{d})^{n}\), \(M(d,D)\) runs in worst-case time polynomial in \(n+d\), satisfies \((1,1/(100n^{2}))\)-differential privacy under replacement of one row, and outputs a finite binary synopsis \(S\). With probability at least \(2/3\) over \(M\)'s random bits, this one synopsis satisfies \[\left|E(d,S,J,a)-q_{J,a}(D)\right|\le\alpha(d)\] simultaneously for every \(J\subseteq[d]\) and \(a\in\{0,1\}^{J}\). The evaluator runs in worst-case time polynomial in \(d+|S|\), outputs a binary-encoded rational, and has no further access to the database. The synopsis may be arbitrary: it need not be synthetic data or describe a consistent probability distribution.
cards.definitions: \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\). A marginal query \((J,a)\) asks for the fraction of rows agreeing with the assignment \(a\) on the coordinates in \(J\): \[q_{J,a}(D)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf 1\{\forall j\in J,\ D_{ij}=a_j\}.\] All orders \(0\le|J|\le d\) are included; the empty query equals one. Each query can be encoded as a length-\(d\) word over \(\{*,0,1\}\), indicating omitted coordinates or required bits; fix any constant-length binary encoding of these symbols. Thus there are \(3^{d}\) queries with descriptions of length \(O(d)\). The database is an ordered \(n\)-by-\(d\) bit matrix. For every ordered pair of equal-size databases \(D,D'\) differing at one row and every set \(O\) of binary output strings, privacy requires \[\Pr[M(d,D)\in O]\le e\Pr[M(d,D')\in O]+1/(100n^{2}).\] It is a guarantee on the whole synopsis distribution. \(M\) and \(E\) are ordinary classical multitape Turing machines with no advice, oracle or shared private database state; \(M\) uses independent fair bits. One fixed polynomial bounds its time, output length and number of random bits on every execution. One fixed polynomial bounds the evaluator's time on every valid query and synopsis. The probability of simultaneous accuracy is required separately for every database, with no input-distribution promise. All of \(C,\alpha,M,E\) and their polynomial bounds are chosen before \(d,D\). The convergence condition means that for every real \(\eta>0\), there is \(d_0\) such that \(\alpha(d)\le\eta\) for all \(d\ge d_0\); no computable convergence rate or procedure for evaluating \(\alpha\) is required. Error is an absolute error in a row fraction in \([0,1]\), not in the unnormalized count. These are the concrete synopsis, privacy and sample-size conventions already selected for this card in September 2026; they are not claimed equivalent to every interactive or fixed-order variant of the source question.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove this existence statement or its logical negation in Lean. A positive answer must exhibit the fixed uniform machines, exponent, polynomial resource bounds and vanishing error function and prove both privacy and simultaneous accuracy on every valid database. A negative answer must exclude all such choices; hardness only under an unproved cryptographic assumption proves the corresponding conditional obstruction, not the unconditional negation. Fixed positive error, accuracy only for most queries or typical databases, a polynomial number of interactive queries, or a runtime polynomial in the exponential number of all query answers does not meet the stated criterion. The target is the existence of a vanishing-error polynomial-time synopsis, rather than a numerical value requiring additive \(1/100\) determination.
cards.why: Marginals are basic summaries of relationships among attributes. The question asks whether the large information-theoretic usefulness of private high-dimensional data can be captured by a compact, efficiently evaluated object using polynomially many records. It isolates a statistical-versus-computational gap for a concrete query family while allowing outputs more flexible than synthetic datasets.

importance.reason: A fundamental statistical-versus-computational gap for a concrete and widely used query family. It complements existing sample-complexity questions and has an explicit specialist open-problem formulation, while allowing non-synthetic outputs avoids a known source of misleading hardness claims.

progress.text: The checked 2013 manuscript, published at ITCS 2014, gives subexponential per-query private marginal answers for small databases at fixed absolute error.

Weighted Fourier factorizations give optimal Gaussian-factorization variance for arbitrary specified marginal workloads with runtime polynomial in explicit output size; this does not bound the time or synopsis size polynomially in dimension for all marginals.

context_blocks.text: A marginal measures how often a selected pattern occurs in a set of attributes. Low-order queries concern small attribute groups; this problem includes every order. There are exponentially many queries, but each query has a short description. Polynomial running time therefore requires a reusable compact synopsis with a query evaluator, rather than an explicit table of all answers.

Privacy and accuracy concern different quantifiers. Changing one person’s entire row must leave the output distribution nearly unchanged. For each fixed database, a single successful synopsis must answer every query accurately at once. Evaluating it after release accesses no additional records. A guarantee for each query separately with a fresh failure probability would not give the requested simultaneous event.

Vadhan’s 2017 open question asks for vanishing error with polynomially many records and polynomial computation. The current card retains the previously approved approximate-privacy parameters and a noninteractive binary synopsis. The survey’s alternative question about some growing but restricted order is not substituted for the all-orders requirement.

Chandrasekaran, Thaler, Ullman and Wan give a subexponential per-query algorithm on small databases. Theorem 1.1 handles a sequence of adaptively chosen marginal queries at fixed absolute error and its database-size guarantee depends on the length of that sequence. This is meaningful progress, but is not a polynomial-time construction of one synopsis answering all orders with vanishing error.

The survey’s synthetic-data hardness theorem assumes one-way functions and restricts the output to a new database, even for two-way marginals. It does not rule out an arbitrary synopsis: the survey explicitly contrasts that obstruction with efficient nonsynthetic answers to low-order marginals. The benchmark deliberately retains this broader output interface.

The checked December 2025 weighted-Fourier paper provides exact optimality for weighted or maximum noise variance within Gaussian factorization mechanisms. Its runtime is polynomial in the dataset and the explicit output/workload size. For the entire \(3^{d}\)-query family that size is exponential, and variance optimality within that mechanism class is not a general polynomial-synopsis theorem or impossibility result.

cards.title: Optimal regret for private stochastic online learning
cards.formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors, the optimal expected pseudo-regret \(R^{*}(K,T,\varepsilon,\Delta)\) for pure differentially private stochastic full-information online learning. The domain is integers \(K\ge2\), \(T\ge1\), and real parameters \(\varepsilon>0\), \(0<\Delta\le1\). For independent loss distributions \(P_1,\ldots,P_K\) on \([0,1]\), let \(\mu_j=\mathbb E_{P_j}[L]\); require a unique minimizer \(j^{*}\) and \(\mu_j-\mu_{j^{*}}\ge\Delta\) for every \(j\ne j^{*}\). At round \(t\), select \(I_t\in[K]\) using only earlier observations and private randomness, incur loss \(L_{I_t,t}\), and then observe the entire vector \(L_t\), where all \(L_{j,t}\sim P_j\) are independent across actions and rounds. Put \[R^{*}(K,T,\varepsilon,\Delta)=\inf_A\sup_{(P_1,\ldots,P_K)}\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}(\mu_{I_t}-\mu_{j^{*}})\right],\] where the supremum ranges over the promised product distributions and the infimum over the causal \(\varepsilon\)-private strategies defined below. The requested rate retains every dependence on \(K,T,\varepsilon,\Delta\), including logarithmic factors and the small-horizon regime.
cards.why: This asks how protecting one round of observations changes the achievable accuracy of sequential decisions even when the environment is stationary and all actions are observed. A sharp rate would identify the statistical price of pure privacy and whether the remaining dependence on the number of actions is necessary.

sentences: A learner repeatedly chooses an action and then observes the losses of every action.
The losses are independent draws from fixed unknown distributions, and one action has strictly smallest mean loss.
The card asks for matching-order expected pseudo-regret under pure privacy protecting one entire round of observations.
A published 2026 upper bound removes the time-horizon factor but leaves a logarithmic gap in the number of actions.
A solution must identify the rate throughout the stated parameter domain and certify both achievable guarantees and unavoidable loss in Lean.

cards.definitions: \([K]=\{1,\ldots,K\}\). The public parameters are \(K,T,\varepsilon,\Delta\); the gap bound \(\Delta\) is a promise supplied to the strategy, while the distributions, their means, and the best-action index are unknown. This is the minimax interpretation of the source's gap-dependent optimal-rate question: the worst case is over all instances whose minimum gap is at least the supplied threshold, rather than one specified vector of means. A strategy is a family of Borel-measurable probability kernels for \(I_t\), given the public parameters, earlier actions, and earlier full loss vectors. It may retain arbitrary private state and use correlated internal randomness; equivalently use the conditional kernels of its observable history. No running-time, memory, or properness restriction is imposed. The output available to a privacy observer is the complete action sequence, not the privately observed losses. For every pair of deterministic sequences \(s,s'\in([0,1]^K)^T\) differing in at most one entire loss vector, and every event \(E\subseteq[K]^T\), require \[\Pr[A(s)\in E]\le e^{\varepsilon}\Pr[A(s')\in E].\] This requirement applies to all loss sequences, including nonstochastic ones, and has no additive privacy slack. Its prefix versions follow by projection. The utility expectation includes both the stochastic losses and the strategy's independent initial randomness. Pseudo-regret compares against the smallest expected loss, not the smallest realized cumulative loss. The first action is selected before any losses are revealed. There is no adversarial dependence of later losses on released actions. Infima need not be attained; approaching strategies qualify.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a nonnegative rate function \(B(K,T,\varepsilon,\Delta)\), an explicit family of admissible private strategies, and universal constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\), with a Lean-checked proof that \(cB\le R^{*}\le CB\) throughout the stated domain. The upper bound must hold for every promised product distribution; the lower bound must apply to every causal private strategy and allow a worst-case promised distribution. If an infimum is not attained, certify arbitrarily close upper bounds instead of requiring an optimal strategy. Constants cannot depend on any of the four parameters. A bound only for deterministic losses, bandit feedback, approximate privacy, or only one side of the rate does not meet this criterion. This is asymptotic precision in unnormalized cumulative pseudo-regret, not an additive \(1/100\) approximation.

source_formulation.text: Determine matching-order bounds for gap-dependent pseudo-regret under pure differential privacy in stochastic full-information decision-theoretic online learning.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase

context_blocks.text: After each decision, the learner sees how every action performed. This makes the problem different from a bandit problem, where it sees only the chosen action. In a stationary environment, the mean-loss gaps measure how much evidence separates the best action from its competitors. The total error from exploring those competitors can remain bounded as the number of rounds grows.

Privacy treats one complete observed loss vector as one record and protects the joint distribution of all released actions. Protecting each action separately would not suffice: an observer can combine decisions across many rounds. Pure privacy also excludes a small additive exceptional-event term, which is explicitly outside the source question.

The 2024 paper compares an upper bound \(O(\log K/\Delta_{\min}+\log K\log T/\varepsilon)\) with a long-horizon lower scale \(\Omega(\log K/\Delta_{\min}+\log K/\varepsilon)\). Its authors expressly do not conjecture that this lower scale is optimal. Those displayed rates describe the nontrivial parameter regime; a lower bound independent of \(T\) cannot hold for arbitrarily short horizons because regret is at most \(T\).

Wu and Wang prove the improved stochastic upper bound \(O(\log K/\Delta_{\min}+\log^{2}K/\varepsilon)\). It removes dependence on \(T\) from the gap-dependent upper bound. A logarithmic factor in \(K\) remains between the stated upper and lower privacy terms. Their matching \(\Theta(\log K/\varepsilon)\) result applies to the separate model with deterministic loss vectors and does not settle the stochastic question.

The card makes the minimax quantifier convention explicit by supplying a lower gap promise \(\Delta\) and retaining finite \(T\). An upper bound using only the actual minimum gap also applies to this promise class. Sharp finite-horizon transitions and boundary gaps are part of the stated rate; the displayed long-horizon literature bounds are not claimed uniformly tight there.

cards.title: Finite-domain promise CSP dichotomy
cards.formal: For every fixed pair of finite relational structures \(A,B\) of the same finite signature, with nonempty domains and a homomorphism \(A\to B\), is the decision promise problem \(\operatorname{PCSP}(A,B)\) either solvable by a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm or NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one promise reductions? Its yes instances are the finite structures \(I\) with \(I\to A\); its no instances are those with \(I\not\to B\). The quantifier ranges over all finite signatures and template pairs. The algorithm or hardness reduction, including its polynomial bound, may depend on the fixed pair.
cards.definitions:
A signature is an ordered finite list \(R_1,\ldots,R_s\), where \(s\geq0\) and each symbol has a fixed positive integer arity \(r_i\). A finite structure \(D\) for this signature has a finite domain and relations \(R_i^D\subseteq D^{r_i}\). The templates have domains \(A=\{1,\ldots,a\}\), \(B=\{1,\ldots,b\}\) for positive integers \(a,b\); their relation tables are fixed, not part of the varying input. Different template domains are allowed. For two structures of the same signature, a homomorphism \(h:D\to E\) is a map of domains satisfying
\[\forall i\;\forall(v_1,\ldots,v_{r_i})\in R_i^D:\ (h(v_1),\ldots,h(v_{r_i}))\in R_i^E.\]
Write \(D\to E\) if such a map exists, and \(D\not\to E\) if none exists. Homomorphisms need not be injective. Empty relations and repeated coordinates in a tuple are allowed.

An input structure \(I\) has domain \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\geq0\), and explicitly listed relation tuples. Fix the following binary encoding. Write \(n\) as the unary prefix \(1^n0\). In signature order, write the number \(t_i\) of listed tuples of relation \(i\) as \(1^{t_i}0\), followed by its tuples in their listed order. Encode each coordinate \(v\) by \(1^{|w|}0w\), where \(w\) is the binary expansion of \(v\) without leading zeros and \(1\leq v\leq n\). Each tuple has exactly \(r_i\) coordinates. Duplicate tuples are permitted in the encoding and denote the same relation member; their bits still count. The input ends after the last relation list, with no trailing bits. Thus \(L\), the length of the entire encoding, accounts for the domain as well as all constraints. The empty-domain structure is valid only with all lists empty and is a yes instance. Any encoding polynomial-time equivalent to this explicit representation gives the same question.

For a fixed pair, define \(Y_{A,B}=\{I:I\to A\}\) and \(N_{A,B}=\{I:I\not\to B\}\). The assumption \(A\to B\) makes these sets disjoint. A valid decision algorithm accepts every input in \(Y_{A,B}\) and rejects every input in \(N_{A,B}\). It may give either answer when \(I\to B\) but \(I\not\to A\). Polynomial time means a single deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program, no advice or oracle, halting on every binary input of length \(L\) within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps for some fixed positive integers \(C,k\). It returns reject on malformed encodings; even instances outside the promise must obey the time bound. Reading, writing and manipulating bits all count. The constants and machine may depend on \(A,B\) and their signature, but not on \(I\).

NP-hardness here means that one uniform deterministic polynomial-time map sends every 3-CNF formula \(\varphi\) to a valid input structure \(I_\varphi\) and satisfies
\[\varphi\text{ satisfiable}\Rightarrow I_\varphi\to A,\qquad
\varphi\text{ unsatisfiable}\Rightarrow I_\varphi\not\to B.\]
A 3-CNF formula is a finite conjunction of clauses, each the disjunction of three signed Boolean variables; repeated variables and literals are allowed. For definiteness, encode its number of clauses in unary followed by three literals per clause, each a sign bit and a positive variable index encoded by the same length-prefixed binary convention as coordinates above. A positive literal is true when its variable is 1, and a negative literal when its variable is 0. The reduction's bound is polynomial in the entire formula encoding, including the time and bits needed to output \(I_\varphi\). Malformed formula encodings may map to the empty input structure. Both satisfiable and unsatisfiable formulas must map into the promise.

The question is the inclusive disjunction of these two possibilities for each fixed pair; it assumes neither \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) nor that the alternatives are disjoint. It does not request an algorithm that, given template tables, identifies the alternative, nor a common polynomial bound over all pairs. Producing a \(B\)-valued homomorphism on every input promised to map to \(A\) is the separate search task. Counting assignments, weighted objectives, allowing a fraction of violated constraints and robustness to broken promises are not part of this decision problem.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated dichotomy for every fixed finite pair, or of its logical negation. A negative answer must establish a fixed finite signature and pair \(A\to B\) whose decision promise problem admits neither any qualifying deterministic polynomial-time decider nor any qualifying polynomial-time many-one reduction from 3-SAT. Both failures must be proved; a presently unclassified pair is not a counterexample. The positive answer need not effectively classify templates, but must establish the full quantified disjunction without an unproved complexity assumption. A dichotomy only for a restricted family, a conditional general classification, or a theorem only about the search task does not settle this target.
cards.why: This asks whether finite local constraint descriptions force a sharp complexity classification even when the accepted and rejected instances are separated by a promise. It encompasses approximate graph colouring and many relaxed feasibility problems. A resolution would determine whether the organizing principle of the finite CSP dichotomy extends beyond exact satisfaction, or whether a fixed finite promise can have intermediate decision complexity.

importance.reason: A broad structural question extending the finite CSP dichotomy into approximation and promise problems, with connections to algebra, topology, and optimization.

progress.text: Bulatov proves the ordinary finite-template CSP dichotomy, covering the special case \(A=B\).
Zhuk independently proves the same ordinary CSP dichotomy; the final arXiv revision is dated 2 October 2020.
Brakensiek and Guruswami give a symmetric Boolean promise-CSP dichotomy with negations; the checked revised manuscript is dated 6 May 2021.
Ficak, Kozik, Olšák and Stankiewicz classify all symmetric Boolean promise CSPs without requiring negations.
Barto establishes a tractable finite promise pair whose every finite intermediate exact CSP is NP-complete.
Krokhin and Opršal survey the open general classification and distinguish decision from search.
The Banakh–Barsukov–Nakajima preprint proves the Promise MMSNP correspondence and states a monochromatic-clique dichotomy with conditional hardness; it subsequently appears at LICS 2026.

The published Krokhin–Vagnozzi theorem proves NP-hardness for \(\operatorname{PCSP}(\mathrm{LO}_2,\mathrm{LO}_3)\) and completes the three-element symmetric ternary target classification for approximations of exactly-one satisfaction.

cards.status_note: An open general classification question in the 2022 survey and the published July 2026 Krokhin–Vagnozzi article. The latter resolves a restricted three-element target family; the May 2026 Promise MMSNP preprint gives a logical correspondence and a conditional monochromatic-clique classification. Bounded checks through 14 September 2026 found no full unconditional finite-pair dichotomy or counterexample. Individual theorem statements and scopes were checked, but their full proofs were not independently verified.

context_blocks.text: A promise CSP uses a stronger and a weaker version of each local requirement. For fixed integers \(2\leq k\leq c\), the templates \(A=K_k\) and \(B=K_c\), with the inequality edge relation, distinguish graphs that admit a proper \(k\)-colouring from graphs that admit no proper \(c\)-colouring. A proper colouring assigns different colours to adjacent vertices. Instances between these two cases impose no answer requirement. This is a qualitative relaxation of every constraint, rather than an objective to maximize the number satisfied.

For \(A=B\), there is no gap between the two cases. Bulatov and Zhuk independently established the finite-template CSP dichotomy in 2017: every such exact satisfaction problem is polynomial-time solvable or NP-complete. Classifying the two endpoint CSPs separately does not classify the promise problem, because the weaker required answer can make it easier than either endpoint.

One concrete polynomial-time example has Boolean domains, the stronger ternary relation \(\{(1,0,0),(0,1,0),(0,0,1)\}\), and the weaker relation \(\{0,1\}^3\setminus\{(0,0,0),(1,1,1)\}\). Thus it relaxes exactly-one satisfaction to not-all-equal satisfaction. Barto proves that every finite intermediate template \(C\) with \(A\to C\to B\) has an NP-complete exact CSP. Consequently this tractable promise pair has no tractable finite intermediate CSP unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).

A \(q\)-ary polymorphism of a pair is a function \(p:A^q\to B\) that sends any \(q\) tuples of each \(R_i^A\), applied coordinate by coordinate, to a tuple of \(R_i^B\). Here \(q\geq1\). This describes operations that combine stronger solutions into a weaker solution. Unlike operations on a single domain, these maps do not generally allow unrestricted self-composition. This distinction helps explain why the classical classification does not directly extend to promises.

Brakensiek and Guruswami obtained a dichotomy for symmetric Boolean promise languages with negations. Ficak, Kozik, Olšák and Stankiewicz subsequently removed that extra requirement and classified all symmetric Boolean pairs: both domains are Boolean and every relation is unchanged under permuting its coordinates. Symmetry remains a substantive restriction; this does not classify arbitrary Boolean relations or arbitrary finite domains.

A 2026 theorem settles another restricted family. Let \(\mathrm{LO}_d\) have domain \(\{0,\ldots,d-1\}\) and the ternary relation consisting of triples whose maximum occurs exactly once. In particular, \(\mathrm{LO}_2\) is the exactly-one Boolean template. Krokhin and Vagnozzi prove that \(\operatorname{PCSP}(\mathrm{LO}_2,\mathrm{LO}_3)\) is NP-hard. Their Corollary 2 classifies every three-element target \(B\) with a single symmetric ternary relation and \(\mathrm{LO}_2\to B\): it is NP-hard if \(B\to\mathrm{LO}_3\), and polynomial-time solvable otherwise. Their hardness concerns the decision promise as well as search.

Banakh, Barsukov and Nakajima relate a logical class called Promise MMSNP to finite-domain promise CSPs. Their 2026 monochromatic-clique classification concerns a specified family and relies on the Rich 2-to-1 Conjecture for its hardness direction. Neither the general logical correspondence nor that conditional family theorem supplies an unconditional dichotomy for all finite pairs.

The 2022 survey explicitly treats a general dichotomy as a question with insufficient evidence for a consensus conjecture. The published ICALP 2026 article makes the same distinction while resolving its own restricted family. Decision and search must also remain separate: the article states that their general polynomial-time equivalence is not known. The present card asks only for the fixed-template decision dichotomy.

Their Corollary 2 classifies every three-element target \(B\) with a single symmetric ternary relation and \(\mathrm{LO}_2\to B\): it is NP-hard if \(B\to\mathrm{LO}_3\), and polynomial-time solvable otherwise. Their hardness concerns the decision promise as well as search.

Banakh, Barsukov and Nakajima relate a logical class called Promise MMSNP to finite-domain promise CSPs. Their 2026 monochromatic-clique classification concerns a specified family and relies on the Rich 2-to-1 Conjecture for its hardness direction. Neither the general logical correspondence nor that conditional family theorem supplies an unconditional dichotomy for all finite pairs.

The 2022 survey explicitly treats a general dichotomy as a question with insufficient evidence for a consensus conjecture. The published ICALP 2026 article makes the same distinction while resolving its own restricted family. Decision and search must also remain separate: the article states that their general polynomial-time equivalence is not known. The present card asks only for the fixed-template decision dichotomy.

cards.title: Bodirsky–Pinsker conjecture
cards.formal:
For every countable finitely bounded homogeneous relational structure \(A\) over a finite signature, and every first-order reduct \(B\) of \(A\) with a finite relational signature, is
\[\operatorname{CSP}(B)\in\mathrm P\quad\lor\quad\operatorname{CSP}(B)\text{ is NP-complete}\ ?\]
NP-completeness uses deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions. The templates are fixed before the finite input is supplied. This is the unconditional complexity dichotomy, without requiring an algebraic criterion identifying the two sides.
cards.definitions:
A finite relational signature is a finite list of relation symbols, each with a fixed positive integer arity. A structure \(D\) interprets an \(r\)-ary symbol as a subset \(R^D\subseteq D^r\) of tuples over its domain. Countable means finite or countably infinite. Empty domains, if admitted, have trivial CSPs and do not affect the question. Nullary relations can likewise be processed separately.

The induced substructure on a subset \(S\) of a domain restricts every relation to tuples from \(S\). An embedding is an injective map \(e:D\to E\) with \(\bar d\in R^D\) if and only if \(e(\bar d)\in R^E\) for every relation and tuple; it preserves both presence and absence of relation tuples. An isomorphism is a bijective embedding, and an automorphism is an isomorphism from a structure to itself. The structure \(A\) is homogeneous when every isomorphism between two finite induced substructures extends to an automorphism of \(A\).

The structure \(A\) is finitely bounded when there is a finite list \(\mathcal N\) of finite structures in its signature such that, for every finite structure \(D\) in that signature,
\[D\text{ embeds into }A\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{no }N\in\mathcal N\text{ embeds into }D.\]
Thus the finite patterns occurring inside \(A\) are precisely those avoiding finitely many forbidden induced patterns. Homogeneity is an additional condition, not part of finite boundedness alone.

A first-order reduct \(B\) has the same domain as \(A\). Each of its finitely many relations is defined by a fixed first-order formula over the relations of \(A\) and logical equality, using Boolean connectives and quantifiers over elements of \(A\), without naming parameters. It may forget original relations and introduce newly definable ones. Both signatures, \(A,B\), the defining formulas and a finite bound list witnessing the hypothesis are fixed; none is an input to the individual CSP.

An input \(I\) has finite domain \([n]\), \(n\geq0\), and an explicit list of tuples for each relation in the signature of \(B\). A homomorphism \(h:I\to B\) is any map such that \((i_1,\ldots,i_r)\in R^I\) implies \((h(i_1),\ldots,h(i_r))\in R^B\). It need not be injective and need not preserve absence of tuples. The decision problem accepts exactly when such a map exists. Repeated coordinates and isolated input elements are allowed; duplicate listed tuples are harmless. The empty input has the empty homomorphism.

Encode \(n\) in unary and each relation by a unary list length followed by binary tuple coordinates, in fixed signature order, with delimiters. Let \(L\) be total bit length. Invalid encodings are rejected. Polynomial time means a deterministic multitape Turing machine halts correctly on every input within \(C(L+1)^k\) bit steps for constants \(C,k\) depending on \(B\). No randomness, infinite-domain oracle, advice, supplied homomorphism, common polynomial exponent or algorithm choosing the correct side from template descriptions is required.

The class \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of languages with polynomial-length certificates checkable in deterministic polynomial time. A problem \(Q\) is NP-hard under the stated reductions when, for every \(K\in\mathrm{NP}\), a total deterministic polynomial-time function \(f\) satisfies \(x\in K\) if and only if \(f(x)\in Q\). NP-complete means NP-hard and in NP. Every CSP in the displayed scope is already known to be in NP. The two alternatives are not required to be disjoint without a separation assumption: if \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), every such problem satisfies the first alternative.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition, or of its logical negation, retaining every permitted structure and reduct. A negative answer must establish one permitted \(A,B\) for which \(\operatorname{CSP}(B)\) is neither in P nor NP-complete under the stated many-one reductions; membership in NP already follows from the hypotheses. No separation assumption is added to the proposition. A classification for one reduct family, the first-order/logarithmic-space-hard boundary, or a procedure deciding an algebraic meta-problem does not prove the full dichotomy. The stronger algebraic tractability conjecture would suffice if proved, but is not substituted for the existing bare complexity target.

context_blocks.text: The finite-domain CSP dichotomy, proved independently by Bulatov and Zhuk in 2017, says that fixing a finite collection of relations on a finite domain leaves no intermediate complexity between polynomial time and NP-completeness. The infinite-domain conjecture asks whether this organizing principle survives when variables can take rational values, positions in a countable graph, or other infinitely many possibilities, provided the template has a finite structural description.

The restrictions explain why the question is computationally meaningful. Homogeneity means that finite patterns completely determine their symmetry type. Finite boundedness gives a finite list of forbidden patterns for checking whether a proposed finite configuration can occur. For a fixed reduct, one can guess a partition of the variables representing equal values and the finite relational pattern on those values, then check the constraints and forbidden patterns. The signature and forbidden sizes are constants, so this yields polynomial-size NP certificates despite the infinite domain. Homogeneity over a finite relational signature also gives quantifier elimination, so each fixed first-order reduct relation can be tested on that finite pattern by a fixed quantifier-free formula.

For a concrete example, the ordered rational numbers \((\mathbb{Q} ;<)\) are homogeneous and finitely bounded. Constraints consisting only of strict inequalities are feasible exactly when their directed inequality graph is acyclic. Adding the definable ternary relation “y lies strictly between x and z” gives the classical NP-complete Betweenness problem. Thus the same domain can support both tractable and hard constraint languages; the choice of allowed relations is decisive.

A central method studies polymorphisms: operations which, applied coordinatewise to several satisfying tuples of any relation, produce another satisfying tuple. Such operations record ways of combining solutions and can prevent standard hardness gadgets. Barto and Pinsker identify a particular algebraic identity that characterizes the absence of the relevant hardness construction for model-complete cores. The missing general step is turning the tractable-side algebraic structure into polynomial-time algorithms. The bare \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{NP}\)-complete dichotomy asked here is weaker than proving that full algebraic classification. A model-complete core is a homomorphically equivalent template in which every endomorphism agrees, on each finite subset, with some automorphism; an endomorphism is a homomorphism from the template to itself.

Pinsker, Rydval, Schöbi, Spiess and Winkler’s May 2026 revision shows that the conjecture can be reduced to templates without algebraicity: fixing finitely many elements does not force any additional element into a finite orbit. Their construction replaces domain elements by infinite families while preserving the relevant constraint complexity. They also connect tractable infinite-domain templates to finite-domain promise CSPs through intermediate structures. These are reductions in the scope of the conjecture, rather than a general tractability algorithm.

Dorochko and Wrona’s July 2026 revision proves a different dichotomy: for first-order expansions of finitely bounded homogeneous model-complete cores, the CSP is first-order definable or hard for deterministic logarithmic space under first-order reductions. An expansion retains all original relations; this hypothesis does not cover arbitrary reducts. Moreover, L-hard problems can still be in P, so the result separates a much lower boundary and leaves the P versus NP-complete question open. Here first-order definability means that one fixed first-order sentence on finite inputs decides the CSP, and L denotes deterministic logarithmic work space.

Feller and Pinsker’s August 2026 revision develops effective tools for comparing templates. In particular, a model-complete core is computable when the structure has a finitely bounded homogeneous Ramsey expansion, an additional structural hypothesis. Their decidability results concern interpretability and equivalent algebraic presentations, not a complete algorithmic classification of all templates in this card. The Ramsey condition says that for every pair of finite patterns P,Q and every finite number of colours, a larger finite pattern exists in which every colouring of embeddings of P has a copy of Q whose internal P-embeddings all receive one colour.

A resolution would say whether a finite description by symmetric local patterns rules out intermediate NP complexity across a large family of logical and combinatorial problems. The difficulty is to find algorithms that exploit this description uniformly within each fixed template, without assuming that the infinitely many possible values can simply be replaced by one fixed finite domain.

cards.title: Constant-colour polynomial-time colouring of 3-colourable graphs
cards.formal: Is there a fixed integer \(C\ge 3\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, on every finite simple undirected graph G promised to be 3-colourable, outputs a proper vertex colouring using at most C colours with probability at least \(2/3\)?
cards.definitions: The input is an explicitly given graph \(G=([n],E), n\ge 1\), with no loops or parallel edges, encoded by its adjacency matrix. A proper k-colouring is a map \(c:[n]\to [k]\) such that \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every \(\{u,v\}\in E\). The promise is existence of a proper 3-colouring; such a colouring is not supplied. There must be one C, one randomized Turing machine A, and fixed constants K,d such that A uses at most \(K(n+1)^{d}\) bit operations on every graph and every random tape. On each promised input, the probability, over independent unbiased internal random bits, of outputting a proper C-colouring is at least \(2/3\). Invalid outputs can be replaced by a failure symbol after checking all edges. No correctness requirement is imposed on non-3-colourable inputs, but the time bound still applies. The algorithm may colour such an input whenever it can; it need not recognize the promise. C is independent of n, degree, density and the input graph. No planarity, bounded-degree, expansion, forbidden-subgraph, random-input or supplied-decomposition promise is available. Randomization is explicitly permitted in this version of the inherited question; a deterministic algorithm would be a stronger positive result. The algorithm must colour every vertex and avoid every monochromatic edge on a successful run.
cards.answer_criterion: Give such an algorithm for at least one fixed C, or prove that no such C and randomized polynomial-time algorithm exist. A growing colour bound, a partial colouring of most vertices, or a guarantee only on a restricted graph family is insufficient. NP-hardness of the 3-versus-C promise for every fixed C would establish the usual complexity-theoretic obstruction; excluding randomized algorithms from that obstruction additionally uses \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{RP}\). Hardness for \(C=5\) alone leaves all larger constants unresolved. Conditional hardness results must keep their assumptions explicit.
cards.why: A defining promise-CSP problem: determine whether relaxing an NP-hard colouring task to any fixed larger palette permits efficient construction of a valid solution.

importance.reason: The paradigmatic approximate graph-colouring question, central to promise CSPs and to the gap between algorithmic relaxations and hardness with perfect completeness.

The February 2026 primary paper retains the gap between five-colour NP-hardness and a growing \(O(n^{0.19539})\) algorithmic bound. context_blocks.text: The input comes with a guarantee that three colours suffice, but not with the partition into three independent sets. Allowing more colours is a relaxation of the output requirements. The question asks whether some fixed amount of this relaxation makes the problem efficiently solvable on every promised input. A mechanism for choosing 100 colours would qualify just as a mechanism for choosing six colours would; the constant need not be close to three.

This promise matters. Strong inapproximability results for the chromatic number on unrestricted graphs can use instances whose chromatic number grows with the graph size. They do not automatically establish hardness when the yes-instances must have chromatic number at most three. Conversely, an algorithm for planar graphs would use a structural assumption missing here. Three-colourable graphs can be dense and can have high-degree vertices.

The problem is a basic example of promise constraint satisfaction. An edge asks its two endpoints to receive different labels. The promise says the constraints have a solution over a three-element domain; the algorithm is allowed to use a larger fixed domain. In graph-homomorphism language, an input maps to \(K_{3}\) and the output must provide a map to \(K_{C}\). The associated decision promise distinguishes graphs mapping to \(K_{3}\) from graphs not mapping to \(K_{C}\).

Barto, Bulín, Krokhin and Opršal prove NP-hardness of finding a five-colouring of a three-colourable graph, as part of a broader algebraic framework. This is far stronger than hardness of finding the promised three-colouring, yet it excludes only particular small output domains under standard complexity assumptions. It does not rule out a successful algorithm using six, 100 or any other larger fixed number of colours.

A useful elementary observation is that the neighbours of any vertex in a three-colourable graph induce a bipartite graph: the vertex’s own colour cannot appear among its neighbours. Thus one can efficiently colour a large neighbourhood using two fresh colours. When all remaining degrees are small, greedy colouring is effective. Balancing these two procedures already gives an \(O(\sqrt{n})\)-colour algorithm. The challenge is to extract much more global information than this local observation provides.

Modern algorithms combine combinatorial reductions with semidefinite relaxations. The relaxation assigns vectors that mimic the separation of colours, and rounding extracts independent sets or other useful progress. Kawarabayashi, Thorup and Yoneda’s STOC 2024 work strengthens the combinatorial side and obtains \(\widetilde{O}\)\((n^{0.19747})\) colours after combining it with the SDP approach. The suppressed factors are polylogarithmic in n.

Bansal, Huang and Lee’s February 2026 preprint improves the SDP analysis using third-level neighbourhoods and a new vector \(5/2\)-colouring construction. Combined with the combinatorial component, its theorem gives \(O(n^{0.19539})\) colours. A vector \(5/2\)-colouring is a geometric relaxation, not an ordinary assignment using a fractional number of colours. The exponent improvement is real progress, while the final number of actual colours still grows with n.

Hardness evidence also goes beyond five colours under additional assumptions. Guruswami and Sandeep show that a fixed d-to-1 Label Cover conjecture implies hardness for every constant output palette. Their premise requires perfectly satisfiable yes-instances. Replacing perfect completeness by near-perfect completeness changes what the reduction guarantees, so established results about almost-satisfiable games cannot simply be substituted into this argument.

Dawar and Molnár’s full version, revised in March 2026, proves that fixed-point logic with counting cannot separate three-colourable graphs from graphs requiring more than any fixed number of colours. This is an unconditional obstruction for that logic on unordered structures, not for all polynomial-time algorithms on explicitly encoded graphs. The card sits at the intersection of approximation algorithms, algebraic reductions and limits of relaxation methods: a resolution would tell us how much a fixed expansion of the solution domain can help.

Kawarabayashi, Thorup and Yoneda’s STOC 2024 work strengthens the combinatorial side and obtains \(\widetilde{O}\)\((n^{0.19747})\) colours after combining it with the SDP approach. The suppressed factors are polylogarithmic in n.

Bansal, Huang and Lee’s February 2026 preprint improves the SDP analysis using third-level neighbourhoods and a new vector \(5/2\)-colouring construction. Combined with the combinatorial component, its theorem gives \(O(n^{0.19539})\) colours. A vector \(5/2\)-colouring is a geometric relaxation, not an ordinary assignment using a fractional number of colours. The exponent improvement is real progress, while the final number of actual colours still grows with n.

Hardness evidence also goes beyond five colours under additional assumptions. Guruswami and Sandeep show that a fixed d-to-1 Label Cover conjecture implies hardness for every constant output palette. Their premise requires perfectly satisfiable yes-instances. Replacing perfect completeness by near-perfect completeness changes what the reduction guarantees, so established results about almost-satisfiable games cannot simply be substituted into this argument.

Dawar and Molnár’s full version, revised in March 2026, proves that fixed-point logic with counting cannot separate three-colourable graphs from graphs requiring more than any fixed number of colours. This is an unconditional obstruction for that logic on unordered structures, not for all polynomial-time algorithms on explicitly encoded graphs. The card sits at the intersection of approximation algorithms, algebraic reductions and limits of relaxation methods: a resolution would tell us how much a fixed expansion of the solution domain can help.

cards.title: Search-to-decision equivalence for finite promise CSPs
cards.formal: For every fixed pair \((A,B)\) of finite nonempty relational structures over the same finite signature with \(A\to B\), does polynomial-time solvability of the decision promise problem \(\operatorname{PCSP}(A,B)\) imply polynomial-time solvability of its search version? Decision must accept every finite \(X\) with \(X\to A\) and reject every \(X\) with \(X\not\to B\). Search receives \(X\) with the promise \(X\to A\) and must output an explicit homomorphism \(X\to B\). Both algorithms are deterministic and have polynomial worst-case running time on all inputs; the programs and polynomial bounds may depend on \(A,B\).
cards.definitions:
A finite relational signature is a finite ordered list of relation symbols, each assigned a positive integer arity. A structure \(D\) consists of a domain and, for each symbol \(R\) of arity \(r\), a relation \(R^D\subseteq D^r\). A homomorphism \(h:D\to E\) is a function satisfying
\[(d_1,\ldots,d_r)\in R^D\ \Longrightarrow\ (h(d_1),\ldots,h(d_r))\in R^E\]
for every relation and tuple. It need not be injective. The notation \(D\to E\) asserts existence of such a map. Templates \(A,B\), including their finite relation tables and a numbering of their domains, are fixed constants, not part of the input. No stronger assignment is supplied with an input.

The input structure \(X\) has domain \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\geq0\), and explicitly listed relation tuples. Repeated coordinates and empty relations are allowed. Encode \(n\) in unary, followed by the tuple lists in signature order with unary list lengths; each coordinate has \(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Let \(L\) be the total bit length, which counts isolated variables. Duplicate listed tuples have no effect. A search output is the list of images of all \(n\) elements in the fixed domain of \(B\), or a failure symbol. The empty input has the empty homomorphism.

A decision algorithm returns one bit. If \(X\not\to A\) but \(X\to B\), either bit is permitted; this is the intermediate region of the promise. Since \(A\to B\), no input simultaneously requires both answers. On search inputs outside the promise \(X\to A\), any output is permitted, including failure. Both machines halt on every binary input within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps for positive integers \(C,k\); malformed strings may be rejected. Cost is measured on a deterministic multitape Turing machine, without advice, oracle or randomness.

The quantifier order is \(\forall(A,B)\,[\exists D\text{ with the decision guarantee}\Rightarrow\exists S\text{ with the search guarantee}]\). Constants and exponents can depend on the fixed template. There is no required effective procedure that recognizes tractable templates or constructs \(S\) from arbitrary \(A,B,D\), no common exponent over templates, and no requirement that \(S\) use \(D\) as a black-box subroutine. The target is the tractability implication between the two fixed-template problems.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the implication for every fixed finite template pair, or of its logical negation. An affirmative proof must establish a search machine with the stated promised output and all-input polynomial bound whenever a qualifying decision machine exists. A negative proof must exhibit a fixed finite \(A\to B\), prove its decision promise solvable in deterministic polynomial time, and prove that no deterministic polynomial-time promised search algorithm exists. Hardness of rounding all inputs accepted by a particular relaxation, undecidability when the template varies, or failure of a particular black-box reduction does not refute this statement. A conditional separation is partial progress and must retain its unproved hypothesis; the target itself is unconditional.
cards.why: Many applications need an assignment rather than recognition that an assignment must exist. A universal implication would connect tractability classifications of promise decision problems to actual construction across finite local constraint languages. A separation would identify a fixed finite promise problem whose decision gap is efficiently recognizable while its promised solutions resist every deterministic polynomial-time search algorithm.

context_blocks.text: The strong template A describes the constraints guaranteed to be simultaneously satisfiable; B describes the weaker constraints an answer must satisfy. The map from A to B proves that a weak answer exists whenever a strong one exists, but the input supplies only that existence promise. A decision algorithm recognizes the promised gap, whereas search must actually construct the weaker assignment.

For graph colouring, one may take A and B to be complete graphs on three and six vertices. Search then asks for a six-colouring of a graph promised to admit a three-colouring. Decision only separates three-colourable graphs from graphs admitting no six-colouring; it has no required behaviour on graphs with chromatic number four, five or six. This example illustrates the promise and does not assert tractability for that particular pair.

A polynomial-time search algorithm implies decision by returning a proposed weak assignment that can be checked. The reverse implication is known for ordinary fixed finite CSPs, where A=B. With two templates, fixing a variable to a weak-domain value can destroy the stronger promise, so ordinary decision self-reducibility does not automatically apply.

Known constructive cases include templates admitting a fixed finite intermediate structure C with A→C→B and tractable CSP(C). The survey also discusses tractable promise problems whose explanation requires more than such a finite intermediate problem, under the usual separation assumptions. Thus the ordinary CSP case does not supply the general statement.

Larrauri studies rounding for three standard decision relaxations: the basic linear program using consistent local distributions, an affine integer program, and their combination. Finding a weak assignment on every input accepted by one of these relaxations can encode arbitrary total NP search problems. A total NP search problem has a polynomially checkable, polynomially bounded witness for every input. Relaxation acceptance is a weaker promise than the existence of a homomorphism to A.

The May 2026 revision explicitly retains the general implication here as open. Its undecidability theorems instead concern recognizing classes of templates when A and B vary as input. A nonuniform choice of one finite program for each fixed template, as allowed here, is compatible with undecidability of that recognition problem.

The February 2026 robust-satisfiability paper gives constructive guarantees for special preservation structures, including Boolean templates preserved by all odd-arity majority operations. Here preservation means that applying coordinatewise majority to strong satisfying tuples produces a weak satisfying tuple. These results handle almost satisfiable instances with quantitative error guarantees, but require an additional structural hypothesis absent from the general implication.

cards.title: Logarithmic-color approximation of 3-colorable graphs
cards.formal:
Is there a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, for every \(n\)-vertex graph promised to be \(3\)-colourable, produces a proper colouring using \(O(\log n)\) colours in expectation? More precisely, do there exist such an algorithm \(A\) and an absolute integer \(K\geq1\) for which
\[
\mathbb E_{\rho}\big[\kappa(A(G;\rho))\big]\leq K\max\{1,\log_2 n\}
\]
for every nonempty \(3\)-colourable graph \(G\), where \(\kappa\) counts distinct colours used? Randomization and expected performance follow the source’s approximation-algorithm convention; deterministic algorithms are included. Properness is always required, and the time bound is worst case as specified below.
cards.why: Logarithmic colouring would be a major improvement for a canonical approximation problem whose positive guarantees still grow as powers of the input size. It would show that a hidden partition into three independent sets can be replaced efficiently by a very small exact partition without needing to recover the original three classes.
cards.status_note: The textbook explicitly poses the logarithmic-colour target as Problem 9. Its randomized approximation convention and colouring chapter support the expected-performance model fixed here. The February 2026 primary paper still gives a power-of-n palette guarantee and records the constant-palette hardness frontier. A bounded search on 16 September 2026 did not identify a resolution of the logarithmic target; this source-open assessment is dated evidence rather than an exhaustive proof of present openness.

cards.definitions:
The input is a finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(V=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). An explicit unary size header is followed by its adjacency matrix, so the input length \(L\) includes isolated vertices and is of order \(n^2+1\). There are no loops or parallel edges and no restriction on degree, connectedness, density or induced subgraphs. The promise says only that some proper colouring with at most three colours exists. The colouring is not supplied, and the input need not be randomly generated.

A proper colouring is an explicit vector \(c=(c_1,\ldots,c_n)\) with \(c_i\in[n]\) and \(c_i\ne c_j\) whenever \(\{i,j\}\in E\). Its palette size is \(\kappa(c)=|\{c_i:i\in[n]\}|\). Colour names can be relabeled without changing \(\kappa\). Output the colour indices in vertex order in binary with delimiters. On the empty graph, the algorithm outputs the empty colouring with palette size zero. The logarithm in the bound has base two; changing its base only changes the absolute constant. Using \(\max\{1,\log_2 n\}\) fixes the cases \(n=1,2\) without imposing an asymptotic exception.

Use a uniform randomized multitape Turing machine. There are fixed integers \(C,d\geq1\) bounding the number of bit operations by \(C(L+1)^d\) on every graph and every random-bit sequence. Independent fair bits are the only random resource, so there are polynomially many random bits per run. There is no advice, oracle, exact-real arithmetic or free infinite-precision sampling. All numerical approximations, verification and output writing count toward time. The program, \(K,C,d\) are independent of \(n\) and \(G\).

The algorithm must output a proper colouring on every valid graph and every random-bit sequence; the palette-size guarantee applies only to the promised \(3\)-colourable graphs. Requiring universal properness introduces no new approximation obstruction: a candidate colouring can be checked in polynomial time, and any failure can be replaced by the trivial colouring assigning a different colour to each vertex. On malformed graph encodings the algorithm may reject in polynomial time. The expectation is over the internal random bits for each fixed promised graph, not over an input distribution.

The asymptotic existential target is equivalent to allowing a polynomial-time randomized algorithm to return a proper \(K'\max\{1,\log_2 n\}\)-colouring with probability at least \(2/3\) for every promised graph, for some absolute \(K'\). An expected bound implies this by Markov’s inequality after multiplying its constant by three. Conversely, a bounded-error algorithm can be run independently \(O(\log n)\) times, retaining a verified small colouring if one appears and otherwise using the \(n\)-colour fallback. Reducing failure probability to at most \(1/n\) makes the expected number of colours at most the successful palette bound plus one. The constant and running-time exponent remain fixed. This equivalence does not require derandomization and does not permit a small fraction of incorrectly coloured edges.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such an algorithm and absolute constants exist, or a proof in Lean that no algorithm in the stated class exists. A positive proof must cover every promised graph, always return a proper colouring, account for worst-case bit complexity and prove the expected logarithmic palette bound with one constant \(K\). The equivalent bounded-error formulation may be used if its conversion to the stated guarantee is proved.

A negative proof must rule out every uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm and every absolute logarithmic-bound constant, rather than only a particular SDP relaxation, local procedure or deterministic subclass. Hardness conditional on an unproved assumption is partial progress on this unconditional target. A bound \(O(n^\alpha)\) for fixed \(\alpha>0\), a bound \(O((\log n)^c)\) for \(c>1\), a colouring of only part of the vertices, or a guarantee for random or structurally restricted graphs does not meet the required logarithmic bound. This is an algorithm-existence question, so there is no replacement of the asymptotic palette guarantee by an additive numerical tolerance.

source_formulation.text: Find a polynomial-time algorithm that uses only logarithmically many colours on every graph known to be three-colourable.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Problem 9. Randomized expected performance is made explicit using the book’s Chapter 5 convention and the randomized colouring context of §13.2; a separate derandomization requirement is not added.

context_blocks.text: The promise guarantees a partition into three independent sets but does not reveal any of them. Finding that exact partition is computationally hard. The question allows a growing palette, asking whether that relaxation is enough to reduce the output from a power of the graph size to a logarithm.

A standard way to build a colouring is to repeatedly remove a large independent set and assign it a fresh colour. Every induced subgraph of a three-colourable graph is still three-colourable. If one could efficiently find an independent set containing a fixed positive fraction of the remaining vertices at every stage, the number of stages would be logarithmic. This is a useful sufficient route, not an asserted equivalence between logarithmic colouring and a particular independent-set approximation.

The textbook develops Wigderson’s combinatorial ideas and semidefinite relaxations with randomized rounding. Its §13.2 analyses the expected size of independent sets produced by such rounding, and Problem 9 isolates the \(O(\log n)\) palette goal. Making randomization explicit preserves this surrounding algorithmic context; it does not demand that an eventual solution also be derandomized.

The February 2026 theorem of Bansal, Huang and Lee reports \(O(n^{0.19539})\) colours, improving the previously stated growing-palette bounds. Its analysis combines combinatorial progress in dense graphs with semidefinite methods in sparse graphs and uses deeper neighborhoods in the rounding argument. For any fixed positive exponent, a power of \(n\) eventually exceeds every constant multiple of \(\log n\), so that improvement leaves the target’s asymptotic form unchanged.

The unconditional three-versus-five hardness theorem concerns a fixed output palette. A logarithmic palette eventually has more than five colours, so that theorem does not rule it out. Conversely, a logarithmic colouring algorithm would not give any fixed constant palette. The constant-colour and logarithmic-colour questions therefore remain distinct despite sharing the same input promise.

Properness is an exact combinatorial condition that can be checked directly. The uncertainty in the randomized formulation concerns the number of colours and is averaged over the algorithm’s coins for each input. A procedure that succeeds only on typical random graphs or leaves a few monochromatic edges would change the mathematical task.

cards.title: Hardness of 6-coloring 3-colorable graphs
cards.formal:
Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction \(R\) from Boolean \(3\)-SAT to finite simple undirected graphs such that, for every \(3\)-CNF formula \(F\),
\[
F\text{ is satisfiable}\ \Longrightarrow\ \chi(R(F))\leq3,
\qquad
F\text{ is unsatisfiable}\ \Longrightarrow\ \chi(R(F))>6?
\]
Equivalently, is the promise decision problem \(\operatorname{PCSP}(K_3,K_6)\) NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? This is the previously approved gap-decision formulation of the six-colouring hardness question.
cards.definitions:
A Boolean \(3\)-CNF formula is a finite conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most three literals. A literal is a Boolean variable or its negation. Variables and clause lists are explicitly encoded with binary indices and fixed delimiters; repeated literals and clauses are allowed. The empty conjunction is true and an empty clause is false. Let \(L\) be the complete encoding length.

The reduction is one deterministic multitape Turing machine. On every valid formula it outputs one graph \(G=R(F)\) on a labeled vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), allowing \(n=0\). Encode \(n\) by an explicit unary size header and then list unordered pairs of distinct binary vertex indices as edges, without repeated edges. Thus isolated vertices are included explicitly in the input size and the graph is not a succinct exponentially large object. There are fixed positive integers \(C,d\) such that the entire computation, including writing the graph, takes at most \(C(L+1)^d\) bit operations. There are no random bits, advice or oracle calls. Malformed formulas may be rejected. The graph need not come with any colouring, satisfying assignment or other witness.

A proper \(k\)-colouring of a graph is a function \(c:[n]\to[k]\) such that \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every edge \(\{u,v\}\). The chromatic number \(\chi(G)\) is the least such \(k\), with \(\chi\) of the empty graph defined as zero. For \(k\geq1\), \(K_k\) is the loopless complete graph on \([k]\). A graph homomorphism maps vertices to vertices and sends each edge to an edge, so a proper \(k\)-colouring is exactly a homomorphism to \(K_k\).

The promise problem \(\operatorname{PCSP}(K_3,K_6)\) requires YES on graphs with \(\chi(G)\leq3\) and NO on graphs with \(\chi(G)>6\). Graphs of chromatic number four, five or six lie outside the promise; a decision algorithm may answer either way on them. The reduction itself must send every satisfiable formula to the YES region and every unsatisfiable formula to the NO region, so its valid outputs never lie in this middle region. It is a many-one reduction: it produces a single instance and does not query a colouring oracle.

The two reduction implications must hold without a Unique Games, Label Cover, or other unproved hypothesis. NP-hardness here denotes the existence of this unconditional reduction; it is not itself the assertion that the problem has no polynomial-time algorithm. Since Boolean \(3\)-SAT is NP-complete, the displayed reduction is equivalent to the standard deterministic many-one NP-hardness requirement for all NP languages.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a reduction exists, or a proof in Lean that no such reduction exists. A positive answer must specify the construction, prove its uniform polynomial bit complexity and verify both chromatic-number implications for every input formula. Hardness only under an unproved conjecture, a reduction with weaker completeness or soundness, or hardness for a different pair of palettes does not settle this target.

A negative answer must rule out all deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions satisfying the two implications. In particular, a polynomial-time algorithm for the promise problem alone does not unconditionally prove nonexistence of the reduction: combining both would imply \(\mathsf P=\mathsf{NP}\). If \(\mathsf P=\mathsf{NP}\), a SAT decider could itself construct such a reduction by returning \(K_3\) or \(K_7\) according to satisfiability. Failure of one algebraic gadget construction, inability to find a particular polymorphism, or a finite list of unsuccessful reductions is insufficient for the negative answer.
cards.why: The three-versus-six gap is a concrete frontier for unconditional approximate-colouring hardness and finite-template promise CSPs. Resolving it would test whether the methods behind the five-colour theorem can cross the next structural obstruction, with implications for every algorithm trying to produce a fixed six-colour solution.
