context_blocks.text: A promise of three-colourability guarantees that a small partition into independent sets exists but does not reveal it. Allowing six colours relaxes the requested output. The associated decision gap separates graphs admitting three colours from graphs that do not admit even six. This is a small fixed-template promise CSP with no growing palette parameter.

Barto, Bulín, Krokhin and Opršal prove hardness for distinguishing \(k\)-colourable graphs from graphs not colourable with \(2k-1\) colours, for every \(k\geq3\). At \(k=3\), the result gives a gap from three to five colours. Its NO-instances may still be six-colourable, so the theorem does not imply the three-versus-six gap.

The algebraic PCSP framework relates the available reductions to operations that preserve the promised constraint relations, called polymorphisms. The source demonstrates the strength of this approach with the five-colour theorem and explains that moving to larger palettes requires additional analysis. A limitation of one reduction family does not by itself show that the requested polynomial-time reduction cannot exist.

Bansal, Huang and Lee’s February 2026 theorem reports a polynomial-time algorithm using \(O(n^{0.19539})\) colours on an \(n\)-vertex three-colourable graph. Their introduction still identifies five colours as the unconditional hardness frontier in its account. A growing-palette algorithm supplies neither a six-colouring algorithm nor a reduction proving hardness at six colours.

A deterministic polynomial-time six-colouring search algorithm on three-colourable inputs would yield a decision algorithm for this gap: run it with a polynomial time cutoff and check whether its output is a proper six-colouring. Every YES-instance would be accepted, while no NO-instance could pass the check. This one-way implication explains the relevance to search without identifying all possible notions of search hardness with the chosen decision reduction.

The separate question of whether some fixed constant palette allows polynomial-time colouring has a different quantifier. Hardness at six colours would not exclude an algorithm using seven, one hundred or another fixed number. Likewise, logarithmically many colours eventually exceed every fixed palette, so that algorithmic target is distinct from this hardness threshold.

cards.title: NP-intermediate \(\omega\)-categorical CSPs
cards.formal:
Assume \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). Does there exist a countable \(\omega\)-categorical relational structure \(\Gamma\) in a finite relational signature such that its fixed-template constraint satisfaction problem is NP-intermediate? Explicitly, the required three conditions are
\[\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\in\mathrm{NP},\qquad\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\notin\mathrm P,\qquad\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\text{ is not NP-complete}.\]
Completeness uses deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, as in the source’s hardness constructions. No effective presentation or uniform construction of the infinite template is required.
cards.why: This asks whether the principal symmetry condition for infinite-domain CSP algebra allows intermediate NP complexity at all. An example would locate a precise limit of tractability-versus-completeness classifications; a negative answer would establish a much broader NP dichotomy than the currently conjectured finitely bounded homogeneous framework.

This is a dated, bounded status review, not exhaustive certification of present openness.

cards.definitions:
A finite relational signature \(\tau\) is a finite list of relation symbols with fixed positive integer arities. A template \(\Gamma\) has a nonempty finite or countably infinite domain and a relation \(R^\Gamma\subseteq\Gamma^r\) for every \(r\)-ary symbol. A homomorphism \(h:I\to\Gamma\) preserves all positive relation tuples: if \((i_1,\ldots,i_r)\in R^I\), then \((h(i_1),\ldots,h(i_r))\in R^\Gamma\). It need not be injective or preserve missing tuples.

An automorphism is a domain bijection preserving both membership and nonmembership in every relation. It acts on ordered \(k\)-tuples coordinate by coordinate. The structure is \(\omega\)-categorical when, for each fixed positive integer \(k\), this action has finitely many orbits on \(\Gamma^k\). For a countably infinite finite-signature structure, this is equivalent to its complete first-order theory having exactly one countably infinite model up to isomorphism. Finite templates satisfy the orbit convention too. The number of orbits may depend on \(k\), and no procedure computing them is assumed.

The language \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\) accepts encodings of finite \(\tau\)-structures \(I\) exactly when there is a homomorphism \(I\to\Gamma\). Encode the instance domain \([n]\) by unary \(n\), then in signature order the explicitly listed relation tuples, each list preceded by a unary length and with binary indices separated by delimiters. This polynomial encoding counts isolated elements; repeated coordinates and duplicate tuples are allowed. The empty domain maps by the empty function. Malformed inputs are rejected. Let \(L\) be the full bit length. The signature and template are fixed before instances arrive and are not supplied as an infinite table or an oracle.

A language is in \(\mathrm P\) when some deterministic multitape Turing machine decides it on every bit string in at most \(C(L+1)^d\) bit steps for fixed positive integers \(C,d\). A language is in \(\mathrm{NP}\) when membership has a certificate of polynomially bounded length checked by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier. No randomness or advice is used. Importantly, a certificate for this infinite-template CSP need not list actual domain elements of \(\Gamma\); it can use any finite encoding and verifier proving the same language is in NP. Omega-categoricity alone does not guarantee NP membership.

A polynomial-time many-one reduction from a language \(K\) to a language \(Q\) is a total polynomial-time computable function \(r\) on binary strings such that \(x\in K\) if and only if \(r(x)\in Q\). A language \(Q\) is NP-complete if it is in NP and every NP language reduces to it in this sense. These reductions make one target instance and do not make adaptive oracle queries. A language is NP-intermediate if it lies in NP but satisfies neither tractability nor completeness. The constants and programs in these class definitions can depend on the fixed language or reduction; no common exponent for all templates is intended.

The question is existence of a mathematical template with all the stated properties, not a metaproblem receiving descriptions of arbitrary infinite structures. No finite list of forbidden patterns, homogeneous expansion, finite domain or algorithm deciding the relations of \(\Gamma\) is imposed. For context, coNP is the class of complements of NP languages; coNP-intermediate means in coNP but neither in P nor coNP-complete under the same reduction convention.
cards.answer_criterion: Under the hypothesis \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean either that such a template exists or that none exists. A positive proof must establish omega-categoricity, a finite relational signature, NP membership, absence of a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm, and absence of polynomial-time many-one NP completeness. An abstract NP-intermediate language or an unrestricted infinite template without omega-categoricity is insufficient. A negative proof must show, under the hypothesis, that every permitted template whose CSP lies in NP has a CSP in P or is NP-complete. CoNP intermediacy, completeness at a higher complexity level, or a dichotomy only for a narrower subclass does not settle this question.

source_formulation.text: Assuming P differs from NP, is there an NP-intermediate CSP with an omega-categorical template?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Question 3, which restates Bodirsky’s Question 49; NP completeness uses the source’s polynomial-time many-one convention.

context_blocks.text: Ladner’s theorem gives NP-intermediate languages if P differs from NP, but it does not automatically place them inside every structured family of computational problems. The issue here is whether an intermediate NP language can be realized as a fixed CSP while retaining finitely many symmetry types at every tuple length.

Finite-template CSPs satisfy the P versus NP-complete dichotomy, so a finite template cannot witness the desired intermediate behavior under the hypothesis. Allowing an infinite domain admits new CSP languages, while omega-categoricity retains the symmetry property supporting many algebraic methods.

Bodirsky and Grohe already construct omega-categorical CSPs in coNP that are neither tractable nor coNP-complete, assuming P differs from coNP. Their construction adapts Ladner’s diagonalization by choosing a suitable infinite family of forbidden tournaments. This demonstrates intermediate complexity on the complementary side, but does not provide NP membership for the required example.

Taking the complement of a coNP-intermediate language produces an NP-intermediate language, but complementing a CSP language need not produce another CSP language. Every CSP is closed under inverse homomorphisms and disjoint unions of finite instances. Such closure properties constrain representation and do not automatically survive complementation.

The 2026 paper constructs omega-categorical CSPs complete for every level of the polynomial hierarchy, the decision classes described by a fixed number of alternating existential and universal blocks of polynomial-length certificates. Its constructions extend the known complementary-side examples, yet Question 3 explicitly retains NP intermediacy as a separate problem.

The Bodirsky–Pinsker dichotomy concerns the narrower class of first-order reducts of finitely bounded homogeneous structures. In that setting a homogeneous structure has all finite induced partial isomorphisms extend to automorphisms, finite boundedness specifies its finite induced substructures by finitely many forbidden patterns, and a first-order reduct retains finitely many parameter-free definable relations. None of these restrictions is imposed here; a dichotomy for that subclass would not rule out an intermediate template elsewhere.

cards.title: VCSP tractability over the countable random graph
cards.formal:
Let \(\mathbb R=(D;E)\) be the countable random graph. Is it true that for every valued structure \(\mathcal A=(D;f_1,\ldots,f_s)\) with a finite signature and \(\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb R)\subseteq\operatorname{Aut}(\mathcal A)\),
\[
\mathcal A\text{ does not pp-construct }K_3
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{VCSP}(\mathcal A)\in\mathsf P?
\]
All cost functions take values in \(\mathbb Q\cup\{\infty\}\). The valued decision problem and the precise pp-construction condition are defined below. The template \(\mathcal A\) is fixed for each decision problem; the claim is not a uniform algorithm taking arbitrary templates as part of its input.
cards.why: This asks whether the known expressibility obstruction completely determines tractability for a major new class of infinite-domain optimization problems. A positive answer would extend the algebraic classification of valued CSPs beyond ordered domains to graph-invariant costs; a counterexample would expose a failure of the proposed general obstruction.

Checked the full versions and foundational definitions on 16 September 2026; a targeted later-work search did not identify a resolution. cards.definitions:
The countable random graph \(\mathbb R=(D;E)\), also called the Rado graph, is the countably infinite simple undirected graph with the extension property: for any disjoint finite sets \(U,V\subseteq D\), there is a vertex outside \(U\cup V\) adjacent to every vertex in \(U\) and to no vertex in \(V\). This property determines the graph up to isomorphism. The symbol \(\mathbb R\) denotes this graph here, not the real-number field. Its automorphisms are bijections \(\alpha:D\to D\) preserving adjacency and nonadjacency. No random graph is sampled in the algorithmic input.

A valued template consists of finitely many symbols \(f_i\), each with a fixed nonnegative finite arity \(k_i\), interpreted as \(f_i:D^{k_i}\to\mathbb Q\cup\{\infty\}\). The automorphism requirement says that \(f_i(\alpha(a_1),\ldots,\alpha(a_{k_i}))=f_i(a_1,\ldots,a_{k_i})\) for every automorphism \(\alpha\) of the graph and every tuple. Equivalently, a cost depends only on the equality pattern of its arguments and the adjacency pattern between their distinct entries. There are finitely many such patterns at each fixed arity, so each cost has a finite table of rational values and possible infinities. Negative rational costs are permitted. There are no distinguished domain constants or input vertex names.

For fixed \(\mathcal A\), an instance of \(\operatorname{VCSP}(\mathcal A)\) is an explicit finite set of variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\), a sum \(\Phi\) of atomic costs applied to these variables, and a rational threshold \(u\). An atomic cost is \(f_i(x_{j_1},\ldots,x_{j_{k_i}})\), the equality cost \(\operatorname{eq}(x,y)\) which is zero for equal arguments and infinity otherwise, or the always-infinite unary cost \(\bot(x)\). Variables may repeat within an atom, and atoms may repeat in the sum. The empty sum has value zero. Summands are explicitly listed with unit multiplicity; there are no binary-encoded external weights multiplying atoms. The question is whether there exists an assignment \(h:\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\to D\) with \(\Phi(h)\leq u\). Any infinite summand makes the sum infinite.

Encode the variable list explicitly, the sum as symbols with binary variable indices, and \(u\) by a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator. Let \(L\) be the total length. The template’s finite tables are fixed and may be built into a machine. Membership in \(\mathsf P\) means that some uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine decides this threshold language correctly on every valid input in at most \(C(L+1)^d\) bit operations for fixed positive integers \(C,d\). Malformed encodings are rejected. There is no randomness, numerical error, advice or oracle access to the infinite graph. The machine and its constants may depend on \(\mathcal A\); a common exponent, a template-classification algorithm and an assignment-output algorithm are not additionally required.

Here is an explicit equivalent form of the source’s valued pp-construction criterion. First define the valued relational clone \(\langle\mathcal A\rangle\): the smallest collection of finite-arity functions on \(D\) containing the template costs, equality and the always-infinite unary cost, and closed under the following operations. One may form finite sums of functions applied to variables with any repetitions, identifications or permutations, including the zero empty sum; add a rational constant; multiply by a nonnegative rational; or project by
\[
g(\mathbf a)=\inf_{\mathbf b\in D^r} f(\mathbf a,\mathbf b).
\]
Use \(0\cdot\infty=0\), \(c\cdot\infty=\infty\) for \(c>0\), and \(c+\infty=\infty\). Only functions valued in \(\mathbb Q\cup\{\infty\}\) are allowed. In this invariant setting every function produced has finitely many orbit values, so these projection infima are attained and remain rational or infinite.

Two further closure operations turn a function \(f\) into a crisp cost, meaning a function taking only zero and infinity. The feasibility cost is zero on \(\operatorname{Feas}(f)=\{\mathbf a:f(\mathbf a)<\infty\}\) and infinity outside it. The optimality cost is zero on
\[
\operatorname{Opt}(f)=\{\mathbf a:f(\mathbf a)<\infty\text{ and } f(\mathbf a)\leq f(\mathbf b)\text{ for every }\mathbf b\},
\]
and infinity outside it. If no tuple has finite cost, both sets are empty. The feasibility and optimality operations are part of the definition; using only sums and projection would give a different expressive closure. Membership in the clone requires a finite expression using these operations; arbitrary limits are not added.

Let \(K_3\) have vertices \(\{1,2,3\}\) and the binary adjacency relation consisting of all ordered pairs of distinct vertices. The template pp-constructs \(K_3\) precisely when there exist a positive integer \(d\), a crisp cost \(r\in\langle\mathcal A\rangle\) of arity \(2d\), and functions
\[
h:D^d\to\{1,2,3\},\qquad g:\{1,2,3\}\to D^d
\]
with the following properties. Define the binary relation \(H\) on \(D^d\) by \(H(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\) if and only if \(r(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)=0\). Whenever \(H(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\), require \(h(\mathbf a)\ne h(\mathbf b)\); and whenever \(i\ne j\), require \(H(g(i),g(j))\). These are homomorphisms in both directions between \((D^d;H)\) and \(K_3\). The functions need not be computable or definable, and \(H\) need not be assumed symmetric in advance. This criterion includes arbitrary finite dimension and arbitrary expressible crisp costs, not only one graph relation from the original signature. Its equivalence with the source’s definition using valued pp-powers and fractional homomorphisms follows from Proposition 25 and the crisp homomorphism lemma in the full version.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal implication, or of its negation. A positive answer must prove polynomial-time decidability for every invariant finite-signature template that has no pp-construction of \(K_3\), under the full cost and input model above. The algorithm may depend on the fixed template, as membership of its language in \(\mathsf P\) permits.

A negative answer must establish a qualifying fixed template with no such pp-construction and prove that its threshold language is not in \(\mathsf P\). Merely proving NP-hardness gives a conditional counterexample under \(\mathsf P\ne\mathsf{NP}\), not an unconditional refutation of the implication. A dichotomy without the specified pp-construction condition, a result only for temporal templates, or a result only for crisp or nonnegative finite-valued costs does not by itself settle this target. No decision procedure for recognizing the tractable templates is required beyond the source’s per-template assertion.

source_formulation.text: For every finite-signature valued structure preserved by all automorphisms of the countable random graph, does the absence of a pp-construction of K3 imply polynomial-time solvability of its VCSP?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the second part of Question 44, with the hypotheses supplied by its preceding sentence; repeated as Question 59 in the January 2026 full version.

context_blocks.text: The short imported question omitted the ambient class stated immediately before it. The countable random graph supplies that class: all costs are invariant under its automorphisms. Restoring this condition recovers the source’s exact scope. Arbitrary infinite-domain valued problems need not share the same tractability behavior.

Despite the infinite domain, every instance has a finite witness format for NP membership. Guess which variables are equal and the adjacency relation among their distinct assigned values. Every resulting finite simple graph embeds into the Rado graph by the extension property. The fixed pattern table evaluates every atomic cost, and exact rational arithmetic checks the threshold. This places each template’s language in NP without treating infinite-domain assignments as input strings or oracle answers.

The source’s pp-construction notion identifies a general reduction mechanism. Expressible costs can be implemented without changing polynomial-time solvability, finite powers encode tuples of domain elements, and homomorphisms transfer feasibility. Constructing the triangle in this way gives NP-hardness of the valued problem. The question asks whether absence of that obstruction always supplies tractability in this particular invariant class.

Feasibility alone discards relative preferences between assignments, while optimality singles out the tuples of minimum finite cost. Their separate presence in the expressive closure matters for the valued hardness criterion. The equivalent crisp construction above uses all crisp relations obtainable from the costs, not merely the feasibility relations of the originally supplied functions.

The temporal theorem concerns cost functions on the rationals invariant under every order-preserving bijection. It proves the corresponding polynomial-time versus NP-complete classification for that class, including the pp-construction criterion. The group of automorphisms of the countable random graph describes a different class, so the temporal theorem motivates the question but does not answer it.

The original Question 44 asks first for a complexity dichotomy and then for this sharper tractability implication. The imported card selects the second question. Combining its positive answer with the known hardness direction and the finite-pattern NP witness would give the broader dichotomy, while merely establishing a dichotomy would not identify its tractable side by this exact criterion.

In the general framework, the authors formulate a related conjecture for valued templates associated with reducts of finitely bounded homogeneous structures. The random graph is a concrete highly symmetric test case. The January 2026 full version still explicitly poses this case after proving the temporal classification.

cards.title: Boolean decision-Holant dichotomy
cards.formal:
Classify the polynomial-time solvable Boolean decision-Holant problems for all fixed finite families of Boolean relations. More precisely, under \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), determine the entire characteristic function
\[\chi_{\mathrm H}(\mathcal F)=\begin{cases}1,&\operatorname{DecHolant}(\mathcal F)\in\mathrm P,\\0,&\operatorname{DecHolant}(\mathcal F)\notin\mathrm P,\end{cases}\]
with absolute error at most \(1/100\) at every finite family \(\mathcal F\). The answer must give a substantive structural criterion on the allowed relations, with algorithms and complementary lower bounds, rather than merely restating the definition of polynomial-time solvability. The model is the source’s Boolean edge-CSP interpretation of decision Holant, specified below.
cards.why: A full classification would explain exactly which local Boolean constraints remain tractable when each variable has two incidences. The unresolved region contains broad generalizations of matching rather than only the standard Boolean CSP algorithms. Resolving it would connect delta-matroid structure with the boundary between polynomial-time graph algorithms and NP-hardness.
cards.status_note: The 2017 survey explicitly leaves the general Boolean decision-Holant classification open. The checked 2023 ISAAC paper, §1 p. 57:4, explicitly retains that question and the all-delta-matroids tractability conjecture. Bounded primary-source searches on 16 September 2026 found later special-case and counting results but no matching full decision classification; this is not exhaustive certification of current openness. The finite-family tractability characteristic function, P≠NP convention and loopless edge-CSP input model are explicit editorial specifications grounded in the cited sources.

The question seeks a structural classification of all fixed finite relation families that admit polynomial-time decision.
The source’s edge-CSP model makes each variable occur in exactly two distinct constraint scopes, without freely adding constants or unary relations.

cards.definitions:
A Boolean relation of arity \(r\geq1\) is a subset \(R\subseteq\{0,1\}^r\), equivalently its zero-one indicator function \(f_R\). A signature family \(\mathcal F\) is a finite ordered list of such relations given by their full finite truth tables; empty relations and the empty family are allowed. For each decision problem the family and all arities are fixed before inputs are supplied. Arbitrarily large fixed arities are covered across the classification.

A signature grid is a finite undirected loopless multigraph \(G=(V,E)\), together with a label \(R_v\in\mathcal F\) at each vertex and an ordering \((e_{v,1},\ldots,e_{v,r_v})\) of its incident edges, where \(r_v\) equals the arity of \(R_v\). Parallel edges are permitted and are separate variables. The graph need not be planar or bipartite. Each edge has two distinct endpoints and appears exactly once at each endpoint. The incidence order is part of the input, since relations need not be symmetric. This is the explicit convention of Definitions 1–3 in the cited edge-CSP paper: a variable is in exactly two distinct constraint scopes, without a repeated coordinate within one scope.

A Boolean assignment is a map \(\sigma:E\to\{0,1\}\). It is satisfying when \((\sigma(e_{v,1}),\ldots,\sigma(e_{v,r_v}))\in R_v\) for every vertex. Define
\[H_{\mathcal F}(G)=\sum_{\sigma:E\to\{0,1\}}\prod_{v\in V} f_{R_v}(\sigma(e_{v,1}),\ldots,\sigma(e_{v,r_v})).\]
The task \(\operatorname{DecHolant}(\mathcal F)\) accepts exactly the grids with \(H_{\mathcal F}(G)>0\). It asks for one yes/no answer, not the number or a list of satisfying assignments. The empty graph has value one, by the empty-product convention. A grid containing an empty relation is unsatisfiable. Nullary indicators, if included, can be processed separately: zero rejects the instance and one is deleted, so restricting the signature tables to positive arities loses no tractability class.

Encode the numbers of vertices and edges in unary; list binary endpoint indices for each numbered edge, the fixed-family index at each vertex, and its ordered list of edge indices. Let \(L\) be total bit length. Validity of the encoding is checked in polynomial time; malformed strings are rejected. A polynomial-time algorithm is a deterministic multitape Turing machine that halts with the correct answer on every input in at most \(C(L+1)^k\) bit steps, for positive constants \(C,k\) depending on \(\mathcal F\). There is no randomness, oracle or advice. Programs may depend on the fixed family, and no common running-time exponent across all families is requested.

No unary relation, pinning constant, equality relation, edge weight or graph restriction is freely added to \(\mathcal F\). The at-most-two-occurrences decision model used in the survey has the same complexity under this scope convention: remove unused variables, take two copies of the instance, and identify corresponding variables that occurred only once. This gives exactly two occurrences and preserves satisfiability without new relations. The target does not impose a uniform input-template algorithm or require a polynomial-time procedure for recognizing the tractable families from their truth tables.

Here \(\mathrm P\) is deterministic polynomial time and \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of languages whose membership has polynomial-length certificates checkable in polynomial time. Every fixed-family problem above is in NP, with the edge assignment as certificate. NP-hardness, when used in the classification, means deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions from every language in NP; NP-complete means both NP-hard and in NP. This is an explicit reduction convention. The separation assumption makes a tractability classification nontrivial; if \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), the function is identically one. A rational answer within \(1/100\) of a zero-one value determines that value, but the requested result is the structural description of the whole function, not numerical experiments on selected families.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of an exhaustive structural characterization of \(\chi_{\mathrm H}\) with the stated absolute \(1/100\) accuracy, under the explicit \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) hypothesis. Prove correct polynomial-time decision algorithms for every family assigned one and a matching exclusion of polynomial time for every family assigned zero; NP-hardness under the stated reductions is a sufficient exclusion. The result must cover all finite Boolean signature families, including arbitrary delta-matroid relations, with the graph and occurrence conventions above. A characterization cannot simply rename the existence of a polynomial-time machine. Classifying only symmetric signatures, only even delta-matroids, planar inputs, weighted counting, or a language enlarged by freely available unary signatures does not answer the full question. If additional complexity cases arise instead of the expected polynomial-time/NP-complete dichotomy, identify and justify them rather than asserting that every nontractable case is NP-complete without proof.

source_formulation.text: Classify Boolean decision-Holant problems; the remaining general obstacle is the complexity of delta-matroid relations.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of §3. The complete fixed-finite-family tractability target, conditional separation convention and cited loopless edge-CSP model are explicit.

context_blocks.text: In ordinary CSP a variable may constrain many locations. In a Holant grid each variable is an edge linking two local constraints. This restriction creates new algorithms: an ExactOne relation accepts precisely tuples with one coordinate equal to one, and using it at every vertex asks for a perfect matching. Thus tractability is not exhausted by the familiar Boolean CSP cases.

For a nonempty relation \(R\subseteq\{0,1\}^r\), the delta-matroid exchange property says: if \(x,y\in R\) differ at coordinate \(i\), then either flipping \(i\) in \(x\) stays in \(R\), or there is a different coordinate \(j\) at which \(x,y\) differ such that flipping both \(i,j\) stays in \(R\). An even delta-matroid additionally has the same parity of Hamming weight for all its tuples; that parity may be odd. Empty relations are handled separately by immediate rejection when used.

The source’s Theorem 8 records Feder’s boundary: if a family contains a relation failing the delta-matroid exchange property, its decision-Holant complexity agrees with that of ordinary CSP on the family. Schaefer’s Boolean CSP dichotomy then supplies a polynomial-time algorithm or NP-completeness. The remaining general region consists of families whose relations all satisfy the exchange property.

For symmetric relations, membership depends only on the number of one coordinates. The delta-matroid condition then says that between consecutive permitted weights there is at most one forbidden integer. Such families are tractable as general factor problems. This permits relations with both parities; it is a different sufficient condition from the even delta-matroid algorithm.

Kazda, Kolmogorov and Rolínek generalize the matching blossom algorithm to arbitrary even delta-matroid relations given by tuple lists, and extend it to a further class they call efficiently coverable. Their planar Boolean CSP classification is a consequence. It does not classify arbitrary delta-matroid constraints in general edge-CSP grids.

The 2023 general-factor paper explicitly retains the general Boolean edge-CSP classification as open, while proving a strongly polynomial algorithm for particular weighted symmetric constraints. It records the conjecture that every delta-matroid family is tractable. The card retains the full classification question, so it does not assume this conjectured answer in its target.

A counting dichotomy concerns computing the entire sum H, which can be harder than deciding whether H is positive. Counting Holant results for real or complex signatures therefore cannot by themselves classify this zero-one decision task. Availability of all unary signatures and restrictions to planar grids also define different problems.

cards.title: Exact exponential-time equivalence for nonnegative Boolean Max-CSP
cards.formal: Does the following extension of the source’s degree-based classification hold? For every fixed finite Boolean constraint language \(\Gamma\) that is neither 0-valid, 1-valid, nor 2-monotone, let \(d=\deg (\Gamma )\). For every fixed real \(\alpha >1\), if Max \(\mathrm{CSP}(\Gamma ,N,c)\) has an exact deterministic algorithm running in \(\alpha ^{n}n^{O(1)}\) time for every fixed constant \(c\ge 1\), must Max d-CNF-SAT with nonnegative integer weights of total weight at most \(n^{c}\) also have an exact deterministic \(\alpha ^{n}n^{O(1)}\)-time algorithm for every fixed \(c\ge 1\)? The same base \(\alpha\) is required. Algorithms and polynomial factors may depend on \(\Gamma ,\alpha ,c\). This formulates the conclusion’s speedup question as extending Theorem 6.2 to all NP-hard nonnegative-weight languages; tractable languages are explicitly excluded.
cards.why: Would show whether the algebraic degree of a Boolean constraint language determines its exact exponential-time complexity even when every constraint has the usual nonnegative weight.
cards.status_note: Checked the conference statement against the March 2024 version of record, including the exact-base quantifiers, all-c convention and tractability dichotomy. Subsequent searches through 12 September 2026 did not locate a general resolution. The displayed statement is the NP-hard-language extension of the source’s Theorem 6.2; this editorial interpretation of the shorter conclusion is explicit. Search is not exhaustive.

cards.definitions: A Boolean predicate f of arity r is a map \(\{0,1\}\)ʳ→\(\{0,1\}\). A language \(\Gamma\) is a fixed finite set of such predicates, not part of an input instance. An instance \(\Phi\) has variables \(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}\) and weighted applications \((f,(i_{1},\ldots ,i_{r}),w)\), where \(f\in \Gamma\), each \(i_{j}\in [n]\) and w is a nonnegative integer. Indices may repeat. Arguments are variables themselves: constants and negated literals are available only if the corresponding predicate can already be expressed by a member of \(\Gamma\) with variable arguments. The value \(\Phi (x)\) is the sum of weights whose predicate applications evaluate to 1. Max \(\mathrm{CSP}(\Gamma ,N,c)\) asks whether \(\max _{x\in \{0,1\}^{n}}\Phi (x)\ge t\) for an input integer t, under the promise that total weight is at most \(n^{c}\). Weights, indices and t use binary encoding; duplicate applications can be combined and zero-weight applications discarded. Trivial thresholds outside the possible objective range are handled during input reading. Polynomial-time normalization is included; equivalently the runtime has an additional input-reading term for a redundantly listed representation. The normalized input has polynomial length for fixed \(\Gamma ,c\). The algorithm must answer every promised instance correctly, and n denotes variables, not clauses, total weight or bit length. For each f there is a unique multilinear real polynomial \(\mathrm{P}_{f}\) agreeing with f on its Boolean cube. Its degree is the largest number of variables in a monomial with nonzero coefficient; \(\deg (\Gamma )=\max _{f\in \Gamma}\deg (\mathrm{P}_{f})\). This is neither maximum predicate arity nor polynomial degree over \(F_{2}\). Constants can be removed with a threshold adjustment. Disregarding constant predicates, a language is 0-valid if every predicate accepts its all-zero input, and 1-valid if every predicate accepts its all-one input. It is 2-monotone if each predicate has a DNF representation with at most two terms, one consisting only of positive variables and one only of negated variables. The excluded three cases are the source’s polynomial-time cases for nonnegative weights; the remaining cases are NP-hard and have \(d\ge 2\). Max d-CNF-SAT is the same threshold maximization problem for disjunctions of at most d literals, with both signs of variables allowed, and nonnegative integer clause weights. Equivalently one may use the source’s d-ary clause language and repeated variables. All complexity statements are worst-case exact running times in an ordinary discrete computation model, up to polynomial factors. The premise is quantified over every fixed polynomial weight bound c; a result for only one small weight range does not supply that premise.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed implication for every eligible fixed language \(\Gamma\) and every \(\alpha >1\), retaining the same exponential base and the all-c weight convention, or refute it by a language and a rigorously established failure of that implication. A theorem comparing only whether both problems are NP-hard, or comparing compression sizes or exponential rates after a constant-factor increase in variable count, does not establish the stated base-preserving classification.

cards.title: Universal representation of NP by \(\omega\)-categorical CSPs
cards.formal:
For every language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\) in \(\mathrm{NP}\), does there exist a countable \(\omega\)-categorical relational structure \(\Gamma\) in a finite relational signature such that
\[L\equiv_T^p\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\ ?\]
The relation \(\equiv_T^p\) means deterministic polynomial-time Turing reductions in both directions. This reduction convention follows the source’s accompanying non-dichotomy results and the explicit definition in the later monograph; Question 2 itself abbreviates it as polynomial-time equivalence.
cards.why: The question tests whether the symmetry framework that supports infinite-domain algebraic CSP methods is computationally universal for NP under the source’s equivalence convention. A positive answer would place every NP degree into that framework; a negative answer would exhibit a complexity limitation imposed by omega-categoricity itself.
cards.status_note: Question 2 is open in the checked 2008 survey. Bounded primary-source searches through 16 September 2026 found no matching general representation theorem or refutation; the 2026 scope results concern a narrower template class. This is a limited status check, not exhaustive certification of present openness. The Turing reduction convention is explicitly recovered from the related theorem and later monograph rather than attributed as verbatim wording of Question 2.

cards.definitions:
A finite relational signature \(\tau\) is a finite list of relation symbols, each with a fixed positive integer arity. A structure \(\Gamma\) has a nonempty finite or countably infinite domain and an interpretation \(R^\Gamma\subseteq\Gamma^r\) for each \(r\)-ary symbol. A homomorphism \(h:I\to\Gamma\) maps elements of \(I\) to domain values and preserves every positive relation tuple. It need not be injective and need not preserve absence of tuples.

An automorphism of \(\Gamma\) is a bijection of its domain preserving both membership and nonmembership in every relation. It acts on an ordered tuple by applying the same bijection to all coordinates. Two tuples are in the same orbit if some automorphism maps one to the other. The structure is \(\omega\)-categorical here if for every positive integer \(k\), there are only finitely many orbits of ordered \(k\)-tuples. For countably infinite structures in a finite signature, this is equivalent to their complete first-order theory having a unique countably infinite model up to isomorphism. Finite structures are admitted by the same orbit convention. The bound on the number of orbits can depend on \(k\); no fixed global bound, algorithm for orbits, homogeneity or finite list of forbidden patterns is assumed.

A CSP instance is a finite \(\tau\)-structure \(I\) with domain \([n]\), \(n\geq0\), and explicitly listed relation tuples. It is accepted exactly when \(I\to\Gamma\). Repeated coordinates and isolated elements are allowed; duplicate tuples are harmless. The empty structure has the empty homomorphism. Encode \(n\) in unary, then in signature order each relation’s unary list length and its tuples of binary indices, with delimiters. Invalid encodings are rejected. This defines a total language \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\) of finite bit strings. The signature and structure are fixed for this language; no infinite table, presentation algorithm or value from \(\Gamma\) is supplied with an instance.

A language lies in \(\mathrm{NP}\) if membership is witnessed by a certificate of length polynomial in the input bit length and checked by a deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine. A reduction \(K\leq_T^p Q\) is a deterministic oracle Turing machine deciding membership in \(K\) using exact yes/no membership queries to \(Q\). On every input \(x\), all its computation, query writing and answer processing take at most \(C(|x|+1)^d\) bit steps for fixed positive constants \(C,d\). Thus query lengths and their number are polynomially bounded. The oracle supplies each membership bit at unit query cost; its own computation is not part of the reduction. Queries may depend on earlier answers, and answers may be negated. No randomness or advice is available.

Polynomial-time Turing equivalence means \(L\leq_T^p\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\) and \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\leq_T^p L\). The two programs and their constants may depend on \(L,\Gamma\), but each works on every finite input. The quantifiers are \(\forall L\in\mathrm{NP}\ \exists\tau,\Gamma,M_1,M_2,C_1,C_2,d_1,d_2\). No uniform algorithm turning an NP verifier into a template or into these reductions is requested. The source explicitly permits defining a fixed CSP without fixing an effective representation of its infinite template.

This is equivalence of computational problems, not equality of their input classes or their logical definitions. Turing equivalence is also weaker than requiring many-one reductions, which produce one target instance with the same membership answer. No additional hypothesis \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\in\mathrm{NP}\) is inserted: Turing equivalence to an NP language alone implies membership in \(\mathrm P^{\mathrm{NP}}\), the class decided by polynomial-time machines with an NP oracle, rather than closure inside NP. The original question does not separately impose that extra condition. Trivial languages are included and cause no difficulty under Turing reductions.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must cover every language in NP and produce existence of a finite-signature omega-categorical template with both deterministic polynomial-time Turing reductions. A negative answer must establish a language in NP for which no permitted template has the required equivalence. Giving an arbitrary infinite template, only one reduction direction, a weaker oracle-complexity upper bound, or a representation for only NP-complete languages does not settle the question. No unproved complexity separation is assumed; conditional constructions or obstructions settle only their conditional statements.

source_formulation.text: Is every problem in NP polynomial-time equivalent to a CSP with an omega-categorical template?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Question 2; deterministic polynomial-time Turing equivalence is made explicit using the accompanying representation theorem and the author’s later Chapter 13 convention.

context_blocks.text: Infinite templates vastly enlarge the class of possible CSPs, but omega-categoricity retains finitely many symmetry types at each tuple length. It is the structural hypothesis behind many preservation theorems used in algebraic CSP theory. The question asks whether imposing this symmetry still permits representation of every NP computational problem up to the stated reductions.

Bodirsky and Grohe prove that every decision language has a polynomial-time Turing equivalent CSP with an unrestricted infinite template. Their construction is not omega-categorical. Thus arbitrary-template universality is an established starting point, and the symmetry condition is the entire additional issue.

For omega-categorical templates their Theorem 2 instead gives, for any decision language \(L\), a template with \(L\leq_m^p\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\) and \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\in\mathrm{coNP}^{L}\). Here the first relation is a polynomial-time many-one reduction and \(\mathrm{coNP}^{L}\) means complements of languages accepted by nondeterministic polynomial-time machines with exact oracle \(L\). This upper bound does not supply the required deterministic polynomial-time oracle reduction back to \(L\).

The same work constructs omega-categorical templates with coNP-complete CSPs and, conditionally, coNP-intermediate CSPs. These results demonstrate broad complexity within the symmetry class, but they do not establish equivalence to each prescribed NP language. The later book separately retains the question of NP-intermediate omega-categorical CSPs; that question explicitly requires NP membership, unlike bare Turing equivalence.

The stronger restrictions in the Bodirsky–Pinsker dichotomy concern reducts of finitely bounded homogeneous structures. They ensure finite-pattern certificates and hence NP membership. The present target quantifies over all omega-categorical templates and imposes neither restriction; proving that narrower dichotomy would not settle this representation question.

Logical representation is also a different issue. Two templates may define different finite-instance CSPs yet have polynomial-time equivalent decision problems. The source’s neighbouring question about whether a particular SNP-definable CSP has an omega-categorical template asks for the same accepted input class, which is stronger than computational equivalence and has separate counterexamples.

cards.title: Dichotomy for finite-domain restricted CSPs
cards.formal:
Assume \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). For every finite relational signature \(\tau\), every finite \(\tau\)-structure \(A\), and every possibly infinite \(\tau\)-structure \(B\) for which \(\operatorname{CSP}(B)\) is decidable, must \(\operatorname{RCSP}(A,B)\) be either polynomial-time solvable or NP-hard in the source’s completion sense? Explicitly, let
\[\mathcal S_{A,B}=\{S\subseteq\{0,1\}^*:S\text{ is decidable and }S\cap\operatorname{CSP}(B)=\operatorname{CSP}(A)\cap\operatorname{CSP}(B)\}.\]
Is it always true that
\[\bigl(\exists S\in\mathcal S_{A,B}:S\in\mathrm P\bigr)\quad\lor\quad\bigl(\forall S\in\mathcal S_{A,B}:S\text{ is NP-hard}\bigr)?\]
The input is a finite structure \(X\) promised to map homomorphically to \(B\); on that promise the decision is whether \(X\) maps to \(A\).
cards.why: This asks whether the finite-domain CSP dichotomy survives every decidable restriction described by homomorphisms into a fixed, possibly infinite structure. A positive answer would sharply constrain the complexity introduced by such promises. A counterexample would demonstrate intermediate promise behaviour even though all satisfying assignments still use a fixed finite domain.

Section 3 supplies the decidability and completion-hardness conventions omitted by the imported excerpt. cards.definitions:
A finite relational signature \(\tau\) is a finite list of relation symbols of positive integer arities. A \(\tau\)-structure \(D\) has a domain and a relation \(R^D\subseteq D^r\) for each \(r\)-ary symbol. The target \(A\) is finite; the restriction \(B\) may have an arbitrary infinite domain. A homomorphism \(h:D\to E\) is a function preserving every relation tuple: \((d_1,\ldots,d_r)\in R^D\) implies \((h(d_1),\ldots,h(d_r))\in R^E\). Write \(D\to E\) for existence of such a map. Maps need not be injective. Neither \(A\to B\) nor \(B\to A\) is assumed.

Input structures have domain \([n]\), \(n\geq0\), and explicitly listed tuples for each relation. Encode \(n\) in unary, then the relation lists in signature order with unary list lengths and binary coordinate indices. Let \(L\) be the total bit length. Empty relations, repeated coordinates and isolated elements are allowed; repeated listed tuples are harmless. Define \(\operatorname{CSP}(D)\) as the set of valid encodings of finite \(X\) with \(X\to D\). Invalid encodings do not belong to this set. Empty template domains may be included; their trivial boundary cases do not alter the question.

For each problem \(A,B,\tau\) are fixed, and only \(X\) is supplied. An input in \(\operatorname{CSP}(B)\) must be accepted exactly when it lies in \(\operatorname{CSP}(A)\); outside the promise either answer is allowed. A completion \(S\) is a total decidable language with precisely this behaviour on the promise. Since \(A\) is finite, \(\operatorname{CSP}(A)\) is a decidable completion, so \(\mathcal S_{A,B}\) is never empty. Decidability of \(\operatorname{CSP}(B)\) is a hypothesis recovered from the source, not a polynomial-time promise-recognition assumption. No description, relation-table algorithm, homomorphism into \(B\), or oracle for \(B\) is supplied. Infinite restrictions are not limited to finitely presented or categorically specified structures.

A completion is in \(\mathrm P\) if a deterministic multitape Turing machine accepts exactly it and halts on every string of length \(L\) within \(C(L+1)^k\) bit steps for fixed positive integers \(C,k\). The machine and constants may depend on \(A,B\). Decidable means a deterministic machine halts and decides membership, without any time bound. No uniform procedure for constructing these machines from templates, common polynomial exponent, advice or randomness is requested.

A language is in \(\mathrm{NP}\) if membership has polynomially bounded certificates checkable in deterministic polynomial time. A language \(S\) is NP-hard here under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions: for every \(K\in\mathrm{NP}\), there is a total polynomial-time function \(f_K\) with \(x\in K\) if and only if \(f_K(x)\in S\). Equivalently, it suffices to reduce Boolean three-clause satisfiability, where each clause has at most three literals. This is hardness of the total language \(S\), not a claim that \(S\) itself lies in NP.

The promise-hardness quantifiers are \(\forall\text{ decidable completions }S\ \exists\text{ suitable reductions to }S\). Reductions may depend on \(S\); no single reduction whose images always satisfy \(X\to B\) is required by this definition. A uniform reduction landing inside the promise would suffice, but is not silently substituted for the source’s definition. Under \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) the two displayed alternatives are disjoint. If \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), the first alternative already holds for every finite \(A\), since its ordinary CSP is in NP.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean, under the stated \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) hypothesis, that the displayed dichotomy holds for every permitted \(A,B\), or that it fails. A negative answer must establish a fixed finite \(A\) and a permitted possibly infinite \(B\) such that no completion is in P and at least one decidable completion is not NP-hard under the stated reductions. A positive answer must cover every infinite restriction with decidable CSP, retaining the completion quantifiers. Proving only the already known finite-restriction case, treating an arbitrary input class that is not \(\operatorname{CSP}(B)\), or disproving a stronger uniform hardness requirement does not settle this question. No additional unproved hypothesis may replace the explicitly stated separation assumption.

source_formulation.text: Under P≠NP, do finite-domain restricted CSPs satisfy a polynomial-time versus NP-hard dichotomy when their restriction structures may be infinite?

context_blocks.text: Restricted CSPs impose a promise on which input structures must be handled. For example, RCSP(K₃,K₄) asks whether a graph promised to be four-colourable is three-colourable; Kᵣ is the complete loopless graph on r vertices. Unlike a promise CSP, the promise here restricts the input class on both yes and no sides rather than relaxing which assignments count as solutions.

The source proves that a finite restriction B permits a reduction to an ordinary CSP on the exponential structure A^B. Its elements are functions from B to A, with relations defined by preservation along relation tuples of B. If A and B are both finite, this is again a finite structure, so the ordinary finite-domain decision dichotomy applies. Theorem 18 records the resulting restricted dichotomy.

An infinite B can impose familiar global input conditions. For directed graphs, the structure on rational numbers with the strict-order relation admits a homomorphism from exactly the finite acyclic digraphs. Such a restriction remains decidable even though its representing structure is infinite. This illustrates why finite assignment domains do not make the promise finite.

The general question preserves arbitrary decidable homomorphism restrictions. It is separate from the source’s neighbouring conjecture asking for a particular algebraic criterion for tractability. The finite exponential construction does not remain a finite template when B is infinite, so the known finite-restriction reduction alone does not prove the target.

The completion definition is essential: an algorithm must be correct only on the promised class, yet it must halt on every input. Hardness quantifies over every decidable total extension of that promised behaviour. Saying merely that the intersection of two CSP languages is NP-hard would describe one particular extension and would not prove the required universal hardness.

cards.title: Search tractability of BLP-solvable promise CSPs
cards.formal: For every fixed pair \((A,B)\) of finite relational structures of the same finite signature, with nonempty domains and a homomorphism \(A\to B\), suppose that the basic linear programming relaxation solves the decision problem \(\operatorname{PCSP}(A,B)\). Must there exist a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, on every finite input structure \(X\) promised to satisfy \(X\to A\), outputs a homomorphism \(X\to B\)? The algorithm and its polynomial bound may depend on \(A,B\); the promised homomorphism to \(A\) is not supplied.
cards.why: BLP is a central general-purpose tractability criterion for promise constraints. Determining whether its decision power always entails efficient promised search would clarify when an efficiently recognizable relaxation gap can also support construction of the relaxed object. A separation would expose a basic limitation of decision-to-search equivalence even for finite local relations.

A bounded primary-source search checked on 15 September 2026 found no matching resolution; the preprint proofs were not independently verified.

sentences: A finite promise CSP asks for weakly satisfying assignments when a strongly satisfying assignment is promised.
BLP can recognize the decision gap using compatible local probability distributions.
The question asks whether every fixed template solved by that relaxation also has a deterministic polynomial-time search algorithm on the original promise.

cards.definitions:
A finite signature is a finite list of relation symbols, each with a positive integer arity. A structure \(D\) consists of a domain and, for each symbol \(R\) of arity \(r\), a relation \(R^{D}\subseteq D^{r}\). A homomorphism \(h:D\to E\) is a map such that \((d_1,\ldots,d_{r})\in R^{D}\) implies \((h(d_1),\ldots,h(d_{r}))\in R^{E}\) for every relation. It need not be injective. Write \(D\to E\) if such a map exists. Templates \(A,B\), including their relation tables and signature, are fixed before inputs are supplied.

An input \(X\) has domain \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\geq0\), and explicitly listed relation tuples. Repeated coordinates and empty relations are allowed. For a definite encoding, write \(n\) in unary followed by the relation lists in signature order, each prefixed by its tuple count in unary; each coordinate uses exactly \(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. The total bit length \(L\) counts isolated variables and all tuples. Duplicate listed tuples are harmless. An output is the list of the \(n\) images in the fixed numbered domain of \(B\), or a distinguished failure symbol. The empty instance has the empty homomorphism.

For each \(x\in X,a\in A\), introduce a rational variable \(p_{x}(a)\). For each constraint \(C=(R,(x_1,\ldots,x_{r}))\) of \(X\) and tuple \(t\in R^{A}\), introduce \(q_{C}(t)\). The basic linear programming relaxation, abbreviated BLP, is feasibility of
\[p_{x}(a)\geq0,\quad \sum_{a\in A}p_{x}(a)=1,\qquad q_{C}(t)\geq0,\quad \sum_{t\in R^{A}}q_{C}(t)=1,\]
\[\sum_{\substack{t\in R^{A}\\t_{i}=a}}q_{C}(t)=p_{x_{i}}(a)\qquad\text{for every }C,\ 1\leq i\leq r,\ a\in A.\]
An empty sum is zero. These conditions are imposed at every coordinate even when a variable repeats in a constraint; no extra constraint forces its coordinates to be equal inside each tuple of a local distribution. Rational and real feasibility coincide for this finite rational system. A homomorphism to \(A\) gives an integral feasible point, but feasibility alone need not give such a homomorphism.

BLP solves the decision problem for \((A,B)\) precisely when, for every finite \(X\), feasibility of the displayed system implies \(X\to B\). This makes feasibility a valid test distinguishing \(X\to A\) from \(X\not\to B\). The search guarantee in the question applies only when \(X\to A\). An input that is BLP-feasible but has no homomorphism to \(A\) is outside that search promise, even though it necessarily has a homomorphism to \(B\).

Polynomial-time search means a single deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program, no oracle or advice, that halts on every binary input of length \(L\) within \(C(L+1)^{k}\) bit steps, for positive integers \(C,k\). On valid promised inputs it returns a \(B\)-homomorphism; on other inputs any output is allowed, and malformed inputs may be rejected. The machine and constants depend only on the fixed template. No common exponent across all templates, algorithm for recognizing BLP-solvable templates, or particular rounding procedure is requested.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal implication, or of its logical negation. An affirmative answer must establish a polynomial-time search machine for every fixed finite BLP-solvable template, with the stated promise, output and worst-case bit bound. A negative answer must establish a fixed finite \(A\to B\) satisfying the BLP-solvability hypothesis for which no such polynomial-time promised search machine exists. Difficulty rounding arbitrary feasible LP solutions, undecidability of recognizing templates, or a conditional obstruction to one prescribed algorithm does not prove this negation. An unproved complexity assumption may describe partial progress but does not settle the unconditional target.

context_blocks.text: A promise CSP separates a stronger local requirement from a weaker one. Decision only distinguishes instances satisfying all strong constraints from those failing even the weak constraints. Search must actually assign weak-domain values when a strong assignment is guaranteed to exist. This distinction is absent from the familiar fixed-template CSP case, where decision and search are polynomial-time equivalent.

BLP replaces each variable value by a probability distribution and each constraint by a compatible local distribution. Compatibility checks one-variable marginals, so different constraints may agree locally without yielding a joint strong assignment. The BLP-solvability hypothesis guarantees the existence of a weak assignment whenever these local checks succeed; the question asks for a polynomial-time construction on the stronger promise.

The quantifier over fixed templates matters. A separate finite program may use all the information in its particular template, and its polynomial exponent may depend on that template. Consequently, the question is different from recognizing the class of BLP-solvable pairs from their relation tables.

Larrauri’s May 2026 preprint establishes hardness of finding weak assignments for every BLP-accepted input, with reductions from arbitrary total NP search problems. Its discussion explicitly leaves open whether search is tractable on inputs promised to map to the strong template. A total NP search problem has polynomially bounded, polynomially checkable witnesses and at least one witness for every input; its hardness is a statement about this broader input guarantee.

cards.title: Characterizing CSP languages with linear non-redundancy
cards.formal: Characterize all finite constraint languages \(\Gamma\) over arbitrary finite nonempty domains for which every \(n\)-variable formula has a subformula with at most \(C_\Gamma n\) constraints and exactly the same set of satisfying assignments, for some constant \(C_\Gamma\) independent of the formula and \(n\). Equivalently, determine the class-membership function \(\chi_{\mathrm{lin}}\) on all such finite languages, taking value \(1\) when this property holds and \(0\) otherwise. The target is the full classification from Question 8; it is not restricted to Boolean domains or to a proposed sufficient condition.
cards.why: A full classification would explain which systems of local relations always have a linear-sized exact description using their own constraints. It would organize connections among logical redundancy, sparsification, preprocessing and algebra across all finite domains. The distinction between existence of a small subformula and efficiently finding it is essential to interpreting the result.
cards.status_note: Question 8 in the July 2024 workshop source poses the full classification. The December 2025 Richness revision and May 2026 shrinking manuscript retain it, and the published July 2026 arity-four paper gives only a restricted near-classification. These primary sources were checked on 15 September 2026; bounded later-work searches did not find a full resolution. Proofs and computational classifications were not independently reproduced.

sentences: Non-redundancy measures how many constraints can remain individually essential in a formula.
The question asks which finite languages always allow a subformula with linearly many constraints and the identical set of satisfying assignments.
The number of variables is the size parameter, and the linear constant may depend on the language.
The classification includes all finite domains and does not require an efficient algorithm to find the subformula.
A solution would identify the structural boundary for compact exact descriptions of constraint systems.

cards.definitions:
A language \(\Gamma\) consists of a finite nonempty domain \(D=\{1,\ldots,d\}\) and a finite list of named relations \(R\subseteq D^{r}\), each with a positive integer arity \(r\). Empty and full relations, and the empty list of relations, are permitted. The domain, arities and relation tables give the entire description. A formula \(F\) on variables \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(n\geq1\), is a finite conjunction of constraints \(R(x_1,\ldots,x_{r})\) from this language. Variable repetitions and repeated constraints are permitted. An assignment \(a:V\to D\) satisfies the constraint when \((a(x_1),\ldots,a(x_{r}))\in R\), and satisfies \(F\) when it satisfies every constraint. Write \(\operatorname{Sol}_{D}(F)\subseteq D^{V}\) for this set; it may be empty.

A subformula \(F'\subseteq F\) is obtained only by deleting constraint occurrences, keeping the same variables and domain. It may have isolated variables and no constraints. The preservation requirement is \(\operatorname{Sol}_{D}(F')=\operatorname{Sol}_{D}(F)\), as sets of assignments on the original \(V\). It is stronger than merely preserving whether a satisfying assignment exists. No new constraints, new variables, weights or relaxation of relations are allowed.

Define
\[\operatorname{nr}_\Gamma(n)=\max_{F}\ \min_{\substack{F'\subseteq F\\\operatorname{Sol}_{D}(F')=\operatorname{Sol}_{D}(F)}} |F'|,\]
where \(F\) ranges over all formulas on these \(n\) variables and \(|F'|\) counts constraint occurrences. This maximum is finite: duplicate occurrences do not change solutions, and there are at most \(\sum_{R\in\Gamma}n^{\operatorname{arity}(R)}\) distinct constraints. An equivalent definition is the maximum size of a formula in which every constraint is non-redundant. A constraint \(C\) is non-redundant when there is an assignment satisfying all other constraints but violating \(C\). Unsatisfiable formulas are included; no satisfiability promise is made.

The numerical function being classified is
\[\chi_{\mathrm{lin}}(\Gamma)=\begin{cases}1,&\exists C\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\ \forall n\geq1:\ \operatorname{nr}_\Gamma(n)\leq Cn,\\0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\]
Its domain consists of every finite language just defined, with no global bound on domain size, arity or number of relations. The hidden constant may depend on the whole fixed language. Requiring the bound at all positive \(n\) is equivalent to asymptotic \(O(n)\), since finitely many exceptions can be absorbed in the constant. A bound of \(n\log n\) or \(n^{1+o(1)}\) does not meet it.

This is a mathematical classification of an extremal property. No polynomial-time procedure for finding \(F'\), recognizing languages, or deciding satisfiability is built into the target. A structural criterion or another substantive unambiguous mathematical description of the membership function can specify an answer without a predetermined syntactic form. Introducing the characteristic function records the same classification target, rather than replacing it with an optimal-growth problem for \(\operatorname{nr}_\Gamma\).
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a real-valued function \(g\) on the stated full domain and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that \(|g(\Gamma)-\chi_{\mathrm{lin}}(\Gamma)|\leq1/100\) for every finite language \(\Gamma\). An exact necessary-and-sufficient characterization of class membership also qualifies. The supplied description must determine membership substantively; merely renaming the defining optimization or repeating that a language is linear exactly when it has linear non-redundancy is not an answer. No efficient recognition algorithm is required. Prove both membership and nonmembership sides of the characterization, including all domains and arities. A sufficient algebraic condition, a finite table of small languages, a near-linear bound or a decision-preserving kernel alone does not settle the full target.

source_formulation.text: Which finite constraint languages allow every formula to be reduced to linearly many of its own constraints while preserving all satisfying assignments?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of PACS 2024 Question 8

context_blocks.text: A constraint can be logically unnecessary even when its relation occurs many times. For example, equality constraints connecting a set of variables can often be deleted while preserving the same equality requirements on all assignments. Non-redundancy asks how large a collection can remain when every member has its own witness to being essential.

This is a question about the amount of information in a system, not the difficulty of finding a satisfying assignment. Some NP-hard fixed predicates have linear non-redundancy. Conversely, the binary positive-OR relation has quadratic non-redundancy despite the simplicity of deciding its satisfiability. These contrasting examples separate this classification from the usual tractability dichotomy.

The 2020 Boolean work supplies linear sparsification through representations by degree-one equations over integer rings. The December 2025 manuscript identifies the Boolean languages admitting the more general Mal’tsev embedding condition with the corresponding balanced class, while exhibiting genuinely noncommutative behavior on larger domains. This clarifies known sufficient conditions without proving that they capture all languages with linear non-redundancy.

The 2025 manuscript realizes every rational non-redundancy exponent at least one over suitable finite domains. The resulting range is much richer than a choice between linear growth and the trivial maximal-arity bound. It does not supply a complete description of the languages at the linear endpoint.
The 2026 shrinking paper develops further superlinear lower bounds while retaining the general linear or near-linear classification as an open question.
The CP 2026 paper almost classifies Boolean arity four, leaving one predicate unresolved and exhibiting non-polynomial asymptotics. This is a restricted family within the all-language target.

cards.title: Common polynomial exponent for tractable digraph CSPs
cards.formal: Does there exist an integer \(c\geq1\) such that, for every fixed finite digraph \(H\) for which \(\operatorname{CSP}(H)\) is in \(\mathrm P\), there are a deterministic algorithm \(M_{H}\) and a constant \(C_{H}\geq1\) that decide whether an input digraph \(G\) admits a homomorphism to \(H\) in at most \(C_{H}(L+1)^{c}\) bit steps, where \(L\) is the input encoding length? The exponent must be independent of \(H\), while both the machine and multiplicative constant may depend on \(H\).
cards.why: The finite CSP dichotomy classifies each fixed set of local relations qualitatively. A common exponent would add a quantitative uniformity principle to this classification. Its failure would show that polynomial-time digraph CSPs can require arbitrarily large exponents even though every individual template is tractable.

cards.definitions:
A finite digraph \(G=(V_{G},E_{G})\) has a finite vertex set and a relation \(E_{G}\subseteq V_{G}\times V_{G}\); loops and both orientations of a pair are permitted. A homomorphism \(h:G\to H\) is a map such that \((u,v)\in E_{G}\) implies \((h(u),h(v))\in E_{H}\). It need not be injective or preserve nonedges. The problem \(\operatorname{CSP}(H)\) asks whether such a map exists. The target \(H\) is finite and nonempty, and is fixed before inputs are supplied. Including the empty target adds only a trivial decision problem and does not change existence of a common exponent.

Number the vertices of \(G\) by \(1,\ldots,n\), with \(n\geq0\). Encode \(n\) in unary followed by the number of listed edges in unary, each terminated by a zero, and then their endpoint pairs, with \(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits per coordinate. Duplicate listed edges denote the same edge and still count toward the bit length \(L\); all labels must be valid. This representation counts isolated vertices. Algorithms reject malformed encodings. They are deterministic multitape Turing machines with finite programs and no oracle or advice; all reading, writing and intermediate bit operations count. Bounds are worst-case and answers must always be correct.

By \(\operatorname{CSP}(H)\in\mathrm P\) we mean existence of such a decider with a polynomial bound whose exponent may depend on \(H\). The question's quantifier order is \(\exists c\geq1\;\forall H\;\exists M_{H},C_{H}\), restricted to tractable \(H\), with correctness and the stated time bound for every input. No procedure producing \(M_{H}\) from \(H\) is required. The graph \(H\) is not part of the varying input or its length \(L\).

The author separately asks for one machine receiving \(G,H\), running in \(f(|H|)(L+1)^{c}\) time for a computable function \(f\) under the tractability promise. That fixed-parameter tractability assertion implies this card's assertion but is stronger. Polynomial time in the combined descriptions is stronger still. The inherited label “uniform” left these distinctions unresolved; this formulation recovers the main fixed-template source question.

The source permits conditional refutation by fine-grained assumptions. This card admits deterministic SETH as one explicitly specified assumption: for every real \(\delta>0\) there is an integer \(k\geq3\) such that Boolean \(k\)-SAT has no deterministic algorithm running in \(O(2^{(1-\delta)v}S^{d})\) time for any constant \(d\). Here \(v\) is the number of variables, \(S\) the explicit input bit length, and \(k\)-SAT asks satisfiability of a conjunction of clauses containing at most \(k\) signed Boolean variables. The assumption concerns worst-case inputs of unbounded size.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the common-exponent assertion or its negation. Following the source's express allowance, a Lean proof that deterministic SETH implies the negation is also an accepted answer and must be labelled conditional on SETH. No other unproved assumption is implicitly accepted. A negative answer must establish that for every proposed exponent \(c\), some tractable finite digraph template \(H\) has no correct deterministic \(O((L+1)^{c})\) decider, even with a template-specific machine and multiplicative constant. Refuting one algorithm or showing superpolynomial dependence on template size is insufficient. An affirmative proof need not give one algorithm receiving arbitrary template tables.

source_formulation.text: Is there one polynomial degree sufficient for every tractable fixed digraph CSP, with the template held fixed when input complexity is measured?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the main source question

context_blocks.text: A graph homomorphism assigns each input vertex a target vertex while respecting every directed edge. Holding the target fixed defines one decision problem. The finite CSP dichotomy says that each problem is polynomial-time solvable or NP-complete, but the existence of separate polynomial algorithms does not itself supply a common exponent.

The question concerns a quantitative distinction within tractability: whether separate template-dependent polynomial degrees can always be replaced by a single constant. The programs and hidden multiplicative factors may remain different, and those factors need not be practical.

Bodirsky and Weiß’s 2026 paper studies the stronger question of time polynomial in both explicitly listed structures and its relationship to finding operations that preserve relations. Its introduction says this fully uniform problem is open even for important subclasses. That does not by itself prove that the weaker common-exponent problem here is open or false.

The source explicitly allows a fine-grained conditional lower bound. Such a result would have to establish unbounded input-exponent requirements among tractable templates, with each individual template fixed while its input graphs grow. A lower bound arising only because the target itself grows has different quantifiers.

cards.title: Polynomial kernels for Boolean MinCSP
cards.formal: Classify all fixed finite Boolean constraint languages \(\Gamma\) for which \(\operatorname{MinCSP}(\Gamma)\), parameterized by the allowed number \(k\) of violated constraints, admits a randomized polynomial kernel. Equivalently, determine the membership function \(\chi_{\mathrm{ker}}(\Gamma)\in\{0,1\}\) of this class for every finite Boolean language. Deterministic kernels also qualify; the target retains the full language classification and the allowance for randomization in PACS 2024 Question 9.
cards.why: This would classify the full preprocessing power of finite Boolean constraint languages after the fixed-parameter solvability boundary is known. It asks which nearly satisfiable systems admit a compact equivalent core whose size depends only polynomially on the repair budget. The source allows randomization so that the classification addresses this compression boundary without also demanding derandomization of established kernels.
cards.status_note: The July 2024 workshop poses the full polynomial-kernel classification. The April 2025 full dichotomy manuscript still treats it as a future classification, and the checked SWAT 2026 theorem concerns a different preprocessing guarantee. Bounded primary-source searches on 15 September 2026 found no full kernelization classification. This is a sourced open-status assessment, not an exhaustive proof that no later resolution exists.
