sentences: Boolean MinCSP asks whether an assignment can violate at most a specified number of constraints.
The question seeks all finite Boolean languages admitting polynomial kernels in that violation budget.
A kernel must run in polynomial time and output a same-problem instance with polynomially many parameter-dependent bits.
Randomization is allowed, and the recorded complexity assumption may support lower bounds for the excluded languages.
A classification would reveal which nearly feasible constraint systems admit efficient compression beyond their known fixed-parameter algorithms.

cards.definitions:
A finite Boolean constraint language \(\Gamma\) is a finite list of named relations \(R\subseteq\{0,1\}^{r}\), each of positive integer arity \(r\), described by its complete finite table. Empty relations, full relations and the empty language are allowed. For each individual decision problem \(\Gamma\) is fixed, including its maximum arity. There is no global bound on arity or on the number of relations when classifying languages.

An instance is \((F,k)\), where \(k\in\mathbb N\) and \(F\) is a finite set of constraints \(R(x_1,\ldots,x_{r})\) on variables \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\geq0\). Coordinates may repeat. The set convention follows §1.1 of the cited dichotomy; repeated listings of the identical named constraint do not create extra cost. An assignment \(a:V\to\{0,1\}\) violates a constraint when \((a(x_1),\ldots,a(x_{r}))\notin R\). Let \(\operatorname{opt}_\Gamma(F)\) be the minimum number of violated constraints over all assignments. The instance is yes exactly when \(\operatorname{opt}_\Gamma(F)\leq k\), equivalently when deleting at most \(k\) constraints makes the rest satisfiable. All constraints have unit cost and may be deleted; there are no separately undeletable constraints or freely supplied constant assignments.

Use an explicit binary input encoding: unary \(n\) and constraint count, each followed by zero; each constraint has a relation index in the fixed language and a tuple of variable indices of width \(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\); finish with the length-prefixed binary representation of \(k\). The full length \(L\) includes isolated variables and the parameter bits. Output instances use the same convention. Encodings can be normalized to remove duplicate constraints in polynomial time.

A randomized polynomial kernel for a fixed \(\Gamma\) is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(K_\Gamma\) using independent fair coin flips, with no oracle or advice. There are positive integer constants \(C,d,e\), depending on \(\Gamma\) only, such that on every valid input \((F,k)\), and for every sequence of coin outcomes, it halts within \(C(L+1)^{e}\) bit steps and outputs a valid instance \((F',k')\) of the same \(\operatorname{MinCSP}(\Gamma)\) with total encoding length at most \(C(k+1)^{d}\). Require
\[\Pr\bigl[\operatorname{opt}_\Gamma(F)\leq k\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \operatorname{opt}_\Gamma(F')\leq k'\bigr]\geq 2/3.\]
This is a worst-case guarantee for each input over the kernel's internal randomness; both kinds of error are allowed. The original workshop permits randomized kernels without fixing an error convention; bounded two-sided error and an all-runs size bound are recorded here explicitly. A deterministic kernel has probability one. The machine may create new variables and constraints from the same fixed language. It need not preserve the optimum or the entire solution set, and need not be a subformula reduction.

Define \(\chi_{\mathrm{ker}}(\Gamma)=1\) if such a machine and constants exist, and \(0\) otherwise. Its classification is over all finite language tables. No uniform machine for recognizing the class is demanded. A polynomial kernel is different from an algorithm taking \(f(k)(L+1)^{e}\) time for an arbitrary computable function \(f\), and from a compression to an instance of a different decision problem. A bound in the variable count \(n\) alone is not a bound in the parameter \(k\).

The source allows standard complexity assumptions for the lower-bound side. This card fixes the customary hypothesis \(\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\) as an admissible conditional premise. Here \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of binary languages with polynomially bounded certificates verifiable by deterministic polynomial-time machines. A language is in \(\mathrm{NP}/\mathrm{poly}\) when such a verifier may also receive an arbitrary advice string of polynomial length depending only on input length; advice need not be computable. A language is in \(\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\) when its complement is in \(\mathrm{NP}/\mathrm{poly}\). The stated noncontainment means that some NP language lacks such a complement verifier. It is an assumption, not a proved theorem or a conclusion automatically obtained from any parameterized hardness result.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a substantive mathematical characterization, represented by a real-valued function \(g\) on all finite Boolean languages, and prove in Lean that \(|g(\Gamma)-\chi_{\mathrm{ker}}(\Gamma)|\leq1/100\) for every \(\Gamma\). An exact necessary-and-sufficient classification also qualifies. For every class identified as admitting a kernel, establish the stated machine, runtime, size and per-input error guarantees without an unproved assumption. For every excluded class, prove nonexistence of such a randomized kernel either unconditionally or under the explicitly stated hypothesis \(\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\), labelling the classification conditional when used. The required lower bounds must cover the allowed randomized model. Merely renaming the defining kernel-existence predicate, classifying only fixed-parameter tractability, excluding only deterministic kernels, or solving finitely many languages does not settle the question. No algorithm efficiently recognizing the class from language tables is required.

source_formulation.text: For which Boolean constraint languages can instances be reduced in polynomial time to equivalent instances of size polynomial in the permitted number of unsatisfied constraints, allowing randomized reductions and standard conditional lower bounds?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of PACS 2024 Question 9

context_blocks.text: A small number of violated constraints represents a small repair to an otherwise feasible system. Fixed-parameter tractability permits expensive work that depends only on that repair budget. A polynomial kernel asks instead for polynomial-time preprocessing that compresses all subsequent difficulty into a number of bits bounded polynomially in the budget. These demands can have different boundaries.

Almost 2-SAT is the language consisting of all Boolean clauses with at most two literals, viewed as individual relations. Its randomized polynomial kernel is an established positive example. The workshop includes it explicitly to allow randomization; requiring deterministic kernels would add a further unresolved issue from that example.

The completed FPT dichotomy of Kim, Kratsch, Pilipczuk and Wahlström distinguishes which Boolean MinCSPs admit algorithms with parameter-dependent overhead. It also distinguishes weighted and unweighted variants. This card uses the unweighted problem and asks the subsequent preprocessing classification, which their revised manuscript still presents as a further question.

The SWAT 2026 essential-constraint theorem concerns identifying constraints that occur in all sufficiently good repair sets. That preprocessing can improve the effective search parameter, but does not assert that the entire instance shrinks to polynomial size in the original violation budget. The same paper distinguishes results about compression measured by the number of variables.

cards.title: Polynomial-time tractability testing for core crisp CSP languages
cards.formal: Is there one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite crisp constraint language \(\Gamma\) over an explicitly given finite domain D and promised that \(\Gamma\) is a core, decides whether \(\Gamma\) admits an idempotent Siggers polymorphism? Equivalently on the core promise, decide whether \(\Gamma\) is solvable in the algebraic sense of the finite-domain CSP dichotomy. The polynomial must be uniform in the entire input, including |D|, the number of relations, their arities and their listed tuples; neither a polymorphism nor a tractability certificate is supplied.
cards.why: Would make the finite-domain CSP tractability criterion efficiently recognizable when the core is already given, connecting the structural dichotomy to algorithms whose template also varies as input.
cards.status_note: Checked the source’s encoding, core definition and algebraic solvability convention, its complete April 2019 version, and the explicit ICALP 2026 discussion following Theorem 4. Broader searches through 12 September 2026 found no polynomial core-crisp Siggers test or matching promised-core hardness result. The 2026 primary source directly supports continued openness; search is not exhaustive.

cards.definitions: A crisp language is a finite set \(\Gamma\) of relations \(R\subseteq D\)ʳ of possibly different finite arities on a finite nonempty explicitly listed domain D. Each relation is given by its arity and a list of its allowed tuples; unlisted tuples are forbidden. This is equivalent to a cost function with value 0 on allowed tuples and +∞ elsewhere. The input size N includes D, relation delimiters, arities and the binary encodings of all listed entries. There is no fixed bound on |D| or arity imposed outside the input. An m-ary operation \(g:D^{m}\to D\) preserves an r-ary relation R if, for every m tuples \(a^{1},\ldots ,a^{m}\in R\), the coordinatewise tuple \((g(a^{1}_{1},\ldots ,a^{m}_{1}),\ldots ,g(a^{1}_{r},\ldots ,a^{m}_{r}))\) lies in R. A polymorphism of \(\Gamma\) preserves every relation in \(\Gamma\). The language is a core if every unary polymorphism \(u:D\to D\) is bijective; for a finite relational structure such a map is an automorphism. Core status is promised rather than something the requested algorithm must verify. An idempotent Siggers polymorphism is a four-ary operation \(s:D^{4}\to D\) that preserves every relation and satisfies \(s(x,x,x,x)=x\) for all \(x\in D\) and \(s(r,a,r,e)=s(a,r,e,a)\) for every \(r,a,e\in D\). On a core, existence of a Siggers operation without the idempotence identity is equivalent to existence of an idempotent one. An ordinary \(\mathrm{CSP}(\Gamma )\) instance has variables and constraints requiring selected variable tuples to belong to relations of \(\Gamma\); it asks for a satisfying assignment from D. In the source’s terminology, solvable means satisfying the dichotomy’s polymorphism criterion. Such languages have polynomial-time CSP algorithms when \(\Gamma\) is fixed; failure of the criterion gives NP-hardness. The present target tests that algebraic criterion and does not assume \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) in order to define its yes/no answers. The requested machine must halt in \(N^{O(1)}\) time on all inputs and be correct on every input satisfying the core promise. Its behavior on non-core inputs is unrestricted. The task only asks to decide existence, not to output the operation table, although a four-ary table has |\(D|^{4}\) entries and gives a polynomial-size, polynomially checkable existence certificate.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a deterministic algorithm with one polynomial running-time bound in N that accepts exactly the promised core languages having such a polymorphism, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A hardness statement requires the core promise to be respected. Testing whether the input is a core, classifying languages without that promise, or solving CSP instances for one fixed tractable template does not settle this meta-decision problem.

cards.definitions:
A finite relational signature \(\tau\) is a finite list of relation symbols of fixed positive integer arities. A template \(\Gamma\) interprets these symbols as relations on a nonempty domain, which may be finite or infinite. A finite input structure \(I\) has domain \([n]\), \(n\geq0\), and an explicit list of tuples for each symbol. A homomorphism \(h:I\to\Gamma\) preserves all listed positive relation tuples; it need not be injective or preserve absence of tuples. The language \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\) accepts exactly such inputs with a homomorphism. Repeated coordinates and isolated elements are allowed, and the empty structure maps to every template.

Encode \(n\) in unary and then each relation’s unary list length followed by binary tuple indices, in signature order, with delimiters. Let \(L\) be total bit length; invalid encodings are rejected. Membership in NP means that there is a deterministic Turing verifier and a polynomial \(p\) such that a valid input is accepted exactly when it has a binary certificate of length at most \(p(L)\) accepted by the verifier within \(p(L)\) bit steps. The template and signature are fixed; no effective presentation or homomorphism oracle for the infinite domain is an input. No complexity separation is assumed.

An SNP sentence over the input signature \(\tau\) has form
\[\Phi=\exists S_1\cdots\exists S_t\ \forall x_1\cdots\forall x_q\ \psi,\]
where the \(S_j\) are fresh relation symbols of fixed finite positive arities and \(\psi\) is a quantifier-free first-order formula using input relations, the new relations, equality, Boolean connectives and the displayed individual variables. Truth constants are allowed. The formula, the numbers \(t,q\) and all arities are fixed independently of input size. On \(I\), the existential quantifiers choose relations on the same domain \([n]\); the universal quantifiers range over all tuples of input elements. There is no built-in order, arithmetic, constant naming input elements, or auxiliary larger universe. General arities are allowed: SNP is not restricted to unary second-order predicates. The empty-domain convention is the usual one for universal sentences, consistent with accepting the empty CSP input.

Exact SNP definability means \(I\models\Phi\) if and only if \(I\to\Gamma\) for every finite \(\tau\)-structure \(I\). There is no reduction or change of input signature hidden in this equivalence. A fixed SNP sentence has polynomial-size guessed relation tables and polynomially many universal tuples to check, so it always defines an NP problem. Arbitrary existential second-order sentences may contain alternating first-order quantifiers; restricting that part to a universal block is the additional requirement here.

For the known structural reformulation, a finite-signature structure \(C\) is finitely bounded if a finite list \(\mathcal N\) of finite structures in its signature satisfies
\[D\text{ embeds into }C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{no }N\in\mathcal N\text{ embeds into }D\]
for every finite \(D\). An embedding is an injective map preserving both relation membership and nonmembership, so the bounds are forbidden induced patterns. The age of \(C\) is the class of its finite induced substructures up to isomorphism. For signatures \(\tau\subseteq\sigma\), the reduct \(C\upharpoonright\tau\) forgets the symbols in \(\sigma\setminus\tau\) and keeps the same domain and remaining relations. No homogeneity or omega-categoricity is required. The representing reduct may differ from the original template; equality of their finite-instance CSPs is what matters.

The source classification direction concerns templates, or equivalently their finite-instance CSP classes. It does not specify an algorithm receiving finite descriptions of infinite structures. A countable representative suffices: choose one solution image for each satisfiable finite instance and take the induced substructure on their countable union.
cards.answer_criterion: A precise completion criterion still requires selecting the additional structural characterization or effectiveness requirement intended beyond the known logical-to-forbidden-pattern representation. The source does not prescribe such a requirement. Merely restating SNP definability by existence of a finite universal expansion is insufficient to certify that this historical research direction is resolved; no particular stronger criterion is selected here.

context_blocks.text:
The following exact representation theorem is known:
\[\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\in\mathrm{SNP}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists\sigma\supseteq\tau\ \exists C\ \bigl[C\text{ is countable and finitely bounded over finite }\sigma\ \land\ \operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)=\operatorname{CSP}(C\upharpoonright\tau)\bigr].\]
This equivalence is a structural reformulation of SNP definability, not a separately stated solution of the historical classification question. The equality is on all finite structures in the original signature. The LICS 2026 introduction explicitly identifies this class correspondence. It allows arbitrary finite bounds and auxiliary relations; homogeneity is not an extra condition.

For the forward direction, every CSP is closed under inverse homomorphisms and under disjoint unions. The monograph shows that an SNP sentence defining such a class can be chosen monotone and connected. Monotone means that input relations occur only negatively in clauses; connected means that each clause’s variables are connected through its negative relation literals. These are normal-form transformations of the given problem, not changes to the accepted inputs.

Consider all finite expanded structures satisfying the universal first-order part of that connected sentence. This class is closed under induced substructures, and connectedness makes it closed under disjoint unions. The disjoint union of one representative of each finite isomorphism type is therefore a countable structure whose age is exactly this class. Since the universal formula mentions only finitely many variables, its failures have finitely many minimal finite induced patterns, giving a finite bound list. Forgetting the guessed relations produces a template with exactly the original CSP.

Conversely, a CSP of a reduct of a finitely bounded structure is described in SNP by guessing equality classes for variables and the missing relational pattern on their prospective values. Universal clauses enforce congruence, the original positive constraints and avoidance of the finitely many forbidden induced patterns. The resulting quotient pattern embeds into the representing structure precisely when those constraints pass. This supplies finite universal certificates even when the domain of the representing template is infinite.

The representation concerns some template with the same CSP. It does not assert that the particular supplied template has a finitely bounded expansion, nor provide a uniform recognition algorithm for arbitrary infinite presentations. The 2008 question specifies neither of these stronger requirements. Choosing one, or choosing a particular algebraic invariant, would supply a new completion target rather than merely unpack its notation.

The monograph’s integer-successor example shows why omega-categoricity must not be added to this answer. Its CSP is definable in connected monotone SNP, but cannot be represented by an omega-categorical template with the same accepted finite structures. Thus SNP definability and the symmetry assumptions of infinite-domain dichotomy conjectures are distinct.

The 2026 paper separately studies extensional SNP and CSPs of finitely bounded structures before forgetting relations. These are distinct settings. Its discussion supplies the exact representation theorem above, but does not explicitly identify it as a resolution of the 2008 classification question. The distinction between a structural reformulation and the intended new classification therefore remains material.

Exact representation by reducts of finitely bounded structures is already known through a translation of the universal existential expansion; no checked later source identifies that reformulation as resolving the historical question. A completion criterion must specify what substantive new invariant or effectiveness requirement is sought beyond this known equivalence. Selecting one would add a target absent from the source.

cards.title: Word equations with linear length constraints
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine which halts on every input consisting of a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\), a finite system of word equations \(U_i=V_i\) and a finite conjunction of integer linear equalities and inequalities on variable lengths, and answers YES exactly when they admit a simultaneous solution in the free monoid \(\Sigma^*\)? The alphabet, equations, variables and arithmetic coefficients are all part of the input. No bound on the running time is prescribed.
cards.definitions: The alphabet \(\Sigma\) is a finite nonempty set of constant letters. The finite set of variables \(X=\{X_1,\ldots,X_k\}\) is disjoint from \(\Sigma\); \(k\) may be zero. Each side \(U_i,V_i\) is an explicitly written finite word over \(\Sigma\cup X\), including the empty word. A substitution \(\sigma:X\to\Sigma^*\) assigns one finite word to each variable and extends by concatenation while fixing each constant letter. Every occurrence of a variable receives the same word, and empty substitutions are allowed. Each equation requires literal equality \(\sigma(U_i)=\sigma(V_i)\). The length \(|w|\) of a word is its number of letters. Each arithmetic atom has the form \(\sum_{j=1}^{k}a_j|\sigma(X_j)|\le b\) or \(\sum_{j=1}^{k}a_j|\sigma(X_j)|=b\), with signed binary integer coefficients and constants. Every supplied atom must hold for the same substitution as every equation. Empty lists of equations or constraints are allowed and mean the empty conjunction. Alphabet and variable symbols have finite identifiers; equation sides are explicit lists and arithmetic atoms are explicit coefficient lists. Nothing is given as a circuit or a compressed word. The machine is one uniform program over all input sizes, alphabet sizes, variable counts, equation counts and coefficient values; it halts on both positive and negative instances. Malformed inputs may be rejected. Only existential choice of the substituted words is involved. There is no variable-times-variable product of lengths, individual-letter count, regular-language predicate, string-to-integer conversion or universal string quantifier. Nonempty-variable requirements are expressible by \(-|\sigma(X_j)|\le-1\), but they are not imposed unless present in the input. This is exact satisfiability, with no random error, oracle, numerical tolerance or complexity bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean proof that a total computable YES/NO procedure exists for exactly the encoded input class above, or that no such procedure exists. A positive answer must verify termination on every input and equivalence of YES with existence of one simultaneous substitution satisfying all word and arithmetic constraints. It need not output a substitution or satisfy a time bound. A negative answer must prove noncomputability for this length-only existential conjunction problem; a result using extra predicates, stronger quantification, or a failure of one particular procedure does not suffice. Acceptance is exact and has no numerical tolerance. This editorial audit does not supply a Lean formalization.
cards.why: A fundamental boundary for reasoning about concatenation and numerical size simultaneously. It governs whether a complete terminating solver can exist for a basic fragment of string constraints used in verification, while connecting free-monoid equations, arithmetic and reachability.

importance.reason: A longstanding decidability question at the intersection of formal languages, number-theoretic constraints and automated verification; even unrestricted termination is unknown, before asking for efficient algorithms.

context_blocks.text: The two ingredients are separately decidable: plain word equations by Makanin’s theorem and integer linear arithmetic by Presburger’s theorem. Their combination constrains both letter alignment and numerical size, and neither theorem alone settles their interaction.

Length identities can omit crucial content. For distinct letters \(a,b\), the word equation \(Xa=bX\) has no finite-word solution, although its induced length equality \(|X|+1=1+|X|\) is always satisfied. This illustrates why the target concerns a common word substitution, not merely a consistent length vector.

Restrictions on counts of individual letters, full Parikh vectors or additional quantifier alternation can yield different decidability results. Those predicates do not occur in the present input language. The distinction is explicit in Ciobanu’s survey.

Day and Konefal prove decidability for quadratic equations with at most two unknowns and semilinear constraints on their solution lengths. Quadratic means each unknown appears at most twice across the equation. Their RP 2025 paper appeared online in November 2025; its proceedings carry a 2026 copyright year. This restricted theorem does not cover an arbitrary system with unrestricted variable occurrences.

The IJCAR 2026 paper gives a sufficient termination condition and a partial converse for extended Nielsen transformations. The theorem concerns a specific procedure and a graph condition on an extended equation; it does not establish that every input of the unrestricted satisfiability problem is decidable. Its full preprint explicitly retains the general open question.

The checked July 2026 preprint states NEXP-hardness for nonerasing satisfiability of positive Boolean combinations of word equations and Presburger length constraints over two letters. Its NEXP-completeness theorem concerns existential arithmetic with divisibility. These are distinct claims, and neither is a decision procedure or an undecidability proof for the current card.

The saved target is a conjunction, while that lower-bound corollary permits disjunctions. Finite expansion relates their decidability questions, but need not preserve polynomial input size; the corollary is therefore not presented here as a checked NEXP lower bound for the exact conjunction encoding. Allowing empty substitutions is likewise kept distinct from the preprint’s nonerasing convention.

cards.title: Decidability of unification in the basic modal logic K
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that halts on every finite modal formula \(\varphi\) and decides whether there exists a substitution \(\sigma\) for its propositional variables such that \(\sigma (\varphi )\) is valid on every Kripke frame?
cards.why: Determines whether automated reasoning can decide the existence of a validity-making substitution in the basic normal modal logic, despite the decidability of checking each individual instance and the poorly behaved structure of its unifiers.

Beklemishev’s 2025 introduction explicitly states it as open. Nullary unification type, undecidability with extra modalities and 2025 decidability for K5 extensions do not settle it.

cards.definitions: Formulas are finite expressions generated by variables \(p_{i} (i\in \mathbb{N} ), \perp\), negation, conjunction and the unary operator □; other Boolean connectives and ◇ are abbreviations. Variable indices use binary notation and formulas are supplied as fully written syntax trees. A substitution assigns a finite formula to each variable occurring in \(\varphi\), may use new propositional variables, and extends simultaneously through the connectives and □; it does not substitute recursively inside its newly inserted formulas. There are no distinguished parameters that must remain unchanged. A frame is a nonempty set W with an arbitrary relation \(R\subseteq \mathrm{W}\times \mathrm{W}\), finite or infinite. A valuation assigns a subset of W to every variable. Satisfaction uses the usual truth tables, ⊥ is false everywhere, and \(w\models\)□\(\psi\) iff \(v\models \psi\) for all v with wRv. Validity means satisfaction at every world in every frame with every valuation. This is the basic normal modal logic K, with no reflexivity, transitivity or seriality requirement on R. The substitution is existentially quantified without a length bound. Only its existence is decided; no running-time bound or output unifier is required. Malformed formula encodings are rejected.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a total decision procedure correct for every finite formula in the stated language, or prove that no such Turing machine exists. The unbounded substitution and arbitrary-frame semantics must remain those of parameter-free, single-modality K.

upgraded_from.title: Decidability of unification in the basic modal logic K

references.title: Research reference · www.mathnet.ru

context_blocks.text: A modal formula talks about truth at a world and at worlds accessible from it. Unification asks whether its variables can be replaced by formulas so that the result becomes valid on every frame. This is a global requirement on one syntactic replacement, shared across all worlds and models. Choosing a satisfying assignment in one model is a different and weaker task.

For example, □p is unifiable: replacing p by ⊤ makes it valid. In contrast, ◇p is satisfiable in a model with an accessible world where p holds, but has no unifier in K. At a world with no successors, ◇\(\psi\) is false for every replacement \(\psi\). Such dead ends are allowed by K’s unrestricted frame semantics. These examples distinguish satisfiability from the existence of a valid substitution instance.

For any proposed finite substitution, validity of the resulting K formula is decidable. Enumerating all finite substitutions therefore eventually finds a witness whenever one exists. The unresolved part is a procedure that also halts and answers no on every nonunifiable formula. A search that works only for positive instances does not give the requested decider. There is no time bound in this question.

Jeřábek’s theorem that K has nullary unification type concerns the organization of all unifiers, not their nonexistence. For the formula \(p\to\)□p, unifiers exist, including \(p\mapsto \top\), but they lack a complete irredundant family under the usual instantiation order. In that order, a unifier is more general when other unifiers arise by further substitution, modulo equivalence in K. The theorem blocks a particularly well-behaved classification of witnesses; it does not prove undecidability of whether any witness exists.

The choice of logic changes the problem. Wolter and Zakharyaschev prove undecidability after adding a universal modality, which can state that a formula holds at every world of a model. That extra operator is absent here. Their other negative results also add modalities and nominals. A decidable validity problem can thus coexist with undecidable unification, but those extension results do not settle basic K.

Positive results for stronger frame conditions likewise require care. Gougeon’s 2025 work computes most general unifiers for extensions of K5, including versions with fixed parameters. K5 imposes a Euclidean condition on accessibility: two successors of one world must be accessible from one another in the appropriate direction. K does not impose that condition. Beklemishev’s 2025 paper explicitly separates the open K case from solved transitive logics.

A resolution would locate a basic limit of automated substitution reasoning: can the simplest normal modal logic recognize when an expression can be made universally valid? The target concerns only existence. Constructing every unifier, deciding admissibility of arbitrary inference rules, or finding a most general unifier asks additional questions.

cards.title: Decidability of Presburger arithmetic with primes
cards.formal: Is the full first-order theory of the fixed structure \[\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{Pr}}=(\mathbb Z;0,1,+,-,<,\mathrm{Pr})\] decidable, where \(\mathrm{Pr}(n)\) means that \(n\ge2\) is a positive prime? Equivalently, does there exist one deterministic Turing machine which halts on every finite encoded sentence \(\varphi\) of this language and returns YES exactly when \(\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{Pr}}\models\varphi\)? The question is unconditional and permits arbitrary finite first-order quantifier alternation.
cards.why: Addition and order alone admit a complete decision procedure, while the prime predicate brings the distribution of primes into quantified arithmetic without directly adding multiplication. This is a classical boundary question linking effective first-order reasoning, definability and deep number theory. The standard ordered structure can express prime-pattern assertions, so a truth decider would have consequences far beyond individual primality tests.
cards.status_note: The FSTTCS 2024 survey explicitly leaves this full decision problem open. The checked 1993 theorem is conditional on linear Schinzel/Dickson prime-tuples assumptions, and the 2017 conditional positive result uses the different unordered symmetric-prime structure. The 16 September 2026 bounded primary-source search found no matching unconditional resolution; source-open is a dated attribution, not certification of present openness.

sentences: Presburger arithmetic describes the standard integers using addition and order and has a decidable first-order theory.
This question adds a predicate for positive primes and asks for one algorithm deciding every sentence, with arbitrary quantifier alternation.

cards.definitions: All variables range over the standard integers \(\mathbb Z\). The symbols \(0,1,+,-,<\) denote their usual constants, addition, unary negation and strict order. The predicate \(\mathrm{Pr}\) is false for negative integers, zero and one; for \(n\ge2\), it is true exactly when the only positive divisors of \(n\) are \(1\) and \(n\). This defines the intended predicate in the mathematical metatheory; multiplication and variable divisibility are not additional symbols of the input language. Terms are variables, integer numerals, sums and negatives. Atoms are term equality, strict inequality and \(\mathrm{Pr}(t)\); formulas use the ordinary Boolean connectives and individual-variable \(\exists,\forall\). A sentence has no free variables. Arbitrary signed integer numerals and multiplication by a specified integer coefficient are harmless abbreviations for expressions in this language, not products of two variables. Inputs are explicit finite syntax trees with variable identifiers and numerals encoded in binary. Malformed encodings may be rejected. The machine is uniform over all formula lengths, variable counts and alternation depths, with no prescribed resource bound, randomness or oracle. It must give exact truth in this one intended structure, rather than satisfiability over arbitrary structures or provability from an unspecified axiom set. There is no numerical tolerance. Removing the definable unary-negation symbol does not change decidability: its graph is \(x+y=0\).
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean proof that such a total computable truth classifier exists, or that none exists. A positive proof must formalize finite syntax, satisfaction in the standard integer structure, the algorithm, termination on every sentence and correctness in both truth directions. A negative proof must establish noncomputability of this exact full theory. A result conditional on an unproved number-theoretic hypothesis must discharge that hypothesis to meet the unconditional criterion. Deciding a quantifier-restricted fragment or testing the primality of a supplied integer does not cover the target. No Lean formalization is supplied by this editorial review.

source_formulation.text: Is Presburger arithmetic extended by the predicate for positive prime numbers decidable?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the source question in its integer-and-order convention

context_blocks.text: Presburger arithmetic allows arbitrary first-order quantification but restricts its numerical operations to addition, order and fixed integer coefficients. Adding one decidable predicate can still change decidability of the full theory: the issue is the interaction with unbounded quantifiers, not the cost of evaluating that predicate at a known integer.

The source works over integers and writes an order-based twin-prime sentence. Accordingly, this card includes order and takes primes to be positive. For example, the twin-prime assertion is \(\forall x\,\exists y\,(x\le y\land\mathrm{Pr}(y)\land\mathrm{Pr}(y+2))\).

The source also invokes Goldbach’s conjecture. Its even-input restriction must be explicit: one correct sentence is \(\forall n\,(n\ge2\Rightarrow\exists p\,\exists q\,(\mathrm{Pr}(p)\land\mathrm{Pr}(q)\land p+q=n+n))\). The printed illustrative sentence on p. 29 omits that restriction; the open decision question itself does not depend on this typo.

Bateman, Jockusch and Woods prove, assuming the linear case of Schinzel’s hypothesis, that multiplication is definable in the natural-number structure with addition and primes, yielding undecidability. The nonnegative integers are definable in the ordered integer structure, so this conditional obstruction applies to the present target too. The hypothesis is essential to the stated theorem.

Dickson’s prime-tuples conjecture is the assertion that finitely many integer affine forms with positive leading coefficients take simultaneous prime values infinitely often whenever no prime divides their product for every integer argument. The card does not assume this conjecture.

Kaplan and Shelah prove conditional decidability for the unordered additive integer structure whose predicate includes both primes and their negatives. Their introduction explicitly retains the number-theoretic assumption on the ordered undecidability result, although the abstract abbreviates that qualification. The absence of order and the symmetric prime convention are substantive differences.

The 2024 survey explicitly retains the present decision question. The September 2026 bounded primary-source search found no matching unconditional resolution; this is dated evidence and a search limit, not a proof that the question remains open.

cards.title: Deterministic polynomial-time equivalence testing for d-DNNFs
cards.formal:
Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given two d-DNNF circuits \(C,D\), returns yes exactly when
\[\forall a:X\to\{0,1\},\qquad f_C(a)=f_D(a),\]
where \(X\) is the union of the variables appearing in the two inputs?

The algorithm must work for all promised pairs, without any requirement that their internal decompositions or variable trees agree. It must give the exact yes/no answer in worst-case time polynomial in their total binary encoding length. The two circuits are supplied explicitly; no truth table, equivalence certificate, common compiled representation or source formula is supplied.
cards.why: Equivalence testing checks whether two compiled representations express the same Boolean knowledge despite different decompositions. A deterministic polynomial-time test would support exact comparison and verification of representation changes without a probabilistic failure event. The gap between known randomized testing and the deterministic target also links this concrete compilation task to broader derandomization questions.

The known general test is randomized, and the 2026 paper retains a restricted cross-tree version as open. A bounded subsequent-work check found no matching deterministic general algorithm or impossibility theorem.

sentences: The problem asks whether two explicit d-DNNF circuits can be tested for exact Boolean equivalence in deterministic polynomial time.
Decomposability requires disjoint variable sets at conjunctions, while determinism requires mutually exclusive inputs at disjunctions.
The circuits may use unrelated internal decompositions and need not share a variable tree.
Randomized polynomial-time equivalence testing is known, but its possibility of error does not satisfy this target.
A resolution would clarify the cost of comparing and verifying succinct compiled Boolean representations.

cards.definitions:
A negation-normal-form Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated output gate. A leaf is a constant \(0\) or \(1\), or a literal \(x\) or \(\neg x\) for a variable in a finite set \(X\). Each internal gate is AND or OR with a finite nonempty input list. Arbitrary fan-in and sharing of subcircuits are allowed, and every input occurrence counts as an edge. Evaluation on an assignment \(a:X\to\{0,1\}\) uses the ordinary Boolean operations. There are no other negation gates. Constants suffice when \(X\) is empty.

For a gate \(g\), let \(\operatorname{var}(g)\) be the variables appearing in the literals reachable by following its input edges. Decomposability requires that the input subcircuits of each AND gate have pairwise disjoint such variable sets. Determinism requires that, for every OR gate, no assignment to \(X\) makes two distinct input occurrences true simultaneously. A d-DNNF satisfies both conditions at every gate. Determinism is a semantic mutual-exclusion property; it is not a restriction to gates that branch on a single variable.

Write \(f_C(a)\) for the output of circuit \(C\) and \(s(C)=|V(C)|+|E(C)|\) for its size, including leaves and all wires. Unused variables in \(X\) do not affect evaluation. Smoothness, which would require all inputs of an OR gate to mention the same variables, is not assumed. There is also no common tree organizing the variable splits of all conjunction gates. Thus the target uses general d-DNNFs, not only the smaller class of structured d-DNNFs. When two circuits are compared, their variable names denote the same coordinates of a common assignment; a missing coordinate is simply ignored by that circuit.

For computational tasks, encode a circuit as a topologically ordered list of gate records, with gate kinds, signed variable indices at literal leaves, input-list lengths and binary indices of earlier input gates. Include the output index. Variables occurring in the input circuit, or jointly in the two input circuits for a comparison, are consistently renamed to \(1,\ldots,n\); the number \(n\) is at most the total number of input literal occurrences. The input length \(b\) is the total number of bits of these records and delimiters. Gate-and-wire size and bit length are polynomially related with this convention.

An algorithm is one deterministic multitape Turing machine with no oracle, advice or randomness. Polynomial time means at most \(K(b+1)^d\) bit steps for fixed constants \(K,d\) independent of the circuits and number of variables. The inputs are promised to be d-DNNFs. The machine must satisfy the time bound on every input encoding, but its output may be arbitrary when the promise fails; it is not required to recognize the semantic determinism promise. All input reading and output writing count toward the bound.

Equivalence concerns the same assignment in the two circuits; it does not allow renaming variables separately to obtain isomorphism. The inputs may have different numbers of gates and may mention different subsets of \(X\). Logical nonequivalence means that at least one assignment makes their outputs differ. Equal numbers of satisfying assignments do not by themselves establish equivalence. The only required output is the decision bit; construction of a distinguishing assignment is not an additional task.

For comparison with the known randomized result, a one-sided randomized equivalence test can always accept equivalent circuits while rejecting each nonequivalent pair with probability at least \(2/3\), in polynomial time using independent random bits. The target here removes randomness entirely. A probabilistic test, even with arbitrarily small failure probability, does not meet its guarantee.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the deterministic polynomial-time existence claim in the stated promise model. A positive answer must give one uniform algorithm, prove exact equivalence decisions on all promised pairs, and establish a polynomial worst-case bit-time bound. A negative answer must exclude every such algorithm; it need not produce a single pair that defeats every algorithm. A randomized algorithm, a procedure requiring a common variable tree, or a hardness result for arbitrary DNNFs without determinism does not by itself settle this problem. Neither does hardness of verifying a proposed conjunction of two circuits, which is a different input-output relation.

context_blocks.text: The 2026 source explicitly leaves equivalence across different variable trees open even for structured representations. This card retains the broader general d-DNNF question, independently stated in the knowledge-compilation map; it does not attribute that broader formulation solely to the structured-circuit paper.

Darwiche and Huang give a one-sided randomized polynomial-time equivalence test for general d-DNNFs. Their analysis includes a polynomial bound on the bit length of arithmetic values; the algorithmic claim is stronger than merely bounding the number of unit-cost arithmetic operations.

The knowledge-compilation map distinguishes exact model counting, equivalence and entailment. Efficient counting does not automatically decide whether two represented sets of assignments coincide, and a common variable order or compatible structured decomposition is an additional restriction.

The 2026 paper establishes efficiently checkable restricted restructuring steps while leaving the one-shot comparison across arbitrary trees open. Its hardness discussion for checking a conjunction relation concerns three representations and does not establish hardness of the two-circuit equivalence problem.

cards.title: Greedy CDCL without restarts versus resolution
cards.formal: Does greedy CDCL without restarts p-simulate resolution in the asserting-learning model below? Precisely, do there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(M\), a constant \(C>0\) and \(k\in\mathbb N\) such that for every finite CNF formula \(F\) and every valid resolution refutation \(\pi\) of \(F\), on the explicit binary input \((F,\pi)\) of length \(L\), \(M\) halts within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps and outputs a legal greedy CDCL refutation of the same \(F\), without restarts, of at most \(C(L+1)^k\) bits? The single program and polynomial must work for all formulas and supplied proofs.
cards.definitions:
Literals are \(x_{i}\) or \(\neg x_{i}\) for \(i\in \{1,\ldots ,n\}\); clauses are sets of literals and F is a finite set of clauses. A resolution inference derives \((C\setminus \{x\})\cup (D\setminus \{\neg x\})\) from clauses C containing x and D containing \(\neg x\). A refutation is a finite sequence ending in the empty clause, each entry being an input clause or an inference from earlier entries, with parent indices and pivot recorded. Variable indices and pointers use binary notation. Clause and formula encodings explicitly list their literals.

A CDCL state consists of a database D containing F and an ordered trail of assignments to distinct variables of F. Each assignment is marked either as a decision or with its reason clause in D. Its decision level is the number of decisions up to that assignment. Initially \(D=F\) and the trail is empty. A clause is falsified if all its literals are false on the trail; it is unit if exactly one literal is unassigned and all others are false. The following priority of actions is mandatory.

If D has a falsified clause, a conflict must be processed before any other action. At decision level zero the run ends with UNSAT. Otherwise choose a falsified clause K and a trivial resolution analysis: start with K and repeatedly resolve the current clause with a reason clause recorded on the current trail, using a distinct pivot at each step. Every intermediate clause must be falsified by the current trail. Stop at a nonempty asserting clause C, meaning that exactly one of its variables has the current highest decision level. The trace records the full analysis. Add C to D and erase the suffix of the trail whose decision levels exceed a, where a is the maximum level of the other literals of C, or zero if there are none. Then perform one legal unit propagation and return to the conflict-first priority check.

If there is no conflict but a unit clause exists, choose such a clause, assign its unassigned literal to true, record that clause as the reason, and repeat the priority check. Only when neither conflicts nor units exist may a new decision assign either value to an unassigned variable. At such a stable state the run may first delete any subset of learned clauses, retaining all input clauses and all reasons appearing on the current trail, and must then make a decision. A satisfying complete trail ends with SAT, not a refutation. There is no independent operation clearing or shortening the trail: backjumping is allowed only after a conflict and only to the assertion level.

All choices of decisions, unit reasons, conflict clauses, trivial asserting analyses and permitted deletions are free components of the output trace. No fixed branching heuristic or first-UIP policy is imposed. No new variables, preprocessed replacement formula, unrecorded learned axioms or restarts are permitted. The only learned clauses are those derived by the recorded conflict analyses. The trace length counts all clauses, literals, assignments, analysis steps and pointers in an explicit binary encoding, so expensive analysis cannot be hidden in one step. This is the restart-free instantiation of the Vinyals model with arbitrary trivial asserting learning. The requested p-simulation is a uniform translation supplied with \(\pi\); mere existence of a short trace, or finding one from F alone, is a different claim.

The input promise is that the explicitly recorded resolution derivation is a valid refutation of the supplied formula; correctness is required for every promised input, including a formula already containing the empty clause. Invalid encodings or derivations may be rejected. All computation and output costs use ordinary sequential bit time. Choices made by the translator are deterministic and fully recorded, with exact clause and Boolean semantics; no randomness, numerical approximation, oracle or nonuniform advice is available. The model permits a conflict-justified backjump to level zero, which does not count as an independent restart.

context_blocks.text: Clause learning stores consequences of encountered conflicts and reuses them during a SAT search. General resolution permits arbitrary reuse of earlier clauses, without requiring that they arise along a current partial assignment. This question asks whether the constraints of a greedy search, even with freely chosen decisions and learning, impose a superpolynomial cost when restarting is unavailable.

The operational model matters. Exhaustive unit propagation and immediate conflict processing constrain which trails are reachable. A restart discards the current trail while retaining learned information, whereas a backjump must be justified by the newly learned asserting clause. The statement specifies those actions separately rather than treating every return to decision level zero as a prohibited restart.

Vinyals gives an execution-trace proof system with explicit propagation reasons, conflict-analysis derivations, deletion rules and cost measures. The present card selects its no-restart policy and allows arbitrary trivial asserting analyses. This avoids making the question depend on a particular solver implementation, while retaining actual greedy search restrictions.

The supplied resolution proof is part of the translator’s input. An affirmative answer therefore would not give a polynomial-time SAT solver or a practical heuristic that discovers short proofs unaided. A theorem guaranteeing only polynomial-size traces, without a polynomial-time translation, would establish the corresponding size-simulation statement rather than the full p-simulation asked here.

Vinyals’ 2022 exposition distinguishes no-restart simulations using non-greedy propagation or preprocessing from the greedy comparison. Such changes alter which search traces are legal, so those positive results do not satisfy the transitions written here.

Buss–Thapen construct formulas with short resolution proofs whose height must nevertheless be large. They discuss these as candidates for separating pool resolution from general resolution, explicitly state that they cannot prove that separation, and give polynomial-size pool proofs for a simpler variant. This is related progress, not a checked identification of pool resolution with every operational CDCL model.

The SAT 2026 graph-backtracking paper proves correctness and termination of a generalized solver and shows how suitable weights reproduce chronological and nonchronological backtracking. Its more general repair operation can retain assignments outside the ordinary retained prefix. These are simulations between backtracking policies; they do not supply the requested translation of arbitrary resolution proofs into the unchanged greedy no-restart model.

The bounded search through 16 September 2026 found no checked proof of the stated p-simulation or its negation. The dated specialist open discussion and subsequent related papers support retaining the target; this search is not an exhaustive proof of current openness.

cards.why: Restarts are a central operation in modern clause-learning SAT solvers. This target isolates whether their removal causes an unavoidable loss in proof generation even when the solver may choose decisions, propagation order and learned asserting clauses with full knowledge of a supplied resolution proof. A resolution would connect an exact operational restriction of search with the polynomial simulation structure studied in proof complexity.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean proof of the displayed uniform p-simulation or its logical negation. A positive answer must formalize the finite clause encoding and resolution proof checker, the stated CDCL state and transition system, and a computable translator with a polynomial bit-time bound, proving that every valid input proof yields a trace on the original formula ending in the permitted UNSAT state. The trace must obey conflict and propagation priority, trivial asserting analysis, assertion-level backjumps, deletion restrictions and the absence of restarts. A negative answer must rule out all such uniform polynomial-time translators; a lower bound for one fixed heuristic or a different backtracking policy is insufficient. Existence of polynomial-size traces alone does not supply the required efficient translator. Conditional theorems settle only their stated conditional variants unless their premises are also proved. No proof-assistant verification of either answer is claimed by this editorial review.

importance.reason: A concrete bridge between SAT solving and proof complexity: it isolates the computational role of restarts while allowing helpful search choices. The significance comes from the unresolved comparison with general resolution and explicit specialist discussion, not from an unspecified explanation of solver performance.

cards.title: Decidability of termination for one-rule string rewriting
cards.formal: Is global termination of a one-rule string rewriting system decidable? The input is a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) and two explicitly written words \(\ell,r\in\Sigma^{*}\). Define \(u\to v\) when \(u=x\ell y\) and \(v=xry\) for some \(x,y\in\Sigma^{*}\). Decide whether there exists no infinite sequence \(w_0\to w_1\to w_2\to\cdots\) of finite words. The quantifier includes every starting word and every choice of replacement position.
cards.why: A single literal replacement is among the simplest possible descriptions of an unbounded computation. Settling its global termination problem would locate a sharp limit on automatic reasoning about repeated symbolic transformations, without relying on a large instruction set or richer term syntax.
cards.status_note: The 2002 primary paper and the August 2026 authored note present arbitrary one-rule termination as unresolved. A bounded check on 13 September 2026 found no later resolution. The note and historical proofs have not been independently verified; source-open status is not an exhaustive certification.

sentences: A one-rule string system repeatedly replaces one fixed substring by another.
The question is whether an algorithm can decide if every reduction sequence from every finite starting word eventually stops.
Replacement positions are unrestricted, and the rule and alphabet are part of the input.
Known decision procedures cover special rule families, while an August 2026 note still lists the arbitrary one-rule question as open.
The answer must prove decidability or undecidability in Lean for global termination, rather than only termination from one supplied word.

definitions: The alphabet is a finite nonempty set listed by distinct binary symbol indices. Both sides of the rule are explicit finite sequences of these symbols, including possibly the empty word \(\varepsilon\). No variables, compressed word descriptions, contexts supplied as inputs, or additional rewrite rules occur.

One rewrite step chooses one contiguous occurrence of \(\ell\) and replaces it with \(r\), preserving the prefix \(x\) and suffix \(y\). If \(\ell=\varepsilon\), any boundary in a word, including its ends, is an occurrence. A rule application counts as a step even when the resulting word is identical to the original word. Thus \(\ell=r\) admits a constant infinite reduction sequence from \(\ell\).

Global termination means that for every \(w_0\in\Sigma^{*}\) there is no function \(w:\mathbb{N}\to\Sigma^{*}\) with first value \(w_0\) and \(w_i\to w_{i+1}\) for all \(i\geq0\). There is no fixed leftmost or rightmost evaluation strategy. Requiring only that each word has some terminating sequence would be a different property.

Decidability asks for a single deterministic Turing machine that halts on every valid finite description and outputs yes exactly for globally terminating systems. No running-time bound is imposed. Malformed descriptions can be rejected. The rule itself varies across instances; neither its length nor the alphabet size is a fixed constant.
cards.answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of a total decision algorithm for all one-rule systems in this model, or a Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists. Deciding termination from one supplied start word, analyzing one strategy, or handling a restricted family of rules alone is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: Geser’s paper gives decidability for grid rules: there is a letter \(b\) occurring on the left whose count on the right is no larger. It explicitly distinguishes this substantial subclass from the unresolved arbitrary one-rule problem.
RTA Problem 21 distinguishes the string case from the more general question for a single linear term-rewriting rule. This card asks only about replacements of contiguous substrings.
Kfoury’s August 2026 note restates global one-rule termination as Open Problem 8. It is a source-status update, rather than a new proof of either answer.

cards.title: Singly exponential shortest solutions of word equations
cards.formal:
Do positive integers \(c,k\) exist such that every satisfiable word equation \(u=v\), over every finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) of constant letters and a disjoint finite set \(\mathcal X\) of variables, has a solution \(h\) satisfying
\[\max_{x\in\mathcal X}|h(x)|\le 2^{c(n+1)^k},\qquad n=|u|+|v|?\]
Here \(\mathcal X\) consists exactly of the variables occurring in the equation, each occurrence contributes one to \(n\), and the maximum over no variables is zero. A solution replaces each variable consistently by a finite word over \(\Sigma\), possibly empty, fixes the constant letters and makes the two expanded words identical.

The same constants \(c,k\) must work independently of the equation, the alphabet and the number of variables. This is the polynomial-exponent meaning of singly exponential. A linear exponent is welcome but is not required.
cards.why: Very short equations can describe solutions whose expanded words are enormous. A universal singly exponential shortest-solution bound would constrain this hidden growth and, by the source’s compression theorem, imply NP membership of general word-equation satisfiability. This links a basic combinatorial question about strings to the unresolved complexity of exact string constraints.

progress.text: ICALP 1998 presents Conjecture B and the theorem showing that its affirmative answer implies NP membership of word-equation satisfiability.
The third arXiv version of Jeż’s paper includes an independent derivation of the doubly exponential shortest-solution bound.
STACS publishes the three-variable structural improvement while retaining the general NP-membership question.

cards.definitions:
For a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\), the free monoid \(\Sigma^*\) consists of all finite sequences of its letters, including the empty word \(\varepsilon\). Multiplication is concatenation, and \(\varepsilon\) is its identity. The length \(|w|\) is the number of letters in the sequence \(w\), with \(|\varepsilon|=0\). Distinct constant letters are distinct symbols, not variables or numbers. The alphabet may have any finite cardinality; if it is empty, its only word is \(\varepsilon\).

An equation is a pair of explicitly written words \(u,v\in(\Sigma\cup\mathcal X)^*\). Each variable and each constant occurrence counts as one symbol in the equation size \(n\). No compressed input, binary-encoded repeat operator, regular-language membership condition, length constraint, inequality, involution or cancellation operation is supplied. Exponent notation in an example of an equation is only shorthand for its fully expanded string, and its expanded length is charged. Variables may occur arbitrarily many times and may appear on either or both sides.

A solution is a monoid morphism \(h:(\Sigma\cup\mathcal X)^*\to\Sigma^*\) that fixes every \(a\in\Sigma\) and satisfies \(h(u)=h(v)\). Equivalently, choose one word \(h(x)\in\Sigma^*\) for each variable, substitute the same word at every occurrence, and concatenate in the original order. Empty substitutions are allowed, and no letter outside \(\Sigma\) may occur in a substitution. This is solving an equation in a free monoid, not in a free group or a semigroup with mandatory nonempty substitutions.

For a satisfiable equation, define
\[m(u,v)=\min_{h:\,h(u)=h(v)}\ \max_{x\in\mathcal X}|h(x)|.\]
The minimum exists because the feasible lengths form a nonempty subset of the nonnegative integers. The claim is \(m(u,v)\le2^{c(n+1)^k}\) for all satisfiable equations. It asks for at least one bounded solution to each equation, not for a bound on every solution. An equation can have infinitely many solutions with unbounded lengths and still satisfy the proposed shortest-solution bound.

The source also measures a solution by the length of the common expanded word \(h(u)=h(v)\). For each solution with \(M=\max_x|h(x)|\), every occurring variable image is a factor of that common word, and
\[M\le |h(u)|\le n\max(1,M).\]
These inequalities also cover the no-variable case using \(M=0\). Thus existence of a singly exponential bound on the shortest common-word length and the displayed variable-image bound are equivalent after changing the universal polynomial in the exponent. The card does not assert equality of these two minimum-length quantities.

The negative answer is the quantified assertion that for every pair of positive integers \(c,k\), some satisfiable equation has no solution meeting \(\max_x|h(x)|\le2^{c(n+1)^k}\). It is not enough to exhibit an exponential-length solution when a shorter one exists, or to beat one chosen polynomial exponent. No efficient construction of a solution or of a counterexample family is part of this nonconstructive length question.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of the universal singly exponential bound. A proof must provide fixed positive integers \(c,k\) and prove the bound for all satisfiable equations under the free-monoid and explicit-symbol conventions. A refutation must prove that every such polynomial-exponent bound fails. Bounds for a fixed number of variables, bounded occurrence counts, a restricted equation family or only compressed solution sizes do not settle the general claim. Proving membership of satisfiability in NP by an unrelated argument does not by itself establish this specific length bound.

context_blocks.text: Conjecture B concerns the length of a shortest solution. Theorem 2 and Corollary 1 establish that this conjecture would imply the separate NP-membership conjecture for satisfiability. The implication depends on the proved compression property; an exponentially long explicit witness alone is not a polynomial-size certificate.

The source fixes letters and permits variable substitutions in the free monoid, hence allows erasing substitutions. The card retains its explicit occurrence-based equation size and uses a universal polynomial exponent to resolve the phrase singly exponential.

Jeż gives an independent proof of a doubly exponential general bound on the shortest common-word length. A bound of that scale does not establish the single-exponential claim, and bounds on repeated periodic blocks are not automatically bounds on the full solution length.

The 2026 paper gives stronger parametric descriptions for constant-free equations on three variables. It still describes membership in NP as open for unrestricted word equations. The fixed-variable, constant-free structural result does not cover the arbitrary equations in this card.

sentences: A word equation asks for consistent substitutions of finite strings that make two concatenations identical.
The conjecture says that every satisfiable equation of size n has some solution whose variable images have length at most two to a fixed polynomial in n.
The bound must hold uniformly over all finite alphabets and arbitrarily many variable occurrences, with empty substitutions allowed.
Known compression results make this length conjecture sufficient for NP membership of general word-equation satisfiability.
Doubly exponential bounds and newer results for restricted equation families do not meet the universal single-exponential target.

cards.title: Decidability of fifth-order \(\beta\)-matching
cards.formal: Is fifth-order \(\beta\)-matching decidable in the source's closed range formulation? Given finite simple types \(\sigma,\tau\) and closed simply typed lambda terms \(F:\sigma\to\tau\) and \(N:\tau\), with \(\operatorname{ord}(\sigma)\le5\), decide whether \[\exists M\;\bigl(\varnothing\vdash M:\sigma\ \land\ F\,M=_\beta N\bigr).\] The unknown \(M\) is a finite closed term. One deterministic Turing machine must halt and decide this predicate for every such input, with no time bound. Type order starts at one, exactly as in the source.
cards.why: Matching is a central restricted form of higher-order unification, with uses in rewriting and symbolic reasoning. The fifth-order boundary asks exactly how much higher-order functional structure is needed for beta-only matching to encode undecidable behavior. It also exposes the substantive effect of extensional eta equality: a change in the equality relation, rather than just the input size, changes the general decidability result.
cards.status_note: The FSCD 2025 source and its 11 August 2026 extended v2 explicitly leave beta-matching at order five open, with ground type order one. Remark 3.24 identifies σ, the candidate term type, as the bounded order in the order-six negative construction. The bounded 16 September search found no matching subsequent resolution. Older low-order decidability is reported with the source attribution; the cited formal development was not rerun.

cards.definitions:
Simple types are the finite trees \(A::=\iota\mid A\to A\), over one fixed ground atom \(\iota\); arrows associate to the right. Their order is \(\operatorname{ord}(\iota)=1\) and \(\operatorname{ord}(A\to B)=\max(\operatorname{ord}(A)+1,\operatorname{ord}(B))\). Thus \(\iota\to\iota\) has order two. The bound five applies to the type \(\sigma\) of the term to be instantiated, rather than to \(\sigma\to\tau\) or to every type in the input derivations; \(\tau\) has no independent order bound. This is the convention made explicit for the order-six construction in the August 2026 source. A convention starting at zero shifts all these order numbers down by one.

Terms are finite expressions \(t::=x\mid(t\,t)\mid\lambda x.t\), up to consistent renaming of bound variables. There are no constants, recursion operators, polymorphic types, additional rewrite rules or extensional equations. A typing context \(\Gamma\) assigns simple types to finitely many distinct variables. Typing has exactly the variable rule \(x:A\in\Gamma\Rightarrow\Gamma\vdash x:A\), application \(\Gamma\vdash t:A\to B,\ \Gamma\vdash u:A\Rightarrow\Gamma\vdash tu:B\), and abstraction \(\Gamma,x:A\vdash t:B\Rightarrow\Gamma\vdash\lambda x.t:A\to B\). Closed means no free variables, as witnessed by the empty context. The input includes finite type trees, term trees and typing derivations for \(F\) and \(N\); the finite encodings use binary variable/de Bruijn indices and explicit trees. A purported input failing typing, closedness or the order bound may be rejected. These syntactic conditions are decidable.

A beta step replaces \((\lambda x.t)u\) by the capture-avoiding substitution \(t[x:=u]\) in any subterm, including underneath lambda abstractions. The relation \(=_\beta\) is the reflexive, symmetric, transitive closure of these steps, modulo bound-variable renaming. The eta equation \(\lambda x.f x=f\), where \(x\) is not free in \(f\), is not an allowed additional equation. The known equivalence of beta convertibility with equality of beta normal forms does not require candidate terms to be eta-expanded. The substitution occurs only at the unknown argument of \(F\); the closed target \(N\) is fixed. The same machine handles all allowed types and all finite term sizes, including types with no closed inhabitant. It returns exact YES/NO answers, with no oracle, random error or numerical tolerance.
cards.answer_criterion: An accepted answer is a complete Lean proof of existence of a total computable decider for the displayed predicate or a proof that none exists. A positive answer must formalize the pure simply typed syntax, typing, the order-one ground convention, capture-avoiding beta conversion and the algorithm's termination and correctness for every allowed instance. A negative answer must prove noncomputability while keeping \(\operatorname{ord}(\sigma)\le5\); undecidability using order-six candidate types does not qualify. Neither a beta-eta decision theorem nor a restriction to eta-long candidates answers the beta-only question. This review does not claim to port or rerun the cited Rocq/Coq development in Lean.

cards.title: Polynomial-time equivalence of free binary decision diagrams
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for equivalence of two explicitly given free binary decision diagrams? In full quantifiers, are there a deterministic Turing machine \(M\), constants \(C>0\) and \(k\in\mathbb N\) such that for every valid pair \((B_1,B_2)\), of total binary encoding length \(L\), the machine halts within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps and returns YES exactly when \[\forall a:X\to\{0,1\},\qquad f_{B_1}(a)=f_{B_2}(a),\] where \(X\) is the union of the variable labels appearing in the two inputs? No shared variable order is promised.
cards.why: FBDDs allow different branches to choose different variable orders and can be much more compact than ordered diagrams. Reliable equivalence testing is needed to compare independently compiled representations or optimized versions of a Boolean function. The question asks whether that representational flexibility can coexist with deterministic exact polynomial-time comparison, beyond the known randomized guarantee.
cards.status_note: Darwiche–Marquis 2002 mark FBDD equivalence as unknown; the checked Darwiche–Huang theorem supplies a randomized one-sided polynomial-time test. The 2026 proof-system discussion concerns stronger join verification and different structured formats, not a checked resolution of two-FBDD deterministic equivalence. A bounded primary-source search through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution; source-open records the dated question, not exhaustive present-status certification.

cards.definitions:
A free binary decision diagram (FBDD) is a finite rooted directed acyclic graph. Each nonterminal vertex is labelled by a Boolean variable and has exactly two outgoing edges, one marked 0 and one marked 1; their targets may coincide. A terminal vertex has no outgoing edge and is labelled by the output bit 0 or 1. All vertices can be taken reachable from the root. On every directed root-to-terminal path, each variable occurs at most once. Different paths, and the two different input diagrams, may inspect variables in different orders. In particular no fixed global linear order or common graph ordering is part of the input. Redundant tests and shared subgraphs are permitted; the diagrams need not be reduced or isomorphic.

For an assignment \(a:X\to\{0,1\}\), start at the root and at a vertex labelled \(x\) follow its edge marked \(a(x)\); acyclicity leads to a terminal, whose label is \(f_B(a)\). Variables absent from a diagram do not affect its value. Constant diagrams consisting of one terminal and the case \(X=\varnothing\) are included. The input is an explicit finite vertex table giving the root, each node's type and label, and its two successor indices when present. Identifiers, labels and indices are binary encoded, and \(L\) counts all bits in both tables. Inputs are promised to meet the graph and path conditions. All arithmetic, preprocessing and reading costs belong to the ordinary sequential deterministic bit-time bound; no unit-cost manipulation of unbounded integers, oracle, random coins or nonuniform advice is allowed. One program and one polynomial work for all pairs. Correctness is exact on every assignment, not agreement on most assignments or numerical approximation. Only the YES/NO equivalence answer is required; canonicalization or construction of a combined diagram is not an additional output.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean proof that such a uniform polynomial-time equivalence decider exists, including the graph semantics, input encoding, runtime and both correctness directions, or prove the negation of the displayed quantified claim. The negative target rules out every deterministic polynomial-time machine on the promised FBDD input class; failure of one graph comparison or one representation-conversion method is insufficient. A randomized polynomial-time test or a deterministic test requiring a common ordering does not meet the full target. A conditional lower bound settles only its conditional version unless its premise is proved. This review supplies no Lean proof of either answer.

source_formulation.text: Does the FBDD representation support polynomial-time equivalence testing?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the unresolved EQ entry in the knowledge-compilation map

context_blocks.text: An FBDD records a branching computation that tests a variable at most once on each path. It generalizes an ordered binary decision diagram by allowing the order to vary between branches. Shared subgraphs make its explicit representation potentially much smaller than the full truth table.

Darwiche–Marquis Table 5 marks equivalence for FBDDs as unknown. This is distinct from entailment between diagrams and from constructing their conjunction; the map treats these as separate operations. The card retains equivalence alone.

Darwiche–Huang give randomized polynomial-time equivalence testing for FBDDs and even for general d-DNNFs. For every fixed equivalent pair the test accepts with certainty; for every fixed inequivalent pair it incorrectly accepts with probability at most one half. This is the one-sided-error class coRP, and their bit-length analysis makes the polynomial-time claim an ordinary finite-arithmetic claim.

That error statement is conditioned on the fixed input, not a posterior probability that the input is equivalent after a positive answer. The source’s informal confidence wording is therefore expressed here as the precise one-sided algorithmic guarantee. The requested deterministic answer admits no such error.

The 2026 structured-circuit paper discusses hardness of verifying a join rule for FBDDs: testing whether a third represented function equals the conjunction of two others. That is a different, three-diagram operation. Its hardness is not presented as a lower bound for the two-diagram equivalence question.

Every FBDD has a polynomial-size translation into deterministic decomposable negation normal form. Thus a deterministic general d-DNNF equivalence algorithm would also solve this card; an FBDD-only algorithm would not by itself settle that broader question. The related cards retain those different targets.

The September 2026 bounded search checked the foundational map, the randomized theorem and the newer proof-system discussion, without finding a matching deterministic solution or impossibility theorem. The dated unknown table cell is not an exhaustive certificate of present openness.

cards.title: Two-sided distributive unification with a unit
cards.formal: Let \(E\) be exactly the four identities \[x\cdot(y+z)=(x\cdot y)+(x\cdot z),\qquad (x+y)\cdot z=(x\cdot z)+(y\cdot z),\qquad x\cdot1=x,\qquad1\cdot x=x.\] Is general first-order \(E\)-unification decidable? Namely, does one deterministic Turing machine halt on every finite signature and finite list of equations \(s_i\doteq t_i\), under the conventions below, and return YES exactly when a single finite-term substitution \(\sigma\) satisfies \(s_i\sigma=_E t_i\sigma\) for every \(i\)?
cards.why: Distributivity couples two operations, so the standard decomposition methods for disjoint equational theories do not immediately apply. The multiplicative unit creates additional identifications between expanded and unexpanded expressions. Determining decidability for exactly this small axiom set would clarify a longstanding boundary in symbolic constraint solving, between known distributive fragments and stronger theories with undecidable unification.
cards.status_note: The 2001 handbook explicitly lists this question as open. Checked the exact axiom sets in the two distinct 1996 positive results, the 1987 associative-extension negative result and the 2010 one-sided algorithm correction. A bounded primary-source search on 16 September 2026 found no verified resolution of the general four-identity target. Because no recent explicit status confirmation was found, scientific status remains uncertain.
