importance.reason: A compact and longstanding equational-unification boundary, situated between decidable distributive fragments and undecidable associative extensions, with relevance to symbolic reasoning and theory combination.

sentences: Unification asks whether a common substitution can make every pair of supplied expressions equal under specified algebraic identities.
Here the identities are both distributive laws together with a two-sided multiplicative unit.
The expressions may also use uninterpreted symbols, and neither operation is assumed associative or commutative.
Known algorithms handle neighboring fragments, while undecidability results with additional associativity do not settle this exact theory.
A resolution would identify a longstanding boundary for symbolic equality reasoning under interacting algebraic laws.

cards.definitions:
The fixed theory signature consists of binary symbols \(+\) and \(\cdot\) and a constant \(1\). An input signature \(F\) is any finite extension by uninterpreted function symbols of specified finite arities, including extra constants; these free symbols have no further equations. This uses the handbook's general-unification convention from §3.1 and §3.2.2 and includes elementary problems and problems with free constants as subcases. A term is a finite ordered rooted tree: a leaf is a variable or a constant, and a node labelled by a symbol of arity \(r\) has exactly \(r\) children. Variables come from a countable set of identifiers; only finitely many occur in an input. The equations form an explicitly written finite list, possibly empty. Signature declarations, arities, identifiers and complete term trees have finite binary encodings; no succinct circuits or infinite rational trees are inputs. A substitution assigns finite terms over \(F\) and variables to the finitely many input variables, fixes the other variables, and extends homomorphically through each function symbol. The same substitution applies to every equation. It is an ordinary simultaneous substitution, not an instruction to unfold terms indefinitely. Additional variables in its range are allowed. A unifier need not be most general, and the decision machine need not output one.

The relation \(=_E\) is the least equivalence relation on terms closed under application of every function symbol and substitutions, and containing every instance of the four displayed identities. Equivalently, equality has a finite equational derivation from exactly these identities, using reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity, congruence and substitution. Parentheses and operand order therefore remain meaningful except where those identities identify them. Neither operation is assumed associative or commutative; no idempotence, additive zero, annihilation, additive inverse or cancellation law is included. The unit is two-sided and belongs to multiplication only. The notation resembles arithmetic, but the target is equality in the presented equational theory, not equality under a chosen integer or semiring interpretation. The same uniform machine must handle every finite input signature, variable count and equation list, halt on both YES and NO inputs, and use no oracle or random error. No time or memory bound is imposed, and no numerical tolerance applies.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean proof that this precisely defined general-unification language is computable, or that it is not. A positive proof must represent finite signatures, terms, substitutions and the generated equational congruence, prove termination of one uniform algorithm on every well-formed input, and show that its YES output is equivalent to existence of a common unifier. A negative proof must establish noncomputability using only the four identities and the permitted free symbols. A result for a different axiom set, a matching problem with variables on only one side, or a nonterminating search for unifiers does not settle the card. The Lean proof must justify the exact signature convention it uses; a constants-only procedure does not automatically prove the general result. This source review is not a completed formal proof.

source_formulation.text: Is unification modulo both distributive laws and a two-sided multiplicative unit decidable?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the handbook question; general finite-signature unification convention stated explicitly

context_blocks.text: The handbook defines the two distributive theories separately, their union D, and the two-sided unit theory U. It then explicitly leaves D combined with U open. This is not an ordinary semiring problem because the associative, commutative and zero axioms of a semiring are absent.

Schmidt-Schauß’s 1996 distributive-unification theorem concerns the two distributive identities without the unit. Its publisher abstract lists those identities explicitly. The mention of unit-bearing auxiliary theories in that algorithm must not be mistaken for a multiplicative-unit axiom in its input theory.

A different 1996 result handles one-sided distributivity with a multiplicative unit. Having an algorithm after omitting either the second distributive law or the unit does not decide their combination.

Adding associativity of addition changes the situation: Tidén and Arnborg obtain undecidability for a theory with one-sided distributivity, associativity of addition and a one-sided multiplicative unit. That theorem does not settle the four-identity target, which lacks associativity.

The handbook separately distinguishes elementary unification, unification with extra constants and general unification with arbitrary free function symbols. The present card keeps the general first-order setting rather than silently restricting the problem to closed arithmetic-shaped terms.

The 2001 discussion repeats an early polynomial-time claim for the original one-sided algorithm. Narendran, Marshall and Mahapatra later give inputs requiring exponentially many steps for that algorithm. This correction concerns a neighboring algorithm’s running time, not a resolution of two-sided unification with a unit.

The September 2026 search checked these primary statements and later work indexed under distributivity and unification, without verifying a resolution of this exact theory. The old open statement is retained as historical evidence; its age and search absence are not proof of current openness.

cards.title: Decidability of subsequence constraints with regular domains
cards.formal: For each fixed finite alphabet \(A\), consider the following decision problem. An input consists of a finite set \(X\) of variables, one regular expression \(r_x\) over \(A\) for every \(x\in X\), and a finite list \(C\) of constraints \(x\preceq y_1\cdots y_k\), where \(x,y_i\in X\) and \(k\ge0\). Does there exist, for every fixed \(A\), a deterministic Turing machine that halts on every such input and decides whether there is an assignment \(h:X\to A^*\) satisfying \[h(x)\in L(r_x)\quad(x\in X),\qquad h(x)\preceq h(y_1)\cdots h(y_k)\quad((x\preceq y_1\cdots y_k)\in C)?\] The same variable may occur repeatedly, and the directed dependencies between variables may contain arbitrary cycles.
cards.why: This question isolates the effect of cyclic reuse of unknown strings in a small constraint language. Regular domains and ordered concatenation are basic operations in string analysis, while subsequence constraints model loss of letters. A resolution would identify whether these ingredients alone retain effective satisfiability testing, clarifying a boundary obscured by undecidability results for richer interfaces.
cards.status_note: Source-open in the checked July 2024 problem statement and March 2024 primary paper. On 15 September 2026 a bounded later-work search found no matching resolution. Acyclic algorithms and richer-model undecidability do not settle this exact syntax; paper proofs were not independently verified.

progress.text: The published STACS paper gives an NEXPTIME decision bound for acyclic regular constraints even in its richer model. Its §6.2 leaves decidability open when regular constraints use only concatenation and arbitrary cycles are allowed; the undecidability constructions discussed there require operations absent here.
Automata Exchange records the exact question with one variable on each left side, a word of variables on each right side, and regular-expression domains.

The original problem page and the precise open passage in STACS 2024 were rechecked. A bounded search of subsequent work did not locate a resolution matching these constraints. This is a dated source-status report, not an independent proof that the question remains open.

sentences: Each variable denotes one finite word constrained to a specified regular language.
A relational constraint requires that word to occur as a scattered subsequence of a concatenation of other assigned words.
The question asks for total decidability over every fixed finite alphabet, allowing repeated variables and arbitrary dependency cycles.
Known algorithms for acyclic systems and undecidability results with shuffle or transducers concern different input classes.
A resolution would locate the decidability boundary of a basic language for relating incomplete and concatenated strings.

cards.definitions: A word over \(A\) is a finite sequence of its letters; \(A^*\) contains the empty word \(\varepsilon\). Concatenation appends sequences in their given order. For words \(u=u_1\cdots u_m\) and \(v=v_1\cdots v_n\), \(u\preceq v\) means that there exist indices \(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_m\le n\) with \(u_j=v_{i_j}\) for every \(j\). Thus it is the scattered-subsequence relation, including \(\varepsilon\preceq v\). For \(k=0\), the right-hand side evaluates to \(\varepsilon\). Every occurrence of a variable receives the same assigned word. A regular expression is a finite syntax tree generated by letters of \(A\), \(\varnothing\), \(\varepsilon\), binary union, concatenation and Kleene star; its language is defined by these operations, with star allowing any finite number of repetitions, including zero. Variables may receive empty words exactly when their domain expressions permit them. The input explicitly lists the expression trees and variable occurrences, using binary integer indices and delimiters; no compressed strings, numeric length predicates or additional relation symbols occur. A dependency edge \(x\to y\) is present if \(y\) occurs on the right of a constraint whose left side is \(x\). No acyclicity promise is imposed. Up to renaming, the alphabet can be written \(A=\{0,\ldots,a-1\}\) for \(a\in\mathbb N\). The quantifier order is \(\forall a\,\exists M_a\,\forall I\): one finite machine for every instance over that fixed alphabet. This preserves the source's fixed-alphabet convention; it does not demand an effective construction of \(M_a\) from \(a\). Machines must terminate with the exact answer on both satisfiable and unsatisfiable inputs. No time or space bound is requested.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the quantified decidability statement or its negation. A positive result must provide total, correct decision procedures covering every finite system over every fixed finite alphabet with exactly the syntax above. A negative result must prove that for at least one fixed finite alphabet no such total computable decision procedure exists. Deciding only systems with acyclic dependencies, or proving undecidability after adding shuffle, transducers, concatenations on the left, or nonregular domain languages, does not settle this statement.

context_blocks.text: A domain expression describes the possible complete value of one variable. A constraint such as \(x\preceq yz\) asks that this value survive as a subsequence after the values of \(y\) and \(z\) are joined. The assignment is shared across the whole system, so different constraints cannot choose independent values for the same variable.

The left side is always one variable, whereas the right side may repeat and concatenate variables. This syntactic asymmetry matters: the card does not ask for arbitrary pairs of concatenated terms related by subsequence. The open question also permits dependencies that return to an earlier variable; results requiring acyclicity cover only part of this domain.

The STACS paper studies a broader language that can interleave strings by shuffle and transform them by finite-state transducers. Its acyclic regular fragment is decidable, while general cyclic fragments of that richer language are undecidable. Section 6.2 explicitly separates the present concatenation-only, transducer-free case as unresolved. Those neighboring theorems therefore do not justify retiring this card.

cards.title: Polynomial-time complementation of d-DNNFs
cards.formal:
Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given any d-DNNF circuit \(C\), outputs a d-DNNF circuit \(D\) over the same variables such that
\[\forall a:X\to\{0,1\},\qquad f_D(a)=1-f_C(a)?\]
The runtime is measured in the explicit binary input encoding and includes writing the entire output. The output may use different decompositions and share subcircuits arbitrarily, subject to the same d-DNNF conditions. It may omit irrelevant input variables, but may not introduce new variables, quantifiers or negation gates above leaves.

One uniform algorithm and one polynomial bound must work for all input sizes and all promised circuits. This is a construction question, distinct from the nonconstructive polynomial-size closure question.
cards.why: Complementation is a basic operation needed to reuse a compiled Boolean representation for exceptions, exclusions and opposite events. General d-DNNFs support useful counting and reasoning tasks, but it is unknown whether this logical transformation can always preserve their computational advantages with polynomial overhead. Resolving the construction question would clarify which operations can be performed directly on this succinct representation.
cards.status_note: Checked on 2026-09-14: the source question, Darwiche–Marquis Sections 2, 4–5, Vinall-Smeeth Theorem 2 and conclusion, and STACS 2026 Section 7. These sources keep arbitrary d-DNNF complementation distinct from the resolved structured-output restriction. A bounded later-work search found no matching general deterministic polynomial-time construction or refutation; openness is not exhaustively certified.

cards.definitions:
A negation-normal-form Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated output gate. A leaf is a constant \(0\) or \(1\), or a literal \(x\) or \(\neg x\) for a variable in a finite set \(X\). Each internal gate is AND or OR with a finite nonempty input list. Arbitrary fan-in and sharing of subcircuits are allowed, and every input occurrence counts as an edge. Evaluation on an assignment \(a:X\to\{0,1\}\) uses the ordinary Boolean operations. There are no other negation gates. Constants suffice when \(X\) is empty.

For a gate \(g\), let \(\operatorname{var}(g)\) be the variables appearing in the literals reachable by following its input edges. Decomposability requires that the input subcircuits of each AND gate have pairwise disjoint such variable sets. Determinism requires that, for every OR gate, no assignment to \(X\) makes two distinct input occurrences true simultaneously. A d-DNNF satisfies both conditions at every gate. Determinism is a semantic mutual-exclusion property; it is not a restriction to gates that branch on a single variable.

Write \(f_C(a)\) for the output of circuit \(C\) and \(s(C)=|V(C)|+|E(C)|\) for its size, including leaves and all wires. Unused variables in \(X\) do not affect evaluation. Smoothness, which would require all inputs of an OR gate to mention the same variables, is not assumed. There is also no common tree organizing the variable splits of all conjunction gates. Thus the target uses general d-DNNFs, not only the smaller class of structured d-DNNFs. When two circuits are compared, their variable names denote the same coordinates of a common assignment; a missing coordinate is simply ignored by that circuit.

For computational tasks, encode a circuit as a topologically ordered list of gate records, with gate kinds, signed variable indices at literal leaves, input-list lengths and binary indices of earlier input gates. Include the output index. Variables occurring in the input circuit, or jointly in the two input circuits for a comparison, are consistently renamed to \(1,\ldots,n\); the number \(n\) is at most the total number of input literal occurrences. The input length \(b\) is the total number of bits of these records and delimiters. Gate-and-wire size and bit length are polynomially related with this convention.

An algorithm is one deterministic multitape Turing machine with no oracle, advice or randomness. Polynomial time means at most \(K(b+1)^d\) bit steps for fixed constants \(K,d\) independent of the circuits and number of variables. The inputs are promised to be d-DNNFs. The machine must satisfy the time bound on every input encoding, but its output may be arbitrary when the promise fails; it is not required to recognize the semantic determinism promise. All input reading and output writing count toward the bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of such a uniform polynomial-time complementing algorithm. A positive answer must prove the output d-DNNF properties, equality to the complement on every assignment and the full bit-time bound. A negative answer must exclude all deterministic polynomial-time algorithms meeting this promise specification, not merely one construction or one output structure. A polynomial-size existence theorem without an efficient construction does not prove the claim. A conditional lower bound establishes only its stated conditional implication unless the needed assumption is also proved.

cards.why: Measures the cost of recognizing algebraic structure that can make entire families of equation systems tractable. cards.definitions:
A finite algebra \(\mathbf A=(A;f_{1},\ldots,f_{m})\) has a nonempty explicitly listed finite universe and a finite signature. Each basic operation \(f_{j}:A^{r_{j}}\to A\) is supplied by its complete table, with its arity. Nullary operations, when present, specify distinguished constants. The universe size, number of operations and arities may vary with the input. Let \(L\) be the total binary length of this description. A large-arity operation is not given by a succinct circuit or program.

A term is an expression made from variables and the given operation symbols; interpreting it on \(\mathbf A\) gives a term operation. Constants not in the given signature are not automatically available as term symbols.

The Taylor promise means that there are an arity \(r\geq2\) and a term operation \(t:A^{r}\to A\) such that \(t(a,\ldots,a)=a\) for every \(a\in A\), and for every coordinate \(i\in\{1,\ldots,r\}\) there are two tuples \(\mathbf u_{i},\mathbf v_{i}\in\{x,y\}^{r}\) with \((\mathbf u_{i})_{i}=x\), \((\mathbf v_{i})_{i}=y\), satisfying
\[t(\mathbf u_{i}(a,b))=t(\mathbf v_{i}(a,b))\qquad\text{for every }a,b\in A.\]
The choices of \(r,t\) and identities may depend on the algebra. This is what the source means by membership in a Taylor variety. A witnessing term or operation table is not supplied, and recognizing whether the promise holds is not part of the task.

An endomorphism of \(\mathbf A\) is a map \(h:A\to A\) preserving every basic operation:
\[h(f_{j}(a_{1},\ldots,a_{r_{j}}))=f_{j}(h(a_{1}),\ldots,h(a_{r_{j}})).\]
It must also fix the interpretation of every nullary symbol. Its image is a subalgebra. A core is an endomorphic image minimal under inclusion among such images, equipped with the restricted operations. For finite algebras these cores are unique up to isomorphism; equivalently, every endomorphism of the core is an automorphism.

Abelianness here is the universal-algebraic term-condition property. A concrete definition uses the algebra of \(2\times2\) matrices over a finite algebra \(\mathbf B\), with each basic operation applied entrywise. Let \(M_{\mathbf B}\) be the smallest subset of \(B^{2\times2}\) closed under these operations and containing all matrices
\[\begin{pmatrix}a&a\\ b&b\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\begin{pmatrix}c&d\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}\qquad(a,b,c,d\in B).\]
Then \(\mathbf B\) is abelian if every matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}x&y\\ z&w\end{pmatrix}\in M_{\mathbf B}\) satisfies \(x=y\Rightarrow z=w\). This is the source’s condition \([1_{\mathbf B},1_{\mathbf B}]=0_{\mathbf B}\). It is not a requirement that each basic operation be commutative.

One uniform deterministic algorithm must run in \(O(L^{k})\) bit operations for a fixed constant \(k\), with a fixed multiplicative constant, on all inputs. It must answer correctly for every well-formed algebra satisfying the Taylor promise. On other inputs the answer is unrestricted, but the polynomial time bound still applies. The requested output is only YES or NO; no particular representative of the core has to be chosen.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a deterministic algorithm with a uniform polynomial bound in the full table encoding length that recognizes abelian cores on every promised input, or prove that none exists. A conditional lower bound must identify its assumption. The source also asks for faster construction of the core and its Mal’cev operation in positive cases; those are additional output tasks and are not silently asserted equivalent to the selected decision question.

cards.title: FO model checking on hereditary monadically dependent graph classes
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal: For every hereditary effectively monadically dependent class C of finite simple graphs, do there exist a deterministic algorithm \(A_{C}, a\) computable function \(f_{C}:N\to N\) and a constant \(d_{C}\) such that \(A_{C}\) decides whether G satisfies a first-order sentence \(\varphi\) in time \(f_{C}(|\varphi |)(|V(G)|+1)^{d_{C}}\) for every \(G\in C\)? The precise effectiveness condition is given below; the graph is supplied without a structural decomposition.
cards.definitions: The class C is fixed, is closed under isomorphism and induced subgraphs, and is not part of each input. First-order sentences use equality, adjacency \(E(x,y)\), Boolean connectives and quantifiers over individual vertices. They do not quantify over sets, and no vertex order or arithmetic is supplied. The input is the explicitly represented graph G and the sentence \(\varphi\); the parameter \(k=|\varphi |\) is its encoded length. The algorithm must halt on every input, and its correctness and stated time bound are required when \(G\in C\); it need not recognize membership in C. To define monadic dependence, let \(\theta (x,y)\) be any fixed first-order formula using adjacency and finitely many additional unary predicates. A graph in \(T_{\theta}(G)\) is obtained by interpreting these predicates as arbitrary vertex subsets, putting an edge between distinct u,v whenever \(\theta (u,v)\) or \(\theta (v,u)\) holds, and taking any induced subgraph. C is monadically dependent when no single \(\theta\) gives all finite graphs among the outputs \(T_{\theta}(G), G\in C\). For an explicit effective version, define \(\mathrm{P}_{s}\) as the bipartite powerset graph with vertices \(a_{1},\ldots ,a_{s}\) and \(b_{S}\) for every \(S\subseteq \{1,\ldots ,s\}\), and edges \(a_{i} b_{S}\) exactly when \(i\in S\). Require a computable function \(b:N\to N_{\ge 1}\) such that, for every formula \(\theta\) and every \(G\in C, \mathrm{P}_{b(|\theta |)}\) is absent from \(T_{\theta}(G)\). Formula length includes its predicate symbols under a fixed effective encoding. This is the computable dependence-function convention of Mählmann’s Definition 12.24. The programs computing b and the eventual algorithm may depend on C; they are not extra per-instance certificates. The exponent \(d_{C}\) is independent of k. The query-evaluation problem here is for the plain graph signature; unary colours occur in the structural definition. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

cards.status_note: Explicitly open in the July 2026 neighborhood-complexity paper. The independent-side hardness and stable-side algorithm are known; radius-one merge-width does not provide the full algorithm. This card fixes the effective dependence-function convention to require a computable FPT bound. No resolution found through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: First-order logic describes many small graph queries with quantifiers over vertices. For example, the existence of a dominating set of size k can be expressed by choosing k vertices and requiring every vertex to equal or be adjacent to one of them. A direct evaluation can try \(n^{k}\) choices. Fixed-parameter tractability asks for the stronger form \(f(k)n^{d}\): the query may be expensive, but its length must not keep increasing the exponent of the graph size.

Graph structure can make this possible. The broad research programme asks which hereditary classes support such evaluation. Hereditary means that deleting vertices keeps a graph inside the class, a natural closure property when a query examines a portion of a database or network. Sparse graph classes gave early positive results, but dense classes with controlled structure also admit efficient model checking. Thus density alone cannot describe the boundary.

Monadic dependence measures whether unrestricted graph structure can be hidden inside a class through a fixed logical interpretation. Unary predicates mark arbitrary vertex subsets. A formula then defines new edges, after which selected vertices may be retained. If this process can generate every finite graph, apparently restricted inputs still contain arbitrary graph complexity in an interpretable form. Monadic dependence forbids that possibility.

The effective hypothesis matters to the exact computational claim. A structural class can have finite obstruction bounds at every logical complexity while those bounds grow faster than any computable function. Mählmann makes the dependence condition quantitative using forbidden powerset graphs and distinguishes computable parameter bounds from weaker conventions for fixed-parameter tractability. This card adopts that explicit effective formulation, so “there exists a finite bound” is not silently substituted for an algorithmically bounded parameter function.

One direction of the broader classification has been established. Dreier, Mählmann and Toruńczyk prove that first-order model checking is AW[*]-hard on every hereditary monadically independent graph class. Under the standard assumption \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{AW}[*]\), this excludes efficient model checking on the independent side. Their structural characterization uses flip-breakability, a separation property allowing controlled changes to adjacency between vertex groups. The missing direction is the algorithm for dependent classes.

A major positive theorem proves fixed-parameter tractability for monadically stable classes. Stability additionally forbids interpreting arbitrarily long linear orders; dependence forbids arbitrary graph encoding and allows more classes. The 2023 preprint by Dreier, Eleftheriadis, Mählmann, McCarty, Pilipczuk and Toruńczyk, published at FOCS 2024, settles the stable case using neighborhood complexity and suitable covers. It does not make the two structural notions equivalent.

Merge-width is a graph parameter used in existing model-checking theorems. Dreier and Toruńczyk describe a graph by a sequence of successively coarser vertex partitions, recording deviations from default adjacencies between parts. Their model-checking theorem applies to bounded merge-width when a witnessing construction sequence is supplied. This theorem assumes that a witnessing sequence is supplied and does not cover the stated input model.

The July 2026 neighborhood-complexity paper proves that, for every fixed positive \(\eta\), the number of distinct sets \(N(v)\cap A\) is \(O(|A|^{1+\eta})\) in a monadically dependent class, with the constant depending on the class and \(\eta\). It also constructs sequences witnessing radius-one merge-width \(n^{o(1)}\) in polynomial time. This supplies a concrete structural and algorithmic step. General first-order formulas require control at radii depending on the formula, so radius one does not complete the model-checking argument.

Related February 2026 work by Dreier and Kuske accelerates the construction of low-crossing orders and neighborhood covers, improving model-checking runtimes within the already tractable monadically stable setting. Such refinements are useful because they make the structural tools more practical, while leaving the dependent-versus-stable boundary in place.

A positive answer would unify several major algorithmic graph frameworks through one logical condition and explain when small declarative queries can avoid repeated high-dimensional enumeration. A counterexample satisfying the effective hypothesis would show that the absence of arbitrary logical graph encoding is insufficient for tractability. Either outcome would sharpen the connection between graph structure and query evaluation.

cards.title: Constant-delay conjunctive-query classification
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal: Is there a total algorithm that, given any conjunctive query q with self-joins allowed, decides whether q admits enumeration of all distinct answers with \(O_{q}(N)\) preprocessing and \(O_{q}(1)\) worst-case delay on every database of size N?
cards.definitions: A query is a finite formula \(q(\bar\{x\})=\exists \bar\{y\} \land _{i} R_{i}(\bar\{z\}_{i})\), with no constants, negation, disequalities or aggregation. The head x̄ lists distinct variables; every variable occurs in a relational atom. Relation symbols have fixed positive finite arities within q and may occur repeatedly; repeated variables within atoms are allowed. Boolean queries have an empty head. A database D explicitly lists finite set-valued relations over a domain \([n]; N=1+n\)+the total number of tuple entries in these lists. Each domain identifier fits in \(O(\log (N+2))\) bits. \(q(D)\) is the set of head tuples extendible to an assignment satisfying all atoms. Fix the deterministic word-RAM convention with addition, multiplication, comparison, Boolean word operations and indirect access costing one step, words of \(O_{q}(\log (N+2))\) bits, and a polynomial address universe of initially zero cells. Accessed cells and operations are charged; no linear-space or constant-extra-space restriction is imposed. This allows direct tuple-membership tables without charging for touching every unused address. Membership in the target class means that for this fixed q there are an enumerator and constants \(C_{q},B_{q}\) whose preprocessing takes at most \(C_{q} N\) steps, whose word length is at most \(B_{q} \log _{2}(N+2)\), and whose time to the first answer, between consecutive answers, and from the last answer to termination is at most \(C_{q}\) after preprocessing. Empty output must be reported within the same delay bound. Output order is arbitrary and each tuple appears exactly once. The classifier takes q, not D, as input and must halt on every query; it has no prescribed runtime bound and need not output the enumerator. This is an explicit effective yes/no formulation of the source’s broader request for a complete tractability classification. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length \(w=\Theta (\log  n)\) (or \(\Theta (\log  N)\) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The checked primary sources leave the general self-join classification unresolved. The exact target is an editorial effective formulation, with a specified RAM and permissive polynomial memory. Known negative classifications use stated fine-grained hypotheses; newer projected-query and dynamic results do not cover the whole class.

context_blocks.text: A conjunctive query combines relational lookups with shared variables, then projects away variables that are not requested in the output. For example, \(q(x,z)=\exists y R(x,y)\land S(y,z)\) asks for all endpoint pairs connected through an intermediate value. It may have many witnesses y for one answer \((x,z)\), but under the set semantics here that answer must be printed only once. A self-join occurs when several atoms use the same relation symbol.

This is data complexity: q is fixed while the database grows. Even a fixed query can produce quadratically or cubically many answers, so linear total running time is often impossible just because of output size. Linear preprocessing followed by constant delay is a more appropriate ideal. It permits total time proportional to input plus output while also controlling the wait for each answer, including the first one and the final termination signal.

The classical positive condition is free-connex acyclicity. Form the query hypergraph with a vertex for each variable and one edge for the variables of each atom. It is acyclic when its edges admit a join tree: the edges containing any particular variable form a connected subtree. Free-connex additionally requires acyclicity after adding one edge containing all output variables. Bagan–Durand–Grandjean develop constant-delay enumeration for this structure.

For the example \(\exists y R(x,y)\land S(y,z)\), the two atom edges form a path, but adding the output edge \(\{x,z\}\) creates a cycle. Its answers are exactly the nonzero entries in the Boolean product of the two relation matrices. This explains why projection is tied to matrix multiplication. Classical hardness for acyclic self-join-free queries relies on a Boolean-matrix-multiplication assumption, rather than an unconditional superlinear lower bound.

Carmeli–Segoufin show that the self-join-free classification does not extend merely by ignoring repeated relation names. Some cyclic queries with self-joins allow constant-delay enumeration. Their paper gives positive and negative conditions, a classification for queries with at most two output variables under stated hyperclique assumptions, and further results for queries whose Boolean cores are cyclic. A general classification remains outside these theorems.

A particularly instructive example is the full query \(R(x,y)\land R(y,z)\land R(x,t)\land R(t,z)\). A two-step path from x to z already yields an answer with \(t=y\). When another middle vertex becomes available for those endpoints, it can be paired with previously stored middle vertices to produce further answers. The paper generalizes this symmetry through mirror queries. Its algorithms may store information proportional to the output, which is why this card explicitly allows growing memory.

Adding a predicate on only one of the two middle vertices can break that symmetry. More generally, assignments can identify several query variables with one database element. This is allowed by the syntax; injective matching would be another task. Such identifications generate extra answers that can invalidate a hardness reduction designed for independent relations. Any complete criterion has to account for the interaction between repeated symbols, variable identifications and the chosen output variables.

Rouvroy’s May 2025 research report studies acyclic queries with self-joins and projections, focusing on atoms of arity at most two. It develops a sufficient condition through a construction called patching, alongside necessary conditions and examples not captured by either side. The report explicitly says it is not yet polished. These are useful additional tractability results, but the report does not claim the full classification; relation arity at most two also differs from having at most two output variables.

The source question asks for a structural classification. To make this card a definite yes/no problem, the formal target asks whether membership in the tractable class is decidable from query syntax. This does not demand a fast classifier, nor one uniform enumerator with constants independent of q. It does demand termination for every query. A finite list of sufficient patterns is progress only if there is also a justified answer for every remaining query.

Recent dichotomies for incremental view maintenance concern another resource tradeoff. There the update cost and the semiring affect tractability. Such a dynamic, annotated classification does not resolve static distinct-answer enumeration with arbitrary self-joins.

A solution would explain exactly when a query can be compiled into an output stream with predictable response time after one linear scan of its data. The significance reaches beyond one faster join implementation: it would provide a general language-level boundary for a basic form of relational computation. The explicit memory, projection and duplicate conventions make proposed classifications comparable instead of allowing the target to change between examples.

sentences: A conjunctive query joins relations and projects the resulting assignments to its output variables.
The question asks for a terminating classifier deciding which queries allow linear preprocessing followed by constant-delay enumeration of distinct answers.
Self-joins are allowed, so repeated uses of one relation can create symmetries and dependencies absent from simpler classifications.
A complete answer would identify the exact boundary for efficiently generating query results in this basic language.
The reviewed formulation fixes the RAM and termination conventions, and the classifier itself need not run quickly or output the enumeration algorithm.

cards.context:
A conjunctive query combines relational lookups with shared variables, then projects away variables that are not requested in the output. For example, \(q(x,z)=\exists y R(x,y)\land S(y,z)\) asks for all endpoint pairs connected through an intermediate value. It may have many witnesses y for one answer \((x,z)\), but under the set semantics here that answer must be printed only once. A self-join occurs when several atoms use the same relation symbol.

This is data complexity: q is fixed while the database grows. Even a fixed query can produce quadratically or cubically many answers, so linear total running time is often impossible just because of output size. Linear preprocessing followed by constant delay is a more appropriate ideal. It permits total time proportional to input plus output while also controlling the wait for each answer, including the first one and the final termination signal.

The classical positive condition is free-connex acyclicity. Form the query hypergraph with a vertex for each variable and one edge for the variables of each atom. It is acyclic when its edges admit a join tree: the edges containing any particular variable form a connected subtree. Free-connex additionally requires acyclicity after adding one edge containing all output variables. Bagan–Durand–Grandjean develop constant-delay enumeration for this structure.

For the example \(\exists y R(x,y)\land S(y,z)\), the two atom edges form a path, but adding the output edge \(\{x,z\}\) creates a cycle. Its answers are exactly the nonzero entries in the Boolean product of the two relation matrices. This explains why projection is tied to matrix multiplication. Classical hardness for acyclic self-join-free queries relies on a Boolean-matrix-multiplication assumption, rather than an unconditional superlinear lower bound.

Carmeli–Segoufin show that the self-join-free classification does not extend merely by ignoring repeated relation names. Some cyclic queries with self-joins allow constant-delay enumeration. Their paper gives positive and negative conditions, a classification for queries with at most two output variables under stated hyperclique assumptions, and further results for queries whose Boolean cores are cyclic. A general classification remains outside these theorems.

A particularly instructive example is the full query \(R(x,y)\land R(y,z)\land R(x,t)\land R(t,z)\). A two-step path from x to z already yields an answer with \(t=y\). When another middle vertex becomes available for those endpoints, it can be paired with previously stored middle vertices to produce further answers. The paper generalizes this symmetry through mirror queries. Its algorithms may store information proportional to the output, which is why this card explicitly allows growing memory.

Adding a predicate on only one of the two middle vertices can break that symmetry. More generally, assignments can identify several query variables with one database element. This is allowed by the syntax; injective matching would be another task. Such identifications generate extra answers that can invalidate a hardness reduction designed for independent relations. Any complete criterion has to account for the interaction between repeated symbols, variable identifications and the chosen output variables.

It develops a sufficient condition through a construction called patching, alongside necessary conditions and examples not captured by either side. The report explicitly says it is not yet polished. These are useful additional tractability results, but the report does not claim the full classification; relation arity at most two also differs from having at most two output variables.

The source question asks for a structural classification. To make this card a definite yes/no problem, the formal target asks whether membership in the tractable class is decidable from query syntax. This does not demand a fast classifier, nor one uniform enumerator with constants independent of q. It does demand termination for every query. A finite list of sufficient patterns is progress only if there is also a justified answer for every remaining query.

cards.definitions: A finite relational vocabulary \(\tau\) lists finitely many relation symbols with fixed positive arities. A finite \(\tau\)-structure A has a nonempty finite domain and interprets each r-ary symbol as a subset of \(A^{r}\). An isomorphism is a bijection between domains that preserves and reflects every relation. For computation, label the n domain elements by \([n]\) and encode the domain explicitly together with all relation tables in binary. Different labelings of the same abstract structure are permitted; the input supplies no distinguished order relation. A Boolean property is an isomorphism-closed class of structures of one vocabulary. It is in PTIME when one deterministic Turing machine decides membership for every encoding in time polynomial in its length. The logic has a decidable set of finite binary sentence encodings with their vocabularies. Each sentence \(\varphi\) has a truth value \(A\models \varphi\) invariant under isomorphism. One total computable compiler, given a valid \((\tau ,\varphi )\), outputs a deterministic machine \(M_{\varphi}\) and integers \(C_{\varphi},k_{\varphi}\ge 1\) such that \(M_{\varphi}\) decides \(A\models \varphi\) in at most \(C_{\varphi}(N+1)^{k_{\varphi}}\) steps on every valid input structure encoding of length N. Finally, for every finite \(\tau\) and every PTIME Boolean property Q of \(\tau\)-structures, some fixed \(\tau\)-sentence \(\varphi\) satisfies \(A\models \varphi\) exactly when \(A\in Q\) for all finite A. Neither sentence construction from an arbitrary machine nor polynomial-time compilation is required. The exponent may depend on the sentence. No uniform polynomial bound for the combined input \((\varphi ,A)\) is imposed. The same syntax and compiler must work across vocabularies; no oracle, advice or externally chosen ordering is supplied to the semantics.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution gives a formalism satisfying decidable syntax, invariant semantics, effective polynomial-time compilation and expressive completeness for every finite relational vocabulary. A negative resolution proves that no formalism can satisfy all these requirements. Failure of one named logic, capture on a restricted class of structures, or capture with an additional input order does not decide general existence.

context_blocks.title: Properties should survive renaming
context_blocks.text: A graph with vertices called 1, 2 and 3 has the same abstract edges after a consistent permutation of those names. The property “the graph is connected” is unchanged; the property “vertex 1 has a neighbour named 2” can change. A logic for structures must express the first kind of property. An ordinary algorithm still receives a labeled encoding and may use its order internally, but its final Boolean answer must depend only on the structure being represented.

context_blocks.title: Why an effective syntax matters
context_blocks.text: One could assign a symbol to each polynomial-time property and declare that the symbol names that property. This supplies no way to evaluate the symbols. The compiler requirement makes the connection operational: from a sentence, one must obtain an actual algorithm and its polynomial clock. Similarly, listing all clocked machines does not ensure that every listed machine gives the same answer after relabeling its input. The task is to combine effective enumeration with invariance and full expressive power.

context_blocks.title: The known ordered theorem
context_blocks.text: The Immerman–Vardi theorem captures polynomial time by fixed-point logic on structures equipped with a linear order. Fixed-point operators express iterative constructions such as repeatedly extending a reachability relation until no new pairs appear. The order allows the logic to organize elements and simulate an ordinary computation. In the present question the order is absent from the mathematical input. Adding one to every structure changes what the sentence is permitted to access, so the ordered theorem does not directly settle the unordered case.

context_blocks.title: Capturing is not one universal time bound
context_blocks.text: One sentence may compile to a quadratic algorithm and another to an algorithm taking the tenth power of the input size. Both are permitted. The sentence is fixed when its data complexity is measured. Conversely, expressive completeness asks for a single sentence for an entire property on all finite input sizes. Writing a separate sentence for each graph, or a different sentence for each domain size, would not supply the required description.

context_blocks.title: The remaining gap
context_blocks.text: Known extensions of fixed-point logic add counting, linear algebra or symmetry-preserving computation, but ruling out a particular candidate is not a proof that no logic exists. Lichter and Schweitzer’s witnessed symmetric choice extends a candidate logic and yields capturing results on classes where isomorphism is definable; the premise is not known for all structures. Dahan’s August 2026 paper explicitly retains the general question. Its obstruction to choosing small symmetric generating sets concerns a structured output task, rather than proving that no logic can express every PTIME Boolean property. Finally, if \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), existential second-order logic would capture P by Fagin’s theorem and would have effective polynomial-time evaluation. Thus a proof that no such logic exists would also separate P from NP.

cards.title: Asser’s problem
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal: For every first-order sentence \(\varphi\) over a finite relational vocabulary, does there exist a first-order sentence \(\psi\) over some finite relational vocabulary such that, for every positive integer \(n, \psi\) has a model with exactly n elements if and only if \(\varphi\) has no model with exactly n elements?
cards.definitions: A vocabulary is a finite list of relation symbols, each with a specified positive integer arity; the list and the arities may vary with the sentence and are not bounded by a fixed global constant. Equality is allowed. Sentences use variables, relation atoms, equality, Boolean connectives and first-order quantification, with no free variables. A finite model has a nonempty domain A and interprets each k-ary relation as a subset of \(A^{k}\), with equality interpreted as equality on A. The spectrum \(Spec(\varphi )\) is {\(n\in N:n\ge 1\) and some finite model of \(\varphi\) has cardinality n}. The required equality is \(Spec(\psi )=N_{>0}\) minus \(Spec(\varphi )\). The vocabulary of \(\psi\) need not be the vocabulary of \(\varphi\). No bound on the length of \(\psi\) and no effective transformation \(\varphi \mapsto \psi\) are required. Restricting to relational vocabularies loses no ordinary first-order spectra: functions and constants can be represented by their graph relations with first-order axioms for totality and uniqueness. This is closure of the class of spectra, not a decision procedure for finite satisfiability.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.

context_blocks.text: A spectrum forgets the internal structure of a model and remembers only its possible finite sizes. A sentence can impose substantial combinatorial conditions on its relations, but the resulting object is just a subset of the positive integers. Asser’s question asks whether sizes excluded by one finite description can themselves be the allowed sizes of another finite description.

Negating the sentence does not solve the problem. If \(\varphi\) describes a graph consisting of disjoint edges covering all vertices, its spectrum contains the positive even numbers. An even-sized edgeless graph nevertheless satisfies \(\neg \varphi\), so even numbers also belong to \(Spec(\neg \varphi )\). Existence of a countermodel at a given size is different from absence of every model at that size.

The quantifier order is therefore essential. The target permits a new sentence \(\psi\), chosen after \(\varphi\) but before n, which represents the entire complement simultaneously. It is not enough to provide a separate sentence for each excluded size. Allowing \(\psi  a\) different vocabulary also prevents an arbitrary choice of representation from imposing an unintended extra restriction.

The spectrum problem helped shape finite model theory and descriptive complexity. The survey by Durand, Jones, Makowsky and More records Asser’s complement question as unresolved and connects the subject with bounded computational resources and structural restrictions on models. The importance here is the closure operation on the full expressive class, rather than one particular encoding of a graph family.

The existing logic-for-PTIME card asks for a logical characterization of efficient properties of individual finite structures. This card instead concerns the sets of cardinalities admitting some structure satisfying a sentence. It adds a different foundational question to the database and finite-model-theory bucket, even though both connect logic with computation.

cards.title: Decidability of conjunctive-query entailment in SROIQ
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal: Does one total algorithm decide, for every finite SROIQ knowledge base K and every Boolean conjunctive query q, whether \(K\models q\) under the standard semantics over all finite or infinite models?
cards.definitions: Fix classical SROIQ without datatypes, using the syntax of Horrocks–Kutz–Sattler (2006), Definitions 1–6. Concept names denote subsets of a nonempty domain; nominal concept names denote singletons; individual names denote elements, without a unique-name assumption. Role names denote binary relations, inverse roles reverse their arguments, and U denotes the universal relation. Concepts are built from names, ⊤, ⊥, Boolean operations, \(\exists r\).C and \(\forall r\).C, qualified number restrictions \(\ge k s\).C and \(\le k s\).C, and \(\exists s\).Self. The last three require a simple role s. They mean, respectively, at least or at most k distinct s-successors satisfying C, and an s-edge from an element to itself. The nonnegative integer k is encoded in binary. K consists of concept inclusions C⊑D, individual assertions \(C(a), r(a,b), \neg r(a,b), a\ne b\), and a legal role box. Role inclusions have form w⊑R, with R a non-universal role name and w a nonempty string of non-universal roles, interpreted by relational composition. Regularity requires a strict partial order ≺ on roles satisfying S≺R iff \(Inv(S)\)≺R, such that each inclusion has \(w=RR, w=Inv(R)\), or \(w=S_{1}\ldots S_{t}, RS_{1}\ldots S_{t}\), or \(S_{1}\ldots S_{t}R\) with every \(S_{i}\)≺R. Equivalent roles can first be identified. Transitivity and symmetry are represented by RR⊑R and \(Inv(R)\)⊑R. A role is non-simple if a composition of length at least two is included in it, or in one of its subroles, closing under inverse; all other roles are simple. Reflexivity assertions are allowed; irreflexivity, strict asymmetry and role-disjointness assertions require simple roles. U cannot occur in role-box assertions. These are the standard global regularity and simplicity restrictions, not unrestricted role-chain rules. The query is \(q=\exists x_{1}\ldots x_{t} \land _{j}\alpha _{j}\), where each atom is \(A(u)\) or \(r(u,v), A\) is a concept name, r is a role name, and terms are variables or individual names. Query roles may be non-simple. Query atoms have no negation, inequality or regular-path operators; variables may receive the same value. A model satisfies q when some assignment makes every atom true. \(K\models q\) means every model of K satisfies q, including infinite models; an inconsistent K entails every query. Both K and q are input, and the sought algorithm must halt on every legal pair, with no prescribed complexity bound.

context_blocks.text: A knowledge base describes incomplete information about a world. Its assertions name some objects, while its general axioms can require additional unnamed objects in every possible world. A Boolean query asks whether a finite relational pattern must exist. The problem is to decide whether the pattern follows from the whole specification, rather than whether it can be found among explicitly stored facts.

For example, let K assert \(Person(a)\) and Person⊑\(\exists\)knows.Person. Every model then contains a person who knows a person, so K entails \(\exists x\exists y\)(\(Person(x)\land knows(x,y)\land Person(y)\)). No named witness for y is needed. The same individual may serve as both variables when the model permits it. More complicated queries reuse variables across several edges, requiring a single assignment that satisfies all joins simultaneously.

SROIQ combines concept negation, existential and universal restrictions, singleton concepts, inverse roles, counting and regular role chains. This expressive combination underlies the logical core of OWL 2 DL. The role restrictions in the definitions are substantive: removing regularity or allowing arbitrary counting over composite roles produces different logics. The original SROIQ paper supplies a decision procedure for consistency, but that alone does not answer arbitrary conjunctive queries.

The conjunction of K with \(\neg q\) is inconsistent exactly when K entails q, but the negation of an arbitrary joined relational pattern need not be expressible as a SROIQ knowledge base. Likewise, a finite graph built by a consistency tableau is usually a compact representation of models, not an ordinary database on which evaluating q automatically gives the right answer. Unfolding repeated nodes can change whether a query cycle exists.

Rudolph and Glimm resolved a major part of the surrounding question in 2010. They handle nominals, inverse roles and counting together, and obtain decidability for SROIQ when all binary query predicates are simple roles. Thus the mere presence of those three constructors is not the remaining obstacle. The full question on this card also allows the query to inspect roles affected by transitivity and more general role compositions.

A different positive frontier comes from Horn restrictions. Ortiz, Rudolph and Šimkus show decidability even for a stronger path-query language over Horn-SROIQ, with doubly exponential combined complexity. Horn knowledge bases exclude forms of disjunctive choice that full SROIQ permits. Their result is therefore highly relevant progress, while leaving the unrestricted combination of knowledge-base features and query joins unresolved.

The distinction between all models and finite models is particularly consequential. Rudolph proves undecidability of finite conjunctive-query entailment already in a fragment of SROIQ. This is not an undecidability proof for the semantics chosen here: the sets of countermodels differ, and the distinction can affect the answer even on a small example.

To see the difference directly, require every domain element to have exactly one r-successor and at most one r-predecessor, and require a named element a to have no predecessor. The role r can be simple. Such a knowledge base has an infinite model, the natural-number successor chain, but no finite model: on a finite set, an injective total successor function would be surjective. A fresh predicate A may be empty in the infinite model, so \(\exists x A(x)\) is not entailed over all models. Over finite models it is vacuously entailed, because there are none.

Steigmiller and Glimm’s 2019 absorption method addresses practical entailment checking in very expressive logics and is implemented in Konclude. Its termination argument depends on a bounded supply of newly generated nominals in the difficult feature combination. Useful empirical behavior and termination on substantial fragments do not establish a total procedure for every SROIQ input. This conditional termination is exactly why the inherited source continues to present full decidability as open.

There is relevant progress as recently as 2026, but on a different slice of the language. Ibáñez-García, Jung, Michielini and Murlak show that conjunctive-query entailment for S, which adds transitive roles to ALC, is 2ExpTime-complete; hardness already uses two transitive roles and a Boolean conjunctive query. Their May 2026 full version also treats restrictions giving smaller upper bounds. This settles a complexity question for S, not the decidability of full SROIQ.

A positive solution would establish that general finite query patterns can always be answered against this expressive ontology language in principle. A negative solution would identify a sharp gap between consistency checking and pattern entailment inside a standard logical framework. Either outcome would clarify which expressive features can be combined while retaining an algorithmic foundation for querying incomplete knowledge.

cards.title: Conjunctive-query containment under bag semantics
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal: Does a Turing machine exist that halts on every pair of finite conjunctive queries \(q_{1}\) and \(q_{2}\) with the same output arity and decides whether $q_1(D)(a)\le q_2(D)(a)$ for every finite bag database D over their common relational signature and every output tuple a? A query $q(x)\!:\!-A_1,\ldots,A_m$ is evaluated by $q(D)(a)=\sum_{h:h(x)=a}\prod_{j=1}^{m}D(A_j[h])$, where h ranges over assignments of its variables to the finite database domain and \(D(A_{j}[h])\) is the nonnegative integer multiplicity of the instantiated tuple. Both input relations and query answers retain multiplicities.
cards.definitions: A relational signature lists finitely many relation names and their arities. A finite bag database supplies a finite domain U and, for each relation symbol of arity r, a function \(U^{r}\) to the nonnegative integers. Zero means the tuple is absent. A query body is a finite list of positive relational atoms with variables or named constants as arguments; constants denote distinct fixed elements of U. Every variable, including every output variable, must occur in a body atom. Repeated occurrences of relation names, variables, or entire atoms are allowed and are interpreted by the displayed sum-product rule. Assignments fix constants. No disjunction, negation, inequality, comparison predicate, aggregation operator, or recursion is permitted. The output tuple lists the values of the head variables in order. Boolean queries have an empty head and return the multiplicity of the single empty tuple. The question is about deciding containment from the queries alone, with no database supplied and no size or multiplicity bound on databases.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a total algorithm deciding exactly this universal multiplicity inequality, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Enumerating counterexample databases only semidecides noncontainment. A procedure for set-valued databases, query equivalence, or a proper subclass of queries is insufficient; undecidability for unions, inequalities, or a modified numerical comparison is insufficient unless reduced to the stated plain-CQ problem.
cards.why: Bag semantics captures duplicate-sensitive query behavior, and containment is a basic correctness test for query optimization. Its unknown decidability marks a fundamental gap between simple positive query syntax and unbounded counting over finite structures. The problem also connects database theory with homomorphism inequalities and arithmetic decision problems.

importance.reason: A longstanding central decidability question for the most basic duplicate-sensitive query language. It has broad consequences for query rewriting and connects finite-model counting with undecidability boundaries.

progress.text: Chaudhuri and Vardi raise the bag-containment decidability question; the 2025 seminar traces the problem to their PODS paper.

Marcinkowski and Orda prove undecidability for nearby generalizations, including comparison after a supplied linear transformation of a Boolean query’s count. This is not the unmodified containment predicate.
Konstantinidis and Mogavero prove decidability when the left query is join-on-free and the right query is a general CQ. This extends the earlier projection-free decidable case.
The revised Marcinkowski–Ostropolski-Nalewaja paper develops techniques connecting CQ and UCQ containment, while explicitly leaving ordinary CQ-versus-CQ bag-containment decidability open.
Amarilli’s maintained question list continues to list bag-containment decidability. Current searches did not locate a resolution of the plain two-CQ formulation.

context_blocks.text: Containment asks whether one query can ever produce more of some answer than another. Under set semantics only presence matters. Under bag semantics, a join multiplies available copies and projection adds contributions from different witnesses. The multiplicities can therefore change even when the two queries return exactly the same set of answers.

For a minimal example, let \(q(x)\) have body \(R(x)\), and let \(r(x)\) have body \(R(x),R(x)\). If \(R(a)\) has multiplicity m, then q returns m copies of a and r returns \(m^{2}\). Their answer sets always coincide, but the reverse bag-containment r contained in q fails as soon as \(m=2\). This demonstrates why duplicate-insensitive rewrites need a different correctness argument.

For one fixed finite database, both values can be computed by enumerating assignments. The challenge is the quantifier over every database of every size and every choice of multiplicities. Noncontainment has a finite witness that can eventually be found by exhaustive enumeration. A decision procedure also needs to halt when no witness exists; a counterexample search by itself does not solve that side.

The 2025 seminar still identifies this as a longstanding unresolved boundary. Recent work establishes decidability for a restricted left-hand query in which existential variables do not participate in joins, while related work proves undecidability after extending the query language or numerical comparison. These results make the precise boundary especially significant: small changes around the basic formulation have known answers, but do not settle two unrestricted plain conjunctive queries.

cards.formal: Does there exist one effective logic \(\mathcal L\), in the precise sense below, whose sentences define exactly all deterministic logarithmic-space Boolean properties of finite unordered relational structures, for every finite relational vocabulary?

importance.reason: A broad descriptive-complexity existence question for a central resource class, with consequences for the expressive limits of order-independent database queries. It is distinct from improving one proposed recursion operator.

sentences: The input is a finite relational structure with no distinguished ordering of its elements.
The question asks for an effective logic expressing exactly all isomorphism-invariant Boolean queries decidable in deterministic logarithmic space.
Each sentence must compile to a halting evaluation algorithm with a certified logarithmic workspace bound.
The proposed CLogspace logic is known to miss some such queries, while ordered structures and strings admit stronger capturing results.
A solution would settle a broad descriptive-complexity question linking small-memory computation to the expressive power of logical queries.

cards.definitions:
A vocabulary \(\tau\) is a finite list of relation symbols, each with a fixed positive integer arity. A \(\tau\)-structure \(A\) has a finite nonempty domain and, for each \(r\)-ary symbol, an \(r\)-ary relation on that domain. An isomorphism is a bijection preserving and reflecting every relation. A Boolean property of \(\tau\)-structures is a class closed under isomorphism. The mathematical input supplies no distinguished ordering of its elements.

For computation, label the domain by \([n]=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\). Encode \(n\) in unary followed by all relation truth tables in the vocabulary order and lexicographic tuple order, using one bit per tuple. Write \(N\) for the full encoding length. All labelings of a structure are valid encodings. A property is in deterministic logarithmic space, denoted \(\mathrm L\), if a fixed deterministic Turing machine halts and decides it correctly on every such encoding using at most \(C\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil\) work-tape cells for some fixed positive integer \(C\). Machines have a read-only two-way input tape, a finite control, and a fixed finite number of work tapes over fixed finite alphabets. Work space counts all cells visited on the work tapes; the input tape is not writable. They have no oracle, advice, auxiliary input, or random bits. A machine may use the encoding order internally, but its answer must be the same on all isomorphic inputs.

The proposed logic has a decidable set of finite binary encodings of pairs \((\tau,\varphi)\), where \(\varphi\) is a sentence over \(\tau\). Each valid sentence has a Boolean satisfaction relation \(A\models\varphi\) on all finite nonempty \(\tau\)-structures, invariant under isomorphism. There must be one total computable compiler that, on a valid pair, outputs a deterministic Turing machine \(M_\varphi\) and a positive integer \(C_\varphi\). For every valid encoding of every \(\tau\)-structure, \(M_\varphi\) must halt, return its satisfaction value, and use at most \(C_\varphi\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil\) work cells. On invalid sentence encodings the compiler may return a fixed error symbol. Syntax checking and compilation are not required to run in logarithmic space or polynomial time.

Expressive completeness requires that for every finite \(\tau\) and every isomorphism-invariant \(\mathrm L\) property \(Q\) of its structures, there is one fixed \(\tau\)-sentence \(\varphi\) such that \[ \forall A:\quad A\models\varphi\iff A\in Q.\] The sentence and its space constant may depend on \(Q\) and \(\tau\), but not on \(A\). The same syntax and compiler work across all vocabularies. No computable translation from arbitrary invariant machines to sentences is required. There is no uniform logarithmic-space requirement when the sentence is part of the evaluation input. A relational query with a fixed tuple of distinguished elements can be represented as a Boolean property in a vocabulary expanded by singleton unary relations marking those elements; the target uses the Boolean convention throughout.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a logic exists, including decidable syntax, invariant semantics, effective evaluation with certified per-sentence space constants, and expressive completeness; or prove that no logic meets all those conditions. The formalism and its semantics must be specified, rather than merely assigning an uninterpreted name to each logarithmic-space property. A result for one candidate logic or for a restricted family of input structures does not settle this general existence question.

context_blocks.text: The source motivation is computation on large relational inputs with very little working memory. A representation necessarily labels the elements, but a query about the abstract structure must not change when those labels are permuted. Capturing asks for both expressive completeness and an effective resource-bounded evaluation of every sentence.

The 2019 paper constructs CLogspace as a logic for computations that preserve input symmetries. Its objects are finite sets built from input elements and further finite sets, equipped with size annotations and restricted recursion. Theorem 27 proves that this particular logic is strictly weaker than logarithmic space. That negative result concerns a candidate, not the existence of any capturing logic.

The saved passage asks whether ideas from CLogspace can yield a stronger logic. It specifies no formal class of permitted extensions. This card makes explicit the general logic-existence objective discussed in the same paper’s introduction and Section 5; it does not require a particular extension grammar or claim that CLogspace itself captures the class. The effective-syntax and compiler requirements follow the standard capturing convention, with the space bound stated separately here.

An externally supplied order changes the descriptive problem. The 2019 source recalls that deterministic transitive-closure logic captures logarithmic space on ordered structures. More recently, Bell, Day and Freydenberger obtain LOGSPACE-capturing fragments for string queries; the June 2026 abstract concerns strings, not arbitrary unordered relational inputs.

cards.title: Computability of entropic query-size bounds
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal:
Is the logarithmic entropic query-size bound uniformly computable? More precisely, does a single deterministic Turing machine, given any finite set of degree constraints \(\mathcal D=\{(X_i,Y_i,b_i):1\leq i\leq k\}\) on \([n]\) with nonnegative rational logarithmic budgets, and any \(m\in\mathbb N\), halt and output either \(+\infty\) when \(E(\mathcal D)=+\infty\), or a rational \(q\) satisfying \(|q-E(\mathcal D)|\leq 2^{-m}\) when
\[E(\mathcal D)=\sup\{h([n]):h\in\overline{\Gamma_n^*},\ h(Y_i)-h(X_i)\leq b_i\ (1\leq i\leq k)\}<+\infty?\]
Here \(\overline{\Gamma_n^*}\) is the closure of the discrete entropy region defined below; \(n\) is part of the input.
cards.why: The strongest information-theoretic query estimates are useful algorithmically only if their numerical values can be obtained effectively. A computability theorem would make this extremal use of arbitrary discrete distributions accessible to uniform algorithms; a noncomputability theorem would identify a fundamental limit on exact information-theoretic database estimation, even with unlimited running time.
cards.status_note: The 2022 seminar asks Question 7.1. Mengel–Romashchenko v1, 27 August 2026, abstract and introduction explicitly say that general entropic-bound computability is not known. A bounded primary-source check on 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution; cited results were read for their statements and scope, not independently proved.

progress.text: Hung Ngo poses computability of the entropic bound as Question 7.1 at Seminar 22301; the report appears in February 2023.

Suciu’s expanded paper gives the cone and duality framework; Theorem 9.7 identifies the entropic upper value with optimization over the almost-entropic closure. It does not provide a general computation procedure.
Im, Moseley, Ngo and Pruhs give a polynomial-size formulation for simple degree constraints, providing a tractable case of the coincident bounds.
Mengel and Romashchenko explicitly retain general entropic-bound computability as unknown while obtaining new results for acyclic constraints and projections.
