sentences: Entropy bounds limit the number of tuples returned by a database join from constraints on conditional degrees.
The entropic bound optimizes total entropy over the closure of all finite discrete entropy vectors.
The question asks for one terminating algorithm that computes this value to every requested absolute accuracy in arbitrary dimension.
Simple constraints admit effective special cases, while the general polymatroid relaxation can overestimate the desired value.
Resolving computability would determine whether the strongest information-theoretic estimate is accessible to algorithms at all.

cards.definitions:
Let \(n\geq1\), \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(2^{[n]}\) be its set of subsets. Given jointly distributed discrete random variables \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n\), each with a finite alphabet, their entropy vector is the real set function
\[h(S)=H(Z_S)=-\sum_z\Pr[Z_S=z]\log_2\Pr[Z_S=z],\qquad h(\varnothing)=0,\]
where \(Z_S\) is the tuple with indices in \(S\), and \(0\log_2 0=0\). Alphabets and real joint probabilities are unrestricted. The set of all such vectors is \(\Gamma_n^*\). Its closure \(\overline{\Gamma_n^*}\) in the finite-dimensional Euclidean space of subset coordinates consists of all limits of sequences of entropy vectors and is the almost-entropic cone. Neither alphabet sizes nor convergence rates are input bounds. Continuous differential entropy is not used.

A degree constraint is a triple \((X,Y,b)\), where \(X\subseteq Y\subseteq[n]\) and \(b\in\mathbb Q_{\geq0}\). It bounds the conditional entropy \(h(Y)-h(X)\). The case \(X=\varnothing\) gives a cardinality-type constraint, and \(b=0\) gives a functional dependency. Equal sets, repeated triples and an empty list are permitted. The all-zero entropy vector is always feasible, so the supremum is in \([0,+\infty]\). The optimization is over the closed almost-entropic cone, not just the nonclosed set of entropy vectors satisfying the constraints exactly; this distinction matters on faces defined by zero budgets.

For a database interpretation, a full conjunctive query returns the natural join of finite relations: an output tuple assigns all variables and its projection onto each relation's columns is present in that relation. There are no duplicate output tuples and no existentially projected variables. A bound of \(N\) on the number of extensions from columns \(X\) to columns \(Y\) gives the entropy budget \(b=\log_2 N\). Drawing a join tuple uniformly makes its full entropy the logarithm of the join size. The quantity \(2^{E(\mathcal D)}\) is the information-theoretic upper bound; the question asks to compute its logarithm, rather than to enumerate joins or compute the exact maximum size of a finite database instance.

The finite encoding used here writes \(n\) and the list length in unary, every subset as an \(n\)-bit mask, and each rational budget as a nonnegative binary numerator and a positive binary denominator, with delimiters. The precision \(m\) is given in unary. This is an explicit rational logarithmic-budget version of the source's numerical problem, with no real-number oracle. At the level of computability it also covers positive integer degree bounds supplied as \(N\): cone homogeneity handles rational budgets by scaling them to integer logarithms, while positive values \(\log_2 N\) can be bracketed multiplicatively by rational numbers, keeping zero budgets exactly zero. This equivalence concerns computability, not polynomial-time equivalence of the two encodings.

Unbounded inputs are included. They can be recognized by starting with \(S=\varnothing\) and repeatedly adjoining \(Y_i\) whenever \(X_i\subseteq S\). The optimum is finite exactly when the resulting closure is \([n]\). In that case conditional-entropy inequalities and subadditivity supply an explicit finite upper bound. If some variables remain outside, let them all share an arbitrarily high-entropy random variable and make the other variables constant; every constraint is satisfied while the objective is unbounded. Thus recognizing infinity is not the unknown part of the problem.

The machine must halt on every valid input, with a finite binary rational output in the bounded case; malformed strings may be rejected. There is no time or space bound, no advice, oracle, fixed dimension or randomness. Accuracy is absolute in base-two entropy units. In particular the machine must achieve error at most \(1/100\), by taking \(m=7\), and also every finer requested accuracy. A one-sided sequence of estimates without a computable error guarantee does not suffice.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that the displayed uniform machine exists, or that it does not. An affirmative proof must provide an effective procedure and prove termination and the requested two-sided absolute error for every finite dimension, rational degree-constraint list and precision, including zero budgets and the stated infinity convention. A negative proof must establish noncomputability of this particular functional, not merely undecidability of a different entropy-region membership or information-inequality problem. An exact symbolic formula is unnecessary, while a computable value for each separately fixed input without one uniform procedure is insufficient. There are no unproved complexity assumptions in the target.

source_formulation.text: Does an algorithm compute the entropic bound on query output size from the supplied constraints?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Question 7.1; entropy closure, numerical representation and accuracy are made explicit in this card.

context_blocks.text: The seminar groups several algorithmic questions about information-theoretic database bounds. Question 7.1 asks for computability of the entropic bound; Question 7.2 separately asks about the complexity of its polymatroid relaxation. The first issue is whether any terminating numerical algorithm exists, before asking whether one is efficient.

Entropy inequalities constrain correlations among columns in a join. Using every valid inequality gives a potentially sharper bound than the familiar Shannon inequalities alone. Suciu formulates the entropic upper bound by such inequalities and identifies its value with optimization over the closed almost-entropic cone. This closure specifies which limiting entropy vectors belong to the target.

Replacing the almost-entropic cone by normalized monotone submodular set functions gives a finite linear program, with exponentially many subset coordinates. This yields a computable upper relaxation, but a gap between that relaxation and the entropic optimum prevents it from settling the question. Restricting alphabet sizes also changes the feasible region unless a sufficient effective approximation theorem is proved.

For simple degree constraints, where every conditioning set has size at most one, the entropic and polymatroid bounds coincide and a polynomial-size linear program is available. This tractable subclass does not cover arbitrary conditioning sets or all zero-budget functional dependencies.

Mengel and Romashchenko still describe general computability as unresolved in August 2026. Their new work examines acyclic dependencies and shows that allowing projected variables can create gaps between entropy and polymatroid bounds. That result concerns the comparison of bounds in a richer query setting, not an algorithm or impossibility proof for the full general numerical target here.

cards.title: Linear-round convergence over stable semirings
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal: Is there a universal constant C such that the following holds for every integer \(p\ge 0\), every \(n\ge 1\), every commutative p-stable semiring S, and every polynomial map \(F:S^{n} -> S^{n}\) with coefficients in S? Starting with \(x^{0}=(0,\ldots ,0)\), perform synchronous iteration \(x^{t+1}=F(x^{t})\). There must exist an integer \(t\le C(p+1)n\) with \(x^{t+1}=x^{t}\). Here p-stability means $1\oplus a\oplus\cdots\oplus a^p=1\oplus a\oplus\cdots\oplus a^{p+1}$ for every a in S. The constant C is independent of the semiring, coefficients, number of monomials, and polynomial degrees. This is the grounded polynomial-system formulation of the source’s proposed linear convergence bound.
cards.definitions: A commutative semiring has associative, commutative addition op-plus with identity 0 and associative, commutative multiplication op-times with identity 1. Multiplication distributes over addition, and 0 times \(a=0\). No additive inverses are assumed. Powers use semiring multiplication and \(a^{0}=1\). Every component of F is a finite sum of finite products of coefficients and variables; repeated variables and constant terms are allowed. S need not be finite. One round evaluates all components using only the previous vector, not partially updated coordinates. Equality means exact equality of semiring elements. The cost measure is the number of rounds, irrespective of the work needed to evaluate a component or represent an element. In a grounded Datalog program, coordinates represent individual derived facts and their values are annotations; using all n coordinates also includes any that remain zero.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal bound, or refute it by constructing systems whose first fixed-point time divided by \((p+1)n\) is unbounded. A fixed example exceeding n rounds does not refute an unspecified constant C. A bound with a growing factor depending on degrees, coefficients, or n does not establish this target. A faster evaluation algorithm with a different update rule does not by itself bound the number of synchronous naive iterations.
cards.why: The problem asks whether local algebraic stability imposes a sharp global limit on recursive evaluation. A universal linear bound would explain why a broad class of annotated recursive computations needs only an output-scale number of rounds, while a separation would expose a fundamental cost of nonlinear interactions.

importance.reason: A foundational convergence question for semiring-valued recursion, with implications beyond one query language. Its historical significance is high, but a newly announced directly relevant paper makes current open status uncertain.

progress.text: Work on convergence of Datalog over pre-semirings establishes stable-semiring convergence and an exponential upper bound in the number of grounded coordinates; the later polynomial paper reviews this starting point.
Im, Moseley, Ngo, and Pruhs establish polynomial convergence for nonlinear programs. The inspected arXiv v2 states the additional sigma and lambda dependencies explicitly.
Ngo records the gap between the polynomial upper bound and \(Omega((p+1)n)\), and proposes a matching linear upper bound.

Author publication pages list Optimal Convergence of Iterative Methods for Datalogo, with a forthcoming PODS 2027 label on Ngo’s page. No theorem text was obtained for that entry. Its relationship to this exact target requires verification.

context_blocks.text: In ordinary Boolean Datalog, a derived fact switches from absent to present at most once. A nonstationary round must add a fact, so the number of possible facts bounds the number of rounds. Annotated recursion can improve the value attached to an already known fact many times. Counting how many coordinates exist therefore ceases to give an immediate termination bound.

The stability assumption controls repeated use of a single semiring element. It says that a sufficiently long truncated geometric sum absorbs the next power. The question asks whether a system of n interacting recurrences can multiply the resulting delay by only \(O(n)\), even when the equations are nonlinear. This is a structural claim about composition of recursive dependencies, not a bound on the time taken by one database join.

The examined Im–Moseley–Ngo–Pruhs preprint proves a polynomial convergence bound, with explicit dependence on sigma, the number of distinct coefficients referenced, and lambda, the maximum number of multiplicands. Its bound is O(sigma \(p n^{2}\) (\(n^{2} \log\)(lambda+1)+log(sigma+1))) for positive p; the 0-stable case has a separate linear bound. Suppressing sigma and lambda would conceal part of the remaining challenge.

The 2025 seminar asks for \(O((p+1)n)\), matching the order of its stated lower bound. A newer paper titled Optimal Convergence of Iterative Methods for Datalogo is now listed by its authors. The inspected listings supply no theorem or accessible manuscript for that entry. This card therefore preserves the precise historical question with an uncertain current status; the title alone does not identify which convergence bound, iteration scheme, or semiring hypotheses it settles.

cards.title: Complexity of polymatroid query-size bounds
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal:
Is computing the general polymatroid query-size bound NP-hard? Use the following exact comparison formulation and deterministic polynomial-time Turing reductions. Given \(n\geq1\), a finite list \(\mathcal D=\{(X_i,Y_i,b_i):1\leq i\leq k\}\) of rational logarithmic degree constraints and a rational threshold \(t\), let
\[P(\mathcal D)=\sup\{h([n]):h\in\Gamma_n,\ h(Y_i)-h(X_i)\leq b_i\text{ for all }i\},\]
where \(\Gamma_n\) is the cone of normalized monotone submodular set functions on \([n]\). Is the language
\[\mathrm{POLYBOUND}=\{\langle n,\mathcal D,t\rangle:P(\mathcal D)\geq t\}\]
NP-hard under the reduction convention below, when dimension and all constraints are part of the input?
cards.why: A general polynomial-time procedure would make a broad information-theoretic relaxation available for query planning without enumerating exponentially many subset entropies. A hardness theorem would explain why the known algorithms require special dependency structure. Determining which conclusion is justified separates a useful compact optimization method from a bound whose direct formulation is mainly an existential certificate.
cards.status_note: The 2022 source explicitly asks whether computing the general polymatroid bound is NP-hard. Im–Moseley–Ngo–Pruhs, 3 April 2025, still describe general polynomial-time computability as open and distinguish their normal-function hardness theorem from the unrestricted cone. A bounded primary-source search checked on 16 September 2026 found no matching general resolution; the exact rational-threshold and Turing-reduction conventions are stated editorial choices, and absence of a located resolution is not a proof of openness.

progress.text: The seminar records Hung Ngo’s question about the general complexity and possible NP-hardness of the polymatroid bound.
The Optimizing Polymatroid Functions preprint reports polynomial-time optimization for simple constraints and NP-hardness for the distinct normal-function optimization.

Theorem 1.1 supplies a polynomial-size LP for simple constraints; Theorem 1.3 gives general-to-restricted reductions, and Theorem 1.4 proves hardness only for normal functions. The introduction and conclusion still leave general polynomial-time computability open.

sentences: Polymatroid query bounds maximize a normalized monotone submodular function subject to supplied degree constraints.
The obvious linear program has exponentially many coordinates even when its input constraint list is short.
The source explicitly asks whether computing this general bound is NP-hard, formalized here through exact rational threshold comparisons.
Simple constraints admit polynomial-time algorithms, while hardness for the smaller cone of normal functions leaves the general question unresolved.
An answer would clarify whether this broad database estimation framework can be computed efficiently from compact dependency descriptions.

cards.definitions:
For \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), a polymatroid function is a real-valued function \(h:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R\) such that
\[h(\varnothing)=0,\qquad h(S)\leq h(T)\quad(S\subseteq T),\]
\[h(S)+h(T)\geq h(S\cup T)+h(S\cap T)\quad(S,T\subseteq[n]).\]
These conditions imply \(h(S)\geq0\). Their cone is \(\Gamma_n\). Coordinates may be arbitrary real numbers; functions need not be integer-valued matroid ranks or entropy vectors. A constraint \((X,Y,b)\) has \(X\subseteq Y\subseteq[n]\) and \(b\in\mathbb Q_{\geq0}\), and means \(h(Y)-h(X)\leq b\). An empty list, zero budgets, equal sets and repeated constraints are allowed. The zero function is feasible. Set \(P(\mathcal D)=+\infty\) for an unbounded objective; in that case every finite threshold is accepted. Otherwise the finite rational linear program attains a rational optimum, and equality with the threshold counts as yes.

The input explicitly lists the constraints, not the \(2^n\) values of a candidate function. Write \(n\) and the list length in unary, each subset as an \(n\)-bit mask, and every rational as a binary integer numerator and a positive binary denominator with delimiters; the threshold numerator may be negative. Let \(L\) be the total number of bits. Invalid strings are rejected. This card fixes the usual rational logarithmic-budget bit model for the source's optimization question: numbers \(b_i\), rather than potentially enormous degree counts \(2^{b_i}\), are supplied. It does not assume unit-cost exact arithmetic on arbitrary real inputs. Comparison is exact, with no numerical tolerance, promise gap, fixed dimension or fixed constraint arity.

The database meaning is as follows. A full conjunctive query joins finite relations by matching common columns and returns all variable columns, with set semantics. A degree bound \(N\) limits how many distinct \(Y\)-tuples extend each fixed \(X\)-tuple. For a uniform random output tuple, conditional entropy is at most \(\log_2 N\), while the entropy of the complete tuple is the logarithm of the result size. Every entropy vector satisfies the displayed polymatroid inequalities, so maximizing over polymatroids yields a valid logarithmic upper estimate. The source's linear-program framework is formalized here with rational logarithmic budgets. No database instance is an input to POLYBOUND, and maximizing the actual finite join size is a different optimization problem.

A language lies in NP when yes instances have binary certificates of polynomially bounded length verified by a deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine. NP-hardness here means that every such language can be decided by a deterministic oracle Turing machine with access to exact POLYBOUND membership and worst-case running time \(C(L+1)^c\), for some constants depending only on the reduced language. An oracle query returns one membership bit; writing the query and all other bit operations count toward the time bound. Equivalently, it suffices to give such a reduction from satisfiability of Boolean formulas in conjunctive normal form with at most three literals per clause. Clauses are disjunctions of variables or their negations, and the formula is the conjunction of its clauses. This explicitly chosen Turing-reduction convention avoids changing hardness when the complementary threshold convention is used. No randomized reduction, advice or entropy oracle is allowed.

The full optimization has \(2^n\) subset variables and exponentially many monotonicity and submodularity inequalities, so explicit rational linear programming gives a terminating algorithm taking time at most exponential in a polynomial of \(L\). That upper bound does not establish NP-hardness. The issue is the cost in the compact input length; with \(n\) fixed the linear program has fixed dimension.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that POLYBOUND is NP-hard under the stated deterministic polynomial-time Turing reductions, or a proof of the logical negation of that assertion. A positive proof must preserve the general polymatroid feasible cone and the finite input encoding, and establish correctness for every source instance. Hardness of a restriction on the admissible functions, such as the cone of normal functions, does not imply this claim unless a valid reduction to POLYBOUND is proved. A polynomial-time algorithm would settle the principal algorithmic side of the source's broader complexity question, but by itself proves the negation of NP-hardness only together with a proved separation of P from NP; an unproved separation must be stated as a conditional result. Neither an exponential-size LP formulation nor difficulty computing a different entropic bound is a negative algorithmic result for this problem.

source_formulation.text: Determine the complexity of computing the polymatroid bound; in particular, is the general computation NP-hard?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Question 7.2. The card retains its explicit NP-hardness question and fixes rational logarithmic inputs, exact comparison and polynomial-time Turing reductions.

context_blocks.text: The source asks both for the complexity of the polymatroid bound and, explicitly, whether it is NP-hard. The displayed yes/no target is this stated hardness question for the entire degree-constraint class. The companion entropic question concerns existence of any computation procedure; the polymatroid bound is already computable by finite linear programming.

Unlike minimizing one supplied submodular function, this problem optimizes over the values of an unknown submodular function. The constraint list is compact but a direct feasible function has exponentially many subset coordinates. Standard polynomial-time solvability of explicit linear programs therefore leaves the desired compact-input complexity unresolved.

A degree constraint is simple when its conditioning set has at most one variable. For this class, Im and coauthors give a linear program with O(k n²) variables and O(k n) constraints, and an efficiently obtainable derivation of the bound using Shannon inequalities. The 2022 preprint already reports the tractability breakthrough; the 2025 paper supplies the formulation and theorem locators used here.

Theorem 1.3 of the 2025 paper reduces the general problem to several apparently restricted degree languages, including constraints with conditioning sets of size at most two and total sets of size at most three. Its statement that these cases are as hard as the general case is a reduction result, not a proof that any of them is NP-hard.

The same paper does prove NP-hardness after restricting feasible polymatroids to normal functions. Such functions have the form h(S)=Σ_T w_T·1[S∩T≠∅], with nonnegative weights indexed by nonempty variable subsets T. This is a smaller cone; its constrained maximum can change when arbitrary polymatroids are permitted. The hardness therefore does not settle Question 7.2.

Theorem 1.3 of the 2025 paper reduces the general problem to several apparently restricted degree languages, including constraints with conditioning sets of size at most two and total sets of size at most three. Its statement that these cases are as hard as the general case is a reduction result, not a proof that any of them is NP-hard.

The same paper does prove NP-hardness after restricting feasible polymatroids to normal functions. Such functions have the form h(S)=Σ_T w_T·1[S∩T≠∅], with nonnegative weights indexed by nonempty variable subsets T. This is a smaller cone; its constrained maximum can change when arbitrary polymatroids are permitted. The hardness therefore does not settle Question 7.2.

cards.title: BDD/FC conjecture
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal: Is every finite set \(R\) of existential tuple-generating dependencies with bounded derivation depth finitely controllable? Use the precise query-rewriting definition of bounded derivation depth below. The required conclusion is that for every finite database \(I\) and every Boolean conjunctive query \(q\), \[(I,R)\models q\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(I,R)\models_{\mathrm{fin}}q.\] The left side quantifies over all models extending \(I\) and satisfying \(R\); the right side quantifies only over finite such models. The conjecture quantifies over every finite relational signature of arbitrary finite arities, and permits conjunctions of several atoms in rule heads.
cards.why: Bounded derivation depth permits queries under existential rules to be answered through finite positive rewritings on the original database. Finite controllability asks whether considering only finite possible worlds changes those answers. Connecting the two would clarify when this useful query-processing property also supports finite-model semantics, across arbitrary relational arities.
cards.status_note: The general conjecture is explicitly open in the checked PODS 2025 paper, which was posted to arXiv in March 2026. Its structural theorem does not imply full finite controllability, and the original binary-signature theorem assumes single-head rules. Bounded later-work checks through 2026-09-15 found no resolution of the unrestricted target; the review is not an exhaustive proof or literature certification.

sentences: The BDD/FC conjecture asks whether every finite existential rule set with bounded derivation depth is finitely controllable.
Bounded derivation depth is expressed by a finite positive rewriting for each conjunctive query that works on every database.
Finite controllability means that a query failing in some unrestricted model also fails in a finite model.
The question allows arbitrary finite relational arities and several atoms in a rule head.
The known binary theorem requires single-head rules, and the checked PODS 2025 result posted in 2026 leaves the general conjecture open.

cards.definitions: A relational signature is a finite collection of relation symbols, each with a fixed nonnegative integer arity. An atom has the form \(P(t_1,\ldots,t_a)\), with repeated arguments allowed. In rules and queries the arguments are variables; there are no function symbols, built-in equality or inequality, negation, or interpreted order. A rule is the sentence \(\forall\bar x\,\forall\bar y\,(B(\bar x,\bar y)\to\exists\bar z\,H(\bar y,\bar z))\), where \(B,H\) are finite nonempty conjunctions of atoms, each universal variable occurs in \(B\), and the only universal variables in \(H\) come from \(\bar y\). The tuples of universal and existential variables are disjoint. The existential tuple may be empty, so ordinary positive Datalog rules are included. A rule set is finite, and rule heads may contain several atoms. A database \(I\) is a finite set of relational facts on finitely many named distinct elements; its active domain is the set of elements appearing in these facts. Empty active domains and nullary facts are allowed. A model extending \(I\) has a nonempty domain containing its named elements and includes every fact of \(I\); it may add elements and facts, including new facts on old elements. It satisfies \(R\) with ordinary first-order semantics, and must preserve the identities of the named database elements. “Finite model” means a finite domain, with no prescribed cardinality bound. A conjunctive query \(q(\bar u)=\exists\bar v\,A(\bar u,\bar v)\) uses a finite nonempty conjunction of relational atoms, with every displayed free variable occurring in an atom. A Boolean query has no free variables. A union of conjunctive queries is a finite disjunction of such queries with the same free variables; the empty disjunction denotes false. Query evaluation on a database means a variable assignment into its active domain satisfying all required facts, and for a union means satisfaction of at least one disjunct. For an answer tuple \(\bar a\) from the active domain, \((I,R)\models q(\bar a)\) means that every model extending \(I\) and satisfying \(R\) satisfies this instantiated query. Define \(R\) to have bounded derivation depth if for every conjunctive query \(q(\bar u)\) there is a finite union of conjunctive queries \(Q(\bar u)\) over the same signature such that, for every finite database \(I\) and every compatible answer tuple \(\bar a\), \((I,R)\models q(\bar a)\) if and only if \(I\models Q(\bar a)\). The rewriting \(Q\) may depend on \(R,q\) but not on the database or answer tuple. This is the source’s equivalent positive query-rewriting formulation of bounded derivation depth; it does not require one depth bound for all queries. Finite controllability is the displayed unrestricted-versus-finite equivalence for every \(I,q\). There is no syntactic guardedness, stickiness, binary-arity or single-head restriction on \(R\), and no time bound for constructing a rewriting or countermodel.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the implication for every finite signature and rule set, or refute it. A positive answer must show that whenever a Boolean conjunctive query fails in some possibly infinite model of \(I,R\), it also fails in some finite model of the same database and rules, assuming only the stated bounded derivation depth property. A negative answer must provide one finite signature and rule set \(R\), prove its rewriting property for every conjunctive query, and provide a finite database \(I\) and Boolean conjunctive query \(q\) such that every finite model of \(I,R\) satisfies \(q\) but some infinite model does not. Showing bounded behavior for a single query does not establish the premise on \(R\). A counterexample whose rules lack bounded derivation depth, or a theorem for binary single-head rules alone, does not settle this target.

cards.definitions:
The base graph is finite, nonempty, simple and undirected. Write \(E(v)\) for the edges incident with \(v\). Use the vertex-parity construction of Section 3 of the primary source. For each base edge \(e\), introduce two distinct vertices \(e_{0},e_{1}\). For each base vertex \(v\), introduce a vertex \(v^{X}\) for every subset \(X\subseteq E(v)\) satisfying
\[|X|\equiv\mathbf1_{v\in T}\pmod2.\]
For each such \(v^{X}\) and each \(e\in E(v)\), join \(v^{X}\) to \(e_{1}\) if \(e\in X\), and to \(e_{0}\) otherwise. These are all the edges in this primary-source convention. Thus an even gadget uses even subsets, and an odd gadget uses odd subsets.

The constructed names describe the mathematical construction; they are not readable labels in the input. The program receives only an unordered graph isomorphic to \(G^{T}\), through its adjacency relation. It receives no order of base vertices, no designation of which edge-gadget vertex is 0 or 1, no set \(T\), and no list of the subsets \(X\). There is no auxiliary coloring, padding or supplied circuit. The source’s parity query distinguishes the two CFI types over each connected base graph. Inputs outside the promised CFI family need not be recognized.

The resource parameter is \(N=|V(G^{T})|\), the size of the explicit expanded input, not \(|V(G)|\). A high-degree base vertex can generate exponentially many gadget vertices. The program and its polynomial resource bound must work uniformly over all base graphs and all twists \(T\).

CPT here includes counting. Its data domain consists of the input vertices as indivisible atoms and hereditarily finite sets built from these atoms: finite sets whose members are atoms or further such finite sets, with finite nesting depth. The available constants include the empty set and the set of all atoms. Operations are unordered pairing \(\{x,y\}\), union, extracting the unique member of a singleton (returning the empty set otherwise), and cardinality. Cardinalities are encoded as von Neumann ordinals, where \(0=\varnothing\) and \(m+1=m\cup\{m\}\). Counting an atom returns the empty set.

Terms are built from variables, these constants and operations, and bounded set comprehensions
\[\{s(\bar x,y):y\in r(\bar x)\text{ and }\varphi(\bar x,y)\}.\]
Tests use equality, membership and input adjacency, combined by Boolean connectives. Comprehensions range over an already constructed finite set; there is no primitive that arbitrarily chooses a member of a non-singleton set or provides an order on the atoms.

A program is fixed finite syntax for a state-update term and two tests, for halting and acceptance. Beginning with empty state, it repeatedly applies the update and checks the tests. There is a fixed polynomial bound in \(N+1\) on the number of iterations and on the number of distinct objects in the transitive closures of the states. A transitive closure includes all recursively nested members, so a huge set cannot be hidden inside a small outer container. Exceeding a bound aborts and rejects. Equivalent standard encodings of the CPT formalism give the same definability question.

All permitted operations respect permutations of the input atoms that preserve adjacency. Numerical ordinals can be ordered, but this does not authorize an arbitrary order of graph vertices. The question permits unbounded finite nesting depth subject to the polynomial size bound; it is not limited to fixed-rank sets or tuples.
cards.answer_criterion: Give one CPT program with counting and prove its polynomial resource bound and correct parity decision on every promised unordered CFI input, or prove no such program exists. A negative result for a restricted family of CPT programs, or failure to construct a particular auxiliary order, does not establish nondefinability in full CPT.

cards.definitions: For an integer \(n\ge2\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A partial order \(\le_P\) is a reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive binary relation on \([n]\). Distinct elements \(x,y\) are incomparable if neither \(x\le_P y\) nor \(y\le_P x\); a total order has no incomparable pair. A linear extension is a bijection \(L:[n]\to[n]\) such that \(L(a)<L(b)\) whenever \(a\le_P b\) and \(a\ne b\). Let \(E(P)\) be the finite nonempty set of all linear extensions, \(e(P)=|E(P)|\), and \(e_P(x,y)=|\{L\in E(P):L(x)<L(y)\}|\). Probabilities use the uniform distribution on the entire set \(E(P)\), so \(\Pr[L(x)<L(y)]=e_P(x,y)/e(P)\). The endpoints \(1/3\) and \(2/3\) are included. The pair may depend on the full finite order; there is no algorithmic or representation restriction. In the context, width is the largest size of a set of pairwise incomparable elements, height the largest size of a totally ordered subset, and the cover graph joins \(x,y\) if one is strictly below the other with no element strictly between them. The balance constant is \(\beta(P)=\max_{x\ne y}\min\{e_P(x,y),e_P(y,x)\}/e(P)\).

context_blocks.text: A partial order records comparisons already known, and its linear extensions are all complete rankings still compatible with that information. The conjecture says that unless only one ranking remains, some unresolved comparison splits these possible rankings into two substantial groups. Neither outcome may leave more than two thirds of them. The distribution is uniform over whole rankings, not over the currently available choices in a stepwise topological sort.

Take three elements with \(a<b\) and c unrelated to both. The three linear extensions are abc, acb and cab. The probability that a precedes c is \(2/3\), while the probability that b precedes c is \(1/3\). No incomparable pair is closer to a half. This small example shows that the universal interval cannot be narrowed to \([1/3+\eta ,2/3- \eta ]\) for any \(\eta >0\). In a total order every pair instead has probability zero or one, which explains the excluded case.

Uniform local choices need not produce uniform extensions. In the same example, choosing randomly between the two initially minimal elements a and c gives cab probability \(1/2\), and gives abc and acb probability \(1/4\) each. Those are different from the required probabilities \(1/3\) each. Fixing the probability space prevents a superficially similar random-ordering question from replacing the conjecture.

Brightwell, Felsner and Trotter prove the weaker universal bound \(\beta (\mathrm{P})\ge (5- \sqrt{5})/10\approx 0.2764\). It already guarantees an informative comparison and improves the earlier \(3/11\) bound of Kahn and Saks. The requested value \(1/3\) is a sharper extremal constant, rather than the first guarantee of any fixed positive balance.

The conjecture is known for substantial classes, including width-two and height-two orders, and orders whose cover graph is a forest. Width limits how many elements can be mutually incomparable; height limits the length of a chain. These are distinct restrictions, and neither covers arbitrary finite orders. The Chan–Pak survey states the general question separately from this collection of positive cases.

Aires and Kahn obtain stronger asymptotic balance under size hypotheses: for example \(\beta (\mathrm{P})\) tends to \(1/2\) when width is at least a fixed positive fraction of the number of elements. Their 2025 paper still states the unrestricted \(1/3\)–\(2/3\) bound as a conjecture. A result for a sequence of sufficiently wide orders leaves narrower and exceptional finite orders uncovered.

Gupta’s July 2026 revision reports an exhaustive verification of the stronger Gold Partition property through fourteen elements, implying the balance conjecture for those sizes. Its arithmetic and archived artifacts are described in the paper; this review did not rerun the census. A verified finite range, however large its enumeration, does not establish the universal statement.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every finite non-total partial order has an incomparable pair with \(e(P)/3\le e_P(x,y)\le2e(P)/3\), or a complete Lean-checked refutation: a finite non-total order for which every incomparable pair violates that closed interval. All extension counts and probabilities must use the full set of linear extensions defined here.

Aires and Kahn obtain stronger asymptotic balance under size hypotheses: for example \(\beta (\mathrm{P})\) tends to \(1/2\) when width is at least a fixed positive fraction of the number of elements. Their 2025 paper still states the unrestricted \(1/3\)–\(2/3\) bound as a conjecture. A result for a sequence of sufficiently wide orders leaves narrower and exceptional finite orders uncovered.

Gupta’s July 2026 revision reports an exhaustive verification of the stronger Gold Partition property through fourteen elements, implying the balance conjecture for those sizes. Its arithmetic and archived artifacts are described in the paper; this review did not rerun the census. A verified finite range, however large its enumeration, does not establish the universal statement.

cards.title: Extremal size of sunflower-free set families
cards.formal: For each fixed integer \(r\ge 3\), determine, up to constant factors as \(k\to \infty , S_{r}(k)\): the largest number of distinct k-element sets in a family containing no r members whose pairwise intersections are all equal, where the finite ground set is unrestricted.
cards.definitions: The r members in a sunflower must be distinct. Their common pairwise intersection is the core, and deleting it leaves pairwise disjoint petals. For each integer \(k\ge 1\), take the maximum cardinality over all sunflower-free families on arbitrary finite universes. The classical sunflower bound makes these cardinalities bounded by an integer depending only on k,r, so the maximum exists despite the unrestricted universe. No algorithm or encoding bound is imposed. The parameter r is fixed before k grows; asymptotic constants may depend on r.

context_blocks.text: The target is the extremal function itself. The sunflower conjecture states that \(S_{r}(k)\) has at most exponential growth in k for each fixed r, a weaker qualitative question than matching its full asymptotic order.
Sunflowers capture a simple repeated pattern inside a large family of small sets. Bounds on their forced occurrence are basic tools in circuit complexity, pseudorandomness and kernelization.

The breakthrough bound of Alweiss, Lovett, Wu and Zhang replaces a much larger dependence by roughly \((\log  k)^{O(k)}\) for fixed r. The conjecture asks for a constant base to the k-th power. This is admitted as a computationally motivated exception to the exclusion of general combinatorics, not to fill a combinatorics category.

cards.why: A general combinatorial principle with established applications to computational lower bounds and parameterized reductions.
cards.answer_criterion: Give functions \(f_{r}(k)\) and, for every fixed integer \(r\ge 3\), constants \(0<c_{r}\le C_{r}<\infty\) with \(c_{r} f_{r}(k)\le S_{r}(k)\le C_{r} f_{r}(k)\) for every \(k\ge 1\), absorbing finitely many small k into the constants if needed. Prove both a universal upper bound and existence of matching sunflower-free families in Lean. An exponential upper bound by itself does not determine the growth within constant factors.
